Position: The AI Conference Peer Review Crisis Demands Author Feedback and Reviewer Rewards

Paper I25-40108 | Kim, Lee and Lee | PMLR 267:81634–81651 (2025). Reviewed: the 18-page publisher-linked proceedings PDF. Page references below are physical PDF pages and match the printed page numbers. Review date: 24 October 2026.

Outcome: Minor — one confirmed, bounded empirical-survey correction. No Major defect is demonstrated. The central feedback-and-rewards proposal remains an untested intervention whose benefits require pilots; this review does not establish that it fails. Human scientific decision is pending; author adoption has not been requested.
# Problem 1. The compensation survey omits a documented ICML 2024 benefit

Location and original claim. Appendix C, Table 2, p.17, records ICML 2024 as O / - and gives a 2024 in-kind-compensation total of one. The table counts benefits restricted to outstanding reviewers, and p.18 explicitly includes registration tickets as in-kind compensation. Section 4.3, p.6, uses the survey to support limited availability of reviewer rewards. The claim being checked is the venue-year classification and its count, not whether a reward improves review quality. [S1]

Evidence. The ICML 2024 program chairs state that financial constraints reduced the group receiving free registration from the originally planned top decile to a smaller group. The official conference reviewer-instructions page links that explanation. The target paper itself recounts this reduced-pool arrangement in §5.2, p.6, footnote 7, so the discrepancy does not depend on a newly introduced post-publication program. [S1, S3]
Quantity | Published coding | Minimal correction
ICML 2024 compensation | Not positively marked | Mark present; annotate limited recipient pool
2024 positive venue count | 1: ICLR | 2: ICLR and ICML, holding other cells fixed
Distinct positive venues over 2020–2024 | 5 in Table 2: ACL, CVPR, ECCV, ICLR, NeurIPS | 6 after adding ICML, if other entries remain unchanged

Reasoning and strongest alternative interpretation. A reduced number of recipients does not remove a benefit from a survey that includes selective awards. The caption acknowledges incomplete public information; a dash could therefore mean not identified rather than proven absent. Even under that interpretation, the table omits a positive program already recognized in the paper and understates its positive count. Section 4.3’s separate statement of four compensated venues also needs a defined time window and reconciliation with the table. That count discrepancy is included in this correction, rather than treated as a second problem.

Bounded impact and repair. This is a Minor empirical classification error in a supporting survey, with no demonstrated damage to the central proposal. Correct the ICML cell, update the 2024 total, define the survey cutoff and counting window, and distinguish unknown entries from verified absence. Do not infer that rewards are widespread or effective from this correction. The remaining venue-year classifications have not been exhaustively revalidated.

Verification class: direct primary-source comparison plus independent exact recounting of the published table. This is not an empirical replication of a reward intervention. Source snapshots, a web-evidence note for the program-chair page, and the reviewer-authored recount script are recorded in provenance.
# Checks that passed and interpretation boundaries
Scope | Result and limit

Figure 1, p.1 | ICLR’s official 2025 fact sheet gives 11,603 submissions and an increase of 4,341. The implied prior count is 7,262; growth is 59.7769%, correctly rounded to 59.8%. Other venue/year points were not independently reconstructed. [S4]

Appendix A, pp.12–14 | The seven top-20 changes sum to 24: 3+4+3+3+4+2+5. The mean turnover is 24/(7\(\times\)20)=17.1429%, supporting the reported 17%. This describes ICLR keyword slots, not a measured loss of reviewer knowledge. [S1]

Appendix B, pp.15–16 | The prompt, model family and error categories are disclosed. The paper explicitly allows spell-checking confounding and describes the evidence as weak and non-conclusive. No LLM-authorship prevalence or causal quality decline follows from Figure 6. The 28.8% versus 28.883% difference from rounded endpoints is immaterial and excluded. [S1]
Figures 2–3, pp.3 and 5 | The diagram matches staged release; the badge image is explicitly illustrative. Neither is evidence of an implemented system’s effectiveness. [S1]

Staging and aggregation. Under §3, authors commit feedback before weaknesses and ratings are released. A legitimate first-stage question about a missing mathematical assumption can still reveal skepticism and induce punitive feedback. This establishes a limit on an absolute prevention guarantee, not that staging cannot reduce bias. Averaging also need not remove shared directional bias. The abstract’s mitigation wording, §5.1’s proposed pilots, §5.3’s gaming discussion and §6’s acknowledged burdens support treating these as Needs Evidence, not additional confirmed Problems. [S1]

Rewards and measurement. Subsequent impact of reviewed papers measures a reviewer’s portfolio, not necessarily the contribution of that review; reviewers of the same papers can provide different-quality reviews. The cited educational badge study reports a favorable course-level observation in a qualitative case study. Its transfer to conference reviewers remains untested. These are measurement and external-validity limits, consistent with the paper’s call for pilots. [S1, S8]
# Selected source corrections and pending evidence

NeurIPS definitions. The 2021 study reports 203/882=23.0% raw accept/reject disagreement; 16.0% results from treating specified borderline opposing decisions as consistent. The 2014 table gives 43/166=25.9%. Clarify these definitions and years when presenting §7.1’s 16–23% range. The primary 2021 report does not establish a temporal increase in noise. This is a scope clarification, not a demonstrated failure of the qualitative inconsistency argument. [S5]

Goldberg study timing. Section 7.1, p.8, describes review evaluations as occurring after the whole submission process. The primary study’s §2 places them after reviews were shown to authors but before final conference decisions. Its author bias concerns reviewer recommendations; the randomized length experiment is a separate analysis. Correcting the timing does not invalidate a proposal that hides recommendations before feedback. [S6]

Liang prevalence attribution. The accessible arXiv v1 uses sentences as its main unit and reports an estimated 17.5% for arXiv computer-science abstracts by February 2024. It does not directly measure an annual paper-level lower bound above 17.5%. A constructed corpus with 35 modified sentences out of 200 can have only two of twenty papers affected, showing why units matter. This is a logical example, not a reconstruction of the data. The cited COLM final version was inaccessible; exact version correspondence remains unresolved, so this attribution is retained as Needs Evidence / Scope Clarification. [S7]

Pending subitems without severity escalation: P01 — effectiveness, residual retaliation, calibration and false-positive LLM flags under staged feedback; P02 — reward alignment and whether paper-impact metrics measure review contributions; P03 — reconstruction of keyword/typo analyses from dated data, mappings, model outputs/settings and detector validation; P04 — final-version verification of the Liang attribution. The exact CVPR count of 19 desk-rejected papers was not independently verified from a primary announcement; the underlying policy was verified and no contrary evidence was found. [S9]
# Coverage, provenance and delivery limits

Read main text pp.1–9 and Appendices A–D, pp.12–18; references pp.9–11 were consulted selectively. Figures 1–6, Table 2 and the illustrative commentary page were visually inspected; Figure 7’s prompt was read as text. The original analyses make code/data reproducibility applicable, but no released implementation or snapshot was identified in the publisher record, manuscript links, arXiv materials or bounded repository searches. No author program, training run or Gemini API experiment was executed. The independent arithmetic checks use only reviewer-authored code.

The primary review target is the proceedings PDF (SHA-256 517064cf99897b87b58a463e4294449ec83c377c2391815de3dcb4ebbf6cd9d3). The related arXiv record shows v1, 8 May 2025; no later revision or erratum was identified in the checked records. OpenReview history was inaccessible. The report PDF was produced with the existing HTML renderer from the same canonical content as the TeX source; the TeX file was not compiled because no TeX compiler was available. PDF pages were rendered for visual inspection.

S3. ICML 2024 program chairs: https://medium.com/@icml2024pc/reviewing-at-icml-2024-a7aa81169d8c; official link: https://icml.cc/Conferences/2024/ReviewerInstructions. The chair post was readable through web retrieval; direct snapshot download returned HTTP 403.

report: Author: ELVIA independent paper verification
Date: Review date: 23 October 2026 (America/Chicago)
Title: Verification report: You Can’t Manufacture a NeRF
# Paper identity, version and outcome

I25-40110 / display 0011. Reviewed the official ICML 2025 proceedings PDF, PMLR 267:81652-81664, downloaded from the PDF link on the publisher record. The first-page author line reads MA Kimmel, Mueed Rehman, Yonatan Bisk, Gary K. Fedder; the publisher and task manifest use different expanded name forms. Identity is fixed by title, PMLR record, OpenReview kJzB6lQmcb and the file hash below, not by silently replacing the manifest names. Locations in this report use printed PDF pages 1-13, equal to one-based PDF page indices.

Supported outcome: Minor, for a bounded discrepancy between the released sampling implementation and the stated method. The connection of that release to the published experiments remains Needs Evidence. Two further quantitative reporting questions remain unresolved. No demonstrated Major defect or refutation of the reported reconstruction failures was established. The engineering motivation and the observed benefit of ground-truth segmentation survive these checks.
# Scope, definitions and checks that passed

Read the complete main text (pp.1-9), references (pp.10-11), and Appendix A (pp.12-13). Inspected the four-file public repository at the pinned commit below, with detailed inspection of sample_mesh.py; the other scripts were inspected as preparation/labeling context. No author code was executed and no training, reconstruction, machining, or dataset-scale reproduction was performed. The Appendix is included in the source PDF. A separate supplement could not be verified through OpenReview because access returned a browser-verification page; a delegated API check returned HTTP 403.

The paper’s operational complexity criterion is satisfied by more than 15 BREP faces, among other alternatives (p.2, section 1.2). A closed manifold condition includes vertex neighborhoods as well as edge incidence; the more complete discussion on p.3 prevents treating the introductory edge-only shorthand as an independently established implementation defect. The arccosine formula in Appendix A is correct for nonzero normals. Distinguish an average point-distance statistic, a worst-case geometric deviation, and a specified dimensional manufacturing tolerance.

Table 2’s F360 Point2CAD rate of 18.9% manifold corresponds to 81.1% non-manifold, agreeing with Table 3’s rounded 81%. The intervention in section 4 lowers the reported non-manifold proportion from about 81% to 47%, a 34-percentage-point change, supporting a segmentation contribution without removing downstream failures. Feature subsets overlap, so subgroup means are not expected to partition the overall row. These are consistency checks of reported values, not independent confirmation of the underlying observations.
# Problem 1. Released sampling differs from the written protocol

Source claim and location: section 4.1, p.8, defines high curvature at an adjacent-normal angle exceeding 0.3 rad, specifies a neighborhood width t=0.035 times the minimum bounding-box dimension, allocates at least 25% of the samples near qualifying edges, and ultimately selects 10,000 points. The earlier paragraph also states a minimum of ten samples per edge. Evidence E1 and E2.

Static check: sample_mesh.py line 75 uses np.deg2rad(2.5); line 89 applies that threshold. Lines 104-112 interpolate on the edge at spacing 0.001. Line 153 requests 150,000 surface points; line 158 concatenates edge and surface samples; lines 177-181 shuffle and save the combined array. This file contains no implementation of the stated distance zone, allocation guarantee, or final 10,000-point selection. The two angular thresholds are 0.0436332313 and 0.3 rad, differing by a factor of 6.87549354.

Complete analytic witness: consider the convex regular 64-gonal prism with vertices (0.5 cos(2 pi j/64), 0.5 sin(2 pi j/64), +/-0.5), j=0,...,63. It has 66 planar BREP faces and is therefore complex under the paper’s face-count criterion. Its closed convex boundary has no self-intersections, every edge has exactly two incident faces, and vertex links are single cycles. All vertices have norm sqrt(1/2), so the whole convex prism lies inside the unit sphere. Triangulate each planar face without altering its surface. Along each vertical prism edge, adjacent outward normals differ by 2 pi/64.

\[0.0436332313 < \theta = 2\pi/64 = 0.0981747704 < 0.3.\] The released threshold selects those vertical edges; the written threshold does not. This verifies a difference on an input satisfying the stated geometry assumptions. It does not predict a published table entry. In particular, no trained model or author sampler was executed.

Alternative reading and impact: this release could be an intermediate preparation script followed by unpublished sampling or experiment-specific code. A later subsampling step could reconcile the point count. The inspected release does not identify that step or connect any commit to the reported tables. The supported defect is a local reproducibility/method discrepancy (Minor); changes to model performance remain Needs Evidence. A threshold-only edit is not a verified repair because the other protocol differences remain. Resolution requires an experiment-producing revision/configuration and matched runs if numerical impact is to be established.
# Problem 2. Dimensional interpretation of Chamfer error is under-specified

Source claim and location: Table 1 and section 2.1, p.5, compare normalized Chamfer values with the absolute tolerances on p.3 and in Appendix Table 5, using a four-inch object as an illustration. The metric equation, power of distance, bidirectional aggregation, and per-object inverse scale are not given. The adjacent prose refers to a median, while Table 1 explicitly reports averages and standard deviations. No released evaluation script resolves these choices. Evidence E1-E2.

Check: for the following explicitly defined illustrative family, scaling follows directly by factoring the norm in every nearest-neighbor term. Here r>0 is the power, a>0 is a uniform scale, and P,Q are nonempty finite point sets.

\[D_r(P,Q)=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p\in P}\min_{q\in Q}\|p-q\|^r+\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\min_{p\in P}\|q-p\|^r,\qquad D_r(aP,aQ)=a^rD_r(P,Q).\] Linear conversion is valid for r=1; r=2 has squared-length units until an appropriate square root is taken. Fitting inside a unit sphere does not, by itself, specify the object’s normalized longest dimension. An average nearest-neighbor value also cannot certify a worst-case tolerance bound or identify the failing manufacturing feature.

Counterevidence: if the actual statistic is an unsquared distance and the normalized longest extent is 2, scaling to four inches gives a=2. Then 0.029 becomes 0.058 inches, 11.6 times 0.005 inches. Thus a plausible interpretation supports the stated order-of-magnitude comparison; this audit does not demonstrate a wrong numerical conversion. Judgment: Needs Evidence. Supply the metric equation, dimensional inverse transforms, exact summary statistic, and feature-appropriate deviation measures. No correction to the table or experimental result is proposed.
# Problem 3. Thang3D percentage needs an explicit denominator

Source claim and location: section 1.4, p.4, describes 200 downloaded Thang3D models; Table 2, p.6, reports 6.9% manifold for Point2CAD. If there is one binary result for each of exactly 200 objects, every percentage is k/2 percent for integer k. Thirteen successes give 6.5%; fourteen give 7.0%; rounding to one decimal cannot give 6.9%. This is an exact finite arithmetic check.

Alternative readings include an evaluated subset after exclusions, multiple bodies per model, or an average over runs. Any could change the denominator or aggregation. The table does not specify which applies. Judgment: Needs Evidence, with bounded reporting impact. The calculation does not establish a false count or a changed comparative conclusion. Resolution requires the evaluated numerator, denominator, exclusions and averaging rule; it does not justify substituting 7.0%.
# Dependence, scope clarification and later material

The finite 256-cubed reconstruction experiment supports a statement about the evaluated pipeline and datasets. It does not establish a representation-wide impossibility for every triangulated shape and tolerance. An independent illustration is an exact triangulation of a convex 16-gonal prism of radius 2 inches and height 1 inch: it has 18 BREP faces, 32 vertices, 60 triangles, 90 mesh edges, Euler characteristic 2, two triangles per edge, and cyclic vertex links. Each triangle lies in and partitions an original planar face, so nominal representation error is exactly zero. This is a scope clarification, not a learned-model or machining reproduction; it does not refute the measured failures or guarantee tool-path feasibility for arbitrary shapes.

The paper discusses alternative manufacturing views in section 5 and distinguishes mechanical validity from geometric validity. These counterweights matter when reading its broad statements. No central conclusion is downgraded solely because a future pipeline might perform better. The released repository’s inspected history, issues and releases did not reveal a correction; exact-title searches found no separate later manuscript or erratum. OpenReview revision contents were not accessible, so this is a bounded search result, not a claim of exhaustive absence.

Chamfer conversion | Needs Evidence | No numeric repair asserted | Metric, scaling and tolerance mapping

Title: Verification report: Build Agent Advocates, Not Platform Agents
# Identity, reviewed version and outcome

I25-40111 / display 0012. Sayash Kapoor, Noam Kolt and Seth Lazar. Official ICML 2025 proceedings, PMLR 267:81617-81633; OpenReview jd1N60VNFE. Reviewed the publisher-linked PDF saved before analysis. Page references use printed pages 1-17, equal to one-based PDF pages. SHA256: cb56276971f459bf7a0062f984a9b04b568b16f59177cd20efc43cea47d32c19.

Inspection outcome: Scope Clarification. No Issue Found within the inspected central argument. No demonstrated Major or Minor scientific defect was established. Two stronger interpretations of supporting language remain Needs Evidence: general verifiable deletion with zero publisher loss, and formal Pareto dominance. These pending claims do not increase the supported severity of the paper.
# Scope and checked reasoning

The complete main argument (pp.1-9), the references as leads for selected checks (pp.10-16), and the explicitly hypothetical appendix (p.17) were inspected. This is a position paper advocating a coordinated institutional and technical program, not a theorem, benchmark, or controlled comparison of deployed ecosystems. No experimental reproduction, author-code execution, exhaustive bibliography audit, or comprehensive legal/current-product audit was performed. No separate target-paper implementation or additional supplement was identified in the inspected publisher record; the appendix is in the PDF.

Sections 2-4 connect incentives, concentrated control, switching costs and data access to proposed user-controlled alternatives. The 2024 FTC source independently supports the surveillance and advertising-incentive background (E5); it does not prove the paper’s forecast of future agent-market structure. The forecast remains conditional. The proposed package combines model/compute access, interoperability and safety infrastructure, and competition policy, so checking only one component would misstate the argument.
Location | Claim actually checked | Result / implication

pp.5-6, sections4.1-4.2 | Local/private-cloud control and open models | p.6 acknowledges on-device capability limits and need for affordable remote compute; no immediate feasibility guarantee established
pp.6-8, sections4.2,5.2 | Openness, loyalty and institutional incentives | Alignment remains unsolved; provider drift is acknowledged. Openness is not presented as sufficient for loyalty
pp.5-8, sections4.1-5.2 | Interoperability reduces dependence | Platform obstruction motivates regulation; prior decentralization failures and new concentration risks are considered
pp.7-8, sections5.1-5.3 | Costs, misuse and multi-agent effects | These are explicit counterarguments, not omitted premises. No causal effect size is claimed
p.17, Appendix Table1 | Three agent examples | Explicitly hypothetical spectrum; not observed comparative performance
# Clarification 1. What the forgetting precedent establishes

The supporting example on p.5, section 4.1, proposes previewing paid information and forgetting rejected content, citing Weiss et al., COLM 2024 (OpenReview Zq9Dfj4nBo). Its strongest reading combines a general deletion guarantee with no loss to the publisher. The exact COLM final PDF was inaccessible: browser verification in the web tool and HTTP 403 in a delegated Lumen request. The accessible earlier preprint, arXiv:2403.14443v1, differs in title and author order and is identified separately, rather than substituted for the final text.

That earlier primary source explicitly assumes a marketplace regulator controlling buyer-agent behavior (section 2) and describes retaining purchased content for later use (section 3.2). The authors’ corresponding public repository was checked statically at commit 62e539900cc3d3d5fd76fef035d6de93bda77171. simulator.py lines349-353 retain rejected Quote objects in _rejected_quotes; lines575-588 include them in evaluation summaries. schema.py lines227-231 includes their answer blocks, whose summaries include raw content at lines402-403. Thus rejection does not erase every copy in that simulator.

Counterevidence is decisive for a fair interpretation: simulator.py lines403-420 gives only _accepted_quotes to final-answer synthesis and follow-up generation. The implementation therefore supports selective information flow within a trusted architecture. Retaining audit data inside a trusted simulator is compatible with restricting an agent’s designated downstream calls; it is not, by itself, a bug in that cited system.

The inference from controlled downstream access to a guarantee for arbitrary user-controlled software requires a defined trust boundary, allowed outputs, retained state and verification mechanism. Economic zero-loss also requires its own assumptions. This report records that stronger interpretation as Needs Evidence, without claiming an impossibility theorem or a broken target-paper experiment. Reading the passage as a conditional future mechanism is consistent with the paper’s acknowledged infrastructure and alignment requirements. No security repair was implemented or verified.
# Clarification 2. Pareto language is not a welfare theorem

The last paragraph of section5.3, p.8, describes the proposal as a Pareto improvement under appropriate safety and governance. A formal comparison would require a specified population, utilities, baseline and no-loss conditions. None is supplied. Reduced platform rents could disadvantage platform owners if they are included, while consumer-only evaluation would still need capability, convenience, cost and security tradeoffs. Those tradeoffs are already acknowledged in section5.

This observation is not an original-assumption counterexample: the formal assumptions are unspecified. The defensible reading is a proposed improvement on targeted platform harms, conditional on governance and technical feasibility. Formal universal dominance remains Needs Evidence. The central recommendation does not depend on a demonstrated welfare theorem, and no numerical or mathematical repair is asserted.
# Dependence, versions and remaining work

The three-part policy program remains coherent within its stated aims. Its practical comparative benefits need deployment and institutional evidence; no study of those effects was reproduced here. The target arXiv record lists v1 on 7 May 2025 and v2 on 19 June 2025. The relevant forgetting passage persists in the inspected v2 HTML. The review target remains the PMLR file; byte identity of the two PDFs was not established. No formal erratum or later replacement was found in the inspected exact-title searches and primary records. OpenReview revision/attachment coverage remains incomplete.

Title: Verification report: Strong Consumer Protection and AI Safety in the United States
# Identity, exact version and outcome

I25-40112 / display0013. Serena Booth, Position: Strong Consumer Protection is an Inalienable Defense for AI Safety in the United States. Reviewed the official ICML 2025 proceedings PDF, PMLR 267:81118-81129; OpenReview j5eEF77JQz. Locations use printed pages 1-12, equal to one-based PDF pages. Source SHA256: 14388ff872856a8c186c0f6d0639e357babe83e182620d69af77dcc247924b53.

Supported outcome: Minor, limited to an overbroad attribution of a model-architecture restriction to CFPB guidance. The paper’s next-page qualification supplies substantial counterevidence and preserves its main lesson. No demonstrated Major defect or central-claim damage was established. The RealPage counterfactual and the fraud statistic are recorded separately as scope/evidence clarifications.
# Scope, assumptions and checked argument

Read the full 12-page paper, including the main argument on pp. 1-9 and the bibliography on pp. 9-12. This policy position paper supplies case studies rather than a quantitative causal estimate or a new algorithm. Selected contemporaneous primary sources were checked for the most material interpretation questions. No target-paper code, experimental supplement or separate appendix was identified in the inspected publisher record. No code execution, statistical reproduction, exhaustive legal audit or present-day compliance assessment was performed.

The broad AI-safety definition and exclusions are explicit in sections 1.1-1.3, p. 2. Gradual harm emergence is expressly speculative in section 2, pp. 2-3, and the following paragraph preserves a case for consumer protection even under abrupt emergence. Section4.1 treats AI-specific rules as potentially complementary; section 4.2 acknowledges compliance costs and regulatory capture; section 5 recognizes enforcement and political fragility. These passages prevent reading the title as a theorem that current law is sufficient or automatically enforced.
# Problem1. Explanation requirements are overstated as a deep-learning restriction

Source claim and exact location: section 3.2, printed p.4, final paragraph, attributes to the CFPB an effective prohibition on deep-learning systems for credit decisions, especially without significant human oversight. The suspect step replaces a functional requirement for explanations with a restriction on model architecture. Evidence E1-E3.

Complete check: the cited19 September 2023 CFPB announcement requires accurate, specific adverse-action reasons that reflect actual decision factors, including when complex models are used. The contemporaneous Circular 2022-03, Response and Analysis, states the prohibition conditionally: a creditor may not use a complex algorithm when it cannot supply the required specific, accurate reasons. Endnote1 discusses post-hoc explanations and requires their accuracy to be validated, recognizing that this may be infeasible for some models. Thus the relevant condition is explanatory compliance, not membership in the deep-learning model class. Neither inspected source makes human oversight a substitute for that requirement.

Alternative reading and counterevidence: the author may mean that many practically inscrutable deep models cannot meet the requirement. The same section on p. 5 explicitly narrows the statement to systems that remain inscrutable and says institutions must be able to provide accurate explanations. That is much closer to the official source. This audit therefore identifies a bounded local overstatement, not an invalidation of the case study or a finding about every deployed credit model.

Impact: the p. 4 formulation can exaggerate the claimed innovation-versus-consumer-protection tradeoff by suggesting a restriction on an entire architecture family. The central example that technology does not remove adverse-action explanation duties remains supported. Judgment: Minor. If interpreted solely as a prediction about practical model capability, the architecture-wide prediction instead Needs Evidence.

Precise source-supported clarification: creditors using complex algorithms remain subject to adverse-action explanation requirements, and may not use a system when doing so prevents them from providing the specific, accurate reasons required for those actions. This restores the conditional scope and agrees with the manuscript’s later qualification. This is a verified source-based clarification, not a proof that any particular credit system complies with all applicable law. The manuscript was not edited and author adoption has not been requested.
# Separate clarifications and unresolved claims
## RealPage: data provenance and agreement structure

Section3.1, pp. 3-4, proposes that replacing private inputs with publicly inferred signals could preserve rent-setting performance and make legal applicability more ambiguous. The original DOJ complaint, filed23 August 2024, alleges information-sharing agreements in paragraphs 225-234 and broader agreements to align pricing in paragraphs 236-241. The latter are not defined only by the privacy of inputs. Complaint printedpp.81-85 correspond to one-based PDF pages86-90. These are allegations, not adjudicated findings.

A public-data substitution alone does not show that a common pricing arrangement lacks an agreement. However, the paper says the case becomes more ambiguous, not that public data guarantees legality. A fair evaluation distinguishes independent responding algorithms from an agreed common pricing service. The suggestion that inferred data would maintain comparable performance also lacks a measured inference error or downstream sensitivity analysis. Both are Needs Evidence within a speculative counterfactual; neither establishes a false reported experiment. No finding about RealPage’s ultimate liability is made.
## Fraud: the measured increase is monetary loss

Section3.5, p. 6, refers to a 30% increase in fraud/scams and nearly9 billion dollars of losses. The cited FTC release reports more than30% growth in reported dollar losses, reaching nearly8.8 billion dollars in 2022. The official explanatory post separately says fraud reports decreased from2.9 million to 2.4 million. The rounded dollar amount in the paper is reasonable; the wording should identify reported monetary loss as the statistic. It does not establish a 30% rise in incident counts, population prevalence, or AI-attributable fraud. Because the surrounding sentence discusses losses, this is retained as metric clarification rather than a separate confirmed defect.
## Remaining case-study coverage

Sections3.3-3.6 on disparate impact, supervisory authority, transfers and privacy were read for argumentative dependence and acknowledged gaps. Their full statutory exceptions, enforcement histories and all economic estimates were not independently audited. No quantitative effectiveness estimate was validated. Later administrative developments are not used retroactively as evidence of an original2025 error.
# Overall dependence, version search and conclusion

The core thesis remains a conditional case for preserving, enforcing and improving technology-neutral protections. It does not require the local architecture-wide interpretation of CFPB guidance. The inspected PMLR record, exact-title searches and an author publication listing did not identify a separate later manuscript, code release, supplement or formal erratum. OpenReview modification metadata is not evidence that a particular substantive correction occurred. No corrected historical issue has been relabeled as a current defect.

report: Author: ELVIA independent paper verification
Date: Review date: 23 October 2026 (America/Chicago)
Title: Verification report: Beyond Assistance
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

Reviewed paper: Abeer Badawi, Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar, Jimmy Xiangji Huang, Shaina Raza, and Elham Dolatabadi, Position: Beyond Assistance – Reimagining LLMs as Ethical and Adaptive Co-Creators in Mental Health Care, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81050–81066 [E1]. The exact proceedings PDF was saved before review. All page locations below use printed pages 1–17, equal to one-based PDF pages; these differ from proceedings pagination. The packet abbreviates Huang’s given names; the PDF author line resolves the identity.

All main-text sections, bibliography, Appendix A, and Appendix B were read. Figure 1 on p.3 was rendered and inspected. This is a claim-focused audit of a position paper, with selected clinical dependencies and independent arithmetic/identification checks. It is not a clinical trial, comprehensive reference audit, regulatory certification, or execution of an author implementation.
# Summary and definitions

Supported outcome: Minor, limited to two empirical-evidence descriptions. The Fraser study cannot demonstrate mental-health-crisis misclassification because its eligibility excluded mental-health presentations. The cited Woebot trial does not establish a comparative anxiety benefit. Neither finding invalidates the proposed SAFE-i implementation principles or the rationale for human-centered evaluation. No Major issue is demonstrated. Additional metric and transfer concerns remain Scope Clarification or Needs Evidence and do not increase supported severity.

SAFE-i is an implementation proposal spanning data, engineering, and integration. HAAS-e proposes criteria, score families, and future validation methods. R_llm denotes a model response; C_user, E_human, C_culture, and U_history denote concerns, expert evaluations, cultural context, and history. Align is a schematic scoring function: Appendix A permits expert, learned, or similarity-based estimators. Thus the four names do not yet identify one standardized, calibrated instrument. The paper’s explicit human oversight, escalation, proposed trials, and Appendix B limitations constrain any literal reading of its assurances.
# Problem 1: Emergency-triage evidence transferred to an excluded population

Source claim and location. The Introduction, p.2, attributes unsafe triage and misclassification of urgent mental-health crises to Fraser et al. (2023). Section 4, Challenge 3, p.5, later characterizes that study as examining only diagnostic accuracy. The suspect step is transferring an emergency-medicine result to a population not included in the cited study [E1, E2].

Complete source check. Fraser’s Methods, Data Source, restricts eligibility to adult, English-speaking emergency patients with nontrauma, nonmental-health problems and ESI levels 2–5. Its Study Design and Table 2 report 37 triage cases; ChatGPT 3.5 was rated unsafe in 15, approximately 41%. The analysis used previously collected patient symptom data entered into the LLM. It measured diagnostic and triage performance, including unsafe triage. Consequently, the study supports a general triage-risk example, but it cannot provide observed mental-crisis performance in an excluded cohort.

Counterreading, impact, and precise clarification. The authors may intend a warning by analogy. Indeed, their p.4 discussion correctly identifies emergency-department diagnostic and triage evaluation; the statement that this was not direct patient–LLM interaction is defensible. Preserve that general caution, but identify the study’s nonmental-health cohort and describe application to mental-health crises as a hypothesis needing its own evidence. This repairs the evidence attribution only. It does not establish that LLM crisis triage is safe, validate a new model, or overturn the framework proposal. Judgment: Minor local evidence-scope defect.
# Problem 2: Anxiety improvement described as demonstrated intervention efficacy

Source claim and location. Section 3, p.4, describes Woebot as having shown efficacy in alleviating depression and anxiety, citing Fitzpatrick et al. (2017). The relevant distinction is improvement observed over time versus a benefit attributable to the intervention compared with its control [E1, E3].

Complete source check. The source randomized 70 young adults to a two-week Woebot intervention or information-only control. Its Results, Table 2, reports a depression difference (PHQ-9, P=.017) but no significant anxiety difference (GAD-7, P=.581). The Completer Analysis reports anxiety improvement over time in both groups (P=.004). A within-time improvement shared by both arms does not establish an intervention-specific anxiety effect. The Methods describe a decision-tree conversational system with embedded NLP, so the study also cannot directly validate generative-LLM efficacy.

Counterreading, impact, and precise clarification. If the target sentence means only that participants’ anxiety improved, the source supports that narrower descriptive reading. The target also introduces Woebot under conversational AI, so merely including this older system is not independently treated as a model-category defect. Replace the efficacy summary with preliminary comparative evidence for depression, alongside anxiety improvement in both arms without a demonstrated between-arm benefit. Nonsignificance is not proof of no anxiety effect. Judgment: Minor bounded overstatement of this study’s efficacy evidence; no change to the general case for evaluating collaborative tools.
# Measurement checks and unresolved transfer claims
## Appendix A: correct arithmetic and explicitly illustrative inputs

On p.16, CES=(1.00+0.80)/2=0.90, CSI=0.90 is an assumed expert score, PAS=3/5=0.60, and ASA=40/50=0.80. Independent rational arithmetic reproduces these values. Equal weighting is a valid linear combination, consistent with §6.2. Dividing a 1–5 score by five maps it into [0.2,1]; a zero-anchored scale is not required by the stated example. The appendix explicitly marks scenario details as illustrative. Its 50-session example is not a reported completed pilot; cultural context, history, and ratings cannot be reconstructed from the dialogue alone. No arithmetic or fabrication finding is supported.
## ASA identifies adherence; safety and causal benefit require other measurements

\[\operatorname{ASA}=P(A=1\mid R_{\rm llm}),\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{ASA}}=40/50=0.80.\] Here A is completion of a prespecified beneficial action. Consider two hypothetical populations of 50 sessions, each with 40 action completions. Their ASA is identical even if an independently defined adverse-outcome count is zero in one population and ten in the other. The recommended action remains beneficial in both; the formula contains no constraint fixing other adverse outcomes. Hence ASA alone does not identify an overall safety profile.

For a separate causal check, let A(1) and A(0) be beneficial-action outcomes with the LLM response and with a specified comparator. In both hypothetical worlds, 40 of 50 users have A(1)=1. In world X, A(0)=A(1) for everyone, so mean[A(1)-A(0)]=0. In world Y, A(0)=0 for everyone, so the mean effect is 0.80. Both have observed ASA=0.80. All outcomes are binary, cohort size and beneficial-action definition are fixed, and no medical data are simulated or claimed. This proves nonidentification from adherence alone, not failure of HAAS-e as a whole.

Decisive counterevidence: §6.3, p.9, separately proposes randomized comparisons, expert safety reviews, and red teaming; §5.3, p.7, includes escalation and monitoring. These can supply information missing from ASA. The proper outcome is Scope Clarification, with measurement validation pending. No invented composite safety score or clinically validated repair is supplied.
## Standardization and clinical transfer remain unverified

The Align estimators, score anchors, aggregation, rater reliability, population sampling, and clinically meaningful thresholds remain implementation choices. Appendix A explicitly allows alternative estimators, while §7 calls the frameworks a starting point. Different implementations should not be assumed directly comparable until those choices and validation are fixed. This is unresolved operationalization of a proposal, not an algebraic contradiction.

Section 5.2, pp.6–7, extends ToT/CoT to reduced hallucinations and safer emotionally sensitive reasoning. Yao et al.’s inspected experimental inventory is Game of 24, creative writing, and mini crosswords; its Discussion explicitly limits the study to three relatively simple tasks [E4]. Wei et al.’s abstract describes arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning [E5]. These sources motivate candidate techniques but do not establish the asserted clinical transfer. Treat the mental-health benefit as Needs Evidence requiring task-specific testing; this audit does not prove that such techniques fail.

Selected supporting checks: Bedi et al.’s 519-study review supports the 5% real-patient-evaluation statistic, across healthcare rather than specifically mental health or training data [E6]. HAILEY supports improved expressed empathy in a nonclinical N=300 peer-support trial, without validating this paper’s new metrics or clinical outcomes [E7]. Varghese’s 53% moderate-trust and 34.8% future-outlook figures appear in a survey of 466 Indian volunteers; they do not identify global clinical adoption or effectiveness [E8]. The original GE/MIT adoption table was inaccessible. The target’s 48%, 21%, and 27% categories need source/denominator clarification; 21+27=48 alone does not establish an error.
# Dependencies, versions, and impact

The official proceedings PDF remains the reviewed object. The arXiv record lists v1 on 21 February 2025 and latest v2 on 30 May 2025 [E9]; the selected v2 Introduction still contains the Fraser mental-crisis attribution. Byte identity with the proceedings PDF was not asserted. No separate target implementation, supplement, or formal erratum was located in the inspected official/arXiv/author records. Appendices A–B are included in the downloaded PDF. OpenReview revision and attachment history could not be inspected behind its verification challenge; absence of a discovered correction is not proof that none exists.

The demonstrated defects narrow two background evidence claims. The position that human-centered, supervised evaluation is needed does not depend on anxiety efficacy in this single trial or a mental-health subgroup in Fraser. Framework effectiveness, subgroup fairness, emergency escalation, and clinical outcomes require fresh validation with specified models, populations, comparators, endpoints, and adverse-event ascertainment. The present audit supplies no deployment recommendation.
# Conclusion ledger

Woebot anxiety efficacy: Minor | Between-arm versus time-effect distinction verified | Not requested; no claim of zero effect

Scientific decision and human-review declarations remain pending. No author adoption has been requested. These outcomes apply only to inspected claims; they do not certify whole-paper correctness.

Title: Verification report: Online–Offline Copyright Risk Management
# Identity, version, and outcome

Reviewed paper: Yanzhou Pan, Jiayi Chen, Jiamin Chen, Zhaozhuo Xu, and Denghui Zhang, Position: Iterative Online-Offline Joint Optimization is Needed to Manage Complex LLM Copyright Risks, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81962–81976 [E1]. The original 15-page proceedings PDF was saved before review. Locations use printed pages 1–15, identical to one-based PDF pages. All main sections, references, and Appendices A–D were read; pages 3, 6, and 15 were rendered to inspect the table and diagrams.

Outcome: Scope Clarification, with substantive stronger interpretations remaining Needs Evidence. No Major or Minor scientific defect is established under the defensible reading of this position paper as a research proposal. Its coordination argument is coherent, but universal necessity, monotonic improvement, and demonstrated system efficiency are not proved here. A complete independent check below disproves a general precision-monotonicity inference under stated fixed-output assumptions; it is not a reproduction or failure demonstration of MemFree, SHIELD, or an implemented joint optimizer.
# What the evidence establishes

Sections 3.1–3.3, pp.3–5, distinguish serving-time interventions from changes to data, training, and model parameters. Runtime output filtering does not retroactively change how a model was trained; retraining alone does not immediately incorporate arbitrary new external rights information. Those observations support coordination. They do not establish impossibility for every isolated method, task, environment, or information source. A model trained offline can still implement a context-conditioned response policy at inference; external updating and responding to an input are different capabilities.

The abstract and §5.5, pp.8–9, describe scalable effectiveness and improvement on successive iterations. The paper supplies a conceptual architecture, borrowed benchmark results, and an illustrative ChatGPT exchange, but no joint objective, update rule, convergence argument, implemented-system evaluation, or latency measurements. Its millisecond-response and per-iteration-improvement descriptions therefore remain design intentions. Appendix C acknowledges resource constraints, and §5.4 makes model updates conditional on need. These are counterevidence to an unconditional guarantee reading. No invented bad optimizer is treated as a counterexample to an algorithm the authors never specified.
# Detailed mathematical scope check: n-gram length and precision

Source claim. Section 5.2, p.7, Log suspicious activities, presents higher n as improving precision while recall drops. Its subsequent sentences acknowledge that flagged cases may be noninfringing and unflagged cases may remain risky. This supports a heuristic reading, but longer matches alone do not mathematically guarantee higher infringement-classification precision.

Definitions and assumptions. Hold fixed the candidate texts, the blocklist, and independent binary evaluation labels. Let the detector flag a candidate if it contains any exact n-gram from the blocklist. With no approximate-filter errors, every longer-match alarm is also a shorter-match alarm. Let T and F be the initial true and false positives; increasing n removes t true and f false positives, with 0<=t<=T, 0<=f<=F and at least one remaining alarm. Recall cannot increase under these assumptions. Precision has a different condition:

\[P_{\rm new}-P_{\rm old}=\frac{T-t}{T+F-t-f}-\frac{T}{T+F}=\frac{Tf-Ft}{(T+F)(T+F-t-f)}.\] The denominator is positive, so precision increases exactly when Tf>Ft. Alarm-set nesting does not imply this condition.

Complete finite witness. Use one reference containing 60 distinct artificial tokens x0,\(\ldots\),x59. Seven positive candidates contain x0,\(\ldots\),x29 followed by distinct unmatched suffixes. An eighth positive contains the full reference plus an unmatched suffix. Two negative candidates also contain the full reference with distinct suffixes. Labels are stipulated independently: the eight positives represent prohibited uses in this hypothetical benchmark and the two negatives represent authorized uses. The artificial tokens are not asserted to constitute a copyrighted work, and no legal decision about actual excerpts is made. This is a classifier countermodel with fixed labels, not a clinical or legal dataset.
Exact detector | True / false alarms | Precision / recall
n=20: all 10 candidates match | TP=8, FP=2 | 8/10=0.80; 8/8=1
n=40: only three full-reference candidates match | TP=1, FP=2 | 1/3\(\approx\)0.333; 1/8=0.125

All structural conditions hold: the same texts and blocklist are used; each 40-gram match contains a matching 20-gram; the seven short positive strings have fewer than 40 tokens; labels do not change. Here T=8, F=2, t=7 and f=0, giving Tf\(-\)Ft=\(-\)14. The independent program reproduces both alarm sets and exact rational scores. Therefore a general promise of increasing precision is false even in this simpler matching setting.

Counterevidence and precise supported statement. The cited MemFree source explains a practical tradeoff and selects n=10 qualitatively (§3.2 and Appendix B.2–B.3), not by proving legal-label precision monotonicity [E3]. SHIELD uses n together with other thresholds and copyright verification; its Appendix D fixes 10-grams [E4]. Changing an actual decoder may change its outputs, while Bloom filtering introduces other assumptions. Thus even recall nesting cannot be transferred automatically to those systems. A defensible clarification is: n changes the matching tradeoff; on fixed texts with nested exact alarms, recall is nonincreasing, while precision can move either way. The actual trend must be measured under specified labels and parameters. This narrows an informal expectation without refuting the recommendation to log and calibrate.
# Benchmark and legal-scope checks

Table 1, p.3, reproduces the copying columns from CopyBench Table 5 (printed p.15142). Negative parenthetical changes indicate reductions, despite the target caption’s reversed legend. This presentation issue is excluded from standalone scientific finding counts under the task contract. Rounded displayed rates do not permit an exact audit of relative changes: hypothetical underlying values 0.08\(\rightarrow\)0.04 display as 0.1\(\rightarrow\)0.0 with \(-\)50%, and 2.4\(\rightarrow\)2.568 displays as 2.4\(\rightarrow\)2.6 with +7%. These are compatibility witnesses, not recovered source data.

The §3.1 summary on p.4 must be read as inconsistent non-literal mitigation across tested settings. For Tulu, system prompts reduce event and character scores by reported 28% and 29%; other combinations improve little or worsen. CopyBench itself uses the same broad qualitative summary, so no altered-data allegation is supported. CopyBench §6 expressly says its behavioral tests do not adjudicate infringement. Therefore neither this table nor the single Figure 2 interaction establishes legal liability, universal failure of online methods, or the efficacy of the proposed joint framework [E2].

For the Figure 2 jurisdiction example, the Canadian guide confirms the former life-plus-50 term and nonrevival after the 2022 extension. Conditional on the paper’s 1961 death year and ordinary applicable term, expiry is at the end of 2011 and public-domain entry is 1 January 2012. The target’s 2011 entry date does not change its 2025 cross-jurisdiction contrast. The US 95-year rule with calendar-year expiry gives end-2047 for a qualifying 1952 copyright; original registration and renewal conditions were not independently established [E5, E6]. These boundary-date observations are not promoted to substantive findings. Current court outcomes or later law were not retroactively used to criticize the 2025 paper.
# Coverage, versions, and remaining work

The inspected appendices give database examples, roles/access and qualitative costs, implementation constraints, and lifecycle mappings. They provide no complete rights oracle or numerical system evaluation. Figure 3 and Figure 5 consistently map mitigation, examination, and calibration; their arrows do not prove convergence. Figure 2 lacks a reproducible model/version/date and sampling protocol for estimating failure rates. Internal-state copyright prediction in §5.2 is explicitly proposed research, not an established detector.

No target-specific public implementation, separate supplement, later edition, or erratum was found in the inspected PMLR/institutional records and targeted searches. Appendices A–D are included in the source PDF. OpenReview’s verification challenge blocked revision/attachment history; a secondary asset-inventory request returned HTTP 404. These are access limits, not proof of absence. The CopyBench dependency repository was located, but no author code was executed. A secondary review of the cited NAF theory found conditional reference-model guarantees, with no specific theorem misattribution established in the target [E7].

Remaining work is concrete: specify the objective and updater, rights-label assumptions and jurisdictions, update acceptance criteria, dataset/sampling design, and compute budget; compare the complete framework with coordinated and isolated baselines on held-out copying, over-filtering, utility, latency, and newly emerging risks. Such experiments would test the stronger efficacy and continuous-improvement interpretations. They were not performed in this audit.

report: # Scientific verification report: I25-40115
# 1. Identity and reviewed version
Paper: Position: Human Baselines in Model Evaluations Need Rigor and Transparency (With Recommendations & Reporting Checklist).

Authors: Kevin L. Wei, Patricia Paskov, Sunishchal Dev, Michael J. Byun, Anka Reuel, Xavier Roberts-Gaal, Rachel Calcott, Evie Coxon, and Chinmay Deshpande. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, proceedings pages 82265-82325. Assigned display number: 0016.

The reviewed object is the 61-page PMLR PDF downloaded from the assigned publication link. All page references below are 1-based PDF pages, which coincide with its printed internal page numbers; they are not the proceedings page range. SHA-256: `24e0aae716ddb6fdcb8c61f8a0e035c9cd0359eab7ffa29f6c96e37e22c6095e`. The immutable matching source is identified in the references. The author repository’s 69-page paper is a distinct file and was not substituted. [Wei-PMLR (2025)]
Task: B001 / [internal task] / attempt-001. Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]. Review performed 23 October 2026, America/Chicago; source timestamps are recorded in UTC.
# 2. Summary and inspection outcome

Supported outcome: Major (P1), with two scoped Minor concerns (P2 and P3). The systematic audit of 115 human baselines is an explicitly stated contribution. Three prominent audit rates describe imputed classifications as reported or observed practices; this materially changes the quantitative evidence supplied by that contribution. P2 concerns the precision-to-power wording, with the source’s conditional precision standard retained. P3 distinguishes operational tool access from the fairness of an asymmetric comparison. The transparency recommendations and the evidence of missing reporting survive; their survival does not determine the severity of the affected audit results. This is a proposed AI acceptance calibration revision, with scientific decisions pending.

The review combines close reading, independent counts from the released raw workbook, static notebook inspection, and a small exact probability calculation. It is not an empirical reproduction of the 115 underlying human studies. The raw data and notebook are pinned to repository commit `46d4b1b9099d32f3580d19e5671ee3c865aaddbe`. [Wei-data (2025/06); independent_results.json]
# 3. Definitions, assumptions, and inspected scope

A baseline is the unit of annotation. The dataset has 115 baseline columns (Final_Data!D:DN), drawn from 109 titled articles. The six additional baselines are explicitly explained in Appendix E, p.57. Counts over baselines are descriptive counts of this selected corpus, not probability-sample estimates of every foundation-model evaluation.

The codebook distinguishes explicit Yes, Partial, No, Unknown/Unreported, and N/A. Appendix B, p.45, says Yes and No require source evidence, Partial is generally rounded to Yes, and selected Unknown/Unreported values are replaced by defaults. Accordingly, an imputed category and an observed report are different estimands. All percentages below state their denominator. [Wei-PMLR (2025), pp.38,45,56-57]

Main sections 1-7, the checklist and selected summary tables, the case-study/expert-baseline reasoning, and the review-method appendix were checked. The review did not independently reopen and recode all 109 source articles. Bibliographic reference pages were used for location and provenance, not comprehensively audited.
# 4. Problem 1: imputed classifications become observed-practice claims
## Source claim and location

Section 4.2, p.5, describes approximately 29% of baselines as having reported recruitment quality control. Section 4.3, p.6, describes approximately 88% and 76% as displaying differences in UI and instructions. Tables 3 and 6, pp.41-42, disclose defaults; Appendix B, pp.45,47-48, defines the coding. The concern is the main-text interpretation, not a hidden imputation procedure. [Wei-PMLR (2025)]
## Complete check

The independent checker reads the XLSX ZIP/XML directly and counts raw, non-formula cells. It does not execute the author notebook or any workbook formula. The following categories reproduce from the pinned raw workbook:
Item and cell range | Yes | Partial | No | Unknown | N/A
Recruitment QC, D34:DN34 | 13 | 0 | 82 | 20 | 0
UI equivalence, D54:DN54 | 7 | 7 | 37 | 62 | 2
Instruction equivalence, D57:DN57 | 23 | 5 | 21 | 66 | 0
All ranges are on Final_Data, and each row totals 115. [Wei-data (2025/06); independent_results.json]

Recruitment QC: the explicit-Yes proportion is 13/115 = 11.30%. The stated default-Yes rule adds 20 unknowns, yielding 33/115 = 28.70%, which explains the main-text 29%. That value describes the classification after imputation; it cannot simultaneously be the proportion that explicitly reported QC.

Instructions: 21/115 = 18.26% are explicitly No, and 66/115 = 57.39% are unknown. Defaulting unknowns to No produces (21+66)/115 = 75.65%, explaining 76%. Five Partial records are separate and are rounded upward under the authors’ rule. This calculation does not establish that 76% were observed to use different instructions.

UI: 37 records are explicitly No, 62 are unknown, and two are N/A. The published Table 6 has 14 Yes and 101 No. Its No total numerically equals 37+62+2; thus it also includes the two N/A records. The explicit-No share is 37/115 = 32.17%, whereas the table’s residual-No share is 101/115 = 87.83%. The formula path that allocated N/A was not inspected. Retaining 115 as the denominator matches the published table; removing N/A would create a different analysis. [Wei-PMLR (2025), Table 6; Wei-data (2025/06)]
## Alternative reading and counterevidence

The authors openly disclose imputation and deliberately choose different defaults for different variables. For example, tool-access unknowns default to Yes. Appendix B frames these defaults as assumptions about prevailing practice; this is evidence against an allegation of concealed or uniformly pessimistic coding. The discrepancy concerns the semantic move from an assumed label to a reported or observed practice.

If the intended outcome is an assumption-dependent assessment of likely rigor, the imputed summaries are interpretable with that qualification. They do not directly measure actual reporting rates or demonstrated procedural differences. The many unknown records independently support concern about transparency.
## Impact and precise repair

Severity: Major. The dependency is explicit: the abstract presents the systematic 115-baseline review as a contribution; sections 4.2 and 4.3 use these rates to describe observed recruitment and evaluation practices; Tables 3 and 6 and the coding defaults generate the cited summaries. Treating unknown records as observations changes the estimand and materially overstates what the released annotations establish about these practices. This is a defect in the core audit’s quantitative evidence, even though the textual correction is bounded. The raw categories establish documented evidence and missingness, not the true practices in unknown cases. The disclosed defaults and the continued support for transparency remain valid counterevidence against stronger accusations.

A verified descriptive repair is to report the explicit counts and missing counts separately, while labeling the 28.70%, 75.65%, and 87.83% values as summaries after the specified coding defaults. A corrected estimate of actual practice cannot be obtained by relabeling unknowns; it requires source re-examination or author information. This repair is arithmetically checked against the frozen workbook, not adopted by the authors.
# 5. Problem 2: precision is used to infer power without a design
## Source claim and suspect step

Section 4.1, p.4, first correctly says that power analysis depends on significance level and a prespecified relevant effect. It then invokes a sample near 1,000 for a survey margin of error and, explicitly conditional on that standard, characterizes the baselines as vastly underpowered using their median sample size of eight. The numerical precision reference does not establish test-specific power across heterogeneous outcomes and effects. The wording must preserve that conditional standard; it is inaccurate to attribute an unqualified universal power theorem to the source. [Wei-PMLR (2025), p.4]

The released data reproduce the descriptive median of 8 and mean of 89.8272 (rounded to 90), using 81 numeric entries in Final_Data!D16:DN16. These are not calculations over 115 fully observed participant counts. The descriptive numbers themselves are not the issue. [Wei-data (2025/06); independent_results.json]
## Fully specified analytic counterexample

Consider eight independent, uniformly sampled humans from a large target population. Each answers one fixed binary task under identical conditions. Let Y_i be independent Bernoulli(p) outcomes and K their sum. Treat the AI reference probability p0 = 0.5 as known; no additional estimated-AI uncertainty is present. Test H0: p=0.5 against a two-sided alternative at nominal alpha=0.05.
The conventional nonrandomized equal-tail exact test rejects at K=0 or K=8:

Every stipulated sampling assumption holds, and the design is a valid human-baseline comparison. Thus n=8 can provide greater than 92% power for a sufficiently large effect even with a conservative exact test. A normal-approximation survey half-width of 1.96*sqrt(0.25/1000) = 0.03099 describes a different target: precision for a proportion near one-half. [Independent analytic calculation; independent_checks.py]

This exact example shows that small sample size alone does not force low power. It uses a known AI probability, independent Bernoulli outcomes, and a very large prespecified alternative. It does not meet a demand for roughly three-percentage-point survey precision and therefore does not refute the source’s conditional precision standard. It is not a counterexample to a theorem asserted in the paper, nor a power estimate for any of the audited studies.
## Alternative reading, impact, and repair

The explicit qualification to the stated standard supports reading the sentence as a warning about survey precision. The earlier effect-specific power-analysis sentence, the sampling-bias discussion on p.5, and the context-dependent framework on p.9 reinforce that reading. The precise supported concern is conflation of precision and statistical power, plus an unestablished transfer of that survey target to heterogeneous baseline studies; the example does not prove those studies adequately powered.

Severity: Minor within this demonstrated scope. The issue bears on the audit’s sample-size diagnostic, but the source’s express precision condition and correct effect-specific guidance prevent the example from establishing a materially false power conclusion under matching assumptions. The descriptive median remains verified. Retain the sample-size evidence, distinguish precision from power, and state the estimand, effect, variance, dependence, sampling design, and test needed for a power assessment. No actual-study power reanalysis was performed.
# 6. Problem 3: the tool-equivalence rule conflates access and fairness
## Source claim and location

Appendix B.3, Q3.5, p.48, asks whether humans and AI have the same technical tools but instructs coders to count Internet-trained AI without Internet access as equivalent to humans with Internet access. Appendix D, p.53, argues that such an asymmetric comparison can be fair because the model has encountered Internet information. Table 6, p.42, and section 4.3, p.6, use the resulting tool-equivalence variable. [Wei-PMLR (2025)]
## Complete check and original assumptions

Prior training does not supply a live retrieval tool. Let model weights Theta be fixed. After training, draw B uniformly from {0,1}, independently of Theta, and publish B at a known URL. Both participants receive the same task identifying the URL but not B. The human is permitted live retrieval; the model has no retrieval or other channel containing B. Model randomization R is independent of B.

For any binary prediction Y=g(Theta,prompt,R), independence gives P(Y=B)=1/2. An idealized human who successfully retrieves and correctly copies the page obtains B with probability 1. The example deliberately assumes successful lookup; it does not assert measured human performance.

All conditions of the codebook exception hold: the human has Internet access, the AI does not, and the AI was Internet-trained. The rule nevertheless labels unequal operational access as equal. The failure of equivalence is already present in the allowed tools; the bit example additionally shows why prior exposure cannot resolve every information-access difference.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair

The authors’ fairness argument can be reasonable for a specified research question. Fairness of an asymmetric design, however, is distinct from literal equality of permitted tools. The report does not claim that every such comparison is scientifically inappropriate.

Severity: Minor within the demonstrated scope. This is a construct-labeling defect in one audit variable: its operational rule permits different live tools while the question asks about the same tools. The rule can instead be understood as a proposed fairness proxy; the report does not disprove that normative choice. No affected observed row or materially changed aggregate rate has been established, so the analytic example does not establish a false corpus-level result. The released row59 has 34 Yes, 12 No, and 69 Unknown/Unreported; default Yes yields 103/115 Yes. The number of explicit-Yes records using the exception and any corrected percentage remain undetermined.

Repair: record operational tool access separately from the rationale for a fair asymmetric comparison. The example must be unequal in the tool-access field; the fairness rationale may remain in a separate field. Recode affected source articles and recompute dependent statistics before publishing a new percentage. The conceptual distinction is verified analytically; corpus-level repair remains unverified.
# 7. Other checked reasoning and dependence

The 109-article/115-baseline distinction is explained and reproduces from the data. Static notebook inspection found hand-entered year, venue, and language frequency arrays rather than an implementation generating the main checklist percentages. Independent year and language counts matched the inspected notebook literals. This is finite data checking, not evidence that the notebook generated the published figures.

The 38 affirmative uncertainty annotations and 42 interval-or-distribution records concern different checklist questions; their difference alone does not prove a contradiction. The same-item recommendation on p.3 is a practical safeguard. Independent representative task samples can also estimate a population-level human-AI difference with suitable unpaired uncertainty; this is recorded as scope clarification, not another error.

Appendix D’s maximum-performance discussion is itemwise. Replacing that target with the best single person’s average would change the estimand and would not refute the stated discussion. No such counterexample is claimed. None of the three supported findings invalidates the overall value of the checklist or establishes that any individual underlying benchmark is wrong.
# 8. Version history, existing corrections, and remaining work

The inspected arXiv record lists arXiv:2506.13776v1, submitted 9 June 2025, under an alternate title. The author repository snapshot is from the same date. Its paper.pdf has 69 pages and a different hash; only its identity/front matter were checked, not its complete semantic equivalence. The inspected public issue list contained a dataset-hosting request (issue #1), not a scientific correction. No relevant author erratum was identified in those inspected records. OpenReview discussion could not be read. [Wei-arXiv (2025/06); Wei-repo (2025/06); Issue-1 (2025/06)]

The linked Google summary spreadsheet was not inspected: automatic approval review rejected the attempted retrieval because the source’s public accessibility and specific access authorization were not verified. It was not retried through another route. Raw GitHub data suffice for the category counts above, but the historical summary-formula lineage remains unresolved.

Fresh empirical work would be needed to measure the effects of improved baseline methods or infer unreported practices. Reassessment of actual power and corrected tool-equivalence percentages requires the relevant original study information. Human scientific decisions and any author adoption are pending.
