report: # Scientific verification report: I25-40116
# 1. Identity and exact reviewed version

Paper: Position: The Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Community Should Adopt a More Transparent and Regulated Peer Review Process. Author: Jing Yang. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82399-82408. Assigned display number: 0017.

The reviewed source is the 10-page final PMLR PDF, SHA-256 `038bff56e4440b9896d64fcc0eb6819cbeb4fd051c48f16f08875b129178723d`, downloaded at 2026-10-24T04:25:43.932578+00:00. Page references below are 1-based PDF pages and match printed internal pages. No appendix is present. [Yang-PMLR (2025)]
Task B001 / [internal task] / attempt-001. Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]. Review date: 23 October 2026, America/Chicago.
# 2. Summary

Supported outcome: Major. The sixfold active-user comparison and the equation of closed visibility with one-time rebuttal materially compromise two parts of the paper’s central review-model analysis. The U.S. patent-disclosure exception remains a Minor local correction. The causal benefits attributed to openness remain Needs Evidence, because the reported comparisons do not isolate disclosure policy from venue, content, timing, and selection effects.

P1 affects the quantitative evidence in Section 4.3, Community Interests Validation; P2 affects the explanatory inference linking public disclosure to iterative author clarification. These are core empirical and procedural dependencies. Major does not require disproving all benefits of open review or reversing the direction of an association. The original full-text, source-policy, visual, and arithmetic checks are retained; acceptance rechecked the relevant source anchors and dependency. The historical website analytics and individual survey responses were not independently reproduced.
# 3. Definitions, data, and scope

The paper defines review modes by timing and extent of public disclosure, while its engagement measures include website views, active users, engagement duration, confidence scores, and reply counts. These outcomes are not interchangeable. Website visitors are not automatically a representative sample of researchers; stated confidence does not by itself measure calibration; reply counts do not directly measure review quality.

The comparison mixes public API records, voluntary community submissions, and website analytics. Figures 7-9 concern accepted papers. Table 3 identifies differing data sources. The survey in section 5.2 is a voluntary front-page survey about anonymous score sharing. These design details are central to interpreting its claims. [Yang-PMLR (2025), pp.3-8]

All ten PDF pages were read. Figures 5-9 were visually checked against relevant narrative statements. Public materials and version histories were inspected, but no paper-specific frozen Google Analytics/Search Console export or complete survey package was located in the inspected links. No author code was run.
# 4. Problem 1: the active-user multiplier does not match Figure 5
## Original claim and location

On p.5, section 4.3, the text gives ICLR 88,220 active users and describes this as approximately six times the NeurIPS count. Figure 5 on the same page displays active users as orange bars against the left logarithmic count axis. [Yang-PMLR (2025), p.5]
## Complete numerical and visual check

The exact source page was rendered with pdftoppm. The NeurIPS orange bar is unambiguously above 10^4.5, or approximately 31,623, rather than near 14,700. Only this conservative graphical bound is used:

Code:
NeurIPS count implied by sixfold statement = 88,220 / 6 = 14,703.3333.
Conservative lower bound from plot = 10^4.5 = 31,622.7766.
Therefore ICLR / NeurIPS < 88,220 / 31,622.7766 = 2.7897614.

Thus the sixfold comparison and the plotted count cannot both describe the same active-user metric, reporting window, and filter. Reading the wording as sevenfold rather than sixfold does not resolve the disagreement. The figure crop is preserved as sources/0017/figure5_crop.png, derived from the hashed original. [Independent arithmetic; independent_results.json]
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair

Possible explanations include different reporting windows, filters, or a mistaken comparator. None is specified in the compared text and caption. The check does not establish which representation contains the correct raw count.

Judgment: Major. Section 4.3 presents this comparison as quantitative validation of community interest across review modes. Under the common measure and population implied by the text and caption, a claimed factor of six is incompatible with the conservative graphical upper bound below 2.79. This materially overstates a core empirical comparison, even though the displayed direction of the association survives. The bound establishes inconsistency, not which raw representation is correct. A precise numerical repair requires both counts for the same population, window, and filters; no exact replacement ratio is inferred from pixel heights. Repair verification remains pending.
# 5. Problem 2: private review is conflated with one-time author response
## Original claim and suspect step

At the opening of p.7, section 4.3, the discussion contrasts extended open-review dialogue with a categorical characterization of fully closed models as allowing a single rebuttal phase. The suspect implication is that non-public reviews necessarily prevent iterative author-reviewer communication. [Yang-PMLR (2025), p.7]
## Complete check against a historical counterexample

The paper classifies ICML in its closed category for the historical period ending in 2024. The official ICML 2024 Author Instructions, under Reviewing and Author Response, specify private reviewing, an initial rebuttal, a subsequent discussion period involving authors, reviewers and area chairs, and permission for multiple responses per submission. This is an example within the paper’s own historical scope, rather than a policy introduced only after publication. [ICML-2024, Reviewing and Author Response]

The relevant variables are distinct: public visibility, number of allowed responses, duration of discussion, and eligibility to participate. A private process can allow multiple exchanges, while excluding the broader public.
## Counterevidence, impact, and precise repair

Open public commenting can still expand participation beyond the author/reviewer group. Nothing here establishes equal interaction volumes or quality across review modes. A charitable reading is that the text intended a particular closed venue, but it did not specify that restriction.

Judgment: Major. The paper defines review modes by public disclosure on p.1 and places ICML in the fully closed category in Figure 5. The within-scope ICML 2024 counterexample therefore invalidates the categorical premise used in Section 4.3 to explain iterative clarification as an advantage of open over closed review. Public visibility and permission for repeated author responses are distinct policy variables. This is a failed core explanatory inference, not an assessment that public participation has no value. Repair by identifying venue/year, response rounds, discussion duration, and eligible participants separately from disclosure. The policy evidence verifies this distinction; it does not estimate the contribution of each variable to the observed reply differences.
# 6. Problem 3: the U.S. patent statement is too absolute
## Original claim and location

Section 6, p.8, Disclosure Policy, describes the U.S. first-to-file system as requiring no public disclosure before filing. The adjacent statement that an open submission can jeopardize patent protection is conditional and broader. [Yang-PMLR (2025), p.8]
## Source check and corrected scope

USPTO MPEP section 2153.01, revision R-01.2024, explains 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A): qualifying inventor-originated disclosures made no more than one year before the effective filing date are excepted from the specified prior-art rule. This pre-existing exception disproves an unconditional U.S. prohibition on all prefiling disclosure. [USPTO-2153.01 (2024)]

For a concrete logical instance, assume an otherwise qualifying inventor-originated disclosure occurs six months before the effective filing date and satisfies the statutory provenance and subject-matter conditions. The paper’s absolute statement would exclude it solely because disclosure preceded filing; the cited exception does not treat that qualifying disclosure as prior art under 102(a)(1). This does not establish patentability under all other requirements.

Judgment: Minor. The defect is local to the legal premise used in the confidentiality discussion. A defensible repair acknowledges the defined U.S. exception and conditions the risk on jurisdiction, timing, disclosure origin, and subject matter. The general concern about disclosure risk remains. No particular invention, application, or filing strategy was evaluated.
# 7. Problem 4: causal effects of openness remain unidentified
## Claim and location

Sections 4.3 and 5, pp.5-8, attribute engagement and oversight advantages to review openness. Website traffic and accepted-paper discussion distributions are offered as supporting observations. [Yang-PMLR (2025)]
## Check of the inferential step

The comparisons vary venue and review mode together. Venue identity also carries topic, audience, calendar, available content, search visibility, and review procedures. The site’s ability to show live information differs by mode. Restricting discussion data to accepted papers introduces venue-specific selection. Similar submission counts do not remove these differences.

A minimal identification argument makes the limit explicit. Let m_c be an observed mean engagement value for venue c and O_c its disclosure indicator. In the decomposition m_c = beta*O_c + gamma_c, gamma_c represents unrestricted venue effects. For any beta, choosing gamma_c = m_c - beta*O_c reproduces every observed mean. The reported cross-venue means therefore do not identify beta without additional assumptions or design information. This is an analytic identification check, not a fitted model or evidence of a zero effect.
## Alternative readings and supported impact

The paper is a position paper and can legitimately use descriptive patterns to motivate policy. Some explanations are tentative, and p.9 acknowledges voluntary-selection bias. Its traffic data can support interest in the particular information service. Those points limit the concern.

Judgment: Needs Evidence. The direction or size of a causal effect, the quality of discussion, the reduction of overconfidence, and population-wide policy preferences are unresolved. They are not elevated into supported Major damage. A verified wording repair would describe associations and hypotheses. A causal repair requires a defensible design or assumptions and relevant data, not merely a new label.
# 8. Additional checked claims and scope clarifications

The basic CVPR 2025 author-reviewer obligation is documented. Its official policy also limits assignments to qualified reviewers, varies load with seniority, and lists exemptions. Therefore the obligation itself is not fabricated, while the paper’s proposed quality consequences require evidence that considers these safeguards. The text already calls some complaints anecdotal. [CVPR-2025; Yang-PMLR (2025), p.7]

The 57% anonymous-score-sharing result is a statement about voluntary respondents, not a representative estimate of support for full, real-time public reviews. The observed age distribution also does not establish every visitor’s occupation or career status. These are interpretation limits, not demonstrations that the raw reported values are false.

The lower-confidence explanation on p.6 is explicitly tentative. Confidence calibration would require comparison with an appropriate correctness or quality outcome. Visual inspection found that the stated reply maxima and increasing ICLR medians are consistent with Figures 8-9; those displays do not independently establish improved rigor.

The four Table 2 percentages sum to 100.8%. This cannot be explained by ordinary one-decimal rounding if they are mutually exclusive exhaustive shares, but overlapping users or differing attribution definitions might explain it. The denominator is unresolved, so this was not promoted to a confirmed arithmetic defect.

Figure 3 explicitly excludes 2025. ICML’s 2025 FAQ describes later publication of accepted-paper reviews, with opt-in publication for rejected papers. That policy change is recorded as time-sensitive context rather than retroactively invalidating the figure’s historical classification. [ICML-2025-FAQ]
# 9. Later versions, public materials, and overall dependence

The arXiv record lists versions v1 (2 February 2025), v2 (24 May 2025), and v3 (15 October 2025). A support agent independently compared extracted text from v2 and v3 with the PMLR file, joining line-break hyphenation, removing the repeated running header, and collapsing whitespace. The differences were the title prefix, arXiv stamp, and added section numbering. No substantive textual repair of the inspected claims was found. Images were not compared across versions, so complete visual identity is not asserted. The downloaded v3 has SHA-256 `f418e3cc8b1213622b7ded7a4fc9f99d9badaeba440779ac2fc6e2a34164c4b0`. [Yang-arXiv-v3]

Public Paper Copilot repositories contain conference and review records, but the documentation inspected did not identify the historical website-analytics exports, demographic missingness/denominators, or complete survey records required to reproduce this paper’s traffic and attitude claims. Current repository contents and later website usage totals are not substitutes for that frozen historical snapshot. [Paperlists; OpenReview-archive; ContactUs]

No matching author erratum was identified in the inspected version record, site documentation, or scoped project-issue search. OpenReview discussion was inaccessible. The separate later Paper Copilot system paper was used only to locate released resources, not reviewed as an additional assigned paper.

The contribution-dependency disposition is explicit: P1 is Major because an internally incompatible magnitude supports the central empirical comparison of review modes; P2 is Major because a false categorical procedural premise supports the interpretation of iterative discussion benefits. P3 remains Minor because its qualified patent-law correction concerns an alternative-view example and does not supply the empirical or procedural comparison. P4 remains Needs Evidence: the data do not identify a causal policy effect, and no effect reversal is claimed. The normative recommendations, public-participation distinction, and descriptive observations can survive these corrections. Their survival does not lower the severity of the failed core steps. Human policy and scientific decisions remain pending.
# 10. Conclusion table
Item | Judgment | Repair verification | Adoption | Remaining work
Active-user multiplier | Major; core magnitude inconsistent | Bound checked; exact repair pending | Not requested | Original counts, common window/filter
Closed review and rebuttals | Major; core premise false | Policy-based correction checked | Not requested | Venue-specific comparative analysis
U.S. prefiling disclosure | Minor; statutory exception omitted | Limited legal correction sourced | Not requested | No specific patent case assessed
Openness causes better outcomes | Needs Evidence | Descriptive wording defensible | Not requested | Causal design and outcome measures

report: # Scientific verification report: I25-40117
# 1. Identity and exact reviewed version

Paper: Position: Principles of Animal Cognition to Improve LLM Evaluations. Authors: Sunayana Rane, Cyrus F. Kirkman, Graham Todd, Amanda Royka, Ryan M. C. Law, Erica A. Cartmill, and Jacob G. Foster. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82051-82061. Assigned display number: 0018.

The reviewed source is the 11-page final PMLR PDF, SHA-256 461ff952375293337551d22b9528546048b186ddb829f43a0e3bde9bdc0cb34b, downloaded at 2026-10-24T04:31:04.670160+00:00. Page references are 1-based PDF pages and match printed internal pages. No appendix is present. The public preliminary drafts are not substituted for this version. [Rane-PMLR (2025)]
Task B001 / [internal task] / attempt-001. Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]. Review date: 24 October 2026 (UTC).
# 2. Summary and supported judgment

Supported outcome: Minor. One concrete reporting incompatibility is demonstrated: the Experiment 2 endpoint-exclusion rule permits test distances 2-4, whereas the results give 2-6. Which description matches the implemented tests remains unresolved. The numerical chance-performance and uncertainty claims require additional evidence for independent verification; no error in the reported accuracy of 0.40 or SD of 0.50 has been established.

The five proposed evaluation principles remain defensible. The case study supports examining sensitivity to task formulation. It does not, by itself, isolate a unique reasoning mechanism. The paper’s own distinction between behavior and mechanism and its contextual discussion are important counterevidence against reading it as a blanket denial of all transitive competence. No Major issue is supported.
# 3. Definitions, coverage, and evidence limits

The empirical question concerns transitive inference (TI): extending an ordinal relation to pairs not explicitly compared. Experiment 1 states ordinal premises in a prompt and varies operators and stimuli. Experiment 2 supplies correct/incorrect feedback on adjacent binary choices without explicitly stating a total-order assumption. These tasks involve overlapping but different demands. Symbolic distance is rank separation: adjacent elements have distance 1. [Rane-PMLR (2025), pp.5-8]

All 11 source pages were read, and Figures 1-2 and Table 1 were visually checked against the exact original. The check included quantifiers, training/test denominators, endpoint exclusions, figure signs, illustrative alternative mechanisms, source identity, and public version/materials searches. It did not reproduce GPT-4o outputs or validate every cited animal experiment.

The PMLR related-material section links the PDF and OpenReview, with no separate software or supplement link. No experiment repository or raw-response package was located in the inspected PDF, author publication links, or targeted searches. This is a bounded availability result, not proof that such records do not exist. OpenReview returned a browser-verification page, leaving its discussion and attachments unverified.
# 4. Problem 1: the stated test rule and distance range cannot both hold
## Original claim and suspect step

On p.7, section 6.2 describes seven ordered stimuli A through G and novel test pairs that exclude the terminal elements. Section 7.3 on the same page reports tests at symbolic distances 2-6. The distance definition in Figure 2, p.8, is rank separation. [Rane-PMLR (2025)]
## Complete finite check
After removing A and G, the available ranks are B, C, D, E, F. Enumerating all unordered nonadjacent pairs gives exactly:
Pair | Distance
B,D | 2
B,E | 3
B,F | 4
C,E | 2
C,F | 3
D,F | 2

Thus the admissible distance set is {2,3,4}, with maximum 4. Distance 5 requires A,F or B,G; distance 6 requires A,G. All of those pairs contain a terminal element. Reversing the display order of a pair does not change its rank separation. The finite enumeration was independently executed using the standard library and saved in verification/0018/independent_results.json.
## Counterevidence and alternative readings

The reported range could be a carryover from Experiment 1, which includes all pairs. Alternatively, the actual Experiment 2 tests may have included endpoints. The abbreviated Figure 1 schematic is not a trial log and cannot decide between these possibilities.

A nearby statement assigning B an always-incorrect status is also inconsistent with B being an interior member of the adjacent chain; it plausibly intends G. This is treated as related descriptive ambiguity, not as a second independent defect or evidence that the experiment used incorrect labels.
## Impact and conditional repair

Judgment: Minor, a bounded methods/results incompatibility. Endpoint exclusion matters because endpoints have uniformly reinforced status, so choices involving them can be answered without general nonadjacent inference. The inconsistency prevents a precise reconstruction of the intended control. It does not show that the reported 0.40 accuracy is false.

If endpoint exclusion describes the implementation, the admissible range is 2-4; this conditional mathematical correction is verified. If distances 5 or 6 were actually tested, the method description and endpoint-free interpretation require revision. The actual pair list must determine the repair, followed by recalculation of any affected summaries. No empirical repair has been verified or adopted.
# 5. Problem 2: chance-performance and uncertainty claims cannot yet be independently verified
## Claim, missing information, and precise uncertainty

Section 7.3 characterizes Experiment 2 performance as at chance and reports no distance differences. Table 1 gives accuracy 0.40 and SD 0.50. Figure 2 presents 95% intervals and fitted lines for Experiment 1. The text specifies ten task iterations and sixty training trials per iteration, but does not establish the independent test-response denominator or the SD’s aggregation unit. The inspected materials also do not identify a reproducible model snapshot, inference settings, complete response history, or sufficient GLM family/link and uncertainty details. [Rane-PMLR (2025), pp.6-8]

Ten iterations cannot automatically be equated with ten test observations, and the six hundred training presentations are not test responses. An SD near 0.50 can be compatible with binary outcomes near accuracy 0.4; it is not evidence of an arithmetic error. The Experiment 2 paragraph’s pointer to Figure 2 does not supply its missing trial data because that figure describes Experiment 1.
## Independent check of what accuracy alone can establish

To illustrate dependence on the missing denominator, consider hypothetical independent Bernoulli responses under a known null probability 0.5. An exact two-sided binomial test sums probabilities no greater than the observed probability. Two hypothetical samples have identical accuracy 0.40:
Hypothetical sample | Accuracy | Exact two-sided p-value

These are independently calculated illustrations, not reconstructions of the paper’s data or its SD. They prove that an accuracy value alone does not determine its statistical relation to chance. Actual observations may also be clustered within conversations or task instances, so an independent-binomial calculation could be inappropriate even after obtaining a raw count.
Failure to reject a chance null is not, by itself, an equivalence result. A formal equivalence claim would additionally require a justified tolerance and suitable uncertainty calculation.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair status

Judgment: Needs Evidence for independent statistical verification. The authors may intend a descriptive characterization of 40% as roughly near a 50% baseline; that reading is acknowledged and is not disproved. Likewise, all six displayed fitted slopes are visually positive, consistent with their sign claim. No contrary numerical result is asserted.

The unresolved material is needed to assess sampling uncertainty, distance effects, and reproducibility. Release the actual test pairs and responses, independent units, aggregation rules, model/inference metadata, and uncertainty procedure. Reanalysis should respect dependence and distinguish estimation, a difference test, and equivalence. The published estimates, intervals, and fitted coefficients have not been independently reproduced.
# 6. Mechanism and scope checks: no additional demonstrated defect
## Inductive transfer versus deduction from declared ordinal premises

Figure 1C asks the system to learn correct word choices through feedback; it does not announce that the hidden relation is transitive. A concrete countermodel shows the resulting inference boundary. Let one rule choose the earlier item in A>B>C>D>E>F>G. Let a second rule agree everywhere except for the unseen B,D pair, where it chooses D. Both rules make identical predictions for all six trained adjacent pairs, and hence for all sixty repetitions, but they disagree on B,D. The second rule has a cycle B>C>D>B.

Therefore, the training labels do not uniquely entail the intended nonadjacent answer without a structural assumption. The independent checker confirms equal training predictions and different B,D predictions. This does not invalidate the task: spontaneous adoption of the intended structure is a legitimate behavioral capacity to test. It means that failed transfer can reflect failure to infer or deploy the hidden ordering, rather than absence of an ordinal computation once suitable premises are represented.

The same reasoning limits the assertion on p.7 that using a common mechanism across contexts would necessarily give similar performance. Encoding, memory, instruction comprehension, and elicitation can affect the observed outcome even when a reasoning component is available. The paper’s P4 and P5 explicitly recognize related behavior/mechanism and performance/competence distinctions. Its discussion also favors context-dependent capability statements. A claim about the observed protocol is supported more directly than a universal mechanism claim.
## A symbolic-distance pattern does not uniquely identify TI

For Experiment 1, consider an illustrative rule that memorizes the adjacent choices, always selects A if present in a novel pair, avoids G if present, and otherwise guesses. It has no general solution for interior novel comparisons. At a nonadjacent distance d, there are 7-d unordered pairs; the expected accuracy is (endpoint_pairs + 0.5 * other_pairs)/(7-d).
Distance | Total pairs | Endpoint-containing pairs | Expected accuracy

The checker independently enumerates this curve. It demonstrates an alternative source of a positive distance association, without claiming that GPT-4o actually used this strategy or that the curve matches every plotted value. Endpoint-free and position-controlled comparisons would help discriminate mechanisms.

The authors describe behavior analogous to the symbolic distance effect; they do not prove a unique animal-like mechanism from the curve alone. All six fitted lines in Figure 2B point upward. Intermediate dips in Figure 2A do not contradict a positive fitted association. These are scope clarifications, not further confirmed errors.
## Causality motivation

The cited Halpern paper studies sufficient conditions for causal transitivity and explicitly discusses failures of transitivity in general. It does not establish ordinal TI as a necessary substrate of every causal judgment. The reviewed article’s motivation should be read with that qualification; it does not explicitly claim that every causal relation is transitive. This source check therefore does not refute the ordinal experiments or create another finding. [Halpern (2016), author PDF pp.2,6-8]
# 7. Versions, known issues, and overall dependence

An immutable PMLR copy was independently downloaded by a support agent and matched the assigned PDF byte for byte. The author publication page links an older-title, 12-page draft bundle with an extra cover page and preliminary/under-review markers. Another author-hosted file is an 11-page anonymous preliminary draft. Neither was established as a later corrected edition. Exact upload dates were not established, and the drafts were not exhaustively diffed against the final article.

No relevant erratum or verified later repair was identified in the inspected primary records and targeted searches. OpenReview revision/discussion history remains inaccessible. The finite inconsistency is independently reproduced here, but no claim of priority or exhaustive absence of prior criticism is made.

The demonstrated problem affects reproducibility of one empirical control. The statistical and mechanistic limits restrict the interpretation of that case study. None demonstrates failure of the paper’s broader recommendation to use adversarial controls, stimulus variation, failure analysis, behavior/mechanism distinctions, and appropriate task accommodations.

# Scientific verification report: I25-40119
# 1. Identity and exact reviewed version
Paper: Position: Generative AI Regulation Can Learn from Social Media Regulation. Author: Ruth Elisabeth Appel. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81035-81049. Assigned display number: 0019.

The reviewed version is the 15-page final proceedings PDF, SHA-256 a8d0ff2846358b38cfa6922b2353fc40feac2f360fab4e98040474bea9c09f08, downloaded at 2026-10-24T04:36:28.808563+00:00. References to the paper use 1-based PDF pages, matching its printed pages. The earlier 11-page arXiv manuscript is distinguished throughout. [Appel-PMLR (2025)]
Task B001 / [internal task] / attempt-001. Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]. Review date: 24 October 2026 (UTC).
# 2. Summary and supported judgment

Supported outcome: No Issue Found within the inspected scope. The review did not establish a substantive defect that invalidates the paper’s central position or warrants a numbered Problem entry. Selected empirical citations support their bounded claims, and historical legal texts support a qualified reading of the legal examples.

This finding is limited. The paper is a policy argument about learning from experience, with particular attention to content moderation and regulation broadly understood to include self-regulation. It does not demonstrate the effectiveness of a finished regulatory package. Several qualifications below matter for interpreting its evidence: model scoring is distinct from generated behavior; research-access mechanisms differ across laws; and medium-level feature comparisons are not universal technological classifications.

All 15 pages were read, including the bibliography. Table 1 on p.3 and Figure 1 on p.5 were visually inspected. Selected empirical sources, original historical legal texts, accessible version records, and public-material links were checked. Not every citation, legal jurisdiction, or policy outcome was independently audited. No new author experiment, theorem, dataset, or executable implementation is presented for this review to reproduce.
# 3. Argument reconstruction and quantifier check

The central inference is that shared content-governance problems make social-media experience informative for generative-AI policy. That inference can support candidate practices and questions without implying that a practice will have identical effects in the two settings. The distinction matters: shared features alone do not identify an intervention’s net benefit when incentives, user populations, failure modes, and implementation costs differ.

The paper limits its comparison to common applications on p.2, discusses differences on pp.3-4, acknowledges institutional shortcomings on pp.5-6, calls for effectiveness research on p.7, and distinguishes learning from copying on p.9. These qualifications directly answer several possible adverse readings. An imperfect analogy is not sufficient to refute the modest proposition that relevant lessons can be drawn. [Appel-PMLR (2025), pp.2-9]

The four recommendations are policy directions. Figure 1 maps them to strategies, possible measures, and social-media precedents; it is not a plot of measured effects. Table 1 is a conceptual classification, not an estimated prevalence table or an experimental comparison. No numerical significance or causal-effect estimate was inferred from either visual.

The review therefore does not convert acknowledged future research into an alleged missing experiment. The broad comparative phrase that this is the best way to avoid mistakes is not established by a comparative policy evaluation; it is most defensibly read as advocacy within a paper that expressly permits other analogies and first-principles analysis.
# 4. Selected empirical-source checks
## 4.1 Opinion distributions and political leaning

The primary Santurkar et al. publication record describes comparisons between language-model responses and opinion distributions from 60 US demographic groups. It reports substantial misalignment and left-leaning tendencies in some human-feedback-tuned models. This supports the reviewed paper’s bounded discussion of opinion mismatch. It does not establish a context-independent orientation for all models. [Santurkar et al. (2023)]

The paper’s p.5 acknowledgment that prompts and question order affect bias measurement is relevant counterevidence against an interpretation that it ignores elicitation dependence. This verification checked the primary publication record and abstract; it did not recompute OpinionQA measurements.
## 4.2 Influence on opinions and decisions

Fisher et al.’s 2024 version describes randomized interactive tasks involving liberal-biased, conservative-biased, and control chatbot conditions. The inspected methods include instruction-induced partisan behavior and tasks involving opinion formation and budget allocation. Those experiments support the possibility that biased chatbot behavior can affect choices in the tested setting. [Fisher et al. (2024), v1, section3.2]

This evidence does not quantify changes in actual election outcomes, establish identical effects for default deployed models, or prove that a proposed regulation removes the effect. The reviewed paper’s possibility claim does not require those stronger conclusions. The 2024 version was inspected, rather than substituting the source’s current 2026 revision.

A support agent also inspected Matz et al.’s original article, which studies personalized generated messages and outcomes involving attitudes and intended behavior. That evidence fits the bounded persuasion claim; it should not be read as direct observation of lasting real-world voting behavior. The parent reader’s Nature-page retrieval failed, so full-text coverage of that source is attributed specifically to the support agent. No reported effect size was independently recalculated. [Matz et al. (2024)]
## 4.3 CrowS-Pairs: measurement and model-class qualification

Nangia et al. evaluate supplied stereotypical and less-stereotypical sentence pairs using masked-language-model scores. Their methods use conditional pseudo-log-likelihood, and the evaluated models are BERT-base, RoBERTa-large, and ALBERT-XXL-v2. [Nangia et al. (2020), sections3-4, PDF pp.4-5 / printed pp.1956-1957]

This is evidence of biases in the tested language models’ sentence-scoring behavior. It is not a direct experiment measuring freely generated depictions from a contemporary conversational or image-generation product. The citation on p.4 is best framed as earlier evidence about language-model biases, with modern deployment-specific claims supported separately.

The charitable reading is that the citation supplies background evidence for the broader bias concern. Other cited studies support that concern, so this source-type qualification does not establish that the policy premise is false or that its main recommendations fail. It is recorded as a scope clarification, without inventing a corrected empirical effect.
# 5. Historical legal-source checks
## 5.1 Access mechanisms must be distinguished

The historical AI Act text permits specified general-purpose-model compliance and systemic-risk evaluations, including independent experts appointed to act for the Commission. Article 92 permits access requests through APIs or other appropriate technical means. This supports a narrow reading of the p.8 reference to researcher access, but does not create a general access entitlement for unaffiliated researchers’ own projects. [AI Act signed text (2024), Article92, printed pp.342-343 / PDF pp.343-344]

The DSA has a different route: Article40 provides conditional access for vetted researchers, through the relevant Digital Services Coordinator, for systemic-risk and mitigation research involving covered very large platforms/search engines. Article37 requires annual independent audits of those covered services. These are bounded mechanisms, not duties applying identically to every service and every research request. [DSA signed text (2022), Articles37 and40]
Legal example | Verified interpretation | Limit on transfer
AI Act Article92 | Regulator-directed evaluation, potentially involving appointed independent experts | Not a general independent-research application right
DSA Article40 | Conditional researcher access for designated purposes and covered providers | Eligibility, procedure, purpose, and provider scope matter
DSA Article37 | Independent audits for covered very large services | Not an undifferentiated audit requirement for all social media

The paper does not expressly say these access mechanisms are legally identical. Its recommendation to improve access remains intelligible under the narrower reading. The appropriate outcome is legal-scope qualification, not a fabricated contradiction.
## 5.2 User-base factors and historical timing

AI Act Annex XIII(f)-(g) includes market reach and registered-user factors, including a presumption based on at least 10,000 registered EU business users. The p.8 reference to user-base size therefore has support; it is not evidence of accidental substitution of a DSA threshold. [AI Act signed text (2024), AnnexXIII, PDF p.419]

The verified legal sources are signed Council/Parliament texts dated 13 June 2024 and 19 October 2022. Direct EUR-Lex retrieval encountered a JavaScript verification page; the official Council copies were accessible. Their precise provenance is retained rather than presenting them as a retrieved current consolidated-law edition.

This review does not certify current compliance, resolve the application of Section230 to generated speech, or equate historical enactment with the date every obligation became applicable. The paper itself presents liability questions as uncertain. Subsequent legal or company-policy changes are not used to manufacture errors in its historical account.
# 6. Technical comparison and policy-effect boundaries

The comparison between deep generative models and traditional recommender systems should not be interpreted as a division between deep learning and all recommendation systems. A primary 2016 YouTube paper already describes deep candidate-generation and ranking models. The distinction between a probabilistic model and a stochastic output-selection procedure also cuts across content types. [Covington et al. (2016)]

For a simple analytic illustration, a fixed distribution assigning probabilities 0.7 and 0.3 to two options can be used with deterministic argmax or with categorical sampling. The options could be text tokens or recommended items. Thus probabilistic representation and randomized selection are separate properties. This is a conceptual illustration, not a simulation of a deployed platform.

The paper’s p.2 caveat about common applications, its comparison of differences in degree, and its limited content-moderation focus prevent a single atypical application from automatically refuting the argument. More precise descriptions would identify the product class, date, sampling and ranking pipeline, and stage of moderation. The present review did not establish a central failure caused by the simplified binary feature labels.

Similarly, transparency, democratic participation, choice, staffing, and global expertise are candidate safeguards, not interchangeable outcomes. An implementation assessment would need to specify the harm, affected population, intervention, comparison, costs, privacy constraints, and success criteria. The paper explicitly requests research on effectiveness, so those unresolved questions are part of its stated agenda.
# 7. Version history, materials, and known-issue status

The original PDF matches an immutable PMLR copy at commit a3e4112da70e3f0623daeb3eeea06e2b34ed5e2f. The arXiv record 2412.11335 lists v1 submitted on 15 December 2024 at 23:00:29 UTC, associated with the NeurIPS2024 Regulatable ML workshop. It is an earlier 11-page manuscript. The saved earlier PDF has SHA-256 8f57b140ed7a74f257211f954d17bcca1ef6e5f3fd819a1c4bafb2cfe3ca1c7b. [Appel-arXiv (2024)]

The author website’s full-text link resolves to that earlier arXiv record. It should not replace the proceedings source or its pagination. An exhaustive semantic or visual comparison of versions was not performed.

No author erratum or later corrected edition was identified in the inspected PMLR, arXiv, or author publication records. This is not a universal absence claim. The official OpenReview forum and a related workshop record returned verification pages, leaving their discussions, attachments, and revision histories unverified. No paper-specific code/data package was found in the inspected links; for this policy position paper, that absence alone is not a reproducibility defect.

The independent retrieval script sources/0019/retrieve_support.py ran with Python -B and exited0. It downloaded five supporting PDFs, checked their PDF headers, calculated hashes, and extracted text successfully: CrowS-Pairs, the 2016 YouTube article, the two signed Council legislative texts, and the earlier arXiv manuscript. The full URL/hash/size/command records are in sources/0019/supporting_downloads.json. These source retrievals are not empirical replications.

report: # Scientific verification report — 0020
# 1. Identity, version, and outcome

Paper: Oliver Eberle, Thomas McGee, Hamza Giaffar, Taylor Webb, and Ida Momennejad, *Position: We Need An Algorithmic Understanding of Generative AI*. ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267:81292–81314. Paper ID I25-40121. [R1]

Reviewed object: the 23-page PMLR proceedings PDF, 2,415,573 bytes; SHA-256 efd6802e5a317e032ea5ee9b1f3d0c411325cf4b387c6da718bde9663956c098. All paper page references below are one-based PDF pages, identical to its printed internal page numbers. Main argument and impact statement occupy pp. 1–11; references extend through p. 19; Appendix A is pp. 20–23.
Review context: B001 / [internal task] / attempt-001; scientific contract 2026-10-23-five-papers; batch token [internal identifier omitted]. Review date: 24 October 2026.

Supported outcome: Minor. One bounded problem concerns the workload and accounting categories in the environmental motivation. Two additional concerns remain Needs Evidence: the interpretation of representation/attention proxies as algorithm identification, and the statistical family underlying the layer counts. No demonstrated central damage supports a Major classification. The proposal to study algorithmic primitives and their composition remains a defensible research agenda within the inspected scope.

The decisive evidence comprises an analytic countermodel to a decoder-to-mechanism implication, an independent recalculation of all 17 tabulated layer-test tails, a primary-source check of environmental quantities, and static inspection of the pinned public case-study script. These are not an empirical reproduction of Llama activations or attention data. Scientific decisions and controller acceptance remain pending; no human endorsement or author adoption is asserted.
# 2. Scope, definitions, and evidence limits

An algorithmic explanation describes operations and their composition; a behavioral result records an answer; a mechanistic explanation links computation to model components. Agreement between any two requires an explicit mapping. In particular, a token representation, a graph node, a search state, and an attention weight are different objects. A search rollout also depends on neighbor ordering, stopping rules, and whether one records visited nodes, traversed edges, or frontier updates.

AlgEval is presented as a methodological program, not a proved identification theorem. The paper includes no formal theorem/proof appendix. Its proposed causal interventions and future tests must not be misrepresented as completed validation. Similarly, proposed improvements in sample efficiency, emissions, safety, and architecture are prospective, rather than measured benefits of the case study.
Coverage | Work actually performed | Result and boundary
Main argument, pp. 1–11 | Definitions, assumptions, distinctions, dependencies, alternatives | No demonstrated contradiction in the central research program
Case study, pp. 6–8 | Decoder and attention inference; Figure 2–3 visuals | Conditional observations do not identify all possible implementations
Appendix A, pp. 20–23 | Tables, prompts, heatmaps, projections, rollout figures | Numerical and scope checks below; no raw-data re-fit
Statistics, p. 20 | All 17 printed layer statistics and Table 1 tail | Conditional 13/2 result; overall-model tail consistent
Environmental passage, p. 10 | Li et al. v5 full-text/source comparison | Workload/accounting mismatch; carbon figure unsubstantiated
Public implementation | Full script inspected by audit agent; parent checked key routines and parsed AST | Partial representation workflow only; no author code executed
Versions and corrections | PMLR bytes, arXiv text, pinned repository/history, primary records | No correction identified in inspected accessible records

All source images for pp. 6, 8, and 20–23 were inspected by the review team; the parent independently inspected pp. 6, 8, 20, and 23. Selected references were checked for the claims at issue; the bibliography was not exhaustively validated. OpenReview discussion was blocked by verification. Missing raw attention arrays, analysis scripts, and model-run records limit what can be reproduced.
# 3. Problem 1 — Algorithm exclusion depends on an unvalidated decoder
Judgment: Needs Evidence / inferential scope qualification.
## Source claim and suspect step

Section 4, p. 6, assumes a layer-to-search-step correspondence. Section 4.2, p. 7, selects the node pair with greatest representation inner product at each layer and compares that sequence with BFS/DFS rollouts. Figure 2, p. 6, labels the comparison as hypothesis rejection. The interpretation on p. 8 extends the attention observations toward absence of exhaustive search or a full world model. [R1]

The missing link is necessity: if a model implemented a particular search procedure, must the chosen maximum-inner-product pair or attention summary reveal its state? A mismatch rejects the procedure together with its assumed observable encoding. It cannot separately reject every implementation of the procedure.
## Complete analytic check
Consider seven token representations at each layer i. For tokens A and B set a_A = a_B = 2; for each other token set a_x = 1/2. Let

Code:
u(i,x) = (a_x, z(i,x)), with -1 <= z(i,x) <= 1.
score(i,x,y) = u(i,x) dot u(i,y), for distinct x and y.

Every A–B score is 4 + z(i,A)z(i,B), hence at least 3. For a pair containing exactly one of A/B, the score is at most 1 + 1 = 2. For a pair containing neither, it is at most 1/4 + 1 = 1.25. Thus the selected distinct pair is always A–B, strictly and without a tie.

A changing finite search state can be encoded by distinct bounded values of z(i,C) for another token C, with downstream computation reading that coordinate and ignoring the fixed first coordinate. For example, three successive states can be assigned 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. Each layer may still correspond to one search step, while the observed maximum pair never changes. The decoder reports a constant pair; the encoded state changes.

This construction satisfies the stated raw-inner-product definition, bounded finite representations, and a layerwise state progression. It grants exclusion of self-pairs, which is favorable to the decoder. It is an abstract countermodel to an unrestricted proxy-to-state implication, not a construction of the inspected pretrained Llama weights and not a refutation of the authors’ explicitly conditional assumption. No assumption that the model must place algorithmic state in its dominant similarity component has been established.

An independent finite check evaluated all 3^7 = 2,187 assignments with z in {-1, 0, 1}. The minimum A–B score was 3, the maximum competing score 2, and the minimum margin 1. The inequalities above establish the continuous case; the grid is only a check on their implementation.

A separate attention boundary follows from the standard head output A V, where A = softmax(Q K-transpose / sqrt(d_k)). [R5, Eq. 1, p. 4] Setting a head’s value output to zero makes its contribution zero for every attention pattern permitted by its queries, keys, and mask. Such heads can influence an unweighted attention average without contributing to the answer. Multi-head output projection further separates attention weight from causal contribution. This does not imply that the actual models contain such zero-value heads.
## Counterevidence, impact, and defensible repair

The paper is substantially more cautious than a universal exclusion theorem: p. 6 states the correspondence as an assumption; p. 7 calls the sequence possible; p. 8 uses tentative interpretation and requests further mechanism verification; p. 5 includes causal intervention in the proposed framework. Figure 6 also treats geometric changes as a candidate signature. These qualifications preserve a useful exploratory case study. The cited attention literature likewise does not justify a blanket claim that attention can never explain a model. [R6]

The defensible conclusion is that the extracted sequences show poor agreement with the tested rollouts under the chosen decoder. A stronger exclusion requires validated state decoding or causal evidence, with sensitivity to representations, token occurrences, layer grouping, stopping rules, and candidate implementations. Positive controls with known algorithms and tests of value/output contributions would help distinguish the possibilities; none was performed in this review.

Repair status: the conditional wording is analytically justified. An empirically verified identification method is not supplied. Impact: the reach of the illustrative mechanism inference is limited; the central research agenda is not invalidated.
# 4. Problem 2 — The direction and family of layer tests need specification
Judgment: Needs Evidence, with a fully specified conditional recalculation.
## Source claim and complete numerical check

Section 4.1, p. 7, counts 14 layers favoring the correct pathway and three favoring the incorrect pathway. Appendix A.1, p. 20, describes Bonferroni correction over layer tests but does not explicitly give sidedness, alpha, or separate directional families. [R1]

Let T have Student’s t distribution with 31 degrees of freedom. Recomputing P(T >= abs(t)) from each printed statistic approximately reproduces the Tables 2–3 p-values, allowing for rounded t values. This is a one-sided tail in the observed direction. For a single two-sided family of 32 layers at an explicitly assumed alpha = .05, the required raw two-sided threshold is .05/32 = .0015625; the two-sided p is twice that tail.
Layer and direction | Printed t; df | Recomputed one-tail p | Two-sided p | Bonferroni 32 adjusted p

These two layers do not pass that two-sided family criterion. Every other listed layer does. Among the published significant layers, the resulting counts are 13 positive and two negative. This is not a reanalysis of omitted layers or a claim that the paper specified the assumed test family.

For a symmetric null, selecting the one-sided tail after observing the sign covers both tails. Controlling a combined family requires accounting for both directions. Equivalently, the two-sided 32-test calculation uses a one-tail threshold .05/64. Bonferroni does not require independence, although the validity of each original t-test still depends on its sampling/model assumptions.
## Strongest alternative and bounded impact

Two separately prespecified directional families could justify a 32-test correction within each family. This would not by itself provide a single .05 bound for their union. The published description does not resolve the intended claim, so the reviewer cannot infer the authors’ prior decisions or declare the 14/3 result unconditionally false. The original observation unit, pairing, full p-value vector, and handling of dependence also require the underlying data and analysis specification.

Table 1 is consistent at the level that can be checked: t = 4.51, df = 2015 yields two-sided p = 6.85561e-6, agreeing with the rounded 7.0e-6. The displayed coefficient .33 and SE .07 need not divide to exactly 4.51 because they are rounded; their rounding intervals permit ratios from about 4.33 to 5.15. No extra error is inferred from that ratio.

Defensible resolution: disclose the planned hypotheses, sidedness, alpha, family definition, analysis unit, and raw/adjusted p-values. If the intended claim is one two-sided 32-layer family at .05, the conditional changes above follow from the printed statistics. If separate directional families were intended, describe them and limit the associated error-control statement.

Repair status: tail arithmetic verified; the original inferential design remains unresolved. Impact: two marginal layer classifications depend on the interpretation. The displayed aggregate-model tail is not contradicted, and none of these significance tests alone identifies a search algorithm.
# 5. Problem 3 — Environmental quantities change workload and accounting scope
Judgment: Minor for the source-attribution/accounting mismatch; the carbon magnitude remains Needs Evidence.
## Claim, primary-source comparison, and units

The p. 10 emission-efficiency paragraph presents half a liter of cooling water and gasoline-equivalent emissions for one interaction, then compares projected global water use with UK consumption, citing Li et al. (2025). [R1]

Li et al. v5, Introduction p. 2, instead estimates 500 mL for approximately 10–50 medium-length responses, dependent on place and time. Table 1, p. 5, includes on-site and electricity-related off-site water. Section 3.3.2, pp. 5–6, describes inputs up to roughly 800 words and outputs of 150–300 words, and acknowledges higher possible consumption. Its 2027 projection distinguishes 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters of withdrawal from .38–.60 billion of consumption; the UK comparison concerns withdrawal. [R4]

The reviewer’s arithmetic is 500/50 = 10 mL and 500/10 = 50 mL per response on the source’s aggregate approximation. Recasting 500 mL as a single medium-response quantity changes that denominator by a factor of 10–50. This calculation is neither a fresh measurement nor a universal bound on heavy requests.

The cited PDF supplies no located per-interaction estimate equivalent to five gallons of gasoline. Full-text checks found no occurrence of gallon, gasoline, petrol, or carbon equivalent. No independently verified replacement carbon number is proposed. Water volume also cannot be converted to carbon emissions without workload, energy, location, and accounting information.
## Alternative reading, impact, and precise repair

An interaction might mean a long session of many responses, and a difficult workload might consume much more than the source’s reference request. These readings prevent an impossibility claim about half a liter or the carbon magnitude. They do not supply the omitted workload definition or justify substituting consumption for withdrawal. Nor does a comparison described as more than half logically disprove every larger fraction; the paper’s near-two-thirds fraction remains untraced rather than independently falsified.

A defensible local revision is to preserve the source’s response count and combined operational-water scope, explicitly distinguish withdrawal from consumption, and remove or separately substantiate the gasoline-equivalent number with a workload-specific calculation. This corrects the attribution without promising that AlgEval itself reduces resources.

Repair status: the workload and accounting clarification is source-verified; a carbon replacement and any emissions benefit require additional evidence. Impact: the quantitative environmental motivation is affected, not the validity of the proposed algorithmic research program.
# 6. Public code, versions, and other inspected boundaries

The directly linked author project is oeberle/AlgEval, pinned at commit 18fdee6097e0dbb193be39073afdde345885baf6 (10 July 2025). The tree contains only README, requirements, and a 557-line representation script. The script is 18,979 bytes, SHA-256 d4910d8ee18416f7bfbf885ac2036ccbcea6cd3c6be61030662ce56f38454ded. [R3]

No released routine computes the mixed model, layer tests, BFS/DFS rollout comparisons, edit distances, or longest subsequences. No recorded raw results are in the inspected tree. This limits reproducibility; it does not prove unpublished analysis was wrong or establish which code generated the figures. Static AST parsing imported or executed none of the author module.

Appendix A.3 shows four reachable leaf-goal prompts on one seven-node tree. A constant affirmative responder gives the correct answer on those displayed questions, so those answers alone do not discriminate general navigation from simpler behavior. This does not explain the observed activations and is a scope clarification, not a replacement empirical theory. report: Position: The Categorization of Race in ML is a Flawed Premise

Claim-focused scientific verification | B001 / [internal task]
Paper I25-40122 | Report 0021 | AI review; human decision pending
# 1. Identity, version and outcome

Miriam Doh, Benedikt Höltgen, Piera Riccio and Nuria M. Oliver. ICML 2025 position paper, PMLR 267:81211-81232. Reviewed source: the publisher-linked 22-page PDF downloaded on 24 October 2026 UTC. All page locators below use the PDF’s printed internal pages 1-22, not the proceedings pagination. OpenReview ID: eI8KegpPyX. Source SHA-256: dfc8307bd43b2ada698a3b9005af7d20e0c7b5a92a8479c7d9b0c234699040fe. [S1]

Outcome: one demonstrated Minor defect in the account of available ACS PUMS race variables, plus a Needs Evidence concern about the literature-survey ledger. Neither establishes damage to the central normative argument for context-sensitive treatment of racialization. The paper’s position is explicitly qualified by circumstances in which categorical information remains useful (§7); this review does not recast it as a theorem that all race categories must always be removed.
# 2. Scope, definitions and checks

The main text (§§1-8), embedded Appendices A-F, and relevant tables were inspected. Checks focused on data representation, the survey’s internal audit trail, the nonempty-subset count, the relation to subgroup fairness, and what the illustrative CLIP and VQA results can establish. Reference pages were used selectively, not exhaustively validated. No separate supplement or paper-specific implementation was located in the publisher record or targeted discovery. A public folktables source file was inspected statically; it was not executed.

A single-valued recode, a vector of yes/no race indicators, perceived race, self-identification, and a person’s broader social identity are different objects. The existence of a multi-label encoding establishes data availability only; it does not establish its ethical suitability or capture all identity complexity. The review distinguishes mathematical reasoning, finite text/count checks, static code inspection, and empirical reproduction. No image-generation, CLIP, t-SNE, VQA, or author-code reproduction was performed.
# 3. Problem 1 - PUMS availability is conflated with a benchmark recode

Source claim and location. Section 4, Approach E, PDF p. 4, states that multiple-race responses collected by the Census are subsequently simplified into single-label categories in ACS PUMS, and invokes this as a data-availability obstacle to multi-label treatment. Appendix C, p. 19, describes the coarse folktables race categories. The suspect step is extending the properties of the RAC1P recode to the information available in the underlying public microdata.

Complete check. The official 2022 ACS 1-year PUMS metadata independently defines RACWHT, RACBLK and RACASN as binary indicators for White, Black and Asian membership respectively, including membership in combination with other races. Each has distinct 0/1 values. RAC1P is a different variable with a combined multiple-race category. The public schema therefore retains combination-capable information in parallel with the coarse recode. These are metadata for a pre-publication data year, not a hypothetical newly proposed representation. [S2-S5]

The sampled public folktables implementation, acs.py lines 84-102, configures ACSIncome with RAC1P as its group variable. This supports the narrower statement that the default benchmark uses a coarse group label. It does not support a claim that PUMS itself lacks the separate indicators. The exact inspected code bytes are saved and hashed; the snapshot was retrieved from the current main branch and is not evidence of which historical revision the paper’s authors used. [S6]

Alternative reading and impact. Read strictly as a statement about a particular RAC1P-only benchmark export, the criticism is reasonable. Read as the stated property of ACS PUMS, it is false. The demonstrated impact is bounded: one practical argument against multi-label analysis is overstated. This check neither proves that all mixed identities are adequately represented nor refutes the paper’s ethical critique or establishes the performance of any alternative fairness method. Severity: Minor.

Supported correction. Specify that standard RAC1P-based folktables tasks collapse multi-race responses, while ACS PUMS also supplies separate race indicators; retaining and analyzing those indicators is distinct from selecting the default benchmark recode. This factual correction is verified against the official schema. No claim is made that it restores all social or methodological objectives of the paper. Author adoption has not been requested.
# 4. Problem 2 - The survey sample cannot be reconciled from its supplied ledger

Source claim and location. Section 3, p. 2, describes a title-screened corpus of 78 ICML/CVPR papers from 2023-2024, a 45-paper group-fairness subset, and 29 papers using racial categories. Appendix A, p. 18, describes 28 papers, while Table 1 contains 37 paper-dataset citation occurrences and 26 distinct identifiable author-year entries after duplicates across datasets are removed.

Complete check. The two-column table was read, its right-hand citation column isolated, and author-year entries normalized and deduplicated by an independent reviewer script. The complete list and result are saved in verification/0021/independent_checks.json. In addition, the table includes Xu and Strohmer (2023); the bibliography and the official publisher record identify that work as JMLR 24(331), rather than either screened conference. This makes the concern broader than a lone numeric typo: the mapping from inclusion criteria to the cited sample remains unclear. [S1, S7]

Alternative readings and impact. Missing table rows, stale text, or an unintended reference could explain the discrepancies. The original screening ledger is needed to distinguish them. The observed 26 is a count of table entries, not a corrected numerator for the survey, and no revised prevalence estimate is warranted. The qualitative observation that racial categories are used in fairness research is not refuted. Judgment: Needs Evidence; no supported Major impact.

Remaining work. Supply the 78 screened records, the 45 group-fairness decisions, the identifiers and inclusion coding for the stated 29 papers, and a mapping to Table 1. No numerical correction is adopted in this report because the evidence does not determine one.
# 5. Checked reasoning and scope clarifications

Combinatorial statement (§4, p. 4). If each of k base labels may be included or excluded independently, and the empty combination is inadmissible, the possible distinct nonempty combinations number 2^k - 1. This follows by subtracting the empty subset from all 2^k subsets. Independent enumeration for k = 1,...,7 returned 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, agreeing with the formula. The formula does not by itself prove that every combination must be instantiated or that all analyses require an exponentially large computation. No issue found in the stated counting step.

Subgroup fairness (§2, p. 2; §6.1, pp. 6-7). Kearns et al.’s formal setup accepts a protected feature vector and a family of Boolean subgroup indicators; categorical race variables are one possible instantiation, not a mathematical prerequisite. Its experimental example does use census-derived attributes. This distinction qualifies a broad reading of the target paper’s characterization but does not resolve which protected features are normatively appropriate. This is recorded as a scope clarification, not a separate central defect. [S8, §2 and §5.2]

Illustrative experiments (§§4-6; Appendices D-E). The reported mean cosine similarities have the stated ordering: the generated-minus-real differences are 0.0811 and 0.0382. These are arithmetic checks of printed summaries, not validation of the underlying embeddings or identification of phenotypic diversity. Pair construction, cropping, image-selection decisions, uncertainty and controls would be needed for that stronger inference. The Figure 1 significance markers could not be reproduced from the supplied summaries.

The VQA illustration records repeated responses to one face pair. It supports a description of those responses under that stimulus and prompt; it does not identify a latent perceptual mechanism or establish population-level discrimination. The text acknowledges important limits, including that the illustration does not imply systematic discrimination. No additional demonstrated error is assigned merely because fresh experiments would be needed to test a broader claim.
# 6. Dependence, later versions and conclusion

The demonstrated defect concerns an empirical premise used to discuss multi-label alternatives. The central proposal also rests on social and normative arguments independent of that premise. The unresolved survey ledger affects reproducibility of the quantified review, without establishing the direction of any corrected estimate. Targeted title/erratum discovery and the publisher record did not identify an erratum. The OpenReview web page presented a verification wall and its public note API returned HTTP 429; revision history and later OpenReview corrections remain unverified. # 1. Identity, reviewed version and outcome

Alan Jeffares and Mihaela van der Schaar. ICML 2025 position paper, PMLR 267:81573-81587. Reviewed: the publisher-linked 15-page PDF, retrieved 24 October 2026 UTC. Page references use the printed internal pages 1-15. OpenReview ID: cw7MYyDL33. Source SHA-256: d8f580196644b9877c01adb8ab157bc7a5e3e20abe5330cfac9fae87f5e51d0c. [S1]

Supported outcome: Minor, for a local mathematical overstatement about the shape of the bias-variance risk curve. A separate discrepancy in the linked upstream grokking implementation is documented, but its connection to the published experiments is unresolved. Neither finding demonstrates failure of the paper’s main recommendation to seek useful, generalizable explanations. No Major issue is supported.
# 2. Scope and interpretation

Inspected the main argument (§§1-6), Figures 1-4, Appendix A and the self-evaluation checklist, with selective checks of cited regularization and lottery-ticket results. The distinction between deliberately selected edge cases, non-edge cases, normative research priorities and empirical prevalence was preserved. The paper expressly describes its literature selection as nonexhaustive and its utility judgments as partly subjective. The review therefore does not treat those judgments as mathematical theorems.

The linked teddykoker/grokking training file was downloaded and read statically, without importing or executing it. No network training, author code, prime-count experiment or ten-seed figure reproduction was run. Conference phrase counts and the dated Google Scholar count were not reconstructed. Only two small, independent checks were executed: exact rational arithmetic for the counterexample below and scalar modular arithmetic for the code observation.
# 3. Problem 1 - The bias-variance decomposition does not imply convex risk

Source claim and location. Section 3.2, PDF p. 6, right column, attributes a convex relationship between model complexity and predictive error to the bias-variance tradeoff and infers that, after increasing complexity begins to worsen performance, further increases should not improve it. The suspect step is the claimed implication from a decomposition of risk into components to a restriction on the shape of their sum.

The source gives no formal theorem or assumptions guaranteeing that implication. The following counterexample uses ordinary nested, full-rank least-squares regression with finite independent Gaussian noise. It addresses the unconditional mathematical wording; it is not a counterexample to an unstated, more restricted theorem about a specific model family.

Parameters and design. Let the four training-design rows be (1,1,1), (1,-1,-1), (-1,1,-1) and (-1,-1,1). Write this 4-by-3 matrix as X. Set beta = (sqrt(2), sqrt(1/10), sqrt(2))^T. Training outcomes are Y = X beta + epsilon, with independent epsilon_i distributed as N(0,4). The independent test covariate is uniform over the same four rows; its response is x^T beta plus independent N(0,4) noise. For k = 0,1,2,3, fit least squares using the first k columns, with the zero predictor for k = 0.

\[X^{\mathsf T}X=4I_3,\qquad \mathbb E_x[xx^{\mathsf T}]=I_3.\] Assumption verification. Every fitted design has full column rank; the feature sets are nested and contain at most three fitted coefficients for four observations. Orthogonal columns make omitted signal components orthogonal to every included column. Training and test noises are mutually independent with mean zero and variance four. All second moments exist. Thus no interpolation singularity, exotic loss, distribution shift, or nonidentifiable fit is needed.

\[\widehat\beta_j=\beta_j+\frac14\sum_{i=1}^{4}X_{ij}\varepsilon_i,\qquad\mathbb E[\widehat\beta_j]=\beta_j,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_j)=1\quad (j\le k).\] Complete calculation. Averaging over training noise, the independent test covariate and test noise gives the exact squared-error risk below. The integrated squared bias is the sum of the omitted coefficient squares; the integrated estimator variance is k because the test second-moment matrix is the identity. The irreducible test-noise contribution is four.
\[R_k=\mathbb E\!\left[(Y_{\rm test}-\widehat f_k(x_{\rm test}))^2\right]=4+\sum_{j>k}\beta_j^2+k.\]
k | Squared bias | Variance | Noise | Test MSE

The squared bias decreases and the variance increases. Nevertheless, test MSE falls from 8.1 to 7.1, rises to 8.0, and falls again to 7.0. The claimed convexity would require the middle value at k = 2 to be at most the average at k = 1 and k = 3. Instead:

\[R_2=8>\frac{R_1+R_3}{2}=7.05,\qquad R_2-\frac{R_1+R_3}{2}=\frac{19}{20}=0.95.\] Alternative reading and impact. The intended reference may be the familiar U-shaped heuristic often used to introduce model selection. That heuristic can be useful under additional assumptions. It is not a consequence of the decomposition alone. The defect is a bounded mathematical overstatement in a motivating example, not evidence that the paper’s main research-policy argument or its empirical figure is false. Severity: Minor.

Precisely supported repair. Replace the alleged implication by a statement that conventional heuristics often depict a U-shaped risk curve, while the exact bias-variance decomposition itself neither forces convexity nor forbids later improvement. The derivation and exact arithmetic verify that narrower statement. No proposed change claims to prove a universal shape theorem or to repair an empirical experiment.
# 4. Static code observation - multiplication in a division-labelled upstream task

Appendix A, p. 14, cites teddykoker/grokking as a base implementation. In the inspected train.py snapshot, division_mod_p_data describes modular division but assigns result = x * y % p and passes y itself as the second input token. For the default prime p = 97, x = 2 and y = 3 satisfy 0 \(\leq\) x < p and 0 < y < p. The implemented expression returns 6. Since the inverse of 3 modulo 97 is 65, modular division returns 2\(\times\)65 mod 97 = 33. The prime, range and invertibility conditions were checked using independent integer arithmetic. [S3, function division_mod_p_data]

This proves a discrepancy between that upstream file’s description and its arithmetic. It does not prove that Jeffares and van der Schaar used that exact snapshot or unchanged dataset generator. Their prime-count implementation and ten-seed run configuration were not found in the linked base file. Also, multiplication and division on the nonzero second operand are related by the bijective input-token relabelling y \(\mapsto\) y^(-1); this substantially limits the implication for the qualitative grokking illustration. No published-result failure is inferred.

The scalar operation x times the modular inverse of y would implement the advertised division, but no tensor-level patch was applied or executed. Publication linkage remains Needs Evidence: the actual experimental snapshot and configuration would be needed. The observation is attributed to the third-party repository, with its exact byte hash, and is not claimed to be a novel discovery or an established defect in the paper’s experiments.
# 5. Other checked claims and dependencies

Regularization (§2.1, p. 3). Nakkiran et al. prove monotonicity under specific linear-model/data assumptions and optimally tuned regularization; their neural-network evidence is empirical and they also present a non-Gaussian counterexample to sample monotonicity. The target paper’s wording expresses an expectation under appropriate regularization, so it should not be read as a guarantee for every practical optimizer and setting. This is a scope clarification, not an additional demonstrated error. [S4, §§1 and 4.1]

Lottery tickets (§2.3, p. 4). Malach et al.’s theorem concerns high-probability pruning approximation of a bounded target ReLU network by a sufficiently large random network under stated depth/width conditions. It is not a universal guarantee about training every dense architecture or identifying useful tickets cheaply. The target paper already distinguishes existence from discovery and hardware utility; no separate central defect is established. [S5, Theorem 2.1]

Prime-count illustration (Figure 4, p. 6; Appendix A, p. 14). The appendix explicitly describes parameter magnitude and parameter count as confounders. It does not claim that primality is a causal explanation. The illustration is consistent with the methodological point that an observed correlate need not be useful or generalizable. The plotted means, standard deviations and prime-count construction remain unreproduced.
