Paper I25-40125 | Report 0023 | AI review; human decision pending
# 1. Identity, reviewed version and outcome

Jacy R. Anthis and colleagues. ICML 2025 position paper, PMLR 267:81005-81034. Reviewed the publisher-linked 30-page PDF retrieved on 24 October 2026 UTC; all target locators below use printed internal pages. OpenReview ID: cRBg1dtj7o. Source SHA-256: `75135835b88ceb84aab6ec62cbcf56a06e8a77cea07650a334f67ec54c90dd31`. [S1]

Supported outcome: Minor. A local statistical interpretation problem affects prominent evidence: correlations and a likelihood-based pseudo-R-squared are described as proportions of variation predicted. Correcting the metric names and interpretations leaves the central claim of a promising, conditional research direction intact. No Major issue is supported. This review does not establish the validity of simulations for any untested population or intervention.
# 2. Inspected scope and strongest alternative reading

Read the main argument and Appendices A-C, and checked the three prominent empirical examples against dated primary sources. Table A1 has 53 rows across pp. 22-25 (15, 16, 14 and 8); Table A2 has 10 selected rows on p. 26. The tables contain no performance-value column. Their row counts are consistent with their framing, but that does not establish exhaustive literature coverage or independence of studies.

The position is prospective and explicitly conditional. Its five challenges, validation recommendations, limitations of the narrative literature search and emphasis on individual-response simulation should constrain interpretation. The paper does not claim that all current simulations can replace human experiments. Its discussion of imperfect transfer and preregistered validation is material counterevidence to a broader accusation of ignoring generalization. This review therefore distinguishes a metric error from disagreement with the authors’ research priorities.
# 3. Problem 1 - Correlation and likelihood fit are not explained variation

Source claims and precise locations. The Introduction, p. 1 right column, describes the Hewitt result as 91% of variation predicted; §4.5.2, p. 8 right column, similarly renders adjusted correlations as percentages of variation. Appendix A.2.2, beginning on p. 28 and continuing on p. 29, describes the Centaur performance range in terms of variation in human data. The invalid step is assigning a variance-explanation interpretation to metrics that measure different quantities.

Primary-source check for Hewitt. The dated 8 August 2024 working paper defines Pearson correlation and its disattenuated counterpart on PDF p. 5; Figure 2, p. 7, reports the comparisons. GPT-4 has raw r = 0.85 and adjusted r = 0.91. The adjusted comparison values are -0.09, 0.25, 0.82, 0.84 and 0.91, matching the target’s percentages. These are correlations, not calibrated prediction R-squared values. The target itself correctly labels r = 0.91 in Appendix A.2.4, p. 29. [S1, S2]

Independent derivation. Let Y and P be centered random variables with unit variance, finite second moments and correlation rho. For a linear calibrated predictor aP, the mean squared error is the following quadratic. Its derivative vanishes at a = rho, and its second derivative is 2, so this is the unique minimum.

\[\mathbb{E}(Y-aP)^2=1-2a\rho+a^2,\qquad a^*=\rho,\qquad R^2_{\rm calibrated}=1-(1-\rho^2)=\rho^2.\] Thus even in this favorable, fully specified calibration example, rho = 0.91 gives R-squared = 0.8281, not 0.91. More generally, a forecast’s out-of-sample R-squared also depends on its scale, offset, comparison baseline and evaluation set. This calculation is an illustration of the invalid inference, not a reanalysis of the source data. In particular, 82.81% must not be substituted as an empirical predictive-variance result: the source’s 0.91 is disattenuated and is not the correlation of a supplied calibrated prediction vector.

Calibration is a substantive distinction here: Hewitt’s PDF p. 8 reports systematic overestimation of effect magnitudes and evaluates a rescaling correction. This does not invalidate the reported association; it shows why association and numerical prediction accuracy should be separately identified. [S2]

Primary-source check for Centaur. Binz et al., arXiv:2410.20268v1, PDF p. 12 Eq. (1), defines a normalized log-likelihood metric relative to uniform guessing. PDF p. 4 names it pseudo-R-squared and describes a participant-level training/test split. The source’s 160-experiment dataset should not be interpreted as 160 unseen experiments. [S3]

\[R^2_{\rm pseudo}=1-\frac{\log p_{\rm model}(D)}{\log p_{\rm guess}(D)}.\] Complete metric-distinction example. Take independent Bernoulli responses with success probability p = 0.9. Let the model assign probability 0.9 to success on every trial and the guessing baseline assign 0.5. Both are valid probability distributions, all likelihoods are nonzero, and expected log likelihoods are finite. On a per-observation expected-log-likelihood basis:

\[H(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p),\quad R^2_{\rm pseudo}=1-\frac{H(0.9)}{\log 2}=0.5310044064\ldots\] The same model’s conditional-mean prediction is the constant 0.9. Its squared-error risk is 0.9(0.1) = 0.09, exactly Var(Y). Therefore its variance-based predictive R-squared relative to the mean baseline is zero. The positive pseudo-R-squared arises from improving over uniform probabilities; it does not mean 53.1% of response variance is explained. This is a population calculation illustrating metric non-equivalence, not an estimate from Centaur’s experiments.

Counterevidence and severity. A charitable reading treats ’variation’ as informal language for statistical correspondence. Section 4.5.2 even explicitly mentions correlation, and the appendix supplies the correct r notation. Those qualifications make a central-invalidity claim unwarranted, but they do not make a numerical percentage-of-variation interpretation correct. The error concerns how supporting evidence is communicated; the high reported association and the motivation to investigate simulation remain. Judgment: Minor.

Repair and verification. Replace the Hewitt wording with a disattenuated correlation of 0.91, optionally accompanied by the raw correlation of 0.85, and label all comparisons as correlations. Describe Centaur using likelihood-based predictive pseudo-R-squared relative to uniform guessing. Do not translate either result into a variance percentage without a separately defined and evaluated variance-based metric. These wording repairs follow directly from the primary metric definitions and require no new experiment. Author adoption has not been requested.
# 4. Checks that did not support additional problems
Claim / location | Check and bounded conclusion

# 1. Identity, reviewed version and outcome

Min-Hsuan Yeh, Jeffrey Wang, Xuefeng Du, Seongheon Park, Leitian Tao, Shawn Im and Yixuan Li. ICML 2025 position paper, PMLR 267:82409-82425. Reviewed the publisher-linked 17-page PDF, retrieved 24 October 2026 UTC. Page numbers below are printed internal pages. OpenReview ID: bXfF6Dqe9s. Source SHA-256: `e439604accb8e208669a55611f154e9db8ee77d57c6c66b5b4fb6db3fe4583a9`. [S1]

Supported outcome: Major. The inference from two unacceptable responses to arbitrary or unreliable pairwise preference materially affects the interpretation of the paper’s stated qualitative contribution. Sources 5 and 6 and the both-bad branch of Table 3 rely on this step. Sample lineage and quantitative denominators remain a separate Needs Evidence finding; no corrected counts or kappa are established. Recommendations to improve feedback data survive independently of the failed inference.
# 2. Scope and interpretation

Inspected Sections 1-6, Tables 1-3, Appendix A.1-A.2 and selected cited primary sources. The abstract and introduction identify the qualitative analysis of unreliable human feedback as a contribution. Its six-source taxonomy and interpretation of the annotation data therefore receive substantive dependency assessment. The calls for broader validation and complementary data and algorithm work are preserved. Population representativeness is not required of the three-person laboratory panel unless the resulting percentages are interpreted as population estimates.
# 3. Problem 1 - Absolute unacceptability does not erase relative preference

Source claim and location. Section 4.1, p. 5, Source 5 infers that when both candidates give harmful advice, there is no justified harmlessness ranking and an annotator without a both-bad option must select randomly. Source 6 makes a similar inference for two poor or inaccurate answers. Appendix A.1, p. 16, treats chosen-better, rejected-better, both-good and both-bad as four alternative labels.

The suspect step is the inference from two threshold failures to equality or incomparability. A binary pairwise preference asks which candidate is better according to a criterion. Absolute acceptability asks whether a candidate meets a threshold. These questions can have different answers without contradiction.

Complete counterexample. Fix one scalar quality criterion q, with larger values better, and an acceptability threshold tau = 0. Choose q(A) = -1 and q(B) = -2. Both candidates fail the threshold, while A strictly outranks B. An annotator who consistently follows this criterion can choose A on every repetition. No random decision is required. All quantities are finite, the criterion and threshold are fixed, and there is no hidden change in context or comparison standard.

\[q(A)=-1<0,\quad q(B)=-2<0,\qquad q(A)-q(B)=1>0.\] The distinction also holds under stochastic preference modeling. For the optional Bradley-Terry-Luce model with unit scale, the probability of selecting A is about 0.731, rather than 0.5. Adding any common constant to both qualities leaves this probability unchanged, while it can change whether the candidates meet a fixed absolute threshold. This is a mathematical illustration, not a fit to the paper’s annotations.

\[P(A\succ B)=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-(q(A)-q(B))]}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-1}}\approx0.731059.\] Primary protocol check. Bai et al., arXiv:2204.05862v1, §2.2 p. 11, describes relative helpfulness or harmfulness comparisons, preference-strength input and exclusion of the weakest comparisons/ties from retained data. Thus it does not mechanically turn every forced-looking pair into a retained arbitrary label. This does not establish that all retained labels are reliable; it narrows the target’s causal claim about the absence of a both-bad category. [S2]

Strongest alternative reading. The authors may intend equally poor, indistinguishable or incomparable candidates. Indeed, the cited historical Yeh v1 uses equal-poorness language in §3.2 p. 6. Under an actual tie, a separate tie/abstention option can be informative. Poor response candidates can also fail to teach acceptable behavior despite supplying a valid relative ranking. These interpretations preserve a useful concern, but require conditions not entailed by both candidates being bad. [S3]

Impact and repair. Judgment: Major. The abstract and introduction identify qualitative analysis of human-feedback unreliability as a contribution. On p. 5, Sources 5 and 6 use the invalid both-bad-to-arbitrary-preference inference to classify harmful or inaccurate response pairs as sources of unreliable feedback. Table 3 assigns these themes 39% and 36% of its both-bad column and uses that branch to argue that poor response quality triggers unreliable supervision. Absolute response quality does not establish that the original relative label lacks information. This breaks the inferential interpretation of a substantial branch of the empirical contribution; it does not establish that the recorded category counts, kappa or every pairwise label are false. Distinguish absolute acceptability from relative preference and tie or insufficient-evidence responses. Amend the causal interpretation and check the original annotation instructions and coding matrix before asserting which cases provide invalid relative labels. If both-bad was operationally defined as equally bad, supply that definition and analyze its use separately. The counterexample verifies the logical distinction; no corrected frequencies, improved agreement or downstream training effect is claimed. Broader feedback-quality recommendations survive. Adoption was not requested.
# 4. Needs Evidence - Annotation lineage and Table 3 denominators

Locations and observed facts. Current Appendix A.1, p. 16, describes 160 samples, 80 from each helpful/harmless split, rated by three laboratory annotators. It reports 25% both-bad and a Fleiss kappa of 0.46. Table 3, p. 5, gives within-subset theme percentages, but the inspected methods do not state the two table denominators or the current low-IAA selection rule. The label matrix, sample identifiers and coding assignments were not available in the inspected paper.
Evidence | Current PMLR paper | Cited historical Yeh v1
Sample selection | Appendix A.1 p. 16: 80 random observations per split | §3 p. 5: 20 per split within each of four reward-model agreement strata
Total qualitative sample | 160 | 160
Low-IAA selection | Appendix A.2 p. 16: named, without a numerical threshold | §3.2 p. 6: groups with Fleiss kappa below 0.4 and evident disagreement
Theme percentage vectors | Table 3 p. 5: low IAA 2/28/29/37/0/4; both-bad 0/0/25/0/39/36 | Table 2 p. 6: identical vectors, columns in a different order

The same arXiv identifier now points to the position paper, but v1 is a differently titled empirical paper: How Reliable Is Human Feedback For Aligning Large Language Models? (2 October 2024). The final paper cites that historical work in §5.2. Identical percentages and the different sampling descriptions justify a lineage question; they do not prove that the same sample was reused or that any procedure was improper. Random sampling within strata is compatible with a broad use of the word random. The current description may simply be abbreviated. [S1, S3, S5]

Conditional arithmetic check. If 25% both-bad means exactly, or rounds to the nearest whole percent of, the 160 observations, the corresponding count is 40. For a single code per item and denominator 40, every percentage is a multiple of 2.5. No integer count rounds to 39% or 36% under ordinary nearest-integer rounding. Therefore the full 25/39/36 vector cannot be reconstructed under those combined assumptions. Each table column does sum to 100%, so this is not a simple addition error.

The assumptions matter. The text could use a rough 25%, a smaller coded subset, weighting, a different unit of analysis or an unreported denominator. For illustration, counts 7, 11 and 10 out of 28 round to 25%, 39% and 36%; those are not asserted to be the actual counts. The independent script enumerates compatible denominators only to demonstrate non-identifiability. It does not recover the authors’ data.

Requested evidence and limits. Provide the sampled record identifiers and dataset revision, whether the final analysis reuses or replaces the v1 sample, the strata and selection probabilities if applicable, the three-rater label matrix, the low-IAA rule, raw theme counts, denominators, any weights and rounding convention. Recompute summaries from that ledger. No corrected prevalence or kappa is supplied here, and no claim of fabricated data is made. Status: Needs Evidence; impact is presently limited to reproducibility and interpretation of descriptive frequencies.
# 5. Scope clarifications and negative checks

The 25% reversed preference labels are disagreements with the original annotators, not independently established objective error rates. Three experienced lab members offer another judgment under an expanded label set. Table 2 itself preserves ambiguity in an example prompt. Likewise, kappa = 0.46 cannot be recalculated without the rating matrix; no inspected evidence independently disproves it. The closing paragraph on p. 5 expressly calls for work to establish how broadly the themes apply.

Section 3, p. 2, categorically describes algorithm-centered alignment as assuming perfect data. That framing should be narrowed: the paper itself cites Provably Robust DPO, whose method explicitly addresses random preference flips. The source assumes a specified noise model and known flip rate below one half; its guarantees require a log-linear policy class and feature coverage. It is a counterexample to the broad characterization, not a demonstration that algorithms solve arbitrary human disagreement. Classify this as a scope clarification supporting the paper’s own complementary framing. [S4]

The proposed four-option annotation is demonstrably more expressive, but the supplied analysis does not isolate a causal improvement in reliability against a matched two-option control. Similarly, data-cleaning recommendations and claims about smaller selected datasets are literature-based, context-dependent arguments. This review did not rerun those experiments or treat these recommendations as established universal guarantees.
# 6. Coverage limits, references and roles

No author code, reward-model inference, relabeling experiment or training run was performed. No raw annotation release was identified on the inspected publisher record or within the final PDF; this is not a claim that none exists elsewhere. OpenReview discussion was not verified. Only selected passages of historical Yeh v1 were inspected to resolve citation and sampling provenance; it was not substituted for the assigned final paper. Paper I25-40127 | Report 0025 | AI review; human decision pending
# 1. Identity, reviewed version and outcome

Sebastian Bordt, Eric Raidl and Ulrike von Luxburg. ICML 2025 position paper, PMLR 267:81130-81142. Reviewed the publisher-linked 13-page PDF retrieved 24 October 2026 UTC. Locators use printed internal pages. OpenReview ID: b2gM1HyAgE. Source SHA-256: `8c2b6f0a3a8a7bfbb88fe0066dbb315ec51ccfbeb1f811e8cdedf41cb0ef37a5`. [S1]

Supported outcome: Minor, limited to missing existence/selection conditions in the closest-counterfactual example. No Major issue is supported. The central analogy between explanation methods and statistical summaries survives this correction. The review also positively verifies the warning that zero feature attribution need not mean local irrelevance, and preserves the paper’s explicit caveat about neural-network parameterization.
# 2. Scope and interpretive commitments

Read §§1-10, Definitions 2.1-2.3 and 4.1, all ten examples in §2.2, the qualifying footnotes, and selected primary citations. The exact PDF has no appendix; references begin on p. 9 and continue through p. 13. The argument proposes a research perspective rather than an empirical benchmark or a theorem equating all explanatory concepts. Its normative preferences about expertise, trust and research priorities are not treated as mathematical claims requiring a universal counterexample.
# 3. Problem 1 - A closest counterfactual need not exist

Source claim and location. Under Definition 2.3, p. 2, statistics of functions have vector-valued outputs. Section 2.2, example 9 on p. 3, lists the nearest point with a different prediction as an example, using the following argmin. The missing step is ensuring that the feasible set contains a distance minimizer and that the expression selects one point when ties occur.

\[\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z:\,f(z)\ne f(x)}\|x-z\|_1.\] Complete counterexample. Set d = 1 and f(z) = 1{z > 0}, and explain x = -1. If a distribution argument is required, fix D to the uniform distribution on [-2,2]; it does not affect the displayed optimization. This is an ordinary measurable binary threshold classifier, with x inside the data support. We do not exploit a nonmeasurable function, infinite loss, or regression output.

\[f(-1)=0,\qquad \{z:f(z)\ne f(-1)\}=(0,\infty),\qquad |-1-z|=1+z\quad(z>0).\] The feasible set is nonempty, yet no candidate is closest. For every feasible z, the point z/2 is also feasible and has strictly smaller distance. Meanwhile the feasible sequence z_n = 1/n has distances 1 + 1/n converging to 1. Thus the infimum is 1, but it is not attained, and the argmin is empty. The same problem remains if candidates are restricted to the distribution support: the feasible set becomes (0,2], with the same unattained infimum.

\[\inf_{z>0}(1+z)=1,\qquad \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z>0}(1+z)=\varnothing.\] This contradicts the unrestricted use of the expression as a point-valued example. It does not contradict the claim that properly specified counterfactual algorithms can be useful statistics, and no later theorem or experiment in this position paper depends on the unrestricted optimization.

Strongest alternative reading and severity. The example may be intended as a sketch with existence, finite numerical precision and tie handling understood. Those assumptions are often supplied in implementations. However, this failure occurs for a routine classification boundary and should be explicit when the example motivates a formal domain and output type. Judgment: Minor, a local well-posedness gap.

Repair and its verification. Specify a nonempty closed target region C and an output-selection convention. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the continuous distance to x attains its minimum on nonempty closed C: choose any point in C, restrict attention to points no farther than that point, and minimize on the resulting closed bounded, hence compact, nonempty set. The minimizing set can still contain multiple points, so a fixed tie rule or a set-valued output must be declared.

For the displayed counterexample, impose a positive margin z >= epsilon > 0. The unique minimizer is z = epsilon, since 1 + z is strictly increasing. At epsilon = 1/10, the repaired optimum is 1/10, its label is 1, and its distance is 11/10. This repair changes the feasible set transparently; merely flipping a threshold convention from strict to non-strict is not a general solution because another class can remain open. Alternatively, return a specified approximate counterfactual and label it approximate. The existence proof and special-case arithmetic verify the proposed mathematical repair; no algorithm implementation was patched or tested. Adoption was not requested.
# 4. Positive check - Zero attribution can coexist with local dependence

Section 5.2, item 1 on p. 6, warns against treating zero feature attribution as irrelevance. The conditional-SHAP formula on p. 3 supports a direct one-feature verification. Take X uniform on [-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)], f(t) = t squared, and x = 1. The function is smooth, the distribution is bounded, all needed moments are finite, and x is interior to the support. For one feature, the only coalition difference is f(x) minus the background expectation, using the natural fully observed conditional value f(x).

\[\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}t^2\,dt=1,\qquad \phi_1=f(1)-\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=0.\] \[f'(1)=2,\qquad f(1+h)-f(1)=2h+h^2>0\quad\text{for }0<h<\sqrt{3}-1.\] The perturbed inputs remain within the data support. Thus this is not an out-of-distribution artifact. At h = 1/10, the exact change is 21/100 despite zero attribution. The result supports the target’s warning: a signed baseline-relative score does not certify local insensitivity. It does not establish that SHAP is useless, nor that every attribution method fails for every task.

Selected source comparison. Bilodeau et al.’s arXiv:2212.11870v2, §§3.1-3.2, places its impossibility result under explicit model-class richness and baseline/domain conditions and completeness/linearity of the attribution. Those assumptions should not be dropped when summarizing the general theorem. The simple calculation above is independently derived and does not depend on re-proving that theorem. The inspected source is the 11 April 2023 preprint version, not an asserted byte-identical copy of the final PNAS article cited by the target. [S2]
# 5. Other checks and scope clarifications
Target location | Evidence and bounded assessment

Definition 2.3 p. 2; footnote 2 p. 3; §7 p. 8 | The authors explicitly replace function space by parameter space for methods depending on network parameterization. Different internal explanations for identical input-output functions would illustrate that acknowledged caveat, not expose an unacknowledged contradiction.

Definitions 2.1-2.3, pp. 2-3 | Individual examples require ordinary domain conditions: finite moments, differentiability, fixed background distributions and conditional-expectation conventions. Outcome-dependent performance/fairness also needs labeled evaluation information. These are scope conditions; no separate major formal failure is alleged.

§4.2 p. 5: anchors | The primary Anchors paper defines conditional prediction precision under a specified perturbation distribution and maximizes coverage subject to a confidence/precision condition (PDF p. 4, Eqs. 2-4). Read the target’s similarity language within that rule-and-distribution scope, not as a universal metric-based individual-fairness guarantee. [S3]

§5.1 pp. 5-6: p-values and confidence intervals | The p-value discussion agrees with the ASA distinction between a tail probability under a statistical model and the posterior probability of a hypothesis. Frequentist interval coverage is a repeated-sampling property; it does not supply a posterior probability for a fixed realized interval. No defect found in the inspected explanatory point. [S4]

§§4.3, 6 and 9: interpretation, trust and benchmarking | The broad prevalence and utility judgments were not independently measured. They remain argued positions. The paper’s acknowledgment that explanations can help debugging and that some methods have clear interpretations should be retained.

No author code, model training, benchmark evaluation or user study was performed. No separate code or supplement was identified on the inspected publisher record. The mathematical checks do not validate every explanation method or all cited empirical examples. No exhaustive citation audit, survey of interpretation practices, or full proof reconstruction of the cited impossibility theorem was performed. John Hewitt; Robert Geirhos; Been Kim
ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81556-81572; publisher-linked 17-page PDF
No Issue Found within inspected scope; scope clarifications recorded

The masked-generation invariance argument and the illustrative number-guessing probabilities survive independent checks. The broad position and the model experiments are not established as universal theorems or independently reproduced empirical results.
# 1. Identity, version and review scope

The reviewed source is the publisher-linked PDF preserved at [S1]. SHA-256: `e6873baee038e095475e51e4ea98f904e99f51547e6dc6abb333b4df1e50e195`. Its hash matches the controller acquisition receipt. The title and all three authors match the publisher record [S2]. Page references below use 1-based PDF pages, which agree with printed pages 1-17; proceedings pages are 81556-81572.

Read the main argument and experiments on pp. 1-9 and the included appendices on pp. 14-17. The bibliography on pp. 9-13 was used for source discovery, not exhaustively fact-checked. Visually inspected pp. 8, 14 and 16, including Figures 5-7 and Eq. (2). No separate supplement or author repository was identified from the inspected publisher page, paper, arXiv metadata and targeted searches. OpenReview forum access reached a browser-verification page, so its discussion and attachment history were not reviewed.
# 2. Checked reasoning and decisive evidence

Unchanged behavior without a neologism. Figure 4 (p. 6), Section 5 step 3 and Section 5.2 (p. 7) promise unchanged model behavior when the new word is absent. A naive vocabulary expansion changes a softmax denominator, but Appendix B (p. 14) explicitly masks the new token during every generation step. That provision resolves the candidate concern.
> p_new(v | x) = exp(z_v(x)) / [sum_{u in V} exp(z_u(x)) + exp(-infinity)] = p_old(v | x), for v in V.

The equality assumes unchanged tokenization of old-token inputs, frozen old embeddings and other parameters, and the same decoding settings. Since the new token cannot be generated, induction gives equality of complete sequence distributions. It does not require independently sampled strings to coincide. An illustrative three-logit calculation returned zero probability difference [E1]. Removing the mask would change the assumptions and is not a counterexample to the stated experimental procedure.

Diversity calculation. Section 5.4 and Figure 6 (p. 8) consider nine possible target numbers. Under a uniformly selected correct target and iid guesses from probabilities p_1,...,p_9, the average success probability is:

Convexity of (1-p)^n and Jensen’s inequality show that uniform guessing maximizes this success probability among fixed iid guessing distributions. Independent computation yields 0.6920538523 at n=10 and 0.9910071137 at n=40, consistent with 69% and above 99% [E1]. Concentrating all mass on two targets has limiting average success 2/9, which explains the approximate low baseline. Adaptive sampling without replacement is outside this iid comparison. Appendix B.2 (p. 16) says the Gemma curves are analytic functions of empirical token probabilities; this review did not reproduce those probabilities.

Preference loss and self-scoring. Equation (2), Appendix A.1 (p. 14), adds a term -log sigmoid(beta log[p_theta(y_c|x)/p_theta0(y_c|x)]) to the DPO loss. At fixed other probabilities it rewards increasing chosen-response likelihood. It is not a proof of monotonic improvement under shared-parameter optimization, and the paper reports empirical stabilization rather than claiming such a theorem. Section 5.5 (pp. 8-9) and Appendix B.3 (pp. 16-17) explicitly target the model’s own expressed preferences. Using that model as scorer matches this target; it does not establish human-assessed quality. The reported 3.8 versus 3.2 means remain descriptive and were not recomputed from raw responses.
# 3. Scope, dependence and unresolved evidence

The paper is a position article with proof-of-concept experiments. Section 3.2 (p. 5) allows that existing language could describe concepts at greater length; Section 4 (p. 6) states that neologisms do not solve faithfulness. Consequently, the experiments should support a proposed interface for communication and control, not a formal impossibility result for all existing vocabulary or proof of human understanding. No distinct substantive defect was demonstrated within this interpretation.

Length-control plots and the example tables were checked for internal consistency with their stated purpose, not independently reproduced. Exact held-out splits, raw generated responses, numerical token probabilities, parsing behavior, prompt variants and training logs were not available in the reviewed materials. Resolving generalization and performance uncertainty would require these artifacts or fresh model experiments. No author code was executed.

The authors’ October 2025 blog identifies a separate follow-on work on controllability and self-verbalization [S4]. That follow-on is not an erratum and was not audited here. No correction was identified in the inspected sources; inaccessible discussion means this is not an exhaustive errata search.

Title: Scientific verification report
I25-40129 / 0027
Position: Medical Large Language Model Benchmarks Should Prioritize Construct Validity
Ahmed Alaa; Thomas Hartvigsen; Niloufar Golchini; Shiladitya Dutta; Frances Dean; Inioluwa Deborah Raji; Travis Zack
ICML 2025, PMLR 267:80991-81004; publisher-linked 14-page PDF
Minor: two bounded defects in the empirical argument; execution provenance unresolved

The documented EHR evaluation retains answer choices, so its performance drop does not isolate their removal. The text also names the wrong MedQA leader relative to Table 1. The recommendation to validate medical benchmarks and the observed ranking discordance are not invalidated.
# 1. Identity, scope and assumptions

The preserved source [S1] is , SHA-256 `682e0ef017c005a8c69086ccaaba2e1cbe2eaab8d1d1fa6a26b61847df8bbd12`, matching the controller receipt. Title and authors were checked against the publisher record [S2]; the full middle name Deborah appears in that record and the PDF. Locations use 1-based PDF pages, also printed pages 1-14. Main text pp. 1-9 and Appendices A-C pp. 12-14 were inspected; references were used for discovery rather than exhaustively audited. Source pp. 6, 7, 8 and 12 were visually checked.

This is a position paper with a proof-of-concept EHR comparison. Its statistical targets include item-level conditional transfer accuracy, aggregate clinical-case accuracy, and agreement of rankings across models. These targets are distinct. Table 1 values are rounded published summaries, not patient-level data. No clinical records were accessed and no author code was run.
# 2. Problem 1: Answer-choice explanation is not isolated by the documented comparison

Source claim and location. Section 4.1, p. 7, paragraph below Figure 5, proposes the contrived MedQA format as a likely explanation of the accuracy drop, specifically referring to answer choices being absent in real-world clinical reasoning. Appendix B, p. 12, instead describes pairing the retrieved EHR note, after removing its Plan section, with the extracted MedQA question and its answer choices [S1].

Complete check. Under the appendix protocol, the benchmark condition uses an MCQ clinical vignette, while the EHR condition uses an MCQ with a retrieved clinical context. Both retain answer choices. Therefore, the comparison changes context and case construction, but does not implement removal of choices. Its accuracy difference cannot identify the effect of a format intervention that was not performed. Figure 5’s separate answer-count experiment does not establish that the EHR comparison lacked choices.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. The main-text sentence can be read as a general ecological criticism of medical MCQs; that criticism is not refuted. It becomes unsupported when used to explain this particular accuracy drop. The appendix could describe a protocol different from the one actually used, but neither execution logs nor prompt records were available to decide that. The displayed measurements themselves have not been disproven.

Judgment and impact. Minor, confined to the methodological interpretation of the accuracy gap. The actual executed protocol is a Needs Evidence subitem, not an additional demonstrated error. If Appendix B is accurate, a supported repair is: ’The comparison shows a performance drop when MedQA questions and choices are paired with EHR-derived contexts; this design does not isolate the effect of removing answer choices.’ This is a conditional interpretation repair, not a validated experimental repair. A paired evaluation with and without choices would be new work.
# 3. Problem 2: The named MedQA leader conflicts with Table 1
Source claim and location. Section 4.3, first paragraph on p. 8, identifies GPT-4 as the model at the top of the MedQA rankings. Table 1 on p. 6 lists the following relevant values [S1]:
Model | MedQA accuracy | EHR accuracy
PMY MedLLama | 0.75 | 0.36

Complete check. The maximum MedQA value among all seven displayed rows is 0.75 for PMY MedLLama, exceeding GPT-4 by 0.04. Llama 3 has the highest displayed EHR accuracy, 0.48 [E1]. These are direct finite comparisons, not significance tests. A pairwise comparison restricted to GPT-4 and Llama 3 would make the ordering correct, but that restriction is absent from the sentence referring to the full table.

Judgment, impact and repair. Minor, a local factual error in the model comparison used to motivate construct-validity concerns. The supported replacement is: ’PMY MedLLama leads Table 1 on MedQA (0.75), whereas Llama 3 leads the EHR-adapted evaluation (0.48).’ The numerical repair is verified against the table. Ranking discordance remains because PMY’s EHR accuracy is 0.36, below Llama 3’s 0.48. This repair does not establish that discordance uniquely diagnoses inadequate medical knowledge.
# 4. Checks that did not establish additional defects

Abstention accounting. Table 1 reports that GPT-4 refrains on 57% of cases and is correct on 64% of answered cases. Counting abstentions as errors gives (1-0.57)*0.64 = 0.2752, consistent with 0.28 after rounding [E1]. Section 4.3 explicitly notes that nonresponse complicates interpretation. It would be incorrect to report this as an undisclosed arithmetic error.

Conditional transfer metric. Section 4.1 defines alpha = P(EHR correct | matched MedQA correct). This is a descriptive item-level measure; it is not interchangeable with across-model score prediction or rank agreement. For example, if model-specific benchmark success is theta and clinical success is theta/2, independently conditional on model, expected clinical score is exactly predicted by benchmark score, yet alpha equals theta/2 rather than one. This analytical distinction does not validate MedQA or refute the paper’s observed values. The alpha-near-one expectation on p. 7 is defensible only for the stronger target of near-deterministic item-wise transfer.

Clinical matching and content. The p. 7 discussion itself acknowledges that matching on a shared answer code may fail to capture clinical similarity. The actual note-question compatibility, adjudicated answers and repeated-patient structure remain unverified. Figure 5 and Appendix C were checked for described task categories, concept counts and perturbation scope, but the classifier outputs and cTAKES extractions were not reproduced. Document-level concept counts alone do not identify every aspect of construct coverage. These are scoped evidence limits, not demonstrated false empirical results.
# 5. Dependence, versions and decision table

The two bounded findings affect the interpretation and named example of the proof of concept. They do not invalidate the normative proposal for benchmark validation, establish that MedQA is valid, or prove that the reported accuracies are wrong. Patient-level outputs, denominators, matching adjudications, model versions and complete prompts are needed for further statistical or clinical conclusions. Repeated notes per benchmark item also need to be retained when estimating uncertainty.

I25-40131 / 0028
Position: Contextual Integrity is Inadequately Applied to Language Models
Yan Shvartzshnaider; Vasisht Duddu
ICML 2025 / PMLR 267, pp. 82200–82210; publisher PDF, 11 pages
Minor — one verified overstatement of prior experimental coverage

The statement that none of three cited studies accounted for prompt variation conflicts with a pre-existing paraphrasing experiment in one of those studies. This is a bounded literature-characterization error; the paper’s central distinction between contextual integrity (CI) and narrower privacy proxies remains supported within the reviewed scope.
# 1. Identity, version and review scope

The original publisher PDF was retained unchanged. Its title, authors and proceedings identity match the task and acquisition receipt. SHA-256: `32a0ea673672ac12848e878c8b94d06a7f1500daedfad9cf819fc41e8ff81589`. Page references below use one-based PDF pages. Main text and Tables 1–2 were read; references occupy pp. 9–11 and there is no included appendix. Theoretical claims and the potentially consequential blanket statement in Section 4 received targeted primary-source checks.

The inspected arXiv record is 2501.19173, with v1 dated 31 January 2025 and v2 dated 15 May 2025. This review applies to the hashed proceedings PDF; identity with either arXiv PDF was not assumed. No correction was identified in the inspected publisher/arXiv records. The OpenReview response was a browser challenge, so reviews and revision discussions were unavailable.
# 2. Problem 1: Prior paraphrasing experiment omitted

F28-01 — Minor; high confidence. Section 4, p. 7, under “Paraphrasing Prompt Sensitivity,” states that none of Mireshghallah et al. (2023), Ghalebikesabi et al. (2024), or Shao et al. (2024) accounted for prompt variation. The cited Ghalebikesabi paper provides a direct counterexample in its historical arXiv:2408.02373v1 version, dated 5 August 2024, before the reviewed paper.

In Operationalizing Contextual Integrity in Privacy-Conscious Assistants, Section 4.2 (PDF p. 6) varies form titles, descriptions and field wording. Section 5 (pp. 8–9) analyzes robustness across paraphrased forms; Figure 5 (p. 9) plots within-form-group variation in privacy leakage and utility. Appendix C.2 (pp. 33–34) gives paraphrasing instructions. These forms enter the assistant’s decision input. The page-9 figure and caption were visually inspected, and the exact historical PDF was archived with SHA-256 `6a6764795f9d19ac2cb7b87cc4655388c5d7550fc7eb4ee317a85bd009320c0c`.

The strongest alternative reading is that the reviewed authors meant variation only in a fixed instruction or assessment template, excluding the wording of form inputs. Section 4 does not state that restriction. The finding therefore concerns the unrestricted published assertion, not a claim that all possible prompt dimensions were previously tested. It is not a missing-citation complaint: the counterexample is already cited.

Supported impact and repair: replace the blanket statement with an explicit acknowledgement that Ghalebikesabi et al. tested form paraphrasing, then identify any distinct instruction-template variation left untested. The assertion of uniformly absent paraphrasing controls must be narrowed. This does not establish adequate coverage of position bias, validate every CI-tenet classification, reproduce the prior experiment, or overturn the social-theoretical position. No Major issue is supported.
# 3. Core argument and candidate objections
Claim / location | Check and result

Four CI tenets; Section 2, pp. 2–3 | Consistent with Nissenbaum’s 2019 primary account: appropriate flows, contextual norms, parameterized flows, and ethical assessment of departures. No Issue Found in this conceptual correspondence.

Legal rules as privacy norms; Section 3 and Table 2, p. 8 | The heading alone could appear absolute. Table 2 and Section 5 explicitly allow institutions that reflect contextual values. A claim that the paper prohibits all legal embodiments of norms is not supported.

Partial use of CI; Section 5, p. 8 | The paper acknowledges useful applications of parts of the framework with limited claims. This qualification avoids interpreting all partial implementations as intrinsically worthless.

ConfAIde flow representation; Section 3 / Table 1 | The targeted 2024 primary version acknowledges five CI parameters but uses a three-factor Tier-2 template. The reviewed critique has a concrete target; no additional verified error was established.

Experimental hygiene; Section 4, p. 7 | Separating repeated-prompt, paraphrasing and option-position variation is useful. F28-01 affects the literature summary for the second dimension; the other universal negatives were not exhaustively verified.

Nissenbaum, Contextual Integrity Up and Down the Data Food Chain (2019), pp. 224, 227 and 231–234, supports the distinction between descriptive departures from prevailing norms and ethically illegitimate flows. It also permits partial use of the framework. The reviewed paper’s qualified discussion is compatible with this account. This is a conceptual consistency check, not an empirical test of privacy protection or a legal compliance opinion.
# 4. Coverage, limits and reproducibility

Coverage includes the complete reviewed PDF and targeted checks of two cited LLM studies plus the primary CI account. It does not independently audit all nine rows and all four tenet labels in Table 1. Claims about every prior study’s lack of position-bias controls therefore remain Needs Evidence for an exhaustive verification. No new empirical experiment, equation-based performance claim, or author implementation is supplied by this position paper; no executable author code was required to test F28-01, and none was run.

The evidence bundle preserves publisher and arXiv metadata, primary-source PDFs/HTML, acquisition hashes, extracted text and page images. is reviewer-authored and only extracts, checks and renders public documents. Its successful check establishes the presence and historical date of the counterexample, not the correctness of the reported experimental measurements. OpenReview discussion and a complete all-study robustness audit remain unavailable or unperformed.
# 5. Conclusion and repair status

Title: Scientific verification report
I25-40132 / 0029
Position: Don’t Use the CLT in LLM Evals With Fewer Than a Few Hundred Datapoints
Sam Bowyer; Laurence Aitchison; Desi R. Ivanova
ICML 2025 / PMLR 267, pp. 81143–81184; publisher PDF, 42 pages
Minor — four bounded scientific/methodological findings

Independent calculations support the central warning about small-sample Wald intervals. Four local errors concern importance-weight normalization, correlation interpretation, a parameter-support argument, and the clustered-bootstrap comparator. They do not establish failure of the central conclusion or of all reported Bayesian intervals.
# 1. Identity and evidence standard

The unchanged publisher PDF matches the controller receipt, title, authors and proceedings record. SHA-256: `d9edc21df36d9e0bde2f2d1ef18f472cd35a90972233e39da3dc4143f8ce2bee`. This report uses one-based PDF page numbers. Main text, included Appendices A–J, targeted formulas and public code were inspected. Two independent AI checks covered the statistical argument and static code. No author code, including printed snippets, was executed.

arXiv:2503.01747 lists v1 on 3 March 2025, v2 on 4 March and v3 on 28 May. The review is pinned to the proceedings hash, without assuming byte identity with arXiv. Code snapshots and the older implementation needed for historical attribution are archived. OpenReview returned a browser challenge; a publication-run commit and full numerical outputs were not established.
# 2. Independently checked central result and coverage scope

For IID Bernoulli outcomes, the paper’s Wald standard error is sqrt[p_hat(1-p_hat)/N]. It vanishes at all-failure or all-success samples, so the stated boundary failure is real. Reviewer-authored exact binomial integration, without simulation or author-code execution, gives the following 95% interval coverage averaged over a uniform true success probability:
N | Wald | Uniform-prior Bayes | Wilson

These calculations corroborate the scale of the main failure; they are not a reproduction of the authors’ sampled simulation or every plotted point. Bayesian average calibration follows from averaging posterior set probability over the joint model. It is different from coverage at each fixed parameter. At N=3 and true theta=0.95, the paper’s Bayesian and Wilson 95% intervals contain theta only for three successes, giving coverage 0.95^3 = 85.7375%; Wald gives 13.5375%.

Accordingly, Table 1’s small-N coverage checkmarks (p. 9) need to be read as a summary of the examined regimes, not a universal pointwise guarantee. Appendix I.1 and Figure 20 explicitly include fixed-theta checks; their existence rules out a claim that the paper concealed or omitted this distinction entirely. This report treats the table wording as a scope clarification, not another independent numerical finding.
# 3. Problem 1: Extra normalization in the importance estimator

Minor; high confidence. Appendix E, p. 21, Eq. (55) defines normalized weights w_hat[k] = w[k]/sum_i w[i], which sum to one. Equation (60) then places a further factor 1/K outside the weighted sum. The correct self-normalized estimate is:
> E_hat[theta | Y] = sum_k theta[k] w_hat[k] (no additional 1/K).

Complete witness: with a uniform Bernoulli prior, one success and one failure, take proposal values 1/4 and 3/4. Both likelihoods equal 3/16, so normalized weights are 1/2 and 1/2. The corrected weighted estimate is 1/2, also the exact Beta(2,2) posterior mean. The printed Eq. (60) returns 1/4. For proposals in [0,1], the printed estimate is bounded by 1/K and therefore cannot consistently estimate a positive posterior mean as K grows.

Repair and impact: remove the extra 1/K. This repairs a quantitative derivation, not merely wording. However, Snippet 4 on p. 22 and the inspected clustered implementation normalize once and resample using those probabilities, then take quantiles. They do not use the erroneous expectation formula to construct their intervals. Thus no reported coverage failure is inferred from this local error.
# 4. Problem 2: Latent correlation is not binary correlation

Minor; high confidence. The final sentence of Appendix C, p. 19, says the binary evals attain the specified correlation rho; p. 20 describes an example with marginal accuracies 0.6 and 0.9 and rho=0.7. Thresholding correlated Gaussians preserves the stated Bernoulli marginals, but generally changes Pearson correlation. Writing Phi2 for the bivariate standard-normal CDF, the induced correlation is:
> Corr(Y_A,Y_B) = [Phi2(Phi^-1(theta_A),Phi^-1(theta_B);rho) - theta_A theta_B] / sqrt[theta_A(1-theta_A) theta_B(1-theta_B)].

For theta_A=theta_B=1/2 and latent rho=1/2, the binary correlation is (2/pi)arcsin(1/2)=1/3. More decisively, the paper’s 0.6 and 0.9 Bernoulli marginals permit correlation at most [0.6-0.54]/sqrt(0.6*0.4*0.9*0.1)=0.408248, so binary correlation 0.7 is impossible. Independent quadrature gives approximately 0.339587 for that latent model.

Repair and impact: consistently call rho the latent Gaussian correlation and report induced binary correlation separately. The main p. 7 construction and Appendix E.2 likelihood can remain valid under this interpretation. This finding changes parameter interpretation; it does not prove that the paired-model simulations or their Bayesian likelihood were incorrectly implemented.
# 5. Problem 3: Wrong full-coverage range for a difference

Minor; high confidence. Figure 7 and Appendix A.1 (pp. 13–14) concern delta=theta_A-theta_B. The continuation on p. 14 dismisses t intervals wider than one because [0,1] supposedly provides 100% coverage. The actual parameter range is [-1,1]. For independent Bernoulli models theta_A=0.2 and theta_B=0.8, delta=-0.6, so the constant interval [0,1] has zero coverage for every N. Under the paper’s independent uniform priors, its average coverage is only 1/2.

Repair and impact: use [-1,1], with width two, as the trivial full-coverage reference and reassess the efficiency statement. Width greater than one alone does not establish domination by a valid full-range interval. This invalidates that specific dismissal; it does not show that the plotted t intervals have acceptable calibration or competitive efficiency.
# 6. Problem 4: The clustered-bootstrap comparator fixes clusters

Minor; high confidence in code behavior, conditional attribution to the published run. Section 3.2 and Figure 3 (pp. 5–6) target the global theta in Eq. (8), with cluster probabilities drawn around theta. In no_clt_paper, eval_lib/src/intervals_clustered.py, bootstrap_subtask_confidence_interval (lines 120–200, especially 159–176 and 191), the algorithm resamples observations within each existing cluster and averages the cluster means. It never resamples clusters. subtask_experiments.py lines 65–68 selects this routine for the named comparator.

The source file is byte-identical at the inspected July 2025 snapshot and the initial 3 March 2025 commit, with SHA-256 `84b2dc23faf2a2a4a5e182d8e7f4a2ad86a5156c657a16dff22ea2d003f3ae3a`. Thus this is not merely a later regression. The exact commit used for the published figure remains unverified.

Analytical witness: take two observed clusters of size five, one all zero and one all one. Every within-cluster resample preserves both cluster means, producing a degenerate [0.5,0.5] interval. Resampling the two clusters instead produces overall means 0, 0.5 and 1 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4, giving a 95% percentile interval [0,1]. This proves omission of between-cluster variation. It does not prove nominal coverage of a corrected bootstrap when only two clusters are available.

A fixed-cluster conditional target would be a possible alternative interpretation, but Eq. (8) explicitly targets a global mean over random clusters. Repair: identify the actual resampling unit, relabel the existing comparator as within-cluster resampling, and add a cluster-resampling comparison before extending its poor results to that alternative. The supported consequence is limited to one comparator and the breadth of the comparison, not the Wald failure or universal superiority of another method.
# 7. Static code, non-findings and outstanding evidence

Pinned code: sambowyer/bayes_evals at `b9711844e00e9664258de321966ecd258a7273d6` (28 May 2025); sambowyer/no_clt_paper at `ab812f29f6508f53352a57b397669b2227f06164` (18 July 2025). The F1 delta variance in Appendix A.5 was independently checked with symbolic algebra. With q=2t/(2t+f+n) and d=2t+f+n>0, the multinomial delta variance equals q(1-q)(2-q)/(N*d), as in Eqs. (38)–(39). Figure 6 and Appendix A explicitly use the delta method; it would be incorrect to report that the paper ignores all asymptotic methods for nonlinear metrics. The beta-binomial cluster likelihood and the paired model’s Bernoulli marginals are also coherent.

Snippet 2 (p. 7) leaves beta undefined locally; with the earlier scipy.stats.beta binding, random draws require .rvs(size=2000), or an explicit numpy.random.beta import. Official SciPy 1.15.2 documentation confirms the interfaces. The relevant repository implementations use appropriate sampling/interval calls, so these notes do not establish erroneous experimental outputs. No author snippet was executed.

The main coverage utility pools over true-parameter draws, consistent with the stated prior-averaged experiment.

Title: Scientific verification report
I25-40133 / 0030
Position: AI Safety Must Embrace an Antifragile Perspective
Ming Jin; Hyunin Lee
ICML 2025 / PMLR 267, pp. 81588–81605; publisher PDF, 18 pages
Major — formal inevitability and fast-loop convergence claims require correction

Theorems 3.2–3.3 are false under the stated general MDP assumptions. Valid counterexamples undermine the formal route to universal inevitability, while leaving the broader case for adaptation and controlled stress-testing open. A second Major finding identifies a failed near-optimality implication in the proposed fast-loop regret framework. Corollary 3.4 is valid under its actual absolute-sensitivity assumptions.
# 1. Identity, version and scope

The original publisher PDF was preserved unchanged and matches the controller receipt, title, authors and publication record. SHA-256: `074f8e79fdf3848284c0cf2149b553b873b3cbb7ab6f15d561e9db3ba33b65d9`. All page references use one-based PDF numbering. Main pp. 1–9 and included Appendices A–H (pp. 15–18) were reviewed; bibliography pp. 9–14 was checked selectively for the formal claims’ source. Two independent AI checks covered the mathematics and source attribution.

The later arXiv record 2509.13339 lists v1 dated 11 September 2025. Its PDF/HTML and the cited Lee et al. ICLR paper were archived separately; they do not replace the hashed proceedings version. No formal erratum was identified in the inspected records. OpenReview was blocked by a browser challenge, so review/revision discussions could not be verified. No author software link was identified in the inspected records or targeted search.
# 2. Conclusion and repair status
Judgment / scope | Repair verification | Adoption / human status | Remaining work
F30-01 / theorem scope: Major | Counterexamples verified; no replacement theorem claimed | Not requested / pending | Restrict assumptions and quantifiers; re-prove formal claims
F30-02 / average gap: Major | Average o(1) and cumulative o(N) equivalence checked | Not requested / pending | Final-iterate convergence needs further assumptions
Corollary 3.4: No Issue Found | Actual absolute-value proof verified; no fix needed | Not requested / pending | Establish hypotheses for any proposed application
Adaptation proposal: Needs Evidence | No empirical repair or universal guarantee supplied | Not requested / pending | Implementation, safety and practical validation

The severity is scoped to the invalid inevitability justification in Section 3 and the failed fast-loop near-optimality implication in the Section 4.1 regret framework. It is not a claim that every practical recommendation is false, or that adaptation cannot help. Section 2 explicitly complements robustness and resilience; Section 5 and Appendices G–H discuss containment, fallback mechanisms and disclosure constraints. The concluding note acknowledges that concrete protocols and reliable implementation remain future work.

Reviewer-authored finite-horizon dynamic programming and symbolic checks verified the counterexamples below. Deterministic transitions in the two-state example avoid ambiguity about probability normalization. The three-state example includes a reachable rare severe loss, avoiding reliance on an all-zero-reward corner case. No author code, model, benchmark or claimed safety deployment was executed.
# 3. Problem 1: The cardinality argument does not prove inevitability

Major; high confidence in the counterexamples. Theorem 3.2 (p. 4) asserts zero robustness gap whenever there are two states or a one-step horizon. The two-state branch already fails. Use initial state s0, discount gamma=1/2 and the following stationary MDP:
State / action | Reward | Deterministic next state
s0 / stay | 1 | s0
s0 / exit | 0 | s1
s1 / either action | 4 | s1

Set u_plus(r)=r/(1+r) for nonnegative r and u_minus(r)=2r for negative r. These satisfy Appendix B.1: the positive branch is increasing and concave with derivative one at zero; the negative branch is increasing and convex with derivative two. All admissible probability distortions preserve 0 and 1, so P_dagger=P. An explicit Appendix-B-compatible pair is w_plus(p)=p+p(1-p)(1/2-p), w_minus(p)=p-p(1-p)(1/2-p), with a=b=1/2.

With the paper’s sum from reward index 0 through T=2, the true-optimal policy exits immediately and has value 3. In the perceived model, staying at s0 has values 0.5, 0.75 and 0.875 for one, two and three remaining reward slots, exceeding exit values 0, 0.4 and 0.6. Thus the perceived-optimal policy stays; its actual value is 1+1/2+1/4=1.75. The gap is 1.25, not zero. The alternate two-reward-slot convention gives gap 0.5, so horizon indexing does not rescue the claim. Scaling rewards by L>=1 gives gap 1.25L. This refutes the explicit zero-gap conclusion; it does not describe an observed negative-reward catastrophe.

Theorem 3.3 (p. 4) asserts that in any environment with at least three states and two steps, some perceived model induces catastrophic true suboptimality. Counterexample: three states s0, good and bad, with two actions having identical true consequences everywhere. At s0 both actions yield reward zero and go to bad with probability epsilon=0.01, otherwise good. Good is absorbing with reward zero; bad is absorbing with reward -1000. With gamma=1/2 and T=2, every policy has true value -7.5. Therefore every perceived-optimal policy has zero true policy gap, for every perceived model. Rare severe outcomes exist, but actions cannot alter them.

The cited Lee et al. source does not fill this gap: its Theorem 2 proof (PDF pp. 26–27) invokes zero intermediate rewards, absent from this paper’s general formulation; its Theorem 3 (p. 6) is an existence claim for some transition/reward functions. Its later same-policy value-discrepancy bound has further assumptions. These are not a universal policy-regret theorem.

Impact and repair: state count is neither necessary nor sufficient for positive policy regret. Replace the universal assertions with correctly restricted, proved claims; identify reward-timing, action-effect and policy-ranking assumptions. Distinguish existence of harmful misperception from inevitability in a specified deployment. Stronger eventual-occurrence conclusions need exposure/reachability conditions. The counterexamples validate the need for restriction, not a complete replacement theorem. The argument for continual monitoring can remain as a motivated position.
# 4. Problem 2: An average gap is assigned a cumulative-regret rate

Major; high confidence. Section 4.1, p. 6, defines the fast-loop average gap A_N=(1/N)sum_i Delta_i and then requires A_N=o(N), stating that this means near-optimality is eventually reached. A sequence with Delta_i=1 for every i has A_N=1 and A_N/N tending to zero. It satisfies the printed condition despite never improving.

A concrete witness is an initial state with actions yielding rewards one and zero, both entering a zero-reward absorbing state; always choosing zero gives gap one at every iteration. Repair the average condition to A_N=o(1), or use cumulative sum_i Delta_i=o(N). This repairs convergence of the average gap; convergence of the final iterate needs an additional argument. Definition 4.1 separately uses decreasing/increasing slow-loop average regret, so this finding does not render that entire definition vacuous.

Core dependency: Section 4.1 introduces the two-timescale regret framework and explicitly uses the fast-loop rate as the condition for reaching near-optimality within the current perception. For bounded persistent suboptimality the printed condition is automatically satisfied, so that optimization conclusion does not follow. This is a demonstrated failure of a formal implication attached to the proposed measurement framework, supporting Major independently of the Section 3 theorem failures. Definition 4.1’s trend criterion and the general case for adaptation can survive. Replacing the rate is a narrow repair; its ease does not reduce the severity of the failed implication.
# 5. Conditional corollary and rejected false positive

Visual inspection of original PDF pp. 4 and 16 confirms absolute-value bars in Delta_1 and Appendix C’s proof. Poppler text extraction omitted them. The apparent signed-gap contradiction was therefore rejected, and there is no basis to call the later arXiv text a correction of that nonexistent error.
> Let A=V_M(pi*), B=V_M(pi_dagger), a=V_Mdagger(pi*), b=V_Mdagger(pi_dagger). Delta=A-B=|A-B| >= |B-b|-|b-a|-|a-A| >= c-delta-epsilon.

True and perceived optimality justify the signs and the margin bound. Thus Corollary 3.4 is algebraically valid when all its stated hypotheses hold. The theorem-scope problem is that neither state count nor the existence of some misperception establishes those hypotheses in every environment.
# Appendix. Remaining evidence, sources, commands and roles

Needs Evidence: quantitative improvement of an implemented antifragile system, stability under new stressors, empirical estimation of the chosen comparator gap, and comprehensive validation of the cross-domain analogies in Appendix F. The notation w(P) should also explicitly identify a distribution-level transform: literal scalar componentwise application need not preserve total probability. This ambiguity is recorded without an additional confirmed finding, and does not affect the deterministic counterexample.

Coverage: main position and formal framework (1–9); source tracing in references (9–14); relations to existing methods A (15–16); distortion definitions B, corollary proof C, and extensions D (16); design principles E (16–17); analogical evidence F (17–18); feasibility G and disclosure H (18). Reading these sections does not establish empirical effectiveness or validate every citation.

report:
ELVIA Scientific Verification Report
I25-40134 / 0031
Paper: Position: Probabilistic Modelling is Sufficient for Causal Inference
Inspection outcome: Major: two demonstrated errors in core-related mathematical claims; scope preserved separately
Reviewed version: ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81810-81840; frozen 31-page publisher-linked PDF
Batch token: `[internal identifier omitted]`
Review date: Original review 23 October 2026; calibration 24 October 2026 (America/Chicago); machine logs use UTC
# 1. Identity, scope and result

Reviewed authors: Bruno Mlodozeniec, David S. Krueger and Richard E. Turner. Source [S1] is the exact publisher-linked PDF already present at papers/0031/0031.pdf. SHA-256: `552cdd7d430b7298895aa8a6d845189075349738326695443326e981f0ade7eb`. Its 823,880 bytes and hash agree with the controller acquisition receipt. The title, author line, proceedings imprint and publisher record agree. Page references below mean one-based PDF/printed local pages 1-31, not the proceedings’ global pagination.

The inspection checked the intervention and counterfactual constructions, the log-normal running example, the adjustment identities and their stated intervention scope, and the treatment of cross-world assumptions and identifiability. Two mathematical errors are demonstrated: the conditional-mean substitutions on pp.2 and14, and the extension of an atomic-intervention equality to parentless stochastic interventions on pp.17 and25. This focused calibration reuses the existing proof and finite-check records; it does not repeat the calculations or add empirical results.

Calibrated outcome: both findings are Major under the user’s clarified criterion for demonstrated derivation errors closely tied to a core contribution. Problem1 concerns the principal worked observational-versus-interventional comparison; Problem2 concerns the advertised generalization of intervention inference. The general joint-model representation and separately valid atomic case are retained as counterevidence, not used to downgrade these failed claims. Scientific decisions remain pending; author adoption has not been requested.
# 2. Definitions and assumptions used in the checks

For the aspirin model, let U=log Z, V=log T and W=log Y. The original model has positive Z,T,Y, independent Gaussian log-noises, a,b>0, and parameters treated as fixed in the conditional-mean calculation. Write sZ=Var(U), sT=Var(log epsilon_T), sY=Var(log epsilon_Y). In the counterexamples all three variances are strictly positive. The model implies V=aU+E_T and W=(b-ac)U-cE_T+E_Y, with U N(muZ,sZ), E_T N(0,sT), E_Y N(0,sY).

An atomic intervention fixes a treatment value. A stochastic parentless intervention replaces the treatment kernel by a distribution g(t) independent of its former parents; it need not make treatment independent of its descendants. For Problem 2 the graph is an acyclic two-node DAG T -> Y, all probabilities are positive, and the outcome mechanism is invariant. This exactly satisfies the paper’s stated parentless-intervention conditions.

The checks distinguish representability from identification: defining a cross-setting joint distribution does not identify that distribution from observational data alone. The paper itself makes this distinction in Appendices F, H and J.1. A posterior can retain prior dependence in a nonidentified problem.
# 3. Problem 1: incorrect log-normal conditional mean

Source claim and location. Section 2.1, p. 2, gives a special-case expression for E[Y|T] when c=0. Appendix B.2, p. 14, Eq. (9), gives its general expression. The latter uses the coefficient [a(b-c)sZ-c sT]/[sZ+c^2 sT+sY] multiplying (T-a muZ). The preceding Gaussian conditioning identity on p. 14 and the covariance matrix in Eq. (8) on p. 14 instead imply a different coefficient multiplying log T. Source pages 2 and 14 were rendered and inspected; this is not a text-extraction artifact [S1, E1].

Suspect step. Substitution from Eq. (8) into the immediately preceding correct Gaussian conditioning formula changes both the covariance numerator and the conditioning variance, and drops the logarithm. Define the following quantities directly from the stated model:

\[D=a^2s_Z+s_T,\quad C=a(b-ac)s_Z-cs_T,\quad H=(b-ac)^2s_Z+c^2s_T+s_Y,\quad \beta=C/D.\] \[\mathbb E[Y\mid T=t]=\exp\!\left((b-ac)\mu_Z+\frac{C}{D}(\log t-a\mu_Z)+\frac12\left(H-\frac{C^2}{D}\right)\right),\quad t>0.\] Complete analytic check. Since (V,W) is jointly Gaussian, E[W|V=log t]=(b-ac)muZ+(C/D)(log t-a muZ) and Var(W|V)=H-C^2/D. The log-normal expectation is the exponential of this conditional mean plus half the conditional variance. This gives the displayed correction without an approximation. D>0 in the stated nondegenerate model.

Assumption-satisfying counterexample. Take a=b=2, c=1, muZ=0, sZ=sT=sY=1. All original positivity and independence conditions hold; doses 1 and 2 both lie in the strictly positive support. Then D=5, C=-1, H=2 and H-C^2/D=9/5. Thus E[Y|T=t]=exp(0.9)t^(-0.2). The correct means at t=1 and t=2 are 2.4596031112 and 2.1412088739, with ratio 0.8705505633. Eq. (9)’s printed coefficient is 1/3; its ratio is exp(1/3)=1.3956124251. Any additive exponent constant independent of T cancels, so no interpretation of ’const.’ repairs this reversal of the trend [E2].

The p. 2 special case is independently wrong even without a trend reversal. For a=b=1, c=0, muZ=0 and all variances 1, the correct mean ratio between doses 4 and 1 is 2; the printed expression gives exp(3/2)=4.4816890703. In general the c=0 coefficient should be ab sZ/(a^2 sZ+sT), multiplying log t, not t.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. Reading T as an already logged variable conflicts with Eq.(1) and the explicit log T in the preceding derivation, and does not repair the coefficient. Eq.(8) and the general Gaussian-conditioning identity remain correct. At c=0, the corrected mean still increases with dose for a,b>0, preserving the qualitative confounding example. At c>0, the paper claims the possibility of positive association, not that every allowed parameter setting has it; the checked reversal does not refute that existential statement. Eq.(4)’s fixed-dose intervention mean also remains valid.

Calibrated judgment: Major at the claim level. The abstract identifies concrete examples as the paper’s demonstration; Section2 introduces this as its running example, and Section2.1/p.3 explicitly invokes Eq.(9) to explain observational versus interventional response. The wrong quantitative function, including a reversed trend for allowed fixed parameters, is therefore a failed derivation closely tied to the core explanatory contribution. The reversal is established for the saved c=1 example, not the c=0 specialization or the paper’s plotted parameters. The existing analytic replacement remains verified. No figure or empirical effect is claimed; the previously checked later version retains the error [S2].
# 4. Problem 2: stochastic intervention marginal confused with a conditional

Source claim and location. Appendix C.1, p. 17, Eq. (35), and Appendix J, p. 25, Eq. (37), assert q(x_y)=q(x_y|x_t) when discussing interventions whose new parent set is empty. Both explicitly extend the result beyond atomic interventions to any such intervention. The parent-adjustment sum that follows is a conditional treatment response; it is not the unconditional outcome under a nondegenerate random treatment [S1, E1].

Suspect step. Removing incoming edges to T makes T independent of its former parents, but it does not remove the edge T -> Y. Therefore it does not imply q(Y)=q(Y|T=t). An atomic treatment is constant, which is why the equality is valid at the assigned value in that special case.

Complete finite check. Let the original graph be T -> Y. Use p(T=1)=1/2 and unchanged outcome probabilities p(Y=1|T=0)=1/5 and p(Y=1|T=1)=4/5. Intervene with g(T=1)=1/4 and no parents. All four original joint cells and all four intervened joint cells have strictly positive mass. There is no hidden confounder, no cycle, no support problem, and the sole original outcome mechanism is preserved.
T | Y | Intervened joint probability q(T,Y)

\[q(Y=1)=\frac34\frac15+\frac14\frac45=\frac7{20},\qquad q(Y=1\mid T=1)=\frac45\ne\frac7{20}.\] Repair. Under the stated valid parent-adjustment setting and positivity on the treatment values used, the fixed-treatment response is obtained first. A stochastic policy then requires averaging over its treatment distribution:

\[q(y)=\sum_t g(t)\sum_z p(y\mid t,z)p(z).\] Here z denotes the original parents of T; for the two-node counterexample this parent set is empty. Summing the four displayed cells verifies the repair exactly. Alternatively, the paper can restrict the equalities in Eqs. (35) and (37) to the atomic case at its assigned treatment. These are two precise repairs, with different scope.

Calibrated judgment: Major at the claim level. Section2.3, p.5, defines general kernel replacement in Eq.(5)/Figure5 and directs readers to Appendix J for adjustment shortcuts. Appendix J expressly asks for q(y) and extends the atomic result to every empty-parent intervention; Appendix C.1’s proof establishes the conditional response only. This failed generalization drops the policy weights and answers a different query from the advertised stochastic marginal. The two-node example also satisfies Y not being a parent of T, and uses positive joint cells and an unchanged outcome kernel. Reading the notation as a family of atomic outcomes would require withdrawing the explicit stochastic extension.

Counterevidence and scope. Eq.(5)’s general stochastic joint factorization remains valid. Appendix I Eq.(36) identifies the treatment-conditional response on the intervention support. Under an atomic intervention, the marginal equals that conditional at the assigned treatment value only; the main fixed-dose aspirin calculation survives. Restoring the outer policy average repairs the stochastic result. Neither this repair’s simplicity nor the survival of the broad expressivity thesis downgrades the failed core generalization. The previously checked arXiv text retains it [S2]; no empirical policy consequence is asserted.
# 5. Dependence, counterevidence and review limits

The two findings are independent: Problem 1 concerns a Gaussian-to-log-normal substitution; Problem 2 concerns marginalization over a stochastic intervention. Neither requires the other. Their correct replacements use the same probability framework advocated by the paper.

Scope clarification, not an additional error finding: Definition 3.2, pp. 7-8, uses full endogenous evidence X=x, whereas Appendix N.1 considers partial evidence (T,Y). Partial evidence can induce dependencies among originally independent noises, so their full posterior joint must be retained. Appendix N.1 does retain that joint and applies interventions to structural equations. A partial-evidence collider example is therefore not an assumption-satisfying refutation of the definition’s literal full-X formulation. The same-G Bayesian-network wording warrants care, but no failed counterfactual result was demonstrated.

The partial-noise-sharing query in Section 3 and the all-noise-sharing SCM query in Appendix N have different model assumptions. The paper identifies that difference. For full sharing, Y*=Y(T/T*)^c follows by eliminating Z^b epsilon_Y; an independent finite illustration agrees. This is an analytic identity plus a finite illustration, not an empirical validation.

The later version checked is arXiv:2512.23408v1, submitted 29 December 2025. Its separate PDF was preserved and the targeted passages compared; it does not replace the frozen publisher PDF. No explicit erratum or dedicated author-code link was located in the examined publisher/arXiv records and scoped searches. The OpenReview forum presented a browser-verification wall; its discussions were not reviewed. No claim is made that no other correction exists.

Not performed: executing author code, fitting the aspirin model, regenerating its plots, testing software used for the publication, exhaustive verification of every cited quotation, or human adjudication. If the displayed formulas generated any published plots, establishing their empirical effect would require the actual plotting source and a fresh controlled regeneration; the formulas alone do not identify the code used.
# 6. Conclusion and decision status
Item | Calibrated judgment and status
Problem1 | Major. Wrong quantitative conditional response in the principal worked comparison; valid-parameter trend reversal. Existing analytic correction verified; figure effects remain unshown.
Problem2 | Major. Invalid advertised extension to a stochastic-policy marginal. Existing outer-mixture repair verified; atomic equality retained only at the assigned value.
What survives | Eq.(5)’s joint representation, the valid atomic calculation, c=0’s qualitative confounding contrast, and c>0’s existential positive-association claim.
Scope | Counterfactual wording remains a clarification with no separate demonstrated defect. Existing version/evidence gaps are unchanged.
Status | Scientific decision and controller acceptance pending; author adoption not requested; publication disabled.
# 7. Consulted sources and stable identifiers

[S1] Mlodozeniec, B.; Krueger, D.; Turner, R. E. Position: Probabilistic Modelling is Sufficient for Causal Inference. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81810-81840. Frozen publisher-linked PDF; local pages 1-31. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/mlodozeniec25a.html
