report: ELVIA Scientific Verification / ICML 2025 / I25-40143
Position: General Intelligence Requires Reward-based Pretraining
Supported judgment: Major. Scientific decision: pending.
Review date: 2026-10-24. Batch token: `[internal identifier omitted]`.
# Identity, source version, and outcome

Reviewed source: Seungwook Han, Jyothish Pari, Samuel J. Gershman and Pulkit Agrawal, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81494-81513; exact publisher-linked 20-page PDF. Page references below use printed pages, identical to 1-based physical PDF pages. The SHA-256 was independently compared with the controller receipt and matches. [E1-E2]

Supported judgment: Major for an invalid causal-isolation inference in the Go comparison (F02), with a separate Minor defect in the published Befunge evaluation prompt (F01). The Go comparison changes both initialization and the KL-anchored objective, so it does not isolate the claimed initialization-induced local-minimum mechanism. The documented Befunge prompt also contains Brainfuck instructions and demonstrations. Reported scores are not shown false, and actual use of the mixed-language prompt remains unresolved.

The review also examined the Go and vector-orthogonality experiments, not only the language benchmark. Their reported comparisons and their broader mechanistic interpretations are distinguished below. Scientific decisions and human review remain pending; adoption has not been requested.
# Scope and checked technical contributions

The main text (pp. 1-9), Tables 1-3, Figures 1-2, and all experimental/proposal appendices (pp. 15-20) were read. The bibliography (pp. 10-14) was consulted selectively. The source page containing the prompt discrepancy was rendered and visually inspected.

The empirical contributions inspected are: six-model evaluations on Brainfuck and Befunge tasks; a 9x9 Go comparison between reward pretraining and supervised-pretraining-plus-RL pipelines; and a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct orthogonality-task comparison of extra SFT-then-RFT versus RFT from the same base. The synthetic-task curriculum and small-context/external-memory architecture are proposed directions. They are not treated as already completed large-scale training experiments.

Section 2’s log-likelihood and expected cumulative-reward objectives have no identified algebraic error. The four dot products in Listing 2 are -10, 0, -1 and 1, confirming option (b). The Listing 8 dot products are -2, -9, -3 and 0, confirming option (d). These are analytic arithmetic checks, not executed model reproductions.

Static resource discovery inspected the publisher link, public project-page response, author-linked sources and a later arXiv version. No author implementation, raw responses or evaluation logs were recovered from the inspected surfaces. No author code, interpreter executing the authors’ snippets, model/API call, training run or paid computation was performed.
# Problem 1: the documented Befunge prompt contains a different-language task

Source claim and location. Section 3.1, p. 4, says models are prompted with the standardized formats in Listings 5 and 6, respectively, including the full language rules and example code. Appendix A.5 is headed ’Befunge Prompt’ (pp. 16-17), but Listing 6 ends with instructions to generate Brainfuck programs for ’ey’, ’ez’ and ’hi’, and the first two programs use Brainfuck arithmetic/loop syntax. The caption also repeats the Brainfuck label. [E1]

Complete check. A.5 first defines Befunge’s ’.’ as numeric output, ’,’ as character output and ’@’ as termination. The appended Brainfuck demonstration programs contain neither ’,’ nor ’@’. Under the very rules supplied in the listing, those programs therefore cannot act as terminating demonstrations that print the stated letter pairs. More directly, the task instructions explicitly ask for the wrong language. Comparing A.4 and A.5 shows the same demonstration tail repeated. This is more than a misspelled heading: the documented executable task and examples conflict with the claimed evaluation language.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. The appendix may contain a copy-and-paste documentation error while the actual evaluated prompts were correct. Indeed, several high reported Befunge printing accuracies make it particularly unsafe to infer that the displayed Brainfuck tail was used verbatim. The released text does not identify the submitted prompt logs or evaluator needed to distinguish the possibilities. The visual source check establishes the published discrepancy only.

Dependence and impact. The listing is explicitly linked to the protocol of the original esoteric-language experiment, a supporting empirical contribution. The inconsistency compromises faithful reproduction and interpretation of that protocol. It does not, on this record, demonstrate a material change in the benchmark scores or in the core comparative conclusions. The supported defect is therefore Minor; the question of actual runtime use remains Needs Evidence.

Repair scope. Replace the erroneous tail with the exact prompts actually used, including demonstration order, decoding settings, input instances and evaluator details; retain any original run logs needed to substantiate the replacement. If wrong-language prompts were actually used, the affected evaluation must be rerun. Neither a corrected protocol nor new scores are claimed verified here.
# Problem 2: the Go comparison does not isolate the claimed mechanism

Source claim and location. Section 4.1, p. 5 (bottom-right), presents the Go comparison as a controlled isolation of whether training with RL from scratch is the major source of the performance gain, and as a rigorous test of whether supervised pretraining impairs escape from local minima. Figure 2 and p. 6 (top-left) interpret the comparison as evidence that passive pretraining restricts exploration. This is an actual interpretation of an executed experiment, not an experiment requirement imposed on a prospective recommendation. [E1]

Design and invalid inference. The comparison changes the initial policy and the KL-anchored objective: p. 6 explicitly introduces a KL penalty for SPT-then-RFT, with coefficients 0.1 and 0.5 in Figure 2. The reported win rates therefore compare complete pipelines. They do not isolate an initialization-created local-minimum mechanism, because the anchoring can change which policy optimizes the objective. Appendix B.1 describes the training stages but supplies no matched-objective control that resolves this distinction.

Decisive identification check. The existing independent mathematical audit provides a strictly concave one-state, two-action illustration, reused here without re-execution. Let q be the probability of the action with reward 1, let the other action have reward 0, let the reference probability p lie strictly between 0 and 1, and let beta > 0. The regularized objective is:

\[J_\beta(q)=q-\beta\left[q\log\frac{q}{p}+(1-q)\log\frac{1-q}{1-p}\right].\] \[J_\beta''(q)=-\beta\!\left(\frac1q+\frac1{1-q}\right)<0,\qquad q_\beta=\frac{p e^{1/\beta}}{1-p+p e^{1/\beta}}<1.\] Thus a lower reward than the unregularized optimum q=1 can arise at the unique global optimum of the regularized problem, with no suboptimal local maximum. This is a witness to non-identification by the reported contrast, not a model of the Go dynamics, a counterexample to the win rates, or proof that the actual Go runs never encountered local minima.

Counterevidence and surviving result. The paper explicitly discusses KL strength, reports 66% and 92% RPT win rates against the two KL-constrained pipelines, and states that removing KL with an infinite training budget can yield the same optimal policy. Those qualifications support the narrower complete-pipeline comparison. They do not establish the stronger claimed isolation of an initialization or local-minimum mechanism. The LLM experiment separately starts all conditions from a pretrained Qwen base and is expressly a finetuning proxy; F02 does not reinterpret it as scratch pretraining or allege false scores.

Dependency, severity, and repair. Section 4.1 uses this inference as a central empirical argument for replacing passive pretraining. The demonstrated invalid causal-isolation inference is therefore Major under the saved calibration standard. Whether initialization-induced trapping actually occurred remains unresolved. Restrict the conclusion to the evaluated pipeline comparison, or provide a comparison that separates initialization from the anchored objective together with evidence specifically identifying optimization trapping. No experiment is demanded for the broader normative proposal, and no corrected scores or fully repaired empirical claim are certified.
# Other evidence questions and counterevidence

Befunge aggregation. The 30 numbers printed in Table 2 sum to 12.94, yielding an unweighted cell mean of 43.13%, whereas the p. 4 overview says about 29%. Appendix A.3 uses different task sizes (100 printing inputs, one Fibonacci example, and 15 factorial inputs), so the intended aggregation or omitted repetition scheme must be specified before the 29% figure can be judged against its intended denominator. This is retained as Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated false table or a higher-severity finding. Table 1’s unweighted mean is 12.4%, consistent with the approximate 12% statement.

Befunge Fibonacci denominator. Appendix A.3 lists one example, while Table 2 includes 0.02 for Llama 3.1 70B. A one-trial binary accuracy could not equal 0.02; however, one unique task evaluated over repeated samples or constituent test inputs could. The paper does not document that denominator in the inspected protocol. Runs, samples and aggregation rules are needed; no fabrication or incorrect scoring is inferred.

Go causal interpretation. F02 above concerns the explicit claim to isolate scratch-RL or initialization-driven local-minimum effects from a comparison that also changes the KL objective. The narrower reported pipeline contrast remains meaningful. The actual optimization mechanism remains unresolved; this does not restore the invalid isolation inference. The existing KL illustration was reused, not rerun.

Orthogonality experiment. Both arms start from a pretrained Qwen model; p. 6 explicitly identifies this as a proxy rather than an experiment training a language model from scratch. Appendix A.6 describes 100 training and 100 test examples, 100 SFT epochs, and 31 RL steps, plus manual post-filtering of evaluator outputs. The reported 93% versus 80% test comparison is conditional on that setup. Raw outputs and correction rules were not available for an independent audit. The paper is not accused of falsely claiming that this proxy is full RPT.

Generalization and architecture. The language tasks test transfer to unfamiliar program semantics and syntax; they do not uniquely identify memorization or knowledge/reasoning coupling as the cause of failure. The broader explanation is explicitly framed as a hypothesis. Algorithm 1 appends to its working context without displaying truncation, but it is high-level proposed pseudocode, not an executed result demonstrating fixed-context performance. Its context-management mechanism remains unspecified. These qualifications do not create an experiment requirement for a normative proposal.
# Version comparison, repair status, and conclusion

The later arXiv:2502.19402v3 record is dated 26 August 2025. Targeted comparison found that it retains the same Brainfuck tail in A.5, the approximate 29% statement, the one-example Fibonacci count and the 0.02 table cell. No relevant repair is verified by that comparison. The conference PDF remains the reviewed target; the later HTML is preserved separately. [E3]

The publisher’s Notion project link returned a web-fetch 404, while direct public HTTP returned a generic JavaScript shell with no substantive page content or repository links. This is an access limitation, not proof that the project or source code never existed. No author repository was substituted by an unrelated third-party project.

Supported judgment: Minor. Scientific decision: pending.
Review date: 2026-10-24. Batch token: `[internal identifier omitted]`.
# Identity, source version, and outcome

Reviewed source: Paul Youssef, Zhixue Zhao, Daniel Braun, Jörg Schlötterer and Christin Seifert, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82426–82440; the exact publisher-linked 15-page PDF. Page references below use printed pages1–15, identical to physical PDF pages. Title and authors match the publisher record. The original SHA-256 was independently compared with the controller receipt and matches. [E1–E2]

Supported judgment: Minor. Three bounded errors are established: a blanket inference-overhead claim conflicts with an included method; a defense summary omits the cited study’s discrete, existing-vocabulary deployment; and two regulatory examples do not have the training/data-only scope attributed to them. These corrections affect the accuracy of the comparative and supporting discussion. The inspected evidence does not establish that the paper’s core warning about malicious editing is false or that the cited attack demonstrations fail. Scientific decisions and human review remain pending; author adoption has not been requested.
# Scope and checked technical contributions

The entire main text (pp. 1–9), Figure 1 and Tables 1–4 were read. Pages10–15 contain references, which were checked selectively. There is no appendix, new model-training experiment, formal theorem, original evaluator or original numerical results table in this source. The contribution is a literature-based risk argument, a stakeholder analysis and a research agenda. Absence of a new experiment is not treated as an error.

Primary-source checks covered ROME’s quoted performance and optimization, IKE’s prompt construction, LoRA’s mergeable inference representation, representative harmful-edit demonstrations, and both cited Youssef2025 detection/reversal papers. Public publisher/arXiv surfaces and linked resource information were inspected. No matching implementation for a new experiment in this position paper was identified or required. Author code was not executed; no model/API calls, training, installations or paid computations were performed.

ROME’s 99.8% efficacy and 88.1% paraphrase/generalization values on GPT2-XL and zsRE match the original ROME Table 1. The original paper also reports a neighborhood metric; these scores are benchmark-conditional and do not measure real-world attack prevalence. BadEdit, Hazra et al. and Chen et al. support the existence of harmful-edit outcomes under their respective threat models. They do not supply a denominator for the qualitative attack-likelihood ratings in this paper. [E3,E6–E8]
# Problem 1: zero inference overhead is overgeneralized

Source claim and location. Section 2, p. 2, states that KEs introduce no inference overhead and therefore leave edited-model latency unchanged. This follows a taxonomy that includes memory-based and in-context methods, and is presented as a distinction from PEFT. Table 1 on p. 3 includes IKE. [E1]

Complete check. The rendered table itself marks IKE with minimal inference overhead, while the MEND, MALMEN, ROME and MEMIT rows are marked none. The original IKE study constructs an inference prompt containing the edited fact and demonstrations, commonly 32 demonstrations and 16 for a shorter context window. Those input tokens must be processed at inference. A lack of additional model parameters therefore does not imply zero inference work or guaranteed unchanged latency. No timing experiment is needed to reject the universal zero-overhead statement; the paper’s own table already records the exception. [E4]

Counterevidence and impact. Weight-only edits that preserve the forward architecture can have no additional inference operations, and Table 1 acknowledges IKE’s exception. The defect is the blanket prose and its latency-based rationale, not a demonstrated failure of the low-cost editing methods or their attacks. The evidence supports Minor: scope the claim to the relevant parameter-modifying methods, and separate edit-time computation, added parameters, prompt length and deployment-time latency. No measured slowdown or reliable timing detector is asserted.

Related comparison limits. ROME optimizes an internal edit value with Adam, so a few forward passes is not a complete cost description; no training may instead mean no conventional base-model retraining. LoRA can merge its update into the original weight matrix without additional inference latency. An unmerged-adapter implementation could explain a nonzero overhead entry, but that deployment assumption must be stated before treating latency as a general KE-versus-PEFT discriminator. These are scope clarifications, not separately counted findings. [E3,E5]
# Problem 2: the reversal summary overstates a vocabulary requirement

Source claim and location. Section 6.1, p. 8, says the cited reversal approach requires adding vocabulary tokens and tuning their embeddings; this model-modification requirement is repeated in the discussion of reversing edits without model access. The citation is Youssef et al. 2025a, the published NAACL paper, rather than an unspecified earlier draft. [E1,E9]

Complete check. In the cited study, Section 5.2 describes continuous reversal tokens, which do require an expanded vocabulary. Section 5.3, physical PDF p. 5 / printed p. 12660, also constructs discrete reversal tokens chosen from the existing vocabulary. Once selected, these tokens can be included in an ordinary prompt without adding vocabulary entries. Table 2 and Section 6.1 evaluate this discrete variant. Thus the claimed deployment requirement is not necessary for every reversal variant in the cited work. [E9]

Counterevidence and impact. Finding the discrete tokens still uses white-box optimization and validation. The discrete results are unstable on GPT2-XL/GPT-J and poor on Llama 3.1; the method only targets in-context edits. This is not evidence for reliable black-box discovery, reversal of weight edits or a general solution to malicious editing. The supported correction is Minor and local to the defense taxonomy: distinguish white-box token discovery from ordinary-prompt deployment, and continuous from discrete tokens. The continued need for improved defenses remains supported. This review verified the distinction in the cited method, not a new implementation or an empirical repair.
# Problem 3: the regulatory examples have a broader scope than claimed

Source claim and location. Section 3.4, p. 6, presents the California AI Transparency Act 2024 and China’s Interim Measures 2023 as examples of regulation focused only on training-process and training-data risks. The original page was rendered and visually inspected. [E1]

Complete check. The cited Chinese regulation addresses generated harmful and discriminatory content, service transparency/accuracy, generated-content labels and action on illegal output or misuse, including Articles 4,12,14 and15. Its coverage is not limited to training data. The California bill sponsor’s official 19 September 2024 signing statement describes disclosures on generated image/video/audio and an AI-detection tool, which are output-provenance measures. The direct official California bill-text endpoint returned403, so no inaccessible clause is claimed to have been inspected. The contemporaneous official statement and the accessible Chinese primary text suffice to contradict the characterization of these particular examples. [E10–E11]

Counterevidence, impact and repair. This check does not establish that either regime comprehensively detects or prevents knowledge editing, nor does it estimate the fraction of all regulations with any given scope. The paper also acknowledges EU safeguards. The narrower question of gaps in KE-specific verification is distinct from a claim that these examples only regulate training/data. The supported impact is Minor: revise the examples and document any remaining editing-specific gap. Later 2026 legal changes are not applied retroactively to the 2025 paper, and no comprehensive legal assessment is claimed.
# Other evidence questions and counterevidence

Attack-method attribution. Chen et al. 2024 Section 2.2 uses an in-context editing baseline without demonstrations, explicitly distinguishing it from Zheng et al.’s demonstration-based IKE. The target paper’s IKE label can be read as family shorthand, but should not transfer the full 33-instance protocol or its measured properties to that attack unchanged. This is retained as Scope Clarification: the primary study still demonstrates harmful outputs with in-context editing. A January 2026 revision of Chen et al. was not substituted for its 2024 version. [E8]

Stealth and likelihood. Section 3.1 explicitly defines stealthiness as preserving unrelated knowledge and general capabilities; Section 6 discusses successful edit detection and its limitations. Treating the paper as claiming universal undetectability would ignore this counterevidence. Table 3’s uniformly high attack-likelihood ratings have no calibrated scale, population, time window or incident denominator. They can be read as qualitative threat judgments; their interpretation as measured frequencies remains Needs Evidence.

Proposals and historical scope. Verifiable updates, weight-based edit inference, conditional editability and remote reversal are proposed directions, not established security guarantees. No impossibility result or missing-experiment requirement is manufactured for these proposals. Contemporary law/platform conditions are not treated as timeless facts. AISI’s cited safety-case discussion emphasizes future autonomy/loss-of-control risks, but one document does not prove the absence of all institutional work on editing threats. No exhaustive policy or hosting-platform audit was performed.
# Version comparison, repair status, and conclusion

The arXiv record lists v3 dated 17 June 2025. Targeted comparison of that version retains the blanket inference-overhead statement, the reversal vocabulary restriction, and the regulatory characterization; no repair of these passages was identified. The reviewed conference PDF remains the fixed target. Public version discovery does not establish that no unobserved correction exists. [E12]
Item | Judgment | Repair / remaining work
Inference-overhead generalization | Minor | Restrict zero-overhead claim and state deployment assumptions; no latency measurement reproduced.
Reversal vocabulary requirement | Minor | Separate continuous/discrete deployment and white-box discovery; no new defense validated.
Regulatory examples | Minor | Correct existing output/service protections; KE-specific gap needs precise evidence.
Attack evidence and likelihood | Existence supported; prevalence Needs Evidence | Conditional published demonstrations retained; no real-world frequency inferred.
Overall | Minor; scientific decision pending | Human review and controller acceptance pending; adoption not requested.

The findings are bounded source-consistency errors. None supplies a counterexample to the existence of the malicious editing techniques cited by the paper. Their repair should improve the accuracy of the supporting argument without being represented as a verified change in attack performance or a completed defense.

report: ELVIA Scientific Verification / ICML 2025 / I25-40145
Position: Causal Machine Learning Requires Rigorous Synthetic Experiments for Broader Adoption
Supported judgment: Major. Scientific decision: pending.
Review date: 2026-10-24. Batch token: `[internal identifier omitted]`.
# Identity, source version, and supported outcome

Target: Poinsot et al., ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81995-82015, 21-page publisher-linked proceedings PDF [R1]. The six-author identity was checked against the publisher. Page references below use the PDF’s printed pages, which coincide with physical pages. The preserved original is papers/0040/0040.pdf (388,219 bytes).

Code:
Original SHA-256:
0618d4eface712111272c6b804ddba156790c5d0c84c3a6c07f35661cd37d345

Supported judgment: Major. Two demonstrated problems affect central empirical arguments: the released CausalNF reproduction recipe does not satisfy the observational-equivalence premise of the chosen SCM pair, and the RealCause filter analysis applies an independent-samples test to overlapping samples. A further Minor issue concerns the counterfactual error metric’s label. These conclusions concern the validity of particular experimental and inferential chains; they do not establish fabricated results or refute the general recommendation for rigorous synthetic evaluation. Scientific decision and human acceptance remain pending.
# Claim coverage and evidence boundary
Claim / location | Checks and result

Position and design framework; Sections 1-2, 4-7, pp.1-9 | Read throughout. The proposed framework and adoption argument are methodological positions; no proof of an adoption effect is claimed or required.
RealCause; Section 3.1, pp.4-5; Appendix B, pp.15-17 | Read all tabulated rows; compared 100 means and 100 standard deviations with archived aggregates. Static filter-code audit identifies F02.
CausalNF; Section 3.2, p.5; Appendix C, pp.17-20 | Checked structural equations, noise law, configuration-to-sampler path, saved notebook outputs, and metric aggregation. F01 and F03.
Definitions / proposed extension; Appendices A and D, pp.14-15,20-21 | Checked identifiability, additive-noise reasoning, and sampling scope. No additional demonstrated major error.

References, pp.10-13; public resources | Selective primary-source checks, full repository-tree inventory, 251 selected archived files, and targeted later-version comparison. Not an exhaustive bibliography or reproduction.

The target text was read in full, with selective reference verification. Original pages 17, 19, and 20 were also visually inspected. Source-code statements below refer to a frozen public commit, not independently observed historical execution. Only reviewer-owned arithmetic, text/JSON parsing, hashing, and document rendering were executed; author programs, notebooks, pickle files, and models were not executed.
# F01 - Major: the released SCM pair is not observationally equivalent

Appendix C, pp.18-20, states that CTF1 and CTF2 share an observational distribution while their counterfactuals differ. Table 3 and the following interpretation connect CTF2’s higher error to CausalNF learning CTF1 instead. Section 3.2 uses this experiment to illustrate failures under violated assumptions [R1]. Both models set X1=U1 and X3=X2+U3. Their second mechanisms are:

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{CTF1}:\quad X_2&=\begin{cases}U_2,&X_1\geq0,\\U_2-1,&X_1<0;\end{cases}\\\mathrm{CTF2}:\quad X_2&=\begin{cases}U_2,&X_1\geq0,\\-U_2,&X_1<0.\end{cases}\end{aligned}\] The chain paragraph does not restate its noise law. The author-linked reproduction recipe resolves that ambiguity: causal-flows/setup.md lines 110-118 directs these experiments to grids/causal_nf/robustness2/base.yaml; line 14 selects dataset.base_version=1. The companion base_ctf.yaml selects the CTF mechanisms. Tracing configuration merging, SCMPreparator, and the three-node noise factory shows that version 1 is independent standard Normal noise in all three coordinates. This is the documented experiment path, not an unrelated default [R2].

\[\begin{aligned}X_2\mid X_1<0,\mathrm{CTF1}&\sim\mathcal N(-1,1),\\X_2\mid X_1<0,\mathrm{CTF2}&\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad P(X_1<0)=\tfrac12.\end{aligned}\] The conditional means differ on an event of positive probability, so the joint observational distributions cannot be equal. CTF3/CTF4 retain this mismatch and introduce the analogous shifted-versus-reflected third mechanism. Thus the released recipe fails a necessary premise of the paper’s selected-pair explanation. An error-score contrast alone also does not identify which structural mechanism a trained flow learned.
SCM | Saved notebook mean / SD | Published Tables 3-4

These values occur in the existing plain-text output of display_comparison_table.ipynb, zero-based cell 4, whose source names comparison_flows_robustness2.pickle. They match every reported mean and standard deviation in Tables 3-4 after rounding. This links the released workflow to the reported numbers, but saved notebook output is not an execution receipt: undocumented historical overrides remain possible. No pickle was opened or notebook executed. The finding establishes a failure of the released reproduction and interpretation chain, without asserting that every historical run necessarily used this configuration.

Counterevidence matters. With Gaussian noise, CTF2 is observationally equivalent to a different model M0 with X2=U2 and the same X1 and X3 equations, by Normal sign symmetry. Its counterfactuals can still be non-identifiable in that broader class, and the measured performance gap may be real. That does not restore equivalence with CTF1 or demonstrate that the learner recovered CTF1. The broader lesson about testing assumption violations therefore remains possible.

An analytic repair is to use U2 uniform on (0,1), retain an independent U1 with positive probability on both sides of zero, and keep the same independent U3 in both chain models. Then U2-1 and -U2 are both uniform on (-1,0). For a factual X1>0 and X2=0.25, intervening to X1<0 yields X2=-0.75 in CTF1 and -0.25 in CTF2. Extending this repair to CTF3/CTF4 also requires uniform U3. Changing all noises to uniform (0,1) while retaining X1=U1 would remove the negative factual branch and would not implement the intended two-branch comparison. The cited original counterexample uses a binary treatment and uniform noise [R3]. These are verified analytic repairs only; performance under a corrected experiment requires new runs.
# F02 - Major: the realism-filter test ignores sample overlap

Appendix B.2, p.17, compares all 20 seed-level ATE errors for each IHDP realization with the subset passing the realism checks. It reports one significant Welch test among 100 realizations and interprets this as realism checks rarely finding meaningfully lower errors. The pinned realcause/equivalencerealism.py confirms the procedure: lines 25-34 insert the same ate_bias_noisy into all_biases and, when both q30 marginal p-values exceed 0.05, filtered_biases; line 50 calls ttest_ind(all_biases, filtered_biases, equal_var=False). Welch permits unequal variances but retains the independent-samples assumption [R4,R5].

Let P be the passing group of size m and F its failing complement of size k, with n=m+k. Conditional on group membership and independent seed outcomes within and across the disjoint groups, the exact contrast and its variance are:

\[\begin{aligned}\bar X_P-\bar X_A&=\frac{k}{n}(\bar X_P-\bar X_F),\\\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_P-\bar X_A)&=\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)^2\left(\frac{\sigma_P^2}{m}+\frac{\sigma_F^2}{k}\right).\end{aligned}\] Under the common-variance null, covariance between the passing mean and the full mean is sigma^2/n. The correct contrast variance is sigma^2(1/m-1/n), whereas treating the means as independent uses sigma^2(1/m+1/n). For n=20 and m=10, the latter is three times larger. The algebra concerns a fixed-membership illustration; actual training dependence and random filtering require a design-aware analysis.

A reviewer-owned calculation used 20 illustrative nonnegative errors: passing values 0.1,0.2,...,1.0 and failing values 0.5,0.6,...,1.4. Their means are 0.55, 0.95, and 0.75 for passing, failing, and all seeds. It yields:
Calculation | t / degrees of freedom | Two-sided p
Independent passing-versus-all Welch | -1.60056 / 21.15524 | 0.1243025
Disjoint passing-versus-failing Welch | -2.95420 / 18 | 0.0084891
Passing-minus-all contrast using overlap covariance | -2.95420 / 18 | 0.0084891

The same 0.05 threshold produces different decisions. For k>0, equality of passing and all means is equivalent to equality of passing and failing means; the weighted contrast supplies the proper scale and standard error under the stated assumptions. This is not the authors’ data, a simulation of their KS checks, or a corrected count of significant realizations. Reviewer-owned standard-library integration independently calculated the p-values; 10,000- and 20,000-panel results agreed within 6e-15.

There is also an inferential gap between non-rejection and negligible benefit. A meaningful-benefit claim needs an effect size, uncertainty, and a practical threshold. The code skips tests with fewer than two passing seeds while retaining 100 as the final denominator; missing per-seed filter records prevent determining whether or how often this happened. If every seed passes, the full/subset difference is identically zero and supplies no selective-filtering evidence.

This is Major because B.2 addresses whether realism filtering remedies the generator errors used in Section 3.1’s central empirical critique. Its appendix location does not reduce that dependency. The published one-of-100 inference requires reanalysis. The demonstrated error does not invalidate the descriptive ATE variability, prove that filtering helps, or overturn the overall position. Repair requires the paired seed-level error and KS records, an explicit selection estimand, disjoint-group analysis or resampling of the complete filtering procedure, effect estimates with uncertainty, acceptance rates, and valid-test denominators. None of that empirical repair is claimed here.
# F03 - Minor: the reported metric is mean Euclidean error

Tables 2-4 label counterfactual performance as RMSE. In causal_nf/models/causal_nf.py lines 176-179, the released code computes a Euclidean error norm separately for every unit. BaseLightning.compute_metrics_stats in models/base_model.py lines 71-94 concatenates these norms and takes their arithmetic mean. scripts/create_comparison_flows.py line 102 averages the counterfactual-query columns; there is no later squaring that restores a root-mean-square across units [R2].

\[\underbrace{\frac1N\sum_i\sqrt{\sum_j e_{ij}^2}}_{\text{implemented mean norm}}\quad\ne\quad\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_i\sum_j e_{ij}^2}}_{\text{vector RMSE in general}}.\] For scalar errors 0 and 2, the former is 1 and the latter is sqrt(2); per-coordinate RMSE additionally specifies coordinate normalization. The released aggregation therefore needs an explicit definition and an accurate label, or recomputation if conventional RMSE was intended. This is Minor because the demonstrated issue concerns interpretation and comparability of the values. No observed ranking reversal, corrected score, or reversal of the larger-error pattern is established.
# Retained evidence, unresolved questions, and qualifications

RealCause’s descriptive variability is supported by committed aggregate JSON: every one of the 100 Appendix B.1 means and 100 standard deviations matches at three decimal places. With seed 123 across 100 realizations, the archived mean error is 0.9540, standard deviation 1.3550, and maximum 9.4467. Realization 84 across 20 seeds has mean 6.2087 and standard deviation 11.3186, consistent with the reported 6.209 +/- 11.319. These are checks of archived numbers, not independent model reproductions. The full tree has no paired per-seed KS/error records sufficient to redo B.2.

The p.5 statement about instability of downstream method rankings needs additional evidence. The archived causal-predictive-analysis.csv has 1,568 rows for Lalonde PSID, Lalonde CPS, and Twins, with no IHDP rows. The new IHDP automation and aggregates concern generator ATE/PEHE; they do not establish downstream estimator-ranking reversals. This is recorded as Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated false ranking claim. Large absolute ATE errors also do not by themselves identify a directional bias or a downstream ranking reversal.

The released evaluate2 routine averages model effects over the test covariates while load_ihdp supplies the full-realization target ATE. Thus the error can include finite-split composition differences as well as model error; the setup explicitly acknowledges seed-dependent data splitting and sampling variation. Without decomposition, the audit does not attribute all variability to optimization or dismiss it as a split artifact. Marginal KS non-rejection is also weaker than full joint observational equality; the causal-hierarchy theorem alone does not diagnose these particular errors.

For the Triangle variants, additive transformed noise can make g(U) sufficient for the tested counterfactuals even when U is not uniquely recoverable. The paper itself explains this and qualifies its robustness interpretation; no universal-robustness error is assigned. Appendix A’s identifiability definition is standard. report: Scientific verification report: 0041
Position: AI Evaluation Should Learn from How We Test Humans
I25-40146 | PMLR 267 (ICML 2025) | AI-assisted review | 24 October 2026
Supported outcome: Major: a core 3PL selection formula is invalid as stated; three bounded Minor findings; empirical provenance questions remain unresolved.
# 1. Identity, reviewed version, and scope

Reviewed source: Yan Zhuang, Qi Liu, Zachary A. Pardos, Patrick C. Kyllonen, Jiyun Zu, Zhenya Huang, Shijin Wang, and Enhong Chen. PMLR 267, pp. 82483-82508 (ICML 2025). All locators below use the PDF’s printed pages 1-26, which coincide with PDF page indices counted from one. Title, author identity, page count, byte count, and SHA-256 were checked against the publisher record and controller receipt before analysis.

Original PDF: papers/0041/0041.pdf; 2,910,663 bytes; SHA-256 `c1aec1c553dd13b22fa39c33421be4de2c4f4e2e365eb5401899a84be7fe15d2`. These bytes were preserved. arXiv:2306.10512v4 (8 May 2025) was additionally checked through official HTML/history; it is not treated as byte-identical to the publisher PDF.

Inspection covered Sections 1-7, Appendix A, Appendix B equations and demonstrations, Appendix C exemplars, and the full meaningful author-linked data tree at commit `25085c8837115138294d77381541f3976e5c9475`. Mathematical checks, exact finite arithmetic, static data comparisons, and source-page visual checks were performed. No author code, LLM experiment, or model fitting was executed. The position itself does not require a new experiment; actual technical prescriptions and supplied empirical support do require faithful evaluation.
# 2. Summary and governing assumptions

The central demonstrated defect is in Section 3.2’s item-selection information formula. The paper introduces a three-parameter logistic (3PL) response model, but its main-text information expression is the two-parameter special case. An admissible two-item example reverses the selected item. Because this directly affects the proposed adaptive-selection mechanism supporting efficient evaluation, Major is supported under the task’s core-derivation standard.

The correct general formula already appears in Appendix B, Eq. (5). This preserves a sound route to the intended mechanism and is explicit counterevidence against alleging that the published experiments necessarily used the wrong expression. Three additional concerns are bounded: a continuous/ordinal response-domain mismatch, an inherited erroneous GSM8K exemplar, and an incorrect MedQA mapping in the released data.

For the analytic check, ability theta and difficulty beta are finite real numbers, discrimination alpha is positive, guessing c lies in [0,1), and the response is Bernoulli with success probability p. Item parameters are held fixed when calculating Fisher information for theta. No empirical calibration or hidden training assumption is required for this local identity.
# 3. Problem 1 - The main 3PL selection rule uses the wrong information (Major)

Source claim and dependency. Page 3, Section 2.1 and page 18, Eq. (1) define the 3PL model. Page 7, Section 3.2 then assigns each candidate item information alpha^2 p(1-p) and selects its maximizer. That is an operational selection prescription, not merely a background mention: it is the mechanism used to explain why adaptive evaluation can use fewer informative items. Section 3.2 does not restrict this prescription to c=0. Appendix Eq. (4), p. 19, explicitly uses the probabilities defined in Eq. (1).

\[\begin{aligned}s&=\sigma(\alpha(\theta-\beta)), & p&=c+(1-c)s,\\p'&=\frac{\alpha(p-c)(1-p)}{1-c},\\ I(\theta)&=\frac{(p')^2}{p(1-p)}=\frac{\alpha^2(p-c)^2(1-p)}{(1-c)^2p}.\end{aligned}\] Complete derivation. For y in {0,1}, the derivative of y log p + (1-y) log(1-p) is (y-p)p’/[p(1-p)]. Its squared expectation equals (p’)^2/[p(1-p)] because the Bernoulli variance is p(1-p). Differentiating the stated 3PL probability yields the displayed expression. The main-text simplification follows for c=0; it does not hold for general c.

Counterexample. Take two distinct candidate items with theta=0, alpha_A=alpha_B=1, beta_A=beta_B=log(2), c_A=1/4, and c_B=1/10. Thus s_A=s_B=1/3. Both discriminations are strictly positive, both guessing probabilities are strictly between zero and one, all parameters are finite, and the paper permits item-specific guessing parameters. All operative conditions are satisfied.
Quantity | Item A | Item B
Success probability p | 1/2 | 2/5
Derivative p’ | 1/6 | 1/5
Main-text information | 1/4 = 0.25 | 6/25 = 0.24
Correct Fisher information | 1/9 = 0.111111... | 1/6 = 0.166666...

The main prescription selects A; the correct maximum-information rule selects B. A supplies only two-thirds of B’s Fisher information in this example. This is an analytic identity failure with an exact finite witness, independently replayed using rational arithmetic. It does not purport to prove a particular change in aggregate benchmark rankings.

Alternative reading and repair. Interpreting Section 3.2 as an unstated 2PL illustration makes its formula correct, but that restriction is absent and excludes the nonzero guessing factors emphasized elsewhere. Appendix B, p. 20, Eq. (5) already states the correct general expression. Replacing the main expression with Eq. (5), or explicitly restricting that passage to c=0, repairs exactly this selection identity. The corrected identity has been analytically checked; experiment-level implementation and results have not been repaired or reproduced. Ease of this correction does not remove the demonstrated damage to the core prescription. Evidence: E1, E2, E3.
# 4. Problem 2 - Raw continuous scores are assigned an ordinal likelihood (Minor)

Source claim. Page 3 describes the graded response model (GRM) as accommodating continuous BLEU scores. Page 18, Appendix B, calls y continuous on [0,M], but sets P(Y=m) equal to P(Y>=m)-P(Y>=m+1). For an arbitrary response variable the difference is P(m<=Y<m+1), not its point probability. In a nondegenerate continuous model, a point has zero probability while such an interval can have positive probability.

Counterevidence and scope. The term polytomous and the finite ordered threshold vector strongly indicate that an ordinal model was intended. For already-discrete categories the stated identity is correct. No discretization step is stated in the inspected text. The supported defect is therefore the claimed direct use on raw continuous scores; no effect on the binary examples or Problem 1 is established.

Scoped correction. Map the raw score explicitly into ordered categories 0,...,M. Define S_0(theta)=1, S_(M+1)(theta)=0, and p_m(theta)=S_m(theta)-S_(m+1)(theta), with positive discrimination and ordered thresholds. The category masses are nonnegative and telescope to one. This repairs the categorical model, without claiming to preserve all information in the original continuous score. Evidence: E1, E2.
# 5. Problem 3 - A known erroneous GSM8K item is used as a clean exemplar (Minor)

Source claim. Appendix C, p. 24, interprets GSM8K ID7876 as a high-difficulty/low-guessing item whose properties arise from complex multistep calculation. The item specifies a 900-watt air conditioner and a reduction in runtime BY five hours per day for 30 days, but prints 81 as the answer.

\[E_{\rm saved}=0.9\,{\rm kW}\times5\,{\rm h/day}\times30\,{\rm day}=135\,{\rm kWh}.\qquad81=0.9(8-5)30.\] The printed value is the remaining energy use under the stated wording; it would be energy saved if runtime were reduced TO five hours. The source also confuses power and energy units. Hence this item is not clean evidence that low guessing/high estimated difficulty is caused by calculation complexity. The fitted parameter values under a corrected scoring key are unknown.

Historical attribution. The same text and wrong key occur in upstream GSM8K test item 404 (zero-based index 403). Kermittt publicly reported the issue in openai/grade-school-math issue #20 on 4 December 2023; the fetched source still retains it. This is a known-issue reproduction and a current local interpretation defect, not a newly discovered original error by these authors.

Correction of the arithmetic to 135 kWh is verified. Interpreting corrected item parameters would require rescoring and refitting. Alternatively changing BY to TO repairs the answer only by changing the task. Neither empirical repair was performed. Evidence: E1, E2, E4.
# 6. Problem 4 - Released MedQA item mapping contains GSM8K questions (Minor)

Source claim and complete static check. Appendix C and the repository README offer intermediate item features. At the pinned commit, both GSM8K_irt_feature.json and MedQA_irt_feature.json contain 1,000 records. An independent comparison found all 1,000 question texts, IDs, and answers identical across the corresponding records; all 1,000 triples of alpha/beta/c differ. The MedQA file therefore pairs medical-labeled features with GSM8K question/answer metadata. For example, id8131 asks about cooking times for rice, beans, and pork in both files.

This invalidates the released mapping as a means to verify the MedQA item-specific analysis. Different numerical parameter triples remain consistent with an accidental metadata-copying error after otherwise valid fitting. The release alone does not establish which data generated the published figures. No demonstrated link supports upgrading this release defect to core empirical damage.

No mapping repair is claimed. A defensible repair requires original MedQA identifiers/text, a checked match to parameter rows, and provenance for the response matrix used in fitting. Evidence: E5, including the complete pinned tree, comparison script, and results.
# 7. Coverage, surviving conclusions, and unresolved evidence

The broad proposal to use psychometric and adaptive assessment remains viable; the correct Fisher formulation is already available internally. Normative recommendations concerning interpretability, efficient item selection, and richer evaluation are not rejected for lacking new experiments. The appendix supplies actual technical claims, which were assessed on their own terms.

Appendix A.3 manipulates contamination by placing items/answers or hints in the test context. This is evidence about a controlled prompt-exposure setup, not direct verification of training-data contamination detection. Released guessing-factor summaries have higher means for label 1 than label 0 in all three files, consistent with the reported direction. The file named output_imdb.txt is described as MATH in the README; the filename without item IDs does not prove a different dataset was used. Its dataset identity remains Needs Evidence.

Appendix B, p. 20, cites Figure 10(a/b) for error and rank curves, but Figure 10 on p. 19 is a schematic. The 20% and 60% efficiency statements therefore lack the claimed plotted evidence at that locator. Released ranking consistency summaries exist, but raw responses, seeds, fitting/selection scripts, and a complete experimental lineage are absent from the inspected release. These are explicit unresolved evidentiary limits, not proof that the numerical statements are false.

Figure 11 (p. 22) was visually inspected by the independent checker, and the released similarity matrices were checked statically: their qualitative increase in overlap is consistent. The ability interval/binary-search analogy was retained as a heuristic, not recast as a deterministic confidence guarantee. Conventional regularity and calibration assumptions are needed for the asymptotic MLE discussion; no separate counterexample to a fully specified theorem is asserted.

Official arXiv history lists v4 (8 May 2025) as latest at inspection; its HTML retains the main-versus-appendix formula inconsistency. The inspected author repository has one commit and no returned issues or tags. This bounded check found no correction of Problem 1; it is not a claim of an exhaustive errata search. OpenReview website access encountered a verification challenge, and the public API request returned HTTP 403.
# 8. Conclusion and repair/adoption status

report: Scientific verification report: 0042
Position: Uncertainty Quantification Needs Reassessment for Large Language Model Agents
I25-40147 | PMLR 267 (ICML 2025) | AI-assisted review | 24 October 2026
Supported outcome: Major: two invalid inferences in the central theoretical case; one bounded formula defect. The interactive-agent research agenda and inspected empirical motivation remain viable.
# 1. Identity, version and review scope

Michael Kirchhof, Gjergji Kasneci and Enkelejda Kasneci. PMLR 267:81665-81677 (ICML 2025). Reviewed the exact 13-page publisher-linked PDF preserved as papers/0042/0042.pdf. SHA-256: 93b27b8eb594c61bfc9cae22b766bd124806e7b926bb0e54135d1774d2db8450; 1,572,972 bytes. This matches the controller acquisition receipt. Page references below mean printed pages 1-13, equal to one-based PDF pages.

The official arXiv record inspected lists 2505.22655v1, submitted 28 May 2025, with no later version listed. Publisher materials expose the paper and OpenReview link; no separate supplement, appendix or author repository was found in the inspected paper, publisher page and arXiv HTML. The publisher PDF controls this review; the preprint is version context, not a silently substituted source. OpenReview discussion was not obtained.

Checked the main argument, Eqs. (1)-(2), Figures 2-4 and their cited technical premises, uncertainty/context distinctions, proposed agent research directions, alternative views and selected empirical claims. References were checked selectively, not exhaustively. This is an AI supporting audit; the scientific decision and human review remain pending. No new experiment is required merely because the paper makes a normative recommendation.
# 2. Definitions and supported findings

Here Q is a second-order probability distribution over a Bernoulli parameter theta in [0,1]. EU denotes epistemic uncertainty as a functional of Q. AU denotes aleatoric uncertainty under the particular definition being discussed. H is Shannon entropy, measured in bits in the independent examples. A distinction between exact probability identities, semantic interpretation, estimator performance and learnability is essential.
Item | Judgment | Demonstrated consequence
F1: Wimmer axioms, p3 §2.1 | Major | The claimed near-zero endpoint-mixture result does not follow; the cited A2/A3 instead imply a maximum under their weak reading.
F2: misspecification, p4 §2.2 | Major | A consistency requirement targeting the true parameter is transferred outside its applicable model class, invalidating the claimed corollary.
F3: task mixture, p6 Eq. (2) | Minor | The formula needs context conditioning or an explicit conditional-independence assumption.
D1: exact decomposition, p5 §2.3 | Scope clarification | Correlation and nonadditive interval width do not disprove an entropy identity; practical disentanglement concerns survive.

Major judgments follow the dependency of the failed steps on the paper’s principal theoretical examples. They do not require disproving every recommendation or showing degraded experimental scores. The Eq. (2) defect is bounded because no algorithm or quantitative guarantee is shown to depend on its omitted condition.
# 3. Problem 1: the Wimmer axioms do not imply near-zero EU

Source claim and location. Section 2.1 and Figure 2, p3, use the equally weighted mixture of Bernoulli parameters zero and one as the first central contrast: disagreement/MI is maximal, while the cited Wimmer axiomatic view is asserted to yield approximately zero EU. The proposed explanation is that only two models remain possible. The questionable step is treating this intuition as a consequence of the cited axioms.

Primary-source check. Wimmer et al., UAI 2023, printed p2285 (PDF p4), A2 makes the uniform distribution on the simplex a global EU maximum. A3 requires a mean-preserving spread not to decrease EU, with a strict alternative also stated. Footnote 3 defines the spread through conditional mean-zero noise. A1 applies to a single Dirac measure; an endpoint mixture is not a single Dirac measure.

\[U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\quad B\mid U=u\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(u),\quad Q_B=\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1.\qquad \mathbb E[B-U\mid U=u]=0.\] Complete assumption check. Both distributions are valid distributions over the binary probability simplex, represented by the scalar Bernoulli parameter. Integrating P(B=1|U=u)=u gives P(B=1)=1/2. Both means are 1/2. Setting Z=B-U supplies exactly the conditional mean-zero noise required by the source definition, so Q_B is a mean-preserving spread of Q_U, with no approximation or limit involved.

\[\mathrm{EU}(Q_B)\geq\mathrm{EU}(Q_U)\geq\mathrm{EU}(Q_B),\qquad \mathrm{EU}(Q_B)=\mathrm{EU}(Q_U)=\max_Q\mathrm{EU}(Q).\] Under the strict A3 reading, this nontrivial spread instead exposes incompatibility with A2 on the same pair. Neither reading gives the nontrivial near-zero value asserted in the reviewed paper. This argument does not claim to construct a functional satisfying an inconsistent full axiom set, and does not use inconsistency to infer arbitrary conclusions.

Independent finite/numerical checks confirm MI(Q_B)=1 bit and MI(Q_U)=1-1/(2 ln 2), approximately 0.27865248 bits; variances of the parameter distributions are 1/4 and 1/12. These checks illustrate the example; the conditional coupling above is the decisive proof.

Alternative reading and counterevidence. Wimmer’s p2286 discussion does support the intuition that knowing the parameter is an endpoint can convey more knowledge than a uniform distribution does. The philosophical tension about knowledge and disagreement is real. It does not establish the reviewed paper’s stronger zero-versus-maximum claim as an axiomatic necessity.

Impact and correction scope. This invalidates the first central technical demonstration used to motivate reassessment, warranting Major. It leaves open independent conceptual disagreements and all empirical questions about useful uncertainty for agents. A defensible revision must remove the purported axiomatic near-zero implication or provide an explicitly specified measure with verified assumptions. No replacement axiom system is claimed to have been repaired or validated. Evidence: independent_math_memo.json, independent_math_checks.py/results.json, and the archived Wimmer PDF and p2285 image.
# 4. Problem 2: a true-parameter consistency requirement is misapplied to model bias

Source claim and location. Section 2.2, p4, contrasts a restricted model class with a richer data-generating mechanism. It then invokes Bengs et al.’s infinite-sample requirement as a corollary forcing remaining model bias out of EU and into AU. Figure 3 and the theoretical framing make this an evidentiary step in the second principal example, not just an unrelated terminology aside.

Actual cited requirement. Bengs et al., NeurIPS 2022, p8, Section 4, Definition 1(A2), considers iid categorical observations with true probability parameter theta*. It requires the learned second-order distribution Q_N to converge in probability to the Dirac measure at theta*. The original simplex contains the true parameter. This is a consistency requirement used to assess second-order loss functions, not a universal theorem that reclassifies arbitrary model misspecification.

\[Y_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.8),\quad \Theta_{\mathcal H}=\{0.5\}\ \Longrightarrow\ Q_N=\delta_{0.5}\ \forall N.\qquad \int\theta\,dQ_N=0.5\ne0.8=\int\theta\,d\delta_{0.8}.\] This is an applicability check, not a counterexample purporting to satisfy Bengs A2. The fixed test-function gap proves the restricted sequence cannot converge to the required true-parameter target. Moving the target to the best approximation would define a different requirement and must be stated. Failure to express the truth does not itself imply that residual model bias must be labeled AU.

Counterevidence and faithful terminology. Hullermeier and Waegeman do call the risk minimizer within a hypothesis class a Bayes predictor; that phrase alone is not an error. Their discussion distinguishes it from the pointwise Bayes predictor, groups model and approximation uncertainty with EU, and assumes correct specification when setting model uncertainty aside. Schweighofer et al., arXiv:2410.10786v1, pp2-3, genuinely offer an alternative selected-model entropy definition of AU. The reviewed quotation is accurate. That source also retains a selected-versus-true KL term, and its setup states representability of the true predictive distribution.

Impact. Legitimate differences between uncertainty conventions therefore survive. What fails is the specific argument that the cited consistency axiom forces misspecification bias to be AU. The inference is central to the paper’s second theoretical example and thus supports Major under the task’s core-derivation standard. This judgment does not assert that all of Section 2.2, Table 1, or the proposed agent agenda is false.

Scoped correction. State the true-parameter target and its expressibility requirement; remove the forced-AU corollary when truth is excluded. Separately name true-distribution entropy, selected-model entropy, estimation uncertainty and model discrepancy. This is a supported correction of the inference, not a verified replacement theory of all uncertainty categories. Evidence and exact historical versions are recorded in source_audit_memo.json and its two acquisition manifests.
# 5. Problem 3: Eq. (2) omits a context condition

Source claim and location. Section 3.1, p6, Eq. (2), expresses output prediction as a mixture over a finite or continuous task variable t, but its within-task factor is P(y|t) while task weights depend on input context x.

\[P(y\mid x)=\int P(y\mid t,x)P(t\mid x)\,dt.\qquad P(y\mid t,x)=P(y\mid t)\ \text{requires}\ Y\perp X\mid T.\] Admissible counterexample. Use the explicitly permitted finite task space with one task T=t0. Let X be equiprobable on two distinct literal contexts 0 and 1, and let the literal output Y equal X deterministically. These are valid normalized probabilities; no task uncertainty is needed. At X=1 the true left-hand side P(Y=1|X=1)=1. The printed mixture has one unit-weight term P(Y=1|T=t0)=1/2. The corrected factor P(Y=1|T=t0,X=1)=1 restores equality.

A charitable interpretation is that context is suppressed in notation or that the task variable includes every relevant context feature. Neither condition is stated in the displayed formula. The surrounding text already recognizes that context can determine the output. Because no algorithm, experiment or quantitative guarantee is shown to rely on the omission, the supported impact is Minor, a local formalization defect. The conditional-probability repair is analytically verified; adoption is pending.
# 6. Scope clarifications and evidence that survives

Section 2.3, p5. Eq. (1) is an exact entropy identity. High correlation of component values across inputs cannot invalidate the identity. Conversely, an exact identity does not establish identifiable or operationally useful AU/EU semantics. The most faithful reading of the surrounding discussion is concern about meaningful disentanglement by practical estimators. A universal impossibility claim should be narrowed accordingly.

\[\mathrm{AU}=q,\quad \mathrm{EU}=h(q/2)-q,\quad\mathrm{TU}=h(q/2),\quad 0<q<0.4;\qquad \mathrm{EU}'(q)=\tfrac12\log_2\!\frac{2-q}{q}-1>0.\] The reviewer calculation independently sums the joint distribution for mutual information. At q=0.1,0.2,0.3, the maximum entropy-identity residual is 1.94e-16. This example establishes the logical distinction; it is not an empirical rebuttal of Mucsanyi et al. Their NeurIPS 2024 study explicitly allows some true-component correlation and reports a dataset-specific gap between it and correlations in assessed estimators. Its empirical concern remains relevant.

Gruber et al.’s cited 2023 v1 distinguishes nonadditive prediction-interval width (p4 Eq. (4)) from exact additive mean-square-error contributions (pp4-5 Eq. (5)). The distinction already exists in that historical version. Nonadditivity on one scale is not evidence of impossibility on every scale. No separate Major is assigned to this scope clarification.

Section 2.4, p6, concerns changing contexts and decisions about clarification. The text acknowledges that input points can change within a fixed string space. This is not a demonstrated contradiction of conditional probability. Sections 3-4 propose research directions and retain roles for numerical uncertainty, active learning and existing categories; no blanket claim that all conventional uncertainty methods are useless is attributed to the paper.

Empirical citation checks. CLAMBER (ACL 2024), Table 3, gives 57.38% ambiguity-detection accuracy for ChatGPT under the specified zero-shot chain-of-thought setting; Table 7 gives 53.29% helpfulness for a different few-shot chain-of-thought setting. The approximate 57% and 53% motivation is supported, with distinct prompting conditions. AmbigQA (EMNLP 2020), Table 2, reports 44% single-answer questions among 2,004 test questions, hence 56% with multiple answers. These are benchmark- and setting-specific results, not estimates for every current LLM or every real-world query.

The paper’s bibliometric illustration was inspected as motivation, but its arXiv query/count pipeline was not rerun. No missing experiment or code is itself treated as an error in the normative recommendations.

report: Scientific verification report: 0043
Position: AI Should Not Be An Imitation Game: Centaur Evaluations
I25-40148 | PMLR 267 (ICML 2025) | AI-assisted review | 24 October 2026

Supported outcome: Major: the proposed randomized encouragement does not identify the full human-pool production function or its derivative as claimed. One empirical comparator attribution is Minor. The case for evaluating human-AI collaboration survives.
# 1. Identity, exact version and scope

Andreas Haupt and Erik Brynjolfsson. PMLR 267:81526-81541 (ICML 2025). Reviewed the exact publisher-linked 16-page PDF preserved as papers/0043/0043.pdf, 271,419 bytes, SHA-256 35131cdbb4a65756a15c2173891de71ecde2bcb34c5fee0ea9c80562ab15c356. The hash matches the controller receipt. All target-paper page references mean printed pages 1-16, equal to one-based PDF pages.

Read the main paper, Sections 1-7, the economic formalization, proposed causal design, alternatives and Appendix A’s proposed benchmarks on pp15-16. Primary-source checks targeted the coding productivity comparison, call-center example, meta-analysis baselines and instrumental-variable interpretation. No exhaustive historical or reference audit was attempted.

The Stanford author publication page links a 15-page copy at a /2025/12/ path. The /2025/06/ copy is byte-identical to it: SHA-256 c5550796223dc351462919a61f1cba778650da232310c116e2fa93df441b7340. Both differ from the publisher PDF but retain the two passages discussed below. Dated upload paths do not establish a formal revision date; no arXiv version record or formal erratum was found in the bounded search. The publisher PDF remains the reviewed version.

Publisher materials and author pages supplied no applicable author code or separate supplement. Appendix A is part of the original PDF. The inspected project page describes further evaluations as being prepared. Absence of such new experiments is not treated as an error in a position paper. Human scientific review, final decision and author adoption remain pending.
# 2. What was checked and what follows

The paper’s proposed benchmark specifies a human selection rule, an interface and scoring, with optional transcripts. Its production-function notation fixes a model i, compute K and human time L, and uses output Y to motivate the marginal contribution of human time. The substantive issue concerns the inference from the suggested randomized incentives to this population-level resource response, not whether collaborative evaluation is useful.
Item | Outcome | Scope
F1: §5.2 p6 causal estimation | Major | Two admissible populations give identical trial data but different production derivatives and comparison rankings.
F2: §2.2 p2 Peng comparator | Minor | The cited trial compares assisted and unassisted humans, without an AI-alone experimental arm.

Economic Eq. (1), Definition 4.1 | Scope clarification / no issue within inspected scope | The stated monetary-proxy and interior competitive-market thought experiment is coherent; it is not a universal wage forecast.
§6.1 meta-analysis language | Scope clarification | Synergy, human-only-baseline augmentation and marginal human contribution are different estimands.
# 3. Problem 1: randomized incentives do not identify the claimed whole-pool derivative

Source claim and exact location. Section 5.2, p6, proposes random treatments that alter compute use or encourage shorter human work, including early-finish bonuses, and then states that the design allows an unbiased estimate of f_i(K,L) or its human-time derivative. Sections 4.3.1-4.3.2, p5, use that derivative to define human augmentation, compare systems and motivate policy-relevant quantities.

Target and assumptions. Fix the model, interface and K. Let U denote a worker drawn from the declared human pool. The economically relevant population response to setting work time to l is f(l)=E_U[Y_U(l)], keeping that pool fixed. A descriptive regression E[Y|L=l] is a different object when realized time depends on worker type. Random assignment of a bonus Z does not make every realized L a randomized intervention.

Counterexample. The pool contains types C and N in equal proportions. Assign Z in {0,1} independently of U, with equal probabilities. Type C responds to the bonus by reducing time from 2 to 1; type N always uses time 2. Work time l ranges over [1,2]. Consider two possible worlds:
Observed event (Z,L,Y) | Probability in A | Probability in B

Every operative design feature is satisfied. The human pool is prespecified and can be heterogeneous under Section 2.1. Assignment is genuinely randomized. All output response functions are smooth, nondecreasing and concave on the relevant interval. Exclusion holds: conditional on U and l, Z has no direct effect on Y. Time responses are monotone. The first stage is nonzero. No direct bonus effect, selection into treatment or noisy finite-sample accident is needed.

\[\Delta\mathbb E[L]=\Delta\mathbb E[Y]=-\tfrac12,\quad \frac{\Delta\mathbb E[Y]}{\Delta\mathbb E[L]}=1;\qquad f_A(l)=l,\ f_A'(l)=1,\quad f_B(l)=\tfrac12l+1,\ f_B'(l)=\tfrac12.\] Both worlds therefore generate exactly the same observable joint distribution for every sample size, but the target derivatives differ. Any statistic computed from those data has the same expectation in both worlds, so it cannot be unbiased for both targets. This is a nonidentification result, stronger than a complaint about sample size or a particular regression implementation.

The error can change an actual comparison: a reference system with f_R(l)=3l/4 has derivative 3/4. The unobservably different worlds rank above and below that reference respectively. More generally, with a smaller positive fraction of responsive workers, the population derivative in World B can be arbitrarily smaller than the identified responsive-worker slope. The displayed equal-proportion construction alone is sufficient for the finding.

Alternative interpretation and counterevidence. Section 5.2 says that causal methods may be used and cites instrumental-variable work. That is a legitimate recommendation. Angrist, Imbens and Rubin’s 1996 abstract explicitly describes identification of the effect for compliers under its restrictions, rather than an unrestricted population response. Here the population Wald ratio correctly captures the slope for C. It does not reveal N’s unobserved response at time 1. The cited methods are not invalid, and randomized time-budget designs can answer useful questions.

Impact and severity. The unsupported step is upgrading a randomized encouragement result to an unbiased estimate of the whole-pool production function or derivative without identifying restrictions. The derivative is a central quantitative output proposed by this paper, so the invalid inference supports Major even though the normative case for more centaur evaluations remains intact. The proof does not assert that any published productivity experiment used the proposed design incorrectly.

Defensible correction. Name the assigned-policy effect or a precisely defined local responder effect, and state its identifying assumptions. If the desired target is instead a fixed-pool response to a controlled resource budget, randomize that budget with common population, interface and other resource settings, and report the resulting budget estimand. A two-budget mean contrast estimates a finite difference, not automatically an exact point derivative. Derivative identification requires suitable support and regularity or a justified response model. Even an identified IV ratio is not generally an unbiased finite-sample estimator. No complete new estimator or empirical repair is claimed.

Evidence: causal_identification_check.py and causal_identification_check.json, causal_evaluation_memo.json, independent_economic_memo.json, and the target source p6 image. The independent check uses rational arithmetic and requires no author program or human-subject experiment.
# 4. Problem 2: the cited coding experiment has no AI-alone comparator

Source claim and location. Section 2.2, p2, attributes the HTTP-server speed comparison in Peng et al. (2023) to a centaur outperforming both a machine-learning model and a human alone. The machine-only comparison is not part of that experiment.

Primary evidence. Peng, Kalliamvakou, Cihon and Demirer, arXiv:2302.06590v1, 13 February 2023, pp2-5, describe 95 recruited developers randomly assigned to Copilot access or no Copilot access (45 and 50 assignments). The task is implementing an HTTP server in JavaScript. The reported speed comparison is between those two human-participant groups; there is no AI-alone arm.

Alternative reading. The main sentence could be read loosely as describing an assisted system and an unassisted person. Its explicit machine-only comparator, however, adds a baseline the citation does not measure. The genuine assisted-human productivity result remains evidence that centaur evaluations are feasible and useful.

Impact and repair. Minor: this is a bounded attribution error in an illustrative example, without a demonstrated failure of the central normative position or the other cited empirical work. Restrict the statement to assisted versus unassisted developers. A claim of superiority to AI alone would require an appropriate additional comparison; that experiment was not performed in this audit. The same wording persists in the inspected Stanford author copy.
# 5. Clarifications and preserved counterevidence

Economic first-order condition, p5. With K fixed and output already expressed in monetary units as the paper assumes, let profit be pi(L)=f_i(K,L)-wL. At a differentiable interior optimum, pi’(L)=0 yields f_{i,L}=w. The standard thought experiment is valid under those conditions. At L=0 only the one-sided inequality f_{i,L}<=w need hold. No general-equilibrium wage forecast follows from a benchmark gradient alone; this is an applicability clarification, not an additional Major.

Definition 4.1 deliberately defines augmentation by marginal human-time contribution. It does not prove that every combined system beats every human-only or AI-only system. Resource units, population and operating range must be fixed when comparing gradients. The 15-versus-30-minute illustration is explicitly a finite-difference approximation; dividing by the time interval gives an average slope under a controlled design. It is not treated as a false exact derivative identity.

Vaccaro, Almaatouq and Malone (2024), published pp2294-2295, distinguish two baselines. Against the better of a human or AI alone, pooled synergy is g=-0.23 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.07). Against humans alone, pooled augmentation is g=0.64 (0.53 to 0.74). Neither is the paper’s marginal-time derivative. Section 6.1 presents a skeptical argument and then emphasizes task dependence; clarify those baselines rather than infer that the paper disproved or entirely misreported the meta-analysis. No raw meta-analysis was rerun.

The call-center example is supported by the inspected primary institutional publication summary of Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond’s Generative AI at Work: assistance improved productivity on average in that setting. It does not itself establish superiority to a fully autonomous call-center system or the labor-market consequences of universal deployment.

Sections 2-4 propose collaboration-specific evaluation affordances and an economic motivation. Sections 5-6 explicitly discuss costs, variability, human selection, interfaces, synthetic calibration and systems that can underperform standalone agents. Appendix A supplies proposed human/interface/scoring configurations, not new experimental results. These qualifications survive the findings. Long-run claims about technology, bargaining power and universal automation remain a motivating position, not empirically established guarantees from this paper.
Figure 2’s caption contains a model-label inconsistency with the plot/prose. It is a presentation-only issue and is excluded from substantive findings under this task’s instructions.
