Position: Lifetime tuning is incompatible with continual reinforcement learning

Claim-focused scientific verification | B001 | [internal task]-r002
Major: the advertised SAC tuning-duration inference is not identified by the reported default-versus-short-tuned comparison.
# 1. Identity, reviewed version, and decision status

Authors: Golnaz Mesbahi, Parham Mohammad Panahi, Olya Mastikhina, Steven Tang, Martha White, and Adam White. Primary version: ICML 2025 position paper, PMLR 267, proceedings pages 81786-81796. The supplied publisher PDF has 11 pages, 1,771,961 bytes, and SHA-256 2e8b767ba54830d8176f923c58611f3b0fd1a452314e98ad3068bda3af0125de. Its title, author list, embedded venue metadata, size, and hash were checked against the publisher page and controller acquisition receipt. [E1-E2]

All page references below use the PDF’s printed, one-based pages 1-11, which agree with physical PDF pages; they are not the PMLR proceedings page numbers. The complete supplied PDF was read: substantive text on pp. 1-9 and references on pp. 10-11. Figures 1-7 and Tables 1-4 were checked in context; decisive figures and tables were also inspected visually.

Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]. This is an AI-assisted verification report, not a human approval or an author-adopted correction. The proposed issue judgment remains pending scientific/controller acceptance. The previous attempt and papers 0046/0047 were not modified.
# 2. Executive assessment

The paper’s methodological position is that continual-RL evaluation should test performance beyond the horizon used to select hyperparameters. It supports this position with Catch, Cartpole, a SAC quadruped task, and Jelly Bean World. The defect established here concerns the advertised SAC extension: p. 2 presents SAC as testing the effects of both limited and lifetime tuning, but the reported SAC comparison uses literature defaults as the reference, while the short-horizon search cannot even select those defaults. [E1, pp. 2, 6-7]

Changing only selection duration within the published SAC candidate set cannot reproduce the reference configuration. Consequently the SAC performance gap mixes selection horizon with candidate-space and default-origin differences. This is a demonstrated inferential defect in an explicitly advertised extension of the paper’s main empirical evidence; Major is assigned to that claim. No deterioration of the published scores, execution bug, or failure of the entire paper is alleged.

The actual Figure 6 default baseline and mitigation comparisons remain valid descriptive results within their stated scope. Separate DQN and Jelly Bean World evidence is not invalidated by the SAC comparison problem. Rejected and unresolved concerns are retained without being converted into additional defects.
# 3. Definitions, operative assumptions, and scope

Lifetime tuning selects hyperparameters using performance over the full experimental horizon n. Limited tuning selects them using an initial horizon j and evaluates the selected configuration over n. For a numerical percentage k, the intended budget is j = floor((k/100)n). Section 5 prints floor(kn) while declaring k in [0,100], but Section 8 correctly gives 150,000 and 300,000 steps for 10% and 20% of 1.5 million. The isolated normalization inconsistency is recorded, not counted as a substantive finding. [E1, pp. 5, 7]

A tuning-duration effect means changing the selection horizon while holding the candidate family and other relevant selection/evaluation conditions fixed. This is the controlled interpretation needed to attribute a performance difference to duration. The review does not invent an explicit same-grid promise in Section 7: the actual, transparently described default comparison does not establish the broader duration attribution advertised on p. 2.

Let H denote candidate configurations, J-hat_t(h) the selection score of h over t steps, and J_n(h) its independent full-horizon evaluation score. The relevant selections are h_short in argmax over H of J-hat_j(h) and h_life in argmax over H of J-hat_n(h). The paper instead reports a comparison involving h_default, an externally supplied configuration. This notation formalizes the comparison; it is not a theorem attributed to the authors.

The review comprises document analysis, visual inspection, an exact finite parameter-membership check, and a targeted later-version comparison. No author code was run, no agent was trained, and no empirical result was reproduced. No dedicated public experiment-code release or raw result bundle was identified through the publisher page, PDF, arXiv record, or inspected author publication entry. OpenReview access failures limit supplement and revision-thread coverage. [E2-E7]
# 4. Problem 1: the SAC comparison does not identify the advertised tuning-duration effect

Source claim and location. In the upper-right paragraph of p. 2, immediately before Section 2, the paper describes the SAC study as an extension to another algorithm and continuous actions that tests the impact of k-percent and lifetime tuning, with similar outcomes. Section 7, p. 6, actually specifies comparison to previously reported default values; Figure 6 on p. 7 labels the reference curve Default. Table 3 defines the short-horizon search and Table 4 gives the configurations. [E1]

Suspect step. The default-versus-short-tuned contrast is used as evidence about the effect of restricting tuning duration. The reference configuration is not a full-horizon selection over the reported short-horizon candidate family. This is not an unknown code-provenance inference: the mismatch follows directly from the reported tables.

Complete finite check. Table 3 contains seven learning rates, five batch sizes, three replay-buffer sizes, two beta2 values, and two Adam epsilon values. Its Cartesian product has 7 x 5 x 3 x 2 x 2 = 420 configurations, if all combinations are used. The conclusion requires only coordinate membership and does not assume all 420 were executed. Exact rational arithmetic confirms the following. [E4]

P0.18P0.32P0.19P0.19 Coordinate & Table 3 candidate values & Table 4 default & Default admissible?
Learning rate & 0.02, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001, 0.00001, 0.000001, 0.0000001 & 0.0003 & No
Batch size & 16, 32, 128, 256, 512 & 256 & Yes
Replay buffer & 512, 1,000, 10,000 & 1,000,000 & No
Adam beta2 & 0.9, 0.999 & 0.999 & Yes
Adam epsilon & 0.00000001, 0.1 & 0.00000001 & Yes

The one-percent-selected configuration is learning rate 0.001, batch size 512, buffer size 10,000, beta2 0.9, and epsilon 0.00000001; every coordinate belongs to the stated search. The default learning rate 0.0003 is absent and its buffer is 100 times the largest available buffer. Thus h_default is not in H, whereas h_short is in H. No increase of tuning duration within H can select h_default. These assertions use printed values, not assumptions about hidden code.

The desired contrast is Delta_duration = J_n(h_life) - J_n(h_short). The reported contrast is Delta_reported = J_n(h_default) - J_n(h_short). Subtraction gives Delta_reported - Delta_duration = J_n(h_default) - J_n(h_life). The reported SAC experiment does not determine this last term. The identity establishes the attribution gap without inventing learning curves or claiming that the observed direction must reverse. [E4]

Alternative reading and counterevidence. Section 7 is explicit about defaults, and Figure 6 labels the curve correctly. As a comparison of transferred defaults against limited-tuning configurations and mitigations, the experiment is legitimate. Historical defaults could themselves have been chosen using long experiments; that does not make them the full-horizon optimum of the same candidate family on the switching quadruped task. If p. 2 is interpreted only as an imprecise roadmap, the appropriate action is to narrow that claim to the default-transfer comparison. The report does not label the Figure 6 legend or descriptive comparison erroneous.

Impact and judgment. The affected dependency is: advertised SAC corroboration across algorithm/action domains -> interpretation of the default gap as an effect of limiting tuning -> claimed empirical support beyond DQN. The second step is unsupported by the actual design, so that specific central extension fails. Major applies to this invalid empirical attribution. A position-paper label, surviving DQN results, or easy textual narrowing does not restore the missing comparison.

Precisely supported repair. Textual narrowing can describe Figure 6 as comparison to published defaults plus mitigation performance under one-percent tuning; this restores fidelity to the experiment but relinquishes the SAC duration-effect demonstration. Restoring that demonstration requires short- and full-horizon selection over a common predeclared candidate family, a consistent selection protocol, and fresh evaluation trials. Including the default would allow its role to be tested. This experiment was not performed here, and no outcome is predicted.

Repair status. The logical adequacy of the narrowing is checked; no manuscript was edited, no adoption was requested, and no empirical repair is verified. An unreported matched experiment could change the assessment, but the review neither assumes it exists nor claims it was never performed.
# 5. Checked evidence that survives; rejected and unresolved candidates

Catch and DQN. Figures 1-3 distinguish default parameters in a changed environment, tuning both algorithms for 500,000 steps, and extending the selected configurations to 10 million steps. The visual trajectories agree with the descriptive account of a later DQN collapse and sustained W0-DQN performance. The SAC defect does not invalidate these separate comparisons. No seed-level reproduction was done. [E1, pp. 3-4]

Cartpole and mitigations. The stationary Cartpole task tests extended learning stability, although Section 2 motivates continual RL using changing optimal behavior. This difference in scope does not falsify the observed long-horizon contrast. Figure 5 describes mixed, environment-dependent mitigation performance and includes failures; the paper does not claim all mitigations work everywhere. [E1, pp. 5-6]

Jelly Bean World. Section 8 explicitly separates five tuning trials from thirty new evaluation trials. The 10%, 20%, and full-horizon budgets are consistent. DQN has 25 learning-rate candidates; W0-DQN and PT-DQN each have 5 x 5 = 25 combinations. Equal candidate count does not prove equal wall-clock cost, but the arithmetic is correct. Figure 7 supports the stated sensitivity of relative performance to tuning window, with acknowledged late recovery differences even under lifetime tuning. [E1, pp. 7-8; E4]

Partial-observability language. Section 3’s suggestion that repeated tuning can remove the need for continual learning is stronger than a general POMDP result. However, no universal theorem is established, and the paper’s own Jelly Bean World discussion acknowledges continued relearning. The operative concern is benchmark-specific designer adaptation. This is recorded as scope clarification rather than a counterexample to an unstated universal theorem.

Unresolved empirical provenance. Earlier experiments do not document every seed-selection and bootstrap detail in the supplied text. That absence does not demonstrate leakage or false intervals. Figure 6 reports standard error over ten runs; Figures 4, 5, and 7 describe bootstrap confidence intervals. These different summaries were not treated as interchangeable. Exact score and interval recalculation remains unperformed.

Normative recommendation. Section 9 treats k-percent tuning as an illustrative alternative, acknowledges its limits as a deployment simulation, and calls for improved methods. No experiment was demanded merely to justify that normative recommendation. The substantive issue concerns empirical support the paper actually advertises.
# 6. Later versions, dependence, and conclusion table

The latest arXiv record inspected lists version 4, dated 8 August 2025. Its PDF SHA-256 is 33628f4f26e359120861419bc16fb0661956605c75618adc0586214b68f98362. A corrected whitespace-insensitive page-by-page comparison found extracted text on pp. 2-11 identical to the publisher copy. The affected claim and Tables 3-4 therefore are not textually repaired in that inspected version. This does not establish byte identity or exhaustive image equivalence. [E3, E5]

No separate erratum was identified in the inspected publisher/arXiv/author-entry sources and targeted searches. OpenReview’s verification challenge and HTTP 429 API responses prevented a complete revision/supplement check. Previous-attempt scientific findings were not supplied in this staging root and were not silently replaced or labeled corrected.

The recommendation to test beyond the tuning horizon survives, as do descriptive SAC mitigation results and the independently supported portions of DQN/Jelly Bean World comparisons. Supported damage is confined to attribution of the SAC reference gap to tuning duration.

Position: Language model developers should report train-test overlap

Claim-focused scientific verification | B001 | [internal task]-r002
Minor: a bounded released-code/specification mismatch and a local unsupported Codeforces inference; no demonstrated failure of the 9/30 census.
# 1. Identity, version, and scope

Authors: Andy K Zhang, Kevin Klyman, Yifan Mai, Yoav Levine, Yian Zhang, Rishi Bommasani, and Percy Liang. Primary source: ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82460-82482, 23-page publisher PDF. SHA-256: 68d3b5338207ce4cd1d47abf7353a7b5ff338297f541bb9058fd37c10d464e26; size: 390,118 bytes. The title, authors, page count, size, and hash were verified against the publisher page and controller receipt. The task manifest’s shortened first-author name resolves to the publisher’s Andy K Zhang. [E1]

Page references are one-based physical/printed PDF pages 1-23, not proceedings numbers. Main Sections 1-8, Tables 1-2, and Appendices A-D including Figure 1, Table 3, and Algorithm 1 were checked. Bibliography pages were used for targeted source discovery, not an exhaustive verification of every cited work. Relevant official code was inspected statically at commit 4d525c1769e8b440d9b13e6579b190940feeb186, dated 27 March 2024. [E2]

Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]. These are proposed AI-assisted judgments pending scientific/controller acceptance. No author code was executed, no model/API expenditure occurred, and no author correction or adoption was requested.
# 2. Summary of checked claims

The paper advocates reporting training/test overlap when publishing model evaluations. Its main descriptive result is a survey of thirty selected flagship models: nine receive a positive transparency score. Recounting the actual Table 1 rows gives 30 total, 9 positive, and 21 zero scores. The three outreach-linked additions are included in those nine. A score measures the paper’s minimum transparency threshold; it is not evidence that every benchmark was covered or that a model is free of overlap. [E1, pp. 4-6, 18-19; E3]

Two bounded concerns are supported. First, the released pipeline does not implement the paper’s concatenated-reference convention consistently. A complete finite example demonstrates missing or understated reference overlap. Second, the Codeforces discussion links a separate old/new-problem anecdote to the published GPT-4 result and then gives a causal interpretation not established by those data. Neither concern demonstrates that the thirty-model census or the general disclosure recommendation is false.

Short-sequence domain handling, scoring completeness, pseudocode variable names, and inaccessible anecdote sources are recorded separately with their counterevidence. They do not raise the supported severity. The review treats the normative recommendation on its own terms and does not demand an experiment merely to justify a transparency norm.
# 3. Definitions and operative assumptions

Appendix B.1 represents training data as token sequences and each test example as an input plus a set of reference sequences. It explicitly concatenates the references into one sequence. Appendix C compares its n-grams to training n-grams. Appendix D.2 fixes n = 13 and defines binary overlap, a test-side n-gram fraction called Jaccard overlap, and coverage of distinct token positions. The explicit test-side denominator is used here; terminology alone is not treated as a numerical defect. [E1, pp. 19, 21-22]

All finite examples below use distinct lowercase words, single spaces, no punctuation or leading/trailing whitespace, a valid nonempty instance ID, one test instance, and one training document. The input can be any nonempty unrelated sequence. The pinned default tokenizer preserves the displayed reference tokens. No frequency filter or duplicate-token ambiguity is needed. The computations are independent set arithmetic written for this review, not execution of the authors’ functions. [E2-E3]
# 4. Problem 1: reference boundaries differ between the specification and released implementation

Source claim and locations. Appendix B.1, p. 19, concatenates references; Appendix C, p. 21, computes reference n-gram intersections; Appendix D.2, p. 22, converts those intersections into scores. The official repository is linked directly in the caption of Table 2, p. 7. [E1]

Suspect implementation step. In the pinned compute_data_overlap_metrics.py, lines 100-108 index each reference separately. Lines 174-186 only record matches against that index, and lines 239-249 emit the recorded entries. By contrast, compute_metrics_from_ngrams.py, lines 278-294, processes emitted entries and joins references at line 292 before computing scores. Therefore the matcher omits cross-reference n-grams that the paper and downstream denominator include. [E2]

Complete case A. Let r1 be ’alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta’ and r2 be ’theta iota kappa lambda mu nu xi’. Set n = 13 and let the sole training document be their fourteen-token concatenation. Under the paper’s definition, the concatenated reference has two 13-grams, both present in training. Binary overlap is 1, n-gram fraction is 2/2 = 1, and the union of their token positions covers all fourteen tokens, giving token overlap 14/14 = 1. Each separately indexed seven-token reference has zero 13-grams. The released matching stage therefore emits no reference-overlap entry for this instance. Missing output is the demonstrated static consequence; it is not mislabeled as a numerical zero returned by a helper. [E3]

Complete case B avoids short individual references. Use the twenty-six-token sequence ’alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota kappa lambda mu nu xi omicron pi rho sigma tau upsilon phi chi psi omega aleph beth’. Split after token thirteen into two references, and use the entire sequence as the training document. The paper’s concatenation has 26 - 13 + 1 = 14 distinct 13-grams, all overlapping, so its n-gram fraction is 1. Per-reference indexing retains only two 13-grams. A reference entry now exists, but downstream scoring uses the concatenated denominator fourteen and only two recorded matches: 2/14 = 1/7. Binary and token coverage remain 1 in this case. All tokens are distinct and both references have length thirteen, so neither zero denominators nor multiplicity conventions explain this discrepancy. [E3]

Alternative reading and counterevidence. Preserving reference boundaries is a legitimate design that avoids artificial matches between separate answer choices. It is not the convention stated in B.1, and it should not be combined silently with a concatenated downstream denominator. The finding is a specification/implementation mismatch, not an assertion that concatenation is scientifically preferable.

Impact and severity. Minor is supported for the inspected release. The official link establishes relevance, but neither the paper nor the retrieved repository proves this exact commit generated Writer’s results or every overlap example. No Table 1 classification is shown to change. The missing publication-run linkage remains Needs Evidence; it is not filled by assuming current public code is the historical executable. The appendix location is not the rationale for Minor.

Scoped repair. To implement the stated concatenation convention, concatenate references before indexing with the same tokenizer used downstream. Alternatively, explicitly adopt per-reference matching and make definitions and downstream denominators consistent. These are precise alternatives with different measurement meanings. No author file was changed, neither alternative was adopted, and no historical result was recomputed.
# 5. Problem 2: the Codeforces example does not establish the claimed causal contribution

Source claim and location. The Introduction, p. 1, and Section 3, p. 3, connect the published GPT-4 Codeforces evaluation to a separate report of success on ten pre-2021 problems and failure on recent problems. Section 3 then states that overlap reporting would have made overlap’s significant contribution to the described breakthroughs clear. The issue is this inference and the linked evaluation populations, not a claim that the anecdotal counts are fabricated. [E1]

Primary-source check. The GPT-4 Technical Report’s Table 1, p. 5, reports a Codeforces rating of 392, below the fifth human percentile. Appendix A.6, p. 25, describes ten recent contests, about six problems each, with ten attempts per problem. Table 9, p. 30, already reports zero measured contamination for that evaluated set. This is a different evaluation from ten old problems. The source’s own contamination test is not treated as proof that every possible form of overlap is absent. [E4]

Complete inference check. Let A be the report’s recent-contest evaluation and B the separate historical-problem comparison. Evidence about scores on B does not establish membership of A in the training data or the causal contribution of overlap to A’s scores. Even accepting the paper’s old/new accuracy numbers, time also changes the sampled problems and potentially their difficulty and selection. The reported comparison contains no identification argument that holds these factors fixed. Furthermore, the specific assertion that missing reporting prevented understanding A is not supported when the cited report already supplies an overlap analysis.

Alternative reading. The historical-problem result can be a useful warning signal and motivation for more transparent evaluation. The original cited social-media source was inaccessible in this review, so the counts were not independently authenticated. Low human percentile also does not by itself rule out best performance among contemporary language models. Neither of those stronger accusations is made here.

Impact, repair, and judgment. Minor is supported for this bounded empirical illustration: the survey count and the protocol definition are not derived from this anecdote, and the demonstrated failure is a local population/causal attribution. A faithful narrowing would present the anecdote as a separate concern about historical problems and avoid treating it as proof that contamination caused the published result. This logical narrowing is supported; no causal effect has been estimated, no author correction has been adopted, and no new experiment was run.
# 6. Counterevidence, domain clarification, and unperformed work

Census and outreach. Table 1’s 30 rows produce 9 positive and 21 zero scores. The p. 2 phrase giving 23 remaining models is a local numerical/editorial inconsistency, not evidence that the 9/30 count is wrong. Section 7 says the nine include three from outreach, so the abstract should not be interpreted as twelve positives. Narrative GPT-NeoX versus Table 1 Pythia is a model-name inconsistency within the EleutherAI entry; no score change is established. These presentation issues do not create additional substantive findings. [E1; E3]

Partial transparency versus complete coverage. Section 5.2 asks about each reported benchmark, but also states an operational minimum of some meaningful information. Appendix A discloses coverage of 6/8 benchmarks for GPT-4, 8/14 for Qwen2, and prefiltering for 12/24 listed Apple benchmarks. The positive scores are defensible as partial-transparency scores. They must not be interpreted as certification of complete benchmark coverage. No unambiguous scoring error is claimed from the broader aspirational criterion. [E1, pp. 4, 18-19]

Short-sequence domain. The stated family of metrics maps token sequences into [0,1], but the n-gram fraction has denominator zero when a nonempty sequence contains fewer than thirteen tokens. For x = (’alpha’), its printed expression is 0/0. This is an omitted domain/convention, preserved as a clarification. Static tracing supplies crucial counterevidence to a crash allegation: no full-length n-gram is indexed for such a component, no match entry is emitted, and the ordinary downstream path therefore does not call the unguarded division on it. No end-to-end crash was demonstrated. A total mathematical definition needs a stated short-sequence convention or restricted domain. [E1-E3]

Other technical checks. The p. 22 toy example is correct: twelve tokens, ten trigrams, three matched trigrams, seven distinct covered token positions, hence 3/10 and 7/12. Algorithm 1 mixes test/train variable names, but static source inspection establishes that test-scenario n-grams are indexed and training documents query the index; an alleged training-versus-itself computation is rejected. The paper openly discusses literal-match limitations, paraphrases, training stages, and the fact that overlap is not automatically harmful. [E1-E3]

Unresolved anecdote. The exact Meng (2025) reference is https://x.com/mengk20/status/1904669936032899434 . Primary access failed. The Claude memorization allegation therefore remains source-access unresolved. A different Transluce account of an exposed flag in a broken benchmark environment is not substituted for that citation, and no finding is based on it. The Horace He source at https://twitter.com/cHHillee/status/1635790330854526981?lang=en was likewise inaccessible through primary endpoints. [E5]

Not performed. No private training data, model runs, author code, published developer outputs, or exact historical execution environment were reproduced. The complete historical documentation behind all thirty scores was not independently reconstructed. The review verified the census arithmetic and stated criteria, inspected relevant sources and code, and checked specific technical consequences.
# 7. Versions, overall dependence, and conclusion

The inspected later author-posted version is arXiv:2410.08385v2, dated 22 July 2025, with 23 pages and SHA-256 1b9456e6d817b26305e562d8854788e1615f8302c05d20b25668ad6fcb83c961. It changes the running title and some text/layout. Targeted inspection confirms that the concatenated-reference definition, 13-gram metric formulation, and Codeforces inference remain. The comparison records do not claim complete version identity. No separate correction was identified in inspected sources. OpenReview’s supplemental attachment returned HTTP 403, leaving that specific historical bundle uninspected. [E6]

The core recommendation to disclose overlap remains a coherent normative position. The 9/30 table count is reproduced. The implementation finding affects agreement between a released protocol and its specification; the anecdote finding narrows an empirical illustration. These bounded impacts support Minor, with unresolved source/run provenance retained separately.

Position: The Right to AI

Claim-focused scientific verification | B001 | [internal task]-r002
Major, narrowly: the healthcare case supplies invalid empirical support for participatory benefits. A separate Dorian outcome attribution is Minor; the normative framework is not refuted.
# 1. Identity, exact version, and review scope

Authors: Rashid Mushkani, Hugo Berard, Allison Cohen, and Shin Koseki. Primary version: ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81876-81896, 21-page publisher PDF. SHA-256: 00fd19aa0783d2c7fcd04b9d213769ef56290cf8e5dac9189d185f23875a0799; size: 485,084 bytes. Title, authors, page count, bytes, and hash were checked against the publisher entry and controller receipt. The receipt retains its original acquisition path; the actual byte-identical copy in this attempt was independently checked. [E1]

Page references to the reviewed paper use one-based physical/printed pages 1-21, not proceedings page numbers. Main Sections 1-9, the Impact Statement, Figures 1-2, Table 1, the consolidated overview, and Appendices A-F were read. The bibliography was used for targeted source discovery, not an exhaustive citation audit. Five of the nine case descriptions received targeted primary-source checks; four remain without independent source reconstruction.

Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]. Findings are proposed AI-assisted judgments pending scientific and controller acceptance. No author code was run, no model/API money was spent, and no author correction or adoption was requested.
# 2. Checked claims and outcome

The paper proposes a governance right for people affected by AI, argues that AI functions as societal infrastructure, develops a four-tier participation framework, and uses nine cases to illustrate opportunities and constraints. The main normative premises are explicit. The paper also makes concrete empirical claims about what particular participatory projects accomplished; those claims require faithful attribution even when the broader governance recommendation is normative. [E1, pp. 1-9, 18-21]

Major is supported for the healthcare inference in Section 6 and Table 1. Correcting this case changes both the attributed intervention and the evidentiary role of its alleged outcomes. The failed link is part of the stated empirical synthesis supporting participation’s ability to mitigate bias. The general right to participate and the four-tier proposal need not be false for that inference to require substantial correction.

A second, bounded concern is Table 1’s attribution of faster resource allocation to Project Dorian. Its cited case description supports a narrower result and does not establish the operational endpoint asserted. Other checked cases provide substantive counterevidence against rejecting the entire synthesis.
# 3. Operative premises and distinctions

The consolidated argument is: AI increasingly functions as infrastructure; affected people have a moral or political entitlement to help govern consequential infrastructure; therefore an AI-specific participatory governance right is warranted. The second premise is normative rather than a consequence of data production alone. Conditional on these declared premises, the inference is coherent. Disagreement about their moral force is not a mathematical counterexample. [E1, pp. 18-19]

The four tiers distinguish consumer access, private-organization leadership, government control, and citizen control through agency, transparency, and inclusivity. They are explicitly nonexhaustive, allow expert/community hybrid governance, and describe an aspirational trajectory. No universal ordering of real systems by measured performance or formal optimization objective is supplied. The p. 2 word ’optimal’ is read in this qualified normative context, not upgraded into a proved effectiveness theorem. [E1, pp. 2, 5-6, 9]

For the case audit, identifying risks, consulting experts, including affected people in design, transferring decision authority, and demonstrating improved outcomes are distinct propositions. An assessment can motivate an intervention without showing that the intervention was implemented or caused a benefit. The checks below are documentary comparisons and logical dependency analysis, not clinical replication or mathematical counterexamples.
# 4. Problem 1: the healthcare case does not support its attributed participatory intervention and benefits

Source claim and location. Section 6, p. 6, presents a healthcare co-design case involving patients, clinicians, and ethicists, with enhanced accountability. Table 1, p. 7, specifies iterative design with patients and clinicians and lists reduced diagnostic bias and enhanced trust as achieved impacts. Appendix B(e.1), p. 20, again invokes Zicari et al. (2021) for collaborative diagnostic-bias tools. These are concrete claims about a cited case, not merely recommendations for future participation. [E1]

Decisive source comparison. The exact cited Frontiers article, DOI 10.3389/fhumd.2021.673104, describes Z-Inspection expert assessment. Its p. 9 states: ’Callers and patients have not been involved in the system design’. Dispatchers were consulted. Fairness concerns remain in p. 12 and issue E4, p. 16; issue E6, p. 17, discusses dispatcher distrust. Recommendation 3, p. 19, proposes future patient/caller involvement. The conclusions, pp. 21-22, describe possible benefits of assessment and transparency, rather than a measured patient-co-design intervention with the two attributed outcomes. [E2]

Complete check. Define P as patient participation in the reported system-design process, B as demonstrated reduction in diagnostic bias from that process, and T as demonstrated increase in trust from it. The reviewed case entry uses P together with B and T as empirical support for participatory healthcare benefits. The source comparison contradicts P and does not establish B or T. Thus the proposed evidentiary chain cannot be obtained from that study. No numerical effect is inferred, and an absence of demonstrated benefit is not converted into a claim that the intervention could never work.

The identity condition is satisfied: the bibliography gives this precise article and DOI, not a different patient co-design trial. The intervention condition is not rescued by changing ’patients’ to any expert or practitioner, because the reviewed paper specifically lists patients and distinguishes affected-community power from expert oversight. The outcome condition is not rescued by a recommendation or by identifying a bias: detecting a problem and showing its reduction are different results.

Alternative reading and counterevidence. A broad usage of ’participation’ could include professional consultation and ethical assessment, and those activities can be valuable. This would support a narrower account of the case. It cannot retain the specific patient-inclusive design claim or treat anticipated improvements as achieved diagnostic-bias and trust results. The source’s positive discussion of assessment is preserved; the review does not allege that the project lacked value.

Dependency and severity. The abstract explicitly advertises nine-case analysis and the ability of grassroots methods to mitigate biased outcomes. Section 6 presents these cases as empirical insights, and Table 1 makes the healthcare intervention/outcome link explicit. Correcting the account removes that claimed successful healthcare demonstration from the synthesis. This is substantive empirical support tied to a stated contribution, so Major is appropriate under the requested standard. It is not merely an incorrect label, and its severity does not depend on overturning the normative proposal or every other case.

Scoped repair. Recast the entry as an expert assessment identifying unmet participation needs, and remove the unsupported achieved-outcome attribution. Alternatively, provide a different, precisely identified study that demonstrates the intervention and benefits claimed. The first option is supported as a narrowing of the evidentiary claim; it does not restore the original successful-case inference. No replacement evidence was supplied, manuscript edited, or author adoption obtained.
# 5. Problem 2: Project Dorian’s achieved allocation-speed outcome is unsupported

Source claim and location. Table 1, p. 7, describes Project Dorian’s key impact as faster resource allocation. The cited source is Berditchevskaia et al. (2021). The question is whether the case description supports an achieved operational effect, not whether faster response would be desirable. [E1]

Primary-source check. Nesta’s case study, printed pp. 18-19, labels Dorian a one-off research proof of concept. Faster response appears as a possible benefit of remote damage assessment. Its impact paragraph reports classification errors identified by community responders, targeted improvements, and better understanding of potential tool value. It does not report an allocation-time comparison or demonstrated acceleration of resource delivery. [E3]

Invalid step and limit. The case supports participation in validating damage classifications. Turning that into a completed resource-allocation speed benefit changes the endpoint and evidentiary status. Error identification can plausibly help later operations, but it does not establish that resource allocation was faster. This review does not conclude that acceleration failed to occur; the attributed outcome is unsupported by the cited account.

Alternative reading, impact, and repair. ’Facilitated’ could be intended as potential usefulness. If so, the table should state that scope. Minor is supported for this local outcome overstatement: the participation process itself remains substantiated, while the specific operational endpoint is not used to derive the four-tier framework or the healthcare bias claim. A supported replacement is that responder validation identified classification weaknesses and informed targeted improvements. # 2. Checked dependencies and counterevidence

Formal soundness and statement fidelity. Section 2.2 (p3) describes sound formal reasoning and says Lean checks a proof relative to its statement. Section 4.2 (p6) explicitly identifies evaluation of autoformalized statements as a bottleneck. Section 4.3 (p7) explicitly requires generated specifications to match developers’ intent. The extended version reinforces this on pp13 and 19 [E2]. Therefore a proof of an unrelated, weakened or mistranslated statement would expose a translation failure, not refute the paper’s conditional proof-checking property. The trusted checker and accepted axioms are operative assumptions; adding an inconsistent axiom would not be a valid counterexample.

Data and self-improvement. Section 3 (p5) reports diminishing gains after a few expert-iteration rounds. Section 4.1 (pp5-6) leaves generalization beyond domains with many human-written problems open. Logical availability of indefinitely many provable statements is distinct from useful diversity or guaranteed learning improvement. The actual text does not promise the latter. This dependency supports treating synthetic-data claims as proposed mechanisms with stated limitations.

Neural verification and indispensability. Section 3 (p5) and Section 5.3 (p8) acknowledge that neural verifiers can improve performance. Section 6 (p9) treats neural-only approaches as an alternative view and expresses uncertainty about rigorous theorem proving. Its prospective advocacy is not a proved impossibility theorem about all future neural systems. Conversely, the paper does not establish a universal necessity theorem for formal reasoning. The position remains a proposed direction supported by examples, not a quantified lower bound.

Roadmap and code verification. Section 5 (pp7-9) proposes capability levels and identifies missing benchmarks. The levels do not assert a mathematically nested hierarchy or a guaranteed development order. The Level 4 proposal in Section 5.4 does not provide an implemented scoring rule that uniquely recovers user intent from code. Such evaluation design remains future work; it is not an observed failing benchmark.
# 3. Independent checks of concrete evidence

Figure 1 (p2) asks for x+y over complex x,y satisfying x^2+y^2=7 and x^3+y^3=10. Write s=x+y and t=xy. The first constraint gives t=(s^2-7)/2; substituting into the second gives the cubic below. Its three roots are -5, 1 and 4. For each root, choose x,y as the roots of z^2-sz+t. Every such quadratic has complex roots, and the symmetric identities recover both original equations. Thus the negative discriminants for s=-5 and s=4 are allowed, not counterexamples. Exact rational calculations return sum-of-squares 7, sum-of-cubes 10 and zero cubic residual for all three cases; see calculation_results.json.

Figure 2 (p3) defines addition recursively in the second argument. For 0+n=n, the base case reduces to 0=0 and the induction step reduces add(0,succ(n)) to succ(add(0,n)), then uses the induction hypothesis. This is an analytic inspection of the displayed example, not execution or verification by Lean.

AlphaProof evidence. The 2024 official infographic visibly labels approximately 1M informal problems and 100M formal problems [E3]; this supports the scale reported in Section 4.1. It does not show that all 100M were successfully proved. The surrounding training description includes proof and disproof search. The later Nature account reports about 80M formal problems [E5, Training], a later account that must not be silently equated with the earlier graphic. No demonstrated core error is inferred from the differing counts or from the paper’s loose use of ’theorems’; a success-count interpretation is not established.

The official 2024 account describes manually translated contest statements and multi-day computation. The paper’s Section 5.3 explicitly distinguishes future evaluation without manual formalization. The silver-medal-level example is therefore not treated as proof of autonomous, human-time-budget performance.

# 2. Problem 1 - Incompatible human-validation statistics

Source claim and assumptions. Appendix D.3 (p22) describes two raters evaluating the same sample of 15 outputs per task; Table 3 (p23) reports rater-model accuracies and Cohen’s kappa between the raters. The Conspiracy (Bad) row gives a=0.73, b=0.44 and kappa=0.78. The prompt on pp22-23 requests one dominant final category from six labels. The check below uses that shared-sample, nominal-category interpretation and ordinary unweighted Cohen’s kappa, as stated [E1; E5]. The values were visually confirmed in the PDF.

Complete check. Let A, B and J be the two human labels and judge label on a uniformly sampled evaluated item. If A and B agree, their agreement indicators with J are equal. Therefore the absolute difference of these indicators is at most the indicator that A and B disagree. Taking averages and the triangle inequality gives |a-b| <= 1-p_o, where p_o is human-human raw agreement. For a defined Cohen kappa, the chance agreement p_e lies in [0,1), so kappa <= p_o. Hence the reported accuracies require kappa <= 0.71, contradicting 0.78.

Rounding cannot explain this. With conventional rounding to two decimals, a is at least 0.725 and b is at most 0.445, so kappa is at most 0.72; a displayed 0.78 requires kappa at least 0.775. The contradiction does not depend on n=15. Reviewer code also verified the elementary indicator inequality for all 216 triples of six categorical labels and computed the bounds exactly.

Alternative readings and impact. Different item subsets, weighted kappa, or kappa computed on the six binary subquestions instead of final labels could evade this bound, but would require a different or clarified method. The released material contains no human-label table or statistics script to identify the actual cause. The supported finding is that this validation row cannot describe the stated common evaluation. Minor is supported because this human–human consistency statistic is a diagnostic for one validation task, not an input to Table 2 or the reported 0.75 human–model mean. The bound also does not force corrected kappa below the authors’ 0.5 convention. Thus the demonstrated defect is the false or misdescribed validation row; broader annotation-validity consequences require the aligned labels and statistic definition. This dependency judgment does not require a change in model ordering.
Repair status. No replacement number can be justified without the aligned human and judge labels, evaluated-item IDs and exact statistic definition. No numerical repair is claimed or applied.
\[\left|\mathbf{1}_{A=J}-\mathbf{1}_{B=J}\right|\leq\mathbf{1}_{A\ne B},\qquad \kappa=\frac{p_o-p_e}{1-p_e}\leq p_o\leq1-|a-b|.\]
# 3. Problem 2 (Major) - The avoidance formula accepts direct answers

Source claim. Section 3.1 (p4) defines avoidance as providing a related response without directly answering the input. Table 1 (p5), explicitly headed Formal Definition, instead uses dist(M(x),{y*}) > k. Its caption calls y* a user-preferred response; Appendix A.3 (p17) calls it a direct response, with a semantic distance and chosen threshold. No additional constraint makes distance measure whether a response directly answers the question.

Admissible counterexample. Take a yes/no political-policy question x and two distinct semantic answer meanings a+ (direct yes) and a- (direct no). Set d(a+,a-)=1 and d(a,a)=0. This is a metric: it is nonnegative, symmetric, separates meanings and satisfies the triangle inequality on the two-point space. Use the induced distance on singleton outputs. Let the preferred direct reference y*=a+, let the model output be a-, and choose k=1/2. These values satisfy every stated requirement. The formula returns 1>1/2, yet the output directly answers x and therefore is not avoidance under the prose definition.

Counterevidence and precise impact. If A.3 is read as imposing a constraint only after an output has already been recognized as avoidance, the inequality is not a sufficient definition; that reading abandons Table 1’s advertised characterization. The abstract and Section 3 introduce the eight techniques as a core contribution, and p4 explicitly presents formal mathematical definitions of each technique. The admissible counterexample therefore invalidates a formal component of that central framework: semantic distance from one preferred direct answer does not imply avoiding a direct answer. This core dependency supports Major. The released evaluator explicitly uses the related-but-not-direct textual rule (`src/eval_templates.py`, line 15), and never computes this metric. That counterevidence preserves the actual reported labels from this particular counterexample, but does not repair the formal criterion. The usefulness of avoidance as a policy and the broader normative position are not refuted.

Scoped correction. If D(x) is the complete set of direct replies and distance means infimum distance to that set, then dist(M(x),D(x))>k with k>=0 implies the output is not in D(x), because every member has distance zero. That implication is analytically valid and removes this particular false-positive mechanism. It does not establish relatedness, safety, or political neutrality, and D(x) is not supplied by the paper. No complete operational repair is claimed.
\[y^\star=a_+,\quad M(x)=\{a_-\},\quad d(a_+,a_-)=1>\tfrac12=k.\]

Position: Certified Robustness Does Not (Yet) Imply Model Security
Outcome: Minor; two bounded technical-background inaccuracies; no demonstrated defect in the inspected core non-implication or norm conversion
Batch token: `[internal identifier omitted]`
Human scientific decision: Pending
# 1. Identity, scope and outcome

The reviewed artifact is the 14-page publisher-linked ICML 2025 paper by Andrew C. Cullen, Paul Montague, Sarah Erfani and Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein [E1]. Its SHA-256 is 3f96194f25866608a43fa8e673f6e6e684ea024b36a0833e3e7f8aa22b04a6a4. The original bytes match the controller receipt. Printed pages 1-14 equal the 1-based PDF pages.

All main-text pages 1-9 were read. Two categorical descriptions of existing certification methods require bounded corrections. The core distinction between local prediction invariance and broader security, and the norm-conversion factor in Theorem 2, survived the checks below. No new experimental reproduction is claimed.
# 2. Supported findings and validated corrections

F1 — Training is not a prerequisite for computing these certificates (Minor). Section 2.2, p3, states that exact approaches require substantial training changes; Section 2.2.2 then makes an augmented training loss a requirement for using IBP or convex-relaxation bounds. This conflates computing a sound bound on a fixed network with training a network to obtain useful bounds. The cited Xu et al. (2020), Section 3.1, treats a supplied computational graph and fixed unperturbed parameters; robust-loss training is a separate application in Section 3.3 [E3].

A complete admissible counterexample uses the fixed network h(t)=ReLU(t), with logits f(t)=(1-h(t),h(t)), input t=1/5 and radius 1/10. The input interval is [1/10,3/10], on which h=t. Ordinary interval propagation gives class-0 logits in [7/10,9/10] and class-1 logits in [1/10,3/10]. Their worst-case separation is 2/5>0, so class 0 is certified throughout that interval. No augmented training objective is required for this computation. Exact Fraction arithmetic independently confirms these bounds in analytic_check_results.json.

The strongest alternative reading is that specialized training is often needed for practically useful tightness, especially for deep-network IBP. That qualified statement is compatible with [E3], but differs from the paper’s categorical prerequisite. The verified correction is to separate post-training verification from training for larger or tighter certificates. The example does not establish useful radii, speed or scalability for arbitrary networks. Minor is supported because the false premise affects the background comparison of methods; it is not used in the proof of either central non-implication or norm conversion.

F2 — Non-ReLU certification predates the cited recent advance (Minor). Section 2.2.2, pp3-4, describes applicability beyond ReLU as only recently demonstrated, citing Shi et al. (2023). Yet its own Zhang et al. (2018) reference develops CROWN for general activation functions. Section 3.2 and Table 5 explicitly cover tanh, sigmoid and arctan, with nonzero certified bounds [E4]. Section 4 also applies CROWN to pretrained ReLU models.

The strongest alternative is that a particular architecture, tightness improvement or practical scale was intended. The passage does not specify such a restriction. A source-supported correction is to acknowledge earlier general-activation certification and identify the narrower advance meant by the 2023 citation. This repairs the historical and capability description; it does not show that all modern architectures are easy to certify. Minor follows from the limited dependency: the paper’s broad concerns about deployment costs and threat-model scope do not require a claim that non-ReLU certification began recently.
# 3. Core mathematical checks and rejected stronger readings

Theorem 1, pp4-5: a valid radius is a prediction-invariance guarantee, not a semantic correctness or input-history guarantee. The constant-probability illustration can show certified misclassification, but its constant predicted class does not itself exhibit a class-flipping attack under Eq. (1). This incompleteness of the illustration does not refute the non-implication.

A complete independent example takes S=[0,1], F(t)=0 for t<1/2 and F(t)=1 otherwise, with semantic truth y(t)=0 throughout. The clean input 1/4 is correctly classified and an attacker can replace it by 3/4, preserving truth but changing the prediction. Each point has valid radius 1/5, below the boundary distance 1/4. The attack magnitude is 1/2, outside the original certified radius. Thus the example demonstrates a certificate at an already-attacked input, without violating any within-radius guarantee. The paper’s p4 expressly acknowledges the real guarantee against correctly bounded attacks and permits heuristic risk ranking. Accordingly, its no-information wording is read as no intrinsic attack-status guarantee, not universal statistical independence.

Theorem 2, p7: for p,q>=1, a radius r_p in the p norm transfers to the q-norm radius shown below. If q<=p, the p norm is at most the q norm. If q>=p, the p norm is at most d^(1/p-1/q) times the q norm. These establish inclusion of the transferred ball; one-coordinate and equal-coordinate vectors respectively make the bounds sharp in ambient space.

Beyond this radius there can be points outside the known certified ball. This does not prove an actual adversarial example for every classifier, and a restricted permissible domain can remove geometric witness directions. The theorem says potential attacks, its proof concludes noncoverage, and nearby prose says attacks may exist. These qualifications support the coverage reading. A constant classifier would refute a stronger universal attack-existence claim, but does not establish a defect in this stated, qualified argument. Merely changing the norm also does not revoke the original certificate.

Eqs. (3)-(4), p3: the lower top-class and upper competing-class probability bounds, inverse-normal signs and sigma/2 factor are consistent with the randomized-smoothing guarantee [E6]. The text explicitly identifies the smoothed classifier as the certified object. Sampling confidence and abstention remain relevant; no Monte Carlo procedure was rerun.
\[R_q=r_p\min\{1,d^{1/q-1/p}\},\qquad B_q(x,R_q)\subseteq B_p(x,r_p).\]
# 4. Security evidence, version comparison and remaining limits

The certificate-guided-attack concern is conditional on access. The paper states this on p5; the cited Cullen et al. (2024), Sections 3.1 and 4.1, assumes relevant model/certificate access and uses certificates to guide search beyond known certified regions [E5]. This supports a conditional information advantage, not a contradiction of the certified-radius guarantee. No claim of universally worse security or measured user complacency is established. Section 6 acknowledges that partial improvements can enhance security.

The inspected publisher material and paper do not identify a new code or data release requiring reproduction for this position paper. Cited prior-work experiments were not rerun. The deployment, user-expectation and governance proposals were evaluated as arguments and research questions; no legal compliance opinion or new experiment was invented.

The latest retrieved arXiv record is v2 dated 11 August 2025 [E2]. Checked pp3-5 and 7 retain the relevant descriptions and arguments. A main-text word comparison found only small text/encoding differences; it is a locator aid, not proof of formula-level version equivalence. No repair to F1/F2 was identified in the checked passages. OpenReview history was inaccessible.
# 5. Conclusion and repair/adoption tracking

report: ELVIA scientific verification report
Position: Graph Matching Systems Deserve Better Benchmarks
Outcome: Major; false extension of a core invariance guarantee and invalid alignment-specific diagnostic inference; bounded local findings and unresolved empirical provenance kept separate

Human scientific decision: Pending
# 1. Identity, scope and supported outcome

The reviewed source is Roy, Meher, Jain, Chakrabarti and De, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82131-82150 [E1]. Printed pages 1-20 equal the 1-based PDF pages. SHA-256: 8c6171896f0dd221ac5a1e4597882ff62d469d7961ca169c1a89c6219ac533ed. Original bytes match the controller receipt and remain unchanged.

The review covered all main text, Appendix A, the core mathematical chain and selected released implementation/data evidence. Major is supported for the broadened invariance guarantee, its invalid supporting proof step, and the alignment-specific evaluation inference. Each lies on a dependency of the advertised augmentation or evaluation contribution. The theorem heading’s zero-substitution regime remains valid. The general case for better benchmarks is not refuted, and no published experimental score is claimed to have changed.
# 2. Problem 1 - The broader cost-invariance guarantee is false (Major)

Source and operative assumptions. Theorem 4.2’s heading on p5 requires cNS=0 and cNA,cND,cEA,cED>0. Its proof-closing sentence instead claims invariance for all five positive costs satisfying cNS<cNA+cND. Section 4.2 uses invariance to justify reusing an optimal alignment to generate ground-truth labels across cost settings. Appendix A.2.1, p14, repeats the weaker inequality. The demonstrated failure concerns the explicit broader conclusion on p5, not the theorem heading.

Complete counterexample. Both graphs are the simple connected undirected path 0-1-2, with source labels (A,A,B) and target labels (A,B,A). Use cost order (node addition, node deletion, node substitution, edge addition, edge deletion). Each graph is padded to six vertices with three isolated artificial vertices, so every partial matching is representable. In both settings below every cost is strictly positive and cNS=1<20=cNA+cND. Ordinary undirected edges are counted once.

All 720 padded permutations were independently enumerated for each cost vector using exact fractions [E3]. The two optimal real-map sets are disjoint. Each has 12 padded optima, accounting for dummy permutations. The minimum cost among alignments with any real-node deletion/insertion is 20.5 in the low-edge setting and 24 in the high-edge setting, so partial mappings do not defeat the example.

A high-edge-cost optimal alignment reused at low cost returns 2 rather than the true GED of 1/2. Reusing a low-edge-cost optimum at high cost returns 4 rather than 2. This is a concrete wrong-label mechanism for the broadened compatibility rule supporting the core augmentation method. Major follows from this dependency, independently of whether any released experiment used the invalid regime.

Counterevidence and exact limits. Every C0-C6 configuration in Table 5 sets cNS=0. Section 5.4 also expressly invokes the zero-substitution regime. Appendix p14 can be read narrowly as referring only to those seven settings. These observations preserve the demonstrated applicability of the restricted theorem to the published configurations; they do not make the p5 universal positive-substitution conclusion true. No corruption of Table 5 labels is inferred from this counterexample.
Cost vector | Optimal real maps | Operations and exact GED
(10,10,1,2,2) | (0,1,2), (2,1,0) | 2 substitutions; no edge edits; GED=2
# 2.1. Problem 1b - Core proof step (Major), with verified repair

The Proposition 4.1 proof on pp4-5 also uses an invalid degree-only equality for substitution cost. Equal degrees do not ensure equal aligned neighborhoods. With source edges {(0,1),(1,2)}, target edges {(0,2),(1,2)}, identity alignment and labels (A,C,D)/(B,C,D), the matched vertex 0 has degree 1 in each graph. Unit substitution/addition/deletion costs give a true cost of 3 (one substitution and two edge edits), whereas the displayed degree formula gives 1. This invalid derivation is a Major subfinding (F1b). The false equality is used to prove Proposition 4.1; Theorem 4.2 invokes that proposition to fix node-edit counts; the theorem then supports reuse of alignments in the augmentation method. The witness can take all five costs equal to 1, so cNS=1<cNA+cND=2. The proposition itself survives the independent repair below. Ease of repair does not reduce the severity of the invalid core proof step.

A correct exchange proof merges one deleted source node with one inserted target node while retaining every other real match. No previously matched edge is destroyed. Node addition and deletion counts each drop by one, while substitutions increase by at most one. Nonnegative edge costs therefore give a total change at most cNS-cNA-cND<0. This proves the no-paired-insertion/deletion result under its original assumptions.

For cNS=0, optimal node counts are consequently fixed by graph-size differences. If m(P) counts preserved edges, the cost is Cnodes+cED|E|+cEA|E’|-(cEA+cED)m(P). Positive cEA+cED means every allowed cost vector selects exactly the same maximum-common-edge alignments. This supplies the missing invariant behind the weighted-edge minimization step and proves the theorem heading’s restricted statement.

The supported correction is to retain cNS=0 with the other four costs positive, or independently solve/validate positive-substitution configurations. Restricting the domain restores a valid guarantee; it does not prove the false broader one. No author files or published experiments were modified.
# 3. Problem 2 - Scalar cost-shift scores do not diagnose alignment recovery (Major)

Source claim. Sections 4.2 (p5) and 5.5 (p8) present the cost-variant tests as assessing whether models recover the optimal alignment P*. Page 9 interprets performance through alignment capability. The stated target is stronger than end-to-end prediction under a changed cost vector.

The inspected C0-trained baseline branch omits cost features, reloads the same learned checkpoint at each cost setting, and changes the GED targets. This is visible in inference_with_diff_ged_cost.ipynb cells 3-5 and utils/data_utils.py lines 223-268 [E2]. GraphEdX separately applies cost coefficients to its output. The manuscript itself acknowledges unchanged predictions on p9, so this is a disclosed interface difference, not an alleged hidden implementation bug. The C1-trained branch supplies four cost features and must be distinguished.

Admissible failure with perfect alignments. Use the paper’s C0=(1,1,0,1,1) and C3=(1,1,0,11,12). For K2 to P3, an optimal alignment adds one node and one edge; exact costs are 2 and 12. A model can recover that alignment perfectly but continue reporting its C0 cost 2, producing squared error 100 at C3. Thus changed-cost error does not imply incorrect alignment.

The two-pair example below also reverses Kendall ordering, so the problem is not merely MSE units. Every graph is simple, connected, undirected and unlabeled. Pair A preserves the source edge and attains the mandatory additions of three nodes and three edges. Pair B deletes exactly the edge-count difference 10-6=4. Each construction attains cardinality lower bounds and is therefore optimal under both cost settings. A perfect C0 predictor returns 6>4, whereas C3 truth is 36<48: Kendall tau is -1 despite exact alignments [E4].

Success is not alignment identification either. Let D0 be exact C0 GED, a=(n’-n)+, d=(n-n’)+ and DeltaE=|E’|-|E|. In the valid zero-substitution regime, edge additions plus deletions equal D0-a-d, and their difference is DeltaE. Problem 3 — Table 1 leakage counts and percentages disagree (Minor). On p6, IMDB intra-test leakage is printed as 26,463 of 45,150 pairs and 34.1%; the ratio is 58.6113%. # 4.1. Problem 5 - Released filtered graphs retain model-visible duplicates (Minor; historical impact unresolved)

The pinned release’s Linux_filtered data contain two train-test isomorphism classes after the edge symmetrization used by the PyG input builder (utils/data_utils.py, lines 95-100). The raw objects are directed graphs; they are distinct under directed isomorphism. The model input builder adds both directions for every stored arc. All inspected train/test node-feature storage contains only 1.0, so features do not distinguish these examples. This establishes a release-level failure of the advertised isomorphic-separation invariant for that model path, independently of whether it affected the published run.

An exact seven-node witness uses zero-based train index 41 and test index 1. Ignoring stored direction, train edges are {(0,1),(0,3),(1,2),(2,4),(2,6),(5,6)}. The narrow conclusion is that 2 of the 19 test graphs in this released filtered set have model-equivalent training counterparts under the checked path. Some adjacency consumers treat direction differently; do not generalize to every architecture. The release contains 98 filtered LINUX graphs, while the paper reports 89 undirected unique graphs, reinforcing the need for a run/version map. Without that map or reruns, the magnitude of any historical Table 2 effect is Needs Evidence. Minor is supported for the verified release inconsistency, without promoting it to a demonstrated paper-wide experimental failure.

A precise prevention rule is to normalize graphs to the actual model-visible edge/feature semantics, form exact feature-preserving isomorphism classes, and split whole classes. ## 2. Scope and decisive result

The review read the argument in Sections 1-6 (pp. 1-9), Table 1, Figure 1, and Appendices A-C (pp. 18-19). Selected bibliography entries were traced; this is not an audit of every cited paper. The central checks concern the move from absolute to relative identifiability, the conditional interpretation of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), and whether a proposed research programme is represented as a completed theorem.

The decisive counterevidence to an overly strong reading is in the paper itself: Section 2 says representation similarity is not universal; Section 4 explicitly presents Singular Identifiability Theory (SITh) as a future blueprint; and Appendix B distinguishes similarity between learned models from recovery of a common ground truth. Different augmentations can select different latent factors. The paper therefore does not claim a theorem that every SSL architecture, dataset or training run converges to one universal representation [E1, pp. 2, 4, 7, 18-19].
No demonstrated central mathematical or empirical error was established in these checks. This conclusion does not certify all cited results or every broad historical assertion.
## 3. Checked reasoning and operative assumptions

Conditional identifiability bridge. Suppose two learned representations refer to the same latent vector z, the same population, and the same dimension, and satisfy f1(x) = A1 z and f2(x) = A2 z with invertible square matrices A1 and A2. Substitution gives f2(x) = A2 A1^-1 f1(x). This is an analytic identity, not a finite-training result. With a fixed equivalence relation, the same implication follows from symmetry and transitivity. It fails as an argument for arbitrary models if the latent variables, admissible transformations or populations differ. Appendix B recognizes these restrictions rather than discharging them universally [E1, p. 18].

Upstream SimCLR result. Section 3.2’s example was compared with Zimmermann et al.’s published Sections 3.1-3.2, Theorems 1-2 [E3]. Their spherical result uses a uniform latent marginal, a von Mises-Fisher conditional, a differentiable injective generative map, a matching conditional model, population loss minimization and an asymptotic number of negative samples. It recovers latents up to an orthogonal linear transformation. The position paper uses this as an idealized example and explicitly identifies the practical gap. This supports its conditional illustration; it does not establish finite-data recovery for deployed SimCLR.

Evidence from Figure 1. The rendered p. 7 was inspected. Its caption specifies RBF-kernel CKA with sigma = 0.4 and attributes the similarity matrix to Ciernik et al.; the right panel is a UMAP depiction. The text acknowledges non-universal similarity. Neither the matrix nor a UMAP projection is a proof of identifiability. The report does not substitute a linear-CKA counterexample for a claim about this different metric. The underlying embeddings and plotting pipeline were not reproduced.

Research agenda and evaluation. Questions 4.1.1-4.8.2, including finite samples, optimization, architecture, projection and compositional generalization, are presented as questions. A theorem proving that SITh will accelerate research is not supplied or assumed. The critique of using one classification score to assess all latent information is logically coherent: a task insensitive to a factor cannot by itself establish recovery of that factor [E1, pp. 4-8].
## 4. Clarifications and unresolved boundaries

C1: Fix the admissible relation in Definition A.2. Literally, the existence of an unrestricted equivalence relation is vacuous: the relation that makes every pair equivalent always satisfies the definition. A nonvacuous reading fixes a scientifically meaningful transformation class before quantifying over learned models. The surrounding discussion repeatedly uses simple or linear transformations, while A.1 refers to a particular relation. No downstream proof was found to depend on the unrestricted reading. This is retained as a definition/scope clarification, without a supported defect severity. A precise clarification would begin: “For a pre-specified admissible equivalence relation …”. This is an editorial interpretation, not a verified repair of a false theorem [E1, p. 18].

C2: Identifiability is not universal metric agreement. Invertible linear equivalence alone does not guarantee high values for every similarity measure or recovery after arbitrary finite training. The paper’s conditional wording and open questions are material counterevidence against treating such a stronger statement as its claim. No counterexample to the actual statement is asserted.

Pending source-level boundary. Appendix B’s statement about non-content factors collapsing needs to be read with the representation dimension, layer and augmentation assumptions of von Kuegelgen et al. Section 4.3.1 itself discusses other factors being learned with larger representations and more training. This review did not reconstruct that upstream theorem in full; it records the boundary as Needs Evidence, without inferring a contradiction or increasing severity [E1, pp. 5, 18].
## 5. Dependence, versions and remaining work
