# Scientific verification report: I25-40164 (0057)

Supported impact: Major, scoped to the advertised public benchmark implementation.
Additional confirmed finding: Minor, reversed inequalities in the printed metric definitions.
Batch B001 / [internal task]. Token: [internal identifier omitted]
Scientific decision: pending human review. Author adoption has not been requested.
## 1. Identity, version and scope

Ossi Raisa, Boris van Breugel and Mihaela van der Schaar, Position: All Current Generative Fidelity and Diversity Metrics are Flawed. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82016-82050 [E1-E2]. The reviewed primary object is the 35-page publisher-linked PDF. Locations use one-based physical PDF pages, matching printed article pages.
Primary PDF SHA-256:

The original bytes matched the controller receipt before analysis and remain preserved. The public repository linked by the publisher was acquired at commit `d30d874bca4581365f5949f875c7cbc9426cfe72`, dated 10 June 2025, 09:48:57 UTC [E3]. Its meaningful 44-file tree is preserved under `sources/0057/repository/`.

The review covered the main argument (pp. 1-9), metric definitions (Appendix A, pp. 12-14), all sanity-check setups and criteria (Appendix B, pp. 15-21), and selected result plots in Appendix C. Static code inspection traced the precision/recall-cover calculation through preprocessing, callers, metric-type assignment, criterion selection and table labels. Other metric code and aggregation were inspected selectively; no author code, notebook or model was executed.
## 2. Summary and scientific dependency

The paper’s core contributions include a reproducible benchmark with programmatically checked passing criteria and guidance on which metrics measure fidelity or diversity [E1, pp. 1-2, 5-9]. The released default path computes recall cover under the key used for precision cover, and vice versa. Those keys then select different fidelity/diversity criteria and determine the table labels. An independent exact finite calculation demonstrates distinct intended and released named outputs under both the paper’s hyperparameters and the release’s defaults.

This is a demonstrated defect in an advertised central implementation, not an inference from a missing file or an unused helper. It supports Major at that contribution level. It does not establish which code generated every number in the published Tables 3-4. That historical provenance question remains unresolved. Other failure cases and the broad argument for more careful metric evaluation are not refuted by this finding.

Separately, the PDF reverses the cross-neighbour count inequalities in Eqs. (11)-(12). The released comparison uses the correct direction, so the printed error is assessed separately rather than being assumed to corrupt the experiments.
## 3. Definitions and assumptions

Let R be the real embedded sample and G the generated embedded sample. For a sample point x in S, let b_S(x) be the distance to its k-prime-th nearest neighbour in S, excluding x itself. Define a ball using distance at most b_S(x). With k positive, the intended empirical cover scores are:
- Precision cover PC: the fraction of g in G whose G-neighbour ball contains at least k points of R.
- Recall cover RC: the fraction of r in R whose R-neighbour ball contains at least k points of G.

These orientations and the “at least” comparison are specified in Cheema and Urner’s Definition 2, Eqs. (3)-(4), physical PDF p. 4 [E4]. They also match the orientation of the target paper’s sums, after correcting its inequality signs.

The finite checks below use distinct, one-dimensional real-valued observations, n = m = 1000, positive real-sample variance, and valid neighbour counts less than n. They test deterministic metric definitions and implementation semantics, not an asymptotic probabilistic theorem. A common affine transformation with positive scale preserves every nearest-neighbour radius and cross-ball membership.
## 4. Problem 1: the released benchmark swaps precision and recall cover
Judgment: Major, scoped to the core public implementation.
### Source claim and exact path

The paper identifies C-Prec as fidelity and C-Rec as diversity in Table 1 (p. 4), and bases the evaluations and practitioner guidance on that distinction. Its publisher-linked README says the released workflow produces Tables 3 and 4 [E1-E3].
The inspected path is:
1. `sanity_checks/gaussian_mixture.py` constructs a metric computer with real data, then calls `compute_metric` with synthetic data.
2. `metrics/metric_computer.py::MetricComputer` fits StandardScaler on the real data and applies that same transformation to both sets.
3. `metrics/precision_recall_cover/precision_recall_cover_computer.py::PrecisionRecallCoverComputer.compute_metric` explicitly sets P to scaled real data and Q to scaled synthetic data.

4. Its first loop counts sufficiently covered real-centred balls and returns that average as `precision_cover`. Its second loop counts sufficiently covered synthetic-centred balls and returns that average as `recall_cover`.

5. `experiment_config.py::metric_types` maps these keys to fidelity and diversity, respectively. `sanity_check_criteria.py::CriterionSeparatorByMetricType` selects the corresponding tests. `aggregate_pass_fail_tables.py::print_metric_names` prints the keys as C-Prec and C-Rec without reversing them.

Thus the computed quantities are the opposite of the intended named measurements. The inspected class is the one registered in the benchmark; the finding does not depend on its unused duplicate function.
### Complete independent finite check
Choose:

The generated sample covers the first real cluster and omits the second. Each set has exactly 1000 distinct finite points. R has nonzero variance. Cross-set distances are odd integers while within-set radii are even, so no cross-ball boundary tie occurs. StandardScaler applies a common translation and positive rescaling in one dimension; every comparison remains unchanged.
The target paper prescribes k-prime = ceil(log(1000) + 6) = 13 and k = ceil(13/3) = 5. The released constructor instead uses a 15-neighbour radius with k = 5. The discrepancy below holds for both:
Radius convention | Cross-counts at retained real points | Cross-counts at omitted real points | Cross-counts at generated points
Printed defaults: k-prime = 13 | -28 |  | -7
Released defaults: k-prime = 15 | -32 |  | -8

Every generated-centred ball contains at least five real points, so PC = 1. Exactly 500 of the 1000 real-centred balls contain at least five generated points, so RC = 1/2. The released dictionary, by its statically established semantics, reports precision_cover = 1/2 and recall_cover = 1.

The reviewer-authored standard-library script `code_audit/independent_cover_check.py` enumerates integer distances and counts. Its saved JSON records these outputs. It never imports or invokes author code [E5].
### Counterevidence, alternatives and precise consequence

Exchanging the arguments could compensate for the reversal, but the actual callers pass real then synthetic, and the base class and local assignments confirm that order. A subsequent relabelling could also compensate, but the inspected aggregation and printing paths preserve the keys. The correct inequality inside `PR_Cover_Indicator` does not fix the orientation error. Nor does the different neighbour-radius rounding: the witness works under both choices.

The wrapper and bundled source acknowledge upstream code. This report attributes the observed behaviour to the acquired release and does not assign personal responsibility for its origin. Cached notebook outputs are historical evidence, not proof of the exact code used for the published PDF.

The dependency is direct: wrong named scalar -> wrong fidelity/diversity branch -> wrong interpretation of a passing or failing test. For example, the mode-dropping test expects fidelity to remain horizontal and diversity to fall. Routing the two measurements oppositely changes which property is being assessed. It invalidates the release’s claim to evaluate the two specified cover metrics under their correct roles, even if other metric columns and the broad position remain useful.
### Scoped repair

Return the generated-centred average as precision cover and the real-centred average as recall cover, then regenerate criterion decisions and tables from correctly named raw measurements. This mapping restores PC = 1 and RC = 1/2 in the exact witness. It is analytically verified for the naming defect; the author implementation was not modified or executed. Matching the stated radius policy and reassessing historical outputs are separate tasks.
## 5. Problem 2: printed cover definitions reverse the inequality
Judgment: Minor, limited to the documented metric specification.
Location. Appendix A, physical p. 13, Eqs. (11)-(12), visually inspected. Each indicator uses a cross-count at most k, whereas the intended method requires at least k [E1, E4].

For a complete check, use r_i = i/1000 and g_i = 10 + i/1000, i = 0,…,999. Both sets contain 1000 distinct points. With the paper’s k-prime = 13 and k = 5, every within-set radius is at most 13/1000, whereas the smallest cross-set distance is 9001/1000. Every cross-count is zero. Therefore:
- Printed Eqs. (11)-(12) give C-Prec = C-Rec = 1.
- The intended cover definitions give PC = RC = 0.

Open versus closed balls does not change this example. The same zero-count argument applies to separated compact supports with all within-support diameters smaller than their separation. The error is established without interpreting a numerical plot [E6].

Reversing both signs to “at least” restores the cited empirical definitions exactly. This repair does not fix Problem 1. The local Minor judgment rests on the demonstrated scope: this is an incorrect printed specification, while the actual predicate in the released implementation already uses the intended direction. No false derived theorem or additional experimental corruption was established from this sign error alone.
## 6. Other checks, counterevidence and remaining boundaries

Checks that passed. The Gaussian mean-separation extremes in B.2 have TV distances 0.9973002, 0.9999779 and 0.9999367. All six scale-separation extremes in B.3 also exceed 0.99; the smallest is 0.9968327. These independent numerical checks support the stated separation settings. Distinct concentric sphere surfaces are disjoint. Translating each coordinate of unit cubes by t = 1 - 0.2^(1/d) gives overlap volume exactly 0.2. Common invertible rescaling and adding independent identical variables preserve population TV [E6]. These checks do not reproduce finite-sample metric curves.

Radius policy discrepancy. At n = 1000 the text specifies k-prime = 13, k = 5, whereas the release uses k = 5 and k-prime = 3k = 15. This is a verified bounded specification mismatch. Its effect on the published results is unresolved; it is not needed for the Major conclusion.

Hypercube explanation. Section 5.3’s decreasing-distance intuition needs qualification. For independent unit-cube samples U and V displaced by t in every coordinate, EU-V^2 = d/6 + d t^2, which grows asymptotically. The distance between centres, sqrt(d)t, decreases. The latter is a defensible interpretation of the conjectural explanation; this is retained as a clarification, not a finding that the experiment is invalid.

Torus setup. Uniform cross-sectional disk sampling followed by uniform rotation does not give uniform volume density on a solid torus: its density is proportional to 1/rho. Nevertheless, the described torus (major radius 1, minor radius 0.1) remains disjoint from the radius-0.8 ball. The disjointness premise survives; no changed pass/fail result was demonstrated.

Scope of the position. The inclusion criteria explicitly exclude curve-valued and prohibitively slow metrics (p. 3). The title should be read with that evaluated scope. The chosen thresholds and notions of acceptable fidelity/diversity are stated desiderata, not universal statistical laws. Disagreement with those choices alone is not recorded as a mathematical error.
## 7. Versions, history and overall impact

The arXiv record inspected lists 2505.22450v1, submitted 28 May 2025 [E7]. The publisher PDF remains the reviewed authority. The acquired repository history includes a June 2025 correction described as a table-aggregation error when not using all metrics; the current aggregation code includes the corresponding metric-presence filter. That historical correction is not relabelled as a current defect.

No complete historical experiment reconstruction was performed. To determine precisely which printed C-Prec/C-Rec cells need revision, obtain the original raw metric outputs, generating revision and configuration, reconcile the labels and radius convention, then recompute the affected criteria. This task did not run that workflow.

The supported result is the current core implementation error plus the independent printed-definition error. It does not establish that all metric criticisms fail, that every published table cell is wrong, or that a corrected implementation would make a particular metric pass every check.
## 8. Conclusion table
Item | Judgment | Repair verification | Adoption and remaining work

Wrong named cover scores and criterion routing | Major, public benchmark implementation | Correct mapping verified analytically and in exact independent witness | Not applied; author adoption not requested
Eqs. (11)-(12) count direction | Minor, printed specification | Greater-or-equal restores cited definition | Not applied
Printed Tables 3-4 historical impact | Needs Evidence | Not reproduced | Original outputs/revision and affected rerun needed
Radius policy; geometry interpretations | Bounded mismatch / clarification | No global repair claimed | Quantitative empirical effect unresolved
Checked Gaussian separation and support premises | No Issue Found in checked calculations | Not applicable | Human scientific decision pending
## 9. References and evidence
- E1: Raisa et al. (2025), exact target PDF and `sources/0057/paper.layout.txt`.
- E2: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/raisa25a.html ; saved publisher snapshot.

- E5: `verification/0057/code_audit/independent_cover_check.py` and its JSON output.
- E6: `verification/0057/math_audit/independent_math_checks.py`, `independent_math_results.json` and `math_audit_notes.md`.

- Workflow: Paper 01 and Paper 02 guidance. Kassis et al. (2026), Scientific Agent Skills, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.00065 ; procedural reference, not scientific evidence for the findings.
## Appendix: actual work, failures and roles

The archive SHA-256 is `269cc0afe8c3fb37d37f7fe9a9ddad95eb8a70ce7a5ef2a28a5d626ba15017b0`; per-file hashes and acquisition URLs are retained in the code acquisition manifest. # Scientific verification report: I25-40165 (0058)

Supported impact: Major, scoped to two central quantitative derivations.
Batch B001 / [internal task]. Token: [internal identifier omitted]
Scientific decision: pending human review. Author adoption has not been requested.
## 1. Identity, version and inspected scope

Yash Goel, Ayan Sengupta and Tanmoy Chakraborty, Position: Enough of Scaling LLMs! Lets Focus on Downscaling, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81375-81392 [E1-E2]. The primary reviewed object is the 18-page publisher-linked PDF. All page references are one-based physical PDF pages, matching the printed article pages.

Primary PDF SHA-256:
`f7645a566ade49e81a277e7e47ad9a69a9ebbacd136c2f8f0c6e56ef3d5fe9f0`

Its bytes match the controller acquisition receipt and remain preserved. The review read the main argument (pp. 1-9), all Appendices A-E (pp. 16-18), and selected cited primary sources. Source pages 4, 7, 16, 17 and 18 were also inspected visually. The publisher-linked repository was acquired at commit `c5c328c359456abbd512bc5d99885315b9a851fb`, dated 2 May 2025, 03:58:47 UTC. Its 11-file tree is preserved in `sources/0058/repository/` [E3].

The arXiv record lists v1 on 2 May, v2 on 5 May, and v3 on 25 May 2025. A separate v3 PDF was acquired; targeted comparison confirms the same factor deletion in Appendix E and the same carbon-performance equations and percentage claim. This is not a complete version diff, and the publisher PDF remains the reviewed authority [E4].
## 2. Summary and scientific dependence

The paper advances a research position favoring smaller, specialized models. It also presents an explicit sufficient condition for an ensemble of pruned models to improve loss at unchanged modeled compute, and a quantitative relationship between downstream performance and carbon emissions. These technical claims supply substantive support for the position.

Two derivations fail even when their surrounding fitted-law assumptions are granted. First, Proposition 4.1 deletes a multiplicative pruning-loss factor that does not cancel. A complete finite countermodel satisfies the printed sufficient condition and the stated compute equality, yet has higher ensemble loss. Section 4.5 explicitly relies on this proposition to prescribe the proposed pipeline. Second, Eqs. (8)-(10) discard an affine intercept and reverse an exponent sign. The stated universal carbon cost of a 10% performance increase does not follow.

These are Major findings because they damage central mathematical guarantees or quantitative conclusions. Neither finding requires proving that every small-model ensemble performs poorly, that the environmental motivation is false, or that the whole downscaling agenda should be rejected. The conditional fixed-hardware carbon proportionality and the elementary ensemble reparameterization have useful valid content, discussed below.
## 3. Definitions and operative assumptions

Let N0 be the pre-pruning model size, D the post-training token count, rho the removed fraction, L0 the original loss, and n the number of equal-size pruned models. The derivation uses rho = (n-1)/n, so n must be at least 2 to avoid the singular no-pruning endpoint. Assume positive N0, D and b, and a common loss scale.
Define the factor retained in Eq. (11):
`Q = NC/N0^alpha + DC/D^beta + E.`
The two fitted relations used by Appendix E are:
- Pruned-model loss: `Lc = L0 + Q/(rho^gamma N0^delta).`
- Ensemble loss: `Le = Lc - b + b/n^a.`

The review grants these relations exactly for the algebraic countermodel. It does not claim that arbitrary coefficients describe a measured LLM. The paper additionally assumes Q is approximately constant at matched budget; the countermodel makes Q exactly constant. Equal modeled compute follows from `n K (1-rho) N0 D = K N0 D`, with fixed positive K. This does not by itself establish equal latency, energy, or orchestration overhead.

For the second finding, write carbon emissions as Ccarb to avoid confusing them with the paper’s computational budget C. The review grants its fixed-data, fixed-hardware simplification `Ccarb = Kc L^(-1/alpha)`, with Kc positive and alpha = 0.08, and its affine performance model `P = w1 + w2 L`.
## 4. Problem 1: the sufficient downscaling condition drops a decisive factor
Judgment: Major, affecting Proposition 4.1 and the pipeline’s claimed guarantee.
### Source claim and invalid step

Section 4.4, p. 7, presents Eq. (13) as a sufficient condition for strictly lower ensemble loss at the same compute. Appendix E, pp. 17-18, begins with the complete pruning law in Eq. (27), then replaces Q by 1 in Eq. (28). The explanation says Q is approximately constant and therefore cancels from both sides of the comparison. Section 4.5, p. 8, expressly directs pruning to obey this condition and uses it to assert better performance at equal cost [E1].
Substituting the two full fitted laws actually gives:
`Le - L0 = Q/(rho^gamma N0^delta) - b(1 - n^(-a)).`
Only L0 cancels. Q multiplies the pruning penalty and has no identical additive counterpart on the right-hand side. Its being constant does not make its magnitude irrelevant.
Let `g(n) = (1 - n^(-a)) ((n-1)/n)^gamma`. The printed condition is `g(n) >= 1/(b N0^delta)`. Under the assumed laws, the correct non-worse condition is:
`g(n) >= Q/(b N0^delta).`
Strict improvement requires a strict inequality. The printed non-strict antecedent cannot guarantee strict improvement even in the special case Q = 1.
### Complete countermodel
Choose the following exact values:
Quantity | Value
a, b, gamma, delta, alpha, beta | all 1
rho | 1/2

Every size and token-count variable is positive; n is a positive integer greater than 1; the pruning fraction lies strictly between 0 and 1; all fitting coefficients here are positive; and Q is exactly fixed. The example is an algebraic countermodel to the claimed implication of the assumed laws, not a purported empirical eight-parameter language model.
The printed condition passes strictly:
But the unabridged relations give:

The modeled compute is unchanged: the two retained-size-4 models each use D = 1, giving total cost 8K, equal to the base model’s 8K. Thus neither a violated budget nor a boundary equality explains the failure. The correct condition fails, as it should: 1/4 is less than 5/8. Exact rational evaluation is preserved with the independent mathematical audit [E5].
### Alternatives, counterevidence and repair

One could introduce an explicit normalization Q = 1, or redefine the ensemble coefficient after rescaling the loss. Neither follows from Q being approximately constant; either changes the hypotheses or coefficients. Similarly, allowing approximation error does not establish a robust sufficient condition without a bound on the omitted factor and on the two fitted laws.

The p. 7 LLaMA illustration also uses coefficients transferred across settings. Upstream Chen arXiv:2411.10272v2 prints gamma = +1.08 in the relevant fitted table, while v3 changes it to -1.08. The target’s positive sign can therefore be faithful to the earlier cited version and is not classified as an independent misquotation. The retained evidence preserves this history; the demonstrated factor omission is independent of it. No claim that the printed threshold is the smallest possible n is needed.

A precise conditional repair is to retain Q, use the corrected threshold above, and distinguish non-worse from strictly better loss. This repairs the algebra exactly. It does not validate transferring CNN ensemble coefficients to domain-specialized, pruned LLMs. Such transfer requires a consistent loss, units, pruning-law version, ensemble diversity assumptions and suitable measurements. If an 8B model is divided under this compute model, each member has size 8B/n; only n = 8 gives 1B members at the same total size.
## 5. Problem 2: the carbon-performance conversion is algebraically invalid
Judgment: Major, affecting the claimed quantitative environmental-performance relationship.
### Source claim and exact derivation

On p. 4, Eq. (7) relates carbon to loss with exponent -1/alpha. Eq. (8) states `P = w1 + w2 L`. Eq. (9) then uses carbon proportional to `P^(-1/alpha)`, and Eq. (10) changes to performance proportional to carbon raised to positive alpha. The text derives a fixed carbon multiplier for a 10% performance gain [E1].
Even granting Eq. (7), correct substitution gives:
`Ccarb = Kc ((P - w1)/w2)^(-1/alpha),`
on the domain `(P - w1)/w2 > 0`, or equivalently:
`P = w1 + w2 (Ccarb/Kc)^(-alpha).`

The additive intercept cannot be absorbed into a proportionality constant. Moreover, even if w1 were zero, inverting Eq. (9) gives a negative exponent, not the positive exponent in Eq. (10). Redefining performance as inverse loss would be a different premise, inconsistent with the displayed affine model.

The cited Chen et al. primary source fits an affine loss-to-performance relation to emerged, above-random observations. It neither sets the intercept to zero nor establishes a universal positive-exponent carbon law. Its current v2 also explicitly discusses limits of composing compute and performance fits across different training trajectories [E6, p. 3, Sections 2.2-2.3].
### Complete numerical check

Choose alpha = 0.08, w1 = 1 and w2 = -1/2. Let performance increase from 0.50 to 0.55, exactly 10% relative. The corresponding positive losses are L1 = 1 and L2 = 0.9. Both performance values lie in [0,1], and the sign expresses the intended improvement as loss decreases.

These values can be realized within the paper’s assumed scalar laws by taking a positive reference size Nr, setting `L = (N/Nr)^(-0.08)`, holding D and hardware fixed, and taking carbon proportional to N. Thus the witness satisfies the premises used in the carbon substitution.
Calculation | Carbon ratio C2/C1
Correct consequence of Eqs. (7)-(8): 0.9^(-12.5) | 3.732232

The three outcomes disagree. This is a check of the claimed implication, not a new measured carbon estimate. More generally, the ratio depends on the intercept and starting performance; there is no task-independent 10% rule from the stated premises. The reviewer-authored scalar calculation and output are preserved [E7].

The displayed arithmetic also confuses percentage of baseline with percentage increase: 3.291611 times the baseline is 329.161% of the baseline, or 229.161% more. This local arithmetic issue is subordinate to the invalid model conversion. A fixed power law is also not an exponential law in performance.
### Impact and precise repair

This removes the stated quantitative carbon-versus-performance conclusion used in the paper’s environmental argument. It does not establish that scaling is environmentally benign. Retaining the affine offset and exponent gives the valid conditional relation above; estimating a practical multiplier additionally requires task-specific coefficients, an operating point, the scaling trajectory for N and D, and appropriate hardware assumptions. No corrected universal percentage is justified.
## 6. Other checked claims and evidence limits

Conditional carbon proportionality. Given the paper’s fixed hardware, power, efficiency, lifetime and data-center coefficients, substituting runtime proportional to ND into its emission formulas does yield carbon proportional to ND. This is a conditional algebraic result. Changes in those coefficients or in the scaling path require separate treatment. The proof does not make K1 + K2 universal across deployments.

What Figures 2-3 show. Static inspection of `analysis.ipynb` identifies a single GPT3 database row in zero-based cell 11. Cells 18-19 vary N or D while reusing its hardware settings, append predicted emissions, and cells 20-21 plot the resulting curves. `model.py`, lines 68-117, computes FLOPs from 6ND and carbon from power times modeled runtime. Cells 14-17 similarly evaluate analytic loss bounds. These are model-generated curves; the figure labels themselves say estimated. A cached single-row residual is not independent validation of the across-size scaling relationship. The p. 4 statement of empirical validation therefore remains unsupported by an independent scaling experiment in the inspected release [E3]. This qualification does not invalidate the conditional algebra.

Ensemble reparameterization. Appendix D correctly derives Eq. (12) from L = c + b/n^a by setting the single-member loss to c + b, provided the member family and fitted coefficients remain fixed. That valid rearrangement does not justify the subsequent deletion of Q or guarantee transfer to heterogeneous domain specialists.

Loss-floor interpretation. A finite-scale lower bound depending on N and D is not a positive bound uniform in both variables. In the displayed Kaplan formula with positive exponents, both terms tend to zero when N and D grow together. Chinchilla’s explicit positive E can supply a floor. The p. 4 statement should keep these cases distinct; the review does not infer that real-world cross-entropy can be driven to zero.

The recommendations for data curation, pruning and domain specialization were read as research proposals. Their merits are not rejected for lacking a new benchmark experiment. Conversely, the empirical applicability of the proposed composed law remains unverified. The review did not reproduce training, inference, carbon measurements, the complete cited literature or every historical source revision.
## 7. Conclusion and remaining work
Item | Judgment | Repair status | Adoption / remaining work
Proposition 4.1 drops Q | Major | Correct conditional threshold proved | Not applied; refit and validate transfer
Carbon-performance conversion | Major | Affine relation restored analytically | No universal multiplier; coefficients needed
Figures 2-3 empirical validation | Needs Evidence | Model-based scope established statically | Independent measurements absent from inspected release
Fixed-coefficient carbon algebra; Appendix D | No Issue Found in checked steps | Not applicable | Keep stated conditions
Broad downscaling recommendation | Not refuted by these checks | Not a mathematical repair | Human scientific assessment pending

The original publisher PDF and the separately saved arXiv v3 preserve the inspected claims. No full errata search or author correspondence was performed. Future experiments are necessary for the proposed LLM guarantee’s applicability; they are not necessary to establish the invalid algebra already demonstrated.

# Scientific verification report: I25-40166 (0059)

Supported impact: Minor, limited to a misreported survey result.
Separate evidence concern: a cited scientific-productivity study was withdrawn; its affected claim needs replacement evidence.
Batch B001 / [internal task]. Token: [internal identifier omitted]
Scientific decision: pending human review. Author adoption has not been requested.
## 1. Identity, version and scope

Sanchaita Hazra, Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder and Tuhin Chakrabarty, Position: AI Safety Should Prioritize the Future of Work, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81542-81555 [E1-E2]. The primary reviewed object is the 14-page publisher-linked PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages, matching printed article pages.

The original 201,203 bytes match the controller receipt and remain preserved. The review read Sections 1-6, all six risk statements P1-P6, recommendations R1-R6, alternative views and selected references. Source pages 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8 were inspected visually. There is no technical appendix in this PDF and no software link on the publisher page; no new implemented method or experiment is claimed by this position paper.

The arXiv record lists v1 on 16 April 2025 and v2 on 11 July 2025. A separate v2 PDF was saved and compared at selected claims. It retains both the survey wording and the Toner-Rodgers paragraph discussed below. This was a targeted comparison, not a full version diff [E3].
## 2. Outcome and evidentiary standard

The paper argues that protection of meaningful work should be part of AI safety, using economic mechanisms, prior studies and policy recommendations. Its P1-P6 statements are argumentative propositions, not formal theorems with a fully specified statistical or equilibrium model. This review did not impose an original experiment requirement on the normative recommendation.

One bounded factual error is demonstrated: a strong survey majority is reported as unanimity. Separately, an empirical source used to support unequal gains among scientists has been formally withdrawn. That invalidates reliance on that source as affirmative evidence, but does not establish the opposite substantive result.

The headline 21%, 17% and 55.8% figures can be traced to the cited primary studies. Their population, outcome and comparison conditions must accompany them. The review found no demonstrated Major invalid derivation or central empirical refutation within the inspected scope. This is not certification of the full paper, every citation, or the effectiveness of the policy package.
## 3. Problem 1: the author survey was not unanimous
Judgment: Minor, a local statistical overstatement.

Claim and location. Section 2.6, p. 6, describes a 2023 Authors Guild survey of more than 2,000 respondents as finding unanimous opposition to uncompensated, unconsented training use. The matching primary report, dated 21 December 2023, gives more than 2,400 respondents and a 96% / 3% / 1% response split: required consent and payment / accepted use without them / unsure [E4].

The observed nonzero dissent contradicts unanimity. This requires no hypothetical counterexample or estimation assumption. Reading the word as rhetorical emphasis explains the intended message but does not make the reported statistic exact.

Impact and repair. The strong-majority rationale survives. Replace unanimity with the stated 96% of survey respondents; do not generalize this sample to every author. This correction is verified against the primary summary. It has not been applied to the source paper, and author adoption remains unrequested.
## 4. Known source withdrawal: the scientific-productivity paragraph
Status: verified source withdrawal; affected empirical inference Needs Evidence.

On p. 5, Section 2.5.1, the paper invokes Toner-Rodgers (2024) for a mechanism in which leading scientists identify useful AI suggestions while others spend effort testing false positives. It then extends the concern to junior researchers. The cited work is Artificial Intelligence, Scientific Discovery, and Product Innovation, arXiv:2412.17866.

The primary record establishes two distinct events. MIT’s statement of 16 May 2025 disavowed confidence in the data and research and requested withdrawal [E5]. The arXiv record separately confirms administrator withdrawal on 20 May 2025, citing data-validity concerns and incomplete Institutional Review Board requirements [E6]. The April target preprint predates those events; the inspected publisher PDF and the separately saved July v2 retain the affected claim. This chronology is recorded without inferring author knowledge or intent.

The withdrawn study cannot presently establish the claimed distributional mechanism. Removing that reliance, or replacing it with independently credible evidence, is warranted. A replacement has not been supplied or validated here. Withdrawal does not prove that experienced scientists never benefit more from AI, nor does it invalidate the paper’s other learning-risk evidence. The unsupported local inference is therefore not upgraded to Major.
## 5. Primary-source checks that constrain interpretation
### Online labor demand

A preserved Demirci, Hannane and Zhu working paper dated 22 April 2024 reports 20.86% and 17.01%, matching the rounded figures. These are relative changes in job-post counts on one freelancing platform against manual-intensive categories, estimated using difference-in-differences. Tables 2-3 are on physical PDF pp. 12 and 14; the demand-versus-employment distinction is explicit on p. 4 [E7].

The target’s p. 3 correctly supplies the comparator. On p. 1, retain “job posts” for image-related work. These estimates are not counts of displaced workers or economy-wide employment losses. The review checked the estimand and numerical transformations, not the underlying dataset or every identifying assumption.
### Programming task performance

Peng et al., arXiv:2302.06590v1, reports a randomized study of 95 developers performing one JavaScript HTTP-server task. The headline figure concerns time among completers: 35 per arm, with means 71.17 and 160.89 minutes, giving a rounded 55.8% reduction [E8, pp. 3-5].

This supports the task-specific result, not a direct estimate of hiring, wages or full-project productivity. The study’s exploratory heterogeneity points toward larger benefits for less-experienced developers; it does not independently support the nearby high-skill-advantage prediction. The authors themselves discuss generalization limits on pp. 7-8. No numerical error in the cited headline was established.
### Learning risk and design dependence

The later published Bastani et al. study reports worse unaided performance after access to an unrestricted tutor, while a guarded tutor largely mitigated the harm. Its abstract and significance statement were checked in the PNAS record and author-hosted manuscript [E9]. This is compatible with the target’s concern that AI can harm learning. It does not justify treating all AI tutoring designs as equivalent. The complete experiment and its raw data were not reanalyzed.
## 6. Argument checks, alternatives and limits

Economic mechanisms. The life-cycle and permanent-income discussion identifies income uncertainty and adjustment costs as plausible pathways. It does not estimate a savings response or supply the preferences, borrowing constraints and income process needed for a unique prediction. Its expanded use of technical debt is a conceptual analogy, not a measured financial liability. These distinctions should remain explicit when presenting P1 as a risk mechanism.

Automation can displace some tasks while creating or complementing others. The paper itself acknowledges new-task mechanisms in Section 2.2 and discusses market adaptation in Section 4.1. Those passages are counterevidence against reading the paper as a formal assertion that every deployment necessarily destroys net employment. The categorical phrasing of P2 and the Section 3 opening should be understood with this context and the narrower empirical studies above. A general distributional forecast still needs more evidence than those studies alone.

Detection and watermarking. The p. 5 statement about impossibility after fine-tuning lacks a specified attack, model distribution, text length, false-positive constraint or detector access model. The subsequent paragraph concerns customized evasion, a narrower and defensible concern. The review therefore records a needed scope qualification rather than constructing a counterexample from an unrelated kind of fine-tuning. It establishes no universal impossibility theorem; the selected detector citations and their limits are recorded in the independent argument audit [E10].

Sections 2.5.2 and 3 explicitly acknowledge detector false positives and watermark bypasses; p. 5 cautions against using detection alone for discipline. Advocating improved watermarking despite imperfect robustness is not a logical contradiction. The collective-action discussion is an incentive analogy without a quantified payoff matrix, not an empirically established unique equilibrium.

Governance recommendations. Worker support, representation, licensing and disclosure are proposed interventions. Their desirability combines empirical expectations with value judgments. The paper does not establish that a single global licensing mechanism already exists or that Shapley allocation is universally fair under every normative criterion. No new proof of that cited mechanism is claimed here. Its technical details, jurisdiction-specific copyright questions, litigation outcomes and practical policy costs were not comprehensively audited in this review.

The retained analysis distinguishes these open questions from demonstrated errors. Absence of a new experiment alone is not used as a defect. Conversely, agreement with the broad aim of worker protection does not validate every factual premise or ensure that the proposed interventions will achieve it.
## 7. Conclusion table
Item | Judgment | Repair verification | Adoption / remaining work
Survey reported as unanimous | Minor | Primary response distribution checked | Correct wording; not applied
Toner-Rodgers empirical support | Known source withdrawal; Needs Evidence | Withdrawal chronology verified | Remove or replace support; no replacement validated
21%, 17%, 55.8% | No numerical issue found | Source estimates and arithmetic checked | Preserve outcome, comparator and task scope
Detection impossibility; broad distributional forecasts | Scope clarification / Needs Evidence | No universal claim established | Specify threat model and evidentiary domain
Pro-worker AI safety recommendation | Normative position not refuted by these checks | Not an empirical repair | Human scientific and policy assessment pending

The demonstrated correction is local. The source withdrawal is material to one cited evidentiary link, but pending claims do not raise the supported severity. No author correspondence, empirical replication, policy deployment or comprehensive errata search was performed.
## 8. References and retained evidence

The Impact of Generative AI on Online Freelancing Platforms, author working paper, 22 April 2024: https://questromworld.bu.edu/platformstrategy/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2024/06/PlatStrat2024_paper_119.pdf . # Scientific verification report: I25-40168 (0060)

Supported impact: Minor, for demonstrated source-characterization and printed-prompt defects.
Central unresolved item: Needs Evidence for the calculation of prediction-based regret.
Batch B001 / [internal task]. Token: [internal identifier omitted]
Scientific decision: pending human review. Author adoption has not been requested.
## 1. Identity, version and scope

Matthew Riemer, Zahra Ashktorab, Djallel Bouneffouf, Payel Das, Miao Liu, Justin D. Weisz and Murray Campbell, Position: Theory of Mind Benchmarks are Broken for Large Language Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82091-82130 [E1-E2]. The primary reviewed object is the 40-page publisher-linked PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages, matching printed article pages.

The original 8,779,996 bytes match the controller receipt and remain preserved. The review covered the main argument, Definitions 2.1-2.2, the regret comparator, Tables 1-10, conceptual Appendices A/B, experimental descriptions in Appendix C, selected prompt images and selected learning curves. Figure captions throughout Appendix C were read; all curves were not numerically reconstructed.

The arXiv record identifies v1 on 27 December 2024, v2 on 5 February 2025, v3 on 6 June 2025 and v4 on 12 June 2025. A separate v4 PDF and its TeX-source archive were preserved. Targeted comparison confirms the same selected nonzero IPD values and comparator description; this is not a complete version diff. The TeX was read statically and was not executed [E3-E4].
## 2. Outcome and evidentiary standard

The paper advocates evaluating actions and adaptation in addition to explicit predictions about other agents. It defines literal and functional theory of mind operationally, permits model-free implementations, and recognizes that prediction alone can suffice for insight-only applications. Its position is therefore strongest when interpreted as a warning against granting agency solely on the strength of predictive benchmarks.

Two bounded defects are demonstrated: an inaccurate description of cited interactive studies, and a prompt example that mixes prediction of the partner’s action with selection of the agent’s own action. Both support Minor corrections. Their historical runtime effects have not been established.

A separate, consequential question concerns `Delta_ToM / T`. A stagewise interpretation contradicts the reported single-action IPD values, but the general policy notation permits a different, counterfactual planning interpretation. The available description does not identify the actual estimator sufficiently to choose between them. This remains Needs Evidence, with an exact conditional diagnostic and an explicit counterexample to overclaiming recorded below.

A demonstrated invalid core metric or implementation would support Major even if the broad recommendation survived or repair were easy. The present limitation is identification of the actual computation, not a requirement to prove that corrected experiments worsen performance. No empirical replication, author-code execution or model/API call was performed.
## 3. Finding 1: cited studies do contain interaction
Judgment: Minor, literature-characterization error.

Claim and location. Section 3, p. 5, groups persona simulation, trust behavior and macroeconomic simulation studies, then says these tasks all lack interactivity. The matching primary sources contain interaction, including feedback used in subsequent decisions.
Cited study | Preserved version and locator | Directly relevant evidence

Xie et al., trust behavior | arXiv:2402.04559v1, PDF p. 3, Game 6; Appendix C, PDF p. 21 | A repeated trust game uses the same players. The next-round prompt supplies the previous amounts sent, received and returned before eliciting another decision.

Ha et al., CloChat | arXiv:2402.15265v1, Section 5.3, PDF p. 9 | Participants conduct live conversations with CloChat and ChatGPT; the procedure permits natural dialogue without imposed time or length limits.
Li et al., macroeconomic agents | arXiv:2310.10436v1, Section 4.2, PDF pp. 7-8 | A memory pool retains prior environments and decisions; periodic reflection informs later decisions.

Xie is the strongest witness because the interaction involves the same partner, outcome feedback and another action. Ha corroborates human-agent interaction; Li corroborates sequential environment interaction. These are evidence for one correction, not three independently inflated findings [E5-E7].

Strongest alternative reading. The authors may mean that these studies do not isolate reward-optimal partner adaptation or compare explicit prediction quality with the quality of resulting actions. That would be a narrower and potentially useful distinction. It does not make the no-interaction description accurate. The present checks do not establish that these earlier studies already implement the proposed paired metrics or achieve low functional regret.

Repair and impact. Acknowledge existing interactive work and specify which controlled diagnostic remains missing. Explain the value added by paired prediction/action measurements and regret. This changes the motivation and literature characterization; it does not establish that the paper’s observed prediction/action discrepancies are false.

The preserved Ha v1 has different presentation and pagination from the final CHI paper, but its title, DOI and procedure identify the study. Li v1 is the earlier four-author work corresponding to the cited 2023 title; the later EconAgent revision is not silently substituted. Xie v1 already contains the repeated-game protocol. All three versions predate the target.
## 4. Finding 2: Figure 13 mixes two prediction targets
Judgment: Minor for the printed example; historical experimental impact Needs Evidence.

Section 4.2, p. 7, cites Figure 13 as the CoT 3-Shot variant of the action-selection prompt. In Figure 13, p. 23, the three examples reason about the focal agent’s own best response. Yet the final prompt states that the focal agent has already chosen Option J and asks which option the other player chose. It then asks for the best action. The final target is therefore ambiguous between predicting the partner and choosing the focal agent’s action.

This is visible in the original page image, so it is not a text-extraction artifact. Figures 4-7 separately illustrate action selection and literal prediction; the distinction is central to the experiment. Figure 13 does not clearly specify the action-selection procedure cited in the main text.

Strongest alternative reading. The figure could be a presentation mistake, or could show the prediction variant without an adequate label. Either possibility limits the demonstrated defect to the printed protocol. No execution trace or experiment implementation was located that establishes which template generated the reported CoT 3-Shot rows.

Repair. Supply separately labeled templates for choosing one’s own action and predicting the partner’s action. For an action-selection template, remove the statement that the action is already chosen and ask directly which action the agent should take. Check the actual run configuration before deciding whether only the figure needs correction or the affected results need recalculation. The proposed textual repair has not been applied to the source paper or validated in an LLM experiment.
## 5. Central pending item: reconcile prediction-based IPD regret
Status: Needs Evidence; conditional contradiction established, unconditional implementation defect not established.
### What must be reconciled

Sections 2.1-2.2, pp. 3-4, describe a rational policy based on predicted partner behavior and ground-truth payoffs, with its regret reported as `Delta_ToM / T`. The active TeX text gives the same description at lines 280 and 284. Table 2, p. 7, nevertheless reports nonzero IPD comparator regrets against single-action partners, including 0.098 for LM prompting and 1.342 for QA prompting. Table 4, p. 9, reports 0.360 for the DeepSeek single-action IPD row; Tables 8-9 also contain nonzero values.
Table 7, p. 18, gives the following focal-agent rewards:
Focal action | Partner cooperates | Partner defects
Cooperate | 8 | 0
Defect | 10 | 5
For any forecast probability q that the partner cooperates, if that forecast is independent of the candidate focal action:
- Expected cooperation reward is `8q`.
- Expected defection reward is `10q + 5(1-q) = 5 + 5q`.
- Defection’s advantage is `5 - 3q >= 2` for every q between 0 and 1.

Thus a stagewise rational response always defects, regardless of whether the next-action forecast is correct. Against the actual fixed-action partners, always defecting is also optimal over the whole episode. Under this specific reading, prediction-based regret must be zero. Sampling error or a confidence interval cannot explain a nonzero value for this exact deterministic identity.
### Why that is not an unconditional proof of a bug

The general notation allows a model of an entire counterfactual partner policy, not only a forecast independent of the focal action. An incorrect model could predict retaliation after defection, making cooperation rational under the model even when the true partner is fixed.

An independent 100-step example makes this distinction concrete. Let the true partner always cooperate. Let the imagined partner cooperate until the focal agent first defects, then defect forever from the next round. The optimal response to the imagined policy is to cooperate for 99 rounds and defect in the last round. Its reward against the true partner is `99*8 + 10 = 802`; the true optimal always-defect policy earns 1,000. Regret is therefore 1.98 per step, despite correct partner predictions along the chosen path. A small independent backward-induction calculation verifies the policy and rewards [E8].

This example satisfies the broader full-policy interpretation and defeats the claim that every possible rational model-based response must have zero regret. It is a diagnostic counterexample, not an explanation of the published numbers.
### What the available artifacts establish

The prompt images elicit the next partner action. Figure 2 includes the focal agent’s already selected current action, while Figure 3 predicts the partner first; Figure 18 passes a single predicted action into an action-selection prompt. These differences matter. They do not by themselves document a counterfactual rollout model, how candidate actions are queried, a planning horizon, or a transition/value computation for the reported comparator.

The preserved arXiv source archive contains manuscript, bibliography/style material and figure assets, with no experiment implementation located. Its active metric text supplies no additional estimator or planner specification. A publisher/paper/author-page search did not locate a clearly linked implementation; OpenReview was blocked by a verification wall. These are bounded search results, not a claim that code does not exist.

Required resolution. Supply the exact estimator or relevant code excerpt, the information supplied to its optimizer, treatment of counterfactual actions and continuation values, and an example episode connecting forecasts to the reported regret. If the comparator is stagewise, correct the single-action IPD values to the appropriate zero-regret baseline and recompute dependent summaries. If it is a full-policy planner, document and validate that procedure. Until then, the numerical comparator and inferences specifically relying on it remain unverified.
This question is central enough to require resolution. It is not labeled a demonstrated Major because the alternative semantics are real and the historical calculation has not been identified.
## 6. Additional checks and interpretation limits

Task relevance. The p. 4 relevance metric compares optimal responses across partners. Under a uniform distribution over the three fixed RPS actions, its expected per-step value is 1, matching the paper. For fixed-action IPD partners it is 0, because the same always-defect policy is optimal for both. Static IPD is consequently a useful control for payoff-directed decision making, but provides no partner-dependent optimal-action distinction under that metric. Dynamic tit-for-tat partners require a separate analysis; the zero result is not transferred to them.

Prediction versus action. A good next-action predictor need not be a good controller, and the paper explicitly permits model-free policies. A constant-action heuristic therefore does not refute its stipulated literal-ToM definition. Likewise, poor oracle-assisted choices can expose payoff reasoning or context-handling problems. They do not, by themselves, isolate a failure to infer another agent’s hidden mental state. The paper’s functional objective intentionally includes decision competence.

Reward versus regret. At a fixed task and comparator, cumulative regret is the optimal return minus the achieved return. The p. 4 wording about a constant factor should be expressed as a sign reversal plus an additive task-specific constant. Rankings correspond when the comparator is fixed; pooling tasks with different comparators needs care. No additional demonstrated table error follows from this wording alone.

Scope of the headline. Section 5, p. 9, explicitly allows insight-only uses of literal ToM and defends its stronger terminology for applications in which AI receives agency. Section 3 also acknowledges prior interactive and behavioral game-theory work. These qualifications constrain the paper’s claim and must remain in a faithful review. The recommendation for direct action evaluation is not refuted by the two local corrections.

Experimental coverage. Appendix C specifies 100-step episodes, a 24-hour or 100-episode limit and at least 30 episodes per model. The review read reported aggregates and selected curves, including Figures 19, 28-29 and 42-43. It did not reproduce model outputs, reconstruct confidence intervals, validate the RMax implementation or recover exact per-condition episode counts. Figure trends over 100 steps should be described at that finite horizon; an asymptotic convergence conclusion would need separate support. The reasoning-model successes reported in Table 4 also preclude an accurate summary that every model always fails.

# 3. Problem 1 - Released subsample does not fully recover the stated analysis input

Source claim and location. Appendix A.2, p.16 describes two time-based samples of 30 draws each, plus all 56 top-4 papers, for 116 sample memberships. The sum is 115, with 111 distinct rows across overlapping groups. Thus the linked public dataset does not encode one of the declared newer-group draws. report: Author: AI-assisted scientific verification; human decision pending
Date: 24 October 2026
Title: 0063 | Scientific Verification Report
I25-40171 | Danhofer, D’Ascenzo, Dubach and Poggio | Position: A Theory of Deep Learning Must Include Compositional Sparsity | PMLR 267:81199-81210 (2025). Reviewed publisher PDF: 12 pages.

Overall finding: Major. Problem 1 is a demonstrated invalid extension of a core approximation theorem; Problem 2 is a bounded Minor error about CNN parameter symmetries. Human scientific decision pending; author adoption not requested.
# 1. Identity, version and review boundary

The original PDF was read from papers/0063/0063.pdf and its SHA-256 matched the controller acquisition receipt before scientific review. Its title, authors, proceedings identity and 12-page length agree with the publisher record. Original bytes were preserved. Page references below use the printed 1-12 pagination.

Code:
SHA-256: 35ac6f45b1dc829139a90f2f18d646d5afc1e6b54ec4ca60c51467feb4d95c36

The main text (pp.1-8) and Appendix A (p.12) were inspected, with focused primary-source checking of the approximation and computability bridges. References were checked selectively. The published PDF remains the review target. The target’s arXiv record shows v1 dated 3 July 2025; no full text comparison with that version was performed.
Claim / location | Verification and result

Definition 3.1, Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.4; p.3 | Compare original 2017 assumptions and give an analytic counterexample to the unrestricted continuous-domain approximation statement: Problem 1, Major.
Theorem 3.2 and Appendix A; pp.2-3,12 | Check Boolean circuit-family interpretation and exact neural gate emulation. Boolean result survives. Real-input precision bridge needs additional hypotheses.
CNN symmetry argument; Section 4.2, p.5 | Construct two distinct convolutional parameterizations with identical outputs for all inputs: Problem 2, Minor.

Learnability, supervision and conjectures; Sections 4-6, pp.4-8 | Inspect dependencies and qualifiers. The manuscript distinguishes representability from efficient learning and assumes constituent supervision where used; no blanket learnability claim is attributed to it.
# 2. Problem 1 (Major): bounded fan-in does not imply the asserted approximation theorem

Claim and location. On p.3, Theorem 3.3(2), labeled an informal statement of Poggio et al. (2017), assigns a graph-mimicking deep network complexity O(d epsilon^-2) for a compositionally sparse function. Definition 3.1 requires only polynomially many constituents with constant fan-in. The paragraph following Corollary 3.4 expressly says that approximation imposes no further restriction on the node-function class. Corollary 3.4 is then derived by combining Theorems 3.2 and 3.3.

Source check. The cited 2017 paper specifies uniform approximation and derivative-bounded function classes. Its Theorem 2, printed p.5, assumes a binary-tree class with constituents in W_m^2 and an infinitely differentiable, nonpolynomial activation; its rate is O((n-1) epsilon^(-2/m)). Its proof uses Lipschitz control. The arbitrary-DAG Theorem 3, p.6, still requires regularity classes for individual nodes and gives a sum of rates depending on their dimensions and smoothness. Its ReLU discussion also retains regularity assumptions. None of these statements establishes a fan-in-only theorem for arbitrary real node functions.

Exact scope of the refutation. The target omits a norm and activation class. The following counterexample uses the uniform norm and continuous activations of the cited approximation setting; it also applies to ReLU networks. Under this natural source-based interpretation the unrestricted statement is false. Choosing a different norm or a discontinuous activation class requires a newly specified theorem and proof.

\[X=[-1,1],\quad d=2^k\geq128,\qquad
f_d(x)=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i\geq0\right\}.\] Build a complete binary tree with constituent A(u,v)=(u+v)/2, then append h(t)=1{t>=0}. The averaging tree computes the mean using d-1 binary nodes; the final threshold is unary. This construction depends on every coordinate and avoids any need to interpret unused input slots.
Original hypothesis | Counterexample check
Function X^d -> X | The output is 0 or 1, both in X.
At most O(poly d) constituents | There are exactly d nodes: d-1 averages and one threshold.
Small constant fan-in c | Every node has fan-in at most 2, independently of d.
Node outputs remain in X | Averages of members of [-1,1] remain in [-1,1]; threshold outputs also belong to X.
No extra node-class restriction | Definition 3.1 and the explicit p.3 explanation admit this threshold constituent.
Network interpretation used | Every finite feedforward network with continuous activations computes a continuous function q.
Proof. Let a=q(0). For x^(j)=(-1/j,0,...,0), the target is zero and x^(j) tends to zero. Continuity gives q(x^(j))->a, whereas f_d(0)=1. Therefore the supremum error obeys:

\[\|q-f_d\|_{\infty}\geq
\max\{|a|,|1-a|\}\geq\frac12,
\qquad 1\leq |a|+|1-a|.\] The constant function q=1/2 attains the lower bound, so the obstruction is exact. Taking epsilon=1/4 contradicts the claimed availability of a finite O(16d)-parameter approximation: no finite continuous-activation network achieves that uniform error, irrespective of size. The proof is analytic. Reviewer-written rational spot checks are supporting arithmetic checks, not substitutes for the limiting argument.

Dependency and severity. This is a substantial invalid derivation in the paper’s central link from compositional structure to approximation complexity, expressly used to obtain Corollary 3.4. That direct dependency warrants Major. The result does not require showing that the entire research agenda fails or that every restricted theorem is false. The position-paper label and informal presentation do not remove the explicit scope mismatch.

Strongest alternative readings. Restricting the claim to the original regular node classes restores a meaningful restricted theorem, but changes the target’s definition-to-theorem implication and its express fan-in-only assertion. A distribution-dependent Lp approximation can behave differently for this discontinuity and is not refuted by this example; it is also not the uniform theorem cited. Threshold activations can represent the example exactly, but require a different network class and an independently justified general rate.

Limits. The threshold function is not claimed to be polynomial-time computable under a Type-2 real-number representation. Thus this example directly refutes the unrestricted Theorem 3.3 reading, not every possible formalization of the real-valued Corollary 3.4. The invalid displayed derivation and a separately false conclusion are distinct claims.
# 3. A bounded repair and the Boolean result that survives

A defensible repair of Theorem 3.3 would restore a precise domain, norm, activation class and constituent smoothness/norm assumptions. Node count, arity and error propagation through the graph must be reflected in the bound. The source’s linear node count for a binary tree cannot simply stand for every polynomial-size DAG. This report verifies the restricted source comparison; it does not certify a replacement theorem for all real-valued FP functions.

Theorem 3.2 has a sound Boolean reading: for a fixed polynomial-time machine and each bit-input length n, a polynomial-size bounded-fan-in Boolean circuit computes its output. Use a standard finite basis such as AND/OR/NOT or NAND, and interpret multiple output bits componentwise or with a multi-output DAG. A polynomial-overhead Turing-machine-to-circuit simulation suffices; the exact sharper simulation rate is unnecessary here. The primary circuit construction in Barak’s text corroborates this implication.
Boolean Corollary 3.4 also has an independent exact construction. For a,b in {0,1}, with R(t)=max(0,t), use:

\[\operatorname{AND}(a,b)=R(a+b-1),\quad
\operatorname{OR}(a,b)=a+b-R(a+b-1),\quad
\operatorname{NOT}(a)=R(1-a).\] Each gate costs constant network size on the Boolean domain; replacing polynomially many gates yields a polynomial-size neural DAG with exact outputs. Layered implementations may need identity relays and still have polynomial size. The full four-row Boolean truth table was checked exactly. This preserves Boolean representability without invoking the defective unrestricted approximation theorem, and says nothing by itself about learning the circuit from input-output examples.

Appendix A’s broad suggestion that any k-input gate can be replaced by k-1 binary gates needs a basis qualification. It is valid for k-input AND/OR gates, not arbitrary truth-table gates. Starting with a standard bounded-fan-in simulation already supplies the needed result. This is a proof-wording clarification, not a separate rejection of Theorem 3.2.

Real-valued scope remains unproved as written. Appendix A controls complexity in bitlength n; the corollary uses coordinate dimension d and error epsilon. A real-input representation, input/output precision, runtime dependence, and a justified connection from encoded-bit networks to raw real inputs in the chosen norm are needed. Those missing links are recorded as a scope/proof gap supporting Problem 1, not counted as an additional independently refuted theorem.
# 4. Problem 2 (Minor): convolution preserves hidden-channel permutation symmetries

Claim and location. Section 4.2, p.5, attributes avoidance of weight-space permutation symmetries to CNN translational equivariance and links that mechanism to a simpler optimization landscape. Standard convolutional networks retain permutations of hidden channels.

Counterexample with actual parameters. At every spatial site z, let a hidden 1x1 convolution have two kernels K=(1,2), zero biases and ReLU activations. Follow it with a linear 1x1 convolution with channel weights L=(3,5). Simultaneously swap the hidden channels and their corresponding output weights, giving K’=(2,1), L’=(5,3). Then:

\[F(z)=3R(z)+5R(2z)=13R(z)
=5R(2z)+3R(z)=F'(z),\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}.\] The parameter vectors are distinct, all operations remain convolutional, and applying the same rule at each location preserves translation equivariance on a periodic or unrestricted spatial domain. The equality is an algebraic identity, not merely an equality on test examples. Independent reviewer checks used a second choice of kernels and biases and confirmed the same phenomenon.

The weaker interpretation that weight sharing restricts arbitrary permutations of individual spatial units is reasonable. It does not eliminate hidden-channel permutations. A correction should identify which symmetries are restricted, retain the channel symmetry, and qualify any optimization advantage rather than infer it from complete symmetry removal.

Severity is Minor because this is a bounded architectural/optimization explanation, with no demonstrated failure of the Boolean circuit result or additional failure of the main approximation bridge. Ease of correction and the paper’s genre are not the grading basis.
# 5. Counterevidence, version checks and unperformed work

The manuscript explicitly separates efficient representation from efficient learnability in Section 4 and acknowledges cryptographic worst-case barriers. Corollary 4.3 assumes training sets for the constituents. These qualifications prevent treating the paper as a claim that arbitrary FP functions are efficiently learnable from ordinary end-to-end examples. Chain-of-thought and optimization discussions include conjectural or agenda-level claims; no new numerical benchmark is presented here.

A later related primary record, Tomaso Poggio’s arXiv:2510.11942v1, was submitted on 13 October 2025. Its description explicitly treats input quantization, output precision and neural emulators of encoded computations. It is not treated as an erratum, an audited repair, or a substitute for the ICML PDF. The chronology and relationship to the target’s 2025 memo citation were not fully reconstructed. The later abstract and HTML have differing title/author displays; bibliographic attribution here follows the official arXiv abstract.

Not performed: a full proof audit of every cited learning/generalization theorem, verification of all Rademacher-complexity constants, a formal real-computability model or certified general repair, training experiments, author-code execution, and full comparisons with OpenReview/arXiv versions. No current-paper implementation or experimental reproduction package was identified in the inspected primary materials. Absence of a new experiment in this position paper is not itself a finding.

Evidence status: the unrestricted uniform approximation counterexample and CNN algebraic counterexample are established within their stated assumptions. Missing real-precision details remain a proof/scope question. Human scientific review and final scientific decisions remain pending; no correction has been adopted by authors.
# 6. Evidence, replay and delivery provenance

The original-source identity and acquisition records are in verification/0063/. The cited 2017 PDF is preserved under sources/0063/peer_poggio2017/ with SHA-256 40b03d9e4fe34a158a146411386ce926d022f38a6a3c59e90e99638fb8dd3b62. Detailed source locators and comparison notes are in peer_theorem_check.json; computability_review_notes.json records the independent circuit and channel-symmetry audit.

Run the reviewer-written verification/0063/reviewer_math_checks.py or computability_exact_checks.py with the existing Python runtime to regenerate the exact finite checks. Their JSON results distinguish finite checks from universal analytic proofs. Supporting source-download manifests record URLs, dates, hashes and failures. No author code, installation or paid model call was used.

The present delivery is compiled from this self-contained TeX using the existing Tectonic runtime and a task-local offline cache.
