report: Author: AI-assisted scientific verification; human decision pending
Date: 24 October 2026
Title: 0064 | Scientific Verification Report
I25-40172 | South et al. | Position: AI Agents Need Authenticated Delegation | PMLR 267:82211-82231 (2025). Reviewed publisher PDF: 21 pages.

Overall finding: Minor. Two bounded corrections are supported: an OIDC token-role misdescription and an incorrect legal-case name in the bibliography. Further protocol details need evidence; no complete-system security failure was demonstrated. Human scientific decision pending; author adoption not requested.
# 1. Identity, version and coverage

The original papers/0064/0064.pdf was hashed before review and matched the controller receipt. Its title, seven-author list, page count and proceedings identity match the official PMLR record. An independently downloaded current publisher-linked PDF was byte-identical to the reviewed file. Original bytes were preserved.

The review covers the main argument and technical proposal (pp.1-9), background and token specification (Appendices A-B, pp.14-17), scoping and limitations (C-D, pp.17-20), and example use cases (E, pp.20-21). References were checked selectively against primary standards and cited feasibility examples. Figures and relevant source text on pp.5 and 10 were visually checked.
Claim group | Check and result
OIDC/OAuth baseline and proposed extension; Sections3.1-3.2 | Compare OIDC Core 1.0 errata set 2, RFC6749 and RFC8252. Minor token-role error; extension details remain partly unspecified.
User, agent and delegation tokens; AppendixB | Inspect key binding, audience, federation and stated threat model. Requirements needing evidence; no invented validator or exploit.
Natural-language-to-policy conversion; Section4,AppendicesC-D | Read explicit future-work and reliability caveats; verify two primary cited examples. No Issue Found within this conceptual scope.
Legal illustration; Section5.3,p7;referencep10 | Case name is incorrect in the bibliography. Publisher’s own case identification and reproduced ruling paragraphs support the Air Canada illustration.
Deployment scenarios; AppendixE | Read as proposed enforcement examples, not empirical tests or proved end-to-end security.

The related arXiv record 2501.09674 shows v1 dated 16 January 2025, under Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents, with eight authors including Dazza Greenwood. That title/author version was not substituted for the seven-author PMLR paper. A full revision comparison was not performed.
# 2. Problem 1 (Minor): the baseline OIDC UserInfo flow uses the wrong token

Location and claim. At the transition from p.4 to p.5, Section 3.1 describes ordinary OIDC as letting a merchant submit an ID token to an OP token-validation endpoint to obtain further user information. This conflates ID-token validation with retrieval of claims through UserInfo.

Primary standard. OpenID Connect Core 1.0 incorporating errata set 2 (15 December 2023), Sections 5.3 and 5.3.1, specifies UserInfo access using an Access Token. Section 3.1.3.7 separately specifies ID-token validation. These provisions do not require a generic endpoint that turns an ID token into a UserInfo request.

Concrete standards-level witness. Consider a conforming provider that issues an ID token I and a distinct access token A to registered client C. Its UserInfo endpoint recognizes A as an access credential and rejects I as an invalid access credential. C can still validate I and obtain UserInfo using A. This provider implements the standard yet does not implement the manuscript’s claimed ID-token exchange. This is an analytic protocol comparison; no live provider, real account or token request was used.
Operation | Credential and responsibility
Validate the user’s authentication result | The relying party validates the ID token according to OIDC rules.
Request additional user claims | The client presents the appropriate Access Token to UserInfo.
Validate the proposed agent delegation | The new credential and verification service require an explicit extension/profile; this behavior does not follow merely from OIDC Core support.

Strongest alternative reading. A particular provider may expose a nonstandard tokeninfo or introspection service. Section 3.2 also explicitly proposes custom registration and newly introduced delegation credentials, so the authors can define additional endpoints. These possibilities preserve the broader design direction but do not make the described background behavior part of ordinary OIDC Core.

Impact and severity. Minor: Section 3.1 incorrectly substitutes an ID token for the access credential used by UserInfo. Section 3.2 instead proposes customized registration and new delegation credentials; Figure 2 explicitly adds delegation mechanisms. Its identity-and-scope architecture does not require the erroneous baseline exchange. ’Standard OP’ therefore needs qualification as an appropriately extended provider with a defined credential-validation profile; ordinary OIDC Core support does not supply that profile. No specific authentication or non-escalation inference in the customized design depends on ID-token access to UserInfo. Missing user-key binding and audience rules remain unresolved design requirements, rather than a demonstrated failed guarantee. Minor is based on this documented dependency and the source’s explicit extension scope.

Local correction supported by the check. Separate ID-token validation from UserInfo retrieval using an access token. Identify any ID-token introspection or custom delegation-verification endpoint as an extension, with its authentication and authorization requirements. This correction was checked against standards; no complete repaired implementation was built or tested.
# 3. Problem 2 (Minor): the cited Air Canada case is misnamed

Location and observed discrepancy. The p.10 reference attributed to the Civil Resolution Tribunal names Patel v. wong while giving neutral citation 2024 BCCRT 149 and a CanLII URL containing that citation. Section 5.3 on p.7 describes the Air Canada chatbot dispute.

Independent source check. CanLII’s own 7 March 2024 publication identifies 2024 BCCRT 149 as Moffatt v. Air Canada and reproduces paragraphs 27-28, addressing the airline’s responsibility for the chatbot information on its website. That source supports the identity of the case and the general example described in the main text.

Correction and impact. Replace the incorrect case name with Moffatt v. Air Canada while retaining the verified neutral citation and appropriate source URL. This is a reference-identity error affecting traceability. The checked main-text illustration remains supported; no demonstrated damage to the proposed delegation mechanism or broader legal motivation follows.

Retrieval limit. The full CanLII decision returned HTTP403 and the direct tribunal page was inaccessible through the web tool. The check uses the legal publisher’s own identification and reproduced decision paragraphs, not an independently reviewed full judgment. No comprehensive doctrinal conclusion, current-law advice or certification of the other legal citations is made.
# 4. Protocol requirements that remain Needs Evidence

User-signature binding (B.1, p.15). Hash references to an OP-issued user ID token and an Agent-ID token do not themselves identify the public key authorized to sign the separate delegation token. OIDC Core’s mandatory ID-token fields do not include an end-user public key. A concrete profile should bind the delegation-verification key to the authenticated user and specify how that binding is established and checked.

Counterevidence and limit. The manuscript’s requirement that the human user signs the delegation token can reasonably presuppose an authenticated user key. Customized registration or an additional credential can provide it. The paper does not present a complete validator accepting arbitrary keys, so this review does not manufacture an impersonation attack by assuming such an implementation.

Audience and cross-service use (B.1-B.3, pp.15-16). Standard ID-token validation requires the relying party’s client identifier to appear in the token audience. Shared trust in the OP alone does not make a token issued to one client a valid login token for any other client. The delegation profile needs defined audiences, issuer trust and permitted cross-service verification semantics.

Counterevidence and limit. Purpose-built delegation credentials, suitable audience values or token exchange can supply a valid design. Wrapping a token in another credential does not by itself explain those rules, but an incomplete profile is not evidence that a deployed verifier disables audience checks.

Further implementation boundaries. A deployable system also needs enforceable scope semantics, replay and freshness handling, revocation behavior and rules for delegation across agents. The manuscript names validity/revocation information and describes a threat model; this review did not verify an implementation or formal security proof. The conditional threat-mitigation discussion in B.5 should be read at that proposal-level resolution.
# 5. Scoping: explicit limitations and positive evidence

Section 4.1, p.6, proposes translation to structured resource policies followed by human review, and expressly defers validation and robustness evaluation. Section 5.1 and Appendix D.2, p.20, acknowledge mistranslation, fallible human review, prompt-injection-driven privilege expansion, contextual drift and dependence on third-party enforcement. These limitations are already disclosed and are not recast as new demonstrated defects.

The cited IBAC-DB work describes generation of PostgreSQL permission rules from natural-language intent. The cited RAGent work describes retrieval-assisted construction of structured JSON access policies. Inspection of the primary papers supports feasibility of those specific approaches; it does not establish universal semantic fidelity for arbitrary instructions, resources or downstream services. The present paper does not provide a universal translation-soundness theorem.

Inter-agent scoping (C.7, p.19) describes forwarding scope, obtaining a structured interpretation, and approval by a user or another agent. It does not supply a formal semantic subset test proving that every downstream permission is contained in the original authorization. This is a remaining verification requirement. The disclosed translation and enforcement assumptions prevent treating an arbitrary mistranslation scenario as a newly demonstrated failure of a claimed complete attenuation algorithm.

Structured permissions constrain actions only when the relevant access paths are actually mediated by their enforcement mechanism. They do not certify the truth of model capability claims, good intentions, correct reasoning or task success inside an authorized resource boundary. The illustrative examples in Appendix E should remain conditioned on the proposed enforcement and policy assumptions.

Outcome for this portion: No Issue Found within the inspected conceptual and feasibility scope. No live policy compiler, cross-agent enforcement system, spending-limit implementation or adversarial benchmark was reproduced.
# 6. Evidence, unperformed work and delivery provenance

Saved evidence includes original extraction and identity records; peer_protocol_audit.json and peer_standards_manifest.json; scope-review notes and primary example/version snapshots; and case_version_source_manifest.json for the CanLII identity check and related preprint. The OIDC snapshot SHA-256 is `4d016752``a645e8a3``c259baa4``173b5a90``cb6c8289``8ce868fc``8444adde``262a5aed`.

Not performed: live OAuth/OIDC login, token issuance or federation tests; author-code execution; penetration testing; a formal proof of the proposed extension; exhaustive review of every standard, legal citation or prototype; full preprint/OpenReview textual comparison. No current-paper implementation was identified and tested. The two Minor findings do not certify security of a future deployment.

Title: 0065 | Scientific Verification Report
I25-40174 | Gressmann, Chen, Xie, Amato and Rauchwerger | Position: It Is Time We Test Neural Computation In Vitro | PMLR 267:81393-81409 (2025). Reviewed publisher PDF: 17 pages.

Overall finding: Minor. The MNIST presentation-time estimate needs a corrected value or an explicit subset size. No substantial core defect was demonstrated in the inspected biological examples or proposed control framework. Human scientific decision pending; author adoption not requested.
# 1. Source identity, version and audit scope

The original papers/0065/0065.pdf was hashed and matched to the controller acquisition receipt before review. The title, author list and proceedings identity agree with PMLR. A current publisher-linked PDF was independently downloaded and found byte-identical to the reviewed 4,090,192-byte, 17-page original. Original bytes were preserved.

Code:
SHA-256: 0ee7f5189d626f915cef175b221c94f63c1af68148fa6429ed5c16b27fc1c4f7

All main-text sections (pp.1-9) were inspected; references on pp.10-17 were checked selectively. The paper has no separate experimental appendix. The audit focuses on the biological proof-of-concept evidence, the proposed control/optimization formulation, the distinction between control and mechanistic identification, and the explicit numerical timing example. Figures 1 and 3 and the p.7 timing passage were visually checked.
Claim group | Verification and result

Biological examples and accessible platforms; Sections1-3 | Check published Kagan2022, Jordan2024, Zhang2024 and Elliott2023 sources, including cell provenance and stated limits. No demonstrated core contradiction.
Control model and optimization; Sections3.1-3.3 | Inspect equations, Figure1 and qualifications. Record Markov-state, computation-attribution and interface requirements as boundaries of the proposal.
MNIST timing; Section3.2,p7 | Check the actual training-label file header and exact arithmetic. Minor unqualified estimate / missing subset size.

Alternative views and long-term implications; Sections4-6 | Distinguish disclosed technical/ethical limitations and energy-efficiency expectations from demonstrated results. No new experiment or proven convergence result is claimed.

The PMLR and author-lab records did not expose an exact benchmark implementation for this position paper. No matching arXiv version was identified in the inspected records. Direct OpenReview access encountered a browser-verification wall, so a full OpenReview revision comparison was not performed. These are bounded search results, not assertions that no related material exists anywhere.
# 2. Problem 1 (Minor): the MNIST epoch duration requires correction or a stated subset

Location and claim. In Section 3.2 on p.7, the paper assumes 500 milliseconds of presentation per image and estimates almost seven hours for one MNIST training epoch. No 50,000-example subset or train-validation partition is stated in the inspected main text.

Dataset check. The standard training split contains 60,000 examples. The audit independently downloaded the original-format train-labels IDX gzip file from the Google-hosted dataset mirror, decompressed it, and read its big-endian header: magic number 2049 and item count 60,000. The decoded file has exactly 60,008 bytes, consistent with an eight-byte header plus one label per example. Official Keras dataset documentation independently specifies the same training size.
Assumed presented examples | Presentation time at500ms each
60,000: complete standard training split | 30,000s = 8h20m00s
50,000: possible training subset | 25,000s = 6h56m40s

Strongest alternative reading. Reserving 10,000 of the training examples for validation would yield a 50,000-example training subset and explain almost seven hours. That interpretation is possible but undocumented here. The evidence establishes a mismatch with the standard full-training-split reading, not an error under every imaginable partition.

Correction. State 8 hours 20 minutes for the full 60,000-example split, or explicitly state a 50,000-example training subset if that is intended. Specify that this is presentation time only, before reset intervals, pauses, data processing, repeated trials or other overhead.

Impact and severity. This is a bounded numerical/setup-description issue. Correcting the full-split estimate increases the required time and preserves the paper’s point that ordinary digital benchmarks can consume substantial biological recording time. It does not invalidate the proposed research program. Severity is Minor because no material central-claim damage has been demonstrated.

Replay. verification/0065/check_mnist_timing.py reproduces the download, header check and exact arithmetic; mnist_timing_check.json and mnist_source_manifest.json record results and hashes. No MNIST training run or wet-lab experiment was performed. The source gzip SHA-256 is `3552534a``0a558bbe``d6aed32b``30c495cc``a23d567e``c52cac8b``e1a0730e``8010255c`.
# 3. Biological evidence: supported claims and their limits

The p.1 footnote narrows the paper’s use of in vitro neurons to iPSC-derived neurons. This makes source-cell provenance relevant, but does not automatically disqualify every citation involving other biological preparations, particularly where the cited contribution is instrumentation or a comparison with in vivo control.
Primary source and target use | What was verified; limit

Kagan etal.2022,DishBrain; targetSection3,p5 | The published study includes human iPSC-derived neurons as well as primary mouse cortical neurons, with closed-loop Pong-like gameplay and control conditions. This supports the target’s basic-gameplay proof of concept. It does not establish persistent across-day learning or a uniquely identified biological learning rule.

Jordan etal.2024,Neuroplatform; targetpp2,8 andFigure1 | The methods specify neural stem cells derived from human iPSCs, and the paper documents remote electrophysiological access. This supports the availability example. The platform source also reports capacity and experimental limitations; universal access, price and task capability were not audited here.

Zhang etal.2024,MindInVitroplatforms; targetpp2,7 | The demonstrations include mouse embryonic-stem-cell-derived and primary preparations, rather than establishing all cited results in human iPSC neurons. The target cites interface availability and recording practicalities. Transfer to its narrower cell scope remains something to validate; the source difference alone does not refute the instrumentation rationale.

Elliott etal.2023,remote closed-loop infrastructure; targetp2 | The published experiments use mouse embryonic stem-cell-derived cultures. They provide a remote-infrastructure precedent; Jordan separately supports human-iPSC platform availability. Neither establishes mature task computation across arbitrary preparations.

The narrow DishBrain claim in the target does not inherit every stronger interpretation suggested by the cited article’s title. In particular, the review does not treat basic task adaptation as established phenomenal consciousness, general intelligence, durable memory or a proof of a particular learning mechanism. The target’s later discussion acknowledges ethical uncertainty and technological immaturity.

Li et al. (2024) is identified in the target as an in vivo C. elegans example, not an iPSC culture experiment. The publisher abstract supports optogenetic integration of a deep-RL agent with the animal on a target-finding task. Full subscription-only methods and the exact offline Soft Actor-Critic training details were not independently reproduced in this audit.

Primary published XML snapshots and extracted text for the four platform/culture papers are preserved under sources/0065/bio_primary/. The check examined what the papers report; it did not reproduce original spike recordings, culture-level statistics, biological replicates, plasticity assays or experimental controls.
# 4. Control, computation and mechanistic inference: verification boundaries

Section 3.1 models the observed neural system with a transition law and a stimulation policy. Such notation is a useful starting point. If two histories produce the same current observation but different future responses, however, the current observation alone is not a sufficient Markov state. A practical formulation may need history, a learned latent state or a belief state. The paper’s proposed sequence models allow that interpretation, so this is a specification requirement rather than a counterexample to a universal theorem supplied in the paper.

Task success also does not by itself determine where the computation occurred. A simple logical example is a digital encoder that computes an XOR label, a fixed biological channel that relays its input, and an identity decoder. The combined system predicts XOR perfectly without the biological channel learning XOR. A four-row exact truth table is saved in model_exact_boundaries.json. This illustrates a measurement boundary, not a biological simulation or a falsification of the proposal.

Counterevidence is explicit. Section 3.1 permits reservoir/random-projection uses of the culture; Section 3.2 calls for objectives that incentivize nontrivial biological use. Thus the manuscript does not prove that any high task score establishes biological computation, internal plasticity or mechanistic identification. Future implementations would need suitable encoder/decoder controls, biological perturbations and attribution criteria to make those stronger inferences.

The suggestion that the artificial policy should ideally approach an identity map is an aspiration. Its mathematical meaning requires matching interfaces or defined encodings between task inputs, recorded activity and stimulation channels; the earlier map from state space to action space does not by itself define that identity. No convergence theorem, limit proof or trained implementation is supplied, and none was assumed in this audit.

The control-to-understanding argument is appropriately narrower when read as discovery of exploitable response properties. It does not identify a unique internal mechanism from arbitrary control success. The report preserves this limited reading rather than claiming that the paper has established or failed a stronger identifiability theorem.

Simulation fidelity, transfer and automatic differentiation are presented as research opportunities. The manuscript acknowledges simulation-to-experiment gaps and requires eventual testing on actual cultures. Results from a differentiable simulator or formal spiking model are not treated here as measured gradients through living tissue.
# 5. Overall assessment, unperformed work and provenance

The inspected evidence supports a research agenda for experimenting with living neural systems through learned controllers. Cost, maturity and longer-term energy benefits remain conditional expectations. This review does not certify net energy savings for a complete installation including stimulation, recording, digital controllers and culture-maintenance infrastructure.

Not performed: wet-lab replication; reanalysis of the cited biological experiments or participant/culture-level statistical data; training a controller; executing author code; validating an exact benchmark, learning rule or causal mechanism; formal convergence/identifiability proofs; exhaustive reference or historical-timeline checking; and a current legal or ethical-policy audit. No general repair or implemented replacement system is claimed.

Independent AI checks of the biology and modeling portions, source hashes, acquisition outcomes and reviewer-written exact checks are saved in verification/0065/ and sources/0065/. The model examples are labeled boundary demonstrations, not newly discovered failures of a published algorithm. Original-source preservation and the five required deliverables are checked in completion_checkpoint.json.

report: # 0066 | Scientific verification report
Position: The Future of Bayesian Prediction Is Prior-Fitted

Samuel Mueller, Arik Reuter, Noah Hollmann, David Ruegamer and Frank Hutter. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81861-81875. Reviewed publisher-linked PDF: 15 pages. Page references below use PDF/printed pages 1-15, not the PMLR volume pagination.
Task [internal task] / B001. Batch token [internal identifier omitted]. AI-assisted draft; scientific decision pending; no author adoption requested.
## Outcome and decisive evidence

Supported severity: Minor. Section 5.1 infers fulfillment of a distribution-valued martingale property from stabilization of a standard-deviation statistic. That scalar cannot establish the stated property. A constant-variance predictive countermodel demonstrates this logical gap. This is a finding about the inference made from the diagnostic, not evidence that the actual trained PFN violates the property.

A separate question remains Needs Evidence: whether the early decrease in Figure 2 is itself a violation. The paper does not specify whether it averages conditional standard deviations, measures the standard deviation of a mixture over rollouts, or plots convergence with the number of Monte Carlo rollouts. These alternatives have different Bayesian null behavior.
## Scope and checked contributions
- Read the complete scientific main text (pp. 1-9), experimental setup and Appendix B (p. 15), and relevant reference entries. Visually inspected Figure 2 (p. 6) and Figure 4 (p. 15).
- Re-derived the cross-entropy/KL relation in Section 2.1 and the discrete-coin posterior in Section 6.5 / Appendix A.1. Checked the identical-token attention argument analytically.

- Compared publisher metadata with the retained source and acquisition receipt. Inspected arXiv v1 TeX and archive contents for the experiment definition; inspected metadata of the cited original PFN repository, not its implementation.

- Extensions and predictions in Sections 4 and 6 were treated as research proposals. No experiments were demanded for normative recommendations. No training, author-code execution, benchmark replication or claim of global correctness was performed.
## Identity and version

The retained PDF has 525443 bytes and SHA-256 7f13f5c03442b51b62c8b420abe2110344d6822a6440cbde5b65d6cd92fa3e50, identical to controller_acquisition_receipt.json. Its title, authors and ICML 2025 footer agree with the publisher record. The arXiv record 2505.23947 lists v1 dated 29 May 2025; it is a secondary version check, not a substitute for the retained publisher PDF.
# Problem 1 | A scalar plateau does not prove a martingale
## Source claim, location and suspect inference

Section 5.1, p. 7, first states a distribution-level rollout identity, then says the reported standard deviations stabilize, ’fulfilling the Martingale property’. Figure 2, p. 6, supplies the scalar trajectory; Appendix A.1 and Appendix B are on p. 15. The problem is the inference from a plateau in one statistic to equality of probability distributions.
## Definitions and complete check

Let Q_D be the predictive distribution at a fixed query x given the observed dataset D. Let Z be an additional observation drawn through the stated sequential predictive sampling procedure. The one-step distribution-valued property requires equality for every measurable set A; longer-horizon identities follow by iterating an appropriate one-step identity.

\[Q_D(A)=\mathbb E\!\left[Q_{D\cup\{Z\}}(A)\mid D\right]\quad\text{for every measurable }A.\] Countermodel to the diagnostic’s sufficiency: define Q_D = Normal(n, 1), where n is the number of observations. This is a proper finite-moment predictive distribution for each finite dataset. Inputs may follow the paper’s independent uniform input distribution; the rule ignores their values. Draw Z from Q_D and append it. The resulting predictive distribution is Normal(n+1, 1) for every sampled Z, so its mixture over Z is also Normal(n+1, 1).

\[\operatorname{SD}(Q_D)=\operatorname{SD}\!\left(\mathbb E_Z Q_{D\cup\{Z\}}\right)=1,\qquad Q_D\ne\mathbb E_Z Q_{D\cup\{Z\}}.\] For A = (-infinity, n+1/2], the two probabilities are Phi(1/2) and Phi(-1/2), which are unequal because the normal CDF is strictly increasing. Repeating this construction gives stable standard deviation at every rollout depth while the distribution keeps changing. Thus even an exactly flat standard-deviation curve cannot imply the paper’s displayed property.

Assumption boundary: this construction refutes the sufficiency of the statistic. It is not asserted to be the trained PFN, its neural implementation, or a counterexample satisfying the specific GP training experiment. The conclusion does not require that assertion. No failure rate or empirical degradation of the actual PFN is inferred.
## Impact and precise correction

The supported correction is to describe stabilization of the reported scalar statistic and leave the full martingale property unresolved. Establishing that property would require a correctly specified distribution-level comparison, or sufficiently justified separating statistics with an explicit tolerance and sampling uncertainty. This report verifies the logical scope of that correction; it does not supply new empirical verification.
# Counterevidence | What Figure 2 may measure
## Conditional uncertainty versus mixture uncertainty

If the plotted quantity is average within-trajectory predictive standard deviation, an exact Bayesian predictor can decrease it. Under the paper’s GP prior (RBF length scale 0.1, output scale 1, observation-noise variance 10^-8, uniform inputs), standard Gaussian conditioning gives the following latent-variance update. C_D is the posterior latent covariance after the initial dataset, and v_D(x) = C_D(x,x).

\[v_{D\cup\{(X,Y)\}}(x)=v_D(x)-\frac{C_D(x,X)^2}{v_D(X)+10^{-8}}.\] The denominator is positive, and the reduction is strict wherever the posterior cross-covariance is nonzero. It is independent of Y. Adding the same observation-noise variance to both sides preserves the predictive-variance reduction. Nevertheless, integrating the entire conditional predictive distribution over the newly sampled Y restores the original predictive distribution by the tower property. Thus shrinking conditional SD is not by itself a martingale violation.

Conversely, the variance of the mixture over trajectories contains both the average conditional variance and the variance of the conditional means. These two terms can compensate. If Figure 2 uses mixture uncertainty, the preceding GP argument does not refute its Bayesian null. If its horizontal axis instead denotes the number of independent Monte Carlo rollouts used to estimate a fixed mixture, estimator convergence must also be separated from predictive inconsistency.
## Why no actual experimental failure is asserted

The plotted x-axis is ’Number of Rollouts’; the caption discusses steps and normalization by the final standard deviation. Appendix B labels a ’Martingale Posterior Epistemic Uncertainty’. These descriptions do not identify the estimator uniquely. The arXiv TeX archive contains figures and manuscript sources but no Python or notebook experiment scripts. The relevant source text repeats the ambiguity.

Figure 4’s caption describes sine and sloped-line training, whereas Appendix A.1 specifies a GP prior. The TeX source shows this caption was reused from a commented-out sine illustration. It is retained here as counterevidence against treating the caption as a reliable description of the plotted experiment. The stale caption alone is outside the substantive finding.
## Severity rationale based on dependencies

Minor is supported for the invalid sufficiency inference. The demonstrated defect concerns a scalar interpretation within Section 5’s proposed diagnostic agenda. It is not used in the cross-entropy/KL derivation, and Section 6.4 proposes iterative sampling without deriving a guarantee from Figure 2. An incorrect actual estimator or failure of a core learning guarantee has not been established. The pending estimator question does not increase the supported severity. The classification does not rest on the position-paper label, ease of repair or survival of an unrelated result.
# Other checked reasoning and conclusion
## Cross-entropy objective (Sections 2.1-2.2)

\[\mathbb E[-\log q(Y\mid X,D)]=\mathbb E[H(p(\cdot\mid X,D))]+\mathbb E[\operatorname{KL}(p(\cdot\mid X,D)\|q(\cdot\mid X,D))].\] This identity follows by adding and subtracting log p, under common measure/support and integrability conditions. The entropy term does not depend on the learned parameters. It justifies the ideal population target; it does not guarantee finite-capacity optimization or out-of-prior accuracy. The paper itself acknowledges these approximation and support limits. No issue was found in this inspected derivation.
## Coin-counting limitation (Section 6.5; Appendix A.1)

For the exact discrete prior p_j = j/100, j = 1,...,99, and n observed heads, Bayes’ rule gives m_n = sum_j p_j^(n+1) / sum_j p_j^n. The next increment equals Var_n(p)/m_n > 0. Independent exact-rational calculation gives m_1 = 199/300 = 0.6633333333, m_10 = 0.9119988890 and m_100 = 0.9844204810.

With identical context embeddings, no positional/count features and the Figure 1 attention mask, normalized attention returns the same value vector independently of the number of duplicate tokens. Tokenwise residual, feed-forward and normalization operations preserve this invariance. A test token attending only to identical training tokens cannot distinguish n from n+1. These conditions explain the stated original-architecture limitation. A special token, positional/count encoding or injected nonidentical features changes the assumptions; the paper explicitly discusses workarounds. No issue was found in the qualitative counting argument; trained numerical outputs were not reproduced.
## Additional scope clarifications

Synthetic pretraining eliminates direct reuse of real evaluation rows in those pretraining examples, provided the generator is independent of the held-out test data. It does not itself certify freedom from evaluation-driven prior design or downstream preprocessing leakage. The paper’s wording was interpreted within this pretraining context; no concrete leakage finding is asserted. Claims about future dominance, latent prediction and new architectures remain proposals.

# Problem 1 | Outcome timing in the reward example
## Claim and exact location

Section 5, p.4, paragraph headed Overjustification Effect, summarizes Lepper, Greene and Nisbett (1973). Its concluding sentence states that ’removing rewards can lead to a decline in both engagement and performance.’ The suspect step assigns a shared post-removal interpretation to two measurements made at different stages.
Primary-source endpoint | Measurement stage / locator | What the comparison supports
Voluntary drawing time | Later classroom observations; printed p.134 / PDF p.6; 7-14 days after the sessions | Subsequent interest under an unrewarded setting
Rated drawing quality | Experimental-session drawings; printed pp.133,135 / PDF pp.5,7 | Immediate performance under the experimental reward conditions

The quality ratings were 2.18, 2.85 and 2.69 for expected, unexpected and no-award groups, respectively. They were not post-withdrawal quality measurements. Reading the methods and results together therefore does not support attributing a measured later quality decline to reward removal. This is a documentary endpoint/timing check, not a new statistical reanalysis.
## Alternative reading and exact impact

The phrase ’These findings suggest’ can be read as proposing an extrapolation. Under that reading, post-removal performance decline is an untested possibility, not a reported result. The review does not claim that such a later effect is impossible or contradicted by other research. The problem is local evidentiary ambiguity in the illustrative example.

Minor is supported because the demonstrated defect changes the interpretation of this one endpoint, rather than invalidating a claimed estimated effect or a formal mechanism used elsewhere. The paper’s design proposal does not depend on a measured post-removal quality coefficient, and its Section 5 discussion explicitly permits beneficial, context-sensitive incentives. A stronger severity would require evidence of damage to the actual central recommendation or its principal empirical basis, which was not demonstrated.
## Verified correction of the attribution

Replace the closing inference with a distinction between immediate drawing quality and later voluntary engagement. Treat any effect on later performance as an extrapolation requiring separate support. The primary-source comparison verifies this narrow correction only; no intervention, empirical repair or author adoption was performed.
## Counterevidence retained

Section 2 explicitly accepts compensation. Section 5 recognizes informational rewards and calibrated incentives as potentially beneficial. Section 6 permits judicious LLM assistance. Sections 7.2 and 8.2 acknowledge feasibility and trust problems; Section 8.3 discusses bias, privacy and manipulation. Thus neither a universal claim that rewards are harmful nor a proven universal advantage of games is an accurate representation of this paper.
# Conclusion, references and evidence appendix
## Other central evidence

Veselovsky et al. (2025) supports prevalent LLM use in the studied crowdwork task and greater output homogeneity; it also reports better keyword-retention scores for LLM-labeled summaries. These findings concern different dimensions of quality. They do not contradict the reviewed paper’s contextual definition of quality and acknowledgement of useful AI assistance. They do not independently establish the entire proposed causal chain from incentive design through motivational crowding-out to LLM use.

report: # 0069 | Scientific verification report
Position: Deep Learning is Not So Mysterious or Different

Andrew Gordon Wilson. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:82326-82346. Reviewed: exact publisher-linked 21-page PDF. Page references use the PDF’s printed numbering: main text 1-9, references 10-14, appendices 15-21.
Task [internal task] / B001. Batch token [internal identifier omitted]. Scientific decisions remain pending.
## Outcome and supported impact

Supported severity: Major. Three mathematical defects are supported: Problems 2 and 3 are Major under the core-dependency criterion, and Problem 1 remains Minor. The overparameterized linear-model discussion needs an explicit generalized-inverse and spectral convention; a displayed single-scale fat-shattering inequality is false; and the exact straight-line minimizer asserted for finite weighted L2 regularization is false. The actual Figure 1(g) covariance estimator remains a separate Needs Evidence item.

The generalized-inverse interpretation has direct support in the cited primary paper and an inspected historical notebook. It preserves the stated minimum-norm proposition, so an allegation of a failed core double-descent theorem is not established. Problem 2 invalidates the quantitative fat-shattering component of the explicitly advertised comparison of generalization frameworks (Section 3.3, Appendix C and Table 1). Problem 3 invalidates the exact optimizer-selection step in the running polynomial example used to explain the core soft-inductive-bias principle (Section 2, reused in Sections 4 and 7). The independent countable-hypothesis proof survives; this does not reduce the severity of those affected technical components. No empirical result is declared invalid on the basis of absent code provenance.

## Checked reasoning that survives

For each fixed hypothesis, Hoeffding bounds the upper deviation by exp(-2nt(h)^2/Delta^2). Choosing this as delta P(h), then taking a countable union, gives total failure probability at most delta and covers data-selected hypotheses. Appendix D explicitly requires the prior to be independent of the sample; the adaptive-prior objection therefore does not apply. Zero-prior hypotheses give no finite certificate.

The complexity discussion was checked with a fixed data-independent decoder/architecture and common log units. A compression certificate must refer to the represented hypothesis and include its coding overhead; the review did not independently recalculate the cited CIFAR/LLM certificates. The paper’s distinctions among fixed representations, learned kernels, and relative rather than exclusive mode connectivity were also read.
## Identity

Original PDF: 1128076 bytes, SHA-256 `c362bba8cedcdbe2ac351e91a72317f97db7d131c9926da7cb1fd68eb3e5850d`, matching the controller receipt. arXiv:2503.02113 lists v1 (3 March 2025) and v2 (10 July 2025); no later version was listed in the inspected record.
# Problem 1 | Inverse and spectral convention
## Claim, location and operative assumptions

Section 6, pp.8-9, describes X as n by d, explicitly enters d>n, writes w*=(X^T X)^(-1)X^T y for the minimum-norm interpolant, and calls parameter covariance the inverse Hessian. Appendix F, p.20, specifies alpha=10 for its effective dimension. The matrix in that inverse is singular in the stated regime.

\[\operatorname{rank}(X^\top X)\le n<d,\qquad \dim\ker(X^\top X)\ge d-n.\] This is a structural failure for every such X, including almost every draw under the stated feature model X_ij=y_i+epsilon_ij with Gaussian noise. A particular support-point matrix illustrates the algebra; the conclusion does not rely on the probability of that exact point.
\[X=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad y=\binom10,\quad \operatorname{spec}(X^\top X)=\{0,1,3\}.\]
## Complete check and precise algebraic repair

\[w_{\min}=X^\top(XX^\top)^{-1}y=X^+y=(2/3,-1/3,1/3)^\top.\] Here Xw_min=y. Every interpolant is w_min+t(-1,-1,1), with squared norm 2/3+3t^2, minimized uniquely at t=0. Thus the minimum-norm proposition is true when the inverse is replaced by the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. References to growing eigenvalues must concern the nonzero spectrum, since the nullspace persists.

The covariance convention also matters. Define N_eff(A,alpha)=sum_i lambda_i(A)/(lambda_i(A)+alpha), and H=X^T X. At alpha=10, N_eff(H^+,10)=42/341. For C_lambda=(H+lambda I)^(-1), N_eff(C_0.1,10)=59/96 and its limit as lambda decreases to zero is 1+42/341. A null mode contributes zero in the first convention and one in the latter limit. Alpha in N_eff does not itself regularize H before inversion.
## Counterevidence, dependency and remaining scope

Maddox et al. (2020), Appendix B.1, Eq.(12), explicitly uses the pseudoinverse and rank-based identity. Its historical random_features_nb.ipynb uses least-squares and singular values, providing a coherent interpretation. This is evidence against treating the printed inverse as a demonstrated failure of the underlying minimum-norm result. The supported judgment is a bounded equation/convention defect, not a disproved generalization guarantee.

The 2020 notebook has different metric/scaling details and is not authenticated as the generator of the 2025 Figure 1(g). No experiment was run. A complete plot audit needs the actual script, covariance definition, normalization, numerical tolerance and plotted data. This separate provenance question remains Needs Evidence and does not raise the supported severity.
# Problem 2 | A false single-scale inequality
## Source claim and exact scope

Appendix C, p.19, displays Rademacher complexity bounded by c gamma sqrt(fat_gamma(H)/n), immediately before a generalization-bound expression; Table 1, p.20, repeats the latter comparison. As a bound on the real-valued class and empirical Rademacher complexity defined on the same page, the displayed inequality is false.
\[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_S(H)=\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{h\in H}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i h(x_i)\ \not\le\ c\gamma\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{fat}_\gamma(H)}{n}}\quad\text{in general}.\]
## Counterexample with every condition specified

Take any nonempty input domain, n=2 fixed sample inputs, H={h0,h1} with h0(x)=0 and h1(x)=1/2 for all x, and gamma=1/2. Both functions are bounded in [0,1], the class is finite and measurable, and the signs are independent uniform {-1,+1}. The sample inputs can also be drawn independently; their values do not change the calculation.

Using the standard margin definition in Alon et al. (1997), Definition 2.2, shattering even one point requires two available values separated by at least 2 gamma=1. The class has maximum gap 1/2. Hence fat_gamma(H)=0.
Signs (sigma1,sigma2) | Supremum over H
\[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_S(H)=\frac{0+0+0+1/2}{4}=\frac18>0=c\,\frac12\sqrt{\frac02}\quad\text{for every finite }c.\]
## Alternative readings and effect on the paper

Changing the multiplicative constant or log convention cannot repair a zero right-hand side. A margin-loss bound or a scale-dependent entropy bound is a different statement and needs its own loss, accuracy/residual, scale and confidence conditions. The cited primary source explicitly makes scale relative to accuracy relevant; it does not justify discarding all within-scale variation.

Major is supported by the affected core dependency. Section 3.3 explicitly introduces the comparison of generalization frameworks and directs the reader to Appendix C and Table 1. The false raw-class inequality is the quantitative link offered for the fat-shattering certificate in that comparison; the counterexample invalidates this technical component, and no finite multiplicative constant repairs it. The direct refutation concerns the displayed complexity inequality, not every entry of Table 1 or all possible margin-loss bounds. A replacement requires a precisely stated and verified loss/scale/accuracy theorem. The independent Hoeffding/weighted-union proof in Appendix D and the minimum-norm argument survive. No empirical bound computation is declared false. No general replacement theorem has been verified; the correction status remains open.

Evidence: primary p.19 visual check; exact reviewer enumeration in independent_fat_check.py and independent_fat_check.json; Alon et al. (1997), pp.619-620. The numerical enumeration is a check of an analytic counterexample, not an empirical reproduction.
# Problem 3 | Weighted L2 does not enforce zeros
## Claim, objective and matched parameters

Section 2, pp.3-4, introduces f(x)=sum_{j=0}^J w_j x^j and penalty sum_j gamma^j w_j^2, gamma>1. It then asserts that for data on a straight line the preferred fit has all w_j=0 for j>=2 because this incurs the lowest penalty. The exact lowest-penalty assertion fails for finite weighted L2 regularization.

Set J=150 and gamma=2, the order and weighting used in Appendix F for Figure 1(a-c). Choose three distinct noiseless samples (x,y)=(-1/2,-1/2),(0,0),(1/2,1/2), all on y=x. Use the stated Gaussian data-fit term with any fixed sigma>0. The basis is the stated monomial basis from degree 0 through J=150. Both candidates set the intercept and all unused coefficients to zero, so penalizing or exempting the intercept does not change the comparison. This is a counterexample to the hypothetical straight-line assertion, not a reproduction of the plotted nonlinear data.
\[f_0(x)=x,\quad f_1(x)=\frac{64}{65}x+\frac{4}{65}x^3,\qquad w_j=0\text{ otherwise}.\]
## Complete fit and penalty comparison

At x=+/-1/2, x^3=x/4, so f1(x)=(64/65+1/65)x=x; at x=0 it is also exact. Both models therefore have identical predictions and identical Gaussian negative log likelihood at every training sample, for any fixed positive noise variance.

\[\Omega(f_0)=2,\qquad \Omega(f_1)=2\left(\frac{64}{65}\right)^2+8\left(\frac4{65}\right)^2=\frac{128}{65}=2-\frac2{65}<2.\] The competing polynomial is in the same J=150 hypothesis space and has strictly smaller total objective because its data fit is identical. Thus the all-zero higher-order interpolant cannot be the claimed minimizer, even before considering other coefficients or noninterpolating solutions.
## Alternative reading, repair and dependency

The weaker interpretation, that increasing weights discourage higher-order coefficients, is valid. A plotted curve can also look nearly linear without having zero cubic and higher coefficients. Neither interpretation makes the exact zero-coefficient statement true. Finite quadratic penalties favor distributed coefficients when monomials agree on the observed samples; they do not generally induce exact sparsity.

A precise supported correction is: order-dependent L2 penalties make high-order terms more expensive, but need not set them to zero or exactly recover the lowest-degree interpolant. The analytic example and exact arithmetic verify this correction’s scope. No claim is made that the corrected sentence proves better test risk.

Major is supported because the failed optimizer-selection step belongs to the paper’s core running example. The abstract and introduction identify simple models and soft inductive biases as central explanatory contributions. Section 2 derives exact straight-line preference from the finite weighted penalty; Sections 4 and 7 reuse this polynomial construction when explaining benign overfitting and the bias-variance discussion. The lower-objective, equal-fit competitor disproves the claimed selection step under its own assumptions. The broad existence of soft preferences and the independent countable-hypothesis theorem survive, but their survival does not repair this exact claim. No change in empirical scores is required for this judgment, and no such change is asserted. Figure 1 and Figure 6 performance were not independently reproduced. Evidence and executable reviewer-only replay are in `verification/0069/agent_math/independent_checks.py` and independent_results.json.

report: # 0070 | Scientific verification report
Position: Constants are Critical in Regret Bounds for Reinforcement Learning
Simone Drago, Marco Mussi and Alberto Maria Metelli. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81233-81275. Reviewed: exact publisher-linked PDF, 43 pages including appendices. Locations use printed/PDF pages 1-43.
Task [internal task] / B001. Batch token [internal identifier omitted]. Scientific decision pending.
## Outcome: Major

The published derivation of the central refined regret guarantee contains a false bonus substitution in the optimism proof and incorrect reciprocal-root summation constants. The first failure has an explicit admissible MDP execution: the claimed intermediate lower bound is about 0.05396 while the actual value difference is about 0.01350. This invalidates a step required to justify the advertised smaller bonus. It does not demonstrate nonoptimism or violation of the final regret inequality.

Independent static inspection also establishes discrepancies between the official software release and the mathematical algorithms. Their effects on the reported empirical ratio and rankings remain Needs Evidence because no raw result provenance or corrected execution was available. The normative position that constants deserve attention is not itself an experimental claim requiring refutation.
Concern | Supported judgment | Repair / remaining work
1. Extra L in optimism proof, Eq.(74) | Major: false core proof step | No complete proof for the stated bonus verified
2. Reciprocal-root sums and constants | Major: invalid constant-sensitive derivation | Scalar corrections checked; some downstream slack survives
3. Released variance and algorithm differences | Minor: confirmed release discrepancies | Exact variance repair checked; no empirical rerun
Reported curves / 1.87 ratio | Needs Evidence | Generating revision, raw results and corrected comparison needed
Signed-weight reduction in D.2 | Needs Evidence; inherited concern | Scalar diagnostic only; no full MDP counterexample retained
Scientific decision / adoption | Pending / not requested | No human review or author acceptance claimed
## Operative scope

The theoretical setting has finite states/actions, stationary transitions, deterministic known rewards in [0,1], horizon H, K episodes and T=HK. The proof witness respects these conditions and the stated greedy policy rule. Claims about exact constants were checked as technical contributions. The review does not certify every concentration event, citation, reported curve or asymptotic guarantee.
## Identity and evidence preservation

Original PDF: 694262 bytes; SHA-256 `89c52167bb0bc6eb54e2c40dd407f6516ae53fcf9b39a89765f3779edecc1620` matches the controller receipt. Original bytes were preserved. The official repository was archived at commit `3434b55b735d674d144eefce392b545425816ca1` (2 June 2025), including all 32 files and its meaningful directory tree.
# Problem 1 | A larger bonus enters the proof
## Source claim and exact mismatch

Theorem 3.2, pp.3-4 and its Appendix F restatement on p.35, defines the Bernstein-Freedman bonus with correction term C below. Lemma F.1 also omits an exterior factor L in its correction, although its minimum is outside the expectation. Write N=max{N_k(x,a),1}, and let expectation be under the empirical next-state distribution.

\[\begin{aligned}L&=\log(5HSAT/\delta),\\ b'(y)&=\min\!\left\{\frac{84^2H^3S^2AL^2}{\max\{1,N'_{k,h+1}(y)\}},H^2\right\},\\ C&=\sqrt{\frac{4\mathbb E_{\widehat P}b'}{N}}.\end{aligned}\] In Eq.(74), p.40, the substitution for this same bonus instead contains sqrt(4 L E_Phat[b’]/N)=sqrt(L) C. The subsequent variance comparison on p.41 relies on this enlarged term to cancel the term containing L times the squared value-estimation gap. Since L>1 and b’ is positive for finite counts, the inserted term is strictly larger. The L^2 already inside b’ does not supply the additional exterior L.

\[\begin{aligned}\text{Stated:}\quad &\sqrt{4L\widehat{\mathcal V}/N}+C-\sqrt{2L\widehat{\mathcal V}^{*}/N},\\ \text{Eq. (74):}\quad &\sqrt{4L\widehat{\mathcal V}/N}+\sqrt L\,C-\sqrt{2L\widehat{\mathcal V}^{*}/N}.\end{aligned}\]
## Dependency and severity

Lemma F.1 is the optimism step used to replace true regret by optimistic regret and invoke the bonus/model-error bounds in Theorem 3.2. The substitution changes the quantity being analyzed. A complete execution on the next page makes the printed lower bound itself false, rather than merely identifying a notational ambiguity. Major is warranted by this invalid derivation of a central technical guarantee; empirical score deterioration is not required for that judgment.
## Alternative readings and historical attribution

There is no stated convention that absorbs the extra L: the main bonus, repeated lemma statement and released correction term agree in omitting it. The counterexample is also insensitive to the H^2/H^3 inconsistency and min/expectation order because it has one state and the b’ cap is active. Retaining a nonnegative future-value gap cannot justify the enlarged lower bound in that execution, where the future gap is zero.

Azar et al. (2017), main Algorithm 4 and supplement Lemma 19, already contain a related missing-L step: their variance-difference lower bound drops L. The current issue therefore has inherited lineage; the 2025 proof inserts L into the correction instead. Both primary versions and exact locations are preserved. No allegation about intent or historical discovery priority is made.
## Repair status

Adding L to the algorithm’s correction would restore this particular cancellation but changes the algorithm and its bonus sum. It does not validate the published constants. A new proof for the stated bonus, or a fully reanalyzed changed bonus, is needed. Neither complete repair was established by this review.
# Problem 1 | Fully admissible execution
## Parameters and policy
Assumption | Concrete choice / verification
Finite stationary MDP | One state s; actions a0,a1; both transition deterministically to s
Rewards | R(s,a0)=R(s,a1)=0, known, deterministic and in [0,1]
Horizon and confidence | H=2, S=1, A=2, K=100000, T=200000, delta=0.05
Tie schedule | Episode 1: a0 at both stages. Later: a1 at stage 1, a0 at stage 2
Stage 2 | Footnote 5 sets terminal bonus to zero; estimated and true values are zero
Other regime conditions | SA=H=2; T>=H^3 S^3 A=16

For the sole state, the unique transition distribution also gives a consistent zero-count convention. Before episode K, N(a0)=K=100000, N(a1)=K-2=99998, and the stage-2 state count is K-1=99999. The raw b’ expression is approximately 373.859, so its cap is H^2=4. These counts follow from the stated schedule, not from freely assigning inconsistent counters.
## Why the schedule obeys Algorithm 1

All stage-2 actions tie at value zero. At stage 1, after the initial cap stops binding, the bonus B(n)+C(n) is decreasing in its visit count n. Action a1 has the smaller count and therefore the larger optimistic value. Earlier episodes can follow the same choices while the initial cap produces ties. Monotone Q clipping preserves this ordering. The independent reviewer calculation checked the closed-form greedy comparisons through all 100000 episodes; no author implementation was executed.
\[B(n)=\frac{7HL}{3(n-1)},\qquad C(n)=\frac{2H}{\sqrt n},\qquad n=99998.\]
## Stated versus correct quantities
Quantity | Value
C(n), from the stated bonus | 0.012649237133677323
Eq.(74) printed lower bound sqrt(L) C | 0.05395983862193981
Claimed lower bound minus actual value | 0.04046135760862298

Both empirical variances in Eq.(74) vanish. Transition-estimation and martingale deviations are zero, so event E and optimism hold deterministically. Yet the printed lower bound exceeds the actual left-hand side. The discrepancy is much larger than numerical rounding and follows directly from the distinct closed forms.

The actual regret is zero because all rewards are zero. This is deliberately an example of a false proof inequality under the algorithm’s assumptions, not a counterexample to the final regret bound or to optimism. Evidence: `verification/0070/agent_math/independent_checks.py`, independent_results.json, and rendered source pages 3, 37, 40 and 41.
# Problem 2 | Incorrect summation constants
## Confirmed scalar failures

Lemma D.7, p.25 after Eq.(34), turns 2H^2 sqrt(SL) times a state-action sum of n^(-1/2) into H^2 S sqrt(A T_k L). With the displayed balanced upper limit N=T_k/(SA), this requires the false bound sum_{n=1}^N n^(-1/2)<=sqrt(N)/2. The same factor error occurs in term (c) on that page and in D.9, p.31, Eqs.(56)-(57). Appendix E, pp.34-35, instead effectively uses sum n^(-1/2)<=sqrt(N).

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-1/2}&\ge\sqrt N>\frac{\sqrt N}{2}&& (N\ge1),\\ \sum_{n=1}^N n^{-1/2}&>\sqrt N&& (N>1).\end{aligned}\] The first inequality holds because every summand is at least 1/sqrt(N); no probabilistic or MDP assumption can make this scalar step valid. For a concrete large-count choice, take H=2,S=2,A=1,K=1000000,delta=0.05. Then T=2000000, N=1000000 and L=20.5001223; K exceeds 250HS^2AL. The sum is 1998.54014549 while the D.7 implied upper bound is 500. This diagnostic concerns the displayed intermediate sum, not an assertion that a stochastic variance attains that sum.
## Verified local correction and downstream dependency

\[\sum_{n=1}^Nn^{-1/2}\le1+\int_1^N x^{-1/2}\,dx=2\sqrt N-1\le2\sqrt N.\] Using this bound in the displayed reindexing changes D.7’s coefficients from 1+4+2 to 4+4+8, giving a conservative combined coefficient 16 instead of 7. D.7 feeds the empirical-variance sum in D.9, which feeds Eq.(75) and the 24e/616e constants in Theorem 3.2. Appendix E has an additional bonus substitution: its summation uses 2H sqrt(L/N), although Theorem 3.1 specifies 2HL/sqrt(N). These are material errors in a contribution explicitly focused on constants.
## Counterevidence and partial repair limits

The final constants are not proved false by these failures. Conditional on the remaining counting steps, replacing 7 by 16 still gives an Eq.(51) normalized envelope of about 2.1438 at the typical threshold, below its stated 4. A corrected CH envelope can also fit within the main 10HL term for nontrivial H>=2 and L>=log(20). These explicit slack checks are retained rather than asserting that every final coefficient must increase.

Other intermediate counting conventions need separate work: D.9 drops a stage index when aggregating stage-specific harmonic sums, and its b’ definition varies between H^2 and H^3. The scalar correction alone does not validate those steps, the probability event, or Problem 1. Major describes the invalid derivation of central constant-sensitive results; a complete repaired theorem remains unverified.

Evidence: primary p.25 image; independent_root_checks.py/json; agent_math/analysis.txt and independent_results.json. These calculations are analytic bounds with finite arithmetic checks, not empirical regret experiments.
# Problem 3 | Released implementation differences
## A different variance is computed

The official repository linked by the publisher is pinned to commit `3434b55b735d674d144eefce392b545425816ca1`. In agents.py, UCBVI.newEpisode (lines 79, 83) and MVP.newEpisode (line 216) compute population variance across the entries p_i V_i. The formulas in the paper require the variance of V under probability weights p.
\[\mu=\sum_i p_iV_i,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_{p}(V)=\sum_i p_i(V_i-\mu)^2.\]

Code:
Released statistic: np.std(Phat[s,a,:] * Vstar[:,h+1])**2

Take p=(1/2,1/2), V=(1,0), admissible next-stage values with deterministic rewards and H>=2. The required variance is 1/4. The entrywise products are (1/2,0), whose population variance is 1/16. More generally, for uniform p over S states, the released statistic is the required variance divided by S^2; the variance-dependent bonus component is therefore divided by S. This is a mathematical function mismatch, not a numerical tolerance issue.
## Other confirmed release-to-paper discrepancies
Item | Inspected release | Paper specification
Terminal UCBVI bonus | Positive B/C still computed; terminal stage-count slot never updated | Footnote 5: zero bonus at stage H
UCBVI initialization/cap | H at all stages | Algorithm 1 starts at H-h+1
UCBVI log factor | log(5SAKH)=log(5SAT) | L=log(5HSAT/delta)
CH flag | improved=True gives 7; False gives 2 | The refined coefficient is 2
BF constant choices | 4, 7 and 84^2 versus 8, 14 and 100^2 | These coefficient choices agree
## Impact, correction and provenance limit

Minor is assigned to the confirmed released-code discrepancy; the paper-level numerical effect is a separate Needs Evidence item. The released computation is not a faithful evaluation of the displayed weighted-variance bonus, and its confidence setting differs. Because both BF variants share several differences, the effect on their empirical ranking or ratio cannot be inferred from the algebra.

The weighted-variance expression above is a precise local correction and was checked by independent rational arithmetic. It is not a validated repair of the entire implementation. No author file was edited or executed. Establishing the reported empirical effect requires the generating revision and raw results, followed by a corrected comparison if authorized.
Evidence: archived agents.py with per-file SHA-256, source_audit.json, and `verification/0070/independent_root_checks.py/json`. The original implementation is preserved for static replay.
# Coverage, counterevidence and pending claims
## Experiment provenance remains unresolved
Experiment | Paper | Archived executable configuration
Main illustrative environments | S=A=3; H=5/10; K=10^5/10^6; 10 runs | Core settings and 10 runs match
RiverSwim, Figure 2 | S=5, H=10; 4 runs | S=10,H=25; 4 runs; comments retain 5/10
Larger environments, Appendix G | 5 runs | All 18 corresponding configurations specify 4
Reported 1.87 +/- 0.03 | Empirical improvement summary | No released raw-result files authenticate the statistic

These are release/provenance discrepancies, not proof that the authors used the wrong configuration in the published experiments. The repository history and raw-data absence prevent identification of the exact plotted runs. Performance claims remain unverified; no corrected numerical ratio is invented.
## Concerns narrowed by primary counterevidence

The allegation that the compared MVP never discards samples was rejected. Zhang et al. (2024), Section 3, Remark 1, explicitly describes a modified MVP using the newest half of the data at each doubling, while distinguishing the original cumulative-data variant. The released baseline resets its batch counts consistently with that description. This supports the concrete cited variant; it does not imply all doubling schemes must discard data.

Lemma D.2, p.17, removes stage-dependent weights from a sum containing signed martingale terms. A scalar recurrence shows that the generic algebraic inference needs justification, and the same step appears in Azar et al. (2017). However, a fully admissible UCBVI witness to that lemma was not established. It is retained as Needs Evidence, with a potential weighted-martingale repair unverified, rather than counted as a false theorem.

report:
ELVIA Scientific Verification Report 0071
Position: Current Model Licensing Practices are Dragging Us into a Quagmire of Legal Noncompliance
Paper I25-40180 | Supported outcome: Minor
Review date: 24 October 2026 | Human scientific decision pending
# 1. Identity, version and review result

Reviewed source: Moming Duan, Mingzhe Du, Rui Zhao, Mengying Wang, Yinghui Wu, Nigel Shadbolt and Bingsheng He. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:81276-81291. The exact 16-page publisher-linked PDF was supplied by the controller and its SHA-256 was independently verified against controller_acquisition_receipt.json. Page references below are 1-based PDF pages, equal to the printed internal page numbers, not the PMLR volume pagination.

Supported outcome: three bounded substantive issues (Minor): a mistaken Creative Commons definition, an unjustified conversion of method composition into method-specific risk, and an inconsistent Table 3 percentage. Compatibility exceptions and the La2E/La3E license-tag rule remain scoped Needs Evidence items. No executed classifier or corrected corpus prevalence is claimed.

The review read all main sections and Appendices A-E, checked the central quantitative definitions against Table 3, inspected primary license texts and current author project information, and independently recalculated the relevant arithmetic. PDF pages 1 and 13 were visually inspected. No author software or models were executed. Scientific acceptance and author adoption remain pending.
# 2. Definitions, dependencies and coverage

The paper crawls a popularity-selected Hugging Face graph in December 2024: 151,302 model nodes and 146,818 relationships from the top 8,000 downloaded models and their trees (Section 2, p.3). Its NCM is the number of distinct flagged models; CTM is the number deemed eligible for a given noncompliance case (Appendix C, p.13). Method columns summarize adjacent dependency types among flagged models. Multiple paths are allowed, so those columns can sum to more than NCM.

The position concerns model licensing standards. Its actual technical support includes a license-clarity rubric, metadata-based conflict rules, descriptive counts, and a proposed license family. No experimental efficacy requirement is imposed on its normative recommendation. Copyrightability, license scope, source provenance, and enforceability are not treated as interchangeable facts.

Coverage: Sections 1-2 and Figures 1-3 were checked for identity, definitions and sampling scope; Section 3 and Tables 1-3 for stated rules and numerical interpretation; Sections 4-6 for alternative positions and dependence; Appendices B-C for classification and counts; Appendix D for metadata limitations; Appendix E for the stated ModelGo sheet. Table 1’s entire legal scoring matrix and individual repository classifications were not independently recoded. The raw December 2024 graph and the exact generating classifier were not obtained from the inspected publisher/project links. No empirical prevalence was reproduced.
# 3. Problem 1 - A conditional CC clause is turned into a definition

Source claim and suspect step: p.1, Introduction, License Mismatch paragraph, represents Licensed Material as limited to music, performance or sound recordings and uses that premise to motivate ambiguity when CC is applied to model weights.

Complete source check: CC BY 4.0 Section 1(a), and BY-SA 4.0 Section 1(a), contain a conditional rule about synchronizing musical material with a moving image. The actual general definition of Licensed Material is in BY Section 1(f) and BY-SA Section 1(h), and encompasses artistic or literary works, databases and other licensed material. Removing the condition changes the logical meaning. Thus this particular scope-based justification is false. [R2-R3]

Alternative reading and impact: ambiguity about model copyright, model-specific governance, software patents or source-code obligations can still be discussed. Those questions do not make the quoted definition accurate. The paper’s broader rationale has other premises and its Table 1 rubric does not explicitly compute scores from this mistaken restriction. The demonstrated damage is to this concrete supporting argument, so Minor is supported; a change to the entire mismatch count is not established.

Scoped correction: replace the claimed definition with the actual general definition and discuss model-specific gaps directly. This restores the local source attribution. It does not validate every Table 1 entry or establish the legal status of model weights.
# 4. Problem 2 - Within-case composition does not determine conditional risk

Source claim: Appendix C, pp.13-14, introduces the method columns as an analysis of which reuse methods are more prone to noncompliance, then concludes that certain methods are more likely to lead to it. In the copyleft-violation row, 296 finetune, 32 merge and 37 quantization flags sum to NCM=365; CTM=949. The displayed 81.1%, 8.8% and 10.1% are fractions within the flagged set.

The suspect inference reverses the conditioning. Counts of flagged methods estimate composition among flagged models, not the probability of a flag among all eligible models using each method. The latter requires method-specific eligible denominators. Neither the row nor the global graph’s method proportions supplies those denominators for this particular eligible subset.

Complete logical counterexample: assign the 949 eligible models to disjoint method groups of 850 finetune, 32 merge and 67 quantization models, with 296, 32 and 37 flags respectively. Every flag count is nonnegative and at most its denominator, the flags total 365, the eligible models total 949, and the row’s three reported composition percentages are preserved. Disjoint labels are an allowed special case: the paper permits multiple paths but does not require them. Yet conditional flag rates are 34.8235%, 100% and 55.2239%, respectively. Finetune has the largest number of flags and the lowest rate. These are reviewer-constructed values demonstrating non-identifiability, not recovered corpus data.

Counterevidence and impact: global finetune prevalence is reported in Section 2, but it concerns the full graph, not the copyleft-eligible subset. Multi-path counting creates an additional denominator choice rather than resolving this one. This invalidates the method-specific comparative-risk inference from the supplied table. It does not change the reported marginal counts or the rule used to detect a case. Minor is assigned because this is a secondary stratified interpretation with no demonstrated dependence of the principal conflict detector or overall prevalence on it; its appendix location is not the reason.

Scoped correction: call the columns the composition of flagged cases, or provide and audit eligible denominators for every method before making a comparative-risk statement. A corrected empirical ranking requires the raw graph; none is invented here. The finite calculation is replayable in independent_checks.py.
# 5. Problem 3 - Table 3’s copyleft-style percentage is internally inconsistent

Source: p.13, Table 3, Copyleft-style Terms row: NCM=26,679, CTM=41,019 and 63.5%; p.7 repeats 63.5%. By the paper’s declared NCM/CTM definition, 100 x 26,679 / 41,019 = 65.04059094565933%, which rounds to 65.0%, a difference of 1.54059 percentage points. This was checked from the rendered original table and with independent scalar arithmetic.

The three entries cannot all be correct simultaneously. The evidence establishes a local inconsistency, not which original integer is wrong. If both printed counts are intended, 65.0% is the precise one-decimal repair. If another denominator generated 63.5%, that denominator and its eligibility definition must be supplied. Minor: this changes one reported rate and its repetition, without demonstrating reversal of the broader descriptive observation that the flagged fraction is large. Raw-data repair remains unverified.
# 6. Unresolved checks, counterevidence and known limitations

Compatibility (Needs Evidence for empirical impact). Section 3.2, p.6, and Appendix B use broad same-license wording; Appendix C, p.13, similarly generalizes OSS copyleft restrictions as CC conflicts. However, p.7 expressly recognizes BY-SA 4.0 to GPLv3 compatibility, and p.12 explicitly permits a compatible license. The official CC compatibility list confirms the exception. A literal rule that rejects every different identifier would be too broad, but the paper contains a defensible exception-aware reading. Without the exact classifier, no confirmed miscount among the 365 copyleft or 76 CCf cases follows. [R3-R4]

La2E/La3E license-tag inference (Needs Evidence). Section 3.3, p.7, flags a Llama2/3 license label when the corresponding base is absent. Meta’s relevant Section 1.b.v concerns using the corresponding Meta materials or outputs to improve another LLM. A tag alone does not establish this antecedent. Conversely, an absent edge does not establish absence of actual use. A constructed independently trained model with an inappropriate Llama tag would be a metadata/license-scope problem; it would not by itself prove a violation of the cited use clause. Because that construction may exploit the very input errors acknowledged by the authors, it is not promoted here to a demonstrated Major defect under verified operative assumptions. The direct dependence on the 1,000 La2E-license and 966 La3E-license flags warrants targeted source-level adjudication. These counts are not added as if disjoint. [R5-R6]

Known-issue reproduction: Appendix D, pp.15-16, already discloses missing/inaccurate dependencies and license metadata, including 276 La3E and 18 La2E candidate identifiers suggestive of false positives. Their disclosure is preserved and attributed to the authors. This review does not identify those models, adjudicate them, subtract them from totals, or relabel that disclosure as a newly discovered error.

Later-version check: the current ModelGo website reports changes in 2026 and a withdrawal of its share-alike variant from OSI review. This is not treated as a retroactive defect or a verified repair of the paper’s November 2024 ModelGo 2.0 comparison. A version-matched historical license text and complete scoring audit remain outstanding. The publisher page was inspected; OpenReview’s forum presented a browser challenge and its public note API returned HTTP 403. No accessible paper erratum was identified in the inspected sources; this is not an exhaustive guarantee of absence. [R1,R7]
# 7. Dependence, repair status and conclusion

The supported errors affect one foundational example, one secondary comparative-risk inference and one table rate. They do not establish that model-license conflicts never occur, that all reported counts are wrong, or that a standardized license proposal cannot be useful. Neither ease of repair nor survival of the position determines severity: the bounded dependencies above do.

The unresolved classifier questions could affect central quantitative evidence, but the missing implementation and alternative readings prevent a demonstrated severity upgrade. Appropriate follow-up is to inspect the frozen graph, versioned classifier, compatibility exceptions and per-case adjudications; this requires source evidence, not model training.
