# 1. Identity, outcome and coverage

Authors: Sifan Yang, Yuanyu Wan, Peijia Li, Yibo Wang, Xiao Zhang, Zhewei Wei and Lijun Zhang. The first-page identity agrees with the task packet and publisher record. The controlling 26-page PDF has SHA-256 `b2c064ec9dd4b1fea903390e83716a06b08a67e41691712de5d3508fd88976c8`. The controller’s bytes were preserved. Page references are 1-based physical PDF pages, matching the paper’s printed pages.

The supported severity is Major. One fundamental stability/constant-control failure invalidates the uniform regret orders in Theorems 4.1 and 4.2, and also affects Theorem 4.4’s matrix extension under its printed assumptions. Complete counterexample families satisfy the stated convexity, comparator and rank requirements. The vector family even has a fixed global gradient cap. These are failures of the claimed orders, not just missing proof details or empirical non-reproduction.

The review checked Algorithms 1-5, the relevant assumptions, vector and matrix proof chains in Appendix A, the stated complexity conditions, Appendix B’s reduction notation, and the experimental descriptions and figures in Sections 5 and Appendix C. It also checked official-source availability and a separately preserved later extension. Author code was not located or executed, and the classification experiments were not reproduced.
# 2. Claims, assumptions and favorable conventions

Write G_t=sum_{i<=t} g_i g_i^T, bar g_t=sum_{i<=t} g_i, and rho_{1:t}=sum of the FD-discarded eigenvalues. FTSL uses A_t=B_t B_t^T+rho_{1:t} I and x_{t+1}=-eta A_t^{-1/2} bar g_t. FTFSL implements the analogous update through a larger basis and delayed compression. Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 assume convex losses and ||x*||<=D, choose eta=D/sqrt(2), and claim O(tr(G_T^{1/2})+sqrt(rho_{1:T})). D is fixed throughout the counterexamples.

Appendix A, p. 12, explicitly defines inverse notation to mean the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse when a matrix is singular. We honor that convention. Startup singularity is therefore not alleged as an undefined-algorithm defect. The counterexamples either use an ordinary positive inverse after the first gradient or act wholly within the observed gradient span.

The matrix theorem assumes convexity, gradient rank at most r, and ||X*||_F<=D_M. It uses eta=D_M/sqrt(r), epsilon>0 and the cumulative-gradient update X_{t+1}=-eta Ltilde_t^{-1/4} bar G_t^X Rtilde_t^{-1/4}. No gradient-norm cap is included among those theorem assumptions.

The uniform interpretation of big-O is essential: with the stated parameters and assumptions fixed, its hidden multiplicative constant cannot grow with the horizon or the realized gradient/preconditioner ratio. Merely renaming an unbounded sequence-dependent factor as a constant changes the claimed data-dependent guarantee.
# 3. Complete vector counterexample to Theorems 4.1 and 4.2
Fix any d>=2, sketch size tau=1, D=1 and eta=1/sqrt(2). Let T=N+1, e1 be the first coordinate vector, and choose the following differentiable convex losses:

\[f_t(x)=-\frac{x^{(1)}}{N}\quad(1\le t\le N),\qquad f_{N+1}(x)=x^{(1)}.\] Every loss is convex and globally Lipschitz with gradient norm at most 1. The cumulative loss of every fixed x is zero, so x*=0 is an attained optimum and satisfies the comparator assumption. Nonuniqueness is permitted by the source. A smooth unique-optimum strengthening is given below.

In FTSL with tau=1, FD discards the only eigenvalue each round, so B_t=0 and rho_{1:t}=sum_{i<=t}||g_i||^2. For the first k gradients, rho_{1:k}=k/N^2 and bar g_k=-(k/N)e1. Hence A_k=(k/N^2)I and the actual next decision is x_{k+1}=eta sqrt(k)e1. These matrices are positive definite for k>=1.

In FTFSL the gradients stay in one direction, so the maintained rank remains 1<2tau and no compression occurs. Its escaped mass is zero; the preconditioner is the exact rank-one G_k. Its prescribed pseudoinverse gives exactly the same decision trajectory. Thus the example also covers the fast method without any sketch approximation error.

\[R_N=\eta\left(\sqrt N-\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\sqrt k\right)\ge\frac{\eta}{3}\sqrt N.\] The inequality follows from sum_{k=0}^{N-1}sqrt(k)<=integral_0^N sqrt(u)du=(2/3)N^{3/2}. At the final horizon G_T=(1+1/N)e1 e1^T. The expression in Theorem 4.1 is exactly 2sqrt(1+1/N)<=2sqrt(2), while that in Theorem 4.2 is sqrt(1+1/N)<=sqrt(2). Actual regret diverges like sqrt(N), while each claimed controlling expression stays bounded. No horizon-independent constant can make the advertised orders hold.
N | Actual vector regret | FTSL claimed expression | Regret / expression

The table is reviewer arithmetic for the displayed formulas, not an author-code experiment. The analytic unbounded ratio is the proof; a finite ratio exceeding one alone would not refute an unspecified big-O constant.

The failure is not restricted to a nonunique optimum. Replace only the last loss by x^(1)+sqrt(1+||x+e1||^2)-1. The total fixed-comparator objective is then sqrt(1+||x+e1||^2)-1, uniquely minimized at x*=-e1, with ||x*||=D=1. All losses remain smooth and convex, and every gradient is globally bounded by 2. The prefix trajectory is unchanged; terminal squared-gradient mass is at most 5, while regret is the preceding R_N plus a nonnegative term and still diverges. This removes both a uniqueness objection and a concern about choosing D larger than a zero comparator’s norm.

For fixed sketch sizes tau>=2, the same rank-one sequence is retained exactly, with zero discarded mass and the same pseudoinverse trajectory. Thus the mechanism is not a one-column sketch artifact. It concerns the unconstrained cumulative-gradient update and its missing stability control.
# 4. Where the proof fails

Appendix A.2, p. 13, compares the lagged preconditioner A_{t-1} with the current covariance G_t through a_t, then sets C1=max_t 1/sqrt(a_t). The publisher PDF actually prints a_t=max{rho_{1:t-1}/(||g_t||^2+rho_{1:t-1}),1} and claims a_t<=1. For nonnegative masses that maximum is 1; the required matrix comparison generally fails. Replacing max by min corrects the immediate expression but does not bound C1.

For the normalized tau=1 counterexample, before the last gradient rho_{1:N}=1/N and ||g_{N+1}||^2=1. Even after ignoring the initial zero-mass issue, the corrected ratio is a_{N+1}=1/(N+1), so C1>=sqrt(N+1). It cannot be absorbed into a uniform constant. In the no-compression fast case rho remains zero, making the same escaped-mass comparison even less informative.

There is also an initialization problem in the imported lagged-regret lemma as printed. For T=1, tau=1, D=1, eta=1/sqrt(2), take f1(x)=|x^(1)+1|, x1=0 and x*=-e1. The queried gradient is e1, A1=I and A0=0. Actual regret is 1. Lemma A.1’s right-hand side is Psi1(x*)/eta+(eta/2)||g1||^2_{A0^{-1/2}}=1/sqrt(2), because the prescribed zero pseudoinverse makes the second term zero. The displayed lemma therefore fails in this admissible instance. A positive initial regularizer requires a different statement and proof treatment.

These diagnostics explain the theorem failure, but the complete trajectory counterexample is independently decisive. Correcting the max/min symbol or an omitted transpose does not alter that trajectory and cannot repair its divergent ratio.
# 5. Matrix extension: Theorem 4.4 fails under its stated assumptions

Fix m=n=2 and tau=r=D_M=epsilon=eta=1. Let E11 denote the matrix with a single 1 in position (1,1). For N>=8 use the first N losses -X_11 and the final loss N X_11+(1/2)||X||_F^2. Their sum is exactly (1/2)||X||_F^2, so X*=0 is the unique optimum. Every gradient queried along the trajectory has rank one, satisfying Assumption 3.3. No gradient-norm bound is assumed by Theorem 4.4.

With tau=1, each left/right sketch discards its sole nonzero eigenvalue. Consequently Lhat=Rhat=0, rho^L=rho^R=S_t (the cumulative squared scalar-gradient mass), and Ltilde=Rtilde=(1+S_t)I_2. After k of the first gradients, the exact decision is X_{k+1}=k/sqrt(k+1) E11. All inverse powers are ordinary positive definite matrix functions.

\[R_N=\frac{N^2}{\sqrt{N+1}}-\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{k}{\sqrt{k+1}}+\frac{N^2}{2(N+1)}\ge\frac14N^{3/2}\quad(N\ge8).\] Let q=N+N/sqrt(N+1) be the final scalar gradient and S=N+q^2. The true terminal left and right covariance matrices each have eigenvalues 1+S and 1. With rho^L=rho^R=S and r=1, the factor displayed in Theorem 4.4 is:

\[B_N=\left((1+S)^{1/4}+1+S^{1/4}\right)^2\le25N,\qquad \frac{R_N}{B_N}\ge\frac{\sqrt N}{100}\longrightarrow\infty.\] A simple bound suffices: q<=2N and S<=5N^2, so the displayed factor is O(N); meanwhile k/sqrt(k+1)<=sqrt(k) and N^2/sqrt(N+1) is at least sqrt(8/9)N^{3/2} for N>=8, giving the stated regret lower bound. Reviewer calculations independently reproduce the exact recurrence. At N=512, 2,048, 8,192 and 32,768 the exact regret/factor ratios are approximately 1.853, 3.734, 7.503 and 15.045.

Page 22 identifies the same missing control explicitly: C3=[min_t sqrt(r epsilon/(||g_t||^2+r epsilon))]^{-1}. Here it grows with N. A separately imposed, horizon-independent gradient cap, or an explicit retained C3 term, would change the matrix theorem and can block this family. The source’s current convexity/rank/comparator assumptions do not supply that cap. This is grouped with the vector failure as one fundamental issue, not counted as a second unrelated discovery.
# 6. A verified restricted repair for a modified vector algorithm

A concrete repair is available under additional conditions, but it changes the original vector method. Add a fixed ridge delta>0 before taking the square root: A_t=delta I+B_t B_t^T+rho_{1:t}I, with A0=delta I, and retain x_{t+1}=-eta A_t^{-1/2} bar g_t. Assume a fixed bound ||g_t||<=G and eta>0. Let C=sqrt(1+G^2/delta). Then the following bound is valid:

\[R(T)\le\frac{D^2}{2\eta}\left(\sqrt\delta+\sqrt{\rho_{1:T}}+\operatorname{tr}G_T^{1/2}\right)+\eta C\,\operatorname{tr}G_T^{1/2}.\] Proof of scope: FD gives A_{t-1}>=delta I+G_{t-1}. For a=delta/(delta+G^2), the ridge implies A_{t-1}>=a(delta I+G_t). Positive definiteness permits inverse-square-root order, so the lagged gradient penalty is bounded by C times the current regularized penalty. Concavity of the trace square root gives sum_t g_t^T(delta I+G_t)^{-1/2}g_t<=2 tr(G_T^{1/2}).

For completeness, monotone H_t=A_t^{1/2} and the conjugate potential Phi_t(s)=(eta/2)s^T H_t^{-1}s give the lagged FTRL bound by telescoping: each linearized loss is at most Phi_{t-1}(bar g_{t-1})-Phi_t(bar g_t)+(eta/2)g_t^T H_{t-1}^{-1}g_t. Fenchel’s inequality bounds the endpoint minus comparator term by x*^T H_T x*/(2eta). Its spectral norm is at most sqrt(delta)+sqrt(rho_{1:T})+tr(G_T^{1/2}), proving the displayed repair.

This derivation was independently checked. It requires both the positive initial ridge and an explicit fixed gradient cap, and keeps their dependence visible. It does not validate the original zero-ridge update, preserve its exact scale behavior, prove a repaired matrix theorem, or establish unchanged experimental performance. Simply clipping gradients is insufficient to fix the original vector result: the first counterexample already has gradient norm at most 1.
# 7. Surviving checks, empirical scope and excluded concerns

The FD covariance sandwich and escaped-mass mechanism remain useful. The spectral compensation preserves PSD monotonicity; the rank/trace handling in the matrix comparator term, Kronecker vectorization, and the structural memory advantage are not refuted by the counterexamples. Appendix A contains local notation slips, including an omitted transpose in Algorithm 3 and a common left/right rank label; favorable symmetric formulations were used rather than treating these as separate central failures.

The advertised O(tau d) fast-update cost is amortized, with an O(tau^3) small-matrix decomposition each round and an O(tau^2 d) basis rotation after sufficiently many basis insertions. The condition tau<=O(sqrt(d)) is needed to absorb the cubic term. A compression round can be more expensive than the amortized cost. This is a complexity qualification, not a refutation of the overall acceleration mechanism.

Theorem 4.3’s mirror-descent variant has a different assumption involving D1=max_t||x_t-x*||. The present cumulative-gradient examples do not establish a false statement of that theorem under its own conditions. Nor do they demonstrate failure on the reported classification datasets or neural-network workloads.

The original experiments compare online classification on Gisette/Epsilon, ResNet training on CIFAR-10/100, and a small Transformer on WikiText-2. The source reports a learning-rate/regularizer grid, eight RTX 3090 GPUs, no momentum in the image comparison, gradient clipping at 0.5 in language modeling, and no preconditioner for the embedding layer. Those empirical settings differ from the unrestricted theorem class. Raw curves, seeds, exact selected settings and author implementation were unavailable, so runtime, statistical repeatability and train/test selection were not reproduced.

Iteration/epoch labels require clarification: CIFAR is described as 200 iterations, while the language-model description uses 40 epochs and the corresponding graph labels iterations. These could be reporting conventions; without logs they do not prove incorrect training. The empirical figures cannot establish a worst-case online regret theorem, and an invalid theorem does not itself show that the plotted comparisons are false.

Appendix B’s reduction was checked against the cited Agarwal et al. supplement and visually inspected at p. 23. Its adaptive-ratio normalization and inner gradient-query notation differ from the cited presentation. These are retained as clarification/provenance limitations, without asserting an independently proved failure of every nonconvex conversion. Any application relying on the refuted online guarantees must first use a valid replacement.
# 8. Later version, source provenance and execution

Official PDFs hosted by the first and corresponding authors match the controlling publisher PDF byte for byte. A later paper, Efficient Preconditioned Optimization Methods with Frequent Directions, arXiv:2610.16792v1, submitted 2026-10-12, explicitly identifies the ICML paper as its preliminary version on p. 4. The separately archived later PDF has SHA-256 `b7ea95eaf5c3b88a0ac1c1176fb547bc372f4c33782d3628212ff29ddc33d149`.

Targeted inspection of that extension finds the same cumulative-gradient FTSL/FTFSL update, zero initial covariance, comparator/convexity assumptions and regret orders. Its p. 21 changes max to min in a_t but still absorbs C1 into the claimed order. It also restores the omitted transpose in the fast algorithm. These are verified changes; they do not exclude the counterexample. The matrix analysis similarly retains the C3 dependence. This is a targeted correction check, not a complete review of all new content.

No official implementation of the original methods was identified in the paper, publisher record, inspected author pages or bounded repository discovery. OpenReview’s public API returned HTTP403. A baseline implementation linked by the later paper is not treated as the 2025 authors’ release. Version and acquisition evidence is retained under sources/0084 and verification/0084.

Reviewer-created scalar recurrences and matrix special cases were executed, with outputs in `agent_claim_calculation.json` and `agent_empirical_matrix_replay_result.json`. They are independent reductions of the printed algorithms, not author-code execution. Source-page images verify the decisive formulas. No model training, installation, paid API calls, external publication or controller modification occurred.

The initial review’s TeX and HTML-rendered PDF derived from the same `report_content.json`; those artifacts and their deferred-compilation record are preserved. This proposed replacement PDF is generated from the submitted TeX with the existing offline Tectonic runtime. Exact TeX/PDF hashes, compiler diagnostics and page-inspection records accompany acceptance. The scientific decision remains pending, human verification is not asserted, and no author adoption is claimed.
# 9. Conclusion and primary references
Item | Supported judgment | Repair / remaining work
Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 | Major. Fixed-parameter bounded-gradient counterexamples refute the uniform regret orders. | A fixed-ridge, gradient-bounded modification has an explicitly verified bound.
Theorem 4.4 | Same Major root cause. Complete rank-one matrix family has unbounded regret/claimed-factor ratio. | State/control gradient dependence and rederive the guarantee.
FD structure / fast complexity | PSD and structural arguments survive; fast cost is conditional and amortized. | Implementation and timing provenance remain unverified.
Empirical and nonconvex claims | Not reproduced or globally refuted by these examples. | Obtain code/logs; use valid online theory before transferring guarantees.
[P1] Yang et al. (2025), PMLR 267:71249-71274. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/yang25ah.html . Original: papers/0084/0084.pdf; SHA-256 in Section 1.

[P2] Yang, Wan, Wang and Zhang (2026), Efficient Preconditioned Optimization Methods with Frequent Directions, arXiv:2610.16792v1. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16792 . Targeted source checks and hashes are recorded in the code/source audit.

[P3] Agarwal et al. (2019), Efficient Full-Matrix Adaptive Regularization, Supplementary Material, pp. 1-3. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/agarwal19b/agarwal19b-supp.pdf . Archived SHA-256 `fc336b96a36a6cdc5598799cf1cbe597f4be70995ced2c8aafccf56e63d4a0f9`.

The finding is substantive because the main mathematical contribution promises uniform data-dependent bounds that the printed algorithms do not satisfy over the stated class. A successful empirical workload or a possible restricted repair does not establish those original guarantees.

report: Scientific Verification Report: 0085
Dynamic Mixture of Curriculum LoRA Experts for Continual Multimodal Instruction Tuning
I25-43454ICML 2025, PMLR 267:19011-19033; publisher-linked 23-page PDF
Inspection outcome: Major: the norm theorem and the published equal-parameter rationale fail
Batch token: `[internal identifier omitted]`
# 1. Identity, outcome and scope

Authors: Chendi Ge, Xin Wang, Zeyang Zhang, Hong Chen, Jiapei Fan, Longtao Huang, Hui Xue and Wenwu Zhu. The first page agrees with the task packet and publisher record. The controlling 23-page PDF has SHA-256 `3a800ba288be998f7165ac570c5ea98fe633fd54f2519cea158dd89861a7f5ef`; its original bytes were preserved. Page references below are physical PDF pages.

The first confirmed Major finding concerns Theorem 3.1 / Theorem K.1. Its assumptions permit equal gradient norms at every layer even though at least one layer has non-collinear expected gradients, so its asserted existence of a layer with different gradient norms is false. A complete token cross-entropy example, compatible transformer realization, and independent arithmetic establish the failure. This damages the claimed formal justification for task-dependent magnitude differences and allocation, without establishing that the benchmark scores or practical heuristic are false.

A second Major finding concerns the published equal-parameter rationale: its rank-times-location calculation is not invariant to unequal matrix costs, and the task-1 allocation in Figure 6 contradicts the asserted equality under the paper’s stated targets. This invalidates the stated justification for interpreting the central comparison as matched in trainable parameters. Exact historical checkpoint counts and any effect on Table 2 remain Needs Evidence. A separate release-level routing mismatch also remains distinct from an established error in the published scores.

Coverage includes the main method, Theorem 3.1 and Appendix K, evaluation definitions and headline arithmetic, appendices on implementation, routing, thresholds, runtime and budgets, the published allocation heatmap, and static inspection of the official code. No author code was executed or imported, and no training, inference or benchmark reproduction was performed.
# 2. The formal claim and its actual assumptions

Theorem 3.1 (p. 3) and Theorem K.1 (p. 22) assume that two tasks have distinct input-output distributions and require different optimal parameter configurations (K.2). They also assume that at least one layer has expected gradients that cannot be related by any real scalar multiplier (K.3). The conclusion is that some layer has different norms of these expected gradients.

\[\exists l^*: \left\|\mathbb E_{T_A}[
abla_{W_{l^*}}\mathcal L]ight\|_2
e\left\|\mathbb E_{T_B}[
abla_{W_{l^*}}\mathcal L]ight\|_2.\] The printed formulas and Definition K.4 use the norm of an expected gradient, not the expectation of individual gradient norms. The decisive pages were inspected as images to avoid a formula-extraction error. Both task expectations are evaluated at a common parameter checkpoint, consistent with the shared pretrained-model proxy in Eq. (3). The statement supplies no convergence condition, optimizer constraint, or temporal quantifier that would force a norm inequality.
# 3. Complete counterexample with finite optima

Use one fixed image-and-text instruction input and three possible next tokens. Task A has probabilities q_A=(1/2,1/3,1/6); task B has q_B=(1/3,1/2,1/6). These can be realized as six-example datasets with token counts (3,2,1) and (2,3,1). Both distributions have full support and are distinct. With logits w in R^3, the ordinary expected token cross-entropy is:

\[F_q(w)=\log\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^3e^{w_j}\right)-q^\top w,\qquad \nabla F_q(w)=\operatorname{softmax}(w)-q.\] Each risk has finite minimizers w=log(q)+c*1. The optimal predictive distribution is uniquely q. Because q_A differs from q_B, no single parameter configuration can achieve both predictive optima on the same input. K.2 is therefore satisfied; uniqueness of every redundant neural parameter is not required.

\[g_A=\left(-\frac16,0,\frac16\right),\quad g_B=\left(0,-\frac16,\frac16\right),\quad \|g_A\|_2^2=\|g_B\|_2^2=\frac1{18}.\] No scalar multiple of g_B equals g_A: their first components already rule this out. Thus K.3 holds. Nevertheless, the two norms both equal sqrt(2)/6. This is a counterexample to the asserted implication, rather than merely a missing justification for it.

To realize the example within the claimed model class, use a bias-free residual transformer with one active feed-forward output projection P. On the fixed instruction, choose its hidden activation u=e1 with unit norm, and a fixed affine readout that subtracts the residual base and maps the active coordinates to logits w=P u. At P=0, the expected gradient of P is g_q u^T; its flattened L2 norm is exactly ||g_q||. Earlier feed-forward gradients vanish because their path contains P=0.

Other attention branches can have both value and output factors zero. Other feed-forward branches can have both factors zero with an activation satisfying phi(0)=0; use bias-free branches or fixed biases. They are identity residual blocks with zero parameter gradients at this checkpoint. A fixed zero visual-to-predictive projector makes the visual transformer’s gradients zero. The theorem contains no requirement that every modality have nonzero influence for every task. Extra inactive dimensions and blocks can be added without changing the example.

Hence the active layer has equal nonzero gradient norms and non-collinear expected gradients, while every other transformer layer has equal zero norms. There is no layer with the claimed inequality. Setting P u=log(q_A) or log(q_B) realizes the respective finite optima while leaving the other blocks unchanged. The witness is a formal admissible model, not a claim about the actual InternVL2 weights used in the experiments.

Sequential presentation does not exclude this checkpoint. With fixed features and only P trained, choose 0<eta<1 and let w_pre solve w_pre=eta(softmax(w_pre)-q_A). The map is a contraction because the softmax Jacobian has operator norm at most 1. A finite fixed point exists, and one legitimate task-A gradient step maps w_pre exactly to zero, where task B may begin. The source imposes no requirement that task A be fully optimized first.
# 4. Proof failure, impact and valid repair limits

The proof on p. 23 first places equal-norm, non-collinear gradients on the same sphere in Eq. (26). That geometry is consistent with all preceding assumptions. It then asserts that equal norms would require reconciling incompatible updates and would violate sequential training. No mathematical condition supplies this purported contradiction.

\[g_A^\top g_B=\frac1{36}>0,\qquad \cos(g_A,g_B)=\frac12,\qquad D_{-g_A}F_B(0)=-\frac1{36}<0.\] The example also shows that non-collinearity does not imply opposing updates. A sufficiently small descent step for either task reduces both losses locally. Independent reviewer arithmetic gives the following values for a task-A step with eta=0.1:
Risk | Before step | After task-A step

The supported impact is the failure of the stated formal foundation for task-specific gradient-magnitude discrepancies. The paper prominently uses this theorem in Section 3.1 and its contribution list to motivate nonuniform allocation. Appendix location or an easy wording edit does not reduce that demonstrated mathematical impact. The empirical sensitivity heatmap and successful benchmark comparisons can still be observations even though this universal theorem is false.

A valid weaker conclusion is that some expected gradient vectors differ; that follows directly from K.3. It does not prove different magnitudes, different layer rankings, or optimal parameter allocation. Even a common positive rescaling of every layer’s gradient norm between tasks preserves all rankings. A defensible revision would remove or weaken the universal norm theorem and describe the measured sensitivity patterns as empirical motivation. A retained norm-separation theorem requires substantive extra assumptions and a new proof; simply relabeling non-collinearity as conflict is insufficient.
# 5. Major: the published equal-parameter rationale is invalid

Appendix A (p. 15) states equal trainable parameter counts, justified by rank 4 on all baseline layers versus rank 8 on half the method’s allocation locations. Eqs. (5), (14) and (15) actually constrain counts of experts/layers. A LoRA adapter on a d_out by d_in matrix has r(d_in+d_out) trainable weights, so selecting half the locations does not in general select half the parameter cost.
Target weight | LoRA parameter cost at rank r
LLM fused qkv: 2048 to 4096 | 6144 r
LLM attention output: 2048 to 2048 | 4096 r
Vision qkv: 1024 to 3072 | 4096 r
Vision attention output: 1024 to 1024 | 2048 r

These dimensions follow the stated InternVL2-2B model and its pinned official configuration: the LLM has 16 query heads and 8 key/value heads, and the vision attention uses ordinary qkv projection. With the paper’s attention-only target description, rank 4 over all 24 LLM and 24 vision blocks gives 1,572,864 LoRA weights.

The published Figure 6 was visually checked and independently sampled at its exact two fill colors. Every task row contains 48 selected attention/output subslots. For task 1, the LLM has 21 first-subslot and 15 second-subslot selections; vision has 11 and 1. Regardless of which subslot is assigned to qkv versus output within each modality, rank 8 yields between 1,638,400 and 1,900,544 weights. This is 4.17% to 20.83% above the stated attention-only baseline. The counts are reproducible from the archived source figure; they are not measured checkpoint tensors.

Thus the published count-based explanation does not establish the claimed equality, and its illustrated task-1 allocation is inconsistent with that equality under the stated target matrices. The public allocator likewise budgets by score-row count and enforces a 25% minimum vision share rather than weighting actual parameter costs. However, the released baseline wrapper also includes feed-forward target modules when no architecture filter is supplied, unlike the manuscript’s attention-only description. This prevents treating the preceding theoretical counts as verified counts of the original experimental runs.

The demonstrated failure of this equality rationale is Major because Appendix A uses it to justify the fairness of the central parameter-constrained comparison. This conclusion does not require an empirical ranking reversal or a claim that the released source produced the original experiments. Actual matched-run counts remain Needs Evidence: supply per-task architecture files and tensor counts for every baseline, distinguishing new trainable adapters, frozen accumulated adapters and auxiliary autoencoders. A cost-constrained allocation can use sum_j I_j r_j(d_in,j+d_out,j)<=B. If that changes the selected architecture, its performance requires a new comparison. Table 11 already reports O-LoRA at nominal 2x and 4x budgets still below D-MoLE; that preserves relevant performance counterevidence, but does not make the published equality calculation valid.
# 6. Official release: routing differs from the manuscript

The official gcd19/D-MoLE repository was pinned at commit `525fe2b788da85ebe3f5f102c4a77b3d37348c18`. Relevant source bytes and Git blob identities were preserved. Eq. (10) defines a threshold-passing candidate set separately for each sample, and Eq. (12) selects up to two lowest-error eligible task experts for that sample. The training description selects a prior expert together with the current task’s new expert.

The public get_task_ids function in internvl/model/internvl_chat/`modeling_internvl_chat.py`, lines 933-979, instead chooses one minimum-error eligible task for each sample, counts those winners over the batch, and returns one or two task IDs based on batch votes and a 0.3 support threshold. The returned IDs are applied through one shared expert mask. The second task requires multiple distinct per-sample winners, so a single sample can never activate two task experts through this function.
Minimal input, thresholds (1,1) | Manuscript per-sample rule | Pinned release trace
One sample with errors (0.1,0.2) | Both experts 1 and 2 are eligible and selected. | Only expert 1 is returned.
Sample x errors (2,2), evaluated alone | No candidate; use pretrained backbone. | No candidate; backbone fallback.
Same x batched with a sample having errors (0.1,0.2) | x still has no eligible expert. | Batch votes return expert 1, whose mask also applies to x.

These are reviewer-created traces of the visible control flow, not author-code execution. Default evaluation batch sizes are larger than one: the VQA evaluator uses 8, and captioning/grounding use 10; the separate run_eval.sh specifies 8 or 16. Therefore batch composition is a material part of the released evaluation behavior. A dataset-homogeneous evaluation batch and independent-example deployment need not route the same sample identically.

This is a confirmed implementation-to-manuscript discrepancy. Its effect on the original tables remains unverified without the original commit, batch construction, thresholds, routing outputs and experiment logs. It does not establish false scores, test-answer leakage, or a reversed comparison. The inspected evaluation calls supply questions and images to generation, with annotations retained for scoring; no reference-answer leakage was found in those paths.

Other code details matter for correspondence: the allocator operates on individual attention linear-module scores, sums these scores by modality, and applies the minimum vision share. The manuscript describes an entire-module gradient L2 norm and no such floor. Exact proxy aggregation and original allocation settings should therefore be documented before claiming that the release reproduces the printed curriculum exactly.

The source’s p. 6 statement that any rejecting autoencoder triggers fallback is best read as a local quantifier error: Eq. (10), p. 5 and the per-sample candidate test in the code support an empty-candidate fallback. The batch-mask issue above is separate. A disabled-adapter flag in one class was also examined; the traced main routing paths explicitly clear expert masks before feature extraction, so that flag alone does not establish a defect in those paths.
# 7. Empirical results: reconstructed gains and limits
Metric | D-MoLE | Best displayed baseline (O-LoRA) | Absolute gain
AVG | 73.87 | 58.79 | 15.08 aggregate-score points
Last | 82.18 | 62.04 | 20.14 aggregate-score points
BWT | -1.49 | -21.31 | 19.82 aggregate-score points

Table 2’s row averages reconstruct within rounding. The quoted 15.08%, 20.14% and 19.82% are arithmetic differences, not relative percentage improvements. AVG and Last mix CIDEr scores with percentage-valued VQA/grounding metrics, so the honest unit is aggregate-score points. Relative changes of the first two displayed aggregates would be about 25.65% and 32.46%, although those mixed-unit aggregates still require careful interpretation. This unit clarification does not erase the displayed score advantage.

The evaluation definitions are explicit: AVG_i averages A_t,i across all N checkpoints, including stages before task i is trained; Last_i is A_N,i; BWT_i averages A_t,i-A_i,i over all later checkpoints. They are not the same as an average over only seen tasks or a final-checkpoint-only backward-transfer metric. The paper deliberately evaluates unseen tasks because it starts from a pretrained model. This is a disclosed protocol choice rather than hidden denominator manipulation.

The nine datasets span captioning, VQA and grounding, and use common templates within output formats. This reduces task-specific template cues, but does not remove dataset-domain information; Appendix F itself describes dataset boundaries as relatively distinct. A t-SNE plot of reconstructions from each task’s own autoencoder does not by itself establish cross-autoencoder routing accuracy or calibration. Router confusion, unknown-task rejection and batch-stratified results would make that interpretation testable.

The v4 ablation removes both dynamic placement and task-specific routing, so its drop cannot isolate the causal contribution of allocation alone. General benchmarks in Table 3 show reduced forgetting relative to the reported adaptation baselines, while MME and MMMU remain below the original zero-shot model. The source supports a comparative retention improvement, not universal preservation of pretrained ability.

The threshold sensitivity table evaluates a fixed final checkpoint and gives aggregate Last scores from 80.34 to 82.18 across the shown multipliers. It supports limited aggregate stability under those settings; individual tasks vary more. Exact thresholds, original calibration data and raw predictions remain unavailable. The author’s threshold-calibration reply (repository issue 2) recommends setting thresholds from training reconstruction-loss distributions, for example above a high percentile; this guidance is not the original run’s threshold file.

The reported preprocessing and routing overheads were inspected rather than assumed absent. Table 9 sums to 44,772 training seconds and 650 proxy-preprocessing seconds (1.4518%); including both gives 12.6172 hours. Table 10’s 0.0552 s routing versus 0.5225 s inference gives 10.5646%, matching its 10.56%. In Table 8, listed task-time sums differ from reported totals by 0.08 h for Seq-FT, 0.07 h for EWC-LoRA and 0.09 h for Dense MoLE, exceeding a 0.05 h independent-rounding allowance. D-MoLE’s 44,772 s is 12.4367 h rather than the displayed 12.40 h. Different timing boundaries or runs could explain these differences; logs and inclusion of autoencoder training are needed. An IconQA epoch discrepancy between Appendices A and H also remains. These issues do not establish a reversal of the broad training-time ordering.

No repeated-run significance test or raw checkpoint-by-task score matrix was reproduced. The word significantly should not be interpreted as an independently verified statistical result. The public issue alleging different reproduced values is an unverified user report; it is not treated as evidence that the paper’s scores are wrong.
# 8. Version, provenance and execution record

The publisher record is PMLR 267:19011-19033. The available arXiv record is 2506.11672v1, submitted 2025-06-13, with a separately preserved 24-page PDF (SHA-256 `d26c6fe9612c637d6cad7e40ed9dbff50074c48cb5034231d72767edb70a02d2`). The repository’s current pinned commit is dated 2026-01-11; its most recent changes concern download links, with the three checked core files (router, allocator and scorer) unchanged since the 2025-06-16 initial release. Forty-six relevant source text files were preserved and their Git blob hashes verified. Paper: I25-43455 / 0086
Reviewed version: ICML 2025 / PMLR 267:37874-37888; publisher-linked 15-page PDF
Supported outcome: Major: invalid response-level derivation of the proposed local decoder; empirical scores not disproved
Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]
Source SHA-256: 861b0e1d6e7d6c5ed783f13e786b7562f1ab50cb33e8e217d2c68ef62907932f
# 1. Identity, scope and supported outcome

Authors: Baijiong Lin, Weisen Jiang, Yuancheng Xu, Hao Chen and Ying-Cong Chen. Review date: 24 October 2026. The local source was hashed before analysis and matched verification/0086/controller_acquisition_receipt.json. Title, authors and publisher PDF link match the PMLR landing page. All locations below use the printed page number, which equals the one-based PDF page number; they do not use the PMLR volume’s page numbering.

The principal supported finding concerns Section 4.4, p. 6: the globally normalized response law in Eq. (12) does not in general have the locally normalized next-token conditional in Eq. (13). An exact two-token example gives a first-token probability of 41/66 under Eq. (12), versus 1/2 under Eq. (13). The omitted continuation partition links the mathematical failure directly to the proposed decoder’s response-level alignment interpretation.

This is a Major finding under the task’s clarified standard for a substantial invalid derivation tied to a core contribution. It does not assert that PARM’s published benchmark scores are false. The local decoder remains a valid heuristic, the PBLoRA architecture remains implementable, and Theorem 4.1 is correct under its stated rank assumptions.
Inspected component | Location and result
Inspected component | Location and result
Reward and inference derivation | Sections 3 and 4.4, Eqs. (1)-(6), (11)-(13): exact conditionalization fails; Problem 1.
Architecture and proof | Section 4.2; Appendix C: outer-product independence verified; expressiveness interpretation qualified.

Empirical evidence | Section 5, Tables 2-5, Figures 1-4, Appendices D-F: definitions, settings and reported percentage arithmetic checked; no model run.

Scientific decisions remain pending. No human verification, author contact, author adoption, experiment reproduction, or whole-paper correctness certification is recorded.
# 2. Problem 1: the stated response law and decoder differ

Source claim and suspect step. Section 4.4, p. 6, defines the reward as the sum of ARM token log probabilities (Eq. 11), substitutes it into a response-level aligned distribution (Eq. 12), and then presents Eq. (13) as the next-token conditional obtained according to Eq. (12). The same transition appears in the GenARM background, p. 3, Eqs. (4)-(5). The defect is the marginalization over unseen suffixes, not the validity of either individual autoregressive model.
\[P^*(y)=Z^{-1}\prod_{t=1}^{T}b(y_t\mid y_{<t})q(y_t\mid y_{<t})^{1/\beta},\qquad Q(u\mid h)=\frac{b(u\mid h)q(u\mid h)^{1/\beta}}{\sum_v b(v\mid h)q(v\mid h)^{1/\beta}}.\]

Counterexample parameters. Fix one prompt, beta = 1, preference alpha = (1/2,1/2), binary tokens 0 and 1, and a horizon of two generated tokens. Let the frozen base b and the ARM q coincide, with the following conditionals. A terminal symbol may be appended after the fixed horizon.
Prefix | b(0 | prefix) = q(0 | prefix) | b(1 | prefix) = q(1 | prefix)
Prefix | b(0 | prefix) = q(0 | prefix) | b(1 | prefix) = q(1 | prefix)

Assumption check. Every allowed token probability is strictly positive and each conditional sums to one. The base is fixed. The ARM is a normalized autoregressive model. The reward is exactly log q(y), beta is positive and matches the experimental setting, alpha lies in the interior of the simplex, and Z is finite. The claimed algebraic implication imposes neither b != q nor exact training optimality. The example audits that implication, not the actual outputs of an Alpaca checkpoint.
Response | b(y) = q(y) | Eq. (12): P*(y) | Eq. (13): Q(y)
Response | b(y) = q(y) | Eq. (12): P*(y) | Eq. (13): Q(y)

The unnormalized Eq. (12) weights are 81/400, 1/400, 1/16 and 1/16; Z = 33/100. Thus P*(first token = 0) = 41/66. Eq. (13) instead gives Q(first token = 0) = 1/2, a discrepancy of 4/33. These values are verified by the saved exact-arithmetic replay, not estimated by simulation.
# 3. Complete derivation, impact and scoped correction

Let w(u|h) = b(u|h) q(u|h)^(1/beta). Define H(h) as the sum over every allowed complete suffix after h of the product of its remaining w factors, and set H(terminal) = 1. Direct summation gives the exact conditional of Eq. (12):
\[H(h)=\sum_v w(v\mid h)H(hv),\qquad P^*(u\mid h)=\frac{w(u\mid h)H(hu)}{H(h)}.\]

Equation (13) drops H(hu). Equality holds only when H(hu) is constant across next tokens with positive weight. Separate normalization of b and q does not enforce that condition. In the example H(0) = 41/50 and H(1) = 1/2, so the missing factor changes the very first conditional.

A second check measures the precise consequence for the response-level regularized objective. For beta = 1 and J(P) = E_P[log q(y)] - KL(P||b), the Gibbs identity gives J(P*) - J(Q) = KL(Q||P*) > 0. The replay obtains J(P*) = -1.1086626245, J(Q) = -1.1389462402 and a gap of 0.03028361568 nats. This finite-model calculation establishes an objective mismatch; it is not a benchmark-performance claim.

Dependency and supported impact. Equation (13) is the proposed inference mechanism. Equation (12) is its connection to the response-level reward-aligned law introduced in Eq. (1). The invalid inference breaks that connection even at a two-token horizon. A demonstration that published HV or MIP scores deteriorate is unnecessary to establish this central derivation failure.

Alternative reading and counterevidence. The tilde on the decoder distribution can be read as indicating an approximate or surrogate policy. Such a policy is well-defined and may work empirically. However, Section 4.4 does not state the continuation-factor approximation and explicitly connects Eq. (13) to Eq. (12). If only a heuristic was intended, that intention narrows the claim; it does not make the exact conditionalization valid. The analogous background formula is attributed to GenARM, so this report does not claim the defect or its discovery originated with PARM.

Precise mathematical correction. Including H(hu) restores the exact conditional by the identity above. This correction is analytically verified for finite horizons, and reduces to Eq. (13) under the stated constant-continuation condition. Computing H generally requires summing over future completions; no equally efficient corrected implementation is claimed. Alternatively, retain Eq. (13) as a local heuristic and withdraw the exact response-level derivation. That is a scope correction, not verification of the original equality.

What survives. The PBLoRA parameterization, Theorem 4.1, the existence and local normalization of the decoder, and the use of one preference-conditioned ARM survive. The reported empirical comparisons have not been independently refuted. Measuring the empirical effect of exact or approximate continuation correction would require fresh experiments, which were not performed.
# 4. Checks that constrain the finding

Theorem 4.1 and Appendix C, pp. 4-5 and 13-14. The theorem assumes B has column rank r and A has row rank r. A zero linear combination of the claimed outer products is BCA = 0. Apply a left inverse of B and a right inverse of A to obtain C = 0. This verifies all r^2 products are independent and agrees with the appendix’s columnwise proof.
\[L B=I_r,\quad A R=I_r,\quad BCA=0\ \Longrightarrow\ C=L(BCA)R=0.\]

Expressiveness scope. With A and B fixed, arbitrary W spans r^2 directions and diagonal W spans r directions. The theorem supports that comparison. With freely trainable factors, however, BWA = B’A with B’ = BW, so no larger unrestricted rank-r matrix class follows. In the actual Eq. (9), a linear/affine W2(alpha) over the (k-1)-dimensional simplex traces at most k-1 affine directions after training. These qualifications preserve the valid theorem and the usefulness of preference conditioning; they are recorded as scope clarification, not another theorem defect.

Loss sign and code counterevidence. On p. 3 the text sets z = 1 when the first response is preferred, while Eq. (3) multiplies its log-probability difference by (-1)^z. Those two conventions disagree. The released trainer instead selects chosen and rejected responses from response IDs and uses the chosen-minus-rejected log-probability direction. This prevents an unsupported allegation that published experiments trained against preference labels. The isolated printed sign/label inconsistency is outside the requested substantive-finding scope.

Scalarization scope. The standard sufficient result uses strictly positive weights and an exact global scalar minimum. At boundary weights a scalar minimizer need only be weakly Pareto optimal; joint optimization over a shared conditioned model need not attain every independent per-preference minimum. Section 4.3’s practical approximation claim is therefore not treated as a verified guarantee of the entire true Pareto set. No additional neural-model counterexample was established here.

Empirical checks. The Table 2 HV improvement is 14.1333%; its MIP improvement is 223.75%. Table 3 improvements versus GenARM are 6.0735% and 91.1602%, and versus MOD-w2s are 26.0536% and 17.6871%. These agree with the reported rounded percentages. Thirty boundary plus six positive-interior preference points gives the stated 36-point evaluation design.

Appendix D gives a minimization-form hypervolume expression, while the reported reward axes favor larger values. A sign conversion and reference point are needed for replay. The inspected release does not supply a complete HV/MIP reproduction pipeline or the per-response outputs used in the tables. This limits empirical verification; it does not prove the reported metric values wrong. Oracle-reward results also do not by themselves establish human preference satisfaction.

report: Scientific Verification Report
Aligning Multimodal Representations through an Information Bottleneck

Paper: I25-43456 / 0087
Reviewed version: ICML2025/PMLR267:1250-1270;21-page publisher-linked PDF
Supported outcome: Major: false information bound, overbroad alignment guarantee and invalid essence uniqueness; bounded additional defects
Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]
Source SHA-256: 10ffd2d2a546dff928447874e446e1d4a2bf92b73144216a6f10c1787a67e63d
# 1. Identity, scope and result

Authors: Antonio Almudevar, Jose Miguel Hernandez-Lobato, Sameer Khurana, Ricard Marxer and Alfonso Ortega. Reviewed on 24 October 2026. The 21-page publisher PDF was hashed before analysis, matched the controller acquisition receipt, and matched the publisher’s title, authors and source link. Page numbers below are the printed numbers, equal to one-based PDF page numbers.

The principal result is a demonstrated failure of Eq. (17), the mutual-information upper bound used to derive the proposed regularizer. Its right-hand side can equal zero while the left-hand side is positive, including within the equal-variance spherical-Gaussian setting. A second finding concerns Theorem 2’s unrestricted kernel-based guarantee: perfect CKA need not imply zero nuisance information. Both bear directly on the paper’s theoretical explanation of alignment.

The proposed agreement loss remains a usable objective, its equal-covariance Gaussian KL calculation is correct, and these findings do not establish that the reported captioning or retrieval scores are false. A precise conditional-information interpretation survives. The essence-uniqueness claim is a third core formal defect. Bounded additional issues concern the appendix’s temperature derivation and a released retrieval evaluator.
Coverage | Actual inspection
Coverage | Actual inspection
Main theory | Definitions 1-5; Lemma 1; Theorems 1-2; Eqs. (3)-(20); Appendix A.
Auxiliary derivation | Appendix B, p. 15: symbolic differentiation and finite numerical check.
Empirical sections | Sections 5-6 and Appendix C: settings, metric definitions and code paths; Appendix D-E caption text and retrieval descriptions screened.
Code and history | Pinned public repository, selected methods/evaluation files, all 72 text/config files archived, version/issue records inspected.

No author program, training job, model inference, paid API or empirical reproduction was run. Figures were not independently rescored, and illustrative image-caption examples are not a quantitative validation. Human verification, scientific decisions and controller acceptance remain pending.
# 2. Problem 1 - false variational upper bound (Major)

Claim and location. Section 4.2, p. 4, Eq. (17), and Appendix A.5, p. 14, Eqs. (25)-(29), state that I(Z_alpha;X_alpha) is upper-bounded by the average KL divergence between the paired modality-conditional representation laws. This bound is then converted into the squared-distance regularizer in Eq. (18), and used in the claimed information-bottleneck objective and loss, Eqs. (19)-(20).
\[I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha)\ \leq\ {\mathbb E}_{X_\alpha,X_\beta}D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p(z\mid X_\alpha)\,\|\,q(z\mid X_\beta)\right)\quad\hbox{(claimed).}\]

Complete counterexample. Let S,A,B be independent fair bits. Take X_alpha=(S,A), X_beta=(S,B), essence Y=S, and nuisances N_alpha=A, N_beta=B. Each encoder outputs the shared bit through the same binary symmetric channel: P(Z=S|S)=9/10 and P(Z!=S|S)=1/10. The two encoder draws can be conditionally independent.

All operative assumptions hold. The inputs are conditionally independent given S; Y is determined by either input, so both essence Markov chains hold. Each nuisance is independent of Y and determined by its own input. In bits, H(X_alpha)=H(X_beta)=2 and H(Y)=H(N_alpha)=H(N_beta)=1, verifying Definition 2’s entropy identity. The encoders are stochastic functions of their own inputs and all their output probabilities are positive.
\[\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)=0,\qquad I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha)=\log 2+\tfrac9{10}\log\tfrac9{10}+\tfrac1{10}\log\tfrac1{10}=0.3680642072>0.\]
The conditional laws coincide on every positive input pair, making KL zero, while Z still encodes S. The claimed inequality is therefore false, independently of any numerical approximation.

Gaussian restriction does not rescue it. Let S instead be a fair sign, retain independent nuisance bits, and use N(S,1) as both encoders’ conditional law. Their means agree for every positive pair, so both KL and the proposed squared-distance term are zero. Yet I(Z;S)>0 because N(-1,1) and N(1,1) are distinct. Reviewer-owned quadrature gives approximately 0.3368308203 nats; strict positivity follows analytically from non-independence.
# 3. Problem 1 - exact repair scope and contribution dependency

Invalid step. Appendix A.5 treats the remainder after inserting q(z|X_beta) as a nonnegative KL term in Eq. (28). The averaging measure still depends on the same z being integrated inside the alleged KL. The stated expression is not the nonnegative KL decomposition needed for Eq. (29). Marginal input information cannot be discarded merely because paired conditional encoders agree.

Correct identity. Under the local-encoder Markov relation Z_alpha - X_alpha - X_beta, let p(z|X_beta) be the conditional distribution induced by the alpha encoder. Directly add and subtract its log density:

\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p(z\mid X_\alpha)\|q(z\mid X_\beta))
&=I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha\mid X_\beta)\\
&\quad+\mathbb E_{X_\beta}D_{\rm KL}(p(z\mid X_\beta)\|q(z\mid X_\beta)).
\end{aligned}\]

Thus the computable cross-modal KL upper-bounds conditional input information, not total input information. Equivalently, total information is bounded by that KL plus I(Z_alpha;X_beta). In the counterexample, conditional information is zero while the shared-information term is positive, exactly accounting for the discrepancy.
\[I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha)\leq \mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)+I(Z_\alpha;X_\beta).\]

Impact. Equation (17) is the stated theoretical bridge from input compression to the proposed distance penalty. Its failure invalidates that bridge and the claimed exact substitution into the ordinary IB objective. This is central derivation damage even if the same agreement regularizer improves practical alignment or captioning.

What a correction does and does not establish. Conditional-information regularization can give a defensible alternative motivation. With exact information quantities, I(Z;X_beta)-beta I(Z;X_alpha|X_beta) equals (1+beta)I(Z;X_beta)-beta I(Z;X_alpha). It changes the coefficient relationship and does not restore the printed Eq. (17). Replacing information terms with InfoNCE lower bounds is also a surrogate optimization, not exact equality of the objectives or their minimizers.

Appendix A.6 survives: equal spherical covariance yields KL = ||mu_alpha-mu_beta||^2/(2 sigma^2). The error occurs before that valid Gaussian algebra. The analytic conditional identity is verified; no corrected training run, performance claim or author-adopted repair is asserted.
# 4. Problem 2 - perfect kernel alignment does not force minimality

Claim and scope. Theorem 2, p. 4, and Appendix A.3, p. 13, assert that alignment in the sense of Eq. (2) implies I(Z_alpha;N_alpha)=I(Z_beta;N_beta)=0. Equation (2), p. 2, permits general kernel functions. The theorem is a necessary-condition claim; this review does not reverse it into a sufficiency claim.

Use independent fair signs S,A,B, inputs (S,A) and (S,B), common essence S, and independent nuisances A,B. Set Z_alpha=(S,A)/sqrt(2), Z_beta=(S,B)/sqrt(2). Both representations are deterministic functions of their own inputs, unit norm, sufficient for S, and preserve one bit of their respective nuisance. The essence and nuisance assumptions verified in Problem 1 also hold in this sign-valued construction.
\[k(z,z')=l(z,z')=z_1z'_1,\qquad K=L=\tfrac12 ss^\top,\qquad {\rm CKA}(K,L)=1.\]

This is a valid positive-semidefinite kernel with nonzero centered Gram norm whenever both signs occur. Nevertheless, I(Z_alpha;N_alpha)=I(Z_beta;N_beta)=1 bit. The Gram equality holds for arbitrary repetitions of the full support and in the population limit. It is not the finite-sample exception already acknowledged by the appendix.

Proof failure. Appendix A.3 infers a deterministic surjection from Z_alpha to Z_beta when nuisance information is present. Here H(Z_beta|Z_alpha)=H(B)=1 bit, so no such function exists. It also assumes that the kernel distinguishes the relevant unequal representations, which a permitted projection kernel need not do.

Counterevidence and exact impact. The actual release uses full-feature linear CKA. In this same example its CKA equals 1/2, so the counterexample does not refute those measured values or the narrower empirical association. The supported Major judgment concerns the central stated theoretical guarantee and its proof under the kernel generality allowed by Eq. (2). Perfect similarity under a kernel cannot certify removal of information that kernel ignores.

Repair remains scoped. A valid guarantee needs explicit restrictions on the kernel and representation coupling, followed by a proof appropriate to them. No blanket repaired theorem for all kernels is claimed. The software’s full-feature linear choice and the empirical trends survive this particular counterexample.
# 5. Problem 3 - essence uniqueness uses an unstated premise (Major)

Source: Definition 1 and Lemma 1, p. 3; Appendix A.1, p. 13. The definition supplies two Markov chains, while the proof immediately treats the essence as a minimal sufficient statistic and infers a bijection. Those Markov chains alone do not supply that premise.

Counterexample. Let independent fair signs S,A,B define X_alpha=(S,A), X_beta=(S,B). Both Y=S and Y’=X_beta satisfy X_beta - Y - X_alpha and Y - X_beta - X_alpha. For Y, this follows from independent nuisances and the fact S is known from X_beta. For Y’=X_beta, both conditional-independence statements are immediate. Yet Y has two states and Y’ four, with H(Y’|Y)=1 bit; no bijection on their supports exists.

Even the displayed nuisance constraints can be met: for Y=S choose A,B; for Y’=X_beta, both input entropies and H(Y’) are two bits, so constant nuisances meet Definition 2’s displayed identities. The latter interpretation shows why the formal definition does not capture the intended common-information meaning.

Alternative reading and calibrated impact. The surrounding prose calls essence the common part, and Appendix A.1 clearly intends a minimal sufficient statistic. That stronger intended definition is not supplied by the two displayed Markov chains. The supported judgment is Major: Section 3.1 explicitly identifies the unique essence-induced input partition as the learning target, treats the essence as unique thereafter, and Section 3.2 uses Lemma 1 to claim that all ideal representations create the same partition. The verified nonbijective essences invalidate this formal uniqueness guarantee within the paper’s central information-theoretic formulation. The finite-discrete repair below and the survival of Theorem 1 and Appendix A.4 do not establish the original lemma under Definition 1.

Precise finite-discrete repair. Add H(Y|X_alpha)=0 for each candidate essence. Equation (5) then forces H(Y|X_beta)=0. Given Eq. (4), any other deterministic variable shared by both conditionally independent inputs must be constant conditional on Y; hence it is a function of Y. Apply the same reasoning in reverse to obtain a bijection on the supports. This repairs the lemma in the stated finite-discrete setting; no unrestricted continuous-variable repair is asserted.

Checked statements that survive. Theorem 1 follows directly by selecting the identity task T=Y in its premise about all deterministic tasks. Its proof’s unnecessary Markov-chain sentence can be replaced by T - Y - Z_alpha, without changing the conclusion. Appendix A.4’s equality I(Z_alpha;Y)=I(Z_alpha;X_beta) follows from the two stated Markov chains and local encoder conditional independence. Neither result is refuted by the uniqueness example.
# 6. Problem 4 - incorrect adaptive-temperature derivation (Minor)

Location: Appendix B, p. 15, Eqs. (34)-(40). The appendix differentiates a variant whose positive-pair numerator uses tau’ and whose denominator uses tau, then claims a sample-dependent effective temperature gap. The printed positive-log signs already disagree with minimization and the displayed gradients. Even after correcting those signs to the intended negative log loss, the positive-pair derivative in Eq. (38) is wrong.

\[D=\sum_k e^{s_{ik}/\tau},\qquad L'_i=-s_{ii}/\tau'+\log D,\qquad
\frac{\partial L'_i}{\partial s_{ii}}=-\frac1{\tau'}+\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\tau D}.\]

The denominator’s positive-pair term differentiates at tau, not tau’. The printed Eq. (38) instead places tau’ in both the prefactor and the numerator exponential of this correction. At s_ii=0.2, one negative similarity s_ij=0.1, tau=0.5 and tau’=0.25, the correct derivative is -2.9003320054; Eq. (38) gives -0.7189762528. These cosine similarities are feasible for unit vectors, for example an anchor e1 and two vectors having first coordinates 0.2 and 0.1.
An exact calculation is simpler than Eq. (40). For unit-norm vectors, the squared-distance penalty is proportional to 2 beta(1-s_ii). Therefore:

\[\begin{aligned}
L_i&=-s_{ii}/\tau+\log D+2\beta(1-s_{ii}),\\
\frac1{\tau'}&=\frac1{\tau}+2\beta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_i=L'_i+2\beta .
\end{aligned}\]

The equivalence uses a constant coefficient mapping for fixed beta and tau; it does not yield the appendix’s claimed sample-dependent adaptive gap. Symbolic differentiation and simplification in regularizer_replay.py verify the derivative and the zero residual of this identity.

Impact and limits. This invalidates the appendix’s particular adaptive-temperature derivation, a bounded secondary explanation. It does not refute the observed learned-temperature trajectories in Section 5.3 or the regularizer’s implementation. The repaired algebra concerns this numerator/denominator variant only; it is not an empirical explanation or a verified dynamical model of information homeostasis.
# 7. Problem 5 - released retrieval evaluator cannot satisfy its caller

Supported judgment: Minor, bounded to the inspected public release. Paper Section 6, Table 3, p. 8, reports both image-to-text and text-to-image recall. The released captioning evaluation path attempts to obtain those directions from an incompatible helper interface.
Source path below multimodal_ib/ | Decisive observation
Source path below multimodal_ib/ | Decisive observation
src/experiments/captioning/train.py, lines 11 and 175-180 | Imports the metrics helper, then unpacks top_k_retrieval into two recall values for each k.
src/helpers/metrics/__init__.py, line 4 | Exports top_k_retrieval from .retrieval; no replacement wrapper in the traced path.
src/helpers/metrics/retrieval.py, line 38 | Only return expression is recall.item(), a scalar; docstring also specifies float.

Complete check. Independent reviewer code, without importing author modules, defines a function returning 0.5 and attempts two-value unpacking. It raises TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable float object. AST inspection confirms that the actual helper’s only return is the scalar expression. Thus, even if preceding tensor operations succeed, the released caller cannot complete as written.

A separate visible shape problem strengthens the scope limit: the caller preserves N-by-32-by-d image query features and passes them to a helper documented for two-dimensional embeddings. The scalar contract alone is decisive, so this review does not assert which exception occurs first in a full environment.

Counterevidence and repair. This snapshot postdates publication; a different historical evaluator could have produced Table 3. The defect does not establish false published recall numbers. A complete repair needs an explicit two-direction, multi-query and multiple-caption metric specification plus matching inputs; merely changing unpacking does not verify that specification. No complete repair, rerun or author adoption was performed.

Other code checks passed within scope. Normalized 1-cosine equals half squared Euclidean distance, so it is not a new cosine-versus-MSE defect. Full linear CKA’s common HSIC scale cancels in the ratio. The toy split uses complementary seeded train/test slices, and the linear probe fits training features and evaluates test features. No train/test overlap was demonstrated by that path.
# 8. Dependence, versions and conclusion table

Core dependence is explicit: Eq. (17) supplies the claimed IB derivation of the distance regularizer; Theorem 2 supplies the claimed necessary connection from perfect alignment to nuisance removal. Those theoretical statements fail at their stated scope. The architecture, normalized agreement penalty, correct Gaussian KL identity, Theorem 1 and the Appendix A.4 equality survive the checks.

Empirical limits. The toy mutual-information proxy is a held-out linear-probe variational estimate under the datasets’ factor assumptions, not exact MI. Captioning scores, retrieval scores, error bars, model selection and the numerical figure arrays were not regenerated. The released captioning path directly uses QFormer generation, while the paper describes a separate frozen decoder LLM; historical model/configuration provenance is needed to resolve that difference. It is not treated as a demonstrated published experiment error.

Reviewed versions. The adjudicated paper is the hash-verified PMLR PDF. The archived arXiv record lists only 2506.04870v1, 5 June 2025. Public code is pinned at 600bc92829ce4fff322ebd6f2491a1929c3b5c3d, 10 September 2025. Inspected issues/comments concern code availability and releases are empty; no scientific correction was identified there. OpenReview discussion history was not inspected. No claim that all possible errata have been excluded is made.

Paper: I25-43457 / 0088
Reviewed version: ICML2025/PMLR267:39405-39419;15-page publisher-linked PDF
Supported outcome: Major: false convergence guarantee; bounded reporting and released-entry-point defects
Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]
Source SHA-256: 40affe61ba3728fd77dec4e1bde7b41edcde55efab3d670ecc4b84f270d55910
# 1. Identity, outcome and inspected scope

Hongyi Liu, Rajarshi Saha, Zhen Jia, Youngsuk Park, Jiaji Huang, Shoham Sabach, Yu-Xiang Wang and George Karypis. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:39405-39419. The reviewed artifact is the 15-page publisher-linked PDF preserved at papers/0088/0088.pdf. Its SHA-256 is recorded above and matches controller_acquisition_receipt.json. Title and authors match the publisher record. All page references below use printed pages, equal to one-based PDF pages.

Outcome: Major for a demonstrated failure of Proposition 7, the core guarantee that the proposed relaxed-objective solver converges to a critical point. An exact, bounded, smooth counterexample with both regularizers positive converges to a noncritical point because the proximal penalty omits the learning-rate factor. This does not require refuting mask learning or showing worse LLM scores.

Two separate bounded concerns are retained: reported zero-shot averages and the highlighted gain do not reconcile with arithmetic aggregation of the displayed task scores; a released full-regularizer launcher references an undefined name. The former leaves the historical aggregation unresolved; the latter does not establish which script generated published experiments.

Read and checked: Sections 2.3-4.4, Propositions 1-2 and 6-8, Corollary 3, Fact 5, Theorem 4’s definitions, Appendix A and experimental Appendices B-G; 45 displayed accuracy rows were independently recalculated. Relevant public code was statically inspected at commit 4a558bc0674cf48b676d2576ecc06dcf087f0023. Coverage.json distinguishes full reads, targeted checks, missing materials and unperformed reproduction.

Scope: Section 2.3 expressly seeks practical heuristics, not a global optimum of the original combinatorial problem. The review respects that qualification. No author code was executed. No models or datasets were downloaded or run. Human verification, scientific decisions and controller acceptance remain pending; author adoption has not been requested.
# 2. Problem 1 — a bounded exact iteration violates Proposition 7

Source claim: Eq. (3), p. 3 defines F=L+lambda1 R+lambda2 Q, where R=Reg2:4 and Q=RegW0. Proposition 7, p. 5 concludes convergence to a limiting-subdifferential critical point of F from a continuously differentiable loss and bounded iterates. The preceding paragraph also requires the inner proximal solver to return the correct solution. The following example meets that additional qualification exactly.
\[R(w)=\sum_{1\le i<j<k\le4}|w_iw_jw_k|,\qquad Q(w)=\sum_i\left[\frac{w_i(w_i-w_{0i})}{w_{0i}+\epsilon\operatorname{sign}(w_{0i})}\right]^2.\]

The suspect step is Eq. (5b) and Algorithm 1, lines 4-5, p. 4: the smooth step uses eta, but the proximal term uses lambda1 directly. For constant eta, a fixed point corresponds to coefficient lambda1/eta, not the stated lambda1.
\[W_0=w=(1,1,1,0),\quad a=(6/5,6/5,6/5,0),\quad L(W)=\tfrac12\|W-a\|^2,\quad \eta=\tfrac12,\quad\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\tfrac1{10},\quad\epsilon=10^{-9}.\]

Use the deterministic exact gradient oracle, which is unbiased with zero variance. L is C-infinity with Lipschitz gradient constant 1. Q has fixed nonzero denominators, is polynomial, and has locally Lipschitz gradient. The full objective is semi-algebraic, so even the extra regularity invoked in Appendix A is satisfied.

Every term of Q and its derivative vanishes at W0: the derivative is 2w_i(w_i-w0_i)(2w_i-w0_i)/d_i^2, with d_i the denominator. For coordinate 4 the term is w4^4/epsilon^2. Consequently V=w-eta grad(L+lambda2 Q)=(11/10,11/10,11/10,0).
# 3. Problem 1 — global proximal solution and false stationarity

Complete global check: replacing any candidate U by |U| cannot increase its distance to the nonnegative V and leaves R unchanged. Setting U4=0 strictly reduces the quadratic unless already zero and cannot increase any triple product. Capping each remaining coordinate at 11/10 also decreases the quadratic and cannot increase the penalty. Thus a global minimizer lies in [0,11/10]^3 with U4=0.
\[g(u)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^{3}(u_i-11/10)^2+\tfrac1{10}u_1u_2u_3,\qquad \nabla^2g(u)\succeq\tfrac{39}{50}I.\]

The Hessian has diagonal 1; each off-diagonal entry is a remaining coordinate divided by 10. Every absolute off-diagonal row sum is at most 0.22, proving the stated positive lower bound. At u=(1,1,1), each derivative is 1-1.1+0.1=0. Strict convexity on the cube, together with the global reductions, proves that w is the unique global proximal minimizer. No finite sampling argument is used.
Algorithm 1 therefore returns Wk=w for every k. Its iterates obey the assumed bound with B=2. Yet, along each of the first three strictly positive coordinates, grad L=-1/5, grad Q=0 and grad R=1.
\[\partial_iF(w)=-\tfrac15+\tfrac1{10}=-\tfrac1{10}\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad 0\notin\partial F(w).\]

Nonsmoothness in coordinate 4 cannot cancel the nonzero derivatives in the other three coordinates. The claimed result is convergence to a critical point; the correct result here is convergence to a noncritical point. The iteration is stationary only for the rescaled sparse coefficient lambda1/eta=1/5.

Dependency and impact: the paper introduces the regularized objective as its learnable mask-selection formulation and advertises an algorithm with convergence theory for that formulation. This exact counterexample invalidates that central solver guarantee. Major is supported even though the algebraic scaling correction is simple and the mask-learning heuristic and experiments may survive. Evidence: math_audit_notes.md and the positive-lambda2 replay/results.
# 4. Problem 1 — alternative interpretation and scoped repair

A defensible alternative is to interpret lambda1 as an independently tuned proximal strength. With constant eta, this defines an iteration for an objective with sparse coefficient lambda1/eta. It does not establish Proposition 7 for Eq. (3). A changing learning-rate schedule makes that effective coefficient time-dependent and needs a separate theorem.
\[W_{k+1}\in\arg\min_U\left\{\tfrac12\|U-V_k\|^2+\eta_k\lambda_1R(U)\right\}.\]

This correction restores the proper proximal-gradient optimality relation for the stated objective. It is not a complete convergence repair. Step-size, noise, regularity and optimizer assumptions must be stated and justified. Appendix A, p. 13 also infers locally Lipschitz gradient and semi-algebraicity from C1 loss without sufficient assumptions; the main counterexample satisfies those stronger properties, so it does not rely on that omission.

Independent exact check of the stochastic scope: take W0=(1,0,0,0), lambda2=0 (explicitly used in Table 8), lambda1=1/10, eta=1/2, L(W)=w1^2/2 and oracle G(W)=(w1+xi)e1 with independent fair signs xi. Every iterate is one-sparse, so the exact proximal step leaves V unchanged and all trajectories stay bounded by 1.
\[t_{k+1}=\tfrac12t_k-\tfrac12\xi_k,\qquad\mathbb E[t_k^2]=\tfrac13+\tfrac23\,4^{-k}\longrightarrow\tfrac13.\]

Almost-sure convergence would force xi_k=t_k-2t_(k+1) to converge, which iid fair signs do not do. Thus inserting eta alone cannot justify the unrestricted stochastic claim. The preserved initial replay supplies this analytic recurrence, not a model simulation.

Static corroboration: main.py passes learning_rate and config.lambda_ separately; patch_transformers_trainer.py lines 642-646 calls optimizer.step() then replace_weight(model, config.lambda_); prox_op.py passes that coefficient unchanged. The implementation uses AdamW and finite inner sweeps, so this is not a reproduction of the exact counterexample or proof of published score deterioration. Fresh experiments would be needed to assess a changed update.
# 5. Problem 2 — reported averages and quantitative gain need reconciliation

Source claim: Section 4.2, p. 6 reports Mistral-v0.1 average accuracy 52.7% versus Wanda’s 44.1%, described as a 20% improvement. Table 2, p. 7 lists seven task scores and an AVG column. Under ordinary arithmetic aggregation of those seven displayed scores, the largest discrepancies are:
Method | Seven-score sum / 7 | Printed AVG
Method | Seven-score sum / 7 | Printed AVG

For ProxSparse the seven inputs are 0.362, 0.698, 0.428, 0.525, 0.232, 0.756 and 0.350. Their mean exceeds Wanda’s by 8.4466%, whereas the printed AVG entries give 19.5011%. Allowing each three-decimal score an independent rounding error of 0.0005 gives a relative-gain range of 8.21%-8.68%, far below 20%. The source table was also visually checked to exclude extraction error.

The reviewer replay checks 45 rows across Tables 2, 9 and 10 and finds 11 mean discrepancies exceeding the combined rounding allowance; the two rows above dominate. This is finite arithmetic on published numbers, not reproduction of the underlying evaluation.

Alternative reading and evidentiary limit: the paper does not give a formula or weights for AVG. A different aggregation, or errors in individual cells, could change which values need correction. The inspected release contains only perplexity evaluation, with no seven-task aggregator or raw zero-shot logs. Therefore the verified result is an internal reporting inconsistency under the conventional macro-average reading; the true intended historical aggregate remains Needs Evidence.

Judgment: Minor for the bounded reporting inconsistency, with explicit quantitative impact on the highlighted gain. The displayed components do not support the quoted 20% arithmetic-average gain. ProxSparse still ranks first by recomputed mean for all seven models; that survival does not resolve the numerical inconsistency. No assertion that historical runs or all reported gains are false is made.

A separate p. 6 Llama-2-7b claim of 35% PPL improvement from 11.42 to 8.51 computes to 25.48% relative to the baseline. The broader up-to-35% PPL claim survives: Table 9’s 20.91 to 13.63 gives 34.82%. Correcting table values requires the intended aggregation and raw results. Evidence: table_arithmetic_replay.py and table_arithmetic_results.json.
# 6. Problem 3 — released full-regularizer launcher fails name resolution

Source: pinned repository commit 4a558bc0674cf48b676d2576ecc06dcf087f0023, 24 June 2025. README identifies *_full.sh scripts as using both regularizers. script/learn_mask_llama2_13b_full.sh sets project_lambda2=1 and passes it to end-to-end/main.py. In that branch, main.py lines 99-100 interpolates {regularizer} into repository_id.

Complete static check: there is no binding, definition or import for regularizer in the module. The sole AST occurrence is a Load at line 100. If that branch is reached after its model/data prerequisites, ordinary Python name resolution raises NameError before trainer construction. A separate reviewer-owned function with a fresh unbound identifier confirms this language-level behavior. Author files were parsed as text, never imported or run.

Counterevidence and impact: the lambda1-only branch avoids the interpolation. An earlier local script or unarchived change could have generated the published full-regularizer results. Supported judgment is Minor: a concrete defect in the released entry point, with historical experiment provenance unresolved. No full pipeline repair was attempted or validated, and no author adoption is asserted. Evidence: prox_static_check.py/results.json, prox_static_line_evidence.txt and prox_code_audit.md.

Other static findings materially limit the interpretation. The released top-three solver uses the correct cubic triple-product derivative, whereas the printed g3 on p. 5 has quadratic pairwise products. It copies the previous iterate at the start of each sweep, avoiding the printed Algorithm 2 placement that would stop after one sweep. It counts each derivative pair once, initializes at zero, visits coordinates in reverse order, caps 100 sweeps and uses an aggregate L1 stopping test. These differences are preserved as scoped formula/pseudocode discrepancies, not imputed to historical runs.

The inspected final mask path selects two indices in every block, reloads the original pretrained model for evaluation and applies the binary mask to original weights. This supports the paper’s final frozen-weight construction despite weight updates during mask exploration. No checkpoint tensors were acquired, so historical weight equality and score generation remain unverified.
# 7. Coverage, dependence and what survives

Regularizer reasoning checked: R is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when each block has at most two nonzeros. Permutation invariance and active-orthant differentiability hold. Each Q term vanishes at zero or the original weight, yielding Proposition 2 and Corollary 3 under fixed nonzero denominators. The ordinary at-most-two convention, versus wording about exactly two, is not treated as a substantive defect. Fact 5’s nonnegative scalar soft threshold is correct.

Inner optimization: exact coordinate minimization of the intended cubic objective has the displayed sufficient-descent structure. The paper’s 20,000-instance comparison is empirical agreement, not a universal global-optimality theorem, and the outer counterexample grants exact proximal solutions. The Proposition 6 proof has constant/transcription mismatches, but tighter cubic bounds may recover its iteration order; no independent substantive finding is assigned from those discrepancies alone. A full reconstruction of every cited convergence theorem was not performed.

Empirical coverage: checked table arithmetic, stated metric directions, calibration-size comparison, regularization ablations, final frozen-weight interpretation and the reported speed/memory measurements. The table values support broad mask-learning advantages as reported; they were not regenerated. The paper itself attributes sparse inference speedup to hardware-supported 2:4 operations, rather than a unique property of its mask selection. Runtime, GPU kernels, error bars, baseline implementations and statistical significance were not reproduced.
