report: Scientific Verification Report
Point-Level Topological Representation Learning on Point Clouds

Paper: I25-43458 / 0089
Reviewed version: ICML2025/PMLR267:20368-20398;31-page publisher-linked PDF
Supported outcome: Major within Theorem C.1(v)’s generalized support guarantee; original sphere case survives inspected checks
Batch token: [internal identifier omitted]
Source SHA-256: 76c7f84cf71da9049646a82db22ba8965e2df58d4d0a6032846033821e42faef
# 1. Identity, outcome and scope

Vincent P. Grande and Michael T. Schaub. ICML 2025, PMLR 267:20368-20398. This review uses the 31-page publisher-linked PDF at papers/0089/0089.pdf. Its SHA-256 above matches controller_acquisition_receipt.json; title and authors match the publisher record. Page references are the printed pages 1-31, equal to one-based PDF pages, not the continuous PMLR pagination.

Supported outcome: Major, scoped to the arbitrary-contractible-region extension in Theorem C.1(v). A complete geometric and linear-algebra counterexample satisfies the explicit boundary conditions and can be embedded in a point cloud satisfying the theorem’s initial random-sphere and separation premises. Its harmonic feature omits two boundary vertices that the generalized support claim includes.

What survives is stated separately: the original sphere argument in C.1(i)-(iv), the Hodge projection construction, the acknowledged finite-field lift correction, and the usefulness of TOPF on the reported data have not been disproved. The counterexample shows a false support guarantee; the algorithm itself correctly removes a cycle already filled at the chosen scale.

Two bounded findings are separate: an unconditional linear simplex-count statement is false already in dimension three; the released default weight exponent differs from the paper’s formula. Neither establishes damage to the published empirical scores. A few timing-summary inconsistencies are retained as local reporting observations.

Scope: main method and experiments, mathematical Appendices B-C, implementation/runtime/experimental Appendices D-F, selection Appendix G, weights Appendix H and limitations Appendix I. Relevant public code, notebooks, historical corrections and a pinned dependency were inspected statically. Exact independent calculations were run; no author code was executed. No models or datasets were downloaded or run. Human verification, scientific decisions and controller acceptance remain pending.
# 2. Problem 1 — the generalized support claim and local construction

Source claim: Theorem C.1(v), p. 18 extends the sphere support result to any contractible union M of (n+1)-simplices whose boundary n-simplices satisfy the empty-circumsphere condition. Its proof, p. 19 infers that a contractible M has boundary homotopy equivalent to an n-sphere, then transfers the support argument. Contractibility alone does not supply either that boundary topology or the common filling scale used for spheres.

Take n=1. In local coordinates define five points and let M be the union of the two filled triangles OAB and OCD. Translation of this entire configuration will be used on the next page to satisfy even the theorem’s opening sphere premises.
Point | Local Euclidean coordinates
Point | Local Euclidean coordinates

M is star-shaped about O and hence contractible. Its boundary is two triangular circles meeting at O; all five points are boundary points. Both filled triangles have strict empty circumdisks and are Delaunay cells. Every one of their six boundary edges is strictly Gabriel relative to the whole local point cloud: no other point is in or on its diameter disk. Exact squared-distance tests are saved; the smallest Gabriel margin is 1/2.
Event | Alpha radius
Event | Alpha radius
Small triangle fills | 1/sqrt(3)
Large triangle boundary edges appear | 3/2
Large triangle fills | sqrt(3)
Any cross edge between nonshared triangle vertices | At least sqrt(13)/2 > sqrt(3)

Throughout the large persistent class’s lifetime (3/2, sqrt(3)), the local complex is therefore a filled small triangle joined at O to an unfilled large circle. Any interpolation gamma in (0,1), including the default 0.3, selects a scale within this same interval. These are actual alpha-filtration events, not an arbitrary abstract complex substituted for the paper’s geometry.
# 3. Problem 1 — preserving the opening random-sphere assumptions

An interpretation concern must be addressed: C.1 begins with random samples S on a unit sphere and allows arbitrary extra points at distance at least 2 from S. The five-point configuration alone is not such a sphere sample. To avoid relying on whether ’more generally’ cancels the opening premise, retain that premise explicitly.

Let S consist of three independent uniform points on the unit circle centered at the origin. Translate the five local points and M by T=(100,0), and define X=S union (T+{O,A,B,C,D}). The external points are fixed independently of the random sample. Every translated point has norm at least 97, so its distance from every point of S is at least 96, far exceeding the required 2.

All relevant local Delaunay circumdisks and Gabriel disks lie strictly to the right of x=95; thus no point of S enters them. Every simplex joining the two components has circumradius at least 48, since it contains an edge of length at least 96. Consequently the local alpha complex and all previous strict inequalities remain unchanged through radius sqrt(3). Almost surely, the three noncollinear sphere samples form a filled triangle at radius 1; this separate component contributes no first homology during the large class’s lifetime.

Even if one additionally imports the Gabriel condition for S itself, there is a positive-probability event on which it holds. Require one sample in each arc of angular radius pi/24 centered at 0, 2pi/3 and 4pi/3. This has probability 6(1/24)^3=1/2304. Consecutive angular gaps are between 105 and 135 degrees, making the triangle acute, hence its edges strictly Gabriel. The failure below persists throughout that event, so it cannot be dismissed as a measure-zero special configuration.

M is a contractible subset of the Delaunay triangles of this full X and meets every explicitly imposed boundary condition. Thus the embedded example also covers inheritance of the initial sampling/separation premises. A further restriction that M must use only vertices of S would exclude it, but that restriction is not stated in the universal ’any contractible subset M’ clause and would narrow the claimed extension.

Evidence: math_audit_embedded_replay.py/results.json proves the uniform bounds and checks an illustrative exact matrix realization. The probability argument uses the full arc event, not a claim that one fixed equilateral sample has positive probability. The earlier local example and its narrower-scope notes remain preserved.
# 4. Problem 1 — exact harmonic output, impact and repair limits

Use edge order OA, OB, AB, OC, OD, CD. Let cs=(1,-1,1,0,0,0) and cl=(0,0,0,1,-1,1). The oriented boundary of M is g=cs+cl. Both are real cycles, so no finite-field lifting failure is involved. During the entire interval above, the local curl space is spanned by cs, the boundary of the filled small triangle.
\[P_{\rm curl}g=c_s,\qquad P_{\rm harm}g=c_l,\qquad F(O,A,B,C,D)=(1/2,0,0,1,1).\]

The first homology is one-dimensional at this scale; every nonzero representative of the surviving class has the same normalized harmonic support. There is no basis-selection ambiguity. Under the printed coface weights, the three small edges have W=1/4 and the large edges W=1. The transformed input is 2cs+cl and the weighted curl direction 2cs; projection again gives cl. The released inverse-first-power weights also remove the small component.

Thus the stated support is all five points of M, whereas the calculated support is only {O,C,D}; all sphere-component values are zero. A and B are boundary vertices, so replacing ’points contained in M’ by ’boundary points’ does not fix this example. The standard algorithm appropriately discards an already-filled component, contradicting the overbroad guarantee rather than the Hodge machinery.

Dependency: Section 3, p. 6 and the conclusion, p. 9 invoke C.1 as theoretical support for recovering point-level topological structure. Part (v) is the step extending that guarantee beyond the common-scale sphere setting. Its invalid boundary inference and missing filtration-scale control yield a demonstrably false support conclusion. Major is supported for this core theoretical extension, independently of whether the empirical clustering scores survive.

Counterevidence and limited repair: the inspected C.1(i)-(iv) sphere proof retains a common filling radius 1, boundary births below 1 and separation from mixed simplices. Those conditions avoid this failure. Withdrawing the arbitrary-contractible extension preserves that supported scope. A new extension requires explicitly justified geometric and filtration assumptions; merely adding contractibility, or changing boundary wording, is insufficient. No complete replacement theorem, author adoption or changed experiment is claimed.
# 5. Problem 2 — fixed dimension does not imply linear complex size

Source claim: Appendix E.2, p. 23, theoretical runtime item 1(a), states that for fixed ambient dimension the alpha complex has a number of simplices linear in the number of points. This is distinct from the preceding empirical observation that Figure 11 appears linear on two particular data families. The unconditional combinatorial statement is false already in dimension three.
\[P_i=(i,0,0),\quad Q_j=(0,j,1),\quad 0\le i,j<m,\qquad N=2m.\]

For every adjacent pair on each line, the four points Pi, P(i+1), Qj, Q(j+1) form a tetrahedron of nonzero determinant -1. Set x=i+1/2, y=j+1/2 and z=(x^2-y^2+1)/2. Their circumsphere has center (x,y,z) and squared radius 1/4+y^2+z^2.

Hence all (m-1)^2 such tetrahedra are strict Delaunay cells, and the full alpha filtration eventually includes them. The size is at least quadratic in N, despite dimension three being fixed. Strict inequalities allow small generic perturbations; the argument does not require an ambiguous cospherical triangulation. The reviewer replay checks exact instances m=3,5,10, while the formulas establish the entire family.

Judgment: Minor for a bounded worst-case complexity assertion. It removes a general linear-size justification for scalability but does not refute measured runtimes or the use of alpha complexes on suitable data. The CGAL 6.2.1 primary manual independently documents quadratic worst-case three-dimensional triangulations and near-linear behavior under appropriate distributions.

Precise correction supported here: distinguish empirical or distribution-dependent near-linear behavior from unrestricted worst-case size, which can be quadratic already in three dimensions. This is a combinatorial correction, not a complete runtime theorem for persistent homology or iterative least squares. Evidence: complexity_and_table_replay.py/results.json and the archived CGAL manual with retrieval receipt.

Reviewed version: ICML 2025 / PMLR 267:27021-27049; 29-page publisher-linked PDF
Supported outcome: Major: two demonstrated core mathematical failures; bounded release defects and unresolved empirical provenance are separate.

# 1. Identity, checked contribution and supported outcome

This report reviews Tejas Jayashankar, Jongha (Jon) Ryu and Gregory Wornell, Score-of-Mixture Training: One-Step Generative Model Training Made Simple via Score Estimation of Mixture Distributions, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:27021–27049 [R1]. The preserved publisher-linked PDF has 29 pages and 13,825,964 bytes. Its title, authors and SHA-256 were checked against the controller acquisition receipt before scientific analysis. All paper locations below use printed page numbers, equal to one-based PDF pages 1–29, rather than the volume folios.

Reviewed on 24 October 2026. Main text, relevant supplementary proofs, method pseudocode, experimental claims and a pinned public implementation were inspected. The method trains one-step generators using scores of real/fake mixtures; its distillation variant explicitly combines a teacher score, a learned fake score and a learned density-ratio gate.
Item | Supported judgment | Precise consequence
Item | Supported judgment | Precise consequence
Problem 1 | Major | The adaptive generator normalization removes the claimed forward-KL limit at exact scores.
Problem 2 | Major | Fixed-\(\alpha\) mixture DSM does not identify both factors asserted by Corollary 4.1; its separate-factor generator update can be wrong.
Problem 3 | Minor | The released FID evaluator adds an erroneous rank-one covariance offset.
Problem 4 | Minor | Documented release paths contain incompatible calls and incomplete entry-point contracts.
Configuration and historical runs | Needs Evidence / clarification | Release differences do not establish which code produced published scores.

The two Major judgments concern derivations directly supporting the central scientific contribution. They do not depend on demonstrating FID deterioration, refuting all experiments, or establishing that repair is difficult. The underlying unweighted divergence gradient and mixture-score regression identities survive the inspected checks. Actual multi-\(\alpha\) training and separate fake-score anchoring provide substantial counterevidence against inferring failure of the implemented training procedure from the fixed-\(\alpha\) theorem.

Scientific decisions, human verification and controller acceptance remain pending. Author adoption has not been requested. No human-review declaration is made. No author code was executed; no models or datasets were downloaded or run. No empirical reproduction or paid model/API calls were performed.
# 2. Definitions, assumptions and reasoning that survives

At a fixed positive Gaussian noise level \(\sigma\), let p and q denote the real and generated noised densities, m\(\alpha\)=\(\alpha\)p+(1\(-\)\(\alpha\))q, and s_r=\(\nabla\)log r. The data distribution before noising is p0; a differentiable generator g\(\theta\) maps an independent latent variable to generated clean samples. Expectations in noised gradient formulas also average over the injected Gaussian noise. Function-space regression claims require realizability and attainment; pathwise differentiation additionally requires differentiation/integration interchange and transport regularity.
\[D_\alpha=\frac{\alpha p}{m_\alpha},\qquad s_{m_\alpha}=D_\alpha s_p+(1-D_\alpha)s_q,\qquad \Delta=s_q-s_p.\]

Proposition 3.1 and Appendix A.1 [R1, pp.3,12] are consistent with direct differentiation of the paper’s scaled \(\alpha\)-JSD. Mass conservation cancels explicit score-mean terms, yielding the pathwise score-difference update. The \(\alpha\)\(\to\)0 and \(\alpha\)\(\to\)1 limits are forward and reverse KL under the needed integrability. At \(\alpha\)=1/2 the paper’s normalization is four times conventional JSD; its own gradient remains internally consistent.

\[\mathcal D_\alpha=\frac{\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert m_\alpha)}{\alpha}+\frac{\mathrm{KL}(p\Vert m_\alpha)}{1-\alpha},\quad
\partial_\theta\mathcal D_\alpha=\frac1\alpha\int(\partial_\theta q)\log(q/m_\alpha).\]

Completing the square verifies Proposition 3.2’s mixture-score regression. Gaussian DSM in Proposition A.1 identifies \(-\)E[\(\epsilon\)|Y]/\(\sigma\)=s_m\(\alpha\)(Y). Proposition A.2 follows by differentiating log m\(\alpha\) [pp.13–14]. These facts identify the combined score, not an arbitrary learned factorization of it. Four independent Gaussian quadrature/finite-difference checks of Proposition 3.1 differ by at most 4.58\(\times\)10^\(-\)10 [E1]. These finite checks support the analytic calculation; they are not a general proof.

Tweedie’s relation s=(f\(-\)y)/\(\sigma\)\({}^{2}\) and the denoiser conversion in Appendix C are correct in the inspected Gaussian setting. Static source inspection confirms the real/fake DSM mixture weights, generator detachment in score training, generator vector-field sign, frozen teacher and correct logistic gate [E2]. Appendix D.3’s discriminator argument assumes both component scores are already correct. Its weighted Brier optimum identifies the gate where their difference is nonzero, under unrestricted realizability; it cannot establish simultaneous recovery of both unknown factors.
# 3. Problem 1 — adaptive weighting eliminates the claimed KL interpolation

Source claim and location. Section 3.5, p.5, Eq.(9)–(10), defines a samplewise adaptive weight and states that it preserves the forward-KL limiting behavior as \(\alpha\)\(\to\)0. This supports the multi-divergence explanation in Section 3.1 and the interpretation of the ablation in Section 5.3. The printed new normalization contains no additive pseudo-Huber constant. Write w=w_DMD w\(\alpha\) and retain the common DMD weight exactly.

\[w_\alpha=\alpha\frac{\|s_q-s_p\|}{\|s_q-s_{m_\alpha}\|},\qquad
\gamma^w=\mathbb E_q\!\left[J_\theta g\, w_{\mathrm{DMD}}w_\alpha\frac{s_q-s_{m_\alpha}}{\alpha}\right].\]

Complete check. For 0<\(\alpha\)<1, positive p,q and \(\Delta\)\(\ne\)0, the valid mixture-score identity from Proposition A.2 gives s_q\(-\)s_m\(\alpha\)=D\(\alpha\)\(\Delta\) with D\(\alpha\)>0. Homogeneity of the norm then gives w\(\alpha\)=\(\alpha\)/D\(\alpha\). Substitution yields the following pointwise identity, before any expectation or limit.

\[w_\alpha\,\frac{s_q-s_{m_\alpha}}{\alpha}=\Delta,\qquad
\gamma^w=\mathbb E_q[J_\theta g\,w_{\mathrm{DMD}}\Delta]\quad(0<\alpha<1).\]

This is the same DMD-weighted reverse-KL direction as at \(\alpha\)=1. Before the new normalizer, the forward limit is (p/q)\(\Delta\): its density ratio changes the generated-data expectation to a real-data expectation. The new normalizer removes precisely that factor. Calling the update weighted does not preserve the missing \(\alpha\) dependence.

Implementation check. At pinned [R2], main/sjsd/sjsd_guidance.py:263–276 computes \[R=\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{mean}((p_\alpha-p_0)^2)}
                   {\operatorname{mean}((p_1-p_0)^2+10^{-6})}},
 \qquad \mathrm{grad}=\frac{p_\alpha-p_0}{A R},
 \qquad A=\operatorname{mean}|p_1|.\] Exact mixture denoisers imply p\(\alpha\)\(-\)p0=D\(\alpha\)(p1\(-\)p0). Hence D\(\alpha\) cancels even with this stabilizer: the remaining factor depends on the reference difference, not \(\alpha\). The current implementation therefore does not rescue the claimed limit [E2].

Supported impact: Major. The failure directly affects the asserted divergence geometry of a central practical update. It leaves the unweighted derivation intact. Alpha can still affect learned-score approximation, amortization and the optional GAN regularizer. The finding does not assert that the whole algorithm, its finite training trajectories or its empirical ablation are \(\alpha\)-independent.
# 4. Problem 1 — complete full-weight example and precise limits

Parameters and assumptions. Use two dimensions, \(\sigma\)=1, p0=\(\tfrac12\)\(\delta\)_(1,0)+\(\tfrac12\)\(\delta\)_(\(-\)1,0), and g\(\theta\)(z)=\(\theta\) at \(\theta\)=(2,1). The latent may be standard normal and ignored. The noised laws are a two-Gaussian mixture p and q=N((2,1),I), both smooth, strictly positive and finite-moment. E_q[\(\partial\)\(\theta\) log q]=0. Only their noised scores are used; the unnoised point masses do not enter the density differentiation.

\[f_p(y)=(\tanh y_1,0),\quad
\Delta(y)=(2-\tanh y_1,1),\quad
w_{\mathrm{DMD}}=\frac1{\|(2,1)-f_p(y)\|_1}=\frac1{3-\tanh y_1}.\]

The second coordinate of \(\Delta\) is one, so the score-difference norms never vanish. The DMD weight lies strictly between 1/4 and 1/2, so all weighted expectations exist. Eq.(32)’s summed L1 norm is used. Replacing that sum by the released per-coordinate mean supplies a common dimension factor and does not restore \(\alpha\) dependence.

Let u(y)=((2\(-\)tanh y)/(3\(-\)tanh y), 1/(3\(-\)tanh y)). The actual weighted update for every interior \(\alpha\) is E_[N(2,1)]u. The forward limit before the new \(\alpha\) normalizer, retaining the same DMD weight, is E_[\(\tfrac12\)N(\(-\)1,1)+\(\tfrac12\)N(1,1)]u. Dominated convergence applies: for \(\alpha\)\(\leq\)1/2, qp/m\(\alpha\)\(\leq\)2p and u is bounded.
Quantity | Coordinate 1 | Coordinate 2
Quantity | Coordinate 1 | Coordinate 2
Forward limit before new normalizer | 0.644389513281 | 0.355610486719

The vectors both sum to one and differ, so even a global rescaling cannot reconcile them. Their inequality also has a direct proof: u2 is strictly increasing. Couple Yq=Z+2 with Yp=Z+B, where Z is standard normal and B is an independent equiprobable \(\pm\)1. Then Yq>Yp always, so E_q u2>E_p u2. Quadrature reports the size; it does not establish the existence of the discrepancy.

Reviewer Simpson quadrature over [\(-\)14,16], refined from 12,000 to 24,000 subintervals, changes results by at most 4.44\(\times\)10^\(-\)15; omitted Gaussian tails are at least 13 standard deviations away [E1]. Scoped repair: describe this normalization as an ideal-score collapse to the common reverse-KL direction. Changing/removing it changes the algorithm; no performance-preserving replacement or fresh empirical repair is verified.
# 5. Problem 2 — Corollary 4.1 does not identify its learned components

Source claim and dependency. Corollary 4.1, p.6, fixes \(\alpha\) and noise and states that a minimizer of Eq.(14) recovers both the fake score and log(p/q). The following text interprets this as density-ratio learning; Eq.(15) uses the factors separately, and Section 4.2 uses the ratio in a generator regularizer. Appendix A establishes only the combined mixture-score optimum. Existence of one correct factorization does not identify all minimizers.

Interior counterexample. Let p0=N(0,1), q0=N(1,1), \(\sigma\)=1 and \(\alpha\)=1/2. A generator is g\(\mu\)(z)=\(\mu\)+z with standard-normal z, at \(\mu\)=1. Then p=N(0,2), q=N(1,2), and m=(p+q)/2. All densities are positive and smooth, moments and DSM risks are finite, and the usual differentiation and score-mean conditions hold. Choose the following smooth, wrong learned factors.

\[\ell_\psi(y)=0,\quad D_\psi=\tfrac12,\quad
s_{\mathrm{fake}}(y)=2s_m(y)-s_p(y),\quad
s_{\mathrm{exp}}=\tfrac12s_p+\tfrac12s_{\mathrm{fake}}=s_m.\]

The DSM conditional-mean decomposition is a constant plus E_m||s_exp\(-\)s_m||\({}^{2}\). Thus this pair attains the global minimum of Eq.(14), not merely a stationary point. It is also a legitimate fake density score, not an arbitrary nonintegrable vector field. With c=e^(1/2), h=N(2,2), one has q\({}^{2}\)/p=c h and

\[r(y)=\frac{p(y)+2q(y)+c h(y)}{3+c},\qquad
\nabla\log r=\nabla\log(m^2/p)=2s_m-s_p.\]

The mixture weights are positive and sum to one. Moreover r is the \(\sigma\)=1 convolution of the same weighted mixture of N(0,1), N(1,1), N(2,1). Even requiring a normalized density score obtained under the same noising process does not exclude the construction. The regression theorem states no architectural or additional identifying constraint that forbids these function-space factors.

Both claimed conclusions fail: the true log ratio is 1/4\(-\)y/2, not zero; at y=0, s_q=0.5 while s_fake=0.437823499114. The replay verifies the density normalization and exact combined-score identity, with numerical score residual below 8.89\(\times\)10^\(-\)16 [E1]. The scientific defect is the invalid inference from mixture-score identification to separate component identification.
# 6. Problem 2 — generator consequence, counterevidence and scoped repair

Generator consequence. Let D*=p/(p+q). For the location parameter \(\mu\), the Jacobian is one and \(\Delta\)=s_q\(-\)s_p=1/2. The correct divergence gradient is E_q[D*]. At the wrong global Eq.(14) minimizer above, Eq.(15) uses D\(\psi\)=1/2 and s_fake separately, producing 1\(-\)E_q[D*].

\[\gamma_{\rm true}=2\mathbb E_q[D^*\Delta]=\mathbb E_q[D^*],
\qquad \gamma_{\rm wrong}=\mathbb E_q[(D_\psi/\alpha)(s_{\rm fake}-s_p)]
=1-\mathbb E_q[D^*].\]
Check | Result
Check | Result
Correct divergence gradient | 0.44406083715653066
Eq.(15) at wrong global DSM minimizer | 0.5559391628434693

Thus even exact estimation of the combined mixture score does not suffice for the proposed separate-factor gradient. Major is supported by a false central identification guarantee and its direct methodological dependency. The fact that the correct pair is also a minimizer is important counterevidence to a stronger allegation of impossible learning, but does not establish the corollary’s identification claim.

Practical counterevidence. The paper trains across \(\alpha\) and emphasizes mass at \(\alpha\)=0. More decisively, the released SMD trainer sums a separate fake-only DSM loss with real/fake interpolated losses (main/sjsd_dist/train_sjsd_dist.py:376–379). Its interpolation detaches component predictions while training the gate [R2,E2]. This richer objective is not identical to the fixed-\(\alpha\) premise. The counterexample is not an empirical failure of that implementation.

A precise restricted replacement is available. Assume exact realizability and simultaneous attainment of a joint objective with positive weight on \(\alpha\)=0 and at least one interior \(\alpha\). The \(\alpha\)=0 term forces s_fake=s_q almost everywhere. The interior term then forces (D\(\psi\)\(-\)D*)(s_p\(-\)s_q)=0. Therefore the log ratio is identified wherever s_p\(\ne\)s_q. This is an analytic statement about exact minima, not a finite-training convergence guarantee.

The nondegeneracy condition matters. If p=q, choosing s_fake=s_p gives the correct mixture score for every \(\alpha\) and any ratio head, so the objective cannot force \(\ell\)=0. The score-based generator gradient is nevertheless zero. Appendix D.3 explicitly assumes accurate component scores and is consistent with this limitation; it is not a proof of the original simultaneous-identification claim. Author adoption and empirical verification of any modified theorem or training protocol remain pending.
# 7. Problems 3 and 4 — bounded current-release defects

Problem 3: covariance accumulation (Minor). In [R2], main/sjsd/test_folder_edm.py:188–190 initializes the 2048\(\times\)2048 second-moment accumulator with ones. Lines 204–213 add feature outer products, subtract N\(\mu\)\(\mu\)\(^{\mathsf T}\) and divide by N\(-\)1. For one evaluation process and N>1, the result is \(\Sigma\)_sample+J/(N\(-\)1), where J is the all-ones matrix. This identity holds regardless of the feature values. The vendored third_party/edm/fid.py instead initializes with zeros.

Independent two-dimensional illustration [E2]: features (1,0),(\(-\)1,0) give the correct covariance diag(2,0), whereas the released formula gives [[3,1],[1,1]]. The universal offset proof does not depend on these being actual Inception outputs. At the configured N=50,000, the added matrix has trace 2048/49,999; that trace is not a predicted FID change. No reference covariance or generated samples were evaluated. A zero initializer precisely removes this algebraic offset, but no evaluator patch or end-to-end repair was run.

Problem 4: incompatible public entry-point contracts (Minor). In main/sjsd/sjsd_guidance.py:207, compute_density_ratio accepts three arguments besides self; compute_cls_logits:396 supplies four. The enabled GAN generator path therefore has a direct Python call mismatch if preceding initialization succeeds. The guidance classifier call also supplies real_image/fake_image/real_label/fake_label keywords to a function declared with x_real/x_fake/label/step. Reviewer-owned argument-binding demonstrations produce TypeError; no author function was executed.

Additional release constraints are preserved in [E2]: SMT reads undeclared args.distillation; the SMD launchers pass parser-unsupported flags; imports reference modules absent from the archived tree. An external overlay could supply modules, so that absence is not treated as proof that historical runs were impossible. Earlier initialization failures do not invalidate the static signature mismatch, but limit claims about the first runtime failure.

Impact and repair limits. These are demonstrated current-source defects, with no established link to the evaluator or training snapshot used for published tables. Their supported impact is bounded release reliability. Historical source/configuration and raw logs are needed to determine paper-level empirical effects. No score deterioration, fabrication, complete repair or author adoption is asserted.
# 8. Coverage, configuration discrepancies and preserved history

Empirical claims were read against Table 2, Figure 2, Section 5 and Appendix E [R1]. ImageNet SMT reports 3.23 FID versus iCT 4.02 and iCT-deep 3.25; SMD reports 1.48 versus DMD2 with GAN 1.51, while the separately identified expensive finetuned DMD2 result is 1.23. CIFAR-10 SMT 3.13 is above iCT 2.83; SMD 2.22 is above SiD 1.92. The paper describes competitiveness and acknowledges important comparison categories. This review does not convert those qualified comparisons into an invented universal-best claim.

Ablations support empirical benefits from the adaptive weighting, multiple \(\alpha\) values and GAN regularization in the reported runs. Such benefits can coexist with Problem 1 because approximate amortized scores and auxiliary losses remain \(\alpha\)-dependent. Stable training is treated as an observation in these experiments, not as an unstated universal convergence theorem. Swiss-roll and interpolation claims were inspected descriptively; samples, metrics and trajectories were not regenerated.

Release configuration: the current SMT score sampler uses a probability-1/2 branch uniform on {0,1/2,1}, otherwise a 1001-point grid. Its \(\alpha\)=0 mass is 1/6+1/2002=502/3003\(\approx\)0.167166, differing from p.5’s 25%. SMD uses a different augmentation helper; the SMT discrepancy is not transferred to it. This is a current configuration difference, with historical-run provenance unresolved [E2].

The p.5 head-only discriminator-training statement is not enforced by the released live-backbone feature graph and all-parameter guidance optimizer. Existing signature failures prevent claiming that this branch actually ran. The resulting paper impact remains Needs Evidence. Main-text batch 40 versus Table 3 batch 280 plausibly reflects seven processes at 40 per process in the launchers; the exact historical distributed configuration and compute comparison remain unverified.

The same-data denoising warmup is explicitly disclosed and is compatible with training from scratch. The release’s checkpoint/warmup configuration is incomplete, but this is not evidence of a secret external teacher. Known corrections are preserved: author commit f1b1fbf2ae2f58776d0739469e788647691575fd (19 August 2025) changes adaptive-weight multiplication to division, present in the pinned current code. Commit 2be705cfbea6f19ddff6076b3c1d29dcc4259d14 corrects an initializer spelling. These are historical author fixes, not current defects.

No OpenReview discussion was inspected. Missing items include exact historical training/evaluation commits, complete launch environments, warmup/checkpoint provenance, raw FID statistics, generated samples, seed variability and complete compute accounting. These omissions do not raise supported severity.

# 2. Checked claims, assumptions and review scope

Checked Sections 1-5 and Appendices A-H for the claim chain: one shared text-encoder pass -> conditional surrogate features -> GI/ID/FG losses and prediction fusion -> efficiency and adaptation evidence. Detailed checks covered Eqs.4-18, Algorithm 1, Tables 1-7, 9, 12, 15-18, source code for feature generation, losses, local top-k pooling and inference, and the public SAM-related issue. References were consulted for identity/context; a complete citation-by-citation novelty audit was not performed.

M is the number of classes, B the image batch size, Z the number of fine-grained conditional signals, and d the feature dimension. The paper uses Z=4 and a local pooling interval of 10. Cosine scores lie in [-1,1], temperature is positive, and the same temperature scales each branch. Table 3 and Table 16 describe base-to-novel ablation averages over the same 11 datasets. Reported accuracies are means over three seeds, but the underlying predictions and per-seed logs were not obtained.

Checks comprise analytic reasoning, reviewer-authored finite arithmetic and static source inspection. Author training/evaluation code was never run or imported. GPU performance, reported accuracies, dataset splits, seed variance and historical experiment provenance were not empirically reproduced. OpenReview’s public API returned HTTP 403 and its web page presented a verification wall; this limits independent version/review-history checks.
# 3. Problem 1 - inconsistent ablation baseline and bounded ranking claim

Source claim and location. Table 3 (p.6) reports the DVLP base/novel/HM triple 79.61/71.63/75.41. Table 16 (p.17), described as the complete per-dataset base-to-novel ablation, reports 82.30/74.25/78.06 for that same named baseline. The other four aggregate rows agree between the two tables. Section 4.2 uses these ablations to explain component gains.

Complete check. Independently averaging Table 16’s eleven DVLP base values yields 82.2963636364 and its novel values yield 74.2472727273. The harmonic mean of these two means is 78.0648858977. These reproduce Table 16 after rounding. Using the shared full-model HM 81.03, the displayed improvement is 5.62 percentage points against Table 3 but 2.97 against Table 16. The difference of 2.65 points is too large to be rounding. The source table on p.17 was visually inspected; the numbers are not a text-extraction artifact [E1].

\[\bar b=82.29636,\quad\bar n=74.24727,\quad H=\frac{2\bar b\bar n}{\bar b+\bar n}=78.06489.\] \[\Delta_{\mathrm{GI}}^{(3)}=78.09-75.41=2.68,\qquad \Delta_{\mathrm{GI}}^{(16)}=78.09-78.06=0.03.\] Counterevidence and alternative reading. The tables could reflect different unreported baseline configurations or a transcription/version error. Neither possibility reconciles the present labels. The check establishes an internal reporting discrepancy, not which training run is correct. It does not disprove the full model’s scores. Table 16 still gives a positive 2.97-point HM gain, and the few-shot full-model mean independently recomputes to 85.11727, consistent with 85.12.

Related bounded statement. Section 4.3 (p.7) says SurPL-G has the best performance on 9/11 datasets. Reading performance as the displayed base-to-novel trade-off metric HM, Table 17 (p.19) gives 8/11: it loses on ImageNet (74.39<74.44), Flowers102 (83.92<86.46) and Food101 (91.36<91.42). The sentence does not specify another metric that would justify nine. This does not change the highest reported aggregate HM of 81.03. The audit therefore qualifies the count by metric instead of asserting a universal nine-versus-eight error.

Impact and repair status. Major: Section 4.2 expressly uses this ablation to verify the effectiveness of the three text-feature components in the proposed method. Its named baseline is the control from which the component gains are inferred. The inconsistent values change the GI-only HM gain from 2.68 to 0.03 points and the full-model gain from 5.62 to 2.97 points. Under Table 16, GI base accuracy decreases from 82.30 to 81.84 while novel accuracy increases from 74.25 to 74.68. The scientific dependency is therefore direct: inconsistent control values produce materially different effect magnitudes in the evidence validating a core component. This is an observed contradiction in the paper’s own central ablation evidence; it is not contingent on proving that the surrogate architecture or efficiency construction fails. An undisclosed configuration change or transcription error could explain the mismatch, but the present tables do not identify one. Correct reconciliation requires matching run/configuration records, and no unverified baseline is adopted. Positive full-model gains under both baselines and the Table 17 HM count of eight are preserved. Scientific decisions and author adoption remain pending.
# 4. Problem 2 - released inference pools logits instead of probabilities

Source claim and location. Equation 10 (p.5) and Algorithm 1, lines 19-20 (p.14), average the GI probability, ID probability and mean of Z FG probabilities. In the pinned public repository, trainers/SurPL.py lines 332-334 first average FG logits and then return (logits_1 + logits_2 + logits_3)/3, without the per-branch softmax required by Eq.10 [S2,E2]. These operations are generally different.

Complete finite check at the scoring interface. Set two classes, Z=4, a common temperature tau=0.1, GI cosine scores (0.5,-0.5), ID scores (-0.2,0.2), and each FG branch to (-0.2,0.2). All scores are valid cosines. For example, a unit image vector e1 and class text vectors with first coordinates equal to these scores realize each pair in dimension at least two. Identical local unit features realize the four top-k FG averages; at least 40 local features suffice for the specified k values. This is an admissible score-interface example, not a claim that a released trained checkpoint realizes these features.

\[\ell^{GI}=(5,-5),\qquad\ell^{ID}=\ell^{FG}_z=(-2,2).\] The public-code arithmetic produces final logits (1/3,-1/3), selecting class 1. Equation 10 gives class-1 probability [sigmoid(10)+2 sigmoid(-4)]/3 = 0.3453090074, selecting class 2. All four FG probabilities are identical, so averaging them introduces no other assumption. The discrepancy is a direct non-equivalence of the two ensemble operators; no author code or model was executed. This report example is separately recalculated in completion_exact_checks.json. The preserved independent_code_checks.json uses another valid example (tau=0.25 and logits (3,-3), (-1,1)); it is supporting non-equivalence evidence, not the numerical output of this example.

Counterevidence, dependency and supported impact. Both are plausible ensemble choices. Either can perform well. The released operation affects the final decision rule, but no experiment log or checkpoint connects this exact release to the paper’s tables. Therefore Minor applies to the demonstrated release/specification mismatch; damage to the reported accuracy, the efficiency benefit or the core surrogate-feature contribution is Needs Evidence. A rerun with frozen checkpoints under both operators, or contemporaneous experiment logs, would resolve that empirical question. Changing the implementation to Eq.10 would restore the documented operator only; improved accuracy is not established.
# 5. Cleared concerns and exact scope clarifications

Singleton attention is not a class-collapse proof. In the complete Appendix A specification, Eq.13 adds the original class-specific w to the attention output, and Eq.14 adds another residual MLP. The public SFG retains these residuals. A singleton key makes its softmax weight one, but w still distinguishes classes. Using simplified Eq.4 alone to allege identical class features would discard operative source terms.

\[C=M O_T+(B+Z)M O_{SFG},\qquad\frac{(B+Z)O_{SFG}}{O_T}\ll1\] Appendix B, Eq.16 (p.12), gives the full cost above. Its inference that the second term is negligible requires (B+Z)O_SFG/O_T much smaller than one; O_SFG much smaller than O_T alone is insufficient uniformly in growing B or Z. This matters to the introduction’s O(M) versus O(BM)/O(ZM) efficiency comparison. Under the paper’s fixed configurations (B=4 or 32, Z=4), the displayed exact cost is still O(M), and the expensive text-encoder component remains M O_T. The record does not justify imposing a universal quantifier over growing batch sizes on the paper. Outcome: explicit scope clarification. Fixed-configuration timing evidence survives separately; it is not used to validate the unrestricted inference.

Appendix C, Eqs.17-18 (p.13), writes a p-norm constraint but gives epsilon=rho*g/||g||, the Euclidean (p=2) linearized SAM solution. For g=(2,1), rho=1 and p=infinity, that formula gives objective increment sqrt(5), while epsilon=(1,1) gives 3. Thus p=2 must be specified. The Taylor step is already marked approximate, and no new universal generalization theorem is claimed. This does not invalidate intended Euclidean SAM.

The SurPL-G implementation gap is preserved as a known public reproducibility question. Issue #1 asked for SAM code. On 9 August 2025 the author linked a SAM optimizer in GCSCoOp; on 11 August the reporter said they had basically reproduced the base-to-novel results using another SAM implementation. That is attributed third-party testimony, not reproduction performed here. It is counterevidence against inferring false results from the missing integrated release [S3].
# 6. Dependence, surviving results and disposition

The shared text-encoder construction, residual architecture and fixed-configuration exact cost survive the checked objections. Scientific Verification Report - I25-43461
Delta Decompression for MoE-based LLMs Compression | ICML 2025 | 24 October 2026 | B001 / [internal task]-r002 / attempt-002 | Scientific decision pending
# 1. Identity, reviewed version and supported outcome

Hao Gu, Wei Li, Lujun Li, Qiyuan Zhu, Mark Lee, Shengjie Sun, Wei Xue and Yike Guo. Delta Decompression for MoE-based LLMs Compression. PMLR 267:20497-20514 (2025), publisher record gu25c; OpenReview ziezViPoN1 [S1]. Reviewed the exact publisher-linked 18-page PDF, including Appendices A-C. Citations below use physical PDF pages, which equal printed pages 1-18. The publisher metadata reverses Qiyuan Zhu’s name and expands Mark Lee; author identity follows the PDF.

Supported severity: Major. The paper’s explicit static-storage derivation is invalid for its stated half-static, half-dynamic pruning scheme. The affected count directly supports the claimed compression budgets and matched-budget efficiency comparisons. Separately, Algorithm 5 uses the Gram matrix where the main method uses a Cholesky factor; a complete finite example demonstrates the difference. That second finding is bounded by the correct main method and correct released SVD path. Released-code limitations are kept separate from historical experiment attribution.

Pinned D2MoE code commit:

# 2. Coverage, assumptions and evidence types

The review covered the shared-base/delta construction (Eq.3), Fisher weighting (Eqs.4-5), activation-weighted SVD (Eqs.6-8), pruning metric and two-phase selection (Eq.9, Algorithm 3), forward interpretation (Eq.10), parameter analysis, Tables 2-12, and the appendix algorithms. Static inspection traced the documented Mixtral preprocessing, SVD, pruning wrappers and parameter calculator. The ledger records the exact inspected files; other model-specific branches and the entire bundled evaluation harness were not exhaustively audited.

For unambiguous accounting, n denotes the number of experts, k the number active per token, P the number of parameters in one uncompressed expert weight matrix, r the retained fraction of delta-factor parameters, and s the total fraction of base columns skipped after both pruning stages. Both stages remove s/2 of the original column count. The corrected count is an ideal packed-weight count: integer rounding, index overhead, unchanged model components and intermediate activations must be added separately when appropriate.

The evidence comprises exact source reading, analytic proofs, independent small Python/NumPy checks and static code inspection. Author code was never executed or imported. No LLM evaluation, GPU timing or memory measurement was reproduced, and no paid model/API calls were made. The raw runs linking checkpoints, hardware measurements and published tables were unavailable.
# 3. Problem 1 - static storage is confused with dynamic activity

Source claim. Section 3.5, p.5, explicitly labels its expression static parameter storage and gives (n*p+s/2)*P after static compression; the active expression is (k*p+s)*P. Section 3.4 and Algorithm 3, p.18, specify permanent pruning of half the target sparsity, followed by input-dependent skipping of the other half among retained columns. Table 12, p.16, fixes the throughput setting at 30% static plus 30% dynamic pruning, and the performance setting at 5% plus 5%.

Invalid step. A column skipped for one batch must remain available for a later batch that selects it. Dynamic skipping therefore cannot be treated as permanent removal. Independently of whether the ambiguous symbol p means retained or removed delta parameters, the printed base terms assign twice as many active base parameters as stored base parameters whenever s>0. That contradicts the specified subset relation. Reinterpreting the ratio convention alone cannot make both expressions correct.

\[P_{stored}=[nr+(1-s/2)]P,\qquad P_{active}=[kr+(1-s)]P.\] Complete realizable count. Choose n=8, k=2, 100-by-100 matrices (P=10,000), rank-25 delta factors of shapes 100-by-25 and 25-by-100 (5,000 parameters each, r=0.5), and s=0.6. Static pruning removes 30 of 100 columns, leaving 7,000 base parameters; each batch skips 30 more, leaving 4,000 active. A full-rank nonzero base and rank-25 deltas satisfy the architecture, and all counts are integers. Since r=0.5 is also the removed delta fraction, this example is unaffected by the paper’s ambiguous p convention. One algebraic realization sets the full-rank base to 2I, four experts to 2I+D and four to 2I-D, where D has 25 unit diagonal entries and all other entries zero, with equal positive Fisher weights. The weighted merge is the stated base and all deltas have rank 25. Calibration row norms can order the 100 base columns strictly, while a later input changes which 30 retained columns are dynamically skipped. This is an admissible parameter-count construction, not a claim about the Fisher statistics of a trained language model.
Quantity | Actual specified scheme | Printed expression
Original expert storage | 80,000 | 80,000

The storage compression in this example is 41.25%, not the printed expression’s 46.25%. The result follows directly from counts, independently of stochastic performance, Fisher values or which columns score lowest. The dynamic set can vary with input; no condition in the paper makes all dynamically omitted columns permanently unnecessary.

Connection to the reported resource budgets. The public cal_params.py, lines 191-211, counts all shared base matrices with factor (1-pp_ratio) in its total-parameter calculation. Its rank mapping is floor(H*I*r/(H+I)). With inspected Mixtral defaults H=4096, I=14336, L=32, n=8 and vocabulary size 32,000, an independent calculation gives 46.702792704B original parameters, 5.637144576B shared-base parameters and 1.605636096B unchanged parameters. No author calculator was run.
Nominal ratio / Table 12 delta retention | Count using 40% base retention | Stored count using 70% base retention

The first count closely tracks Table 4’s rounded model sizes 18.68B, 14.01B and 9.33B; the small mismatches remain visible. Under Table 12’s delta-retention interpretation and stated two-phase pruning, the omitted persistent allocation is about 1.69114B parameters, or 3.6211 percentage points of the original model. The corresponding ideal static compression fractions are approximately 56.41%, 66.35% and 76.35%. Fractional entries here result from percentage-based budget arithmetic; integer channel allocation changes the last digits, not the omitted allocation.

Counterevidence and limits. These are independent accounting results under the stated architecture and ratio definitions, not reproduced GPU-memory measurements. Alternative historical pruning configurations, offloading or storage formats require their own provenance. The released default pruning path retains full registered base tensors and slices temporary weights; that is additional release-level evidence, not proof of the hardware path behind Table 4. The public issue asking about compression hyperparameters is an unresolved question, not evidence of invalid experiments.

Impact: Major. The dependency is two-phase pruning -> persistent parameter allocation -> stated compression/memory budget -> performance comparisons at that budget. The incorrect resource accounting damages a central efficiency claim even if accuracy at the actual configuration survives. It does not refute delta decomposition or dynamic compute savings.

Precise scoped repair. Separate stored and active expressions. To match the table/helper budget [nr+(1-s)]P while storing the dynamically skipped columns, decrease delta retention by s/(2n); this applies only if the resulting retention is nonnegative and realizable after rank rounding. For n=8,s=0.6 the decrement is 0.0375, so the 0.1218 setting becomes approximately 0.0843. This does not match the different, literal printed static expression [nr+s/2]P. Matching that expression instead requires a decrement (1-s)/n, which is 0.05 in the small example. Both identities are verified below; neither is an empirical repair. Actual persistent storage must first be established, and changed ranks require fresh performance evaluation. Author adoption remains pending.
\[n\left(r-\frac{s}{2n}\right)+1-\frac{s}{2}=nr+1-s,\qquad n\left(r-\frac{1-s}{n}\right)+1-\frac{s}{2}=nr+\frac{s}{2}.\]
# 4. Problem 2 - Algorithm 5 changes the SVD objective

Source claim and discrepancy. Section 3.3, p.4, Eqs.6-8 defines S as a Cholesky factor of G=X*X^T and approximates D*S before inverse scaling. Appendix C.5, p.18, Algorithm 5 instead sets S=X*X^T directly. The original rendered p.18 confirms that this is present in the PDF, not extraction noise. These prescriptions are different [E2].

\[\|(D-A)X\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}((D-A)G(D-A)^\top)=\|(D-A)S\|_F^2,\quad G=SS^\top.\] When G is positive definite, right multiplication by invertible S preserves rank. Truncating the SVD of D*S and undoing S therefore solves the activation-weighted rank constraint. Using G itself instead weights the squared error by G squared. The paper does not state a separate universal optimality theorem for Algorithm 5; the finding is the demonstrated non-equivalence of its recipe to the actual main method.

\[X=\operatorname{diag}(1,2),\quad D=\operatorname{diag}(3,1),\quad rank(A)\le1.\] All assumptions hold: dimensions are 2-by-2; G=diag(1,4) is positive definite; all inverses exist; retained rank 1 is valid; singular values are distinct. The Cholesky factor is diag(1,2). D*S=diag(3,2), so rank-one truncation returns A=diag(3,0). Its output squared Frobenius error is 4. Algorithm 5 uses D*G=diag(3,4), keeps the other direction and returns A=diag(0,1), whose output squared error is 9. The independent calculation confirms both ranks, reconstructions and errors.

Counterevidence and classification. The correct Cholesky construction is already stated in the main text. It is also implemented in preprocess/get_scale.py lines 46-69 and model/merge_mixtral.py lines 224-243. This confines the demonstrated error to a contradictory published algorithm specification; Minor is supported for this finding. The classification rests on that substantive counterevidence, not on appendix location, ease of repair or a requirement to show empirical degradation.

Scoped correction. First compute G=X*X^T, then S=chol(G) with G=S*S^T, and retain the existing SVD/inverse-scale steps. The proof above verifies the correction for G positive definite. Singular or regularized calibration matrices require an explicitly chosen regularization/pseudoinverse policy; no unverified universal fix is proposed.
# 5. Problem 3 - released perplexity evaluation omits later batches

Source and verified call path. D2-mixtral.py line 144 calls utils.ppl_eval_sharing. utils.py line 338 imports get_test_data; model/data_utils.py line 229 returns a loader with shuffle=False. Yet utils.py lines 61-62 create next(iter(data)) anew on every iteration. Each iteration therefore selects the first batch; the number of iterations does not provide dataset coverage.

Complete independent check. Consider two equal-length batches with deterministic average negative log-likelihoods log(2) and log(8). Correct full-data perplexity is exp((log(2)+log(8))/2)=4. Reinitializing the iterator visits batch indices [0,0] and yields perplexity 2. The reviewer replay uses only a Python list and arithmetic. Dynamic pruning could change predictions on the repeated batch, but cannot make subsequent batches enter this loop.

Judgment: Minor within the public-release scope, with potentially material evaluation consequences. This is a definite evaluation-path defect, not an unresolved interpretation of Python iterators. Its connection to the published benchmark numbers remains Needs Evidence because no run manifest binds those numbers to this source snapshot. A scoped repair is to traverse the loader once and accumulate loss by the actual nonignored target-token count. No published-score repair is claimed or applied. This inspected path is the perplexity call; the separate downstream run_lm_eval accuracy path is not shown to have the same iterator defect.
# 6. Problem 4 - released Fisher calibration shifts targets twice

Source and assumptions. preprocess/get_fisher.py lines 226-229 supplies tokens[:-1] as inputs and tokens[1:] as labels. It loads AutoModelForCausalLM at line 375. The pinned requirements specify Transformers 4.42.4; its stock MixtralForCausalLM shifts logits and labels internally at lines 1426-1434. The exact official dependency source was acquired and hashed, not executed [S4]. This finding concerns that documented stock Mixtral path. The script’s default model is mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-v0.1 (line 495), but from_pretrained uses trust_remote_code=True and allows another base path. The conclusion is therefore explicitly confined to the documented stock Mixtral branch; custom loss behavior is not assumed.

Complete index check. Original tokens [0,1,2,3,4] become input [0,1,2,3] and supplied labels [1,2,3,4]. The internal shift compares outputs whose contexts end at [0,1,2] with targets [2,3,4]. Correct next-token targets for those contexts are [1,2,3]. Thus the squared gradients accumulated by the released Fisher routine come from a two-token-ahead objective. This is a source/index proof, not a claim about an observed model score.

Judgment: Minor release-objective error; published-run attribution and empirical damage are Needs Evidence. A custom model that deliberately omitted internal shifting would be a different path, and no such modification is assumed here. Supplying unshifted inputs and same-position labels to the stock causal model, with the intended masking, restores one next-token shift. That repairs alignment only; other Fisher approximations and resulting compression quality require their own verification.
# 7. Other checks, counterevidence and release scope

Fisher averaging: with nonnegative diagonal/per-coordinate Fisher weights whose sums are positive, Eq.5 is the minimizer of the corresponding weighted quadratic objective. The paper does not claim a new global optimality theorem for Fisher merging, guaranteed low rank of every delta matrix, or globally optimal multi-column pruning. The single-column norm product in Eq.9 equals that column’s rank-one output contribution norm; it does not require an unstated multi-column theorem.

Nonlinear forward interpretation: Eq.10 is valid as a normalized-gating identity for a shared linear projection. It should not be promoted into a claim that an arbitrary gated nonlinear FFN can be moved outside expert selection. The released Mixtral path retains shared-plus-delta projections inside the expert nonlinearity and disables the shared_infer option by default. This is counterevidence to an alleged mandatory linearization failure.

Empirical arithmetic: the displayed seven-task Mixtral D2-MoE means at 20% and 60% compression recompute to 0.60 and 0.52. Calibration, task evaluation and speed/memory claims were read but not reproduced. Table 7 associates base pruning 10% and delta removal 52.66% with perplexity 5.63, whereas Appendix A.5/Table 12 describe the 10% base configuration as selected and other tables report 5.28. This configuration-to-result provenance remains unresolved; no value is silently corrected.

Further bounded release deviations were retained without raising paper severity: cal_params.py lines 1120-1127 hardcode target/pruning values for the Mixtral helper despite parsing CLI options; the default ppwandasp scoring path uses a different weight moment from Eq.9. At equal unit activation norms, columns (1,1) and (1.3,0) score (sqrt(2),1.3) under Eq.9 but (sqrt(2),1.69) under the inspected release metric, reversing their ordering. These are static helper/metric discrepancies; no claim is made that the published calibration selected different channels. Full traces and the known open hyperparameter question are preserved in independent_code_notes.md.
# 8. Overall disposition and surviving results

The core shared-base/delta representation, the main-text Cholesky SVD method and possible reductions in arithmetic work survive this review. Published performance values may remain observations at their actual configurations. What fails is the demonstrated derivation connecting the stated dynamic pruning scheme to static storage and therefore to the nominal resource budget. A correct efficiency comparison must match persistent storage, active computation and hardware memory definitions separately.

report:
Scientific Verification Report - I25-43462
DynaMind | ICML 2025 | 24 October 2026 | B001 / [internal task]-r002 / attempt-002 | Scientific decision pending
# 1. Identity, reviewed version and outcome

Ziru Wang, Mengmeng Wang, Jade Dai, Teli Ma, Guo-Jun Qi, Yong Liu, Guang Dai and Jingdong Wang. DynaMind: Reasoning over Abstract Video Dynamics for Embodied Decision-Making. PMLR 267:64586-64603 (2025), wang25cz; OpenReview ziDKPXJBYL [S1]. The reviewed publisher PDF contains 18 pages, including Appendices A-F. All page references use physical PDF pages, equal to printed pages 1-18. The title, authors, publisher link and original PDF hash were checked.

Code:
Publisher PDF SHA-256:
0f57b24b278795b4956b4132562b482afd7c6ef4d20fa824a1204afdcbb5b2a7
Batch token:
[internal identifier omitted]

Supported impact: Minor. The main text and appendix specify incompatible action-gradient routes into the FrameScorer. This affects the reproducibility of a central module’s training, but does not establish which route generated the reported results. The exact gradient graph remains Needs Evidence. Checked table arithmetic is consistent. No attributable public implementation was located, so no implementation error or empirical reproduction is claimed.
# 2. Claims, definitions and operative scope

DynaMind combines frame abstraction, temporal prediction of dynamic representations and action generation. Section 3 and Appendices C.1-C.3 were checked against each other; the evaluation protocols, Tables 1-9 and Figures 3-17 were read for quantitative consistency and claim scope. The coverage ledger distinguishes calculation, source inspection and unresolved implementation details. References were read as context; a full novelty audit was not performed.

Let e_t denote an encoded image, q a frozen DistilBERT language embedding, F_theta the two-layer sigmoid FrameScorer, and C the window length. For a defined nonempty window I_n with positive total weight, the pooling rule is

\[w_t=F_\theta(e_t),\qquad h_n=\frac{\sum_{t\in I_n}w_t e_t}{\sum_{t\in I_n}w_t},\qquad \mathcal{L}_{fs}=\mathcal{L}_{consistency}+\mathcal{L}_{saliency}.\] Finite sigmoid logits give strictly positive weights in exact arithmetic. The two auxiliary losses use cosine similarity and a zero-margin relative-similarity hinge, with equal weights. The temporal transformer conditions on q and historical dynamics; the action transformer uses visual/action history and a goal representation. This report does not add a universal anti-collapse, causal-identification or closed-loop stability theorem to these empirical design claims.

The actual training graph, masking implementation, sequence-to-vector cosine reduction, final partial-window policy, checkpoints, per-seed outputs and raw trial logs were not available. No author code, model execution, paid API, installation or robot experiment was used. Reviewer arithmetic below is finite and independent.
# 3. Problem 1 - incompatible FrameScorer training prescriptions

Faithful source claims and exact locations. Section 3.1, p.4, immediately after Eq.(5), says that downstream modules receive fixed dynamic inputs and do not influence optimization of F. Appendix C.1, p.13, in its second paragraph on behavioral grounding, explicitly says the FrameScorer importance scores are optimized through the downstream action loss, with loss weight 1.0. Both passages describe the same FrameScorer. Source pages 4 and 13 were visually checked [E1].

Suspect step and complete check. These descriptions prescribe different derivatives with respect to the scorer parameters theta. Detachment yields no action-loss gradient through the pooled dynamics. The appendix’s differentiable route includes a chain-rule term. For one window, holding the image embeddings fixed,

\[\left.\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{action}\right|_{\mathrm{detached}}=0,\qquad
\left.\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{action}\right|_{\mathrm{connected}}
=J_\theta(H)^\top \nabla_H \mathcal{L}_{action},\qquad
\frac{\partial h_n}{\partial w_j}=\frac{e_j-h_n}{\sum_{t\in I_n}w_t}.\] A small exact computational-graph illustration makes the distinction explicit. Take C=2, scalar nonzero embeddings e_1=1 and e_2=3, sigmoid logits z_1=z_2=0, hence w_1=w_2=1/2, and a differentiable downstream scalar loss L=h^2. Then h=2, dh/dw_1=-1, dw_1/dz_1=1/4, and dL/dz_1=-1 through the connected route, versus zero through detachment. The denominator is positive, both weights are admissible and every derivative is exact. This illustrates non-equivalent gradient prescriptions; it is not presented as a realization of a trained action transformer or as a counterexample to the reported task scores [E2].

Counterevidence and alternative readings. The end of Section 3.1 also describes broader end-to-end action supervision, which is compatible with the appendix’s route. Shared image encoders can receive action supervision while F is detached; that does not reconcile the appendix’s explicit claim about F itself. An unstated freeze/unfreeze schedule could reconcile the passages. The documented hybrid assignment changes the source of the goal token, and does not specify such a schedule. Incidental zero gradients on particular examples also do not make the two general training procedures identical.

Dependency and supported impact. FrameScorer parameters determine importance weights, which determine dynamic prediction targets and policy conditions. The conflict therefore matters to reproducing the scientific method and interpreting its behavioral grounding. It establishes a bounded method-specification inconsistency, classified Minor. It does not determine the implemented procedure or demonstrate invalid task scores. Repair requires the actual computational graph, detachment points and phase schedule, followed by consistent documentation. No training variant is adopted as a guessed correction.
# 4. Empirical checks and metric scope

Table 1, p.6: DynaMind’s six displayed task rates sum to 322%, giving 53.6667%, which rounds to 53.67%. The corresponding means for Random, Vanilla BC, RL, DT, LISA and SkillDiffuser are 20.3333%, 28.6667%, 13.1667%, 15%, 40% and 43%, consistent with their displayed precision. The 3-seed statement is preserved; run-level uncertainty was not reconstructed.

Tables 2 and 7, pp.7 and 15: the reported averages are reproduced by averaging all five categories, including the category labelled seen. DynaMind’s mean is 53.73%. Averaging only the four non-seen categories gives 52.7175%; corresponding means are 18.835% for DT, 27.67% for LISA and 38.7225% for SkillDiffuser. Table 7 openly identifies the categories, so this is a scope clarification, not evidence of fabricated outcomes. The overall reported mean should not be relabelled as an unseen-only estimate. DynaMind remains highest under either displayed-category summary.

Table 9, p.18, and Figure 9: five tasks with ten trials per task yield 40/50 successes for DT, 41/50 for LISA and 47/50 for DynaMind, giving 80%, 82% and 94%. This verifies the arithmetic and its denominator, not independent trial execution. The observation that DynaMind succeeds more often on the listed tasks is distinct from a causal explanation of why competing policies fail.

The Kitchen and BabyAI protocols, low-data and unseen-composition experiments, ablations and parameter/memory comparison were read. No trained policy, split manifest, hardware trace or statistical significance test was independently reproduced. Figure 8’s mutual-information estimator, aggregation and uncertainty are not specified sufficiently in the inspected material to recalculate the curve or treat it as causal identification. That remains an evidence limitation rather than a demonstrated numerical error.
# 5. Counterevidence and cleared interpretations

Language conditioning. Equation (1) and Appendix C.1 define F(e_t) as a frame-local function, without q as a current input. Language helps train the scorer and explicitly conditions temporal reasoning. Thus the score of the same encoded frame is not instruction-adaptive at inference under this specification, but the complete policy remains language-conditioned. No claim that it ignores instructions is supported.

Temporal abstraction and saliency. Pooling in Eq.(2) is invariant to a joint permutation of features and weights inside one window. The ordered window sequence and historical frame inputs still carry temporal information. The paper does not claim lossless or injective video representation. Likewise, Eq.(5)’s hinge can be zero at equal similarities; the surrounding p.4 discussion explicitly treats the losses as soft guidance. Degenerate admissible representations would not by themselves refute a stated universal collapse-prevention theorem, because none is given.

Future targets and inference. Figure 2, p.3, Sections 3.2-3.3, p.5, and Appendix C.2-C.3, p.14, separate future-frame supervision and early training goal assignment from inference using observed history and predicted goals. This does not demonstrate future-information leakage. Re-anchoring predictions to newly observed frames avoids recursively rolling out predicted latents; it does not prove that all policy/environment errors vanish. Exact masks and token-head alignment remain implementation questions.
# 6. Version comparison, surviving evidence and disposition

The corresponding author’s page supplies an 11-page main-paper PDF [S2], SHA-256 b25a70bcd91f381f09a304ba0e54f36eff4a7b3a2be3ffc39baec580b70f432a. It differs from the 18-page publisher artifact and is undated. Its p.4 retains the fixed-input/no-FrameScorer-optimization statement, while it has no Appendix C.1. It therefore does not resolve the reviewed conflict and is not established as a later correction.

No attributable public code or resolving erratum was found in the bounded publisher, author-page, GitHub and arXiv checks. An unrelated EEG paper with the same short name was excluded. OpenReview API access returned HTTP 403 and the forum presented browser verification; inaccessible revision/review history is not represented as searched successfully [E3].

The empirical architecture, reported task results and arithmetic checks survive this inspection. The demonstrated failure is nonunique training specification for the scorer. Actual score consequences, gradient-route adoption and mutual-information reproduction remain unresolved. Scientific decisions stay pending; no author adoption or human approval is recorded.
Item | Judgment | Repair / adoption / remaining work
FrameScorer gradient route | Minor | Conflict demonstrated; actual graph and schedule needed; no correction adopted

# 7. Consulted sources and reproducible evidence

[S1] Wang et al., PMLR 267:64586-64603, 2025. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wang25cz.html ; exact publisher PDF: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlresearch/v267/main/assets/wang25cz/wang25cz.pdf . Preserved original: papers/0093/0093.pdf.
