report:
Scientific Verification Report 0094
I25-43463 — Enhancing Parallelism in Decentralized Stochastic Convex Optimization
# 1. Identity, version and review outcome

Ofri Eisen, Ron Dorfman and Kfir Yehuda Levy; ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267:15105–15129. Primary version: the 25-page publisher PDF linked from https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/eisen25a.html, SHA-256 0a614ae075bc309f5ca2021df88d1d4213ab2e00b8b87a64c570205389620700. All page references below use physical PDF pages, which equal printed pages 1–25. OpenReview identifier: zgeoOFyIyb. Batch B001; task [internal task]-r002; isolated attempt-002; batch token [internal identifier omitted].

Outcome: Major. Two independently verified mathematical failures directly affect the central convergence contribution. Theorem 4.1 omits a network transient term and is false as a uniform all-horizon bound under its displayed parameter dependence. Separately, Lemma A.1 is incompatible with the averaging recursion it explicitly assumes; its invalid inequality starts the proof chain used for Theorem 4.1. A released neural-network launcher also reverses the stated exponential-average coefficient; that bounded implementation finding is Minor because its connection to the published runs is unresolved.

The review covers the algorithm and assumptions, convergence and parallelism claims, Appendices A–D, the experimental design and Appendix E, and static inspection of pinned public code. No author code was imported or executed. The experiments were not reproduced. Scientific decisions, controller acceptance and adoption of any proposed correction remain pending; no human scientific review is recorded.
# 2. Definitions, assumptions and dependencies

The objective is the mean of M local expected losses, with a global minimizer x*. The theory assumes convexity, L-smooth local objectives, unbiased fresh stochastic gradients with per-node noise second moment bounded by sigma squared, globally bounded gradient heterogeneity zeta squared, and a symmetric doubly stochastic gossip matrix P. Its spectral gap is rho = 1 - |lambda_2(P)| in (0,1]. Common initialization is imposed. Conditional expectation and conditionally independent fresh samples are the standard reading used in the variance calculations; an unconditional-expectation notation ambiguity is not treated as a demonstrated defect.

\[f(x)=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^{M}f_i(x),\qquad
D_1=\|w_1-x^*\|,\qquad
\widetilde{\sigma}^{\,2}=2\sigma^2+\zeta^2,\qquad K^2=5120L^2.\] Algorithm 2, p.5, updates an auxiliary iterate w using a stochastic gradient evaluated at a query x, averages these iterates, and gossips both sequences. With A_t = sum of alpha_1 through alpha_t and alpha_t = t, its consensus trajectory has the following recursion. The same averaging indices appear in Appendix A, Eq.(16), p.12.

\[w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta\alpha_tg_t,\qquad
x_{t+1}=\frac{A_{t-1}}{A_t}x_t+\frac{\alpha_t}{A_t}w_{t+1},
\qquad x_1=w_1.\] Theorem 4.1, p.6, repeated on p.14, prescribes the following step size and states its convergence rate for every T >= 1. In the fourth candidate, rho/T is outside the square root; this was checked against the PDF image rather than inferred from flattened text.

\[\eta=\min\left\{\frac1{24LT},\frac{\rho^2}{K},
\frac{D_1\sqrt M}{\sqrt3\,\sigma T^{3/2}},
\sqrt{\frac{D_1}{2K\widetilde{\sigma}}}\frac{\rho}{T}\right\}.\] \[\mathbb E[f(\bar x_T)-f^*]\le
O\!\left(\frac{\sigma D_1}{\sqrt{MT}}+
\frac{D_1^{3/2}\sqrt{L\widetilde{\sigma}}}{\rho T}
+\frac{LD_1^2}{T}\right).\] The asserted topology-dependent rate is read in its usual uniform sense: the hidden numerical constant does not absorb an additional unbounded dependence on the displayed parameters rho or T. Allowing arbitrary rho-dependent constants would remove the advertised explicit network comparison and would not be the same claim.
# 3. Problem 1 — A missing transient term falsifies the uniform convergence guarantee

Source claim and suspect step. Theorem 4.1, p.6, and its restatement on p.14 omit a term that the last displayed calculation of Appendix B, p.16, explicitly retains. Corollary 4.2, p.6, has the same omission; the finite expression in its proof on p.17 contains the corresponding term. The omitted contribution in the theorem proof is

\[\frac{4KD_1^2}{\rho^2T^2},
\quad\text{equivalently of order}\quad
\frac{LD_1^2}{\rho^2T^2}.\] A complete admissible family. For each integer horizon T >= 2, take two nodes and one real coordinate. Set L = D_1 = 1, x* = 0, and initialize all w_1 and x_1 at 1. Both local stochastic functions are identically f_i(x,z) = x^2/2, independently of z. Use rho = 1/T and the positive declared upper bounds sigma = zeta = T^(-2). Define

\[P=\begin{pmatrix}1-\rho/2&\rho/2\\ \rho/2&1-\rho/2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad f_1(x,z)=f_2(x,z)=\frac{x^2}{2}.\] Every operative condition holds. The functions are globally convex and 1-smooth, with minimizer zero. The exact gradient x is unbiased; actual stochastic variance and gradient heterogeneity are both zero, so the strictly positive supplied bounds are valid and avoid any division-by-zero convention. Deterministic samples satisfy independence. P is symmetric, nonnegative and doubly stochastic, with eigenvalues 1 and 1-rho, so its gap is exactly rho. The dimension, number of nodes, smoothness and initial distance remain fixed across the family.
The prescribed step size can now be evaluated without approximation. Since K = sqrt(5120) and tilde-sigma = sqrt(3)/T^2, the four candidates are

\[\frac1{24T},\qquad \frac1{KT^2},\qquad
\sqrt{\frac23}\sqrt T,\qquad
\frac1{\sqrt{2K\sqrt3}\,T}.\] For every T >= 2 their minimum is eta = 1/(KT^2). Identical initial states and identical deterministic gradients preserve consensus exactly, hence gossip leaves the common trajectory unchanged. The algorithm reduces to

\[w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta t x_t,\qquad
x_{t+1}=\frac{t-1}{t+1}x_t+\frac{2}{t+1}w_{t+1}.\] Complete analytic check. Induction shows that all iterates through horizon T are positive and at most 1. Indeed, assuming earlier x_s <= 1 gives w_{t+1} >= 1 - eta sum_{s=1}^t s, and x_{t+1} is a convex combination of x_t and w_{t+1}. The common lower bound below is positive, so this argument closes the induction. Using a harmless extra final update in the bound gives

\[x_T\ge 1-\frac{\eta T(T+1)}2
\ge 1-\frac3{4K},\qquad
f(x_T)-f^*\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac3{4K}\right)^2
>0.489.\] By contrast, the sum inside the theorem’s O notation on exactly the same instance is

\[R_T=\frac1{\sqrt2\,T^{5/2}}+
\frac{3^{1/4}+1}{T}\longrightarrow0.\] Thus no fixed numerical constant C can give the asserted inequality gap <= C R_T for all these admissible instances and horizons. This is an analytic family counterexample, not a claim based on a large finite ratio. The extra term in Corollary 4.2 is 2 sqrt(3)/T^2 for this family and also vanishes. The omitted unscaled term 1/(rho^2 T^2), however, equals 1, precisely preventing the contradiction if it is retained.

Counterevidence and alternative readings. For each fixed rho, the omitted term eventually becomes smaller than the 1/T term. The main statement could therefore be read as a large-horizon simplification after a network-dependent threshold, but the paper states every T >= 1 and does not impose that threshold. The appendix itself retains the term, confirming the issue is a mismatch between a substantive theorem statement and its displayed calculation. The family does not violate symmetry or use a graph excluded by the theorem.

Core dependency and impact. The prescribed network-dependent step cap makes the iterates move very little in this family. Dropping its transient penalty then claims convergence that does not occur at the specified horizon. This materially falsifies a core finite-sample theoretical guarantee and supports Major, even if the qualitative benefit of parallelism or empirical comparisons survives.

Precisely scoped correction. Retaining the additional order-LD_1^2/(rho^2 T^2) term restores correspondence with the displayed calculation. Alternatively, T >= rho^(-2) suffices to absorb it into LD_1^2/T. These are algebraic repairs to this omission only: Problem 2 prevents certifying the entire resulting theorem without repairing the upstream proof.
# 4. Problem 2 — The central averaging lemma uses inconsistent indices
Source claim. Lemma A.1, p.12, asserts for a convex function with global minimizer and the sequence defined by Eq.(16) that

\[A_t\bigl(f(x_t)-f^*\bigr)
\le\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\alpha_\tau
\nabla f(x_\tau)^\top(w_\tau-x^*).\] The suspect step is the identification of Eq.(16) with the standard weighted-average construction. At t = 1, the printed recurrence gives x_2 = w_2, omitting w_1 from that average. The displayed lemma instead assigns the left side the mass alpha_1 + alpha_2 while assigning the w_2 gradient term only alpha_2.
A fully specified exact counterexample. Work in one dimension with positive linear weights alpha_t = t, w_1 = x_1 = x* = 0, and w_2 = x_2 = 2. Choose the differentiable Huber function

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2/2,&|x|\le1,\\ |x|-1/2,&|x|>1.\end{cases}\] Its derivative is clip(x,-1,1), which is continuous, monotone and globally 1-Lipschitz. Therefore f is convex and 1-smooth, is nonnegative and has global minimizer zero. Eq.(16) is satisfied exactly at the required step. If compatibility with Eq.(15) is also requested, eta = 1 and g_1 = -2 produce w_2 = 2. Appendix A explicitly allows biased estimates, and Lemma A.1 imposes no unbiased-oracle condition. This example refutes that stated lemma; it is not asserted to be an unbiased-gradient counterexample to Theorem 4.1.

\[f(0)=0,\quad f'(0)=0,\quad f(2)=\frac32,\quad f'(2)=1.\] \[\underbrace{(1+2)f(2)}_{9/2}
>\underbrace{1\,f'(0)\,0+2\,f'(2)\,2}_{4}.\] The failure is a positive exact discrepancy of 1/2. Neither numerical error, a nonsmooth objective, zero averaging weights nor an absent minimizer explains it.

Core dependency. Lemma A.3 on pp.12–13 begins by invoking precisely this A.1 inequality. Appendix B, Eq.(19), p.14, then applies A.3 as the initial excess-loss bound for the decentralized average. Thus the invalid inference is directly in the central convergence proof, independently of Problem 1. Major is supported by this substantial invalid derivation; it does not require proving that no replacement proof could work.

Counterevidence. The usual correctly indexed weighted-average inequality is valid. Lemma A.2’s separate online-gradient regret identity is also valid. A local indexing or constant change may be sufficient to rebuild the proof, and this example does not establish empirical deterioration. The finding is attributed only to this paper’s recurrence–lemma pairing, not to the original Cutkosky or Dahan–Levy results cited by the paper.

A verified local correction for the actual linear weights. Let F_t = f(x_t)-f*. For t >= 2 the printed averaging recursion gives the identity below. Applying convexity twice yields the following inequality.

\[w_t=x_t+\frac{t-2}{2}(x_t-x_{t-1}),\] \[t\nabla f(x_t)^\top(w_t-x^*)
\ge tF_t+\frac{t(t-2)}2(F_t-F_{t-1}).\] The t = 1 term is at least F_1. Summing and collecting coefficients proves, for every T >= 2,

\[\sum_{t=1}^{T}t\nabla f(x_t)^\top(w_t-x^*)
\ge\frac{T^2}{2}F_T+F_1+\frac12\sum_{t=2}^{T-1}F_t.\] All the extra terms are nonnegative. Consequently T^2/2, rather than T(T+1)/2, is a valid left-side coefficient for linear weights in this local lemma. A separate general-weight repair is also available: the actual average uses weights alpha_(tau-1) on w_tau for tau = 2,...,t. Telescoping convexity gives
# 5. Problem 3 — Released neural EMA coefficient disagrees with the stated protocol

Source and scope. Section 5.2, p.9, defines an exponential moving average with gamma_t = 0.9 multiplying the previous query. The inspected public release is https://github.com/ofrieisen/DAT-SGD at commit 8070dd37f09e74dd164d1e9622323d654bd79a75. This finding concerns the unmodified released Fashion-MNIST launcher, the anytime-sgd optimizer, and no external gamma override.

\[x_{\mathrm{paper,new}}=0.9X+0.1W,\qquad
x_{\mathrm{release,new}}=0.1X+0.9W.\] Exact implementation path. deep_learning/optimizers/anytime_optimizer.py:69–75 updates W and then uses (1-gamma)X + gamma W. deep_learning/main.py:52 defaults –anytime_gamma to 0.9, and lines 113–114 pass it to the optimizer. deep_learning/run_fashion_mnist.sh:67–71 does not override the flag. For the same old X = 0 and chosen updated W = 1, the two affine combinations are 1/10 and 9/10, differing by 4/5. This isolates the coefficient convention and does not resolve the separate w_t time-index notation or simulate an entire training step.

Dependency and counterevidence. Query positions determine later sampled gradients, so these protocols are not numerically equivalent. However, the optimizer class’s direct default at line 8 is gamma = 0.1, which gives the paper’s affine coefficients. The current launcher may not be the launcher used for Figures 2–3. The repository was created on 10 December 2025 although this commit carries a 31 March 2025 timestamp; a commit timestamp alone does not establish historical experiment provenance.

Judgment: Minor, release-only specification discrepancy. No measured score change or published-run failure has been established. Passing –anytime_gamma 0.1 restores this local coefficient correspondence analytically. It does not verify the entire experimental setup or reproduce the paper’s results.
# 6. Coverage, counterevidence and what survives

Mathematical coverage. The main definitions, Algorithm 2, Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2, Table 1 and the dependencies in Appendices A–D were inspected. The gossip contraction, invariant averages, smoothness self-bound, conditional variance decomposition, Young inequalities and geometric consensus recursion were checked. Under the stated standard sampling interpretation, no additional substantive defect was established in Lemmas C.1–C.5 or D.1–D.6. The mapping c_1^2 = 80L^2, c_2^2 = 80 tilde-sigma^2 and kappa = rho/2 yields the stated consensus bound 2560 tilde-sigma^2 eta^2/rho^4. The formal zero-parameter boundary in D.6 was not developed into a substantive finding.

The consensus contraction may use (1-rho) in place of the tighter (1-rho)^2; this is a valid relaxation. A history sum including one additional nonnegative term is also a valid looser bound. These were considered and rejected as alleged counterexamples.

Parallelism scope. With N = MT, the missing term becomes order LD_1^2 M^2/(rho^2 N^2). In the advertised regime M = O(rho sqrt(N)), it is order 1/N. Thus the asymptotic parallelism exponents can remain consistent after a sound proof repair. Substituting the stated graph gaps gives N^(1/6) for rings, N^(1/4) for the two-dimensional torus, and sqrt(N) for well-connected graphs. An upper convergence bound supplies a certified sufficient regime; it is not an impossibility theorem outside that regime.

Experimental scope. Section 5.1 explicitly uses constant alpha_t = 1 in the synthetic least-squares experiments, while the theorem uses linear weights. Different local quadratic Hessians need not satisfy a global bounded-heterogeneity condition on all of R^d; the experiment’s footnote instead describes heterogeneity at the optimum. Section 5.2 deliberately studies a nonconvex network with momentum, exponential averaging and time-varying communication. These disclosures mean the experiments are illustrations beyond the exact theorem assumptions; their existence neither refutes nor repairs Problems 1 and 2.

Static release coverage. The synthetic gradient construction, optimum calculation, mean local squared-distance metric and disclosed constant-weight update match their described roles. Neural communication carries both query and auxiliary weights. Other release-scope differences were retained in the audit: least_sqaures/utils.py:66–82 creates a static multi-neighbor exponential matrix, while the paper describes a one-peer schedule; deep_learning/main.py:95–103 and the launcher use class-count partitions while the paper describes Dirichlet partitions. These differences limit direct reproduction from the release. A nonsymmetric released graph is not used as a counterexample to a theorem requiring symmetry. Historical figure configurations remain unresolved.

Figures 1–6, baseline descriptions, topology settings, seeds and error metrics were read for consistency and scope, without raw-data reanalysis, training, wall-clock benchmarking or statistical significance reconstruction. No absence of an additional experiment is treated as a demonstrated error.
# 7. Versions, dependence and remaining work

The arXiv record 2506.00961 lists v1 dated 1 June 2025. The acquired v1 PDF has SHA-256 b9f13073db2bf000a31ea13c19766fafc67833fb557d8815581777d72793d996. Its 25-page extracted token sequence agrees with the publisher’s except for the inserted five-token arXiv banner. No later version or erratum was located in the checked publisher, arXiv and repository issue sources. OpenReview API access returned HTTP 403 and the web page required verification; discussion history was not inspected. Absence within this search scope is not proof that no private or unindexed correction exists.

The two Major findings have distinct evidentiary bases. Problem 1 directly falsifies the published uniform rate under every operative assumption. Problem 2 directly falsifies an auxiliary inequality and its use in the core proof, but is not itself asserted to falsify all possible convergence rates. The Minor code finding is static evidence about a particular release path. Published empirical scores, broader optimization research claims and practical benefits are not declared invalid on that basis.

A complete mathematical repair requires choosing a consistent averaging statement, propagating it through A.3 and B, and retaining or explicitly restricting away the transient term. Historical code and run configuration would be needed to resolve which neural protocol produced the figures; new experiments would be needed to measure the effect of any code correction. These tasks remain pending.
# 8. Conclusion and decision status
Finding / judgment | Repair verification | Adoption and remaining work

1. Uniform convergence rate: Major | Counterexample proved; omitted-term restoration is an algebraic correction only. | Scientific decision pending. Reconcile the complete proof and state the horizon regime.
2. Averaging lemma: Major | Exact 9/2 > 4 violation. Linear-weight and shifted-weight local inequalities proved. | No whole-theorem certification. Propagate constants and distance/bias bounds.
3. Released EMA: Minor | Static path and exact affine check verified; gamma 0.1 matches local coefficients. | Historical experiment linkage and empirical effects unresolved; adoption not requested.
Overall: Major | Analytic proof, finite checks and static inspection are separately identified. | human_reviews is empty; controller acceptance pending.

Scientific Verification Report 0095
I25-43464 — Exploring and Mitigating Adversarial Manipulation of Voting-Based Leaderboards
# 1. Identity, reviewed versions and outcome

Yangsibo Huang, Milad Nasr, Anastasios Angelopoulos, Nicholas Carlini, Wei-Lin Chiang, Christopher A. Choquette-Choo, Daphne Ippolito, Matthew Jagielski, Katherine Lee, Ken Ziyu Liu, Ion Stoica, Florian Tramer and Chiyuan Zhang. ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267:25654–25671. Primary source: the 18-page publisher PDF linked from https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/huang25z.html; SHA-256 706d54245d20e448ba0167c01c815da6b66fd6b7a10c3117939f1ebc416f4dc4. Page numbers below mean physical PDF pages, equal to printed pages 1–18. OpenReview identifier: zf9zwCRKyP.

This is batch B001, task [internal task]-r002, isolated attempt-002; batch token [internal identifier omitted]. The inspected earlier preprint is arXiv:2501.07493v1, 13 January 2025, 21 pages, SHA-256 d3e150f07ed2f29f028cf3e2cfb7d94d58b744839619fcdf1634da63c41c82d0. The publisher and preprint are separately identified rather than treated as byte-identical versions.

Outcome: Major. Appendix B constructs the likelihood-ratio defense from an invalid categorical vote distribution. A fully specified Bradley–Terry example shows that the proposed product formula is not a vote probability law; charitable normalization still gives wrong probabilities and can reverse the ordering of likelihood ratios for observed vote sequences. This is a substantial invalid statistical derivation supporting a core proposed mitigation. Two additional Minor findings concern Figure 3 aggregates and an overly strong numerical summary of Table 4.

The review does not refute the existence of response de-anonymization or offline ranking manipulation, and does not establish that Figure 4 was generated by the incorrect formula. Those limits are separate from the severity of the failed derivation. Scientific decisions and controller acceptance remain pending; human_reviews is empty; no correction adoption has been requested.
# 2. Checked claims, definitions and review limits

The paper studies a system that samples two models, presents their responses anonymously, and receives a preference vote. An attacker may control the prompt, directly query candidate models, train a binary target-model detector, and preferentially vote after identifying the target. The study explicitly uses simulated environments and does not claim an unmitigated live-production attack. Existing identity filters and bot defenses, model-family versus exact-version identification, model-owner advantages and watermark exceptions are acknowledged in the source.

The training-based experiment uses 22 models, eight prompt categories, 200 prompts per category and 50 responses per model per prompt. Its stated binary dataset has 50 positive target responses and 50 uniformly sampled negative responses, split 80/20 for logistic regression. Figure 3 concerns test accuracy for this balanced per-target task, not 22-way model identification or positive predictive value in the full leaderboard. Section 3.1 separately assumes 95% accuracy with symmetric 5% false-positive and false-negative rates for the reranking simulation.

A vote and an interaction are distinct: an interaction includes a query on which the attacker abstains. The simulation recomputes rankings at intervals of 1,000 interactions using a historical testbed described in Appendix C.4 as 1,670,250 votes from 477,322 users. The reported win and tie counts, 1,093,875 and 576,375, sum correctly to that total. No historical ratings or raw vote logs were independently refitted here.

For the defense, Appendix B considers independent observations under a known benign profile, and then a second scenario with known benign and malicious profiles. The latter uses true versus perturbed Bradley–Terry ratings to form a likelihood ratio and invokes Neyman–Pearson optimality. The following verification concerns that actual probability construction. It does not invent a universal model-identification theorem or an optimal adversarial-voting theorem that the paper does not state.

Main paper pp.1–9 and Appendices A–D pp.13–18 were read. Critical formulas and tables were checked against rendered source pages. Relevant public-source searches found no attributable detector, simulator or defense implementation to pin and inspect. That is a reproducibility limit, not evidence of a code defect. No author code was executed or imported, no model/API queries or training were performed, and no live leaderboard was interacted with.
# 3. Problem 1 — Invalid vote probabilities undermine the likelihood-ratio mitigation

Faithful source claim and location. Section 4.2.3, p.7, and Appendix B Scenario 2, p.14, define Pr_B(i) as the probability that a benign user votes for model i, with a corresponding adversarial distribution based on perturbed ratings. Equations (4)–(6) construct the likelihood ratio from these distributions. Eq.(5) gives the usual Bradley–Terry pairwise probability, but Eq.(6) forms each supposed categorical component by multiplying over opponents:

\[p_{ij}(Q)=\frac1{1+\exp(-(Q_i-Q_j)/s)},\qquad
q_i(Q)=\prod_{j\ne i}p_{ij}(Q).\] The product is written here with self-comparisons excluded, the most charitable interpretation of the paper’s product over j. Including a self-comparison merely supplies another factor of 1/2 and does not resolve the problem. The invalid inference replaces the event that model i wins one sampled duel by the event that it wins every hypothetical duel.

Complete counterexample and all operative assumptions. Use three available models, positive scale s = 1, finite benign ratings Q = (log(1), log(2), log(4)), and uniformly select one of the three unordered non-self pairs at each interaction. Conditional on the chosen pair, select its winner by exactly Eq.(5). Successive pairs and votes are independent. There are no ties, a permissible decisive-vote subcase of the stated binary comparison model. Both profiles in the example below are fixed and known, as required by the simple-hypothesis likelihood argument. No assumption about a detector or model-response classifier is needed for this downstream statistical step.

\[(p_{12},p_{13},p_{21},p_{23},p_{31},p_{32})
=\left(\frac13,\frac15,\frac23,\frac13,\frac45,\frac23\right).\] Direct multiplication produces the paper’s alleged probabilities, which fail to sum to one:

\[q_B=\left(\frac1{15},\frac29,\frac8{15}\right),\qquad
\sum_i q_{B,i}=\frac{37}{45}.\] Normalizing these products would give the following vector. The actual probability of a winner, however, is obtained by summing over the mutually exclusive sampled pairs, giving a different vector:

\[\widetilde q_B=\left(\frac3{37},\frac{10}{37},\frac{24}{37}\right),\qquad
p_B=\left(\frac8{45},\frac13,\frac{22}{45}\right).\] For example, model 1 wins only when pair {1,2} or {1,3} is selected, so its probability is (1/3)(1/3) + (1/3)(1/5) = 8/45. The three actual probabilities sum to one. With equal ratings the product would give 1/4 for each model, summing to 3/4; that simpler example shows missing mass but is insufficient alone because normalization happens to fix the symmetric case. The unequal-rating calculation establishes that this is not merely an omitted normalizer.

A stronger exact check: the likelihood-ratio ordering reverses. Let the malicious user’s perturbed strengths be (1,4,4), or ratings Q_M = (log(1), log(4), log(4)), under the same independent uniform-pair sampling. This is an admissible finite perturbation of the known ratings. Its true and normalized-product winner laws are

\[p_M=\left(\frac2{15},\frac{13}{30},\frac{13}{30}\right),\qquad
\widetilde q_M=\left(\frac1{21},\frac{10}{21},\frac{10}{21}\right).\] Consider two positive-probability four-vote winner sequences, A = (1,1,1,2) and B = (3,3,3,3). The alternative-to-benign likelihood ratios using the correct categorical laws are

\[\Lambda_{\mathrm{true}}(A)=
\left(\frac34\right)^3\frac{13}{10}
=\frac{351}{640}=0.5484375,\] \[\Lambda_{\mathrm{true}}(B)=
\left(\frac{39}{44}\right)^4
\approx0.617230989.\] The normalized-product construction instead gives

\[\Lambda_{\mathrm{product}}(A)=
\left(\frac{37}{63}\right)^3\frac{37}{21}
\approx0.356915947,\] \[\Lambda_{\mathrm{product}}(B)=
\left(\frac{185}{252}\right)^4
\approx0.290458942.\] Thus the correct likelihood ranks B above A as evidence for the alternative, whereas the paper’s construction ranks A above B. For sequences of the same length, an omitted normalizing constant can be absorbed into the rejection threshold; it cannot repair this strict reversal. Equivalently, the true A/B ratio is 29282/32955 < 1, while the product-based ratio is 768/625 > 1.

Alternative interpretations and counterevidence. Under additional independence assumptions, the product could describe winning separate hypothetical matches against every opponent. Those events are not the categorical outcomes of the single duel actually presented, and they need not exhaust the sample space. A separately normalized artificial distribution is mathematically definable, but it is not the stated Bradley–Terry voting law. A practical detector based on a different, empirically calibrated score could still work. The standard Neyman–Pearson lemma itself remains correct for properly specified simple hypotheses.

Core dependency and impact. Pairwise ratings feed the purported full vote distributions; those distributions feed the likelihood ratio and the proposed optimal detector for ranking-aware attackers. That construction supports the Scenario 2 mitigation discussed with Figure 4b–c and the attack-cost analysis. The exact invalid inference is therefore linked to a scientific contribution, even though it appears in the publisher’s appendix. In the earlier preprint it appears in the main mitigation section, pp.9–10, with Eq.(6) on p.10; the publisher version relocates rather than repairs this step.

Judgment: Major for the substantial invalid statistical derivation. No evidence establishes which formula generated Figure 4, so the review does not declare its plotted detection rates false. The attack, authentication and rate-limit mechanisms do not depend on Eq.(6) and are not refuted.

A precise local repair. If only winner identities are retained, use the pair-sampling probabilities pi_ij to marginalize correctly. If actual pairs and their binary outcomes are retained, use the conditional Bernoulli likelihood:
# 4. Problem 2 — Figure 3 aggregates do not match its displayed data

Source claim and check. Figure 3, p.5, displays an 8-by-22 matrix of prompt-category accuracies, a Max row and a Model Avg column. Section 2.4.2 uses the best prompt performance to motivate high target-model detectability. The matrix was transcribed and checked against the PDF image, and the aggregates were recomputed using reviewer-authored arithmetic.
Target model | Contributing displayed accuracy | Displayed Max / correct category maximum
gemini-1.5-flash | Indonesian and Code: 95.8% | 94.7% / 95.8%
gemma-2-2b-it | Indonesian and Spanish: 97.5% | 96.3% / 97.5%

These discrepancies meet all relevant interpretation conditions. A maximum over the displayed category means cannot be below one of those means. Even if Max meant the best individual prompt rather than the best category mean, it still could not be below an included category average. One-decimal rounding cannot explain discrepancies of 1.1–2.4 percentage points. Eighteen of the 22 Max entries differ from the maximum of the displayed category values, and ten are below a contributing entry.

Four Model Avg entries also disagree beyond rounding with the ordinary across-model mean. The equal per-model sampling description supports that unweighted interpretation, and no different weighting rule is supplied. The exact means of the displayed cells are
Category | Displayed Model Avg | Mean of the 22 displayed cells
Safety-violating | 95.9% | 94.154545...%

Counterevidence and dependency. All 22 recomputed column maxima still exceed 95%; the smallest is 95.4%. Therefore the matrix body continues to support high best-category detectability in the reported setting. An undocumented aggregation, plotting order or data version might explain the reporting mismatch, but cannot make a displayed maximum below an included value valid. The small discrepancy for the Indonesian average can be explained by rounding and is not counted as an error.

Judgment: Minor. The demonstrated damage is to aggregate quantitative reporting and comparisons among prompt categories; the underlying detector measurements have not been invalidated. A scoped correction is to recompute Max and Model Avg from the intended matrix body, if that body is authoritative. This arithmetic is verified; the raw classifier outputs and plotting provenance are needed to determine which published values should be retained, and no full empirical repair is claimed.
# 5. Problem 3 — The one-position vote bound overstates the reported results

Source claim and location. Section 3.2, p.5, states that moving a model up or down by one position requires fewer than 1,000 votes in the simulated setting just discussed. Table 4(a), p.6, contradicts this blanket numerical statement in two directly checkable cases:
Model and one-position move | Published adversarial votes | Conflict with strict bound

Operative assumptions are exactly the reported Section 3.1 scenario: the historical voting testbed, the stated 95% detector with symmetric error assumption, passive behavior when the target is not detected, and the table’s own simulation results. A one-position change means an absolute rank difference of one. The quantities above are votes from Table 4(a), not the larger interaction counts in Table 4(b).

The eight adjacent movements available among the five models in Table 4 use 557, 454, 3,125, 163, 696, 903, 1,236 and 322 votes. Six of eight are below 1,000, and the full range is 163–3,125. Thus a statement about most tested movements is defensible; the strict universal bound is not.

Judgment: Minor. This is a bounded overstatement of a quantitative empirical summary. The approximate thousand-vote scale in the abstract and the broader conclusion that a few thousand simulated adversarial votes can change rankings remain compatible with the table. The repair is to state the observed range or qualify the sub-1,000 statement as applying to most tested adjacent movements. This is a direct consistency check, not a rerun validating the reported counts or an allegation about live voting.
# 6. Scope clarifications and unresolved evidence

Detector accuracy and simulation errors. In a balanced test set, accuracy = 1 - (FPR + FNR)/2. Accuracy of 95% does not identify both conditional error rates as 5%. The paper explicitly makes symmetry a simulation assumption in Section 3.1 and footnote 3; it is not treated here as a demonstrated false inference. Confusion matrices, prompt-selection validation and transfer from the 22-model detector pool to the larger ranking testbed would be needed to establish realized operating rates. Repeated values near 95.7–95.8% in Figure 3 alone do not prove class imbalance or a majority-class classifier, especially given the stated balanced construction. The split is not stated to be stratified, so the balanced-accuracy identity is not asserted to hold exactly for every 20-example test subset.

Vote versus interaction counts. Several table ratios are close to the target’s pair-inclusion probability in a large uniformly sampled model pool. Independent false positives on both non-target responses would ordinarily produce additional votes. The paper does not fully specify dependence between detector outputs, both-positive handling, or exactly which votes enter each count, and no simulation implementation was located. These ratios are a diagnostic requiring provenance, not a demonstrated omission of false positives or a basis for increasing severity.

Finite-sample calibration. Appendix B Eq.(3), p.13, reports an empirical Monte Carlo tail proportion K/m and rejects when it is below 0.01. Such a proportion is not automatically an exact finite-sample p-value. For exchangeable null statistics, the standard rank construction (K+1)/(m+1), with an appropriate conservative treatment of ties, avoids zero-probability Monte Carlo tail claims. The actual m used in Figure 4 is not reported, so no specific false-positive inflation in that figure is established. A bounded illustration and its limits appear in Appendix A below.

Benign-user assumptions and utility. Scenario 1 assumes known benign probabilities and independent votes. Persistent personal preferences, sampling changes and repeated looks would require corresponding calibration, but are not counterexamples satisfying that fixed null. The paper itself shows weak power against ranking-aware attackers and acknowledges that larger rating perturbations harm leaderboard utility. No claim of protection against every well-resourced adversary is attributed to it.

Cost model. The additive form ceil(N/m)c_account + N c_action + c_detector correctly separates accounts, actions and a one-time detector cost under its stated definitions. The approximately $2.20 per prompt follows the illustrative 10-proprietary/20-open-model pool, 512 output tokens and 50 responses using the price inputs supplied in Appendix C.3. This is a conditional output-token calculation, not a verified historical invoice or a current-price estimate. The 200-prompt budget and full eight-category acquisition scope should be distinguished; no unsupported claim of a measured total cost error is made.

Other experimental checks. The Table 8 difference for a 50-position move, from 1,246 votes at accuracy 1.0 to 1,383 at 0.9, is 137 and supports the text’s approximate 150-vote statement. Table 9 supplies alternative non-detection actions, but its full configuration and historical provenance are unavailable. Identity-probing results are appropriately limited by family-level names, disclosed post-processing filters and model-specific failures. A purely normative recommendation to use authentication or rate limiting is not assigned an invented experimental requirement.
# 7. Version, source-code and repair status

The arXiv record inspected lists v1 dated 13 January 2025. The publisher is an 18-page layout, while that preprint has 21 pages. The selected version comparison preserves the same balanced detector construction, the symmetric-error simulation premise, and the nine Figure 3 numeric rows. The Scenario 2 probability-product derivation appears in the earlier main Section 4.2.3, pp.9–10, and in the publisher’s Appendix B, pp.13–14. Its relocation is not a correction.

The checked publisher and arXiv pages, author publication pages, embedded paper links and bounded exact-title/arXiv repository searches did not identify a publicly released implementation attributable to this paper. General bibliographic repositories are not treated as author code. No code pin or release-to-experiment linkage is invented. No later correction was located within the inspected sources; unavailable discussion history and unindexed materials remain outside that statement.

A mathematical repair of Problem 1 requires specifying the actual observation and pair-selection law, constructing a valid likelihood under each hypothesis, and recalibrating the detector. Its effect on Figure 4 would require the historical implementation or a fresh correctly specified experiment. Problems 2 and 3 admit local arithmetic or wording repairs based on the displayed data, while underlying measurement validity and author adoption remain unverified. The overall Major judgment rests on the demonstrated derivation error, not on unresolved code provenance or a required quota.

# Appendix A. Actual checks, commands and finite-calibration limits

The following reviewer-authored rational calculation was executed using installed Python. It uses no author implementation and no model or platform interaction. Full inputs and exact fraction outputs are saved in the verification bundle.

Code:
from fractions import Fraction as F
from functools import reduce
from operator import mul

def prod(xs):
    return reduce(mul, xs, F(1))

def laws(w):
    k = len(w)
    q = [prod(F(w[i], w[i]+w[j])
              for j in range(k) if j != i) for i in range(k)]
    pair = F(1, k*(k-1)//2)
    p = [sum((pair*F(w[i], w[i]+w[j])
              for j in range(k) if j != i), F(0)) for i in range(k)]
    return p, q, [x/sum(q) for x in q]

pB, qB, zB = laws([1, 2, 4])
pM, qM, zM = laws([1, 4, 4])
r = [a/b for a, b in zip(pM, pB)]
z = [a/b for a, b in zip(zM, zB)]
assert sum(qB) == F(37, 45)
assert r[0]**3*r[1] < r[2]**4
assert z[0]**3*z[1] > z[2]**4

ELVIA Scientific Verification Report
0096 / I25-43465
From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology: Training, Evaluating, and Interpreting Sparse Autoencoders on Protein Language Models

Reviewed version: PMLR 267 (ICML 2025), pp. 460-476, publisher-linked 17-page PDF. Review date: 24 October 2026. PDF physical pages 1-17 equal printed article pages 1-17; proceedings pagination is not used below.
Source SHA-256: cf3326a7c0dcfce98a6e66c5fd63891e2ebaaaf93e1f963dd8329f169cfedc37. Hash and title match the controller acquisition receipt; original bytes preserved.

Outcome: No Issue Found within the inspected scientific scope, with scope clarifications and unresolved evidence questions. Public implementation discrepancies are recorded separately; no demonstrated central-claim damage. Scientific decisions remain pending.
# 1. Scope and decisive assessment

The inspected contribution is a method for extracting and characterizing ESM-2 SAE latents, comparing their interpretability with ESM coordinates, and using linear probes to nominate biologically meaningful features. The abstract and discussion explicitly frame unknown mechanisms as hypotheses for subsequent experimental testing. The ATP-binding/CHO-expression suggestion is not presented as an experimentally established causal mechanism.

Main text pp. 1-9 and technical appendix pp. 12-17 were read. Figures 4, 5 and 7 were visually inspected from the preserved PDF. Selected publisher-linked repository files were inspected statically at current commit fae2d3ae90220781289e27a26cb3b0826cf2b07e (23 April 2026) and publication-period commit 287c373817b06178603fc3a97bec95ebabb17ecc (19 May 2025). Availability of a commit does not establish that it generated the paper’s results.
No proof or empirical result was falsified by the checks below. This outcome is bounded by the coverage ledger; it is not certification of the whole paper.
# 2. Definitions, dependencies and checked reasoning
Claim and location | Check and result

SAE and sparsity; Sec. 3.1, p. 3 | Checked encoder/decoder definitions against released model and training code. Top-k followed by ReLU yields at most k active latents. Release also normalizes inputs, uses an encoder bias and an auxiliary loss; simplified paper equations are insufficient to reconstruct every implementation detail, but this does not demonstrate failure of the learned features.

Family specificity; Secs. 4.2-4.4, p. 5; A.6, p. 13 | The operational label is F1 > 0.7 for a latent predicting a selected InterPro family. The inspected code tunes the threshold on training rows and evaluates F1 on test rows. Candidate families and normalization maxima are selected before this split; the stronger interpretation of fully independent target-family selection is not established.

Probe performance; Secs. 3.2-3.3 and 5.1; Fig. 5 | Read task metrics and stated homology-based splits; checked plotted direction of comparisons. Subcellular demo separates train/test and uses validation flags with PredefinedSplit and GridSearchCV. No test-label hyperparameter tuning was found in that path. Published scores and homology clustering were not reproduced.

Biological interpretation; Sec. 5.2, pp. 6-8; discussion | Specific motif associations are illustrative and the layer selection is explicitly qualitative. Unknown functional associations are hypotheses. Their causal validation would require fresh experiments; absence of those experiments does not refute the stated hypothesis-generation contribution.
# 3. Scoped unresolved questions and counterevidence

Human ratings (Sec. 3.4, p. 4; Fig. 4, p. 5). Seven participants are reported; the figure explicitly uses binomial one-versus-all confidence intervals and shows about 80% SAE ’yes’ ratings. Original rater/feature assignments and exports are needed to assess dependence and interval calibration. Dependence is not assumed to have a particular magnitude, and neither the descriptive fraction nor its direction was disproved. A publication-period UI advertises 100 features per model, whereas the text says 100 total, and uses randomized sorting rather than a uniform shuffle. These source discrepancies do not establish the actual deployed protocol or numerical effect.

Steering (Sec. 4.2, p. 5; A.5/Fig. 7, p. 13). The plot supports the reported descriptive ordering. With the other latents fixed, a single latent clamp changes the normalized decoded stream by the decoder direction times the latent increment. report:
ELVIA Scientific Verification Report
0097 / I25-43466
LARM: Large Auto-Regressive Model for Long-Horizon Embodied Intelligence
Reviewed version: publisher-linked PMLR 267 (ICML 2025), pp. 36614-36623, ten-page PDF. Locations below use 1-based physical PDF pages. Review date: 24 October 2026.
Source SHA-256: c87416df10832f016e996a70113977a6d4a6ef90d0f95bd190dd6f385123c35e. Independently matched to the controller receipt and title; original bytes preserved.

Supported issue judgment: Major. One central mathematical argument contains demonstrated invalid inferences. The reported Minecraft successes and ablation results are not refuted. Scientific decisions and controller acceptance remain pending.
# 1. Summary and coverage

The paper motivates Referee RL by a mathematical explanation that ordinary PPO feedback vanishes on long successful trajectories and that nonconstant referee rewards prevent this behavior. The failure is in deriving the TD-residual pattern from reward imbalance and in the proposed nonzero-residual guarantee. The geometric discounting identity itself is valid.

Read the complete ten-page publisher PDF, including the methods, Algorithm 1 and Tables 1-5. Equations on pp. 4-5 and all five tables on p. 7 were visually inspected. Reviewer-authored exact-arithmetic calculations were executed. Official project links and the website repository were inspected; no training/evaluation implementation was located within that search. No author code or model was run.
# 2. Definitions and operative assumptions

Sections 3.1-3.2 define a finite-state MDP, a policy, and a critic intended to estimate expected discounted return. Section 4.1 considers a successful trajectory with a small negative time penalty -epsilon before a final positive task reward R. It assumes gamma and lambda lie strictly between zero and one. It does not specify the duration or continuation value of failed trajectories, require a constant critic, or impose a critic approximation-error bound.

The source places its terminal reward at r_T, while GAE is summed through T-1. The construction below retains that reward convention and uses the terminal state’s continuation value. A consistent one-step reindexing gives the same conclusion; the finding does not depend on this indexing discrepancy.
\[\delta_k=r_k+\gamma V(s_{k+1})-V(s_k),\qquad A_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}(\gamma\lambda)^{k-t}\delta_k.\]
# 3. Problem 1 (Major): reward imbalance does not determine actor feedback

Source claim and location. On PDF p. 4, between Eqs. (5) and (6), the paper infers from the predominance of -epsilon rewards that critic optimization yields approximately zero preterminal TD errors and one terminal residual R. It then concludes that the early GAE and useful actor feedback vanish. PDF p. 5 further argues that changing the rewards with a referee prevents TD errors and GAE from converging to zero.

Suspect step. The realized rewards of a successful rollout do not determine its state values. Those values depend on the current policy and other possible continuations. Likewise, reward variation is not a lower bound on a Bellman residual. These are substantive gaps in the mathematical rationale advertised in the abstract, introduction and method.
# 3.1 Complete counterexample for the sparse-reward inference

MDP and policy. There is one target and fully observed states s0,s1,...,sT, plus absorbing termination. At s0 the policy chooses continue with probability p=1/2 and abort with probability 1/2. Both choices earn -epsilon at s0. Abort then terminates with zero continuation. Continue advances through every required success-chain state in order, with a deterministic action thereafter. Each nonterminal success state earns -epsilon and the target state sT earns R-epsilon. The initial distribution is concentrated at s0. All transition probabilities and policy probabilities are valid.

Choose epsilon=0.01, R=1, gamma=0.9, lambda=0.8 and T=100; the same construction applies to arbitrary T. Every successful trajectory has exactly the rewards specified by Eq. (5). The abort behavior is not constrained by that successful-trajectory condition or by Sec. 3.1. The critic is the exact expected discounted return defined by the paper.

Calculate the two initial action values and the state value as follows. Downstream values satisfy the deterministic Bellman recurrence, with V(sT)=R-epsilon. Hence every later successful-path TD residual is zero, but the initial residual is an action advantage.

\[Q_g=-\varepsilon\frac{1-\gamma^{T+1}}{1-\gamma}+\gamma^T R,\qquad Q_b=-\varepsilon,\qquad V(s_0)=pQ_g+(1-p)Q_b.\] \[A_0=\delta_0=(1-p)(Q_g-Q_b)=(1-p)\left[-\frac{\varepsilon\gamma(1-\gamma^T)}{1-\gamma}+\gamma^T R\right]\ \longrightarrow\ -\frac{(1-p)\varepsilon\gamma}{1-\gamma}=-0.045.\]
# 3.2 Numerical check, consequence and alternative reading

The initial-state conditional PPO actor-logit derivative at the old policy is p(1-p)(Qg-Qb), approximately -0.022492762; clipping is inactive at probability ratio one. This is a conditional initial-state contribution, not a claim that the time-averaged whole-rollout gradient has a nonzero limit. The direct contradiction is the claimed vanishing initial GAE.

The negative sign is essential: with a distant discounted reward, the accumulated time penalties favor aborting. The construction disproves the stated implication to vanishing feedback. It does not show positive feedback for task completion, establish that ordinary PPO solves Minecraft, or disprove the practical utility of shaping.

If every unsuccessful trajectory were required to last exactly as long and incur exactly the same intermediate penalties, the abort construction would be excluded. Under that stronger model the two-action initial advantage can instead be (1-p) gamma^T R and vanish. Those extra assumptions are not in the paper. The exact-critic argument uses the source’s expected-return definition and conventional fixed-target TD regression, not an assertion about a global minimum of a fully differentiated stochastic residual objective.
Quantity at T=100 | Independently computed value
Q_abort | -0.01
Actual initial GAE | -0.04498552403760626
Paper’s terminal-only approximation: (0.72)^99 R | 0.000000000000007514795
Maximum absolute later TD residual | 0 (80-digit Decimal replay)
# 3.3 Nonconstant referee rewards do not guarantee nonzero TD errors

For any deterministic finite chain, including an arbitrarily long one, add a nonconstant sequence of allowed referee bonuses and define the critic by backward recursion. Select category rewards ra=0.2, rb=0.1, rc=-0.1 and rd=-0.2, satisfying the stated ordering. Correct actions can alternate positive-outcome and no-immediate-progress states before eventual success. An illustrative four-step total reward sequence is [0.19,0.09,0.19,1.19]; the same alternating prefix can be extended to T=100.

With the exact shaped return, every TD residual is identically zero, GAE is zero, and Eq. (1)’s squared residual loss is zero. Thus the p. 5 categorical inference from changed/nonconstant rewards to nonzero TD/GAE is false, even at a global zero of the deterministic squared loss. This does not imply that shaped rewards are ineffective during learning; no such conclusion is drawn.
\[V'_k=r'_k+\gamma V'_{k+1},\quad V'_{T+1}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \delta'_k=r'_k+\gamma V'_{k+1}-V'_k=0.\]
# 4. Dependence, surviving evidence and scoped correction

The paper explicitly promotes the vanishment argument as a theoretical explanation for classic RL failure and uses its proposed removal to motivate Referee RL. Invalidating that derivation therefore directly affects a central contribution and supports Major. This judgment does not require a drop in empirical scores, failure of the architecture, or inability to repair the exposition.

What survives is precise. If all preterminal TD errors are zero and a bounded terminal residual is the only contribution, GAE equals a discounted terminal residual and decays when the remaining distance tends to infinity. This conditional identity is analytically valid. It is not a verified repair of the broader theorem-like rationale, because the paper has not established that residual pattern or a nonzero-residual guarantee for its referee.

Tables 1-5 remain empirical evidence. Table 1 has 13 strict point-estimate wins and one tie; Table 2 has three 100% ties, 28/30 diamond successes versus STEVE’s 3/3, and 16/30 enchanted successes versus each listed baseline’s 0/3. These disclosed unequal sample sizes do not establish universal rate dominance, but they do preserve the observed enchanted-sword capability. The reward ablation’s improvements do not independently validate the defective derivation.

The 0.58-second claim concerns high-level skill selection on an RTX4090, not low-level control or full task completion. No independent timing or benchmark replication was performed. The public code search found a website repository, not training/evaluation code. Missing logs, exact reward values, referee versions/prompts, seeds and deployment configuration remain explicit evidence gaps.
# 5. Versions, repair and decision table

The latest arXiv metadata observed is 2405.17424v2, revised 5 February 2025. Its Sec. 4.1 contains the same relevant inference and nonzero-TD assertion. A targeted primary-source search found no relevant formal erratum or later repair; no exhaustive absence claim is made. The publisher PDF is the reviewed source.

Problem 1: central vanishment/referee derivation | Major; analytic counterexamples | Restricted discounting identity verified only. Full scientific repair not verified; author adoption not requested.

# Appendix. Replay, provenance and review roles

The 80-digit Decimal replay agrees with the analytic values at T=10,100,1000. Its fixed-duration countercontrol preserves the legitimate sparse-reward intuition; its dense-reward check verifies the Bellman identity. These are independent reviewer calculations, not author-code execution or empirical reproduction.

Adversarial Combinatorial Semi-bandits with Graph Feedback

Inspection outcome: Major. The explicit lower-bound theorem has admissible failures; the single-arm upper-bound proof contains a false second-moment identity; the additional stochastic elimination algorithm permits a linear-regret execution; the adaptive-hindsight upper proof makes an invalid comparator inference; and the truncation step uses a false L1 inequality. These are separate dependencies. None establishes that the full-set OSMD-G algorithm with S >= 2 has a false numerical regret rate.

Scientific decision pending. Author adoption has not been requested; human review is not asserted. Prepared by AI reviewers under the authorized B001 / [internal task] contract and the user’s 24 October 2026 severity clarification. Batch token: [internal identifier omitted].
# 1. Identity, version and evidence scope

Yuxiao Wen, PMLR 267:66419-66436 (ICML 2025), publisher record wen25a, OpenReview zcOCXlvsk1. The exact publisher-linked 18-page PDF was verified against verification/0098/controller_acquisition_receipt.json before analysis. SHA-256: 14f26a7c7f8fac500d6c423ae3b88d31a7f5b4d3ef18e2a5f2c0a04dec66fea1. The original bytes were preserved.

Locations below use 1-based physical PDF pages, which match the article’s printed page numbers 1-18, not the proceedings’ continuous pagination. The proceedings PDF includes Appendices A-F. Targeted later-version comparisons used arXiv 2502.18826v7, submitted 16 September 2025, SHA-256 1e221fcb61c4bfa9f628582fe71cefa7721526df5bbb08ea8dae4ecbbfdb8704. It is a separate preserved source.

Checked: the model and quantifiers, Theorems 1.1/1.3/3.2/3.4, the core estimator and negative-correlation arguments, Appendix A lower-bound calculations, Appendix C, Algorithm 3 and Theorem D.1, and selected capacity/general-set extensions. These checks combine analytic arguments, exact reviewer arithmetic and static source inspection. No author implementation, training or experiment was run. No publicly linked implementation was found in the inspected publisher materials; this theoretical paper is not assigned an artificial experiment requirement.
# 2. Definitions and operative assumptions

The full decision set A consists of binary K-vectors with exactly S selected arms. A0 is an arbitrary nonempty subset when a statement says so. Rewards are in [0,1]^K; graph edges indicate which rewards a selected arm reveals. A strongly observable graph gives every vertex either a self-loop or incoming edges from every other vertex. Its independence number alpha ignores edge direction in testing whether distinct vertices are adjacent.

Equation (1) uses expected regret against the best fixed feasible decision in hindsight, with the maximum inside expectation. Adversarial rewards may depend on past actions. Appendix D instead assumes stationary i.i.d. rewards for each arm; deterministic rewards satisfy that condition. All counterexamples below use the same decision domain for the learner and its comparator.

Big-O/Omega parameter comparisons below use the conventional uniform multivariate interpretation of the stated dimension/horizon bounds. Where a weaker fixed-dimension asymptotic reading avoids a counterexample, that limitation is stated explicitly. A false proof identity is distinguished from a counterexample to an algorithm’s actual regret.
# 3. Problem 1 — The explicit minimax lower bound exceeds its valid scope

Source claim. Theorem 1.3, p.3, states the following bound for any decision subset A0 contained in A, any strongly observable graph, T >= max{S, alpha^3/S}, and S <= K/2. Appendix A, p.12, imports the logarithmic full-information term. [R1, R3]

Subset counterexample. Set K=2, S=1, alpha=1, T any integer at least one, use a complete directed graph with all self-loops, and A0={(1,0)}. The graph is strongly observable; S=K/2 and the horizon condition holds. The learner and comparator are identical on every reward sequence, so the minimax regret is exactly zero. The displayed positive lower bound cannot hold.

Counterevidence to the breadth of that first objection: Section 1.2 and the contribution list explicitly focus on the full set. Restricting the theorem to A0=A removes the singleton example. It does not remove the next example.

Full-set counterexample. For every integer n >= 2, take T=n, S=1, K=2^(n^2), A0=A, and the complete self-loop graph with alpha=1. All printed conditions hold. For every reward sequence the comparator receives at most n and the learner at least zero, so R* <= n. The claimed scale is sqrt(log 2) n^(3/2) + sqrt(n), and n divided by this scale tends to zero. No positive uniform Omega constant can satisfy the stated result.

The correct order on this family is Theta(n), not just an unknown quantity below the claimed expression. Give every arm independent Bernoulli(1/2) rewards across all n rounds. Any learner’s expected reward is n/2. The probability that at least one arm has all n rewards equal to one is at least 1-exp(-2^(n^2-n)), which is at least 1-exp(-4). Thus the expected hindsight reward is at least n(1-exp(-4)). This randomized oblivious construction supplies a lower bound on the worst-case regret by averaging, and the deterministic upper bound supplies the other direction.

Impact and alternatives. Theorem 1.3 supplies the lower-bound half of the paper’s minimax characterization; its explicit full-set parameter guarantee is materially false. This supports Major under the user’s standard. The new graph-dependent sqrt(alpha S T) term is not refuted, nor is the intended sufficiently-long-horizon rate with logarithms suppressed. If Omega meant only fixed K,S,G followed by T tending to infinity, the growing-K family would not challenge that weaker assertion; the stated parameter conditions do not express that restriction.

Repair status. A full-set restriction and a finite-horizon saturation or an additional logarithmic horizon condition would exclude these examples. No complete repaired theorem is certified here. The later v7 statement still includes the any-subset quantifier and the same displayed range. Evidence: lower_bound_audit.json and lower_bound_checks.py/json.

\[R^*=\Omega\!\left(S\sqrt{T\log(K/\allowbreak{}S)}+\sqrt{\alpha ST}\right).\] \[\left(\tfrac12-e^{-4}\right)n\ \le R^*\le n,\qquad \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log2}\,n^{3/\allowbreak{}2}+\sqrt n}\longrightarrow0.\]
# 4. Problem 2 — The S=1 upper proof uses a false variance identity

Source claim and suspect step. Algorithm 1 (p.5) and Appendix C (pp.14-15, after Eq.16) define the loss estimator rhat, gain estimate rtilde=1-rhat, m=sum over Ut of x_a rhat_a, and rbar=1+m. The proof replaces the squared centered gain by a weighted second moment minus m^2. With Ut equal to all arms and sum x=1, the supplied definitions instead give a plus 3m^2 term. The next asserted variance bound therefore does not follow. [R1, R4]

Complete feasible-target check. Use K=2, S=1, T=50, epsilon=1/(KT)=0.01, x=(0.99,0.01), rewards (0,0), and graph edges 1->2 and 2->1 with no self-loops. Each vertex receives an edge from every other vertex, so the graph is strongly observable and alpha=1. The target lies in the truncated simplex. Singleton sampling has the required means and automatic negative pairwise correlation. Ut contains both arms because both possible loss estimates are at most 100, its threshold.

Selecting arm 2, with probability 0.01, yields rhat=(100,0), m=99, rbar=100 and centered gains (-199,-99). The actual squared sum is 39303; the claimed variance expression is 99. Selecting arm 1, with probability 0.99, yields rhat=(0,100/99), m=1/99; the corresponding values are 103/9801 and 1/99. Exact averaging gives 38911/99 versus 1, as displayed below.

Precise consequence. This refutes a universally asserted algebraic/conditional step in the proof. Reachability of this exact target from the specified initialization within 50 rounds has not been established. The all-zero reward example has zero actual regret. Consequently this is not presented as a counterexample to OSMD-G’s numerical regret rate.

Core dependency and judgment. Theorem 3.2 explicitly includes S=1 and delegates that case to Appendix C; Theorem 1.1 inherits its all-S guarantee. The variance reduction is an essential step in the supplied proof, so a substantial invalid derivation closely tied to the core upper guarantee supports Major even without an algorithmic regret counterexample.

Alternative reading and repair limit. Changing rbar to 1-m repairs this square expansion locally. A common shift cancels from the projected exponential-weights decision, but the subsequent exponential-moment inequalities still require valid step-size/gain conditions. Centered positive gains can be of order 1/epsilon. A sign replacement alone is therefore not certified as a complete proof repair. The same definitions and false transformation persist in v7 Appendix C, pp.14-16. Evidence: upper_bound_audit.json and exact Fraction calculations in upper_bound_checks.py/results.

\[\sum_a x_a(\widetilde r_a-\bar r)^2=\sum_a x_a(\widehat r_a+m)^2=\sum_a x_a\widehat r_a^2+3m^2\ne\sum_a x_a\widehat r_a^2-m^2.\] \[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_a x_a(\widetilde r_a-\bar r)^2\right]=\frac{38911}{99}\approx393.0404,\qquad \mathbb E\!\left[\sum_a x_a(1-x_a)\widehat r_a^2\right]=1.\]
# 5. Problem 3 — Algorithm 3 admits linear regret

Source claim. Section 5.1 (p.9) advertises a stochastic elimination algorithm for general decision subsets. Algorithm 3 and Theorem D.1 (pp.16-17) claim an Otilde(S alpha + S sqrt(log(KT/epsilon) alpha T)) guarantee. The proof bounds each minimum-count phase by 50 log(K)(1+log(K)) alpha using greedy domination. [R1, R5]

Suspect step. AN contains active decisions whose minimum constituent-arm observation count is N. Ut is the union of all arms in these decisions. A well-observed arm stays in Ut if it shares a decision with an unobserved arm. Thus the algorithm’s repeated maximum-outdegree choice does not implement a greedy cover that removes already covered vertices.

Parameters and graph. For any integer m >= 2, set S=2, T=m, K=3m+2, A0=A (all pairs), and epsilon=1/4. There is one hub h, a set H={H0,...,H(2m)} of size 2m+1, and L={L1,...,Lm}. Every vertex has a self-loop. Direct h to every H and every L to h. On H use the regular tournament Hi->Hj iff (j-i) modulo (2m+1) belongs to {1,...,m}. On L direct Li->Lj iff i<j. Choose a fixed m-element set Hminus; every L points to Hminus, and all remaining m+1 vertices Hplus point to every L.

All graph assumptions hold. Every distinct pair has exactly one directed edge, hence alpha=1. Self-loops imply strong observability. Including self-loops, h has outdegree 2m+2; Hminus has m+1, Hplus has 2m+1, and Li has 2m+2-i. Therefore h is the unique maximum-outdegree vertex.

Permitted execution. Choose the pairs {h,Lm}, {h,L(m-1)}, ..., {h,L1}. This is allowed by Algorithm 3’s instruction to pull any decision in AN containing the chosen arm. Before each of these rounds at least one L remains unobserved, and N=0. Any other vertex can pair with an unobserved L; that L itself pairs with h. Therefore Ut is the entire graph. The uniquely selected hub remains h. At the round using Li, h reveals H, while Li reveals itself, h, Hminus and Lj for j>i. Those larger-index L vertices have already been observed. Exactly one new L is revealed each round.

By induction the phase lasts m rounds. Elimination is triggered only once every least-observed decision exceeds N, so none occurs before round m. Elimination after that round cannot change the incurred regret. The example does not depend on a tie in the maximum-outdegree arm; only the expressly permitted companion-decision choice is used.

Rewards and exact regret. Every L has deterministic reward one; h and H have deterministic reward zero. These degenerate stationary distributions are in [0,1] and i.i.d. over time. Every pulled pair earns one; a fixed pair of distinct L vertices earns two every round. All available concentration events hold exactly. The regret is therefore deterministically T=m.

Contradiction. With fixed S=2, alpha=1, epsilon=1/4 and K=3T+2, the claimed bound is Otilde(sqrt(T)); fixed powers of logarithms in K,T cannot absorb linear regret. The explicit phase bound also fails finitely: at m=20000, K=60002, its proposed bound is about 6602.4534 while the phase lasts 20000 rounds. The large comparison evaluates the formula, not a huge simulated graph.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. Different companion choices can cover L much faster. The result falsifies the guarantee for Algorithm 3 as specified, which permits the displayed execution; it does not prove all elimination variants fail. Section 5.1 explicitly claims this extension, so its appendix location does not make the failed algorithmic guarantee peripheral. Judgment: Major. No revised exploration/companion rule or regret proof is certified. The main full-set OSMD-G algorithm is a different algorithm and is not falsified by this construction.

Independent reviewer code checked m=2,3,5,10,20, including graph orientation, self-loops, unique hub, legal actions, full Ut, new observations and exact regret. The all-m induction supplies the general argument. Targeted comparison confirms the same rules, theorem and phase bound in v7 Algorithm 3 p.16 and proof p.17. Evidence: capacity_audit.json, capacity_counterexample.py/results.json, capacity_v7_comparison.json.
\[T_0=m,\qquad R_T=\sum_{t=1}^{m}(2-1)=m=T,\qquad \alpha=1,\quad K=3T+2.\]
# 6. Adaptive-comparator derivation and additional checks

Adaptive-hindsight inference — Major; numerical rate not falsified. Page 1 explicitly allows rewards to depend on the learner’s past decisions, and Eq.(1) places the hindsight maximum inside expectation. Theorem 3.2’s proof fixes a comparator before Eq.(7), applies fixed-comparator unbiasedness in Eq.(8), and concludes the adaptive-hindsight bound on p.7. That conclusion does not follow from the fixed-comparator calculation. The issue affects the stated adaptive upper guarantee and its inheritance by Theorem 1.1; it is not resolved by the correctness of the variance calculation.

Exact witness and assumptions. Take K=2, S=1, T=2, the full singleton action set, and the graph with both self-loops and no cross edges (strongly observable, alpha=2). Use the prescribed truncation epsilon=1/(KT)=1/4 and entropy initialization x=(1/2,1/2); the first action A1 is therefore uniform. Let r1=(0,0) and r2=e(A1). These rewards lie in [0,1] and the second vector depends only on the past action, not the current one. The unique best fixed arm in hindsight is A1. Its first-round gain estimate from Eqs.(3)-(4) is -1 although its true reward is zero. In fact the first-round true comparator-regret term is zero, whereas the estimated term against the conditional mean action is -1. The common centering shift cancels because both decisions have unit mass. Thus the required fixed-to-random comparator substitution fails in a permitted execution.

Evidence and scope. The exact two-round estimator result is reused from upper_bound_check_results.json; no unchanged arithmetic was rerun. This is a demonstrated invalid inference in the core adaptive-regret derivation, so the severity is Major under the saved calibration criterion. It does not establish that the numerical regret rate is false. Oblivious deterministic sequences and a fixed comparator avoid this particular obstruction; a valid uniform or martingale analysis could restore the adaptive guarantee, but none is verified here. The correction must either supply that argument or explicitly restrict the proved claim’s comparator/adversary scope.

Local truncation derivation — Major; scoped correction verified. The S>=2 proof on p.6 explicitly uses the chain (v-v_epsilon) transpose r <= the L1 distance <= K epsilon to obtain Eq.(7). A counterexample within that subcase is K=5, S=2, T=2, epsilon=1/(KT)=0.1, v=(1,1,0,0,0) and v_epsilon=(0.85,0.85,0.1,0.1,0.1). The latter is feasible, has total mass two, and minimizes L1 distance: the three unselected coordinates must receive at least 0.3 total mass, so the selected coordinates must lose at least 0.3. Its distance is therefore 0.6, exceeding K epsilon=0.5.

Dependency and repair are separate. The false inequality is used to establish the epsilon KT term in Eq.(7), which feeds directly into Theorem 3.2 and then Theorem 1.1. The source does not independently derive the needed one-sided bound; thus this is an operative invalid core-proof step, not an unused stronger assertion. Under the saved calibration it supports Major even though the reviewer-supplied correction is verified. Since the two decisions have equal mass and rewards lie in [0,1], their one-sided reward difference is at most the total positive mass (K-S)epsilon <= K epsilon. This proves the exact needed truncation estimate under the same assumptions. The numerical regret rate is not falsified by this finding, and this scoped repair does not repair any other finding.

Appendix A local corrections. A displayed sum must exclude the optimal arm index to equal the number of suboptimal pulls. The unconditional sentence T <= Nm(tau_m) is false on paths that never reach the threshold, but the subsequent maximum inequality follows by splitting hit/non-hit paths. The KL/Pinsker range, averaging, Delta choice and final constant were checked without a further demonstrated failure of the new graph-dependent term. Nondivisible rounding was not fully reconstructed.

What checked out within scope. The multiplicity-weighted estimator is conditionally unbiased; it need not use the probability of any observation. Negative pairwise correlation gives E[count^2] <= E[count]^2+E[count]. For S>=2, no-self-loop vertices have denominator S-x_a >= S-1. Theorem 3.4’s correlated-clique reduction is coherent for K divisible by S with the intended initialization x=(S/K)1; the printed (1/K)1 is a local initialization error. The theorem does not establish that negative correlation is uniquely necessary.

The intended zero-inclusive capacity-copy construction in Section 4 and the basic Appendix E bound Z^2 <= SZ for 0<=Z<=S were checked. The partition example supports the needed negative correlations.
