ELVIA Scientific Verification Report
0099 / I25-43468
Transfer Learning for Nonparametric Contextual Dynamic Pricing

Inspection outcome: Major. The published TLDP algorithm has an unavoidable first-round expected loss on a valid instance while Theorem 4.1 requires its total regret to approach zero as source information grows. The matching lower-bound proof also contains separate invalid construction/information steps. The reported empirical scores and the truth of an appropriately formulated minimax rate are not refuted by these checks.

Scientific decisions remain pending. No author adoption has been requested and no human-review approval is asserted. B001 / [internal task]; batch token [internal identifier omitted]; review governed by the user’s 24 October 2026 evidentiary clarification.
# 1. Identity, reviewed versions and scope

Fan Wang, Feiyu Jiang, Zifeng Zhao and Yi Yu. PMLR 267:63211-63244, ICML 2025, publisher record wang25aq; OpenReview zbFiEmkFNP. The 34-page publisher-linked PDF was verified against verification/0099/controller_acquisition_receipt.json before analysis and preserved unchanged. SHA-256: 62562db92f11f2c402f8d9641e0cadff39773dae890975a3fac3bfd075bc1b59.

All paper locations use 1-based physical PDF pages, which match printed pages 1-34. Main text, applicable Appendices A-D, and the publisher-linked code were inspected within the coverage ledger. The earlier arXiv:2501.18836v1 (31 January 2025) was separately acquired: SHA-256 daa76bd488db902d43a65a1e3003898ce3fd1a992b590d412a5f26e989e4a59f. Its observed submission history showed only v1; no later correction was found in the targeted primary-source search. This is a scoped search result, not a guarantee that no other correction exists.

The official repository chrisfanwang/dynamic-pricing was pinned to commit 411886602687fb4fbf55443c1fece250b81a46d2 (31 January 2025). Its 14-file tree, code, source-data archive and acquisition manifests are preserved in sources/0099. Inspection was static. Only reviewer-created arithmetic, text inspection and CSV counting were executed; no author program or model fitting was run.
# 2. Model, quantifiers and evidence boundaries

The covariate space is [0,1]^d and the price space [0,1]. Target contexts have marginal QX and source contexts PX. Source triplets are independent across time. The mean revenue function f(x,p), bounded in [0,1], is shared between domains and is Lipschitz in the infinity norm. Target small-ball masses are between cQ r^d and CQ r^d. Regret sums expected differences from the best price at each observed context.

Definition 2.3 defines gamma as the infimum of all nonnegative exponents for which some positive constant gives PX(B) >= c r^gamma QX(B) for every target-support-centered ball. Definition 2.4 defines kappa through the infimum of source covariate-price mass ratios over interior price intervals. Both the exponent quantifier and the range of interval centers matter to the arguments below.

Theorem 4.1 claims a constant C depending only on its displayed fixed problem/tuning constants, not on nQ or nP. Its effective sample size is N=nQ+(kappa nP)^((d+3)/(d+3+gamma)), with radius rtilde=Cr(log N/N)^(1/(d+3)) and upper regret C nQ(log N/N)^(1/(d+3)). Theorem 4.4 supplies the claimed matching minimax lower bound over a model class indexed by gamma,c_gamma,kappa,CLip,cQ.

Analytic counterexamples to an algorithmic guarantee are distinguished from failures of a supplied proof. A release configuration discrepancy does not identify the implementation or settings that generated a published figure. A model-based auto-loan evaluation does not constitute an actual pricing intervention.
# 3. Problem 1 — The first target price contradicts the source-rich upper guarantee

Source claim and location. Theorem 4.1, p.5, gives the source-dependent upper rate described above for Algorithm 1, p.4. Initialization sets A1={Z}. The unique root ball is selected and p1 is sampled uniformly on its full price domain [0,1]. The source-driven refinement loop comes after this draw. It changes the selected ball and counters but never assigns a new price. [R1, R3]

Complete instance. Set d=1, let target contexts be i.i.d. Uniform[0,1], let the source covariate density be gP(x)=1/2+x, and draw source prices independently and uniformly on [0,1]. Source triplets are i.i.d. with deterministic revenue YP=pP. Target revenue is also deterministically Yt=pt. Thus f(x,p)=p in both domains and the optimal price is one.

Every operative condition is satisfied. The source density integrates to one, lies between 1/2 and 3/2, and differs from QX, giving genuine covariate shift. PX(B) >= (1/2)QX(B) on every ball, so the exact nonnegative transfer exponent is gamma=0 with c_gamma=1/2. Independent uniform source prices give kappa=1 exactly. Uniform target mass obeys r <= QX(BX(x,r)) <= 2r, so cQ=1,CQ=2. The revenue is bounded and Lipschitz with CLip=1. Set CI=1 and Cr=2; then Cr^4 c_gamma cQ=8, exactly the tuning requirement.

Correct result. The first price remains Uniform[0,1] for every possible source dataset and every nP. Its expected regret is integral from zero to one of (1-p) dp = 1/2. All later regret terms are nonnegative. Therefore total expected regret is at least 1/2, independently of the source sample size.

Contradiction with the stated bound. Take integer m>=10, nQ=m and nP=m^8. All constants above stay fixed and the prescribed radius is positive and less than 1/2. The claimed bound is C m[log(m+m^8)/(m+m^8)]^(1/4), asymptotic to C(8 log m)^(1/4)/m, which tends to zero. No allowed fixed C can dominate the first-round loss. This growing-target sequence avoids relying on a fixed-horizon asymptotic reading.

Proof dependency. Appendix B.1, Eq.(16), pp.13-14, uses the optimistic index-maximizing property of the initially selected ball. Algorithm 1 then replaces that ball by a child centered on the already selected context/price. Eqs.(20)-(21) and the source-rich counting step charge regret to the small final-child radius as though it retained the same argmax property. If the symbol means the original root, it may have no parent and cannot receive the child’s radius bound; if it means the final child, it was not chosen by that argmax. The distinction is essential to the claimed transfer benefit.

Static code corroboration. All five released TLDP routines preserve the same timing. In dynamic pricing functions for Scenario_1.1.R, the price assignment is line 95 and refinement begins at line 111; in the auto-loan routine the corresponding lines are 96 and 118. The shared utility returns the full initial interval and samples it uniformly. These line numbers refer to the pinned commit and are recorded in tldp_first_price_static_check.json. This corroborates the written algorithm; it does not establish which commit produced the paper’s scores.

Alternative readings and impact. No source-only pre-partitioning or re-selection/repricing step appears in the reviewed algorithm. Treating the draw as provisional adds an operation absent from the specification. An additive startup term would cover this particular first-loss obstruction, but the rest of the bound and later rounds have not been re-proved. No complete repair is certified. The counterexample defeats a core quantitative guarantee used to establish minimax-optimal transfer, so Major is supported. It does not establish linear regret in nQ, refute target-only performance, or falsify the experiments.

The earlier arXiv v1 Algorithm 1 p.6 and Theorem 1 p.7 have the same order and rate. This is historical persistence, not a later corrected issue. Independent exact expectation/asymptotic calculations and a small numerical scaling check are saved in first_price_check.py and first_price_check_results.json.

\[\mathbb E[1-p_1]=\int_0^1(1-p)\,dp=\tfrac12,\qquad R_{\rm TLDP}\ge\tfrac12.\] \[C\,m\left[\frac{\log(m+m^8)}{m+m^8}\right]^{1/\allowbreak{}4}\sim C\,\frac{(8\log m)^{1/\allowbreak{}4}}{m}\longrightarrow0.\]
# 4. Problem 2 — The hard family has exact transfer exponent zero

Source claim. Appendix C Step 2, p.25, claims that the distributions constructed in Eqs.(68)-(69), p.23, have transfer exponent equal to the prescribed gamma and hence belong to the class used in Theorem 4.4. Definition 2.3, p.3, defines the exponent by an infimum over all admissible positive constants. [R1, R4]

Complete check of that inference. Write a=c_gamma rtilde^gamma, which is strictly positive for any fixed constructed instance with finite gamma and positive rtilde. On each inner covariate box the source density is a times the target density; outside the outer boxes the two densities agree; in the remaining regions the target density is zero. Therefore pX(x) >= a qX(x) pointwise everywhere, and PX(B) >= a QX(B) for every measurable ball B. Exponent zero is admissible with constant a. Nonnegative exponents then imply that the infimum in Definition 2.3 is exactly zero.

For example, with prescribed gamma=1, c_gamma=1 and rtilde=1/32, the constructed density ratio on the target’s inner support is 1/32, and outside the boxes it is one. The correct exact exponent is zero, while the proof asserts one. This is a countercheck of the construction’s membership claim, not an admissible instance used to falsify the final lower rate.

Alternative interpretation. In transfer-learning bounds it is often useful to index a class by any exponent satisfying a fixed-constant mass inequality, rather than by the smallest exponent. On that larger admissible-exponent interpretation, the construction may satisfy the intended inequality with the advertised fixed c_gamma. But that is different from the literal infimum definition, and the proof explicitly claims equality. The fact that a depends on the horizon does not prevent exponent zero for each fixed distribution; it does explain why a uniform fixed-constant class is a different object.

Dependency and judgment. Under the paper’s literal exact-exponent class, the proposed hard instances with gamma>0 do not establish the claimed minimax lower bound for that class. This is a substantial invalid membership step in the core optimality derivation and supports Major with that precise interpretation. Recasting the model as an admissible-exponent class removes this specific objection, but the separate information-bound failure below remains. No complete corrected lower theorem or replacement exact-exponent construction is verified.
\[p_X(x)\ge a\,q_X(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_X(B)\ge a\,Q_X(B),\qquad a=c_\gamma\widetilde r^\gamma>0,\qquad \gamma_{\inf}=0.\]
# 5. Problem 3 — The low-visit bin is selected under a distribution it then changes

Source claim. Appendix C Step 3.2, p.27, Eq.(79), uses a counting argument to choose a price-bin index u visited at most 2nQ/L times in expectation for many alternatives, where L=floor(1/rtilde). It then sets the common bump center ptilde to that bin and defines the source price density in Eq.(70). The resulting visit bound is used in the target KL calculation, Eq.(82), and ultimately in the matching lower-bound rate. [R1, R4]

Invalid inference. A pigeonhole argument is valid under a fixed collection of probability laws. Here the laws of the adaptive action counts already depend on the bump center through both the reward function and the source-price distribution. After selecting u, redefining the center changes those laws. The preceding average over bins does not supply a self-consistent low-visit center.

A concrete fixed-policy witness makes the failure explicit. Set rtilde=1/32, L=32, kappa=0 and nP=1000. In the candidate family whose center is bin u, Eq.(70) gives zero source-price probability to that bin and equal probability 1/31 to each of the other 31 bins. Use one policy for every possible u and every sign vector: count all source prices in the 32 bins; choose the center of the uniquely empty bin, breaking multiple-empty ties by a fixed rule; then use that price on every target round. The policy uses only observed source data and is admissible.

With probability at least 1-31(30/31)^1000, every nonempty bin has appeared in the source data. On this event the policy identifies the true empty bin u. Thus, for every candidate u and every sign vector, its expected count in the subsequently declared bump bin is at least [1-31(30/31)^1000]nQ. This exceeds 0.9999999999998 nQ, whereas Eq.(79) requires at most nQ/16. There is no candidate center satisfying the needed inference for this fixed policy.

Assumption and scope checks. Kappa=0 is explicitly allowed. Source prices are independent of source contexts and signs, and source triplets remain independent across time. The witness works with the paper’s covariate construction at gamma=0,c_gamma=1/2: the inner density ratio is 1/2, the outside ratio is one, and positive shell mass gives genuine covariate shift. Its exact exponent is zero, so the witness does not rely on Problem 2. Rewards can be the paper’s bounded Lipschitz Bernoulli bump family. It refutes the selection/count inference at this construction step; it is not asserted to refute the minimax lower theorem itself.

Impact and repair. The extra small-bin visitation factor is used to obtain the target information budget and hence the claimed continuous-price minimax exponent. Replacing the argument requires a valid fixed-reference change-of-measure or another hard family; neither is supplied by the displayed pigeonhole step. This substantial invalid derivation supports Major. The abstract possibility of the same minimax rate, and the target-only lower-rate claim with a different proof, remain open within this inspection. No full repair is certified.
# 6. Core canonicalization defect and verified local repair

Price canonicalization in Appendix C Step 3.1, p.26, uses the unknown sign omega_i to choose a replacement core price. That displayed oracle-dependent argument does not establish one admissible policy for all alternatives. This is a Major defect in the printed core derivation: the reduction restricts all admissible policies to plateau prices, identifies regret with the semi-metric, and enables Proposition C.1(i) through Eq.(77) in the proof of Theorem 4.4. Its severity is assessed separately from the scoped correction. A precise local replacement is available for a fixed hard-family center: on an inner target box, write the mean at a slope price as 1/2+omega_i a s, with a=Cphi rtilde and s in [0,1]. Select the bump’s core price with probability s and a different baseline core price with probability 1-s.

The mixture reward is Bernoulli(1/2+omega_i a s) for both signs, exactly the original reward law. Feed the original requested price and resulting reward into a virtual history and let the original policy continue on that history, ignoring the rounding coin and actual replacement price. Outside the target boxes every price has baseline mean. By induction the virtual observations have the original law and expected regret is equal for every sign vector. This proves a universal randomized canonicalization for a fixed family with at least two price bins.

Repair status is deliberately narrow: this replaces the sign-dependent local reduction; it does not fix the later changing-center argument, exact-exponent membership or TLDP upper guarantee. The reviewer supplied the replacement; author adoption was not requested.

Other scoped points are retained without increasing severity. In Eq.(82), factoring an unconditional price-bin count from a context event needs care because the policy observes the current context; a direct joint-count bound may retain the rate with different constants, but the full lower proof was not repaired. In Lemma B.4, the interior-price mass bound is applied to arbitrary adaptive centers; a uniform example near the price boundary invalidates the displayed factor-two lower-mass step. A boundary-adjusted full probability proof was not established.

Source-dependent ball selection also calls for a uniform or predictable concentration argument beyond a fixed selected ball; no additional probability-level counterexample was completed. The main prose counts every historical point geometrically inside a ball whereas the pseudocode counts selected-ball updates. Problem 1 is independent of either convention. Conditional on a valid per-play gap and count estimate, the packing and target-dominated radius balances have the expected d+1-dimensional form. The Holder extension in Remark 4.2 is explicitly conjectural and was not misrepresented as a proven theorem.
# 7. Empirical and implementation evidence

The numerical study compares TLDP with target-only TLDP, ABE and ExUCB. The manuscript explicitly studies posterior drift in Scenario 3 as a robustness test outside the covariate-shift theorem; it is not a proof of that broader setting. Scenario 2 uses Gaussian reward noise, so those simulations do not literally satisfy bounded revenues, although they can still illustrate behavior. No empirical score deterioration was demonstrated or required to establish the theoretical findings.

Table 1’s reported means decrease with added source data: target-only TLDP is 71.95; full Mountain transfer is 50.23 and full Pacific transfer 48.72. Target-only TLDP is worse than the reported ABE and ExUCB means, which the text acknowledges. Static CSV counting confirms the overall 208085 applications and the five division counts used in the manuscript. The plotted/table comparisons were checked as reported summaries, not reproduced training runs.

The auto-loan evaluation fits a random-forest surrogate on target observations and numerically optimizes that model to define comparator prices. Thus its regret is model-based. The use of target data for this disclosed simulator is not by itself evidence of fraudulent leakage into a real deployment. Fresh policy evaluation or a validated counterfactual model would be needed to establish actual deployment revenue.

Release-only discrepancies remain bounded. In Scenario_2.1.R, released defaults use nQ=100, nP=200 and noise sigma=0.05 instead of the paper’s principal nQ=10000, nP=20000 and sigma=0.01 setting; one specified bump center also differs. This establishes configuration mismatch, not that those defaults generated the figures. The simulation-generation settings and outputs needed to resolve that provenance were not available in the inspected release.

The auto-loan release clips the random-forest-derived f/p to a probability in [0,1] when generating an acceptance outcome but computes regret against the unclipped surrogate. If the fitted surrogate exceeds p, those means differ. Whether that condition occurs materially in the actual reported runs was not established without fitting/executing the model. It remains Needs Evidence, with the static paths retained in empirical_code_audit.json. It is not used to elevate the theoretical severity.

Additional bounded release checks: the Scenario 2 price sampler uses a central interval of width 0.1 instead of the paper’s 0.25 and fixed mixture counts rather than i.i.d. component draws. At kappa=0.6 the central density is 4.6 instead of 2.2; at kappa=1 this distribution discrepancy disappears. Scenario_2.2’s sixth positional argument binds sigma=0.05 to ABE’s M parameter instead of the stated M=0.1, multiplying its threshold factor by four. These are release-only Minor discrepancies without demonstrated publication-score effects. Missing result CSVs and an unidentified posterior-drift run script leave experiment provenance unresolved.

The random-forest price oracle uses numerical optimization without a global certificate for a potentially non-unimodal piecewise-constant predictor. No actual missed optimum was demonstrated, so this remains Needs Evidence. The source density normalization and the stated concave-quadratic and separated-bump simulation oracles were independently checked and found consistent within their specified assumptions.
# 8. Overall dependence and conclusion

The upper counterexample directly defeats Algorithm 1’s stated source-rich guarantee. Problems 2 and 3 invalidate distinct steps of the supplied matching lower proof, while leaving the truth of a properly specified minimax rate unresolved. The printed canonicalization reduction is also a Major core proof defect; the fixed-family randomized replacement in Section 6 repairs that specific step. The covariate-shift formulation, practical value of source information, reported simulation comparisons and potential usefulness of contextual zooming survive these particular checks.

No later repair was found in the inspected materials. The earlier preprint and current pinned release preserve the first-price ordering. A repaired algorithm would need an exact specification and a new proof; a local additive startup allowance or source initialization change has not been verified to restore the full theorem. Empirical reproduction would be relevant to configuration and surrogate concerns, but cannot repair a uniform mathematical guarantee.

problems.title: Stationarity of the SAM surrogate does not imply vanishing directional curvature
problems.source_location: Section4, p4, paragraph immediately afterEq8; dependency on Eqs5-7 and subsequent smoothness/CR motivation.
claim: The paper states that solving problem(5) drives convergence to a stationary point, which consequently reduces curvature in the sense ||Hv||_2 ->0, with H the original forget-loss Hessian and v its normalized gradient.
analysis: Status: Analytic counterexamples to a stated implication, with exact symbolic and finite verification

Suspect step: At a stationary point of ell+rho||grad ell||, the correct first-order condition is g+rho H v=0 (plus any retain-loss gradient), not Hv=0. For Eq5 itself, the outer derivative includes the shifted gradient and the Jacobian of v; its vanishing likewise does not require the original directional curvature to vanish.
Correct local identities: For a twice differentiable scalar loss with g!=0, grad||g||_2=H v. This is Eq7 and is correct.
Correct local identities: For F(theta)=ell(theta+rho v(theta)), grad F=[I+rho Dv(theta)]^T grad ell(theta+rho v(theta)), with Dv=(I-vv^T)H/||g||.
Correct local identities: For GP(theta)=ell(theta)+rho||g||, grad GP=g+rho H v.
Correct local identities: These verified identities describe curvature involvement; they do not establish curvature annihilation or an empirical robustness guarantee.
Main counterexample. Rho: Any fixed positive rho; take0.01 for a concrete numerical instance.
Main counterexample. Retain: lambda=0,allowed inEq1; alternatively any lambda with a constant retain loss.

Main counterexample. Assumptions checked: The loss is a smooth polynomial onR, is coercive and globally nonnegative. Its critical points are -rho,rho/2,rho, with values5rho^2/12,215rho^2/192,13rho^2/12, respectively; global minimum5rho^2/12>0.
Main counterexample. Assumptions checked: The original gradient factors as (x-rho/2)(x-rho)(x+rho)/rho^2.

Main counterexample. Assumptions checked: On the open neighborhood(-rho,rho/2) of0, the original gradient is positive, so v=1 and the source's explicit nonzero-gradient assumption holds at and near the candidate solution.
Main counterexample. Assumptions checked: At x=0, g=rho/2!=0 and H=-1, hence ||Hv||=1.

Main counterexample. Assumptions checked: LocallyEq5 is exactly F(x)=ell(x+rho), since the linearized SAM direction v is constant. This treats Eq5 as the paper's approximate-SAM surrogate, not as an exact solution of its original inner max.

Main counterexample. Calculation: F'(0)=ell'(rho)=0 and F''(0)=ell''(rho)=1>0. Thus0 is a strict local minimum of the statedEq5 surrogate, while||Hv||=1. Gradient descent from sufficiently near0 converges toward this point with nonvanishing directional curvature.

Main counterexample. Finite check: At rho=.01,eta=.25 and x0=.001,80 reviewer-generated scalar iterations yield x≈7.45278e-14, g≈.00499999999993 and||Hv||≈1.00000000000745. The independent finite-difference formula at mu=1e-6 equals-1.00004999 and tends to H v=-1 asmu->0.

Main counterexample. Consequence: This directly falsifies the stationarity-implies-zero-curvature inference under its stated nonzero-gradient conditions, without using an undefined normalized gradient or a stationary maximum.
Alternative eq6 counterexample. Purpose: Addresses an interpretation that the paragraph intended the first-order GP objective(6), rather thanEq5.
Alternative eq6 counterexample. Definition: Let t=x/rho, h(t)=1+3t+(9/2)t^2+7t^3+100t^4, F(t)=(t-1)^2 h(t), and ell(x)=rho^2 F(x/rho).
Alternative eq6 counterexample. Positivity: h=(1+3t/2)^2+t^2(9/4+7t+100t^2)>0 because the quadratic has positive leading coefficient and discriminant-851. Henceell>=0.

Alternative eq6 counterexample. Checks: Atx0=0, g=rho>0,H=-1,v=1. Eq5 locallyell(x+rho) has derivative0 and second derivative231. Eq6 locallyell(x)+rho ell'(x) has derivative rho*(1-1)=0 and second derivative-1+6=5. Both are strict local minima, yet||Hv||=1.

Alternative eq6 counterexample. Limits: This is a generic smooth-loss counterexample to the mathematical implication. It is not a simulated LLM loss, not an NPO benchmark reproduction, and not a claim that a real unlearned model follows this trajectory.

Counterevidence and limits: Eq4 explicitly linearizes the inner maximization; its closed-form optimizer of the linearized problem is correct. The audit does not misrepresent it as an exact maximizer of arbitrary nonlinear losses.
Counterevidence and limits: Eq6 is explicitly a first-order Taylor approximation and Eq8 a finite-difference approximation. These local relations are retained.

Counterevidence and limits: The conditional min-max formulation requires a relearning objective counteracting the forget objective and a bounded weight-perturbation threat set; it can remain a useful robust surrogate.
Counterevidence and limits: AlgorithmA1 intentionally bypasses higher-order derivatives. In the scalar counterexample v is locally constant, so this bypass does not remove the counterexample.
Counterevidence and limits: The analysis does not demonstrate diminished empirical UE/UT, failure of all smoothing, or ineffective unlearning. Empirical score verification is separate.

Counterevidence and limits: Even a valid local directional-curvature reduction would not itself be a certificate against unrestricted fine-tuning or every attack; the paper's measured attack results remain empirical.

Dependency: The abstract/introduction list an optimization foundation and a curvature/smoothness explanation as principal contributions. The unsupported implication is the explicit mathematical bridge from SAM stationarity to curvature suppression and motivates the further CR/smoothing methods. It is therefore a substantial derivation closely tied to the core contribution, supportingMajor while allowing experiments and the broader qualitative hypothesis to survive.

Version status: The same claim afterEq8 is present in the observed preconference arXivv4 p4. This is persistence across the compared preconference and publisher versions, not a postpublication erratum.

Repair status: The derivative identities above are verified scoped replacements. No additional assumptions have been shown to restore the claimed||Hv||->0 guarantee; no full repair or author adoption is verified.

Complete check: Conditional-likelihood NPO depends on the log probability of the negative/forget response relative to the reference. A common shift of all vocabulary logits leaves all softmax probabilities and every response likelihood unchanged, so it must leave such an NPO loss unchanged. The released expression changes under that shift. It does not normalize logits or gather the forget labels for this term, although labels are supplied in the forward pass.
Counterexample. Proper likelihood ratio loss before and after: 13.862943611198906

Counterexample. Assumptions: Finite real logits, beta>0, the same reference and forget label in both cases; a common shift is an admissible logit representation of exactly the same categorical distribution.

Counterexample. Precise consequence: The released function is not invariant to an irrelevant logit offset and therefore is not the conditional-likelihood-ratio objective. This does not claim that a particular LLM training trajectory follows only the common-offset direction.

Counterevidence: Both baseline and SAM MUSE code use the same raw-logit objective. That does not make it NPO, but it prevents inferring the sign or magnitude of bias in the SAM comparison without new evidence. The WMDP NPO path instead uses model loss differences, so the MUSE raw-logit defect must not be generalized to WMDP.

Wmdp scope note: WMDP GA.py 118–132 and 148–156 use current/ref model aggregate cross-entropy loss differences before logsigmoid. This differs from an explicitly per-example sequence reduction. The paper does not give enough reduction details to label that alternative normalization a separate demonstrated defect here.
Publication result impact: Needs Evidence; released-source facts do not establish publication run linkage.

report:
ELVIA Scientific Verification Report
0100 / I25-43469
Towards LLM Unlearning Resilient to Relearning Attacks: A Sharpness-Aware Minimization Perspective and Beyond

Inspection outcome: Major. The implication from SAM stationarity to vanishing directional curvature is false under the stated smoothness and nonzero-gradient conditions. Complete counterexamples demonstrate a substantial invalid derivation tied to a principal contribution. The reported relative empirical improvements are not refuted.

Additional outcomes: Minor for a bounded rho-ablation interpretation and for concrete public-release defects; Needs Evidence for linkage to published runs and inconsistent settings/values. Scientific decisions and controller acceptance remain pending. Author adoption has not been requested.
Batch B001 / [internal task]; token [internal identifier omitted]. Review date: 24 October 2026. AI-assisted verification; no human-review approval is asserted.
# 1. Identity, versions and scope

Authors: Chongyu Fan, Jinghan Jia, Yihua Zhang, Anil Ramakrishna, Mingyi Hong and Sijia Liu. Exact source: PMLR 267 (ICML 2025), pp. 15762-15778, publisher-linked fan25e.pdf, 17 pages [R1]. Locations use one-based PDF pages, equal to printed article pages 1-17, rather than volume pagination.

The existing papers/0100/0100.pdf was identified and SHA-256 matched to verification/0100/controller_acquisition_receipt.json before analysis; its bytes were preserved. SHA-256: 77fc07b5fbaff3f32605be16547ac8e131441ada2a05c0e7bb04f8f866a34c29.

The latest arXiv version observed was 2502.05374v4, 27 May 2025 [R2], a preconference comparison rather than a postpublication correction. Its p. 4 retains the affected inference. The official repository was pinned at ea25a74b509b25ece06e65d59bbff01e6d2239da (27 September 2025); 40 selected source/configuration files were acquired preserving their directory tree and verified against Git blobs [R3]. Relevant expressions are unchanged from the first-code tree, a4ec8e730052b2014c8a5d4875b11ec18dcd374c (23 February 2025). Release history does not identify publication-generating code.

Checked: Eqs. (1)-(12), Algorithm A1, main results, appendices A-F, metric directions, table arithmetic, threat descriptions, selected training/evaluation paths and targeted version comparisons. Calculations are analytic, symbolic or finite reviewer checks. No author code was run/imported; no model, training, attack, paid API or empirical reproduction was used. Raw trials, checkpoints and publication-run mappings were not obtained. Coverage and exclusions are itemized in coverage.json and the specialist audits [R6].
# 2. Definitions and valid reasoning retained

Write ell for the forget loss, g for its gradient, H for its Hessian, and v=g/||g|| where g is nonzero, as explicitly assumed on p. 4. The robust formulation restricts weight perturbations to a norm ball, with default Euclidean radius rho>0, and relates relearning to an objective counteracting the forget objective. This is a conditional threat model, not an equivalence to every fine-tuning attack.

Equation (4) explicitly linearizes the inner maximization; rho*v correctly optimizes that linearized problem. Equation (6) is explicitly a first-order Taylor approximation. Equation (7), gradient of the gradient norm equals H*v, is correct for nonzero g. Equation (8) is a local finite-difference approximation. Equations (9)-(11) define coherent smoothing/regularization objectives under ordinary integrability/differentiability conditions. These valid steps survive.

Algorithm A1 perturbs the forget loss, computes its gradient at perturbed weights, and combines it with the retain gradient at original weights. The public SAM paths follow this ordering: WMDP base.py lines 764-775, restoration/retain backward at 834-849, combination at 853-864; MUSE sam_iterative.py lines 129-138 and helpers through 226. This positive static check assumes nonzero forget gradients, relevant gradient entries for trainable parameters and one accumulation step, explicitly configured in WMDP. General multi-microbatch accumulation, AMP and distributed equivalence were not certified [R3,R6].

WMDP UE is 1 minus benchmark accuracy, so higher is better; UT is MMLU accuracy. MUSE forget-set VerbMem and KnowMem are lower-is-better; retain-set KnowMem is higher-is-better. Relative resistance, utility, total information erasure and universal attack robustness are distinct claims.
# 3. Problem 1 - Stationarity does not force curvature to vanish

Source claim and location. Section 4, p. 4, immediately after Eq. (8), concludes from solving Eq. (5) toward stationarity that ||H*v|| tends to zero. This is the mathematical bridge from SAM optimization to curvature suppression and the subsequent CR/smoothing motivation, closely tied to a principal contribution [R1,R2].

Suspect step. A zero gradient of the full surrogate does not force one component to vanish. For the Eq. (6) surrogate G, stationarity permits cancellation between g and rho*H*v. For F in Eq. (5), the derivative contains the shifted gradient and the Jacobian of v. The correct identities appear below. Adding a retain gradient cannot justify dropping the other terms.

Complete counterexample. Fix any rho>0, for example 0.01, and take the scalar polynomial ell displayed below. Choose lambda=0, permitted by the nonnegative retain coefficient, or a constant retain loss with any lambda. The loss is smooth, coercive and globally nonnegative. Its only critical points are -rho, rho/2 and rho, with values 5*rho^2/12, 215*rho^2/192 and 13*rho^2/12, so its global minimum is positive.

The factored gradient is positive on (-rho,rho/2), hence v=1 near x=0. The source’s nonzero-gradient condition holds at and near the solution. At zero, g=rho/2, H=-1 and ||H*v||=1. Locally Eq. (5) is exactly F(x)=ell(x+rho). Thus F’(0)=ell’(rho)=0 and F”(0)=ell”(rho)=1>0: zero is a strict local minimum of the stated surrogate, but directional curvature does not vanish. No undefined normalization or stationary maximum is used.

Independent verification. With rho=0.01, step size 0.25 and x0=0.001, 80 reviewer scalar iterations yield x=7.45278e-14, g=0.00499999999993 and ||H*v||=1.00000000000745. At zero, the Eq. (8) finite difference with mu=1e-6 is -1.00004999, tending to -1. Exact symbolic checks and the complete replay script are preserved [R6].

Alternative readings and counterevidence. This tests Eq. (5) as the paper’s approximate-SAM surrogate; it does not claim its perturbation is an exact nonlinear inner maximizer. Algorithm A1’s deliberate omission of higher derivatives cannot remove the example because v is locally constant. Appendix A supplies a second smooth nonnegative loss with strict local minima for both Eq. (5) and Eq. (6), while ||H*v||=1, closing the alternative interpretation of the paragraph. These are generic mathematical witnesses, not simulated LLM losses or NPO training runs.

Impact and repair. Major: a core-connected inference is false even if the experiments and broader smoothing hypothesis survive. Valid local approximations and conditional robust optimization remain available. The derivative identities below are verified scoped replacements; no complete argument restoring the claimed zero-curvature conclusion has been verified.

\[g=\nabla\ell,\quad v=g/\|g\|_2,\quad Dv=(I-vv^\top)H/\|g\|_2.\] \[\begin{aligned}F(\theta)&=\ell(\theta+\rho v(\theta)),&
\nabla F&=(I+\rho Dv)^\top\nabla\ell(\theta+\rho v),\\
G(\theta)&=\ell(\theta)+\rho\|g\|_2,&
\nabla G&=g+\rho Hv.\end{aligned}\] \[\begin{aligned}\ell(x)&=\rho^2+\frac{x^4}{4\rho^2}-\frac{x^3}{6\rho}-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{\rho x}{2},\\
\ell'(x)&=\frac{(x-\rho/\allowbreak{}2)(x-\rho)(x+\rho)}{\rho^2}.\end{aligned}\]
# 4. Problem 2 - The large-radius ablation confuses forgetting with utility

Source claim. The rho-ablation discussion on p. 9 and Appendix E, p. 15, attributes rho=0.1 to ineffective forgetting. Table A3 instead shows identical pre-attack forget scores, substantial utility deterioration and mixed post-attack changes [R1,R6].

Complete check. Pre-attack forget VerbMem and KnowMem are both 0.00 at both radii. Increasing rho from 0.01 to 0.1 reduces retain KnowMem by 11.57 points; after attack, forget VerbMem improves by 5.42 while KnowMem worsens by 2.19. Directions follow the paper’s explicit UE/UT definitions.

Alternative reading and impact. If effectiveness informally means the joint forget/retain objective, the utility loss supports a worse tradeoff; the specific assertion about preventing forgetting does not follow. Minor: a bounded interpretation error, with no demonstrated failure of the selected rho=0.01 comparison. A verified replacement is: pre-attack forgetting is unchanged at displayed precision, retain utility falls substantially, and post-attack metrics show a mixed tradeoff. This repairs the description, without asserting new experimental results.
Table A3 metric | rho=0.01 | rho=0.1 | Change
Retain KnowMem (higher) | 35.48 | 23.91 | -11.57; worse
Pre-attack VerbMem / KnowMem (lower) | 0.00 / 0.00 | 0.00 / 0.00 | No displayed change
Post-attack VerbMem (lower) | 58.38 | 52.96 | -5.42; better
Post-attack KnowMem (lower) | 38.33 | 40.52 | +2.19; worse
# 5. Problem 3 - The public GP penalty is detached

Source claim and location. Equation (10), p. 5, defines a differentiable gradient-norm penalty. The public WMDP path is NPO_FT_GNR, WMDP/src/unlearn/GA.py lines 218-264, reachable through __init__.py lines 24-25 and the supplied GP command [R3].

Complete static check. Lines 255-257 request differentiable gradients with create_graph=True, but line 258 converts squared-gradient sums using .item(). The accumulated norm and its square root are Python scalar values. Adding that value at line 262 contributes zero parameter derivative. The official Tensor.item documentation confirms nondifferentiability [R5]. For the reviewer example ell(theta)=theta^2/2 at theta=1 and rho=0.01, the intended derivative of ell+rho*|ell’| is 1.01; a detached penalty leaves 1.0. No author or Torch training code was executed.

The command supplies gnr_rho=10, while this loss hardcodes 0.01. A changed logged loss is distinct from a changed optimization gradient. The expression is present in the first code release, so it is not only a recent edit.

Impact and counterevidence. Minor for the demonstrated release defect; published GP-result implications remain Needs Evidence because run-source linkage is missing. Objective identity would matter even if scores remained favorable after such linkage were established. Preserving a differentiable tensor norm and using the intended coefficient are necessary local requirements, but no complete repaired trainer or empirical restoration was verified.
# 6. Problem 4 - The supplied CR route has no dispatch branch

Source claim and location. Equation (11), p. 5, defines curvature regularization. WMDP/run_wmdp_unlearn.sh lines 38-48 selects NPO+FT+CR, but the complete dispatch function in WMDP/src/unlearn/__init__.py lines 5-28 has no branch for that name and falls through to ValueError. Importing its class does not make the command reach it [R3,R6].

Separately, the stored NPO_FT_CR class, GA.py lines 267-346, calls backward inside compute_loss at line 299 and detaches the gradient-difference norm with .item() at line 340, adding a scalar at 344. Adding dispatch alone would not validate the penalty or gradient accounting.

Impact and counterevidence. Minor for this public release path; published-result impact Needs Evidence. The unreachable command is counterevidence against asserting that this class certainly generated the reported CR measurements. Another execution path remains possible. No command was run, no training failure was reproduced, and no complete repair is claimed.
# 7. Problem 5 - The released MUSE objective is not likelihood-ratio NPO

Source claim and location. The paper identifies NPO as the MUSE baseline on pp. 3 and 7-8. The original NPO definition depends on the conditional probability of a forget response relative to a reference, Eq. (3) in Zhang et al. [R4]. The saved MUSE/baselines/baselines/iterative.py lines 155-157 and sam_iterative.py lines 256-258 instead apply logsigmoid to reference.logits-current.logits over the full tensor, without probability normalization or selecting the forget labels for that term [R3,R6].

Complete invariant check. Set beta=0.1, reference and initial current logits (1,-1), and subsequent current logits (-1,-3), a common shift of -2. All logits are finite, beta is positive, and the reference and forget label remain fixed. Both current softmax distributions equal (0.88079707798,0.11920292202), hence every response likelihood is unchanged. Proper likelihood-ratio NPO remains 13.8629436112; the released loss changes from 13.8629436112 to 11.9627773876. This establishes objective mismatch without assuming a real model follows a common-offset trajectory.

Counterevidence and impact. Both MUSE baseline and SAM use the expression, so a relative advantage can survive. WMDP uses cross-entropy loss differences and is outside this raw-logit counterexample; its reduction convention is a separate scope question. Minor for the released objective mismatch; actual published MUSE objective remains Needs Evidence. If the released expression generated the named NPO comparison, that identity failure would need assessment without requiring score deterioration. No run mapping or complete replacement with verified label shifting, masking, sequence reduction and beta convention was obtained.
\[L_{\rm NPO}=-\frac{2}{\beta}\mathbb E\log\sigma\!\left(-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\rm ref}(y\mid x)}\right),\qquad \beta>0.\]
# 8. Empirical checks and unresolved evidence

Reported arithmetic supports relative robustness in the tested settings. Every smoothing variant in Table 2 exceeds NPO in all displayed attack columns. SAM-minus-NPO UE gains are 0.13/0.11/0.08 at 20/40/60 samples and 0.13/0.23/0.22 at 1/2/3 epochs. Table A1 improves every displayed attacked entry for NPO, GradDiff and RMU with SAM. Table A2 reduces post-attack VerbMem/KnowMem by 5.10/2.84 points for News and 9.14/7.00 for Books. These verify published arithmetic, not independent experiments [R1,R6].

Tradeoffs survive alongside the gains. Table 2 UT is 0.42 for NPO+SAM versus 0.44 for NPO; SAM UE falls from 0.74 before attack to 0.45 after the 60-sample attack. Table 1 gives identical SAM/TAR UE (0.74 before, 0.70 after), but SAM UT=0.51 versus TAR=0.54. Reported runtimes yield approximately 647.12 times TAR/SAM and 1.98 times SAM/NPO; hardware-normalized timings were not reproduced. Favorable resistance and efficiency do not imply immunity or dominance on all metrics.

Figure 5’s p. 8 caption lists Books 200/300/400 and News 400/500/600 samples; neighboring prose says 75/100/125. Released commands use Books 50/75/100 steps and News 100/125/150 with batch size 4. With one process, no accumulation and full batches, processed-example counts match the caption; distinct-sample counts and publication settings remain unresolved. Figure 2a gives NPO+WA Relearn60 UE=0.42, while Table 2 gives 0.40. Both exceed NPO=0.37 and remain below SAM=0.45, preserving that ordering. Original run settings and aggregates are needed.

The Books SAM shell command uses retain coefficient 2.5, outside Appendix C’s stated [0.25,1.0] search range. WMDP shell overrides mean JSON defaults alone cannot identify final settings. These are provenance/configuration concerns, not demonstrated changes in published scores. Trial outputs, training-seed uncertainty and complete selected configurations remain unavailable.

The README’s enhanced-GCG command is parameterized by the chosen unlearned model and specifies optimization. This supports intended per-model attack adaptation and is counterevidence to a transferred-prefix-only accusation. Actual prefixes, seeds, external attack revision and logs were not verified. Two-dimensional loss landscapes and token-distribution changes are evidence in the displayed settings, not certificates of all-direction curvature suppression or total information erasure. No new attack requirement has been imposed.

Public issue #1 asked about MUSE GPU count and model availability. Collaborator a-F1 replied on 17 June 2025 that experiments used eight A6000 GPUs; it closed on 18 June. The all-states issue endpoint returned only this issue, and both comments were inspected [R7]. This is historical hardware clarification, not a correction of Problems 1 or 3-5. It does not specify data-parallel world size versus model sharding (the release uses device_map=’auto’), accumulation or run mapping; multiplying step-times-batch counts by eight is therefore not justified. Private/external correspondence was not assessed.

Other observations were not promoted to substantive findings: Eq. (12)’s averaging index and p. 6’s printed prediction-loss sign appear inconsistent with surrounding descriptions, but the evidence does not establish resulting numerical damage or explain the plots.
# 9. Dependence, version status and conclusions

The Major judgment rests on Problem 1 alone: a substantial invalid inference in the central SAM-to-curvature explanation. It does not depend on a quota, release discrepancies, difficulty of repair or empirical-score failure. Curvature involvement in differentiation is established; convergence to zero directional curvature is not. The theoretical claim and empirical observations have separate evidentiary status.

The observed preconference arXiv v4 retains the inference. Repository history preserves the release defects from its first code release; the public hardware clarification does not repair them or establish which source generated published scores. No complete theoretical/implementation repair or author adoption is verified. Determining actual GP/CR/NPO experimental implications requires original run-source/checkpoint records and, if corrected objectives change the evaluated method, fresh experiments.

# Appendix A. A witness also covering Eq. (6)

Let t=x/rho, h(t)=1+3t+(9/2)t^2+7t^3+100t^4, q(t)=(t-1)^2*h(t), and ell(x)=rho^2*q(x/rho). The identity h(t)=(1+3t/2)^2+t^2*(9/4+7t+100t^2) proves h>0: the quadratic has positive leading coefficient and discriminant -851. Thus ell is smooth and nonnegative.

Exact derivatives: q’(0)=1, q”(0)=-1, q”’(0)=6, q’(1)=0, q”(1)=231. At x=0, g=rho>0, H=-1 and v=1 nearby. The Eq. (5) surrogate ell(x+rho) has derivative zero and second derivative 231. The Eq. (6) surrogate ell(x)+rho*ell’(x) has derivative rho*(1-1)=0 and second derivative -1+6=5. Both have strict local minima while ||H*v||=1. Constant retain loss leaves the calculation unchanged. This closes the Eq. (6) reading without invoking a zero base gradient [R6].

Title: Technical Verification of SketchTune
# Identity, version, and review scope

This report concerns Tianyi Zhang, Junda Su, Aditya Desai, Oscar Wu, Zhaozhuo Xu, and Anshumali Shrivastava, Sketch to Adapt: Fine-Tunable Sketches for Efficient LLM Adaptation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 76088–76110 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assigned identifier is I25-43470 (0101). All page references below mean the 1-based PDF pages, which agree with the printed local page numbers 1–23, not the PMLR volume pagination.

The reviewed original has SHA-256 `af45d375c09415671dd3303ce020434eddf899aeab1a80bfa9fc86b8aff2720c`. The main argument and Appendices A–L were read at the level recorded in the coverage ledger. The strongest checks concern equations (3)–(6), Algorithm 1, Appendix B, and the assumptions of Appendix F. Tables and experiment descriptions were checked for interpretation and selected arithmetic, not reproduced. The acquired repository is a selective snapshot at commit `1cb21921a7b6a152b8034f1e49d1edbde7d2f03a`; its README and `tailor_utils.py` were inspected statically [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Author code was not executed.

The supplied manifest records that separate OpenReview material could not be determined because metadata access returned HTTP 403. The embedded appendices are present. Training data, model checkpoints, historical experiment logs, and the full compression implementation were not available for an end-to-end reproduction. No later revision or erratum was acquired and assessed; the findings attach to the specified published PDF, not automatically to every version.
# Definitions and checked dependencies

Equation reference: eq:objective, eq:centers. For a row \(w\in\mathbb R^{1\times c}\), the paper defines \(S\in\mathbb R^{c\times k}\), a one-hot reconstruction matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{k\times c}\), and \[z=wS,\qquad \widehat w=zM.\] With a positive definite Hessian \(H\), let \(q_i=(1/(H^{-1})_{ii})^s>0\), where the experimental choice is \(s=3\). Equation (4) minimizes \[
 J(z)=\sum_{i=1}^c q_i\bigl(\operatorname{RTN}(w_i,z)-w_i\bigr)^2 .\] For fixed nonempty clusters \(C_j=\{i:a_i=j\}\), their weighted least-squares centers are \[
 z_j^*=\frac{\sum_{i\in C_j}q_iw_i}{\sum_{i\in C_j}q_i}.\] The distinction between a scalar center \(z_j\) and the entries of a matrix \(S\) that subsequently multiplies \(w\) is essential.

The gradient in equation (6) is consistent with differentiation through a fixed \(M\). Likewise, the static forward/backward structure in `tailor_utils.py`, lines 13–36, reconstructs a weight matrix and sums weight gradients into shared parameters. This observation does not verify the CUDA kernels, their numerical accuracy, or the provenance of the initial quantization grids.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The printed sketch matrix does not implement weighted clustering).
## Source claim and suspect step

Equation reference: eq:printed. On PDF page 4, equation (5) specifies, for \(a_i=j\), \[
 S_{ij}=\frac{q_iw_i}{\sum_lq_l},\] and zero otherwise. The surrounding text says that weighted \(k\)-means produces the sketched parameters and that these parameters are obtained as \(wS\). Algorithm 1 repeats both the entry formula (line 3) and multiplication (line 13) on page 5. The same dimensions are stated in Table 5, page 14.

As printed, the multiplication introduces a second factor of \(w_i\): \[(wS)_j=\frac{\sum_{i\in C_j}q_iw_i^2}{\sum_lq_l}.\] This is not equation [eq:centers] (#eq:centers). Even interpreting the unqualified denominator as cluster-restricted leaves a weighted second moment instead of a center.
## An admissible, complete check

Take \(c=128\), \(k=4\), one group per row, \(s=3\), and \(X=I_{128}/\sqrt2\). Then \(H=2XX^\top=I_{128}\) is positive definite and all \(q_i=1\). Four codebook values correspond to the paper’s permitted INT2 setting. The row length is also compatible with the stated block size \(B=128\).

Let \(w\) consist of 32 copies each of \(1,2,3,4\), with \(C_j\) containing the copies of \(j\). Every cluster is nonempty, the centers \(z^*=(1,2,3,4)\) are a global minimizer of [eq:objective] (#eq:objective), and the minimum is zero because every weight equals a center.

Under the literal denominator \(\sum_{l=1}^{128}q_l=128\), equation [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) instead yields \[wS=(1/4,1,9/4,4).\] Keeping the original cluster assignments gives a squared error of \[32\{(1-1/4)^2+(2-1)^2+(3-9/4)^2+(4-4)^2\}=68.\] Allowing the round-to-nearest reassignment actually specified in [eq:objective] (#eq:objective) does not fix the discrepancy: \(1\) maps to \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\) map to \(9/4\), and \(4\) maps to \(4\). Thus \[J(wS)=32\{0+(1/4)^2+(3/4)^2+0\}=20>0.\] If the denominator is read charitably as \(\sum_{l\in C_j}q_l=32\), the resulting centers are \((1,4,9,16)\) and \(J(wS)=64>0\). The extra factor of \(w_i\) therefore causes failure under either interpretation.

The independent check in `independent_check.py` constructs this example, evaluates both interpretations, and checks the stated Hessian and cluster counts. Its actual output is preserved in `independent_check_execution.json`. These finite calculations instantiate the algebraic discrepancy; they are not model-training experiments.
## Alternative interpretations and counterevidence

The formula was checked in a rendering of the original PDF page 4, so the extra factor is not an extraction artifact. Treating \(S_{ij}\) as a precomputed contribution to a center, followed by summation of its column, could explain the numerator. It contradicts the explicit definition \(z=wS\) and Algorithm 1 line 13. Simply deleting \(w_i\) is insufficient if the denominator still includes all clusters.

The inspected repository loads precomputed quantization grids and codes and provides fine-tuning/inference operations. It does not demonstrate that the erroneous formula was used to generate those grids. Correct empirical results and an unreported correct preprocessing implementation can therefore coexist with this incorrect published algorithm.
## Impact and supported correction

This is Major under the supplied scientific contract: the failed derivation specifies the initial sketched parameters at the center of the claimed compression-and-adaptation method. The conclusion does not require a measured drop in downstream accuracy or failure of the whole research program.

Equation reference: eq:fixedS. For nonempty fixed clusters, the supported correction is \[
 S_{ij}=\frac{q_i}{\sum_{l\in C_j}q_l}\,\mathbf1_{\{i\in C_j\}}.\] Then direct multiplication gives [eq:centers] (#eq:centers). Differentiating \(\sum_{i\in C_j}q_i(z_j-w_i)^2\) gives \(2\sum_{i\in C_j}q_i(z_j-w_i)\); its zero is [eq:centers] (#eq:centers), and its second derivative is positive. This proves the fixed-assignment weighted least-squares statement. It does not certify global optimality of an arbitrary \(k\)-means run or the complete sequential Hessian-compensation algorithm. The correction passes the stated example; author adoption and historical implementation correspondence remain unknown.
Problem 2 (The update-projection formula has incompatible dimensions and a singular inverse).
## Source claim and complete analysis

Appendix B, page 14, equation (10), gives the purported optimal update approximation as \[\widehat\delta=M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top\delta .\] The paper declares \(M\) to be \(k\times c\) with \(k<c\). Consequently, \(M^\top M\) is \(c\times c\) and has rank at most \(k<c\); its ordinary inverse does not exist. The displayed left factor \(M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top\), even if an inverse were possible, would be \(k\times k\), whereas an update in the original row has \(c\) coordinates. A row-versus-column convention alone cannot remove both errors.

For the explicit nonempty assignment matrix with rows \((1,1,0,0)\) and \((0,0,1,1)\), \(M^\top M\) has rank 2 and \(MM^\top=2I_2\). A column update \(\delta=(1,3,2,6)^\top\) projects onto the reconstruction subspace as \((2,2,4,4)^\top\), with residual squared norm \(10\). The independent calculation records these values.

For the stated orientation, the valid column projection is \[\widehat\delta=M^\top(MM^\top)^{-1}M\delta,\] provided all clusters are nonempty. For a row update, it is \(\delta M^\top(MM^\top)^{-1}M\). The inverse is replaced by the Moore–Penrose inverse if empty clusters are permitted.
## Counterevidence and impact

The familiar formula in the paper would be valid if its \(M\) meant the transposed design matrix, rather than the explicitly defined reconstruction matrix. That is a plausible notation error, but it must be made explicit. Figure 1 is said to use this projection, yet no acquired computation trace establishes that the plotted values used the literal invalid expression.

This finding is Major: the undefined projection is the stated calculation behind Figure 1’s comparison of sketching with low-rank update approximation, which directly motivates the core adaptation method. The rank and dimension failure invalidates that supporting computation under its printed definitions. The transpose correction restores a valid projection identity, but no acquired trace binds it to the plotted curves. The figure’s numerical provenance therefore remains Needs Evidence; no changed benchmark or curve value is inferred.
# Other checked claims and interpretation boundaries

Appendix F introduces both balanced hashing and random sign factors \(g(i)\) in equation (17). Under independent mean-zero signs, the cross terms in the squared error vanish and the factor \((\alpha-1)/\alpha\) follows. That calculation is coherent for the signed random sketch. The algorithmic matrix in Section 2 is unsigned and learned; replacing it by the signed random model is an additional modeling assumption, not a verified property of the learned mapping. This review treats the result as a stylized comparison and does not claim to have falsified the power-law theorem with an example that violates its signed-hash assumptions.

The low-rank comparison must use rank \(n/(2\alpha)\) under a budget of \(n^2/\alpha\) factor entries, as equation (29) does. The appearances of \(n/(2k)\) elsewhere need a consistent notation convention. The present report does not infer an incorrect empirical conclusion solely from those index inconsistencies.

Appendix C’s example count is \(87{,}031{,}808\) trainable sketch parameters, which agrees with its stated arithmetic. Table 4’s 2-bit Llama-2-13B GSM8K difference is \(39.88-25.40=14.48\) percentage points. These arithmetic checks do not reproduce model accuracy. The aggregate counts in Appendix K give 60 ties out of 300 comparisons, hence a tie fraction of \(0.20\); the printed \(0.39/0.61\) values correspond approximately to decisive-outcome shares. The win advantage survives this labeling inconsistency, which is not used to increase the supported severity.

The selection protocol for hyperparameters, historical checkpoint identities behind Figure 1, the exact judge configuration, and GPU performance measurements were not independently reconstructed. Appendix L itself documents sensitivity to answer extraction, which is relevant counterevidence against interpreting all score differences as changes in reasoning ability.
# Overall impact and recorded state

The core compression specification requires correction before it is independently implementable as the stated weighted-clustering method. The separate projection expression also requires an orientation/inverse correction. Neither result demonstrates that the reported trained models or hardware results are invalid.

Title: Scientific Review of
Text-to-LoRA: Instant Transformer Adaption
# Identity, scope, and necessary background

The reviewed paper is Rujikorn Charakorn, Edoardo Cetin, Yujin Tang, and Robert T. Lange, Text-to-LoRA: Instant Transformer Adaption, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, identifier I25-43471 (0102) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which agree with the article’s printed page numbers.

T2L maps a task description, layer index, and module identity to low-rank adaptation factors. Its reconstruction objective learns from existing adapters, whereas its supervised fine-tuning objective learns through downstream language-model loss. For a rectangular weight matrix, write \[\Delta W=BA,\qquad A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d_{\rm in}},\quad
B\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm out}\times r}.\] Appendix F explicitly accommodates the unequal input and output dimensions used by grouped-query attention. Consequently the simplified equal-dimensional notation in the main exposition does not establish a dimension error.

The main text, pp. 1–10, Appendices A–I on pp. 13–17, the dataset/evaluation and description discussions on pp. 20–22, and the scaling and architecture material on pp. 28–30 were inspected. The long task lists and description examples on pp. 18–19 and 23–27 were not exhaustively checked; the active task list was independently counted in the pinned configuration instead. References were not independently audited. Static code inspection covers selected hypernetwork branches and two utility files; it is not execution or a complete repository audit. Exact coverage is recorded in `verification/0102/coverage.json`.
# Problem 1: the medium hypernetwork’s output projection is omitted from its FLOP count
Assessment: Major; invalid accounting of the core adaptation mechanism.
#### Claim and location.

Appendix I.1, PDF p. 17, states, for the M hypernetwork, the following expression (transcribed as an equation): \[C_{\rm printed}=2(1024)(64)+4(4)(128)(512)+128(4096)(8).\] It reports approximately \(0.000005\) TFLOPs per instance and adds this to text-embedding and base-model costs. Appendix I.2 then concludes a greater-than-fourfold saving over three-shot in-context learning. The rendered source page was inspected to exclude a text-extraction error.
#### Assumptions and decisive calculation.

Use the paper’s own multiply-plus-add convention of two FLOPs per dense-matrix coefficient. Appendix F and Listing 2 (p. 29) specify a final hidden width of 512; the M head outputs \(rd=8\cdot4096=32768\) values. There are 32 layers, two target module types, and separate A/B-conditioned evaluations. Thus 128 hidden vectors pass through such output heads. The pinned implementation corroborates this reading: `gen_lora` loops over target modules, and the shared-A/B branch of `_hypernet_forward` evaluates the head twice for each layer batch [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. For the narrower value projection, this branch truncates the output after evaluating the head.
Claim 1.  Under this stated architecture and operation convention, the dense output heads alone require \(4{,}294{,}967{,}296\) FLOPs.

Proof. A dense map from 512 features to 32768 outputs requires \(2\cdot512\cdot32768\) FLOPs per vector in this convention. Applying it to 128 vectors gives \[C_{\rm heads}=2\cdot128\cdot512\cdot(4096\cdot8)
=4{,}294{,}967{,}296.\] In contrast, direct integer evaluation gives \(C_{\rm printed}=5{,}373{,}952\). Therefore \(C_{\rm heads}/C_{\rm printed}=799.2195\ldots\). A complete network cannot cost less than its evaluated dense heads. This discrepancy does not depend on costs of activation functions or normalization. ◻
#### Independent correction and its limits.

For the published backbone, count the task projection once, mixer and first residual block for 64 layer/module vectors, and the subsequent A/B-dependent blocks for 128 vectors. The resulting dense-matrix count is \[\begin{aligned}
C_{\rm M}&=131{,}072+33{,}554{,}432+33{,}554{,}432\\
&\quad+83{,}886{,}080+4{,}294{,}967{,}296
=4{,}446{,}093{,}312.\nonumber\end{aligned}\] These terms correspond respectively to the task projection, mixer plus first residual block, second residual block, final hidden block, and output heads. The reviewer-written integer calculation and exact output are in `independent_check.py` and `check_results.json` within this paper’s verification directory.

This is a correction to the dense-GEMM approximation under the stated evaluation path, not a measured hardware latency. It excludes biases, nonlinearities, normalization, adapter application, decoding, training, and offline description generation. The paper itself explicitly restricts Appendix I to input tokens. A different caching policy changes per-instance amortization and must be stated separately.
#### Counterevidence and bounded impact.

The omitted heads account for approximately \(96.6\%\) of the corrected hypernetwork GEMM cost. Thus the error removes the dominant operation of the proposed adapter-generation mechanism, even though that mechanism’s cost is a small part of the whole-system total. The main text on p. 6 identifies efficiency as a principal advantage and invokes Appendix I to substantiate it. The invalid derivation of adaptation overhead is therefore tied directly to a core contribution and supports Major. The corrected \(>4\times\) comparison and the untested accuracy results remain explicit limits: neither the existence of an efficiency advantage nor the reported scores is refuted.
# Other checks and unresolved evidence
#### Reconstruction is explicitly a seen-task experiment.

The nine-task reconstruction results and Table 5’s description-alignment experiment are explicitly described as using adapters or training descriptions from those benchmark tasks (pp. 5 and 7). Their distinction from supervised-training generalization experiments is material. Treating those reconstruction scores as an undisclosed unseen-task experiment would misrepresent the paper.
#### Task exclusions and validation separation.

Static parsing of `hyper_lora_decontam_lol_tasks.yaml` at the acquired commit found 479 distinct active training task identifiers, ten commented exclusions, and no overlap with the eleven validation identifiers listed in Appendix J. This supports the stated count and identifier separation. It does not prove absence of semantic duplicates, pretraining contamination, or actual historical run compliance. The struck-through entries in Figure 9 are described as exclusions, so their appearance in extracted text is not itself evidence of inclusion.
#### Adapter geometry.

The factorization admits the invariance \((A,B)\mapsto(QA,BQ^{-1})\) for invertible \(Q\), making raw factor-space distances non-identifiable without a convention. Appendix K discusses the associated ambiguity and also compares full \(\Delta W\) matrices. Accordingly this review does not present gauge ambiguity as an unacknowledged counterexample to the whole analysis. The reported correlations and visual embeddings are descriptive evidence, not a universal impossibility theorem for reconstruction.
#### Description-source provenance: Needs Evidence.

Appendix L (pp. 21–22) constructs task descriptions from five question–answer examples per prompt, generating 200 candidates and using 128 for training. The prompt asks for general task descriptions rather than reproduction of particular answers. Appendix J notes that HumanEval has only a test split. The inspected material does not resolve, at sample-ID level, which split/examples generated every benchmark description, or what overlap those examples had with evaluated items. This is a provenance question for the interpretation of unseen-task performance, not demonstrated answer leakage. Resolving it requires the exact description-generation inputs, selected descriptions, sample IDs, and split policy. No claim of changed benchmark scores follows without that evidence.
# Overall impact and disposition

The proposed adapter-generation mechanism has a demonstrated Major cost-derivation defect: its dominant dense output projection was omitted from the claimed overhead. The greater-than-fourfold whole-system prefill comparison survives the displayed repair; the accuracy results were not reproduced. No author correction or adoption was verified, and later revisions were not investigated. The defect in the core efficiency argument does not establish that the practical efficiency advantage or benchmark results fail.

Title: Scientific Review of
STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
# Identity and inspected scope

Kefan Dong and Tengyu Ma, STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, identifier I25-43472 (0103), is reviewed in its acquired published version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. All page references are one-based PDF pages and agree with printed numbering.

STP alternates conjecture generation and proof generation, retaining verified proofs and conjectures with low but positive empirical success rates. The theoretical reweighting places mass on generated conjectures to match a distribution over currently unproved statements. A separate practical procedure limits repeatedly selected conjectures.

The main paper (pp. 1–9) and embedded Appendices A–B (pp. 13–23) were read. Particular attention was given to the data filters, transport calculation, training-versus-test metrics, verifier restrictions, and manually assessed dataset statements. The twenty audit statements were read, but only selected elementary cases were mathematically checked; no assertion of complete formal verification is made. The bibliography was not independently audited. Static source inspection covered the README, metric aggregation, embedding construction, the matching function, and the initial 260 lines of the Lean verifier wrapper. No author code, training, or Lean/Isabelle proof replay was executed.
# Problem 1: a zero mask does not exclude a conjecture for signed cosine costs
Assessment: Major; failure of the core reweighting mechanism.
#### Claim, assumptions, and location.

Appendix A.5, pp. 16–18, defines matching cost as negative cosine similarity. The discussion after the unconstrained solution says that the practical method limits overly large conjecture weights to avoid unstable weighted training. Algorithm 4, p. 18, line 6 selects the smallest values of \(d(x,y)M(x)\); lines 9–10 set \(M(x)=0\) when \(nP(x)>3\). The source page was rendered and inspected. No restriction to nonnegative cosine similarities is stated.
#### Complete admissible construction.

Let \(n=m=8\), with matching weight one for every target statement. In \(\mathbb R^2\), give conjecture \(j\) the unit embedding \[x_j=\left(-\frac{j}{10},\sqrt{1-\frac{j^2}{100}}\right),\quad 1\le j\le8,\] and give each of the eight target statement identifiers the unit embedding \(y_i=(1,0)\). The statements may be distinct while their embeddings agree; injectivity is not an assumption of the algorithm. All norms are one and all costs are finite, with \[d(x_j,y_i)=-\langle x_j,y_i\rangle=j/10.\] The weight increment \(n/m\) is exactly one.
Claim 1.  Algorithm 4 returns weights \((8,0,0,0,0,0,0,0)\) on this input, including four assignments to the first conjecture after its mask has become zero.

Proof. Initially the unique minimum cost is \(1/10\), so the first four targets are assigned to \(x_1\). The fourth assignment makes \(nP(x_1)=4>3\) and sets \(M(x_1)=0\). Thereafter its masked cost is zero, whereas all other masked costs remain at least \(2/10\). It is therefore the unique minimum at every remaining step. Its final weight is eight. ◻

This is failure of the masking mechanism, rather than merely a one-increment overshoot caused by the strict threshold. For arbitrary larger \(n=m\), replacing \(j/10\) by \(j/(n+1)\) yields the analogous concentration on one item.
#### Source correspondence and alternatives.

At the pinned commit, `RL/utils/RL_utils.py`, lines 607–638, normalizes embeddings and selects the largest values of `similarity * mask`. It sets the mask to zero once a weight is at least three. The reviewer independently translated this scalar rule; it has the same output on the construction, setting the mask after the third assignment instead of the fourth. The code uses total matching mass rather than \(m\) when target weights differ; that difference disappears in the weight-one example. The source was read, not executed.

If every unmasked candidate has positive cosine similarity, a zero mask ranks below those candidates. This is a valid favorable regime, but it is not a general property of normalized or mean-pooled embeddings. No sign statistics or training artifacts were acquired to determine whether the counterexample’s regime occurred historically. Therefore no benchmark reduction or training instability is claimed.
#### Repair and boundaries.

Use explicit exclusion, such as an infinite minimization cost for ineligible items, rather than multiplying a signed score by zero. If the intended maximum is three, eligibility must also be checked before the increment and sufficient feasible capacity must be ensured. For this example such a rule gives \((3,3,2,0,0,0,0,0)\), which was independently checked. This local repair does not prove that an ordered greedy algorithm solves a globally capacity-constrained transport problem. The paper’s unconstrained transport derivation is a different, valid calculation. Main-text p. 5 identifies reweighting as the mechanism that preserves conjecture diversity and prevents concentration, and Algorithm 2 invokes this practical reweighting routine. The admissible construction defeats that mechanism and can leave all matching mass on one conjecture, continuing to select it after it is marked ineligible. This is a Major defect in a core algorithmic component. Whether historical embeddings entered the failing sign regime remains unresolved; no empirical score reduction is inferred.
# Problem 2: a statement labeled correct in the manual audit is false over \(\mathbb N\)
Assessment: Minor; exact counterexample to an audit label.
#### Claim and location.

Appendix B.3, PDF p. 21, row 10 labels the following Lean statement as correct: \[a,b\in\mathbb N,\quad a\ne b,\quad a+b\mid a^2+b^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad ab+4\le\gcd(a,b)^4.\] The displayed formal statement has no positivity assumptions. The original row and its Yes label were visually inspected.
#### Counterexample and all hypotheses.

Take \(a=0\), \(b=1\), both admitted by Lean’s natural-number type. Then \(a\ne b\), and \(a+b=1\) divides \(a^2+b^2=1\). However \[ab+4=4,\qquad \gcd(0,1)^4=1,\] so the conclusion is false. This exact integer computation is independent of training behavior or a formal prover’s timeout.
#### Counterevidence, impact, and possible repair.

A positive-integer convention in an informal source would exclude this example, but the actual formal statement uses \(\mathbb N\) without \(a>0,b>0\). Adding those assumptions removes this counterexample; the full amended theorem was not proved here and is not certified as a repair. The immediate correction is to change this row’s formal-statement correctness label to No.

Section 4.2, p. 6, reports seven provable statements among the twenty sampled unproved statements. One of those seven is therefore incorrectly included; the reported count requires revision and the other labels require checking before a corrected total is asserted. This strengthens, rather than undermines, the qualitative observation that some benchmark statements are unprovable. It does not change the recorded fraction of statements actually proved by STP.
# Checks that limit the findings
#### Theoretical transport solution.
#### Metric and split distinctions.

The reported 28.5% on LeanWorkbook is explicitly a cumulative training pass rate, not held-out accuracy. The base model’s exposure to miniF2F-valid and ProofNet-valid is disclosed, including for the variant without those sets in subsequent STP training (p. 6, footnote 7). Table 1 explicitly warns that tree-search and whole-proof generation budgets are not fully comparable. These facts prevent treating the corresponding qualifications as hidden leakage or exact compute equivalence. The 2.9 and 2.1 percentage-point gains in Table 3 agree with the stated roughly 2–3 point ablation gain.
#### Verifier and sampling boundaries.

The inspected Lean wrapper distinguishes absence of errors from completion and additionally rejects reported sorries and relevant warnings. This is consistent with filtering completed proofs; it is not an independent kernel audit of historical outputs. The metric code aggregates unique successful statement identifiers across sampling rounds. Benchmark data, generated proofs, checkpoints, and run logs were excluded from or not supplied with the acquired source-only snapshot, so exact pass rates, their uncertainty estimates, and the historical verifier environment remain unverified. This is an evidence limitation, not a demonstrated invalid score.
# Disposition

The highest supported assessment is Major because the practical reweighting mechanism fails on admissible signed costs, directly compromising its stated role in preserving conjecture diversity. The separate manual-audit label remains Minor. Both should be corrected; historical training effects and the central held-out improvement were not reproduced. No prior correction or author adoption was verified.
