Title: Scientific Review of
ENAHPool: The Edge-Node Attention-based Hierarchical Pooling for Graph Neural Networks
# Paper identity, scope, and background

The reviewed paper is by Zhehan Zhao, Lu Bai, Lixin Cui, Ming Li, Ziyu Lyu, Lixiang Xu, Yue Wang, and Edwin R. Hancock, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 77310–77320, identifier I25-43473 (0104) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The acquired published PDF contains eleven pages and no embedded appendix. References below use one-based PDF page numbers, matching the printed numbers.

The scientific text on pp. 1–8, Eqs. (1)–(16), Tables 1–5, and accompanying figure explanations were read. Pages 5–7 were also visually inspected. Page 9’s acknowledgement/impact material was read; the bibliography was not independently audited. No repository or separate supplement was acquired according to the supplied manifest, so there is no code-to-formula correspondence or experimental replay.

At layer \(l\), a hard assignment \(S_H\) maps vertices to clusters. Node attention forms weighted cluster features. Edge attention constructs \[A^{(l+1)}=S_H^\top(E^{(l)}\odot A^{(l)})S_H.\] The first pooling layer intentionally omits edge attention (p. 5). The MD-MPNN then uses powers of \(A^{(l)}\), masked to retain vertex pairs at a specified shortest support distance. These numerical edge weights and ordinary unweighted path counts must be distinguished.
# Problem 1: path-count interpretation does not extend to weighted coarsened graphs
Assessment: Minor; incorrect literal interpretation, without a demonstrated operator failure.
#### Claim and location.

Section 3.3, p. 6, states that \((A^{(l)})^h(i,j)\) represents the number of \(h\)-step walk paths and that the nonzero strengths in \(T_h^{(l)}\), Eq. (15), reflect the number of shortest paths. This is correct for a binary adjacency matrix. The same architecture is expressly applied to weighted coarsened graphs, whose entries are sums or attention-weighted averages of connectivity strengths.
#### Admissible counterexample.

Consider three coarse vertices \(a,b,c\), with nonnegative symmetric adjacency \[A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&0&2\\1&2&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
S_H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] These integer weights are consistent with prior aggregation of one and two original edges. Every vertex is assigned to exactly one nonempty cluster, \(P=\{a,b\}\) and \(Q=\{c\}\). Set all attention logits to zero, achievable by a zero attention vector. There are two actual directed edges per ordered cluster pair, so each has weight \(1/2\) under the stated actual-edge normalization. Eq. (12) yields \[A_{\rm new}=\begin{pmatrix}0&3/2\\3/2&0\end{pmatrix}.\] At \(h=1\), the support graph has exactly one shortest path from \(P\) to \(Q\), but \(T_1(P,Q)=3/2\). A fractional value is not the number of ordinary paths, even under a parallel-edge counting interpretation. This example also avoids the normalization-domain ambiguity discussed below, since all pairs across \(P,Q\) are actual edges.
#### Correct calculation, alternatives, and impact.

For a weighted matrix the exact identity is \[(A^h)_{ij}=\sum_{v_0=i,\ v_h=j}\prod_{t=0}^{h-1}A_{v_t v_{t+1}},\] where the sum runs over length-\(h\) walks. At the shortest support distance, it is a sum of products along shortest paths. This gives the correct weighted-connectivity interpretation and reduces to ordinary counting when all participating weights are one. It can still provide a useful message-passing strength. Thus the witness refutes the literal count assertion on the paper’s weighted domain, not the usefulness or computability of its operator. Reading the prose as an informal weighted path-strength description supplies a natural clarification; no benchmark change is inferred. The rational calculation is preserved in `check_results.json`.
# Problem 2: edge attention is not generally \(O(N)\)
Assessment: Minor; local complexity undercount.
#### Claim and assumptions.

Section 3.4, p. 6, states that both node and edge attention have complexity \(O(N)\), because they are computed from node embeddings. Eqs. (9)–(11), however, define pairwise scores and normalization over edges between clusters, with an explicit \(N\times N\) coefficient matrix. No bounded-degree assumption is given; the method also constructs coarsened and multi-distance graphs.
#### Decisive scaling argument.

Fix feature widths and the maximum distance \(H\). A complete undirected graph on \(N\) vertices has \(N(N-1)/2\) edges. An explicit coefficient for every directed orientation has \(N(N-1)\) entries, requiring \(\Omega(N^2)\) work simply to write them. Even restricting attention to actual edges requires work proportional to \(|E|\), which is quadratic in this admissible family. Sharing node projections or writing the score as a sum of endpoint terms does not make explicit evaluation and storage of all pair coefficients linear.
#### Repair and bounded conclusion.

Separate the node projection cost from edge scoring and normalization. For fixed widths, actual-edge attention can be described as \(O(N+|E|)\); dense pair materialization is \(O(N^2)\). A linear bound needs a stated \(|E|=O(N)\) restriction or a different implicit algorithm with its own proof. The paper’s overall \(O(N^3)\) dense bound can still hold because matrix powers and pooling dominate the corrected quadratic term. This defect does not by itself invalidate the claimed total cubic order or any measured classification result. Neither runtime nor memory was benchmarked here.
# Verified structure and unresolved evidence
#### Shortest-distance mask: No Issue Found within scope.

Let \(A\ge0\), \(R_h(i,j)=\mathbf1[(A^h)_{ij}>0]\), and \[U_h=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\left(R_h-\sum_{t=0}^{h-1}R_t\right).\] If the support distance is \(h\), there is a length-\(h\) walk and none shorter, so \(U_h=1\). If the distance is smaller, at least one earlier indicator is one, forcing the clipped value to zero; if larger or infinite, \(R_h=0\). Thus Eq. (14) selects exactly distance \(h\), including \(h=0\) on the diagonal. Nonnegative weights are essential to this support argument and are consistent with the stated connectivity and softmax construction. The nearby prose’s description of \(R_h\) as reachability within \(h\) steps is imprecise, but it does not invalidate the actual mask. An independent enumeration of all 64 simple undirected graphs on four vertices, for \(h=0,\ldots,4\), agreed with breadth-first-search distances in all 5120 entry comparisons.
#### Edge-normalization domain: Needs Evidence for implementation.

The text before Eq. (10) says to normalize actual edges, and Figure 4 normalizes two present edges. The displayed denominator sums over every \(x\in p,y\in q\), without an adjacency restriction, while Eq. (9) scores every pair. With two present unit edges among four possible pairs and all logits zero, actual-edge normalization gives a coarsened strength of one; literal all-pair normalization gives \(1/2\). The prose, figure, and first-layer explanation provide strong evidence for the intended actual-edge interpretation. Consequently this is recorded as a formula-to-implementation ambiguity, not a second demonstrated failure of the edge-attention method. An explicit support mask or adjacency-qualified denominator would resolve the written specification; historical code is needed to determine what was used.
#### Experimental interpretation.

Table 2’s means support seven wins among eight listed datasets; COLLAB is the exception. Section 4.1 says standard deviation over ten runs, while Table 2’s caption says standard error. Section 4.3 similarly says standard deviation over five cross-validation runs, while Tables 4–5 say standard error. These statistics differ by a factor of \(\sqrt r\) for \(r\) independent run estimates under the usual convention; the relevant unit of replication is itself important for cross-validation. Without raw fold/run results, neither interpretation can be selected confidently and significance cannot be reconstructed. This is Needs Evidence, not proof of a false mean or test-set leakage.

The proposed use of a straight-through estimator for hard assignment is explicit (p. 4). Classification improvements and depth sensitivity support an empirical benefit, but do not independently isolate over-squashing as its causal mechanism. No formal guarantee of eliminating all over-squashing is verified or required by this review.
# Overall disposition

Both established findings are local. The weighted operator and shortest-distance support construction remain mathematically usable; the total cubic complexity can survive the correction. No author correction or adoption was checked.

Title: Scientific Review of
GCAL: Adapting Graph Models to Evolving Domain Shifts
# Identity and scope

The reviewed work is Ziyue Qiao, Qianyi Cai, Hao Dong, Jiawei Gu, Pengyang Wang, Meng Xiao, Xiao Luo, and Hui Xiong, GCAL: Adapting Graph Models to Evolving Domain Shifts, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 50113–50129, identifier I25-43474 (0105) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The seventeen-page published PDF and pinned ten-file repository were available. PDF page numbers below are one-based and match the printed numbers.

The main scientific text (pp. 1–9), proof in Appendix A (pp. 13–14), experimental setup and additional results (pp. 14–16), and related-work appendix (pp. 16–17) were read. The bibliography was not independently audited. The README, complete `GCAL.py`, `main.py`, and `validation.py` were statically inspected. Other source files, datasets, checkpoints, and historical run logs were not audited or executed. Source pp. 4 and 13–14 were additionally rendered and visually checked.

Write \(G\) for an original graph, \(Z\) for its latent representation, \(M=\widehat G\) for a generated memory graph, and \(Y\) for its discrete training signal. By the mutual-information chain rule, the objective inside Eq. (4) is \[J=I(M;Y)-\beta I(M;G,Z)+\beta I(M;Z\mid G)
 =I(M;Y)-\beta I(M;G).\] Graph features are real-valued: the generator uses Gaussian latent variables and a Gaussian feature prior (pp. 4–5). Continuous densities therefore cannot be treated as probability masses bounded by one.
# Problem 1: Theorem 3.1 drops a potentially negative conditional entropy
Assessment: Major; false core theoretical bound.
#### Claim and exact failed step.

Theorem 3.1, p. 4, Eq. (5), repeated as Theorem A.1, p. 13, claims the lower bound \[B=\mathbb E\log P_f(Y\mid M)
-\beta\mathbb E\operatorname{KL}\bigl(P_g(M\mid G,Z)\Vert Q(M)\bigr)
+\beta\mathbb E\log P_g(M\mid G,Z).\] Appendix A, Eq. (21), replaces \[I(M;Z\mid G)=\mathbb E\log P_g(M\mid G,Z)+h(M\mid G)\] by the first term alone. The first sentence on p. 14 explicitly justifies this by nonnegativity of the conditional entropy. That justification holds for discrete Shannon entropy. Conditional differential entropy of Gaussian node features may be negative.
#### Counterexample satisfying the stated probabilistic assumptions.

Let \(G\) be a fixed graph with one hundred vertices and fixed features; let the memory graph have one vertex, fixed empty edge structure, and a real feature \(M\). This also permits a smaller memory than the original. Set \(\beta=1\). Let \(Z,V\) be independent standard normals and define \[s=0.01,\qquad M=\frac{s}{\sqrt2}(Z+V).\] The memory is genuinely conditioned on the latent variable: \(M\mid G,Z\sim N(sZ/\sqrt2,s^2/2)\). Its marginal is \(N(0,s^2)\), and choose \(Q\) equal to this exact marginal, a valid variational approximation under the theorem. Let \(Y=0\) deterministically and use a binary classifier with \(P_f(0\mid M)=1/2\). The theorem does not require a nondegenerate label distribution or an optimal classifier.

All densities are nonsingular, and every entropy, mutual information, and KL term used below is finite. The source and label are constant, so \(J=0\). Moreover, \[\begin{aligned}
I(M;Z)&=\tfrac12\log2,\\
\mathbb E\operatorname{KL}(P_g(M\mid G,Z)\Vert Q)
 &=\tfrac12\log2,\\
\mathbb E\log P_g(M\mid G,Z)
 &=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi e\,s^2/2).\end{aligned}\] Consequently the stated lower bound evaluates to \[B=-\log2-\tfrac12\log(2\pi e\,s^2)
=2.493084472\ldots>0=J.\] This is a false final inequality, not merely a missing justification. Equation (4) also prints an outer maximization: if read literally as an optimum rather than a pointwise objective, the same example still refutes it, since fixed \(G\) and fixed \(Y\) make \(J=0\) for every generator. Its maximum remains zero.
#### The fixed standard-normal prior does not rescue the pointwise bound.
#### Dependencies, counterevidence, and severity.

The mutual-information chain rule and the KL upper bound in Eq. (20) are valid. A fully discrete model with finite entropies would also justify the disputed entropy drop, but the paper specifies continuous Gaussian features and does not discretize them or assume nonnegative conditional differential entropy. Quantization would define a different bound with its reference measure and resolution; it is not an implicit cure.

The abstract, contribution statement on p. 2, and Sections 3.2.3–3.2.5 explicitly use this lower bound to motivate three generator losses. In particular, the positive conditional log-density term is the proposed basis for the generation loss. The false bound removes that theoretical justification. This dependency warrants Major even if the practical heuristic, ablations, and empirical improvements remain useful. No reduction in reported AP or retention is established by these constructions.
#### What a valid repair would and would not restore.

For discrete \(Y\), \(\beta\ge0\), appropriate absolute continuity, and finite quantities, a valid looser bound is \[J\ge
\mathbb E\log P_f(Y\mid M)
-\beta\mathbb E\operatorname{KL}(P_g(M\mid G,Z)\Vert Q).\] Indeed \(I(M;Y)\ge\mathbb E\log P_f(Y\mid M)\); \(I(M;G)\le I(M;G,Z)\); and the expected KL is \(I(M;G,Z)+\operatorname{KL}(P_M\Vert Q)\). Alternatively retain the missing \(\beta h(M\mid G)\) in the original derivation. Both options change the theoretical objective or require an additional entropy calculation. They do not establish the paper’s original three-term bound or justify substituting the embedding discrepancy of Eq. (14) for a likelihood without further assumptions. No repaired algorithm or performance guarantee is certified.
# Problem 2: Eq. (7) samples the wrong Gaussian variance
Assessment: Minor; local formula error, with corrective source evidence.

The text on p. 4 defines \(\log\sigma\) as log standard deviation. Eq. (7) states a sample from \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) but writes \(\mu+\sigma^2\odot\varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,I)\). For one dimension, \(\mu=0,\sigma=2\), the stated law has variance four, whereas the displayed expression has variance sixteen. Every assumption is satisfied. The correct expression is \(\mu+\sigma\varepsilon\), or \(\mu+\exp(v/2)\varepsilon\) for log variance \(v\).

The released `VGAE.reparameter` function actually computes `exp(0.5*logvar)` and multiplies Gaussian noise by it, consistent with the corrected law. Renaming \(\sigma^2\) as the standard deviation would conflict with the printed distribution and explicit definition. This establishes a local mathematical specification error, not a demonstrated error in sampled training features. The variance identity and exact values are in the independent check output.
# Problem 3: the released edge sampler is categorical rather than independent Bernoulli
Assessment: Major; core graph-generation distribution mismatch in the pinned release.

Section 3.2.2, p. 4, describes an independent Bernoulli edge for each pair, with a per-edge continuous relaxation. In the pinned `GCAL.py`, `PGE.forward`, lines 30–68, instead applies `gumbel_softmax` to the \(K\times K\) matrix and retains entries exceeding \(0.8\). The PyTorch v2.2.1 source, matching the supplied dependency version, confirms the default last-axis normalization and one-hot hard branch [Retained latex: \cite{torch}]. The operation therefore normalizes across each row. Thus if \(p_j\) are a row’s relaxed entries, \[p_j\ge0,\quad\sum_jp_j=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\#\{j:p_j>0.8\}\le1.\] The hard branch likewise chooses one category per row. In contrast, two independent Bernoulli edges of probability \(1/2\) are simultaneously present with probability \(1/4\). The distributions are therefore different, even before comparing training results. No author function was run; the conclusion follows from row normalization and the inspected threshold.

The file contains a later two-category-per-edge sampling block, but it follows an unconditional return and is unreachable in this function. That block is counterevidence about possible intended design, not proof that the earlier executed branch implements it. A repair would apply a binary relaxation independently to each edge with the appropriate probability/logit convention and validate the resulting graph distribution. This was not implemented or tested.

The affected sampler is on the active memory-generation path: `VGAE.decoder` calls it at lines 148–152, and memory replay calls the same generator at lines 165–167. Its synthetic adjacency enters the generation losses at lines 253–269, while the edge regularizer uses a Bernoulli model at lines 157–158. The support restriction therefore changes the graph distributions available to a central component, rather than an unused helper. This demonstrated core method mismatch supports Major for the pinned implementation. Without historical code identity and logs, no assertion is made that the reported tables used this branch or would lose accuracy.
# Additional scope and empirical boundaries

The AP and AF definitions on p. 6 were checked; AF uses final-minus-initial performance and is therefore oriented upward as shown. Table 2’s reported GCAL means exceed the listed baselines on the four datasets, and Table 3 supports improvements in the reported ablations. These are checks of the displayed results, not independent reproductions.

Several source-correspondence questions require evidence. The release passes `argmax` labels into Twitch’s `roc_auc_score`, so that path computes AUC from binary decisions rather than continuous prediction scores. A simple ranking example gives score AUC one but hard-decision AUC one-half; this does not identify which path produced the paper’s table. The release also includes the source-domain test column in its aggregate performance matrix, while the formal setup describes a target-domain sequence. The exact domain list and aggregation used historically should be supplied.

Furthermore, Eq. (14) uses a norm of sums of embeddings, whereas the released `MMD_loss` compares means by mean squared error. The paper says that a new generator is used at each step and memory graphs are retained (p. 6); the inspected class instead retains latent parameter pairs and reuses its generator to reconstruct replay edges. These are version-bound observations, not assertions that historical results used the current implementation. Resolving their empirical importance requires the experiment commit, configuration, per-domain predictions, and saved memories.
# Disposition

The overall assessment is Major. Problem 1 refutes the core theoretical lower bound, and Problem 3 demonstrates a different graph distribution on the pinned release’s central memory-generation and replay path. Problem 2 remains Minor because the released Gaussian sampler implements the corrected law. Historical experimental effects remain unresolved.

The public repository [Retained latex: \cite{code}] was inspected statically at commit `1c0e151007f5e08a9bf88efe5b94ee7151c4a926`. The inspected files are the README, `FedHBN_main.py`, and the three files `MyBNtool.py`, `clients.py`, and `server.py` under `FedBaseline/models/FedHBN/`. No author code was imported or executed. No training, raw-run reconstruction, or independent benchmark reproduction was performed. No separate OpenReview supplement was acquired; its availability was unresolved in the supplied acquisition record. The original PDF does contain Appendices A–B despite the manifest’s negative appendix detector flag.

The core dependency is the sequence: collect raw local moments under a common feature map, pool those moments by Equation (8), and use the resulting global statistics in Equation (9). The adaptive convex combination in Equation (9) is an operational normalization rule; it need not equal the variance of a probabilistic mixture to be well-defined.
# Numbered findings

Problem 1 (Major: the released collection step supplies the wrong moments).  The abstract, contribution 1 on page 2, Section 3.2 on pages 4–5, and Appendix A.2 claim recovery of the previous global model’s statistics. Equation (15) requires \[\mu_k=N_k^{-1}\sum_i f(\omega,x_{ki}),\qquad
 v_k=N_k^{-1}\sum_i(f(\omega,x_{ki})-\mu_k)^2 .\] However, `HybridBatchNorm.forward` first computes raw `curr_mean` and `curr_var`, then forms hybrid `mean` and `var`, and adds those hybrid quantities to the collection buffers. These are not the required raw moments.

Specifically, writing \(a=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\alpha)\), the collected quantities in the first batch after clearing are \[m_k=(1-a)\mu_{\rm old}+a\mu_{b,k},\qquad
 u_k=(1-a)v_{\rm old}+av_{b,k}.\] In `Client.buffer_update`, the network is in training mode, the buffers are cleared, and the forward call enters this branch. The main driver calls this function before local SGD, then passes its outputs to `Sever.aggregate_only_buffer`. The server applies the pooled formula to \(m_k,u_k\), not to \(\mu_{b,k},v_{b,k}\).
#### Decisive admissible check.
#### Impact and counterevidence.

The release does perform a separate collection pass before SGD, and its server includes the correct between-client term. These are positive design elements. They do not repair incorrect inputs to the pooled identity. The finding materially contradicts the exact-statistics component of the method as publicly implemented, and its use during evaluation makes it more than an unused helper defect. The historical code used for Tables 1–8 is not established; this review does not infer lost accuracy or fabricated results.

The collection function additionally stops after the first unshuffled batch of at most 64 examples. Section 5 discusses random subsampling of 128 images, while Equation (7) uses the whole local dataset. The server weights by the collected counts rather than the supplied full-client weights. Those differences require a precise sampling/estimand specification. They are unnecessary for the counterexample above, which uses every example.
#### Repair and verification boundary.

Collect raw input counts, sums, and sums of squares before hybrid normalization, or use a mathematically correct merge of raw batch moments. The merge must include both old-mean and new-mean displacement terms. Choose and document the feature map used during collection at every layer, since client-specific normalization in earlier layers can otherwise make deeper features differ even at fixed shared weights. Establish the connection to the historical experiments and reevaluate affected statistics. None of those implementation or empirical repairs was performed here.

Problem 2 (Minor: an absolute-value equality overstates the motivation).  Appendix A.1, Equation (14), page 13, replaces the absolute value of a sum of feature differences by the sum of their absolute values using an equality sign. Only a triangle inequality holds in general. The following prose asserts that greater data-distribution differences imply greater statistical offset; the calculation does not establish that assertion.

For an explicit one-step model consistent with the setup, take \(f(w,x)=w\), equal client sizes, \(w_0=0\), learning rate 1, and losses \[L_1(w)=\tfrac12(w-1)^2,\qquad L_2(w)=\tfrac12(w+1)^2.\] The local weights are \(1,-1\), their global average is 0, and the aggregated local feature mean equals the global feature mean. Thus the left side in the disputed step is 0, while the average absolute discrepancy is 1. Scaling the targets to \(\pm c\) increases the local discrepancy without changing the mean offset. Heterogeneity can cause a mismatch, but cancellation prevents the claimed universal conclusion. Replace the equality by an upper bound and qualify the prose. This repairs a supporting motivation argument; it does not refute the valid pooled-moment identity.

For clarity, that identity follows directly by writing \(z_{ki}-\bar z=(z_{ki}-\bar z_k)+(\bar z_k-\bar z)\), summing the square, and using \(\sum_i(z_{ki}-\bar z_k)=0\): \[\sum_{k,i}(z_{ki}-\bar z)^2
 =\sum_kN_k\{v_k+(\bar z_k-\bar z)^2\}.\] An independent unequal-group example verifies it numerically. In the rendered Equation (16), the between-client term \(N_k(\bar z_k-\bar z)^2\) is outside the inner sum over \(i\), inside the brackets of the outer sum over \(k\). It is not multiplied by \(N_k\) a second time. The first displayed variance line places an indexed \(N_k\) before the sum over \(k\); placing it inside that sum resolves this local notation issue, and the subsequent grouped expansion gives the valid pooled identity above. Exact equality to the finite-data sample statistic should be distinguished from unbiasedness for a superpopulation, which additionally requires a specified sampling model.

Problem 3 (Minor: one cross-batch superiority claim contradicts Table 2).  Page 8 states that HBN with batch size 2 exceeds BN with batch size 32. At \(\phi=0.6\), Table 2 gives 48.86 for HBN at \(B=2\), versus 49.63 for BN at \(B=32\): a deficit of 0.77 percentage points. The statement does hold in the displayed \(\phi=0.3\) column.

Restrict that sentence to the supported condition. The neighboring claimed drops, \(51.05-48.86=2.19\) and \(49.63-43.89=5.74\), are correct, and HBN is higher than BN and GN at matched batch sizes in the table. The local error does not erase the reported overall pattern.
# Coverage, counterevidence, and remaining evidence

Equations (1)–(11), Algorithm 1, both appendix derivations, Tables 1–8, and the experimental descriptions were examined. The primary empirical comparisons support the reported ordering of HBN in the displayed settings. No general convergence or universal accuracy theorem is asserted or certified by this review. The displayed learning-rate searches disclose method-specific tuning; different rates alone are not a fairness defect.

Needs Evidence: provide the actual historical source revision, seeds, per-run results, validation/test selection protocol, and collection settings. Table 3’s \(K=100\) FixBN value is 75.65, whereas Table 1’s corresponding stated setting gives 77.34; Table 8 contains both values at different learning rates. This suggests a configuration explanation but does not establish one. The main driver tracks best test accuracy, so the reported checkpoint/grid selection protocol requires clarification. The code uses a training buffer momentum of 0.002, while Section 4.1 specifies 0.01. The hybrid sigmoid coefficient uses the opposite sign convention from Equation (9); with an unconstrained learnable parameter initialized at zero this is a reparameterization, not an independent functional defect.

The page 7 discussion acknowledges evaluation recalibration and Section 3.4 describes the use of moving averages under stragglers. Consequently the paper does not claim exact current-global statistics under arbitrary partial participation, and this review does not impose that claim. Likewise, Figure 2 illustrates behavior; it is not a theorem guaranteeing preservation of every geometry.
# Overall impact and review state

The central statistical collection claim fails for the pinned release even under a particularly favorable complete-data case. This supports a Major initial assessment with a precise implementation boundary. The pooled mathematical identity and adaptive normalization idea remain viable. Repair difficulty and benchmark-score loss are not prerequisites for the Major assessment, but neither is assumed.

report: Abstract: The Bradley–Terry training objective is internally consistent. Three defects are demonstrated: a reversed inequality in the published algorithm, undefined hard-negative selection at admissible boundaries, and two incorrect aggregate entries in a results table. The broader human-preference and false-negative interpretations need additional evidence. The assessment is Major for a failure of the pinned release’s core hard-negative selection routine on admissible inputs, including cases with sufficient candidates and valid separated endpoints. Title: Initial scientific review of
QuRe: Query-Relevant Retrieval through Hard Negative Sampling in Composed Image Retrieval
# Identity and inspected scope

This is paper 0107, I25-43476, by Jaehyun Kwak, Ramahdani Muhammad Izaaz Inhar, Se-Young Yun, and Sung-Ju Lee [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied 15-page published PDF, including Appendices A–C, was read. The algorithm on page 11 and survey material on pages 13–15 were visually inspected. Page references are 1-based PDF pages.

Static source inspection used the supplied public tree [Retained latex: \cite{code}], commit `6a50a27c307e151b95533d05ffdfa126fbe5550a`. The inspected scope covers the README, training driver, HP-FashionIQ documentation and evaluator, FashionIQ data file, CIRR selection portion, FashionIQ training configuration, and BLIP-2 construction/forward portion. Most of the 1,239-file acquired tree was not reviewed. No author code was run. The HP-FashionIQ annotation JSON, images, checkpoints, and historical per-query scores were excluded from source acquisition and were not available for reanalysis. No separate supplement was acquired; the original includes its appendices.

The method learns a query-conditioned relevance score, ranks a corpus, selects a region between two large score drops below the target, and trains a pairwise preference loss. Its substantive dependencies are the semantic quality of that selected region and the validity of the evaluation used to support human alignment.
# Numbered findings

Problem 1 (Minor: Algorithm 1 reverses the target-score condition).  Appendix A, Algorithm 1, line 6, page 11, requires \(s(x_I,x_T,y_I)<s(x_I,x_T,I)\). Equation (7), page 4, instead requires the candidate score to be strictly below the target score. The directions contradict each other.

Take the descending scores \(10,9,8,4,3,0\), with target score 10. Among consecutive scores strictly below the target, the two largest drops are \(8-4=4\) and \(3-0=3\). Equation (7) selects the scores \(4,3\). Applying Algorithm 1’s displayed inequality to that same region eliminates both candidates, leaving an empty set from which line 9 cannot sample.

The surrounding prose, Equation (7), and both inspected dataset implementations start after the target rank. They consistently support the intended lower-score rule. This counterevidence limits the finding to a pseudocode error, rather than demonstrating reversal in the historical training objective. Correct line 6 to \(s(I)<s(y_I)\), with the query arguments understood. No change in reported performance is inferred.

Problem 2 (Major: the core selector can fail despite available endpoints).  Equations (5)–(7), page 4, require two adjacent-score drops strictly below the target. No assumption guarantees enough below-target candidates, and no fallback is stated. For scores \(3,2,1\) with target score 1, the eligible subset is empty and the top-two operation is undefined.

The pinned implementation introduces an additional separation condition. In `data/fashionIQ.py`, `FashionIQDataset.rerank_score`, and the corresponding CIRR method, it searches for two drop indices whose separation exceeds `consecutive_threshold`; the FashionIQ configuration sets that threshold to 1. For a target score 10 and below-target scores \(9,7,1\), the only drop indices are 0 and 1, so no pair is accepted. The endpoint variables are assigned only inside the successful branch, but used afterward. On the first query this leaves them undefined; later queries can retain preceding values. This conclusion follows from static control flow, not from executing the release.

The failure is not limited to tails too short to supply a valid pair. Take target score \(0.95\) and below-target scores \[(0.9,\,0.8,\,0.6,\,0.3,\,-0.1).\] These strictly ordered scores lie in \([-1,1]\) and are realizable as dot products between a unit query \(e_1\) and unit candidates \((s,\sqrt{1-s^2})\). Their successive differences are \((-0.1,-0.2,-0.3,-0.4)\), with ascending sort indices \((3,2,1,0)\). Lines 231–244 compare only adjacent entries of this sorted index list: \((3,2),(2,1),(1,0)\). Each pair has separation one, so the strict \(>1\) condition always fails. Yet original drop indices 0 and 3 form a valid separated pair. Line 248 then uses endpoints that were never assigned for this query. This exact scalar construction is recorded in `check_results.json`; no author function was executed.

Arbitrarily long tails have the same behavior: choose \(s_j=b-\delta j(j+1)/2\) with sufficiently small \(\delta>0\). The scores remain within the valid interval while drop magnitudes increase strictly, so neighboring sorted drop indices remain one apart. Corpus size alone therefore does not supply a completeness guarantee.

The training driver calls this selector at `train_qure.py`, lines 37–40, when configured reranking is active. Query-specific hard-negative selection is a core contribution, and the released search can fail to complete that update or reuse another query’s endpoints despite admissible available choices. This supports Major for the pinned implementation. The pairwise loss identity remains valid; historical occurrence, experiment commit and score effects remain unknown. Define a complete endpoint search or explicit fallback, reset per-query state, and specify short-tail and tie policies. No implementation repair or empirical rerun is certified.

Problem 3 (Minor: two Table 3 aggregate entries do not match their components).  Table 3, page 6, labels the final column as the average of \(R@5\) and \(R_{\rm subset}@1\). The CosMo row gives 23.11 and 20.29, whose average is 21.70, but prints 43.55. The MGUR row gives 21.45 and 20.29, whose average is 20.87, but prints 42.91.

The QuRe aggregate is correctly \((82.53+78.51)/2=80.52\), and the stronger comparison rows are consistent up to displayed rounding. Reconcile the two erroneous rows with the underlying runs. If the component entries are correct, the corrected aggregates above follow; if the aggregate entries are correct, their components require correction. QuRe’s displayed ordering over those two methods survives either simple aggregate correction. This review does not infer the true historical component scores.
# Needs Evidence: interpretation of human alignment

Section 5.3, Equation (9), page 6, evaluates \[r=P(Y=1\mid \Delta s>0),\qquad
 \Delta s=s_{\rm rel}({\rm Set}\ 1)-s_{\rm rel}({\rm Set}\ 2),\] where \(Y=1\) denotes human preference for Set 1. The pinned `evaluate_preference_ratio` implements exactly that condition, counting only pairs with score 1 greater than score 2. This is not a coding disagreement. It is a restriction on what the statistic measures.

For a fixed evaluated set, the conditional statistic need not rank models in the same order as all-pair preference accuracy. Here is a deterministic example with no score ties: \[\begin{array}{c|cccc|cc}
 &1&2&3&4&r&\text{all-pair accuracy}\\ \hline
 \text{human preferred set}&1&1&1&2&--&--\\
 \text{model A preferred set}&1&2&2&2&1&1/2\\
 \text{model B preferred set}&1&1&1&1&3/4&3/4
\end{array}\] Moreover, swapping the labels of both sets throughout changes A’s conditional rate from 1 to \(1/3\), while leaving every substantive decision and its accuracy unchanged. This establishes a finite-sample identification boundary; it does not establish that QuRe’s actual model ranking is reversed.

There is relevant counterevidence. The paper randomly selects two generating baseline models per question. If set orientation is independently randomized and exchangeable, the population conditional rate can equal overall accuracy. The inspected description does not establish the orientation protocol or provide denominators and paired outcomes needed to assess that condition and its finite-sample precision. Request the conditional denominators, tie handling, both directional rates, all-pair accuracy, and uncertainty accounting for participant grouping. Table 4’s 74.55 versus 74.45 is a 0.10 percentage-point point-estimate difference; it alone establishes neither statistical separation nor a reversed ordering.

A second scope limitation is explicit in Section 4: the annotated sets come from CLIP4CIR, Bi-BLIP4CIR, CoVR-BLIP, and SPRC. QuRe’s own retrieval sets were not among the survey candidates. Thus Table 4 tests QuRe as a scorer of fixed baseline-produced sets. It does not directly measure whether users prefer QuRe’s retrieved sets. A direct, blinded comparison of those outputs would support that stronger claim. The CIRCO results with multiple relevant ground truths provide independent positive retrieval evidence and must not be discarded because of this survey limitation.
# Other checks and counterevidence

The data totals reconcile: \(61\cdot50=3050\), and \(3050-307-28=2715\). Appendix C states no overlap between participants’ queries. The survey asks about sets as wholes and says within-set image order does not matter, consistent with an average set score. Single-query annotations do not supply inter-rater agreement; none is certified here.

Appendix B includes comparisons with consistent BLIP and BLIP-2 backbones, so unequal backbone capacity is not left wholly unaddressed. Tables 2, 5–8 and the ablation descriptions support positive results in the displayed conditions; independent experimental replication and complete baseline provenance remain outside the evidence available.

Needs Evidence for the sampling mechanism. Model score drops alone do not logically ensure a semantic attribute mismatch or absence of false negatives. Figures 6–8 and the ablations are supporting examples, not an exhaustive semantic guarantee. Quantify false-negative rates against relevance annotations and report sensitivity to selection details. In the release, FashionIQ mining uses the list of training targets, potentially with duplicates, rather than every corpus image; it adds the separation condition and negative-selection history. Those details differ from the simplest whole-corpus, uniform-per-epoch description. Their effect and historical use need configuration-bound evidence. There is no demonstrated contamination or historical semantic failure in this review.
# Overall assessment and separate states

Problem 2 establishes a Major failure of the released core sampling routine on admissible, nonempty candidate sets. The separate reversed pseudocode inequality and inconsistent table entries are Minor. The pairwise loss identity is valid, and the preference interpretation and historical experimental effects remain unresolved.

Title: Initial scientific review of
On the Tension between Byzantine Robustness and No-Attack Accuracy in Distributed Learning
# Identity, scope, and mathematical setting

Paper 0108, I25-43477, by Yi-Rui Yang, Chang-Wei Shi, and Wu-Jun Li, is the supplied ICML 2025/PMLR publication [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], 22 pages. Main text and Appendix A.1–A.7 were read. Page references below are 1-based PDF pages, identical to printed article pages. The critical expressions on pages 4, 6, 20, and 21 were additionally checked against page images.

The supplied manifest identifies no acquired author repository, and separate OpenReview supplement availability is unresolved. The appendix is present in the original PDF. No author code, raw experiment outputs, or later author correction was inspected. The review is an exact mathematical/static assessment with independent scalar diagnostics, not a reproduction of the ResNet experiments.

An \((f,\kappa)\)-robust aggregator must satisfy its error inequality for every subset of \(n-f\) inputs. An \(\epsilon\)-accurate aggregator bounds squared distance to the all-worker mean by \(\epsilon\) times all-worker variance. Here \(f\) is a tolerated number of Byzantine workers; all examples in this review have no actual Byzantine workers. The convergence assumptions are a lower-bounded \(L\)-smooth global objective, globally bounded gradient heterogeneity \(G^2\), and, for the PL conclusions, the stated PL inequality. Theorem 4.5 uses a constant positive step size and an arbitrarily-late-existence quantifier for \(T\), rather than a lower bound at every finite \(T\).
# Numbered findings

Equation reference: eq:bad. Problem 1 (Major: Theorem 4.6 has a false finite-time upper bound).  On page 6, the first display in Theorem 4.6 asserts, for step size \(1/L\), \[
 \frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\|\nabla F(w_t)\|^2
 \leq \frac{2L[F^*-F(w_T)]}{T}+\epsilon G^2 .\] The initial objective value has been replaced by a lower bound in the wrong position. The printed nonpositive transient term is not a valid upper bound.
#### Counterexample and every operative assumption.

Set \(n=3\), \(f=1\), \(d=1\), and use the scalar median. For any selected pair of inputs, their median with the third input lies between the pair’s endpoints; its squared deviation from that pair’s mean is at most the pair variance. Thus the aggregator is \((1,1)\)-robust. It is also \(1/2\)-accurate, as follows from the checked trimmed-mean bound with \(n=3,f=1\).

Choose \[F_1(w)=	frac12w^2,\qquad F_2(w)=F_3(w)=	frac12w^2-w .\] Then \[F(w)=	frac12(w-	frac23)^2-	frac29,\qquad
 F^*=-	frac29,\qquad L=\mu=1 .\] The three gradients are \(w,w-1,w-1\), so \[
abla F(w)=w-	frac23,\qquad
 	frac13\sum_{i=1}^{3}|
abla F_i(w)-
abla F(w)|^2=	frac29=G^2\] for every real \(w\). All assumptions, including global bounded heterogeneity, smoothness, bounded loss, and PL, hold. The functions are convex, which is permitted by the general smooth-objective theorem.

Let \(w_0=0\), \(\eta=1=1/L\), and \(T=1\). The aggregated gradient is \(-1\), hence \(w_1=1\) and \(F(w_1)=-1/6\). The two sides of [eq:bad] (#eq:bad) are \[\text{left}=\tfrac49,\qquad
 \text{right}=2(-\tfrac29+\tfrac16)+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac29=0 .\] The independently written exact-rational check records this discrepancy. It involves neither a limiting argument nor a vanishing-heterogeneity edge case.
#### Correction and counterevidence.

Equation reference: eq:correct. Appendix A.7, page 21, correctly derives \[F(w_{t+1})-F(w_t)
 \leq-\frac{\|\nabla F(w_t)\|^2}{2L}+\frac{\epsilon G^2}{2L}\] and then the valid telescoping bound with \(F(w_0)-F(w_T)\). The next appeal to \(F(w_T)\geq F^*\) supports \[
 \frac1T\sum_{t<T}\|\nabla F(w_t)\|^2
 \leq\frac{2L[F(w_0)-F^*]}{T}+\epsilon G^2,\] not [eq:bad] (#eq:bad). The telescoping version is exactly tight in the counterexample: both sides equal \(4/9\); the uniform lower-bound version has right side \(5/9\).

Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) is proved by summing the displayed one-step bound and substituting the lower bound in the correct term. It uses the same assumptions and restores the asymptotic constant \(\epsilon G^2\). The separate PL upper bound follows from the usual scalar recurrence and is not refuted. The error is plausibly an endpoint substitution mistake, but it changes a principal finite-time guarantee in the paper’s core tightness argument. Its short repair and survival of the qualitative tradeoff do not reduce this finding below Major.

Problem 2 (Major: the lower-bound proof’s unstable-step argument is invalid as stated).  Appendix A.6, case (iii), page 21, claims \(w_t\to+\infty\) whenever \(\eta>2\sqrt{f(n-f)}/(nG)\), and concludes the lower bound from divergence. This omits an admissible fixed initialization and also ignores alternating signs. Theorem 4.5 explicitly quantifies over every initial point.

The proof has already obtained \[w_t=1+r^t(w_0-1),\qquad
 r=1-\frac{nG\eta}{\sqrt{f(n-f)}}.\] Use the same quadratic example above, for which \(nG/\sqrt{f(n-f)}=1\), but set \(\eta=3>2\) and \(w_0=1\). Then \(r=-2\) and \(w_t=1\) for all \(t\). Neither the objective nor the squared gradient diverges. Their actual values are \[|\nabla F(w_t)|^2=\tfrac19,\qquad F(w_t)-F^*=\tfrac1{18}.\] The invalid divergence step is used to complete the arbitrary-step, arbitrary-initialization lower-bound proof, a core contribution. This is a demonstrated proof defect, not a counterexample to the theorem’s conclusion.
#### Full case repair for the construction.

For \(f>0,G>0\), put \[a=\frac{nG}{\sqrt{f(n-f)}}=\mu,\quad
 d=\frac fn,\quad u=w_0-1,\quad
 c=a^2d^2=\frac{f}{n-f}G^2,\quad r=1-a\eta.\] Then \[|\nabla F(w_t)|^2=a^2(d+r^tu)^2,\qquad
 F(w_t)-F^*=\frac a2(d+r^tu)^2 .\] If \(u=0\), these equal \(c\) and \(c/(2\mu)\) at every time, for every positive step size. If \(|r|<1\), they converge to those same limits, so both required strict inequalities hold eventually for every \(C_1<c\). If \(r=-1\), the average squared gradient converges to \(a^2(d^2+u^2)\geq c\); choosing the infinitely repeated parity with the larger terminal gap gives at least \(c/(2\mu)\). If \(r<-1\) and \(u\ne0\), \(|w_t|\) diverges, and both squared-gradient averages and objective gaps diverge. This proves the desired simultaneous inequalities at arbitrarily large \(T\). The zero-floor cases can be handled separately since \(C_1<0\) and both relevant quantities are nonnegative.

This case analysis also avoids Appendix A.6’s self-referential formula for \(T\) on page 20. The proof there treats a lower bound on each two-step squared-gradient sum as an equality. Using the period average as above supplies the missing justification without that formula. Thus the lower-bound result survives the explicit repair. Major attaches to the invalid core derivation, not to a claim that its underlying theorem is false.

Problem 3 (Minor: the main-text middle-group variance uses the wrong divisor).  Page 4, Section 3.4.1, defines \(s_{I_0}^2\) with divisor \(f\), even though \(I_0\) has \(n-2f\) elements. Equation (7) on page 5 then weights it by \((n-2f)/n\), as though it were the usual middle-group variance. The resulting printed identity is false when the middle group has nonzero variance and \(n\ne3f\).

Let \(n=5,f=1\) and \(x=(0,1,2,3,4)\). Both the full mean and trimmed mean are 2. The full variance is 2, the two mean gaps are both 2, and the printed middle variance is 2. Equation (7)’s right side is \[0+\frac25(2\cdot2)+\frac35(2)=\frac{14}{5}\ne2 .\] The correct middle variance is \(2/3\), giving the correct right side 2. Appendix A.3, page 16, explicitly uses the correct divisor \(n-2f\), and its subsequent derivation is valid. Thus this is a local inconsistency in the proof sketch with a valid supplied full proof as counterevidence. Correct the main-text definition; the trimmed-mean theorem and its equality conditions remain supported.
# Results checked without a substantive issue

For Theorem 3.1, the \(n-f\) identical zero inputs force the robust aggregator to return zero. With the remaining \(f\) inputs equal to \(A\), its squared error is \(f^2A^2/n^2\), and all-input variance is \(f(n-f)A^2/n^2\). Their ratio is exactly \(f/(n-f)\). This establishes the universal no-attack floor under the stated robustness definition.

For Theorem 3.2, averaging over all subsets of size \(m=n-f\) gives expected within-subset variance \[\frac{n(m-1)}{m(n-1)}\,V\leq V,\qquad
 V=\frac1n\sum_i\|x_i-\bar x\|^2 .\] Jensen’s inequality for the average subset mean then proves the \(\kappa\)-accuracy statement. The exact finite subset check agrees with the identity.

With the corrected variance definition, Appendix A.3 establishes \[V=\frac{n-f}{f}(\mathrm{TM}_{f/n}-\bar x)^2+
 \frac{2f}{n}\Delta_-\Delta_++\widetilde s^2\] in one dimension, with all remainder terms nonnegative. Summing coordinate inequalities gives the vector bound. A finite exact-arithmetic check over sorted inputs from \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), \(3\leq n\leq9\), and every positive integer \(f<n/2\) finds no violation and attains the claimed ratio for each \((n,f)\). This diagnostic supplements the proof rather than replacing it. The \(f=0\) case is the exact mean and should be treated separately from formulas dividing by \(f\).

The coordinate median result follows for the usual convention averaging the two central values at even \(n\). The geometric-median upper bound follows from its minimizing property, the triangle inequality, and Cauchy–Schwarz, as in Appendix A.5. Its displayed tightness example allows any minimizer in the nonunique scalar even-sample case; it should not be read as proving that every fixed tie-breaking rule attains that same example.
# Empirical scope and overall impact

Section 5 and Tables 3–6 were read and checked for their reported direction and arithmetic. They show worse displayed no-attack accuracies as the specified robustness parameters increase in the tested setups. They do not prove monotonic degradation on every dataset. The mathematical result concerns the sharp worst-case envelope, rather than an ordering of every possible pair of robust algorithms.

The paper explicitly selects the best final test accuracy among initial learning rates. For claims beyond those reported tuned comparisons, per-seed results, fixed validation selection, uncertainty, and exact aggregation/NNM configurations are needed. No code or run logs were acquired, so experimental robustness conditions, historical implementation choices, and reproducibility remain unverified. External provenance for inherited Table 1 constants and the full priority claim was not independently audited.

The strongest supported assessment is Major because a central upper guarantee is false and a central lower-bound proof contains invalid case reasoning. The corrected upper bound, repaired lower construction, aggregation floor, trimmed-mean optimal constant, and qualitative worst-case tension survive. No benchmark-score loss or whole-paper failure is claimed.

report: Abstract: This initial review concerns paper 0109 (I25-43478), the published ICML 2025 proceedings version, including its appendices. The provisional assessment is Major. Four demonstrated defects affect the mathematical justification of trajectory tracking and feature rectification: camera-centered depth is used in an object-centered rotation formula; a feature-norm bound is replaced by a coordinate-norm bound; the unregularized dual-anchor loss admits a nonvanishing Jacobian-omission error; and the fusion composition law fails for uniform local averaging. Explicit constructions and conditional repairs are given. The reported image-quality improvements and Jacobian ablations remain positive empirical evidence within the tested settings. No author code or generative model was executed. Scientific adjudication is pending and no human review is recorded.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
MIRROR: Make Your Object-Level Multi-View Generation More Consistent with Training-Free Rectification
# Version, contribution, and scope
The source is Xing et al., PMLR 267, pp. 68900–68927 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Locations below use PDF pages 1–28 and source equation numbers. The original PDF SHA-256 is
Its supplied manifest SHA-256 is
Neither source was modified.

MIRROR first generates clean views, estimates monocular depth, and inverts the views. It then rectifies a second denoising trajectory using fixed first-stage depth, correspondences between adjacent fixed-elevation views, and a dual-anchor weighted feature loss. Removing the noise-predictor Jacobian reduces correction cost. Thus the geometric correspondence rule, stability argument, and Jacobian approximation directly support the central method and its theoretical explanation.

All 28 pages were read as extracted text, including Appendices A–L. The original geometry and critical derivations on pp. 5, 13–16, convergence/ablation figures on pp. 18–19, and failure examples on p. 28 were visually inspected. This is not an exhaustive examination of all gallery images. No repository was acquired. The manifest records an OpenReview metadata access failure (HTTP 403); the existence of a separate supplement is undetermined. These limitations do not establish that code or supplements do not exist.
# Demonstrated findings

Problem 1 (Major: the depth convention does not give the claimed correspondence).  Location and claim. Definition 4.1, Eq. (4), p. 5, describes a camera moving horizontally around the object at fixed elevation and uses \[x_\alpha=(x-W/2)\cos\alpha+W/2-z\sin\alpha,\qquad y_\alpha=y.\] The same page defines \(z\) as distance from the camera center to the object. The depth prior is converted by multiplication, \(Z_{\rm absolute}=rZ_{\rm relative}\). This equation supplies the point correspondences used by TTM and the rectification loss.

Decisive check. Consider a visible point marker at the orbit’s look-at pivot, two level cameras looking at that pivot, common principal point \(W/2=100\), and camera distance \(D=4\). Choose compatible length and image units with local scale one. The marker lies on both optical axes, so its horizontal coordinate is 100 in both views, under either centered perspective projection or an orthographic camera. Its camera-centered depth/range is \(z=D\). For \(\alpha=\pi/6\), Eq. (4) gives \[x_\alpha=100-4\sin(\pi/6)=98.\] This example stays within the fixed-elevation circular setting; it requires neither unrestricted poses nor occlusion.

Dependency and interpretation. Rotation about the object pivot needs a coordinate measured relative to that pivot. The equation rotates camera-centered depth without the translation that changes the rotation origin. Setting the pivot’s depth to zero repairs this example but changes the stated convention. Multiplication by a scale factor alone cannot generally provide the missing offset. These coordinates select the neighboring feature block, making this a core correspondence issue.

Repair and boundaries. Calibrated perspective geometry with optical-axis depth uses \[\widetilde u'\ \sim\ K'\bigl(R(zK^{-1}\widetilde u)+t\bigr),\] followed by homogeneous division. Radial range instead requires a unit ray. Alternatively, Eq. (4) can be restricted to an explicitly orthographic, object-centered model with matched coordinate units and a defined depth offset. Visibility needs separate treatment. No acquired implementation establishes whether an unreported centering step was used historically. This counterexample invalidates the printed formula under its convention; it does not determine reported metric changes.

Problem 2 (Major: the trajectory-stability proof bounds different objects).  Location and claim. Proposition 4.2, Eq. (5), p. 5, claims stability and convergence of \(T_\alpha(\widehat x_0)\) to \(T_\alpha(x_0)\). Appendix B.1, Eq. (15), p. 13, first bounds the squared difference of transformed images/features by the squared difference of transformed coordinates, then bounds the latter by depth-estimation error.

Decisive check. The declared operator is \(T_\alpha:V\to V\), with \(V=L^2(\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R)\). At \(\alpha=0\), \(T_0\) is the identity. Let \(x_0=\phi\), \(\widehat x_0=1.1\phi\), and \(\|\phi\|_2=1\), with \(\phi\) smooth and compactly supported. Use the same constant-depth scene for both images; a constant depth estimator is continuous and has bounded derivative zero. Coordinate displacement is zero, whereas \[\|T_0(\widehat x_0)-T_0(x_0)\|_2^2=0.01.\] The first inequality of Eq. (15) requires \(0.01\leq0\). Varying scene appearance with fixed depth suffices; inaccurate depth is not needed.

Scope of the refutation. This disproves the proof step. It does not disprove the conclusion for \(T_0\), whose identity action is Lipschitz. Interpreting \(T_\alpha\) as a coordinate map alone changes the declared image/feature operator. Coordinate displacement can satisfy a conditional estimate \[\|u_\alpha(\widehat x_0)-u_\alpha(x_0)\|
 \leq r|\sin\alpha|L_{\mathcal H}\|\widehat x_0-x_0\|\] when the depth estimator \(\mathcal H\) is Lipschitz. A feature-resampling estimate additionally needs appearance differences, spatial regularity, warp distortion, and visibility control. These terms cannot be removed by bounding coordinates.

Core dependency and repair. The invalid step bridges diffusion prediction error to TTM feature stability. The algorithm also freezes first-stage depth, while the proof compares depth estimates of changing predicted images. A corrected theorem must specify the fixed depth map, operator and norm, and residual depth bias. The training-loss/KL discussion around Eq. (19) does not itself provide a per-instance inference error bound. Appendix E and Fig. 12 give favorable tested trajectories but cannot validate the false inequality. Additional regularity may support a revised conclusion; no global impossibility is asserted.

Problem 3 (Major: Jacobian omission need not have vanishing gradient error).  Location and claim. Theorem 4.4, Eq. (13), p. 7, claims that the gradient error from omitting the UNet Jacobian tends to zero as \(t\to0\), justifying Eq. (14). Appendix B.3, pp. 14–15, treats the relevant gradient factors as bounded and argues that the predicted-noise Jacobian vanishes. Neither independence from the data nor a uniform dual-anchor loss-gradient bound follows from the formulation.

Construction using the specified loss. Put \(\sigma=\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\), \(\alpha_t=1-\sigma^2\), and take the fixed linear predictor \(\epsilon_\theta(z,t)=z\). Its Jacobian is the bounded identity. At the current spatial point choose predicted clean feature \(u=(h,0)\), \(h=\sigma>0\), by setting \[z_t=\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}h}{1-\sigma}(1,0).\] This satisfies Eq. (6) exactly. In each adjacent \(3\times3\) block put seven copies of \(e_1=(1,0)\) and two of \(e_2=(0,1)\), placing the latter away from all four corners. Both adjacent blocks are identical. The negative anchor is therefore \(e_1\), and the positive anchor is \(u\). Choose \(m^+=m^-=1/2\), the setting in Appendix C.1. All cosine similarities are defined for every \(\sigma>0\).

The exact chain factor is \((1-\sigma)/\sqrt{\alpha_t}\); omission uses \(1/\sqrt{\alpha_t}\). The \(y\)-component of their gradient difference therefore tends to \[-\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}g_y
 \longrightarrow c(A-B)
 \approx0.0402565818\neq0.\] An independent centered finite difference agrees with the analytic \(g_y\) at \(h=0.01\): \(-4.47184791807\) versus \(-4.47184791824\). For \(\sigma=10^{-2},10^{-3},10^{-4},10^{-5}\), the error components are approximately \(0.0447207,0.0407028,0.0403012,0.0402610\). These verify the construction; they are not model evaluation results.

Assumptions and scope. The example uses the unregularized cosine and local gradient map defined in Eqs. (7)–(11). The current anchor approaches zero but is never zero at a positive noise level. A uniform positive lower bound on limiting anchor norms, explicit cosine regularization, or detached fusion weights changes the assumptions or gradient. None is specified in the theorem, and no acquired code settles the implementation. This is an explicit failure under a missing mathematical condition, not a claim that typical latent trajectories must realize it. The construction is a functional counterexample under the printed assumptions. It has not been shown to constitute a complete sampling trajectory of a particular trained denoiser. A trajectory-restricted guarantee requires explicit control of the loss gradient along that trajectory.

Counterevidence and consequence. Figures 10–11, p. 18, show small errors and similar results with/without the Jacobian in tested configurations. Those observations remain relevant, as do Table 2’s speed improvements. The theorem does not establish unconditional negligible correction error. Its one-step limit also does not control accumulated trajectory error or finite early denoising steps. This is Major because the invalid general justification directly supports the central acceleration; observed empirical score loss is not required for that classification.

Problem 4 (Major: the feature-fusion composition law is false).  Location and claim. After Definition 4.3, p. 6, \(M\circ T\) is called a group homomorphism. Appendix B.4, Proposition B.2, Eq. (29), p. 15, asserts for all \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in\mathbb R\) \[(M T_{\alpha_1})(M T_{\alpha_2})=M T_{\alpha_1+\alpha_2}.\] The p. 16 proof removes a copy of \(M\) because \(T\) acts on coordinates and \(M\) on features.

Decisive check with the actual weights. Set \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0\); the claim requires \(M^2=M\). On a large enough image interior, use scalar positive features \(Z(x,y)=1+x^2+y^2\), or this scalar times a common nonzero feature direction. Extend the field positively with a decaying tail if an \(L^2\) domain is required. Anchor similarities are constant across each block: \(C^+=1\), \(C^-=0\). Eq. (7) gives \(W_v=1/9\), regardless of the mixture coefficients summing to one. This remains true after fusion.

Thus \(M\) is ordinary \(3\times3\) averaging. At the origin, \[(MZ)(0,0)=\frac73,\qquad (M^2Z)(0,0)=\frac{11}3.\] These unequal exact values disprove Eq. (29), without inaccurate warping or numerical approximation.

Dependency and repair. Coordinate/feature separation does not imply idempotence; even commutativity leaves \(M^2\), not \(M\). This algebra explicitly justifies the adjacent operator underlying the core loss and its composition across views. The ordinary rotation-group identity for full 3D coordinates is not disputed. One may remove the homomorphism claim and retain a heuristic local loss, or prove a different statement under explicit projection/idempotence and equivariance conditions on a specified space. Generic dual-anchor averaging lacks those conditions. Empirical consistency improvements can coexist with the false algebraic claim.
# Empirical checks, counterevidence, and unresolved questions

Supported within the material. Table 1 reports improvements for all four baseline/task configurations across its listed metrics, and Table 3’s reconstruction comparisons are favorable. Table 2 gives with/without-Jacobian times \(91/43\), \(112/52\), \(103/64\), and \(154/98\) seconds, giving ratios about \(2.12,2.15,1.61,1.57\). These support useful speed reduction with variation across baselines; the description of a nearly twofold speedup is not treated as a separate defect. Depth-estimator ablations and Figs. 10–13 provide positive tested evidence. In Table 5, DUSt3R improves some metrics while DA2 is stronger on others; no universal estimator ranking is inferred.

Needs Evidence. Appendix C.3, p. 17, describes 100 GSO objects and 100 T3Bench prompts, and states that half the 24 generated text-conditioned views are used for neural-field reconstruction and as pseudo ground truth. Shared versus method-specific references, held-out evaluation views, object/prompt IDs, seeds, and sample-level uncertainty are needed to interpret text-conditioned image and geometry metrics. This is an evaluation-definition and reproducibility gap, not proof of invented measurements or leakage. Appendix D’s 50-prompt Jacobian comparison also needs its prompt list and aggregation record to establish its relationship to the 100-prompt main evaluation.

Boundaries and rejected overclaims. Appendix I discloses fixed-elevation object-level scope. Appendix L and Fig. 21 show failure with poor initial geometry. Changing seeds may help, but no acquired selection log supports an allegation of selective reporting. Downstream NeuS optimization is disclosed; training-free concerns the rectification mechanism. No fresh generation, checkpoint evaluation, author-code execution, or timing reproduction was performed. Algorithm 1’s loss argument and differentiation variable should be reconciled with the predicted-clean features in Eq. (11); the main text gives a plausible intended interpretation, so this is not an additional demonstrated defect.
# Evidence, repair status, and review state

Reviewer-written arithmetic and finite-difference checks are saved in `verification/0109/independent_check.py`; actual results are in `check_results.json`, with execution metadata in `independent_check_execution.json`. Source extraction, selected renders, coverage, findings, provenance, build records, final-PDF renders, and visual inspection records are under `verification/0109/`. No new external source was downloaded for this paper.

The pivot calculation, identity counterexample, nonzero gradient-error limit, and nonidempotence calculation were independently checked. Suggested repairs are mathematical conditions or revised statements, not author-adopted changes. No corrected author implementation or complete repaired theorem was experimentally verified.
