report: Abstract: This initial review concerns paper 0110 (I25-43479), the published ICML 2025 version and the acquired public EMERALD source at a fixed commit. The provisional assessment is Minor. A static control-flow counterexample shows that the released temporal model can reuse attention values from a previous episode when the current fragment contains no reset. The release also differs materially from the printed loss and imagination-batch specification. These findings are version-bound; the available source is not established as the historical experiment revision. Arithmetic checks support the public twenty-seed aggregate and the principal reported comparisons. The human reference aggregation and attribution of gains to individual architectural changes require further evidence. No author code or environment was executed. Adjudication is pending and no human review is recorded.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Accurate and Efficient World Modeling with Masked Latent Transformers
# Reviewed version and central dependencies
The source is Burchi and Timofte, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 5894–5912 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Locations use its 1-based PDF pages. The original PDF SHA-256 is
The supplied manifest SHA-256 is
The public source commit is
> `665948d8cd619ccc960abe54ffdfc785ce95f18b`.
These sources remain unchanged. The commit identifies the acquired release, not the paper’s historical runs.

EMERALD combines \(4\times4\) spatial categorical latents with 32 groups, a causal temporal Transformer, and a spatial MaskGIT predictor. The world model is trained with reconstruction, reward, continuation, dynamics, representation-regularization, and masked-prediction losses. Actor–critic learning uses imagined latent trajectories rather than decoded pixels. Its main empirical claims depend on accurate spatial representations, usable temporal context, coherent multi-step prediction, and favorable performance per unit training time.

All 19 source pages were read as text, including Appendix A.1–A.7 on pp. 12–19. The manifest’s automatic appendix flag is false, but appendices are actually present. Original pages 9, 13, 18, and 19 were visually checked. The acquired source inventory has 82 files; selected central source files were read statically, not the entire dependency stack. The inspected set includes the main model and configuration, TSSM, MaskGIT, encoder/decoder, attention masking and relative attention, replay buffer, relevant distributions, Crafter wrapper, README, and released results. No checkpoint, per-seed historical logs, Atari implementation, or separate supplement was acquired. OpenReview metadata access failed with HTTP 403, leaving separate-supplement availability undetermined.
# Demonstrated findings

Problem 1 (Minor: cached episode boundaries can be ignored).  Location and intended behavior. Section 3.1, pp. 5–6, defines temporal states from preceding states/actions and describes cached keys and values across consecutive training fragments. In the pinned source, `nnet/modules/emerald/tssm.py`, both `forward_obs` (lines 341–363) and `forward` (lines 459–481) apply the episode-separation mask only inside \[\texttt{if is\_firsts.any():}\] where `is_firsts` contains current-fragment flags. The separate argument `is_firsts_hidden` can contain a reset inside the cached context. The ordinary causal/context mask does not encode episode identity.

Reachable condition. Suppose all current flags are zero, while cached flags are \((0,1)\): one old-episode value followed by the first value of the new episode. With a context limit of 64, both cached positions remain visible to the next one-step query. The guard is false, so the release uses the key mask \[(1,1,1),\] although the episode-separation helper would produce \[(0,1,1).\] This situation can occur in online collection after an environment reset. The main model’s `env_step` retains the attention cache, resets the other state fields, constructs cached reset flags, and passes them to TSSM. When no environment has a reset in the current call, the guard skips those flags. The replay buffer also concatenates successive episodes across sequence fragments, so a reset may lie in a prior cached fragment.

Decisive consequence. Choose an attention head with equal logits and value components \((2,0,0)\). Such logits are obtainable by zero query and positional-score contributions. The released mask gives output component \(2/3\), whereas correct episode isolation gives zero. With the full default cache, take 63 old-episode entries followed by the new episode’s initial entry, put the value 2 in one old entry and zero elsewhere, and use equal logits. The next query gives \(2/65\) rather than zero, so the same failure occurs with the default 64-entry cache. Thus a previous episode can influence the current representation even with identical observations/actions in the current episode. This is a mathematical attention/control-flow check written by the reviewer; the author implementation was not executed.

Counterevidence and boundary. The guard works when a current reset is present. Moreover, `imagine` applies the episode mask whenever cached flags are supplied (lines 251–255), and `play` starts each evaluation episode with a fresh state/cache. These paths limit the finding and rule out a claim that every evaluated episode necessarily has cross-episode memory. A fully empty cache also avoids the issue. The source is not bound to the historical five-seed experiments.

Impact and repair. The defect affects episode isolation in released world-model learning/collection and can create a train/evaluation state-distribution difference. Apply the episode-separation mask whenever current or cached reset information is present; keep resetting current states/actions conditional on current resets. Alternatively, explicitly discard prior-episode cache entries per environment. Check a reset at the end of one fragment followed by a fragment with no reset. The supported impact is a localized episode-isolation defect in the inspected release. The direct evaluation path starts each episode with a fresh state, and the release has not been bound to the historical experiments. The available evidence establishes a boundary-condition defect but does not establish material harm to the core scientific conclusions; the supported assessment is Minor, with historical experimental attribution remaining Needs Evidence. No repair was applied to the author’s source.

Problem 2 (Minor: the released training specification differs from the paper).  Locations. Eqs. (2)–(3) and (6), pp. 6–7; Section 3.2, p. 7; Tables 6 and 10, pp. 15 and 17. The corresponding release locations are `nnet/models/emerald.py`, default configuration and `WorldModel.forward`, and `nnet/modules/emerald/decoder_network.py`.

Loss difference with a nontrivial gradient consequence. Eq. (2) states a KL masked-prediction objective and Eq. (6) adds it without an explicit extra coefficient. The release averages KL over masked positions, multiplies by 32, clips that quantity from below at one free nat, and applies weight \(0.5\). Dynamics/representation KL terms also use a free-nat threshold. For equal per-token divergences \(\kappa\), the released masked contribution reduces to \[L_{\rm mask}^{\rm release}=\frac12\max(1,32\kappa).\] Let \(q\) be uniform on 32 categories, and let \(p_x\) assign probability \(x/16\) to each of its first 16 categories and \((1-x)/16\) to each remaining category. Then \[\kappa(x)=\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{x}
           +\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{1-x}.\] At \(x=0.6\), \(\kappa=0.0204109973\), \(32\kappa=0.6531519123<1\), and \(\kappa'(x)=5/12\neq0\), whereas the released clipped contribution has derivative zero. A centered finite-difference calculation confirms the flat released loss. Thus the missing operation is not merely an additive constant or notation change. Free-nat regularization can be a reasonable design choice; the issue is the unbound specification, not proof that regularization is intrinsically wrong.

Imagination workload. Section 3.2 says that flattening all batch/time positions produces \(B^{\rm img}=BT\). With Table 10’s \(B=16,T=64\), this means 1,024 starting trajectories. The release defaults to `img_stride=4` and selects time indices \(0,4,\ldots,60\) when constructing `detached_posts` and their caches. It therefore starts \(16\cdot16=256\) trajectories. Both use horizon 15, but their sample count per update differs by a factor of four. This matters when reproducing training throughput and the actor/critic data volume.

Decoder channel count. Table 6 projects temporal hidden state to \(4\times4\times256\) before concatenation with 1,024 latent channels, giving 1,280 channels. The released main model passes `dim_cnn=32` to `DecoderNetwork`; its hidden projection outputs 32 channels and its concatenation has 1,056 channels. This is a concrete version difference, not a claim of a tensor-shape crash: the released projection is internally dimensioned for 1,056.

Interpretation, counterevidence, and repair. The README explicitly describes twenty-seed results from the public repository, while the paper reports five-seed aggregates. Later changes could explain these differences. No historical configuration was acquired, so the findings do not establish which objective, workload, or decoder produced the paper’s numbers. The public results retain strong performance. Supply a historical commit/configuration or a documented release-to-paper change record; state the mask reduction, free-nat clipping, loss weights, imagination stride, and actual channel widths. This is a Minor reproducibility/specification issue for the available version pairing; historical experimental attribution remains Needs Evidence.
# Quantitative checks and evidence that supports the method
## Crafter aggregate and individual achievements

The p. 7 score definition is \[\mathcal{S}(s)=\exp\left(\frac1{22}\sum_{i=1}^{22}\log(1+s_i)\right)-1,
 \qquad s_i\in[0,100].\] Recalculation from Table 5’s rounded rates gives \(34.9374\), \(39.6132\), and \(42.4970\) for DreamerV3 M, XL, and \(\Delta\)-IRIS, respectively, agreeing with \(34.9,39.6,42.5\). EMERALD gives \(58.2535\); allowing each displayed rate its \(0.05\)-percentage-point rounding interval gives approximately \([58.0052,58.4942]\), consistent with the reported \(58.1\). It would be incorrect to label this small difference an arithmetic error.

The acquired `results/EMERALD.json` reports twenty-seed aggregate return \(16.4824220\) and score \(57.0356286\). Applying the same formula to its 22 aggregate achievement rates reproduces the stored score to numerical precision. All 22 rates are positive. This supports the released aggregate and the pooled statement that every achievement occurred, while not establishing success in every seed or every episode. The paper’s rare-event rates, including \(0.5\%\) for diamonds and \(0.1\%\) for eating a plant, also do not imply reliable mastery of every individual task.

Needs Evidence: human aggregation. The rounded human rates in Table 5 give \(52.0497\), with a rounding interval approximately \([51.9822,52.1123]\), rather than the listed \(50.5\). Rate rounding alone cannot explain that difference. Averaging scores over people/runs before aggregating rates could explain it, because the nonlinear score and averaging do not commute. The original human episode/person data and exact aggregation order were not acquired. Clarify the shared human/agent aggregation protocol rather than presume the reference is fabricated or mathematically invalid. Both the paper’s \(58.1\) and the public \(57.0356\) remain above either displayed/recomputed human reference; this discrepancy does not reverse the observed ordering.
## Architecture, decoding, and efficiency

Table 3 shows that spatial latents plus MaskGIT improve score within both compared architectures. The spatial TSSM scores \(58.1\) versus the spatial RSSM’s \(40.4\). However, vector TSSM scores \(31.8\), below vector RSSM’s \(34.9\). Spatial RSSM also has slightly smaller pixel reconstruction loss, \(0.000231\), than spatial TSSM’s \(0.000241\). These facts support an interaction between architecture and representation, and do not support a universal claim that a Transformer always improves reconstruction or control.

Needs Evidence: isolated causal attribution. The text on p. 8 describes one modification at a time, but Table 3 changes spatial layout and MaskGIT together and changes the RSSM size label/parameter count. Table 4 supplies a useful separate MaskGIT comparison within the spatial TSSM: no MaskGIT \(51.6\), one step \(53.8\), three steps \(58.1\), eight steps \(55.1\). Thus the evidence favors the chosen combined system and three-step tradeoff; it does not fully isolate every component or establish monotonic final control improvement with more refinement. Matched architectures/capacities, seed-level results, and the definition of the reported return variation would resolve the stronger attribution claims.

The released three-step scheduler operates on 512 grouped spatial tokens, with \(512,443,256\) positions masked before successive forward predictions. The final forward samples the remaining positions, so the absence of an additional zero-mask forward pass is not a missing-token defect. Causal token shifting, grouped latent output shapes, the two-step \(\lambda\)-return recurrence, the actor sign/stop-gradient convention, and the \(0.98\) old-value EMA convention were checked without finding a contradiction in these inspected parts. This scoped result is not a certification of all source code.

Table 2’s FPS comparison supports EMERALD over \(\Delta\)-IRIS (\(27\) versus \(12\)) and DreamerV3 XL (\(27\) versus \(23\)), while DreamerV3 M is faster (\(38\)). The paper identifies FPS as collected environment frames divided by total training duration, on an RTX 3090. No hardware run or end-to-end timing was reproduced.
## Atari and limits of aggregate reconstruction

Table 11’s 26 displayed EMERALD scores yield mean/median human-normalized performance approximately \(133.378\%/51.322\%\) and 11 strictly superhuman games using the rounded cells. The paper prints \(134\%/51\%\) and 11. Integer rounding of agent, random, and human reference cells permits a conservative mean interval \([131.023,136.088]\), so these displays do not demonstrate an inconsistency. The other columns were also recomputed; near-ties and rounded normalization denominators prevent treating small differences as established errors.

The Atari comparison is explicitly restricted to model-based methods without look-ahead search; it does not claim the best overall Atari result. The 17-hour timing concerns Breakout on one RTX 3090, not a measured uniform time for every game. The pinned repository is Crafter-focused and provides no acquired Atari run/configuration set. Per-seed Atari results, exact normalization references, environment settings, and historical timing logs remain necessary for independent reproduction.
# Coverage, evidence, and review state

Actual reviewer-written checks are in `verification/0110/independent_check.py`, with results in `check_results.json`. Numbered source excerpts and hashes are in `selected_source_excerpts.txt`; the original acquisition manifest, extracted pages, selected source renders, coverage, findings, provenance, build and visual-QA records remain version-bound under the same assigned root. No new source was downloaded. No author module was imported or executed.

The attention example proves a mask-level functional difference under the stated reachable cache condition. The KL and workload checks establish the released specifications. They do not reproduce a trained network or estimate performance damage. Suggested repairs were checked only algebraically/control-flow-wise; author adoption is unknown. Scientific adjudication remains pending and no human review is recorded.

Title: Technical Verification of
Quantum Speedup for Hypergraph Sparsification
# Identity, version and inspected scope

This report concerns Chenghua Liu, Minbo Gao, Zhengfeng Ji and Mingsheng Ying, Quantum Speedup for Hypergraph Sparsification, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 38448–38466 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; assignment 0111 / I25-43480. The reviewed file is the supplied 19-page published PDF. Page references below mean the printed PDF pages 1–19, not the proceedings page numbers. Its SHA-256 is recorded in the accompanying provenance and input-verification files.

The review covers the definitions, Algorithms 1–2, Theorems 3.4 and 4.1, their Appendices A–C, and the stated runtime dependencies in Section 5. The quantum primitives cited from other papers were treated as their stated interfaces, not re-proved or empirically implemented. Exact rational checks were independently written and run; no author code was run. The supplied manifest identifies no available author repository and records an OpenReview access gap for separate supplements. The embedded appendices were available and inspected.
# Definitions and dependencies

For a hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\), \[Q_H(x)=\sum_{e\in E}w_e\max_{i,j\in e}(x_i-x_j)^2.\] A spectral sparsifier must approximate this energy multiplicatively for every \(x\). A sparse underlying graph assigns conductances \(c_{e,f}\) to a star \(S_e\) inside each hyperedge, with \(\sum_{f\in S_e}c_{e,f}=w_e\) (Definition 3.3, p. 6). A leverage-score overestimate must dominate \(w_e\max_{i,j\in e}R_{ij}\) for some underlying graph satisfying those groupwise constraints, and have total mass \(O(n)\) (Definition 3.2).

Algorithm 1 sparsifies each underlying graph, stores the resulting conductances, and uses them in the next weight update and the final overestimate. Algorithm 2 samples according to the resulting scores and estimates their sum before reweighting. Thus both interfaces are direct dependencies of Theorem 4.1; the cut applications inherit them.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Loss of hyperedge mass invalidates the leverage-score construction — Major).
## Claim and exact location

Algorithm 1, lines 3–6 and 9 (p. 7), stores \(\widetilde G^{(t)}\) and passes that stored graph to WeightCompute and QOverestimate. Proposition B.5, equation (7) (p. 14), divides by \[\Delta_e=\sum_{g\in S_e}\widetilde c_{e,g}^{(t)}\widetilde R_g^{(t)}.\] Proposition B.7 (pp. 15–16) treats the averaged sparsified conductances as an underlying graph of \(H\) and telescopes ratios of successive sparsified conductances to establish domination.
## Complete check

Take \(n=201\) vertices. Include every two-vertex hyperedge with weight one, and one additional hyperedge \(e_0=\{1,2,3\}\) of weight \(d=1/100\). This is a simple weighted hypergraph of rank three with \(m=20101\). Choose vertex 1 as the center of the star for \(e_0\). WeightInitialize produces the multigraph \[L_G=L_{K_n}+\frac d2 L_{\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\}\}}.\] All required weights are nonnegative, and the groupwise sums equal the original hyperedge weights.

Consider the graph-sparsifier output \(\widetilde G=K_n\), retaining the unit edges with their original labels and removing the two edges labelled by \(e_0\). On \(\mathbf1^\perp\), \(L_{K_n}=nI\) and the star Laplacian has largest eigenvalue three. Consequently, \[0\preceq L_G-L_{\widetilde G}\preceq
 \frac{3d/2}{n+3d/2}L_G=\frac1{13401}L_G.\] This output is therefore a valid \(0.1\)-spectral sparsifier. The input has 20102 underlying edges, so \(0.1\ge\sqrt{201/20102}\), as required by the stated graph-sparsification interface. The output has 20100 edges, exactly \(n/(0.1)^2\), and meets its size requirement.

Nevertheless, both stored conductances for \(e_0\) vanish. Equation (7) is \(0/0\) for that hyperedge. Moreover, already with \(T=1\), QOverestimate returns \(z_{e_0}=0\) regardless of its positive prefactor. Its purported underlying graph has group mass zero instead of \(1/100\). If that graph is interpreted as \(K_n\), its effective resistance between any two distinct vertices is \(2/n\), and \[w_{e_0}R_{e_0}=\frac1{10050}>0=z_{e_0}.\] This is not an issue about floating-point accuracy.

There are two further manifestations of the same failed invariant. A spectral approximation preserves aggregate quadratic forms, not the sum of conductances with each hyperedge label. Also, WeightCompute defines the pre-sparsification next conductances \(c^{(t+1)}\); equality (b) on p. 16 substitutes the independently reweighted \(\widetilde c^{(t+1)}\) into the recurrence. The proposed telescoping identity does not follow.
## Counterevidence and bounded consequence

The example is an admissible output of the stated graph-sparsifier interface; it is not a measurement of the distribution produced by a specific implementation of that primitive. That distinction does not rescue the proof: no group-preservation property is supplied, and a sparsifier with fewer edges than positive-weight hyperedges cannot retain a labelled edge from every group. Retaining the unsparsified conductances could change the construction, but would require a new query-cost and domination argument. No such repaired algorithm is verified here.

The demonstrated failure directly affects Theorem 3.4, which supplies the core overestimates for Theorem 4.1. This supports Major even without claiming that quantum hypergraph sparsification is impossible or that every execution fails.
Problem 2 (Constant normalizer error survives sampling and invalidates the symmetrization — Major).
## Claim and exact location

Algorithm 2, line 4 (p. 7), calls SumEstimate with accuracy \(0.1\), while line 8 uses the returned sum in the output weights. Appendix C, pp. 17–19, explicitly retains this fixed accuracy and claims an arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon\)-error after choosing a sufficiently large sample size. The equality introducing Rademacher signs in the uncentered second term on p. 18 is invalid.
## Derivation and an admissible family

Grant an exact valid score oracle, so this finding is independent of Problem 1. Put \(s=\sum_e z_e\), \(p_e=z_e/s\), and let \(\widehat s=(1+\delta)s\). Conditional on this normalizer, the returned energy is \[\widehat Q(x)=\frac1M\sum_{t=1}^M
       \frac{\widehat s\,w_{e_t}}{z_{e_t}}Q_{e_t}(x),
 \qquad \mathbb E[\widehat Q(x)\mid\widehat s]=(1+\delta)Q_H(x).\] Jensen’s inequality already gives \(\mathbb E|\widehat Q(x)-Q_H(x)|\ge|\delta|Q_H(x)\). Increasing \(M\) cannot remove this bias.

A family makes the failure deterministic conditional on an allowed normalizer value. Let \[V=\{0,\ldots,n-1\},\quad
 E=\{\{0,i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n-1\},\quad w_e=1.\] Every hyperedge has rank three. Use the star centered at 0 with conductance \(1/2\) on each of its two edges. The resulting graph is a star whose leaf conductances are \((n-2)/2\). Hence each hyperedge has maximum resistance \(4/(n-2)\). Set \(z_e=4/(n-2)\), a valid overestimate with \[m=\binom{n-1}{2},\qquad s=2(n-1),\qquad p_e=1/m.\] For \(x_0=1\) and all other coordinates zero, every \(Q_e(x)=1\) and \(Q_H(x)=m\). Every possible sampled sequence yields \[\widehat Q(x)=\frac{\widehat s}{s}m.\] The normalizer \(\widehat s=21s/20\) satisfies the stated 10% accuracy guarantee but produces relative error \(1/20\), exceeding \(\varepsilon=1/100\) for every sample sequence. For any fixed hidden constant in \(M=\Theta(n\log n\log3/\varepsilon^2)\), choose \(n\) sufficiently large that \(M\le\binom{n-1}{2}\); such an integer exists since \(n/\log n\to\infty\). Then the sampling primitive’s \(M\le m\) condition and the sparsification regime \(\varepsilon\ge\sqrt{n/m}\) are both met. No single-edge example outside that regime is needed.

On p. 18, the uncentered mean term is replaced by a Rademacher-signed sum. Those quantities do not have the same expectation: in the displayed family the former is a nonzero constant while the latter decreases with sample size. The preceding triangle-inequality coefficient also needs \(|s/\widehat s-1|\), rather than a signed coefficient.
## Counterevidence and correction bound

A particular normalizer implementation could return a much more accurate value on a particular input. The result above disproves the claimed consequence of the stated \(0.1\) interface and the displayed proof, not a universal lower bound on all implementations.

A defensible partial correction is to estimate \(s\) to \(\eta=O(\varepsilon)\) and allocate error to the unbiased sampling step. If an unbiased-sum estimator has relative error at most \(\beta\), the rescaled estimator has error at most \[\eta+(1+\eta)\beta.\] For \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), taking \(\eta=\beta=\varepsilon/3\) makes this at most \(7\varepsilon/9<\varepsilon\). The additional stated sum-estimation cost is \(\widetilde O(r\sqrt m/\varepsilon)\), within the sampling term. This verifies the normalization repair only; it does not fix Problem 1 or prove the required simultaneous high-probability sampling bound. Appendix C ends with an expectation bound, so that probability upgrade remains unverified.
Problem 3 (The density conditions do not justify the advertised runtime simplification — Major).

Remark 4.2 (p. 7) drops \(r\sqrt{mnr}\) under \(\varepsilon\ge\sqrt{n/m}\) and \(m\ge nr\). The exact ratio of this term to \(r\sqrt{mn}/\varepsilon\) is \(\varepsilon\sqrt r\); density cancels. With rank growing polynomially, fixed \(\varepsilon\) and a sufficiently dense simple hypergraph, that ratio need not be polylogarithmic. For example, include all three-vertex hyperedges and the full vertex set, with \(n>3\). Then \(r=n\) and \(m=\binom n3+1=\Theta(n^3)\); both stated inequalities hold for sufficiently large \(n\) and \(\varepsilon=1/2\). The ratio is \(\sqrt n/2\), which is not polylogarithmic in any of the stated parameters.

The abstract (p. 1) advertises the simplified bound as the main algorithmic runtime for rank \(r\), and Remark 4.2 supplies its stated justification. Thus the lost nonpolylogarithmic factor affects a core complexity claim and supports Major. The full two-term complexity in Theorem 4.1 and Table 1 is not contradicted by this arithmetic. Retain both terms in the advertised bound or explicitly restrict, for example, to \(\varepsilon\le1/\sqrt r\) (up to suppressed logarithms). The validity of the unsimplified bound and the availability of this local correction do not validate the stronger claim.
Problem 4 (Proposition C.2 leaves a core chaining hypothesis unjustified — Major).

Proposition C.2 (p. 17) asserts \(Q_H(L_G^{+/2}x)\ge\|x\|^2\) for every \(x\perp\mathbf1\). For the graph with one unit edge \(\{1,2\}\) and isolated vertex 3, take \(x=(1,1,-2)\). This satisfies \(x\perp\mathbf1\) but lies in \(\ker L_G\), giving left side zero and right side six.

The proof establishes only \[Q_H(L_G^{+/2}x)\ge x^\top P_{\operatorname{range}L_G}x.\] Thus \(x\in(\ker L_G)^\perp\) is a sufficient corrected assumption. Even for a connected graph, the set \(T\) on p. 18 as literally defined contains arbitrary kernel directions and is not contained in the Euclidean unit ball. Restricting the chaining domain to the range leaves the represented energy unchanged whenever the underlying graph has the same nullspace as \(H\). The proof on p. 19 explicitly invokes Proposition C.2 to assert \(T\subseteq B_2^n\), the hypothesis needed to apply Lemma C.1 in the proof of Theorem 4.1. This false statement and its invalid application therefore affect a core derivation and support Major. The range restriction verifies a local domain correction, not the remaining chaining argument. Disconnected inputs are allowed by the paper; connectivity must not be silently imposed.
# Overall impact, open scope and conclusion

Problems 1, 2 and 4 invalidate steps directly supporting the main algorithmic guarantee. Problem 3 independently invalidates the advertised rank-dependent runtime simplification. Each supports Major through its stated core dependency; the shortness of a local repair does not change the impact of the original claim or derivation. The general sparsification objective, imported quantum primitives, and possibility of a corrected algorithm remain open within this review.

The Section 5 substitutions also retain unresolved accuracy dependence: inserting \(M=\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^2)\) into the stated classical mincut and flow runtimes yields respectively \(\widetilde O(rn^2/\varepsilon^2)\) and \(\widetilde O(rn^{3/2}/\varepsilon^3)\) under direct composition. No alternative accuracy-independent downstream algorithm was verified. This is recorded as Needs Evidence for those corollaries, rather than a claim that the asserted algorithms cannot exist.

A bounded search of the official proceedings page and arXiv submission history found the latter listing v1 (3 May 2025); no later correction was identified in the material consulted [Retained latex: \cite{record}]. This is not an exhaustive errata search, and no author adoption is claimed.

Title: Technical Verification of
Alberta Wells Dataset
# Identity and scope

Assignment 0112 / I25-43481 concerns P. Seth, M. Lin, B. D. Yaw, J. Boutot, M. Kang and D. Rolnick, Alberta Wells Dataset: Pinpointing Oil and Gas Wells from Satellite Imagery, PMLR 267 (2025), 54030–54057 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed version is the supplied 28-page proceedings PDF; page numbers below are its printed pages. Embedded Appendices A–E are present even though the supplied acquisition metadata’s automated appendix flag is false.

The source tree inspected is `RolnickLab/Alberta_Wells_Dataset`, commit `12fc71bc0be5aab5b1cc1255af16cedb906fd3d3`. The review covers data construction and splitting, label geometry, Tables 2–13, the main performance interpretation, relevant datasheet entries, and selected data-loading and evaluation code. In particular, `trainer/FRCNN_Od_Agent.py`, `trainer/Seg_Trainer_lrs.py`, the binary segmentation loader and inference configuration, and averaging utilities were read statically.

No author code, training, checkpoint inference or data-processing pipeline was executed. The large image/HDF5 dataset, per-seed prediction files and experiment-to-table logs were not present in the assigned source tree and were not downloaded. These are explicit limits on numerical reproduction, not evidence that those materials do not exist.
# Task definitions and checked construction

The labels are generated from recorded well coordinates, using standardized 90-metre sites: disks for binary segmentation and boxes for detection (Section 3.3, p. 5; Appendix B.7, p. 19). Consequently, segmentation measures agreement with a constructed well-proximity mask, not independently traced physical infrastructure boundaries. The paper describes this construction; it is not itself an undisclosed annotation error.

Algorithm 1 (p. 4) assigns spatial clusters, rather than individual random patches, to splits. Selecting small clusters within every larger region creates a within-Alberta spatial holdout, not an evaluation on entirely unseen provinces. The paper does not supply an independently verified minimum train–test distance. The review found no demonstrated duplicate-patch leakage from the supplied evidence, but did not verify the actual spatial memberships.

The split counts \(167436+9463+11789=188688\) and the well counts \(194231+8243+10973=213447\) reconcile across Tables 2 and 9. The individual-well columns of Tables 11–13 also match those split totals. The inclusion of inactive wells and the NIR ablations are identifiable experimental contrasts; the reported directions of the NIR differences are not contradicted by simple arithmetic. Confidence-interval construction and historical execution provenance remain unverified.
# Supported finding
Problem 1 (Incommensurate and conditional metrics do not establish a better task framing — Minor).
## Source claim and dependency

Section 5.2 (p. 7) interprets lower object-detection performance than segmentation performance as evidence that segmentation may be a better real-world framing. Section 5.1 also discusses the segmentation recall as capturing actual well instances. Tables 4 and 5 provide different endpoints: mask IoU/precision/recall/F1 versus box overlap and confidence-ranked average precision.

The first conclusion is a proposed comparative interpretation, not a theorem, but its evidentiary step is invalid: these endpoint values are not on a common operational scale. A segmentation pixel recall is not a fraction of individually localized well sites, and a box-overlap average does not measure either that quantity or detection AP.
## Static implementation and exact check

For a concrete permitted input, take one unit-square target \(G=[0,1]\times[0,1]\) and two same-class predicted unit squares shifted horizontally by \(d_1=1/9\) and \(d_2=2/3\). For \(0\le d<1\), \[\operatorname{IoU}(G,G+(d,0))=\frac{1-d}{1+d}.\] Their IoUs are exactly \(4/5\) and \(1/5\). The same unchanged predictions give \[J_{0.1}=\frac12,\qquad J_{0.5}=\frac45.\] Arbitrarily many additional disjoint same-class false-positive boxes leave both conditional means unchanged. Thus increasing scores across thresholds cannot establish improved detection accuracy or missed-well performance. These are exact geometric calculations, independently checked with rational arithmetic, not a run of the authors’ metric code.

The segmentation trainer computes per-batch metrics and feeds them to `AverageValueMeter`. The supplied ResNet50 inference configuration sets `bs_evalt`=1, so the corresponding evaluation path averages image-level scores. Its recall concerns foreground pixels and the treatment of empty masks; it cannot be reinterpreted as a count of detected individual wells without an instance-extraction rule and matching criterion.
## Counterevidence, impact and correction bounds

Conditional IoU is useful for describing localization among qualifying overlaps, and the authors separately report AP, which is intended to penalize detection errors. No defect in the library is alleged. Nor do these calculations establish that all published numbers came from the currently pinned tree. The paper-level comparison is nevertheless unsupported even if each task-specific number was computed correctly.

The correction is to label the endpoints and aggregation explicitly, restrict comparisons to the same endpoint, and evaluate both task framings on a common well-localization outcome before ranking their real-world utility. For segmentation this requires a specified conversion from masks to site candidates, followed by the same matching and false-positive criterion as detection. That new comparison was not performed here. The demonstrated damage is to a local comparative interpretation; the dataset’s existence, coverage and value are not refuted. Minor is therefore the supported severity.
# Unresolved numerical and provenance questions
## Average-precision columns: Needs Evidence

Tables 5 and 6 label the smaller column \(\mathrm{mAP}_{50}\) and the larger one \(\mathrm{mAP}_{50:95}\); for DETR the values are 15.22 and 38.45 (p. 7, visually checked). The prose on p. 8 explicitly interprets the larger value as improvement under broader IoU thresholds. The detection trainer logs distinct `map` and `map_50` keys, in that order (lines 50–54 and 208–210). A transposition of table labels is a plausible explanation, but raw outputs and the table-construction step are unavailable. This review does not infer a corrected column mapping from convention alone, or use an unproved universal AP monotonicity assertion as a substitute for tracing the actual evaluator. Numerical conclusions tied to those labels remain unresolved.
## Historical methods and denominator: Needs Evidence

Section 4.2 (p. 6) describes AdamW for all detection models, whereas the pinned FRCNN trainer initializes SGD with momentum and Nesterov acceleration (lines 39–43). This is a documented paper–current-source discrepancy, not proof of which optimizer produced the published experiments.

The positive test-patch counts in Table 10 and the detailed Table 11 sum to 5984, while Table 2 gives 5894. The well total remains 10973. Checking the actual release split would resolve the patch denominator; a speculative choice between the two numbers is not offered as a correction. No standalone typographical finding is assigned.

Without image-level outputs, this review cannot validate benchmark variances, inactive-well subset performance, unlabeled-well error rates, or independent real-world site recall. These pending questions do not raise the supported severity.
# Conclusion and version status

The retrieved arXiv history lists v3, dated 25 May 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}]; that metadata check did not replace the proceedings version reviewed here. No erratum was verified. The current pinned source is separately identified, and any future repair must retain that distinction.

Title: Scientific Review of
Contextual Linear Bandits with Delay as Payoff
# Identity and scope

Paper 0113 / I25-43482, by Mengxiao Zhang, Yingfei Wang and Haipeng Luo, is reviewed in the published ICML 2025 version, PMLR 267:76246–76272 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page references use the PDF’s printed pages 1–27. The supplied original and manifest were read and hash-checked. Sections 2–5, Algorithms 1–5 and Appendices A–D were inspected, with emphasis on the concentration and elimination arguments. No released repository is present in the assigned manifest. The original contains the appendices; availability of a separate OpenReview supplement remains unresolved after the acquisition-stage access failure.

The central construction uses a volumetric spanner \(S_m\) with \(|S_m|=3n\): each action has a representation \(a=\sum_i\lambda_i a_{m,i}\) with \(\|\lambda\|_2\leq1\). Each spanner action is pulled \(q=2^m\) times per epoch. Losses satisfy \(u_t=\langle a_t,\theta\rangle+\eta_t\in[0,1]\), with zero-mean noise, \(a_t,\theta\) in the nonnegative unit ball, and delay \(D u_t\). The review uses independent noises, a stronger condition than needed to expose the failure, and no misspecification.
# Supported findings

Problem 1 (Major: unjustified norm scaling of confidence radii).  Algorithm 1, equations (7)–(11), p. 4, and Algorithm 3, equations (22)–(26), p. 12, use radii \(\beta\|a\|_2/\sqrt q\) or \(\beta\|a\|_2/\sqrt{c_m(a)}\). Lemma A.2, pp. 11 and 13, attributes the corresponding concentration statement to Azuma’s inequality. The scalar bounded-noise model on p. 3 does not supply the additional factor \(\|a\|_2\).
#### Decisive construction.

Set \[n=1,\quad K=3,\quad T=1000,\quad D=1,\quad
\theta=1,\quad A=\{\rho,2\rho,3\rho\},\quad \rho=10^{-3}.\] On every pull of \(a\), draw an independent Bernoulli random variable of mean \(a\). Thus \(u\in[0,1]\), \(\mathbb E[u-a]=0\), and \(d=u\). All actions and \(\theta\) satisfy the specified norm and positivity restrictions. Choose \(S_1=A\) and represent its members by the coordinate vectors of \(\mathbb R^3\). This is an admissible volumetric spanner with exactly \(3n\) members and representation norms equal to one.

In epoch \(m=1\), use the permitted round-robin order \((\rho,2\rho,3\rho,\rho,2\rho,3\rho)\). At its end, both observations of the first two actions belong to \(C_1\): their pull times are at most five and \(D=1\). Consider the event \(E\) that exactly one of the two outcomes for \(\rho\) equals one and all four outcomes for the other actions equal zero. Its probability is exactly \[\mathbb P(E)=2\rho(1-\rho)(1-2\rho)^2(1-3\rho)^2
=0.001978093806191928.\] All realized payoffs in this event have been observed by the end of round six, including the last zero payoff. With \(\beta=\sqrt{2\log(3\cdot1000^3)}=6.606342123\ldots\), the published formulas give \[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{LCB}_1(\rho)
&=\tfrac12-\beta\rho/\sqrt2
=0.4953286107\ldots,\\
\operatorname{UCB}_1(2\rho)
&=\beta(2\rho)/\sqrt2
=0.0093427786\ldots .\end{aligned}\] The first action is uniquely optimal in the loss model, yet Algorithm 1 eliminates it: its LCB exceeds the other UCB and the guess is \(B=1\). There is no zero-denominator convention involved in these two estimates. For the optimal action, the empirical deviation is \(0.499\), against a reported radius of \(0.0046713893\ldots\). The event probability exceeds the \(2/T^2=0.000002\) failure budget used in the proof by a factor exceeding 989.
#### Logical consequence and counterevidence.

This is a failure of the asserted confidence mechanism and its optimal-action protection, not a finite-instance numerical refutation of an unspecified big-\(O\) constant. Event 1 itself, equations (32)–(33), has wider bounds without the action norms. It consequently does not justify the narrower intervals used in Lemma A.3. The absolute-value bars on the coefficients in Event 1 are present in the actual PDF; a contrary text-extraction impression was rejected after visual inspection.

Section 5 normalizes experimental actions to unit norm, so those particular experiments avoid this counterexample. That experimental restriction does not change the theorem’s unit-ball domain. A noise assumption scaling with \(\|a\|_2\) would be materially stronger than the stated bounded scalar noise model.
#### Dependency and bounded repair.

The confidence intervals feed Lemma A.3, the elimination bounds A.4–A.6, Theorem A.1, its special case Theorem 3.3, and the contextual reduction’s invocation of A.1 in Theorem 4.1. Appendix B also invokes this confidence analysis. The demonstrated failure therefore concerns the core theoretical contribution.

For bounded scalar noise, radii \(\beta/\sqrt q\) and \(\beta/\sqrt{c_m(a)}\), with the usual simultaneous-probability choice of \(\beta\), are defensible. Propagating them as \(\sum_i|\lambda_i|r_i\) gives the spanner confidence bounds. This repairs the particular concentration defect; it does not certify all later accounting, boundary cases, or the complete stated regret theorem.

Problem 2 (Major: the reward proof uses a different aggregation rule).  Algorithm 4, equation (50), p. 21, defines \[U_m(a)=\max\{U_{m,1}(a),U_{m,2}(a)\}.\] Lemma B.3, p. 22, instead explicitly assumes a minimum and uses \(U_m(a)\leq U_{m,2}(a)\). Lemma B.4, p. 24, likewise infers a component lower bound from survival that is valid for a minimum but not for a maximum.
#### Complete comparison check.

Conditional on both component bounds being valid, a maximum is indeed an upper confidence bound. However, \[\max\{x,y\}\leq y \quad\text{holds only if }x\leq y,\] a restriction neither required by Algorithm 4 nor established in B.3. For example \(x=0.8\), \(y=0.6\) falsifies the used comparison. These numbers illustrate the invalid algebra; they are not presented as a fully specified bandit trajectory.

More directly, the proof’s non-elimination premise with \(\varepsilon=0\) is \(U_m(a)> B\) (and the corresponding comparator condition). A maximum exceeding \(B\) need not have its first component exceed \(B\). Thus B.4’s inference \(U_{m,1}(a)\geq B\) also requires the opposite aggregation rule. Both of these failures persist as logical mismatches even after granting valid component confidence intervals, so they are distinct from Problem 1.
#### Impact, alternatives, and correction boundary.

Theorem B.1, pp. 22 and 25, directly combines B.3 and B.5; B.5 in turn uses the component bound in B.4. The reward guarantee and the stated loss/reward comparison depend on this chain. Its core role supports Major even if the intended repair is a one-word change.

A transcription error is plausible. Replacing the maximum by the minimum preserves optimism when both component upper bounds are valid, and it provides both comparisons above. That local repair is verified algebraically. A different proof might also bound the maximum rule. Neither a complete repaired theorem nor an impossibility result is established here. The supplied materials do not determine which rule generated the experiments.
# Additional coverage and unresolved work

The delayed-loss construction’s replacement of missing observations by zero or one, and its sign-sensitive use of spanner coefficients, are conceptually appropriate once valid component bounds are available. No independent defect is claimed for those ideas.

Several remaining proof details require evidence or further derivation. On p. 18 the discarded early-epoch block is bounded using \(\sum_m2^m\Delta_{\max}\) although a complete epoch has \(3n\,2^m\) pulls. An explicit argument removing that action-count factor is needed; this review does not assert that the final rate is thereby disproved. The contextual proof on p. 26 also transfers instance-dependent gaps between empirical reduced actions and population actions without a fully audited perturbation argument. These pending concerns do not increase the supported severity.

The algorithms need conventions for \(c_m(a)=0\), final partial epochs and small arguments of logarithms. The concrete counterexample above avoids the relevant zero denominators. No separate finding is assigned to notation or typographical details alone.

The empirical scope is synthetic, non-contextual, with \(K=70\), \(n\in\{6,8,10\}\), beta-distributed payoffs, eight seeds and omitted guess \(B\) (pp. 8–9). The paper expressly discloses this simplification. The figures were not independently reproduced, and no claim of empirical failure follows from the proof findings.

The arXiv metadata for 2502.12528 reports v2 dated 20 February 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}]. This is not a verified later correction to the inspected proceedings version. A bounded search did not yield a confirmed erratum; an inaccessible subsequent-paper lead was not relied upon.
# Conclusion
Item | Judgment | Repair / remaining work
Norm-scaled intervals | Major | Local radius repair supported; complete theorem pending
Reward max/min rule | Major | Local minimum-rule repair supported; full analysis pending
Epoch/gap accounting | Needs Evidence | Additional derivation required
Scientific decision | Pending | No acceptance or author adoption

Title: Scientific Review of
Lightweight Protocols for Distributed
Private Quantile Estimation
# Identity, material and assumptions

Paper 0114 / I25-43483 is the ICML 2025 paper by Anders Aamand, Fabrizio Boninsegna, Abigail Gentle, Jacob Imola and Rasmus Pagh, PMLR 267:27–58 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. References below use printed PDF pages 1–32. The immutable supplied PDF and manifest were read and checked. The supplied source snapshot is pinned to `1301f6cdf662befb443dbfa7a94394b6a87bbdcf` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. It is selective: dataset and experimental-result binaries listed as excluded in the manifest were not reacquired.

The paper estimates one quantile of a fixed dataset \(X\in[B]^n\), with each user queried at most once. The adaptive local protocol privately reports one comparison bit; the shuffle protocol groups users into \(r=\log_2B\) disjoint batches. The review inspected the definitions, empirical-CDF drift proof, the noisy-search reduction, the potential argument, lower-bound reductions, shuffle analysis and relevant implementation paths. External sharp-capacity and nonadaptive lower-bound results were not fully rederived.
# Core confidence dependence

Problem 1 (Major: the shuffle analysis drops a nonvanishing tail term).  Theorem 1.4, p. 3, and its restatement G.6, p. 25, give \[n=O\!\left((\alpha^{-2}+\varepsilon^{-2})\log B
 \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)\log(\log B/\beta)}\right)\] for success probability \(1-\beta\). The proof enters this bound through the high-\(\varepsilon_L\) simplification of Theorem G.3, p. 24. That simplification discards a term already present in Lemma G.2.
#### A complete protocol-level check.

Fix \[B=4,\quad r=2,\quad \alpha=1/10,\quad
 \varepsilon=1/2,\quad \delta=1/100,
 \qquad x_1=\cdots=x_n=4,\] where \(n\) is even and tends to infinity. Grant the proof its correct batch-size calibration, rather than exploiting the different total-\(n\) formula printed in Algorithm 3: \[\begin{aligned}
&s=n/2,\quad c=80\log(4/\delta),\quad
 e^{\varepsilon_L}=\varepsilon^2s/c,\\
&q_n=\frac{1}{1+e^{\varepsilon_L}}
     =\frac{c}{\varepsilon^2s+c}.
\end{aligned}\] Here \(q_n\) is the probability that a zero comparison is reported as one. For all sufficiently large \(n\), \(\varepsilon_L>1\) and the condition \(\varepsilon>16\sqrt{\log(4/\delta)/s}\) in Lemma G.5 holds. The data lie in \([B]\), every user is queried once, and permutation of this constant dataset has no effect.

The first midpoint of Algorithm 3 is 2. All its true comparisons are zero. If every one of the \(s\) independent randomized responses is one, the debiased estimate exceeds \(1/2\), so the algorithm sets \(R=1\). Its second midpoint, and returned value, is then 1 regardless of the second batch’s responses. This is an incorrect answer: \(F_X(1)=F_X(2)=0\), so the interval in the paper’s own success predicate misses \((0.4,0.6)\). It is also incorrect under the conventional quantile-value predicate. Shuffling preserves the all-one message multiset. Therefore \[\Pr(\text{failure})\ \geq\ q_n^{n/2}
 =\exp[-\Theta(n\log n)].\] For the confidence sequence \(\beta_L=\exp(-L^2)\), (2.1) with the other parameters fixed prescribes \(n=O(L)\). For every fixed hidden constant and sufficiently large \(L\), the event in (2.5) has probability greater than \(\beta_L\), since \(O(L\log L)=o(L^2)\). Rounding \(n\) to an even integer does not change this conclusion. This is an asymptotic check against every fixed constant, not a numerical comparison to an unknown constant.
#### Impact and alternatives.

The invalid step links G.3 directly to G.6 and the headline shuffle guarantee. It therefore warrants Major. The construction refutes this protocol’s stated unrestricted confidence dependence, not the existence of every conceivable shuffle protocol with such a rate. Fixed-confidence results, or a suitably restricted joint regime of \(\delta\) and \(\beta\), may survive. Section 2 (p. 4) describes \(\beta=1/\operatorname{poly}(B)\) as the typically interesting regime, but neither Theorem 1.4 nor G.6 imposes that restriction. The counterexample addresses their unrestricted statement; a restricted theorem would need to specify its joint parameter regime. This confidence-dependence counterexample does not refute the intended adaptive LDP upper bound or adaptivity separation.

A full correction must retain the tail term and recheck finite-population sampling and parameter regimes. The example proves the necessary condition \(n\log n=\Omega(\log(1/\beta))\) for this calibration. Retaining the Bernstein term gives a conservative local sufficient-batch condition with an additional \(\alpha^{-1}\log(1/\beta')\) term; this review does not certify a complete revised shuffle theorem.
# Implementation and output-contract findings

Problem 2 (Minor: the pinned endpoint selector always chooses left).  Algorithm 2, lines 4–5, p. 17, selects the left endpoint when \((q-W(j-1))/w_j\leq q\), otherwise the right endpoint. In `BaySS/bayesian_learning.py`, the function `get_interval_coin_from_quantile` passes the inclusive \(W(j)\) to `round_interval_to_coin`. The latter computes \((q-W(j))/w_j-q\).
Because the selected interval satisfies \(W(j)\geq q\) and \(w_j>0\), the implemented expression is always nonpositive for \(q>0\). Thus its right-endpoint branch cannot be taken in exact arithmetic.

A reachable state demonstrates a substantive query change. Start from three uniform interval weights and take update parameter \(\alpha=1/10\). After the first private bit is zero, the code’s update gives \[(w_1,w_2,w_3)=(4/15,\,1/3,\,2/5).\] At \(q=1/2\), the next selected interval is the second. The intended ratio is \((1/2-4/15)/(1/3)=7/10>1/2\), selecting right; the code’s flag is \(-4/5\), selecting left. The first private outcome has positive probability under randomized response, so this is not an unreachable weight vector.

Passing \(W(j)-w_j\) instead supplies the intended left cumulative mass and fixes this branch algebraically. No author code was run. The inspected experimental driver calls this mechanism, but no immutable execution-to-figure link was supplied. A different heuristic could still work empirically; neither a score reduction nor invalid local privacy follows from this query-selection discrepancy. The supported finding is a local implementation/fidelity defect, with empirical magnitude unresolved.

Problem 3 (Minor: the stated unary-encoding baseline consumes twice its budget).  Appendix D, pp. 14–15, describes one-hot encoding with independent symmetric randomized response on every bit, each retaining its input with probability \(p=e^\varepsilon/(1+e^\varepsilon)\), and describes the resulting protocol as \(\varepsilon\)-LDP.

Two possible values of one user’s data encode as \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) at a two-category level. The event that the released vector is \((1,0)\) has probabilities \(p^2\) and \((1-p)^2\), respectively. Their ratio is \[\frac{p^2}{(1-p)^2}=e^{2\varepsilon}>e^\varepsilon
 \qquad(\varepsilon>0).\] Thus the described symmetric mechanism is \(2\varepsilon\)-LDP in the worst case. Per-bit parameter \(\varepsilon/2\) fixes the user-level guarantee exactly and changes this baseline’s rate only by a constant factor.

This does not establish a privacy failure in the experiments: the pinned `hierarchical_mechanism/ldp_protocol.py` requests `UEClient(...,use_oue=True)`, an optimized unary-encoding path, rather than the symmetric construction analyzed above. The main proposed algorithm’s single comparison bit is also unaffected. The scope and severity are consequently local.

Problem 4 (Major: the formal quantile contract has no legal output on an allowed input).  Section 2, p. 4, requires \([F_X(m),F_X(m+1)]\) to intersect \((q-\alpha,q+\alpha)\), while Definitions 2.2–2.4, p. 5, constrain \(m\) to \([B]=\{1,\ldots,B\}\). The proof of Theorem 1.1, p. 8, returns \(j+1\) after establishing bounds at \(j,j+1\); Appendix C, p. 14, returns \(j\).

For \(B=4\), all \(x_i=1\), \(q=1/2\) and \(\alpha=1/10\), every allowed \(m\) has \(F_X(m)=F_X(m+1)=1\). Hence no allowed output meets the stated contract, regardless of sample size or privacy. This is an output-domain defect, not a noise limitation.

Two coherent conventions are possible: output a gap index in \(\{0,\ldots,B-1\}\) with \(F_X(0)=0\), or output a quantile value in \([B]\) and use \([F_X(m-1),F_X(m)]\). The latter gives a valid answer \(m=1\) in this example. Definitions 2.2–2.4 supply the success contract for the central empirical, statistical and shuffle guarantees. An allowed dataset for which every legal output fails makes those as-written guarantees unattainable, independently of privacy or sample complexity, and therefore supports Major. A uniform indexing shift can preserve the intended statistical objective and rates, but this possible repair does not validate the original success statement. All algorithms, padding reductions and success evaluators must use the chosen convention consistently; that full conversion and the resulting complete guarantees have not been verified. No impossibility of the intended adaptivity separation is asserted.
# Other checks and limits

The first-half random-permutation drift argument in Lemmas 3.1 and 4.1 has the expected martingale structure: the fraction of remaining zeros has conditional mean equal to its current value and increments at most \(1/n\) during the first half of a \(2n\)-element permutation. The stated maximum-deviation bound and union bound support this scoped step. Randomized response maps a probability \(q\) to \((e^\varepsilon q+1-q)/(e^\varepsilon+1)\), with slope \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\); the reduction’s small-\(\varepsilon\) scaling is consistent.

The main potential argument’s separation into good and bad queries and the information-theoretic lower-bound constructions were inspected, but the sharp external constants and every reduction detail were not independently certified. No issue is asserted merely because those external arguments were not reproduced.

Further evidence is needed for the shuffle argument’s use of remaining-user CDFs through all batches, since Lemma 3.1 explicitly covers only the first half. Algorithm 3’s total-\(n\) calibration also differs from the batch-size calibration in the proof. The pinned utility includes a \(\log B\) factor; this does not by itself certify its complete privacy configuration. These pending points add no severity to the demonstrated finding.

The experiments disclose use of all users, a tuned update parameter and 200 runs. Their error-bar formula on p. 27 is the standard error of a Bernoulli sample average. No claim of empirical reversal is made. The excluded data and result binaries prevent a provenance-complete reproduction, and author-code execution was prohibited. The arXiv metadata lists only v1, 5 February 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}]; no later correction was verified.

Title: Scientific review of Data-Juicer Sandbox
# Identity, materials, and scope

Paper 0115, I25-43484: D. Chen, H. Wang, Y. Huang, C. Ge, Y. Li, B. Ding, and J. Zhou, Data-Juicer Sandbox: A Feedback-Driven Suite for Multimodal Data-Model Co-development, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 9198–9230 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed supplied original has 33 pages; all page references below use its printed pages 1–33. Its SHA-256 is recorded in Appendix 5 (#app:record).

The review covers the Probe–Analyze–Refine workflow, the cost/transfer argument in Section 3.2.4 and Appendix C, the metric definition, training controls, combination and scaling experiments, and the published tables. The pinned source snapshot [Retained latex: \cite{code}] was inspected statically for the image–text filtering operator and project documentation. It is an October 2026 snapshot, not an established historical experiment commit. No author code was executed, imported, or installed. Original training datasets, checkpoints, per-seed predictions and full experiment logs were not reconstructed. Numerical checks below are independent reviewer calculations.

The system samples operator-conditioned pools, trains inexpensive probe models, combines useful operators, and tests repetition/scaling. Its empirical evidence includes several modalities, matched pool sizes in specified experiments, repeated seeds, and explicitly reported negative combination effects. These are meaningful counterweights to any claim that all conclusions fail.
# Definitions and dependence

Equation reference: eq:valid. Write \(X_r=\Delta_{\rm pool}\) for the gain of a probe trained using sampling fraction \(r\), and \(\mu=\mathbb E\Delta_{\rm full}\). Appendix C.1 (pp. 16–17) assumes bounded \(X_r\in[a_r,b_r]\) and, for positive operators, \(\mathbb E X_r\leq\mu\). The displayed one-sided inequality \[\Pr(X_r-\mu\geq\epsilon)
 \leq \Pr(X_r-\mathbb EX_r\geq\epsilon)
 \leq \exp\!\left[-\frac{2\epsilon^2}{(b_r-a_r)^2}\right]
 \] is valid under these assumptions. It need not be an average of independent training runs for this bounded-single-variable inequality to hold. The suspect step is what is inferred about \(r\) and about useful full-scale feedback, not the algebra of [eq:valid] (#eq:valid).

Section 3.2.4 (p. 5) uses this argument to support a cost reduction from \(M T_{\rm full}\) to \((1+mr)T_{\rm full}\), assuming probe cost proportional to \(r\) and informative transfer. The arithmetic cost identity is conditional and unobjectionable; a quantitative accuracy–cost guarantee additionally needs a justified relation between \(r\) and the distribution of \(X_r\).
# Supported problems

Problem 1 (Major: variance does not establish the claimed transfer rate).  Claim and location. Section 3.2.4, p. 5, and Appendix C.1, pp. 16–17, conclude that the probability of error exceeding \(\epsilon\) decreases exponentially as \(r\) increases. The final paragraph of C.1 argues that increasing \(r\) reduces variance, that variance is positively related to \((b-a)^2\), and hence that the Hoeffding right-hand side decreases.

Decisive check. Even granting decreasing variance, the range need not shrink. Here is an exact finite uniform-subsampling example satisfying all stated probabilistic assumptions. Take a population of \(20\) distinct items, full-data gain identically \(1/2\), and \(\epsilon=1/4\). For a uniformly sampled singleton, let the probe gain be \(2/5\) on ten items and \(3/5\) on ten items. For a uniformly sampled unordered pair, let the gain be \(9/10\) on exactly the pair \(\{0,1\}\) and \(9/20\) on each other pair. These gains specify one training-response function of the selected pool and its size; no stated stability or additivity hypothesis excludes it. All gains are positive and bounded. Direct enumeration gives \[\begin{aligned}
 r_1&=1/20,&\mathbb E X_{r_1}&=1/2,&
 \operatorname{Var}(X_{r_1})&=1/100,\\
 r_2&=2/20,&\mathbb E X_{r_2}&=1719/3800<1/2,&
 \operatorname{Var}(X_{r_2})&=15309/14440000<1/100.\end{aligned}\] Thus both the positive-gain mean ordering and the stated variance decrease hold; the absolute-mean ordering also holds because gains are positive. Nevertheless the support width increases from \(1/5\) to \(9/20\). The right side of [eq:valid] (#eq:valid) increases from \(0.043937\) to \(0.539408\), and the actual tail increases from \(0\) to \(1/190\). This contradicts the asserted implication from the stated assumptions, including a monotone decrease, before any exponential rate can be justified.

Moreover, an overestimation tail does not establish useful ranking or two-sided transfer. Deterministic operator gains \[(X^A,\Delta^A_{\rm full})=(0.1,0.8),\qquad
 (X^B,\Delta^B_{\rm full})=(0.5,0.6)\] satisfy positive gains, the assumed mean ordering and zero probe variance. Both upper-tail errors are zero for every positive \(\epsilon\), yet the probe ranking is reversed. This is a logical limitation of the supplied criterion, not a claim that these numbers describe the paper’s models.

Alternatives and counterevidence. The authors may intend variance as an informal proxy for a concentration scale or may have an empirically stable training regime in mind. Neither interpretation supplies a relationship between the support width, bias, sample fraction, and full-model ranking. The reported successful transfers remain experimental observations. Appendix location and the absence of a named theorem do not remove the dependence: the main text repeats this quantitative rate in its central cost argument.

Impact and correction bounds. The exponential transfer justification and any resulting certified choice of \(r\) are unsupported. This is Major because cheap, informative feedback is a central claimed contribution and its quantitative justification uses the invalid step. It does not refute the implementation, cost identity, or measured benchmark scores. A defensible local correction is to retain [eq:valid] (#eq:valid) only as a conditional one-sided bound and remove the claimed \(r\)-rate. A useful replacement guarantee would require explicit bias/stability and concentration assumptions, with their validity established; no complete replacement theorem is certified here. Evidence: `source_p17.png` and `independent_checks.py/json`.

Problem 2 (Minor: reported aggregate and defined aggregate disagree).  Claim and location. Appendix D.2, Eq. (1), p. 17, defines overall relative change as \[R=\frac{\sum_i(s_i-s'_i)}{\sum_i s'_i}.\] Table 10, p. 27, reports a \(+2.12\%\) average change for MGM-2B using the four displayed metrics. The corresponding claim also appears in Tables 2 and the scaling discussion.

Complete calculation. The displayed baseline vector is \((59.2,51.6,1334,302)\) and the Data-Juicer vector is \((62.08,52.32,1323.37,311.07)\). Their total difference is \(2.04\), so Eq. (1) yields \[100R=100(2.04/1746.8)=0.116785\%.\] Instead, the mean of the four separate relative improvements is \[\frac{100}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{4}\frac{s_i-s'_i}{s'_i}
 =2.116668\%,\] which rounds to the published \(2.12\%\). These functionals are generally different: the former weights relative changes by baseline score magnitude and changes under independent changes of metric units.

Alternatives and impact. If the authors normalized every input score by its own baseline before applying Eq. (1), the reported number is reconciled, but this preprocessing is not the stated definition of \(s_i\). The exact numerical agreement strongly favors a formula/documentation mismatch, rather than a demonstrated false score. This is Minor: the aggregate must be specified consistently, but the four component measurements and the direction of their combined gain are not refuted. A verified local repair for this table is to state the mean-relative formula above. Whether every other aggregate, operator ranking and plot used that same formula requires original calculation records and is not certified. Evidence: Eq. (1) visually inspected on original p. 17; Table 10 transcription and independent arithmetic in `independent_checks.json`.
# Unresolved evidence and overall impact

Cost accounting. Tables 3 and 13 (pp. 9 and 29) list \(7.68\alpha\) EFLOPs for each of two successive Data-Juicer stages. Table 12 explicitly says the 228k stage further self-distills the 147k-stage model. Comparing \(167.3\alpha\) for VEnhancer with one such stage gives \(21.784\), consistent with the approximately \(22\)-fold statement; adding both listed stages gives \(10.892\) under the same-factor assumption. However, these are estimates from inference FLOPs multiplied by an unspecified \(\alpha\), not a verified, common accounting of end-to-end training. Teacher/reward computation, the upstream T2V-Turbo checkpoint, probe runs, and architecture-specific training factors matter. A per-incremental-stage interpretation remains possible. This is Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated reversal of model efficiency. Supply the intended cost boundary and actual stage-specific accounting before treating the factor as a total workflow saving.

Empirical scope. Held-out benchmark gains, operator selection and diversity interpretations were checked against the disclosed protocols, not reproduced. Correlated proxy attributes and combined-operator effects are not a causal identification of diversity. Negative combination results are acknowledged in the paper. No universal improvement guarantee was inferred from them. Differences between probe models and full-scale models, reuse of validation feedback, uncertainty across many candidate recipes, and final independent evaluation need experiment-level records to quantify.

Source provenance and versions. The pinned tree contains the inspected filter implementation, but the linked `docs/Sandbox.md` is absent from that tree. The current DJ-SORA document is not a substitute for the historical Sandbox runner. No scientific defect is inferred merely from that absence. The supplied manifest records unresolved separate-supplement availability after an OpenReview 403 response. The original contains its appendices. Official arXiv metadata [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}] lists v3 dated 4 June 2025; only version metadata was checked, not a full version diff. No verified erratum or author adoption is asserted.

report: Abstract: The published dynamic allocation rule can assign more than 100 percent pruning to a block, even with positive entropy scores and an exactly satisfied compensation budget. Date: Initial review, 24 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of multi-structure LLM pruning
# Identity and inspected scope

Paper 0116, I25-43485: M. Yang, S. Lin, C. Li, and X. Chang, Let LLM Tell What to Prune and How Much to Prune, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 70833–70849 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied original contains 17 pages; page numbers below are its printed pages 1–17.

The main method (Sections 3.1–3.4), experiments (Section 4), and Appendices A–C were inspected, including block grouping, compensation, dynamic ratios, row/column scoring, attention-group consistency, and ablations. All four files in the pinned public tree [Retained latex: \cite{code}] were read statically. They contain evaluation/data-loading code and a README, but no implementation of the proposed pruning procedure. The README explicitly attributes its released models to reruns on different hardware and acknowledges seed-dependent differences from the paper. This is a recorded provenance qualification, not evidence that either set of reported results is false.

The review uses independent exact arithmetic, not author-code execution or new model experiments. Benchmark training/evaluation, latency measurements, external model downloads and statistical reruns were not performed. The original and supplied-file hashes were checked.
# Definitions and checked reasoning

For \(N\) blocks let \(s_i\) denote the entropy difference in Eq. (1), p. 3. Equation (4), p. 4, divides scores at \(\mu_s\pm\alpha\sigma_s\) into \(S_L,S_M,S_H\). High-score blocks are preserved, medium-score blocks receive \(p_{\rm low}\), and Eq. (5) calculates their leftover pruning load. Candidate full-block removals \(F\) are the \(|S_H|\) lowest-score members of \(S_L\); candidate layer removals \(E\) depend on \(S_M\). The depth-first search minimizes excess compensation subject to covering the leftover, preferring more full-block removals among ties.

Equation reference: eq:allocation. For \(G\) remaining blocks, Eq. (8), p. 5, assigns \[p_g=\frac{G\omega_g}{\sum_h\omega_h}\widehat p,\qquad
 \omega_g=(\bar s/s_g)^\beta,\qquad
 \widehat p=\frac{G p_{\rm target}-p_{\rm compensation}^{*}+p_{\rm leftover}}{G}.
 \] For positive weights this preserves the sum \(\sum_g p_g=G\widehat p\). It does not by itself enforce the necessary individual constraint \(0\leq p_g\leq1\). The following example tests precisely that missing implication.

The Gaussian entropy formula’s final expression, \(H=\log\sigma+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)+\tfrac12\), and Figure 4’s approximate scores were independently checked. No substantive defect was found in that finite example. The output-entropy difference is treated here as the paper’s operational heuristic; no general causal or rank-preservation theorem is assumed.
# Supported problems

Problem 1 (Major: a reachable allocation exceeds the feasible pruning range).  Claim and location. Section 3.2, Eqs. (4)–(8), pp. 4–5, and Algorithm 1 purport to assign a pruning ratio to each block while meeting the target budget. Dynamic allocation is a named central contribution.

Parameters and assumptions. Take eight equal-size blocks with scores \[(10^{-6},2\cdot10^{-6},3\cdot10^{-6},0.1,0.1,2,2,2).\] Set \(\alpha=1/2\), \(\beta=1\), \(p_{\rm target}=0.4\) and \(p_{\rm low}=0.2\). All scores and both scaling parameters are positive; \(0<p_{\rm low}<p_{\rm target}<1\). The paper supplies no further restriction excluding these values. The scores are compatible with the stated Gaussian entropy calculation: output standard deviation \(1\) and masked standard deviations \(e^{-s_i}\) give exactly the designated differences. This is an allocation-level counterexample on admissible score inputs, not a claim to have measured these scores in the published LLaMA checkpoints.

Complete path through the algorithm. With population standard deviation as specified in Eq. (4), \[\mu_s=0.77500075,\quad \sigma_s=0.949670384,\quad
 T_l=0.300165558,\quad T_h=1.249835942.\] Consequently \(S_L\) contains the first five blocks, \(S_H\) the last three, and \(S_M\) is empty. Thus \(E\) is empty, \(F\) consists of the first three blocks, and \[p_{\rm leftover}=3(0.4)=1.2.\] Each full-block removal contributes \(1-0.4=0.6\) in Eq. (7). Every optimal search solution removes exactly two members of \(F\), giving compensation exactly \(1.2\) and excess zero. Removing one is infeasible; removing three has positive excess. Thus neither tie-breaking nor an approximation in the search can evade the case.

Equation reference: eq:invalid. The remaining set has scores \((\varepsilon,0.1,0.1)\), where \(\varepsilon\in\{10^{-6},2\cdot10^{-6},3\cdot10^{-6}\}\), and \(G=3\), \(\widehat p=0.4\). Cancelling the common \(\bar s\) factor in the weights gives \[p_\varepsilon=\frac{1.2}{1+20\varepsilon}>1,\qquad
 p_{0.1}=\frac{12\varepsilon}{1+20\varepsilon}.
 \] For \(\varepsilon=3\cdot10^{-6}\) these are \((1.1999280043,0.0000359978,0.0000359978)\). The total over all eight blocks is the intended \(3.2\), but a block cannot lose \(119.99\%\) of its parameters. The independent script enumerates all three optimal search solutions; each has the same violation. This example avoids zero scores, negative scores, empty remaining sets, infeasible compensation and unequal block sizes.

Alternative readings and impact. A hidden clipping or redistribution step could make an implementation usable. No such step occurs in the published formula or pseudocode, and the pinned repository contains no pruning implementation to establish one. Clipping alone breaks the intended total: the displayed case then removes about \(3.000072\) block-equivalents, or \(37.5009\%\), instead of \(40\%\). Actual experimental scores need not have entered this regime. The finding establishes a defect in the core algorithmic specification, not a benchmark collapse or a claim that the released checkpoints contain impossible sparsity.

Precisely bounded correction. For positive weights and a feasible residual budget \(B=G\widehat p\in[0,G]\), choose \[p_g=\min\{1,\lambda\omega_g\},\qquad \sum_g p_g=B.\] The sum is continuous, nondecreasing from \(0\) to \(G\), so a solution exists; it is unique for \(0<B<G\). Here it yields \((1,0.1,0.1)\) and restores the total \(3.2\). This verifies box feasibility and budget conservation only. It does not prove optimal accuracy, reproduce the authors’ implementation, handle nonpositive entropy scores, or account for indivisible heads and actual layer parameter costs. Those require additional specification.

Severity and evidence. Major: Eqs. (4)–(7) feed Eq. (8), which feeds the within-block pruning stage. A valid ratio is essential to the proposed dynamic method. Evidence is the original p. 5 image, the exact arithmetic script, and its complete output in `independent_checks.json`.

Problem 2 (Minor: a baseline’s reported average understates its displayed performance).  Claim and location. Appendix B, Table 4, p. 14, gives SliceGPT at \(40\%\) sparsity on LLaMA2-13B the five scores \((60.69,59.30,42.50,56.44,34.13)\) and average \(47.30\).

Check. The equally weighted mean is \[(60.69+59.30+42.50+56.44+34.13)/5=50.612.\] Rounding the displayed component scores cannot explain a \(3.312\)-point difference. The released evaluation script’s `calculate_avg_accuracy` also uses an unweighted task mean, although this later script is not proof of the historical computation.

Alternatives and bounded impact. A copied aggregate or a mistaken component cell could explain the discrepancy; raw result records are required to establish which. If the five component scores are correct, the aggregate is approximately \(50.61\), and the reported method’s advantage over this baseline falls from approximately \(8.74\) to \(5.44\) points. Its mean remains higher, so this does not overturn the within-table winner. The issue is Minor because it overstates a numerical comparison without demonstrated damage to the central comparative conclusion. The correction is conditional on the component scores, not a reconstruction of unobserved runs. Original p. 14 was visually checked to exclude an extraction or row-alignment error.
# Evidence limits, counterevidence, and remaining work

Dynamic-ratio evidence. Table 13 reports static and dynamic means \(45.45\) and \(45.52\). The displayed components reproduce a \(0.068\) percentage-point difference; some tasks improve and others decline. This is an observed single-table difference, not established statistical robustness. The paper’s released-model README expressly notes seed sensitivity. Replicated pruning seeds and matched uncertainty estimates are needed to quantify the incremental dynamic-ratio benefit. This uncertainty does not supply the evidence for P1; the algebraic counterexample does.

Implementation boundaries. Actual \(\alpha,\beta,p_{\rm low}\) choices, clipping/renormalization, clustering counts, discrete head rounding, and handling of zero or signed entropy differences were not recovered from pruning source. The compensation formula for partial layer removal also needs actual parameter-count accounting when attention and MLP sizes differ. These are Needs Evidence, not additional demonstrated benchmark errors.

The bias-compensation notation in Eqs. (12)–(13) requires a dimensionally explicit mask. A column-mask vector with broadcasting can make the intended expression coherent; a full weight-shaped mask would instead suggest \(((1-M)\odot W)\widehat X\). That alternative prevents treating the notation alone as a demonstrated implemented defect. Weighting by activation variability is a heuristic, not a proven optimum asserted by this review.

No issue found within a specific code check. The evaluation’s multiplication of per-batch mean loss by sequence length \(S\), followed by division by the total number of sequences times \(S\), cancels. Since each scored sequence has the same \(S-1\) prediction positions, this correctly averages those mean losses; an apparent off-by-one issue was rejected. WikiText2 training and test splits are separate in the read loader. This does not certify preprocessing equivalence across every baseline.

Versions and missing evidence. A bounded official-publication/repository search did not identify a verified corrective version for these findings. This is not an exhaustive erratum claim. The public source is a later evaluation release, with the rerun caveat preserved. Separate supplement availability remains undetermined after the supplied OpenReview 403 access failure. No author response, adoption or human assessment is present.
