Title: Scientific review of Generalists vs. Specialists
# Identity and scope

Paper 0117, I25-43486: A. Chen et al., Generalists vs. Specialists: Evaluating LLMs on Highly-Constrained Biophysical Sequence Optimization Tasks, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 9029–9072 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied proceedings original has 44 pages; references below use its printed pages 1–44. Its main text, relevant benchmark construction, proofs, loss derivations, algorithm descriptions, training settings, and additional-result claims were inspected. The pinned repository commit is `c15ef89dba98193110eda2b000c9cd30a73f3fd3` [Retained latex: \cite{code}].

The scientific checks are analytic, finite numerical, and static source inspections. No author program was run or imported, no model was trained, and no paid API or wet-lab experiment was used. Exact historical training configurations, checkpoints, raw predictions and plotting records were not supplied. Static source evidence establishes behavior of the inspected code path, not which historical run produced a paper figure.

The paper introduces constrained Ehrlich functions, a bilevel LLOME optimizer, and a MargE preference objective. It explicitly discusses failures on difficult tasks, specialist compute advantages, miscalibration, DPO collapse and artificially favorable early-stop hypervolumes. These qualifications are preserved in this review.
# Definitions and dependencies

Equation reference: eq:pure. For one prompt, write \(p=\pi_\theta\), \(q=\pi_{\rm ref}\), \(p^*\propto\exp(\beta r)\), and \(n_y=|y|\). Sections 4.2–4.3 and Appendix A.3 consider \[F_\lambda(p)=D_{\rm KL}(p\|p^*)+\lambda D_{\rm KL}(q\|p).
 \] On a finite response set with positive \(q,p^*\) and a sufficiently flexible policy family, its endpoint limits are valid. Indeed, comparing its minimum against \(p^*\) bounds \(D_{\rm KL}(p_\lambda\|p^*)\) by \(\lambda D_{\rm KL}(q\|p^*)\), and comparing against \(q\) bounds \(D_{\rm KL}(q\|p_\lambda)\) by \(D_{\rm KL}(q\|p^*)/\lambda\). Thus the respective KL divergences tend to zero. This scoped result is not challenged.

Equation reference: eq:implemented. The implemented form in Eq. (2), p. 5, instead contains \[\mathbb E_{y\sim q}
 \left[\frac{p_y}{q_y}\left(\frac{\log p_y}{n_y}-\beta r_y\right)
       -\lambda\frac{\log p_y}{n_y}\right].
 \] Appendix A.4, Eq. (17), p. 30, identifies the length-weighted cross-entropy with the reverse KL after dropping constants. Appendix A.7, Eqs. (30)–(33), p. 36, adds within-batch self-normalization. These modifications are precisely where transfer of the theoretical guarantee and the code behavior need checking.
# Supported problems

Problem 1 (Major: the modified loss does not have the stated interpolation endpoint).  Claim and location. Section 4.2, p. 5, Appendix A.3, pp. 28–29, and Section 6.2, p. 9, attribute Strong Interpolation Criteria (SIC) to MargE, including return to the reference distribution as \(\lambda\to\infty\). The dependence is Eq. (1) to the computational Eq. (2), via Appendix A.4, especially Eq. (17).

Complete finite counterexample. Take two responses, lengths \(n_1=1,n_2=2\), a full-support reference \(q=(1/2,1/2)\), and zero rewards. Zero margin rewards are consistent with equal objective values. Let the policy family contain every Bernoulli distribution \(p=(t,1-t)\), \(0<t<1\). There is no infinite response-space or partition-function issue. The Boltzmann target is \(p^*=q\), so [eq:pure] (#eq:pure) has the unique minimum \(q\) for every \(\lambda\geq0\).

The term dominating [eq:implemented] (#eq:implemented) as \(\lambda\to\infty\) is instead \[C(t)=-\tfrac12\log t-\tfrac14\log(1-t).\] It is strictly convex, with \(C'(t)=-1/(2t)+1/[4(1-t)]\), hence its unique minimizer is \(t=2/3\). Numerically \(C(1/2)=0.5198603854\) whereas \(C(2/3)=0.4773856262\). The remaining finite-action entropy/reward term is bounded, so minimizing the full objective converges to this unique minimum of \(C\). Thus the limit is \((2/3,1/3)\), not \((1/2,1/2)\). Generally the reference limit becomes \[p_y=\frac{q_y/n_y}{\sum_z q_z/n_z}.\] Self-normalizing the first term does not repair a different reference-dominant term.

Alternative readings. Appendix A.4 explicitly calls part of the first-KL manipulation an approximation. That acknowledgement is relevant, but no approximation error bound preserves SIC, and Eq. (17)’s claimed equivalence is itself false for unequal lengths. If all output token lengths are exactly equal, the reference endpoint objection disappears; this restricted case does not justify the stated general LLM loss. At the other endpoint a common length \(L\) also changes the reward temperature unless \(\beta\) is rescaled. The counterexample tests the general policy objective, not a claim that the particular Ehrlich runs emitted these two responses.

A genuinely normalized distribution proportional to \(p_y^{1/n_y}\) has an additional parameter-dependent normalizer. It cannot be replaced by a log-likelihood divided by length while dropping that normalizer as a constant, nor sampled as though it were \(p\) without correction.

Impact and correction. Major: the claimed theoretical property is part of the motivation and causal interpretation of MargE, including the SIC ablation. The valid proof for [eq:pure] (#eq:pure) is not a proof for the modified objective. Removing the length factors and using the exact population objective restores the finite, full-support endpoint argument given above. This is a verified mathematical repair for that objective only; it does not certify a practical estimator, length control, or improved performance. Alternatively, the present loss may be presented as a heuristic without the inherited SIC claim. Original p. 30 was visually checked; calculations are in `independent_checks.py/json`.

Problem 2 (Major: the advertised reproduction configuration removes the direct reward gradient).  Claim and exact source. The paper presents MargE as using reward magnitudes to improve policy training (Sections 4.4 and 6.2). The README’s reproduction command selects `config/pipeline_marge_f2.yaml`. In that file, lines 151–167 set code coefficients `alpha=1.0`, `beta=10.0`, `self_normalize_weights=True`, and `per_device_train_batch_size=1`; gradient accumulation is 32 and training uses two processes. Here the code’s `beta` is the reference-term coefficient, not the paper’s Boltzmann temperature.

The settings are passed through `run_pipeline.py`, lines 347–366, and instantiated in `marge.py`. The decoder-only path of `marge_trainer.py`, lines 994–1047, preserves the single target example. Lines 1049–1094 normalize the ratio by its local tensor sum; lines 1198–1234 compute ratios, call the loss, and return its mean. There is no cross-process or cross-accumulation normalization before this loss.

Decisive calculation. For a singleton microbatch and a finite positive ratio \(w=p_y/q_y\), \[\widetilde w=w/w=1,\qquad \nabla_\theta\widetilde w=0.\] Writing \(\ell=\log p_y\) and \(n=|y|\), the code’s loss is exactly \[\alpha(\ell/n-r)+\beta_{\rm code}(-\ell/n)
 =-9\ell/n-r.\] Thus its direct reward term has zero parameter gradient. For a binary logit \(z\) with \(p_y=1/4\) and \(n=32\), the gradient is \(-9(1-p_y)/32=-0.2109375\) for each of \(r=0,0.5,1\). Independent central differences reproduce this value. Accumulating 32 such gradients and averaging across two devices cannot restore the missing dependence: normalization has already occurred separately.

Alternatives and impact. Rewards can still affect which pairs enter the dataset and checkpoint selection; the entire pipeline is not reward-blind. The demonstrated problem is loss of reward-magnitude influence on each parameter update, leaving a scaled token cross-entropy gradient. The effective optimization batch size is not the batch over which the ratios are normalized. Larger actual local batches, a different normalization implementation, or historical overrides could avoid this particular collapse; none is established by the inspected reproduction configuration.

This is Major for the supplied core-method reproduction: the designated MargE training path does not implement the claimed direct reward-driven learning mechanism. It does not prove that the paper’s Figure 3 or Figure 5 runs used this exact path. Historical configuration-to-figure provenance remains Needs Evidence.

Correction bounds. Normalization would have to use multiple examples jointly, with a correctly defined sampling law and objective scaling, or be replaced by an otherwise justified estimator. Merely increasing gradient accumulation does not do so. No complete distributed-training repair or performance recovery has been verified; the report does not recommend executing the author pipeline as a check.

Problem 3 (Minor: the released REINFORCE control drops its stated importance weights).  Location and check. Section 6.2, p. 9, and Appendix A.7, Eq. (31), p. 36, describe an importance-weighted REINFORCE control. In `marge_trainer.py`, lines 1080–1090, the `reinforce_style` branch returns \(-\log p_y\,r_y+\beta_{\rm code}(-\log p_y/n_y)\) and does not use the ratio argument at all. The calculated running reward baseline is logged but also absent from this loss.

With fixed off-policy data \(q=(0.9,0.1)\) and positive rewards \((0.5,1)\), the unregularized returned objective is weighted maximum likelihood: \[-0.45\log p_1-0.1\log p_2.\] Its minimizer is \((9/11,2/11)\), whereas maximizing the policy’s expected reward puts all mass on response 2. This is an exact two-action comparison under a full-support proposal, not an author-code run.

Alternatives, scope, and correction. An on-policy resampling scheme could justify an unweighted score-function estimator, but this branch is used in a fixed-data training procedure, and the paper expressly specifies importance weights. The supported judgment is Minor for the released ablation path; whether it materially changes the published SIC ablation cannot be established without its actual run configuration and data. Restoring a valid off-policy estimator also requires specifying the proposal law and differentiating the intended score-function surrogate correctly. A full repaired ablation is not certified, and the reported empirical curve is not declared false.
# Other checked claims and unresolved evidence

The feasible-set construction and the self-transition filler argument for jointly satisfiable motifs (Appendix A.2.5, p. 26) were checked. A small independent motif construction reaches value 1 and satisfies every selected transition. The quantization condition \(q\mid k\) is explicitly present on p. 23; no false counterexample using incompatible \(q\) is asserted. The real-benchmark rank-correlation comparison on p. 27 uses 64 variants of one genetic algorithm and is evidence about those variants, not a universal guarantee of biological validity. No wet-lab extrapolation is certified.

The sign of `get_ehrlich_rewards` was checked against `negate: true` in the supplied test-function configuration. Its apparent reversed subtraction is consistent with minimizing the negated objective and is not reported as a bug. Lemma A.1’s cancellation of a prompt-only reward offset is also valid on a finite domain with a common response set and finite partition function.

Budget and sampling provenance remain Needs Evidence. Algorithm 4 (p. 33) uses oracle feasibility labels while filtering before the nominal \(j\) evaluations. The released generation code scores each parsed candidate; some such evaluations may be diagnostics only. The inspected formatter also samples candidates before later pair-level infeasibility filtering, differing from that pseudocode order. A trace distinguishing optimization-used oracle calls from retrospective diagnostic scoring is required to audit the claimed evaluation budget. No numerical budget inflation factor is established here.

Similarly, PropEn matching, likelihood filtering, greedy generation and temperature mixtures change the empirical proposal law; the derivation’s \(y\sim q\) assumption is not established merely by evaluating \(q(y|x)\) on those pairs. This limits estimator interpretation without proving the empirical optimizer cannot work. External `pytorch-holo==0.0.1` and LaMBO-2 implementations were not fully audited. Reproducing all comparative curves, confidence intervals and historical configurations remains outside the available evidence.

# Identity, coverage, and definitions

Paper 0118, I25-43487: X. Li et al., KVTuner: Sensitivity-Aware Layer-Wise Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for Efficient and Nearly Lossless LLM Inference, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 36451–36485 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied original contains 35 pages; page references below use its printed pages 1–35. The pinned repository is commit `96dd05eb2fe350c72c1a3dfdca04e878506f7c17` [Retained latex: \cite{code}].

The main argument, Appendix A, calibration/search settings, layer-group tables, benchmark tables, and appendix figure captions were read. Original p. 16 was rendered and visually inspected to verify the equations. Plot curves were not digitized. Source inspection was static; no author code was executed or imported, no model inference was run, and no installation was attempted. Independent checks use elementary arithmetic and parsing of literal configuration data.

For one attention head, absorb the usual \(1/\sqrt D\) into the effective query \(u\), and write \[z_j=uK_j,\quad \delta_j=u(\widehat K_j-K_j),\quad
 a_j=\frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}},\quad
 \widehat a_j=\frac{a_je^{\delta_j}}{\sum_k a_ke^{\delta_k}}.
 \tag{1.1}\] Section 3.2, Eq. (2), quantizes each selected group by \[\widehat x=z+s\,\operatorname{round}((x-z)/s),\qquad
 z=\min x,\quad s=(\max x-\min x)/(2^B-1).
 \tag{1.2}\] The method searches layer precision pairs using calibration accuracy and average nominal bit width, then reuses the chosen configuration online. The arithmetic mean bit objective is appropriate as a nominal payload measure when the layers have equal KV tensor sizes; it is not itself an accounting of metadata, residual tokens, packing, or peak allocations.
# Supported Problems

Problem 1 (Major: the attention-concentration proof drops an uncontrolled factor).  Claim and dependency. Lemma 1 in Section 4.4, p. 5, asserts an exclusivity relation between sparse, concentrated attention and consistent low-precision robustness. Appendix A, p. 16, Eqs. (5)–(6), is its proof. Case 2 drops every non-dominant term because \(e^{z_j-z_i}\) is small, even though that term is multiplied by \(e^{\delta_j-\delta_i}\). This theoretical explanation is advertised in the abstract and introduction and used to interpret sensitive layers in Sections 4.4–4.5 and Appendix E. No bound on \(u\), on the projected errors, or on their size relative to logit margins is supplied.

A finite counterexample to the actual quantization argument. Use two keys in dimension three, per-token asymmetric quantization with \(B=2\), and \[K_1=(0.49,0,1),\quad K_2=(0.48,0,1.2),\quad u=(1000,0,0).\] These groups have positive ranges and no rounding ties. The original query in Eq. (1) can be \(q=\sqrt3\,u\), so the scale convention causes no discrepancy. The two group scales are \(1/3\) and \(0.4\). Thus \[\widehat K_1=(1/3,0,1),\qquad \widehat K_2=(0.4,0,1.2).\] The original logit margin is \(490-480=10\), whereas the quantized margin is \(1000(1/3-0.4)=-200/3\). Consequently \[a_1=0.9999546021313,\qquad
 \widehat a_1=1.11438315784\times10^{-29},
 \quad \operatorname{TV}(a,\widehat a)=0.9999546021313.\] The initial attention is extremely concentrated, but the quantized distribution is almost reversed. All coordinates and errors are finite. Replacing 1000 by \(c\to\infty\) makes the original attention arbitrarily concentrated while the quantized attention converges to the other token. This is not a rounding-level discrepancy. Values such as \(V_1=(0,0,1)\), \(V_2=(1,0,0)\) are exactly representable by the same per-token rule and transmit the attention reversal to the output. This construction is an attention-level counterexample, not a claim that these exact activations occurred in a tested LLM.

The Gaussian assumption does not rescue the derivation. Appendix A also models coordinate errors as Gaussian with \(\sigma=(\max K-\min K)/(2^B-1)\). This is an additional stochastic model, not the distributional law of deterministic rounding. Even granting independent Gaussian coordinates, take \(K_1=(0.001,0)\), \(K_2=(0,1)\), \(u=(10000,0)\), \(B=2\), and \(\sigma=1/3\). Again \(a_1=0.9999546\). Now the noisy margin is \[10+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,2(10000/3)^2).\] Its probability of reversing sign is \[\Phi\!\left(-\frac{10}{\sqrt2(10000/3)}\right)=0.4991537163.\] Thus even a natural interpretation of the appendix’s own noise assumption gives almost one-half probability of overturning the dominant token. The two examples test separate interpretations and are not conflated.

Necessity, alternatives, and scope. For finite logits, equality of the entire two softmax distributions holds exactly if and only if every \(\delta_j\) is the same: compare their pairwise probability ratios. The paper acknowledges this as Case 1 but dismisses it as atypical without an assumption that excludes it. For instance, \(K_j=(x_j,0,1)\), \(0<x_j<1\), and \(u=(0,0,1)\) give a uniform, non-concentrated distribution that is preserved exactly for every such \(x_j\) and every positive integer bit width, although the first coordinates may have nonzero rounding errors. This is a whole family with a nonzero query, not only \(q=0\).

A fixed, bounded perturbation becomes harmless when a margin tends to infinity. That restricted reading is correct; it is precisely the missing condition. Empirical correlations in Figures 4 and 11–19 may still hold for the measured models. They do not prove the exclusive or general robustness statement. The finding is Major because the paper’s central theoretical explanation is invalid as derived, without requiring a failure of its entire search framework or a lower benchmark score.

Verified correction bound. If \(z_i-z_j\ge m\) and \(\delta_j-\delta_i\le\rho\) for every \(j\ne i\), then (1.1) gives \[\widehat a_i\ge \frac{1}{1+(S-1)e^{-m+\rho}}. \tag{2.1}\] Each denominator ratio is at most \(e^{-m+\rho}\), proving the bound directly. The sufficient condition must therefore compare the margin with projected error and sequence length. With \(|\delta_j|\le\eta\), one may use \(\rho=2\eta\). This repairs a conditional single-head statement only; it proves neither prompt-independent layer sensitivity nor full-model accuracy preservation. Targeted inspection of arXiv v5, dated 20 November 2025, found the same Lemma 1 and Case 2 approximation still present [Retained latex: \cite{later}]; no full-version diff or author correction is asserted.

Problem 2 (Minor: released layer groups are not partitions for two model settings).  Location and assumptions. Section 5.3 and Appendix D.1.2 group layers to define one precision pair per layer. In the supplied `search_optuna_adaptive.py`, lines 37–43, the Qwen2.5-14B per-channel configuration repeats layer 25, and the Qwen2.5-32B per-channel configuration repeats layers 22, 24, and 25. The independent static audit checks all twelve model/mode combinations; these are the two failures.

For the 14B setting, 49 memberships are used for 48 distinct layers. Lines 218–228 construct a dictionary that overwrites a repeated layer, but accumulate bit cost over every membership and divide by \(2L\). If every group uses KV4, the actual dictionary assigns four nominal bits per element while the returned objective is \[\frac{49(4+4)}{2\cdot48}=4.083333\ldots.\] Thus even the uniform configuration’s reported objective and constraint value are wrong.

For the 32B setting, the group at zero-based index 2 contains 22, 24, and 25 outside its designated special candidate set. Assuming required dependencies are available, the explicit consistency condition at lines 176–185 raises `ValueError` before the search starts. This is a static control-flow deduction, not an executed author program.

Impact and correction bounds. These defects obstruct or mismeasure the released extensions to these settings. They do not establish that the main 3B/7B/8B results used these groups, and they do not invalidate the separately reported uniform-precision 14B/32B measurements. That limited impact supports Minor. For 32B, removing 22, 24, and 25 from group index 2 yields a complete disjoint 64-layer partition compatible with the supplied special sets; this exact data-level repair was checked. For any setting, computing the nominal bit sum from the final distinct-layer mapping avoids double counting, but the grouping still must be made unambiguous. No corrected search performance has been verified.

Problem 3 (Minor: the forced-prefilling path mishandles zero remainder).  Claim and source. Section 5.3, p. 7, and Appendix E.1, p. 23, emphasize applying quantized KV during prefilling. In `flexible_quant/flexible_quant/flexible_quantized_cache.py`, lines 173–190, the `force_quant=True` path with nonzero residual length \(R\) computes \(r=S\bmod R\), passes the slice `:-r` for quantization, and retains `-r:` at full precision.

For \(S=64,R=32\), \(r=0\). Python’s `:-0` is empty and `-0:` is the entire sequence. Hence this path sends zero tokens to quantization and retains all 64, rather than quantizing the complete prefix and retaining an empty suffix. If a backend rejects the empty input, it can fail earlier; that runtime outcome was not tested. The source-level slice defect is independent of such backend behavior.

Alternatives, impact, and bounded repair. The defect is confined to this flag and boundary condition, and does not occur for the same reason when \(r>0\) or \(R=0\). The released search file itself sets `force_quant=False`; its historical relation to the prefilling-enabled paper runs is unresolved. Therefore no numerical table damage is asserted, and the supported severity is Minor. Computing \(c=S-r\), using prefix `:c` and suffix `c:`, restores the intended partition at this boundary. Only the slicing identity is verified; backend empty-input handling and complete inference behavior require separate evidence.
# Other checks and unresolved evidence

Search is a heuristic, and its empirical scope matters. The enormous search-space counts \(9^{32}\) and \(5^6=15625\) are consistent with the stated configurations. Local Pareto pruning and shared group precision do not by themselves certify the global accuracy frontier under nonlinear layer interactions. The paper evaluates final model accuracy and reports a finite-search ablation; those are useful empirical checks. No global-optimality or universal prompt-independence theorem is established. The twenty-prompt observations in two datasets support limited transfer evidence, not independence for arbitrary prompts.

Held-out validation and historical configuration remain Needs Evidence. Appendix C/D uses the first 200 GSM8K samples for search. The released script calls the external `gsm8k` task with a sample limit; the pinned adapter/task submodule is not present in the supplied tree. Exact calibration/evaluation sample identifiers and a disjoint held-out account were not available, so test overlap is not asserted as a demonstrated finding. The paper specifies MOEA/D, while the inspected script selects `NSGAIISampler`; it also has defaults of 20 samples and 100 trials rather than the paper’s 200/200, which could be overridden. Historical commands and search databases are needed to resolve these differences. Appendix D explicitly discloses 500 iterations for one Qwen7B KIVI run; that disclosure is retained.

Arithmetic and performance interpretation. From the displayed integer throughput counts in Table 8, the C3.25 gains over KV8 are approximately \(21.2722\%\), \(17.6044\%\), and \(16.7577\%\). These are close to the reported \(21.25\%\), \(17.55\%\), and \(16.79\%\), within plausible rounding of the displayed rates; no substantive arithmetic finding is supported. The six Llama3.1 C3.25 accuracies in Table 5 average \(0.7925\), versus approximately \(0.8038\) for BF16. The interpretation of nearly lossless needs an explicit tolerance and paired uncertainty; the numerical loss is already visible in the table. No significance claim or wholesale empirical failure is inferred.

Thirty-two supplied YAML presets were checked arithmetically for nominal average bits. The vanilla quantizer stores integers in `int8`, so that simulation path alone does not demonstrate packed two-bit memory savings. Section 6.4 explicitly uses a KIVI GPU-kernel implementation for throughput; those run records and a complete corresponding kernel package were not available here. The analysis preserves that distinction. LongBench aggregate scoring, run-specific model revisions, raw predictions, and the exact treatment of residual/metadata overhead remain unverified. Separate OpenReview supplements could not be determined because the acquisition metadata reports HTTP 403.
# Conclusion
Item | Judgment | Established result | Remaining scope
P1 | Major | Concentration alone fails; conditional bound proved | Model-level and empirical guarantees
P2 | Minor | Duplicate groups; wrong cost or rejected setup | Corrected searches and historical use
P3 | Minor | Zero-remainder slice defect | Backend and historical-run effects
Other | Needs Evidence | Arithmetic checks retained | Raw runs, held-out split, scoring

The overall supported severity is Major. Scientific decisions remain pending and human reviews are empty. This is an initial scientific review, not acceptance. The theoretical finding is material to the paper’s claimed explanation; it does not establish that offline mixed-precision search cannot be useful.

report: Abstract: Two supported Problems are identified. A Major construct-validity problem affects the execution-reasoning task: on the intended domain of valid reference-program tests, a constant `pass` predictor attains perfect label accuracy without inspecting the intermediate representation. This limits what the reported success rates can establish about execution understanding. A Minor reporting problem concerns inconsistent counts, denominators, and pass rates. Concrete examples of incorrect model reasoning remain informative, and the other three tasks are not invalidated by the shortcut. Historical model identity, evaluation scripts, unmatched completion sets, and missing result payloads are recorded as evidence limits rather than inferred experimental failures.
Date: Initial review, 24 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of LLMs and compiler intermediate representations
# Identity, scope, and evaluation objects

Paper 0119, I25-43488: H. Jiang, J. Zhu, Y. Wan, B. Fang, H. Zhang, R. Jin, and Q. Guan, Can Large Language Models Understand Intermediate Representations in Compilers?, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 27851–27872 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page references use the supplied 22-page proceedings PDF. The main study and substantive Appendices A–F were read; original pp. 7 and 17 were visually checked. Despite the acquisition metadata’s negative detection flag, the original contains Appendices A–F.

The study examines CFG construction, IR decompilation, code summarization, and execution reasoning on 164 C++ HumanEval tasks. Structural correctness, executable correctness, text similarity, and assertion truth require separate interpretation.

The pinned repository commit is `af9d4e2a781b3910637903862f5d8ee343995b86` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. All 15 supplied source files were statically indexed and hashed; relevant generation, extraction, evaluation, and compilation code was read. Historical notebook outputs were sampled. The manifest excludes 18,886 upstream paths, including most benchmark and result payloads. One previously excluded 303,498-byte JSONL was acquired at this commit for Problem 1; its Git blob hash matches the supplied remote-tree inventory [Retained latex: \cite{data}]. No unchanged input was redownloaded, author code executed, or model API called.
# Supported Problems

Problem 1 (Major: valid reference assertions admit a perfect label-only shortcut).  Claim and location. Section 3.1, p. 3, describes Task 4 as requiring dynamic interpretation of IR and accurate tracking of state. Section 3.5, p. 5, scores assertion predictions; Section 4.3, pp. 7–8, uses these scores to interpret execution understanding and the source-code/IR gap. Appendix C.4, p. 16, supplies IR and an assertion and requests a pass/fail answer with reasoning. Sections 3.3 and Appendix D identify the inputs as reference C++ programs and their HumanEval unit tests.

Construction and assumptions. Cell 0 of `src/Task4_Execute_Reasoning.ipynb` extracts lines beginning with `assert` from each JSONL record’s `test` field. It does not generate false assertions or mutate the tested reference program. The acquired file contains 164 distinct tasks; that exact line-selection rule yields 1,140 assertion lines, with at least one per task. This is a static inventory, not an execution audit. The paper’s stated average of 7.7 assertions and the inventory’s 6.951 require historical dataset reconciliation; neither number is silently substituted for the other.

The decisive argument assumes that these assertions are valid tests of their canonical reference implementations, that compilation preserves the relevant semantics, and that the quantitative score judges the final pass/fail label. These are the intended golden-data and scoring premises of the published design. No stronger assertion that all 164 programs were independently executed is made.

Decisive argument. Let \(A_{ij}\) be test \(j\) of reference program \(i\), with ground-truth label \(y_{ij}\). Under those premises, \(y_{ij}=1\) for every supplied test. The predictor \[h(\mathrm{IR}_i,A_{ij})=1\] ignores both inputs yet has \[\frac{\sum_{i,j}{\bf1}\{h=y_{ij}\}}{\sum_i m_i}=1,\qquad
 \frac{1}{N}\sum_i{\bf1}\{\forall j,\ h=y_{ij}\}=1.
 \tag{2.1}\] Thus both assertion-level accuracy and all-assertions-correct task accuracy can be perfect without any IR understanding. The result is independent of which of the two inconsistent rate definitions in Problem 2 is selected.

Three concrete cases were checked by direct reasoning from the pinned records. In CPP/2, \(3.5-\operatorname{int}(3.5)=0.5\), exactly representable. In CPP/121, the odd values at even positions of \((5,8,7,1)\) are 5 and 7, giving the asserted 12. In CPP/149, filtering odd-length strings from \((\texttt{aa},\texttt{a},\texttt{aaa})\) leaves only `aa`. These cases agree with the intended positive-test construction; they are not offered as a proof of every program’s correctness.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. An assertion testing that a Boolean function returns false is still a true assertion when its reference implementation is correct. It therefore does not supply a negative label for this task. Requesting a reasoning trace also does not remove (2.1) from a label-only score. The notebook’s cells 4 and 7 extract a pass/fail string; the reported quantitative metric does not independently verify every intermediate state.

Conversely, a model that answers incorrectly on a valid positive test has made a real prediction error. The paper’s qualitative examples of missed filtering or incorrect arithmetic remain useful evidence about those particular traces. This review does not claim that the tested models exploited the shortcut, that their recorded scores are fabricated, or that all their qualitative analyses fail. If the actual historical evaluation contains genuinely false oracle labels, its case-level labels and construction must be supplied; the retained construction does not document such a negative-test mechanism. Invalid canonical tests would instead call for an oracle audit.

Core dependency and precise impact. The construction underlies one of four core tasks and the RQ3 interpretation of measured execution reasoning. It demonstrates that high success, or a source-code/IR difference in such success, cannot by itself discriminate instruction-level understanding from a representation-dependent tendency to answer `pass`. The observed positive-case error rates remain descriptive. CFG, decompilation, and summarization results are outside this counterexample. The Major severity attaches to the task’s ability to measure its stated core construct, not to a claimed collapse of the whole study.

Correction boundary. Add independently verified false assertions or semantics-changing counterfactuals, remove trivial label cues, report label balance and a constant-predictor baseline, and verify selected execution states separately from the final label. With a balanced binary label set, a constant predictor’s accuracy is exactly \(1/2\); this removes this particular perfect-score shortcut, not every possible shortcut or ambiguity about understanding. New measurements are required before attributing a corrected score gap to execution capability.

Problem 2 (Minor: incompatible execution counts and pass-rate definitions).  Claim and location. Section 3.5, p. 5, defines overall pass rate using correctly predicted assertions across cases. Table 5, p. 7, instead says its denominator is the number of completed tasks and presents full-pass counts. Table 9, p. 17, repeats the counts and rates for three runs. The original pages were visually inspected to exclude an extraction artifact.

Arithmetic under the table definition. For a completed-task denominator, full-pass rate is \(n_{\rm pass}/n_{\rm completed}\). Independent exact-fraction calculation gives: \[\begin{array}{lrrr}
\hline
\text{Row}&n_{\rm pass}/n_{\rm completed}&\text{Recomputed}&\text{Reported}\\
\hline
\text{Table 5, DeepSeek SC}&119/164&0.725610&0.804\\
\text{Table 9, Run 1 SC}&133/164&0.810976&0.811\\
\text{Table 9, Run 2 SC}&146/164&0.890244&0.817\\
\text{Table 9, Run 3 SC}&139/164&0.847561&0.804\\
\hline
\end{array}\] The first, third, and fourth discrepancies are approximately 7.84, 7.32, and 4.36 percentage points, respectively, far larger than rounding at the displayed precision. Run 1 is a useful countercheck that the ratio interpretation is numerically consistent for an adjacent row. Table 9 also prints \(119/164\) as \(0.720\) for Llama 3.1; ordinary rounding to three decimals gives \(0.726\).

Alternative reading. An assertion-weighted rate need not equal the proportion of fully correct programs. That reading could explain some numerical differences, but would contradict Table 5’s stated denominator and cannot be reconstructed from its pass/partial counts without per-case assertion totals and correct-label counts. Thus at least one of the definition, counts, or reported rates needs correction; the evidence does not identify the intended replacement for every cell.

Dependency, impact, and correction. These numbers feed Section 4.3’s quantitative comparisons and Appendix E’s stability claim. The appendix’s DeepSeek SC counts exceed Code Llama’s main-table count of 131, whereas the main text calls Code Llama the SC leader. Different runs or metrics might explain this, but the historical mapping is not supplied. Repair requires a case-level ledger and a declared aggregation rule, not choosing whichever number supports a ranking. Under the displayed alternative full-pass counts, the broad SC-over-IR direction still holds; this arithmetic finding alone does not reverse that direction or invalidate the other tasks. Its supported severity is Minor.
# Other checks, counterevidence, and unresolved evidence

CFG construction and attribution. The compile/CFG script uses Clang and LLVM’s CFG pass, consistent with the stated ground-truth strategy. Figure 4 is an example of model output, not explicitly a certified correct CFG: its one-basic-block explanation followed by three DOT nodes is not treated as proof of a wrong golden graph. The standalone graph-similarity script is a demonstration, not a verified reconstruction of Table 2’s full evaluator. Node-label normalization, single-node density handling, loop counts based on metadata, and case-level scoring need the actual evaluation records. The causal claim that CoT improves CFG accuracy needs a within-model controlled comparison; cross-model results alone do not isolate prompting.

Decompilation. The distinction between producing text, compiling/running, and passing tests is scientifically meaningful. The read notebooks generate outputs and record processing, but do not supply the full historical re-execution scoring pipeline. No executed-code replication was attempted. Figure 5’s semantic mismatch is qualitatively plausible; a global claim that every reported successful reconstruction preserves all program semantics would require more than finitely many tests.

Summarization and completion. Table 4’s best average for DeepSeek is conditional on 49 completed cases, while GPT-4 completes 164. It supports a conditional-score statement, not an unqualified comparison on a common population. For illustration only, assigning zero to the uncompleted DeepSeek cases changes a conditional BLEU of \(0.42\) to \(0.42(49/164)=0.12549\), while GPT-4’s \(0.35\) is unchanged. This is not a replacement metric or an assertion that the missing outputs should scientifically receive zero; it demonstrates why the completion policy matters. A common-case comparison, coverage-aware reporting, and independent semantic judgment are needed to interpret score rankings. Table 4’s DeepSeek metric tuple also does not reproduce a single displayed Appendix E run exactly; raw aggregation provenance is needed before diagnosing the cause.

Model and prompt identity. The retained notebooks name `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B-free`, while tables use the broader label DeepSeek R1. They also contain specific temperatures and prompts whose exact historical relationship to every model/table is not documented. This is an unresolved mapping, not proof that an incorrectly named model produced every result. Current documentation gives additional illustrative scores that are not the proceedings tables. The snapshot is pinned for this audit, not asserted to be the experiment-time commit.

Source and version limits. Separate supplement availability was undetermined after the acquisition’s OpenReview HTTP 403 response; embedded appendices were available and read. Most result payloads are excluded from the supplied source snapshot; the single new JSONL does not restore them. Metadata identifies arXiv:2502.06854v2, 5 June 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{version}]; no complete cross-version scientific audit is claimed. Novelty against all prior IR research was not exhaustively checked. Missing historical logs, oracle labels, exact checkpoints, evaluator code paths, and prompt-selection records remain Needs Evidence.

report: Abstract: Three Major findings concern the identification of ground-truth posteriors, the strict CE-bias proposition, and test-set independence in the released CIFAR evaluation path. Two Minor findings concern loss normalization and metric implementation. Finite counterexamples, exact arithmetic, and static control-flow arguments establish the stated scopes without executing author code. The L2 two-point balance result survives independent verification. Historical table corruption, a reversal of the reported empirical advantages, and failure of semantic augmentation in general are not established.
Date: Initial review, 24 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of semantic mixing for model calibration
# Identity and scope

Paper 0120, I25-43489: H. Luo, L. Tao, M. Dong, and C. Xu, Beyond One-Hot Labels: Semantic Mixing for Model Calibration, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 41346–41367 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page references use the supplied 22-page proceedings PDF. Main pp. 1–9 and Appendices A–C, pp. 13–22, were read. Original pp. 4, 5, 8, 9, 16, and 22 were visually inspected, including the equations and figures whose extracted text was unreliable. Figure curves were not digitized.

The supplied repository has 117 files at commit `c8fb26e2e79ec2dd72601e275c801704fced5f82` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Fifteen relevant source/configuration files were separately hashed and read: reannotation, diffusion sampling, data loading, loss, training, metrics, temperature scaling, and entry points. This is not an audit of every line in all 117 files. Author modules were neither executed nor imported; calculations and static parsing were independently written for this review. Model checkpoints, generated labels, historical sample ledgers, and evaluation logits were unavailable.
# Supported Problems

Problem 1 (Major: posterior identification does not follow from the reannotation argument).  Claim and dependency. The abstract, Sections 3.2–3.3, pp. 3–5, and the conclusion describe soft annotations as ground-truth uncertainty or accurate class posteriors. Section 3.3 introduces a classification-optimal encoder \(E\), asserts Eq. (7), and then removes prototype norm/distance terms to obtain the allegedly bias-free Eq. (11). This is a core justification for the proposed reannotation, not merely an ancillary motivation.

First implication: classification optimality does not identify Eq. (7). Consider a finite population of 40 equally weighted observations with \(E(x)=x\), ten observations at each of \(x=-2,-1,1,2\). Their class-1 counts are \((1,4,6,9)\), and class-0 counts are \((9,6,4,1)\). The true posteriors are therefore \[\eta(-2)=0.1,\quad\eta(-1)=0.4,\quad
 \eta(1)=0.6,\quad\eta(2)=0.9.\] The prototype sums specified in Eq. (7) are \(P_1=18\) and \(P_0=-18\). Class counts and prototype norms are equal. The prototype classifier predicts class 1 precisely when \(x>0\), attaining Bayes-optimal classification accuracy. Yet Eq. (7) prescribes \[\eta_{\rm proto}(x)=\sigma(36x/\tau).\] No single \(\tau>0\) gives both \(\eta_{\rm proto}(1)=0.6\) and \(\eta_{\rm proto}(2)=0.9\). Matching the former forces odds \(3/2\) at \(x=1\), hence odds \(9/4\) and probability \(9/13\) at \(x=2\), rather than \(9/10\). The discrepancy is \(27/130\). Dividing both prototypes by their equal class counts changes the scale but not this impossibility. Thus the example satisfies the stated classification-optimality premise and even equal prototype norms; it refutes the claimed implication to calibrated probabilities.

Second implication: removing norm terms can change a correct posterior. For a separate test, grant the stronger premise that Eq. (7) already equals the true posterior. Use finite distinct prototypes and a nonzero residual \[P_i=(2,0,0),\quad P_j=(0,1,0),\quad
 r=(0,0,1),\quad \tau=1,\quad
 E=\lambda_E P_i+(1-\lambda_E)P_j+r.\] The residual is orthogonal to both prototypes, so it meets the orthogonality requirement in Eq. (8). Equations (7) and (10) give \[\lambda_{\rm true}=\sigma(5\lambda_E-1),
 \qquad
 \lambda_{\rm CSM}=\sigma\bigl(s(\lambda_E-\tfrac12)\bigr)
 \quad\text{from Eq.~(11)}.
 \tag{2.1}\] At \(\lambda_E=1/2\), the correct probability is \(\sigma(1.5)=0.8175744762\), while Eq. (11) gives \(1/2\) for every \(s>0\). At \(\lambda_E=1/4\) and \(s=4\), the two values are \(0.5621765009\) and \(0.2689414214\). More generally, every \(\lambda_E\in(0.2,0.5)\) reverses the preferred class for any positive \(s\). The failure therefore extends beyond an isolated midpoint.

Under the mean-prototype convention used in the source, a probabilistic realization is available: take class-conditional Gaussians with these means and common identity covariance, and prior odds \(e^{3/2}\). Bayes’ log odds are \(E^\top(P_i-P_j)\), because the prior log odds cancel half the norm difference. Equation (7) is then an exact posterior, while the norm-removal rule changes it.

Alternative readings and boundary of the objection. Appendix A.1 explicitly postulates Eq. (15), equivalent to Eq. (7). If this is intended as an additional probability-calibration assumption, the first counterexample does not refute that assumption-conditioned identity; it shows why classification optimality alone cannot justify it. Similarly, equal prototype norms plus a common squared inter-prototype distance \(d^2\), with \(s=d^2/\tau\), make Eq. (11) agree with Eq. (10). The second example does not satisfy equal norms and is not presented as a counterexample under that extra restriction. It tests the advertised removal of unequal-norm effects in the general setting that motivates the method.

The norm-invariant rule may be a useful heuristic for imperfect CLIP features. Reported downstream gains do not establish that its labels equal true conditional probabilities, and the counterexamples do not disprove those gains. The precise correction is to state the extra assumptions or describe the labels as model-derived targets, retaining the norm/scale terms when the assumed posterior model is used. Independent probability validation is needed for the stronger ground-truth claim. This limits a central theoretical/evidentiary justification while leaving practical augmentation benefits open.

Exact calculation. Feasibility forces \(p_1=p_2=p\). The objective is \[-\frac85\log p_s-\frac25\log(1-p_s),\] whose unique minimum is \(p_s=4/5\). Both squared errors equal \(1/50\), so \[\beta(p,p)=\|p-q_1\|^2-\|p-q_2\|^2=0,\] contradicting strict negativity. This is the exactly indistinguishable case that the proximity model explicitly allows.

Counterevidence, impact, and correction scope. Restricting the strict-negative branch to \(0<\delta<\|q_1-q_2\|^2\), and including equality at \(\delta=0\), repairs this boundary claim. Positive-\(\delta\) checks support the intended sharper-label tendency, and Proposition 3.4 remains valid as shown below. The finding does not establish that CE is balanced for every \(\delta\), that L2 lacks practical advantages, or that the ablation scores are wrong. Its Major severity concerns the demonstrated invalid derivation and false statement in the central loss-selection argument; the local nature of the correction does not remove that dependency.

Problem 3 (Major: the released test path includes the training pool).  Claim and exact path. Appendix B.2, p. 20, describes separate CIFAR training/validation/test data. In both released `configs/data/cifar10.yaml` and `configs/data/cifar100.yaml`, training/validation and test loaders receive the same `data.data_root`. In `calibrate/data/cifar100.py`, lines 187–198, the former partitions indices from that directory; lines 268–277 construct the test dataset from the whole same directory without a held-out sampler. The trainer’s `test()` uses this configured loader.

Decisive set argument. Assume an unchanged readable directory with unique contiguous image IDs and the supplied `valid_size=0.1`, with no unrecorded test-path override. Let its image identities be \(S\), the training sampler pool \(T\), validation pool \(V\), and test pool \(U\). Then \[T\mathbin{\dot\cup}V=S,\qquad U=S,\qquad T\cap U=T,\quad V\cap U=V.\] For \(50{,}000\) images this is a \(45{,}000\)-image training pool, \(5{,}000\)-image validation pool, and \(50{,}000\)-image test pool. Thus 90% of test identities belong to the training pool and all validation identities are reused in testing. Shuffling changes membership selection but not these inclusions. Dropping a partial training batch does not make the resulting test set independent; different input normalizations do not create new image identities.

Alternatives and bounded impact. This is a static result about the released path, not proof that the proceedings tables used overlapping data. A historical override of the test directory could avoid it. CIFAR-100 additionally encounters a hardcoded ten-class target size, so no completed CIFAR-100 execution is inferred; the same overlap argument applies to the supplied ten-class configuration when its prerequisites are supplied. No author training was run.

Core dependency and correction. Independent test evaluation is essential to the central accuracy/calibration comparison. Following the displayed path does not measure that quantity, giving a Major validity defect in the released evaluation route. A separate test directory or immutable disjoint identity lists, with verified intersections, repairs the route. Historical split IDs and configurations are required to determine whether any published table needs recomputation; no score decrease is asserted without them.
# Local implementation and definition discrepancies

Problem 4 (Minor: the combined loss has an unspecified relative normalization).  Location and calculation. Equation (13), p. 5, defines \(L_2=K^{-1}\|p-q\|^2\), and Eq. (14) sums CE and this loss. Released `calibrate/losses/csm.py`, lines 18–19 and 35–44, instead averages the sum of squared class errors over augmented examples and adds mean CE. For \(B\) originals and \(gB\) augmentations, the code uses \[\frac1B\sum_i L_{{\rm CE},i}
 +\frac1{gB}\sum_a\|p_a-q_a\|^2 .\] Relative to a literal minibatch-sum version of Eq. (14), the L2-to-CE coefficient differs by \(K/g\), not a common multiplicative scale. The supplied loader returns one endpoint plus one interior augmentation, so \(g=2\): factors 5 and 50 arise for \(K=10\) and 100, respectively. The latter is an algebraic comparison, not a claim that the unmodified 100-class path runs.

Why the distinction can matter. For one hard label of class 1 and two identical soft labels \((0.6,0.4,0,\ldots)\), suppose all share \(p=(t,1-t,0,\ldots)\). With \(K=10\), the literal paper objective is \(-\log t+0.4(t-0.6)^2\), minimized at \(t=1\) on the closed simplex. The source objective is \(-\log t+2(t-0.6)^2\), minimized at \[t=(0.6+\sqrt{1.36})/2=0.8830951895.\] These are probability-space calculations, not trained-network measurements.

Alternative interpretation and scope. An intended expectation/mean convention or an explicit loss weight could reconcile the implementation, but the exact coefficient must be stated. For a literal full-dataset sum with \(N\) originals and \(A\) augmentations, the analogous relative factor is \(KN/A\). The standalone two-point L2 balance theorem is invariant under positive scaling and is not refuted. This is a local specification/reproducibility discrepancy; its effect on historical comparisons is unresolved. Correct the objective’s reductions and coefficient, and record the actual training weight.

Problem 5 (Minor: metric formulas and adaptive-bin coverage need correction).  Locations. Section 3.1, p. 3, Eq. (2), Appendix B.3, pp. 20–21, and `calibrate/evaluation/metrics.py` do not fully agree.

ECE normalization and counterevidence. Eq. (2) weights raw bin counts by \(1/M\), where \(M\) is the number of bins, instead of \(1/N\). Thirty wrong predictions of confidence \(0.8\), with 15 bins, give 1.6 under that formula and 0.8 under normalized ECE. Appendix Eq. (65) and the source ECE implementation use the correct sample normalization. Thus this printed definition error does not establish that the ECE tables were computed incorrectly.

Adaptive-bin omission. The source’s `AdaptiveECELoss`, lines 216–237, starts its quantile boundaries at the minimum confidence but tests \(\texttt{lower}<c\leq\texttt{upper}\) for every bin. Every minimum-confidence observation is excluded. With thirty identical confidences \(c=0.8\) and all predictions wrong, every boundary is 0.8, all bin predicates are false, and the implemented accumulation is zero. Correct bin coverage gives a discrepancy of 0.8. This conclusion follows from the predicates without calling the author function.

If the omitted minimum group has size \(m_{\min}\), correcting only that omission with fixed boundaries changes the metric by at most \(m_{\min}/N\). With a unique minimum among 5,000 cases, the bound is 0.02 percentage points; with ties the effect can be larger. This is not a bound on arbitrary alternative rebinning methods. Raw logits are needed to quantify the actual table impact.

OE/UE convention and repair. The source also multiplies each OE/UE contribution by bin confidence, unlike Eqs. (66)–(67). A bin with confidence 0.8 and accuracy 0.5 contributes 0.24 under the source convention and 0.30 under Eq. (66). Either convention can be named, but they are distinct metrics. Specify the definitions consistently and assign every sample exactly once, including tied minima. These local discrepancies do not by themselves demonstrate a changed historical method ranking.
# Verified results and remaining evidence limits

L2 balance: scoped No Issue Found. Let \(d=q_1-q_2\), \(m=(q_1+q_2)/2\), and \(t=\min(1,\sqrt{\delta}/\|d\|)\). Direct projection of the pair onto the distance constraint gives \[p_1=m+\tfrac12td,\qquad p_2=m-\tfrac12td,\qquad
 \|p_1-q_1\|^2=\|p_2-q_2\|^2
 =\tfrac14(1-t)^2\|d\|^2.\] Both outputs lie on the segment joining the labels and hence in the simplex. This independently verifies Proposition 3.4’s balance conclusion, including \(\delta=0\). It does not imply calibrated predictions on a new distribution. A separate numerical minimization of the binary Focal objective at \(\gamma=1\), over 60 specified label/constraint cases, found positive \(\beta\) throughout; this finite check is not a universal independent proof of Proposition 3.3.

One-hot labels and uncertainty. One-hot observations need not imply a conditionally deterministic label. For \(Y\mid X=x\sim{\rm Bernoulli}(\eta)\), expected CE has derivative \((p-\eta)/(p(1-p))\) and is minimized at \(p=\eta\). Thus finite-data overfitting or missing soft annotations should not be conflated with an information-theoretic impossibility of learning uncertainty from one-hot observations. This qualification preserves the possible practical value of additional synthetic supervision.

Release completeness. The annotation utility defines but never invokes `main`; its helper reads `model`, `preprocess`, and `device` as globals although they are local to `main`. In addition, line 84 reuses the last filename from the image loop for every feature coefficient, leaving one key per intended group. These are static obstacles to the advertised command producing complete annotations; they do not establish corruption of the historical labels. The loader hardcodes ten-class targets despite the 100-class configuration. The four-process generation command and the sampler’s single-device assumptions also require reconciliation before reproducing generation. No distributed failure or historical loss of samples is inferred from an unexecuted run.

Experimental accounting. The main CIFAR-10/100 augmentation counts \(159{,}840/158{,}400\) match the seed counts in the run script. Appendix B instead gives \(550\cdot45\cdot8=198{,}000\) for CIFAR-10 and describes five sets per CIFAR-100 pair, which yields \(5\cdot4950\cdot8=198{,}000\), not its printed \(198{,}400\). Different versions or subsets could explain part of this; an immutable sample ledger is needed. Table 10 also has CIFAR100-LT, \(\rho=10\), ACC 62.35 for CSM versus 63.83 for RankMixup, so an across-all-settings accuracy-superiority claim is too broad, while the displayed ECE advantage survives.

The visual examples show semantic transitions, but appearance alone is not an oracle for numerical class probabilities. Table 6 supports a benefit from the reported reannotation/loss combination within its measured setup; it cannot establish exact posterior truth. The EQ-DATA comparison usefully addresses training exposure, but generation/annotation cost and the experiment-time settings remain separate quantities. Historical logits, seeds, full configurations, model checkpoints, and the ImageNet evaluation implementation are needed to resolve remaining reproducibility and uncertainty questions.

Versions and scope. The reviewed original is the proceedings version. Official metadata lists arXiv:2504.13548v2, 26 May 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{version}]; a full version diff was not performed. Separate OpenReview supplement availability remained undetermined after the recorded HTTP 403 response; the embedded appendices were read. No whole-paper invalidity, universal failure of CSM, or fabricated experimental result is asserted.
# Assessment

The supported outcome is Major, based independently on the core posterior argument, the false CE-bias statement/derivation, and the conditional but fully specified released evaluation path. Local loss and metric discrepancies are reported separately with bounded impact; unresolved historical questions do not increase their supported severity. The scientific decision remains `pending`, `human_reviews` is empty, and no acceptance step has been performed.

Coverage, findings, source provenance, independent arithmetic, exact rational checks, and source-page inspections are recorded in the accompanying verification files. The final report PDF is compiled from the exact final TeX and visually inspected page by page; hashes and compiler records are in provenance. The reviewed original SHA-256 is `c39bb401144decb8c45d34bfdf21e624d617dd1ecff17af80255a0abc09653d4`.

report: Abstract: The published procedural generator admits a Forced Coordination layout in which all required facilities are individually accessible, yet onions cannot reach any pot. This invalidates the claimed solvability guarantee, a core infrastructure contribution. A separate calculation identifies an attracting non-CEC equilibrium in the published cross-play matrix. Title: Technical Verification of
Cross-environment Cooperation
# Identity, version, and scope

This report concerns Kunal Jha, Wilka Carvalho, Yancheng Liang, Simon S. Du, Max Kleiman-Weiner, and Natasha Jaques, Cross-environment Cooperation Enables Zero-shot Multi-agent Coordination, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 27198–27220, identifier I25-43490 (0121), OpenReview zBBYsVGKuB [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page references below are the PDF’s printed pages 1–23, which equal its one-based physical page numbers. The complete original-PDF hash is recorded in the reproducibility appendix. The complete main text and substantive appendix were read. Checks concentrated on the generator, cross-play interpretation, evaluation separation, and the distinction between human ratings and game reward. The released source snapshot is commit `2a74a761f2fe044aae1f4232367bf918fbc8de73` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]; it was inspected statically, never executed.

The appendix is present on pp. 14–23 despite the acquisition manifest’s automatic appendix detector reporting false. No separate supplement was acquired. OpenReview metadata access returned HTTP 403, so separate-material availability could not be resolved; the full proceedings PDF remains available. Raw participant records, original experiment configurations, and trained policies were not inspected. Thus p-values and historical task contamination are not reproduced here.
# Necessary definitions

A generated task retains a base layout’s impassable wall cells, places plate piles, onion piles, pots and delivery goals on those cells, and puts one agent in each side of the split Forced Coordination layout. Agents move on free cells and interact with adjacent facilities. Under the standard empty initialization, a completed soup requires transporting onions to a pot before collecting and delivering it. A plate pile or goal cannot serve as an empty counter on which an onion can be deposited. This distinction is explicit in the inspected interaction code.

Equation reference: eq:rep. For the empirical meta-game, use the symmetric matrix \(A\) printed in Fig. 21 and the ordinary single-population replicator equation \[
 \dot x_i=x_i\bigl((Ax)_i-x^\top Ax\bigr),\qquad x\geq0,\quad {\bf1}^\top x=1.\] This is a deterministic analysis of the published mean matrix, not a confidence statement about the underlying empirical population.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Individual facility reachability does not guarantee solvability: Major).
## Source claim and suspect step

The abstract and contribution 2 (pp. 1–2) advertise solvable coordination challenges. Appendix A.1 (p. 14) claims that making at least one facility of each required type reachable by at least one agent guarantees a solvable task. Algorithm 1 (p. 15) implements that criterion. The missing step is reachability of the material flow from onions to pots: separate access to each facility does not ensure that ingredients can move between the agents’ disconnected walking regions.
## Admissible input

Use the \(5\times5\) Forced Coordination base with zero-based row-major cell index \(5r+c\). Its free cells are \(\{6,11,16\}\) and \(\{8,13,18\}\). Put agents at 6 and 8. Choose facilities as follows:
Facility | Mandatory cell | Supplemental cell
Plate pile | 7 | 12
Onion pile | 5 | 10
Pot | 3 | 9
Delivery goal | 17 | 19

These are eight distinct wall cells. The mandatory sequence \((7,5,3,17)\) is an admissible ordered selection from the source’s `need_one` set \[\{1,5,10,15,21,17,12,7,3,9,14,19,23\}.\] The supplementary sequence \((12,10,9,19)\) uses distinct remaining wall cells. Agent 6 is an allowed left-side start and agent 8 an allowed right-side start. These facts follow directly from `layouts.py`, lines 815–883; the independent script additionally checks them as finite set statements.

Every facility is reachable by at least one agent. In particular, both onion piles touch the left walking component, both pots touch the right one, the two plate piles touch both components, and the goal at 17 touches both. Take the permitted no-rotation/no-flip choice and pad with walls. Neither operation creates a passage. Empty inventories and empty pots are the ordinary reset setting, explicitly supported by `overcooked.py`, lines 451–455 and 500–508. The arrangement differs from the five canonical held-out tasks, so Algorithm 1 with those tasks as its held-out set accepts it. This is an admissible input to the stated generation procedure; the argument does not assert that this exact task appears in the authors’ additional 100-task sample.
## Decisive argument

Proof. Let \(L=\{6,11,16\}\) and \(R=\{8,13,18\}\). Walls prevent an agent from moving from \(L\) to \(R\). The only wall cells adjacent to both components are \(\{7,12,17\}\). They contain, respectively, a plate pile, a plate pile, and a goal. None is an empty counter, onion dispenser, or pot.

Initially there is no onion in \(R\), in either pot, or in the right agent’s inventory. An onion can originate only at cells 5 or 10, adjacent solely to \(L\). Movement preserves the component containing its carrier. Dropping an onion across the cut is impossible because all shared cells are permanent piles/goals, and those facilities are not empty counters. No direct transfer between agents exists across a wall. Therefore the stated absence of onions on the right is an invariant of every action sequence. Both pots remain empty, and no completed soup or delivery is reachable, even with an unlimited horizon. ◻

The exact interaction conditions are `table_is_empty` at line 825 and `successful_drop` at line 862 of `overcooked.py`; pile pickup preserves the pile at lines 866–872. The proof is analytic. The reviewer-written script validates the coordinates, permitted selections, walking components, and shared boundary; it does not run or emulate the author’s training code. Its output is `independent_results.json`.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and correction bounds

A shared pot or shared onion dispenser can make some split layouts solvable without an empty counter. Neither occurs here. Random initial food could also defeat this invariant, but the counterexample uses the supported empty initialization. The rule’s two copies of each facility are present; the example does not exploit missing objects, duplicate placement, or an inaccessible mandatory item.

This is Major because the constructive solvability guarantee is a named core contribution and differentiator from generators permitting impossible tasks. It does not require proving that the average reward changes. The empirical benefit of environmental diversity may survive. The proportion of generated unsolvable tasks and their effects on the published comparisons require new enumeration or experiment records. Individual reachability must be replaced or supplemented by a condition certifying feasible ingredient transfer and delivery; no complete corrected generator is claimed or verified here.
Problem 2 (The published meta-game has an attracting non-CEC mixture: Minor).
## Source claim and calculation

Section 6, Q1 (p. 7), interprets Fig. 8 as having vector directions toward CEC or CEC-Finetune in both task settings and uses this as evidence of robust cross-algorithm generalization. Appendix A.8 (p. 19) identifies Fig. 21 as the original-task payoff matrix. With order IPPO, E3T, FCP, CEC, CEC-FT, that matrix is \[A=\begin{pmatrix}
 .51&.29&.77&.47&.49\\
 .29&.43&.41&.38&.33\\
 .77&.41&.55&.58&.71\\
 .47&.38&.58&.61&.67\\
 .49&.33&.71&.67&.78
 \end{pmatrix}.\] On the IPPO–FCP edge, putting IPPO mass \(p\) gives payoffs \(.77-.26p\) and \(.55+.22p\). They agree at \(p=11/24\), so \[x^*=(11/24,0,13/24,0,0),\qquad x^{*\top}Ax^*=781/1200.\] The E3T, CEC, and CEC-FT payoffs are \(71/200\), \(1271/2400\), and \(731/1200\), respectively. Their invasion growth rates in [eq:rep] (#eq:rep) are \[-71/240,\qquad -97/800,\qquad -1/24,\] all strictly negative. The tangent eigenvalue on the IPPO–FCP edge is \(-143/1200<0\). Thus \(x^*\) is locally asymptotically stable, including against small positive invasions by every excluded strategy. It is not merely a zero-mass absorbing boundary point.

The conclusion is robust to independent symmetric rounding errors of at most \(.005\) per displayed payoff. The perturbed edge equilibrium has \(p\in[.42,.50]\). Its resident payoff is at least \(.635\), while CEC-FT’s payoff there is at most \(.6226\), and CEC’s is at most \(.5388\). The negative invasion margins persist. This rounding bound does not account for empirical sampling uncertainty.
## Alternative reading and bounded impact

A narrower reading that CEC-FT is one attracting equilibrium is correct: at its pure vertex, \(.78\) exceeds every alternative payoff against CEC-FT. Figure 8’s top-left panel also visibly contains directions toward the lower edge. Therefore the discrepancy is an overbroad dynamical interpretation, not evidence that the displayed matrix was fabricated. The original-task meta-game has multiple basins; the argument does not challenge the distinct procedural-task matrix in Fig. 22 or the human-study results. This local interpretation defect is Minor. The defensible correction is to state coexistence of CEC-FT attraction and a stable IPPO–FCP mixture rather than a general directional preference.
Problem 3 (Released held-out filtering does not implement repeated rejection: Needs Evidence for historical impact).

Appendix A.1 and Algorithm 1 (pp. 14–15) resample until the generated task is outside the held-out set. In the pinned `overcooked.py`, lines 243–257 test the initial draw and conditionally take one replacement, returning that replacement without another membership check. With independently drawn membership probability \(q>0\), one-shot replacement leaves probability \(q^2\) of returning a held-out task, whereas repeated rejection with \(q<1\) returns none. The formula is an analytic control-flow illustration, not a measured probability for JAX’s deterministic key schedule.

The training initialization does build a held-out collection (`ippo_general.py`, lines 38–80), which is counterevidence against claiming that no exclusion was attempted. The example configuration also sets `check_held_out: False`, but it defaults to a different single-task setup; that default is not proof of the setting used in CEC experiments. The inspected release therefore cannot certify the paper’s strict train/test disjointness. Actual recorded configurations, keys, and generated tasks are required to determine historical overlap and its materiality. Neither contamination nor a benchmark reduction is established. A repeated rejection loop would restore the stated exclusion property under positive probability of an admissible task; its integration and runtime behavior were not tested.
# Overall impact and remaining evidence

Problem 1 establishes failure of a core construction guarantee and determines the overall assessment, Major. Problem 2 is a bounded correction to the original-task dynamical interpretation. Problem 3 remains unresolved for the published experiments. The finite oracle arithmetic on p. 5 is consistent: \([-3+97(3-1)]/200=.955\), and the difference from \(.931\) is approximately \(2.51\%\) of the oracle value.

The paper explicitly distinguishes higher human preference ratings from lower reward than E3T; that distinction was preserved. The within-participant protocol and seven-item ratings were checked descriptively, but the unit used for statistical tests cannot be reconstructed from the supplied aggregated plots. No significance finding is manufactured from that gap. No correction is documented in the inspected paper or README; a comprehensive search of later versions/errata was not performed. The pinned source’s correspondence to historical experiment code is unverified.
# Conclusion
Dimension | State
Inspection assessment | Major: invalid generator solvability guarantee; separate Minor meta-game interpretation issue.
Scientific adjudication | Pending; this is an initial review.
Repair verification | No corrected generator tested; precise meta-game qualification derived above.
Author adoption | Not requested; unknown.
Remaining work | Historical generated-task audit, held-out configurations, raw human-study inference, later-version search.

report: Abstract: Two theoretical conclusions require correction. Title: Technical Verification of
Survival Analysis via Density Estimation
# Identity and inspected scope

Hiroki Yanagisawa and Shunta Akiyama, Survival Analysis via Density Estimation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43491 (0122), OpenReview z9SRjXPf8T [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. References to pp. 1–30 use one-based physical PDF pages, equal to printed page numbers. The complete proceedings-PDF hash is recorded in the reproducibility appendix. Main methods, Theorem 5.3, Appendix B’s construction, the assumptions and proof structure in Appendix C, and Appendices D–F were read. The decisive checks below concern strict propriety and the conditional-error inference; the long induction in Proposition C.3 is not independently certified in every algebraic detail.

The assigned `cenreg` snapshot is commit `0849580744d5d5dbb3119abfda469a226b0f2bd6`. Its README includes 2026 work, so it is a later release, not established as the original experiment implementation. The copula and continuous-loss files were read statically. No author code or training was executed. Separate supplements could not be resolved because acquisition encountered an OpenReview access challenge.
# Definitions and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:v. The observations are \(T=\min(T_1,T_2)\) and \(\Delta=\arg\min(T_1,T_2)\). The targets are latent CDFs \((F_1,F_2)\), and the observable subdensities satisfy \(v_k(t)\,dt=\Pr(T\in dt,\Delta=k)\). For a known copula density \(c\) and differentiable marginals, \[
 v_1(t)=f_1(t)\int_{F_2(t)}^1c(F_1(t),w)\,dw,\] with the analogous formula for cause 2. Fixing \(X\) to a constant is a valid conditional model. Theorem 5.3 assumes finite KL divergence but does not impose the positive copula-density lower bound of Assumption C.1, which appears later for a different theorem.
# Findings
Problem 1 (Strict propriety for observables does not imply strict propriety for latent marginals: Major).
## Claim and failed implication

Theorem 5.3 and its proof (p. 7) conclude that equality of all \(v_k\) and \(\widehat v_k\) is equivalent to equality of all \(F_k\) and \(\widehat F_k\). The KL calculation preceding that statement is correct for normalized observable distributions. The equivalence requires injectivity of the observation map; finite KL divergence alone does not provide it.
## A known smooth copula

For \(z\in[0,1]\), define \[h(z)=
 \begin{cases}
 6\sin^2(3\pi z),&1/3<z<2/3,\\
 0,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
 \qquad c(u,v)=h((v-u)\bmod 1).\] Extend \(h\) periodically. Both \(h\) and its first derivative match zero at the support endpoints, and \(h\) vanishes near 0 and 1. Consequently \(c\) is continuously differentiable and its double integral defines a \(C^2\) copula. It is nonnegative, and \[\int_0^1c(u,v)\,dv=\int_0^1c(u,v)\,du
 =6\int_{1/3}^{2/3}\sin^2(3\pi z)\,dz=1.\] Thus both copula marginals are uniform. The joint law is absolutely continuous and has no tie mass.

Equation reference: eq:alt. Use \(\zeta_B=1\) and true marginals \(F_1(t)=F_2(t)=t\) on \([0,1]\). Keep \(\widehat F_2(t)=t\), and define \[
 \widehat F_1(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 t,&0\leq t\leq2/3,\\
 t+\frac13s^2(1-s)^2,\quad s=3t-2,&2/3<t\leq1.
 \end{cases}\] Both endpoints are correct. In the upper interval, \(\widehat f_1(t)=1+2s(1-s)(1-2s)\geq1/2\), and the derivative matches 1 at both joins. Hence every marginal is continuous and strictly increasing, with positive density throughout the interior. The candidate differs at \[F_1(5/6)=40/48,\qquad \widehat F_1(5/6)=41/48.\] The same fixed copula is used for the true and candidate joint laws.
## Observed distributions and score

Proof. If \(u>2/3\) and \(v>2/3\), then \((v-u)\bmod1\) lies outside \((1/3,2/3)\). Thus \(c(u,v)=0\): no pair of copula coordinates lies in the upper-right square. Both models satisfy \(T\leq2/3\) almost surely. For \(t\leq2/3\), their marginal CDFs and densities are identical, so [eq:v] (#eq:v) gives identical observable subdensities. For \(t>2/3\), both subdensities vanish in both models.

For completeness, under either model the two subdensities are each \[v_k(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&0<t\leq1/3,\\
 2-3t+\sin(6\pi t)/(2\pi),&1/3<t<2/3,\\
 0,&t\geq2/3.
 \end{cases}\] Each integrates to \(1/2\). Both causes are observed with positive probability; this is not an example with an entirely absent cause. The observable laws agree exactly, their KL divergence is zero and finite, and their expected NLL-SC scores agree. Yet their latent marginals differ by \(1/48\) at \(5/6\). The claimed strict equality condition is false. ◻

The expected score is well defined: the subdensities are bounded, and \(-v\log v\) has a finite integral on compact support. Zero-density observations contribute zero in the usual limiting convention.
## Counterevidence and correction

Assumption C.1(2) on p. 14 requires \(\inf c>0\). This example deliberately does not satisfy that condition and does not refute Theorem C.2. It satisfies the conditions actually stated for Theorem 5.3, even with smoothness and strict marginal monotonicity added. It also does not show that the independent or finite-parameter Frank copulas used in experiments are nonidentifiable on their relevant domains.

The corrected general statement is: NLL-SC is proper for latent models through their induced observable law, and strictly proper for that observable law, up to equality almost everywhere. It is strictly proper for a specified latent model class only if the fixed-copula observation map is injective on that class. This follows from the same KL identity plus injectivity; no particular additional copula condition is asserted sufficient here without proof. The universal strict-propriety contribution and claimed latent-distribution guarantee for SC-Net require this restriction. The severity is Major even though the loss remains useful and empirical scores need not change.
Problem 2 (Integrated error is substituted for a pointwise conditional bound: Major).
## Source claim

Appendix D.2 (p. 25), after Proposition D.2, defines error by an integral over \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\) and claims that Eq. (18) follows by taking \(\epsilon\) to be that total variation distance. Equation (18), p. 14, is the cell-probability error required for the conditional Step 2 analysis. The inference changes an integrated-in-\(x\) quantity into a bound at a particular \(x\).
## Independent counterexample

Let \(X\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), and let the true four conditional bin/cause probabilities be \[r(x)=(3/8,3/8,1/8,1/8)\] for every \(x\). These are the two-bin observable probabilities of independent uniform latent event times, with boundary \(1/2\). Let \(A_\eta\) be the interval of length \(\eta\) centered at \(1/2\), and put \[\widehat r(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 (23/40,7/40,1/8,1/8),&x\in A_\eta,\\
 r(x),&x\notin A_\eta.
 \end{cases}\] All probabilities are positive and sum to one. These piecewise constant conditional densities fit the histogram setting; they can equivalently be spread uniformly within the time/cause cells for a continuous reference measure. The integrated unhalved \(L^1\) distance denoted TV in the paper is \[\int_0^1\sum_j|r_j(x)-\widehat r_j(x)|\,dx=\frac25\eta.\] At the fixed supported covariate \(x=1/2\), the first two cell errors are each \(1/5\). For \(\eta=1/100\), Eq. (18) would be claimed with \(\epsilon=1/250\), although the actual conditional error is \(1/5\). As \(\eta\downarrow0\), integrated error tends to zero and this pointwise error persists.

This refutes the stated deterministic implication from an integrated guarantee. It does not claim that the particular histogram estimator necessarily produces this sequence or that its cited oracle inequality is false.
## Norm issue and defensible replacement
# Surviving checks and scope limits

The distribution-free bounds in Eq. (15) and Appendix E follow from \[\{T\leq t,\Delta=k\}\subseteq\{T_k\leq t\}
 \subseteq\{T\leq t\},\] and are valid without a copula assumption. They are identification bounds, not confidence intervals; the paper makes that distinction. Replacing unknown probabilities by estimated CIFs adds estimation uncertainty, also acknowledged in Appendix E.

Finite-bin equal-weight allocation is explicitly an approximation, with sensitivity studied in Appendix F; it is not an exact within-bin ordering identity for arbitrary densities. The scoped checks do not reproduce the eight-dataset experiments or certify numerical optimization. The inspected code implements the conventional negative sign in the Frank copula; the sign discrepancy in displayed Eq. (2) was not promoted to an empirical implementation finding. No correction to the two findings is documented in the consulted original or README. Later-release features do not establish an erratum, and a complete later-version search was not performed.
# Conclusion
Dimension | State
Assessment | Major: missing injectivity in strict propriety, and invalid integrated-to-conditional error inference.
Scientific adjudication | Pending, initial review only.
Repair verification | Identifiable-class qualification and norm bound proved; no revised model trained.
