Title: Initial Scientific Review of
No Free Lunch from Random Feature Ensembles:
Scaling Laws and Near-Optimality Conditions
# Identity, materials, and scope

This review concerns paper 0123, I25-43492, by Benjamin S. Ruben, William L. Tong, Hamza Tahir Chaudhry, and Cengiz Pehlevan, in the supplied 27-page ICML 2025 proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering. The original and source-manifest hashes were checked; neither file was changed. The pinned repository is `benruben87/Random_Feature_Ensembles`, commit . Its theory functions and selected experiment notebook cells were read statically. No author code was executed.

The main text, mathematical appendices A–E, and supplementary figure captions were inspected. The review independently checks the fixed-effective-ridge comparisons, the leading zero-ridge overparameterized expansion, and the width-scaling inference. It does not certify Gaussian universality, concentration results imported from other papers, empirical risk values, or every plotted point. The paper itself distinguishes its deterministic equivalent from finite-sample random risk in Section 3 and Appendix B; the findings respect that distinction.
# Model and checks that hold

Write \(d_i=\mathrm{Df}_i(\kappa)\), \(A=-\kappa^2\mathrm{tf}'_1(\kappa)\), and \(B=\kappa\mathrm{tf}_1(\kappa)\). Equations (12)–(20) give \[\rho=\frac{N-d_1}{N-d_2},\quad
 \gamma_1=\frac{(1-\rho)d_1+\rho d_2}{P},\quad
 \gamma_2=\frac{d_2}{P},\qquad
 E_K=B_z+\frac{E_1-B_z}{K},\] where \(B_z=(A+\sigma_\epsilon^2)/(1-\gamma_2)\) and \(E_1=[\rho A+(1-\rho)B+\sigma_\epsilon^2]/(1-\gamma_1)\). For positive effective ridge and a learnable task, \(B>A\geq0\) and \(d_1>d_2\). At fixed \(\kappa,P\), increasing \(N\) increases \(\rho\), decreases both the signal numerator and \(\gamma_1\), and leaves \(B_z\) fixed. Increasing \(P\) at fixed \(\kappa,N\) decreases both risk denominators’ inflation factors. These observations supply the numerator step implicit in Appendix C.1, as well as the stated monotonicity.

For the fixed-total-size comparison, put \(
u=1/K\) and \(N=
u M\). The decomposition in (C.15) has two nonpositive terms: the derivative in (C.7) is negative, and \[
u(1-ho)= rac{
u(d_1-d_2)}{
u M-d_2}\] decreases with \(
u\), while \(1-\gamma_1\) increases. Thus the core comparison in Theorem 5.1 is supported within this deterministic-equivalent model. This is not a theorem about every realization of a finite feature ensemble or about feature-learning networks.

There is also a useful exact check on Section 6.1. For \(\lambda=0\), \(N>P\), and \(\sigma_\epsilon=0\), the fixed point has \(d_1=P\), independent of \(N\). Direct substitution gives \[\operatorname{Var}_z=\frac{P\kappa\,\mathrm{tf}_1(\kappa)}{N-P}.\] Its leading term is \(P\kappa\,\mathrm{tf}_1(\kappa)/N\), agreeing with (D.21) and the \(1/(KN)\) correction in (24). No issue was found in that specific leading-order assertion.
# Problem

Problem 1 (Missing ridge regime in the core width-scaling derivation).  Assessment: Major, scoped to the stated derivation and its unqualified scaling law. Section 6.2, equations (26)–(27), gives a risk exponent under \(N\ll P\) and source/capacity power laws. Appendix D, equations (D.1)–(D.6), retains a general ridge \(\lambda\). The first paragraph on page 25 then infers that the left side of (D.6) is large from \(P\gg N\), and concludes \(\kappa\sim N^{-\alpha}\). The displayed assumptions do not imply that inference.
## Assumptions and decisive calculation

Work entirely inside the paper’s deterministic-equivalent equations, with \[\eta_t=t^{-2},\qquad \bar w_t=1,\qquad
 \sigma_\epsilon=0,\qquad K=1,\qquad
 P=N^{3/2},\qquad \lambda=1.\] One may take \(N=m^2\) to make \(P=m^3\) integral. The spectrum has infinite rank, finite trace, and \(\alpha=2\). The target has finite variance \(\sum_t t^{-2}\) and satisfies \(\bar w_t^2\eta_t=t^{-(1+2\alpha r)}\) with \(r=1/4\). In particular \(P/N\to\infty\), as required in the printed argument.

The exact fixed-point equation (14) can be rewritten as \[\kappa\left(1-\frac{d_1}{P}\right)
        \left(1-\frac{d_1}{N}\right)=\frac1P.
 \tag{1}\] For this spectrum, integral comparison gives \[d_1(\kappa)\sim \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{\kappa}},
 \qquad
 d_2(\kappa)\sim \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{\kappa}}.
 \tag{2}\] The right side of (1) bounds \(\kappa\) from below by \(P^{-1}\). Since \(d_1\) decreases, this implies \(d_1/N=O(\sqrt P/N)=O(N^{-1/4})\to0\), and also \(d_1/P\to0\). Returning to (1) therefore proves \[\kappa\sim P^{-1}=N^{-3/2},\] rather than \(N^{-2}\). This is a self-consistent asymptotic solution, not a claim based on a finite numerical fit.

Here \(\mathrm{tf}_1=d_1\), so \[A=-\kappa^2d_1'(\kappa)\sim\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{\kappa},
 \qquad
 B=\kappa d_1(\kappa)\sim\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\kappa}.\] Furthermore \(\rho\to1\) and \(\gamma_1\to0\). Equation (12) thus yields \[E_1\sim \frac{\pi}{4}N^{-3/4}.
 \tag{3}\] In contrast, equation (27) at \(\ell=1,\alpha=2,r=1/4\) gives \(s=1\) and equation (26) gives \(E_1\sim N^{-1}\). The discrepancy is in the leading power, not a prefactor.

An independent scalar script solves (1), using the closed-form sum \(d_1=[(\pi/\sqrt\kappa)\coth(\pi/\sqrt\kappa)-1]/2\). For \(N=10^4,10^6,10^8\), it obtains respectively \(\kappa N^{3/2}=1.1714,1.0510,1.0158\) and \(E_1N^{3/4}=0.9172,0.8252,0.7978\), approaching the analytic limits \(1\) and \(\pi/4\). The script imports no author module. These numbers corroborate the proof; they are not new benchmark results.
## Alternative reading and counterevidence

The strongest favorable reading is that Section 6.2 intends the noiseless, sufficiently small, or optimally tuned ridge regime throughout. That interpretation is consistent with the broader paper’s emphasis on optimized risk. It is also supported by the pinned experiment notebook: cells 48–50 use a ridge sweep and set \(\sigma_\epsilon=0\) for the synthetic scaling experiment. Figure 4 explicitly says optimal ridge. Under that strengthened reading, the counterexample with fixed \(\lambda=1\) is outside the intended scope. This review does not claim that optimized risk has exponent \(3/4\) or that a reported fitted exponent is wrong.

Nevertheless, the printed inference from \(P\gg N\) to the large-left-side claim is invalid even at zero label noise, and the displayed derivation does not state the necessary ridge restriction. The restriction must enter the mathematical claim, not merely a numerical configuration.
## Dependency, correction, and bounds on impact

The inference supplies \(\kappa\sim N^{-\alpha}\), which is then substituted into (D.7)–(D.12) to obtain the central joint-growth exponent and near-optimality discussion. This is why the defect is assessed as Major for that derivation, despite its repair being potentially short. It does not depend on lower benchmark scores or failure of the other main theorem.

A sufficient regime for the intended width scaling is noiseless prediction with \(P/N\to\infty\) and \(\lambda/(PN^{-\alpha})\to0\); then the width constraint dominates the ridge constraint. A precise optimized-risk claim can instead specify its optimization and prove that the selected ridge enters the appropriate regime. A fixed positive noise floor must also be removed or accounted for before asserting decay of the full risk in equation (10). These are analytic scope corrections, not a verified revision of the entire paper. Boundary source exponents may introduce logarithmic factors, so exponent statements should distinguish leading log-slopes from strict asymptotic equivalence.
# Overall assessment and unresolved checks

The supported result is one scoped Major mathematical derivation issue. Theorem 5.1 and the checked leading overparameterized expansion remain supported. The Gaussian-universality and concentration assumptions are acknowledged limitations in the original paper, not newly established failures. Numerical reproduction, historical correspondence of the pinned source to each figure, and a comprehensive errata search remain unverified.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
SparseLoRA: Accelerating LLM Fine-Tuning
with Contextual Sparsity
# Identity and scope

Paper 0124, I25-43493, is by Samir Khaki, Xiuyu Li, Junxian Guo, Ligeng Zhu, Konstantinos N. Plataniotis, Amir Yazdanbakhsh, Kurt Keutzer, Song Han, and Zhijian Liu. The reviewed original is the supplied 16-page ICML 2025 PDF. Page numbers are one-based PDF pages, matching printed numbers. The pinned release is `z-lab/sparselora`, commit `a2fd69de93b1168080346ec113c99501f0bb58b1`. Original and inspected-source hashes were verified against their supplied records. No author code, training, or benchmark was run.

The main method and experiments on pp. 1–9 and Appendix A on pp. 14–16 were read. Source inspection covered the sparse linear layer, adapters, registry, token handling, predictor definitions, callback, and training configuration. External evidence was limited to primary PyTorch documentation for the semantics of `no_grad`. No comprehensive novelty, later-version, or errata search was performed.
# Method and supported checks

The proposed computation preserves dense low-rank adapters while selecting channels in the frozen base projections, using low-rank SVD predictors and layer-specific sparsity. It keeps output tokens dense, delays sparsification by an initial dense interval, and applies dense inference after fine-tuning. These are empirical approximation choices; the paper does not prove that SVD selection exactly reproduces dense outputs or globally optimizes attention error.

The source registry explicitly returns `None` for LoRA adapter sparsity modes, consistent with the dense-adapter design. It assigns `out_scatter` to PEFT base layers for query, key, value, gate, and up projections, and `in_gather` to output and down projections. The Math10K script sets the initial dense fraction to \(0.05\), consistent with the relevant appendix configuration.

Independent arithmetic gives \[\frac{623+679}{384+436}=1.5878,\qquad \frac1{0.46}=2.1739.\] These agree, after rounding, with Figure 1’s approximately \(1.6\times\) combined forward/backward ratio and the approximately \(2.2\times\) FLOP reduction associated with Table 2. These calculations do not establish an independently measured wall-clock speedup.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Selected base-projection gradients are detached in the pinned implementation).  Assessment: Major for the core released implementation; historical experimental attribution Needs Evidence. Section 3 and Figure 3, p. 3, motivate sparse loss and gradient computation through selected base-model weights while retaining dense LoRA branches. The pinned `sparselora/modules/linear.py`, lines 19–22 and 30–40, instead performs activation gather and output scatter inside `torch.no_grad()` blocks. This removes the selected base path from reverse-mode differentiation.
## Exact paths and assumptions

The source path is not an unreachable utility. In `registry.py`, lines 33–47, a PEFT base projection is assigned `out_scatter` or `in_gather`. The API replaces eligible linear modules at `api.py`, lines 101–123. The attention module passes selected indices to those projections at `llama.py`, lines 71–88 and 104–108. In `linear.py`, lines 51–71, the patched adapter forward adds the base result to the dense LoRA result.

The finding assumes an enabled sparse layer with a nonempty proper subset of channels, a frozen base weight, and an input that depends on an upstream trainable adapter. These are ordinary fine-tuning circumstances. The selected index set can be held fixed locally; no derivative of a top-\(k\) decision is required.

For `out_scatter`, the selected matrix multiplication is initially differentiable with respect to its input. The subsequent `scatter_add` is evaluated under `no_grad`, so the assembled output loses that graph. For `in_gather`, the input gather itself is detached. Multiplication by a frozen base weight cannot restore the missing dependency. PyTorch’s primary documentation confirms that computations inside this context are excluded from the reverse-mode graph even when inputs require gradients. Neither gather nor scatter-add is a factory-function exception.
## Decisive derivative

Let an upstream scalar adapter parameter produce \(x(\theta)=(\theta,0)^\top\). Take frozen \(W=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)\) and retain channel 0. The intended selected base computation produces \(y=(2\theta,0)^\top\), with \[L(\theta)=\tfrac12\|y\|^2=2\theta^2,\qquad
 \left.\frac{dL}{d\theta}\right|_{\theta=1}=4.\] A fixed-index scatter or gather must preserve this derivative. Treating the selected result as detached gives contribution zero instead. An independent rational-arithmetic central difference at \(\theta=1\), with step \(10^{-6}\), is exactly \(4\). No author function was imported or executed, and this is not represented as a PyTorch runtime test.

The same reasoning applies if residual or LoRA branches are present: those branches can still carry gradients, but the selected frozen-base contribution is missing. Freezing a weight eliminates its own parameter update; it does not eliminate the Jacobian needed to train parameters preceding that weight.
## Counterevidence and impact limits

Keeping LoRA dense does permit learning, and dense tokens and other paths remain active. Thus this finding does not show that training completely stops, that all gradients vanish, or that any printed benchmark number is false. Deliberately using a stop-gradient approximation is another possible algorithm, but it is not the selected-weight backpropagation described in the paper and requires explicit characterization.

The acquired release is pinned, but no historical training commit or raw run log ties these exact lines to the reported experiments. That part of the conclusion is Needs Evidence. The release-level defect is nevertheless material: it changes the optimization mechanism and may reduce backward work beyond channel sparsification. It therefore affects both algorithmic fidelity and the interpretation of a speed measurement made with this implementation. Major is supported for the core implementation without requiring an observed accuracy loss.

The scoped correction is to leave mask prediction or index selection outside autograd if desired while retaining differentiable activation gather/scatter operations. This restores the selected base Jacobian. No source was modified, no repaired training run was performed, and neither corrected accuracy nor corrected speed is claimed.

Problem 2 (The MT-Bench all-category caption exceeds the displayed evidence).  Assessment: Minor. Table 4, p. 8, claims matching or exceeding LoRA across all categories. Its own entries instead decrease from \(5.50\) to \(5.45\) for Extraction, from \(2.25\) to \(2.20\) for Math, and from \(7.78\) to \(7.70\) for STEM.

The decisive check is subtraction of the reported entries, yielding \(-0.05,-0.05,-0.08\). The averages are consistent: the eight-category means are \(6.035\) for LoRA and \(6.0625\) for SparseLoRA. Thus the caption should say comparable aggregate performance, with mixed category changes. The decreases are small and no paired uncertainty information establishes statistical deterioration. This is a bounded reporting correction, not evidence against the core acceleration result.
# Additional evidence boundaries
## Aggregate definition

Table 3 lists nine GLUE tasks but its average is not the mean of all nine displayed columns: those means are \(82.7\) and \(84.2\). Excluding WNLI gives \(87.35\) and \(87.7375\), which approximately explain the printed \(87.3\) and \(87.7\); rounding of underlying scores may explain the first final digit. An eight-task aggregate is a plausible intended convention, but the exclusion should be specified. The relative direction of the reported comparison is preserved under either aggregation. This ambiguity is recorded separately from a proved core failure.
## Lossless performance and measurement scope

The paper reports five runs with highest and lowest discarded for the principal reasoning experiments (p. 6). Without raw runs, covariance, and a stated equivalence margin, small differences do not establish statistical equivalence. Conversely, small negative point estimates alone do not establish material harm.

The SVD factors are explicitly prepared offline (p. 5), while Table 8 measures online estimator overhead. The main timing evidence would be stronger with raw synchronized measurements and a clear inclusion list for warmup, data handling, offline setup, and dense initial steps. For example, if a sparse-step speedup is \(s\), an initial dense fraction \(f\) and one-time setup time \(T_0\) give total relative cost \[f+(1-f)/s+T_0/T_{\rm dense}.\] This identity is a scope check, not proof that the authors omitted any term. Precomputed factors can legitimately be amortized across runs. No timing falsification is inferred from absent logs.
# Overall assessment

The review supports a Major issue in the current source’s gradient path, with historical experiment attribution unresolved, and one Minor literal reporting issue. The headline ratios pass arithmetic checks. SVD approximation quality, task performance, and runtime remain empirical claims not independently reproduced here. The gradient correction must be tested before attributing the original performance–speed tradeoff to a repaired implementation.

# Identity, materials, and review scope

This is paper 0125, I25-43494, by Qingqing Cao, Mahyar Najibi, and Sachin Mehta, reviewed in the supplied 20-page ICML 2025 proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and printed page numbers. The original PDF and source-manifest hashes were recorded and checked without modification.

The main text on pp. 1–9, Appendix A.1–A.8 on pp. 14–20, prompt templates, synthesis paths, training schedules, filtering descriptions, and reported ablations were read. The supplied manifest records no author-released repository identified by the bounded acquisition search; this is not proof that no code exists. Separate OpenReview supplementary availability was undetermined because metadata access returned HTTP 403. Embedded appendices were available and used. No author code, model inference, or benchmark training was executed.
# Method reconstruction and supported checks

The pipeline decomposes an image into object, attribute, and relation tags, transforms those tags through text-control instructions, and optionally generates images through a diffusion model. Its principal CLIP setting mixes original-image/synthetic-text pairs with synthetic-image/synthetic-text pairs. The text explicitly distinguishes this from image synthesis based only on noisy original captions.

The filtering rule compares tag overlap with a selected threshold. It is a useful computable proxy for alignment, not a mathematical guarantee of semantic fidelity. For example, exchanging subject and object can preserve an unordered tag set; the paper’s downstream compositional evaluation, rather than tag overlap alone, is the relevant empirical evidence. This observation does not demonstrate failure of the actual generated dataset or contradict a formal theorem, since no such theorem is supplied.

Appendix A.3 proposes \(E'=EN/(N+N')\) epochs on an augmented dataset of size \(N+N'\). The sample-budget identity \[E'(N+N')=EN\] is correct. It matches total observed training examples under the stated equal-batch convention. It does not equate synthesis compute, pretrained-teacher data, or number of unique real samples. The paper’s data-efficiency claim should be read at that downstream-training level; it does not report a verified full-system compute saving.

For Table 3, the four retrieval scores average to \(13.65\) versus \(37.10\) for CC3M and \(45.40\) versus \(54.35\) for CC12M. These support improvements of approximately \(23.4\) and \(9.0\) percentage points. The main text often writes percentages where percentage points are meant; these should not be interpreted as relative percentage increases. Table 5’s tail gains are exactly \(35.1-13.8=21.3\) and \(24.4-8.2=16.2\) percentage points. It also shows head-class decreases, which the main text acknowledges.

The tag ablation in Table 6 provides evidence that the full object/attribute/relation setting is more useful on SugarCrepe than object-only tags: \(68.5\) versus \(64.3\). The object-plus-attribute value is \(65.4\), so the additional gain over that intermediate ablation is \(3.1\) points. This supports a benefit of relations under the reported settings; it does not isolate all possible differences in generated sample distribution.
# Problem

Problem 1 (The long-tail reproduction protocol is internally inconsistent).  Assessment: Minor for the written protocol; actual generation counts and matched training budgets Needs Evidence. Appendix A.2, p. 15, says seven synthetic samples are generated per tail class, yet reports 80.4K ImageNet-LT samples and 55.2K Places-LT samples. Section 4.3, p. 7, specifies ten baseline epochs or matched iterations for CtrlSynth, while Table 8(b), p. 16, lists iteration budgets incompatible with that description under its own batch and device settings.
## Generation-count contradiction

The paper states that ImageNet-LT has 1,000 classes and Places-LT has 365 classes. Even if every class were a tail class, seven generated images per class would give at most \[7(1000)=7000,\qquad 7(365)=2555.\] The reported 80,400 and 55,200 exceed those upper bounds by factors exceeding 11 and 21. Restricting to the actual tail subset only tightens the bounds. Filtering can remove generated images but cannot increase these maxima.

A plausible alternative is seven images per original tail example, or an omitted repeated-generation factor. Either can describe a substantially larger synthesis process. Neither appears in the quoted generation rule, and no generation manifest was available to determine which correction is intended. The observation proves a contradiction in the description, not that the reported dataset sizes or scores are fabricated.
## Training-budget contradiction

Table 8(b) specifies one GPU and batch size 128. Using the stated real-dataset sizes, ten epochs correspond approximately to \[\frac{10(115800)}{128}=9046.875
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \frac{10(62500)}{128}=4882.8125\] iterations for ImageNet-LT and Places-LT, respectively. Rounding, last-batch conventions, and modest uncertainty in the dataset sizes do not explain the table’s 55,429 and 56,429 iterations. Those budgets instead imply about \(61.27\) and \(115.57\) passes over the real datasets. Even ten epochs over the reported enlarged datasets would not reconcile the table.

An unstated sampler or a different definition of an iteration could change this arithmetic, but would itself require specification. Another plausible explanation is a copied table entry: the long-tail total and warmup iteration numbers repeat the adjacent pretraining table. This is counterevidence against assuming a substantive execution error; it is not proof that a copying error occurred.
## Dependency, correction, and bounded impact

The long-tail result is a central empirical use case, but neither inconsistency demonstrates unequal training between baseline and method. Both could have used the same actual iteration budget, and Table 5’s accuracy differences can remain valid after correcting the written protocol. The demonstrated defect is an internally contradictory protocol description. Because the executed generation counts and optimizer steps are unavailable, the evidence does not establish that either experimental arm violated the stated matched-budget design; that execution question remains Needs Evidence.

The correction requires the actual generation unit and count by class, post-filter totals, sampler definition, effective batch size, and executed optimizer-step counts for both arms. Those records would determine whether the disagreement is purely descriptive or changes the matched-budget interpretation. This review cannot fill in missing values by guessing. No corrected experiment or impact on accuracy is claimed.
# Unresolved evidence and alternative explanations
## Validation-set reuse

Appendix A.6, p. 17, openly states that the filtering threshold is selected using CLIP accuracy on the ImageNet validation set. Figure 6 and the principal ImageNet evaluation use that set. Consequently the selected ImageNet result is not an evaluation on labels completely untouched by pipeline selection. This can create selection optimism, but neither its magnitude nor the disappearance of a gain is established here. The term zero-shot can refer to the absence of target-task classifier training, which is compatible with this disclosed hyperparameter-selection procedure. An independent held-out evaluation would be needed for a stronger claim of untouched-test generalization.
## Cross-paper comparisons

The paper itself acknowledges that training software, recovered CC3M samples, and hardware hinder a fully controlled comparison with prior work (p. 7, footnote 4). Appendix A.7 uses Datacomp subsets at larger scale, and the review did not independently inspect the original VeCLIP or LaCLIP training artifacts. The superiority tables therefore support the reported setting comparison, while causal attribution of every cross-paper improvement to this pipeline alone remains unverified. This limitation does not invalidate within-paper matched-baseline results.
## Other scope limitations

The review did not generate fresh synthetic samples, audit dataset contamination, measure synthesis cost, independently judge the Figure 8 sample quality, or obtain run-level uncertainty. It also did not verify later errata or all cited literature. The numerical gains, ablations, and prompts constitute meaningful supplied evidence, but do not substitute for unavailable execution artifacts.
# Overall assessment

The supported assessment is Minor for a contradictory long-tail protocol. No core scientific failure was established within the inspected pipeline and arithmetic scope. That scoped outcome is not acceptance or certification of all empirical claims.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Thinking LLMs: General Instruction Following
with Thought Generation
# Identity and scope

Paper 0126, I25-43495, is by Tianhao Wu, Janice Lan, Weizhe Yuan, Jiantao Jiao, Jason Weston, and Sainbayar Sukhbaatar. The reviewed original is the supplied 26-page ICML 2025 PDF, whose hash was checked against the preserved source manifest. Locations refer to one-based PDF pages, equal to printed pages.

The review covered Sections 1–5, the fine-grained evaluation and ELO specification, Tables 1–6, and the supplied judge/category prompt descriptions. The extended qualitative examples and plots on pp. 19–26 were not independently validated as benchmark evidence; their existence or plausibility is not treated as proof of aggregate gains. No author code was available in the acquired packet. The acquisition’s bounded search and OpenReview metadata access failure are availability limits, not evidence that a release does not exist.
# Method reconstruction and checks

TPO generates \(K=8\) thought/response pairs for an instruction, scores only the response, selects preferred and rejected full sequences, and applies iterative DPO. Its default setup uses ArmoRM scalar scores and UltraFeedback instructions. The pairwise STE judge is a separate experimental path.

Optimizing a joint sequence \((z,y)\) using response-based preferences is a coherent training objective. It does not establish that the text \(z\) is a faithful causal explanation of the model’s computation, and the paper supplies no formal theorem of that kind. A thought-intervention study would be needed to isolate whether particular thought content is necessary, but its absence is not itself a counterexample to the reported treatment-level benchmark advantage.

The headline differences are \(52.5-48.4=4.1\) and \(37.3-33.0=4.3\) percentage points. Table 5 identifies the \(52.5\) AlpacaEval result at iteration 3 of the specific-prompt setup, while Table 6 identifies \(37.3\) Arena-Hard at iteration 4. Thus Table 1 should be interpreted as reported best results, not proof that one checkpoint attains both maxima simultaneously. The text explicitly discusses the highest rates.

Table 4’s thought-length changes are \(1-314/815=61.47\%\) for generic prompting and \(1-1494/2125=29.69\%\) for specific prompting. These agree with the rounded reductions in the text. Table 2 also reproduces the reported character-length comparisons: approximately \(-12.58\%\) and \(+21.37\%\) before training, and \(-19.48\%\) and \(+9.22\%\) after one iteration, for generic and specific prompting respectively.

These are character-length calculations, not measured FLOPs or latency. Tokenization, prompt length, generation retries, pairwise judging, attention computation, and training padding can change actual cost. The arithmetic supports the stated length differences while the stronger conclusion that total computational impact is minor remains unverified without resource measurements.
# Problem

Problem 1 (The specified pairwise ELO estimator can have no finite maximizer).  Assessment: Minor, limited to the optional pairwise-judge scoring branch. Section 2.2, p. 3, uses pairwise comparisons to obtain scalar scores for selecting preference pairs. Appendix B, pp. 12–13, defines the battle matrix and says scores are obtained by maximizing an unregularized logistic likelihood. No connectivity condition, penalty, score bound, or finite-iteration fallback is specified. Valid, unanimous comparison outcomes can make this optimization lack a finite solution.
## Exact assumptions and counterexample

Let \(B_{mn}\) count wins of response \(m\) over response \(n\) across the two presentation orders. The printed objective is \[\ell(s)=\sum_{m,n}B_{mn}\log\sigma(s_m-s_n),\qquad
 \sigma(u)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-u}}.\] Take two responses for which the judge prefers response 1 in both orders. This gives \(B_{12}=2\) and \(B_{21}=0\), with no ties or parse errors. If \(d=s_1-s_2\), \[\ell(d)=2\log\sigma(d),\qquad
 \ell'(d)=2(1-\sigma(d))>0\] at every finite \(d\). The supremum is zero as \(d\to+\infty\), but it is unattained. Fixing \(s_1+s_2=0\) removes translation ambiguity without curing this separation.

The issue also applies to the paper’s usual eight candidates. Suppose both presentation orders agree with the strict ranking \(1\succ2\succ\cdots\succ8\). Then \(B_{mn}=2\) for \(m<n\) and zero otherwise. Choose centered scores \[s_i=t\left(\frac72-(i-1)\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,8.\] Their sum is zero, and \[\ell(t)=2\sum_{m<n}\log\sigma(t(n-m))<0\] for every finite \(t\), increasing to zero as \(t\to\infty\). No finite maximum exists. Such an outcome is allowed by the described procedure and does not require a pathological empty comparison graph.

An independent scalar script evaluates this eight-candidate likelihood as \(-38.8162\) at \(t=0\), \(-6.5919\) at \(t=1\), \(-0.09456\) at \(t=5\), and approximately \(-2.89\cdot10^{-8}\) at \(t=20\). These computations confirm the analytic argument; they do not execute an author solver.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

A practical library may impose regularization, artificial comparisons, numerical bounds, or terminate before divergence. Any such choice can yield finite scores. The paper references another implementation procedure, but neither that external implementation nor a pinned author source was available for this review. It would be incorrect to infer an actual runtime crash or infinite loop.

Moreover, a perfectly transitive ranking already identifies best and worst responses without finite ELO values. If the implementation only used that ordering, the final pair could remain unchanged. However, the length-control step in Section 2.2 standardizes scalar scores before subtracting a normalized length penalty, so finite score construction and its scale/shape can affect selection beyond pure ordering.

The common TPO objective and response-based preference-pair construction accept scalar scores and do not require this particular unregularized estimator. ArmoRM supplies such scores directly and is the stated default. The demonstrated defect is therefore in an auxiliary, interchangeable score-conversion specification; the source does not establish that a finite unregularized ELO maximizer is a necessary core theoretical guarantee of TPO. The actual STE solver and the effect on length-controlled preference selection remain unresolved.
## Correction and impact bounds

Specify a well-defined estimator and its exact hyperparameters. For example, \[\ell_\lambda(s)=\ell(s)-\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_i s_i^2,\qquad \lambda>0,\] is strictly concave and tends to \(-\infty\) as \(\|s\|\to\infty\), hence has a unique finite maximizer. A bounded-score optimization or an explicitly documented fallback is another possibility. The chosen method must be stated because it can affect length-penalized scores and preference pairs.

This is an analytic existence repair, not a verified replication or a modification of supplied code. The frequency of separable comparisons and the impact on STE-trained models remain Needs Evidence. The default scalar-score results are outside the demonstrated impact.
# Evaluation limits and counterevidence

Appendix A uses five-valued judge scores \(1,0.75,0.5,0.25,0\) and averages them over 200 instructions per category. These are preference scores, not raw Bernoulli win fractions. Without the individual verdicts, paired uncertainty and multiple-category uncertainty cannot be reconstructed. The paper itself says category rankings vary across judges and prompts. The review therefore does not infer a stable universal ordering of which domains benefit most.

Table 3 and the impact statement explicitly disclose degraded GSM8K performance, including large drops under the answer-only prompting condition. This limits any claim of universal reasoning improvement, but it is not a hidden result newly contradicted by this review. The direct baseline may also produce chain-of-thought in its visible response, as the paper states; the comparison is between training/output formats, not an assured absence of all reasoning in the baseline.

Parsing failures are also disclosed. Sampling again after a parse failure changes the inference protocol and can add cost; the rate and retry cap would be needed to quantify the effect. No evidence here shows that retries selected answers by quality. Likewise, existing human instructions and pretrained reward models are compatible with the narrower claim of requiring no newly annotated human thought data.
No training-seed replication, raw evaluation audit, independent human judging, or later-errata search was completed. These are explicit boundaries rather than negative scientific findings.
# Overall assessment

One Minor defect is supported in the pairwise scoring specification. Within the inspected main pipeline, headline arithmetic, and disclosed limitations, no core scientific failure was established. This scoped outcome is not an acceptance decision.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
DRAG: Data Reconstruction Attack
using Guided Diffusion
# Identity, materials, and scope

This review concerns paper 0127, I25-43496, by Wa-Kin Lei, Jun-Cheng Chen, and Shang-Tse Chen, in the supplied 19-page ICML 2025 PDF. Page locations are one-based PDF pages and match printed numbering. The original hash and inspected source hashes were checked against the acquired manifests. The pinned repository is `ntuaislab/DRAG`, commit `96788024346302e8481a56871d6c4b4b2c26ba63`.

The main method, threat model, quantitative tables, defense descriptions, and implementation appendices were read. Static source tracing covered the guided step, diffusion wrapper, optimizer-state extraction, metric feature selection, and selected defense code. Original inputs were preserved. The review performs only analytic and scalar calculations, without running reconstruction, author scripts, downloading models, or accessing private data.
# Supported scope and experimental checks

The attack assumes complete knowledge of the client encoder. The inverse-network extension additionally uses public training data; the paper separates this from private fine-tuning data and distinguishes DRAG from DRAG++. These assumptions matter: the evidence is not a demonstration of a query-free attack against an unknown private encoder.

Table 1 supports a substantial deepest-layer advantage under its reported metrics. For CLIP-ViT-B/16 at layer 12, DRAG reports MS-SSIM \(0.6735\) versus the best displayed alternative \(0.3884\), LPIPS \(0.1857\) versus \(0.5790\), and DINO similarity \(0.9331\) versus \(0.6524\). Shallow-layer superiority is not universal, and the paper acknowledges that. The \(T=250\), \(k=16\) schedule gives 4,000 refinement steps, consistent with Appendix A.3’s iteration count. That count does not imply faster wall-clock performance than every baseline; the execution table supplies separate times.

The evaluation uses ten images from each of three datasets, with sample indices listed in the release README. This is enough to establish examples of vulnerability but is a limited basis for population-level privacy rates. No confidence intervals, repeated seeds, or raw per-image results were independently reconstructed. No conclusion of differential-privacy failure is inferred from a defense that never claimed such a guarantee.
# Problems

Problem 1 (The printed guided step has the wrong minimization sign and inconsistent noise units).  Assessment: Major for the core algorithm as printed. Equation (1), p. 3, minimizes representation distance plus regularization. Equation (8), p. 4, defines \(g_t=\nabla_{x_t}L\) but adds its positive unit direction in the guided noise. Algorithm 1, p. 5, repeats that sign after positive Adam-style moment scaling. Moreover, equation (8) gives the replacement noise norm \(\sqrt n\,\sigma_t\), whereas equation (3) multiplies the noise by \(\sigma_t\) again.
## Assumptions and decisive sign check

Hold the selected guidance vector nonzero, use positive \(\sigma_t\), and consider a fixed denoising mean. At full guidance \(w=1\), the printed equation is \[\epsilon_t=r\,\frac{g_t}{\|g_t\|},\qquad r=\sqrt n\,\sigma_t.\] Its component along the loss gradient is positive. In a local coordinate where the guidance gradient is the objective gradient at the current mean, the linearized loss change from a positive displacement is positive. For the elementary smooth example \(L(u)=u^2/2\) at \(u=1\), a displacement \(+0.01\) increases the loss from \(0.5\) to \(0.51005\). A displacement \(-0.1\) decreases it to \(0.405\).

This scalar calculation does not claim that a nonconvex diffusion trajectory must decrease its loss at every step. It isolates the sign of the intended guidance component, which is the issue. It also does not rely on differentiating a discontinuous operation or on an actual image. On the first optimizer-state update in Algorithm 1, Adam’s positive normalization preserves each nonzero gradient sign; it does not supply the missing minus sign.
## Noise-scale check

Equation (3) writes the stochastic DDIM displacement as \(\sigma_t\epsilon_t\) for standard-normal \(\epsilon_t\). Equation (8), read literally as a replacement for that symbol, assigns it norm \(r=\sqrt n\,\sigma_t\). The resulting displacement consequently has norm \(\sqrt n\,\sigma_t^2\), rather than \(r\). For \(n=4\) and \(\sigma_t=0.1\), the two radii are \(0.02\) and \(0.2\). This affects every nonunit noise scale, independently of the sign issue.

The two consistent conventions are either a unit-variance noise variable subsequently multiplied by \(\sigma_t\), or an already scaled displacement added directly. The paper mixes those conventions. Simply changing the gradient sign without clarifying the stochastic variable leaves this inconsistency.
## Pinned-source counterevidence

The implementation does not use the printed sign and double scaling. In `run_drag_ldm.py`, lines 301–319, the scalar loss is differentiated, a normalized optimizer direction \(v\) is extracted, and the guided endpoint is explicitly `d_star = -r * v`. The final displacement \(d\) is normalized to radius \(r\) and passed as `noise=d`. In `models/diffusion.py`, lines 81–98, supplied noise is added directly, without another \(\sigma_t\) multiplier. The pixel-space path in `run_drag_dm.py`, lines 280–298, uses the same convention.

This is strong evidence for a publication/implementation mismatch, not proof of failed historical reconstructions. The original experiments may have used the correct release behavior. The review does not replace that counterevidence with a claim that the reported images or metrics must be wrong.
## Core dependency and correction bounds

The affected rule is the central operation that makes diffusion conditional on the target representation. A reader implementing the stated equations obtains a different guidance direction and stochastic scale. This is a material core-algorithm error, assessed Major even though a notation/sign repair is short and other empirical results may survive.

A precise repair is to define the guided quantity as a displacement, use a negative loss-gradient direction, and add that displacement directly to the DDIM mean, consistently with the inspected release. Alternatively, retain the standardized-noise convention throughout. No author code was changed, no reconstruction was run, and no corrected score or convergence guarantee is claimed.

Problem 2 (The DINO feature used for evaluation needs provenance clarification).  Assessment: Needs Evidence. Section 4.3, p. 5, describes DINO ViT-S/16 image similarity as a semantic metric. The pinned `models/distance.py`, lines 20–57, returns `pooler_output`, replaces the final layer normalization with the identity, and includes an explicit warning that pooler dense weights and bias were newly initialized rather than loaded from the checkpoint.
## What is observed and what is not

The provider’s model card describes the last hidden state of the CLS token as an image representation and gives an example reading `last_hidden_state`. It does not establish that the release’s extra pooled output is a pretrained semantic head. The release pins Transformers 4.50.3, but direct retrieval of that version’s implementation failed during this review. No checkpoint tensors were loaded, and the actual metric outputs used in the historical runs were unavailable.

The concern is scientifically meaningful because an unverified projection need not preserve cosine geometry. For example, \(u=(1,0)\) and \(v=(1,1)\) have cosine \(1/\sqrt2\), whereas applying \(\operatorname{diag}(10,1)\) to both gives \(10/\sqrt{101}\approx0.995\). This is an illustrative non-isometry, not an assertion that the released pooler equals that matrix or that its numerical errors have that size.
## Counterevidence, impact, and needed resolution

A fixed, shared projection can still preserve useful information, and using the same transform across methods can retain comparative value. In addition, MS-SSIM and LPIPS independently support many of the reported improvements. Neither the benchmark ordering nor the magnitude of DINO-score distortion has been demonstrated to change.

Resolution requires the actual feature-extraction definition, loaded-state key report, checkpoint identity, random initialization/seed information if applicable, and a comparison against the intended pretrained descriptor on the existing reconstructions. Until then, the DINO column’s interpretation and reproducibility remain uncertain. No claim that every metric or the privacy-risk conclusion fails is warranted.
# Additional limits and overall assessment

The token-permutation discussion is compatible with permutation-equivariant transformer blocks when shuffling occurs after positional embeddings and the CLS token is fixed. Dropping tokens is a separate operation that can affect utility. The adaptive token-reordering source maximizes sums of log probabilities through assignment, which matches the stated joint-probability interpretation; no issue was found in that scoped correspondence.

NoPeek is explicitly adapted from pretraining to fine-tuning and to the selected feature-distance setting in Appendix D. The reported defense comparison therefore concerns that implemented adaptation. The review does not establish failure of every possible NoPeek training procedure or future defense. The \(\ell_2\) penalty’s informal range language also should not be mistaken for a hard box constraint; the release separately clamps images before encoder evaluation.

The supported recommendation is Major for the printed guided sampler, with a distinct Needs Evidence metric concern. The historical empirical results remain unreplicated and are not disproved by these checks.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of Paper 0128
Editable Noise Map Inversion
# Identity, scope, and evidence

The assigned paper is I25-43497 (0128), by Mingyu Kang and Yong Suk Choi, Editable Noise Map Inversion: Encoding Target-image into Noise For High-Fidelity Image Manipulation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The review uses the assigned staging original; its complete hash is recorded in the reproducibility appendix. It matches the frozen acquisition manifest. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, equivalent to the printed page numbers. The original and manifest were not modified.

The main text on pp. 1–9, method equations and algorithm on pp. 3–5, Tables 1–7, and appendices on pp. 12–17 were read. The reference list was inspected for context; imported methods were not rederived. Figure captions and the extracted content of the qualitative appendices were inspected, but no full visual audit of all displayed edits or videos was performed. The original p. 4 was rendered and visually inspected to confirm equation notation and loop placement.

No source tree was acquired for this paper. The supplied manifest states that bounded discovery did not identify an author repository; this is not proof that none exists. OpenReview metadata access returned HTTP 403, leaving separate-supplement availability undetermined. No author code, checkpoints, image-generation pipelines, or downloaded inputs were executed. The reviewer-authored algebra script was executed successfully and its exact command, exit status, and numerical output are recorded in the evidence directory.
# Scientific contribution and dependencies

ENM inversion refines each DDIM inversion latent using source reconstruction and target-prompt alignment losses. It is then combined with existing attention-control editors. Its distinguishing operation is not merely using another editor: it introduces a target-conditioned inversion optimization, at additional per-target cost acknowledged in Appendix A (p. 12). The evidential chain is \[\begin{gathered}
\text{noise-gap observation}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{defined optimization}\\
\longrightarrow\ \text{implemented refinement}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{editing comparisons}.
\end{gathered}\] The noise-gap observations in Figure 3 and Appendix B motivate a heuristic; they are not a theorem that reducing the gap must improve editing. The paper supplies empirical comparisons rather than a universal convergence or editing-success guarantee. The problem below arises in the definition-to-algorithm link itself, without demanding such a guarantee.
# Demonstrated problem

Equation reference: eq:true, eq:cached. Problem 1 (Major: the cached-target algorithm does not implement the stated core loss).  Source claim and location. Equation (5), p. 4, defines \[L_{\mathrm{edit}}(z)=\|s(z)-q(z)\|_2,\qquad
s(z)=f(z,t,C_{\mathrm{src}}),\quad q(z)=f(z,t,C_{\mathrm{tgt}}).\] Equation (6) and the adjoining paragraph propose minimizing \[
F(z)=\|a-s(z)\|_2+\lambda\|s(z)-q(z)\|_2\] with respect to the current latent, with \(a=z_{t-1}\) fixed during that refinement. Algorithm 1 on the same page instead computes \(z^e_{t-1}=q(z^{(0)})\) before entering the \(K\)-step loop. Within the loop it recomputes only the source branch and updates \(z_t\). Read as a cached numerical target, it uses \[
G(z)=\|a-s(z)\|_2+\lambda\|s(z)-q(z^{(0)})\|_2.\] The rendered original confirms this placement; it is not an extraction artifact.

Assumptions and decisive calculation. Fix one inversion step, use the ordinary Euclidean norm exactly as printed, and consider differentiable points with nonzero residuals. There is no assumption in the paper that the target branch has zero Jacobian. For the alignment residual \(r=s(z)-q(z)\), the gradient of its norm is \[(J_s-J_q)^\top r/\|r\|_2.\] Treating the target output as fixed removes the \(J_q\) term and, after updates, also evaluates the residual against a stale target value.

A scalar affine diagnostic makes the consequence exact. Let \[s(z)=z,\quad q(z)=2z+1,\quad a=0,\quad z^{(0)}=1,\quad\lambda=10.\] The weight is the default reported in Appendix C. In a neighborhood of \(z=1\), \[F(z)=|z|+10|z+1|,\qquad G(z)=|z|+10|z-3|,\] so \(F'(1)=11\) and \(G'(1)=-9\). For a small refinement step \(\eta=0.01\), cached-target descent gives \(z^{(1)}=1.09\), with \[F(1)=21,\quad F(1.09)=21.99,\qquad G(1.09)=20.19<G(1).\] It therefore increases the claimed objective while decreasing the cached surrogate. This is a direction error, not a large-step overshoot. The global minimizers also differ: \(F\) is minimized at \(-1\), whereas \(G\) is minimized at \(3\); the latter has \(F(3)=43\). If the displayed norm was intended to be squared, the same example gives derivatives \(42\) and \(-38\), again with opposite signs. The independent script checks both readings using finite differences and explicit loss values.

This diagnostic is admissible for the method definition: at a fixed nontrivial DDIM step, Equation (3) has the form \(A z+B\epsilon_\theta(z,t,C)\), with nonzero \(B\), so affine prompt-conditioned maps are not excluded by its algebra. It is not an assertion that a particular trained Stable Diffusion network realizes these maps or that an observed benchmark sample exhibits this trajectory.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. The target assignment might be an omitted recomputation in the pseudocode, while the implementation actually differentiates both current branches. Alternatively, the authors may intend a deliberately frozen target and a different surrogate objective. Either could define a useful empirical method, but they are distinct methods and the paper does not identify which produced the tables. Retaining an old computational graph is also not a specification of repeated evaluation of \(q\) at the current iterate. Even moving the target evaluation inside the loop while stopping its gradient would generally differ from the full gradient of [eq:true] (#eq:true). The example establishes non-equivalence of the printed prescriptions, not failure of all these possible algorithms.

Core dependency, impact, and correction bounds. The target-conditioned refinement is the central new operation, and the update direction and optimization endpoint can change. This supports Major for the mathematical specification as printed. It does not imply that background-preservation gains, CLIP scores, or qualitative edits are fabricated or numerically false.

A repair must choose and document the actual operation. To optimize [eq:true] (#eq:true), recompute both branches at each iterate and include both Jacobians, with an explicit optimizer/step rule. To use a fixed target, state [eq:cached] (#eq:cached) and justify that surrogate instead. Also provide the refinement limit \(K\), threshold \(\tau\), and optimization settings used in the experiments; the inspected implementation section and appendices do not settle these details. Compare the clarified specification with the actual implementation before asserting which existing results require a rerun. No repair implementation or empirical rerun was performed here.
# Other checks and bounded no-issue findings

Equations (3)–(4) have the expected DDIM coefficient structure, with the inversion treated as an approximation. This review found no separate algebraic contradiction in those coefficients. Reconstruction and edit alignment can legitimately compete; that tradeoff alone is not an error.

The majority of Table 1’s reported comparisons support improvement on its stated preservation metrics. For P2P, the reported background MSE falls from 32.86 for PNPInv to 27.02, a \(17.77\%\) reduction in the displayed scaled units. The edited-region CLIP score is 22.12 versus DDIM’s 22.44, however, so the table does not show universal dominance on every metric. Section 4.2 explicitly says most metrics, which is a supported narrower reading. For MasaCtrl and PnP, the reported rows favor ENM on the listed metrics. These are checks of printed values, not reproductions of their computation.

Table 2 shows 38.87 seconds for ENM, versus 18.22 for DDIM and 148.48 for NTI: ENM is approximately \(2.13\) times DDIM’s time and NTI is approximately \(3.82\) times ENM’s time. The specific efficiency comparison with NTI and StyleD in Section 4.2 is consistent with the table. Appendix A expressly acknowledges additional per-target inversion and optimization costs; no hidden claim of cost-free reuse was inferred.

For video editing, Table 4 reports improved CLIP, LPIPS, and SSIM relative to both listed baselines. TEMP is \(0.9454\), above NTI’s \(0.9451\) but below DDIM+TAV’s \(0.9464\). Thus the evidence supports a tradeoff, not best temporal consistency against every baseline. The main quantitative paragraph identifies the former three metrics. There are no raw videos, dispersion estimates, or historical execution records in the available inputs from which to establish statistical reliability or general superiority.

Appendix C shows an increasing whole-image CLIP score with \(\lambda\), while the edited-region score is not monotone. Its default \(\lambda=10\) and \(T=50\) are a practical tradeoff selection, not a mathematical optimum. Appendix E compares source and null prompts in aggregate; close reported metrics are not a formal equivalence test. These qualifications do not independently demonstrate a failed core empirical conclusion.

The cross-attention overlap score in Section 4.5 measures localization of attention within a supplied mask. It can motivate editability, but it is a proxy rather than a proof of correct semantic edits. The paper’s additional CLIP and qualitative evidence are relevant counterevidence to interpreting that proxy as its sole evaluation. No stronger universal claim is certified here.

report: Abstract: The paper develops a constrained referral model for multiple diseases and conditional structural results for two diseases. This review identifies two Major discrepancies in the connection between that model and its experimental implementation: the pinned simulator uses a different, nonadditive stopping convention for screening costs, and its observation generator introduces dependence excluded by the factorized survival analysis. The main text also incorrectly infers temporal independence from independent errors around a shared random patient signal. Further evidence is needed to reconstruct the independent baseline and historical experiment configuration. Title: Initial Scientific Review of Paper 0129
Unified Screening for Multiple Diseases
# Paper, sources, and scope

The assigned paper is 0129, I25-43498, by Yiğit Narter, Alihan Hüyük, Mihaela van der Schaar, and Cem Tekin, Unified Screening for Multiple Diseases, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original is the assigned 33-page proceedings PDF; its complete hash is recorded in the reproducibility appendix. It matches the assigned acquisition manifest. The source tree is pinned at
in the author-linked UniScreen repository [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. A pinned current tree is not evidence that exactly that revision produced the published figures.
Page references use one-based physical PDF pages, matching the printed numbering.

The main scientific text (pp. 1–9), additional related-work discussion, all mathematical proofs in Appendix B (pp. 15–25), experimental appendices C–E (pp. 26–31), and notation tables (pp. 32–33) were read. References on pp. 10–14 were only partially inspected; clinical literature claims were not independently audited. All four source files and the README were read statically. Original pp. 8 and 30 were rendered and actually viewed. The review does not claim visual inspection of every plotted boundary or raw simulation trajectory.
# Contribution and dependency structure

The general objective is expected survival up to a fixed horizon, with a screening budget and diagnostic-error constraints. Rather than optimize every sequential policy, the referral problem chooses which supplied single-disease programs to activate. This restriction and the resulting lower bound on the unrestricted policy optimum are stated clearly in Section 3.2.

For two diseases, the analysis uses product survival probabilities and additive disease-specific screening costs to obtain marginal reward–cost gaps. Those gap inequalities support Proposition 4.1’s Boolean characterization and the conditional boundary geometry of Proposition 4.5. The latter explicitly assumes a decreasing boundary and a unique intersection; Appendix C offers empirical support rather than a general proof. It would be incorrect to treat those acknowledged assumptions as proved universally.

For fixed valid rewards and costs, the finite-grid optimization is a linear program, and the pointwise Lagrangian maximization over actions is sound. This review independently verified Proposition 4.1’s Boolean selection rule on 389 non-tied scalar product-survival/additive-cost cases. That check supports the algebraic rule within those premises; it neither proves all regularity conditions of the continuum problem nor validates a simulator with different premises.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Major: the experimental cost convention breaks the additivity used by the core characterization).  Exact claim and locations. Equation (1), p. 5, charges disease \(n\) until \(\min\{T_0,T_n,t_n^*\}\). Appendix B.1, p. 19, therefore sets \(m_{4,x}=m_{2,x}+m_{3,x}\), and Lemma B.7, p. 20, uses \[\Delta^C_{4,3}(x)=\Delta^C_{2,1}(x).\] The appendix additionally excludes the first sample’s cost for its subsequent analysis; that subtraction does not remove additivity. The equality is used in the proof of Proposition 4.1 (pp. 22–23) and in the boundary comparisons.

In contrast, Section 5.1, p. 8, describes estimating costs up to \(\min\{T_0,T^*\}\), involving the first unprevented event from either disease. The pinned , lines 81–104, implements this joint stopping: the cost of screening disease 1 uses `survival_10` or `survival_11`, each of which depends on disease 2. The independent simulator, lines 49–66, uses the single disease’s survival instead.

Assumptions and decisive calculation. Consider unit annual costs, a 40-year cap, no disease-1 event or diagnosis, a disease-2 event at time \(20.5\), and diagnosis of disease 2 at time \(1\) if its program is activated. This is a deterministic pathwise diagnostic of the displayed source formulas, not an execution of the author simulator. Using the source’s floor/count convention gives \[C_{10}=20,\qquad C_{01}=1,\qquad C_{11}=40+1=41.\] Thus \(C_{11}-C_{01}=40\ne20=C_{10}\). Under the formal own-disease stopping convention, the disease-1 cost would instead be 40 whether or not disease 2 is screened. Subtracting a fixed first-sample charge from each active program does not restore the missing equality in the joint-stopping version. The discrepancy is not an endpoint counting ambiguity.

More generally, under joint stopping, activating the second program can prevent an early adverse event and permit additional screening of the first disease. Its expected cost can consequently depend on the other program’s activation and the other disease’s risk. The proof’s constant-in-\(x_2\) disease-1 cost gap and additive-cost identity no longer follow.

Counterevidence and alternative interpretation. Stopping all screening at an unprevented event may be an intentional and clinically sensible alternative model. It is nevertheless a different optimization model from Equation (1) and the additive-cost theorem. A linear program can still optimize such nonadditive action costs, and it may still yield similar-looking boundaries. Those facts do not transfer the particular gap proof to it. An unreleased historical revision could also have used the formal costs.

Core impact and repair bounds. This is Major because the claimed empirical validation of the core boundary analysis uses a cost definition that need not satisfy its necessary structural identity. It also makes the stated common-budget comparison difficult to interpret when the two simulators account for costs differently. This review does not prove that every reported boundary, or the overall survival advantage, is numerically wrong.

Either use the disease-specific stopping model consistently in theory, simulator, baseline, and budget evaluation, or state joint stopping explicitly and rederive any structural claims that rely on cost additivity. Existing policies must then be checked under one common cost function. No corrected optimization or empirical rerun was performed.

Problem 2 (Major: the stated and implemented observation laws do not support the asserted independence).  Exact claims and locations. Section 3.1, p. 4, assumes that observations at distinct times are independent given the disease states. Lemma B.1, p. 16, factors the joint survival probability into disease-specific terms. Section 5.1, p. 8, claims that sampling a random patient signal once, then adding fresh independent Gaussian errors, gives the temporal conditional independence assumed in the model.

Published signal model. For a diseased patient the text specifies \(S\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\), fixed across visits, and \(Y_t=S+\epsilon_t\), with independent \(\epsilon_t\sim N(0,0.5^2)\). For distinct visits, \[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_u\mid\Theta=1)=\operatorname{Var}(S)=1/12,\] and the correlation is \[\frac{1/12}{1/12+1/4}=\frac14.\] Thus independent measurement errors do not give conditional independence after the common signal has been marginalized. The correct diseased likelihood of a history is \[\int_0^1\prod_t\phi_{0.5}(y_t-s)\,ds,\] rather than the product of its separately marginalized one-visit densities. The likelihood-ratio product in Equation (4), p. 6, would require the appropriate independence model, or history-conditional factors.

Pinned implementation and a different dependence. The release does not implement that uniform signal. In , lines 54–71, its mean is the binary disease indicator and its Gaussian likelihood uses means 1 and 0. Temporal independence is therefore compatible with that particular fixed-mean implementation; the preceding shared-signal calculation is not asserted to describe its temporal behavior.

However, `sample_sizes` is set to shape \((1,40)\) at line 147. Line 56 adds a single Gaussian row of that shape to disease indicators of shape \((2,1)\). Broadcasting reuses the same noise at each visit for both diseases. Conditional on their states, their same-visit errors have covariance \(0.25\) and correlation one, rather than the independence needed for the disease-wise product survival calculation. The independent simulator repeats this construction at lines 31–41 and 98.

A local diagnostic shows why this changes a joint payoff, not merely Monte Carlo variance. With equal risks \(1/2\), both disease states equal to one, and threshold \(0.95\), a one-observation Gaussian posterior crosses the threshold when \[y>\frac{\log 19+2}{4}=1.2361097\ldots .\] The single-disease crossing probability is \(p=0.3183851\ldots\). Shared errors make the two crossings identical, with joint probability \(p\); independent errors would give \(p^2=0.1013690\ldots\). If both adverse events occur after that opportunity, the probability of preventing both is therefore different. This is an illustrative one-opportunity calculation, not a claim that the published 40-visit result has that numerical difference.

Counterevidence and correction scope. Common random numbers across alternative actions or estimators can reduce variance without changing an estimand. The inspected construction instead couples two disease processes within a single patient’s simulated world. Dependence can also be a legitimate intended model, but then the joint-survival factorization and any analysis using it require revision. Historical experiment code may differ from the pinned release, and no resulting reversal of the method ranking has been demonstrated.

The dependency mismatch affects the likelihood model, joint-survival coefficients, and the claimed agreement between theory and simulation, supporting Major. A repair must specify whether patient signals are fixed and latent, fixed and known, or redrawn at each visit, and whether diseases share observation errors. For the factorized model, draw separate disease noise rows and use a consistent temporal likelihood. For a dependent model, integrate the joint law explicitly. No author-code execution, replacement simulation, or clinical validation was performed.

Problem 3 (Needs Evidence: the independent comparator and historical evaluation cannot be reconstructed as the stated experiment).  Locations and claim. Section 5.2, p. 9, reports mean survival 37.70 versus 37.47 under joint budget 10 and separate budgets 5 each. Appendix D.3, p. 30, says that the independent model’s two separately determined expected survival times are combined by taking their minimum. Appendix E, p. 31, reports 50 outer repetitions and small standard deviations.

Decisive distinction. For capped per-disease survival variables \(U,V\), the desired patient survival is \(E[\min(U,V)]\), whereas the literal aggregation of separately computed expectations is \(\min(EU,EV)\). These are not generally equal: \[E[\min(U,V)]\leq \min(EU,EV).\] For independent \(U,V\) each equal to 10 or 40 with equal probabilities, the two values are 17.5 and 25. The original paragraph was visually inspected. It could nevertheless be shorthand for a correct minimum within each simulated trajectory; the relevant final comparison evaluator and raw outputs are absent from the acquired five-file tree.

The direction matters: if the literal minimum-of-means calculation was used only for the independent comparator, with everything else held equal, it overestimates its survival. Correcting that isolated operation would not erase a positive unified-minus-independent mean difference; it could enlarge it. It would still change reported values and pointwise comparisons. Other protocol mismatches prevent turning this one-sided fact into a certification of the overall comparison.

Additional reproducibility constraints. The pinned , lines 71–133, creates separate decision variables for all 10,000 two-dimensional grid points. It does not tie disease-1 decisions sharing the same \(x_1\), or disease-2 decisions sharing the same \(x_2\). The finite Monte Carlo coefficient arrays can therefore permit nuisance-risk-dependent decisions, outside the formally defined independent class. In the exact noiseless population limit, identical coefficients across the nuisance dimension could mask this discrepancy; this review has not measured its extent in stored policies.

The release passes budget 5 to the unified optimizer (line 136), while passing 5 to each independent optimizer (line 133); the paper describes 10 for the unified model. This visible configuration disadvantages the unified model in nominal budget and must not be represented as evidence of a deliberately favorable budget. It is evidence that this checkout is not a complete recorded reproduction of the stated comparison. Other visible differences include Gaussian event-time standard deviation 3 rather than the text’s variance 1.6, means 30 versus 30.1 between the two scripts, and 100 outer iterations rather than the stated 50.

Both optimization paths replace the LP probability vector with its most probable action (lines 62–64 and 124–126). Such rounding need not preserve the budget: with reward and cost one for screening, zero otherwise, and budget \(0.6\), the optimal mixture screens with probability \(0.6\), while argmax rounding screens always and costs one. This establishes a general risk in the implementation, not an observed violation in these reported policies.

Impact and needed evidence. The arithmetic difference \(37.70-37.47=0.23\) is correct. To establish its precise estimand and fairness, the missing evidence is the figure-producing configuration/revision, per-trajectory or correctly joint reward evaluator, independent-policy constraints, final policy costs after rounding, and uncertainty evaluation on fresh trajectories. No fabricated numerical correction is offered. The status is Needs Evidence for the historical result; the concrete formula and configuration discrepancies are documented without asserting an unobserved score reversal.
# Additional verification and limits

The reward-gap inequalities and Boolean combination used in Proposition 4.1 are compatible with the stipulated product survival law and additive costs. The proof’s technical assumptions B.2 and B.8, exclusion of first-sample costs, and conditional intersection assumptions are material restrictions, not optional details. Similarity between an LP policy and a pointwise maximum computed from the same estimated reward/cost arrays checks optimization consistency; it does not independently establish those modeling assumptions.

Appendix E’s intervals use mean plus or minus twice the replicate standard deviation. They are not the usual confidence interval for a mean based on 50 independent replicates, which would use a standard error. The displayed twice-standard-deviation ranges are indeed separated: approximately \([37.6822,37.7178]\) and \([37.4466,37.4934]\). Their separation supports stability under the reported repetition scheme, but cannot remove model mismatch, selection bias from evaluating a fitted policy on the fitting estimates, or the unresolved survival estimand.

The paper expressly limits its claims to a model in which successful early diagnosis removes the corresponding adverse event and acknowledges unmodeled screening harms in Section 6. This review does not convert simulated survival into demonstrated clinical benefit and does not independently challenge those acknowledged modeling choices. No patient records, clinical recommendations, or external medical data were used.

report: Abstract: SOAR alternates language-model program search and learning from search traces, using hindsight relabeling and refinement examples. This review demonstrates a Major defect in the pinned implementation of its central greedy-diverse data selection: an empty-dictionary invariant removes the entire intended low-performing half of the sampling dataset. A second Major specification discrepancy concerns the weighted-voting rule, for which the main text, appendix, and release give non-equivalent formulas that can select different submitted outputs. The exact computational matching claim additionally Needs Evidence. These findings are scoped to the inspected method specification and source revision; they do not establish that historical runs used that revision, invalidate all self-improvement results, or demonstrate test-answer leakage. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
