report: Abstract: The finite-graph typicality equation and its linear-time evaluation after sorting are valid. Four substantive findings concern the claimed all-pairs statistical superiority, the equivalence between the printed path similarity and graph contraction, the claimed complexity bound, and the stated power-law theorem. Each affects an advertised empirical or theoretical contribution and is assessed Major with explicit scope. The released similarity normalization is significant counterevidence: it repairs the demonstrated path-contraction discrepancy. No author code or benchmark was executed.
Date: Initial review: 24 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of TANGO clustering
# Identity and inspected material

Haowen Ma, Zhiguo Long, and Hua Meng, TANGO: Clustering with Typicality-Aware Nonlocal Mode-Seeking and Graph-Cut Optimization, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 42062–42080; I25-43507 (0138) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page numbers below refer to the 19-page proceedings PDF. Original SHA-256:
The source snapshot is pinned to

The full manifest and all 18 inventoried tree files were byte-verified. The README, main driver, all 294 lines of , and evaluation code were read statically. Main pp. 1–9 and Appendix pp. 12–16 were read; additional ablation and limitation text on pp. 18–19 was inspected. Image-segmentation panels were not independently audited or reproduced. Existing source bytes were preserved.
# Valid finite-graph construction

Each point has at most one leader, of strictly higher density. After sorting by density, \(B\) is strictly upper triangular, so \(B^n=0\) and \[T=(I-B^\top)^{-1}\rho
   =\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}(B^\top)^\ell\rho.\] This proves existence and uniqueness without a stochastic stationarity assumption. Each edge is visited once in forward propagation; hence evaluation is \(O(n)\) after leaders and density order are known, with sorting separately costing \(O(n\log n)\). The independent 24-point example below satisfies the defining equation to maximum absolute residual \(2.23\times10^{-16}\).

The final number of clusters is supplied to spectral clustering. The paper explicitly uses the ground-truth count for methods requiring it and searches \(k=2,\ldots,100\). Thus automatic mode detection is distinct from automatic selection of every clustering input. These disclosed choices are retained in interpreting the empirical results.
# Problem 1: The all-pairs significance threshold is incorrect

Supported impact: Major for the stated superiority over all competitors. Section 5.2 (p. 9) and Appendix C.3 (p. 15) claim that TANGO’s differences from all other algorithms exceed the Nemenyi critical difference. With \(K=11\) algorithms and \(N=16\) datasets, the paper computes \[{\rm CD}=q_{.05}\sqrt{\frac{K(K+1)}{6N}},\qquad q_{.05}=1.96,\] giving approximately \(2.30\). The value \(1.96\) is a two-sided standard-normal critical value, not the all-pairs Nemenyi critical value for eleven algorithms.
## Independent distribution calculation

For the standard asymptotic Nemenyi comparison, \(q_{.05}\) is the 95th percentile of the range of \(K\) independent standard normals divided by \(\sqrt2\). This can be calculated without a lookup table. If \(\phi,\Phi\) denote the standard-normal density and distribution, \[F_{\rm range}(r)=K\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
       \phi(z)[\Phi(z+r)-\Phi(z)]^{K-1}\,dz.\] Reviewer-written quadrature and root finding give \(r_{.95}=4.5518635841\), \(q_{.05}=3.2186536073\), and \[\sqrt{\frac{132}{96}}=1.1726039400,\qquad {\rm CD}=3.7742059013.\] The original Figure 7, visually checked on p. 16, reports:
Comparison with TANGO | Mean-rank gap | Passes correct CD?
LDP-SC | 3.66 | No
QKSPP | 3.19 | No
USPEC | 3.38 | No
CPF | 3.94 | Yes
KNN-SC | 4.22 | Yes

The other five printed gaps exceed \(5.6\) and also pass this threshold. Rounding at two decimal places cannot account for the three failures. Approximate adjusted \(p\)-values from the rounded gaps are respectively \(0.0668\), \(0.1905\), and \(0.1285\) for the first three rows.
## Scope and counterevidence

This check holds the paper’s reported rank differences fixed; it does not reconstruct missing-result handling, raw ranks, or the Friedman statistic. An omnibus Friedman rejection does not establish every pairwise difference. A separately justified comparison procedure would need its own analysis and cannot be called the printed all-pairs Nemenyi test.

The numerical clustering scores and favorable average rank may remain valid. The specific claim of statistically supported superiority over all competitors is nevertheless contradicted by the paper’s own differences under its named test. Because that claim directly supports the central empirical conclusion, the impact is Major. No claim is made that TANGO is inferior to those three methods.
# Problem 2: The printed path definition is not the contracted computation

Supported impact: Major for the formal algorithm and equivalence proof; released normalization is a repair. Definition 1 (pp. 4–5) defines \(A_{ij}\) as a sum of shared-neighbor exponentials; it need not be at most one. Definition 5 (p. 7) sets intra-subcluster edge capacities to one and inter-subcluster capacities to \(A_{ij}\rho_i\rho_j\). Appendix A.2 then contracts every subcluster, arguing that intra-subcluster capacities cannot determine a path minimum. This requires them to dominate the inter-subcluster capacities, which the printed definition does not ensure.
## A complete finite input

Use the following 24 points, numbered from zero, \(k=7\), Euclidean neighbors excluding the point itself, and the printed definitions. Ranks are one-based; positive-similarity ties, if any, use increasing point index.

Independent evaluation of Definitions 1–4 and Algorithm 2 gives modes \(5,17,19\), with subclusters \[\begin{split}
 G_5&=\{0,1,3,4,5,6,7,8\},\\
 G_{17}&=\{2,9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17\},\\
 G_{19}&=\{18,19,20,21,22,23\}.
\end{split}\] The largest raw similarity is \(5.4874387419\). The strongest edge between the first two groups is \((5,2)\), with weighted capacity \(1.4163329640\). Exact max–min path closure on the original graph gives \[{\rm PBSim}_{\rm Definition\,5}(5,17)=1,
 \qquad
 {\rm PBSim}_{\rm contracted}(5,17)=1.4163329640.\] The intra-group path from point 2 to its mode provides the unit bottleneck discarded by contraction. The third group’s inter-group maxima are \(0.4908708587\) and \(0.9930155287\), so they do not restore the asserted equivalence.

The independent implementation uses the recurrence \(D_{ij}\leftarrow\max(D_{ij},\min(D_{ih},D_{hj}))\) to compute the widest paths, both before and after contraction. It uses no author code. Full coordinates, matrices, densities, ranks, leaders, typicalities, and mode bindings are saved. A second independently generated input including self in nearest-neighbor sets also demonstrates the discrepancy, so the issue does not rest on that convention.
## Released correction and limits

Lines 70–73 of symmetrize and normalize the matrix by its maximum before later operations. The normalization is absent from Definition 1. With \(A/\max A\), all inter-group capacities are at most one, and the contraction argument becomes valid. On both stored examples, independent original-graph and contracted computations then agree to the recorded numerical precision. Positive global scaling preserves the density normalization, similarity ordering, and leaders in the printed construction.

This is material to a central similarity definition and correctness argument, supporting Major even though the correction is small and present in the release. The finding does not establish a defect in the normalized released path computation or invalidate historical benchmark numbers. Self-loop padding, self-neighbor convention, and historical code version must also be specified for full reproduction.
# Problem 3: The path-matrix output cost is omitted

Supported impact: Major for the advertised efficiency guarantee. Theorem 3 (p. 7) claims \(O(nk\log(nk))\) for the path-based similarities. Its proof on p. 12 first correctly writes \(O(|E|\log|E|+q^2)\), where \(q\) is the number of subclusters, then drops \(q^2\) merely because \(q\ll n\).

Algorithm 3, lines 10–11, writes every newly connected pair of subclusters. In a connected graph, each unordered pair becomes connected exactly once, totaling \(q(q-1)/2\) entries. The released code explicitly allocates a dense \(q\times q\) matrix at line 232 and writes pair blocks at line 270. These are actual output costs, not implementation overhead that disappears in an asymptotic argument.

No theorem assumption bounds \(q^2\) by \(nk\log(nk)\). For example, on a regular polygon with sufficiently many points and fixed \(k=4\) excluding self, rotational symmetry makes the positive density scores equal. Strictly higher-density leaders do not exist, so every point is a mode: \(q=n\). Adjacent vertices have shared neighbors, making the sparse similarity graph connected. The output therefore requires quadratic size while \(nk\log(nk)\) is only \(O(n\log n)\). Ties are not excluded by the stated theorem. Even an assumption \(q=o(n)\) is insufficient: \(q=n^{3/4}\) gives \(q^2=n^{3/2}\).

Retaining the explicit output term gives \[O(nk\log(nk)+q^2)\] for the described contraction stage, assuming its graph operations are implemented appropriately. Section 4.5 separately lists an \(O(q^3)\) spectral step. Its subsequent claim of overall \(O(nk^2d)\) also needs quantitative domination conditions, including \(q^3=O(nk^2d)\), rather than only \(k,q\ll n\). The stated KD-tree cost likewise is not a universal guarantee in arbitrary dimension.

A compressed tree representation can support path queries without writing every pair; the paper’s algorithm and dense spectral input are not that representation. The observed image-segmentation times may be entirely accurate when \(q\) is small. The issue is the general computational guarantee attached to a core efficient aggregation contribution, hence Major, without asserting that the reported runs were slow.
# Problem 4: The stated power-law result lacks required normalization and model assumptions
## A scaling contradiction within the stated stochastic model

Let the offspring distribution be mixed Poisson with mixing variable \(X\) having Pareto tail index two and minimum \(1/4\). Then \(\mathbb EN=\mathbb EX=1/2\), matching the regularly varying mixed-Poisson setup assumed by the paper. Let every edge weight equal \(c=e^{-1}\). Consider two constant additive terms, \(\rho=1\) and \(\rho=1/2\).

Both satisfy \(B<1\), bounded density, and \(\Pr(\rho>x)=o(\Pr(N>x))\). A subcritical branching construction gives finite solutions \[T_a=a\sum_{v\ {\rm in\ the\ tree}}c^{\operatorname{depth}(v)},
 \qquad \mathbb ET_a=\frac{a}{1-c/2},\qquad a\in\{1,1/2\}.\] On the same tree \(T_{1/2}=T_1/2\) exactly. The paper predicts the same positive constant \(c^2/(1-c^2/2)=0.1451577670\) for both distributions. But regular variation with index two and that common \(L_N\) requires the second tail constant to be one quarter of the first: \[\Pr(T_{1/2}>x)=\Pr(T_1>2x)
 \sim \frac14 C_N x^{-2}L_N(x).\] Both claimed conclusions cannot hold. This is an analytic contradiction to the universally stated constant, not a simulation or a claim about a specific benchmark’s fitted tail. Additional normalization would need to be stated and justified.
## Application and counterevidence

Hierarchy alone does not make child typicalities independent copies of a typical uniformly sampled vertex, nor make ranks, density, and degree independent. Theorem 1 establishes uniqueness of a finite triangular linear system, not existence or uniqueness of the independent distributional fixed point. Bounded \(B,\rho\) do not establish heavy-tailed in-degree or the other stochastic hypotheses.

For a fixed finite dataset, the path expansion above also gives \(0\le T_i\le n\) because each descendant contributes at most one along its unique path. An asymptotic power law needs a specified growing-graph or population model; the finite calculation alone supplies none. A suitable infinite random-tree model could admit a power law, and no claim is made that such a model is impossible. The cited external tail theorem was not retrieved, so the finding is about this paper’s stated result and application, not its source literature.

The statistical behavior of the newly introduced typicality measure is explicitly advertised in the contributions and Remark 4. The scale contradiction and unsupported passage from finite dependency to an independent stochastic equation therefore concern that core theoretical validation. The clustering computation and its empirical scores do not depend on this asymptotic proof. A complete corrected tail theorem remains unverified.

report: Abstract: The inspected core update derivations contain two substantive problems. The proposed stop-gradient implementation does not induce the parameter-space update claimed in Appendix E: refreshing detached values at the next forward pass leaves gate weights to the power \(3/2\), rather than the claimed first power. Separately, replacing squared gate weights by linear weights need not move the update closer to full fine-tuning. A two-expert rank-one example establishes both points with invertible Gram matrices and exact finite-step formulas. These are Major findings about the method’s central theoretical justification. The reported benchmark improvements were not reproduced and are not refuted by these calculations.

Title: Scientific Review of Gate-Rescaled MoE-LoRA
# Identity, sources, and scope

The reviewed paper is M. Sun, Y. Wang, T. Feng, D. Zhang, Y. Zhu, and J. Tang, A Stronger Mixture of Low-Rank Experts for Fine-Tuning Foundation Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 57712–57727 [1]. The assignment is 0139 / I25-43508. Page references below use the one-based pages of the staged 16-page proceedings PDF; its internal page labels also run from 1 to 16.
The original PDF, complete source manifest, and staged repository inventory were actually read and hash-checked. The released source is , commit

This release is separately versioned evidence, not proof of which revision produced the historical experiments. The review covers the main update argument, Equations (1)–(13), Appendix E, Algorithm 1, the experiment descriptions and tabulated comparisons on pp. 6–9 and 13–16, and the relevant released forward and optimizer code. Benchmark data, weights, full training, and statistical variability were not reconstructed. References on pp. 10–12 were not exhaustively checked. No author code was executed.
# Definitions and valid preliminary algebra

For fixed positive gates \(g_i\) summing to one, let \[X=W+\sum_i g_iB_iA_i,\qquad G=\nabla_X\mathcal L,\qquad
 P_i=B_i(B_i^TB_i)^{-1}B_i^T,\quad
 Q_i=A_i^T(A_iA_i^T)^{-1}A_i.\] Here \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{r\times d}\), \(B_i\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\); the example below has full row/column rank, so both inverses exist. We use simultaneous preconditioned SGD, matching the derivation, and distinguish the first-order update from the \(O(\eta^2)\) product term.

Equation reference: ordinary, target. With the ordinary forward rule, the factor gradients are \(g_iB_i^TG\) and \(g_iGA_i^T\). Applying Equation (6) gives \[
 X_{\rm new}=X-\eta\sum_i g_i^2(P_iG+GQ_i)+O(\eta^2).\] This is the substantive content of Equation (10), with dimensions made explicit. Dividing both preconditioned factor gradients by \(g_i\), as in Equation (11), indeed gives, in this fixed-gate single-example setting, \[
 X_{\rm new}=X-\eta\sum_i g_i(P_iG+GQ_i)+O(\eta^2).\] These valid identities provide the baseline for the two findings.
# Problem 1: Detached values are incorrectly frozen across an update

Equation reference: stop. Supported impact: Major. Section 3.3, Equation (13), and Appendix E on p. 15 claim that the engineering forward rule achieves Equation (12) while preserving the normal forward value. Write \(\operatorname{sg}\) for a stop-gradient operation. The proposed contribution of an expert is \[
 \sqrt{\operatorname{sg}(g_i)}\,B_iA_i+
 \bigl(g_i-\sqrt{\operatorname{sg}(g_i)}\bigr)
          \operatorname{sg}(B_i)\operatorname{sg}(A_i).\] Numerically this equals \(g_iB_iA_i\). Its autodifferentiation rule with respect to \(A_i,B_i\), however, uses \(\sqrt{g_i}\), not \(g_i\). After Equation (6), the factor increments are therefore \[\Delta A_i=\sqrt{g_i}(B_i^TB_i)^{-1}B_i^TG,\qquad
 \Delta B_i=\sqrt{g_i}GA_i^T(A_iA_i^T)^{-1}.\]
## The invalid step and the actual next forward

Equation reference: actual. Appendix E’s first line substitutes updated \(A_i,B_i\) only into the first term of [stop] (#stop), leaving the detached product at its old value. This is a local surrogate with frozen numerical constants. It is not the output of Algorithm 1 evaluated after an optimizer step. In that algorithm, `exp_out.detach()` is recomputed from the current `exp_out` on every forward pass. Consequently the next numerical value, with gates fixed as assumed in the paper’s derivation, is \[W+\sum_i g_i(B_i-\eta\Delta B_i)(A_i-\eta\Delta A_i).\] Its correct first-order expansion is \[
 X_{\rm new}=X-\eta\sum_i g_i^{3/2}(P_iG+GQ_i)+O(\eta^2),\] not [target] (#target). The error is first order in the step size and survives the paper’s deliberate omission of second-order terms.

The released , lines 97–108, computes the same rule with cloned, detached values on each call. The alternate branch at lines 123–133 does likewise. The released , lines 165–208, supplies the simultaneous preconditioned SGD updates. Static inspection therefore corroborates the recomputation semantics, without executing either program.
## Complete admissible example

Let \(d=2,r=1,N_{\rm Expert}=2\), with both experts active, \[A_1=A_2=(1,0),\quad B_1=B_2=(1,0)^T,\quad
 g_1=g_2=\tfrac12,\quad W=0,\quad
 \mathcal L(X)=\tfrac12\|X\|_F^2.\] Thus \(X=G=P=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) and all four Gram matrices are the scalar one. Gates are positive and normalized; equal softmax logits realize them. Identical expert outputs give zero gradient to those gate logits, so holding them fixed is also consistent with their actual update in this example. The example uses the deterministic algebra of Section 3 and Appendix E, not an assumption about a stochastic benchmark training trajectory.

Equation reference: example. For each factor, the engineering update multiplies its nonzero entry by \(1-\eta/\sqrt2\). Re-evaluating the ordinary numerical forward gives exactly \[
 X_{\rm engineering}
   =\left(1-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}\right)^2P
   =\left(1-\sqrt2\eta+\frac{\eta^2}{2}\right)P.\] Equation (11), by contrast, gives \((1-\eta)^2P\), whose first-order coefficient is \(2\). Freezing the detached old products as in Appendix E gives the different surrogate \[\left[\sqrt2\left(1-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}\right)^2+1-\sqrt2\right]P
 =\left(1-2\eta+\frac{\eta^2}{\sqrt2}\right)P.\] At \(\eta=10^{-4}\), the actual engineering value has coefficient \(0.9998585836437626\) on \(P\), while Equation (11)’s value is \(0.9998000100000001\). Reviewer-written symbolic expansion and finite arithmetic verified these formulas and the limit of the engineering descent coefficient, \(\sqrt2\), as \(\eta\to0\). The script and outputs are in and its JSON/stdout companions.
## Counterevidence, repair status, and dependency

The forward-value identity in [stop] (#stop) is correct. Its direct derivative with respect to a gate also remains \(B_iA_i\) at the current forward. Neither fact permits treating detached numerical values as persistent state. If the intended object were only the frozen local computational surrogate, Appendix E’s linear coefficient would be appropriate; the claimed behavior of the next model forward would still require a different argument.

The paper explicitly calls the implementation an approximation, but supplies an equality derivation and says that Equation (12) is achieved. The exhibited difference does not become a second-order approximation error. The released SGD’s ridge regularizer \(10^{-6}\) perturbs the example’s coefficients to \(\sqrt2/(1+10^{-6})\) and \(2/(1+10^{-6})\); it does not remove the discrepancy. For \(g_i=1\), the powers agree, a valid special case with no multi-expert rescaling.

Equation [actual] (#actual) is a verified correction to the local SGD description, not a certified replacement algorithm. Multi-token shared parameters, changing gates, upstream gradients, adaptive AdamW moments, and a full revised training method require separate analysis. The engineering mechanism is the paper’s central implementable contribution and Appendix E is its explicit link to the ideal update. That invalid link supports Major independently of benchmark effects.
# Problem 2: Increasing gate weights does not establish closer full fine-tuning

Supported impact: Major for the central theoretical justification. Section 3.2, p. 5, asserts that Equation (12) further approaches global full fine-tuning. The preceding argument, p. 4, uses the sum-of-squares inequality for the gates to diagnose underestimation. That scalar inequality does not compare the matrix update with \(G\), because each term is a sum of overlapping projections.

In the same admissible example, \(P_i=Q_i=P=G\). The three first-order descent directions are \[D_{\rm ordinary}=G,\qquad
 D_{\rm Eq.(12)}=2G,\qquad
 D_{\rm engineering}=\sqrt2\,G .\] Full fine-tuning at the same learning rate uses \(D_{\rm FFT}=G\). Since \(\|G\|_F=1\), the corresponding errors are
Update | Descent coefficient on \(G\) | \(\|D-G\|_F\)
Ordinary preconditioned MoE | \(1\) | \(0\)
Proposed ideal Equation (12) | \(2\) | \(1\)
Actual engineering implementation | \(\sqrt2\) | \(\sqrt2-1\)

Thus the proposed ideal rescaling moves an already exact first-order full-gradient update away from that gradient. For completeness, the ordinary finite update is \((1-\eta/2)^2P\), while full fine-tuning gives \((1-\eta)P\); their discrepancy is \(O(\eta^2)\). The proposed changes instead have nonzero first-order discrepancies.

There is no assumption in the relevant argument that the experts’ subspaces or the row/column projections are disjoint. The two projection terms count their shared component twice. Even a normalized weighted average of these sums is not thereby an orthogonal projection or an unbiased approximation to \(G\). This invalidates the stated inference from gate normalization to systematically better full-gradient approximation.

The scope matters. The prose can be read as a qualitative heuristic about common training configurations rather than a quantified theorem. The example does not disprove such an empirical tendency. It does show that the mathematical reasons offered for the central closeness claim do not establish it under the stated conditions. Retuning the learning rate can match this one direction; that would change the comparison and does not verify a general claim with heterogeneous subspaces or token-dependent gates. The theory therefore needs a specified metric, conditions, and a valid argument. The Major assessment concerns this core justification, not an assertion that the method must train poorly.
# Overall impact and unresolved empirical questions

The intact forward-value identity and the genuine gradient modification can explain why the implementation remains usable. Both findings leave the published QA, GLUE, vision-language, and ablation measurements unresolved. Numerical gains do not prove the particular derivation, while the counterexample does not estimate a score change. The paper reports different behavior for SGD and AdamW and some non-improving settings; those qualifications were retained.

Static inspection of all 208 lines of , all 135 lines of , the README, and selected optimizer/training connections in the three training drivers established which released branches are relevant. It did not establish historical run provenance. The available manifest does not supply an independent historical source binding or an erratum resolving these findings. No later-version comparison or comprehensive correction search was performed.

# Identity, version, and inspected scope

This report concerns 0140 / I25-43509, P. Qin and J. Zhang, Learning to Quantize for Training Vector-Quantized Networks, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 50435–50447 [1]. The reviewed original is the staged 13-page proceedings PDF. References below use one-based PDF pages, which agree with the paper’s internal page labels. The main text runs through p. 9; pp. 10–13 contain references and end matter, with no embedded technical appendix.
The complete source manifest was read. The PDF and staged source bytes were checked against their recorded hashes. The released source is , commit

Its 17-file tree is evidence about that release, not a historical execution receipt. The review covers the method on pp. 1–6, the experiment and ablation descriptions and tables on pp. 6–9, the full quantizer and training driver, and relevant loss and argument definitions. Visual examples and benchmark results were not regenerated; the bibliography was not exhaustively audited. No author code was executed.
# Necessary distinction between three derivatives

Let \(\operatorname{sg}(u)\) have numerical value \(u\) but zero assigned derivatives, as explicitly defined on p. 4. With a locally fixed selected code \(q\), the released implementation supplies the task loss with \[q_{\rm ST}=z_e+\operatorname{sg}(q-z_e).\] It also computes commitment and codebook losses with opposite stopped arguments, matching Equations (4)–(7). Thus numerical values, assigned backward derivatives, and derivatives of a freshly re-evaluated gradient field need not coincide.

For an ordinary twice continuously differentiable scalar objective, the chain rule and the central difference in Equations (12)–(16), p. 5, have the familiar justification. Here that justification must be established for the actual stop-gradient computation. In particular, a finite perturbation re-evaluates the numerical contents of stopped expressions, whereas differentiating their existing computational graph does not. This distinction is separate from the explicitly acknowledged one-step approximation to a fully solved inner problem.
# Problem 1: The finite difference does not approximate the stated unrolled hypergradient

Supported impact: Major. Equations (12)–(14) identify the one-step upper gradient with a direct term and two mixed-derivative products. Equations (15)–(16) approximate those products by differences of \(\nabla_\psi\mathcal L\) under perturbations of \(\phi\) and \(\theta\). Section 4.3 and Figure 2 then use these terms to explain how task feedback reaches the quantizer. The suspect step is applying this finite-difference identity to a gradient field containing the specified stop-gradient operations.
## Admissible parameters and unchanged quantization branch

Take one scalar training input and target \(x=y=0\), encoder \(F_\phi(x)=\phi\), and decoder \(G_\theta(z)=\theta z\). Let the two codes be \[C_\psi=(\psi,\psi+10).\] This is an affine hyper-net \(H_\psi(e)=e+\psi\) acting on embedding values \(0,10\). The other hyper-net or embedding coordinates can be held fixed when examining this parameter component. Affine reparameterization is within the method’s stated framework and its linear ablations. No claim is made that this small network is a benchmark architecture.

Use squared reconstruction loss, squared Euclidean commitment and codebook losses, \(\alpha=\beta=1\), and \[\phi=\theta=\psi=1,\qquad \xi=\tfrac1{10}.\] These positive loss weights and learning rate are not excluded by the derivation. At the initial point the code \(q=\psi=1\) is uniquely nearest; after the inner step the encoder value will be \(4/5\), still uniquely nearest to that code. All perturbations below remain in the same cell: the other code is \(11\), and the assignment boundary is at \(6\). There is no argmin tie or boundary crossing.

Equation reference: loss, field. In this branch the actual forward graph is \[
 \mathcal L=
  \bigl[\theta\{\phi+\operatorname{sg}(\psi-\phi)\}\bigr]^2
 +\alpha\{\phi-\operatorname{sg}(\psi)\}^2
 +\beta\{\psi-\operatorname{sg}(\phi)\}^2 .\] The assigned first-order gradients, evaluated numerically at general points of this branch, are \[
 g_\phi=2\theta^2\psi+2\alpha(\phi-\psi),\qquad
 g_\theta=2\theta\psi^2,\qquad
 g_\psi=2\beta(\psi-\phi).\] Equation [field] (#field) describes their values after reevaluation. It is not permission to erase stop-gradient nodes when taking higher derivatives.
## Literal unrolled differentiation
## The paper’s central difference

Equation reference: fd. At the outer point, the two directions prescribed below Equation (16) are \[v_\phi=g_\phi(\phi',\theta',\psi)
       =2(\tfrac45)^2+2(\tfrac45-1)=\tfrac{22}{25},
 \qquad
 v_\theta=g_\theta(\phi',\theta',\psi)=\tfrac85.\] Recomputing the codebook gradient at \(\phi^\pm=1\pm\epsilon v_\phi\) gives \[\frac{g_\psi(\phi^+,\theta,\psi)
           -g_\psi(\phi^-,\theta,\psi)}{2\epsilon}
       =-2v_\phi=-\frac{44}{25}.\] The corresponding \(\theta\)-difference is zero. Therefore the finite-difference hypergradient in Equation (16) is exactly \[
 \frac25-\frac1{10}\left(-\frac{44}{25}\right)
   =\boxed{\frac{72}{125}=0.576}.\] This holds for every sufficiently small nonzero \(\epsilon\), not just a poorly chosen perturbation size. The difference \(22/125=0.176\) from the stated graph derivative does not tend to zero. The linearity of \(g_\psi\) makes the finite difference exact for its own, different target.

Reviewer-written exact rational calculations checked \(\epsilon=10^{-2},10^{-4},10^{-6}\) and the frozen-symbol mixed derivatives. An independent scalar differentiation implementation propagated values, gradients, and Hessians with zero derivatives at stop-gradient nodes. It gave the same \(0.4\) unrolled result. With effective weights \(\alpha=\beta=0.1\), matching the quantization weighting style in the released FFHQ configuration, the two results remain different: \(0.04\) versus \(0.0648\). These checks are in and its JSON/stdout outputs.
## Alternative interpretations and counterevidence

One could instead differentiate the freshly recomputed numerical gradient field [field] (#field) to describe how actual inner updates change with \(\psi\). That also does not justify the transpose used in Equation (16). At the stated point with unit weights, \[\frac{d(g_\phi,g_\theta)}{d\psi}=(0,4),\qquad
 \frac{d g_\psi}{d(\phi,\theta)}=(-2,0).\] These are not transposes of one another. The stopped backward field is not the gradient of a common smooth scalar potential across reevaluations, so symmetry of mixed partials cannot be imported.

For further separation of the objects, the ordinary numerical loss after the one-step inner update has \[\phi'(\psi)=\tfrac45,\quad \theta'(\psi)=1-\tfrac15\psi^2,\quad
 V(\psi)=\{(1-\tfrac15\psi^2)\psi\}^2+
                2(\tfrac45-\psi)^2 .\] It satisfies \(V'(1)=36/25=1.44\), also not [fd] (#fd). This is not an assertion that STE must equal an ordinary forward derivative; STE is deliberately a surrogate. It shows why a precise choice of differentiated object is essential.

The finite perturbation update does contain task information through \(v_\phi\); it can therefore be a task-aware heuristic with nonzero indirect-update plots. The finding does not say that this update has no useful feedback, nor that the method cannot improve reconstruction. A different explicit smooth surrogate, or a separately defined higher-order estimator, may support a valid derivation. Neither was specified in the inspected argument to restore the asserted identity. No complete corrective objective or training algorithm is certified here.
# Source correspondence and bounded consequences

The relevant released operations are in , lines 100–105: discrete nearest-code selection, the two oppositely detached squared losses, and the STE. Lines 115–120 add an optional entropy term; its default coefficient is zero, as used in the example. The hyper-net permits linear and MLP forms at lines 32–56. These facts corroborate the mathematical graph examined above.

The full training driver was read statically. It selects a Betty-based method using `hyper_gradient_type`, whose default is `darts` (, lines 34–36), and connects generator and codebook problems at , lines 421–426. The externally provided Betty implementation was not staged or pinned by the unversioned requirements list. Accordingly this report evaluates the paper’s explicit Equation (16), not an unobserved library runtime or historical job.

Other current-release details require provenance clarification: the codebook optimizer is SGD at lines 389–392 of the training driver, whereas the paper’s experiment descriptions discuss Adam; the shared reconstruction routine in , line 91, computes absolute error, whereas the VQVAE experiment description specifies MSE. The staged release principally supplies an FFHQ MQGAN configuration. These observations do not establish what ran in the VQVAE studies or that published results are invalid. They remain Needs Evidence for reproduction and version correspondence, not additional graded Problems.

The failed derivative equivalence directly affects the central optimization construction, the claimed best-response interpretation in Section 4.3, and the meaning attached to indirect gradients in Section 5.5. This core dependence supports Major under the assigned standard, without requiring score degradation or a whole-paper refutation. The hyper-net representation, constant inference cost after materializing its codebook, and the possibility of empirical usefulness survive. Reported benchmark comparisons, their uncertainty, training histories, and cited baseline comparability were not independently reproduced.

Title: Technical Verification of
Approximate Differential Privacy of the \(\ell_2\) Mechanism
# Paper identity and inspected scope

This report concerns Matthew Joseph, Alex Kulesza, and Alexander Yu, Approximate Differential Privacy of the \(\ell_2\) Mechanism, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 28377–28392 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], input identifier I25-43510 (0141). The reviewed file is the staged, published proceedings PDF; the source manifest records publisher date 6 October 2025. PDF pages 1–16 coincide with the internal printed pages used below. The published PDF, embedded Appendix A, and staged released implementation were consulted. Source and check hashes are recorded in the matching verification directory.

The mathematical checks cover the high-loss set, cap heights and monotonicity in Section 3.1 and Appendix A.1–A.2; the left-sum upper/lower bounding logic; the sampler in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.3; and the moment and Laplace-comparator claims in Section 4.2 and Appendix A.4. The code inspection covers `l2.py`, `laplace.py`, `gaussian.py`, `utils.py`, and `experiments.py` at commit `8bedbbd982e7dcf5c5280e6ae2f0769295c3369e` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Author code, timing experiments, and Monte Carlo experiments were not executed. No assertion is made that this October 2026 repository snapshot generated the published figures. OpenReview-only attachments were inaccessible in the supplied acquisition record.
# Definitions and valid parts of the calculation

Let \(T\) have global \(\ell_2\) sensitivity at most one. The new mechanism releases \(T(X)+Y\), with density proportional to \(\exp(-\|Y\|_2/\sigma)\). For a unit displacement \(e_1\), put \(\tau=\epsilon\sigma\) and \[V=\{y:\|y-e_1\|_2-\|y\|_2\geq\tau\}.\] Under \(d\geq2\) and \(0<\tau<1\), its intersection with a radius-\(r\) sphere about zero is described by \[y_1\leq \frac{1-\tau^2}{2}-\tau r.\] The cap height is therefore \(\min\{r(1-\tau)+(1-\tau^2)/2,2r\}\), as in Lemma 3.6. On a radius-\(R\) sphere about \(e_1\), the cutoff becomes \((1+\tau^2)/2-\tau R\), and the nonzero cap has height \(R(1-\tau)-(1-\tau^2)/2\) for \(R\geq(1+\tau)/2\). These formulas follow by squaring the respective nonnegative distance inequalities, with the stated radius restrictions.

The normalized first cutoff is \(-\tau+(1-\tau^2)/(2r)\), decreasing in \(r\); the normalized second cutoff relative to \(e_1\) is \(-\tau-(1-\tau^2)/(2R)\), increasing in \(R\). This directly confirms the cap-fraction monotonicities needed for Lemmas 3.13 and 3.21. The radial law is \(\mathrm{Gamma}(d,\sigma)\), so the corresponding gamma-mass weighted left sums have the stated directions when the grids meet the lemmas’ increasing-radius assumptions. These analytic observations do not certify floating-point rounding or every parameter choice of the implementation.

For the sampler, a uniform ball radius has distribution function \(u^d\), and an independent \(\mathrm{Gamma}(d+1,\sigma)\) scale yields the stated radial density. In particular, the squared-error identities \(d(d+1)\sigma^2\) for the \(\ell_2\) mechanism and \(2db^2\) for independent \(\mathrm{Laplace}(0,b)\) coordinates are consistent. Here \(b\) always denotes the coordinate Laplace scale, avoiding the rescaled \(\sigma\) notation surrounding Corollary 4.2.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The Laplace comparator is not nearly optimally calibrated under unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity).  Section 4.2, PDF p. 8, says the comparison uses the smallest possible scales, sets the Laplace coordinate scale to \(b_{\rm paper}=\sqrt d/(\epsilon+\delta)\), and footnote 2 asserts that the actual minimum differs only negligibly. Appendix A.4, Lemma A.2, pp. 15–16, is offered as the supporting argument. This optimality justification does not hold for the paper’s \(\ell_2\) sensitivity class.
## The suspect dependence

Lemma A.2 considers a displacement \(e_1\), with \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) norm both one. For this pair, its exact privacy deficit is \[1-\exp\!\left(\frac{\epsilon-1/b}{2}\right)
 \quad\text{when }\epsilon\leq1/b.\] Lemma A.2 remains valid for its stated axis pair. It gives a necessary lower bound near \(1/\epsilon\) on \(b\), not near \(\sqrt d/\epsilon\). Applying a unit-\(\ell_1\) worst-case interpretation after replacing sensitivity by \(\sqrt d\) enlarges the neighboring-displacement class: that larger class includes concentration of the whole \(\ell_1\) displacement in one coordinate, which need not have unit \(\ell_2\) norm. The following valid calibration for the original class provides a direct disproof; it does not rely on this interpretation of the appendix.
## A uniform guarantee satisfying every original sensitivity condition

Let \(Z_i\) be independent \(\mathrm{Laplace}(0,b)\) variables. For any ordered neighboring pair let \(v=T(X')-T(X)\), so \(\|v\|_2\leq1\). Its privacy loss under output \(T(X)+Z\) is \[L=\sum_{i=1}^d L_i,\qquad
 L_i=\frac{|Z_i-v_i|-|Z_i|}{b},\qquad
 a_i=\frac{|v_i|}{b}.\] Independence of the \(Z_i\) makes the \(L_i\) independent. The triangle inequality gives \(-a_i\leq L_i\leq a_i\). Direct integration of the Laplace density yields \[\mathbb E L_i=a_i+e^{-a_i}-1\leq a_i^2/2,\qquad
 \sum_i a_i^2=\|v\|_2^2/b^2\leq b^{-2}.\] The inequality uses \(e^{-a}\leq1-a+a^2/2\) for \(a\geq0\). The elementary bounded-variable exponential-moment inequality gives \[\mathbb E e^{t(L-\mathbb E L)}
 \leq \exp\!\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_i a_i^2\right).\] For completeness, each centered summand lies in an interval of width \(2a_i\); convexity bounds its exponential moment by that of the two endpoints, whose log moment is bounded by \(t^2(2a_i)^2/8\). Multiplication over independent coordinates gives the display.

Equation reference: eq:bound. Chernoff minimization, followed by the two bounds above, proves that for \(\epsilon>1/(2b^2)\), \[
 \Pr(L>\epsilon)
 \leq \exp\!\left[-\frac{b^2}{2}
       \left(\epsilon-\frac{1}{2b^2}\right)^2\right].\] The case \(v=0\) has zero privacy loss and is immediate. Equation [eq:bound] (#eq:bound) holds for every direction and every allowed displacement, including the reverse ordered pair. Splitting any event into \(L\leq\epsilon\) and \(L>\epsilon\) proves \((\epsilon,\delta)\)-DP whenever its right side is at most \(\delta\). Thus the calculation verifies the entire adjacency condition, rather than only a convenient shift.

Take \[d=100,\qquad \epsilon=1,\qquad \delta=10^{-5},\qquad b=5.\] This dimension and privacy pair are used in Section 4.2. All noise coordinates are independent and use the same scale; no extra restriction is imposed on \(T\). Equation [eq:bound] (#eq:bound) evaluates to \[\exp[-25(1-1/50)^2/2]
 =6.1135679664\times10^{-6}<10^{-5}.\] This is a valid Laplace comparator. Nevertheless, \[\begin{aligned}
 b_{\rm paper}&=\frac{10}{1.00001}=9.999900001,\\
 \mathbb E\|Z_{\rm paper}\|_2^2&=2(100)b_{\rm paper}^2
       =19999.600006,\\
 \mathbb E\|Z\|_2^2&=2(100)(5)^2=5000.\end{aligned}\] The ratio is \(0.250005000025\). Hence the optimum is no greater than \(5\), at most approximately half the stated scale, and the achievable mean squared error is approximately one quarter of the stated comparator error. The numerical evaluation is preserved in `independent_check.py` and `independent_check_results.json`; the guarantee itself is analytic.
## Counterevidence, impact, and a supported correction

The paper’s Laplace calibration remains a valid conservative calibration, and the formula in its released `laplace.py` agrees with the printed value. Under a unit \(\ell_1\) neighboring-displacement class, the axis argument is relevant to near-pure-DP optimality. Neither fact rescues the asserted near optimality for all unit-\(\ell_2\) statistics.

This is assessed Major for the invalid optimal-comparator justification, which directly supports the central error comparison in Section 4.2 and the minimum-scale characterization of Figure 5. The example does not establish that Laplace beats the \(\ell_2\) mechanism, does not refute the reported \(\ell_2\) versus analytic-Gaussian advantage, and does not refute the peak advantage quoted at \(d=7\). Figure 1 deliberately truncates the Laplace curve after \(d=8\), so the present \(d=100\) calculation is not represented as a correction to an actually plotted Laplace point at that dimension.

A precise supported replacement is: the evaluated Laplace baseline uses the conservative scale \(\sqrt d/(\epsilon+\delta)\); equation [eq:bound] (#eq:bound) supplies another sufficient calibration under unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. It is not claimed to be the exact optimum. Recomputing comparisons against an optimized approximate-DP Laplace baseline requires additional privacy calibration and regenerated numerical comparisons; the present bound alone does not determine that optimum.

Problem 2 (The closed high-loss event is mishandled at the one-dimensional pure-DP boundary).  Lemma 3.2 on p. 3 and Corollary 3.14 on p. 5 assert zero probability of the closed high-loss event when \(\sigma\geq1/\epsilon\). At \(d=1\) and \(\sigma=1/\epsilon\), the negative half-line has positive probability. The two printed algorithms handle this equality differently.
## Exact endpoint check

Set \(d=1\), \(\epsilon=1\), \(\sigma=1\), \(T(X)=0\), and \(T(X')=1\). This is an allowed unit-sensitivity pair. The definition on p. 3 gives \[V=\{y:|y-1|-|y|\geq1\}=(-\infty,0].\] Consequently, \[\Pr_{M(0)}(V)=\tfrac12,\qquad
 \Pr_{M(1)}(V)=\tfrac{1}{2e},\qquad
 \Pr_{M(0)}(V)-e\Pr_{M(1)}(V)=0.\] The mechanism is therefore pure \(1\)-DP, as also follows from Lemma 2.4. The measure-zero assertion in the proof of Lemma 3.2 is valid for the negative axis in \(d\geq2\), but not for a half-line in \(d=1\).

Printed Algorithm 1, p. 5, uses \(\sigma>1/\epsilon\) for its shortcut and therefore returns \(1/2\) at this input. Algorithm 2, p. 6, uses \(\sigma\geq1/\epsilon\) and returns zero. Algorithm 3 consequently compares \(1/2\) to \(\delta\) and rejects this valid mechanism for \(0<\delta<1/2\). At \(\delta=0\), its preliminary finite-radius truncation cannot achieve zero tail probability, so this executable false-negative claim is restricted to positive \(\delta\). This is a false negative of the sufficient checker, not an unsafe privacy acceptance.

The staged `l2.py` uses \(\sigma\geq1/\epsilon\) in both term routines, giving a combined value zero. Its individual probability-bound interpretation still needs the closed-versus-strict-event qualification, but its combined result at this endpoint is correct. Thus the printed pseudocode behavior is not attributed to the available implementation or to historical experiment runs.

The issue is Minor: it is a localized boundary inconsistency, with no demonstrated failure of the interior spherical-cap guarantee. One exact correction is to return a positive DP verdict in the overall checker whenever \(\sigma\geq1/\epsilon\), using the pure-DP theorem, and retain the actual endpoint probabilities in any separately stated closed-event probability lemmas. Another consistent convention uses a strict high-loss event throughout; changing only one term is insufficient. These endpoint corrections are analytically verified only in their stated scope.
# Overall dependence and recorded state

The cap geometry, radial sampling, and moment identities survive these findings. The first finding concerns the optimality of a comparator central to the empirical justification; the second concerns a boundary in the printed checker. No floating-point certification, experimental rerun, later-version erratum search, or author response was performed. The available repository commit is a separate version from the 2025 PDF; no documented author adoption of the proposed corrections was supplied.

report: Abstract: This review checks the published representation-based weak-to-strong generalization analysis, its Gaussian benign-overfitting example, and the scope of the empirical predictor. A Gaussian family satisfying the stated example premises fails the kernel-isotropy condition needed by the supplied proof. Its error is of order \(\gamma^2\), whereas the definition requires \(o(\gamma^2)\). This establishes a Major defect in the applicability derivation underlying the advertised benign-overfitting application, without refuting the main theorem under its actual assumptions or the example’s final risk formulas. A separate finite perturbation inequality is false, although a verified denominator correction preserves the asymptotic uses inspected here. No author code or original experiments were executed. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:

Title: Technical Verification of
Representations Shape Weak-to-Strong Generalization
# Identity, reviewed version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Yihao Xue, Jiping Li, and Baharan Mirzasoleiman, Representations Shape Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Theoretical Insights and Empirical Predictions, ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, pp. 70120–70159, publisher version dated 6 October 2025; internal identifiers are 0142 and I25-43511, and OpenReview identifier is `ypEW077kle` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. All page references below are one-based pages of the 40-page PDF; its printed local page numbers agree with these PDF numbers. The staged original and source manifest were read directly. The actual original PDF hash is recorded in Appendix 6 (#sec:reproduction) and the verification records.

The principal inspected chain is Definition 3.3 \(\to\) Assumption 3.7 \(\to\) Theorem 3.8, including Appendix A’s ridge-regression factorization and Lemmas A.5–A.13. The review also inspected Theorem 4.1, Example 4.2 and Corollary 4.3 with Appendix B.3, the Gaussian verification in Appendix C.2.1, the construction in Theorem 3.6/Appendix C.3, and the definitions, training protocol and tuning discussion for the empirical metric in Section 5 and Appendix D.1–D.2.

Problem 1 disproves the claim that the stated Gaussian example meets the prescribed decomposability conditions over its full parameter range. It does not supply a counterexample satisfying Assumption 3.7 to Theorem 3.8. The exact high-probability argument, rather than finite simulation, establishes the defect.

The provided manifest records no located paper-specific implementation and an OpenReview attachment access challenge. These are inherited source-availability facts, not independently resolved by new network requests. Experiments, pretrained models, raw predictions, and numerical figure correlations were not reproduced. No later paper revision or erratum was supplied or checked; first-discovery status is not asserted.
# Definitions and inspected conditional reasoning

Equation reference: eq:main. Theorem 3.8, PDF p. 5, assumes these conditions for both models and \(\delta_j\le\beta_j=O(1)\). With \(G_j=\widehat K(\Pi_{V_j}h_j)/\widehat n\), set \[P_w=G_w(G_w+(\beta_w+\widetilde\gamma_w)I)^{-1},
 \qquad P_s=G_s(G_s+(\beta_s+\widehat\gamma_s)I)^{-1}.\] The conclusion is \[
 \mathrm{PredGap}=\left\|P_s(I-P_w)\frac{\widehat y}{\sqrt{\widehat n}}\right\|^2\pm o(1).\] The ridge solutions and population quadratic form in Appendix A.4 give the appropriate starting expression. Lemma A.12 approximates weak predictions on the strong-training split; Lemma A.13 transfers the strong population quadratic form to its principal kernel. Subject to genuine decomposability and the corrected inverse bound in Problem 2, this inspected structure does not establish a new defect in [eq:main] (#eq:main).
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The Gaussian applicability proof misses the required isotropy rate).  The Gaussian premises in Appendix C.2.1 and Example 4.2 permit a family for which [eq:required] (#eq:required) fails. The published route from that example to the advertised benign-overfitting guarantee therefore does not cover the full stated parameter range.
## Original claim, location, and dependency

This claim is used in Example 4.2, PDF p. 6, and explicitly in Appendix B.3.2, PDF pp. 24–25: the Gaussian representations are declared decomposable, allowing Lemmas A.12, B.5 and Theorem 3.8 to determine the risks in Corollary 4.3. This dependency connects the defect to the core explanation of benign overfitting.
## Admissible family and all example premises

Equation reference: eq:parameters. Let \(n\to\infty\) through integers, and take \[
 \widehat n=\widetilde n=n,\quad k=1,\quad
 m=d-k=n^3,\quad \sigma^2=1,\quad
 \eta=\frac35,\quad \beta_w=\beta_s=n^{-2}.\] For each independent sample, let \(y,z\sim N(0,1)\) independently, and take \[h_w=(\sqrt\eta\,y+\sqrt{1-\eta}\,z,\ \xi_w^\top)^\top,
 \qquad h_s=(y,\ \xi_s^\top)^\top,\] where \(\xi_w,\xi_s\sim N(0,I_m/m)\) are independent of each other and of \(y,z\). Samples and the two training splits are independent.

These choices satisfy every explicit premise of the Gaussian specialization and Example 4.2: first-coordinate variance one; nonprincipal-coordinate variance \(\sigma^2/(d-1)=1/m\); independent coordinates within each representation; \(\mathbb E[y^2]=1\); \(\eta\in(0,1)\); equal sample sizes tending to infinity; \(d/n^2\to\infty\); nonzero \(\sigma^2=o(n)\); and \(\beta_j=o(\sigma^2/n)\). The first coordinate is an exact population eigenspace with \(\rho=1\). We target the unambiguous Gaussian specialization rather than rely on the inconsistent variance-versus-standard-deviation convention for the sub-Gaussian parameter between Example 3.5 and Definition C.5.
## Exact independent calculation

Equation [eq:lower] (#eq:lower) proves a lower bound, so the issue is not merely a loose printed upper bound. Independent finite diagnostics gave \(\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}/\gamma^2=2.138,1.902,1.762\) for \(n=8,16,32\). These illustrate the analytic result and do not substitute for it.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

Replacing \(o(\gamma^2)\) by \(o(\gamma)\) avoids this contradiction, since \(\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}/\gamma\) vanishes. The square is nevertheless explicit in the rendered source on PDF p. 4 and in Lemma A.5’s absolute inverse-error argument. Such a replacement requires revisiting that proof.

The special regime \(\sigma^2=\Theta(n)\) mentioned after Example 3.5 has \(\gamma=\Theta(1)\), and ordinary Gram concentration can suffice. It does not cover the permitted \(\sigma^2=1\) family or the entire \(\sigma^2=o(n)\) regime in Example 4.2.

The final risk formulas \(\mathrm{Err}_w\approx1-\eta\) and \(\mathrm{Err}_{w2s}\approx(1-\eta)^2\) may survive through a different or sharper analysis. They are not disproved here. The refuted assertion is decomposability under the example’s original full parameter range, which is the stated gateway to those conditional results.
## Supported impact and limited repair

The supported impact is Major: a demonstrably invalid applicability derivation is used to justify the advertised benign-overfitting application of the framework. Neither Theorem 3.8 under genuine Assumption 3.7 nor the measured empirical correlations are refuted by this argument.

Problem 2 (The finite inverse-perturbation bound omits a denominator).  Lemma A.3, PDF p. 13, states \(\|(A+\Delta)^{-1}-A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le
\|A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) for invertible \(A\). This finite inequality is false.
## Complete scalar check and correction
## Dependency and severity

Lemmas A.5 and A.6 invoke the false bound. Under their genuine hypotheses, however, \(\|A^{-1}\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}}=o(1)\): perturbations are \(o((\gamma+\delta)^2)\) or \(o((\gamma+\delta+\rho)^2)\), while the relevant inverse scale is at most reciprocal to the corresponding sum up to a constant; those sums are bounded and \(\beta\ge\delta\). Thus the denominator in [eq:resolvent] (#eq:resolvent) is \(1-o(1)\), preserving the required absolute \(o(1)\) inverse errors. This supported Minor finite-bound defect therefore does not independently invalidate the inspected asymptotic conclusions. The grading follows this verified consequence.
# Empirical interpretation and remaining boundaries

Corollaries 5.1–5.2 give operator-norm upper bounds, not universal equalities between a label-free score and prediction gap. Their inspected inequalities follow from submultiplicativity and the residual term under the stated assumptions. The paper separately tests finite nonlinear correlations.

Appendix D.2, PDF p. 37, discloses dataset-specific hyperparameter selection and best-result reporting in experiment III, as well as labeled performance measurements for tuning. Table 2 reports held-out-model tuning transfer for Justice and Commonsense in experiment II: \(0.885\pm0.16\) and \(0.67\pm0.20\). This is counterevidence to a blanket claim that all correlations are unvalidated selection artifacts. The metric is label-free after calibration; the supplied experiment III results do not by themselves establish a fully untuned, label-free deployment procedure. Raw metric/error pairs were unavailable for recomputation.

Theorem 3.6’s exact eigenspace preservation remains an additional unresolved boundary: Appendix C.3 bounds, but does not set to zero, \(\mathbb E[h\xi^\top]\), which does not by itself establish that the proposed subspace is a population eigenspace. No separate severity is assigned because intended dependence assumptions and the sub-Gaussian parameter convention need clarification. This does not increase Problem 1’s supported impact.
# Conclusion and recorded state
Dimension | Recorded state
Inspection outcome | Established Gaussian applicability and finite perturbation-bound defects.
Supported impact | Major for Problem 1; Minor for Problem 2.
Repair verification | Stronger Gaussian scaling verified for the displayed family; inverse-bound denominator verified.
Author adoption | Unknown; no contact or adoption request.
Scientific adjudication | Pending; no human review supplied.
Remaining work | General-range repair, unresolved construction assumptions, empirical reproduction and later-version check.

Problem 1’s chi-squared argument is analytic. The independent script uses NumPy 2.4.3 on Python 3.13.5, seed 20261024, float64 arithmetic. It constructs Gaussian matrices only for \(n=8,16,32\). Diagnostics for \(n=100,1000,10000\) instead sample the exact chi-squared representation and do not allocate \(n^3\)-row matrices. Actual results and script/source hashes are in . report: Abstract: The advertised third-party causal-inference release includes a data-dependent debiasing vector in addition to randomized labels. An exact two-category counterexample shows that this joint release violates its claimed differential-privacy budget at strictly positive noise scale. The released vector reveals the perturbed prior, for which the proof understates replacement-label histogram sensitivity and incorrectly extends a label-only privacy branch. This is a Major defect in the privacy certificate supporting the central privacy–variance comparison. The estimator’s conditional unbiasedness is not refuted. A separate Minor defect concerns omitted design weights in the stated population interpretation of cluster homogeneity. A conservative corrected privacy certificate and the correct population normalization are verified analytically. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of
Improving the Variance of Differentially Private Randomized Experiments through Clustering
# Identity and checked scope

The reviewed paper is Adel Javanmard, Vahab Mirrokni, and Jean Pouget-Abadie, Improving the Variance of Differentially Private Randomized Experiments through Clustering, ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, pp. 26946–26980, published proceedings version dated 6 October 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Internal identifiers are 0143 and I25-43512; the OpenReview identifier is `ypDMPB0qY2`. References below use one-based PDF pages, which coincide with printed local page numbers in the 35-page original.

The actual staged PDF and complete source manifest were read. The review inspected the main objective and mechanisms, Algorithm 2, Theorems 3.1–3.2 and their privacy/unbiasedness derivations, Definition 3.4, the total-variance structure of Theorem 3.5, and the experimental calibration protocol. Appendix A.15 was read through the algebraic variance decomposition and auxiliary bounds; no independent certification of every bound or baseline proof is asserted.

No paper-specific author implementation was available in the staged materials. The manifest’s unsuccessful source search and blocked OpenReview attachment access are source-preparation facts, not new searches performed here. No author code, original datasets, original experiments, later revisions, or errata were executed or obtained. The results below are exact mathematical checks, supplemented by independently written numerical evaluations; no first-discovery claim is made.
# Setting and essential definitions

The public treatment assignment and cluster membership are held fixed for label-DP. Neighboring datasets differ in one observed outcome, as specified in Definition 2.2, PDF p. 4. The finite response space is \(\mathcal Y\) of size \(K\). Within each treatment–cluster group, Algorithm 2 perturbs each empirical response probability by independent Laplace noise of scale \(\sigma/n_{a,c}\), clips it to \([\gamma,1]\), and renormalizes it to a probability vector \(\widetilde q\) whose coordinates remain at least \(\gamma\).

Equation reference: eq:q, eq:inv. Writing \(q_j\) for clipped coordinates and \(s=\sum_jq_j\), the renormalization is \[\widetilde q_j
 =q_j+\frac{\zeta_j}{\sum_\ell\zeta_\ell}(1-s),
 \quad
 \zeta_j=\begin{cases}q_j-\gamma,&s>1,\\1-q_j,&s\le1.\end{cases}\] A unit retains its original label with probability \(1-\lambda\) and is otherwise resampled from \(\widetilde q\). Its randomization matrix is \[
 Q=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda\widetilde q\mathbf1^\top .\] For \(\lambda<1\), \[
 Q^{-1}=\frac{I-\lambda\widetilde q\mathbf1^\top}{1-\lambda}.\] The correction vector \(y^\top Q^{-1}\) is used to recover an unbiased outcome estimate from the randomized label. Conditional on the noise and true labels, \(\mathbb E[y^\top Q^{-1}e_{\widetilde y_i}]=y^\top Q^{-1}Qe_{y_i}=y_i\). This algebra supports the unbiasedness argument in Appendix A.14; it does not establish privacy of the correction vector.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The disclosed debiasing vector breaks the advertised privacy budget).  The privacy claim in Section 3.2 for all information passed to the third party is false under the stated parameters and adjacency. Theorem 3.1’s budget cannot be transferred to that joint release as done in the paper.
## Source claim, exact location, and suspect step

Algorithm 2, PDF p. 5, formally returns randomized labels. Section 3.2, PDF p. 6, additionally requires the curator to pass each unit’s cluster assignment, treatment assignment, randomized response, and the vector \(y^\top Q^{-1}_{c,z_i}\) to the third party. The paragraph below Figure 1 claims that all this information, and any estimates based on it, are \(\varepsilon\)-DP by postprocessing.

Equation reference: eq:paperbudget. Theorem 3.1 assigns \[
 \varepsilon=\min(1/\sigma,2/\gamma)+\widetilde\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \delta=\max\{0,1-\lambda+\lambda\gamma(1-e^{\widetilde\varepsilon})\}.\] Appendix A.13, PDF p. 21, justifies the first term by calling the empirical distribution’s sensitivity \(1/n\). Under the paper’s replacement-label adjacency, changing one category to another alters two histogram coordinates, with vector \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(2/n\). Its second, noise-independent branch on PDF pp. 22–23 bounds probabilities of randomized-label outputs in \(\mathcal Y^n\); it does not certify disclosure of the data-dependent prior or correction vector.
The following exact calculation demonstrates a failure after clipping and renormalization, not just a missing sensitivity argument.
## Neighboring datasets and verification of every condition

Use one public cluster of four units, with two assigned control and two treatment. Fix this nonsensitive assignment. Let \(K=2\), \(\mathcal Y=\{0,1\}\), and let the treatment-group labels be identical in both datasets. The control labels are \[D:(0,0),\qquad D':(1,0).\] They differ in precisely one observed outcome. The empirical control distributions, ordered as \((0,1)\), are \((1,0)\) and \((1/2,1/2)\). The population can have fixed, no-interference potential outcomes consistent with these observed labels, so the causal setup imposes no further obstacle.

Equation reference: eq:params, eq:claimednumbers. Choose \[
 \gamma=\frac14,\qquad \sigma=10,\qquad
 \lambda=\frac{99}{100},\qquad
 \widetilde\varepsilon=\log(103/99).\] All groups have positive sizes, the cluster exceeds the required size two, \(0<\gamma<1/K\), \(\sigma>0\), and \(0<\lambda<1\) makes \(Q\) invertible. The noise scale in the control group is \(b=\sigma/2=5\). Substitution in [eq:paperbudget] (#eq:paperbudget) gives \[
 \delta=0,\qquad
 \varepsilon=\frac1{10}+\log(103/99)
 =0.139609138095\ldots .\] Thus neither zero noise nor a singular inverse is involved.
## An observable event in the actual release

Equation reference: eq:reveal. For \(\mathcal Y=\{0,1\}\), let \(t=\widetilde q_1\). Equations [eq:q] (#eq:q)–[eq:inv] (#eq:inv) imply \[
 y^\top Q^{-1}
 =\left(-\frac{\lambda t}{1-\lambda},
             \frac{1-\lambda t}{1-\lambda}\right).\] The released vector determines \(t\) exactly. In particular, the event \[E=\{t=1/4\}\] is the observable event that its first coordinate equals \(-24.75\); the full vector is then \((-24.75,75.25)\). Randomized labels and treatment-group outputs can be unrestricted in \(E\).

Equation reference: eq:event. For completeness, the clipping mechanism creates an atom at this event. If \(s=q_0+q_1>1\), Algorithm 2 gives \[\widetilde q_1=\gamma+(q_1-\gamma)
                    \frac{1-2\gamma}{s-2\gamma}.\] Since \(0<\gamma<1/2\), equality to \(\gamma\) occurs exactly when \(q_1=\gamma\). If \(s<1\), renormalization strictly raises any coordinate equal to \(\gamma\). The boundary \(s=1,q_1=\gamma\) requires the continuously distributed coordinate \(q_0=1-\gamma\) and has probability zero. Therefore \[
 E=\{q_1=\gamma,\ q_0\ge1-\gamma\}\] up to null events. The two coordinates use independent Laplace noise.
## Exact probabilities and violated inequality

Equation reference: eq:p, eq:pprime, eq:ratio, eq:violation. Under \(D\), equation [eq:event] (#eq:event) requires \(w_1\le1/4\) and \(w_0\ge-1/4\). Under \(D'\), it requires \(w_1\le-1/4\) and \(w_0\ge1/4\). Since \(b=\sigma/2\), \[\begin{aligned}
 P_D(E)&=\left(1-\frac12e^{-1/(2\sigma)}\right)^2,
 \\
 P_{D'}(E)&=\frac14e^{-1/\sigma},
 \\
 \log\frac{P_D(E)}{P_{D'}(E)}
 &=2\log\left(2e^{1/(2\sigma)}-1\right).
 \end{aligned}\] For \(\sigma=10\), the probabilities are respectively \(0.274979930008\ldots\) and \(0.226209354509\ldots\). Their log ratio is \(0.195237195353\ldots\), strictly larger than the claimed \(\varepsilon\) in [eq:claimednumbers] (#eq:claimednumbers). Equivalently, \[
 P_D(E)-e^\varepsilon P_{D'}(E)
 =0.014878919907\ldots>0=\delta.\] This disproves the advertised pure-DP guarantee for the joint causal-inference release.

The same event also disproves the noise-independent cap for the joint release. With \(\sigma=0.01\), \(\lambda=1/2\), and the same \(\gamma\), choose \(\widetilde\varepsilon=\log5\), giving \(\delta=0\) and claimed \(\varepsilon=8+\log5=9.6094\ldots\). Equation [eq:ratio] (#eq:ratio) instead gives \(101.3863\ldots\). This second example shows why replacing \(1/\sigma\) by \(2/\sigma\) while retaining the same minimum would not repair the joint-release certificate.
## Counterevidence, precise scope, and core impact

This event concerns the prior exposed through \(y^\top Q^{-1}\), not merely the randomized labels formally returned by Algorithm 2. The calculation does not claim to refute every possible label-only privacy bound. Keeping the prior secret could avoid this specific event, but would also remove the information explicitly supplied for the third party’s estimator; it is a different release protocol.

At \(\gamma=1/K\), the normalized prior is uniform and data-independent. That special case avoids this disclosure issue and supports the paper’s uniform-prior reduction. The counterexample uses \(\gamma<1/K\). It also uses replacement adjacency exactly as defined, rather than silently switching to an add/remove or single-bin adjacency convention.

The supported severity is Major. The user-level causal release and its privacy–variance trade-off are core contributions. The debiasing information required for that release invalidates the claimed privacy certificate. Conditional unbiasedness and potential variance reductions at fixed algorithm parameters may survive; no benchmark-score decline is inferred. Comparisons at a fixed certified privacy budget need recertification, parameter recalibration and, where parameters change, fresh numerical evaluation.
## A conservative, verified privacy correction

Equation reference: eq:repair. For fixed public groups of positive size, \(\sigma>0\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and \(0<\gamma\le1/K\), the full joint release is certified by \[
 \varepsilon_{\rm joint}=2/\sigma+\widetilde\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \delta=\max\{0,1-\lambda+\lambda\gamma(1-e^{\widetilde\varepsilon})\}.\] To verify this statement, the empirical histogram’s \(\ell_1\) sensitivity in the one affected group is \(2/n_{a,c}\). The product Laplace density ratio is bounded by \[\exp\!\left(\frac{\|p-p'\|_1}{\sigma/n_{a,c}}\right)
 \le e^{2/\sigma}.\] Clipping and normalization are postprocessing. Different public groups are disjoint, so one changed label affects only one such release.

For a fixed released prior, only the changed unit’s categorical output differs between neighboring datasets. The positive excess probability at its original category is at most \(1-\lambda+\lambda\gamma(1-e^{\widetilde\varepsilon})\); the other changed category contributes no positive excess. Thus this second-stage channel is \((\widetilde\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP. Adaptive composition gives [eq:repair] (#eq:repair). The correction vectors are then deterministic functions of the released prior and add no further cost. This proves a sufficient certificate; it does not claim optimal privacy loss, retain the invalid minimum, or revalidate the published experiments under their original advertised budgets.

Problem 2 (The population interpretation of homogeneity omits design weights).  The equality following Definition 3.4, at the top of PDF p. 7, identifies the expected finite-sample homogeneity quantity with \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(y(a)\mid c)]\). Its own definition retains sample-size and treatment-allocation factors, so this equality is false in general.
## Definition, complete check, and correction

Equation reference: eq:phi. The paper defines \[
 \phi_a=\sum_c\frac{n_c^2}{n^2n_{a,c}}S^2(\boldsymbol y_c(a)),
 \qquad
 S^2(\boldsymbol u)=\frac1{d-1}\sum_{i=1}^d(u_i-\overline u)^2.\] Take one cluster, \(n=n_c=4\), \(n_{a,c}=2\), and independent Bernoulli\((1/2)\) potential outcomes within the cluster. They lie in the required finite response space \(\{0,1\}\); the design is balanced and cluster membership is fixed. The unbiased sample variance has expectation \(1/4\). Equation [eq:phi] (#eq:phi) therefore gives \[\mathbb E[\phi_a]=\tfrac12\,\mathbb E[S^2]=\frac18,\] whereas the displayed population expression is \(1/4\). Independent exhaustive enumeration of all 16 equally likely outcome vectors confirms these values.

Equation reference: eq:phicorrect. Conditional on fixed cluster sizes and treatment counts, the corrected expression for iid draws within each cluster is \[
 \mathbb E[\phi_a\mid(n_c,n_{a,c})_c]
 =\sum_c\frac{n_c^2}{n^2n_{a,c}}\operatorname{Var}(y(a)\mid c).\] If every cluster uses the same treatment fraction \(p_a=n_{a,c}/n_c\), this becomes \[\frac1{np_a}\sum_c\frac{n_c}{n}\operatorname{Var}(y(a)\mid c).\] A further population interpretation must specify how the cluster weights are sampled or fixed.
## Impact and alternative reading

For a fixed design with constant fractions, the omitted factor is constant, so the qualitative ordering by within-cluster outcome variance can survive. The exact finite-sample definition in [eq:phi] (#eq:phi) is retained in the variance derivation, and this issue does not by itself refute Theorem 3.5. Its supported severity is Minor: the erroneous equality changes the normalization and its dependence on sample size and allocation. Reading it as informal proportionality explains the intended intuition, but not the displayed identity.
# Overall dependence, limitations, and state

The conditional mean calculation and inverse formula were checked independently and do not repair the privacy problem. The decomposition \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{DP},z}(\widehat\tau_Q)
 =\mathbb E_z[\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{DP}}(\widehat\tau_Q\mid z)]
  +\operatorname{Var}_z(\widehat\tau_{\rm NO\text{-}DP})\] is compatible with the established conditional unbiasedness. The detailed constants of the full variance upper bound, all aggregate baselines, and numerical figure values have not been independently certified. No empirical replication is implied by the finite checks.

The stated experiments calibrate parameters using Theorem 3.1, including \(\sigma=10\) and fixed target privacy in Section 4. Those empirical variances may be measured correctly, but the advertised privacy certificate for the full third-party release requires correction. The present counterexample does not measure the amount of privacy leakage or variance change in any particular original dataset.

Title: Technical Verification of
Generative Point Cloud Registration
# Identity and reviewed material

The reviewed work is Haobo Jiang, Jin Xie, Jian Yang, Liang Yu, and Jianmin Zheng, Generative Point Cloud Registration, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 27710–27723 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Its input identifier is I25-43513, local number 0144. This report uses PDF pages 1–14, equal to the internally printed page numbers. The exact staged published PDF and embedded Appendices A–B were read as extracted text. The original page 8 was also rendered and visually inspected, including Table 3.

The staged repository [Retained latex: \cite{repo}] is pinned to commit `c53a047833bfd47aa3b39c3bd93545b749fd8f11`, dated 26 May 2025. Its sole file is a 15-byte `README.md` containing the project title. Thus a successful repository retrieval is not availability of an implementation. No author code, data, model weights, training, or GPU evaluation was executed. Additional OpenReview attachments were not accessible in the supplied source-preparation record.
# Checked reasoning and assumptions
## Registration and coupled attention

Equation (1), p. 3, defines a rigid alignment objective with \(R\in SO(3)\), \(t\in\mathbb R^3\), and ground-truth correspondences used to state the target problem. The text explicitly acknowledges that these correspondences are unavailable at deployment; this equation is not evidence of ground-truth correspondence leakage in the claimed algorithm.

The method projects depth-camera point clouds through known camera intrinsics and stacks the source and target depth maps and noisy latents vertically (Section 3.2–3.3, pp. 3–4). If each latent contains \(H'W'\) tokens in \(\mathbb R^d\), the combined representation contains \(2H'W'\) tokens. Equation (4) then has a \((2H'W')\times(2H'W')\) attention matrix, allowing cross-view terms. This verifies the claimed capacity for feature interaction. It is not a mathematical proof that arbitrary stochastic generations preserve exact correspondence colors. Section 3.4, p. 5, expressly recognizes remaining geometric and texture inconsistencies and motivates fine-tuning; that admission is relevant counterevidence against reading the architecture discussion as a universal consistency theorem.

The training description selects 3,000 pairs from the ScanNet training split, while the evaluation describes official dataset splits and wider frame spacing (Section 4.1–4.2, pp. 5–7). No contradiction establishing train–test overlap was found in that description. Pair identifiers and training logs were unavailable, so independence of the actual splits was not independently reconstructed.
## Feature fusion

Equation (6), p. 5, concatenates weighted geometric and compressed image descriptors. For comparable descriptors \(g,c\) and \(g',c'\), the resulting squared Euclidean distance is \[\|[\omega g;(1-\omega)c]-[\omega g';(1-\omega)c']\|_2^2
 =\omega^2\|g-g'\|_2^2+(1-\omega)^2\|c-c'\|_2^2 .\] The squares follow from concatenation and do not constitute an error: the paper specifies feature weights, not an unsquared linear mixture of distances.

A shared PCA transform and common feature normalization would make corresponding image descriptors comparable. The prose does not establish precisely how the PCA basis is fitted and shared in the released experiment pipeline; the staged repository cannot resolve this. Independent per-cloud PCA fitting could cause a coordinate-basis mismatch, but the paper does not require such a fitting procedure. It is therefore an unresolved implementation detail, not a demonstrated defect.
# Published comparisons and a rejected candidate concern

Tables 1–4 and their associated ablation descriptions were inspected. Changes across rotation accuracy, translation accuracy, error means, and medians should not be read as improvement in every column for every variant. In particular, the ColorPCR block of Table 3, PDF p. 8, contains the following changes:
Metric | Baseline | Generative | Signed benefit
Median rotation error (degrees) | 1.8 | 1.9 | \(-0.1\)
Translation accuracy at 5 cm (%) | 48.3 | 47.3 | \(-1.0\)
Median translation error (cm) | 5.2 | 5.3 | \(-0.1\)
Rotation accuracy at 5 degrees (%) | 79.9 | 83.6 | \(+3.7\)
Mean translation error (cm) | 41.8 | 28.3 | \(+13.5\)
For errors, signed benefit means baseline minus generative; for accuracies, it means generative minus baseline. Independent exact-decimal calculations confirm these values.

In extracted plain text, the row labeled improvement contains positive magnitudes for the first three changes. The original PDF, however, shows those three magnitudes in red, and improved quantities in cyan; the best baseline entries are also bolded. Thus the actual visual evidence distinguishes the deteriorations. No signed-calculation Problem is assigned on the basis of the text extraction. The broad comparative claim is supported by many improved aggregate entries in the published table, while the displayed adverse entries limit any stronger all-metrics reading. This establishes internal reporting consistency only, not independent reproduction or statistical significance of the gains.
# Outcome and remaining evidence

The supported assessment is No Issue Found within the inspected scope, with inspection outcome scope clarification. There are no numbered Problems and no proposed scientific correction. Source availability remains an important limit: the exact trained model, implementation of PCA/normalization, pair lists, random seeds, and raw per-pair registration outputs were not available for inspection. Claims that depend on them remain unverified, rather than certified or disproved.

No new empirical study is needed to understand the table-color clarification. Verifying published performance, the causal contribution of the coupled prompt, or comparative robustness would require the corresponding implementation, model configuration, and evaluation outputs. Such reproduction was neither performed nor inferred from the aggregate tables. Later revisions and errata were not independently searched; the dated repository snapshot supplies no implementation or correction record.

report: Abstract: Two independent defects affect the paper’s core safety derivation. The printed explicit-QP gates have the wrong truncation sign and can return an infeasible control from a strictly safe state. The available implementation uses the opposite truncation, which corrects that example and prevents attributing the printed defect to the experimental implementation. Separately, even an exact QP head cannot guarantee higher-order safety from the theorem’s stated initial condition alone. A closed-form double-integrator trajectory satisfies the enforced inequality yet immediately exits the safe set. Both issues support Major technical assessments in their stated scopes. The shared-constraint convex-combination step remains valid under the appropriate initial-domain conditions. Scientific adjudication is pending.
