Title: Technical Verification of
ABNet: Adaptive explicit-Barrier Net for Safe and Scalable Robot Learning
# Identity, version, and checked scope

This report concerns Wei Xiao, Tsun-Hsuan Wang, Chuang Gan, and Daniela Rus, ABNet: Adaptive explicit-Barrier Net for Safe and Scalable Robot Learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 68472–68490 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assigned identifiers are 0145 and I25-43514. The reviewed original is the 19-page published proceedings PDF, publisher date 6 October 2025. One-based PDF pages agree with its printed local page numbers.

The review inspected the problem formulation, explicit-QP and fusion definitions in Section 3, Theorems 3.1–3.2 and Appendices A–B, and the experimental and limitation descriptions in Sections 4–6 and Appendix C. The selected source-page images 12–14 were actually rendered and read to verify the signs and proof steps. Figure descriptions and reported tables were read; all graphical trajectories and raw runs were not independently reconstructed.

The released source snapshot is pinned to commit `00c09812cf66bc4428eb9341af0cf81a34b77755` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The README and all 212 lines of were inspected statically. That file implements the three explicit solvers. Source inspection is not execution, and this later available commit is not presumed to be the experiment-time version. No author code, training, tests, datasets, or simulation was executed. Extra OpenReview-only attachments were unavailable in the staged acquisition record; no new download or later-erratum search was made.
# Definitions and the valid local fusion argument

Equation reference: eq:cbf. The system is \(\dot x=f(x)+g(x)u\), with locally Lipschitz \(f,g\). For each safety specification \(b_j\), the paper defines \[\psi_{j,0}=b_j,\qquad
 \psi_{j,i}=\dot\psi_{j,i-1}+p_i\alpha_{j,i}(\psi_{j,i-1}),
 \quad 1\le i<m.\] The lower-order penalties \(p_i\ge0\) are shared among heads; \(\alpha_{j,i}\) are strictly increasing and pass through zero. Each head minimizes a strictly convex quadratic objective with positive-definite \(H\), subject to \[
 L_f\psi_{j,m-1}+L_g\psi_{j,m-1}u_k+
 p_{m,k}\alpha_{j,m}(\psi_{j,m-1})\ge0.\] The final control is \(u=\sum_k w_ku_k\), where \(w_k\ge0\) and \(\sum_k w_k=1\).

When the same \(\psi_{j,m-1}\) and Lie derivatives are shared, summing [eq:cbf] (#eq:cbf) with these weights is valid: \[L_f\psi_{j,m-1}+L_g\psi_{j,m-1}u+
 \Big(\sum_k w_kp_{m,k}\Big)\alpha_{j,m}(\psi_{j,m-1})\ge0.\] This algebra is not refuted below. The issues concern whether the printed explicit head actually solves its QP, and whether the stated initial domain permits the subsequent invariance conclusion.

The counterexamples use precisely two specifications, singleton partitions \(S_1=\{1\}\) and \(S_2=\{2\}\), constant observations and parameters, and two identical heads with \(w_1=w_2=1/2\). Thus soft-min aggregation, switching of selected constraints, observation noise, discretization, heterogeneous heads, and singular Gram matrices do not explain either failure.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The printed gate functions need the opposite truncation sign).  Appendix A, PDF p. 12, equations (14)–(15), use \(\max(\cdot,0)\) in gate formulas whose sign must be nonpositive. For a nonsingular feasible QP these formulas can produce an infeasible control. This invalidates the printed explicit solution used in equation (4) and its exact-QP safety justification.
## Exact source convention and dependency

Equations (8)–(13) define \[g_i=-L_g\psi_{i,m-1},\quad
 h_i=L_f\psi_{i,m-1}+p_m\alpha_{i,m}(\psi_{i,m-1}),\quad
 \widehat u=-H^{-1}F,\] \[\widehat g_i=H^{-1}g_i,\qquad
 \widehat h_i=h_i-g_i^\top\widehat u,\qquad
 G_{ij}=\widehat g_i^\top H\widehat g_j.\] The transformed problem minimizes \(v^\top Hv\) subject to \(\langle\widehat g_i,v\rangle_H\le\widehat h_i\), and the displayed solution is \(v=\lambda_1\widehat g_1+\lambda_2\widehat g_2\). The main text, PDF p. 3, explicitly specifies \(\lambda_i\le0\). The first gate branch tests \(G_{21}\max(\widehat h_2,0)-G_{22}\widehat h_1<0\); the second tests \(G_{12}\max(\widehat h_1,0)-G_{11}\widehat h_2<0\). In the second branch the printed gates are \(\lambda_1=\max(\widehat h_1,0)/G_{11}\) and \(\lambda_2=0\). These conventions rule out rescuing the formula by changing the meaning of the inequalities.

The new explicit head in equation (4) depends on these gates. Appendix B, PDF p. 13, then explicitly invokes its claimed identity with the exact QP solution to conclude that each head satisfies the safety constraints. This is a direct dependency of the core safety argument.
## Complete first-order counterexample

Equation reference: eq:qp1. Let \[\dot x=(-1,0)^\top+u,\quad
 b_1(x)=x_1,\quad b_2(x)=x_2,\quad
 x(0)=(1/4,1)^\top.\] Take \(m=1\), \(\alpha(r)=r\), \(p_{m,k}=1\), \(H=I_2\), and \(F=0\). All coefficients are smooth, the initial state is strictly safe, and the two relative degrees are one. The head QP is \[
 \min_u \tfrac12(u_1^2+u_2^2)
 \quad\text{subject to}\quad
 u_1\ge1-x_1,\quad u_2\ge-x_2.\] It is feasible everywhere and has a unique solution. At the stated initial state, \[\widehat g_1=-e_1,\quad\widehat g_2=-e_2,\quad
 G=I_2,\quad \widehat h=(-3/4,1)^\top,\quad\widehat u=0.\] The first branch test equals \(3/4<0\), which is false; the second equals \(-1<0\), which is true. The printed formula consequently gives \[\lambda_1=\max(-3/4,0)=0,\quad\lambda_2=0,\quad u=(0,0).\] The first constraint residual is \(-3/4\), so this is not a QP solution. The actual minimizer is \((3/4,0)\) with gates \((-3/4,0)\).

The same printed branch persists along \(x_2(t)=1\), \(x_1(t)=1/4-t\). It therefore crosses the safety boundary at \(t=1/4\) and is negative immediately afterward. In contrast, the actual QP feedback has \(u_1=1-x_1\), so its trajectory is \(x_1(t)=e^{-t}/4>0\), \(x_2(t)=1\). The witness isolates the gate error without higher-order initialization complications.
## Counterevidence, repair scope, and assessment

The current uses in the branch tests and numerators of `eBQP`, `eBQP_I`, and `eBQP_g`. This operation is \(\min(\cdot,0)\), not \(\max(\cdot,0)\). It gives the correct control in [eq:qp1] (#eq:qp1). This is actual implementation counterevidence: the finding does not establish that the available implementation or original experiments used the wrong sign.

Replacing the printed positive truncations by negative truncations repairs this witness and agrees with the required multiplier sign. A complete solver certification would additionally require a full KKT analysis and explicit treatment of dependent constraints and zero denominators; it is not supplied by this one example or by static code inspection.

The supported impact is Major. A demonstrated invalid closed-form derivation is the defining explicit layer and is used directly to establish safety. The easy local sign correction and the current implementation’s correction limit the affected version and claims, but do not make the printed core derivation valid. No benchmark degradation or unsafe experimental run is inferred.

Problem 2 (The initial condition omits the higher-order barrier domain).  Theorem 3.1, PDF p. 4 and repeated p. 13, assumes initial safety solely as \(b_j(x(0))\ge0\) for every \(j\). This does not suffice for its high-order invariance conclusion. Even granting an exact, sign-corrected QP head, the enforced inequality can hold while the system leaves that set immediately.
## Admissible second-order system and exact QP solution

Equation reference: eq:initial. Use two independent double integrators: \[\dot q_j=v_j,\quad \dot v_j=u_j,\quad b_j=q_j,\qquad j=1,2.\] Set \(m=2\), all penalties equal to one, \(\alpha_{j,i}(r)=r\), \(H=I_2\), \(F=0\), and constant observations. The relative degree is two; the coefficients are smooth and the exact QP feedback is locally Lipschitz. The shared first-order barrier functions and constraints become \[\psi_{j,1}=v_j+q_j,\qquad
 u_j+2v_j+q_j\ge0,\qquad
 u_j=\max(0,-2v_j-q_j).\] The QP is always feasible. Let the initial state be \[
 (q_1,v_1,q_2,v_2)(0)=(0,-1,1,0).\] Both \(b_j(0)\ge0\), as required by the printed theorem.

Equation reference: eq:traj. For \(0<t<1\), the actual QP-controlled solution is \[
 q_1=-te^{-t},\qquad v_1=(t-1)e^{-t},\qquad
 u_1=(2-t)e^{-t},\qquad (q_2,v_2,u_2)=(1,0,0).\] Differentiation verifies both differential equations. Moreover \(u_1>0\) and \(u_1+2v_1+q_1=0\), so [eq:traj] (#eq:traj) is the unique pointwise QP minimum, not an arbitrary feasible control. Nevertheless \(q_1(t)<0\) immediately. Two identical heads and their convex mixture produce the same trajectory.

The obstruction is already visible at the boundary: \[\psi_{1,1}(0)=-1,\qquad
 \psi_{1,1}(t)=-e^{-t}<0,\qquad
 \dot\psi_{1,1}(t)=e^{-t}>0.\] Appendix B, PDF p. 14, claims that \(b_j(x(0))\ge0\) allows initialization with \(\dot\psi_{j,m-1}(x(0))\ge0\), then invokes Nagumo to conclude \(\psi_{j,m-1}\ge0\). The displayed trajectory already has that positive derivative. A positive derivative cannot establish membership of a set from an initial point outside it.

No finite lower-order penalty can correct this boundary initialization: every zero-passing \(\alpha\) gives \(v_1(0)+p_1\alpha(q_1(0))=-1\). The outward velocity also makes \(\dot q_1(0)=-1\), independently of any finite acceleration. Thus this is not a poor choice of a tunable finite initialization that the stated theorem can always repair.
## Alternative interpretation and verified limited correction

A conventional higher-order barrier result restricted to \[\psi_{j,i}(x(0))\ge0\quad
 \text{for every }j\text{ and }i=0,\ldots,m-1\] excludes this witness. Importing that condition changes the theorem’s explicit \(b\)-only hypothesis; the paper’s own initialization argument attempts, unsuccessfully, to bridge the difference. This report does not refute a correctly restricted HOCBF theorem.

For the constant, unit-linear, second-order setting above, the correction is directly verifiable. The QP ensures \(\dot\psi_{j,1}+\psi_{j,1}\ge0\). If \(\psi_{j,1}(0)\ge0\), integrating factors yield \(\psi_{j,1}(t)\ge e^{-t}\psi_{j,1}(0)\ge0\). Then \(\dot q_j+q_j=\psi_{j,1}\ge0\) implies \(q_j(t)\ge e^{-t}q_j(0)\ge0\). This proves safety on the corrected initial domain for this setting and for convex mixtures sharing these constraints. It does not certify arbitrary observation resets, varying penalties, or all of the paper’s merging claims.

The supported impact is Major, independently of Problem 1: an invalid inference is needed by the central safety theorem. This does not invalidate the measured success of the reported trajectories or safety guarantees on a properly restricted initial domain. Experimental trajectories alone cannot prove the theorem’s broader quantifier.
# Remaining scope and recorded state

The reported robot, manipulator and driving comparisons were inspected at the level of their descriptions and aggregate tables. Their raw trajectories, runtime claims, uncertainty estimates and training stability were not independently reproduced. The paper’s same-constraint limitation in Section 6 is relevant to heterogeneous-task merging; the counterexamples above already satisfy identical constraints. No separate finding is assigned to soft-min conservatism, selecting the two most risky constraints, finite sampling, or the natural-noise-filter explanation without a completed adverse case.

# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Gal Dalal, Assaf Hallak, Gugan Thoppe, Shie Mannor and Gal Chechik, Policy Gradient with Tree Expansion, ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, 12229–12255 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The local identity is 0146 / I25-43515; OpenReview identifier `yiZtLtvW9S`. The reviewed file is the staged published proceedings PDF, whose publisher metadata records 6 October 2025. It has 27 PDF pages. All page references below use the PDF’s printed local numbering, which agrees with physical PDF pages 1–27, rather than the proceedings’ continuous numbering.

The review checks the definitions in Sections 2–3, the variance object in (1), Lemmas 4.1–4.6, Theorems 4.4 and 4.7 and their proof dependencies in Appendices A.1–A.8. Sections 5–6 and Appendix B were inspected for the theoretical–implementation relationship and experimental protocol, without reproducing Atari experiments. Theorem 4.8 and Appendix A.9 were read for scope and dependence but were not completely verified. The convergence conjecture in Section 3, all cited external theorems, all possible defects and the empirical rankings are outside the established conclusions.

The staged released repository is `NVlabs/SoftTreeMax`, commit `b40f5013a261537e93f677433cdf7f78d36f8680`, dated 14 March 2023 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Static inspection covered , and . This release is not assumed to be the source of the 2025 results. Additional OpenReview-only attachments were unavailable to source preparation because of a documented access challenge. No author code was executed.
# Definitions and common assumptions

The paper considers a finite discounted MDP with rewards in \([0,1]\), discount \(0<\gamma<1\) and a fixed behavior policy \(\pi_b\). Write \(P=P^{\pi_b}\) for its state transition matrix and \(P_s\) for the action-by-next-state matrix at a root state \(s\). The parameter \(\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^S\) assigns a scalar to each leaf state. The trajectory logit is \[\ell_{s,a}(d;\Theta)=
 \gamma^{-d}\sum_{t=0}^{d-1}\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)+\Theta(s_d).\] C-SoftTreeMax normalizes \(\exp(\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_b}\ell_{s,a})\) over actions; E-SoftTreeMax normalizes \(\mathbb{E}_{\pi_b}\exp(\beta\ell_{s,a})\). Here \(\beta>0\). The paper assumes \(P\) irreducible and aperiodic in Section 4. E-SoftTreeMax’s analysis additionally assumes state-only rewards.

Equation reference: eq:variance. The variance under review is exactly the trace covariance in the paper’s (1): \[
 \operatorname{Var}(G)=\mathbb{E}\|G\|_2^2-\|\mathbb{E}G\|_2^2,\qquad
 G=\nabla_\Theta\log\pi_{d,\Theta}(a\mid s)\,Q^\pi(s,a),\] where \(s\) has the normalized discounted visitation distribution and \(a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)\). Both examples use an actual MDP \(Q^\pi\), not an arbitrarily rescaled function. Both set \(\gamma=1/2\), \(\beta=1\), \(\Theta=0\), two actions \(a\in\{+,-\}\) and an initially uniform state distribution.

Equation reference: eq:Cgradient. For C-SoftTreeMax, differentiating the finite softmax gives the paper’s Lemma 4.3: \[
 \nabla_\Theta\log\pi^C_{d,\Theta}(\cdot\mid s)
 =\beta(I_A-\mathbf{1}_A\pi_s^\top)P_sP^{d-1}.\] This identity is valid and is used directly below. For E-SoftTreeMax, differentiation of the positive finite trajectory sum likewise gives Lemma 4.6. The counterexamples concern the subsequent spectral bounds, rather than these derivative identities.
# Problem 1: the C-SoftTreeMax eigenvalue bound fails

Problem 1 (Theorem 4.4 omits the effect of nonorthogonal spectral projections).  Under its stated irreducibility and aperiodicity assumptions, Theorem 4.4 does not provide a valid finite-depth variance upper bound, even when all eigenvalues are distinct.
## Claim and suspect step

Equation reference: eq:claimedC. Theorem 4.4, p. 4, states \[
 \operatorname{Var}(G_C)\le
 \frac{2A^2S^2\beta^2}{(1-\gamma)^2}
 |\lambda_2(P)|^{2(d-1)}.\] Here eigenvalues are ordered by modulus. The proof outline on pp. 4–5 first assumes simple eigenvalues and says repeated eigenvalues can be handled by Jordan decomposition. Appendix A.4, pp. 14–15, expands \(P\) in spectral rank-one matrices and replaces the sum of their Frobenius norms by \(S-1\). Biorthogonally normalized left and right eigenvectors of a general stochastic matrix do not make every spectral projection have Frobenius norm one. The following example lies within the simple-eigenvalue case itself.
## Complete counterexample

Equation reference: eq:PC, eq:actionsC. Let \[u=(1,-1,0)^\top,\quad v=(1,1,-2)^\top,\quad
 J=\frac{\mathbf{1}_3\mathbf{1}_3^\top}{3},\quad
 \delta=\frac1{10000},\quad \eta=\frac1{24},\] and define \[
 P=J+\frac{uv^\top}{12}
       +\delta\frac{uu^\top}{2}
       +2\delta\frac{vv^\top}{6}.\] At each state \(s\), define the two action transition rows by \[
 P(s'\mid s,\pm)=P_{s,s'}\pm\eta u_{s'}.\] Use uniform \(\pi_b(\pm\mid s)=1/2\), and \(r(s,a)=1\) for every state and action.

Every operative hypothesis can be checked explicitly. The vectors \(u,v\) are orthogonal to \(\mathbf{1}_3\) and to each other. Thus \(P\) is doubly stochastic and the two rows in [eq:actionsC] (#eq:actionsC) each sum to one. The smallest probability among all action transitions is \(833/5000>0\). Consequently all action kernels, and in particular \(P^{\pi_b}=P\), are irreducible and aperiodic. In the basis \((\mathbf{1}_3,u,v)\), the action of \(P\) is triangular with diagonal entries \(1,\delta,2\delta\). These three eigenvalues are distinct, so \(P\) is diagonalizable and \[|\lambda_2(P)|=2\delta=\frac1{5000}.\] The rewards meet the \([0,1]\) requirement. At \(\Theta=0\), all trajectory rewards and hence both C-SoftTreeMax action logits coincide. Thus \(\pi^C(\pm\mid s)=1/2\), \(Q^\pi(s,a)=2\), the induced kernel is \(P\) and the discounted state distribution remains uniform.
## Counterevidence and bounded correction

The discrepancy is not caused by a repeated eigenvalue, an unbounded \(Q\), a nonergodic kernel, a neural parameterization or a sampled trajectory approximation. The special rank-one case discussed on p. 5 and in Appendix C.1 is valid for \(d\ge2\): then \(P^{d-1}=\mathbf{1}\mu^\top\), and the left projection in [eq:Cgradient] (#eq:Cgradient) cancels it. That special case does not justify the stated bound for nonnormal \(P\).

Equation reference: eq:repairC. A valid replacement retaining the relevant matrix dependence follows directly from [eq:Cgradient] (#eq:Cgradient). If \(\mu\) is the stationary distribution and \(|Q|\le Q_{\max}\), then \[
 \operatorname{Var}(G_C)\le
 2A^2\beta^2 Q_{\max}^2
 \left\|P^{d-1}-\mathbf{1}_S\mu^\top\right\|_2^2.\] Indeed, the stationary rank-one term is annihilated, \(\|I_A-\mathbf{1}_A\pi_s^\top\|_F\le\sqrt{2A}\) and \(\|P_s\|_2\le\|P_s\|_F\le\sqrt A\). Applying these bounds to Lemma 4.1 proves [eq:repairC] (#eq:repairC). This repairs this variance inequality only. Obtaining a pure eigenvalue rate requires appropriate matrix-dependent constants or additional structural assumptions; Jordan blocks can also require polynomial factors. No corrected theorem for the full algorithm is claimed.
## Impact

Theorem 4.4 is identified as the first main result in Section 4 and supports the claimed quantitative dependence on the expansion policy’s second eigenvalue. The finite-depth guarantee is false as written; the repair changes the quantity governing that guarantee. This is a Major finding. Long-run mixing and useful tree expansion may still occur, and the counterexample does not measure Atari performance.
# Problem 2: reversibility does not give the claimed E-SoftTreeMax rate

Problem 2 (The reversible clause of Theorem 4.7 is false).  A symmetric irreducible aperiodic transition matrix satisfies all stated assumptions, but its E-SoftTreeMax gradient variance decays with a strictly slower exponential rate than the rate asserted in Theorem 4.7.
## Claim and proof dependence

Theorem 4.7, p. 5, asserts the existence of \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) such that \[\operatorname{Var}(G_E)\in O(\beta^2\alpha^{2d}),\] and states that if \(P^{\pi_b}\) is reversible or rewards are constant then \(\alpha=|\lambda_2(P^{\pi_b})|\). Appendix A.8, pp. 17–20, works with normalized products associated with reward-weighted transitions. Its displayed lower bound (31) depends on \(\gamma^{-d}\); it is not a positive constant uniform in depth. The subsequent convergence invocation therefore does not establish the claimed depth-uniform result. Moreover, the appendix’s own theorem restatement retains the constant-reward case but omits the reversible clause. The main-text reversible claim can be refuted directly without relying on either observation.
## Parameters and every assumption

Equation reference: eq:PE. Take \[
 P=\begin{pmatrix}
  9/20&1/20&1/2\\
  1/20&9/20&1/2\\
  1/2&1/2&0
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 r=(1,1,0)^\top,\qquad \eta=\frac1{100}.\] Use the two action kernels \[P(s'\mid s,\pm)=P_{s,s'}\pm\eta u_{s'},\qquad
 u=(1,-1,0)^\top,\] uniform behavior, \(\gamma=1/2\), \(\beta=1\), \(\Theta=0\) and uniform initial distribution. Every action probability is nonnegative and every row sums to one; the smallest modified positive entry is \(1/20-1/100=1/25\). The only zero is the original \((3,3)\) entry. The behavior average is exactly \(P\). It is irreducible and aperiodic because every state communicates with the other states and states 1 and 2 have positive self-loops. It is symmetric, hence reversible with uniform stationary distribution. Its eigenvalues are \[1,\quad -\frac12,\quad \frac25;
 \qquad |\lambda_2(P)|=\frac12.\] The state-only rewards are in \([0,1]\). Thus the additional E-SoftTreeMax and reversibility hypotheses are satisfied.
## Exact weighted-product calculation

Let \(n=d-1\), and define \[D_k=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,e^{-2^k}),\qquad
 M_n=D_nP\,D_{n-1}P\cdots D_1P,\qquad M_0=I.\] The positive scalar factors removed from the original reward matrices are common to both actions and cancel in the policy and its derivative. This is exactly the product in Lemma 4.5 after that cancellation.

Equation reference: eq:ab, eq:antisym. By symmetry write \(M_n\mathbf{1}=(a_n,a_n,b_n)^\top\). Starting at \(a_0=b_0=1\), multiplication gives \[
 a_n=\frac{a_{n-1}+b_{n-1}}2,\qquad
 b_n=e^{-2^n}a_{n-1}.\] Since \(u^\top D_k=u^\top\) and \(u^\top P=(2/5)u^\top\), \[
 u^\top M_n=(2/5)^n u^\top.\] The two action sums are equal because \(u^\top M_n\mathbf{1}=0\). Therefore \(\pi^E(\pm\mid s)=1/2\) for every \(s,d\). The true kernel is consequently \(P\) and the discounted visitation is uniform. Solving the Bellman equations gives \[V_1=V_2=\frac85,\qquad V_3=\frac45.\] The action perturbation only shifts mass between states 1 and 2, whose values are equal, so \(Q^\pi(s,+)=Q^\pi(s,-)=V_s\) exactly.

Equation reference: eq:Eactual. Put \[Z_H=\frac{a_n+b_n}{2},\qquad Z_L=a_n.\] Differentiating the normalized positive sums at \(\Theta=0\) and using [eq:antisym] (#eq:antisym) gives \[\nabla_\Theta\log\pi^E(\pm\mid s)
 =\pm\frac{\eta(2/5)^n u^\top}{Z_s},
 \qquad Z_1=Z_2=Z_H,\quad Z_3=Z_L.\] The mean gradient again vanishes conditionally on each state. The exact variance is \[
 \operatorname{Var}(G_E)=
 \frac{2\eta^2}{3}(2/5)^{2n}
 \left\{\frac{2(8/5)^2}{Z_H^2}
                  +\frac{(4/5)^2}{Z_L^2}\right\}.\]
## An asymptotic contradiction, not just finite numerics

Define \(A_n=2^na_n\). Then \(A_0=1\), \(A_1=2\), and for \(n\ge2\), [eq:ab] (#eq:ab) yields \[A_n=A_{n-1}+2e^{-2^{n-1}}A_{n-2}.\] This is an increasing positive sequence, and \[A_n\le A_{n-1}(1+2e^{-2^{n-1}}).\] Because \(\sum_{n\ge2}e^{-2^{n-1}}<\infty\), the associated infinite product is finite. Thus \(A_n\) tends to a finite positive \(A_\infty\). Also \[0\le b_n/a_n\le2e^{-2^n}\longrightarrow0.\] Consequently \(Z_H\sim A_\infty 2^{-n-1}\), \(Z_L\sim A_\infty2^{-n}\) and \[\operatorname{Var}(G_E)=\Theta\bigl((4/5)^{2n}\bigr)
          =\Theta\bigl((4/5)^{2d}\bigr).\] Its ratio to \((1/2)^{2d}\) diverges exponentially. No finite depth-independent big-\(O\) constant repairs the asserted \(\alpha=1/2\) rate.

The independent check evaluates [eq:ab] (#eq:ab) and [eq:Eactual] (#eq:Eactual), verifies the rational spectrum and Bellman values, and separately compares the scaled matrix-product derivative with finite differences. For illustration, \(\operatorname{Var}(G_E)/(1/4)^d\) is approximately \(4.8347\) at \(d=10\), \(5.8448\times10^4\) at \(d=20\) and \(8.5421\times10^{12}\) at \(d=40\). These diagnostics support the analytic argument; the proof of divergence is the recurrence above, not a finite fit.
## Counterevidence, impact and correction status

This example has nonconstant rewards, so it does not challenge the separate constant-reward special case. It is reversible and uses exact trajectory sums; neither nonnormality nor sampling error explains it. It continues to exhibit exponential variance decay with \(\alpha=4/5\). Therefore the finding refutes the claimed reversible eigenvalue rate, not the existence of some exponential rate in every setting.

The reversible case is part of a central theoretical guarantee and underlies the interpretation that the ordinary transition spectrum determines the relevant decay rate. Reward weighting changes that rate even for a symmetric kernel. This is a second Major finding. Removing the reversible clause would remove the directly contradicted assertion, but this report does not certify a repaired general E-SoftTreeMax theorem. A complete proof must control the reward-weighted products and all depth-dependent constants.
# Overall dependence and unresolved scope

The two Problems concern separate variants and different failures: nonorthogonal spectral projections invalidate the stated C-SoftTreeMax constant, while reward weighting invalidates the E-SoftTreeMax reversible rate itself. They directly affect contribution (ii) on p. 2 and the expansion-policy guidance in Sections 3–4. The gradient identities and the general idea of differentiable planning survive these checks. The paper’s approximate-model result is a distinct claim and is not resolved by either counterexample.

The static source implements neural logits with a factor \(\gamma^d\) and caches leaves, and implements bounded-width sampling/pruning. These facts require care when relating the exact tabular theory to the release. The release’s full relationship to the conference experiments, including effective temperature and cached observations, was not established; it is recorded as Needs Evidence rather than used to infer an experimental failure. The Atari comparisons and gradient-variance measurements require original run data or fresh authorized experiments for verification. No such experiments were run.

No later paper revision or author erratum was independently retrieved in this review. The staged release and manifest were consulted; this is not an assertion that no correction exists, and no priority claim is made.

Title: Technical Verification of
Hyper-Transforming Latent Diffusion Models
# Paper identity and review scope

This report concerns Ignacio Peis, Batuhan Koyuncu, Isabel Valera, and Jes Frellsen, Hyper-Transforming Latent Diffusion Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 48714–48733, paper I25-43516 (0147) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed source is the 20-page published proceedings PDF staged for this assignment. Page references below use PDF pages, whose printed local numbers agree. Appendix A begins on page 13.

The complete paper text, including appendices, was read. Substantive checks cover the HD reconstruction operators (7)–(9), the latent-variable construction and objectives (10)–(15), stated experimental comparisons, and selected released decoder/metric code. Source inspection used `ipeis/LDMI` commit `e2db5966f2c5287c0bdcbaface5fe8c02b2c4dc2`, dated 9 August 2025 in the acquired manifest [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. This is a pinned released snapshot, not an attested record of the code that produced the publication.

No training, sampling, author-code execution, dataset acquisition, or empirical benchmark reproduction was performed. Reading figure captions and extracted tables does not independently verify image quality or reported measurements. The relevant equation on page 5 was additionally checked against a rendered source page. The inspected and uninspected items are enumerated in `coverage.json`.
# Definitions and dependencies

Equation reference: eq:operators. For a generated weight column, write \(u=w^o_{\lceil c/k\rceil}\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(b=\bar w^b_c\in\mathbb R^m\). The paper compares \[R_{\mathrm{norm}}(u,b)=\frac{u\odot b}{\|u\odot b\|_2},
 \qquad
 R_{\mathrm{scale}}(u,b)=(\mathbf 1+u)\odot b.
 \] The normalized expression requires \(u\odot b\ne0\). Grouping requires divisibility of the input width by the group count; it imposes no additional restriction that changes the following per-column calculation. Periodic activations occur downstream.

The latent code is sampled from an encoder posterior and mapped to INR parameters by the HD. A deterministic map of a random latent code can induce a nontrivial distribution of functions; no contradiction follows from implementing that map deterministically. The paper expressly distinguishes the ordinary ELBO at \(\beta=1\) from its modified objective at other \(\beta\). This review does not treat the latter as a new exact likelihood bound. Diffusion training and conditional completion performance were not independently reproduced.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The stated normalized-weight mechanism is incorrect).  The discussion following equation (8), page 5, attributes instability near \(u=0\) to normalized weights and their gradients vanishing. As an explanation of the displayed operator, that behavior is incorrect in general.
## Original claim and complete check

The authors frame this as a hypothesis motivated by training behavior, not a proved theorem. The displayed normalization nevertheless admits an exact calculation. Set \(m=2\), \(b=(1,1)^\top\), and \(u=(r,0)^\top\) for any \(r>0\). A single column and one group satisfy the grouping condition. The base weight is nonzero, the denominator is \(r\), and the operator is defined. No stated restriction in the operator prevents these values. Rescaling the nonzero base-weight direction gives the same output-norm conclusion.

Equation reference: eq:jacobian. For \(v=u\odot b\ne0\), let \(\widehat v=v/\|v\|_2\). Differentiation gives \[D_u R_{\mathrm{norm}}(u,b)
 =\frac{I-\widehat v\widehat v^\top}{\|v\|_2}\operatorname{diag}(b).
 \] The admissible example yields \[R_{\mathrm{norm}}((r,0)^\top,(1,1)^\top)=(1,0)^\top,\qquad
 D_uR_{\mathrm{norm}}=
 \begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&r^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.\] The output norm is exactly one for every \(r>0\), while transverse sensitivity grows as \(r^{-1}\). For \(r=10^{-2},10^{-6},10^{-10}\), the independent diagnostic returns output norm \(1\) and derivative norm \(10^2,10^6,10^{10}\). The formula evaluation and output are preserved in `independent_check.py` and `independent_check.json`.
## Counterevidence and supported impact

There is a null derivative in the radial direction, and a downstream loss may annihilate other derivative directions. Neither fact implies vanishing normalized weights or a vanishing full Jacobian near zero. At \(v=0\), equation (8) is undefined. An implementation using \(\max(\|v\|,\varepsilon)\) can make the output approach zero within the floor region, but its local derivative is then \(\operatorname{diag}(b)/\varepsilon\), again generally nonzero. The inspected `normalize_weights` function calls `F.normalize`; it does not establish the claimed general mechanism.

A defensible replacement is that exact normalization removes radial information, is undefined at zero, and can have large transverse sensitivity near zero. In contrast, \[R_{\mathrm{scale}}(0,b)=b,\qquad
 D_uR_{\mathrm{scale}}=\operatorname{diag}(b).\] These identities support a local conditioning distinction. They do not prove globally stable optimization or measured improvements. Equation (9) and the reported empirical gains are not refuted. The assessment is Minor: this is a local mathematical explanation error, and no logical dependence of the core performance conclusion on the erroneous vanishing argument has been established.

Problem 2 (The released metric CSV repeats cumulative observations).  The arrays in `experiments/image_metrics.py` accumulate all observations seen so far, but the entire cumulative dataframe is appended after every batch. The saved rows therefore do not form a once-per-example evaluation dataset.
## Source location and complete check

Metric accumulation occurs at lines 85–92; prefix FID calculation and broadcasting at lines 94–102; dataframe construction and `to_csv(..., mode=’a’)` at lines 105–108 in the pinned snapshot [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The defect matters when a run has at least two nonempty batches and its CSV is interpreted as an ordinary table of evaluation observations.

For \(B\) equal-size batches of \(b\) examples, the file receives \(b,2b,\ldots,Bb\) rows, totaling \[b\sum_{i=1}^B i=\frac{bB(B+1)}2\] instead of \(bB\). An observation from batch \(j\) appears \(B-j+1\) times. With two one-example batches whose PSNR values are \(10\) and \(30\) dB, the written rows are \(10,10,30\); their mean is \(50/3\) dB instead of \(20\) dB.

FID is recomputed on each cumulative prefix and broadcast over that prefix’s rows. For illustrative prefix FIDs \(5\) and \(3\), the file contains \(5,3,3\); its mean is \(11/3\), whereas the final full-set statistic is \(3\). Averaging prefix FIDs does not produce a full-set FID. These numbers are synthetic serialization inputs, not measured LDMI activations. The independent diagnostic records them without importing or executing repository code.
## Counterevidence, correction, and scope

The in-memory arrays accumulate each observation once. The final progress-bar PSNR and FID can therefore be correct despite duplicated serialized rows. The final appended block also contains every PSNR once together with the final FID, so a reader deliberately selecting that block can recover a valid summary. Neither the paper nor the inspected files establishes that Tables 1–4 were computed by averaging the entire CSV.

For a fresh evaluation file, a precise correction is to write the completed PSNR array once after the loop and store the final global FID separately as a summary scalar. Alternatively, per-prefix records must be explicitly labeled and cannot be interpreted as independent observations. This correction is justified for serialization only; no modified author program was executed. The released-code defect is Minor. Historical impact on published conclusions remains Needs Evidence and does not raise supported severity.
# Overall dependence and remaining evidence

The HD architecture, equation (9), and two training routes survive these checks. Scale modulation is selected in the inspected CelebA-HQ configuration; the transformer implements encoder self-attention and decoder self/cross-attention. The CSV defect occurs after inference and does not alter parameter updates.

Tables 1 and 4 report different CelebA-HQ HD PSNR values, \(24.80\) and \(27.72\) dB. The description does not establish that they refer to the same run; this review does not label their difference an error. Metric provenance would require the relevant configuration, checkpoint, evaluation population, output records, and aggregation rule. Quantifying a changed score would require a new evaluation. No dataset or checkpoint was acquired here.

No supplied erratum or later paper version was reviewed. The repository date and commit are separate from the proceedings version. The acquired manifest records an OpenReview access challenge; additional OpenReview-only attachments remain unassessed. This does not assert that no correction or supplement exists elsewhere.

Problem 1 repair | Correct operator/Jacobian identities proved; training behavior unverified.
Problem 2 repair | Once-only serialization justified; modified author code not run.
Published metrics | Needs Evidence concerning historical aggregation.

# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Anne Ouyang, Simon Guo, Simran Arora, Alex L. Zhang, William Hu, Christopher Ré, and Azalia Mirhoseini, KernelBench: Can LLMs Write Efficient GPU Kernels?, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 47356–47415, I25-43517 (0148) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. # Checks of the core score

The independent arithmetic diagnostic used \(c=(1,1,0,0)\) and \(s=(2,1,1/2,4)\). It returned \[\operatorname{fast}_0=\tfrac12,\qquad
 \operatorname{fast}_1=\tfrac14,\qquad
 \operatorname{fast}_2=0.\] The incorrect fourth entry does not contribute despite its large speedup. These are independently calculated examples, not executions of the authors’ scoring function.

The level sizes in Section 3.2 are \(100,100,50\), so overall task averages require weights \(0.4,0.4,0.2\). Table 1’s DeepSeek-R1 Eager scores \(12\%,36\%,2\%\) imply \(49/250=19.6\%\), consistent with the reported overall result below \(20\%\). OpenAI o1’s \(10\%,24\%,12\%\) imply \(40/250=16\%\). No inconsistency is established by an unweighted average across levels. The best-of-\(k\) and best-through-turn-\(N\) definitions in Section 5.1 deliberately count whether any candidate succeeded; their nondecreasing trajectories are not claims that every successive generated kernel improved.
# Correctness and timing: what the protocol establishes

Section 3.3 and Appendix B describe five randomized input tests, three warm-up iterations, and 100 CUDA-event timing trials, with comparison of mean runtimes. Appendix B.2 explicitly treats random testing as a heuristic and reports a finite comparison between five and 100 tests. Thus the appropriate interpretation of \(c_i=1\) is passage of the specified tests at the specified precision and tolerance. It is not a proof of equivalence for every input, tensor shape, or execution environment.

Appendix K.1 specifies fixed task shapes and an FP32 tolerance of \(10^{-2}\). Fixed-shape specialization is part of the task definition; failure at an unrequested shape would not refute a benchmark success. The inspected later `eval.py` instead defines FP32 tolerance \(10^{-4}\), while its comments identify \(10^{-2}\) with earlier versions. This is an explicit version difference, not a demonstrated defect in the paper. The exact evaluation source revision, prompts, generations, and environment must accompany any reproduction.

The current correctness routine checks output shape and `allclose`, counts successful trials, and requires all trials to pass. The inspected code and `EVAL.md` also describe ongoing defenses against input modification, cached results, and nondefault streams. The supplied adversarial tests were read statically and were not run; their existence is not evidence that every failure mode is handled.

The trial routine does not visibly reset the RNG between the reference and candidate forward calls. Selected tasks contain stochastic operations, including nonzero dropout in Level 2 task 66 and random initial states in a released LSTM task. This motivates a focused state/RNG check in a future execution-based reproduction. No fixed-seed task-specific mismatch was demonstrated here; no false-negative rate, affected published score, or severity is inferred from this observation alone. An execution of identical stochastic distributions is also not automatically a paired samplewise equivalence test.
# A released task admits exact constant folding

The acquired Level 2 task sets \(\texttt{min\_value}=0\), \(\texttt{max\_value}=1\), and dropout probability \(0.2\). Its forward path applies convolution, group normalization, an elementwise minimum with zero, a clamp to \([0,1]\), and dropout. Let \(z\) be any finite scalar output of the normalization. Then \[\min(z,0)\le0,\qquad
 \operatorname{clamp}_{[0,1]}(\min(z,0))=0.\] Dropout preserves this zero regardless of its mask. This is an exact algebraic conclusion for finite intermediate values, not an assertion about NaNs or infinities. The declared input shape is \(128\times3\times16\times64\times64\); the unpadded size-three convolution gives output shape \(128\times16\times14\times62\times62\). Filling that shape with zeros reproduces the functional output under the stated finite-value condition.

This observation is retained as a scope clarification, not a numbered Problem. Eliminating unnecessary computation is a legitimate optimization under the paper’s explicit allowance for algorithmic changes. A speedup on this particular specification can reflect constant folding rather than efficient execution of its nominal convolution and normalization. That distinction does not invalidate the benchmark’s permission to optimize semantics, nor does it establish a defective published aggregate. The paper lists the same task name on page 42 and an associated result on page 56, but the historical parameter bytes were not supplied separately; the current snapshot cannot establish their identity. The independent check file evaluates representative finite scalars, while the universal zero-output statement follows from the inequalities above.
# Conclusion and limits

No supported Major or Minor problem is established by these checks. The score formula and inspected scoring code agree within the stated valid-timing domain. Finite testing, fixed shapes, and source-version changes must remain explicit when interpreting correctness and performance. The numerical kernel benchmarks, model rankings, hardware comparisons, and full generated-program population remain unreplicated.

report: Abstract: The stated optimal linear-adapter theorem is false under its own invertibility assumption: its proposed solution is singular for every multivariate instance. A feasible exact counterexample, a nonattainment example, and a curvature calculation establish the defect independently of experimental reproduction. This is a Major issue in a theoretical contribution explicitly used to motivate the method. A tabulated MAE is also incompatible with the corresponding MSE. Static checks identify two further issues in the acquired released software, concerning decoded predictive summaries and cross-validation training labels; their effect on the historical experiments is unresolved. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of AdaPTS
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Abdelhakim Benechehab, Vasilii Feofanov, Giuseppe Paolo, Albert Thomas, Maurizio Filippone, and Balázs Kégl, AdaPTS: Adapting Univariate Foundation Models to Probabilistic Multivariate Time Series Forecasting, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 3731–3748, I25-43518 (0149) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The input is the 18-page proceedings PDF. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which match the printed local page numbers.

The complete extracted text, including Appendices A–D, was read. Original PDF pages 3, 6, 14, and 18 were additionally rendered and visually inspected to verify the theorem, proof, and table entries. The source manifest was parsed; the parent reviewer separately performed the complete staged source hash inventory. This reviewer independently hashed the original PDF, manifest, and the files used in the numerical and code findings.

The acquired released repository is `abenechehab/AdaPTS`, commit `8bf57c7ee3b97bfd3f1852ad8dc8d0695a806278`, dated 13 January 2026 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The manifest identifies it as the current released commit at acquisition, without asserting that it generated the paper’s experiments. The review preserves that distinction. No author code, training pipeline, foundation model, supplied test suite, or notebook was executed. Only independently written small calculations were run.
# Problems supported by the inspected evidence

Problem 1 (Major: the optimal linear-adapter theorem returns an inadmissible matrix).  Proposition 3.3, Eq. (4), and its proof in Appendix A.1 claim an optimizer over invertible adapters but produce a singular matrix whenever \(D>1\). The ridge expression in Remark 3.4 does not remove this obstruction.
## Claim and complete assumptions

Equation reference: eq:loss, eq:claimed. Section 3 assumes \(W=W_\phi\in {\rm GL}_D(\mathbb R)\) and a shared univariate affine foundation model \[f_{\rm FM}(X)=W_{\rm FM}^{\mathsf T}X+b\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}.\] No nonzero-rank assumption on \(W_{\rm FM}\), no restriction on \(Y\), and no nonorthogonality requirement involving \(b\) and \(Y-W_{\rm FM}^{\mathsf T}X\) are stated. Put \[A=Y-W_{\rm FM}^{\mathsf T}X,\qquad B=b\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}.\] The loss reduces exactly to \[L(W)=\|A-BW^{-1}\|_F^2.
 \] The paper proposes \[W_*=(B^{\mathsf T}A)^+B^{\mathsf T}B.
 \] Appendix A.1 explicitly writes the optimization domain as \({\rm GL}_D(\mathbb R)\).
## Rank obstruction and explicit counterexample

Because \(B=b\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\), its rank is at most one. Consequently \[\operatorname{rank}(W_*)\leq
 \operatorname{rank}(B^{\mathsf T}B)\leq1.\] For every \(D>1\), Eq. [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) is outside the optimization domain; the inverse required by Eq. [eq:loss] (#eq:loss) is undefined. This is an exact structural obstruction, not a numerical conditioning issue. Whenever the left inverse in the proposed ridge modification exists, \[W_\lambda=(B^{\mathsf T}A+\lambda I)^{-1}B^{\mathsf T}B\] also has rank at most one.

For a fully specified admissible instance, take \(L=H=1\), \(D=2\), \(X=(0,0)\), \(W_{\rm FM}=0\), \(b=1\), and \(Y=(1,2)\). These satisfy the paper’s model assumptions. Then \(A=(1,2)\), \(B=(1,1)\), and independent exact arithmetic gives \[W_*=\begin{pmatrix}1/5&1/5\\2/5&2/5\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 W_{\lambda=1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/4&1/4\\1/4&1/4\end{pmatrix}.\] Both determinants are zero. In contrast, \[W_{\rm feasible}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/2)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 BW_{\rm feasible}^{-1}=(1,2)=A,\qquad L(W_{\rm feasible})=0,\] while \(L(I)=1\). Thus an invertible optimum exists in this example, but the reported formula does not produce it.
## Existence and convexity also require correction

The theorem does not always have any attained minimum. With the same dimensions, \(A=0\), and \(B=(1,1)\), every invertible \(W\) gives \(BW^{-1}\ne0\), hence \(L(W)>0\). The sequence \(W=tI\), \(t\to\infty\), has \(L(W)=2/t^2\to0\). The infimum is zero and is not attained.

The final paragraph of Appendix A.1 asserts convexity in \(W\), citing the inverse operation. Even on a convex positive scalar domain this is false. For \(A=B=1\) and \(w>0\), \[f(w)=(1-w^{-1})^2,\qquad
 f''(w)=\frac{6-4w}{w^4},\qquad f''(2)=-\frac18.\] Equivalently, \(f(2)=1/4>53/225=[f(3/2)+f(5/2)]/2\). The loss is a quadratic in \(M=W^{-1}\), but this does not make it convex in \(W\), and invertibility still restricts the admissible \(M\).
## Diagnosis, correction, and counterevidence

The stationary equation \(B^{\mathsf T}AW=B^{\mathsf T}B\) does not justify discarding its null-space freedom and selecting a singular minimum-norm matrix. The omitted freedom is precisely what can make a solution invertible. Remark A.4 proposes channel-dependent biases to obtain full-rank \(B\). This changes the shared-univariate-model assumption and therefore does not establish Proposition 3.3 as stated. Full-rank \(B\) by itself also does not guarantee a full-rank \(B^{\mathsf T}A\).

A corrected characterization for the stated shared-bias case is simple. If \(b\ne0\), write \(q^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}\), which must be nonzero. Every nonzero row \(q^{\mathsf T}\) can be realized by some invertible \(W\), by extending nonzero row vectors to bases. The unconstrained least-squares row is \[q_*^{\mathsf T}=\frac{b^{\mathsf T}A}{b^{\mathsf T}b}.\] If \(q_*\ne0\), any invertible completion satisfying \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}=q_*^{\mathsf T}\) attains the minimum. If \(q_*=0\), the infimum is not attained. If \(b=0\), the loss is constant on all invertible \(W\). This characterization is an analytic correction, not an author-adopted repair.

The paper explicitly identifies theoretical foundations as a contribution on page 2, calls Proposition 3.3 its foundational motivation on page 3, and claims to evaluate Eq. (4) in Figure 2 on page 4. The demonstrated invalid derivation therefore affects a core theoretical contribution and its synthetic optimality interpretation. This supports Major. It does not establish that the separately trained encoder–decoder method fails or that any real-data score is wrong. The useful existence of better adapters in some cases is compatible with this counterexample; the theorem and its advertised optimizer are nevertheless invalid. Historical Figure 2 code and outputs would be needed to determine how an inverse of the displayed singular expression was handled.

Problem 2 (Minor: incompatible MSE and MAE entries).  The Illness, \(H=24\), LinearAE entry is \(2.624\pm0.035\) in both Table 1 (MSE, page 6) and Table 6 (MAE, page 18). These cannot be the stated metrics of the same residual arrays with the same normalization and run averaging.

The released `compute_metrics` applies MSE and L1 loss to the same targets and predictions, consistent with the conventional interpretation, but its later provenance does not identify the historical table-generation process. Different runs or scales would require explicit relabeling and would defeat the current like-for-like presentation. The correct MAE cannot be reconstructed from MSE alone and must be recomputed from original predictions. This is a localized reporting issue; it does not by itself overturn the main MSE comparisons. Separately, the page-6 ETTh1 improvement from \(0.411\) to \(0.395\) is \(3.89\%\), not the stated \(8\%\); this arithmetic discrepancy likewise does not reverse the ranking.

Problem 3 (Minor, released implementation: predictive summaries are transformed incorrectly).  The acquired `ADAPTS.predict_multi_step` summarizes latent predictions before applying the decoder, although a nonlinear or sign-mixing decoder does not preserve those summaries. The effect on the proceedings experiments remains Needs Evidence.

In `src/adapts/adapts.py`, lines 217–254, the program obtains latent sample means and standard deviations, then applies `inverse_transform` to the mean and to componentwise mean-plus/minus-standard-deviation vectors. With decoder \(g\) and latent forecast \(U\), it therefore returns \(g(\widehat{\mathbb E}U)\), whereas the Monte Carlo predictive mean is \(\widehat{\mathbb E}[g(U)]\). These differ for nonlinear \(g\). For equal samples \(U=0,2\) and \(g(u)=\tanh u\), independent arithmetic gives \[g(\bar U)=0.761594,\qquad
 \frac{g(0)+g(2)}2=0.482014.\] The released VAE decoder contains nonlinear LeakyReLU and Tanh layers, so the required affine identity is not imposed.

Even an affine decoder can invalidate the returned bounds. For \(g(u)=-u\), latent mean zero and standard deviation one, the returned lower value is \(g(-1)=1\), and the upper value is \(g(1)=-1\). A negative decoder weight is permitted by the released linear decoder classes. More generally, a multivariate linear decoder requires propagation of the covariance, not simultaneous transformation of componentwise endpoints.

The proper computation is to decode each joint sample with consistent decoder and normalization state, then calculate the desired means, standard deviations, or quantiles in the original space. The supplied `compute_ks_metric` already decodes individual draws before its calibration calculation; this is material counterevidence against claiming that the identified summary-order defect automatically invalidates every ECE value. No historical plot or score was reproduced. The established result concerns the current returned summaries and their interpretation, not a measured loss of the paper’s empirical advantage.

Problem 4 (Minor, released implementation: outer validation labels enter Moment head fitting).  The current hyperparameter-search script constructs outer folds but fits the Moment forecasting head on the complete pooled data, including the current outer validation fold.

In `scripts/hyperopt.py`, lines 145–148 combine the original training and validation arrays. Lines 290–316 construct fold-specific train and validation subsets. However, lines 334–345 call `fine_tune_iclearner` with `X=X_train` and `y=y_train`, not the fold-training arrays. The subsequent adapter fit does use the fold subsets. The forecast model and learner are created before the fold loop; only the adapter is re-created inside it.

This is supervised label access, not merely fitting a feature scaler on contexts. The Moment wrapper creates a tensor dataset from every supplied pair and, without explicit validation arguments, randomly splits that entire dataset 90/10 before optimizing the unfrozen forecasting head. For a concrete 30-example, three-fold case, each outer validation set has ten elements and the inner head-training set has 27. Their intersection must contain at least \(27+10-30=7\) elements, regardless of the random split. Thus at least 70% of that outer validation set’s labels enter supervised head training. The independent check verifies this set bound; no training was executed.

This defeats the interpretation of the resulting fold metric as validation of the entire fitted forecasting pipeline. It does not prove that test labels were trained on: the separate test arrays remain outside this pool, and the inspected search objective selects by validation MSE, not the saved test score. The corrected procedure must reinitialize the trainable head and adapter for each outer fold and confine all supervised fitting to the outer training portion, with a suitable inner validation split. The released snapshot demonstrates the protocol defect; experiment-time configurations and logs are needed to determine whether it affected the paper’s selected hyperparameters or final scores.
# Other checks and unresolved claims

The adapter definition initially requires an inverse, while Section 2 explicitly relaxes that requirement to separately trained encoders and decoders. Consequently a noninvertible practical autoencoder alone is not an additional contradiction. It also does not repair the invertible linear theorem.

The Jensen steps in Proposition 4.1 and Appendix A.2 give a valid ELBO for the written latent-variable likelihood when the density/support assumptions hold. The paper separately identifies the tunable \(\beta\)-weighted objective; this was not confused with an unmodified ELBO. However, with the concrete decoder mean \(\operatorname{dec}_\theta(f_{\rm FM}(Z))\) and an unconditional prior \(p(Z)\), the displayed generative marginal has no explicit \(X\) dependence beyond any dependence separately retained in the likelihood. Predictions sampled using \(q_\phi(Z\mid X)\) need a careful distinction from that prior-based marginal. The paper’s appeal to universal conditional-density results likewise requires conditions on the fixed intervening foundation model. A constant fixed model can erase encoder stochasticity. No full audit of the cited external theorem or a quantified consequence for the trained models was performed; these interpretations remain Needs Evidence, not an additional established Major finding.

The main forecasting tables explicitly include settings in which adapters match or worsen the baseline. Table 2 labels results on additional foundation models as preliminary. Three runs and reported standard errors do not by themselves establish significance across tasks. The review checked the reported arithmetic and identified the impossible MAE cell; it did not independently reconstruct datasets, training, forecasts, or uncertainty calibration.

The current forecasting data reader fits its initial StandardScaler on the training partition. This is counterevidence against inferring target leakage solely from the prose order of preprocessing and splitting in Appendix C. The `ADAPTS.transform` path refits its scaler on supplied forecast contexts, which is a distinct transductive preprocessing choice requiring experimental protocol clarity. It is not by itself proof that future targets were supplied to that scaler.
# Initial assessment

The paper has a Major issue in Proposition 3.3 and its advertised theoretical optimality argument. The remaining supported problems have the narrower scopes stated above. No conclusion is drawn that the complete practical approach fails, that all published numerical results are invalid, or that the authors intended to mislead. Correction of the theoretical statement and clarification or repair of the affected reporting and released protocols are required. All scientific decisions remain pending; the human-review record is empty. This is an initial review, not batch acceptance.

report: Abstract: The inspected proof of the central maximum-posterior-variance lemma is consistent with an independent determinant and good-index argument. A separate counterexample invalidates the squared-exponential cumulative-regret guarantee of Theorem 6.3 on its stated variance domain. For an admissible fixed noise sequence with \(V_T=T^2-1/2\), the published rate tends to zero, whereas a legal two-point instance incurs a fixed positive first-round regret. The proof applies an information-gain asymptotic outside its valid range and then absorbs a positive startup term into a vanishing expression. This supports Major impact for the stated core guarantee; the lower-noise applications and other kernels are not refuted by this example. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of Improved Regret Analysis in Gaussian Process Bandits
# Identity, version and scope

The reviewed work is Shogo Iwazaki and Shion Takeno, Improved Regret Analysis in Gaussian Process Bandits: Optimality for Noiseless Reward, RKHS norm, and Non-Stationary Variance, ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, 26642–26672 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Its assigned identifiers are 0150 / I25-43519 and OpenReview `ybno0ZP44z`. The reviewed file is the staged published proceedings PDF; the publisher metadata records 6 October 2025. Its 31 physical pages are numbered 1–31 internally. References below use those internal/physical page numbers, not proceedings page numbers.

The review inspected the main definitions and results, the proof of Lemma 3.1 and the elementary part of Lemma C.1, the variance-rate substitutions in Corollary 3.2, the noiseless proof structure in Appendix D, and the nonstationary squared-exponential argument in Appendix F.1. The RKHS-norm results in Appendix E, the simple-regret proof in Appendix F.2, the baseline VA-GP-UCB analysis in Appendix I, and the external lower-bound literature were read for dependence but not completely independently verified. The pseudocode in Appendices G–H was inspected, including the initial action used below.

No paper-specific implementation was available in the staged source preparation. That availability result is not interpreted as evidence of mathematical correctness or as proof that no implementation exists. Additional OpenReview-only material was inaccessible to acquisition because of an access challenge. No new sources, software, datasets or model weights were downloaded, and no author code was executed. Later revisions and errata were not independently searched.
# Definitions and the checked central lemma

Assumption 2.1 requires a compact \(\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d\), a positive definite kernel with \(k(x,x)\le1\), and a reward function \(f\in\mathcal H_k\) with \(\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\). Assumption 2.2 requires independent zero-mean noises satisfying \[\mathbb E e^{a\epsilon_t}\le e^{a^2\rho_t^2/2}
 \quad\text{for every }a\in\mathbb R.\] The cumulative variance proxy is \(V_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\rho_t^2\). In Section 6 the learner learns \(\rho_t^2\) after round \(t\). It is not assumed there that each \(\rho_t\) is bounded by a fixed constant.
## Independent check of the argument

Let \(s_t\) be the posterior standard deviation at the selected point, computed with the virtual noises, and set \[\mathcal G=\{t:s_t/\widetilde\lambda_t\le1\}.\] The determinant identity for adding one observation gives \[\sum_{t=1}^T\log(1+s_t^2/\widetilde\lambda_t^2)
 \le2\gamma_T(\widetilde\Sigma_T).\] Each index outside \(\mathcal G\) contributes more than \(\log2\). Consequently \[|\mathcal G^c|
 \le\frac{2}{\log2}\gamma_T(\widetilde\Sigma_T)
 <3\gamma_T(\widetilde\Sigma_T).\] This in particular justifies the weaker factor 4 used for the nonstationary good-index count.

Actual posterior standard deviations are no larger than their virtual-noise counterparts when \(\lambda_t\le\widetilde\lambda_t\). The greedy selection and posterior variance monotonicity also imply that the final maximum is no larger than any earlier selected actual standard deviation. On \(\mathcal G\), use \(z\le2\log(1+z)\) for \(0\le z\le1\), followed by Cauchy–Schwarz, to obtain \[\sum_{t\in\mathcal G}s_t
 \le2\sqrt{\left(\sum_{t=1}^T\widetilde\lambda_t^2\right)
                  \gamma_T(\widetilde\Sigma_T)}.\] When the lemma’s horizon condition gives \(|\mathcal G|\ge T/2\), averaging over \(\mathcal G\) yields the stated factor \(4/T\) bound. This argument verifies the part of Lemma 3.1 used in Appendix F.1; it does not certify every strengthened count bound or every later theorem.

Two independently written finite diagnostics also checked stationary and nonstationary greedy posterior updates on a two-point squared-exponential kernel. At \(T=64\), the final maximum standard deviations were approximately \(0.08785\) and \(0.10265\), below conservative valid bounds \(0.72236\) and \(0.77818\), respectively. The horizon and good-index count conditions held. These are finite sanity checks, distinct from the argument above.

The substitutions producing the noiseless posterior-variance exponents were also checked: the proposed virtual noise makes the information-gain bound \(o(T)\) in the intended small-noise regime. No substantive defect in that particular argument was established.
# Problem 1: the nonstationary SE cumulative-regret theorem has an invalid variance domain
Problem 1 (Theorem 6.3 predicts vanishing cumulative regret for an allowed noise sequence).  The squared-exponential conclusion of Theorem 6.3 is false under the assumptions stated in that theorem.
## Original claim and precise location

Equation reference: eq:claim. Theorem 6.3, p. 8, assumes Assumptions 2.1–2.2, finite \(\mathcal X\), and \(V_T=\Omega(1)\). For Algorithm 3 with its specified confidence width, it states with probability at least \(1-\delta\) that \[
 R_T=O\!\left((\log T)
       \sqrt{V_T\log^{d+1}(T^2/V_T)\log(|\mathcal X|/\delta)}\right)
 \qquad(k=k_{\rm SE}).\] There is no upper restriction \(V_T\le cT^2\) in this theorem. The separately stated lower-bound Corollary 6.1 on p. 7 does impose \(V_T=O(T^2)\) with a sufficiently small implied constant; Theorem 6.3 does not incorporate that corollary’s assumptions.

In Appendix F.1, p. 23, (102)–(103) replace \(\gamma_T((V_T/T)I_T)\) by \(O(\log^{d+1}(T^2/V_T))\) without restricting the ratio \(T^2/V_T\) away from one. On p. 24, (107)–(108) also absorb the positive startup-regret term into that final expression. Both operations fail for the admissible sequence below.
## A fixed instance satisfying every assumption

Let \[d=1,\quad \mathcal X=\{0,1\},\quad
 k(x,x')=\exp\bigl(-(x-x')^2/2\bigr),\quad
 B=1,\quad f(x)=k(x,1).\] This finite set is compact. The squared-exponential lengthscale is \(\ell=1\), the kernel is positive definite, and \(k(x,x)=1\). The kernel section \(k(\cdot,1)\) belongs to its RKHS with norm \(\sqrt{k(1,1)}=1\), so the reward meets Assumption 2.1 exactly. Its unique maximizer on \(\mathcal X\) is 1, with \[f(1)=1,\qquad f(0)=e^{-1/2}.\] Set \(\delta=1/4\) and initial batch size \(N_1=1\). Before the first observation both points have posterior standard deviation 1. Resolve the first maximum-variance tie in Algorithm 3 by selecting \(x_1=0\). This is a legal deterministic execution of the stated algorithm. For any alternative deterministic first tie convention, interchange the two point labels and the kernel section, obtaining the same construction.

Equation reference: eq:noise, eq:VT. Let the noises be mutually independent Gaussian variables with \[
 \epsilon_t\sim N(0,\rho_t^2),\qquad
 \rho_1^2=\frac12,\qquad
 \rho_t^2=2t-1\quad(t\ge2).\] This is one fixed infinite variance sequence, not a horizon-dependent choice of different experiments. Each proxy is positive, every noise is mean zero, and its moment-generating function equals the required sub-Gaussian bound. The learner can be given the deterministic proxy at the end of each round, exactly as assumed. The total is \[
 V_T=\frac12+\sum_{t=2}^T(2t-1)=T^2-\frac12.\] It satisfies \(V_T=\Omega(1)\). Moreover, \(T^2/V_T>1\), so every logarithm in the disputed formula is strictly positive. The contradiction does not depend on evaluating \(\log0\), on a negative logarithm, or on setting the claimed rate identically to zero.
## Stated versus actual result

Equation reference: eq:positive. The first-round regret is \[
 \Delta=1-e^{-1/2}\simeq0.3934693403.\] Every subsequent instantaneous regret is nonnegative. Therefore \[R_T\ge\Delta\qquad\text{for every }T\ge1\] on every noise realization, irrespective of any later elimination decisions or confidence events.

Equation reference: eq:factor. For the fixed parameters above, the quantity inside the big-\(O\) in [eq:claim] (#eq:claim) is \[
 F_T=(\log T)\sqrt{T^2-\tfrac12}\,
          \log\!\left(\frac{T^2}{T^2-\tfrac12}\right)\sqrt{\log8}.\] Using \(\log(1+z)\sim z\) at \(z=0\) gives \[F_T\sim\frac{\sqrt{\log8}}{2}\frac{\log T}{T}
       \longrightarrow0.\] No finite multiplicative constant can bound the fixed positive \(\Delta\) by \(F_T\) for all sufficiently large \(T\). Thus the asserted high-probability cumulative-regret bound fails pathwise for this instance; changing the confidence constant cannot fix it.

The independent script evaluates the positive logarithm stably with `log1p`. For example, \(F_{1000}\simeq0.00498058\) and \(F_{10^6}\simeq9.96117\times10^{-6}\), while the lower bound [eq:positive] (#eq:positive) is unchanged. The analytic limit, rather than those finite values alone, establishes the big-\(O\) contradiction.
## Independent diagnosis of the information-gain step

Equation reference: eq:IGlower. The defect in (103) can also be shown without analyzing the algorithm. In [eq:IG] (#eq:IG), choose all \(T\) inputs equal to one point, and set the virtual stationary noise to \(\lambda^2=V_T/T\). The Gram matrix is \(\mathbf1_T\mathbf1_T^\top\), so \[
 \gamma_T((V_T/T)I_T)
 \ge\frac12\log\!\left(1+\frac{T^2}{V_T}\right)
 \longrightarrow\frac12\log2>0.\] In contrast, \(\log^2(T^2/V_T)\to0\). Hence the claimed information-gain replacement is itself false on this admissible sequence. A large-signal-to-noise asymptotic has been used in a regime where its argument approaches one.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

The prose emphasizes small or sublinearly increasing cumulative variance, and that interpretation would exclude [eq:noise] (#eq:noise). Under a fixed separation \(V_T\le cT^2\) with \(c<1\), the specific vanishing-log mechanism also disappears. These are meaningful possible restrictions, but neither is an assumption of Theorem 6.3 as printed. Assumption 2.2 permits the independent Gaussian sequence above, and the explicit upper restriction in the nearby lower-bound corollary demonstrates that the two statements have different written domains.

Likewise, replacing \(\log z\) by a floored logarithm or by \(\log(1+z)\) changes the displayed theorem. No such convention was identified in the inspected definitions. The source theorem and proof pages were visually inspected to rule out extraction loss of an added \(1\) or a variance upper bound.

This counterexample leaves the inspected Lemma 3.1 intact. It also does not refute the low-variance rates, the noiseless conclusions, the Matérn clauses, or the RKHS-norm results. A separate assessment would be needed for each.
## Supported repair scope

A universally valid elementary fallback is \[0\le R_T\le2BT,\] which follows from \(|f(x)|\le B\sqrt{k(x,x)}\le B\). It restores a valid upper bound in the problematic regime but does not preserve the disputed asymptotic rate.

Equation reference: eq:IGrepair. For a finite input set of size \(m\), the information-gain step itself admits the valid bound \[
 \gamma_T(\lambda^2I_T)
 \le\frac m2\log\!\left(1+\frac{T}{m\lambda^2}\right)
 =\frac m2\log\!\left(1+\frac{T^2}{mV_T}\right)
 \quad\text{when }\lambda^2=V_T/T.\] To verify it, the Gram matrix has rank at most \(m\) and trace at most \(T\). Concavity of \(\log(1+x)\) bounds the sum over its nonzero eigenvalues by the displayed expression; padding with zeros and using monotonicity in the rank gives the same bound if \(m>T\). This repair is global but introduces explicit dependence on \(m\) and must be carried through the rest of the proof with the startup term retained. It is not a certification of a complete replacement for Theorem 6.3. Restricting the theorem’s domain is another possible route, whose remaining constants and confidence factors still require checking.
## Impact

Theorem 6.3 is one of the principal nonstationary-variance results described as contribution 4 in the introduction and summarized in Table 6. The identified source step is part of its actual derivation, and its conclusion is false for an instance satisfying every listed assumption. This supports Major impact for the stated core guarantee under instruction 0.7.1. The affected regime is precisely bounded above; the report does not infer failure of the paper’s entire research program or of its low-noise results. No new experiment is needed to decide this mathematical counterexample.
# Remaining evidence and recorded states

Theorem 6.4 contains the same raw logarithmic information-gain substitution in (123)–(124). That dependence was identified, but the first-round cumulative-regret argument is not a proof about simple regret. This report therefore does not count the simple-regret conclusion as independently refuted. The validity of its stated domain remains a Needs Evidence item.

The finer asymptotic constants in Corollary 3.2 and all logarithmic factors in the RKHS-norm results were not exhaustively verified. External lower bounds were not independently retrieved. No empirical reproduction or static implementation audit was possible from the staged availability record. The coverage ledger distinguishes these limits from the claims actually checked.

Title: Technical Verification of PatchPilot
# Paper identity and scope

Hongwei Li, Yuheng Tang, Shiqi Wang and Wenbo Guo, PatchPilot: A Cost-Efficient Software Engineering Agent with Early Attempts on Formal Verification, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 35922–35941 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed published proceedings PDF has 20 pages. References below use 1-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed article numbers. The software snapshot is commit `84ec3d3fbc34269078f9f9b62b9d390947344944` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]; its equivalence to historical experimental code is unknown.

Inspection covered the five-component workflow, patch-success definition, cost and stability arithmetic, the formal-verification procedure, Appendix A’s ranking rule, implementation settings, case studies and prompts. The complete formal-verification source file was read statically; other components were not exhaustively audited. No author code, model API, container, dataset or trained model was executed.
# Necessary distinctions

Equation reference: eq:proof, eq:adequacy. Let \(P(x)\) specify admissible inputs, \(Q(x,f(x))\) a generated postcondition, and \(S(x,f(x))\) the behavior required by the issue. A correctness guarantee needs both \[\begin{aligned}
\text{verification evidence}&\Longrightarrow
 \forall x\,[P(x)\Rightarrow Q(x,f(x))],\\
P(x)\wedge Q(x,f(x))&\Longrightarrow S(x,f(x)).
\end{aligned}\] A proof of a weak contract does not establish the intended repair without the second implication and the appropriate domain. Section 3.1 additionally requires preservation of unaffected functionality. Section 5 (pp. 8–9) generates contracts, calls a contract set plausible when an original function produces an assertion counterexample, and calls a patched instance verified when no patched function produces a counterexample. Page 2 advertises a formal guarantee of patch correctness; p. 9 reports eleven formally verified patches.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The negative search result does not establish the formal guarantee).  The Section 5 rule fails to establish the two implications above. The supported assessment is Major for the advertised formal-guarantee component.
## Original claim and implementation

The paragraph headed Formal Verification, p. 9, was checked in the rendered PDF and extracted text. In , lines 193–196 recognize an assertion by the substring `AssertionError`. Lines 350–392 and 395–416 initialize an assertion flag to false and set it only for that substring. They run time-limited `crosshair check` without requesting explicit confirmation of all conditions. The default timeout is 20 seconds (line 814). The before/after flags enter the success-shaped condition at line 482. This is static source inspection, not author-code execution.

CrossHair’s maintainer and documentation distinguish exhaustive confirmation, unknown results and execution errors [Retained latex: \cite{chmaint,chdocs}]. A search can stop with unexamined paths and no counterexample. With a pre-patch assertion already established, either empty post-patch output or an import-error string yields a false assertion flag in the release. An unsuccessful import cannot establish a property of the unexecuted function. The independent diagnostic evaluates this Boolean truth table on explicitly constructed strings; these are not claimed to be actual CrossHair runs or outputs from the eleven published cases. The constructed-status calculation is preserved in .

Even if infrastructure errors were discarded manually, an unknown search result would not imply the universal statement in [eq:proof] (#eq:proof). The current documentation interprets the status semantics; the historical CrossHair version is not pinned by the paper and was not reconstructed.
## Complete contract-adequacy counterexample

The second gap remains even with a perfect verifier. Consider \[x\in\mathbb Z,\quad P(x)\equiv\mathrm{true},\quad
S(x,y)\equiv y=|x|.\] Let the buggy function be \(b(x)=x\), the generated postcondition be \(Q(x,y)\equiv y\geq0\), and the candidate patch be \(f(x)=0\). All functions are deterministic and total, all inputs and outputs have the declared integer type, and the precondition excludes nothing. No branch removal, approximation or external library is involved.

The plausibility gate succeeds because \(Q(-1,b(-1))\) is false. The patched contract holds universally because \(Q(x,0)\) is true for every integer. Yet at \(x=1\) the candidate returns \(0\) instead of \(1\), also damaging previously correct nonnegative-input behavior. Thus both semantic gates in the stated procedure can hold while the intended repair fails. A finite list of checked integers is supplied for reproducibility, but the universal identity \(0\geq0\) and the counterexample \(x=1\) provide the analytic argument. The finite diagnostic output is .

Nonnegativity is a necessary property of absolute value, not an unrelated assertion. The described plausibility test fails to establish its sufficiency. This example refutes an inference from that test; it does not claim that this contract or patch appeared in a published trial.
## Counterevidence, dependency and supported correction

The authors describe an early exploration, acknowledge verifier limitations, and also use empirical patch tests. These facts support a weaker contract-testing interpretation. They do not establish complete specifications or proofs for the eleven cases. The guarantee is a named contribution in the title and introduction, and its support depends directly on the invalid inference. The finding does not require failure of the rest of the patching system.

The release defaults to applying the benchmark’s golden patch when no external patch file is supplied (lines 687–690 and 729–732), and its default model is `o4-mini` (line 816); the paper’s formal experiment names o3. These observations raise provenance questions, not evidence that the authors actually evaluated golden patches. The actual command, patches, contracts and full condition statuses are needed.

A supported reporting repair separates refuted, unresolved/error and explicitly confirmed contracts; documents verifier assumptions; and validates specification adequacy separately. Unresolved cases must remain unresolved. Strengthening the illustrative postcondition to \(y=|x|\) restores adequacy for this example only. No general repaired pipeline or historical certification was verified here.

Problem 2 (The minimum-cost claim conflicts with Table 1).  Page 2 claims the lowest cost among leading compared methods, but Table 1 on p. 6 reports $0.99 for PatchPilot and $0.78 for OpenHands on Verified, both labeled Claude-3.5-Sonnet.

Consequently, \[0.99>0.78,\qquad (0.99-0.78)/0.78=0.269230769\ldots.\] PatchPilot is about 26.9% more expensive in that comparison. On Lite, $0.97 exceeds AutoCodeRover’s $0.65, although those models differ. The matched-model Verified comparison alone refutes the universal minimum claim. Arithmetic output: .

This is a supported Minor comparison defect: the table’s measurements, sub-dollar mean cost and useful accuracy–cost balance remain intact. No underlying API-accounting error is established. The narrower tradeoff claim is supported; actual cost reproduction would require historical usage records.
# Other checks and bounded impact

The PatchPilot fractions \(136/300=45.33\%\) and \(268/500=53.60\%\) are consistent. Sample standard deviations for \((30,32,35)\) and \((15,20,21)\) are \(2.5166\) and \(3.2146\), agreeing with Section 4.2. Appendix C.2’s intersection/union ratios are \(25/38=0.6579\) and \(12/25=0.48\). These descriptive checks concern the disclosed selected 45-instance subset, drawn from cases previously solved by both methods. They do not establish a general causal effect of planning style. These consistency calculations are recorded in .

Appendix A’s rank \(1_{\mathrm{PoC\ fails}}+n_{\mathrm{failed}}/n_{\mathrm{executed}}\) has the stated broad ordering for positive denominators. Its boundary tie between passing only PoC and passing only all benign tests is resolved by an LLM; strict universal PoC priority would therefore be too strong. No material effect was established, so this is retained as clarification.

The measured patching performance is not falsified by the formal-guarantee concern. The eleven verification cases require traceable records. No correction was identified in the inspected README; no exhaustive later-version/erratum search or discovery-priority claim was made.
