Title: Technical Verification of Dynamical Phases of Short-Term Memory
# Identity and scope

B. Kurtkaya, F. Dinc, M. Yuksekgonul, M. Blanco-Pozo, E. Cirakman, M. Schnitzer, Y. Yemez, H. Tanaka, P. Yuan and N. Miolane, Dynamical phases of short-term memory mechanisms in RNNs, PMLR 267 (2025), 32032–32062 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The staged proceedings PDF has 31 pages; page numbers below are 1-based PDF/internal article pages. The source snapshot is commit `3d5d7de50173c5885946dcc3e4030457fb63114b` [Retained latex: \cite{code}].

The native auxiliary inspected the main analysis, Methods and supplement, including low-rank projection, ghost/limit-cycle toy losses and local scaling arguments, training definitions, mechanism classification, and selected plotting/training source. The parent independently checked the decisive classification and loss definitions, source code, original p. 21 image, and finite Fourier calculation. Neither reviewer trained an RNN or executed author code.
# Claims and domains

Section 3.4 (p. 7), Section S3.4.1 (pp. 21–22), and Eq. (S38) use the low-frequency fraction of a correlation matrix’s spectral power, \[D=\mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{lf}}/\mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{total}},\] to distinguish successful networks into limit-cycle (\(D<0.5\)) and slow/ghost-point (\(D\geq0.5\)) categories. The classification also has learning-success gates involving reaction accuracy and reliability. Figure 4 and Figure S3 use these categories as empirical evidence for mechanism-specific behavior.

The relevant release file is . Lines 120–140 project a time-by-neuron trajectory to a time-by-two matrix and apply `torch.corrcoef` directly, then a two-dimensional FFT and centered radius-3 frequency mask. The following analysis concerns that stated implementation.
# Concerns requiring evidence

Problem 1 (PCA-sign dependence of the released discriminator).  The statistic is not an intrinsic property of the neural trajectory. The exact algebra is established; its effect on the paper’s successful networks and empirical conclusions is unresolved.
## Exact calculation

For rows \(z_t=(u_t,v_t)\) with \(u_t\ne v_t\), centering the two coordinates gives \[z_t-\overline z_t(1,1)
=\tfrac12(u_t-v_t)(1,-1).\] Thus the Pearson matrix is exactly \[C_{ts}=\operatorname{sgn}(u_t-v_t)
        \operatorname{sgn}(u_s-v_s).\] It has rank one and discards the magnitudes and most geometry of the scores. A permissible sign change of the second PCA eigenvector replaces this sign signal by \(\operatorname{sgn}(u_t+v_t)\). Distinct eigenvalues do not remove eigenvector-sign freedom.

For a reproducible finite example, let \(N=400\) and \[\theta_j=2\pi(j+0.123)/400,\quad
u_j=0.2625(\sin\theta_j+\sin8\theta_j),\quad
v_j=0.25(\sin\theta_j-\sin8\theta_j).\] Set the first three columns of a 100-column trajectory to \((u_j,v_j,0.1\cos\theta_j)\) and all others to zero. Its columns are centered and orthogonal; their sample variances are approximately \(0.06907895\), \(0.06265664\), and \(0.00501253\). The first two PCs therefore have distinct leading eigenvalues. All entries lie in \([-1,1]\); the largest absolute entry is \(0.519961\). The minimum absolute coordinate differences are nonzero under both signs, so no undefined Pearson entry is used.

The auxiliary’s direct two-dimensional FFT and the parent’s independent factorization of the Fourier transform of \(ss^\top\) agree: \[D(u,v)=8.8729396253\,10^{-7},\qquad
D(u,-v)=0.6570498839.\] The same data and principal subspace therefore receive opposite classes under the released threshold. Independent outputs are and .
## Assumption boundary and counterevidence

This is a valid counterexample to PCA-sign invariance of the statistic. It is not a verified counterexample satisfying every condition of the complete trained-RNN experiment: no weights realizing this trajectory under the paper’s tanh dynamics were constructed, and the reaction-accuracy/reliability gates were not demonstrated. The published claim describes reliable separation in sampled successful networks; it does not state a universal coordinate-invariance theorem.

Consequently, a Major finding against the phase diagram is not established by this construction. A deterministic sign convention could make one implementation reproducible, and the actual sampled trajectories could be insensitive to signs. Representative dynamical examples and the toy-model theory provide evidence independent of the bulk classifier. Conversely, reproducible signs alone would not establish that the resulting classification tracks the intended dynamics.

The supported outcome is Needs Evidence for empirical classification reliability. Resolving it requires the historical trajectory/provenance records and a sign-sensitivity assessment against a dynamical reference classification. A sign-invariant Gram/distance statistic is a possible alternative, not a verified correction offered by this review.

Problem 2 (Delay-dependent normalization complicates the theory-to-training comparison).  The toy loss and an inspected released training loss differ by a delay-dependent factor. The algebra is exact; its contribution to reported empirical exponents remains unresolved.

Equations (S7) and (S17) add separately normalized delay- and response-window mean losses. In , lines 144–148 assign response weight \(1-M/N\) and other-time weight \(M/N\), with \(M=10\) response samples and \(N\) total samples. Line 65 averages the weighted loss over the whole sequence.

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be the respective mean squared errors outside and inside the response window, using the same batch/output averaging. The release computes \[L_{\mathrm{release}}
=\frac{1}{N}\left[(N-M)\frac{M}{N}A
+M\left(1-\frac{M}{N}\right)B\right]
=\frac{M(N-M)}{N^2}(A+B).\] For \(N=20,40,80\), the factors are \(0.25,0.1875,0.109375\). Rebalancing the windows thus does not keep the overall loss scale fixed as delay varies. Under otherwise identical gradient dynamics, a nominal learning rate \(\eta\) corresponds to balanced-loss rate \(\eta M(N-M)/N^2\). The finite scale values are recorded in .

This is a comparison requiring explanation, not proof that the empirical exponent is wrong: cue windows, momentum and different toy/full-RNN dynamics remain, and the historical execution-to-commit correspondence is unverified. Dividing by the displayed factor removes this algebraic scale difference only; it is not a validated full training repair.
# Other checks and overall interpretation

The auxiliary found no substantive defect in the inspected exact low-rank projection or the stated-domain ghost and limit-cycle toy-loss calculations, including their local kink scales. That scoped result does not certify the complete theory. The supplement distinguishes a local escape scale from a global impossibility region; that distinction was retained.

An apparent missing absolute value in extracted Eq. (S36) was rejected: parent visual inspection of p. 21 confirms the bars in the original PDF. It is not a paper defect. No historical numerical regression, trained-model classification, or raw experimental output was reproduced. The two concerns above should remain separate from the existence of the illustrated dynamical mechanisms.
# Conclusion and state
Dimension | State
Assessment | Needs Evidence for empirical classification and scaling reconciliation.
Established checks | PCA-sign dependence; exact loss scale factor.
Not established | Failure of actual trained networks or falsity of phase fractions/exponents.
Repair | No replacement classifier or revised training pipeline validated.
Adjudication/adoption | Pending; no human review; adoption unknown.
Remaining work | Historical trajectories and provenance.

problems.title: The reported step-count breakdown violates the weighted-mean identity
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (The step-count breakdown does not satisfy the partition identity).
claim: Section 5.1, p.7, defines binary complete-task success; Appendix A.14, Figure 4, p.43, reports number of tasks, average steps over all tasks, over successful tasks and over failures, plus success rate, for a common task breakdown. Overall: N=165, all=11.12, successful=7.52, failed=13.43, success rate=53.9%.
analysis: Complete check: Let successful count be S and failed count F=N-S. Summing the step counts by this partition gives N*m_all=S*m_success+F*m_fail identically, without probabilistic assumptions. The table implies (89*7.52+76*13.43)/165=10.242181818..., whereas it prints 11.12. Each rounded mean can differ from its underlying mean by at most 0.005; the weighted prediction can differ by at most 0.005 and the printed all-mean by at most 0.005, so the discrepancy 0.877818... cannot be rounding. The six per-website rows also all fail this identity, as independently computed in independent_checks.json. Weighting the six displayed all-means by their task counts gives 11.17684848..., which is also inconsistent with overall 11.12 beyond the 0.01 combined rounding tolerance.

Counterevidence: Rendered and visually inspected the exact original PDF p.43; table numerals are genuine and not a text-extraction error. Separately averaging conditional means across runs with unequal success counts, using different populations, or an undisclosed step-count convention could explain different numbers, but none is stated for this table. Such a reading would itself require relabeling the reported common breakdown and supplying denominators. Success counts themselves are mutually consistent (16,16,17,25,12,3 sum to 89); therefore this does not show the 53.94% main success rate is wrong.

Correction: Do not choose one column to overwrite based solely on this identity. Recompute all three means and denominators from the same per-task trace records, or explicitly describe distinct weighting/populations if intentional. The displayed other columns imply an overall all-mean of approximately 10.24 only conditionally; this is an arithmetic implication, not a verified replacement for the empirical table.
result: Impact: The supplemental step-count/trajectory-length evidence is not reconstructible from the printed summaries. This is a supported local quantitative inconsistency. No demonstrated dependency makes the central comparative success-rate result false; classify Minor. The fact it is in the appendix is not the reason for the classification; the absence of demonstrated damage to the central success-rate claim is.
assumptions: All/Success/Fail columns summarize the same finite trial population, with success and failure exhaustive and disjoint, as their labels and the binary success definition indicate.
Means are ordinary task means and displayed decimal means round to 0.01; displayed success percentages round to 0.1 percentage point.
The 165 overall tasks are the sum of the six website rows; 53.9% is compatible with exactly 89 successful tasks at that denominator.

problems.title: Released exact matching loses the association between keys and numeric values
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Released matching erases key–value associations).
claim: Section 5.1, p.7, evaluates complete task success with binary success/failure. The pinned repository exposes an exact_match utility whose implementation returns equality of alphanumeric token Counters after simple normalized-string variants fail (utils.py lines 1037-1051). The string evaluator calls this utility (previous_rounds_evaluators.py lines 136-137,174-175); its must_include rule calls a token-set-subset utility (utils.py lines 1011-1025; evaluator lines 195-201).
analysis: Complete check: Set reference r='01:11, 02:16' and prediction p='01:16, 02:11'. The reference mapping is {01:11,02:16}; the predicted mapping has both values assigned to the wrong month. String equality and all separator variants fail, since no considered separator changes the strings. Tokenization returns respectively [01,11,02,16] and [01,16,02,11], whose Counters are equal; utils.py therefore returns 1.0. Under the required task semantics the prediction is wrong. Moreover, when each required pair is checked through must_include, both token sets {01,11} and {02,16} are subsets of the wrong answer's token set, so the set fallback also passes both. The independent Python check records these exact token lists and outcomes, without importing the author implementation.

Counterevidence: Order-insensitive matching can be correct for an unordered collection, but here the order establishes which month has which count; sorting the complete key-value pairs is different from erasing their internal bindings. Unicode or punctuation normalization cannot justify swapping values. Released run scripts call a previous_rounds evaluator, but import it from evaluation_harness; the inspected repository file is delivered under plan_and_act. This path mapping and the actual historical runtime are not established. The commit was observed in 2026 and no statement equates it to the publication-time revision. Therefore no number of false positives in published experiments, and no lowered benchmark score, has been established.

Correction: For a fixed month:count output schema, parse into a mapping and compare the full key-value relation (after allowed canonicalization). This restores the exhibited pairing requirement. It is not a universal replacement for all benchmark string or fuzzy matching, and no revised benchmark implementation is certified.
result: Impact: The released matching routine has a definite semantic false-positive case on the paper's illustrated output class. Treat this as a supported release-level Minor finding while leaving the effect on Tables 1-4 and the SOTA claim Needs Evidence. Establishing historical usage and scoring the original logs would be necessary to elevate the paper-level impact; the current evidence does not support that elevation.
assumptions: Both reference and proposed answer are ordinary ASCII strings, with no diacritics, unusual spaces, dash/slash/dot separators or control characters, so canonicalize leaves them unchanged.
Choose a task asking for a mapping from month IDs to counts; the paper itself illustrates this output form in Appendix A.5.2, pp.19-21.
For the finite counterexample, evaluate the exact_match branch on a reference and proposed answer, without claiming the actual benchmark uses this specific configuration or recorded erroneous answer.

Title: Technical Verification of Plan-and-Act
# Identity, version and scope

Lutfi Eren Erdogan, Nicholas Lee, Sehoon Kim, Suhong Moon, Hiroki Furuta, Gopala Anumanchipalli, Kurt Keutzer and Amir Gholami, Plan-and-Act: Improving Planning of Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The 44-page published proceedings PDF is reviewed; references use 1-based PDF pages, matching printed page numbers. Actual author names follow the PDF rather than transcription errors in the input worksheet. The pinned source is commit `534ed56f0d75e3059e54907859b89c901094f293` [Retained latex: \cite{code}].

The native auxiliary inspected the planner/executor architecture, synthetic and targeted data generation, evaluation design, main comparisons, appendix results/settings and selected evaluator code. Prompt examples were sampled rather than audited line by line. The parent independently checked the two decisive arguments, code branches, p. 7 evaluation definition and rendered p. 43. No browser task, LLM, dataset or author module was executed.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The step-count breakdown does not satisfy the partition identity).  Appendix A.14, Figure 4 (p. 43), reports mutually inconsistent all-task, successful-task and failed-task mean step counts under the table’s stated common-population interpretation.
## Claim, assumptions and calculation

Section 5.1 (p. 7) specifies binary complete-task success on 165 WebArena-Lite test cases. Figure 4 reports \(N=165\), success rate \(53.9\%\), all-task mean \(11.12\), success mean \(7.52\), and failure mean \(13.43\). Its original rendered page confirms these values.
## Counterevidence, impact and correction

Conditional means averaged separately across multiple runs, different denominators, or different step conventions could yield different aggregates. Such conventions are not stated for this table and would require revised labels and denominators. The website success counts themselves are consistent: \((16,16,17,25,12,3)\) sum to \(89\). Therefore the check does not contradict the principal \(53.94\%\) success rate.

The supported assessment is Minor because the established error concerns the step-length summary, with no demonstrated dependency invalidating the central task-success comparison. Appendix location is not the basis for this grading. Do not overwrite one column merely to satisfy the identity: the raw traces must establish which quantity or population was intended. The number \(10.24\) is a conditional arithmetic implication, not a verified replacement measurement.

Problem 2 (Released matching erases key–value associations).  The pinned exact-match utility has a definite semantic false positive for the monthly-count output form illustrated on pp. 19–21. Historical benchmark impact remains unresolved.
## Source and complete finite check

In , lines 1037–1051, failed normalized-string comparisons fall back to equality of alphanumeric token multisets. Lines 1011–1025 similarly use token-set inclusion for `must_include`. The consuming , lines 136–141 and 174–201, routes exact and inclusion evaluations through these helpers.

Take the ordinary ASCII reference and prediction \[r=\texttt{01:11, 02:16},\qquad
p=\texttt{01:16, 02:11}.\] The task requests month-to-count associations. The independent mapping/token diagnostic is . The prediction assigns both counts to the wrong month. Both strings are unaffected by case, Unicode or separator normalization relevant here; string equality fails. Their token sequences are respectively \[(01,11,02,16),\qquad(01,16,02,11),\] which have identical multisets. The release therefore returns \(1.0\) through the fallback, although the mappings differ. For the inclusion branch, both required token sets \(\{01,11\}\) and \(\{02,16\}\) are subsets of the wrong prediction’s token set, so that fallback also accepts. The independent scripts enumerate these strings and mappings without importing or calling author code.
## Alternatives and bounded consequence

Order-insensitive matching is valid for an unordered set of independent answers. A month-to-count mapping requires preserving each internal association; sorting complete pairs would preserve this information, whereas sorting all tokens does not. Punctuation normalization cannot justify swapping values.

This is a supported Minor defect in the release. The run script imports an evaluator under , while the inspected file is delivered under ; runtime path mapping and publication-time commit correspondence are not established. The existence of the helper is therefore not proof that it scored the historical runs, nor that any particular published answer exploited it. No false-positive count or adjusted benchmark rate was measured.

For a fixed month:count schema, comparing parsed mappings restores the illustrated semantic requirement. This is an example-specific correction, not a universal replacement or a validated rerun of the benchmark evaluator.
# Other checks and overall impact

The architecture, synthetic data strategy and main result tables were read without establishing a further core invalidity. The paper explicitly describes a held-out validation set for targeted augmentation (Section 4.3); a generic source variable named `test_set_path` does not establish test leakage. No leakage finding is made without split identities and traceable overlap evidence.

The first finding affects the supplemental trajectory-length evidence. The second affects a released matching procedure; any impact on the central comparative success rate remains Needs Evidence. Raw step traces and historical evaluator/configuration provenance are the decisive missing evidence. Later errata were not exhaustively searched, and no first-discovery claim is made.

Unresolved impact | Effect of released matcher on published benchmark scores.
Repair verification | Mapping example checked analytically; no corrected table or benchmark rerun.
Adjudication | Pending; no human reviews.

Title: Technical Verification of EEG–Language Pretraining
# Identity and inspected material

Sam Gijsen and Kerstin Ritter, EEG-Language Pretraining for Highly Label-Efficient Clinical Phenotyping, PMLR 267 (2025), 19480–19504 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed proceedings PDF has 25 pages; page references use 1-based PDF/internal article numbering. The source snapshot is `fcd929a57ce3dc9a409be37a71f4ee80ee59979d` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its historical experiment correspondence is not established.

The auxiliary inspected the main model definitions, losses (1)–(13), data splits, pretraining/downstream evaluation and appendix details, plus the loss/configuration/trainer call chain. The parent checked the original p. 4 rendering, preceding definitions, complete loss source, and independent analytic/numerical examples. The review does not reproduce clinical metrics, inspect private patient data or execute author code.
# Definitions and assumptions
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The published contrastive objective discards pair identity).  Equation (9), p. 4, does not implement the paired alignment described in Section 2.1.1. The supported assessment is Major for this central mathematical definition.
## Complete analytic check

For any strictly positive probability vector \((p_1,\ldots,p_B)\) summing to one, concavity of the logarithm gives \[-\sum_{k=1}^B\log p_k\geq B\log B,\] with equality exactly at \(p_k=1/B\). Applying this to every row in both directions yields \[L_{\mathrm{align}}\geq B\log B.\] Equal cross-modal similarities attain the bound. In particular, setting all normalized embeddings equal is allowed and is a global minimizer. Independently permuting text examples only permutes entries/rows in the full sums, leaving the objective unchanged. It therefore contains no information about which EEG belongs to which text.

A complete admissible finite example has \(B=2\), \(d=256\), \(\tau=0.3\) and \[\hat e_1=\hat l_1=(1,0,\ldots,0),\qquad
\hat e_2=\hat l_2=(-1,0,\ldots,0).\] All norms are one, all cosine similarities lie in \([-1,1]\), and the correct-pair probability is \(q=(1+\exp(-2/\tau))^{-1}\). Equation [eq:literal] (#eq:literal) gives \[-\log q-\log(1-q)=6.6692103160.\] Setting all four unit vectors equal gives \(2\log2=1.3862943611\), strictly lower. Minimizing the stated objective thus favors losing discrimination rather than retaining the strongly correct pairings in this legal example. Parent calculation output: .
## Alternative reading, dependency and correction

The prose makes the intended positive-pair interpretation plausible. Replacing the double sum by the diagonal sum \[L_{\mathrm{paired}}=
\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{j=1}^B
[-\log p_{jj}-\log\widetilde p_{jj}]\] gives \(0.0012718247\) for the aligned example and \(\log2=0.6931471806\) for collapse, restoring the intended distinction in this check. This is a precise algebraic repair of the stated paired objective, not proof that optimization reproduces reported clinical results.

The release’s , lines 59–65, instead constructs similarity-derived soft targets for ELM\(_{e,l}\). That is evidence against assuming literal Eq. (9) generated the historical results, and it prevents claiming the diagonal replacement reconstructs the actual algorithm. An intended soft-target variant must be stated and reconciled separately.

The defect is not merely an inconsequential symbol: it changes the optimum and removes pair information from a central representation-learning strategy. The MIL extension and other empirical observations may survive independently; no whole-paper failure or empirical score decrease is asserted.
Problem 2 (Released MIL aggregation differs from the published loss).  Equations (10)–(11), p. 4, and the pinned loss implementation apply different objectives to multiple positives.
## Source, domain and calculation

For an anchor with \(m\geq1\) positive samples \(\mathcal P\) and softmax probabilities \(p_j\), the paper uses \[L_{\mathrm{paper}}
=-\log\left(\frac1m\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}p_j\right).\] In , lines 90–100, masked `log_softmax` values are averaged, giving \[L_{\mathrm{release}}=-\frac1m\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}\log p_j.\] The configured MIL training route calls this class (trainer/configuration evidence is bound in verification). Jensen’s inequality gives \(L_{\mathrm{release}}\geq L_{\mathrm{paper}}\), with equality for equal positive probabilities, including \(m=1\).
## Impact and alternatives

The paper motivates MIL as relaxing alignment of every individual positive pair. The release uses an all-positive log loss with a different weighting preference. This is a supported Minor release-to-method discrepancy; the effect on the published metrics and positive-aggregation ablation remains Needs Evidence. A later source change or a miswritten publication formula could explain the mismatch. No historical run was reconstructed.

The exact expression \[\log\sum_j e^{z_j}-\log\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}e^{z_j}+\log m\] implements the paper’s per-anchor loss. Its algebra is verified here; changing the historical algorithm or claiming restored benchmark performance is not.
# Other checked interpretations and overall impact

The disclosed TUAB/pretraining overlap and post-hoc subject-split analysis were read; no additional test-leakage claim was established. External NMT evaluation involves a downstream linear probe and should not be misread as zero-shot deployment without target labels. The review did not turn disclosed crop/model differences into demonstrated mathematical failures.

Problem 1 invalidates the published mathematical specification of one principal alignment strategy. Problem 2 records a separate implementation discrepancy. Neither determines which objective generated the reported scores. The decisive next evidence is a version-bound training configuration/code record, followed by any experiments needed to distinguish the alternatives. No external erratum search or discovery-priority claim is made.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
NEAR: Neural Electromagnetic Array Response
# Paper identity and reviewed version

Yinyan Bu, Jiajie Yu, Kai Zheng, Xinyu Zhang, and Piya Pal, NEAR: Neural Electromagnetic Array Response, ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, pp. 5749–5774 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment: 0155 / I25-43524. The frozen published PDF has 26 pages, including appendices. Page references below use the one-based PDF page number, equal to its internal printed number. The manifest records the publisher date as 6 October 2025 and retrieval on 24 October 2026. The release [Retained latex: \cite{release}] is pinned separately; its conference-time equivalence is unknown.
# Summary, scope, and necessary background

NEAR represents a radar array response with an implicit neural representation and a learned recurrence regularizer. The reviewed material includes the signal model, principal representation and recurrence claims, their appendices, experimental descriptions and tables, and substantive released source. Coverage is itemized in the accompanying ledger. This is not exhaustive verification of every cited work, image, implementation path, or historical experiment.

Equation reference: eq:response. The relevant noiseless response in Eq. (8), p. 6, is \[
Y_{m,n}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}x_k
 \exp\!\left\{\frac{2\pi i}{\lambda}
 [(m-1)d_1\sin\phi_k\cos\theta_k+
  (n-1)d_2\sin\phi_k\sin\theta_k]\right\}.\] The targets are in the far field and the spacings obey \(d_1,d_2\leq\lambda/2\). For a row \(y_m\), \(H_{N_2}(y_m)\) is the \(N_2\)-by-\((M_2-N_2+1)\) sliding Hankel matrix. Definition 4.3 stacks these blocks into \(\mathcal H_{N_1,N_2}(Y)\). In particular, \(\mathcal H_{M_1,M_2-K}(Y)\) vertically stacks the row Hankel blocks and has \(K+1\) columns. Let \(S=[I_K\;0]^\top\) select its first \(K\) columns and let \(b\) select its last column.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Theorem 4.5 does not ensure unique recurrence coefficients).  Assessment: Major. Theorem 4.5, p. 6, asserts that for the response in Eq. (8), if \(K\leq\min\{\lceil M_1/2\rceil,\lceil M_2/2\rceil\}\), the last column of \(\mathcal H_{M_1,M_2-K}(Y)\) is uniquely representable by its first \(K\) columns. The analogous assertion is made for the other axis. This is a paraphrase of the printed claim, visually verified in the original PDF.
## An admissible counterexample

Equation reference: eq:parameters. Take \[
\begin{aligned}
&K=2,\quad M_1=M_2=4,\quad \lambda=1,\quad d_1=d_2=\tfrac12,\\
&x_1=x_2=1,\quad \theta_1=\theta_2=0,\quad
\phi_1=\tfrac{\pi}{6},\quad \phi_2=\tfrac{\pi}{4}.
\end{aligned}\] The size bound holds with equality. Both amplitudes are nonzero, the physical directions are different, and the spacings meet the stated half-wavelength requirement. The target ranges can be chosen arbitrarily large compared with the finite aperture, satisfying the far-field assumption. Neither the setup nor Theorem 4.5 requires distinct projected frequencies on each axis.

Substitution into [eq:response] (#eq:response) gives \[Y_{m,n}=c_m
 =e^{i\pi(m-1)/2}+e^{i\pi(m-1)/\sqrt2},
\qquad 1\leq m,n\leq4.\] The response is independent of \(n\), and \(c_1=2\). Therefore \[H_2(y_m)=
\begin{pmatrix}c_m&c_m&c_m\\c_m&c_m&c_m\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathcal H_{4,2}(Y)=[\,h\ h\ h\,],
\quad h=(c_1,c_1,c_2,c_2,c_3,c_3,c_4,c_4)^\top\ne0.\] Consequently both \(m_1=(1,0)^\top\) and \(m_1=(0,1)^\top\) satisfy \(\mathcal H_{4,2}(Y)Sm_1=\mathcal H_{4,2}(Y)b\). Every vector \((a,1-a)^\top\), \(a\in\mathbb C\), does so. This is an exact failure of uniqueness, independent of numerical tolerances.

The reviewer-written parent calculation constructs Eq. (8) and Definition 4.3 directly. It obtains an \(8\times3\) matrix of rank one, first-two-column rank one, and residual norm zero for both displayed coefficient vectors. An independently written auxiliary check gives the same result. These computations corroborate, rather than replace, the algebraic argument. The independent outputs are and .
## Where the proof fails and why the dependency matters

Appendix B, pp. 20–22, establishes Lemmas B.1–B.3 and then invokes them to prove Theorem 4.5. Lemma B.2 treats a Vandermonde factorization as sufficient for rank \(K\) and first-\(K\)-column independence. Lemma B.3 then inverts the transpose of the \(K\)-row Vandermonde matrix. However, the sampled nodes \[z_{2k}=\exp(2\pi i d_2\sin\phi_k\sin\theta_k/\lambda)\] all equal one in [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters). The required inverse does not exist.

This is not solely a consequence of the whole block Hankel matrix losing rank. With the same response and \(N_1=N_2=2\), all size conditions of Lemma B.1 hold: \(K=2\leq N_i=2\leq M_i-K+1=3\). The \(4\times9\) matrix \(\mathcal H_{2,2}(Y)\) has rank two but its first two columns coincide and have rank one. Thus the claimed basis property fails even while the claimed total rank is retained.

Theorem 4.5 explicitly motivates the learned coefficients and least-squares regularization in §4.4, Eqs. (9)–(11). It is a central theoretical guarantee, not an unrelated appendix observation. A demonstrated false guarantee with this dependency supports Major under the stipulated calibration.
## Counterevidence and bounded impact

The exact recurrence still exists in this example: its coefficient set is nonempty and nonunique. Generic random directions can avoid repeated projected nodes. Noise can perturb numerical ranks. None of these facts proves the deterministic uniqueness statement as written, which contains no almost-sure qualifier or coordinatewise distinctness premise.

The example does not establish failure of the trained response predictor, loss of a reported benchmark gain, or failure of every regularizer optimum. In particular, an optimization penalty can be useful without a uniquely identifiable auxiliary coefficient vector. These surviving possibilities are distinct from the false theorem.

The proof also uses \(N_2=M_2-K\) in a lemma requiring \(N_2\geq K\), whereas the published ceiling bound allows \(M_2=2K-1\). This is an additional boundary in the proof’s applicability; no second Major claim is needed for it.
## A sufficient restricted repair

One sufficient revised statement adds all of the following assumptions: \(M_1,M_2\geq2K\), every \(x_k\ne0\), and the sampled nodes \[z_{1k}=e^{2\pi i d_1\sin\phi_k\cos\theta_k/\lambda},
\qquad
z_{2k}=e^{2\pi i d_2\sin\phi_k\sin\theta_k/\lambda}\] are pairwise distinct on each respective axis. Under these strengthened conditions, the two recurrence coefficient vectors are unique.

Indeed, write \(A_q(z)_{jk}=z_k^{j-1}\). The first \(K\) columns of each row Hankel block factor as \[A_{M_2-K}(z_2)
\operatorname{diag}(x_k z_{1k}^{m-1}) A_K(z_2)^\top.\] The first factor has full column rank and the remaining two factors are invertible. The coefficient \[m_1=(A_K(z_2)^\top)^{-1}(z_{21}^{K},\ldots,z_{2K}^{K})^\top\] is unique and independent of \(m\). Stacking the blocks preserves this conclusion. Swapping axes proves the other direction. This verifies only the stated restricted algebraic repair; it certifies neither training convergence nor experimental performance. No author adoption is known.

Problem 2 (The inspected release changes the residual norm).  Assessment: Minor. Eq. (10), p. 7, defines the regularizer as the sum of two Euclidean norms of stacked recurrence residuals. The original \(2\) subscripts were visually confirmed. In the pinned release, , lines 88–99, the row and column loops instead accumulate `torch.abs(pred - H @ coeff).sum()`; the loss is called in the training loop near line 203 [Retained latex: \cite{release}].

For nonzero residuals these are different objectives. The real residual vectors \(a=(3,0)\) and \(b=(2,2)\) satisfy \[\|a\|_2=3>\sqrt8=\|b\|_2,
\qquad
\|a\|_1=3<4=\|b\|_1.\] Thus even candidate preference can reverse. The exact-zero sets agree, so this discrepancy does not refute recurrence feasibility. The inspected release is not proven to be the exact code used for the historical tables. Its quantitative experimental effect remains Needs Evidence. A documented choice of norm and an aligned equation or implementation would resolve the specification discrepancy; a replacement training outcome has not been verified.
# Additional inspected claims and limitations

Theorem 4.1 and Appendix A were examined for the harmonic-support induction. Multiplying trigonometric polynomials gives the stated type of upper support bound. This one-way support result should not automatically be read as arbitrary coefficient and phase attainability for a fixed input mapping. For example, a mapping consisting only of \(\sin(\pi r)\) identifies \(r=1/6\) and \(r=5/6\), whereas \(\cos(\pi r)\) distinguishes them. The implementation includes sine and cosine features, and the proof also uses a one-way representability formulation. This observation is retained as a scope clarification, not a further false-theorem verdict.

Main experimental descriptions, Tables 1–6, figure captions, and Appendix C were read for consistency and for the scope of the claimed response-recovery, resolution, and denoising benefits. No independent radar measurements, raw-data audit, training run, confidence-interval reconstruction, or benchmark reproduction was performed. The evidence here does not refute those numerical results. External cited theorems and later errata were not comprehensively audited.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The highest supported impact is Major, because the stated uniqueness guarantee underpinning the central recurrence regularizer is false under the published assumptions. Recurrence existence and empirical utility may survive. The \(L_1/L_2\) discrepancy is a separate Minor release issue whose historical effect is unresolved.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
P(all-atom) Is Unlocking New Path For Protein Design
# Paper identity and reviewed version

Wei Qu, Jiawei Guan, Rui Ma, Ke Zhai, Weikun Wu, and Haobo Wang, P(all-atom) Is Unlocking New Path For Protein Design, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 50786–50816 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment 0156 / I25-43525 concerns the frozen 31-page proceedings PDF, including appendices. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, coincident with internal printed numbers. The publisher landing page is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/qu25c.html; source retrieval and version details are preserved in the manifest. The public Pallatom release is independently pinned to commit [Retained latex: \cite{release}], without a claim that it generated the historical tables.
# Scope and necessary background

Pallatom models protein coordinates using an atom14 representation, a diffusion denoiser and a sequence decoder. The main scientific text, key metric definitions and tables, sampling and representation appendices, and the source paths needed to trace noise conditioning were inspected. Coverage of dense graphical panels is limited to their descriptions and reported comparisons; there was no new quantitative image analysis or protein generation.

Equation reference: eq:inflate. Write \(\sigma\) for the current coordinate noise level and \(\gamma\) for churn. In Algorithm 1, p. 5, the noisy coordinates are perturbed at the inflated level \[
\widehat{\sigma}=\sigma(1+\gamma).\] Both MainTrunk calls receive this inflated level. The reverse direction also divides by \(\widehat{\sigma}\). Eq. (5) and Appendix Algorithm 2 use the denoiser noise argument in its input, skip and output preconditioning. Thus it is an operative numerical input.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The released sampler does not propagate churn inflation to the denoiser).  Assessment: Minor. Algorithm 1, lines 12–24, p. 5, specifies that the denoiser receives the same inflated level used to form its noisy input and reverse update. In the pinned source, the model receives the uninflated level. This is a static specification-to-release discrepancy, with unresolved impact on the historical experiments.
## Exact source correspondence
The relevant chain in [Retained latex: \cite{release}] is:
1. , lines 155–162, computes the normalized perturbed time and stores the original noise in both `batch[’t_hat’]` and the derived time feature.

2. Lines 170–174 call `add_additional_noise`, which returns noisy coordinates and the inflated `r3_t_hat`. Lines 176–179 replace the coordinates and call the model, without replacing its stored noise condition.
3. Lines 185–187 pass the inflated level to the reverse update.
4. , lines 53–60, gives \(\widehat{\sigma}_{\rm release}=\sigma(1+\gamma+10^{-6})\). Lines 72–73 use this inflated denominator in the reverse step.
5. The model actually consumes the unchanged condition: , line 1318, scales coordinates with it; lines 1507–1508 compute skip/output factors with it; line 1609 transfers it into the trunk.

The parent read these code regions and the complete diffusion module. The full sampler and driver were independently read by the auxiliary reviewer. The discrepancy is therefore not based solely on a suggestive variable name.
## A legal default-parameter calculation

The documented defaults are \(T=200\), \(\gamma=0.2\), churn window \([0.01,1]\), and \(\sigma_{\rm data}=16\). The release uses \[t=\frac{j}{T-1}-\frac{U}{T},
\qquad
\sigma(t)=16\exp\{-1.2+1.5\Phi^{-1}(t)\},
\quad U\in[0,1),\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution. Set \(j=157\) and choose \[U=200\left(\frac{157}{199}-\Phi(0.8)\right)
  \simeq0.1600244402974349.\] This is a valid uniform variate. It gives \(t=\Phi(0.8)\simeq0.7881446014166033\), inside the churn window, and hence \(\sigma(t)=16\). At that step the arguments are \[\begin{array}{ll}
\text{condition actually sent to the model:}&16,\\
\text{condition specified by Algorithm 1:}&19.2,\\
\text{condition used in the released reverse update:}&19.200016.
\end{array}\] All masks may select a real atom, and no special sequence length is needed. The \(10^{-6}\) epsilon does not explain the 20% inflation omitted from the model argument.

Separate parent and auxiliary reviewer-owned calculations reproduce these values. Their outputs are and . They do not import or execute the author repository. The argument mismatch itself follows directly from the code path.
## Why the argument can matter

The preconditioning formulas already show that replacing 16 by 19.2 changes the denoiser computation. An elementary illustration makes the distinction explicit. If a scalar clean coordinate has prior variance \(v=256\) and is corrupted with independent Gaussian noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), its posterior-mean denoiser is \[D(x;\sigma)=\frac{v}{v+\sigma^2}x.\] At \(x=1\), the two arguments yield \[D(1;16)=0.5,\qquad
D(1;19.2)=0.4098360655737705.\] This analytic example proves that the arguments are not interchangeable in general. It is not a measured error of Pallatom, a model of its exact training distribution, or an estimate of a protein-design score change.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

When \(\gamma=0\), the discrepancy reduces to the release’s small epsilon. Outside the churn window there is no substantial inflation. The documented defaults activate the discrepancy for the legal example above.

A deliberately different sampler heuristic could be valid or useful. However, the paper’s Algorithm 1 passes the inflated level, and the release does not document this particular departure. Weights and historical run logs were not inspected. Consequently the result supports a current-release reproducibility concern; it does not establish that Tables 1–16 used this implementation or that the published metrics are wrong.

There are further correspondence questions: the printed algorithm uses two within-step trunk calls with updated self-conditioning, whereas the inspected source uses one and updates the template for the next step. Its Fourier time embedding also overwrites an initially logarithmic quantity with a raw-noise expression. These are retained as historical provenance limitations, not additional unbounded experimental allegations.
## Correction and what it would establish

For correspondence with the published noise argument, update the denoiser’s noise-level field and its derived features from \(\widehat{\sigma}\), preserving masks, shapes and numerical types. This restores that one argument relationship algebraically. It does not validate a complete repaired sampler or guarantee better samples. A full reconciliation must also address the self-conditioning and time-embedding differences, followed by evaluation with the actual trained weights. No code modification, model rerun or author adoption was performed.
# Checked counterevidence and surviving conclusions

Appendix C.1, p. 13, explicitly acknowledges that the atom14 geometry can be ambiguous among chemically different residues. Main §3.3 and its SeqHead address sequence decoding. This review therefore does not allege an undisclosed one-to-one geometry-to-sequence theorem.

claim: Section 3.4, PDF p.6, defines cos(z_output,y^k) as ordinary cosine similarity. Eq.(8) has the conventional NEGATIVE prefactor -1/|K_gt union K_n|. It omits a sigmoid, another probability conversion, a positivity restriction and positive-class reweighting, and is stated to drive training. The minus is visible in the reliable PyMuPDF recovery rendering of the same original page.
analysis: Complete check: For unit vectors z=(1,0), y_positive=(-1/2,sqrt(3)/2), and y_negative=(1/2,sqrt(3)/2), the cosine scores are -1/2 and +1/2. All vectors are nonzero and normalized and can be embedded in any larger feature space; no original domain condition is violated. Eq.(8) then includes log(-1/2), which is undefined as a real training loss. After retaining the printed negative sign and inserting sigmoid scores, the repaired unweighted BCE has the finite value log(1+exp(1/2))=0.974076984... for this one-positive/one-negative illustration. Static trainer.py lines213-232 shows sigmoid(cos) and an additional factor N/P multiplying the summed positive log terms. The source implements L_src= -[(N/P)sum_pos log sigma(c_k)+sum_neg log(1-sigma(c_k))]/(P+N). Retaining the printed negative sign and inserting sigma in Eq.(8) gives the charitable repaired comparator L_unw= -[sum_pos log sigma(c_k)+sum_neg log(1-sigma(c_k))]/(P+N), a different objective. To prove non-equivalence, choose P=2, N=100, all item embeddings equal a unit vector y, and output z(c) a unit vector with dot product c in [-1,1]; this is allowed because no distinctness restriction is placed on embeddings. Then dL_unw/dc=sigma(c)-2/102>0 throughout [-1,1] (sigma(-1)>2/102), so its unique constrained minimum is c=-1. In contrast dL_src/dc=(100/102)(2sigma(c)-1), giving a unique minimum c=0. Thus even the favorable sigmoid-link repair does not describe the released optimization problem. The comparison uses the actual printed negative sign; the original raw-cosine domain defect and the additional released reweighting are separate.

Counterevidence: The published equation already has a conventional negative sign; the previous contrary reading was caused by a missing glyph in the initial raster and is withdrawn. An implicit sigmoid interpretation would repair the domain but conflicts with the explicit ordinary-cosine definition and still omits positive reweighting. If P=N, the weight is one; the multi-answer task with N=100 does not require P=N. The complete embedding-to-loss path uses LayerNorm followed by unconstrained affine representation layers (model.py64,75,86,102,111; applied255-265 before concatenation267), with the same affine maps for item embeddings at trainer.py183-194. No final positivity constraint precedes CosineSimilarity at trainer.py62,213. claim: Appendix O.4, p.21, states that monthly product lists are beginning-of-month availability snapshots used with purchase dates to determine which products can be offered. mainfinal.py lines116-135 loads lists in sorted filename order; dataloader.py lines33-39 converts their keys to corresponding first-of-month dates. The sampler comments that it selects the candidate products during the purchase date (lines201-209), but its loop overwrites the selection through the final month.
analysis: Complete check: Let snapshots be dated 2024-01-01, 2024-02-01, 2024-03-01, and purchase date 2024-02-15. Give each snapshot common IDs1,2,3,4 plus 100 unique month-specific IDs: January101..200, February201..300, March301..400. Let history=[1,2,3], positive set=[4], N=100 and seed79. All purchased/history items exist in each catalog and every catalog has exactly 100 eligible negatives. At k=0, buydate>January sets candidateproducts=monthproduct[-1], i.e. March. At k=1, buydate>February sets monthproduct[0], January. At final k=2, the condition buydate<=ym and k!=last is false because k=last; buydate>March is false; the else assigns March again. The final pool is March301..400, while the correct contemporaneous snapshot is February201..300. With 100 unique negatives drawn from 100 eligible IDs, the pool discrepancy is deterministic even though no random author sampler was executed. More generally, the final iteration alone yields the last snapshot for t<=last_date, and the penultimate snapshot for t>last_date, independently of intervening dates.

Counterevidence: If every month has identical item membership, this bug is dormant. If the intended evaluation deliberately uses a fixed global catalog, no temporal lookup is needed, but that is not the stated monthly-availability convention and does not explain the penultimate-month behavior after the last date. Missing historical source provenance prevents attributing numerical benchmark damage. This is separate from the TST module's relative positional alignment and does not refute its attention-mask design.

report: Abstract: The published training expression applies a logarithm directly to ordinary cosine similarity, which can be negative for allowed embeddings. It is therefore not a real-valued loss on its stated domain. The inspected release uses a sigmoid and additionally reweights positive terms. Even after inserting the missing sigmoid link, the unweighted expression and released objective have different minimizers in an admissible finite construction. This is a Major issue in the core mathematical training specification, without a demonstrated failure of the reported benchmark gains. A separate Minor release defect overwrites the time-appropriate negative-sampling catalog with a later catalog. Exact examples, original-page visual inspection and static source tracing support these bounded conclusions.
Author: AI-assisted scientific review
Date: 24 October 2026

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
MTSTRec: Multimodal Time-Aligned Shared Token Recommender
# Paper identity and reviewed version

Ming-Yi Hong, Yen-Jung Hsu, Miao-Chen Chiang, and Che Lin, MTSTRec: Multimodal Time-Aligned Shared Token Recommender, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 23640–23661 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment: 0157 / I25-43526. The reviewed frozen proceedings PDF contains 22 pages including appendices. References below use one-based PDF/internal printed page numbers. The source manifest records publication on 6 October 2025 and retrieval on 24 October 2026. The release [Retained latex: \cite{release}] is pinned separately; equivalence to the historical experimental build is not established.
# Summary, scope, and background

MTSTRec combines modality-specific and shared tokens to represent user sequences and predict purchased items. The review inspected its main method and experiments, appended feature and metric descriptions, and relevant release logic. It did not reproduce training, audit raw interaction data, verify every external reference, or estimate empirical effects of the issues.

Equation reference: eq:printed. For a sequence representation \(z\) and an item embedding \(y^k\), §3.4, p. 6, explicitly defines \(\cos(z,y^k)\) as cosine similarity. Let \(P\) be the number of positive items and \(N\) the number of negative items, with disjoint item identities. The published Eq. (8) is \[
L_{\rm printed}=-\frac{1}{P+N}
 \left[\sum_{k\in K_{\rm gt}}\log c_k+
       \sum_{k\in K_n}\log(1-c_k)\right],
\qquad c_k=\cos(z,y^k).\] The original Eq. (8) has the conventional negative prefactor, but no sigmoid link or positive-class weight. A reliable recovery rendering of p. 6 confirms the negative sign; an earlier rendering omitted that glyph. The cosine is explicitly defined as ordinary cosine similarity.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The operative training expression is undefined on its domain and does not specify the released objective).  Assessment: Major. The paper presents Eq. (8) as the formula driving training. For ordinary nonzero real embeddings, cosine lies in \([-1,1]\), whereas the positive logarithmic term requires a positive argument. Neither normalization nor the model description imposes the needed positivity constraint.
## An admissible domain counterexample

Choose unit vectors \[z=(1,0),\qquad
y^+=(-1/2,\sqrt3/2),\qquad
y^-=(1/2,\sqrt3/2).\] Their cosine scores are \(-1/2\) and \(1/2\). The positive term in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) is \(\log(-1/2)\), which is not real. The vectors are nonzero and normalized. They can be embedded in a larger feature space by zero padding, or repeated across modality blocks without changing the cosine. Distinct item identities need not have injective embeddings.

The release provides no countervailing positivity condition. In , final affine representation layers are applied to the modality outputs before concatenation, lines 255–267. , lines 183–194, applies the corresponding affine maps to target-item features. The auxiliary inspection also traced the layer definitions and LayerNorm operations: neither restricts cosine scores to \((0,1)\). The shared-token architecture therefore does not supply the missing assumption.
## A charitable correction still differs from the release

Equation reference: eq:unweighted, eq:weighted. Let \(\sigma(c)=1/(1+e^{-c})\). Retain the printed negative sign and insert a sigmoid link in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed). The resulting unweighted criterion is \[
L_{\rm unw}=-\frac{
 \sum_{k\in K_{\rm gt}}\log\sigma(c_k)
 +\sum_{k\in K_n}\log(1-\sigma(c_k))}{P+N}.\] The pinned source instead implements \[
L_{\rm src}=-\frac{
 (N/P)\sum_{k\in K_{\rm gt}}\log\sigma(c_k)
 +\sum_{k\in K_n}\log(1-\sigma(c_k))}{P+N}.\] In , lines 213–232, the cosine scores are mapped through sigmoids; the positive sum is divided by the positive count and multiplied by the configured negative count before the overall average. The parent inspected this full calculation. The default negative count is \(N=100\), recorded in , lines 69–73. A sequence with \(P=2\) positives is permitted by the multi-answer task.

Parent calculation outputs in corroborate the derivative bound and give \[\begin{array}{c|rr}
c& L_{\rm unw}&L_{\rm src}\\ \hline
-1&0.3328695307&1.5946307598\\
0&0.6931471806&1.3591121187\\
1&1.2936538444&1.5946307598
\end{array}\] The exact derivatives, rather than this three-point table, establish the minima. The independent auxiliary output is ; its unweighted comparison likewise assumes the conventional negative sign.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and correction

The release’s sigmoid makes its objective finite for the exhibited scores. This review does not infer that training the released code necessarily produces NaNs. Nor is a benchmark decline established. If \(P=N\), the weighting factor happens to be one; the stated task does not require that equality. Treating \(\cos\) as an implicit sigmoid score would contradict the explicit definition and would still leave the missing reweighting unresolved.

The finding concerns the mathematical rule used to train the central recommender, not a peripheral typographical claim. The domain failure and non-equivalent optimization criterion demonstrate an invalid core method specification, supporting Major under the required calibration even if a short correction is possible. The proposed token architecture and empirical comparisons may still be useful and correct under the actual implemented loss.

A source-aligned correction is [eq:weighted] (#eq:weighted), for nonzero embeddings and \(P,N>0\). It is finite on the cosine domain and matches the statically inspected per-sequence weighting. This verifies algebraic correspondence only. It does not identify the historical training objective or certify a retrained model. If unweighted BCE was intended, the code and historical provenance instead require reconciliation. The earlier missing-minus allegation is withdrawn: it arose from a missing glyph in the initial source rendering. The domain counterexample and weighted-objective comparison do not depend on that allegation.

Problem 2 (The release overwrites the contemporaneous negative-sampling catalog).  Assessment: Minor; historical impact Needs Evidence. Appendix O.4, p. 21, describes monthly product lists as beginning-of-month availability snapshots to be used with each session’s purchase date. The released lookup can instead finish with a future or penultimate catalog.
## Source and complete finite example

, lines 116–135, reads monthly filenames in sorted order. , lines 33–39, converts the ordered keys to first-of-month dates. Its negative-sampling loop, lines 193–220, does not stop after selecting a date interval; each later iteration may overwrite the pool. At the final iteration it selects the last catalog if the purchase date is no later than that last snapshot, and the penultimate catalog otherwise.

Consider snapshots on 1 January, 1 February and 1 March 2024, and a purchase on 15 February. Each catalog contains common IDs \(1,2,3,4\) plus 100 month-specific IDs: January \(101,\ldots,200\), February \(201,\ldots,300\), and March \(301,\ldots,400\). Let the history be \([1,2,3]\), the positive item be \([4]\), and the requested number of negatives be 100. All history and positive IDs occur in every catalog. Removing them leaves exactly 100 unique eligible candidates in each pool, so the example does not depend on an infeasible draw or duplicate exhaustion.

The successive assignments are March at the January iteration, January at the February iteration, and March at the final iteration. The final eligible pool is therefore \(301,\ldots,400\), while the contemporaneous pool is \(201,\ldots,300\). A draw of 100 distinct items must select the whole chosen pool; randomness cannot repair the mismatch. The independently constructed date/catalog result is saved in . No author sampler or dataset was executed.
## Scope and repair

If all monthly memberships are identical, this defect is dormant. A deliberately global catalog would be a different protocol and would not explain the penultimate-catalog behavior after the last date. The observed code can change the negative-sampling problem, but actual score direction and magnitude remain unknown. The pinned source is not proved to have produced the paper’s tables. The issue does not refute the relative-position shared-token mechanism.

For ordered snapshot dates \(d_0<\cdots<d_{m-1}\) and \(t\geq d_0\), choose \[j=\max\{i:d_i\leq t\}\] once, then sample from catalog \(j\) after exclusions. Sessions before \(d_0\) and insufficient candidate sets require explicit handling. This rule selects February in the example and follows directly from the stated availability convention. Historical metrics would require replaying the actual data and evaluation; that repair has not been performed or adopted.
# Other inspected claims and surviving results

The shared-token attention masks and output slicing in , including lines 121–191, were examined. No separate invalidity of their direct token pairing was established. The paper expressly distinguishes relative temporal alignment from absolute timestamp modeling; the review does not impose an unstated timestamp objective.

The multiple-positive HR/MRR protocol explicitly removes the other positives while ranking each answer. The corresponding released metric logic follows that convention. A tempting criticism based on an assumed ordinary single-positive denominator was therefore excluded. The missing top-\(k\) indicator in one printed metric expression is bounded by the surrounding explanation and implemented cutoff, and is not promoted into another substantive Problem.

Tables 1–4, ablation descriptions, dataset splits, feature construction, baseline settings and computational-cost descriptions were inspected as recorded in the coverage ledger. Raw-data leakage checks, statistical-significance reconstruction, full training, benchmark reproduction and complete external citation/erratum review were not performed.
# Overall impact and state

The highest supported impact is Major, for the published operative loss definition. The catalog defect is a separate Minor finding in the inspected release. Neither establishes that the historical benchmark improvements are false.

A finite matrix calculation demonstrates that the orders do not generally agree. Both findings are assessed Minor; no historical image-quality degradation or measured hardware slowdown is established. The rank/frequency explanation is treated with explicit empirical scope.

# Summary, scope, and notation

The method augments a binary matrix branch (BMB) with a full-precision low-rank branch (LRMB) and a sparse branch (SMB). The review inspected the main scientific text, Eqs. (1)–(12), Tables 1–3, figure descriptions, the complete released supplement, and relevant source. Dense qualitative-image claims were not independently scored, and training or restoration was not rerun.

For a weight matrix \(W\), write \(L_r(W)\) for its truncated rank-\(r\) SVD approximation and \(T_k(W)\) for the matrix retaining its \(k\) largest-magnitude entries. The paper uses rank \(r=8\) and \(k=2\max(C_{\rm in},C_{\rm out})\) in the described configuration. The branch costs are reported as effective parameter counts and equivalent operations, using the paper’s bit-precision accounting convention.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Auxiliary overhead is substantial relative to the binary baseline).  Assessment: Minor. The abstract and the end of §3.5, p. 5, describe the auxiliary storage/computation overhead as ignorable. Eq. (2), p. 4, compares full-precision low-rank storage \(Br(m+n)\) with binary storage \(mnB'\), where \(B'=1\) and \(B\) is 16 or 32.

The exact storage ratio in this simple matrix model is \[\frac{Br(m+n)}{mnB'}.\] For a square matrix and \(B'=1\), it is \(2Br/n\). Merely describing \(r\) as small relative to the matrix width does not give a numerically negligible ratio at finite dimensions; the precision factor remains relevant.
The decisive internal evidence is Table 3(a), p. 8, visually checked in the original:
Configuration | Equivalent operations (G) | Effective parameters (M)
BMB + LRMB + SMB | 1.83 | 4.98

The low-rank branch’s increments are therefore \[\frac{1.83-0.78}{0.78}=1.3461538\ldots,\qquad
\frac{4.98-3.69}{3.69}=0.3495935\ldots.\] These are approximately 134.6% of the binary baseline’s operations and 35.0% of its effective parameters. LRMB accounts for about 57.4% of the resulting operation budget. These are calculations from rounded published totals, not newly measured costs. Parent and auxiliary output bindings are and .
## Counterevidence and correction

The paper openly reports these totals, and the rank ablation explicitly recognizes the effect of rank on complexity. SMB produces no visible increment at the table’s precision. Relative to the full-precision baseline, the LRMB increment can be small; that is a plausible intended interpretation of acceptable overhead.

The overall reductions in Table 2 remain arithmetically consistent: \[50.23/1.83=27.4480874\ldots,\qquad
118.59/4.98=23.8132530\ldots.\] Thus the finding does not invalidate the reported total compression advantage or show a restoration-quality failure. The appropriate correction is to state the baseline: auxiliary costs are small relative to the full-precision backbone but substantial relative to BMB. They must be included in compressed-model comparisons. No empirical repair is required for this arithmetic clarification, and no author adoption is known.

Problem 2 (The text and figure/release specify opposite initialization orders).  Assessment: Minor. Main §3.4, pp. 4–5, Eqs. (5)–(8), first extracts a rank-\(r\) approximation, then selects sparse entries from its residual. Figure 3, p. 4, instead extracts sparse entries before taking the low-rank approximation. Parent visual inspection confirms the diagram’s ordering.

Equation reference: eq:textorder, eq:releaseorder. The text specifies \[
L_{\rm text}=L_r(W),\quad
S_{\rm text}=T_k(W-L_{\rm text}),\quad
R_{\rm text}=W-L_{\rm text}-S_{\rm text}.\] The release and diagram specify \[
S_{\rm rel}=T_k(W),\quad
L_{\rm rel}=L_r(W-S_{\rm rel}),\quad
R_{\rm rel}=W-S_{\rm rel}-L_{\rm rel}.\] In , lines 654–658, the linear constructor extracts and subtracts sparse entries; lines 662–667 then initialize the low-rank branch from the residual. The convolution constructor follows the same broad ordering with its spatial-kernel handling. The shipped , lines 73–78, enables both branches at rank eight. The training configuration and , lines 264–270, load the pretrained model before replacement. , lines 474–480, dispatches that replacement. These source paths were traced statically; they were not run.
## Independent finite calculation

The operations \(L_r\) and \(T_k\) do not commute. To check a nontrivial scale compatible with the stated rank and sparse-entry rule, construct a \(160\times160\) matrix \[W_{ij}=\sin((i+1)(j+2))+0.03(i+1)+0.007(j+1)

\|L_{\rm text}-L_{\rm rel}\|_F&434.6541495\\
\|S_{\rm text}-S_{\rm rel}\|_F&420.9855802\\
\|R_{\rm text}-R_{\rm rel}\|_F&135.1607553.
\end{array}\] Both unquantized sums reconstruct \(W\), to residual norms \(0\) and \(5.62\times10^{-14}\). Equality of the unquantized sum therefore does not imply equality of the branch parameters or residuals.

For an additional weight-level diagnostic, quantize the residual using per-row mean-absolute scaling, \[Q(R)_{ij}=\left(\frac1{160}\sum_{\ell}|R_{i\ell}|\right)
                    \operatorname{sign}(R_{ij}).\] Then \[\|L_{\rm text}+S_{\rm text}+Q(R_{\rm text})
 -L_{\rm rel}-S_{\rm rel}-Q(R_{\rm rel})\|_F
=106.0913795\ldots.\] The full matrix definition, settings and outputs are saved in and . This is a synthetic weight-decomposition calculation, not a full neural forward pass, trained-image test, or reconstruction of historical checkpoints. In particular, it does not bypass the separate activation quantization present in the real network.
## Counterevidence and correction

The release agrees with Figure 3. Both orders are coherent initialization algorithms; it would be inaccurate to say the code contradicts the whole paper. The ablations may reflect either particular historical implementation, and they are not invalidated by the finite example.

The demonstrated consequence is an underspecified initialization procedure whose two readings can yield different branch parameters and quantized weight approximations. To resolve it, specify one sequence consistently in text, equations, diagram and code, and identify the sequence used for the reported experiments. No retraining, historical checkpoint matching, or author-adopted correction was performed.
# Scope clarifications and excluded allegations
## Rank versus frequency

Low matrix rank alone does not imply low spatial frequency. For example, \(A_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\) on a \(16\times16\) grid is rank one, with all two-dimensional Fourier energy at the Nyquist pair. The parent and auxiliary finite checks confirm both properties. A rank-one channel map can likewise transmit an oscillatory spatial signal.

This limits a universal interpretation of the rank/frequency explanation around Eqs. (5)–(7), but does not refute the measured tendency in trained branches. Main §4.4 and Figure 5 describe an empirical division of contributions and explicitly acknowledge high-frequency LRMB output in some layers. The original p. 8 image confirms this qualification. Historical branch-frequency distributions were not recomputed, so a stronger empirical conclusion remains Needs Evidence.
## Equivalent operations and hardware timing

The paper’s operation convention divides binary operations by 64. The approximately \(27.4\times\) figure is consequently an equivalent-operation ratio, not an independently measured wall-clock acceleration. The released supplement, E.1–E.2 on supplement p. 3, explicitly states that practical hardware deployment has not been tested and lists it as future work [Retained latex: \cite{supplement}]. The parent read that passage. No hardware-speed failure is alleged.

Eq. (10)’s XNOR/popcount shorthand omits the explicit signed-dot conversion \(2\,\mathrm{popcount}-\mathrm{fan\_in}\). However, Figure 2 includes postprocessing and the inspected release uses signed, scaled floating convolution/linear operations. This is counterevidence against asserting an actual missing-popcount-correction implementation bug. The full hardware operation-count implementation was not audited.
## Empirical results

Tables 1–3, supplement training-time data and qualitative-comparison descriptions were examined for the stated comparisons and scope. No raw metric recomputation, data audit, confidence assessment, image restoration, or full model inference was performed. The random-binary-rank discussion in supplement B is a heuristic for trained weights; its independence assumptions were not established empirically. No additional core theorem failure is asserted from that heuristic alone.
# Overall impact and state

The highest supported assessment is Minor. The auxiliary-overhead comparison needs a clear denominator and the initialization specification needs reconciliation. The arithmetic total compression advantages survive; image-quality and practical timing consequences remain unresolved.
