# Paper identity and reviewed version

Jingyang Ke, Feiyang Wu, Jiyi Wang, Jeffrey E. Markowitz, and Anqi Wu, Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Switching Rewards and History Dependency for Characterizing Animal Behaviors, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 29608–29625 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment: 0159 / I25-43528. The frozen published PDF has 18 pages including Appendices A–C; page references use one-based PDF/internal printed numbers. The source manifest records publication on 6 October 2025 and retrieval on 24 October 2026. The independently pinned release is [Retained latex: \cite{release}]. Its exact historical code-to-result correspondence is unknown.
# Scope and necessary background

SWIRL combines hidden reward modes with inverse reinforcement learning and finite state-history dependence. Main §3.1 defines finite mode, state and action spaces and a discounted decision process. §3.3 allows a state-dependent hidden-mode transition kernel and history length \(L\); state-only rewards are used for simplicity. §3.4 learns rewards and mode dynamics by EM, with an auxiliary function \(G\) that is the expected log joint under the current latent posterior.

The full paper text and relevant appendix descriptions were read. Detailed checking focused on the generative factorization, forward/backward boundaries, posterior normalization, and M-step direction. Static released source was inspected as enumerated in the coverage ledger. Empirical plots were read through descriptions/captions, not digitized or independently recomputed. No model training, animal-data inference, or author-code execution was performed.

Equation reference: eq:joint. For a trajectory \(\xi=((s_1,a_1),\ldots,(s_T,a_T))\), let \(z_t\) be its hidden mode. The published joint on p. 13 includes \[
p(s_1)p(z_1)\pi_{z_1}(a_1\mid s_1)
 \prod_{t=2}^{T}
 P(s_t\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1})
 P_z(z_t\mid z_{t-1},s_{t-1})
 \pi_{z_t}(a_t\mid s_t^L).\] This factorization supplies the appropriate reference for the message-passing formulas.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The forward initialization omits a mode-dependent first emission).  Assessment: Major. Appendix A.2, p. 14, defines \(\alpha_{t,z}=p(s_{1:t},a_{1:t},z_t=z\mid\widehat\theta)\) but initializes \(\alpha_{1,z}=p(z_1=z\mid\widehat\theta)\). The recursion starts with the current action likelihood at \(t=2\). The stated terminal likelihood is \(\sum_z\alpha_{T,z}\), and the terminal posterior uses \(\beta_{T,z}=1\).

Equation reference: eq:alpha. By [eq:joint] (#eq:joint), the required initialization is \[
\alpha_{1,z}=p(s_1)p(z_1=z)\pi_z(a_1\mid s_1^L).\] A common initial-state factor can be dropped from normalized mode posteriors if handled consistently, but a mode-dependent action probability cannot. The example below sets \(p(s_1)=1\), eliminating that possible distraction.
## An admissible soft-MDP construction

Use three states \(S=\{o,u,v\}\), two actions \(A=\{a,b\}\), two modes \(\{A,B\}\), history length \(L=1\), discount \(\gamma=0.95\), and entropy temperature one. The initial state is \(o\), and the initial modes have probability \(1/2\) each. From \(o\), action \(a\) reaches \(u\) deterministically and action \(b\) reaches \(v\). Both \(u\) and \(v\) are absorbing under either action. The hidden-mode kernel is the identity at every state.

This kernel is a valid state-independent special case of the stated state-conditioned model; no strict-positivity or irreducibility premise is imposed in the paper. It also makes the mode-specific policy optimal for the full process, removing any separate question about anticipated future mode changes.

Set \[d=\frac{1-\gamma}{\gamma}\log3,
\qquad
r_A(o,u,v)=(0,d,0),\qquad
r_B(o,u,v)=(0,0,d).\] Rewards are bounded, real and state-only. At an absorbing state \(s\), entropy-regularized optimal value is \[V_z(s)=\frac{r_z(s)+\log2}{1-\gamma}.\] At \(o\), the difference between the two mode-A action values is \(\gamma d/(1-\gamma)=\log3\), with the opposite sign in mode B. The Boltzmann policy therefore has \[\pi_A(a\mid o)=\tfrac34,\qquad
\pi_B(a\mid o)=\tfrac14,\] and each action at \(u\) or \(v\) has probability \(1/2\) in either mode. These emissions are derived from the paper’s soft-policy construction, rather than assigned arbitrarily.

The independent parent script constructs the soft values and action probabilities and checks their Bellman residuals. The reported maximum residual is zero at the used floating precision, below \(10^{-12}\); the auxiliary calculation independently confirms the construction. Inputs and outputs are in , , and .
## Exact enumeration versus the printed recursion

Observe \(\xi=((o,a),(u,a))\). The environment transition factor is one. Exact joint weights are \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &z_2=A&z_2=B\\ \hline
z_1=A&3/16&0\\
z_1=B&0&1/16
\end{array}\] and hence \[p(\xi)=\tfrac14,\qquad
p(z_2\mid\xi)=(\tfrac34,\tfrac14).\] The printed initialization gives \(\alpha_1=(1/2,1/2)\). Even applying the subsequent recurrence correctly gives \[\alpha_2=(1/4,1/4),\qquad
p_{\rm printed}(\xi)=\tfrac12,\qquad
p_{\rm printed}(z_2\mid\xi)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12).\] Thus the sequence likelihood doubles and the terminal mode-A posterior differs by \(1/4\). This calculation uses only the unambiguous terminal condition; it does not depend on the separate problematic backward boundary expression on the same page.

With [eq:alpha] (#eq:alpha), \(\alpha_1=(3/8,1/8)\) and \(\alpha_2=(3/16,1/16)\), restoring the enumerated likelihood and posterior exactly. These fractions are independently evaluated with exact rational arithmetic in the parent output cited above.
## Dependency, alternative readings, and repair

The E-step posterior weights determine reward fitting, hidden-mode transition fitting, and the inferred behavioral segmentation in main Eqs. (1)–(4) and Appendix A.1 Eqs. (5)–(7). The printed recurrence therefore fails at a central inference step for an allowed model. This supports Major even though the omission is short and a correct intended factorization is available elsewhere.

A reinterpretation of \(\alpha_1\) as a pre-emission message would require the recursion to multiply the first action before proceeding; the printed formulas do not do that. The joint on p. 13 is internal counterevidence about intended correctness, not a validation of the conflicting boundary formula.

The inspected release is correct on this point: , lines 171–182, initializes log-forward values as `log(pi0) + log_likes[0]`. Lines 184–200 use the next emission in the backward scan; lines 202–224 construct normalized marginals and wire the E-step. Analogous first-emission terms occur in the inspected labyrinth and spontaneous-behavior routes. No released or historical run is claimed to omit the first action.

A consistent backward recursion from [eq:joint] (#eq:joint) is \[\beta_{t,z}
=P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)
 \sum_{z'}P_z(z'\mid z,s_t)
 \pi_{z'}(a_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1}^L)\beta_{t+1,z'},
\qquad \beta_{T,z}=1.\] The printed p. 14 expression instead uses current-action and shifted state-conditioning indices, with a separate self-referential first-boundary line. Correcting all boundaries and indices to the joint resolves the specification. The forward correction is verified exactly on the finite case; no empirical performance repair or complete implementation rerun is certified.

Problem 2 (Algorithm 1 descends the auxiliary function it must maximize).  Assessment: Major. Appendix A.1, p. 12, defines \(G\) with positive expected log-policy, log-prior and log-transition terms. Both prose and Algorithm 1 then prescribe gradient descent: \[\theta^{k+1}=\theta^k-\eta_k\nabla_\theta G(\theta,\theta^k).\] Appendix A.2, p. 13, correctly specifies the M-step target as \(\arg\max_\theta G(\theta,\theta^k)\). These directions conflict.

For \(g=\nabla_\theta G(\theta^k,\theta^k)\ne0\) and sufficiently small positive \(\eta\), \[G(\theta^k-\eta g,\theta^k)
=G(\theta^k,\theta^k)-\eta\|g\|^2+O(\eta^2).\] The printed step therefore decreases the maximization target. Even generalized EM seeks an increase rather than necessarily an exact maximizer; the sign does not implement that weaker requirement either.
## A legal parameter block and numerical check

Use the exact posterior in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:forward), so this finding is independent of its erroneous E-step. The paper includes \(p(z_1)\) among the learned parameters. Holding the remaining model components fixed, parameterize \(p(z_1=A)=\sigma(\theta)\), where \(\sigma\) is logistic. For posterior \(q_A=3/4\), the varying part of \(G\) is \[G(\theta)=\tfrac34\log\sigma(\theta)
+\tfrac14\log(1-\sigma(\theta)).\] At \(\theta=0\), \(G(0)=-\log2\) and \(G'(0)=1/4\). The exact maximizer is \(\theta=\log3\). Parent independent arithmetic gives:
\(\eta\) | \(G(-\eta/4)\), printed descent | \(G(+\eta/4)\), ascent

Every descent value is below \(-0.6931471806\), while ascent increases it. The small-step example avoids dependence on an excessive learning rate. The block calculation is one valid optimization subproblem, and the preceding differential argument supplies the general sign conclusion. Actual values and source bindings are in .
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair

The error is in the operative EM learning derivation, not an unrelated remark. It supports Major under the core-contribution standard without requiring an empirically observed failure or a difficult correction.

The source again provides important counterevidence. In , lines 257–275, the transition objective returns negative expected log joint divided by trajectory length to a minimizer. The emission loss in lines 334–365 uses the same sign, and lines 401–403 update the initial prior from posterior counts. The parent statically inspected these paths. The auxiliary checked corresponding negative objectives in the labyrinth and spontaneous-behavior routes. These observations prevent attributing the printed sign error to the actual published fitted models.

The correction is gradient ascent on \(G\), or gradient descent on a clearly defined loss \(-G\). The finite calculation verifies the corrected direction at the displayed step sizes. It does not prove global convergence, fitted reward recovery, or restoration of an empirical result. No author adoption is known.
# Other inspected claims and boundaries

Finite-history augmentation was checked at the stated structural level. The gridworld source shifts augmented states from (current, previous) to (next, current), consistent with the construction. First-history padding and every empirical boundary case were not exhaustively rechecked.

Deterministic next-state dynamics alone do not make actions identifiable, but the spontaneous-behavior experiment defines actions by the next syllable/state. That explicit convention prevents a generic non-injectivity criticism from being treated as a demonstrated defect of the described experiment. No unsupported reward-uniqueness theorem was identified, so generic inverse-RL ambiguities were not substituted for a specific invalid claim.

Held-out likelihood, mode/history/temperature selection, reported behavioral correlations, and noise analyses were read in their stated scope. Original split files, trained outputs, raw neural traces, complete preprocessing and causal biological mechanisms were not verified. Appendix C’s IQ-Learn extension was read but its cited external derivation was not independently rederived. No wet-lab requirement or quantified selection bias is invented.
# Overall impact and state

The highest supported impact is Major. The published E-step and M-step each contain a demonstrated error directly affecting the central inference/learning specification. Correct released code and the correct intended joint/argmax formulations preserve a plausible implementation path; the empirical findings are not disproved here.

report: Abstract: The printed value-preservation argument fails when poisoned states can follow poisoned states. Under the admissible reward-history range explicitly used in the appendix, and after granting normalization and domain repairs, an exact finite construction gives a benign-state value \(15/16\) instead of \(1\). Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Adversarial Inception Backdoor Attacks against Reinforcement Learning
# Paper identity and reviewed version

Ethan Rathbun, Alina Oprea, and Christopher Amato, Adversarial Inception Backdoor Attacks against Reinforcement Learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 51273–51296 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment: 0160 / I25-43529. The reviewed published PDF contains 24 pages, including Appendix A. Page references below use one-based PDF pages, which agree with the internal printed page numbers. The frozen manifest records publisher publication on 6 October 2025 and retrieval on 24 October 2026. The inspected released source is pinned to [Retained latex: \cite{release}]. That pin identifies the available release; correspondence to the historical experimental executable is not established.
# Scope and necessary background

The paper proposes bounded-reward backdoor attacks against reinforcement learning. The theoretical construction changes transition and reward functions, while Q-Incept approximates the attack through changes to collected training trajectories. The abstract, main §4.3, and conclusion present simultaneous attack-success and stealth guarantees as central contributions.

The complete paper text, including the main method and experimental descriptions and Appendix A, was read by a native auxiliary reviewer. Independent calculations concentrated on the formal guarantees and relevant source branches. The parent checked the decisive original equations, proof dependency, reward-domain assumptions, and source lines. Original PDF pages 2, 5, and 16 were rendered and actually viewed. Numerical curves were not digitized, experiments were not rerun, and author code was neither imported nor executed.

Let \(S\) be the benign state set, \(S_p\) a disjoint poisoned copy, and \(\delta:S\to S_p\) a bijection. The action set contains the target \(a^+\). A discount \(0<\gamma<1\), poisoning probability \(0<\beta<1\), and policy \(\pi\) define the values under comparison. Equation (9), p. 5, remaps \(a^+\) at a poisoned state to an action maximizing a benign-state action value; other actions are unchanged. Equation (10) assigns probability \(1-\beta\) to benign successors and \(\beta\) to poisoned successors, including when the current state is poisoned.

Equation reference: eq:tau. With \(L=\inf R\), \(U=\sup R\), the published reward perturbation is \[
\tau(a,r,\widehat r)=
\begin{cases}
\min\{r+(\widehat r-L)/\gamma,U\}, & a=a^+,\\
\max\{r-(U-\widehat r)/\gamma,L\}, & a\ne a^+.
\end{cases}\] The prose identifies \(\widehat r\) as the previous received reward. Equation (12) adds a correction \(\gamma\mathbb E[r-\tau]\) only to benign-to-poisoned transitions; poisoned-origin transitions receive \(\tau\). Equation (7), p. 4, requires \(\inf R'\ge L\) and \(\sup R'\le U\). This is a condition to check, not a premise that can be omitted.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Consecutive poisoned states break the value-preservation derivation).  Assessment: Major. Lemma 2, main p. 6 and Appendix A.1.4, p. 16, asserts, in paraphrase, \[V_\pi^{M'}(s)\ge V_\pi^M(s)
\qquad\text{for every }s\in S,\ \pi\in\Pi.\] Its base case asserts equality when action remapping is replaced by the identity. The step leading to Appendix equation (52) substitutes a poisoned action value by its benign counterpart plus \(\tau-r\). That substitution does not account for the different correction rewards when the successor is itself poisoned.
## Explicit interpretation and granted repairs

Three choices are stated before evaluating the claim. First, use the normalized full kernel in equation (10), granting the local normalization repair in Problem Problem 2 (#prob:normalization). Second, pull a poisoned successor back through \(\delta^{-1}\) when a benign reward function is called on it. The poisoned-origin row of equation (12) does not explicitly write that successor pullback.

Third, use the admissible previous-reward domain \(\widehat r\in[L,U]\) explicitly assumed in Appendix equation (15), p. 13. In the benign-to-poisoned correction, evaluate the future \(\tau\) using the incoming reward of that next poisoned step. This is the forward-consistent interpretation of the prose’s cancellation of the next perturbation. The unmodified-incoming and corrected-received-incoming readings agree in the finite construction below; its consistency equation is verified explicitly.

These qualifications matter. Equations (11)–(12) print real argument domains without restricting \(\widehat r\). Taken literally on all real inputs, [eq:tau] (#eq:tau) is not bounded: at \(L=0,U=1,\gamma=1/2,r=1/2\), \[\tau(a^+,1/2,-1)=-3/2,\qquad
\tau(a_0,1/2,2)=5/2 .\] Thus the example below is not claimed to satisfy an unrestricted-real-domain version of equation (7). It meets the bound on all state/action/successor triples for every admissible prior reward in \([0,1]\), under the stated incoming-reward interpretation. Other interpretations of the unspecified dot arguments require a complete definition; no invariance under every possible repair is asserted.
## Finite model and verification of assumptions

Equation reference: eq:benignreward. Take \[S=\{\ell,b,h\},\quad S_p=\{p_\ell,p_b,p_h\},\quad
\delta(q)=p_q,\quad A=\{a^+,a_0\},\quad
\beta=\gamma=\tfrac12 .\] The sets are finite and disjoint, and \(\delta\) is bijective. Both benign actions self-loop: \(T(q,a,q)=1\). Define the complete benign reward function, including impossible cross-component transitions, by \[
R(q,a,q')=r(q'),\qquad
r(\ell)=0,\quad r(b)=\tfrac12,\quad r(h)=1 .\] Consequently \(L=0,U=1\) are attained on actual self-loops. A uniform benign initial distribution, if needed, gives both extrema positive probability. The off-support definition in [eq:benignreward] (#eq:benignreward) is part of this final construction; it strengthens the earlier auxiliary candidate without changing any operative benign transition.

Let \(\pi\) always take \(a_0\), at both benign and poisoned states. This is a valid policy in the universal quantifier. The argmax branch of \(\phi\) is never used on policy, and the actual remapping equals the identity. Off policy, the two benign actions have the same transition and reward functions, so action selection does not change those components.

For each \(q\), equation (10) gives the closed two-state transition matrix \[P_q=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{on }(q,p_q).\] In particular \(p_q\to p_q\) has positive probability. No inspected assumption excludes consecutive poisoned states; deleting that branch would change the published kernel.

Equation reference: eq:entry. The benign-to-poisoned entry rewards are \[c_\ell=0,\qquad c_b=\tfrac34,\qquad c_h=1.\] Each satisfies both the nominal incoming calculation and the received-reward consistency equation \[
c_q=r(q)+\tfrac12\bigl[r(q)-\tau(a_0,r(q),c_q)\bigr].\] For \(b\), \(\tau(a_0,1/2,3/4)=0\), giving \(c_b=3/4\). For \(\ell\) and \(h\), the corresponding perturbations are \(0\) and \(1\).

The reward constraint holds over all \(6\cdot2\cdot6=72\) state/action/successor triples, not only positive-probability transitions. Benign-to-benign rewards are \(r(\text{destination})\). Benign-to-poisoned rewards are the corresponding \(c_q\), all in \([0,1]\). For poisoned origins and any \(\widehat r\in[0,1]\), the target branch of [eq:tau] (#eq:tau) lies in \([r,1]\) and the other branch in \([0,r]\), including actions not taken by the fixed policy. These clipped affine functions are nondecreasing in \(\widehat r\), so checking their endpoints also bounds the full interval. The parent’s exact calculation enumerated all 72 triples at both endpoints and verified [eq:entry] (#eq:entry). Actual output: . The independent auxiliary challenge reaches the same result in .
## Correct values and failed substitution

Equation reference: eq:vb, eq:vp, eq:counter. Start the central component from a benign state with a compatible prior reward \(1/2\). Its operative reward histories remain in \(\{0,1/2,3/4\}\), and \(\tau(a_0,1/2,\widehat r)=0\) for every such history. Thus the following two-state Bellman calculation is valid even if the previous reward is explicitly included in the underlying process: \[(R'_{b b},R'_{b p_b},R'_{p_b b},R'_{p_b p_b})
=\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac34,0,0\right).\] Writing \(v=V_\pi^{M'}(b)\), \(w=V_\pi^{M'}(p_b)\), with the latter understood on those consistent operative histories, \[\begin{aligned}
v&=\tfrac12(\tfrac12+\tfrac12v)+
   \tfrac12(\tfrac34+\tfrac12w)
 =\tfrac58+\tfrac14(v+w),\\
w&=\tfrac12(\tfrac12v)+\tfrac12(\tfrac12w)
 =\tfrac14(v+w).\end{aligned}\] Subtracting gives \(v-w=5/8\), while [eq:vp] (#eq:vp) gives \(v=3w\). Therefore \[
v=\tfrac{15}{16}<1=\frac{1/2}{1-1/2}=V_\pi^M(b),
\qquad w=\tfrac5{16}.\] Both Bellman residuals are exactly zero in rational arithmetic. The original value is \(1\); the asserted nondecrease is violated by \(1/16\). The base-case equality also fails because remapping is already the identity on policy.

In this one-action-on-policy component, the equation-(52) substitution would require \[Q_\pi^{M'}(p_b,a_0)
=Q_\pi^{M'}(b,a_0)+\tau-r
=\tfrac{15}{16}-\tfrac12=\tfrac7{16}.\] The correct left side is \(5/16\), a residual of \(-1/8\). This identifies the failed step rather than merely reporting a different numerical value. The parent independently solved the exact system and checked all three reward components in . Its original reachable-history calculation is supplemented, not retroactively replaced, by the full admissible-domain check above.
## Dependency, counterevidence, and repair limits

Appendix A.1.5, p. 18, explicitly invokes Lemmas 1 and 2 in the forward proof of Theorem 2, which claims preservation of benign optimal policies. A false supporting lemma and invalid value substitution invalidate that central derivation. This is the reason for Major. The result does not depend on the proof’s appendix location or on demonstrating a benchmark decrease.

No direct counterexample to the final optimality biconditional is claimed here. The construction is policy dependent, and a valid replacement theorem would require its own fully specified reward/history semantics and proof. Other theoretical statements and empirical successes may survive.

The practical procedure is relevant counterevidence. Algorithm 1, p. 6, and the inspected release correct the previous sampled transition regardless of whether it was poisoned; p. 7 also explains a stronger practical reward choice. They are not identical to the three-row theoretical reward definition. Consequently the formal counterexample is not evidence that the reported Q-Incept attack-success or benign-return measurements are false.

In the finite central example, adding \(1/4\) to the \(p_b\to p_b\) reward gives \(v=1,w=1/2\); this diagnostic restores the local cancellation. It is not a proposed globally valid bounded-reward repair. The checker records this finite result separately. A full repair must specify history dependence and all transition types, recheck the global bound, and prove the resulting optimality statement.

Problem 2 (The transition constraint weights the mixture twice).  Assessment: Minor. Main §3, p. 2, equation (1), states the constraint \[(1-\beta)T'(s'\mid a,s)+
\beta T'(\delta(s')\mid a,s)=T(s'\mid a,s).\] At the same time \(T'\) is the full transition kernel on \(S\cup S_p\), as made explicit in equation (10), p. 5.

For a fixed row, let \(P_B=\sum_{s'\in S}T'(s'\mid a,s)\) and \(P_P=\sum_{s'\in S}T'(\delta(s')\mid a,s)\). Disjointness and bijectivity give \(P_B+P_P=1\). Summing the printed constraint instead requires \[(1-\beta)P_B+\beta P_P=1.\] For \(0<\beta<1\), its left side is at most \(\max\{\beta,1-\beta\}<1\), a contradiction. With \(\beta=1/2\), equation (10)’s valid row is \((1/2,1/2)\), but equation (1)’s left side is \(1/2\) rather than \(1\). The exact calculation is recorded in ; original pages 2 and 5 were visually checked.

The intended local repair is clear from the prose and equation (10): \[T'(s'\mid a,s)+T'(\delta(s')\mid a,s)=T(s'\mid a,s).\] Interpreting the displayed \(T'\) terms as branch-conditional kernels would require different notation and would conflict with their actual equation-(10) values. This is a supported local specification inconsistency. The report grants its repair in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:value); it does not use the inconsistency to claim that every practical experiment is impossible. Subsequent probability expansions must be synchronized with whichever convention is adopted.

Problem 3 (The release uses a future rollout reward as the predecessor at index zero).  Assessment: Minor; historical impact Needs Evidence. In the pinned release, , lines 85–100, samples indices from a categorical distribution over the supplied states. Lines 140–150 then access without excluding index zero. The caller in , lines 241–248, passes chronological per-environment rollout slices, including .

The code path is conditional on attack activation, the caller’s attack-success condition, and the selection budget. Index zero is included in the finite categorical support. Finite scores give it positive probability; positive selected scores cause the target action to be assigned. For example, finite two-action Q rows \((1,0),(0,0),(0,0)\), with the first action selected, yield a positive centered score at the first step and finite clipped logits. Such values are an illustrative legal branch condition, not a measured network output.

A larger rollout may reduce the frequency of selecting a particular boundary index, but it does not change this branch’s temporal meaning. No historical logs establish its occurrence or effect on published scores. A correction must explicitly handle the actual previous transition and episode/rollout boundaries; merely indexing the current slice cannot recover that transition. The general repair and its empirical impact remain unverified.
# Overall impact and unresolved claims

The supported overall assessment is Major, arising from Problem Problem 1 (#prob:value)’s core theoretical dependency. Problems Problem 2 (#prob:normalization) and Problem 3 (#prob:boundary) remain local Minor findings with separate evidence. The finite model establishes a failure of the value-preservation claim under explicitly stated, source-supported semantics; it does not establish that all variants of adversarial inception fail.

The theoretical and practical algorithms differ in ways that prevent transferring the formal defect directly to measured attack success or benign return. Historical commit provenance, raw rollout logs, exact configuration-to-table correspondence, and reruns would be required to assess empirical effects. The full original text and selected release were inspected, but no comprehensive later-version or external-erratum search was performed. No priority or first-discovery claim is made.

# Checked reasoning
## Operational method

The top-down stage retrieves question–subquestion examples from AGQA-Decomp and recursively asks an MLLM whether each subquestion is perceptual. The bottom-up stage answers leaves, combines their answers with the original video, and checks intermediate answers. These prompts define an inference procedure, not a formal soundness theorem. Because the video remains an input at internal nodes, a parent answer need not follow from textual leaf answers alone. This agrees with Section 3.2.2 (p. 5), Figure 3 and Section 5 (pp. 8–9), and the loss of accuracy when video is removed from bottom-up reasoning in Table 5 (p. 9).
## Selected comparisons

The four matched backbone pairs in Table 1 give main-question accuracy gains of 3.8, 3.5, 3.5, and 3.7 percentage points and subquestion gains of 6.1, 6.0, 6.3, and 6.9 points. Independent decimal arithmetic reproduces these differences. Table 5 gives full-method gains of 2.2 and 2.3 points over the baseline on Causal-VidQA and NExT-QA. Removing answer verification lowers the full method by 0.5 and 0.7 points; removing video from bottom-up reasoning lowers it by 17.6 and 21.6 points. These checks support the direction of the displayed comparisons, without validating predictions or identifying a causal cognitive mechanism.

The qualitative failure case acknowledges that a missed book count propagates to an incorrect final answer. The paper is therefore not reasonably interpreted as claiming a correctness guarantee for the verification prompt. The sixteen-frame limitation for long videos is explicit in Appendix A.2 and C.1.
# Scope clarification and unresolved evidence
## Supplied graph in AGQA-Decomp

Section 4.3 (p. 6) expressly states that the DAG from the AGQA-Decomp test set is used for bottom-up reasoning when evaluating compositional consistency. Table 1 therefore measures reasoning with that supplied structure. It does not alone establish the complete generated-tree pipeline’s AGQA-Decomp accuracy. This is a disclosed protocol distinction, not demonstrated answer leakage. Other benchmarks and first-stage ablations supply separate evidence for the complete pipeline.

Section 3.1.1 (p. 4) describes embedding all non-leaf question–subquestion tuples in the retrieval database, but does not identify the retrieval split, exclusions, top-\(K\) value, or item-level retrieval records in the inspected materials. The supplied-graph protocol and retrieval database must be distinguished. The wording alone does not establish leakage. That question requires the exact retrieval inventory and evaluated question identifiers.
## Interpretability and uncertainty

The tree exposes intermediate questions, answers, and explanations. That operational transparency is supported by the examples, but does not establish causal faithfulness of every explanation to the model’s internal computation. No quantitative faithfulness evaluation was available in this inspection.

Table captions distinguish copied results from reproduced backbone results. Matched pairs are the appropriate evidence for the framework’s incremental effect. Prediction records, judge configuration, and run-level uncertainty were unavailable. The compositional-score aggregation cannot be reconstructed from rounded entries alone: a harmonic mean of aggregate precision and recall need not equal an average of per-item harmonic means. The review does not label such an aggregation ambiguity a demonstrated arithmetic defect.
# Assessment

No substantive invalid derivation or demonstrated core-result failure was established. The outcome is scope clarification, with No Issue Found in the declared inspected scope. The generated-tree AGQA-Decomp interpretation, retrieval split, exact compositional aggregation, and empirical reproducibility remain evidence-dependent. No correction is proposed. Later revisions and errata were not independently established in this inspection.

Title: Technical Verification of Representation Preserving Multiclass Agnostic to Realizable Reduction
# Identity, scope, and outcome

Steve Hanneke, Qinglin Meng, and Amirreza Shaeiri’s Representation Preserving Multiclass Agnostic to Realizable Reduction, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 21995–22008, is reviewed in its staged published-proceedings version (I25-43531). References to pages below mean the PDF’s printed pages 1–14, equal to the one-based PDF index. The source manifest and actual file hashes are retained with the verification records.

Two substantive problems are established. First, the partial-class extension is false under its printed loss and agnostic-comparator definitions. Second, Section 6’s lower-bound construction does not establish the claimed cost of representation preservation, even after a charitable reversal of its displayed ratio. Both concern advertised theoretical contributions. The ordinary reduction for total predictors is not refuted.

An auxiliary scientist examined the scientific text and appendices. The parent independently checked the decisive definitions and statements, visually inspected source pages 7, 10, and 11, verified the counterexample, and reran an independently written finite calculation. The coverage ledger distinguishes this targeted parent verification from the auxiliary’s wider reading. External theorems used for dimension and compression bounds were not independently re-proved.
# Definitions needed for the checks

The framework specifies a tuple \((X,Y,A,L,C,H)\) and requires the learner’s output to belong to \(H\). Appendix B.1 (p. 10) allows partial concepts \(c:X\to A\cup\{\star\}\), defines \(\operatorname{supp}(c)=c^{-1}(A)\), and explicitly sets \(L(\star,y)=0\). A distribution is realizable only if, almost surely for every finite sample, some concept both covers every sampled input by its support and has zero loss on that sample.

The agnostic approximation error is instead \[L_D(C)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E_{S\sim D^n}\min_{c\in C}L_S(c).\] Definition B.2 (p. 11) quantifies over every distribution on \(X\times Y\). Its minimization is not restricted to concepts whose support contains the sample. This distinction is essential.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Zero-loss abstention invalidates the partial-class reduction).  Theorem B.3 (p. 11) claims that Algorithm 1 converts every realizable unified partial learner into an agnostic unified partial learner with finite sample complexity. Under the printed definitions, a realizable learner can exist while no permitted agnostic learner exists.
## Complete admissible construction

Let \(X=Y=A=\{0,1\}\), equip these finite sets with their full sigma algebras, and take \(\star\notin A\). Set \[L(a,y)=\mathbf1\{a\ne y\}\quad(a\in A),\qquad L(\star,y)=0.\] Let \(C=\{c_0,c_1\}\) and \(H=\{h_0\}\), with
Predictor | \(x=0\) | \(x=1\)

All spaces and functions are finite and measurable, both classes are nonempty, and the definitions do not require \(C\subseteq H\). Define the supplied learner to return \(h_0\) on every sample, including the empty sample.

The only \(C\)-realizable distributions are \(\delta_{(0,0)}\) and \(\delta_{(1,0)}\). A point with label 1 cannot be supported and correctly labeled by any concept, already at sample size one. If both zero-labeled input points have positive mass, a size-two sample containing both has positive probability, and no concept supports both. Conversely, each displayed point mass is supported and correctly labeled by one concept. The supplied learner has risk zero on every realizable distribution. Thus a finite realizable sample bound of one is valid for every \(\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)\).

Now take \(D=\delta_{(0,1)}\). Every nonempty sample contains only \((0,1)\). Because \(c_1(0)=\star\), every sample satisfies \(L_S(c_1)=0\). Therefore \[L_D(C)=0,\qquad L_D(h_0)=1.\] Algorithm 1’s candidates all equal \(h_0\), whatever subsets and sample sizes it uses. At \(\epsilon=1/2\) and \(\delta=1/4\), its required success event is \(1\le1/2\), which has probability zero instead of at least \(3/4\). The same contradiction holds for every \(\epsilon<1\), every \(\delta<1\), and every sample size.

The independent finite calculation reproduces the four point-mass losses, verifies the mixed-input support failure, and checks samples of sizes 1, 2, 5, and 20. The argument above, not that finite list alone, proves the all-sample-size conclusion.
## Failing proof step and alternative readings

Before the proof on p. 11 and following Eq. (15) on p. 12, the argument treats the zero-loss portion of an empirical minimizer as realizable and invokes the supplied learner. In this example the empirical minimizer has zero loss only because it is undefined on every observation. Zero loss does not imply the required support condition. Equivalently, if one defines the selected portion using actual support, Eq. (14)’s loss decomposition no longer equals the claimed \(1-\mu^\ast\) under zero-loss abstention.

Changing \(L(\star,y)\) to one, or changing the agnostic comparator to include a support restriction, would alter an explicit definition and remove this particular witness. Neither alteration appears in Definition B.2. No complete repaired theorem under either convention has been verified.
## Impact

This is Major: Theorem B.3 is false as stated, and partial-learning corollaries relying on it cannot inherit its guarantee without reconciliation. The partial extension is advertised as a contribution; its appendix location does not limit its importance. The counterexample does not refute Theorem 4.1 for total predictors, where the support mismatch is absent.

Problem 2 (The lower-bound example does not isolate a representation-preservation cost).  Section 6 (p. 7) states that an extra \(1/\epsilon\) factor relative to compression-based learning can be unavoidable because representation is preserved. Theorem 6.1 and its proof do not establish that conclusion.
## Literal statement
## Why reversing the ratio is insufficient

Grant the charitable reading that the ratio should be reversed. In the theorem’s construction take \(n=1\) and \(m=2\): one input point, two labels, and the two constant predictors as \(C=H\). This \(H\) is the entire predictor space. Representation preservation imposes no output restriction at all.

Let \(p=\Pr(Y=1)\). Empirical majority outputs a member of \(H\). If the wrong label has excess risk greater than \(\epsilon\), then \(|p-1/2|>\epsilon/2\). The elementary bounded-sample tail inequality gives a wrong-majority probability at most \(\exp(-N\epsilon^2/2)\). Thus \[N\ge 2\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)\] suffices while preserving representation. If \(|2p-1|\le\epsilon\), either label already meets the excess-risk target.

This example therefore distinguishes realizable and noisy learning, not restricted and unrestricted representations. In particular, it cannot demonstrate a necessary \(\epsilon^{-3}\) cost or an extra \(\epsilon^{-1}\) penalty relative to an \(\epsilon^{-2}\) comparison. No lower-bound result external to the reviewed paper is needed for this conclusion: the predictor spaces coincide exactly, and the explicit upper bound suffices.
## Impact and correction limits

The reversed ratio is a plausible writing error, but the representation-cost interpretation remains unsupported after that local edit. The defect is Major for the stated lower-bound rationale connected to the central sample-complexity contribution. It does not invalidate the reduction algorithm’s upper bound. A different construction might establish a representation-dependent cost; this review does not show that such a lower bound is impossible. The supported correction is to describe the example as a realizable-versus-agnostic sampling comparison, without claiming that it isolates representation cost. No replacement optimality theorem has been verified.
# Other checks, dependence, and limitations

The total-predictor conditioning argument in Lemma 4.2 and the finite validation-class selection in Theorem 4.1 were examined without finding a corresponding counterexample. This is an argument-level check, not certification of every logarithmic factor, external dimension theorem, or measurability detail.

The noise-model analysis was also examined. Equation (5)’s displayed arbitrary-pair bound omits an empirical-risk difference, whereas its actual empirical-minimizer application can use that difference’s nonpositive sign. A further factor in the conditioned-error comparison can be absorbed by a smaller internal accuracy. These observations are retained as proof details requiring care, rather than asserted false noise-model rates. Appendix C relies on external compression results not independently verified here.

No paper-specific implementation was available in the frozen acquisition. The manifest records inaccessible additional OpenReview attachments. No later full-text revision or erratum was independently checked, and no absence of a correction is claimed. The findings attach to the hash-bound published PDF.
# Conclusion

Title: Technical Verification of Promoting Ensemble Diversity with Interactive Bayesian Distributional Robustness for Fine-tuning Foundation Models
# Identity and inspected material

This report reviews Ngoc Quan Pham, Tuan Truong, Quyen Tran, Tan Nguyen, Dinh Phung and Trung Le, Promoting Ensemble Diversity with Interactive Bayesian Distributional Robustness for Fine-tuning Foundation Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 49259–49276 (I25-43532). The original proceedings PDF contains 18 pages. Page numbers below refer to that original, including the embedded supplement. The publisher reference is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/pham25b.html.

The preserved public release is https://github.com/quanphamnus/IBDR, commit `1d628ca3e538e729631a6f22836ddf365aa6e563`. Its equivalence to the conference experiment code is not established. The auxiliary reviewed the main scientific text, theoretical supplement and relevant implementation/configuration paths. The parent visually checked original pp. 4, 5, 7 and 18, read the p. 6 definitions and decisive code sections, rehashed all manifest-listed sources, and independently recalculated the examples. No author code or benchmark was executed.
# Definitions and contribution

Equation reference: eq:loss, eq:gram. The paper seeks particle diversity while retaining low loss and low sharpness in Bayesian parameter-efficient fine-tuning. On p. 4, its joint loss for \(K\) particles is \[
 \ell(\theta_{1:K};x,y)
 =\frac1K\sum_{i=1}^K l(\theta_i;x,y)
   +\alpha l_{\rm div}(\theta_{1:K};x,y),
 \qquad \alpha>0.\] Let \(f^i_{-y}\) contain the prediction probabilities after deleting the true-label coordinate, and let \[
 F=\left[\frac{f^1_{-y}}{\|f^1_{-y}\|},\ldots,
          \frac{f^K_{-y}}{\|f^K_{-y}\|}\right]
 \in\mathbb R^{(C-1)\times K}.\] Section 4.3, p. 5, defines \(l_{\rm div}=\det(F^\top F)\). Page 6 identifies this with squared spanned volume and states the intention to maximize that volume, while retaining the positive sign in the minimized objective.

The statistical development uses an independent joint distribution \(Q^K\), with \(Q\) subsequently represented as \(K^{-1}\sum_i\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2I)\) and prior \(P=\mathcal N(0,I)\). Corollary 4.3 supplies the Gaussian complexity term used to motivate the practical objective. These are central links between the proposed mechanism and its formal justification.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The printed minimization has the opposite diversity preference).  Assessment: Major. The positive determinant term in [eq:loss] (#eq:loss) rewards less diversity when minimized, contrary to its stated role in the central method.
## Decisive example and assumptions

Consider one input, three classes, true label \(0\), and two particles. All probabilities below are strictly positive and sum to one, so they are attainable softmax outputs. Compare \[\begin{aligned}
 f^1=f^2&=(0.8,0.1,0.1), &&\text{collapsed case},\\
 f^1&=(0.8,0.19,0.01),\quad
 f^2=(0.8,0.01,0.19), &&\text{diverse case}.\end{aligned}\] The mean cross-entropy is \(-\log0.8\) in both cases. In the collapsed case the normalized non-target columns coincide, giving determinant zero. In the diverse case their inner product is \(19/181\), hence \[\det(F^\top F)=1-\left(\frac{19}{181}\right)^2
 =\frac{32400}{32761}\simeq0.9889808.\] At the paper’s \(\alpha=0.02\), the printed losses are \[\ell_{\rm collapsed}=0.2231435513,\qquad
 \ell_{\rm diverse}=0.2429231673.\] Thus the printed minimization strictly prefers the collapsed pair while the supervised component is held fixed. The example directly tests the defined diversity loss; it does not assume a complete optimization trajectory or replace the DRO problem with an empirical claim.
## Counterevidence and correction

The preserved release differs: , lines 290–296, uses a negative log-determinant; , lines 33–54, forms the normalized Gram matrix, adds \(10^{-7}I\) and computes its log-determinant. Minimizing this negative quantity encourages a larger regularized determinant. This is substantive counterevidence against claiming that the inspected code literally minimizes the wrong-sign determinant.

It does not reconcile the published equations with their stated meaning or establish which implementation produced the reported tables. Reversing the determinant’s sign, or specifying the actual negative log-determinant and its regularization throughout, addresses the local direction. The latter also changes the objective and its range, so the theorem’s loss-bound assumptions need rechecking. No complete theoretical repair or historical-code binding is certified.
The finding is Major because the incorrect optimization preference is in the mechanism named as the central contribution, independently of any benchmark reversal or difficulty of repair.

Problem 2 (The binary-task diversity mechanism is constant).  Assessment: Major. For binary classification, the normalized non-target construction cannot supply the claimed particle-diversity pressure, including for the reported Camelyon task.
## Exact rank calculation

For \(C=2\), every non-target vector is a positive scalar \(a_i\). Its normalization is \(a_i/|a_i|=1\). Therefore \[F=[1,\ldots,1],\qquad F^\top F=\mathbf1_K\mathbf1_K^\top.\] For \(K>1\), the printed determinant is identically zero, independent of all particle predictions. More generally, the printed determinant vanishes whenever \(K>C-1\), because the Gram matrix lacks full rank.

The release’s jitter does not restore a binary prediction signal. For a hard-label binary example, \[\det(\mathbf1_K\mathbf1_K^\top+\varepsilon I)
 =\varepsilon^{K-1}(K+\varepsilon).\] This is positive but constant. At \(K=4\), \(\varepsilon=10^{-7}\), its negative logarithm is \(46.9679925668\), with zero prediction derivative in exact arithmetic. This conclusion concerns mathematical signal, not floating-point residuals.
## Connection to the reported task

Page 7 states that the Bayesian methods use four particles. The staged , lines 103–108, assigns two classes to `patch_camelyon`, and , line 27, sets four particles. Camelyon appears in the main comparisons and diversity ablations. The counterexample is therefore tied to an actual low-class-count setting of the core mechanism, rather than an unrelated unsupported application.

The source masks coordinates using the target tensor. The exact code corroboration above uses hard labels, matching the mathematical definition of removing the ground-truth label. Soft-label masking conventions require separate care and are not used to claim an executed training result.
## Counterevidence, impact and correction

Robustness regularization, supervised loss, ensembling and other training differences may still improve Camelyon accuracy. The calculation does not falsify the reported score. Nor does it prove that all multiclass settings lack a diversity signal: regularized Gram objectives can vary in higher-dimensional cases.

The supported Major finding is the absence of the claimed explicit interaction signal in a reported application of the principal mechanism. Fixing the sign in Problem 1 alone does not fix it. A rank-aware diversity construction, a different representation, or a stated restricted domain would be needed. No replacement method or its empirical behavior is verified here.
Problem 3 (The Gaussian KL substitution is incorrect).  Assessment: Major. Corollary 4.3 and its p. 18 proof use a false Gaussian KL expression in a central generalization-bound derivation.
## Original and correct quantities

Equation reference: eq:wrongkl, eq:rightkl. Convexity in the first argument gives the valid mixture inequality \[\mathrm{KL}\left(\frac1K\sum_i\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2I)
       \,\middle\Vert\,\mathcal N(0,I)\right)
 \le\frac1K\sum_i
   \mathrm{KL}(\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2I)\Vert\mathcal N(0,I)).\] The proof then replaces the right side by \[
 \frac1{2K}\sum_i(\|\mu_i\|^2+d\sigma-d\log\sigma).\] For standard deviation \(\sigma>0\), direct expectation of the Gaussian log-density ratio instead gives \[
 \frac1{2K}\sum_i
 \bigl(\|\mu_i\|^2+d(\sigma^2-1-2\log\sigma)\bigr).\] The paper’s covariance notation and reparameterization \(\theta_i=\mu_i+\sigma\epsilon_i\) both identify \(\sigma\) as a standard deviation; interpreting it as a variance would not reproduce [eq:wrongkl] (#eq:wrongkl) either.
## Admissible finite witness

Take \(d=1\), all \(\mu_i=0\), and the practical value \(\sigma=0.1\). Coincident mixture means are not excluded by the stated family, and the mixture is then exactly \(\mathcal N(0,0.01)\), so the mixture inequality is equality. Its actual KL is \[\tfrac12(0.01-1-2\log0.1)=1.8075850930.\] The printed substitution gives \(\tfrac12(0.1-\log0.1)=1.2012925465\), an underestimate of \(0.6062925465\). Thus the substituted expression is neither the asserted equality nor a valid upper bound in this case. This checks the Gaussian substitution itself; it does not purport to construct an entire statistical experiment violating every possible version of the final bound.
## Impact, counterevidence and bounded repair

Conditional on the preceding theorem and its hypotheses, replacing the Gaussian term would produce the complexity contribution \[L\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i\|\mu_i\|^2+
       Kd(\sigma^2-1-2\log\sigma)+2\log(1/\delta)}{4N}}.\] The full PAC-Bayesian/DRO argument is not certified by this local correction. In particular, uniformity requirements, the loss bound, and the relationship between iid mixture draws and one draw from each component deserve separate checking.

The practical fixed-\(\sigma\) setting makes the erroneous part a constant with respect to the means, so this error alone need not alter their gradients or measured accuracy. It nevertheless invalidates the displayed derivation of a central formal bound. That supports Major under the requested standard without asserting that the final statistical inequality is false in every setting.
# Empirical arithmetic and unresolved correspondence
The parent transcribed the 19 Table 1 entries per method from original p. 7 and independently calculated their ordinary unweighted means:
Method | Printed AVG | Mean of displayed tasks
BayesTune | 68.5 | 72.1474

Several discrepancies are much larger than rounding of one-decimal task entries. Under equal task weighting, BayesTune is the strongest listed baseline and the IBDR margin is \(1.6421\) percentage points, compared with \(2.7\) from the printed AVG column. IBDR remains first under that recomputation.

This is a demonstrated mismatch with the ordinary 19-task mean, but the raw aggregation records are unavailable. The review therefore records Needs Evidence for whether stale entries, an unstated weighting convention or another reporting issue explains the column; it does not silently choose which individual task results are correct. The small SAM discrepancy is not independently elevated, because rounding can matter at that scale.

Static inspection also shows that the release averages prediction logits before cross-entropy, whereas the displayed joint loss averages individual losses. The inspected code imports a `swag` component not supplied in the bounded snapshot and contains configuration/interface differences. These observations limit exact reproducibility and paper–release correspondence; no runtime failure or historical training error is claimed. Dataset code’s class count is used above, but no datasets were downloaded.
# Conclusion and limitations

Three Major Problems are supported, with distinct dependencies and counterevidence: the sign of the central diversity objective, the absence of binary diversity signal, and the invalid Gaussian KL substitution. They are not a claim that all results fail. Title: Technical Verification of Transformer Training Dynamics for Regular Language Recognition
# Identity and scope

This report reviews Ruiquan Huang, Yingbin Liang, and Jing Yang, How Transformers Learn Regular Language Recognition: A Theoretical Study on Training Dynamics and Implicit Bias, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 25516–25549 (I25-43533), in the exact staged published-proceedings PDF. Page numbers mean printed internal pages 1–34, equal to the one-based PDF index.

The main training formulation, Phase 1 and Phase 2 claims, mathematical appendices, and experiment descriptions were examined by an auxiliary scientist. The parent independently checked the operative training rule, assumptions, margin definition, horizon and proof dependencies, and the two-step counterexample. Source pages 3, 4, 6, 13, 23, 26, and 28 were visually inspected by the parent. One central derivation problem supports Major; a separate local false symmetry statement supports Minor. These findings do not establish that the tasks cannot be learned or that the experiments are false.
# Model and assumptions

For every binary string \(s\) of length \(L\le L_{\max}\), write \(X_s\) for its matrix of orthonormal position–token embeddings, and \(x_{s,L}\) for its last token. The attention representation and scalar prediction are \[v_s(W)=X_s\operatorname{softmax}(X_s^\top W x_{s,L}/\lambda),
\qquad f_s(u,W)=\langle u,v_s(W)\rangle.\] The even-pairs label is \(y_s=1\) if the first and last tokens agree, and \(-1\) otherwise. The loss sums the average logistic loss at each length: \[\mathcal L(u,W)=\sum_{L=1}^{L_{\max}}2^{-L}
\sum_{s\in\{a,b\}^L}\log(1+e^{-y_sf_s(u,W)}).\] Initialization is \(u_0=W_0=0\). In Phase 1, \[u_{t+1}=u_t-\eta\nabla_u\mathcal L_t,\qquad
W_{t+1}=W_t-\eta\lambda\nabla_W\mathcal L_t.\] Theorem 4.1 (p. 5) chooses \(\lambda=\Omega(L_{\max}^2)\), \(t_0=O((\eta L_{\max})^{-1})\), and \(\eta=O(\min\{L_{\max}^{-1},\lambda^{-2/3}\})\). Phase 2 uses learning rate \(\eta\) for both parameter blocks. The max-margin vector \(u^\ast\) is the minimum-norm vector satisfying \(y_s\langle u^\ast,v_s(W_{t_0})\rangle\ge1\) for every training string. The following analysis grants the claimed Phase 1 separability.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Incompatible margin dependence and Phase 2 proof horizon).  The horizon used to prove the central Phase 2 claims is inconsistent with the margin dependence generated by the stated Phase 1 dynamics.
## Original claims and proof dependency
## Complete check of the parameter dependence

Equation reference: eq:Wbound. The logistic derivative has absolute value at most one, \(\|v_s(W)\|\le1\), and the softmax Jacobian has operator norm at most one. Since the loss has one average term per length, \[\|\nabla_u\mathcal L_t\|\le L_{\max},\qquad
\|\nabla_W\mathcal L_t\|\le L_{\max}\|u_t\|/\lambda.\] Thus \(\|u_t\|\le\eta L_{\max}t\), and the actual Phase 1 update gives \[
\|W_{t_0}\|\le
\eta L_{\max}\sum_{s=0}^{t_0-1}\|u_s\|
\le \frac{\eta^2L_{\max}^2t_0(t_0-1)}2=:B.\] Write \(t_0\le c/(\eta L_{\max})\) with the fixed constant allowed by the stated asymptotic regime. Then \(B\le c^2/2\), independently of \(\lambda\).

Equation reference: eq:margin. Now retain only the four length-two strings \(aa,bb,ab,ba\), with labels \(+,+,-,-\). At uniform attention, \[v_{aa}(0)+v_{bb}(0)-v_{ab}(0)-v_{ba}(0)=0.\] Orthonormal columns and the softmax Lipschitz bound imply \(\|v_s(W)-v_s(0)\|\le\|W\|/\lambda\). For any feasible unit-margin separator, summing its four margin inequalities yields \[4\le\left\langle u,\sum_s y_s v_s(W)\right\rangle
=\left\langle u,\sum_s y_s(v_s(W)-v_s(0))\right\rangle
\le4\|u\|\|W\|/\lambda.\] Consequently, whenever the promised separator exists, \[
\|u^\ast\|\ge\lambda/\|W_{t_0}\|
\ge\lambda/B\ge2\lambda/c^2.\] If \(W_{t_0}=0\), these four features are not separable; this cannot rescue the asserted Phase 2 argument.

For the second entry to be the minimum in [eq:T] (#eq:T), one needs \[\|u^\ast\|\le \frac{2^{4/3}}{3}\lambda^{2/3}.\] This contradicts [eq:margin] (#eq:margin) as \(\lambda\) grows with fixed \(c\) and \(L_{\max}\ge2\). The condition \(\lambda=\Omega(L_{\max}^2)\) does not provide the missing upper bound on the margin norm. An admissible scaling family is \(L_{\max}=2\), \(\lambda=n\), \(\eta=1/n\), and \(t_0=\lfloor cn/2\rfloor\), with fixed sufficiently small \(c>0\); it satisfies the stated step-size and Phase 1 orders.

Furthermore, [eq:t1] (#eq:t1) implies \[t_1>\frac{14\|u^\ast\|^2}{\eta}
\ge\frac{56\lambda^2}{c^4\eta},
\qquad
\frac{t_1}{T}>
\frac{56\,2^{2/3}L_{\max}}{c^4}\lambda^{4/3}.\] The proof’s chosen sufficient threshold therefore exceeds the proved horizon in that regime. Restoring the literal minimum in [eq:T] (#eq:T) only makes the horizon smaller. The proof has not established a nonempty time interval where all its premises apply.
## Finite diagnostic and loss implication

For \(\eta=10^{-3}\), \(\lambda=100\), \(L_{\max}=2\), and \(t_0=50\), the independent calculation gives \(B=0.0049\), \(\|u^\ast\|\ge20408.1633\), second horizon \(6786.0440\), first horizon at most \(202.0726\), and \(t_1>5.8309\times10^{12}\). These are evaluations of analytic bounds, not a claimed numerical solution of the max-margin problem. The asymptotic argument is the decisive contradiction and does not depend on choosing unspecified constants for this illustration.
## Impact and counterevidence

This is Major: a demonstrated invalid derivation directly supports the central alignment, loss-convergence, and reused parity guarantees. Phase 1 separability was granted, and the experiments and qualitative two-phase behavior are not refuted. Hidden constants that depend arbitrarily on \(\lambda\) cannot justify a conclusion obtained by sending \(\lambda\) upward. A replacement result needs a proved compatible time regime and complete margin dependence. No such complete repair is certified.

Problem 2 (Query-position symmetry in Lemma B.1 is false).  Lemma B.1 (p. 13) asserts \[\langle E_\ell^w,W_tE_L^w\rangle
=\langle E_\ell^{-w},W_tE_L^w\rangle
\quad\text{for all }\ell\ge2.\] Its sample-pairing argument incorrectly treats flipping the last token as label-preserving.
## Admissible two-step counterexample

Set \(L_{\max}=2\), use the full six-string training set with the stated length weights and orthonormal embeddings, and start from zero. Choose positive \(\eta,\lambda\) in the stated regime with two Phase 1 updates. Direct differentiation gives \[u_1=\frac{\eta}{4}(E_1^a+E_1^b),\qquad W_1=0.\] At the next update, \[\langle E_2^a,W_2E_2^a\rangle
=\frac{\eta^2}{64}\tanh(\eta/16)>0,\qquad
\langle E_2^b,W_2E_2^a\rangle=0.\] Indeed, the latter coordinate never appears with query \(E_2^a\): a length-two sequence with last token \(a\) has no position-two token \(b\). The two same-query sequences produce the stated nonzero diagonal after their logistic contributions are combined.

The independently written enumeration at \(\eta=0.001,\lambda=100\) returns \(9.76562498728945\times10^{-13}\) versus zero; the analytic diagonal is \(9.765624987284342\times10^{-13}\). The tiny rounding difference between the two nonzero evaluations does not affect the strict inequality.
## Bounded impact

This is Minor. The false equality concerns a query-position coordinate that is inactive for that query. Interior-position and global token-flip symmetries may still support the intended sample reduction; no additional core failure is established from this defect. Correcting the position domain is necessary, but a boundary edit has not been certified to repair every downstream proof. This judgment is based on functional dependence, not appendix location.

Title: Technical Verification of Think Twice, Act Once: A Co-Evolution Framework of LLM and RL for Large-Scale Decision Making
# Identity, sources and scope

This report concerns Xu Wan, Wenyue Xu, Chao Yang and Mingyang Sun, Think Twice, Act Once: A Co-Evolution Framework of LLM and RL for Large-Scale Decision Making, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 62102–62120 (I25-43534). The supplied proceedings PDF contains 19 pages, with embedded appendices. References below use one-based PDF pages. The publisher reference is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wan25g.html.

The complete manifest, source-availability record, scientific text and appendices were read by native auxiliary `/root/review_0162`. The parent verified manifest-listed file hashes, rechecked the decisive original formulas and tables, visually inspected pp. 5, 8, 9 and 18, and independently recalculated the normalization example and reported ratios.

No paper-specific released implementation was located in the staged source preparation. This is a bounded availability statement, not proof that no private or unindexed code exists. Additional OpenReview-only attachments were inaccessible. There was no author-code execution, model call, installation or download by this reviewer.
# Scientific reconstruction

ACE uses an RL policy for environment actions and deployment. During training, an LLM Actor refines selected low-reward actions, and an LLM Critic adjusts selected trajectory rewards. Refined one-step transitions are checked by simulation, collected in a separate buffer and used in weighted replay; the mixed buffer also supports LLM fine-tuning.

The paper is an empirical framework. It does not state a general convergence theorem, a theorem preserving the original optimal policy under arbitrary reward edits, or an unbiased importance-sampling guarantee for its exponential reward weights. Those stronger claims are not imposed as premises of this review.

Using a simulated replacement action to form a fresh off-policy transition is coherent in principle. It does not require treating an unchanged remainder of the old trajectory as though the replacement action had generated it. The described learning unit is a transition. The scientific questions instead concern the validity and normalization of the actual sampling rule, the meaning of modified rewards, and comparable measurement of interaction budgets.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (Mixed replay is undefined when the LLM validity normalizer is zero).  Assessment: Minor, published specification. Historical implementation handling and empirical consequences remain Needs Evidence.
## Original definition and dependencies

Equation reference: eq:mix. Equation (7), p. 4, defines \[I_v(\tau)=\mathbf1\{\widehat r(s,\widehat a)\ge0
                  \ \land\ \neg d(\widehat s')\}.\] Equations (8)–(9), p. 5, then define \[w_r(\tau)=
 \frac{\exp(\widehat r(s,\widehat a)/\beta)}
      {\exp(r(s,a)/\beta)}\] and, with \(Z_{\rm LLM}=\sum_{\tau'\in D_{\rm LLM}}I_v(\tau')w_r(\tau')\), \[
 p_{\rm mix}(\tau)=
 \begin{cases}
 (1-\beta)/|D_{\rm RL}|,&\tau\in D_{\rm RL},\\
 \beta I_v(\tau)w_r(\tau)/Z_{\rm LLM},&
                          \tau\in D_{\rm LLM}.
 \end{cases}\] The buffer components are interpreted as tagged replay entries. Algorithm 1, p. 5, lines 21 and 27, invokes this distribution for RL updates and construction of the fine-tuning buffer. The practical refinement process allows at most five attempts when proposed actions remain inferior (Section 4.3, p. 6). A finite attempt limit does not ensure a valid refinement.
## A permitted zero-normalizer case

Take a nonempty RL buffer and \(\beta=1/2\). Let the LLM buffer contain one unsuccessful refinement with \(r=-1\), \(\widehat r=-1\) and terminal flag \(\widehat d=1\). Negative rewards and terminal outcomes are explicitly part of the gate’s domain, and unsuccessful finite refinement attempts are not excluded. Then \[w_r=1,\qquad I_v=0,\qquad Z_{\rm LLM}=0.\] The LLM branch in [eq:mix] (#eq:mix) is \(0/0\). Meanwhile, summing the RL branch gives only \(1-\beta=1/2\). The displayed rule therefore does not define a probability distribution.

Discarding invalid candidates before storage does not by itself complete the specification. In that case \(D_{\rm LLM}\) can be empty, but the stated RL branch still carries only mass \(1-\beta\) unless an explicit fallback changes it. The issue also applies before any valid refinement has been collected.
## Counterevidence and verified local completion

An actual implementation could delay mixed updates, fall back to RL-only replay, or adapt a separate mixture weight. No available executable source establishes whether it did so. The finding is not an observed crash and does not show that published trajectories used an invalid distribution.

For nonempty \(D_{\rm RL}\), a sufficient mathematical completion is to use \[p(\tau)=|D_{\rm RL}|^{-1}\quad(\tau\in D_{\rm RL}),\qquad
 p(\tau)=0\quad(\tau\in D_{\rm LLM})\] when \(Z_{\rm LLM}=0\), retaining [eq:mix] (#eq:mix) when \(Z_{\rm LLM}>0\). This fallback has total mass one, while the positive-normalizer branch has component masses \(1-\beta\) and \(\beta\). This completion does not require substituting \(\beta=0\) into the exponential temperature expression.

Only the normalization property of this local completion has been verified. It is not an executed code repair, a proof of learning performance or evidence of author adoption. Its bounded missing-case character supports Minor; no unsupported larger impact is assigned.
# Checked empirical statements
The main percentage claims in Section 4.4 agree with Table 1, original p. 8, to the stated precision:
Comparison | Values | Relative gain
WCCI 2020: ACE Qwen+SFT versus expert RL | 69.8/57.1 | 22.2417%
WCCI 2020: ACE Qwen+SFT versus GPT-4 | 69.8/29.5 | 136.6102%
NeurIPS 2020: ACE versus best listed non-ACE baseline | 145.3/131.5 | 10.4943%
WCCI 2022: ACE Qwen+SFT versus expert RL | 75.9/31.0 | 144.8387%
The calculation is \(100(a-b)/b\) in each row. This validates numerical correspondence between the text and table, not the underlying experiments.

Figure 8, p. 18, shows substantial ACE gains on difficult scenarios, but some easier scenarios favor RL slightly. The evidence supports an aggregate improvement with heterogeneous scenario effects. It does not support literal superiority on every individual scenario; this is retained as a scope clarification.

The ablation tables, computational-overhead table and example prompts were read. Their reported comparisons are not independently reproduced because raw runs, training code and model traces are unavailable.
# Needs Evidence: units and interaction accounting

Section 4.6, original p. 9, describes the expert-RL budget as 100K timesteps. Figure 8, p. 18, calls the ACE and RL budgets 40K episodes and 100K episodes; Figures 9–10 and Table 6 also use episodes. Table 1 instead labels its column Sample Requirements, with entries such as \(40\mathrm K+287\).

These units cannot be interchanged. Described episodes can last 864 or 2016 steps and may terminate early. Without the actual counters or logs, the review cannot select timesteps or episodes as the correct interpretation, or reconstruct the total number of environment calls. The 287 refinements should likewise not be described as the entire training budget: the table expressly includes the additional \(40\mathrm K\) term.

The missing evidence is a definition and accounting of ordinary environment transitions, completed or attempted episodes, accepted LLM refinements, rejected simulated refinements within the up-to-five-round process, and the units of the training curves. This uncertainty affects interpretation of absolute sample efficiency. It does not demonstrate that the reported reward improvements are false.
# Other assumptions and limits
## Terminal handling and weighting

The displayed SAC target in Eq. (2), p. 3, omits an explicit terminal mask even though transitions have a terminal flag. An absorbing-state convention or implementation mask could make the intended target correct; no code is available to distinguish these cases. An implementation error is not established from the shorthand alone.

The reward weight enters both the sampling distribution and the policy objective in Eq. (10), amplifying selected refinements. That is a heuristic change of objective. The paper does not establish it as an unbiased density-ratio correction, so the absence of such a theorem is not labeled a refuted guarantee.
## Reward changes and deployment cost

The Critic’s discretized reward modifications need additional conditions to preserve the optimum of the original reward function. The inspected text presents its relationship to TD(\(\lambda\)) as a conceptual connection, not a proved exact equivalence or policy-invariance theorem. The relation between modified training rewards and raw evaluation rewards remains evidence-dependent.

For WCCI 2022, Table 1’s total test times are 1440.0 seconds for expert RL, 3627.2 for ACE Qwen+SFT and 7478.9 for ACE GPT-4. The latter ratios are \(2.5189\) and \(5.1937\). These are total evaluation times, potentially affected by different survival lengths and numbers of executed decisions. They do not alone determine per-decision latency or refute a real-time deployment claim. A full latency distribution was not available.
## Action inventory and external validity

Appendix A describes large action spaces and a cardinality expression. Exact allowed-action inventories and per-substation element counts were not supplied for independent enumeration of the 60K/70K figures. No action-pruning optimality guarantee was established or refuted. The external baseline papers and Grid2Op implementation were not independently audited, and later revisions or errata were not checked.
# Conclusion

One Minor specification defect is demonstrated. No Major error was established in the declared inspected scope. The main gain arithmetic is consistent; sample-efficiency units, total interaction accounting, terminal conventions and historical implementation handling need additional evidence.

Scientific adjudication is pending, and `human_reviews` is empty. The only verified repair is the probability normalization of an explicit RL-only fallback. No empirical reproduction, accepted scientific correction or author adoption is claimed.
