Title: Technical Verification of Importance Corrected Neural JKO Sampling
# Paper identity, version and review scope

This report concerns Johannes Hertrich and Robert Gruhlke, Importance Corrected Neural JKO Sampling, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 23083–23119 (I25-43535). The inspected proceedings PDF has 37 pages, including appendices; page references below are one-based PDF pages. The exact original hash is reproduced in the appendix and recorded in the accompanying provenance file. The source landing reference is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/hertrich25a.html. The preserved public implementation is commit `74fe27a2d5472bd25fc2bc58a7a3fe59edd8e488` of https://github.com/johertrich/neural_JKO_ic; its equivalence to the historical experimental code is unverified.

The auxiliary task read the full original extraction, including the proofs and experimental appendices, and statically traced the principal model, training, CNF, evaluation and configuration files. The parent checked the decisive original pages, re-read the relevant implementation paths, verified all manifest-listed source hashes, and independently recomputed the witnesses below. No author code, model, dataset or benchmark was executed. Additional OpenReview attachments were inaccessible during source preparation. Later revisions and errata have not been assessed.
# Scientific reconstruction and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:jko. The paper represents a JKO update by a continuous normalizing flow and interleaves learned transport with importance-based rejection corrections. The exact proximal update is \[
 \mu_\tau^{k+1}\in\arg\min_\mu
 \left\{\mathcal F(\mu)+\frac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\mu,\mu_\tau^k)\right\}.\] The theoretical velocity fields in Theorem 3.3 are minimizers of the exact dynamic problem. They should not be identified with arbitrary approximate neural-network optimizers.

Assumption 3.1 requires \(\mathcal F:\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) to be proper, narrowly lower semicontinuous, coercive, bounded below and \(\lambda\)-convex along generalized geodesics. Its finite-slope domain is required to lie in \(\mathcal P_2^{ac}\), and the initial absolutely continuous measure must have finite metric slope. Theorem 3.3 asserts strong convergence of the exact concatenated velocities as \(\tau\downarrow0\). Corollary 3.2 identifies their interpolated curves with geodesic interpolation.

The rejection correction is a separate contribution. For acceptance function \(\alpha\) and \(a=\mathbb E_\mu\alpha\), its density has the form \[\widetilde p(x)=p(x)\bigl(\alpha(x)+1-a\bigr).\] It is normalized, and can be written as \(a\eta+(1-a)\mu\) with \(\eta\) the normalized accepted distribution when \(a>0\). The auxiliary review checked the corresponding mixture algebra and the stated KL argument under the paper’s exact-distribution assumptions. This does not certify numerical ODE densities, estimated normalizers or trained neural flows.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Missing time-step factor in the strong-convergence proof).  Assessment: Major. Appendix B.3, PDF p. 20, uses an invalid action identity in the proof supporting Theorem 3.3, a central theoretical contribution.
## Original claim and dependency

Equation reference: eq:action, eq:correctaction. Corollary 3.2(i), p. 5, correctly states \[
 W_2^2(\mu_\tau^k,\mu_\tau^{k+1})
 =\tau\int_{k\tau}^{(k+1)\tau}
     \|v_\tau(\cdot,t)\|_{L^2(\gamma_\tau(t))}^2\,dt .\] The velocity convention in Eq. (9), p. 16, is also \((T_\tau^k-I)/\tau\). Nevertheless, the p. 20 proof replaces the total integral by an unscaled sum of squared distances. With \(K\) steps the correct identity is \[
 A_\tau:=\int_0^{K\tau}\|v_\tau\|^2\,dt
 =\frac1\tau\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}
       W_2^2(\mu_\tau^k,\mu_\tau^{k+1}).\] There is also a local index mismatch in the displayed sum. The missing factor, rather than the index typography, is the material issue.
## An admissible exact witness

Take \(d=1\), \(\nu=\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\mathcal F(\mu)=\mathrm{KL}(\mu\Vert\nu)\), and \(\mu^0=\mathcal N(1,1)\). Relative entropy to this Gaussian is nonnegative, proper, narrowly lower semicontinuous, coercive and \(1\)-convex in the stated sense. Its finite-slope domain is absolutely continuous; the initial squared slope is \(1\). Thus this is within the paper’s assumptions.

The global minimizer in [eq:jko] (#eq:jko) is \(\mathcal N(m/(1+\tau),1)\) when the previous measure is \(\mathcal N(m,1)\). This is not merely a restriction to an arbitrarily chosen Gaussian subfamily. For a competitor of mean \(a\), write \(\bar\mu\) for its centered translate. Then \[\begin{aligned}
 W_2^2(\mu,\mathcal N(m,1))
  &=(a-m)^2+W_2^2(\bar\mu,\mathcal N(0,1)),\\
 \mathrm{KL}(\mu\Vert\mathcal N(0,1))
  &=\frac{a^2}{2}+\mathrm{KL}(\bar\mu\Vert\mathcal N(0,1)).\end{aligned}\] The centered terms are nonnegative and jointly minimized by \(\bar\mu=\mathcal N(0,1)\). Minimizing the remaining scalar quadratic gives \(a=m/(1+\tau)\).

For \(\tau=1/2\), \(K=2\) and \(T=1\), the successive means are \(1,2/3,4/9\). Consequently \[\sum_{k=0}^1W_2^2(\mu_\tau^k,\mu_\tau^{k+1})
 =\frac19+\frac4{81}=\frac{13}{81},
 \qquad A_\tau=\frac{26}{81}.\] The p. 20 equality is therefore false by a factor of two in this instance. More decisively, for \(\tau=1/K\), \[A_\tau=\frac{1-(1+\tau)^{-2K}}{2+\tau}
 \longrightarrow \frac{1-e^{-2}}2>0,
 \qquad \sum_k W_2^2=\tau A_\tau\longrightarrow0.\] The unscaled sum and the actual action have different limits.
## Why restoring the factor does not complete the printed proof

The proof uses endpoint error \(W_2(\mu_\tau^k,\gamma(k\tau))\le C\tau\). Put \(b_k=W_2(\gamma(k\tau),\gamma((k+1)\tau))\) and \(I_\tau=\int_0^{K\tau}\|\widehat v\|^2\,dt\). After restoring [eq:correctaction] (#eq:correctaction), the displayed triangle-inequality strategy yields only \[\begin{aligned}
 A_\tau
 &\le 4KC^2\tau+4C\sum_k b_k+\frac1\tau\sum_k b_k^2\\
 &\le 4KC^2\tau+4C\sqrt{K\tau I_\tau}+I_\tau.\end{aligned}\] Here \(b_k^2\le\tau\int_{k\tau}^{(k+1)\tau}\|\widehat v\|^2dt\) follows from the dynamic distance bound. The first two excess terms do not vanish merely from \(K\tau\to T\). The square expansion in the original proof also loses a factor of two in its cross term. Thus the printed reasoning does not establish the limsup estimate used in its next, strong-convergence step.
## Counterevidence, impact and correction

The Gaussian witness does not refute strong convergence; its exact velocities converge to the Gaussian gradient flow. A different energy-dissipation argument may prove the theorem. No complete repaired proof is certified here. The supported Major conclusion is that a demonstrated invalid derivation lies directly in the proof of the core velocity-convergence claim. Neither failed benchmarks nor impossibility of repair is needed for that assessment. The rejection-density identity and empirical results are not refuted by this finding.

Problem 2 (The appendix’s explicit velocity has the ascent sign).  Assessment: Minor. Appendix B.1, pp. 15–16, gives \(v=+
abla(\delta\mathcal F/\delta\mu)\) and, for reverse KL, \(v=
abla\log p-
abla\log q\).

The main definition on p. 4 instead uses the descent convention \(v\in-\partial\mathcal F\), with continuity equation \(\partial_t p+
abla\cdot(pv)=0\). For \(p=\mathcal N(m,1)\) and \(q=\mathcal N(0,1)\), \[
abla\log p-
abla\log q=m.\] The appendix’s sign therefore gives \(m'=m\) and \( rac{d}{dt}\mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q)=m^2>0\) for \(m
e0\); descent requires \(m'=-m\). This directly checks the stated formula under smooth positive densities satisfying the assumptions.

The main negative-subgradient definition and variational minimization are counterevidence against alleging that the trained algorithm follows ascent. The local correction is a minus sign in the explicit gradient-flow formulas. No observed implementation reversal or additional core dependency was established, so the assessment remains Minor.

Problem 3 (The neural objective does not implement the stated JKO step).  Assessment: Major. The objective in Eq. (5), p. 5, and the first objective on p. 6 contains \(\frac12\int\|v\|^2\). On p. 6, \(\dot\omega=\|v\|^2\), but Eq. (6) adds \(\omega\) rather than \(\omega/2\).

For the same one-dimensional Gaussian family, the defined JKO objective minimizes \[\frac{a^2}{2}+\frac{(a-m)^2}{2\tau},
 \qquad a_{\rm JKO}=\frac{m}{1+\tau}.\] Doubling its transport penalty instead gives \(a=m/(1+\tau/2)\). At \(\tau=1/2\), \(m=1\), these are \(2/3\) and \(4/5\).

Algorithm 3 in Appendix D.1 (p. 23) explicitly optimizes Eq. (6), so this objective is on the central neural-JKO training path. The release statically corroborates the discrepancy: accumulates the squared velocity norm; with its unit integration duration, , lines 98–104, adds the resulting penalty divided by `tau`, without a factor \(1/2\). No author code was executed.

This is a Major derivation defect in the correspondence between the defined JKO step and the central neural training objective: Eq. (6) doubles the kinetic term derived from Eq. (5), and the Gaussian witness changes the exact optimizer at the same stated step size. Adding the missing half, or explicitly setting \(\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau/2\), supplies a local reconciliation. This reparameterization preserves a JKO family and may preserve convergence and practical performance; it does not make the printed derivation valid. The severity follows the demonstrated core dependency, without requiring benchmark loss or a difficult repair. No benchmark degradation or complete verified implementation patch is claimed.

Problem 4 (Shifted latent densities are evaluated without recentering).  Assessment: Minor, release-specific. In , the zero-centered `latent_energy` expression is also used by `energy_evaluation` on a recovered latent coordinate without subtracting `latent_mean`.

Lines 22–39 define the latent mean, zero-centered energy, and sampling path. Sampling computes energy before translating the sample and is consistent. Lines 91–92 of the evaluation path instead pass the shifted coordinate directly to the zero-centered expression.

A valid zero-layer instance with \(d=1\), scale \(1\), latent mean \(1\) and evaluation point \(x=1\) has density \(\mathcal N(1,1)\). The correct negative log density is \[\frac12\log(2\pi)=0.9189385332,\] whereas the released evaluation expression gives \(\frac12[1+\log(2\pi)]=1.4189385332\). Its reported-to-true density ratio is \(e^{-1/2}=0.6065306597\).

The default zero-mean configuration is unaffected. The LGCP configuration enables finding a nonzero latent mean, making the option substantive; however, the inspected evaluation routine in , lines 156–162, calls `model.sample`, whose latent-energy handling is different and correct for this translation. Historical benchmark harm is consequently unproved. A local correction is to recenter the argument at the `energy_evaluation` call. Changing the shared energy function without adjusting sampling would require additional review.
# Other checks and unresolved evidence

The exact-density rejection correction should be distinguished from numerical density evaluation. The release uses stochastic trace estimation in dimensions above its configured threshold, and the appendix discusses the approximation. Its existence is not an undisclosed defect. The inspected theory does not establish arbitrary neural approximation or finite-optimization guarantees.

The auxiliary task read the reported target examples, ablations and evaluation procedures, and traced the CNF, training, metrics, configurations and loading paths statically. Raw model outputs, normalization estimates, run-to-run variation and empirical tables were not independently reproduced. This review makes no claim that the reported comparisons are numerically false.

Only the supplied proceedings version and preserved release were assessed. Additional attachments, later corrections and historical source correspondence remain unavailable or unchecked. A local corrected equation is not a certified repaired theorem, an executed implementation patch, or evidence of author adoption.
# Conclusion

The highest supported assessment is Major: the invalid action estimate supports Theorem 3.3, and the missing kinetic half breaks the derivation of the central neural training objective. The appendix velocity sign and shifted latent-evaluation defects remain Minor, with their distinct dependencies and counterevidence. All scientific adjudication is pending; there are no human review entries. Repair verification is limited to the scalar and algebraic calculations explicitly shown, and author adoption is unknown.

Title: Technical Verification of Diffusion Sampling Correction via Approximately 10 Parameters
# Identity, version and scope

This report concerns Guangyi Wang, Wei Peng, Lijiang Li, Wenyu Chen, Yuren Cai and Songzhi Su, Diffusion Sampling Correction via Approximately 10 Parameters, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 64023–64043 (I25-43536). The inspected proceedings PDF has 21 pages including appendices. Page references below use the one-based original PDF index. The publisher reference is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wang25cd.html.

The preserved implementation is https://github.com/onefly123/PAS, commit ea6951bf815e30852d564e40399bb60d9b3a2ee3. Its correspondence to historical conference runs is unverified. The auxiliary read the complete original extraction and relevant source paths; the parent rehashed all manifest-listed files, visually inspected original pp. 4–5, read the decisive PCA/training/sampling code, and independently executed the saved linear-algebra checks. No author modules, diffusion models or benchmark code were run.
# Method and operative assumptions

PAS learns a small vector of correction coordinates shared across samples at selected diffusion sampling steps. It pins the first basis vector to the current update direction, obtains three principal components from history augmented with that direction, and orthogonalizes the four vectors. It fits coordinates to states on a more finely discretized teacher trajectory and retains corrections whose teacher-state loss improvement exceeds a threshold.

Equation reference: eq:basis. Write \(d\ne0\) for the current direction, \(X'\) for the augmented history, and \(v'_1,v'_2,v'_3\) for its leading right singular vectors. Equation (14), p. 4, specifies \[
 U=[u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4]
 =\operatorname{Schmidt}\left(
      \frac d{\|d\|},v'_1,v'_2,v'_3\right),
 \qquad U\in\mathbb R^{D\times4},\] describing its columns as four orthogonal unit vectors. Equations (15)–(18) and Algorithms 1–2 use their four coordinates for the actual correction.

The geometric explanation is expressly heuristic. This review does not invent a universal theorem that all diffusion trajectories have rank three or that lower teacher-state error must improve FID. It does check the unqualified mathematical construction on which the four-coordinate procedure itself depends.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The core four-vector basis construction is undefined on admissible dependent inputs).  Assessment: Major. The specified orthogonalization cannot produce four orthogonal unit vectors from the dependent inputs that arise in the exact low-rank setting.
## Exact counterexample and all relevant conditions

Take \(D=4\) and \[X'=\begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&0\\
 0&2&0&0\\
 0&0&3&0\\
 1&0&0&0
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad d=e_1.\] There are four history rows, the current direction is nonzero and is included as a row, and the positive singular values are distinct: \(3,2,\sqrt2\). The leading right singular vectors can be chosen as \(e_3,e_2,e_1\). Thus [eq:basis] (#eq:basis) receives \[e_1,\ e_3,\ e_2,\ e_1.\] After the pinned vector, the Gram–Schmidt residual norms are exactly \(1,1,0\). Normalizing the last residual is undefined. Sign choices for singular vectors do not remove the dependence.

More generally, if \(X'\) has rank three and contains \(d\) as a row, then \(d\) lies in the span of its leading three principal components. Appending the normalized \(d\) to those three components cannot increase their span to dimension four. The p. 4 observation that adding a third PC suffices to span the relevant low-dimensional trajectory does not establish the independence required for four unit vectors.
## An admissible smooth diffusion case

This is not only a matrix detached from diffusion. For centered Gaussian data of variance one under the variance-exploding/EDM convention, \[q_t=\mathcal N(0,(1+t^2)I),\qquad
 \nabla_x\log q_t(x)=-\frac{x}{1+t^2},\qquad
 d(x,t)=-t\nabla_x\log q_t(x)=\frac{t}{1+t^2}x.\] At finite positive times, each nonzero trajectory stays on a radial line. Its initial state and update directions are collinear. Accumulating enough history rows does not remove this rank-one structure. A leading PCA direction is parallel to the pinned direction and gives a zero orthogonalization residual in exact arithmetic.

The example uses a smooth positive density and well-defined finite nonzero times. It does not rely on a zero current direction, an undefined score or an insufficient number of rows. Centering the radial history likewise leaves at most a one-dimensional span.
## Implementation and core dependency

The preserved , lines 109–126, implements the four-vector branch with divisions by all three residual norms and no rank guard. Lines 69–70 also normalize the current direction. The initial exclusions in , lines 311–320, address too few rows, not dependence of later rows. The adaptive improvement test occurs after basis construction, so it does not make the invalid construction defined.

The paper states no restriction requiring the pinned direction to lie outside the leading three-PC span or every residual norm to be positive. This defect therefore concerns an actual mathematical step in the core correction method, not an unused local identity.
## Counterevidence, severity and possible repair

Empirical image histories may be only approximately low rank, leaving enough independent components for the four-vector calculation to run. No NaN, exception, unstable image or failed benchmark was observed in this review; author code was not executed. The exact construction’s invalidity nevertheless follows from the stated inputs and is closely tied to the central method, supporting Major without requiring benchmark score loss.

A rank-revealing basis or an explicit orthogonal-complement completion could supply a well-defined alternative. Its relation to fixed learned coordinate vectors and its inference convention would need specification. Neither alternative is the algorithm currently written, and no complete repair is verified.
Problem 2 (Inference retains extra uncorrected directions absent from the training history).  Assessment: Minor, preserved release. Historical experiment impact remains Needs Evidence.
## Static dataflow

In , `correction_d` passes the original list to `PCA_process` (lines 27–34), which appends the raw current direction at line 54. Training’s `pre_PCA_process` instead passes a copy at line 164; after an accepted correction, , lines 369–371, stores only the corrected direction.

Euler inference in , lines 80–85, passes its persistent list directly to `correction_d` and then appends the returned corrected direction. The iPNDM path repeats this at lines 169–174. Therefore, writing \(\Vert\) for list concatenation, \[H_{\rm train}^{+}=H\Vert[\widetilde d],
 \qquad H_{\rm infer}^{+}=H\Vert[d,\widetilde d].\] An earlier selected correction can add an extra raw row to a later inference PCA. Because coordinates are learned in a history-dependent basis, this is a substantive correspondence discrepancy.
## Independent numerical witness

Let \(e_1,\ldots,e_5\) be coordinate vectors and compare histories \[X_{\rm train}=[2e_2;3e_3;4e_4;e_1],\qquad
 X_{\rm infer}=[10e_5;2e_2;3e_3;4e_4;e_1].\] Pin \(e_1\), use the same coordinates \((1,0.2,0.3,0.4)\), and orient basis signs with reference vector \(-2e_2-3e_3-4e_4\). Independently computed SVD and Gram–Schmidt give corrected-direction differences
SVD convention | Euclidean difference
All residuals used in this witness are nonzero, so it is independent of Problem 1. Full inputs, singular values, residual norms and output vectors are saved.
This demonstrates that the extra row can change the correction. It is not a reproduction of PyTorch’s randomized PCA or a claim that this synthetic history occurred in the published image runs.
## Limits and correction

The first selected correction is unaffected by a previous selected-step mutation; a configuration with only one selected correction need not encounter this discrepancy at all. Some histories make the extra row immaterial. No historical commit binding, saved trajectories or independently recomputed FID results are available.

A local repair is to construct a local augmented history or pass a copy during inference, retaining each actual update direction once. No source was modified and no executed patch is certified. These limitations support a release-specific Minor finding.
# Other checked claims and scope
## Parameter count

There are four scalars per retained correction step. Table 1, p. 7, contains one-to-three-step configurations, giving 4–12 scalars; its DDIM 10-NFE example uses three selected timesteps and hence 12. Table 6, p. 15, includes configurations with five selected steps, or 20 scalars. The appendix discloses that variation. The approximate title is not evidence of an exact-ten-parameter falsification.
## Adaptive selection and teacher accuracy

Equation (20)’s comparison \(L_2-(L_1+\tau)>0\) matches the release’s loss-improvement test. Separate tolerances for the first and later accepted corrections are described in Appendix C.2. The teacher uses more numerical steps and remains an approximation, not an exact solution of the continuous ODE.
## FID and time accounting

Appendix C.3 explicitly states that smaller L1/L2 state error need not improve FID. Table 11, p. 17, includes an iPNDM case changing from 2.77 to 2.97. This is disclosed counterevidence to a universal improvement interpretation, not independently demonstrated false experiments.

The release separates teacher-trajectory generation from coordinate search. , lines 69–83, invokes the former before the latter; the search timer in , lines 306 and 433–434, excludes earlier setup and teacher generation. This identifies a timing boundary. Full end-to-end cost, amortized teacher reuse and hardware-specific performance require measured records; no fabricated runtime is alleged.
# Conclusion

The core four-vector construction has a demonstrated invalid domain case and is assessed Major. The separate training/inference history discrepancy is Minor within the inspected release. The assessment does not imply that reported image benchmarks fail, and no complete repaired PAS method or empirical result is certified.

All scientific adjudication is pending; `human_reviews` is empty. Models, weights and datasets were not downloaded or executed. Later revisions, additional OpenReview-only attachments and historical experiment correspondence remain unassessed.

Title: Technical Verification of Robust Autonomy Emerges from Self-Play
# Identity and actual review scope

This report concerns Marco Cusumano-Towner et al., Robust Autonomy Emerges from Self-Play, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 11710–11737 (I25-43537). The inspected proceedings PDF has 28 pages, including its appendices. References below use one-based original PDF pages. The publisher record is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/cusumano-towner25a.html.

The native auxiliary read the complete manifest, source-availability record, scientific text and appendices. The parent rehashed all manifest-listed inputs, re-read the benchmark metric definitions and protocols, visually inspected original pp. 2, 17, 19, 21, 22 and 24, and independently computed the witnesses and scale checks. The staged preparation located no paper-specific released implementation. No private implementation, raw evaluation records or individual incident videos were inspected.

The contribution concerns planning and control from structured observations in simulation, using a single conditioned policy across traffic participants and evaluation environments. It largely abstracts perception, and the paper explicitly states that its work is entirely in simulation. The review does not turn these results into a physical-world safety certification or allege an undisclosed physical deployment claim.
# Scientific reconstruction

Training randomizes maps, goals, actor dimensions, dynamics, rewards, traffic signals and other-agent behavior. A policy observes its own conditioning but not all intentions of nearby actors. The empirical evidence has three distinct parts: transfer to external simulated driving benchmarks, behavior-realism metrics in WOSAC, and incident rates in a modified long-form self-play evaluation distribution.

Those parts support different conclusions. Benchmark transfer tests control behavior under specified interfaces. WOSAC measures a likelihood-style realism criterion using a hybrid rollout procedure. Long-form evaluation estimates a rate under a more conservative configuration. The distinctions matter to the interpretation of robustness, even where no demonstrated error is found.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The displayed bicycle displacement does not vanish at zero motion).  Assessment: Minor, displayed dynamics specification. An implementation error or empirical consequence is not established.
## Original equation and an admissible witness

Equation reference: eq:bicycle. Appendix B.2, original p. 17, states that the resulting vehicle movement is calculated by \[
 d=\tfrac12(v^{(t)}+v^{(t-1)})\Delta t,\qquad
 \theta=d/\rho,\qquad
 \Delta x=\rho\sin\theta,\qquad
 \Delta y=\rho\cos\theta.\] The prose identifies \(d\) as displacement along the arc and \(\theta\) as angular displacement.

Take the stated training step \(\Delta t=0.3\) s and an allowed vehicle length \(l=5\) m, hence wheelbase \(l_{\mathrm{wb}}=0.6l=3\) m. Set both velocities, the previous longitudinal and lateral accelerations, and the selected jerks to zero. Choose \[\phi^{(t-1)}=\arctan(0.3)+0.6(0.3)
\simeq0.4714568<0.55 .\] The p. 16 acceleration and velocity updates remain zero, and the requested steering is zero. The rate limit in Eq. (3) therefore gives \(\delta_\phi=-0.18\); Eq. (4) gives \(\phi^{(t)}=\arctan(0.3)\simeq0.2914568\), also within the angle limit. Thus the effective curvature is \(\tan(\phi^{(t)})/3=0.1\ {\rm m}^{-1}\), yielding \(\rho=10\) m, while the recomputed lateral acceleration remains zero. This respects both the steering-rate and steering-angle constraints. Hence \(d=\theta=0\), yet [eq:bicycle] (#eq:bicycle) gives \[\Delta x=0,\qquad \Delta y=10\ {\rm m}.\] More generally, the norm of the displayed displacement is \(|\rho|\), independent of \(\theta\), so it does not tend to zero with the arc length.

For the forward/lateral convention suggested by \(\Delta x\), a relative circular-arc displacement has lateral component \(\rho(1-\cos\theta)\), up to a lateral sign convention. It is zero at \(\theta=0\). The parent independently checked the displayed and relative formulas.
## Impact, counterevidence and correction

This is a definite displayed movement error, not merely an OCR ambiguity; the original page was visually checked. However, the simulator source is unavailable, and the described ordinary driving behavior would be difficult to reconcile with literal repeated application of the displayed expression. A missing origin-offset term in the manuscript is a plausible explanation.

The review therefore confines the finding to the published equation. It does not assert that the simulator displaced stationary vehicles, that training was invalid, or that any benchmark score changes. The local correction must be reconciled with the simulator’s coordinate convention; no executed code repair or author adoption is verified.
# Needs Evidence: Waymax aggregate and tabulated rates
## What is actually defined

Table A7, p. 24, lists collision and off-road rates, total distance ratios and scores. Its caption says that other-agent scores assume full progress and mutually exclusive collision and off-road events. The headline figure uses the derived scores. The manuscript also says that its results use Waymax’s provided agent-overlap and off-road metrics.
## A conditional check, with its missing assumption explicit

If the two \(0.43\%\) entries for GIGAFLOW were the marginals of the same scenario events \(C_s,O_s\), and progress were one, then \[\Pr(C\cap O)\le\min(0.43\%,0.43\%)=0.43\%\] would make the literal score at least \(99.57\%\), while the table lists \(99.16\%\).

The necessary identification of denominators is not established. The available text does not specify the reduction over agents and timesteps that connects the table’s provided metrics to Eq. (5)’s scenario indicators. A statement about 187 collisions in 44,097 scenarios is suggestive but does not define the table’s averaged metric or its aggregation. If a table entry is an agent/time rate, substituting it as a scenario-event marginal is invalid. Consequently this review does not claim that the actual 99.16% score is mathematically impossible. The displayed calculation is retained only as a conditional diagnostic.

Likewise, for a possible intended union-success definition, \[{\rm success}_{\cup}=1-c-o+j,\qquad j=\Pr(C\cap O),\] the caption’s explicit disjointness assumption gives \(1-c-o\). That conditional arithmetic is valid. An overlapping-events example cannot refute a statement expressly conditioned on disjointness.
For reference, under common scenario marginals and full progress, the compatible union-success intervals would be:
Method | Conditional union-success interval
Expert demonstration | 99.07–99.39%
Wayformer | 81.43–89.32%

These are not corrected experimental scores. If that interpretation were intended, the listed learned baselines’ upper bounds would remain below the reported GIGAFLOW value; it would not demonstrate a ranking reversal.
## Required evidence and final disposition

The relationship between the intersection formula, the caption’s failure-event assumption and the numerical aggregate requires the implemented aggregation or equivalent per-scenario records. The needed evidence comprises event units, joint event counts, progress values and the actual formula used for each compared method. If the caption refers to the same scenario events as Eq. (5), disjointness would make the literal intersection success one; this reinforces the correspondence question without deciding which formula was used.

An initial candidate Major inference was withdrawn after the parent challenged the denominator assumption and the auxiliary confirmed that it could not be verified. The final disposition is Needs Evidence for metric correspondence and score correctness. No invalid historical ranking, fabricated result or unconditional false bound is claimed.
# Evaluation scope and checked arithmetic
## Training scale

Independent dimensional calculations give \[\begin{aligned}
 1900/(8\cdot24)&=9.8958\ {\rm days},\\
 (1900/8)\,3600\,(1.2\times10^6)
   &=1.026\times10^{12}\ {\rm transitions},\\
 (1900/8)\,3600\,(1850)
   &=1.58175\times10^9\ {\rm km},\\
 \frac{10^{12}(0.3)}{365.25\cdot24\cdot3600}
   &=9506.43\ {\rm subjective\ years}.\end{aligned}\] These agree with the paper’s rounded under-ten-day, trillion-transition, 1.6-billion-kilometer and approximately-9500-year descriptions. They do not verify measured throughput or actual compute logs.
## Long-form incident-rate interpretation

Section F.3, p. 22, and Table A4 disclose a different evaluation configuration: dynamics noise is removed, there are 50 drivers, initialization ensures clearance, traffic-light randomization is removed, perceived vehicle dimensions are enlarged by 10 cm on each side, reward conditioning is conservative and decision frequency is approximately 15 Hz. Episodes are approximately 600 seconds, with up to 40 observed actors.

The main text also acknowledges important configuration changes. This is a disclosed distribution restriction, not evidence of a hidden protocol. The 17.5-year expression is an aggregate interval/rate interpretation across simulated exposure, not proof that one vehicle completed an uninterrupted 17.5-year trajectory. The implied speed from three million kilometers over 17.5 years is about 19.56 km/h, which is arithmetically coherent.

Total evaluation exposure, raw incident counts, episode/seed counts, pooling rules and uncertainty intervals were unavailable. Their absence leaves the strength and precision of the rate claim unresolved; it does not alone demonstrate a false incident rate.
## External simulated benchmarks

The nuPlan evaluation uses Val14 and closed-loop reactive Challenge 3, with IDM traffic vehicles and replayed pedestrian trajectories. The paper discloses this setup and the unavailable online leaderboard. These are recorded human-driving scenarios with specified simulated actors, not live interaction with physical human drivers.

For CARLA, the paper describes privileged state/map access and a pedestrian-state workaround, and states that comparators were rerun in the same setup. The displayed means give \((93+99+92)/3=94.6667\) for GIGAFLOW and \((90+92+83)/3=88.3333\) for the rerun expert, matching the rounded headline values. Implementation parity and raw run uncertainty were not independently verified.

For Waymax, the paper specifies WOMD 1.2.0 validation, 44,097 eight-second scenarios, 10 Hz, up to 128 objects, a particular IDM patch and goal construction from logged endpoints plus projected/snapped goals. Route-progress and total-distance ratios are distinct disclosed quantities. They must not be silently interchanged.
## WOSAC and advantage filtering

WOSAC realism evaluation uses GIGAFLOW for vehicles and bicycles, an IDM-like pedestrian rule, goal sampling based on initial history and value estimates, and added Gaussian position noise. The paper reports a two-point realism improvement from that noise. Table A8 also labels a validation-versus-public-test comparison. This supports a disclosed hybrid realism result; component-level attribution to self-play alone and an exact same-split ranking require additional evidence.

The parent visually checked Algorithm 1 and the surrounding p. 19 text. They contain absolute-value bars in the advantage filter. Those bars were lost in plain-text extraction; no signed-advantage filtering error is supported. This check prevented an extraction artifact from becoming a scientific finding.
# Conclusion and limitations

One bounded Minor displayed-equation error is established. No Major problem is established in the inspected evidence after the unsupported metric inference was withdrawn. Waymax metric correspondence and long-form rate uncertainty remain Needs Evidence. Training-scale arithmetic and several protocol descriptions are internally coherent within their stated scope.

Scientific adjudication is pending, with no human reviews. No author code, model execution, dataset download, physical safety validation or empirical replication was performed. Individual incident videos, additional OpenReview-only attachments, external benchmark implementations and later revisions remain unassessed.

Title: Technical Verification of Rethinking the Stability-Plasticity Trade-off in Continual Learning from an Architectural Perspective
# Identity and reviewed version

This report reviews Aojun Lu, Hangjie Yuan, Tao Feng and Yanan Sun, Rethinking the Stability-Plasticity Trade-off in Continual Learning from an Architectural Perspective, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 40888–40902 (I25-43538). The inspected original has 15 pages including appendices. Page references are one-based PDF pages. The publisher record is https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/lu25t.html.

The staged public repository is https://github.com/byyx666/Dual-Arch, commit `6a6f80ca4229d88aa29cf44d5079310d7e945fe5`. It is not established as the exact code that produced the conference results. The parent rehashed every manifest-listed file and checked the decisive metric definition, original tables and release lines. The auxiliary performed broader method, experiment and static-source review. Original pp. 4 and 8 were visually inspected by both roles.

No author code was executed. Additional OpenReview-only attachments were inaccessible during preparation; no later full-text revision or erratum was compared. The findings apply to the preserved versions.
# Scientific reconstruction and scope

The paper empirically studies architecture-dependent plasticity and stability in class-incremental learning. It proposes a stable learner and a plastic learner with different architecture choices, using the latter during learning and the former for inference. The study concerns observed trade-offs under specified parameter budgets and training protocols; it is not a universal theorem that depth or width determines forgetting for all data and optimizers.

The inspected implementation uses a stable configuration with depth 10, width 64 and a larger final pooled representation, and a plastic configuration with depth 18, width 42 and unit final pooling. The auxiliary traced the iCaRL integration, teacher distillation, replay use and ResNet construction. The distillation soft cross-entropy has the same student gradient as KL when the teacher distribution is held fixed; the missing teacher-entropy constant is not an optimization error.

The architecture, distillation and replay checks are static correspondence checks. Other integrations such as WA, DER, FOSTER and MEMO were not all traced end to end, and the reported learned behavior was not independently reproduced.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (Intermediate forgetting uses future accuracy maxima).  Assessment: Minor, released implementation. The mathematical error is demonstrated, but its historical use in the reported curves remains Needs Evidence.
## Defined metric and exact code

Equation reference: eq:af. Section 3.1, original p. 4, defines average forgetting after task \(k\) as \[
 AF_k=\frac1{k-1}\sum_{b=1}^{k-1}(a_b^\ast-a_b),\] where \(a_b^\ast\) is the peak past accuracy on task \(b\) and \(a_b\) is its current accuracy. Figures 1 and 4 include intermediate forgetting curves, so the time restriction has a concrete interpretation.
The preserved , lines 142 and 165, computes CNN and NME forgetting after the complete trajectory has been assembled:

> `np.mean((np.max(np_acctable, axis=1)`
> `- np_acctable[:, i])[:i])`.

The maximum spans every column of the completed accuracy matrix, including stages later than \(i\). Restricting the final task slice `[:i]` selects old tasks, but does not restrict the time index over which the maxima were calculated.
## Finite witness with valid accuracy entries

Let rows index evaluation tasks and columns index the completed training stage: \[A=\begin{pmatrix}
 60&50&80\\
 0&70&60\\
 0&0&90
 \end{pmatrix}.\] All entries are valid percentages; the zeros before a task is introduced are placeholders and are not used in the decisive past maximum. After the second task, task 1 has current accuracy \(50\) and past peak \(60\), so its forgetting is \(10\) percentage points. The released expression instead uses its later peak \(80\) and returns \(30\).

This is not a reproduced learning trajectory. It is an independent finite input demonstrating that the released statistic differs from the defined past-only metric. Both strict-past and past-including-current conventions give \(10\) at this stage, so the witness does not rely on that separate convention.
## Dependency, counterevidence and correction

The erroneous statistic can alter intermediate forgetting curves when an old task improves later. It does not alter AIA or last-stage accuracy calculations in this path. At the final stage there are no future columns, so this particular future-dependence argument does not automatically invalidate the paper’s final forgetting numbers. Whether the final convention clips negative forgetting is a separate issue not resolved here.

A local time-respecting formula at zero-based stage \(i>0\) is \[\frac1i\sum_{b=0}^{i-1}
       \left(\max_{b\le s<i}A_{b,s}-A_{b,i}\right).\] If the intended convention includes the current stage in the peak, it should be stated explicitly; either convention must exclude future stages for an online metric.

No saved paper-run matrices or historical plotting-script binding were supplied. The finding is therefore confined to the inspected release. It does not establish that the published architecture comparison was computed with this expression or that its ranking changes. A complete executed patch and benchmark recomputation were outside authorization.
# Checked numerical and methodological claims
## Ablation averages

The parent visually checked Table 3, p. 8, and independently averaged the five displayed method scores in each row. The results are \[72.924,\quad70.288,\quad71.182,\quad72.274,\quad71.238.\] They agree with the printed two-decimal row averages. This checks arithmetic, not the three-run variability or original training outputs.
## Parameter accounting and compute

The two prominently annotated reductions in Figure 3 follow from \[100\left(1-\frac{14.6}{112.2}\right)=86.9875\%,\qquad
 100\left(1-\frac{4.2}{22.5}\right)=81.3333\%.\] These support the rounded 87% and 81% statements. The auxiliary inspected Appendix A.1’s model-count accounting; it includes the plastic learner and the retained networks relevant to the stated comparison. No omission of the entire plastic learner was established.

Parameter count and forward FLOPs do not imply equal training time. The paper expressly reports increased training time for two learners, including ratios around \(1.39\)–\(1.77\) in Section 5.5 and Table 4. That disclosed limitation is counterevidence against alleging that reduced parameters were presented as measured training-time savings.
## Architecture and loss correspondence

The relevant ResNet block counts, pooling configurations, replay usage and distillation coefficients were statically compared with the method description. No demonstrated invalid distillation derivation or architectural contradiction was found within that checked iCaRL path. This scoped result is not certification of every implementation variant.
# Needs Evidence and coverage boundaries

Table 3 describes three runs with different initializations. The inspected , lines 196–199, fixes Torch random seeds to 1, while configured seeds may affect data/task order elsewhere. This creates a reproducibility question about how initialization variation was produced in the historical experiments. Different scripts, changed versions or external seeding could explain it. Without run records, this review does not assert that the stated variability is false.

The auxiliary read the main architectural study, Tables 1–3, Figure 3, the computational discussion and Appendix A.1, with partial inspection of the remaining appendix analyses. Its static review covered , , , , , the relevant experiment configuration and portions of the base learner. It did not trace every continual-learning integration or externally cited baseline.

The parent independently checked the original forgetting definition and table arithmetic and read the decisive full-trajectory metric loop and seed function. No model training, accuracy extraction from raw predictions, or benchmark reproduction was performed. Later revisions, additional attachments and the exact conference-time source version remain unverified.
# Conclusion

One implementation-scoped Minor Problem is supported. No Major invalid derivation or demonstrated harm to the core architectural conclusion was established within the inspected material. The future-maximum defect should be corrected in the released metric path and checked against historical curves if those records become available.
Scientific adjudication is pending; `human_reviews` is empty. The review supplies a finite witness and a local metric correction, not an executed repair, author adoption or acceptance decision.

Title: Scientific review of
Fleet of Agents: Coordinated Problem Solving
with Large Language Models
# Identity, version, and review scope

The reviewed paper is Lars Klein, Nearchos Potamitis, Roland Aydin, Robert West, Caglar Gulcehre, and Akhil Arora, Fleet of Agents: Coordinated Problem Solving with Large Language Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 30986–31019 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assignment identifiers are 0170 and I25-43539; the OpenReview identifier is `yNpYb376zf`. Page references mean one-based pages of the 34-page proceedings PDF, including its embedded appendices.

The review covers the main scientific claims, algorithm and resampling definitions, experimental setup and prompts, cost accounting, reported tables, and appendices A–D. Relevant released files were read statically from `au-clan/FoA`, commit
|6a06e2ecac3683cd56d4979d0c07a58b287acadf|.

That frozen source snapshot was acquired on 24 October 2026. No evidence binds this exact commit to the historical experimental runs. The bounded snapshot contains 37 source files; an assigned SciBench execution path and raw provider billing records are not available. The separate OpenReview attachment was unavailable in the acquisition record; this does not prevent inspection of the substantial embedded supplement.

No author code, language model, environment benchmark, or paid API was executed. Finite calculations below were implemented independently using the existing Python standard library. They demonstrate specified mathematical and dataflow consequences, not empirical reproduction. The source PDF was read again through the installed Poppler extractor; its extracted text hash matched the retained extraction.
# Claims, definitions, and dependencies

FoA maintains a population of agents, advances each by mutation, evaluates states, and resamples promising states, with optional backtracking to earlier states. Caching and grouping identical prompts are intended to improve the cost–quality trade-off. These are the operative claims in Sections 3–6, the extended algorithm on pp. 13–16, and Appendix C.

Equation reference: eq:cost. A logical group asks for several completions of one prompt. A physical request is one successful call to the provider. The distinction matters when a provider adapter splits a logical group. Let request \(j\) report \(P_j\) input tokens and \(O_j\) output tokens. Under the stated usage-based prices \(r_{\rm in}\) and \(r_{\rm out}\), in dollars per million tokens, the applicable cost is \[
 C=\frac{r_{\rm in}\sum_jP_j+r_{\rm out}\sum_jO_j}{10^6}.\] This expression assumes that each request’s reported tokens are billable at those rates. It is not a claim about a provider’s present-day discounts or an unseen invoice.

For WebShop, the evaluator prompt asks for an explanation followed by a final correctness score \(s\in\{1,\ldots,10\}\). The released implementation maps this to a value in \([0,1]\), caches it, and uses values in selection. Thus both the completeness of the evaluator response and the extraction of its final score are dependencies of the main coordination mechanism.
# Problem 1: physical request usage is lost when responses are merged
## Source claim and suspect step

Appendix C.3, p. 26, attributes a batching saving to paying for the common input once while obtaining multiple outputs. A single physical multi-completion request can have precisely that property. The released adapter, however, also merges multiple physical requests.

In `async_engine/api.py`, `together_request` (starting at line 252) sets `max_n=16`, partitions \(n>16\), calls the provider separately for each part, and then invokes `merge_responses`. The Groq adapter similarly makes \(n\) separate requests with one completion each. In `utils.py`, lines 738–773, `merge_responses` retains the first response’s input-token count and adds subsequent output-token counts, but explicitly adds zero to input-token usage. The ordinary `API.request` accounting then receives this merged usage. The experiment drivers use |api.cost(tab_name=...)| to record costs; a tab labels accounting and does not restore discarded physical usage.

Consequently, the saved ordinary usage estimate can represent an idealized shared-input call rather than the calls actually made. The relevant failure is not that batching itself is invalid, but that its physical-request boundary is removed from the accounting.
## Complete finite check

The cardinality is supported by the released interface rather than an out-of-range synthetic call. The Game of 24 driver sets evaluation batch size to \(3N\), while the agent evaluator requests three judgments per state. Appendix C.4 uses \(N=9\). A group of 27 identical evaluation prompts is therefore possible when the population contains the same state, which resampling and cloning permit. The example proves a reachable accounting defect; it does not establish how often such a group occurred in the unpublished runs.
## Counterevidence and precise limits

If a logical group is handled by one physical request, retaining its one input-token count is appropriate. The OpenAI single-call route is not subject to this particular multi-call loss. Smaller groups, differing prompts, cache hits, or different provider charging rules can reduce or remove the example’s effect. The source snapshot need not be the historical experimental version. Neither the paper’s total token logs nor provider invoices are available to determine the frequency or aggregate magnitude.

A related unresolved version question is that Table 5, p. 19, lists a Llama-3.2-90B output rate of \(0.06\), whereas the reviewed code catalog uses \(1.2\) per million. The ratio is 20, but the relevant historical price and the rate used for each published result have not been established. That discrepancy is Needs Evidence; it is not substituted for the demonstrated merge defect or used to calculate a corrected published table.
## Core impact, severity, and bounded correction

Dollar cost is a central comparison axis and part of the paper’s principal efficiency claim. Dropping physical input usage directly changes that axis for the supported execution path. The finding is Major for the released cost-measurement implementation. It does not establish that every reported cost is wrong, that a quality ranking reverses, or that the overall coordination idea fails.

A precise repair is to retain and sum usage for every physical request under an explicit pricing model, and to report any hypothetical shared-input cost separately. Summing both responses restores \(0.002724\) in the fixture and, by additivity, restores [eq:cost] (#eq:cost) for the stated model. Provider discounts, cached-token classes, retries, and invoice reconciliation need their own recorded rules. No source patch or historical rerun was performed, and author adoption has not been requested.
# Problem 2: the WebShop evaluator does not implement its stated score interface
## Claim, configuration, and parser

Table 6, p. 19, distinguishes the WebShop action-generation stop sequence `["\n"]` from the evaluation setting `null`. Prompt 7 on pp. 23–25 asks for analysis and a final line of the form Thus the correctness score is \(s\).

The driver `run/webshop.py`, lines 32–62, defines both configurations but constructs one `API` with `step_api_config`. Its action and evaluation batchers both receive that instance (lines 131–132). The evaluation configuration is not supplied to the actual call; changing the accounting tab to `eval` does not change the API configuration. Thus the evaluator inherits the action’s newline stop and may lose the final score line.

There is a second, independent failure at `src/agents/ws.py`, |value_outputs_unwrap|, lines 197–219. The parser searches the entire reply for `"10"`, then `"9"`, down to `"1"`, returning the first match divided by ten. It does not locate the score declaration. Digits in prices, quantities, or the explanation can become the state value even without truncation.
## A valid-response counterexample
Consider two evaluator responses whose intended scores obey the required range and final-line format:

> A: The item costs 100 dollars, exceeding the budget.
> Thus the correctness score is 1

> B: The task is not yet complete.
> Thus the correctness score is 9

The numerical values specified by the final lines are \((0.1,0.9)\). With the full replies, the released substring rule returns \((1.0,0.9)\), because `100` contains `10`. If the newline stop truncates each reply to its first line, the same rule returns \((1.0,0.0)\): A contains `10`, and B contains no digit. Thus one defect persists when the other is removed.

For two equal-age candidate states and ideal linear weighting, the intended probability of selecting A is \(0.1/(0.1+0.9)=0.1\). The full-reply parser instead gives \(1/(1+0.9)=10/19\), about \(0.5263\). The driver adds \(10^{-6}\) to retained weights; including it changes the two probabilities only to approximately \(0.1000008\) and \(0.5263158\). With truncation, B is assigned zero; the driver excludes newly evaluated zero-valued states from its retained records. With no other retained state, A is selected with probability one. If zero-valued states were retained instead, the epsilon-smoothed probability would still be approximately \(0.999999\).

All assumptions are explicit: ordinary nonterminal WebShop states, a valid one-to-ten evaluation, an explanation containing an ordinary price, no previous cached evaluation, equal age for the comparison, and the driver’s linear resampling path. No claim is made about the probability that a particular model emits these exact sentences. The interface must correctly handle them if its final-line score contract is to hold. The independently written parser and configuration fixtures are saved with the review.
## Counterevidence and alternative interpretations

A model can sometimes place its score before the first newline or omit digits from the explanation, in which case this fixture’s failure may not occur. Such outputs do not repair an interface that explicitly permits analysis before the final score. The implementation might also differ from the one used for the historical tables. The comment above the parser attributes it to LATS; this review reproduces the defect in the supplied FoA snapshot and makes no first-discovery claim about that code pattern.

This check does not show that the environment reward or the final success indicator is directly parsed by this function. The established path is evaluator value, caching, and resampling. A system can retain substantial benchmark success despite erroneous selection weights. Those facts limit the empirical conclusion but do not remove the algorithmic dependency.
## Core impact, severity, and correction

Evaluation-guided selection is part of FoA’s defining coordination mechanism. The implementation can invert the evaluator’s expressed preference and discard the higher-scored state. This is Major for the released WebShop evaluation path. The source evidence does not identify how much the published WebShop score would change after correction.

Use the evaluation configuration for evaluation calls and extract a validated final score with an anchored grammar or a structured response. A missing score should be distinguished from a genuine zero-valued state. An independently written anchored final-line extractor returns \((0.1,0.9)\) for the complete replies above. It cannot recover a score that was never received, so fixing the parser alone is insufficient. These statements verify a narrowly specified interface repair, not a repaired benchmark or a deployed author implementation.
# Additional checked claims and counterevidence

The four main comparisons in Section 5 and Figure 4 were recalculated from the displayed aggregate values. The quality increases are \(2.0,4.8,9.5,1.7\) percentage points, averaging \(4.5\), compatible with an approximately five-point summary. The corresponding FoA-to-comparator cost ratios average approximately \(0.35749\), supporting an approximately \(35\%\) cost summary for those four selected comparisons. That computation does not establish the same average over every model–task combination.

Two local percentage statements need clarification. The change from \(75.02\) to \(62.93\) dollars is a \(16.12\%\) reduction relative to \(75.02\), not \(25\%\); the SciBench ratio \(0.80/5.11\) is \(15.66\%\), not \(14\%\). These are bounded arithmetic inconsistencies in the displayed-value narrative. They do not change the shown order of those methods or supply an additional core failure.

The Game of 24 and crosswords test/validation indexing in the inspected data module agrees with the paper after converting zero-based indices to the paper’s one-based convention. The WebShop test set agrees. The released validation range contains ten tasks (55–64), whereas the paper states fifteen (55–69); historical tuning provenance is unresolved. The paper discloses single-run GPT-4 results, and five trials for the other models. Aggregate means alone do not establish paired significance or a universal improvement; no such test was fabricated here.

Uniform resampling need not preserve every distinct state, but the paper says it may maintain diversity, not that it guarantees preservation. This candidate criticism is therefore rejected. The main method makes no formal convergence or global optimality theorem requiring a newly invented guarantee. The appendix explicitly discusses the RAFA score comparison and its metric differences; that disclosed distinction is not relabeled as an undiscovered error. Ablation trends and figure context were read, but raw trajectories, all plotted numerical coordinates, and independent runs were unavailable.

No verified later-version correction or author erratum was found in the supplied version-bound materials. No exhaustive external erratum search is claimed. Establishing the effects of either main Problem on the published tables requires the historical commit, requests and responses, usage/pricing records, and a controlled rerun.
# Conclusion and separate decision states

The overall supported initial assessment is Major, driven by two demonstrated defects in released core implementation paths. The exact historical experiment provenance remains unresolved. The scientific assessment, proposed repair checks, and author adoption are distinct:

Title: Technical Verification of GPR-GAE
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Woohyun Lee and Hogun Park, Self-supervised Adversarial Purification for Graph Neural Networks, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, identifier I25-43540 (local number 0171), OpenReview yMhkpJ1K01 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied proceedings PDF has 21 pages. All page references count PDF pages from one, agreeing with the paper’s printed internal page numbers. The reviewed repository is `woodavid31/GPR-GAE`, commit `c67df283c5ab` (9 July 2025); its relationship to the original experiment run is not documented by the inspected snapshot. The claim-focused inspection covers Sections 2–6, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 and Appendix A, the cost expressions in Appendix B, experimental settings in Appendix C, and Algorithms 1–2 in Appendix E. The ablation and representation-analysis descriptions in Appendices F–G were read but the experiments were not rerun. The central model file and training-loss construction were inspected statically. Hash comparison verified all 35 manifest-listed source files without changing their bytes. No author code was executed.
# Definitions and valid conditional reasoning

The paper predicts link probabilities \(\widehat A_{ij}\in(0,1)\) using sigmoid outputs. The positive set \(E\) contains original edges; \(E_{\rm inject}\) contains sampled nonedges. These roles are explicit in Section 5.1 and in the training code. Bidirectional predictions are averaged; a symmetry penalty compares the two directions. The iteration in Equation (12) is \[A^{t+1}=(1-\alpha)A^t+\alpha f_\theta(A^t,X),\qquad 0<\alpha\leq1.\] If \(f_\theta\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(L<1\), on a closed invariant domain, the relaxed operator has Lipschitz constant at most \(q=1-\alpha(1-L)<1\). This triangle-inequality calculation in Appendix A.2 is valid. On a closed ball about a fixed clean graph \(A_\star\), the conditions \(f_\theta(A_\star)=A_\star\) and uniform contraction throughout that ball imply invariance and linear convergence. Mere local contraction at an initial point does not itself supply invariance. The explanatory fixed-point condition on p. 4 provides a possible intended setting, so this review does not assert a false convergence theorem. The empirical maximum of 100 sampled pairwise ratios in Section 6.2 is a lower bound on the supremum defining a Lipschitz constant, not a certificate of a uniform upper bound. It is evidence for the sampled behavior. Likewise, Theorem 3.1’s maximization decomposition is valid for a fixed partition whose unaffected losses remain constant over the entire perturbation set. A partition defined separately for each candidate graph cannot automatically be pulled outside the maximum. This quantifier issue is recorded as a scope clarification, not an established counterexample or an additional severity-bearing Problem.
# Substantive findings

Equation reference: eq:paperloss, eq:bcerepair. Problem 1 (The specified restoration loss differs from the released objective).  The restoration formula on p. 6, Equation (9), and minimization in Algorithm 1, p. 18, specify \[
L_{\rm paper}=\frac1{|E|}\sum_{e\in E}\log(1-p_e)
+\frac1{|E_{\rm inject}|}\sum_{e\in E_{\rm inject}}\log p_e.\] The released `experiment.py`, lines 240–250, instead minimizes binary cross-entropy with target one for original edges and zero for injected edges: \[
L_{\rm BCE}=-\frac1{|E|}\sum_{e\in E}\log p_e
-\frac1{|E_{\rm inject}|}\sum_{e\in E_{\rm inject}}\log(1-p_e).\]
## Complete check

Take one equally weighted positive and one negative prediction sharing \(p=\sigma(z)\). In the released decoder, final weights can be zero and the common bias can be \(z\), with equal directional predictions and zero symmetry penalty. A bias is not needed for the literal paper architecture either: in Equations (4)–(7), take identical node features with \(H_i^{(0)}=e_1\), let \(W_e\) copy only the first endpoint’s zero-hop coordinate into \(e_1\) and annihilate all other inputs, including higher-hop coordinates, and set \(W_d=ze_1\). The ELU activation used by the released configuration fixes 0 and 1, so all directed scores are \(\sigma(z)\) and the symmetry penalty is zero. The two objectives reduce to \[L_{\rm paper}(p)=\log p+\log(1-p),\qquad
L_{\rm BCE}(p)=-\log p-\log(1-p).\] At \(p=1/2\) their values are \(-1.38629436\) and \(1.38629436\); at \(p=0.9\) they are \(-2.40794561\) and \(2.40794561\). Moreover, \[\frac{dL_{\rm paper}}{dz}=1-2p,\qquad
\frac{dL_{\rm BCE}}{dz}=2p-1.\] At \(p=0.9\) the derivatives are \(-0.8\) and \(0.8\): minimization moves the shared logit in opposite directions. The first expression tends to \(-\infty\) at either boundary; the second has its unique shared-probability minimum at \(1/2\). These identities were independently evaluated in `independent_checks.py`; actual output and source excerpts are retained in `verification/0171/independent_checks.json`.
## Alternative readings, impact and correction

For independently adjustable positive and negative scores, minimizing the printed terms pushes each score toward its correct boundary. Thus a claim that every individual gradient has the wrong class direction would be false. The demonstrated discrepancy concerns the objective under parameter sharing. Reversing only the optimization sign or only the edge labels does not make the specifications identical. Inspection of the original p. 6 image confirms the printed logarithms. Equation [eq:bcerepair] (#eq:bcerepair) is the precise objective supported by the released training calls, with the symmetry term retained. Substituting it restores agreement with those calls. This is a specification repair, not a validation of the learned purifier. The paper does not explicitly identify Equation (9) as BCE, and a different objective can still move independently adjustable class scores toward the intended boundaries. The shared-probability example establishes non-equivalence; it does not refute a stated universal optimization or restoration guarantee, nor force a trained model to remain in that parameter restriction. A core invalid derivation has therefore not been established from this discrepancy. Its supported assessment is Minor. Historical experiment provenance and score effects are separately unresolved; absence of a measured score change is not the reason for this severity.

Problem 2 (The released stopping rule permits cancellation of edge updates).  Section 5.3, p. 6, and Algorithm 2, p. 18, stop when \(\|\Delta A^t\|/\|A^t\|\leq\tau\), with practical \(\tau=10^{-3}\). The pinned `gprgae.py`, lines 151–157, records the old sum of edge weights and tests the relative absolute change of that sum against \(10^{-4}\).
## Complete check
## Alternative readings, impact and correction

For nonnegative weights, their sum is an entrywise \(\ell_1\) norm, but the absolute difference of sums is not the \(\ell_1\) norm of the difference. Equal total mass does not imply a small update in any norm. Both paper and release use an outer five-step cap, and full replacement in the release is consistent with the default \(\alpha=1\). A faithful implementation must retain the old vector and test a declared norm of \(w'-w\) divided by the same norm of \(w\), using the stated threshold and an explicit zero-denominator convention. The correction is verified algebraically for the predicate only. It was not applied to author code. This is a Minor release discrepancy; its effect on historical experiments requires the execution version and, if relevant, a rerun.
# Overall dependence and remaining work

Both Problems affect exact algorithm reproduction. They do not refute the multi-filter architecture, the valid conditional contraction calculation, or any particular reported accuracy. A released-code discrepancy does not identify which implementation produced a table. Section 6 and Appendix C distinguish adaptive attacks from transfer-only evaluation on OGB-arXiv; that disclosed limitation is not treated as a defect. The Appendix B simplification requires \(K|E|Z\) to dominate \(NZ^2+K^2NZ\); the preceding unsimplified expression should be used outside that regime. No separate OpenReview supplement was accessible in the staged acquisition, which records HTTP 403. Embedded appendices were available. No later manuscript version or erratum was inspected, so no current-version or discovery-priority claim is made. Benchmark reproduction, global contraction certification and identification of the experiment commit remain unperformed.

Restoration objective | Minor | Matching BCE stated; analytical check only
Stopping predicate | Minor | Norm predicate specified; no code change
Convergence/partition scope | Clarification | Uniform-domain conditions stated
Scientific adjudication | Pending | No human review supplied

report: Abstract: The joint training objective and the probabilistic justification of Inner-Guidance were inspected in the ICML 2025 proceedings version. A central derivation confuses differentiation with respect to the sampled state with differentiation with respect to model parameters. Consequently, dependence of a conditioning signal on model weights does not establish the claimed obstruction to ordinary conditional-score algebra. An explicit smooth Gaussian model verifies this distinction, even with correlated conditions whose distribution depends on the weights. The supported impact is Major for the justification of a principal method component; the empirical advantages of VideoJAM are not refuted by this check.

Title: Technical Verification of VideoJAM
# Identity and scope

The paper is Hila Chefer, Uriel Singer, Amit Zohar, Yuval Kirstain, Adam Polyak, Yaniv Taigman, Lior Wolf and Shelly Sheynin, VideoJAM: Joint Appearance-Motion Representations for Enhanced Motion Generation in Video Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 7595–7616, I25-43541, local number 0172, OpenReview yMJcHWcb2Z [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. References below use one-based PDF pages (1–22), agreeing with internal printed pages. The inspection covers the motivation in Section 3, flow-matching and joint representation objectives in Sections 4.1–4.2, the complete Section 4.3 derivation, Appendix A, evaluation design and ablation claims in Section 5, and the implementation and metric descriptions in Appendices C–E. Original PDF pages 5 and 12 were rendered and actually viewed. No training, sampling, human-evaluation replication or author-code execution was performed. The staged source acquisition contains no available implementation of VideoJAM; that is an availability limitation rather than proof that no implementation exists. The arXiv version history was checked on 24 October 2026 and listed v2, dated 26 May 2025, as the latest revision. Its Section 4.3 and Appendix A retain the reasoning at issue. The frozen proceedings PDF remains the principal reviewed artifact.
# Definitions and checks that survive

Equation reference: eq:target. For a fixed model parameter \(\theta\) and realized condition \(c\), the state score is \(\nabla_x\log p_\theta(x\mid c)\). It lies in the state space. The parameter score \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x\mid c)\) lies in parameter space and is a different derivative. The cited classifier-free guidance paper explicitly uses the noisy-state derivative [Retained latex: \cite{cfg}]. The paper uses the interpolation \(x_t=t x_1+(1-t)x_0\), with velocity \(x_1-x_0\). Equations (1)–(3) follow from differentiation in time, and the concatenated squared-error objective in Equation (6) is a coherent joint appearance–motion regression target. There is no contradiction in learning correlated appearance and motion, or in employing the generated motion state as an auxiliary signal. Write \(z=(x,d)\) and suppress time. For positive differentiable densities, Equation (7) defines the unnormalized quantity \[
\widetilde p_\theta(z\mid y)\ \propto\
p_\theta(z\mid y)\,p_\theta(y\mid z)^{w_1}\,
p_\theta(d\mid x,y)^{w_2}.\] Whenever it is normalizable, it is a legitimate modified density. Its state-score calculation can be performed without independence from model weights.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (Parameter dependence does not invalidate the conditional-score identity).  Section 2 (p. 3), Section 4.3 (p. 5), and Appendix A (p. 12) argue that existing conditioning constructions require independence of the conditions from model weights, and that generated motion violates this requirement. Appendix A ties omission of \(p_\theta(c_1,c_2)\) in Equations (9)–(11) to that independence. Equation (8) on p. 5 then explicitly writes \(\nabla_{\theta'}\) while identifying the result as a diffusion score and subsequently substituting state-sized velocity predictions.
## Exact mathematical check

Equation reference: eq:bayes, eq:statescore. For any positive differentiable joint density and fixed realized \(c\), \[
\log p_\theta(x\mid c)=\log p_\theta(x,c)-\log p_\theta(c).\] Thus, with \(\theta\) and \(c\) held fixed, \[
\nabla_x\log p_\theta(x\mid c)=\nabla_x\log p_\theta(x,c),
\qquad \nabla_x\log p_\theta(c)=0.\] The marginal may depend arbitrarily on \(\theta\) and the components of \(c\) may be dependent. Neither changes Equation [eq:statescore] (#eq:statescore). In contrast, \[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x\mid c)
=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x,c)-\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(c),\] and the last term need not vanish. This identity concerns a parameter derivative, not a sampling direction. For a fully specified example take independent standard Gaussian noises and \[C_1=\theta+\varepsilon_1,\qquad
C_2=C_1+\varepsilon_2,\qquad
X=C_1+C_2+\varepsilon_x.\] All conditional variances are one. The joint density is smooth, strictly positive and normalized, the two conditions are correlated, and their marginal depends on \(\theta\). At \[\theta=0.4,\qquad c_1=1,\qquad c_2=0.2,\qquad x=2,\] direct evaluation gives \[\begin{aligned}
\partial_x\log p_\theta(x\mid c_1,c_2)
&=\partial_x\log p_\theta(x,c_1,c_2)=-0.8,\\
\partial_x\log p_\theta(c_1,c_2)&=0,\\
\partial_\theta\log p_\theta(x\mid c_1,c_2)&=0,\\
\partial_\theta\log p_\theta(x,c_1,c_2)
&=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta(c_1,c_2)=0.6.\end{aligned}\] An independent finite-difference calculation with step \(10^{-5}\) returned \(-0.8000000000008\), \(0\), and \(0.5999999999950\) for the corresponding nonzero/zero derivatives. These numerical results confirm the exact algebra; they are not its proof. The input model, source script and actual output are retained in `verification/0172/independent_checks.json`.
## Alternative interpretations and counterevidence

Treating the subscript \(\theta'\) in Equation (8) as a notational error repairs that symbol but does not repair the repeated verbal argument about weight independence in Sections 2, 4.3 and Appendix A. Conversely, reading it literally as a parameter derivative makes the immediate substitution of velocity predictions invalid: the vectors live in different spaces, and a parameter-dependent normalizing constant can no longer simply be omitted. A generated conditioning value can change between inference steps. Its origin does not alter a partial derivative at a fixed realized condition. If instead one deliberately differentiates through a state-dependent function \(c(x)\), the chain rule introduces \(D c(x)\) terms. That is a different derivative and is not justified merely by saying that the condition depends on model weights. The joint state interpretation matters. For \(z=(x,d)\), a marginal involving \(d\) can depend on the differentiated coordinates. This can distinguish a joint-state construction from a conditional appearance score; it does not validate the stated weight-independence argument. Likewise, the product factorization in Appendix A’s Equation (9) requires conditional independence of conditions given \(x\). Dropping the conditioning marginal from an \(x\)-derivative requires no such factorization. Appendix A’s Equation (10) is an exact chain factorization without an independence assumption.
## Verified correction and boundaries

Equation reference: eq:correct. Taking the state gradient of Equation [eq:target] (#eq:target) and applying Bayes’ rule gives the precise identity \[
\begin{split}
\nabla_z\log\widetilde p_\theta(z\mid y)
={}&(1+w_1+w_2)\nabla_z\log p_\theta(z\mid y)\\
&-w_1\nabla_z\log p_\theta(z)
-w_2\begin{pmatrix}\nabla_x\log p_\theta(x\mid y)\\0_d\end{pmatrix}.
\end{split}\] The omitted normalizer and \(p_\theta(y)\) are constant in \(z\) at fixed \(\theta,y\). Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) restores the density-level derivation. It makes no claim that an arbitrary motion output of the flow-dropped network equals the padded marginal score. Section 4.3 states that the dropped-motion branch is trained with appearance loss only, so its motion component requires a separate convention if the whole concatenated update is to implement this exact joint-score identity. The staged materials do not resolve that implementation question. The score-to-velocity relation also uses state derivatives. For the stated Gaussian interpolation, the exact conditional-mean velocity at \(0<t<1\) satisfies \[u_t(z)=\frac{z+(1-t)\nabla_z\log p_t(z)}{t}.\] This follows by differentiating the Gaussian convolution and substituting \(\mathbb E[z_0\mid z_t=z]\) into the interpolation. In particular, the padded marginal score \((s_x,0_d)\) maps pointwise to \((u_x,d/t)\), not \((u_x,0_d)\). The independent native challenge checked this affine mapping with exact rational arithmetic. This pointwise identity alone does not show that an arbitrary tilted score family transports its proposed marginals. A complete corrected sampler requires consistent treatment of these relations. No fully repaired implementation is asserted here.
# Core dependence and impact

Inner-Guidance is one of the paper’s two principal method components. The failed reasoning is used to declare existing guidance inapplicable, motivate the new construction, and attribute the IP2P ablation difference to a theoretical gap (Appendix A). This is a demonstrated invalid argument directly tied to that contribution, supporting Major under the review contract. The density in Equation (7), the joint regression architecture, and reported preference improvements can remain useful. A different empirical result from another weighting rule cannot establish the erroneous derivative premise. The comparison tests complete update rules and coefficients; it does not isolate independence from model parameters as a causal mechanism. No video-quality loss, false benchmark value, or whole-paper failure is inferred. The available arXiv v2 contains the same targeted reasoning; no correction was found in the inspected version and no exhaustive erratum search is claimed. The inaccessible reference fetches and absence of staged VideoJAM implementation are recorded as missing evidence, not additional defects.
