Title: Technical Verification of
LieRE: Lie Rotational Positional Encodings
# Paper identity and inspected scope

This report concerns Sophie Ostmeier, Brian Axelrod, Maya Varma, Michael Moseley, Akshay Chaudhari, and Curtis Langlotz, LieRE: Lie Rotational Positional Encodings, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, identifier I25-43542, assigned number 0173 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed proceedings PDF has 17 pages. Locations below use PDF page numbers, which agree with the printed scientific page numbers. The appendix is embedded in this original PDF. The released source snapshot is commit `b27b41ba0d27331ec0774de852939c6d407889aa`, dated 13 August 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. It is not assumed to be the historical experiment commit.

The review inspected the main mathematical definitions and method, the empirical protocols and reported comparisons at a descriptive level, the one-dimensional argument in Appendix A, experimental settings in Appendix B, the implementation in Appendix C, and the stated compute, validation-loss, parameter-scaling and attention-map material in Appendices D–G. Detailed static source inspection covered the positional encoder and attention path in `models/rope_vit.py`. It did not execute author code, train models, load checkpoints, reconstruct individual predictions, verify confidence-interval coverage, or measure runtime/FLOPs. Figures and tables are evidence of reported results, not independently reproduced observations. Separate OpenReview attachments were not accessible in the prepared-source record.
# Mathematical construction and verified reasoning

Let \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) be a position and let \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) satisfy \(A_i^\top=-A_i\). The method forms \[B(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_iA_i,\qquad R(p)=\exp B(p),
 \qquad q_p'=R(p)q_p,\quad k_p'=R(p)k_p.\] For real positions \(B(p)\) remains skew-symmetric, so \[R(p)^\top R(p)=\exp(-B(p))\exp B(p)=I,\qquad
 \det R(p)=\exp(\operatorname{tr}B(p))=1.\] Thus the positional operation preserves vector norms and lies in \(\mathrm{SO}(d)\). The static implementation constructs a strictly upper-triangular parameter matrix, subtracts its transpose, linearly combines these bases with positions, and calls the matrix exponential. Both keys and queries receive the transformations before their inner product [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The subtraction of the same constant from every entry before antisymmetrization cancels and does not invalidate skew-symmetry.

Equation reference: eq:oned. For a single position coordinate, choose an orthogonal \(S\) with \(A=S^\top\Lambda S\), where \(\Lambda\) is a direct sum of planar skew blocks (and a zero block if needed). Then \[
 R(t)^\top R(t')=S^\top\exp\big((t'-t)\Lambda\big)S.\] The constant factors \(S\) can be absorbed into unconstrained learned key and query projections. This verifies the substance of Appendix A for RoPE with learned frequencies/phases. Section 7, PDF page 8, explicitly gives this qualification. The same statement would not hold for an arbitrary learned spectrum if the comparator were restricted to fixed preset frequencies, but that unfavorable reading is not needed in view of the stated qualification. Transpose and repeated-line irregularities in the displayed appendix do not defeat the corrected identity [eq:oned] (#eq:oned).
# Established local finding

Problem 1 (The exponential map is not a global bijective coordinate system).  The background’s universal global statement about the matrix exponential is false, including on the rotation group actually used by the method. Assessment: Minor.
## Original claim and precise scope

Section 3.1, PDF page 4, describes, in paraphrase, the matrix exponential as a smooth bijection from the Lie algebra to every Lie group and calls it a diffeomorphism. No neighborhood restriction is attached to this global assertion. The later phrase about \(U,V\) being close accompanies Equation (1), not a restriction of the exponential’s domain or codomain. The original page image was inspected to rule out an extraction artifact.
## Complete counterexample

Take the matrix Lie group \(\mathrm{SO}(2)\) and its Lie algebra \[\mathfrak{so}(2)=\{\theta J:\theta\in\mathbb R\},
 \qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This is exactly the real skew-symmetric rotation setting, with no additional regularity or learning assumptions. Since \(J^2=-I\), expansion of the absolutely convergent exponential series gives \[\exp(\theta J)=I\cos\theta+J\sin\theta.\] The distinct Lie algebra elements \(0\) and \(2\pi J\) therefore both map to \(I\). The map is not injective and hence cannot be a global bijection or diffeomorphism. The independent numerical calculation reproduced this identity to a maximum entrywise residual of \(4.44\times10^{-16}\), but the series calculation is the decisive exact argument; floating-point equality is not being substituted for proof.
## Alternative readings, correction and impact

A valid local statement is that the exponential maps a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(0\) diffeomorphically onto a neighborhood of the identity. In the planar case this is explicit: restricting \(\theta\) to \((-\pi,\pi)\) gives a smooth inverse angle on the rotation group with the rotation by \(\pi\) removed. This is not a global coordinate system for the full group. A half-open interval that covers every planar rotation still has a discontinuous inverse at the cut and is not the full vector-space Lie algebra.

The construction in Section 4 only evaluates the smooth forward exponential. It neither computes a global logarithm nor relies on distinct skew parameters producing distinct rotations. The static code agrees with this forward-only use. Consequently the false background assertion is a supported local mathematical defect, but no dependency that invalidates the central learned rotation method, its empirical comparisons, or its optimization has been established. The repair is to state local invertibility and retain the globally smooth forward map. It does not require changing the encoder, and it has not been adopted by the authors on any source checked here.
# Scope clarifications and unresolved empirical checks
## Relative versus absolute information

If the generators commute, \(R(p)^\top R(q)=R(q-p)\) exactly. For general noncommuting generators the product can depend on \(p\) and \(q\) separately. A reviewer-written diagnostic with two skew \(3\times3\) generators gave a Frobenius change of \(0.0935176458872\) after jointly translating two positions. This is a diagnostic of the model class, not a defect under the paper’s stated scope: the abstract and conclusion expressly allow absolute information, and Section 3.1 explicitly contrasts the stronger commuting identity with a weaker relation.

Equation (1)’s approximation is not supplied with a quantitative error bound. Closeness of \(U\) and \(V\) should not be interpreted as a first-order identity with a uniform small remainder at arbitrary nonzero base points. The review does not infer an empirical extrapolation failure from this unspecified approximation. A quantitative relative-position guarantee would need a domain and an error bound. None was independently established here.
## Empirical and implementation boundaries

Reported CIFAR-100 improvements and the resolution-retention plots support the paper’s stated experimental narrative at the level of the displayed observations. Claims of significance require the actual resampling unit, predictions, and sampling procedure, which were not re-created. The released code implements the principal algebraic construction, but static agreement cannot certify training provenance or reported scores. Appendix D’s FLOP and training-compute numbers were not independently profiled. The confidence-interval and table transcription details are not treated as substantive mathematical defects without a demonstrated consequential discrepancy.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The highest supported assessment is Minor, confined to the global exponential-map assertion. No additional substantive issue was established in the inspected construction, its qualified one-dimensional reduction, or the selected source path. This is a scope-bounded result and not whole-paper certification. Empirical reproducibility and any uninspected implementation paths remain outside the completed checks.

Title: Technical Verification of
Convex Markov Games
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Ian Gemp, Andreas Haupt, Luke Marris, Siqi Liu, and Georgios Piliouras, Convex Markov Games: A New Frontier for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:19137–19160, OpenReview identifier `yIfCq03hsM` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The exact input is the staged 24-page proceedings PDF whose SHA-256 is recorded in Appendix 5 (#app:repro). All page references below are one-based PDF pages; they coincide with the paper’s printed page labels 1–24, rather than the volume page range.

The claim-focused inspection covered Definition 1, the policy–occupancy correspondence, Theorem 1 and Appendix A, the rank and differentiability arguments in Appendix B, Lemma 3 in Appendix C, Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 in Appendix D, and the domain descriptions in Section 5 and Appendix F. The robot-warehouse listing was inspected statically; it was not executed. The independent arithmetic below uses only a separately written standard-library script. No training, rollout, author-code execution, or empirical replication was performed. A paper-specific released implementation was unavailable in the staged acquisition record. Separate OpenReview attachments were unresolved after the acquisition process encountered HTTP 403. The remaining experimental tables were inspected as descriptions, not recomputed from original data.
# Definitions and checked reasoning

For player \(i\), the stationary policy space is the product of finite action simplexes, \(\Pi_i=\prod_{s\in S}\Delta(A_i)\). The normalized discounted occupancy is \[\mu_i^\pi(s,a_i)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\geq0}\gamma^t
 \Pr_\pi(s_t=s,a_{i,t}=a_i),\qquad 0\leq\gamma<1.\] For fixed opponents it satisfies \(A_i(\pi_{-i})\mu_i=(1-\gamma)\mu_0\) and \(\mu_i\geq0\), and the utility is concave in this occupancy. Continuity is interpreted jointly in the variables on which the utility depends, as required and used in Appendix A’s existence argument.
## Exploitability certificate

The derivation in Appendix D is valid when the displayed gradient or supergradient exists. For feasible \(z,\mu_i\), concavity gives \[u_i(z,\pi_{-i})-u_i(\mu_i,\pi_{-i})
 \leq g^\top(z-\mu_i)
 =(\Pi_{\ker A_i}g)^\top(z-\mu_i)
 \leq\sqrt2\,\|\Pi_{\ker A_i}g\|_2.\] The last inequality follows because normalized occupancies lie in a simplex of Euclidean diameter \(\sqrt2\). Adding an entropy bonus changes each utility difference by at most \(\tau\log(|S||A_i|)\), yielding the stated upper bound. This is a sufficient small-exploitability certificate. It does not require every equilibrium to have zero loss for every supergradient selection.

The rank argument is also sound: a block \(I-\gamma P_a\) is invertible because \(P_a\) is stochastic and \(\gamma<1\); consequently the full flow matrix has full row rank. The matrix entries depend on opponents’ policies, as Section 4 explicitly recognizes. No claim of global convergence of Algorithm 1 is attributed to the paper; page 5 expressly disclaims it. At zero occupancy entries the ordinary Shannon-entropy gradient is not finite. The smooth formula therefore needs positive occupancy or an explicit restriction to the reachable support. This domain qualification is not a counterexample to the certificate where its gradient exists.
## Equilibrium existence: a checked clarification

Appendix A, page 14, passes from convex optimal-occupancy sets to contractible policy best-response sets by invoking upper hemicontinuity. Upper hemicontinuity alone does not imply preservation of contractibility. For a full-support initial distribution the inverse normalization is a homeomorphism, but with zero initial masses some states can have zero occupancy and arbitrary policies. An additional argument is then needed. This review does not infer that the existence theorem is false from that omission. The following independent argument verifies the theorem’s conclusion without relying on the asserted topological preservation.

For \(\delta>0\), set \[\mu_0^\delta=(1-\delta)\mu_0+\delta\,\mathrm{Unif}(S),
 \qquad
 u_i^\delta(\mu_i,\pi_{-i})=u_i(\mu_i,\pi_{-i})+\delta H(\mu_i).\] Use \(0<\delta<1\). Every state marginal is at least \((1-\gamma)\delta/|S|>0\). The feasible occupancy set against fixed opponents is compact and convex, and strict concavity of entropy gives a unique maximizing occupancy. Its dependence on opponents is continuous: the feasible correspondence is the continuous image of the fixed compact policy set, hence continuous, and the maximum theorem with a unique optimizer applies. Normalizing the positive state marginals gives a unique continuous policy best response. Brouwer’s theorem on the compact convex product \(\prod_i\Pi_i\) gives a fixed point \(\pi^\delta\).

Take a subsequence \(\delta_k\downarrow0\) with \(\pi^{\delta_k}\to\pi^*\). Discounted occupancy is jointly continuous in the initial distribution and policies because \((I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\) exists throughout the compact policy domain. The perturbation of utilities converges uniformly: the unregularized utilities are uniformly continuous on the relevant compact domain and \(0\leq H(\mu_i)\leq\log(|S||A_i|)\). The best-response inequality for each fixed alternative policy therefore passes to the limit. Thus \(\pi^*\) is a pure strategy in the paper’s policy-level sense: one stationary stochastic policy per player. This analytic argument verifies existence, including initial distributions with zero entries; it makes no algorithmic convergence claim. The topological observation is recorded as a scope clarification, not a false-theorem finding.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The published warehouse kernel contains negative probabilities).  The Appendix F.2 robot-warehouse specification does not define a stochastic transition kernel for the two mixed-speed actions at the joint pickup state.
## Original specification and location

Pages 21–24 describe four joint states and two actions per player, with state \(s=0\) meaning both robots are at pickup. Page 21 sets \(p_{\mathrm{low}}=0.2\), \(p_{\mathrm{mid}}=0.5\), and \(p_{\mathrm{high}}=0.8\). For \((a_1,a_2)=(0,1)\), page 22 assigns the transition to state 1 probability \(p_{\mathrm{high}}\); page 23 assigns transitions to states 2 and 3 probability \(p_{\mathrm{low}}\) each. Page 24 defines the remaining transition to state 0 by subtraction from one.
## Complete check and counterevidence

The displayed values give, in destination-state order \(0,1,2,3\), \[P(\cdot\mid0,0,1)=
 \left(1-\frac45-\frac15-\frac15,\frac45,\frac15,\frac15\right)
 =\left(-\frac15,\frac45,\frac15,\frac15\right).\] The reversed mixed-speed action yields \((-1/5,1/5,4/5,1/5)\). Both columns sum to one but violate nonnegativity. The final assertion on page 24 checks column sums only, so it cannot detect these entries. The parameter values and assignments were checked in rendered source pages 21–24; this is not an extraction artifact. The exact rational calculation is preserved in `verification/0174/independent_results.json`.

The source explicitly labels these entries transition probabilities, and Definition 1 requires \(P:S\times A\to\Delta(S)\). No signed-kernel interpretation is compatible with those conditions. The paper could have used a different internal implementation, but the available sources do not establish that provenance. This finding concerns the literal published domain, not an assertion about which code produced the reported numbers.
## Impact and repair state

The specification must be corrected before the warehouse example can be reproduced as the stated Markov game. The reported 69% versus 42% action probabilities and exploitabilities in Section 5.4 have not been independently falsified: connecting their numerical values to this listing requires the actual experimental implementation or a rerun on an author-specified valid kernel. The general cMG definition, existence theorem, other domains, and the abstract exploitability bound are unaffected. The supported assessment is Minor, with the provenance of the warehouse experiment Needs Evidence. There is no uniquely justified numerical repair: changing one entry, renormalizing, or changing the joint-event model defines different games. No corrected experimental result is claimed.

Problem 2 (Nonsmooth optimality does not force every selected projected gradient to vanish).  The necessity direction of Appendix C, Lemma 3, fails for an arbitrary selected supergradient of a concave nondifferentiable utility.
## Original claim and location

Lemma 3 on page 17 states that a strictly positive primal-feasible strategy is a best response if and only if its projected-gradient norm is zero. The proof uses a KKT set inclusion in Equation (32), then treats an element of the utility’s generalized differential as lying in the row space of the equality-constraint matrix, and concludes zero projection in Equations (33)–(37). For concave utilities, the relevant supporting vectors are supergradients; the paper calls them subgradients.
## A counterexample satisfying the stated conditions

Take one player, one state, two actions, \(\gamma=0\), initial state mass one, and a valid self-loop transition under either action. The feasible occupancy simplex is \[\mu_1+\mu_2=1,\qquad \mu_1,\mu_2\geq0.\] Let \(u(\mu)=-\max(\mu_1,\mu_2)\), a continuous concave utility. The unique maximizer is \(\mu^*=(1/2,1/2)\), which is strictly positive, with utility \(-1/2\). The vector \(g=(-1,0)\) is a valid supergradient: for every \(z\), \(u(z)\leq-z_1=u(\mu^*)+g^\top(z-\mu^*)\). For \(A=(1,1)\), \[\Pi_{\ker A}g
 =\left(I-\frac12
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\right)
 \binom{-1}{0}
 =\binom{-1/2}{1/2},
 \qquad
 \|\Pi_{\ker A}g\|_2^2=\frac12.\] Thus an admissible selected gradient has a nonzero projected norm at a strictly positive best response. Adding the paper’s entropy bonus does not change this example’s optimizer; the entropy gradient at the uniform point is constant across actions and has zero tangent projection.
## Alternative reading, correction, and bounded impact

KKT gives an existential condition: at an interior optimum there is a supporting vector in \(\operatorname{range}(A^\top)\). Indeed, \(g_0=(-1/2,-1/2)\) is also a valid supergradient here and has zero projection. If Lemma 3 means that there exists such a selection, rather than that a previously selected one must vanish, the example is consistent with it. The proof’s passage from an existence statement to an arbitrary differential element is the defect.

The precise supported repair is to state the equivalence with existence of a supergradient having zero tangent projection, under the usual finite-supergradient/KKT conditions at the strictly positive point. For differentiable utilities the gradient is unique, so the original form is valid. This repair follows directly from concavity and the normal-space optimality condition; it does not certify a particular autodifferentiation rule or a modified optimizer.

This is a Minor local lemma defect. Appendix D’s upper bound uses the supporting inequality and remains valid for every admissible finite supergradient. Algorithm 1 has no advertised convergence guarantee, and the present check does not establish that any published run selected the counterexample’s differential element. No core bound is refuted.
# Overall dependence and conclusion

Two concrete local defects require correction or clarification, while the main existence conclusion and exploitability certificate survive the checks performed here. The existence discussion is supported by a complete independent analytic argument. The unresolved experimental provenance does not increase the severity of the demonstrated transition-table defect. No later revision or author erratum was inspected in this review, and no novelty or first-discovery claim is made.

report: Abstract: The finite-sample high-feedback derivation assigns a binomial tie to the opposite branch from the estimator explicitly defined in its proof. For an admissible two-sample example, this changes the expected risk from \(9/128\) to \(15/128\) and reverses both reported impact signs. This is a Major error in the exact finite-sample analysis under the stated tie rule; a consistent alternative tie rule restores the printed formulas. Three separate Minor concerns concern a main-text formula already correct in the appendix, a released uncertainty-band scale, and use of a true unknown parameter in a released exploratory policy. The full-information framework and the qualitative possibility of performative side effects are not refuted. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:

Title: Technical Verification of
Performative Risk Impact for Binary Variables
# Identity, version, and review scope

The reviewed article is Nikita Tsoy, Ivan Kirev, Negin Rahimiyazdi (the PDF byline prints Negin Rahimi), and Nikola Konstantinov, On the Impact of Performative Risk Minimization for Binary Random Variables, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:60336–60361, OpenReview `yIL0WEiGNo` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The source is the 26-page proceedings PDF with embedded appendices, identified by its actual hash in Appendix 5 (#app:repro). Page numbers here are one-based PDF pages, equal to the paper’s printed labels 1–26.

The inspection covers the binary response model, the one- and two-period full-information formulas, the finite-sample moment and risk derivations, the structure of the infinite-horizon recurrences, and static reading of all three released notebooks [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The notebooks were parsed as JSON and their source cells read; no notebook cell or author function was executed. Exact independently written rational enumeration was used for the counterexample. Four bounded infinite-horizon paths were checked numerically against necessary Euler equations; those finite diagnostics are not a proof of global infinite-horizon optimality. No complete reproduction of Figures 1–6, training, or simulation run was performed. The staged record leaves separate OpenReview attachments unresolved following an acquisition HTTP 403. No later revision or erratum was inspected.
# Model and checked baseline

Equation reference: eq:risk. The observation \(z\) takes values \(\{-1/2,1/2\}\), with mean \(p\in[-1/2,1/2]\). Predictions lie in the same interval. The response is \[p_{t+1}=\alpha\theta_t+(1-|\alpha|)
 \{\lambda p_t+(1-\lambda)\pi\},
 \quad -1<\alpha<1,\quad 0\leq\lambda<1.\] In the one-period slow-deployment experiment with \(p_0=\pi\), the test mean conditional on the prediction is \(p_1=\alpha\theta+(1-|\alpha|)p_0\), so the exact risk is \[
 R=(1-2\alpha)\mathbb E\theta^2
   -2(1-|\alpha|)p_0\mathbb E\theta+\frac14.\] This follows directly from \(z^2=1/4\) and agrees with the paper’s Appendix B.4. Its error–uncertainty decomposition is also valid.

For \(\alpha<1/2\), minimizing the deterministic quadratic gives the clipped formula in Proposition 4.1. For \(\alpha>1/2\), a zero sample mean makes the two endpoints equally optimal for the plug-in problem; which endpoint is selected must be specified when calculating moments and impact. For the two-period rapid case, backward substitution gives \(\theta_1=p_1\) and a quadratic in \(\theta_0\) with coefficient \(1-\gamma\alpha^2>0\), supporting Proposition 4.2. These analytic checks do not depend on the disputed binomial boundary.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The binomial boundary changes the estimator whose moments are computed).  The high-feedback branch of Lemma B.1 and Theorem A.2 uses a different tie rule from the estimator explicitly defined in its proof.
## Source claim, domain, and suspect step

Equation reference: eq:positive, eq:source-moment. Section 4.2.1, page 5, defines the plug-in estimator using the empirical mean of \(m\) independent observations from \(D_0\), with \(p_0=\pi\). Appendix B.4, page 19, case (ii), explicitly defines, for \(\alpha\in[1/2,1)\), \[
 \widehat\theta_+=
 \begin{cases}
  1/2,&\overline p_0\geq0,\\
  -1/2,&\overline p_0<0.
 \end{cases}\] Let \(K=m(\overline p_0+1/2)\sim\mathrm{Bin}(m,1/2+p_0)\). The same page converts the strict event \(K<m/2\) to the inclusive binomial CDF \(F(m/2)=\Pr(K\leq\lfloor m/2\rfloor)\), and consequently states \[
 \mathbb E\widehat\theta=\frac12-F(m/2).\] For even \(m\), this assigns \(K=m/2\) to the negative branch. The error propagates through Equation [eq:risk] (#eq:risk) into the \(\alpha\geq1/2\) risk branch of Theorem A.2, page 16, and into the bias and shift identities of Appendix A.3.1, page 15.
## Complete admissible counterexample

Set \[\alpha=\frac34,\qquad p_0=\pi=\frac14,\qquad
 \lambda=\frac15,\qquad m=2,\qquad T=1.\] All parameters are inside their stated domains. Any \(0<\gamma<1\), for example \(1/2\), is admissible and irrelevant for this one-period risk. The observations are independent with \(\Pr(z=1/2)=3/4\). Because \(p_0=\pi\), the response baseline is \(s_1=1/4\), independently of \(\lambda\). The complete sample-space calculation is \[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 K&0&1&2\\ \hline
 \Pr(K)&1/16&6/16&9/16\\
 \overline p_0&-1/2&0&1/2\\
 \widehat\theta_+&-1/2&1/2&1/2\\
 p_1(\widehat\theta_+)&-5/16&7/16&7/16\\
 \mathbb E[(\widehat\theta_+-z)^2\mid K]&3/16&1/16&1/16
\end{array}\] Every induced mean remains in \([-1/2,1/2]\), so the test distributions are valid. The sample tie selects a legitimate endpoint minimizer; the positive tie rule is not an inadmissible policy. It follows exactly that \[\mathbb E\widehat\theta_+=\frac7{16},\qquad
 \mathbb E\widehat\theta_+^2=\frac14,\qquad
 R_+=\frac9{128}.\] In contrast, \(F(1)=7/16\), so Equation [eq:source-moment] (#eq:source-moment) gives \(1/16\), and Theorem A.2 gives \(15/128\). The bias and shift are, from the paper’s definitions, \[b=(1-\alpha)\mathbb E\theta-(1-|\alpha|)p_0,\qquad
 d=\alpha\mathbb E\theta-|\alpha|p_0.\] Thus the stated estimator has \((b,d)=(3/64,9/64)\), whereas the printed moment yields \((-3/64,-9/64)\). Both signs reverse. The independently written exact enumeration and its full table are saved in `verification/0175/independent_results.json`. The source’s inclusive inequality and CDF conversion were verified visually on page 19.
## Counterevidence and precise repair alternatives

For odd \(m\), \(K=m/2\) is impossible and the formulas agree. An exact \(m=3\) check at the same parameters confirms this. Moreover, the printed formulas are correct for the negative tie estimator \[\widehat\theta_-=
 \begin{cases}1/2,&\overline p_0>0,\\-1/2,&\overline p_0\leq0.\end{cases}\] The released imperfect-information notebook, source cell 1, calculates the printed moment; its cell 2 calculates the corresponding printed risk. This is evidence for a consistent alternative intended convention. It does not make that convention identical to Equation [eq:positive] (#eq:positive).

There are two exact repairs. If the stated positive tie rule is retained, replace Equation [eq:source-moment] (#eq:source-moment) by \[\mathbb E\widehat\theta_+
 =\frac12-\Pr(K<m/2)
 =\frac12-F\bigl(\lceil m/2\rceil-1\bigr).\] Equivalently, add \[q_m=\mathbf1_{\{m\ {\rm even}\}}
 \binom{m}{m/2}(1/2+p_0)^{m/2}(1/2-p_0)^{m/2}\] to the printed first moment. The second moment remains \(1/4\). The risk correction is \(-2(1-\alpha)p_0q_m\), and the bias and shift corrections are \((1-\alpha)q_m\) and \(\alpha q_m\). Alternatively, explicitly define the estimator with the negative tie rule throughout; the printed formulas then apply. Both statements follow analytically by assigning the single tie event to its intended branch. Neither repair is an empirical rerun.
## Core dependence and assessment

The affected objects are the exact moments, risk, and impact measures for the proposed finite-sample estimator, one of the paper’s central contributions. The counterexample demonstrates a false derivation and changes the direction of both impact measures under the explicitly stated estimator. The supported impact is Major for this finite-sample result. That judgment does not require a failure of the full-information theory or of the broad claim that performative optimization can have side effects. An endpoint convention can repair the result, but it must be chosen consistently. The comparison does not establish which convention generated every historical plot.
Problem 2 (Theorem 4.3’s displayed risk omits the squared mean).  The main-text risk formula differs from the correct expression already given in the paper’s appendix.

The correct expression follows from \(\widehat\theta=(1-|\alpha|)\overline p_0/(1-2\alpha)\), \(\mathbb E\overline p_0=p_0\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline p_0)=(1/4-p_0^2)/m\). Independent exact enumeration agreed with the appendix expression in 27 selected cases, in addition to this analytic derivation. This is Minor: the same source already contains the correct general result and the released code uses it. The correction is to restore \(p_0^2\) in the main display. It is not presented as a failure of the appendix derivation or a new author-adopted correction.
Problem 3 (The released shift band uses the bias standard-deviation factor).  The plotting implementation scales the random mean shift by \(1-\alpha\) instead of \(|\alpha|\).

In the released notebook `c2-figures-2-3-imperfect-info.ipynb`, source cell 4, both the bias and shift band widths are set to \((1-\alpha)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)}\). But for fixed true parameters the random shift is \(D=\alpha\widehat\theta-|\alpha|p_0\), whereas the random bias is \(B=(1-\alpha)\widehat\theta-(1-|\alpha|)p_0\). Therefore \[\operatorname{sd}(D)=|\alpha|\operatorname{sd}(\widehat\theta),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{sd}(B)=|1-\alpha|\operatorname{sd}(\widehat\theta).\] The released shift width is too large by \(7/3\) for the plotted \(\alpha=0.3\), and by \(7/2\) for \(\alpha=-0.4\), at nondegenerate points. These ratios were checked with exact rational arithmetic. For example, at \(\alpha=-0.4,p_0=0,m=10\), the correct shift standard deviation is \(0.4/(6\sqrt{10})\), while the released width is \(1.4/(6\sqrt{10})\).

Figure 2 and the page 5 discussion interpret the shaded bands as one-standard-deviation ranges; they are not 95% confidence intervals. The published image was inspected and is consistent in appearance with the released scaling, but no original plotting arrays or hash-bound generation receipt was available. Accordingly, the established Minor finding is a release implementation discrepancy. The exact historical figure-generation provenance remains Needs Evidence; no precise digitization or reproduction of the paper’s figure is claimed. Replacing the shift multiplier with \(|\alpha|\) restores the variance identity for fixed parameters. No new simulation is needed to prove that identity, although regenerating and checking the affected figure is remaining work.

Problem 4 (A released exploratory policy uses the true unknown feedback parameter).  The released one-period exploration routine’s action depends on the environment’s true \(\alpha\), despite its unknown-parameter setting.

The true parameter is properly needed to simulate the response after the action; this does not justify its use inside the unknown-parameter decision rule. The discrepancy disappears when \(|\widehat\alpha|=|\alpha|\), so convergence to the same final point may still occur. The finite learning trajectory can nevertheless differ. This is a Minor static implementation finding: the release does not implement the declared information restriction. Its use in the historical Figure 4 run has not been established independently, and no claim is made that the reported convergence disappears after correction. Substituting \(|\widehat\alpha|\) in this numerator restores this local information constraint; rerunning the exploratory experiment would be needed to assess the numerical consequence.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The highest supported impact is Major because the finite-sample moment calculation for its explicitly defined estimator is wrong on an allowed event of positive probability, with a demonstrated effect on the paper’s principal impact metrics. The consistent negative-tie convention is substantive counterevidence: it recovers the printed formulas and is compatible with the released risk notebook. The report therefore identifies exactly what must be made consistent and does not reject all possible PRM estimators.

The binary risk identity, full-information one-period quadratic minimization away from the tie ambiguity, and two-period rapid calculation survive inspection. Four finite checks of bounded infinite-horizon paths gave necessary-Euler residuals below \(2\times10^{-17}\); this verifies those substitutions at the selected parameters, not a general sufficiency or boundary-regime theorem. The two code concerns remain separated from unproved historical experiment provenance.

report: Abstract: This claim-focused review identifies a failure of the bounded-estimator argument used to establish deterministic target-arm selection in the linear reward analysis. An admissible noise event of probability one half violates Lemma G.6 while satisfying its stated confidence event. This is a Major defect in the derivation of the core linear guarantee, without establishing that the stated regret rate is false. Separately, an exact bounded-reward example exceeds Algorithm 3’s stated round limit; its logarithmic order survives, so this finding is Minor. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of Principal-Agent Bandit Games
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Junyan Liu and Lillian J. Ratliff, Principal-Agent Bandit Games with Self-Interested and Exploratory Learning Agents, ICML 2025, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267:39318–39365, paper identifier I25-43545 and OpenReview identifier `yI24Wy5YaN` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed file is the 48-page PMLR proceedings PDF staged as `papers/0176/0176.pdf`. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the document’s printed 1–48 page numbers; they are not the PMLR volume page range.

The review inspected the model, benchmark and main claims in Sections 2–5; the incentive-search pseudocode and selected proof dependencies in Appendix D; and the algorithms, confidence event and complete linear proof dependency chain in Appendix G. The exploration results in Section 4 were read at the statement and construction level, but Appendices E–F were not independently verified line by line. No author code or empirical experiment was executed. No paper-specific implementation was supplied in the staged acquisition. A separate OpenReview attachment could not be established by source preparation, which recorded an HTTP 403 response. These missing materials do not prevent the calculations below.
# Model and necessary distinctions

In the linear model on page 4, the finite arm set satisfies \(\mathcal A\subseteq B(0,1)\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and spans \(\mathbb R^d\). The true agent and principal parameters \(s^\star,\nu^\star\) lie in \(B(0,1)\). The observations are \[R_{A_t}(t)=\langle s^\star,A_t\rangle+\eta^A(t),\qquad
 X_{A_t}(t)=\langle\nu^\star,A_t\rangle+\eta^P(t),\] where the noises are conditionally 1-subgaussian. This linear model does not impose the \([0,1]\) reward restriction that the adjacent paragraph imposes on the separate i.i.d. model. The agent uses ordinary least squares, initialized by an arbitrary \(\widehat s_1\in B(0,1)\), and selects an empirical maximizer of \(\langle\widehat s_t,a\rangle+\pi_a(t)\). No projection or clipping of later estimates is specified.

To avoid the source’s inclusive-\(t\) observation-index ambiguity, \(\widehat s\) below means the estimate formed from the observations already received before the next action. The counterexample therefore applies under the usual causal reading of the learning model.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The target-selection lemma assumes an absent OLS norm bound).  The proof of Lemma G.6 (page 46) uses \(\pi_a^\star\leq\max_b\|\widehat s_t\|\|b-a\|\leq 2d\) to conclude that the capped offer strictly exceeds the minimum incentive. The corresponding norm claim also appears in the explanation of Algorithm 8 on page 9. The stated OLS model does not imply \(\|\widehat s_t\|\leq d\).
## Source claim and dependency

Lemma G.6 asserts, conditional on the event \(\mathcal E\) defined on page 42, that every target offer in every phase strictly exceeds the target’s minimum incentive. Its base case is phase 1, when the offer is \(2d+T^{-1}\) for all target arms. The page 42 notation then identifies intended target rounds \(\mathcal T^E_{m,a}\) with actual arm rounds \(\mathcal T_{m,a}\). Algorithm 7, Equation (45), and Lemmas G.7–G.10 use the resulting sample allocation and design matrices. The proof of Theorem 5.1 on pages 43–44 expressly invokes Lemma G.6 in its regret decomposition and sample counts.
## An exact-design counterexample

Equation reference: eq:linear-example. Set \[
 d=1,\quad \mathcal A=\{+1,-1\},\quad
 s^\star=-1,\quad \nu^\star=0,\quad
 \widehat s_1=0,\quad T=65536,\quad \delta=T^{-1}.\] Both arms and both parameters satisfy the unit-ball restrictions, and the arms span \(\mathbb R\). Let the first agent noise be a Rademacher random variable, taking \(+1\) and \(-1\) with probability \(1/2\) each, and let every later agent noise and every principal noise be zero. The first noise is conditionally 1-subgaussian because \(\mathbb E e^{\lambda\eta}=\cosh\lambda\leq e^{\lambda^2/2}\); the later zero noises also meet the condition. The linear model permits this time-dependent noise sequence. There is no exploratory behavior.

Choose the phase-1 design \(\rho_1(+1)=\rho_1(-1)=1/2\) and list the \(+1\) arm first in Algorithm 7’s target loop. Its design matrix is \(G=1\), and \(\max_a a^2/G=1\); thus it is even an exact optimal design and certainly satisfies the stated 2-approximation requirement. Its phase-1 block has at least two rounds. There is an initial-index ambiguity in Algorithm8: it defines \(z_i\) for \(i\in\mathbb N\), but its initial unit ball has width2 in the normalized direction. Thus line3 has no admissible nonnegative index. Under the natural intended dyadic extension to \(i=-1\), one has \(z_{-1}=1/4\) and, with \(\epsilon_0=1\), line4’s threshold is \(4/\|a_1-a_2\|=2\). The algorithm therefore breaks before any incentive or observation and returns \(c_1\in[-1,1]\). For the variant \(\{1,-1/4\}\) below the threshold is \(16/5\), so the same immediate return holds. The execution witness uses this explicit intended reading; the literal natural-number indexing instead leaves the initial search undefined. It does not silently assume that a nonempty search has already occurred.

For every such permitted output, the \(33\epsilon_0\) term with \(\epsilon_0=1\) makes Algorithm7’s first-phase offer equal to the cap. The subsequent false norm bound and target rejection are independent of which \(c_1\in[-1,1]\) is returned.

Initially, the incentive \(2+T^{-1}\) makes the agent choose \(+1\). On the event \(\{\eta^A(1)=-1\}\), of probability \(1/2\), its first reward is \(-2\). After that observation, \[U=1,\qquad \widehat s=1^{-1}(1)(-2)=-2.\] At the next intended \(+1\) round, Equation [eq:optimal] (#eq:optimal) yields \[\pi^\star_{+1}=(-2)(-1-1)=4.\] The actual offer is \(2+T^{-1}<4\). Equivalently, the two scores are \[\widehat s(+1)+2+T^{-1}=T^{-1},
 \qquad \widehat s(-1)=2.\] The agent strictly prefers \(-1\), so arbitrary tie-breaking is immaterial. The claimed inequality \(\pi_{+1}>\pi^\star_{+1}\) is false.
## The confidence event does not exclude this path

Equation reference: eq:ols-path. This is not merely an example outside the good event. After any \(n\geq1\) observations on the specified branch, all arms have squared value one and all later noises vanish. Therefore \[
 U_n=n,\qquad
 \widehat s_n=s^\star-\frac1n,\qquad
 |a(\widehat s_n-s^\star)|=\frac1n
 \quad(a\in\mathcal A).\] Writing \(L_0=\log(4KT/\delta)\) with \(K=2\), we have \[\frac1n \leq \sqrt{\frac{2L_0}{n}}\qquad(n\geq1).\] Thus the path satisfies even the conventional confidence radius using the squared Mahalanobis norm. The event displayed on page 42 uses a norm under the square root; its radius is no smaller on this example. The agent part of \(\mathcal E\) holds at every later time, including all times after phase 1 to which that event applies. All principal observations and the principal estimate are zero, so the principal part holds exactly. Consequently \(\mathcal E\) holds on the probability-\(1/2\) branch that violates Lemma G.6.
## A variant makes the design mismatch explicit

For the two symmetric arms, a wrong sign happens to preserve the scalar Gram increment. This coincidence does not rescue the target-selection lemma. Replace the arm set by \(\{1,-1/4\}\) and retain all other parameters, the half-half design, and the same first noise. Now \[G=\frac{17}{32},\qquad
 \max_a\frac{a^2}{G}=\frac{32}{17}<2,\] so this remains an admissible design. After the first reward, \(\widehat s=-2\) and the minimum incentive for target \(1\) is \(5/2\), again larger than \(2+T^{-1}\). The agent selects \(-1/4\); its actual Gram increment is \(1/16\), whereas the prescribed target allocation uses \(1\). For every continuation, \(U\geq1\) and \(\widehat s-s^\star=-1/U\), so \(|a|/U\leq |a|\sqrt{2L_0/U}\) proves that the confidence event remains satisfied. Principal observations remain zero. This variant directly invalidates identifying the designed and actual sample allocations.
## Alternative readings, impact, and repair status

The norm restriction in the model is on the true parameter and the initial estimate, not on every later OLS estimate. Interpreting the agent as using projected OLS would change the specified behavior. Conditioning on \(\mathcal E\), taking a large horizon, or allowing arbitrary tie-breaking does not remove the counterexample. The comparison concerns the linear model, so it does not impose an unbounded reward on the paper’s separate bounded i.i.d. model.

The supported assessment is Major: a false lemma and invalid bounded-estimator step sit directly in the proof of the paper’s core linear regret guarantee. The calculation does not prove that the rate in Theorem 5.1 is unattainable, nor that the i.i.d. guarantees fail. A bounded-estimator assumption would restore the particular cap argument, but it would alter the agent model and would require a new analysis; no complete repair of Theorem 5.1 is verified here.

Problem 2 (The stated search-round limit is exceeded).  Lemma 3.1 (page 6), repeated as Lemma D.6 (page 18), states that Algorithm 3 uses at most \(2\lceil\log_2 T\rceil\) rounds. The two counters in the page 14 pseudocode permit more rounds, even with constant bounded rewards and no exploration.
## Exact construction and complete count

Let \(T=2^L\) with \(L\geq2\), and define \[h=2^{-(L-1)},\qquad q=h-2^{-2L}.\] Give the target arm constant reward zero and its only competitor constant reward \(q\). Both are valid \([0,1]\)-bounded i.i.d. distributions. Consider a call after the competitor has been sampled once, with target empirical mean zero and competitor empirical mean \(q\). Such a state is reachable from zero initial estimates in Algorithm 1: list the competitor first, complete its first search and first-phase block, and then search for the target. For \(T=65536\) the relevant first-phase block is much shorter than the horizon. The principal rewards may be identically zero. All later empirical means stay constant.

Equation reference: eq:duration. The first \(L-1\) midpoint bids are \(1/2,1/4,\ldots,h\). Each is strictly above \(q\), so each selects the target. The midpoint counter is then \(C_1=L-1\) and the stored upper offer is \(h\). The next \(L\) midpoint bids are \[h(1-2^{-j}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,L.\] They are all strictly below \(q\), since even the largest equals \(h-2^{-(2L-1)}<h-2^{-2L}=q\). Each therefore fails and triggers an asymmetric check at bid \(h\), which strictly succeeds. The algorithm does not test its \(C_1\) stopping condition on those failed midpoint rounds. It returns at line 17 when the successful-check counter reaches \(C_2=L\). The total is exactly \[
 (L-1)+2L=3L-1>2L.\] No tie-breaking convention is needed. The independently written exact rational diagnostic, with \(L=16\), recorded 47 offer rounds against the stated limit of 32. Its entire bid/action transcript is retained in `verification/0176/check_results.json`.
## Counterevidence and bounded impact

This example does not establish an error in the returned incentive bound: the returned offer is \(h+2/T\), with overpayment \(2/T+2^{-2L}\). Its runtime also remains \(O(\log T)\). The issue is therefore Minor: the precise round bound and the duration argument in Lemma D.6 are false, but a change of the constant does not by itself refute the asymptotic regret orders. The source proof’s proposed worst case, in which every midpoint fails, misses the initial successful midpoint rounds accumulated before the repeated checks. No new universal sharp bound is asserted in this report.
# Overall dependence and conclusion

The linear analysis needs a valid guarantee linking its offered incentives, the agent’s actual choices, and its designed sample counts. The failure of Lemma G.6 is not a peripheral appendix observation: its conclusion is used by the principal theoretical result in Section 5. A corrected model or algorithm would require fresh proofs, including the associated concentration and elimination steps. Empirical reruns cannot establish that missing universal guarantee.

The search-duration error is logically separate and has narrower supported impact. This review does not infer that the other regret theorems are false, and it does not certify their complete proofs. No later version or erratum was supplied or independently compared; absence of a known correction here is not a claim that no correction exists.

Title: Technical Verification of GA-Planes
# Identity, version, and review scope

This report concerns Irmak Sivgin, Sara Fridovich-Keil, Gordon Wetzstein, and Mert Pilanci, Geometric Algebra Planes: Convex Implicit Neural Volumes, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 55828–55853, paper I25-43546 (local number 0177) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed source is the staged 26-page proceedings PDF. Page references below use one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the displayed article page numbers.

The review checks the parameterizations in Sections 3.1–3.3, their optimization claims in the introduction and Appendix A.1, the algebraic forms of Theorems 1–4 and Appendix A.2, and the lower bound in Appendix A.4, Equation (50). Sections 5–6 and the experiment descriptions were read to locate dependencies and distinguish theoretical guarantees from measured results. The XYZ and XYT implementations were inspected statically at the pinned commits in the references. No author program, training procedure, dataset evaluation, or empirical replication was run. The complete coverage ledger distinguishes read material from fully checked claims.

The main supported finding is a failure of a core optimization guarantee for Equation (4), not a claim that the representation family or its reported empirical performance is invalid. The isolated lower-bound defect is assessed separately.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Equation reference: eq:paper. Section 3.1 defines three line grids, three plane grids, and one volume grid. Features are obtained by linear, bilinear, or trilinear interpolation and concatenated as \[f(q)=e_1\odot e_2\odot e_3\odot e_{12}\odot e_{13}\odot e_{23}\odot e_{123}.\] The grids and decoder weights are trainable real parameters. For the semiconvex model, Section 3.2, Equation (4), gives \[
\widetilde y(q)=\sum_{i=1}^{h} (W_i^\top f(q))\,
       \mathbf{1}[\overline W_i^\top f(q)\geq0],\] where only \(\overline W\) is stated to be frozen at initialization. The same trainable \(f(q)\) occurs in both factors. The claim immediately below Equation (4) is that the objective is separately convex in the feature grids and in \(W\); the introduction and Appendix A.1 additionally attribute global optimization and absence of nonglobal local optima to the semiconvex formulation.

Our counterexample uses direct mean-squared-error supervision, one of the paper’s explicitly admitted convex objectives. The construction requires no feature multiplication, missing grid, nonconvex measurement operator, parameter sign constraint, or additional regularizer. Section 3.2 imposes no width or data restriction that excludes it. The radiance-field loss is already identified as nonconvex by the paper and is outside this guarantee.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Trainable features make the purported fixed gates change).  The separate-convexity argument for Equation (4) and its associated guarantee that all local minima are global are invalid for the stated model. Supported impact: Major.
## Source claim and dependency

Equation (4) and the separate-convexity assertion are on PDF page 4. The initialization-independent optimization contribution is stated on pages 1–2; Appendix A.1, page 14, expressly states that the semiconvex formulation has no nonglobal local optima. Section 5.4 and Figure 6 interpret the observed stability through this favorable landscape. Thus the affected claim is one of the paper’s advertised theoretical advantages.

Freezing \(\overline W\) does not freeze the binary pattern in [eq:paper] (#eq:paper): \(f(q)\) changes when the grids are optimized. Convexity in \(W\) for fixed grids survives, but convexity in the grids for fixed \(W\) does not.
## Admissible construction and exact calculation

Set all feature dimensions to one and all spatial grid resolutions to two. Retain all seven grids. Assign the first line grid the constant value \(z\), and assign the other two line grids, all three plane grids, and the volume grid the constant value zero. Choose any nonempty finite set of training coordinates within the grids’ interpolation domain, with target value one at every coordinate. Constant grids are preserved by each stated interpolation rule, so \[f(q)=(z,0,0,0,0,0,0)^\top\] at every training point. Choose \(h=1\) and \(W=\overline W=(1,0,0,0,0,0,0)^\top\). This also respects the requirement that the fixed gating weight be the initial value of the trainable weight. There is no parameter constraint violated by these choices.

Equation reference: eq:loss, eq:jensen. The mean squared loss is exactly \[
L(z)=\left(1-z\mathbf{1}[z\geq0]\right)^2.\] With \(W\) held fixed, \[L(-1)=1,\qquad L(0)=1,\qquad L(1)=0.\] Hence \[
 L\!\left(\frac{-1+1}{2}\right)=1>
 \frac{L(-1)+L(1)}2=\frac12.\] The restriction to this affine line in the grid parameters is nonconvex, disproving separate convexity in the grids.

There is also a nonglobal local minimum in the full parameter space, not merely on that line. At the constant-grid point \(z=-1\), every gate has a strictly negative argument. At a finite set of sampled coordinates, interpolation is a continuous linear function of the grid values. A sufficiently small open neighborhood of all trainable grid and decoder parameters therefore keeps every gate closed. The prediction remains zero and the loss remains one throughout that neighborhood. This is a non-strict local minimum. The admissible point \(z=1\), with the same decoder and fixed gate weight, has loss zero. Thus the local minimum is not global.

The construction is not dependent on an exceptional zero gating weight. For \(h=1\) and any nonzero frozen vector \(a\), constant grids can realize \(f=-a\) at initialization with \(W=\overline W=a\); the gate is strictly negative. The same model fits the constant target at \(f=a/\|a\|^2\). Strict negativity is stable under small perturbations, so interpreting the weights as random initial draws does not establish the asserted universal guarantee.
## Static implementation evidence and alternative readings

The released XYZ implementation [Retained latex: \cite{xyz}], `triplane_models.py`, defines `ConvexNet` on lines 6–22. It freezes `fc2.weight`, then evaluates \[\texttt{fc1(x) * (fc2(x) >= 0)}.\] The `MiniTriplane` forward path concatenates trainable interpolated grids and passes those same features to the decoder. The XYT implementation [Retained latex: \cite{xyt}], lines 7–24 and 72–105 of its corresponding file, uses the same structure. These observations were obtained by reading source; no author code was executed. The code has biases beyond the displayed mathematical model, but it does not supply the missing frozen feature copy. We do not infer which commit generated the paper’s experiments.

The most charitable alternative is to read the gate as \(\mathbf{1}[\overline W_i^\top\overline f(q)\geq0]\) with a frozen feature map. The PDF image on page 4 shows no bar on \(f\) in Equation (4), and the released forward path uses the moving features. Moreover, Equation (5), Figure 1, and the adjoining Section 3.3 text explicitly freeze separate gate grids for the fully convex variant. That distinction supports the literal reading of Equation (4).

For Equation (5), fixed gating grids make predictions linear in trainable grid values; composing with a convex loss preserves convexity. This positive check is counterevidence against extending the finding to the fully convex method.
## Impact and bounded correction

The counterexample invalidates the stated semiconvex landscape guarantee and the separate-convexity justification. It does not establish frequent training failure, altered benchmark scores, or invalidity of the fully convex and explicitly nonconvex models. The observed multi-seed stability in Section 5.4 may remain accurate as an empirical observation; it is not a proof of the claimed landscape.

Freezing both the gating weights and gating features would restore separate convexity for the resulting bilinear model under a convex loss. That is a change of model. Separate convexity alone does not prove that all local minima are global, so no complete repair of the original optimization guarantee is certified here. Equation (5) already provides the paper’s distinct fully convex alternative.

Problem 2 (The printed singular-value lower bound excludes an exact fit).  Appendix A.4, Equation (50), on PDF page 19 gives \(E_{\rm linear}(D(e_1\circ e_2))\geq \sigma_k(M)\). Under the conventional one-based descending singular-value notation, this is false. Supported impact: Minor.
## Assumptions and complete counterexample

Use the stated two-dimensional linear-decoder model with matching spatial resolutions \(m=n=r_1=2\), feature dimension \(k=1\), and \[M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 g_1=g_2=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad \alpha=1.\] These are unconstrained real grids of the stipulated sizes, evaluated at their grid coordinates. There is no interpolation mismatch. Equation (18) of the paper gives \(\widehat M=g_1\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)g_2^\top=M\). The attained Frobenius error is zero, and therefore the optimal error is zero. The singular values are \((1,0)\), so Equation (50) requires \(0\geq\sigma_1(M)=1\). The contradiction is unchanged if the loss is interpreted as the squared Frobenius norm.
## Counterevidence, correction, and impact

Theorem 1 and its explicit factorization, Equations (7) and (18), agree with the exact fit. Thus this check preserves the main factorization identity and identifies a defect in the subsequent lower-bound expression. Appendix A.4 does not define \(\sigma_k\) as a residual-tail quantity; its discussion refers to singular-value decay. An intended nonstandard meaning would require an explicit definition. The rendered page confirms that the printed index is \(k\), not \(k+1\).

Equation reference: eq:svd. For the unrestricted rank-\(k\) model with complete Frobenius supervision, the correct optimal error is \[
 \min_{U,V}\|M-UV^\top\|_F
 =\left(\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j(M)^2\right)^{1/2}.\] Indeed, the truncated singular-value decomposition attains the right-hand side, and no rank-\(k\) approximation can retain more than \(k\) singular directions. In particular the simple bound is \(E\geq\sigma_{k+1}(M)\), with absent singular values set to zero. For squared error, square the right-hand side of [eq:svd] (#eq:svd). This correction is restricted to Equation (50); it does not certify the neighboring bounds involving a downsampled, rather than optimized, low-resolution component.

The supported harm is a false local theoretical bound. No dependence of the main parameterization identity or the reported experiments on that numerical bound has been established, which is why this item is Minor independently of Problem Problem 1 (#prob:gates).
# Overall assessment and remaining work

The highest supported impact is Major because the semiconvex global-optimality claim is a central contribution and fails for an admissible instance. The fully convex formulation retains its direct convexity argument. The linear factorization identities checked in Theorems 1–2 survive, and the algebraic rearrangements in Theorems 3–4 do not resolve the optimization defect.

The available source manifest reports embedded appendices and pinned repositories; access to possible additional OpenReview attachments was unresolved in source preparation. No later revision or author erratum was supplied or independently located in this review, and no priority or first-discovery claim is made. Fresh experiments would be needed to measure the effect of changing the semiconvex gates or the frequency of training failures.

report: Abstract: The Gaussian marginal construction and deterministic reverse-step algebra of MA-TSD pass the checks described here. Two aspects of the training rationale need a more precise interpretation: the hybrid-loss upper bound depends on whether sequence errors are summed or averaged, and the exact Gaussian variational term has a matrix-weighted error rather than the unweighted denoising error. A literal Euclidean reading of the hybrid proof admits a counterexample, whereas the mean-squared-error convention used in the released code admits a valid bound. These alternatives prevent a supported Major or Minor defect judgment in this review. The outcome is Needs Evidence within the declared scope; empirical results were not reproduced.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of MA-TSD
# Paper identity and scope

The reviewed paper is Chenxi Wang, Linxiao Yang, Zhixian Wang, Liang Sun, and Yi Wang, A Non-isotropic Time Series Diffusion Model with Moving Average Transitions, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 65144–65166, paper I25-43547 (local number 0178) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The source is the staged 23-page proceedings PDF. References to pages below mean one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the displayed article page numbers.

The claim-focused review covered the forward marginal and conditional Gaussian construction in Section 4.2 and Appendix B.3.2; the deterministic reverse algebra in Section 4.3 and Appendix B.3.3; the denoising objective in Equation (15); and the hybrid bound in Section 4.4 and Appendix B.3.4. Experiment descriptions were read for task definitions and the relation of the theory to the implementation. Relevant released source files were inspected at commit `6b80af723e5ac285f27ace2e63a284e694b90cc0` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. No author code, training, data loading, or benchmark evaluation was executed.
This is not a full review of every numerical result or a certification of the entire method. The coverage ledger records partially inspected and unexamined material separately.
# Definitions and checks that passed

The paper normalizes each nonconstant target series \(x_0\in\mathbb R^L\) using scalar temporal mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), giving \(z_0=(x_0-\mu)/\sigma\). Its marginal is \[q(z_t\mid z_0)=\mathcal N(K_tz_0,\beta_t^2 I).\] The interpolated nonoverlapping moving-average matrices \(K_t\) need not be invertible. For \(\beta_t>0\) and \(0\leq\eta_t^2\leq\beta_{t-1}^2\), define \[a_t=\frac{\sqrt{\beta_{t-1}^2-\eta_t^2}}{\beta_t}.\] Equation (14) is the Gaussian conditional with mean \(K_{t-1}z_0+a_t(z_t-K_tz_0)\) and covariance \(\eta_t^2 I\).

Conditional on \(z_0\), write \(z_t=K_tz_0+\beta_t\epsilon\) and add independent Gaussian innovation \(\eta_t\xi\). Then \[z_{t-1}=K_{t-1}z_0+
\sqrt{\beta_{t-1}^2-\eta_t^2}\,\epsilon+\eta_t\xi.\] Its mean and covariance are exactly \(K_{t-1}z_0\) and \(\beta_{t-1}^2 I\). This verifies the claimed marginal consistency without requiring an inverse for \(K_t\). The independent arithmetic check with \(\beta_{t-1}=0.6,\beta_t=0.8,\eta_t=0.3\) returns the required covariance coefficient \(0.36\). A subscript inconsistency in the displayed covariance expansion in Equation (21) does not invalidate this direct calculation.

The normalization argument in Appendix B.3.1 is valid when \(K_t\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1\): scalar shifts commute with such a matrix, and standard deviations are shift invariant. This check does not certify every claimed variance-preservation interpretation of the dataset-based noise schedule.
# Training claims requiring clarification

Problem 1 (The hybrid bound depends on the sequence-loss convention).  The literal Euclidean-norm proof and the mean-squared-error implementation lead to different constants. Assessment: Needs Evidence, with a conditional counterexample and a valid alternative reading.
## Claim, source, and core dependency

Section 4.4, page 6, states that appropriately chosen coefficients in \[L_{\rm hybrid}=\lambda_z L_z+\lambda_\mu L_\mu+\lambda_\sigma L_\sigma\] make this objective an upper bound on the conditional diffusion loss without instance normalization. Appendix B.3.4, page 15, Equations (26)–(38), supplies the proof and prescribes a common coefficient based on maxima of normalized target amplitude and predicted standard deviation.

This is a theoretical rationale for jointly training the normalized denoiser and the two statistic predictors, not an unrelated appendix observation. A demonstrated failure under the intended convention would concern that training guarantee. The issue cannot be graded merely from its location or the ease of changing a constant.
## Literal Euclidean reading: exact counterexample

As written, Equations (15) and (26) use \(\|\cdot\|_2^2\) for length-\(L\) vectors, while the errors in the scalar mean and standard deviation are scalar squares. Let the dataset consist of the single length-eight series \[x_0=z_0=(1,-1,1,-1,1,-1,1,-1)^\top.\] Its temporal population mean is zero and standard deviation is one. Let \(f_\theta(z_t,t,c)=z_0\) for every input, let \(g^\sigma_\omega(c)=1\), and let \(g^\mu_\omega(c)=1\). A constant-output denoiser is admissible, and the standard-deviation predictor satisfies the proposed cap at the dataset maximum \(\sigma_{\max}=1\). A singleton dataset and constant predictors also make the following calculation valid after expectation over all diffusion steps and noises.

The reconstructed series is \(\widehat x_0=z_0+\mathbf 1\). Thus \[L_x=\|\mathbf 1\|_2^2=8,\qquad L_z=0,\qquad
L_\sigma=0,\qquad L_\mu=1.\] Even using the generous squared-maxima interpretation of the proposed coefficient, \(\lambda=\max\|z_0\|_\infty^2+\max|g^\sigma_\omega|^2+1=3\), the hybrid loss is three. The purported inequality becomes \(8\leq3\).

Equation reference: eq:sumcorrect. The source of this discrepancy is the broadcast of scalar errors. With Euclidean vector errors, the exact decomposition is \[\widehat x_0-x_0=
\widehat\sigma(f_\theta-z_0)+z_0(\widehat\sigma-\sigma)
 +(\widehat\mu-\mu)\mathbf 1,\] so its norm obeys \[
\|\widehat x_0-x_0\|_2
\leq |\widehat\sigma|\,\|f_\theta-z_0\|_2
 +\|z_0\|_2|\widehat\sigma-\sigma|
 +\sqrt L|\widehat\mu-\mu|.\] The corresponding factors are absent from the substitutions leading to Equations (30)–(34). This calculation uses neither a constant series with undefined normalization nor an uncapped variance predictor.
## Counterevidence: the released code uses averaged losses

The paper describes its fitting objective as mean squared error. More decisively, the released `src/models/matsd.py` assigns `F.mse_loss` to the reconstruction loss and also uses it for the scalar mean and standard-deviation losses in `_get_loss`. The temporal statistic predictors in `src/backbone/mlp.py` have output length one. The default mean reduction therefore gives an averaged sequence error, not the summed Euclidean error used in the literal calculation above.

Equation reference: eq:meancorrect. Under that convention, define \[\ell_{z,\mathrm{rms}}=L^{-1/2}\|f_\theta-z_0\|_2,\qquad
\ell_{x,\mathrm{rms}}=L^{-1/2}\|\widehat x_0-x_0\|_2,\] and let \(A\) and \(B\) bound \(\|z_0\|_\infty\) and \(|\widehat\sigma|\) on the domain being claimed. Dividing [eq:sumcorrect] (#eq:sumcorrect) by \(\sqrt L\) and using \(\|z_0\|_2/\sqrt L\leq A\) gives \[\ell_{x,\mathrm{rms}}\leq
B\ell_{z,\mathrm{rms}}+A|\widehat\sigma-\sigma|
+|\widehat\mu-\mu|.\] Cauchy–Schwarz now proves \[
L_{x,\mathrm{MSE}}\leq
(B^2+A^2+1)
\bigl(L_{z,\mathrm{MSE}}+L_\sigma+L_\mu\bigr).\] For the example above, this reads \(1\leq3\) and is valid.

This is an admissible reading of the intended method, supported by actual source inspection. It prevents treating the literal-norm contradiction as a demonstrated defect of the implemented training objective. Conversely, the code’s average reduction does not make the written Euclidean calculation literally correct. An explicit convention in the mathematical statement is needed.

The bounded-predictor condition is part of [eq:meancorrect] (#eq:meancorrect); it should not be silently inferred from an unconstrained linear network output. The reviewed backbone does not visibly impose the cap contemplated in Appendix B.3.4. The paper’s experiments also use coefficients equal to one, whereas the theorem discussion conditions the bound on suitable coefficients. We do not infer that the paper promised its bound for those experimental settings.
## Impact and precisely verified alternatives

The supported result is conditional: the displayed summed-norm reading fails; the averaged-MSE reading has a valid pointwise and expected bound when the stated amplitude caps hold. For summed errors, Cauchy–Schwarz applied to [eq:sumcorrect] (#eq:sumcorrect) instead gives the sufficient common coefficient \(B^2+LA^2+L\). Either statement is precise. Neither verifies author adoption or the historical implementation used for the reported results.
A clarification of the intended losses and boundedness domain would resolve this concern. No benchmark deterioration, invalid Gaussian sampler, or universal failure of hybrid training is established.

Problem 2 (An exact variational term is matrix weighted).  Equation (15) is a defensible denoising surrogate, but it is not in general an algebraic scalar reweighting of the Gaussian KL term induced by Equation (14). Assessment: Needs Evidence about the intended strength of the derivation, with the distinction proved below.
## Original statement and exact calculation

Equation reference: eq:kl. Section 4.3, page 5, introduces the ordinary squared-error objective in Equation (15) by analogy with DDIM. The preceding background, pages 2–3, motivates training through Gaussian variational terms. For \(\eta_t>0\), substitute \(f_\theta\) for \(z_0\) in Equation (14), as the paper prescribes. At fixed \((z_t,z_0,c)\), the two Gaussian covariances coincide and their means differ by \[A_t(z_0-f_\theta),\qquad A_t=K_{t-1}-a_tK_t.\] The exact conditional divergence is therefore \[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(z_{t-1}\mid z_t,z_0)
 \,\|\,p_\theta(z_{t-1}\mid z_t)\right)
=\frac{\|A_t(z_0-f_\theta)\|_2^2}{2\eta_t^2}.\] The matrix \(A_t^\top A_t\) need not be a scalar multiple of the identity.

For an admissible explicit example, use length four, the two nonoverlapping pair averages followed by linear interpolation, and the final all-series average: \[K_1=\begin{pmatrix}
1/2&1/2&0&0\\3/8&3/8&1/8&1/8\\
1/8&1/8&3/8&3/8\\0&0&1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad K_2=\tfrac14\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top.\] These matrices preserve constants and the temporal mean. For the normalized singleton series \((1,1,-1,-1)^\top\), the paper’s schedule gives \(\gamma_1=\sqrt{5/8}\), \(\beta_1^2=3/8\), and \(\beta_2^2=1\). Choose \(\eta_2^2=\beta_1^2\), which satisfies the admissible noise constraint. Then \(a_2=0\) and \(A_2=K_1\). The errors \[d_1=(1,-1,0,0)^\top,\qquad d_2=(1,1,0,0)^\top\] both have squared norm two, but [eq:kl] (#eq:kl) equals zero for \(d_1\) and \(13/6\) for \(d_2\). Thus no scalar time weighting makes the individual KL term identical to the ordinary squared error in this example. This is a finite calculation supporting an exact algebraic distinction, not an author-code execution.
## Alternative reading and limits

The source says it derives a similar optimization target by analogy; it does not provide a detailed equality proof for the non-isotropic metric. An ordinary squared-error loss can instead be chosen as a surrogate. More directly, for a fixed deterministic positive-semidefinite matrix \(H=A_t^\top A_t\), the conditional mean \(m=\mathbb E[z_0\mid z_t,t,c]\) minimizes both ordinary MSE and \[\mathbb E[(z_0-f)^\top H(z_0-f)\mid z_t,t,c].\] Indeed, writing \(z_0-f=(z_0-m)+(m-f)\) eliminates the conditional cross term and leaves a nonnegative quadratic in \(m-f\). If \(H\) is singular, the weighted loss can have additional minimizers. With a restricted network and shared parameters, equivalence of optimizers is not automatic.

Consequently, [eq:kl] (#eq:kl) does not refute the use of Equation (15), the marginal consistency proof, or the reported experiments. It rules out only an exact scalar-reweighting interpretation without additional assumptions. The report requests explicit identification of the surrogate objective and the level at which the analogy is intended, rather than assigning a Major issue from an interpretation the paper may not assert.
# Overall assessment

The checked Gaussian construction is valid under its variance and nonzero-denominator conditions. No supported core sampler failure or empirical error was established. The two concerns concern the formal interpretation of the training rationale and remain Needs Evidence because an admissible interpretation is supported by the text or implementation.

The staged manifest includes the appendix and a pinned repository snapshot. Potential additional OpenReview attachments were unresolved during source preparation. Later revisions and errata were not independently searched; none is claimed to have been excluded or incorporated. Determining historical experimental impact would require provenance and, if the actual objective changes, fresh training and evaluation.
