report: Abstract: This initial review identifies two Major problems in the inspected scope. The Heston application invokes a global diffusion regularity condition that fails and claims moments and asymptotic properties that need not hold under its stated Feller condition. An explicit admissible Heston model has a second-level price-signature coordinate with finite mean and infinite variance, independently of the observation mesh. Separately, three pinned released implementations select signature words starting, rather than ending, in a designated martingale coordinate. An exact Brownian example shows persistent bias in this core partial-martingale estimator. The conditional convergence theorems and the paper’s mathematical last-coordinate criterion are not refuted by these findings. No historical benchmark-score effect is established. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:

Title: Technical Verification of
Learning with Expected Signatures: Theory and Applications
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The paper is by Lorenzo Lucchese, Mikko S. Pakkanen and Almut E. D. Veraart, published in PMLR volume 267, ICML 2025 (OpenReview identifier `yDTwamN4LQ`) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The preserved original is the 61-page proceedings PDF. Page references below mean the one-based PDF page, which agrees with its printed page numbering. The original SHA-256 is
The staged original, complete source manifest, and selected released source files were actually read. Existing bytes and versions were preserved.

The inspection covered the main mathematical definitions and claims in Sections 2–3, the long-span proof and covariance-estimation argument in Appendices B.2–B.3, the diffusion conditions in Appendix D.1, and the estimator and application paths listed below. This is not a line-by-line certification of every rough-path estimate in Appendix B.1 or of every result in Appendices C, E and F. The report gives a separate scope decision for unchecked questions instead of treating their absence here as validation.

The released code snapshots are `esig` at commit , at , at , and at . They are the pinned sources supplied with this review. Their identity with the historical runs underlying the tables has not been established. The distribution-regression snapshot intentionally excludes some data and binary files; no new download or author-code execution was performed.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Theorem 2.8, p. 4, sets \(p=mk\) for the largest inspected word length \(k\). In case(ii) it requires, among other conditions, \[\|X_t-X_s\|_{L^p}\lesssim |t-s|^{1/2},
 \qquad
 \|\mathbb E[X_t-X_s\mid\mathcal F_{0,s}]\|_{L^p}
       \lesssim |t-s|^\delta,\quad \delta\ge1.\] Theorem 2.10, p. 5, assumes these conditions with \(m>2\), suitable stationarity/ergodicity, and sufficiently fine refining partitions. Its central-limit conclusion further requires mixing and a finite, strictly positive covariance matrix. Independent repeated paths satisfy the relevant inter-path dependence requirements but do not, by themselves, supply the required moments.

Equation reference: eq:control. Section 2.2, p. 6, defines the control \[
 C_I^\pi
 =\sum_{[u,v]\in\pi} S^{I^-}(X^\pi)_{0,u}
          (X_v^{i_k}-X_u^{i_k}),\qquad I^-=(i_1,\ldots,i_{k-1}).\] For an integrable adapted prefix and martingale final coordinate, \(\mathbb EC_I^\pi=0\) by conditional expectation. Remark 2.15 correctly identifies the last coordinate as the requirement when only some components are martingales. For a fixed coefficient \(c\), subtracting \(cC_I^\pi\) then preserves the discretized target expectation. These facts are central to distinguishing the mathematical method from its released implementation.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Major: the Feller-only Heston application has insufficient moments).  The Heston claim in Section 3.1, p. 7, does not follow from the stated Feller condition and is false for permitted parameters. The affected derivation is the asserted application of the central convergence theory to this model, not a counterexample to the conditional statement of Theorem 2.10.
## Original claim and exact failed step

Equation reference: eq:heston. The model on p. 7 is \[
 dS_t=S_t\sqrt{V_t}\,dW^S_t,\qquad
 dV_t=\kappa(\theta-V_t)\,dt+\xi\sqrt{V_t}\,dW^V_t,
 \qquad d\langle W^S,W^V\rangle_t=\rho\,dt .\] For deterministic initial values and \(2\kappa\theta>\xi^2\), the paragraph asserts that the joint diffusion coefficient is \(1/2\)-Hölder and invokes the third case of Appendix D.1.2 to obtain the increment conditions for any \(p>2\), then consistency and asymptotic normality under independent sampling. The invoked condition on p. 43 is global: \[\|\sigma(x)-\sigma(y)\|\le K_\sigma\|x-y\|^{1/2}
 \quad\hbox{for all }x,y.\] Already at \(V=1\) and \(\rho=0\), the price entry is \(S\), so taking \(x=(a,1)\), \(y=(1,1)\) would require \[|a-1|\le K_\sigma |a-1|^{1/2}\quad\hbox{for every }a>1,\] which is impossible. Positivity of \(V\) does not bound this product coefficient globally. This is more than an unavailable proof technique: the moments it is used to obtain can actually be infinite.
## An admissible model and a decisive signature coordinate

Equation reference: eq:parameters. Set \[
 \kappa=\theta=\xi=1,\quad \rho=0,\quad S_0=V_0=1,\quad T=2 .\] All parameters and initial values have the stated domains, and \(2\kappa\theta=2>1=\xi^2\). Take independent repetitions of this model and any endpoint-preserving dyadic observation scheme. Thus the observational and independence choices used in Section 3.1 are available.

Equation reference: eq:conditional. Here is a direct moment calculation, requiring no simulation or external moment-explosion formula. Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_4\) be independent processes \[dY_j=-\tfrac12 Y_j\,dt+\tfrac12\,dB_j,\qquad
 (Y_1(0),Y_2(0),Y_3(0),Y_4(0))=(1,0,0,0).\] Itô’s formula shows that \(V=\sum_jY_j^2\) has drift \(1-V\) and quadratic variation \(V\,dt\), hence the variance dynamics in [eq:heston] (#eq:heston). Use a Brownian motion \(W^S\) independent of the \(B_j\)’s. Conditional on the whole variance path, \[
 \mathbb E[S_T^p\mid V]
 =\exp\left\{\frac{p(p-1)}2\int_0^T V_s\,ds\right\}.\] In particular \(\mathbb ES_t=1\), so this example does not exploit a price process with a defective first moment.

Let \(Z=\int_0^2Y_1(s)\,ds\). It is Gaussian, with \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb EZ&=2(1-e^{-1}),\\
 v_Z:=\operatorname{Var}Z
 &=\int_0^2(1-e^{-(2-u)/2})^2\,du
   =-1+4e^{-1}-e^{-2}\simeq0.33618248 .\end{aligned}\] Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[\int_0^2 V_s\,ds\ge\int_0^2Y_1(s)^2\,ds\ge \tfrac12 Z^2.\] Consequently, \[\mathbb ES_2^4=\mathbb E\exp\left(6\int_0^2 V_s\,ds\right)
       \ge \mathbb Ee^{3Z^2}=\infty ,\] because \(6v_Z\simeq2.01709489>1\). This last criterion follows directly by multiplying the Gaussian density by \(e^{3z^2}\): the resulting quadratic coefficient in the exponent is positive.

Equation reference: eq:secondmoment. For completeness, \(\mathbb ES_2^2\) is finite. Put \[B(t)=1+\tan(t/2-\pi/4),\qquad
 A(t)=t-2\log\frac{\cos(t/2-\pi/4)}{\cos(-\pi/4)} .\] For \(0\le t\le2<3\pi/2\), these are finite and satisfy \[B'=\tfrac12B^2-B+1,\quad A'=B,\quad A(0)=B(0)=0.\] With the CIR generator \(L=(1-v)\partial_v+\tfrac12v\partial_{vv}\), the positive function \(u(t,v)=e^{A(t)+B(t)v}\) satisfies \(\partial_tu=Lu+vu\). Applying Itô’s formula to \(e^{\int_0^t V_sds}u(2-t,V_t)\), stopping, and using Fatou’s lemma yields \[
 \mathbb ES_2^2=\mathbb Ee^{\int_0^2 V_sds}\le u(2,1)<\infty .\]

Equation reference: eq:ss. Now choose the repeated price word \(I=(S,S)\). The chain rule gives \[
 Y:=S^{(S,S)}(X)_{0,2}=\tfrac12(S_2-1)^2.\] Exactly the same identity holds for every piecewise linear interpolation containing both endpoints. Equations[eq:conditional] (#eq:conditional)–[eq:secondmoment] (#eq:secondmoment) give \(\mathbb EY<\infty\) but \(\mathbb EY^2=\infty\); the latter follows, for example, from \((S_2-1)^4\ge S_2^4/16\) when \(S_2\ge2\). Thus the discretized and continuous statistics agree exactly, yet their sample average has infinite mean-squared error for every finite \(N\). The advertised \(L^2\) consistency is unavailable. There is also no ordinary \(\sqrt N\) central limit with finite Gaussian variance, as shown in Appendix A below. Finer observations cannot remove this obstruction.
## Impact, counterevidence and bounded correction

This is a demonstrated invalid application of the core convergence theory, with a concrete failure of its asserted moment and asymptotic guarantees. That supports Major severity even though other models and the conditional theorems may remain valid. The paper expressly uses Section 3.1 as the probabilistic foundation for the applications (pp. 7–8).

The example does not satisfy the high-\(p\) assumptions of Theorems 2.8–2.10: that is precisely why their application here is invalid, rather than why those conditional theorems are false. The ordinary strong law still applies to \(Y\), because its mean is finite; the finding does not deny every form of consistency. Nor does it establish failure at the particular parameter and horizon choices in Figure 3 or a change in any reported score.

A valid revision must impose and prove adequate moments for the chosen word length, parameters and horizon, or weaken the application claim. Stopping or truncating the model would change the object being estimated. No complete replacement theorem for unrestricted Heston parameters is verified here. Repair verification is therefore limited to identifying the necessary missing condition; author adoption is unknown.

Problem 2 (Major: released partial-martingale correction selects the first letter).  The supplied implementations of the central corrected estimator select words whose first letter is a designated martingale coordinate. Remark 2.15 requires the last letter. This can subtract a control with nonzero mean and destroy consistency for the intended expected-signature coordinate.
## Source binding and core dependency

In the pinned `esig` source, , lines 10–20, appends the index interval \[o_k+j d^{k-1},\ldots,o_k+(j+1)d^{k-1}-1\] for every selected coordinate \(j\), where \(o_k=\sum_{\ell<k}d^\ell\). The repository’s own , lines 4–18, maps words by C-order `ravel_multi_index`; the first letter is the most significant base-\(d\) digit. The interval above therefore fixes the first letter. Meanwhile the correction tensor in , lines 30–46 and62–78, is prefix signature times final increment, with that increment on the last, fastest-varying axis before flattening. There is no compensating word reversal.

The same mask is present in /, method , and /, function . The latter is called by `compute_signature`. In , adding time puts time first and shifts the supplied martingale indices by one; the pathwise expected-signature transformer then calls the affected routine. The released invokes this branch with `at=True`, depths 2,3,4, and `martingale_indices=[0]`. Thus this is part of the released core estimator and application workflow, not an unused helper.
## Exact independent calculation

Let \(X=(t,B_t)\) on \([0,1]\), with standard Brownian \(B_0=0\), grid \(\pi=\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\), truncation depth 3, and only coordinate1 designated martingale. This process has all needed polynomial moments; the designation is correct. Write \[U=B_{1/2},\qquad V=B_1-B_{1/2},
 \qquad U,V\ \hbox{independent }N(0,\tfrac12).\] The released mask selects the level-three words \[100,\ 101,\ 110,\ 111,\] whereas the last-coordinate rule selects \[001,\ 011,\ 101,\ 111.\] In particular, it incorrectly corrects \(I=(1,1,0)\), the word \((B,B,t)\), whose zero-based flat signature index is12.

Equation reference: eq:bias. The signature coordinate and its implemented control are \[\begin{aligned}
 Y&=S^{(B,B,t)}(X^\pi)_{0,1}
   =\frac12\int_0^1(B_t^\pi)^2\,dt
   =\frac{U^2}{3}+\frac{UV}{4}+\frac{V^2}{12},\\
 C&=\sum_{[u,v]\in\pi}S^{(B,B)}(X^\pi)_{0,u}(v-u)
   =\frac{U^2}{4}.\end{aligned}\] The control has mean \(1/8\), so its subtraction is not justified by the martingale argument. The exact Gaussian moments are \[\mathbb EY=\frac5{24},\quad \mathbb EC=\frac18,\quad
 \mathbb E[YC]=\frac{13}{192},\quad \mathbb E[C^2]=\frac3{64}.\] The source uses the through-origin coefficient \(\widehat c=\sum_nY_nC_n/\sum_nC_n^2\). For independent paths, the strong law therefore gives \[
 \widehat c\longrightarrow\frac{13}{9},\qquad
 \frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N(Y_n-\widehat c C_n)
 \longrightarrow\frac5{24}-\frac{13}{9}\frac18=\frac1{36}.\] The target at this fixed mesh is \(5/24\), so the persistent difference is \(-13/72\). This is not a finite-sample coefficient-estimation effect.

There is also a continuous-time obstruction. On successively fine uniform grids, both \(Y^\pi\) and the erroneously selected left-sum control \(C^\pi\) converge in the requisite moments to \(\tfrac12\int_0^1B_t^2dt\). Their population coefficient tends to 1 and the corrected population coordinate tends to 0, whereas the true expectation is \(1/4\). Brownian continuity and finite moments of its supremum justify these Riemann-sum limits. This also gives a joint sample-size/infill counterexample: \(Y^\pi,C^\pi\) are bounded in absolute value by \(\tfrac12\sup_{t\le1}|B_t|^2\), uniformly in the grid. Their products and squares consequently have uniformly bounded variances. For any refining sequence \(\pi_N\), Chebyshev’s inequality gives triangular laws of large numbers for the sample averages of \(Y^{\pi_N},C^{\pi_N},Y^{\pi_N}C^{\pi_N},(C^{\pi_N})^2\). The last denominator converges to a positive second moment; hence \(\widehat c_N\to 1\) and the empirical corrected coordinate converges in probability to 0. Thus this mask does not approximate the intended continuous expected-signature coordinate even with increasing resolution.
## Counterevidence and precise repair scope

The mathematics in Remark 2.15 is correct. When all coordinates are selected, the two masks coincide, and at level 1 the first and last letter coincide. The supplied `esig`/ selects all channels in its generic simulation call; the finding must not be projected onto that call as a subset-mask failure.

The paper also openly permits deliberate use of correction on nonmartingale data as a potentially biased transformation (p. 7). That does not repair the present mismatch: the counterexample supplies a correctly identified martingale subset, and the implementation modifies a coordinate outside the stated last-letter rule. This directly harms the promised estimator behavior, supporting Major severity. No accuracy or MSE change in a historical table is claimed. Establishing that change would require the actual historical run provenance and additional empirical work.

For C-order indexing, the local mask correction is \[\{\,o_k+dq+j:
       0\le q<d^{k-1},\ j\in M\,\},\] where \(M\) is the martingale-coordinate set. The base-\(d\) representation proves that this fixes the last digit. Independent exhaustive enumeration for dimensions 2–4, depths 1–4 and three representative subsets confirmed this local identity in 36 cases. No released file was modified or executed. This verifies the indexing repair only; it does not certify every implementation branch, coefficient estimator, or empirical result.
# Coverage decisions and conclusion

Within the inspected scope, the finite-grid mean-zero control argument for a correctly chosen martingale final coordinate and fixed coefficient has No Issue Found: the adapted prefix and martingale increment give zero conditional mean term by term. This is a bounded mathematical check, not a certificate for all claims in Section 2.2.

The complete long-span covariance estimator, the full Appendix B.1 rough-path proof, every auxiliary result in Appendix C, and historical experiment reproducibility remain Needs Evidence beyond the checks described. In particular, the two findings do not substitute for a full audit of those results. The distinct statuses are:
Dimension | Recorded state
Scientific assessment | Major within the demonstrated scope
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Heston repair verification | Missing moment condition identified; full repair unverified
Indexing repair verification | Last-digit mask verified analytically and finitely
Historical score impact | Not established
Author adoption | Unknown
Human review declarations | None recorded
# Why infinite variance excludes the asserted square-root limit

Here is a short justification independent of moment-convergence assumptions. Let \(Y'\) be an independent copy of the nonnegative, finite-mean variable \(Y\) in [eq:ss] (#eq:ss), and set \(D=Y-Y'\). Then \(\mathbb ED^2=\infty\). Its characteristic function is real and nonnegative: \(\psi(t)=|\mathbb Ee^{itY}|^2\). For fixed \(t\ne0\), the elementary inequality \(1-\cos x\ge x^2/4\) for \(|x|\le1\) gives \[N[1-\psi(t/\sqrt N)]
 \ge\frac{t^2}{4}
      \mathbb E\!\left[D^2\mathbf1_{\{|D|\le\sqrt N/|t|\}}\right]
 \longrightarrow\infty.\] Therefore \(\psi(t/\sqrt N)^N\to 0\). If the centered average of \(Y\), multiplied by \(\sqrt N\), converged to a finite-variance Gaussian, subtracting an independent copy would give a Gaussian difference with a strictly positive characteristic function. The displayed limit contradicts this. Since [eq:ss] (#eq:ss) is mesh-independent, a triangular array of increasingly fine observations cannot avoid the argument.
# Reproducibility, evidence and actual roles

The independent standard-library script constructs the two-segment signature by Chen multiplication, integrates exact Gaussian polynomial moments using rational arithmetic, checks the mask enumeration, and computes the explicit Heston scalar bounds. It imports no author module. Its actual output is preserved in . These finite diagnostics support the calculations; the universal and infinite-moment arguments are supplied in the report itself.

The original PDF was extracted with an existing local `pdftotext`. Pages5,6,7 and43 were rendered with existing `pdftoppm` and actually viewed to check the formulas and operative quantifiers. Source file hashes, the frozen prompt/template/contract, and output bindings are recorded in and the companion coverage and findings files. No supplementary OpenReview attachment was available from the completed source preparation, which records HTTP403. No separate accessible Space reference was supplied, and no cloud copy is asserted.

A native auxiliary task, `/root/review_0176_0179`, performed the source reading, analysis, independent calculations and scientific drafting inside the parent conversation. The inherited runtime instruction identifies GPT-6 Astra Pro; the auxiliary tool does not expose a separate model label or verify the parent UI’s selected model. The parent owns integration, independent decisive-evidence checks, final TeX compilation and report-PDF visual inspection. Their actual completion records belong in the final provenance; this scientific draft does not impersonate those later checks. No human review or author adoption is claimed.

report: Abstract: The proceedings paper, its embedded appendices, and the pinned released implementation were inspected. A bounded, continuous, controllable and stabilizable example disproves the discounted Bellman-optimality-to-stabilization implication used in Theorem F.4. Exact Bellman iterates converge and their unique greedy actor is identically zero, yet a nonzero state never approaches the designated equilibrium. This is a demonstrated failure of a core theoretical derivation, supporting Major. It is not a reproduction of the finite neural critic’s training trajectory or evidence of harm in the human experiments. Differences between the published configuration and released code leave experiment-level correspondence and enforcement of the printed timing bounds unresolved.

Title: Technical Verification of AIP Exosuit Control
# Identity, version, and inspection scope

The paper is Junmin Zhong, Emiliano Quinones Yumbla, Seyed Yousef Soltanian, Ruofan Wu, Wenlong Zhang and Jennie Si, Reinforcement Learning Control of a Physical Robot Device for Assisted Human Walking without a Simulator, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 78575–78601; local number 0180, identifier I25-43549, OpenReview yAdcCADXqH [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original is the 27-page proceedings PDF. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the internal printed numbering.

All 27 pages of extracted text were read, including Appendices A–I and the bibliography. Figures 1–10 were visually inspected on rendered original pages. The analysis focuses on the offline/online objective and protocol, the assumptions and proofs in Appendix F, the relation between reported performance and its baselines, and static correspondence with the release. The reviewed repository is commit , dated 25 May 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. All four available Python files and the README were read; both small released CSV files were parsed for dimensions and finite values. No author code was executed.

This is an initial scientific review. It does not certify the hardware, reproduce human trials, validate raw EMG processing, or re-establish all results of the cited literature. The release does not include the full real-time sensor/pressure-control pipeline, experiment checkpoints or complete online trial records. Those limitations matter for attributing a source discrepancy to the historical experiments.
# Mathematical setting and contribution dependencies

The method learns a policy from five gait-state variables to four inflation/deflation timing variables, using offline normative walking data followed by online actor–critic adaptation. Equations (8)–(10), pp. 5–6, define a discounted cost with \(0<\gamma<1\), combining a kinematic error term and an EMG-effort term. Tables 7–8 use \(\gamma=0.95\).

Appendix F writes a deterministic model \[s_{k+1}=f(s_k,u_k),\qquad s_k\in\mathbb R^5,\quad u_k\in\mathbb R^4,\] as a device for analysis, while the actual method is described as data-driven. Definition 1, p. 22, uses stabilization to mean convergence of the state to a designated equilibrium \(s^e\). Assumption F.1 requires controllability and stabilizability, an equilibrium pair \((s^e,u^e)\), and bounded feedback controls. Assumption F.2 requires a finite continuous nonnegative stage cost, with zero cost if and only if \((s,u)=(s^e,u^e)\).

Theorems F.3–F.4 are presented as the theoretical basis for convergence, optimality and dynamic stability. These properties are advertised in the abstract and introduction, and Sections 3.3 and 3.6 connect them to the control and safety rationale. Consequently, the stability proof is a dependency of a principal assurance, despite its appendix location.
# Problem 1: discounted optimality does not give the claimed stabilization

Problem 1 (Invalid stability inference in Theorem F.4).  Theorem F.4, p. 24, asserts under F.1–F.2 that a converged value sequence and converged policy, with the stated policy-gradient actor updates, yield a stabilizing limiting policy. Its proof compares the learned value with the value of a stabilizing policy in Equations (41)–(43), then transfers decay along the stabilizing policy’s trajectory to the learned trajectory. That transfer is invalid. The failure persists even when the exact Bellman minimization and convergence used by the proof are granted.
## A complete bounded example

Equation reference: eq:plant. Let \[\Omega=[-1,1]^5,\qquad U=[-1,1]^4,\qquad
 \gamma=\frac{19}{20},\qquad s^e=0,\quad u^e=0,\] and let \(S(a)=\max(-1,\min(1,a))\). Define \[
 f(s,u)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 S(s_1+3u_1^3)\\
 S(2u_2)\\
 S(2u_3)\\
 S(2u_4)\\
 s_4
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 c(s,u)=\|s\|_2^2+200\|u\|_2^2.\] Both functions are continuous, \(\Omega\) is invariant, controls are bounded, and the cost is at most \(805\). The cost is zero precisely at the designated equilibrium pair. Thus F.2 holds, with boundedness stronger than the finiteness required there.

The system is controllable on \(\Omega\) in two steps. For any initial state and desired target \(r\in\Omega\), choose \(u_4=r_5/2\) on the first step. At the second step, with current state \(s'\), choose \[u_1=\sqrt[3]{(r_1-s'_1)/3},\qquad
 u_2=r_2/2,\qquad u_3=r_3/2,\qquad u_4=r_4/2.\] The final state is exactly \(r\). The first action has magnitude at most \(1/2\) in its only nonzero coordinate; the second has \(|u_1|\le(2/3)^{1/3}<1\) and \(|u_j|\le1/2\) for \(j>1\).

Equation reference: eq:stabilizer. A stabilizing feedback is \[
 \mu(s)=(-\tanh(s_1/2),0,0,0).\] For \(0<x\le1\), \[0<3\tanh^3(x/2)<\frac{3x^3}{8}\le\frac{3x}{8}<x.\] Thus the first coordinate decreases in absolute value without changing sign; its only possible limiting value is zero. The other coordinates vanish in at most two steps. This verifies stabilizability, not merely boundedness. The feedback in [eq:stabilizer] (#eq:stabilizer) is exactly representable by two ReLU features followed by a tanh output: the preactivation is \(-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReLU}(s_1)+\tfrac12\operatorname{ReLU}(-s_1)\). The identically-zero actor is also exactly representable. F.1’s bounded actor and equilibrium requirements therefore do not exclude these policies.
## Exact discounted-optimality certificate

Equation reference: eq:value. Consider the zero policy \(\pi^0(s)=0\). Its discounted value is \[
 V(s)=20s_1^2+s_2^2+s_3^2+(1+\gamma)s_4^2+s_5^2.\] Indeed, \(s_1\) remains constant, \(s_2,s_3,s_4\) disappear after one step, and \(s_5\) receives \(s_4\) for one additional step.

Equation reference: eq:gap, eq:certificate. Define \(Q^0(s,u)=c(s,u)+\gamma V(f(s,u))\). Direct substitution gives \[\begin{aligned}
 Q^0(s,u)-V(s)
 ={}&200\|u\|_2^2
 +19\{S(s_1+3u_1^3)^2-s_1^2\}\notag\\
 &+\gamma S(2u_2)^2+\gamma S(2u_3)^2
   +\gamma(1+\gamma)S(2u_4)^2. \end{aligned}\] Because \(S\) is 1-Lipschitz and \(a\mapsto a^2\) is 2-Lipschitz on \([-1,1]\), \[|S(s_1+3u_1^3)^2-s_1^2|
 \le6|u_1|^3\le6u_1^2.\] Consequently, \[
 Q^0(s,u)-V(s)
 \ge86u_1^2+200(u_2^2+u_3^2+u_4^2)\ge0.\] Equality is attained only at \(u=0\). Thus \(V\) satisfies the discounted Bellman optimality equation and \(\pi^0\) is its unique greedy policy.

The conclusion can also be established without appealing to a fixed-point theorem. For every control sequence, the Bellman inequality implies \[V(s_0)\le\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\gamma^k c(s_k,u_k)+\gamma^N V(s_N).\] The last term tends to zero because \(V\) is bounded on \(\Omega\). The zero policy achieves equality. It is therefore globally discounted-optimal.
## The exact iteration and actor-gradient antecedents

Equation reference: eq:finite. Starting from \(Q_0=0\), let \[Q_{n+1}(s,u)=c(s,u)+\gamma\min_vQ_n(f(s,u),v),
 \qquad V_n(s)=\min_u Q_n(s,u).\] At the initial all-tied step choose the zero policy. It remains uniquely greedy thereafter. Specifically, \(V_1(s)=\|s\|^2\), and for \(n\ge2\), \[
 V_n(s)=A_n s_1^2+s_2^2+s_3^2+(1+\gamma)s_4^2+s_5^2,
 \qquad A_n=\frac{1-\gamma^n}{1-\gamma}\le20.\] Induction follows from the same calculation as [eq:gap] (#eq:gap); the possibly negative term is bounded by \(6\gamma A_{n-1}u_1^2\le114u_1^2\), leaving the same positive margin. Hence \(Q_n\) and \(V_n\) converge uniformly to their exact optimal limits, while \(\pi_n\equiv0\).

For every finite exact \(Q_n\), \(\nabla_uQ_n(s,0)=0\). The first coordinate’s state effect is of order \(u_1^3\), even where clipping has a corner; the other new-state terms and the action cost are quadratic at zero. A zero actor therefore remains zero under the policy-gradient actor update. This observation is independent of the sign convention in the printed update.

Page 21 describes stabilization together with cost minimization as the control goal. A favorable alternative reading would restrict optimization to stabilizing policies. However, Equations (17)–(20) take unrestricted pointwise action minima and allow an arbitrary initial policy; they do not impose that admissibility restriction. Adding such a restriction changes the premises and the learning procedure. It does not justify the displayed inference that a converged discounted-optimal policy must stabilize.

There is a necessary realization boundary. These are the exact Bellman functions used in the paper’s proof. The released finite ReLU critic is not claimed to represent them exactly, and its Adam training was not executed. The example establishes failure of the proof’s discounted-optimality-to-stabilization inference even under its idealized exact-value assumptions. It is not a claimed reproduction of every network-specific premise through an actual training run.
## Contradiction and the failed proof step

At \[s_0=e_1=(1,0,0,0,0),\qquad u_k=\pi^0(s_k)=0,\] one has \(s_k=e_1\) for every \(k\), \(c(s_k,u_k)=1\), and \[V(e_1)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(19/20)^k=20.\] The policy is optimal and the exact value iteration converges, but the state does not approach \(s^e=0\). It is non-stabilizing in Definition 1’s convergence sense; this is not a claim of Lyapunov instability or unbounded state growth.

The value of a stabilizing comparison policy tends to zero when evaluated along that policy’s trajectory approaching the equilibrium. It need not tend to zero when evaluated at states generated by another policy. In this example those latter states are always \(e_1\). A pointwise value inequality such as Equation (43) does not transfer the former trajectory limit to the latter.

Equation reference: eq:lyapunov. The discounted Bellman identity itself exposes the missing requirement: \[
 V(f(s,\pi(s)))-V(s)
 =\frac{(1-\gamma)V(s)-c(s,\pi(s))}{\gamma}.\] Positive stage cost does not force this difference to be negative. At \(e_1\) the numerator is exactly zero.
## Counterevidence, impact, and a bounded repair statement

This witness uses the five-state/four-control dimensions, finite bounded domains, continuous dynamics and a continuous positive-definite cost. It has a simple neural stabilizer and a unique optimal action. It does not depend on divergent values, lack of a stabilizing controller, approximate minimization, policy ties after initialization, or a discount other than the paper’s \(0.95\).

The system is a mathematical counterexample to the general analysis, not a model of the pneumatic device or a human participant. The five reported experiments can remain successful. The result does not establish an unsafe physical deployment or negate the reported EMG reductions.

A genuine additional sufficient condition can be stated precisely. Suppose an invariant compact domain contains the equilibrium, \(V\) is continuous and positive definite, the policy satisfies the Bellman identity, and \[c(s,\pi(s))-(1-\gamma)V(s)\ge\gamma W(s)\] for a continuous positive-definite \(W\). Then [eq:lyapunov] (#eq:lyapunov) gives \(V(s_{k+1})-V(s_k)\le-W(s_k)\). Summation and compactness imply \(s_k\to s^e\). This supplies the missing strict decrease condition; it is not present in F.1–F.2 and has not been verified for AIP. It does not repair neural-learning convergence or certify physical safety.

The supported assessment is Major: the invalid derivation underpins a core advertised stability assurance. Appendix placement, an empirical success, or the possibility of a strengthened theorem does not remove that dependence.
# Other theoretical and empirical checks
## Exact Bellman recursion versus learned actor–critic updates

Theorem F.3, pp. 22–24, studies exact minimization in Equations (18)–(20), while its statement invokes policy-gradient weight updates. A gradient step on a parameterized actor is not an exact global argmin; a sampled critic regression is not an exact Bellman backup. The proof does not establish the equivalence needed to transfer its monotonicity, boundedness and optimality conclusions to the stated neural training process. This is an unresolved guarantee for the actual algorithm, separately from the decisive failure of F.4’s idealized stability inference.

The positive signs in printed Equation (14), p. 21, also conflict with the stated minimization objectives when read literally. Static inspection of `DHDP.py`, lines 68–85, shows ordinary optimizer minimization of the critic MSE and mean critic value. A sign typo is therefore an admissible reading; this review does not elevate the printed sign alone into a separate substantive finding.

F.2 additionally requires zero stage cost at the equilibrium. The application cost includes an uncentered nonnegative EMG-effort term, and the reported final EMG values remain positive. The paper does not establish a zero-cost equilibrium for that exact physical objective. This is an application-assumption boundary; it is not needed for the counterexample, which satisfies F.2 exactly.
## Human experiments and the scope of their evidence

The experiment description reports five healthy participants, offline data from one participant, three online sessions per participant, constant treadmill speed, and five consecutive steps aggregated into each online sample. Figure 10 explicitly shows the incline extension for two participants. These constitute finite feasibility evidence within the stated tasks, not a proof of the general stability theorem or of adaptation across arbitrary users and terrain.

An independent arithmetic check of Table 1 reproduced the reported training-end reductions relative to the no-assistance baseline, approximately \(14.4\%,48.2\%,36.8\%,5.0\%,8.5\%\). The separate evaluation improvement from the initial offline policy is approximately \(21.2\%\), \(66.7\%\), \(23.6\%\), \(52.5\%\), \(55.4\%\). Accordingly, the text about at least \(20\%\) improvement has an admissible initial-policy reference; this review does not force a contradiction by substituting the no-assistance baseline.

The EMG metric is the processed muscle-activity measure described in Appendix D. No independent metabolic expenditure measurement was verified. The figures support observed changes of timing and EMG under online adaptation. Isolating human learning from immediate mechanical responses, fatigue, session effects, and robot-policy changes would require more evidence than the plotted aggregate trajectories. Complete per-trial data and the confidence-interval calculation were unavailable for independent statistical reconstruction.
# Problem 2: correspondence of the release to the reported configuration

Problem 2 (Unresolved configuration and timing-bound correspondence).  The pinned release contains observable differences from the paper’s specified network, training procedure and timing ranges. Their historical experimental impact remains Needs Evidence.

Table 4, p. 19, states gait-fraction limits \[t_1\in[0,.20],\quad d_1\in[0,.20],\quad
 t_2\in[.60,.80],\quad d_2\in[0,.20].\] In `AIP_Online_training.py`, the action conversion instead permits \[t_1\in[0,.20],\quad d_1\in[0,.25],\quad
 t_2\in[.50,.74],\quad d_2\in[0,.28].\] For the strictly interior normalized actor output \(a=(0,.8,-.5,.8)\), the conversion gives \[(t_1,d_1,t_2,d_2)=(.10,.225,.56,.252).\] Three components lie outside the printed Table 4 intervals. This is an exact calculation of the released formula, not an executed author-code test. Figure 8(c), p. 25, also visibly includes \(t_2\) values below \(.60\) and early \(d_1\) values above \(.20\), so clarification of the printed intervals is warranted.

The release refers to an external `pressure_commands.py` and sensor-reading processes that are absent from the snapshot. Additional downstream bounds, a different historical configuration, or corrected tabulated limits may explain the difference. Thus the published interval description and release are not currently reconciled; no injury, physical limit breach, or historical deployed action is inferred from the static example.
Other concrete correspondence limits are:
- Appendix E.3 describes 256 hidden nodes, whereas the actor and critic in `DHDP.py` use a single hidden layer of 1024 nodes.

- The released offline path constructs a replay buffer and calls the actor–critic trainer, rather than directly differentiating the supervised cloning loss in Equation (7). Its stored noisy action and its cost computed from the noiseless actor also require an explicit interpretation.
- Published online hyperparameters differ from several script defaults; command-line overrides could resolve some of them. The actual invocation records were not supplied.
- Each released CSV has 107 rows, while the paper describes \(N=150\) offline samples. The release may be a subset; its size alone does not refute the experiment description.

These are evidence gaps for reproducibility and implementation correspondence. They do not establish that this commit generated the reported figures. No additional supported Major or Minor is assigned from unresolved historical provenance.
# Overall assessment and remaining boundaries

The report’s supported highest impact is Major, confined to the false stabilization inference in a core theoretical analysis. The offline initialization strategy, online adaptation experiments and observed EMG improvements are not disproved. Demonstrating a corrected guarantee would require additional stabilization conditions and a justified connection from the actual learning algorithm to those conditions.

The current official proceedings page and public repository landing page were inspected on 24 October 2026. No correction was identified in those inspected materials; no exhaustive erratum search is claimed. A targeted search did not establish an alternative arXiv revision of this paper. OpenReview returned a browser-verification wall, so its discussion and possible additional material were not inspected. The frozen proceedings version and pinned release remain the evidence base.

# Reproducibility and source binding

The original PDF SHA-256 is . All manifest-listed staged source hashes were independently recomputed and matched. The source identity manifest, line-numbered static excerpts, detailed coverage and calculation output are retained under `verification/0180`.

The reviewer-written `independent_checks.py` imports only Python standard-library modules and never imports or executes the author release. It verifies the exact rational margin \(200-6\gamma/(1-\gamma)=86\), evaluates 10,000 bounded state/action pairs, checks 200 two-step controllability constructions, records the constant non-stabilizing trajectory, and evaluates the proposed stabilizing feedback. The analytical proof, not finite sampling, establishes the universal claims.

With seed 18043549, the minimum sampled slack above the analytical bound was \(0.12530393515902438\). The largest numerical terminal error in the controllability check was \(4.44\times10^{-16}\). The exact finite-horizon values at \(e_1\) approach 20; at horizon 100 the value was \(19.881589415593318\), and at horizon 500 it was \(19.99999999985451\). These computations confirm the derivation without estimating an effect in the human experiments.

Original PDF pages 3, 7–9, 16, 19, 22, 24–27 were rendered and actually viewed, covering every numbered figure and the decisive theorem pages. Rendering commands and image hashes are retained in provenance. Viewing source-page images is distinct from visual inspection of a compiled review report.
# Roles and limitations

A native auxiliary within the assigned parent conversation performed the source reading, static inspection, calculations and draft report. A second native auxiliary independently challenged the counterexample; its actual checks and limits are retained separately. The parent owns integration and final report checks. No separate runtime model identity was exposed for these auxiliaries; no independent Chat or Work conversation was created for this review.

No author-code execution, hardware operation, trial reproduction, training-data download, software installation, human adjudication or author contact occurred. The exact critic sequence in the mathematical witness is not represented as a reproduced finite-network learning run. Full experimental provenance, unavailable lower-level control files, the OpenReview discussion, and any uninspected later correction remain explicit limits.

Title: Technical Verification of Contrastive Visual Data Augmentation
# Identity and scope

This report concerns Yu Zhou, Bingxuan Li, Mohan Tang, Xiaomeng Jin, Te-Lin Wu, Kuan-Hao Huang, Heng Ji, Kai-Wei Chang, and Nanyun Peng, Contrastive Visual Data Augmentation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 78812–78826 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The identifier is 0181/I25-43550. The reviewed 15-page proceedings PDF includes its appendix. Page references are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed page labels.

The inspection covered NovelSpecies construction and interpretation, feature filtering, reported comparison arithmetic, Appendix A.2–A.4, and relevant code in the pinned release. The source was read statically; it was not executed. No model was trained or queried. Dataset images, pretraining corpora, and per-run predictions or human annotation records were not independently audited. Separate OpenReview attachment availability is unresolved in the source-preparation record.
# Definitions and dependencies

CoDA extracts contrastive attributes, filters them, synthesizes and verifies images, and updates a target model. Table 2 tests SUN, iNaturalist, and NovelSpecies. The empirical contribution therefore extends beyond the novel-species interpretation.

For target and confusing classes \(C_T,C_M\), Section 3.2 defines a sum of pairwise CLIP-score ratios and uses a fixed cutoff of \(0.6\). Section 4 claims that selecting concepts discovered after the latest component-training cutoff guarantees novelty. Formal recognition date, first availability of relevant records, and actual training-corpus membership are distinct quantities.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Recognition date does not guarantee absence from pretraining).  The temporal implication underlying the asserted novelty guarantee is invalid. The supported impact is Major for this core benchmark interpretation; actual contamination remains unestablished.
## Claim and location

The abstract and introduction (pp. 1–2), Section 4 (pp. 5–6), and Section 5.1 (p. 6) assert that species selected after a model’s cutoff were never encountered during training. Section 4 offers the date rule specifically as a guarantee despite unavailable corpora. Figure 1 and Section 3.1 motivate the approach with the clouded tiger cat, Leopardus pardinoides.
## Complete check

Let \(t_r\) be recognition under the selected taxonomic status, \(t_p\) the first availability of relevant visual or descriptive records, and \(t_c\) the model’s latest training cutoff. The rule requires \(t_r>t_c\). It does not require \(t_p>t_c\). The ordering \[t_p<t_c<t_r\] satisfies the rule while allowing pretraining on an older record, including a photograph captioned with a historical subspecies name. Construct a model whose pre-cutoff training corpus contains that record. Its cutoff and the species’ recognition date meet the stated selection conditions, yet the underlying appearance has been encountered. Section 4 imposes no condition excluding this case.

The paper’s own example illustrates the distinction. The primary study published on 29 January 2024 groups previously recognized subspecies, including L. t. pardinoides and L. t. oncilla, as the clouded tiger cat, using historical museum and photographic material [Retained latex: \cite{taxonomy}]. Recognition of a grouping is not creation of its underlying visual information. This evidence refutes the claimed implication; it does not identify an image in a particular closed training corpus.
## Counterevidence, impact, and correction

A task of learning a newly adopted label or taxonomic distinction remains meaningful, as does low-resource adaptation. Those narrower interpretations support useful experiments but cannot provide the advertised unseen-concept guarantee. Conversely, unavailable corpora do not prove contamination.

NovelSpecies is an explicit principal contribution and the central unseen-concept test. The invalid implication thus affects a core interpretation. It does not invalidate the numerical accuracy tables, SUN/iNaturalist results, or the usefulness of CoDA. A supported correction is to describe recently recognized taxa under documented cutoffs and remove the unconditional guarantee. Establishing stricter novelty requires record dates, synonym-aware checks, and training provenance; no such comprehensive audit was performed here.

Problem 2 (The printed discriminability score differs from the released filter).  The published unnormalized sum fails its accompanying fixed-threshold interpretation. The supported finding is a local specification defect; experimental impact remains unresolved.
## Claim and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:sum. Section 3.2, p. 4, defines \[
D=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{a_i}{a_i+b_i},
\quad a_i=\operatorname{CLIP}(f,i_{C_T}),\quad
b_i=\operatorname{CLIP}(f,i_{C_M}),\] for equally many images per class. It states that scores below \(0.5\) favor the confusing class and filters at \(0.6\). Appendix A.3.2 identifies cosine similarity. The actual rendered page confirms the sum.
## Calculation and source comparison

Take two images per class with \(a_i=b_i=0.2\). These positive cosine values have nonzero denominators and can be realized by unit vectors with first coordinate \(0.2\) against a unit text vector. Neither class is preferred, but ([eq:sum] (#eq:sum)) gives \(D=1>0.6\). Five equal-score pairs give \(2.5\). With \(n=2,a_i=0.1,b_i=0.2\), every pair favors the confusing class, yet \(D=2/3>0.6\).

On the normal path where all image pairs are processed successfully, the pinned release [Retained latex: \cite{code}], `filter.py`, lines 320–351, instead averages over all pairs after a softmax of scaled cosine scores: \[D_{\mathrm{release}}=\frac{1}{nm}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m}
\frac{\exp(100a_i)}{\exp(100a_i)+\exp(100b_j)}.\] `generation.py`, lines 101–105, thresholds this statistic. Equal scores give \(0.5\) for every sample count, so that feature is rejected. Independent scalar calculations confirm the examples; no embeddings were computed and no author code was executed.
## Counterevidence and impact

The probability-like interpretation and fixed thresholds suggest a normalized statistic, and the released code explicitly averages. That is substantial counterevidence against alleging that the experiments used the printed sum. Adding \(1/n\) alone also would not reproduce the code: softmax and all-pairs averaging differ from the published raw paired ratios. Raw cosine ratios need treatment of negative scores and zero denominators.

The finding is Minor as a demonstrated publication/release mismatch without an established failure of the operative experimental filter. The release already avoids the demonstrated sample-count failure. A precise documentation correction is the displayed release formula, if that was the experimental implementation. Historical commit provenance and benchmark effects remain Needs Evidence. This does not certify the entire pipeline.
# Other checked claims and overall assessment

Table 2’s advertised 5:1 absolute gains check exactly: \[73.0-60.7=12.3,\quad83.4-78.3=5.1,\quad67.0-61.0=6.0\] percentage points. The setting uses one synthetic plus five real images per class. Table 3’s best LLaVA value, \(79.2\), is 18.0 points above \(61.2\). The relative calculation \(100(78.8-61.2)/61.2=28.758\%\) explains the roughly \(28.7\%\) improvement reported for a different comparison. Such arithmetic does not verify statistical significance; original run and annotation records remain unavailable.

The overall supported impact is Major for the unconditional novelty inference, with the score mismatch separately Minor. Actual contamination, historical training implementation, and effects of stricter novelty screening remain unresolved. The arXiv metadata identifies v2 (5 June 2025), whose abstract retains the guarantee. That was a metadata inspection, not a complete alternate-version comparison; no exhaustive erratum search was performed. Scientific adjudication remains pending; human reviews are empty. Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Modulated Diffusion: Accelerating Generative Modeling with Modulated Quantization
# Identity, scope, and assessment
Paper 0182, I25-43551, is by Weizhi Gao, Zhichao Hou, Junqi Yin, Feiyi Wang, Linyu Peng and Xiaorui Liu, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. The reviewed original is the staged 26-page proceedings PDF with SHA-256

Locations use one-based PDF/printed pages. The available release is https://github.com/WeizhiGao/MoDiff, pinned to `b4db613546e7e6ea974544d9d641f2cbd9f0222e`, dated 2025-09-27. This is not a proven historical table-generation checkout.

Overall assessment: Major. The native auxiliary agent read the complete extracted PDF text and selected release paths. The parent read the complete scientific analysis, visually inspected pp. 6, 13 and 14, checked the assumptions, independently reconstructed the exact quantizer witnesses, and inspected the activation quantizer and its calling configuration statically. Source identity checks passed. No author code was imported or executed. Adjudication is pending and human reviews are empty.
# Method and dependency

MoDiff caches layer states and computes quantized changes across diffusion steps, using error compensation to reduce accumulated approximation error. For a fixed linear operator \(A\), standard modulation uses \[\widetilde o_t=AQ(a_t-a_{t+1})+\widetilde o_{t+1},
 \quad \widetilde o_T=Aa_T.\] The compensated version maintains \[\widehat a_t=Q(a_t-\widehat a_{t+1})+\widehat a_{t+1},
 \quad
 \widehat o_t=AQ(a_t-\widehat a_{t+1})+\widehat o_{t+1},\] initialized by \(\widehat a_T=a_T\) and \(\widehat o_T=Aa_T\). Theorem 4.4’s bounds are the paper’s principal quantitative justification for error accumulation versus suppression. Its scope is a fixed linear operator, not an end-to-end nonlinear diffusion distribution theorem.
# Problem 1: both core error bounds are false
Rating: Major. Locations: p. 6, Theorem 4.4, Eqs. (24)–(31); p. 13, Theorem A.2, Eqs. (43)–(50) and recurrence (59); p. 14, Eqs. (65)–(68).
## Exact claim and assumptions

Write \(\Delta_k=a_k-a_{k+1}\) and \(o_t=Aa_t\). Under \(\|u-Q(u)\|^2\le c\|u\|^2\), the claimed conclusions are \[\|o_t-\widetilde o_t\|^2
 \le c\|A\|^2\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}2^{T-k-1}\|\Delta_k\|^2, \tag{R1}\] \[\|o_t-\widehat o_t\|^2
 \le\|A\|^2\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}(2c)^{T-k-1}\|\Delta_k\|^2. \tag{R2}\] Main Eq. (29) permits \(0<c<1\); the appendix and accompanying prose use the stronger \(c<1/2\). The following examples satisfy both. The exponent directions were verified from the original page images.
## A globally admissible quantizer

Use the two-dimensional, four-bit max–min floor/clamp quantizer of Eqs. (19)–(22). For a nonconstant vector \(u\), set \(m=\min u\), \(M=\max u\), \(s=(M-m)/15\), \(z=\lfloor-m/s\rfloor\), and \[Q(u)_i=s\{\operatorname{clamp}(\lfloor u_i/s\rfloor+z,0,15)-z\}.\] Define \(Q(u)=u\) for constant vectors, including zero. This supplies the zero-range case left undefined by the scale formula and satisfies the abstract theorem’s requirement \(Q(0)=0\).

Here is a global check of the hypothesis. Write \(m/s=j+\theta\), \(j\in\mathbb Z\), \(0\le\theta<1\). For \(\theta=0\) both extrema are exact. For \(0<\theta<1\), the two coordinate errors, up to permutation, are \(-s(1-\theta)\) and \(s\theta\). Thus \[\|u-Q(u)\|^2
 =s^2[(1-\theta)^2+\theta^2]\le s^2
 \le\frac2{225}\|u\|^2<\frac1{100}\|u\|^2.\] Constant vectors are exact, so \(c=1/100\) is valid uniformly. This is an analytic bound for all vectors, not a hypothesis inferred from finite testing.

Take \(A=[1,0]:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\), whose spectral and Frobenius norms both equal one, and \[x=(-6.999,8.001),\quad Q(x)=(-6,8),\quad
 \|x\|^2=113.002002,\quad
 |A(x-Q(x))|^2=0.998001.\] The scale is one and zero point six. All decimal inputs here are exact terminating rationals.
## Standard and compensated counterexamples

For (R1), take \(T=3\), \(a_3=0\), \(a_2=x\), \(a_1=2x\), and evaluate \(t=1\). Both increments are \(x\), giving \(\widetilde o_1=-12\) and \(o_1=-13.998\). Therefore \[\|o_1-\widetilde o_1\|^2=3.992004
 >3c\|x\|^2=3.39006006.\] This strictly violates Eq. (30)/(49).

For (R2), take \(T=4\), \(a_4=a_3=a_2=0\) and \(a_1=x\). All earlier updates are zero; the final compensated output is \(AQ(x)=-6\). Therefore \[\|o_1-\widehat o_1\|^2=0.998001
 >(2c)^2\|x\|^2=0.0452008008.\] This strictly violates Eq. (31)/(50).

The auxiliary exact-Fraction computation and the parent’s separate implementation agree on all values and assertions. These sequences can be independent degenerate random variables, so the pre-theorem independence sentence does not exclude them. No unbiased quantization, random error cancellation, nonzero initialization or diffusion-specific input restriction appears among the theorem’s hypotheses. The norm-one projection removes matrix-norm ambiguity. The bandwidth corollary gives a sufficient generic bound, not an additional restriction excluding a quantizer whose stronger global bound has been proved directly.
## Proof diagnosis and verified correction

The displayed standard recurrence is \[E_t^2\le2c\|A\|^2\|\Delta_t\|^2+2E_{t+1}^2.\] It does not yield (R1). Direct unrolling gives the looser but correctly indexed weights \(c\,2^{k-t+1}\). A sharper useful standard bound follows from telescoping: \[o_t-\widetilde o_t=A\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}(\Delta_k-Q(\Delta_k)),\] \[\|o_t-\widetilde o_t\|^2
 \le c\|A\|^2\left(\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\|\Delta_k\|\right)^2
 \le c(T-t)\|A\|^2\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\|\Delta_k\|^2. \tag{R3}\]

For compensation, linearity and initialization imply \(\widehat o_t=A\widehat a_t\). Define \(r_t=a_t-\widehat a_t\), \(r_T=0\). Then \[r_t=(I-Q)(\Delta_t+r_{t+1}),\qquad
 \|r_t\|\le\sqrt c(\|\Delta_t\|+\|r_{t+1}\|).\] Consequently valid bounds include \[\|o_t-\widehat o_t\|^2
 \le c\|A\|^2
 \left(\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}c^{(k-t)/2}\|\Delta_k\|\right)^2, \tag{R4}\] \[\|o_t-\widehat o_t\|^2
 \le\|A\|^2\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}(2c)^{k-t+1}\|\Delta_k\|^2. \tag{R5}\] Equation (R5) follows from \(\|r_t\|^2\le2c\|\Delta_t\|^2+2c\|r_{t+1}\|^2\). Older increments can be forgotten geometrically, but the newest increment has coefficient \(2c\) independently of the total timeline. If \(\|\Delta_k\|\le B\), (R5) gives \(2c\|A\|^2B^2/(1-2c)\) for \(c<1/2\), and (R4) gives \(c\|A\|^2B^2/(1-\sqrt c)^2\) for \(c<1\).

The proof’s Eq. (67) also prints a plus sign before a quantized term where the residual requires a minus sign. Correcting that sign alone does not repair the reversed geometric weights. These replacement bounds are reviewer derivations, not claimed author corrections.
## Bounded impact and counterevidence

Both core quantitative inequalities and their derivation are invalid. This merits Major without requiring a benchmark score reduction or difficulty of repair. The corrected recurrences preserve a substantial part of the method’s qualitative rationale. No conclusion is drawn that all generated images fail, that reported quality scores are false, or that compensation cannot be useful. The paper itself notes that nonlinear feedback in a full diffusion network goes beyond this fixed-operator model.
# Problem 2: released activation scaling does not implement the described channel axis
Rating: Minor, release-scoped. Locations: Section 5.1, p. 7; Appendix D.2, p. 17; README lines 61–85; ; ; .

The paper distinguishes channel-wise activation LCQ from tensor-wise LTQ and says the main activation scale uses each channel’s minimum and maximum. The pinned entry points pass `args.act_tensor` directly to `channel_wise`; the flag is false by default and described as enabling tensor-wise activation quantization. The documented CIFAR and LSUN dynamic commands omit it.

For an activation of shape \(N\times C\times H\times W\), the quantizer’s true branch reduces all three trailing dimensions and reshapes the remaining scales to \((N,1,1,1)\). The false branch takes extrema over the entire input and produces one scalar. The wrapper sends conventional convolution activations, possibly split along channels, without moving the channel axis to dimension zero. Thus neither route creates the advertised \(C\)-axis scales: for \((N,C,H,W)=(2,3,1,1)\) the scale shape is \((2,1,1,1)\) or scalar, not \((1,3,1,1)\).

Preserving axis zero is appropriate for output-channel weight tensors, and per-example quantization can reasonably be called tensor-wise. The defect concerns the described activation channel axis and default reproduction commands, not terminology alone. Stable Diffusion’s deliberately tensor-wise setting is also not refuted.

This static discrepancy prevents equating the pinned documented route with the stated LCQ configuration. Historical experimental impact remains Needs Evidence because exact experiment commits/configurations and logs were not supplied. A repair should make the activation channel axis explicit and align defaults and flag meanings. No author-code or patched-code run was performed.
# Other inspected claims and coverage

The fixed-linear modulation identity and compensated state relation were checked without finding an issue in their stated scope. For affine layers the inspected release includes the bias at initialization and omits it on subsequent residual calls before adding the cached output; this also preserves a fixed affine map. No repeated-bias defect is alleged.

Theorem 4.3’s no-clipping intermediate claim is too strong: for nonintegral \(m/s\), \(\lfloor m/s\rfloor+\lfloor-m/s\rfloor=-1\), so the lower endpoint clips. The clipped endpoint still has error at most \(s\), preserving the theorem’s final \(\|x-Q(x)\|^2\le ds^2\) bound for nonconstant vectors. This local correction was considered when checking Problem 1’s quantizer and is not represented as a second false error theorem. The theory’s flooring and the release’s rounding conventions were kept distinct.

Experimental tables, setup and stated limitations were read, but FID, sFID, IS, BOP counts and image quality were not recomputed. The source explicitly says wall-clock runtime was not evaluated; its BOP proxy is not misrepresented here as a runtime measurement. Apparent table-label ambiguities remain unresolved rather than claims of fabricated scores. Not all 55 acquired code files were fully audited; bibliography and later errata were not independently checked.

FedPHA: Federated Prompt Learning for Heterogeneous Client Adaptation
# Identity, source version, and review status
The paper authors are Chengying Fang, Wenke Huang, Guancheng Wan, Yihao Yang and Mang Ye.

This initial review covers 0183, I25-43552, FedPHA: Federated Prompt Learning for Heterogeneous Client Adaptation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, official record https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/fang25e.html. The staged 16-page proceedings PDF has SHA-256
> 99e5addc8c09e9814fcba385a39eadc8ec8b7e406d2734e1d5cd8e4fb813b47e.

Page references use one-based PDF/printed pages. The released repository https://github.com/CYFang6/FedPHA is pinned to `316004f77b98673c474c0282d19075f64c4a0c12`, dated 2025-09-02. It is an accessible source snapshot, not a proven historical experiment checkout.

Overall assessment: Major. The native auxiliary agent examined the paper and relevant training/federation sources. The parent read its complete analysis, visually inspected original pp. 5, 6 and 16, read the runtime passage on p. 8, inspected the projection and sequence code, and independently checked the linear algebra and sequence indices. No author code was imported or executed. Scientific decisions remain pending and human reviews are empty.
# Method and central dependency

FedPHA uses a global prompt with fixed length \(T_g\) and personalized local prompts with client-dependent lengths \(T_i\) in a frozen CLIP backbone. Only global prompts are aggregated; local prompts remain personalized. The central interaction projects local prompts with \(Q=V_2V_2^\top\), obtained from the global prompt’s SVD. A pull loss brings local features toward projected-local features, while a margin-based push loss separates local and global features. Both classification losses and regularizers enter Eq. (13). The definition of \(Q\) therefore determines a training target central to the proposed method.
# Problem 1: incompatible projection operators and a failed null-space claim
Rating: Major. Locations: Figure 2, p. 4; Section 3.3, p. 5, Eqs. (8)–(10); Algorithm 1, p. 6; Table 8, p. 16; `trainers/GL_SVDMSE.py:129–165` and `trainers/GL_SVDMSE_HE.py:131–169`.
## The three constructions

The paper specifies a global prompt \(P_g\in\mathbb R^{T_g\times d}\) and a full SVD \(P_g=USV^\top\) with \(V\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). It selects the last \[d'=\lfloor(1-\rho)d\rfloor\] columns as \(V_2\). Algorithm 1 instead takes the slice \(V[:,d(1-\rho):d]\), retaining approximately \(\rho d\) columns. The release calls `torch.svd(global_ctx)` with its default reduced SVD, then uses `cutoff=int(S.shape[0]*(1-ratio))` and `V[:,cutoff:]`. Thus it counts from \(\min(T_g,d)\) singular directions, not from \(d\) full-SVD directions.

The locally installed primary PyTorch documentation explicitly states `some=True` by default and \(\min(m,n)\) columns in \(V\). Its exact excerpt and hash were read and preserved by the parent. The auxiliary agent also ran a small installed-library shape diagnostic using PyTorch 2.9.0+cu128, with no author import. This checks available-library behavior; it is not asserted to identify the historical training environment.
## A complete legal matrix witness

Use standard dimensions \(T_g=16\), \(d=512\) and \[P=[\operatorname{diag}(16,15,\ldots,1)\mid0_{16\times496}].\] This is an allowed real global prompt, with rank 16 and nullity 496. Its nonzero singular values are distinct; \(V=I_{512}\) is a valid full right basis and the reduced basis is \((e_1,\ldots,e_{16})\).
At the default \(\rho=4/5\):
- Eq. (9) selects the last 102 full-basis columns; \(Q\) has rank 102 and \(PQ=0\).
- Algorithm 1 starts at index 102 under floor indexing and keeps 410 columns, also with \(PQ=0\) on this example. A ceiling convention changes this count to 409, not to 102.

- The release cuts the 16 reduced directions at index 3 and keeps \(e_4,\ldots,e_{16}\). Its rank-13 projector lies in the global row space and \[\|PQ_{\rm release}\|_F^2=1^2+\cdots+13^2=819,
 \quad \|PQ_{\rm release}\|_F\approx28.618176.\]
A local prompt row \(p=e_{16}^{\top}\) is preserved by the released projector and annihilated by both full-basis alternatives. It can be repeated to any legal local prompt length.

At \(\rho=1\), explicitly tested in Table 8, rounding ambiguity disappears: \[Q_{\rm equation}=0,\qquad Q_{\rm Algorithm\,1}=I_{512},\qquad
 Q_{\rm release}=\text{projector onto the row space of }P.\] The latter two give \(PQ=P\ne0\), with \(\|P\|_F=\sqrt{1496}\approx38.678159\). More generally, Algorithm 1 returns the identity for every nonzero \(P\) at this setting; its range cannot lie in \(\ker P\). The equation and pseudocode thus prescribe opposite operations at a legal evaluated parameter.

These identities were checked analytically and with independent reviewer calculations. The parent recomputed all ranks, squared norms and boundary cases; no learned-prompt distribution or benchmark execution is needed to refute the general construction claim.
## Counterevidence and bounded significance

Section 3.3 also discusses retaining smaller singular-value components, which might motivate an approximate low-energy spectral filter. The released operator is a valid orthogonal projector onto such a reduced subspace; it is not undefined. This interpretation nevertheless does not reconcile the full-\(d\) equation, complementary slice and reduced-\(T_g\) cutoff. At \(\rho=1\), the published full-basis algorithm removes no global directions at all.

The finding is Major because a principal method component and the target of the pull loss are not mathematically defined consistently. A score decrease, whole-paper collapse or difficult repair is not required for that conclusion. The witness is a lawful prompt matrix, not a claim that training reached it. Which operator produced Tables 1–8 and whether their accuracy values remain valid require historical configurations and outputs.
## Local correction and unverified repair scope

If an exact null-space projector is intended, let \(V_r\) contain right singular vectors for nonzero singular values. Then \[Q_{\rm null}=I_d-V_rV_r^\top,\quad
 Q_{\rm null}^2=Q_{\rm null}=Q_{\rm null}^\top,\quad
 PQ_{\rm null}=0.\] This fixes the linear-algebra property. It does not preserve an arbitrary selected null-subspace dimension or settle differentiation/rank-tolerance choices and empirical behavior. If an approximate row-space filter is intended, it should instead be named and specified consistently with its \(\rho\) semantics. Merely requesting a full SVD is insufficient while the cutoffs disagree. No corrected FedPHA model was trained or certified.
# Problem 2: heterogeneous sequence pooling uses a stale EOS index
Rating: Minor, pinned-release scope. Locations: ; heterogeneous sequence construction, p. 5, Eq. (7).

Token IDs are created using the maximum prompt length \(T_{\max}\) and retained. The text encoder pools at `tokenized_prompts.argmax`, the EOS position in that maximum-length tokenization. The embedded sequence, however, concatenates the common prefix, a shorter learned context, and the shared suffix. EOS moves earlier by \(T_{\max}-T_i\), and zero-padding is appended only at the end. The pooling IDs are not adjusted.

For a class name with one token and a punctuation token, \(T_{\max}=32\) gives fixed zero-based pooling index 35. A length-four context has actual EOS at index 7; a length-16 context at index 19. Both are still pooled at index 35. Only length 32 has matching EOS and pooling positions. Other class-token lengths change the absolute indices but not the displacement.

This is a deterministic sequence-bookkeeping discrepancy, independently reconstructed without executing CLIP. A later padding-position hidden state may still attend to preceding content, so it is not evidence of an empty representation or a measured accuracy loss. A deliberate shared readout position is another possible design, but it would need a consistent description rather than mismatched token and embedding sequences. Historical experimental impact remains Needs Evidence. Updating each pooling index consistently is a local implementation correction, not a validated method repair.
# Problem 3: the release recomputes SVD per forward call
Rating: Minor, source/documentation discrepancy. Locations: p. 8, Table 3 and cost paragraph; both released trainers’ prompt-learner and model-forward paths.

The paper reports decomposition 4.2 ms, projection 2.8 ms and training 4536.8 ms per round, and explicitly says decomposition/projection happen once per round rather than per batch. The released `CustomCLIP.forward` invokes the prompt learner, whose forward unconditionally computes the SVD and projection. Its training path calls the model on each batch; there is no cached-round guard in these methods. The computation also precedes the training-mode branch.

This is a static call-path conflict, not a measurement of total overhead. The release might differ from the timed historical implementation, and no synchronized GPU timing or batch count was obtained. Multiplying the quoted milliseconds by an assumed number of batches would be unjustified. The remedy is to identify the timed implementation and counting unit, or measure the actual per-forward release. The historical Table 3 values remain Needs Evidence rather than established false measurements.
# Counterevidence, empirical scope, and unresolved claims

The inspected non-AMP loss path includes both classification losses, pull MSE and mean hinge push. The backbone is frozen, client local prompts are retained, and the inspected aggregator normalizes global-prompt weights by participating clients’ data counts. No Issue Found is appropriate for these scoped checks; other configurations, including all AMP branches, are not certified.

Auxiliary arithmetic verified the stated Food101 difference \(96.42-92.96=3.46\) percentage points and selected Office31/OfficeHome averages. Table 4 openly shows slightly lower results for randomly heterogeneous lengths than fixed lengths, so the disclosure does not support an allegation of hidden universal improvement.

The Office31 search evaluates \(8^3=512\) combinations, only eight fully uniform. A separate held-out selection protocol was not established from the inspected sources; whether the selected optimum predicts prospective gains remains Needs Evidence. This is not a demonstrated test-leakage claim. Differences between described three-seed/last-ten-round reporting and selected released script/summary conventions likewise require logs before attributing an error to published results.

The exact experiment commit, per-seed outputs, actual projection used in the tables and timing implementation are missing. Separate OpenReview attachment access remains unresolved after the preparation failure. No complete independent bibliography or later-erratum audit, benchmark reproduction, training, dataset download or model execution was performed.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Breaking Barriers: Combinatorial Algorithms for Non-Monotone Submodular Maximization with Sublinear Adaptivity and \(1/e\) Approximation
# Identity, reviewed materials, and assessment
Paper 0184, I25-43553, is by Yixin Chen, Wenjing Chen and Alan Kuhnle, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. This review uses the staged 40-page proceedings PDF, with SHA-256

Page references are one-based PDF pages, matching printed numbers. The available repository is https://gitlab.com/luciacyx/size-constraints-parallel-algorithms, commit `a92b07ed0486ce004cae300bf5d69b83c8e99aea`, dated 2025-10-10 in the source manifest. The manifest and relevant source hashes match. This snapshot is not established as the historical experimental checkout.

Overall assessment: Major. Scientific decisions remain pending and human reviews are empty. The native auxiliary agent inspected the main method, relevant appendices and the complete 540-line `algs_pig.cpp`. The parent read the complete auxiliary analysis, visually checked original pp. 4, 6 and 8, read the decisive proof on p. 15 and Algorithm 11 on p. 37, inspected the cited code, and independently recomputed the witnesses. No author program was run.
# Contribution and core dependencies

The paper develops combinatorial methods for maximizing a nonnegative, potentially nonmonotone submodular function subject to a cardinality constraint. Its simplified interpolated greedy procedure is a theoretical foundation for a parallel threshold-based construction. The headline guarantees combine a \(1/e-\epsilon\) approximation with sublinear adaptivity and controlled oracle-query complexity.

Theorem 3.1 concerns Algorithm 2’s simplified serial procedure. Theorems 4.1–4.2 concern PIG and PItG, sharing UPDATE as a threshold maintenance subroutine. A claimed approximation for a precisely stated algorithm requires its candidate availability invariants; a finite adaptive/query bound requires that each subroutine returns. The following examples attack these exact dependencies, without asserting that a corrected intended algorithm cannot achieve the paper’s goals.
# Problem 1: permanent candidate deletion defeats Theorem 3.1
Rating: Major. Locations: Algorithm 2 and Theorem 3.1, p. 4; Claim 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, p. 5; proof of Lemma 3.2, p. 15, Eq. (8); final theorem analysis, p. 19.
## Printed algorithm and claim

Algorithm 2 initializes \(G=\varnothing\), \(V=U\), and \(m=\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor\). For each of \(\ell\) outer rounds, it starts \(\ell\) solutions \(A_l=G\). It selects \(m\) elements for each solution by greedy marginal maximization over the shared \(V\), deleting each selected element from \(V\). It retains a random \(A_l\) as the new \(G\). There is no reset of \(V\) inside the outer loop.

Theorem 3.1 claims \[\mathbb E f(G)\ge(1/e-\epsilon)f(O),
 \qquad
 \ell\ge\frac{2}{e\epsilon},\quad
 k\ge\frac{2(e\ell-2)}{e\epsilon-2/\ell},
 \quad \ell=O(\epsilon^{-1}).\] Theorem hypotheses allow modular objectives, since these are nonnegative submodular functions and the monotone subclass is not excluded.
## Complete counterexample

Take \(\epsilon=1/10\), \(\ell=10\), \(k=1000\), \(m=100\) and \(|U|=10000\). Let \(H\subset U\) contain 1000 elements and set \[f(S)=|S\cap H|.\] All other elements, including the added dummy elements, have weight zero. This objective is normalized, nonnegative and modular. Its optimum is \(f(O)=1000\). The parameter bounds hold: \[10>7.3575888234=\frac{2}{e\epsilon},\qquad
 1000>701.1960288238=\frac{2(e\ell-2)}{e\epsilon-2/\ell}.\] There are enough ordinary zero-weight elements to complete all selections, so the example does not depend on whether dummy elements are included in \(V\) at initialization.

In round one the \(\ell m=1000\) selections exhaust all of \(H\): every useful element has marginal one and every other element has marginal zero. Each candidate solution receives exactly 100 useful elements. Whichever candidate is selected, \(f(G_1)=100\). The other 900 useful elements were deleted from \(V\) and are never restored. All later additions have zero marginal value. Therefore every random branch returns value 100, and \[\mathbb E f(G)=100<(1/e-0.1)1000=267.8794411714\ldots.\] The parent’s independent finite calculation reproduces the ten-round value sequence \((100,\ldots,100)\). The all-branch assertion follows from the invariant that all candidate values are equal in every round, rather than from an incomplete enumeration of random runs.
## Proof failure and counterevidence

At round two, partition the 900 remaining optimal elements into ten sets \(O_l\) of size 90. This meets Claim 3.1’s requirements: newly selected zero-weight elements do not intersect \(O\). Yet \[\Delta(A_l\mid G_1)=0,\qquad
 \Delta(O_l\mid A_l)=90,\] contradicting Lemma 3.2’s first inequality. The proof’s p. 15 assertion that an optimal element outside the current solution sets remains in the candidate pool is false for elements discarded in an earlier round.

Resetting \(V\) to \(U\setminus G\) at the beginning of each round is a plausible intended correction. It fixes this example and the exhibited availability failure. It is absent from the visually inspected pseudocode, however, and the complete corrected proof has not been certified. The parallel implementation’s repeated `parallel_tg` calls reconstruct candidate sets from the current \(G\); hence this serial counterexample is not evidence that the released parallel experiments made the same permanent deletion.

The demonstrated theorem-to-algorithm mismatch is central and supports Major even though the apparent specification repair is short. It does not establish a lower bound against the intended reset algorithm or falsify empirical objective values.
# Problem 2: UPDATE can fail to terminate

Rating: Major. Locations: Algorithm 5, p. 6, lines 4–6; Algorithm 6, p. 8, calls in lines 4 and 8 and cutoff tests in lines 5 and 9; Lemma G.1 termination argument, p. 36; Theorems 4.1–4.2 and Algorithm 11, pp. 6 and 37–39.
## Unreachable stopping test

UPDATE filters candidates at threshold \(\tau\). While its pool is empty, it replaces \(\tau\) by \((1-\epsilon)\tau\) and searches for elements with marginal at least \(\tau\). It has no \(\tau_{\min}\) input or internal cutoff. Its caller tests whether \(\tau<\tau_{\min}\) only after UPDATE returns.

For Theorem 4.1 take \(n=8\), \(k=2\), \(\ell=2\), \(\epsilon=1/10\) and \[f(S)=\mathbf1\{x\in S\}\] for a distinguished element \(x\). This is normalized, nonnegative and modular, with \(M=f(O)=1\) and \(\tau_{\min}=\epsilon M/k=1/20\). Both initial pools become \(\{x\}\) at threshold one. Their sizes are below \(2\ell\), so Algorithm 6 uses its sequential branch. The first solution selects \(x\), and line 13 removes it from all other pools. The next solution calls UPDATE on the restricted ground set excluding selected elements.

Every remaining marginal is zero. After \(r\) threshold reductions, \[\tau_r=(9/10)^r>0\] for every finite integer \(r\ge0\). No remaining element passes the threshold. UPDATE never returns, and the caller’s cutoff test cannot be reached. The threshold crosses \(1/20\) after 29 reductions, which is irrelevant to the unmodified inner loop. This is an exact-arithmetic nontermination proof, not an inference from a timeout. Eventual floating-point underflow is neither specified nor a proof of the claimed oracle-model complexity.
## The main parallel claim is directly affected

The proof on p. 36 counts only logarithmically many threshold levels by asserting deactivation below \(\tau_{\min}\). That deactivation is implemented in the caller and cannot interrupt the inner loop as written. Therefore both termination and finite adaptivity/query claims for the printed algorithms fail on admissible inputs.
## Released-code counterevidence and local correction
The pinned source contains an internal guard. In `src/algs/algs_pig.cpp:505–540`, `Pig::update` receives `tau_min` and uses
> while (tau > margeGains[0].gain && tau > tau_min)

before returning to its caller. The parent read these bytes directly. This prevents the demonstrated infinite loop in that release on the present instance, whose restricted ground set is nonempty. It does not establish the historical provenance of the experimental checkout or certify the entire implementation.

Passing \(\tau_{\min}\) to the pseudocode UPDATE and returning once it falls below the cutoff repairs this local nontermination and enables the existing caller to retire the solution. Full proof and implementation repair verification remains separate. Major reflects invalid central termination and complexity guarantees, not difficulty of repair or demonstrated benchmark degradation.
# Problem 3: released distributor violates disjointness

Rating: Minor, restricted to the pinned release. Algorithm 3 and Lemma 4.3 on p. 6 require pairwise disjoint output candidate subsets. In `Pig::dist`, source lines 433–464, the implementation declares an exclusion set `added_u` and checks membership, but never inserts chosen elements into it.

Take \(\ell=2\) and \(V_1=V_2=(0,1,2,3)\). Each pool has size \(2\ell\) and satisfies the lemma’s cardinality condition. These are legal initial candidate pools for \(f(S)=|S|\) with four elements and \(k=2\). Both iterations select the first two elements because the exclusion set remains empty. The returned subsets are \(\{0,1\}\) and \(\{0,1\}\) and have nonempty intersection.

This finite witness, independently derived from static source semantics, defeats the released function’s required invariant. It does not disprove the mathematical distributor in Algorithm 3. It also does not determine final objective loss or show that this snapshot generated the paper’s plots. Those historical and empirical implications remain Needs Evidence. Inserting chosen elements into the exclusion set is a local candidate correction; no patched author program was executed or globally certified.
