report: Abstract: The paper studies whether gradient flow learns nearly optimally robust classifiers for an orthonormal Gaussian mixture. Two demonstrated errors affect the central argument. Lemma 17 converts a cosine deficit into a directional error without a square root; an exact balanced two-neuron example violates its bound by a factor of approximately \(30.9\). The proof of the main uniform approximation theorem explicitly invokes this lemma. Separately, the robustness bridge treats a degree-\(p\) function as degree one. Both are classified Major because they invalidate derivations on the core dependency path. Neither counterexample proves that an actual sampled gradient-flow trajectory fails to become robust. A corrected directional bound and a replacement homogeneity argument delimit what remains plausible.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Gradient Flow Provably Learns Robust Classifiers for Orthonormal GMMs
# Identity, scope, and result

This is the initial review of paper 0185, I25-43554, by Hancheng Min and René Vidal, in the ICML 2025 proceedings, PMLR 267, pp. 44292–44350. The reviewed artifact is the staged 59-page proceedings PDF, identified by SHA-256

All locations below use its one-based PDF page numbers. The source manifest and original PDF identity were checked; no replacement version was downloaded. No paper-specific code was identified in the staged preparation. Access to a separate OpenReview attachment remains unresolved, rather than evidence that no attachment exists.

Assessment: Major. The findings concern explicit false inequalities and an invalid core proof step. Scientific adjudication remains pending; no human review or author adoption is recorded. The auxiliary agent examined the main text and selected appendices. The parent checked the decisive original equations, source images on pp. 4, 22, 35 and 59, the main-theorem dependency on pp. 6 and 36, and independently recomputed the exact counterexample. This is not a certification of every dynamical lemma in the 59-page paper.
# Contribution and dependency structure

For orthonormal cluster centers \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\), the paper considers a balanced Gaussian-mixture training set and the network \[f^{(p)}(x;\theta)=\sum_j v_j
 \frac{[\langle x,w_j\rangle]_+^p}{\|w_j\|^{p-1}},\qquad p>2,\] with small, balanced, nondegenerate initialization. Under balance \(|v_j|=\|w_j\|\), each neuron contributes \(\operatorname{sign}(v_j)\|w_j\|^2[\langle x,u_j\rangle]_+^p\), where \(u_j=w_j/\|w_j\|\). The target classifier is \[F^{(p)}(x)=\sum_{k\le K_1}[\langle x,\mu_k\rangle]_+^p
 -\sum_{k>K_1}[\langle x,\mu_k\rangle]_+^p.\] Theorem 1, Eq. (12), asserts uniform sphere approximation of order \(\widetilde O(\alpha_0^2)\) over a training interval, under its dimension, sample-size, initialization and variance assumptions. Proposition 3 converts suitable sphere approximation into near-optimal adversarial robustness. Lemma 17 is the stated conversion from directional alignment and cluster weight control to the uniform approximation. These dependencies make both problems central despite their detailed derivations appearing in appendices.
# Problem 1: a false angular-to-uniform error bound
Rating: Major. Locations: Lemma 17, p. 35 and pp. 58–59; Theorem 1, p. 6, Eq. (12); restated theorem, p. 35, Eq. (G.5); explicit application of Lemma 17, p. 36.
## Claim and assumptions

The lemma assumes cosine alignment within a deficit \(\delta\), per-cluster squared-weight sums within \(
u\) of one, and total void-neuron squared weight at most \(\zeta\). It concludes \[\sup_{\|x\|=1}|f^{(p)}(x;	heta)-F^{(p)}(x)|
 \le K(1+
u)(2^p-1)2\delta+K
u+\zeta. 	ag{R1}\] The printed alignment hypothesis uses maxima; the following counterexample satisfies the stronger, intended condition for every neuron, so correcting that quantifier does not remove the violation.
## Exact admissible counterexample

Set \(D=3\), \(K=2\), \(K_1=K_2=1\), \(p=3\), and use two neurons. Let \[t=\frac1{1000},\quad a=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\quad
 b=\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\quad
 \mu_1=e_1,\quad\mu_2=e_2,\] \[w_1=(a,0,b),\quad v_1=1,\qquad w_2=e_2,\quad v_2=-1.\] Take \(\mathcal N_1=\{1\}\), \(\mathcal N_2=\{2\}\), no void neurons, \(\delta=1-a=2/1000001\), and \(\nu=\zeta=t^4>0\). Both neurons have unit norm and satisfy balance; each cluster has squared-weight sum exactly one. Their corresponding cosines are \(a\) and one, respectively. The centers are orthonormal. At the unit vector \(x=(3/5,0,4/5)\), \[|f^{(3)}(x)-F^{(3)}(x)|
 =\left(\frac{3a+4b}{5}\right)^3-\left(\frac35\right)^3
 =\frac{216414079424215946}{125000375000375000125}
 \approx0.001731307441466209.\] In contrast, the right side of (R1) is \[28(1+t^4)(1-a)+3t^4
 =\frac{56000003000059}{1000001000000000000}
 \approx0.000055999947000112.\] The ratio is approximately \(30.9162\). Both an auxiliary exact-rational diagnostic and the parent’s separately written Fraction calculation reproduced this violation. No author code was executed.
## Failure mechanism and bounded consequence

The displayed proof on p. 59 replaces \(\|u_j-\mu_k\|\) by \(2(1-c_{kj})\). The correct identity for unit vectors is \[\|u_j-\mu_k\|^2=2(1-c_{kj}),\qquad
 \|u_j-\mu_k\|=\sqrt{2(1-c_{kj})}.\] The example’s output difference is \(216t/125+O(t^2)\), whereas (R1) is \(56t^2+O(t^4)\). This is a rate error, not rounding or a loose constant.

The theorem proof on p. 36 explicitly uses Lemma 17 after obtaining cosine deficits of order \(\widetilde O(\alpha^2)\). Thus its stated deduction of the core uniform \(\widetilde O(\alpha_0^2)\) rate is invalid. This is sufficient for Major under a core-derivation standard. The example is a configuration satisfying the lemma, not a constructed sampled gradient-flow trajectory satisfying every assumption of Theorem 1. It therefore does not independently disprove that theorem’s conclusion or the paper’s qualitative learning mechanism. Extra dynamical cancellation or a stronger alignment estimate could in principle recover a sharper rate, but it is not supplied by this lemma.
## Verified local correction

Since \(z\mapsto[z]_+^p\) is \(p\)-Lipschitz on \([-1,1]\), a direct replacement, under the all-neuron alignment hypothesis, is \[\sup_{\|x\|=1}|f^{(p)}(x)-F^{(p)}(x)|
 \le K(1+\nu)p\sqrt{2\delta}+K\nu+\zeta. \tag{R2}\] This follows by summing each neuron’s directional perturbation and then bounding the cluster mass errors. The void contribution is at most \(\zeta\). Retaining the cluster-count dependence, angular and mass errors of order \(\widetilde O(\alpha_0^2)\) make this generic route certify a sphere-error upper bound \(\widetilde O(K\alpha_0)\) for fixed \(p\). At fixed \(K,p\), this is \(\widetilde O(\alpha_0)\), whereas the printed route claims \(\widetilde O(\alpha_0^2)\). Conditional on all other dynamical hypotheses and a sufficiently small tolerance for the repaired robustness bridge, the corresponding certified radius deficit is \(\widetilde O(K^{1/p}\alpha_0^{1/p})\), or \(\widetilde O(\alpha_0^{1/p})\) at fixed \(K,p\). The paper’s tilde convention does not hide polynomial dependence on \(K\). These are upper bounds supplied by the replacement route, not lower bounds excluding a faster rate on actual trajectories and not a replacement theorem for the full dynamics.
# Problem 2: incorrect homogeneity in the robustness bridge
Rating: Major. Locations: Proposition 3 and the paragraph following it, p. 5; Appendix D, p. 22, especially Eq. (D.2).
## Demonstrated invalid step

Proposition 3 assumes \(f(\gamma x)=\gamma f(x)\). Its proof states that the same holds for \(F^{(p)}\), and uses a sphere discrepancy at most \(\nu\) to infer an off-sphere discrepancy at most \(\|x\|\nu\). The main text also calls the actual network degree one in its input. From the definitions, however, \[f^{(p)}(\gamma x;\theta)=\gamma^p f^{(p)}(x;\theta),\qquad
 F^{(p)}(\gamma x)=\gamma^p F^{(p)}(x).\] The denominator in the network depends on the weights, not on the input, and does not change this input homogeneity.

There is a direct counterexample to the proof step even under Proposition 3’s stated degree-one premise. Define \(f(x)=\|x\|^{1-p}F^{(p)}(x)\) for \(x\ne0\) and \(f(0)=0\). It is degree one and has zero sphere discrepancy from \(F^{(p)}\). For \(p=3\), \(\mu_1=e_1,\mu_2=e_2\), and \(x=2e_1\), its value is 2 while \(F^{(3)}(x)=8\). The discrepancy is 6. Choosing \(\nu=0.001<(\sqrt2/8)^3\) satisfies the proposition’s tolerance assumption, while the claimed off-sphere bound is only \(0.002\).

This disproves Eq. (D.2)’s inference and shows that Proposition 3 as stated cannot directly be applied to the degree-\(p\) network. It does not by itself disprove Proposition 3’s robustness conclusion, because classification signs are invariant under positive radial rescaling.
## A replacement bridge and its limits

A local repair is possible. For a positively homogeneous classifier of any positive degree, let \(g(z)=\|z\|^p f(z/\|z\|)\), with \(g(0)=0\). Then \(g\) has the same sign as \(f\) and the same unit-sphere values. If \(\sup_{\|u\|=1}|cf(u)-F^{(p)}(u)|\le
u\) for \(c>0\), the correct extension is \[|cg(z)-F^{(p)}(z)|\le\|z\|^p
u.\] The distance definition can be handled by a limiting argument, or by attainment: the relevant supremum norm is coercive in \(c\) for nonzero bounded \(f\), and \(\|F^{(p)}\|_\infty=1>
u\) excludes a zero minimizing scale.

For completeness, put \(q=\nu^{1/p}\) and \(r=(\sqrt2-8q)/2\), so \(0<q\le\sqrt2/8\). Write a test sample as \(\mu_k+\varepsilon\) and restrict to \[\max_l|\langle\varepsilon,\mu_l\rangle|\le q/K,\qquad
 \|\varepsilon\|\le\sqrt{17/2}-1.\] For any \(\|d\|\le1\), \(z=\mu_k+\varepsilon+rd\) satisfies \(\|z\|\le R=\sqrt{17/2}+\sqrt2/2\). The correct-class coordinate minus the opposite-class \(\ell_p\) norm is at least \[1-q-r\sqrt2=(4\sqrt2-1)q>Rq.\] Writing \(J\) for the opposite-label clusters, \(m=|J|\le K-1\), and \(\varepsilon_l=\langle\varepsilon,\mu_l\rangle\), the two bounds used here are \[|\varepsilon_k|+\|\varepsilon_J\|_p
 \le (1+m^{1/p})q/K\le q,\qquad
 |d_k|+\|d_J\|_2\le\sqrt2.\] The second uses orthonormality and \(\|d\|_2\le1\); the first uses \(p>1\) and both classes being represented. For nonnegative \(A\ge B\) and \(p>1\), \(A^p-B^p\ge(A-B)^p\). Thus the correct-class margin exceeds \(R^p\nu\), which dominates the approximation error. The same argument applies to either class. Combining this deterministic argument with the Gaussian projection and norm tail bounds gives the stated probability form \[1-2K\exp\!\left(-\frac{D\nu^{2/p}}{2K^2\alpha^2}\right)
 -4\exp\!\left(-\frac{3}{8\alpha^2}\right).\] The constants satisfy \(4\sqrt2-1\approx4.65685>R\approx3.62258\) and \((\sqrt{17/2}-1)^2>3\), independently checked numerically. The replacement also avoids the original proof’s unjustified norm-three restriction. The norm-tail bound needs no small-\(\alpha\) condition: for \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\alpha^2I/D)\), \[{\mathbb E}\exp\!\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|^2}{4\alpha^2}\right)
 =(1-1/(2D))^{-D/2}\le\sqrt2.\] Markov’s inequality and \((\sqrt{17/2}-1)^2>3\) give the displayed weaker \(4\exp[-3/(8\alpha^2)]\) tail for every \(\alpha>0\) and integer \(D\ge1\). The deterministic margin is uniformly at least \(\{(4\sqrt2-1)^p-R^p\}\nu>0\) before division by the positive scale. Attacked inputs stay in an annulus bounded away from zero, so transferring this margin back to any positive homogeneity degree is valid. For arbitrary discontinuous classifiers, use an infimum over attacks; the actual network is continuous.

This repair explains why the robustness conclusion can survive the homogeneity error. It does not retroactively validate the printed derivation and does not repair Problem 1’s main approximation rate. Major here records a demonstrated invalid core bridge, with unusually strong counterevidence against claiming the robustness principle itself false.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
video-SALMONN-o1: Reasoning-enhanced Audio-visual Large Language Model
# Identity, reviewed scope, and status
The paper authors are Guangzhi Sun, Yudong Yang, Jimin Zhuang, Changli Tang, Yixuan Li, Wei Li, Zejun MA and Chao Zhang.
This initial review covers 0186, I25-43555, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, official record https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/sun25x.html. The reviewed original is the staged 20-page proceedings PDF, SHA-256

All page references are one-based PDF/printed pages. The available release is https://github.com/BriansIDP/video-SALMONN-o1, commit `4cf978fa9f48942432c959ab7d7eaff80a339d91`, dated 2025-08-26. Its exact connection to the reported historical training runs is unproven.

Overall assessment: Minor. No demonstrated Major problem was found in the inspected core. This is a scope-bounded result, not certification of the full empirical study. The auxiliary agent examined the main text, selected appendix material and relevant source paths. The parent read the full notes, visually inspected original pp. 4, 5 and 7, read the cited KL code and mathematical demo, and independently recalculated the key identities and numerical discrepancies. Scientific decisions remain pending and human reviews are empty.
# Contribution and checked core reasoning

The method combines an audio-visual model with reasoning-focused supervised training, then forms preference pairs between alternative reasoning steps sharing a prefix. Rollout answer correctness estimates a prefix’s utility; an input-perturbation score selects steps for more expensive comparisons. Full-path preference examples complement process-level pairs. The empirical claims depend on both the optimizer and the quality of rollout judging, annotations and evaluation.
## Process-DPO: No Issue Found within the checked algebra

The assumptions are positive \(\beta\), finite normalization, positive reference support, identical prefix and multimodal conditioning for both alternatives, and consistent likelihood evaluation. A reward defined up to a context offset must not be confused with an absolutely calibrated probability of correct reasoning. Eq. (2)’s rollout average estimates continuation-policy-specific answer success given an accurate evaluator; it does not prove every intermediate statement is logically correct.

An independent numerical check with \(\beta=0.7\), reference probabilities \((0.4,0.6)\) and rewards \((1.2,-0.3)\) yields \(Z=2.6119465848\), policy \((0.8503555024,0.1496444976)\), reconstructed reward difference 1.5 and preference probability \(0.8175744762\). The parent independently reproduced the auxiliary calculation. This verifies algebra, not training.
## Contrastive selection and counterevidence

Section 4.3, p. 5, averages the token-level divergence \[D_{\rm KL}(P_{\rm original}\|P_{\rm perturbed})\] over a step’s token positions. The inspected `contrast_probs` function in uses predictive logits aligned to current tokens, sums \(\exp(\log p)(\log p-\log q)\) over vocabulary, then averages token positions. This agrees with the stated direction and normalization. Image perturbation is active while audio zeroing is commented; image-only sensitivity is not by itself a contradiction of the stated video-focused heuristic.

The source presents high sensitivity as a useful selection heuristic, not a theorem identifying all erroneous steps. Six-rollout noise, judge error and soft-label construction remain empirical questions. The main pDPO loss visibly includes the minus sign absent from the separate PRM expression below.
# Problem 1: SynthDec metrics need a consistent definition or correction
Rating: Minor, reporting scope. Location: Table 2 and its caption, p. 7.

The caption describes SynthDec as F1-score (Precision/Recall). Its own-model rows report \[\text{SFT: }5.8\%\ (97\%/5\%),\qquad
 \text{pDPO: }17.8\%\ (87\%/13\%).\] For a common positive class, predictions and aggregation, ordinary \(F_1=2PR/(P+R)\) gives \(9.5098039\%\) and \(22.62\%\). Rounding cannot explain the differences. Allowing precision and recall their full nearest-integer-percent intervals yields \[F_{1,\rm SFT}\in[8.59901,10.41262]\%,\qquad
 F_{1,\rm pDPO}\in[21.84343,23.39109]\%.\] These are disjoint from the respective nearest-tenth intervals \([5.75,5.85]\%\) and \([17.75,17.85]\%\). The harmonic mean is increasing in both positive inputs, so the endpoint check covers the full rounding rectangles.

Separate macro-averages, per-run averages or different class conventions can make averaged F1 differ from the harmonic mean of averaged precision and recall. No such alternative was specified in the inspected caption/discussion. The established problem is incomplete or inconsistent quantitative reporting under the ordinary interpretation, not an unconditional recovery of the true scores. The conditional values above are not rerun evaluation results.

The pDPO-over-SFT ordering survives both the displayed F1s and those conditional harmonic means. This finding does not invalidate the other accuracy columns or the central loss. Exact scoring code, confusion matrices and predictions are needed to resolve the magnitude of the synthetic-detection result. Four nonzero commercial-model entries were compatible with ordinary F1 after rounding, supporting but not proving a common convention. The bounded repair is to provide a precise averaging definition or correct the affected entries.
# Problem 2: the printed PRM loss has the wrong minimization sign
Rating: Minor. Location: p. 4, Eq. (3), labelled as the PRM training loss.

For target success probability \(p\) and prediction \(0<r<1\), the printed summand is \[L(r)=p\log r+(1-p)\log(1-r).\] Its derivative is \((p-r)/(r(1-r))\) and \[L''(r)=-p/r^2-(1-p)/(1-r)^2<0.\] Thus \(r=p\) maximizes this expression; minimizing it drives predictions toward a boundary, with arbitrarily negative value when \(0<p<1\). For \(p=1\), minimizing \(\log r\) drives \(r\) toward zero rather than one.

A leading minus sign yields minimized binary cross-entropy, or the expression may be explicitly called a maximized log likelihood. This is a local specification error under the stated loss interpretation. The main pDPO Eq. (6) is correctly signed, and no actual PRM optimization implementation or historical log was bound to the literal sign in Eq. (3). Consequently this does not establish that the reported PRM baseline was trained incorrectly. The distinct binary target described for the baseline in Section 7.3 also needs implementation clarification rather than an assumption that it must match the earlier soft target.
# Problem 3: a released mathematical demo makes a false inference

Rating: Minor for the public demo; scored-benchmark effect Needs Evidence. The pinned README, lines 66–84, presents a RivaBench mathematics example. Its selected answer and explanation infer from \(w_t-w_{xx}\le0\) that the function can only decrease or remain constant over time at interior points.

Take \[w(x,t)=x^2+t,\qquad (x,t)\in(-1,1)\times(0,1].\] Then \(w_t=1\), \(w_{xx}=2\), and \(w_t-w_{xx}=-1\le0\), while the function increases at every fixed \(x\). The asserted implication is false. A parabolic maximum principle concerns extrema relative to an appropriate parabolic boundary under its assumptions; it does not imply pointwise temporal monotonicity. Non-strict formulations also allow a constant solution to attain its maximum inside.

The demo was directly read from the source bytes. Its exact inclusion in the frozen scored Academic test set was not established; the original PDF’s illustrated Academic cases are different. The linked video and full annotation dataset were not downloaded. Therefore one faulty released explanation does not establish a dataset-wide label-error rate or invalidate the reported Academic accuracy. Repair the explanation and answer, and provide item-level benchmark provenance before drawing broader evaluation conclusions.
# Empirical checks, counterevidence, and unresolved provenance

The reported benchmark sizes \(1912+2128+200=4240\) are internally consistent. Selected pDPO-minus-SFT improvements in Table 2 are 2.7, 4.1, 8.1 and 5.8 percentage points for VideoMME, NExT-QA, StandUp and Academic. Table 3 openly reports that direct-answer SFT outperforms reasoning-output SFT on the listed tasks, and pDPO remains above both displayed variants. This is disclosed counterevidence, not an omitted baseline.

The auxiliary visual check of Figure 5 found relevant full-path-only versus added-process-pair controls. They support the paper’s reported comparison in scope, while no uncertainty or significance was independently recomputed. Neither the algebra nor these table checks isolate exposure-bias mitigation as the sole causal explanation of improvements.

Static inspection found pair-formatted model/collator paths and rollout code, but did not identify a complete historically bound process-DPO training driver with all masks, reference settings and soft labels. A released top-two branch does not prove that the described top-three training run used the wrong value. Missing training configuration is a reproducibility gap, not evidence of a scientific failure by itself.

Title: Technical Verification of RoPE
# Identity and scope

The reviewed paper is Antoine Wehenkel, Juan L. Gamella, Ozan Sener, Jens Behrmann, Guillermo Sapiro, Jörn-Henrik Jacobsen, and Marco Cuturi, Addressing Misspecification in Simulation-based Inference through Data-driven Calibration, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 65949–65980 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; local identifier 0187/I25-43556. The source is the 32-page proceedings PDF with embedded appendices. Page references are one-based PDF pages, matching printed labels.

The check covered Sections 2–3, the metric and interpretation passages in Sections 5–6, Algorithm 1, Appendices E–H, and Algorithm 9. Selected experimental settings and figures were read for scope. A matching RoPE implementation was not available in the staged sources. No author code, datasets, model weights, or experiments were executed or downloaded. The causal-chamber repository mentioned by the paper is not treated as a RoPE implementation. Separate OpenReview attachment access remains unresolved.
# Correct core identities and their limits

For \(n_o\) observations and \(n_s\) simulations, the transport matrix satisfies \[\sum_jP_{ij}=1/n_o.\] Thus Equation (5)’s weights \(\alpha_{ij}=n_oP_{ij}\) are nonnegative and sum to one. The mixture of normalized simulation posteriors is consequently a normalized posterior.

Equation reference: eq:marginal. For balanced transport, \(\sum_iP_{ij}=1/n_s\). Direct summation gives the exact empirical identity \[
\frac1{n_o}\sum_i\widetilde p(\theta\mid x_o^i)
=\frac1{n_s}\sum_j\widetilde p(\theta\mid x_s^j).\] Under the assumed simulator-marginal calibration and the simulation-sampling limit, the right side approaches the prior. Appendix F appropriately calls this a necessary marginal-calibration property; it is not a guarantee of conditional calibration, joint credible-region coverage, or correct coupling. The paper also explicitly acknowledges that ACAUC does not assess joint calibration. No defect is established in ([eq:marginal] (#eq:marginal)) under these conditions.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Algorithm 1 produces a sub-probability density as printed).
## Claim, assumptions, and calculation

Algorithm 1, Step 5, p. 17, uses \(\sum_jP_{ij}\widetilde p(\theta\mid x_s^j)\) as its posterior, although its Step 4 retains the row constraint defining \(\mathcal B_o\) on p. 3. For normalized components and any \(n_o>1\), \[\int\sum_jP_{ij}\widetilde p(\theta\mid x_s^j)\,d\theta
=\sum_jP_{ij}=1/n_o\ne1.\] For the explicit admissible balanced matrix \(P_{ij}=1/16\) with \(n_o=n_s=4\), the integral is \(1/4\). Multiplying by \(n_o\) gives one. If interpreted as a log-density, the unnormalized quantity differs by \(-\log n_o\); this is a conditional implication, not an observed experimental offset.
## Counterevidence, impact, and correction

Main Equation (5) and Appendix F both include the missing factor. They supply a precise, analytically verified repair: use \(\alpha_{ij}=n_oP_{ij}\). The intact core identity is important counterevidence against attributing this omission to the experiments. The supported grade is Minor for inconsistent executable specification, with historical implementation impact Needs Evidence. The grade is not based on the appendix location; it reflects that the main mathematical definition and its proof already give the normalized algorithm.
Problem 2 (Algorithm 9’s unnormalized rank sum does not estimate an average calibration area).
## Claim and source

Section 5, p. 7, defines ACAUC as an average over observations, parameter dimensions, and credible levels. Appendix J, Algorithm 9, p. 28, instead sums ordered rank-derived levels minus \(i/N\) at line 16, then divides only by the parameter count \(K\). The original page image confirms the absence of a sample-count normalization. There are also inconsistent \(M/N\) names and list/scalar assignments; the check below grants those elementary implementation repairs and gives the algorithm its most favorable coherent interpretation.
## Complete analytic check

Take one parameter, continuous correctly specified posteriors, independent observations, and exact posterior ranks (the infinite posterior-draw limit). Then the probability integral transforms \(U_i\) are independent uniform variables. Interpret \(N\) as the number of evaluated observations and line 16 as \[A_N=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(U_{(i)}-\frac{i}{N}\right).\] Sorting preserves the sum. Therefore \[\mathbb E A_N=-\frac12,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(A_N)=\frac{N}{12}.\] The estimator neither converges to zero for a calibrated model nor has the scale of an average area. The concrete grid \(U_i=(i-\frac12)/N\) gives \(A_N=-1/2\) for every \(N\). With \(N=4\), the independent exact-fraction calculation obtains \(-1/2\) rather than a normalized average.
## Counterevidence and bounded repair

The main metric definition includes the correct observation averaging. Its displayed scores and calibration curves cannot be assumed to come from the literal pseudocode, especially because the latter also contains implementation ambiguities. No original implementation or metric arrays were available, so the empirical calibration claims remain unverified rather than disproved by this finding.

The exact connection to the main metric requires an interval convention. For any nested credible-level family \(C_i(\alpha)\), set \[V_i=\inf\bigl(\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\theta_i\in C_i(\alpha)\}\cup\{1\}\bigr).\] Apart from endpoints of zero integration measure, membership is \(\mathbf{1}\{V_i\le\alpha\}\). The single-coordinate empirical signed area in the main definition is therefore exactly \[\frac1N\sum_i\int_0^1
 [\alpha-\mathbf{1}\{\theta_i\in C_i(\alpha)\}]\,d\alpha
 =\frac1N\sum_i V_i-\frac12.\] For one-sided lower credible intervals, \(V_i=U_i=F_i(\theta_i)\); for central equal-tailed intervals, \(V_i=|2U_i-1|\). Both are uniform under a correct continuous posterior, so the normalization diagnosis survives either convention. Under misspecification their distributions differ, and the intended interval definition must be stated.

For the corresponding ordered \(V_i\), dividing the right-endpoint rank sum by \(N\) removes the divergent scale; replacing \(i/N\) by \((i-\frac12)/N\) then gives exactly \(\overline V-1/2\). Under independent correct posteriors, the right-endpoint version has mean \(-1/(2N)\) and variance \(1/(12N)\). For \(N=4\) with every \(V_i=0.99\), the literal sum is \(1.46\), outside the signed area’s range \([-1/2,1/2]\), while the exact area is \(0.49\). The metric can also cancel positive and negative calibration errors; it is not alone a complete calibration certificate. The supported defect is Minor, with historical metric implementation and interval semantics Needs Evidence.
Problem 3 (Disjoint support does not ensure an automatic uniform-transport fallback).
## Claim and assumptions

Section 6, p. 9, discusses disjoint calibration/test support and states that a lack of meaningful matches will make the transport uniform and return the prior. This extrapolation is outside the principal i.i.d. calibration setting. The issue is whether the transport objective itself supplies the claimed detection mechanism. Section 3.1 specifies an unsquared Euclidean feature distance; the counterexample uses exactly that distance.
## An admissible transport calculation

Let the two simulation representations be \((-R,0),(R,0)\) and two test representations be \((-R,R),(R,R)\), with uniform marginals, \(R>0\), balanced transport, and entropy weight \(\gamma>0\). The supports are disjoint, with minimum distance \(R\). The Euclidean cost matrix is \[C=R\begin{pmatrix}1&\sqrt5\\\sqrt5&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Every feasible coupling with these two uniform marginals has the form \[P=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}q&1-q\\1-q&q\end{pmatrix}.\] Strict convexity of entropy ensures uniqueness. Differentiating the objective in \(q\) yields \[-R(\sqrt5-1)+\gamma\log\frac q{1-q}=0,\qquad
q=\frac1{1+\exp[-R(\sqrt5-1)/\gamma]}.\] For \(R=10,\gamma=0.5\), \(q=0.9999999999816493\). Uniform conditional weights would be \(1/2\). As the supports become farther apart, \(q\) tends to one, not to \(1/2\). The assumptions impose no feature-norm bound or constraint on the out-of-distribution extension of the learned representation that excludes this configuration. Semantic correctness of the near-diagonal matching is not determined by its distance ranking. To connect this geometry to the paper’s calibration/test claim, let the calibration representation lie on the same lower line as the simulation representation. It can match the parameter perfectly there. A test distribution on the disjoint upper line may reverse the parameter-to-position association while the representation map retains the displayed geometric positions. Fine-tuning on the lower calibration support constrains neither that out-of-support association nor the relative test costs. The same objective then yields a confident but semantically wrong match. This is an admissible finite transport illustration of the claimed fallback mechanism; it is not a reproduced neural-density experiment.
## Scope and correction

This disproves automatic fallback from separation or poor generalization alone; it does not disprove the paper’s observed light-tunnel results. Large \(\gamma\) relative to cost differences, or essentially equal transport-relevant costs, can produce a uniform coupling. Increasing all distances is insufficient. The supported correction is to make fallback conditional on the cost geometry/regularization, or to provide a separately validated mismatch detector. No such detector is invented here. This is Minor for the unsupported extrapolation beyond the evaluated conditions, with no demonstrated failure of the principal i.i.d. results.
# Overall impact and unexamined work

The highest supported grade is Minor. Main Equation (5), its normalization, and the balanced empirical marginal identity survive. Algorithmic normalization and metric correspondence require correction or clarification; actual experimental provenance is unavailable. The distribution-shift example bounds a discussion claim rather than asserting failure on the published benchmarks.

Appendix G explicitly states that unrestricted NPE optimality cannot establish minimality of its representation. Its information-bottleneck proposal is therefore not treated here as a proved minimal-sufficiency theorem. Experimental LPP, full calibration curves, hyperparameter choices, neural training, and raw data splits were not independently reproduced. Later revisions and errata were not exhaustively checked. Scientific adjudication remains pending; human reviews are empty. The issue grades below are unchanged. Adoption has not been requested or verified. For P2, \(V=U\) for lower one-sided intervals and \(V=|2U-1|\) for equal-tailed central intervals; the interval convention is part of the unresolved implementation binding.

Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
# Identity, scope, and status
The paper authors are Yukang Yang, Declan Campbell, Kaixuan Huang, Mengdi Wang, Jonathan Cohen and Taylor Webb.
This is the initial review of 0188, I25-43557, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, official record https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/yang25c.html. The staged 35-page proceedings PDF has SHA-256

Locations use one-based PDF/printed pages. The available release https://github.com/yukang123/LLMSymbMech is pinned to `7dfaf791cc3916cc95d646f88d7d2909bf6f9588`, dated 2026-07-13. It is later than the paper and is not an established original experiment checkout.

Overall assessment: Minor. Core No Issue Found statements below are bounded to inspected methods and evidence. The auxiliary agent examined main Sections 2–3, relevant discussion and appendix controls, and selected complete analysis paths. The parent read the full notes, visually inspected original pp. 4, 24 and 25, directly checked the decisive release statements, and separately reconstructed the index and confidence-interval examples. Scientific decisions remain pending and human reviews are empty.
# Contribution and causal scope

The paper proposes a sequence of symbol abstraction, symbolic induction and token retrieval during relational reasoning. Its primary task uses arbitrary tokens in ABA/ABB patterns, followed by letter-string and verbal analogies. Activation transplantation, attention patterns, representational similarity, ablation and decoding provide different forms of evidence.

A causal intervention can show influence within a tested computation without proving a unique minimal circuit or universal symbolic reasoning. Similarly, linear decoding across tested disjoint token sets is not exact invariance under every possible token replacement. The paper itself acknowledges mixed token/variable information, additional computation for nonidentity relations and imperfect cross-task agreement. These restrictions matter when interpreting its central claim.
# Core checks and relevant counterevidence
## Contrasts and effect score

The abstract contrast swaps within-example token roles while preserving the literal unpatched answer. For example, an ABA donor with query \((x,y)\) answers \(x\), while an ABB recipient with swapped query \((y,x)\) also answers \(x\); transplanting the donor role is expected to favor \(y\). The token contrast preserves the abstract rule while swapping query tokens, so the literal answer changes. The auxiliary’s enumeration checks both ABA and ABB directions.

Equation (5), p. 4, is a difference of logit differences: \[s=(f(c^*)_{\rm target}-f(c^*)_{\rm original})
 -(f(c)_{\rm target}-f(c)_{\rm original}).\] The original rendered page visibly contains a subtraction, not a ratio. Algorithm 1 and the inspected causal-mediation code agree with it. A misleading text-extraction layout was therefore not promoted into a formula error.

Positive \(s\) measures movement toward the targeted alternative; it does not require an argmax flip. For example, original/target logits \((10,0)\) changing to \((9,0)\) give \(s=1\) while retaining the original top answer. This limits interpretation without contradicting the paper’s effect-magnitude definition. Main analyses condition on successful answers, a disclosed restriction; error-trial analyses provide additional but unreproduced counterevidence.
## RSA, ablation and decoding controls

The paper and `rsa.py:546–552` compare strict lower triangles of similarity matrices, excluding diagonals. The parent checked both the source and p. 24. There is no supported self-similarity-diagonal inflation allegation.

Table 2 reports abstract/token output RSA of \(0.56/0.24\) for abstraction heads, \(0.69/0.03\) for induction heads and \(0.11/0.35\) for retrieval heads. A modified length-four task distinguishes within-instance position from a previous-variable hypothesis that the simpler ABA/ABB task alone cannot distinguish. This is meaningful counterevidence against treating an unresolved simple-task confound as an unaddressed universal flaw.

The auxiliary’s static check found that layer-matched ablation controls select the same number of distinct low-score heads within each selected layer. The random control also selects distinct heads, and the paper describes held-out ablation prompts. Figure 15 visibly shows substantially faster degradation for ranked heads than controls. These observations support importance under the tested zero-ablation procedure; they do not establish an exclusive minimal circuit or every proposed interstage causal edge.

The reported disjoint-token linear probe and error-trial comparisons are relevant controls. Their learned parameters, exact splits and raw outputs were not reproduced. Teacher-forced conditional-token interventions in the analogy extensions are described in the source and should not be mistaken for verified free-running sequence conversion or hidden test leakage.
# Problem 1: final-token RSA commands select BOS or fail
Rating: Minor, pinned-release scope. Locations: ; .

The supplied induction and retrieval RSA commands use `–sel_pos_list -1` to select the final token. The script sets `prepend_bos=True`, then applies `pos+1` to every selected position. Python’s final-token index \(-1\) becomes zero, selecting the beginning-of-sequence token rather than the final token.

For an illustrative 17-token sequence including BOS, the intended final index is 16. The abstract-role tables have keys at positive token positions and at the final position; key zero is absent. The subsequent list construction `ABA_abs_table[pos]` therefore reaches `KeyError: 0`. The token-comparison route instead selects BOS across contexts; its token-identity hypothesis matrix is constant, yielding undefined Pearson correlation rather than the intended final-position RSA.

The parent directly read the command, index conversion, role dictionaries and lookup, then independently reconstructed them with a list and dictionary. This is a verified static-semantic failure of the documented route, without execution of the author script or model.
## Counterevidence and repair boundary

Positive positions used for abstraction heads are shifted appropriately. Moreover, `cma.py:817` and `ablation.py:644` explicitly preserve \(-1\) using `pos+1 if pos!=-1 else pos`. The error is therefore not transferred to the causal-mediation or ablation routes.

The published nontrivial RSA results could come from earlier code, corrected arguments or another invocation. No historical run binding was found, so this defect does not establish that Table 2 or Figure 4 is numerically false. Preserving valid negative indices or selecting a suitable explicit positive position repairs the identified indexing route, but does not certify the full regenerated analysis. The claimed scientific mechanism remains a separate question.
# Problem 2: duplicated greedy responses understate uncertainty
Rating: Minor, released uncertainty calculation. Locations: `run_identity.sh:16–17`; `tasks/identity_rules/eval.py:182,221–238`; Figures 16–17 captions, p. 25.

The documented greedy route uses 500 prompts and `sample_size 4`. The evaluator duplicates each prompt four times, increments success and total counts for every response, and calls a Wilson interval function with those duplicated counts. Under deterministic greedy decoding the four responses to one prompt are identical outcomes, not four independent samples from the prompt population.
For success rate \(0.95\), the parent independently evaluated the 95% Wilson formula using \(z=1.95996398454\):
Unit counted | Successes/observations | Interval

The second width is about \(0.49549\) times the first, although no independent prompt information was added. The point estimate remains unchanged. Small implementation-dependent variation in duplicated generations would still not make the shared prompts independent population samples.
## Scope, counterevidence, and correction

Figures 16–17 label their bands as 95% binomial intervals and describe 500 prompts per rule. However, the above numbers are constructed diagnostics, not recovered figure observations. Raw logs and the exact plot-generation checkout were unavailable. The supported finding is an uncertainty-calculation error in the documented release, with exact published-interval impact Needs Evidence.

This does not establish a changed model ranking, incorrect mean accuracy or invalid head-wise significance test. The main head selection uses a separate prompt-pair permutation procedure; no evidence connects its sample size to this duplicate-count route. A correction should count independent prompts for greedy accuracy or use an appropriate clustered treatment for repeated stochastic responses. No corrected model evaluation was run.
# Statistics and other unresolved evidence

Appendix B.2 describes 5000 paired permutations and a maximum-across-heads threshold. Under a suitable paired exchangeability/symmetry null and consistent joint permutations, this is a recognizable familywise-error approach. The exact implementation, raw tensors and dependence handling were not available in the staged source, so no p-value, significant-head count or familywise guarantee was independently reproduced. Absence from the staged package does not prove nonrelease or an invalid test.

The auxiliary also noted a multiple-activation RSA accumulator limitation. The supplied main RSA commands use only one activation type, so this optional-mode issue is not elevated into a demonstrated published-result failure. A 45-row staged verbal-analogy CSV versus a 46-item paper description similarly lacks historical binding. Neither observation is used to infer fabricated data.

The source openly reports weak or negative cross-task correlations for some retrieval/induction comparisons and adds late MLP computation for nonidentity relations. The reviewed evidence therefore supports a task-qualified mechanism account more directly than one identical exclusive circuit across all reasoning. No demonstrated counterexample to a stronger formal theorem is alleged, because no such theorem was established in the inspected paper.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
ADHMR: Aligning Diffusion-based Human Mesh Recovery via Direct Preference Optimization
# Identity, scope, and pending status
The paper authors are Wenhao Shen, Wanqi Yin, Xiaofeng Yang, Cheng Chen, Chaoyue Song, Zhongang Cai, Lei Yang, Hao Wang and Guosheng Lin.
This initial review covers 0189, I25-43558, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, official record https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/shen25m.html. The reviewed staged 12-page proceedings PDF has SHA-256
Locations use one-based PDF/printed pages. No embedded appendix was located; access to a separate supplement remains unresolved after the preparation’s OpenReview failure, rather than proven absent.

The available https://github.com/shenwenhao01/ADHMR release is pinned to , dated 2026-06-28. It is not established as the original experimental code. Overall assessment: Minor, with scope-bounded No Issue Found and Needs Evidence distinctions below. The auxiliary read the complete extracted proceedings text and relevant source paths. The parent read its full notes, visually inspected original pp. 3, 5 and 7, read the p. 4 ranking definition and decisive release code, and separately computed objective and control-flow checks. Scientific decisions remain pending and human reviews are empty.
# Contribution and checked objective direction

HMR-Scorer learns relative reconstruction quality from perturbed poses using geometric error metrics. It ranks generated mesh candidates to create synthetic winner/loser pairs; diffusion preference optimization then adapts a base reconstruction model. The scorer is also used to filter noisy training labels. These are automatically generated metric/scorer preferences, not demonstrated human-annotated judgments.

The KL-regularized reward formulation motivates a density-ratio preference objective; the diffusion loss is its denoising surrogate. This review does not promote that surrogate into an exact marginal-likelihood identity. The external Diffusion-DPO derivation was not independently audited. Its latent-trajectory and weighting assumptions would be needed for a complete equivalence claim, which is not invented here.
# Problem 1: the release optimizes separate component losses
Rating: Minor, current-release scope. Locations: p. 3, Section 3.2; p. 5, Eq. (5); `ADHMR/lib/models/loss.py:96–146`; `ADHMR/lib/runners/hyponet.py:174–184`.

The paper combines joint/swing and twist representations into one data sample and places one log-sigmoid around the total squared-residual difference. The release separately averages joint and twist errors, computes separate log-sigmoid losses, and adds them. A rescaling of component means versus sums cannot make these two nonlinear objectives equivalent.

Let \(d_j,d_t\) be the model-minus-reference winner/loser error differences averaged over joint and twist coordinates. In the shipped 29-joint/23-twist configuration there are 87 joint coordinates and 46 twist coordinates. With all visibility masks one, the paper’s total difference is \(87d_j+46d_t\), while the released loss has the form \[\operatorname{softplus}(c d_j)+\operatorname{softplus}(c d_t),
 \qquad c=\beta_{\rm dpo}/2>0.\] Take any \(a\ge0\). Set reference squared residuals to zero, model winner joint errors to zero, model loser joint errors to \(46a/87\) on each coordinate, model winner twist errors to \(a\) and model loser twist errors to zero. These are nonnegative squared errors. Then \[d_j=-46a/87,\quad d_t=a,\quad 87d_j+46d_t=0.\] The single combined loss stays \(\log2\) for every \(a\) and every positive \(\gamma\). For normalized \(c=1\), the release’s split loss is:
\(a\) | Combined loss | Split loss
The nonconstant change, not merely the additive difference at zero, proves inequivalence. Both the auxiliary and parent independently computed these values without author imports.

The split loss imposes component-level preferences even when total candidate advantage cancels. It can be an intentional alternative objective; it is not necessarily inferior. The required correction is to identify which objective generated the results and either combine weighted components before one log-sigmoid or explicitly document/evaluate the separate form.

The auxiliary also found an active image-condition optimizer in the release despite the paper’s denoiser-only description. Selecting evaluation mode does not itself freeze parameters. These observations strengthen the need for exact historical configuration binding, but do not establish that the reported training used the later implementation or that benchmark scores are false. No replacement training recipe was run or validated.
# Problem 2: scorer test mode falls through without a return
Rating: Minor, release reproducibility. Locations: ; .

The test entry calls the scorer with mode `’test’` and then reads `model_out[’img’]`. The forward method directly returns outputs for `’clean’` and `’dpo’`. Its final output dictionary and return are nested inside `if mode == ’train’`, with no later test or unconditional return.

Assuming preceding model/tensor operations succeed, the test call therefore returns `None`, and the entry point cannot access the expected dictionary. The parent directly read the source and independently parsed its syntax tree. The only return branches in the method are at lines 286, 307 and 335, conditioned on clean, dpo and train respectively. Parsing and static reasoning did not execute the author program.

A suitable test-mode dictionary/return would fix this local path. No checkpoint or repaired author code was run. The defect is demonstrated for the pinned release, not for the historical scorer experiments, which could have used another implementation.
# Problem 3: correlation signs need an explicit reporting convention
Rating: Minor reporting inconsistency; actual ranking direction Needs Evidence. Locations: p. 4, Eq. (2) and scorer description; p. 5, Table 1 and caption; `HMR-Scorer/data/dataset.py:82–112`.

The scorer assigns higher values to better meshes, and its pairwise label is one when the first candidate has lower reconstruction error. A perfect quality score therefore correlates negatively with raw error: errors \((1,2,3)\) and scores \((3,2,1)\) have Pearson and Spearman correlation \(-1\).

Table 1 nevertheless reports positive PLCC/SRCC values with upward arrows and describes correlations with reconstruction errors. For example, its PVE entries are \(0.63/0.62\) for GTA-Human and \(0.66/0.64\) for DNA-Rendering. The release calls signed Pearson and Spearman functions directly on raw score and positive error arrays, without an explicit negation or absolute value in that routine.

A benign omitted convention—negative-error correlation or magnitude—could reconcile the table. A later source mismatch is also possible. The existing evidence therefore requires clarification, not a claim that the trained scorer actually rewards bad meshes. Signed evaluation arrays and the exact reporting transformation are needed. The caption’s PA-PVE versus header’s PA-MPJPE naming also needs resolution. No scorer prediction was independently evaluated.
# Needs Evidence: global cleaning calibration

The ranking loss compares candidates within the same input image. Adding an arbitrary image-dependent offset \(b(I)\) to all its candidate scores leaves every pairwise difference and the ranking loss unchanged. A single threshold across images need not be invariant.

For example, image-one scores \((2,1)\) and image-two scores \((-1,-2)\) each yield within-image preference probability \(\sigma(1)\approx0.73105858\). Offsets \(-10\) and \(+10\) change the score sets to \((-8,-9)\) and \((9,8)\) without changing either preference. Their retention at a raw threshold \(0.6\) reverses. Applying a monotone sigmoid does not remove the unidentified image-dependent offset.

This demonstrates that within-image ranking alone does not identify a globally calibrated cleaning threshold. It does not prove that a particular trained network lacks useful calibration or that the measured cleaning improvements fail. The paper supplies downstream empirical evidence, while the exact training/cleaning pipeline and calibration records remain unavailable. The inspected release returns raw scores in clean mode despite other paths computing a sigmoid score; resolving which quantity and threshold generated the reported cleaned set requires historical artifacts.
# Empirical checks and counterevidence

Page 7 explicitly reports minimum MPJPE and PVE over \(M\) generated candidates. These are disclosed oracle set-quality metrics. There is no supported concealed-oracle allegation. They do not alone establish the error of a single deployable prediction selected without ground truth. Page 8 identifies target-benchmark training sets for finetuning; shared dataset names are not by themselves evidence of test leakage.

Selected same-\(M\) arithmetic supports the reported improvements. On 3DPW at \(M=100\), HypoNet to ADHMR decreases PVE by 8.0 mm, MPJPE by 5.8 mm and PA-MPJPE by 4.1 mm. These are table arithmetic checks, not rerun evaluations.

The claim that ADHMR(ITW) with \(M=10\) outperforms HypoNet with \(M=200\) requires a metric qualifier: the listed PVE and MPJPE improve, but PA-MPJPE is 37.1 versus 36.1 mm, worse by 1.0 mm. The cleaning table likewise has a disclosed exception: SMPLer-X EHF PA-PVE rises from 51.0 to 51.4, while 20 of 21 inspected model/metric cells improve. These bounded qualifications do not refute the matched-\(M\) gains or imply fabricated results.

The scorer’s perturbed-pose evaluation distribution differs from actual generated candidates and noisy pseudo-labels. Tail-ranking reliability and calibration for those downstream uses are not established by aggregate correlations alone. The supervised-extra-data baseline is relevant counterevidence, but does not isolate every effect of external data versus the preference objective. Raw predictions, per-seed results, exact checkpoints and configurations would be needed for stronger causal or uncertainty conclusions.

Covered Forest: Fine-grained Generalization Analysis of Graph Neural Networks
# Identity, evidence, and review status

This is the initial review of 0190, I25-43559, by Antonis Vasileiou, Ben Finkelshtein, Floris Geerts, Ron Levie and Christopher Morris, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. The reviewed 51-page proceedings PDF has SHA-256
> fab002501f02b8ae36bd69992bca84e8aa8316e8d8dab5eeb74b1a89dca33cfd.

All page numbers are one-based PDF/printed pages. Released material is the staged https://github.com/benfinkelshtein/CoveredForests snapshot at commit , dated 2024-12-08 in the acquisition record. Its bytes and source identities were preserved and checked. The exact historical experiment checkout is not established.

Overall assessment: Major. The native auxiliary agent examined the main text, definitions, robustness arguments, equicontinuity argument, relevant Forest-distance proofs and empirical protocol. The parent read the full scientific notes, independently checked original definitions and decisive formulas, visually inspected pp. 3, 5, 6, 44 and 45, read the table-producing code statically, and executed a separately written arithmetic diagnostic. All adjudication is pending and human reviews are empty.
# Scientific contribution and dependencies

The paper uses graph pseudometrics and covering numbers to study generalization of message-passing neural networks (MPNNs). It seeks a finer account of graph similarity than a discrete distinguishability metric, including normalized-sum, sum and mean aggregation settings. A robustness framework connects small within-cell loss variation to generalization; continuity of the network class controls cell size; metric covering estimates control the number of cells. Table 1 then presents estimated bounds for real datasets as evidence that this analysis can be quantitatively tight.

The four findings address distinct links in this chain. They are not consequences inferred from poor empirical performance. Their impact is bounded separately so that a defect in the general framework is not automatically attributed to every special case.
# Problem 1: Table 1 uses an incorrect statistical normalization
Rating: Major. Locations: Propositions 15–16, p. 8; Table 1 and Section 6 Q3, p. 9; Table 3, p. 51; released `utils/plot/q3_print_generalization_bound.py`, lines 4–29 and 32–49.
## Claim and exact discrepancy

Proposition 15’s statistical term is \[M\sqrt{\frac{4\mathcal N\log2+2\log(1/\delta)}{|S|}},\] and Proposition 16 substitutes \(m/(k+1)\) for the covering-number upper bound. The released script defines the sample-size array \(S=(150,3288,22216,32902)\) but never uses it. Its implemented term is \[\frac{M\sqrt{4m\log2/(k+1)+2\log(1/\delta)}}{m}.\] The required denominator outside the square root is \(\sqrt{|S|}\), not \(m\). The ratio of the correctly normalized statistical term to the released term is \(m/\sqrt{|S|}\), independently of \(k\).

Using the script’s coefficients and \(\delta=0.05\), let \(A_k=4m\log2/(k+1)+2\log20\) and \(\widetilde C=2C_{FD}/n\). The script minimizes \(4\widetilde Ck+M\sqrt{A_k}/m\) over integer \(1\le k\le100\). The auxiliary agent and parent independently reconstructed these scalar formulas without importing or executing the author script.
Dataset | Released optimum | Published | Correct denominator, same \(k\)

Every released optimum is at \(k=1\). Reoptimizing after changing only the denominator gives, respectively, \(4.153607\) at \(k=11\), \(1.211665\) at \(k=27\), \(0.256739\) at \(k=25\) and \(0.601926\) at \(k=51\).

The script’s comparison expression reconstructs the four Table 1 entries labelled \(\epsilon=0\) as \(0.946016\), \(0.078787\), \(0.008498\) and \(0.019067\), each agreeing with the published three-decimal value. Thus all eight printed bound entries are reproduced by the defective arithmetic. The comparison also includes positive \(4\widetilde Ck\) with \(k\ge1\), which is inconsistent with a literal zero-radius label.
## Impact and counterevidence

The all-eight numerical match is strong evidence connecting the released formula to the reported table, while not proving which checkout produced the historical outputs. The table explicitly labels the constants as estimates, and Table 3 says its equivalence counts are dataset-dependent rather than counts over the full graph class. Those honest qualifications do not change the missing square root of sample size.

The source’s counts \((139,\allowbreak 3838,\allowbreak 25465,\allowbreak 34794)\) also differ slightly from Table 3’s \((139,\allowbreak 3808,\allowbreak 25448,\allowbreak 34433)\); that discrepancy cannot explain the normalization error. The reported observed training/test losses and gaps are not refuted. The supported conclusion is that these displayed bound values do not instantiate the stated statistical formula and cannot support the claimed same-order tightness on this evidence.

This is Major because quantitative tightness in real-world settings is a core empirical conclusion. The corrected numbers above are diagnostics, not certified repaired generalization bounds. Repair requires correct normalization plus validation of global constants, cover scope, readout normalization and any data-dependent radius selection. No model or dataset was rerun.
# Problem 2: sample-selected partitions defeat the robustness theorem
Rating: Major. Locations: robustness definition and Theorem 4, p. 5; Definition 34/Theorem 35, p. 32; Theorem 37 proof and Proposition 38, p. 33.
## Claim and admissible construction

The definition permits, for every training sample \(S\), a partition into \(K(S)\) cells with within-cell loss oscillation less than \(\epsilon(S)\). It does not require a partition fixed before the sample is drawn. Theorem 4 claims, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \[|\ell_{\exp}(h_S)-\ell_{\mathrm{emp}}(h_S)|
 \le\epsilon(S)+M\sqrt{\frac{2K(S)\log2+2\log(1/\delta)}{|S|}}. \tag{R1}\] Consider a domain of 1000 distinct graph isomorphism classes, the paths \(P_1,\ldots,P_{1000}\) distinguished by their orders. Draw 100 training examples independently and uniformly, all with label zero. Let the hypothesis class contain all functions from this finite graph domain to \(\{0,1\}\), and take loss \(\ell(x,0)=x\), bounded by \(M=1\).

Let \(h_S\) be zero on the graph orders seen in \(S\) and one on all unseen orders. Choose \(C_1(S)\) to be the observed orders and \(C_2(S)\) their complement. Both cells are nonempty, \(K(S)=2\), and within-cell loss is constant. The strict robustness condition is satisfied with \(\epsilon(S)=0.001\). To define the learner for arbitrary nonempty sample sizes, if every domain order has been observed, use the identically zero predictor and any fixed nonempty two-cell partition; otherwise retain the observed/unseen partition. Thus \(K=2\) remains well defined beyond the size-100 construction.

Empirical loss is zero. If \(u\le100\) distinct graph orders were observed, population loss is \(1-u/1000\ge0.9\). Yet at \(\delta=0.05\), (R1) equals \[0.001+\sqrt{(4\log2+2\log20)/100}
 =0.29704143746015965.\] The bound fails for every sample, not merely with a small exceptional probability. Under the same per-sample-partition interpretation used in the main definition, giving both cells the same positive tolerance also refutes the cell-specific version in Theorems 35/37. Appendix Definition 34 places the partition phrase before the words such that for all samples, permitting a fixed-partition reading. That narrower reading excludes this example but does not repair the broader main definition. Every hypothesis is uniformly continuous on the finite discrete metric domain; the general theorem is not restricted to MPNNs.
## Failure mechanism, dependency, and possible repair

Theorem 37’s proof declares the counts in the cells to have a multinomial distribution with fixed probabilities \(\mu(C_i)\) and applies a fixed-partition concentration inequality. This step cannot justify the per-sample-partition interpretation; it is compatible with the narrower fixed-partition reading of Definition 34. Here \(K\) is even the constant two; variability of \(K\) is not the essential problem.

A fixed, sample-independent partition would exclude this counterexample. That is an additional hypothesis, and Proposition 5/38 expressly considers a scale depending on \(h_S\), so the paper’s broader sample-dependent formulation cannot be justified by silently adding it. One can instead require a fixed partition, or establish concentration uniformly over the allowable selected partitions with an appropriate complexity penalty.

The finding is Major for the stated foundational theorem and proof. It does not automatically refute later applications using a deterministic metric, radius and cover fixed independently of the sample. No complete replacement framework is certified here.
# Problem 3: unrestricted internal gains prevent a common modulus
Rating: Major. Locations: class definitions and Eqs. (1)–(2), p. 3; Theorem 8 and equicontinuity interpretation, p. 6; Theorem 43 and its proof, pp. 35–36.
## Quantifiers and witness

The stated normalized-sum layer is \[h_v^{(t)}=\phi_t\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{u\in N(v)}h_u^{(t-1)}\right),
 \qquad h_G=\psi\!\left(\frac1n\sum_v h_v^{(L)}\right).\] Each internal \(\phi_t\) is Lipschitz, without a common bound on its Lipschitz constant across the class. The readout/FNN has boundedness and Lipschitz constraints. Theorem 8 nevertheless claims a single \(\gamma(\epsilon)>0\) for all graph orders and all these architectures: \[\delta_\square^T(G,H)<n^2\gamma(\epsilon)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \|h_G-h_H\|_2\le\epsilon. \tag{R2}\]

Fix \(L=1\), initial scalar features equal to one, and \(\epsilon=1/2\). Let \(H_n\) be empty and \(G_n\) have one edge and \(n-2\) isolated vertices. Use \(\phi_1(x)=n^2x\) and \(\psi(x)=\tanh x\). The internal map is Lipschitz and allowed; the readout is bounded by one and is 1-Lipschitz.

For every doubly stochastic \(S\), the nonnegative matrix \(A(G_n)S\) has total sum two, while \(SA(H_n)=0\). Its cut norm is exactly two, hence \(\delta_\square^T(G_n,H_n)=2\). Each edge endpoint’s first-layer feature is \(n\), and the normalized readout input is two. Therefore \[h_{G_n}=\tanh2,\quad h_{H_n}=0,\quad
 |h_{G_n}-h_{H_n}|\approx0.96402758>1/2.\] If the class notation is read as including an additional bounded FNN after this readout, another \(\tanh\) still gives approximately \(0.746068>1/2\).

For any purported positive \(\gamma(1/2)\), choose \(n>\sqrt{2/\gamma(1/2)}\). The antecedent of (R2) holds and its conclusion fails. This analytic family disproves the universal claim; finite numerical evaluations merely corroborate its values.
## Scope and correction

An individual network can be uniformly continuous, and a fixed finite graph quotient can have a common small scale. Neither provides the claimed scale uniformly over all \(n\) and unbounded internal gains. Restricting internal Lipschitz constants and initial feature size, or allowing the modulus to depend on the complete architecture, removes this obstruction. A full repaired theorem would need to state these dependencies and propagate them into covering bounds.

Theorem 8 is explicitly used to construct a common modulus for subsequent unlabeled-graph results, including Proposition 9 and Theorem 10, making this a Major core issue. Graph pseudometric definitions and unrelated fixed-network claims are not refuted. The external theorem cited in the proof was not independently audited; this review attributes the verified error only to the statement and class in the reviewed paper.
# Problem 4: padding proof assumes zero preservation
Rating: Major. Locations: sum-aggregation Eq. (3), p. 3; Lemma 14, p. 8; Lemma 57 and its \(L=2\) proof, pp. 43–45.
## Claim and missing condition

The claimed Forest-distance bound has the form \[\|h_G-h_H\|_2\le\frac{C(L)}n L_\psi
 \prod_{i=1}^L L_{\phi_i}\,FD_L(G,H), \tag{R3}\] where \(C(L)\) depends on depth and layer Lipschitz constants. The printed \(L=2\) proof with identity self/neighbor weights gives \(C(2)=2\).

On p. 44 a missing neighbor is matched to a padded vertex whose first-layer value is set to zero. The next step bounds differences through \(L_{\phi_1}\) times differences of original features. Lipschitz continuity controls \(|\phi(x)-\phi(0)|\), not \(|\phi(x)-0|\) when \(\phi(0)\ne0\). Sum aggregation allows general Lipschitz updates. Positive homogeneity is imposed separately for mean aggregation and cannot be imported into the sum setting.
## A fixed-network contradiction

Let \(n=2\), \(d=1\), \(L=2\), all self/neighbor scalar weights equal one, \(\phi_1(x)=x+1\), \(\phi_2(x)=x\) and \(\psi(x)=\tanh x\). All Lipschitz constants are one. Give every original vertex the positive feature \(a>0\). Let \(G\) be an edge and \(H\) be empty. The edge graph’s first- and second-layer vertex values are \(1+2a\) and \(2+4a\); the empty graph’s are \(1+a\) at both layers. Thus \[h_G=\tanh(2+4a),\qquad h_H=\tanh(1+a).\] The two depth-two trees of \(G\) have four non-root attributes equal to \(a\); their matched padded attributes in \(H\) are zero. Root attributes match. Every allowed level- and edge-preserving matching has the same total cost \(FD_2(G,H)=4a\).

As \(a\downarrow0\), all original features remain nonzero, \(FD_2\to0\), while \[|h_G-h_H|\longrightarrow\tanh2-\tanh1
 \approx0.2024334241>0.\] No finite Forest-distance Lipschitz constant works for this fixed network on the stated real-feature domain. For \(a=0.01\), the printed \(C(2)=2\) bound is \(0.04\), versus actual difference \(0.2009852695\).
## Connection to one-hot labels

The obstruction is not confined to arbitrarily small real labels. Take \(n=100\), all original features equal to the one-dimensional one-hot vector 1, one edge versus no edges, and degree bound \(q=2\). Set \[\phi_1(x)=x+B,\quad \phi_2(x)=x-(B+1),\quad
 B=100,\quad\psi(x)=\tanh x.\] All layer Lipschitz constants and identity weights remain one. The empty graph’s final features are zero; the edge endpoints have final feature \(B+3\), all other features zero. The normalized readout input is \(2(B+3)/n=2.06\), giving output difference \(0.9680303033\). Here \(FD_2=4\), while the stated \(L=2\) proof gives \(2FD_2/n=0.08\). Letting \(B=n\) also defeats a constant depending only on depth and the fixed Lipschitz constants.

These constructions establish the missing offset dependence in the sum-aggregation theorem supporting Propositions 15–16. Mean aggregation’s explicit positive homogeneity and bias-free zero-preserving updates avoid this particular obstruction. Adding \(\phi_t(0)=0\) is a precise candidate restriction, but no complete corrected arbitrary-depth/arbitrary-weight theorem has been certified.

Title: Technical Verification of FlexiClip
# Identity, scope, and result

This report concerns Anant Khandelwal, FlexiClip: Locality-Preserving Free-Form Character Animation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 29784–29798, identifier I25-43560 (local number 0191), OpenReview `xtxCM4XZ82` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original is the staged 15-page proceedings PDF, not an inferred later revision. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with printed pages 1–15. The code is the public FlexiClip snapshot at commit `9d476aa1aa25b227265730958190b6fa3386bf4e`, dated 23 June 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}].

The main objectives and their mathematical dependencies, numerical tables, embedded appendices, and relevant implementation paths were inspected. Original pages 6 and 14 were rendered and visually checked to exclude text-extraction errors. Problems 1 and 2 are demonstrated invalid derivations connected to named central contributions. Problem 3 establishes a Major defect in the released implementation of the central score-related objective and a Minor initialization discrepancy; historical experimental consequences remain unresolved. None establishes that the displayed animations or reported scores are false.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

The paper writes the total deformation Jacobian as \(J_t=J_t^P+J_t^R\), where \(J_t^P\) is the spatial component and \(J_t^R\) is the temporal correction. Equations (12)–(13), p. 5, use a learned ODE and prescribe \(J_0^R=0\). The auxiliary loss in Eq. (18), p. 6, compares scores associated with the total and spatial-only sequences and adds a squared correction penalty. Equation (19) combines it with video SDS.

For a Gaussian perturbation \(Y=X+n\), \(n\sim N(0,c)\), a denoiser \(D(y)\) is a pointwise map, its mean squared error is an expectation, and a score is the derivative of a log density with respect to its argument. These objects must not be interchanged. The diffusion check below uses fixed kernel mean, differentiable positive covariance for \(t>0\), zero drift, and spatially homogeneous noise, exactly the specialization invoked in Appendix C.3.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Denoising risk is not the score used to justify the central loss).  The passage following Eq. (16), p. 6, identifies its normalized expected denoising error with a score function, then uses this identification to motivate Eq. (17). This derivation is invalid. Assessment: Major for the mathematical rationale of the central flow loss.
## Claim and complete check

In scalar notation the quantity in Eq. (16) is \[R(c)=\frac{1}{c}\mathbb E\left[(D(X+n;c)-X)^2\right].\] The following paragraph treats it as the score \(\nabla_X\log p(X)\); the next paragraph introduces a difference of scores to preserve dimension and invokes detailed-balance inspiration.

Take independent \(X\sim N(0,1)\) and \(n\sim N(0,c)\), with \(c>0\), and the optimal denoiser \(D(y;c)=y/(1+c)\). This is a smooth data density, positive scalar Gaussian covariance, and a valid denoised estimate satisfying the definitions in the passage. Since \[D(X+n;c)-X=\frac{n-cX}{1+c},\] independence gives \[R(c)=\frac{c+c^2}{c(1+c)^2}=\frac1{1+c}.\] However, the noisy-data density is \(N(0,1+c)\), whose score is \(s_c(y)=-y/(1+c)\). At \(c=1\), \(R(c)=1/2\), while \(s_c(0)=0\) and \(s_c(1)=-1/2\). The clean-data score, if intended instead, is \(-y\) and also differs. More generally a scalar expected risk cannot equal a pointwise vector field.

Equation reference: eq:denoiser. The correct Gaussian Bayes-denoiser relation is \[
 D(y;c)-y=c\,s_c(y).\] It can be verified directly here; generally it follows by differentiating the Gaussian convolution under suitable integrability. It relates the residual, not its expected squared magnitude, to the score. The independent arithmetic in `independent_check_results.json` reproduces the values above; the algebra, not finite testing, is decisive.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and boundaries

The loss is described as inspired by GFlowNet rather than a formal implementation of its transition probabilities. A score-comparison regularizer can therefore be used as a heuristic even though the stated derivation fails. Nevertheless the explicit transition from Eq. (16) to Eq. (17) is the paper’s justification of a named core component, not peripheral notation. This supports Major without requiring a decline in benchmark performance.

There is a related exact limitation: setting the permitted neural vector field \(f_R\) to zero, with the prescribed \(J_0^R=0\), gives \(J_t=J_t^P\) and makes both terms of Eq. (18) zero for every spatial trajectory. Thus zero auxiliary loss alone does not certify removal of temporal artifacts. Joint optimization with SDS could still be useful; failure of the full optimizer is not established. Equation [eq:denoiser] (#eq:denoiser) repairs the mistaken identity only. It does not by itself prove dimension preservation, GFlowNet detailed balance, or the proposed neural ODE’s claimed denoising behavior. Those stronger conclusions need additional evidence.

Problem 2 (The diffusion derivation deletes a nonzero density derivative).  Appendix C.2.3, p. 14, moves both spatial derivatives onto \(GG^\top\) alone. The result is false even under the homogeneous-diffusion specialization of C.3. Assessment: Major for the derivation explicitly invoked on p. 4 to support the probability-flow component.
## Claim, assumptions, and counterexample

In dimension one the printed step equates \[\frac12\partial_{xx}(G^2p)
 \quad\hbox{with}\quad
 \frac12(p_0*\kappa)\,\partial_{xx}(G^2).\] Choose \(p_0=N(0,1)\), \(\mu=0\), \(C(t)=t\) for \(t>0\), \(f=0\), and \(G=1\). The covariance is positive and differentiable, the drift vanishes, the diffusion is spatially homogeneous, and \(G^2=1=\dot C(t)\) satisfies even the final condition on p. 15. The convolution is \[p(x,t)=\frac{\exp[-x^2/(2(1+t))]}{\sqrt{2\pi(1+t)}}.\] At \(x=0,t=1\) the true values are \[p=\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi}},\qquad
 \partial_t p=\frac12\partial_{xx}p=-\frac{p}{4}
 =-0.07052369794346953.\] The printed right-hand side is zero. All hypotheses remain satisfied, so this is a counterexample to the displayed derivation, not a boundary-case objection. The original formula was visually confirmed on p. 14.
## Surviving result and supported correction

For fixed mean and spatially homogeneous covariance the correct calculation retains the kernel derivatives: \[\partial_t p=p_0*\partial_t\kappa
 =\frac12\sum_{ij}\dot C_{ij}\,\partial_{ij}p.\] For its interpretation as an Itô diffusion one additionally needs \(\dot C\succeq0\). This restores the standard Gaussian-convolution identity and shows that the final condition \(GG^\top=\dot C\) is itself correct. Consequently this finding does not refute the standard probability-flow ODE.

C.2.2 also prints a minus sign where the product rule requires \(
abla\cdot(f\kappa)=(
abla\cdot f)\kappa+f\cdot
abla\kappa\). Its interchange of spatially varying drift multiplication and convolution also needs restrictions. The drift errors disappear in the later \(f=0\) specialization and are not used to exaggerate the counterexample. Severity concerns the invalid supporting derivation and its explicit dependency on the core pfODE construction; it does not depend on appendix placement or repair difficulty.

Problem 3 (The released flow objective and initial state differ from the paper).  Static source inspection establishes inactive score-related gradients and nonzero first-frame corrections in the pinned release. Assessment: Major for the disabled central score-related objective in this released implementation; Minor for the nonzero initialization. Impact on the historical published experiments remains Needs Evidence.
## Gradient path and numerical meaning

At `animate_clipart.py:211–218`, the code obtains `logp` and `logp_p`, detaches the latter, and adds their mean squared difference to SDS and an L1 Jacobian penalty. In `losses.py:136–198`, both log-probability tensors are constructed and returned inside `torch.no_grad()`. The ordinary backward graph therefore does not contain this score-related term [Retained latex: \cite{torch}]. The SDS implementation separately constructs a gradient-bearing surrogate at lines 214–215; there is no analogous construction for `logp`. The score-related MSE contributes zero parameter gradient, although the SDS and Jacobian penalties can train the model. This removes the training contribution of the named central score-comparison component in Eqs. (17)–(18), whose gradient is explicitly required on p. 6. That direct dependency supports Major within the pinned implementation; it does not require a demonstrated decrease in benchmark scores or proof that this release generated the historical experiments.

Independently, the quantity returned at `losses.py:177–193` has the form \[y=m+sz,\qquad
 \ell=-\frac{(y-m)^2}{2s^2}-\log s-\frac12\log(2\pi)
      =-\frac{z^2}{2}-\log s-\frac12\log(2\pi),\quad s>0.\] The predicted mean cancels. This is a Gaussian transition log density evaluated at its own sampled point, not the data score in Eq. (17). With \(s=0.5,z=0.7\), changing \(m\) from 0 to 2 leaves the computed result at approximately \(-0.4707913526447274\). Removing a detach or no-gradient context alone would not establish the intended objective.
## Initial correction

In `painter_clipart.py:917–928`, the first correction is initialized with \(F\) identity blocks and then normalized and added to the spatial Jacobian. At the initial integration time the correction per face is \(I_2/\sqrt{2F}\ne0\), contrary to \(J_0^R=0\). The layered branch repeats this at lines 1033–1046. This is a statement about the Jacobian passed to reconstruction; it does not quantify visible distortion after constraints and reconstruction.
## Provenance and counterevidence

The inspected release has not been established as the code that produced Tables 1–4.
