Title: Technical Verification of Novelty Detection with World Models
# Identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Geigh Zollicoffer, Kenneth Eaton, Jonathan Balloch, Julia Kim, Wei Zhou, Robert Wright, and Mark Riedl, Novelty Detection in Reinforcement Learning with World Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43561, OpenReview `xtlixzbcfV` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The staged proceedings PDF has 19 pages. All page numbers in this report are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering.

The review covered the definition of the adaptive detector, Propositions 3.1–3.2, Appendix D, experimental metrics and Tables 2–9, and the embedded descriptions of environments, alternative architectures and exploration limitations. No implementation specifically released for this paper was located in the prepared sources. Dependency links are not treated as that implementation. The assessment is Major for the demonstrated invalid derivation of the central rule; it is not a rejection of every empirical result.
# Definitions and assumptions

Use the paper’s four latent distributions \[P=p_\phi(z_t\mid h_t,x_t),\quad Q=p_\phi(z_t\mid h_t),\quad
 R=p_\phi(z_t\mid h_0),\quad S=p_\phi(z_t\mid h_0,x_t).\] All KL divergences below use natural logarithms. Write \[a=D(P\Vert Q),\qquad
 \Delta=D(P\Vert R)-D(P\Vert S).\] Equation (4), p. 4, declares the nominal decision condition \(a\le\Delta\). Since \[H(P,R)-H(P,S)=D(P\Vert R)-D(P\Vert S),\] the cross-entropy conversion is correct. The finite training assumption in Appendix D, p. 16, is \(a\le\epsilon\). Common support and finite divergences are necessary; the counterexample below satisfies both.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (An unjustified margin enters the derivation of the KL bound).  Appendix D, Eq. (7), p. 16, infers \(\Delta\ge\epsilon\) from \(\Delta\ge0\), then uses \(a\le\epsilon\) to infer \(a\le\Delta\). The first implication is false. Assessment: Major for the derivation of the core adaptive boundary.
## Source claim and decisive calculation

The suspect implication is visible in the original p. 16 rendering, not an extraction artifact. Nonnegativity provides no positive lower bound comparable to the training error. Take full-support binary distributions, writing \(\mathrm{Ber}(p)\) for probability \(p\) of the first state: \[P=S=\mathrm{Ber}(0.8),\quad Q=\mathrm{Ber}(0.75),\quad
 R=\mathrm{Ber}(0.79),\quad\epsilon=0.01.\] Each probability lies strictly between zero and one, all distributions sum to one, and all divergences are finite. Direct calculation gives \[\begin{aligned}
 a&=\frac45\log\frac{16}{15}+\frac15\log\frac45
   =0.00700210664721499<0.01,\\
 D(P\Vert S)&=0,\\
 \Delta&=\frac45\log\frac{80}{79}+\frac15\log\frac{20}{21}
   =0.000304992931601758>0.\end{aligned}\] Thus both the finite training assumption and nonnegative cross-entropy comparison hold, while \(a>\Delta\) and \(\Delta<\epsilon\). The strict violation also has the exact form \[5(a-\Delta)=\log\frac{79^4\,21}{75^4\,25}>0,\] because the numerator is \(817951701\) and the denominator \(791015625\). The saved independent calculation evaluates these explicit formulas; it is not an experiment with author code.
## A consistent conditional model
The four distributions need not be inconsistent outputs of unrelated networks. Let history \(H\) and observation \(X\) be independent fair binary variables, and specify

Here the paper’s \(h_0\) denotes missing history, not the binary event \(H=0\). At \((H,X)=(1,1)\), the full conditional is 0.8, the history-only conditional is 0.75, the no-history marginal is 0.79, and the observation-only conditional is 0.8, giving precisely \(P,Q,R,S\) above. All eight joint atoms have positive probability. The four context-specific posterior-to-history KLs are approximately \[0.00700211,\quad0.00640146,\quad0.00305261,\quad0.00335391,\] each below \(\epsilon=0.01\). A correctly represented stationary discrete model can therefore satisfy the finite local training condition everywhere and still violate the proposed nominal inequality at this context. It can be embedded in a stationary POMDP with an uninformative action and a reward independent of these observations, so no policy optimality requirement repairs the distributional step.
## Counterevidence and the exact scope of failure

Appendix D, p. 17, expressly describes the bound as an approximation rather than a strict mathematical guarantee and acknowledges nominal violations. Section 5 makes a related qualification. These passages prevent attributing an unqualified false-positive guarantee to the whole paper. They do not make the displayed implication in Eq. (7) valid.

The same appendix separately discusses an exactly zero KL assumption and derives \[\Delta=\mathbb E_P\log\frac{S}{R}.\] That identity is correct where the expectations exist. Our example has \(a>0\) and does not refute a statement conditioned on \(a=0\). Under \(a=0\) and the additional condition \(\Delta\ge0\), \(a\le\Delta\) follows trivially. Neither that special case nor the likelihood-ratio identity supplies the missing positive margin for a finite \(\epsilon\).

The detector remains a definable heuristic and can retain the reported empirical utility. The invalid proof is nonetheless closely tied to Eqs. (4)–(5), the main threshold-free contribution; this is the basis for Major. It is not based on appendix placement, ease of repair, or a claim that performance must fall.
## Supported repair boundary

The implication is valid if one explicitly assumes \(\Delta\ge\epsilon\) together with \(a\le\epsilon\). This is an additional margin assumption, not a consequence of \(\Delta\ge0\) or the stated training objective. The algebraic implication is verified; no general method of enforcing the extra assumption or calibrating false alarms was established.

Problem 2 (Universal comparative wording exceeds the tabulated evidence).  The p. 6 comparison says the proposed methods attain higher AUC than RIQN across all MiniGrid and Atari environments. Specific reported entries contradict that universal wording. Assessment: Minor.

In Table 5, p. 7, LavaGap AUC is 0.732 for KL Bound and 0.760 for RIQN. In Table 3, p. 6, Kangaroo FloorSwap AUC is 0.281 for PP-Mare and 0.541 for RIQN. These are direct comparisons of the paper’s own values, not rerun results. The statement should be restricted to supported environments or aggregate comparisons. Numerous favorable entries and the authors’ explicit discussion of DMC trade-offs survive. There is no evidence here that the tabulated numbers themselves are wrong.
# Evaluation checks and unresolved evidence

The paper states nominal-only training, no policy retraining after novelty, and use of common policy trajectories across detectors. Appendix E specifies first-observable novelty times. No demonstrated novelty leakage was established from those descriptions. The reported 300 episodes and 50000 steps need not contradict each other; precise per-environment counts and stopping rules remain unavailable.

AUC in Sec. 4.2 is computed from \(a\), while the actual decision compares \(a\) with the state-dependent \(\Delta\). AUC of \(a\) evaluates raw-surprise ranking, not necessarily ranking of \(a-\Delta\) or calibration of that adaptive rule. Actual delay and nominal false-positive metrics also provide decision-level evidence. Without the paired scores and labels, no numerical AUC error or deterioration is inferred.

Table 6’s RIQN false-positive averages agree with Table 2: DMC averages to 0.275 and Atari to 0.3075, rounded to 0.308. Runtime speedups, false-positive denominators, delay censoring for missed or early triggers, and sampling uncertainty could not be independently reconstructed. The diffusion-world-model experiment uses PP-Mare, as the text explicitly discloses; it is not evidence that the identical latent KL rule was used unchanged in every architecture. Table 8’s exploration limitation, including KL accuracy 0.49 versus KLExplored 0.91, is retained.
# Conclusion

Assessment | Major core derivation; Minor universal comparison
Adjudication | Pending; human reviews empty
Repair verification | Added-margin implication only, analytically checked
Author adoption | Not requested
Remaining work | Calibration evidence, raw decisions and timings, historical implementation

No author correction was supplied in the inspected materials. Later revisions were not comprehensively compared. Fresh experiments would be needed to quantify consequences of any revised detector; the mathematical counterexample itself needs none.

Title: Initial scientific review: Fluctuations of the Largest Eigenvalues of Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices
# Paper identity and summary

This initial review concerns Aro Lee and Ji Oon Lee, Fluctuations of the Largest Eigenvalues of Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, paper 0193 (I25-43562), OpenReview xraEFvFHR4 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The unchanged staged proceedings PDF has 30 pages. References below use one-based PDF pages, which agree with printed page numbers. Exact source hashes are recorded in the reproducibility appendix and adjacent verification records.

Three Major findings are supported: an incorrect sign in a core sticking proposition, an incorrect edge count in its proof, and a wrong fluctuation mean in the growing-SNR extension. Local concerns affect an iid-prior example and numerical parameter descriptions. The fixed-SNR main limiting theorem is not disproved by these checks. All judgments remain pending human adjudication.
# Scope and necessary background

The main assumptions, theorem statements, proof strategy, numerical examples, Taylor reduction, subcritical argument, and growing-SNR extension were inspected. Selected supercritical proof steps were cross-checked; this is not an independent reconstruction of every local-law estimate. No released implementation or raw simulation draws were available in the staged package. Separate supplementary-file availability remains unresolved.

For normalized noise \(Z_{ij}=\sqrt N W_{ij}\), the fixed-\(\lambda\) effective SNR is \[\lambda_e=\lambda\bigl(\mathbb E f'(Z_{12})\bigr)^2.\] The main theorem gives an outlier Gaussian limit for \(\lambda_e>1\) and a Tracy–Widom limit for \(\lambda_e<1\). The critical case is explicitly outside its scope. The reduced transformed matrix retains a secondary rank-one term involving \(f''\); its sign and scale matter below.
# Problem 1: an invalid signed sticking assertion
## Claim, assumptions, and dependency

Proposition 4.1 (p. 7) states, in paraphrase, \[0\leq \mu_1(H)-\mu_1(V)\leq N^{-3/4}\] with overwhelming probability in the subcritical regime. The proof on p. 24 declares the lower bound immediate from min–max. This proposition is a core bridge between the reduced transformed matrix and the noise matrix in the subcritical fluctuation proof.

Assumption 2.4 requires \(\mathbb E f'\geq0\), but not \(\mathbb E f''\geq0\). The temporary nonnegative-curvature assumption in Appendix B.3 simplifies that calculation and mentions the negative case separately; it is not a global restriction.
## Decisive admissible counterexample

Take even \(N\), independent standard Gaussian \(Z_{ij}\) for \(i\leq j\), including the diagonal, and a deterministic balanced vector \(x_i\in\{-N^{-1/2},N^{-1/2}\}\). Then \[\|x\|=1,\qquad \sum_i x_i=\sum_i x_i^3=0.\] Choose fixed \(\lambda>0\) and \[f(z)=-\frac{z^2-1}{\sqrt2}.\] This polynomial has the required regularity and moments: \[\mathbb E f=0,\quad \mathbb E f^2=1,\quad
 \mathbb E f'=0,\quad \mathbb E f''=-\sqrt2,\quad \lambda_e=0<1.\] Writing \(u=N^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^\top\), the retained term is \[H-V=-\frac{\lambda\sqrt N}{\sqrt2}x^2(x^2)^\top
     =-\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{2N}}uu^\top.\] There is no Taylor remainder for this quadratic function. Thus min–max gives \(\mu_1(H)\leq\mu_1(V)\), in the opposite direction. Strict inequality holds almost surely: the independent entries have continuous laws, and equality would require the top eigenspace to be orthogonal to \(u\), an exceptional algebraic condition.

An independently written NumPy illustration with \(N=64\), \(\lambda=1\), and seed 193 returned \[\mu_1(V)=1.874218386760028,\qquad
 \mu_1(H)=1.8727533380544827.\] The analytic family, rather than this one draw, establishes the failure. The script and actual output are evidence E3–E4; the original proof page is E5.
## Counterevidence, impact, and correction

A two-sided sticking estimate may remain true, and the fixed-\(\lambda\) Tracy–Widom conclusion is not refuted. The displayed proposition and its first proof step are nevertheless false under the stated hypotheses. Assessment: Major, because this invalid derivation lies directly on the main subcritical proof path.

A correction must prove the requisite two-sided estimate for both signs or explicitly restrict all affected statements. Reversing the inequality in this example is not a general repair. No complete replacement proof is certified.

The sign also affects Proposition 3.5’s ordered-spectrum wording. For \(f(z)=(-z^2+3z+1)/\sqrt{11}\), Gaussian noise, the balanced spike, and \(\lambda=4\), the nonzero eigenvalues of the deterministic perturbation are \(6/\sqrt{11}\) and \(-4/\sqrt{11N}\). The negative one is last in decreasing order, not second. The weaker assertion of at most two nonzero eigenvalues is compatible with the intended positive-outlier argument.
# Problem 2: an incorrect edge count in the core sticking proof

Appendix C.1, p. 25, defines \[E_3=\{\mu_i(V):N^{-5/9}<\mu_1(V)-\mu_i(V)\leq N^{-2/9}\}\] and asserts \(|E_3|=O(N^{1/3})\). Equation (71) uses this cardinality to control the imaginary part of the unnormalized resolvent trace.

With the corrected count, but otherwise retaining the displayed crude calculation, the contribution is controlled only at scale \[N^{2/3}N^{-5/6}N^{10/9}=N^{17/18}.\] This exceeds the \(N^{5/6}\) lower scale needed for the intended contradiction. The displayed argument therefore does not prove its conclusion. The original page and independent exponent calculation are E6 and E4.

A finer summation over edge distances can improve this crude bound substantially. The review does not claim that the actual trace reaches \(N^{17/18}\), that the limiting theorem is false, or that repair is impossible. Assessment: Major, for an invalid derivation in the main sticking proof. A full repaired summation with its probability and spectral-parameter control remains unverified.
# Problem 3: a wrong fluctuation mean in the growing-SNR extension
## An exact admissible quadratic construction
Appendix D, pp. 27–30, separately considers \(\mathbb E f'=0\) and \(\lambda=\lambda_0\sqrt N\). This problem concerns that extension, not the fixed-\(\lambda\) main theorem.

Let \(Z_{ij}\) be independent and uniform on \[\{-\sqrt{3/2},-\sqrt{1/2},\sqrt{1/2},\sqrt{3/2}\}.\] Let \(s_i\) be independent Rademacher variables independent of the noise, and set \[x_i=s_i/\sqrt N,\qquad f(z)=2(z^2-1),\qquad \lambda_0=1.\] The noise has mean zero, variance one, fourth moment \(5/4\), and bounded moments of every order. The transformation satisfies \[\mathbb E f=0,\quad \mathbb E f^2=1,\quad
 \mathbb E f'=0,\quad \mathbb E f''=4.\] The spike has norm exactly one and satisfies all delocalization and sum conditions with overwhelming probability. Indeed \(\sum_i x_i^3=N^{-1}\sum_i x_i=O_\prec(N^{-1})\). Remark 2.8 gives the effective SNR directly as \[\widetilde\lambda_e=\tfrac14N^2(4)^2\|x^2\|^4=4.\] No reliance on the ambiguous fourth-moment notation on p. 30 is needed.

The exact transformed matrix is \[\widetilde M=V+2uu^\top,\qquad
 V_{ij}=\frac{2(Z_{ij}^2-1)}{\sqrt N}
       +4Z_{ij}s_is_jN^{-3/4}.\] Symmetry of \(Z_{ij}\) makes the conditional joint distribution of \(V\) independent of the signs; its upper-triangle entries remain iid. With \(d=N^{-1/2}\), \[\mathbb E V_{ij}=0,\qquad
 \mathbb E V_{ij}^2=\frac{1+16d}{N}.\] The true variance correction coefficient is 16.
## Variance coefficient and normalized-spike errors

Equation (75), p. 28, literally begins its variance coefficient with \(\mathbb E[f_{12}^2]\), without a prime, as confirmed on the rendered original page E7. Its printed coefficient equals 1 in this example. Substituting the likely intended \(\mathbb E[(f'_{12})^2]\) gives 16.

Even after that charitable correction, Eq. (79) has a distinct centering error. Define \[a_N=\sqrt{1+16d},\quad W_N=V/a_N,\quad \theta_N=2/a_N.\] Then \(\widetilde M=a_N(W_N+\theta_Nuu^\top)\): the normalized spike changes with the noise scale. Exact algebra gives \[\theta_N+\theta_N^{-1}=\frac52-12d+O(d^2),\qquad
 a_N(\theta_N+\theta_N^{-1})=\frac52+8d.\] Multiplying only the fixed center \(5/2\), as in the paper, yields instead \(5/2+20d+O(d^2)\). The omitted spike change is precisely at the fluctuation scale.
## The discrepancy survives in the limiting law

The normalized entries of \(W_N\) are uniformly bounded, centered, and variance one. Their third moment is \[\gamma_{3,N}=\frac{24d}{(1+16d)^{3/2}}\to0.\] The fixed-spike delocalized-outlier theorem of Renfrew and Soshnikov [Retained latex: \cite{rs}], Theorem 1.3 under (1.1)–(1.6), applies to \(B_N=W_N+2uu^\top\). Its third-moment correction vanishes here, and its variance conversion gives \[\sqrt N\left(\lambda_{\max}(B_N)-\frac52\right)
       \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,3/2).\] The external theorem’s fixed-spike requirement is respected; no unverified varying-spike extension is assumed.

For the remaining change, put \(q_N(z)=u^\top(z-W_N)^{-1}u\). Its outliers satisfy \(q_N(\lambda(\theta))=1/\theta\). The quadratic-form semicircle limit, obtained from Theorem 1.6 of [Retained latex: \cite{rs}] using a smooth cutoff of the squared resolvent, gives \(q'_N(\zeta_N)\to-1/3\) for intermediate points \(\zeta_N\to5/2\); the bulk remains separated. Since \[\theta_N^{-1}-\tfrac12=4d+O(d^2),\] the mean-value theorem gives \[\lambda(\theta_N)-\lambda(2)=-12d+o_p(d).\] Multiplying back by \(a_N=1+8d+O(d^2)\) therefore proves \[\boxed{\sqrt N\left(\lambda_{\max}(\widetilde M)-\frac52\right)
          \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(8,3/2).}\] The parent checked the primary theorem hypotheses and derivative argument. An independent SymPy calculation verified the exact moments and center expansions (E3–E4). The external-source check is preserved in E12. This is an analytical conclusion supported by a primary theorem, not a claim of empirical reproduction.

Equation (79) predicts mean \(5/4\) with the literal Eq. (75), or 20 after the missing-prime correction. The correct mean is 8. Assessment: Major: this extension’s quantitative conclusion is false in a fully admissible case. The verified correction applies to this example; a general replacement theorem has not been proved.
# Problem 4: the iid-prior example omits a third-moment condition

The remark following Assumption 2.3 (p. 4) supplies iid mean-zero, unit-variance, finite-moment coordinates as an example. The assumption additionally requires \(\sum_i x_i^3=O(N^{-1+\varepsilon})\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

Let \(Y=\sqrt2\) with probability \(1/3\), and \(Y=-1/\sqrt2\) with probability \(2/3\). Then \[\mathbb EY=0,\qquad\mathbb EY^2=1,\qquad\mathbb EY^3=1/\sqrt2.\] For \(x_i=Y_i/\sqrt N\), the law of large numbers gives \[\sqrt N\sum_i x_i^3\to1/\sqrt2.\] The same holds after exact normalization \(x_i=Y_i/\sqrt{\sum_jY_j^2}\). Hence the cubic sum has order \(N^{-1/2}\), violating the claimed condition when \(\varepsilon<1/2\).

Assessment: Minor, a local scope error. The theorem itself explicitly assumes the stronger condition; the symmetric Rademacher simulation prior satisfies it. A zero-third-moment restriction, with appropriate normalization and moment control, repairs this example. The review does not extend the theorem to inadmissible asymmetric priors.
# Problem 5: inconsistent numerical parameter descriptions

For the Gaussian example on pp. 9 and 13, \[f(z)=\frac{z^2+3z-1}{\sqrt{11}},\qquad\lambda_e=\frac9{11}\lambda.\] Thus \(\lambda=2.5\) gives \(\lambda_e=45/22\approx2.04545\), not the printed 1.294. The prose’s \(\lambda=0.1\) gives approximately 0.081818, not 0.350. Figure 3 instead captions the subcritical experiment with \(\lambda=0.15\), giving approximately 0.122727. These discrepancies change the stated experiment and, in the supercritical case, the theoretical Gaussian variance.

There is substantial counterevidence against inferring that the plots used the wrong theory: the visually inspected upper Gaussian curve peaks near 0.4, consistent with the correct variance \(46/45\). Without code or raw draws, the actual generating settings remain unresolved. Assessment: Minor, for a reproducibility and calculation-description defect, not a demonstrated failed empirical fit.

For completeness, Eq. (25), p. 13, has another local normalization error. The stated mixture \((G+2R)/\sqrt5\) needs prefactor \(\sqrt5/(2\sqrt{2\pi})\), whereas the printed \(5/(2\sqrt{2\pi})\) integrates to \(\sqrt5\). A constant cancels in the score \(-p'/p\), and sampling from the stated mixture can remain correct. This typographical observation is not a separate substantive finding. Source pages 9 and 13 and the independent arithmetic are E9–E10 and E4.
# Overall impact, positive checks, and remaining scope

The invalid sign and edge count affect the displayed derivation of core subcritical sticking. They do not establish a false Tracy–Widom limit. The Appendix D counterexample does establish a wrong limiting mean for the stated growing-SNR scaling. Its appendix location does not diminish that quantitative defect, but its different scaling limits its effect on the main theorem.

The specialization \(f(z)=z\), \(\lambda=4\) agrees with ordinary spiked Wigner behavior: center \(5/2\), variance \(3/2\). The main Taylor reduction correctly retains the quadratic rank term; its remaining \(O_\prec(N^{-1})\) error is smaller than both relevant fluctuation scales. Polynomial \(C^3\) control supports the remainder rate.

All supercritical comparison estimates, every histogram, and a repaired subcritical proof were not independently reproduced. No author correction or adoption was established in the inspected sources. No inference of first discovery is made.

Title: Initial scientific review: OWLS scaling laws for multilingual speech models
# Paper identity and summary

This initial review concerns William Chen, Jinchuan Tian, Yifan Peng, Brian Yan, Chao-Han Huck Yang, and Shinji Watanabe, OWLS: Scaling Laws for Multilingual Speech Recognition and Translation Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, paper 0194 (I25-43563), OpenReview xnPW7yYomF [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original is the unchanged 25-page proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with printed pages.

The broad empirical benefit of scaling is supported within the inspected results. Four local discrepancies are established: the reported model-scaling \(R^2\) conflicts with its cited figure; contextual-biasing size exclusivity conflicts with the reported errors; the top-two benchmark count is overstated; and the mondegreen perplexities are not monotone at every model size. These support an overall Minor assessment. Predictive extrapolation and full historical reproducibility remain Needs Evidence, without being promoted to demonstrated failures.
# Scope, versions, and checked reasoning

The paper supplies 13 models across seven sizes, data subsets and a larger-data variant. Its central empirical form is \[{\rm WER}(x)=\beta_x x^{\alpha_x},\] with an analogous BLEU relation. A finite-range empirical power law is not a universal theorem about arbitrarily large models; the bounded BLEU range alone does not refute this use.

The review inspected main sections 1–6, relevant Appendix A–H protocols, the reported aggregate tables, and selected original figures. The full 102-row model-scaling tables were parsed for independent numerical diagnostics. Training, speech inference, corpus overlap audits, latency measurements, and human ratings were not reproduced.

The staged model metadata/configuration for `espnet/owls_025B_180K` is pinned to commit `f47a25a1bee253af80cdbb2da7708e0c358346f6`, with metadata modification date 3 May 2025. The available ESPnet source is a later snapshot, commit `11446ccf94d7df0a433588e4b8d7390cda2af3a1`, dated 24 October 2026. These are distinct evidence objects; the later toolkit is not assumed to reproduce the exact historical training implementation.

Positive scope checks matter. The paper explicitly separates same-distribution data scaling from added YODAS diversity, restricts compute scaling to English, Spanish and Turkish, discloses its weaker emergence definition in footnote 3, and specifies a speaker-disjoint Quechua split in Appendix H.1. None of these was treated as an undisclosed condition.
# Problem 1: the reported scaling-fit strength disagrees with Figure 3
## Original claim and direct check

Section 4.1, p. 4, describes language-specific model-size fits as highly predictive and gives \(R^2\simeq0.95\), citing Figure 3. On the same original page, the visible Figure 3 legend reports values such as English 0.82, Russian 0.81, Japanese 0.75, Dutch 0.91, Persian 0.73, and Turkish 0.90. The visible legend spans approximately 0.73–0.91, with none near 0.95. This is a direct text-to-figure discrepancy, confirmed visually on E5; it does not depend on an attempted reproduction of an undisclosed regression.

An independent diagnostic fitted the literal two-parameter power law to the rounded Tables 15–16 values at nominal sizes \(0.25,0.5,1,2,4,9,18\) billion. Raw-space nonlinear least squares yielded a mean top-20 \(R^2\) of approximately 0.8105; English gave 0.8171, consistent with its displayed 0.82. The exact script, settings, and output are E11–E12.
## Alternative interpretation and bounded impact

Adding a nonnegative error floor gives substantially higher fits: the same top-20 rows have mean \(R^2\) approximately 0.9892. This is important counterevidence against claiming that no plausible scaling relation fits the observations. However, that alternative is not the literal Eq. (2), and it does not reconcile the stated 0.95 with the cited figure’s own labels without further explanation.

Assessment: Minor. The quantitative description of the reported fit strength is wrong or insufficiently identified. The correction should state which fit and sample produced 0.95, or replace it with the actual Figure 3 values. The observed broad scaling trend survives.

An in-sample \(R^2\) also does not by itself certify prediction of unseen larger models or late checkpoints. The inspected materials do not expose a complete held-out forecasting protocol. Our separately chosen endpoint diagnostic, fitting six smaller sizes and predicting 18B, gives median absolute relative errors of about 20.2% for log-space fitting and 27.9% for raw-space fitting across 102 rows. These are reviewer diagnostics, not reproductions of an identified author forecasting method. The predictive-reliability claim therefore remains Needs Evidence; it is not independently graded as a proven algorithmic failure.
# Problem 2: contextual-biasing size exclusivity is contradicted by Table 12

Appendix G, pp. 17–18, says in paraphrase that the 0.5B model suffers degradation and that only 9B sufficiently maintains unbiased WER while reducing biased WER to obtain lower overall WER. Table 12, p. 19, supplies direct counterexamples:
Model | Test-clean WER, before/after | Test-other WER, before/after

Lower WER is better. Thus three smaller models also improve overall WER on both splits. For 2B on test-other, all three quantities improve: \[{\rm WER}:5.18\to4.63,\quad
 {\rm U\!-\!WER}:3.73\to3.70,\quad
 {\rm B\!-\!WER}:18.70\to13.23.\] The original prose and table were visually checked on E8–E10; independent arithmetic is E3–E4.

The strongest charitable reading is that the 0.5B degradation refers only to U-WER: it does worsen slightly, \(1.77\to1.83\) and \(4.85\to4.94\). That reading cannot rescue the overall-WER exclusivity, and the 2B test-other case even satisfies strict U-WER improvement. Conversely, 9B test-other U-WER worsens \(2.97\to3.67\).

Assessment: Minor. This invalidates a local scale-threshold interpretation in the auxiliary contextual-biasing study. It does not invalidate the suite or the newly studied orthographic, code-switching, and mondegreen observations as a group. A corrected description should report model- and split-specific tradeoffs. No significance claim follows from these rounded aggregates alone.
# Problem 3: the best-or-second-best benchmark count is four, not five
Section 4.4, p. 7, states that OWLS 18B v2 is best or second best on five of the seven Table 1 benchmarks. Ranking the actual model rows, with lower WER/CER better, gives:
Benchmark | Rank | Models strictly ahead
FLEURS English | 2 | Whisper v3
LibriSpeech clean | 4 | Canary, Qwen2Audio, OWLS 9B
FLEURS Japanese | 2 | Whisper v3
ReazonSpeech | 1 | None
FLEURS Chinese | 4 | Qwen2Audio, Whisper v3, SenseVoice S
AISHELL | 3 | SenseVoice L, SenseVoice S
KsponSpeech | 2 | Whisper v3

The qualifying set has four members. Both ordinary competition rank and distinct-score rank give the same top-two count. Even excluding other OWLS variants does not rescue LibriSpeech clean: Canary 1.5 and Qwen2Audio 1.6 remain better than 2.0.

On AISHELL, the reported 4.8 is worse than SenseVoice L’s 2.1 and SenseVoice S’s 3.0, despite its bold formatting. Collapsing all SenseVoice variants into a single family could make it a second-best family; the paper neither defines that convention nor applies such a family-level statement. That alternative cannot be silently substituted for ranking the displayed models.

Assessment: Minor. The practical comparison summary is overstated by one benchmark; the many competitive results remain. Correct the count and highlighting or state a justified comparison population. The check uses the paper’s own numbers (E4, E6), with no inference about the correctness of the underlying recognition runs.
# Problem 4: mondegreen perplexity is not monotone across all sizes

Section 5.2, p. 8, says that larger models obtain consistently better perplexity across all model sizes. Table 4, p. 9, reports \[{\rm PPL}_{9B}=372,\qquad {\rm PPL}_{18B}=429.\] The larger model is worse by \(429/372-1=15.32\%\). MOS likewise decreases from 4.8 to 4.4, and the earlier 0.5B-to-1B MOS changes from 4.1 to 3.5. These table entries were visually checked (E7); arithmetic is E4.

The broad favorable trend remains substantial: perplexity falls from 1338 at 0.25B to 429 at 18B, and the paper describes MOS as a trend rather than a strict theorem. The study also explicitly filters utterances according to average MOS across models; its result concerns that selected subset. This shared filtering rule alone does not establish a biased ranking or fabrication.

Assessment: Minor. Replace the all-sizes monotonic claim with the observed trend and exceptions. Without utterance-level outcomes, sample counts after filtering, and uncertainty estimates, neither significance nor a general population effect can be established.
# Static-source correspondence and unresolved reproducibility

The staged 0.25B configuration agrees with key paper settings: eight encoder and decoder blocks, hidden size 768, FFN size 3072, 16 heads, CTC weight 0.3, and 30-second speech input. Its 45 epochs times 15,000 iterations matches 675,000 configured steps; this arithmetic does not prove that training actually completed.

The same config contains default-looking Adadelta/null-scheduler fields, but also enables DeepSpeed and points to an external `conf/deepspeed.json`. The inspected later trainer loads that file and passes it to `deepspeed.initialize`. The referenced historical JSON is absent from the inspected model package. It would be unsound to infer that the actual training used Adadelta instead of the paper’s Adam merely from the default fields. Optimizer and schedule correspondence remains Needs Evidence.

Complete historical fitting, inference-budget, ICL and mondegreen scripts were not located in the bounded inspection. The model weights were deliberately excluded from preparation and were not downloaded or run. The 2026 toolkit and baseline OWSM recipes cannot certify the entire 2025 OWLS pipeline.

The 102-row diagnostic finds 76 improvements, 25 degradations and one tie from 9B to 18B. This supports a broad trend while limiting literal universal monotonicity. The named 50-language group in Table 14 averages about 58.728, 48.104 and 44.844 at 1B, 9B and 18B, respectively. The prose’s 59-to-45 summary may use a different subgroup or misidentify the final model; subgroup correspondence remains unresolved and is not an additional graded finding.
# Conclusion and state table
Item | Assessment | Repair verification | Author adoption | Remaining work
P1 | Minor | Figure discrepancy and diagnostic fits checked | Not requested | Identify actual fit and validation
P2 | Minor | Table-based correction verified | Not requested | Revise scale-threshold prose
P3 | Minor | Four-of-seven count verified | Not requested | Correct summary/highlighting
P4 | Minor | Nonmonotonic step verified | Not requested | Report exceptions/uncertainty
Reproduction | Needs Evidence | No full rerun | Not requested | Historical configs and scripts

No Major defect is established by this scoped initial review. The central model suite and broad scaling trends survive the checked local corrections. Scientific adjudication remains pending; human reviews are empty. Author corrections or adoption were not established. Focused recovery acceptance does not constitute human adjudication.

Title: Scientific review of
Demystifying Cost-Efficiency in LLM Serving over Heterogeneous GPUs
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed work is Youhe Jiang, Fangcheng Fu, Xiaozhe Yao, Guoliang He, Xupeng Miao, Ana Klimovic, Bin Cui, Binhang Yuan, and Eiko Yoneki, Demystifying Cost-Efficiency in LLM Serving over Heterogeneous GPUs, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 27534–27552 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assignment identifiers are 0195 and I25-43564; the OpenReview identifier is `xnEv5pq4cB`. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the document’s internal pages 1–19.

The inspection covers the main text, equations, worked example, tables, figure captions and accompanying quantitative claims, and embedded Appendices A–M. The source pages containing the decisive formulas were rendered and inspected. The available source manifest identifies no assigned-version implementation snapshot. A later project-family repository was not substituted for this paper. Separate OpenReview supplements were unavailable in the acquisition record; the embedded appendices were available and read. No author code, model, GPU experiment, cloud API, or benchmark was executed.

The paper’s empirical contribution is a study of workload-aware GPU composition, model deployment, and request assignment. Its mathematical contribution is the optimization specification that coordinates those choices. The review tests that specification on its own assumptions and audits the numerical evidence that can be checked from the published document. It does not claim an exhaustive reproduction of the experimental system.
# Model and operative assumptions

For configuration \(c\), \(h_{c,w}>0\) is the profiled request throughput for workload \(w\), \(f_w\geq0\) is its request count, \(x_{c,w}\in[0,1]\) is the assigned fraction, and \(y_c\) is a nonnegative integer number of copies. The paper requires \[\sum_c x_{c,w}=1,\qquad x_{c,w}\leq y_c,
 \qquad \sum_c o_cy_c\leq B,\qquad
 \sum_c d_n(c)y_c\leq a_n .\] Configurations have already passed the memory and connectivity filters; the budget is an hourly rental budget. The model assumes divisible aggregate workload, identical throughput for copies of a configuration, additive processing times across workload types, and parallel operation across configurations. These are the assumptions used below. They are not a claim that actual batched inference, request arrival times, or tail latency obeys the same exact fluid model.
# Problem 1: the central optimization is not the stated MILP
## Source claim and affected step

Equation reference: eq:printed, eq:short. Section 4.3, p. 7, labels equations (1)–(7) a mixed-integer linear program and describes a solver that converges to an optimal fractional assignment. Its equation (3) is \[
 \sum_w\frac{x_{c,w}f_w}{y_ch_{c,w}}\leq T
 \quad\text{for all }c ,\] while equation (7) explicitly permits \(y_c=0,1,2,\ldots\). Appendix E, pp. 15–16, repeats this quotient in the multi-model formulation. Appendix F, p. 16, then displays the binary-search load test \[
 \sum_w\frac{x_{c,w}}{h_{c,w}}\leq \widehat T ,\] and its multi-model analogue. The source PDF itself contains these expressions; they are not extraction artifacts.
## Complete algebraic check

Equation reference: eq:product. For \(y_c>0\), multiplying [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) by \(y_c\) gives \[
 \sum_w \frac{f_w}{h_{c,w}}x_{c,w}\leq y_cT .\] Both \(y_c\) and \(T\) are decision variables in the direct minimization. Their product is bilinear. Treating \(y_c\) as integer rather than continuous does not make the displayed expression linear. An auxiliary-variable construction or an equivalent discrete reformulation is required, but none is specified in the paper. Thus the formulation as printed is not a MILP. This conclusion does not assert that the underlying scheduling problem cannot have a MILP representation.

The inactive case is separate. Activation coupling gives \(x_{c,w}=0\) when \(y_c=0\), but the left-hand side of [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) then contains \(0/0\), which is undefined. One feasible configuration being unused is part of the intended search, rather than an exceptional input excluded by the paper. Defining an inactive configuration’s load to be zero is sensible, but that definition or an equivalent constraint must be supplied.

Finally, [eq:short] (#eq:short) cannot by itself replace the makespan constraint. Consider one GPU type, one feasible single-GPU configuration, and one workload. Set its availability, hourly price, budget, GPU memory, and model memory requirement all to \(1\). The single GPU is connected to itself, so all resource filters are met. Let \[f=100,\quad h=1\ {\rm request/s},\quad x=1,\quad y=1,
 \quad \widehat T=1\ {\rm s}.\] Assignment, integrality, activation, budget, memory, and availability constraints are all satisfied. The displayed shortened test returns \(x/h=1\leq1\), whereas the required load is \(xf/(yh)=100\) seconds. The discrepancy is exactly the missing request-count factor; the example uses no zero denominator or fractional request. Omitting \(y_c\) can likewise remove the benefit of activating multiple copies. The finite fixture is saved in `initial_checks.json`; the derivation is exact.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

Appendix F also says that the candidate must satisfy all constraints in Section 4.3. If this phrase includes the original makespan constraint at fixed \(T=\widehat T\), the full test rejects the example above; the shortened expression is then an incorrect or redundant description rather than evidence that the actual oracle accepted the example. This alternative is important. The report does not infer the implementation from that displayed expression.

Likewise, a competent implementation could have expanded replica counts, linearized bounded products, used a nonlinear solver, or used a correct fixed-\(T\) feasibility problem. These possibilities preserve the overall systems idea. No implementation snapshot or solver model was available to determine which occurred. The printed formulation nevertheless does not specify the claimed direct MILP, and Appendix E inherits the same problem. Appendix F’s approximate knapsack feasibility check supplies no stated false-positive/false-negative guarantee, so its approximation cannot be assumed to preserve a certified binary-search bracket.
## A precisely bounded correction

Equation reference: eq:fixed. A correct aggregate feasibility formulation for a fixed candidate \(\widehat T\geq0\) replaces [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) by \[
 \sum_w \frac{f_w}{h_{c,w}}x_{c,w}\leq \widehat T\,y_c .\] This is linear because \(\widehat T\) is constant. At \(y_c=0\), activation coupling forces all corresponding assignments to zero and [eq:fixed] (#eq:fixed) is well-defined. With an exact feasibility oracle, a genuinely feasible upper bound, and a valid lower bound, monotonicity in \(\widehat T\) gives ordinary binary-search certification. A heuristic’s failure to find a schedule is not automatically a proof of infeasibility.

The direct minimization also has an exact MILP repair under the stated divisible-load model. Let \(K_c\) be any finite upper bound on the copies of configuration \(c\) from GPU availability. Introduce potential replicas \(r=1,\ldots,K_c\), binary variables \(z_{c,r}\), and fractions \(u_{c,r,w}\geq0\). Minimize \(T\) subject to \[\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{c,r}u_{c,r,w}=1,\qquad u_{c,r,w}\leq z_{c,r},\\
 &\sum_w \frac{f_w}{h_{c,w}}u_{c,r,w}\leq T
       &&\text{for every }(c,r),\\
 &\sum_{c,r}o_cz_{c,r}\leq B,\qquad
   \sum_{c,r}d_n(c)z_{c,r}\leq a_n,\qquad T\geq0 .\end{aligned}\] Every constraint is linear. Given a valid aggregate schedule with \(y_c>0\), activate \(y_c\) replicas and set \(u_{c,r,w}=x_{c,w}/y_c\) on each: their loads equal the aggregate per-copy load. Conversely, summing replica assignments gives \(x_{c,w}\) and \(y_c=\sum_rz_{c,r}\); summing their load bounds yields [eq:product] (#eq:product). Thus the two models have the same feasible makespans once inactive configurations are defined correctly. The proof extends by adding the model index. This repair establishes mathematical equivalence only; it does not verify runtime, numerical conditioning, workload prediction, or equivalence to the unpublished implementation.
## Impact and severity

The invalid classification and incomplete feasibility specification concern the central scheduling derivation, not a peripheral equation. They prevent a reader from reconstructing the advertised direct MILP and interpreting its comparison with binary search in Figure 9 without additional information. The supported severity is Major. The basis is the invalid core formulation and its dependency in the multi-model and solver-efficiency claims. No whole-paper failure, empirical score decrease, or difficult repair is required for that assessment. The GPU benchmarking observations can remain valid, and no numerical experiment is declared false on this evidence.
# Problem 2: the published profiling-error range is not reproduced by Table 6
## Claim and calculation

Appendix L, pp. 18–19, uses Table 6 to support the statement that estimation errors range from \(4\%\) to \(7\%\), followed by a claim that the estimates suffice for selecting optimal configurations. Using the displayed measured throughput \(a\) as reference, the usual relative error is \[e=100\,\frac{|\widehat a-a|}{a}.\] For the seven rows in their published order, exact arithmetic on the displayed values gives \[(7.143,\ 6.818,\ 4.762,\ 9.524,\ 4.762,\ 5.556,\ 8.333)\%.\] In particular, the L40 \((2,4)\) row is \(a=0.42\), \(\widehat a=0.46\) requests/s, hence \(e=9.524\%\). Using the estimate in the denominator instead gives \(8.696\%\), also above \(7\%\). The H100+A100 row gives \(8.333\%\) or \(7.692\%\), respectively. Therefore neither common denominator reproduces the asserted range from the published table.
## Counterevidence, scope, and correction

The table rounds throughput to two decimals and does not state the denominator used for the quoted range. Unrounded measurements or a different metric could explain some difference. The check therefore establishes an inconsistency between the displayed evidence and the reported range, not the true raw-measurement error distribution. It also does not prove that a selected configuration was wrong. The highest measured-throughput row and highest estimated-throughput row in this small table coincide.

The supported Minor finding is the inaccurate or insufficiently specified quantitative support for profiling accuracy. A defensible correction is to report the calculation convention and unrounded measurements, or to describe the displayed-table range as approximately \(4.76\%\)–\(9.52\%\) relative to measured throughput. Whether the profiler preserves the optimum over the full configuration search requires rank-sensitive validation beyond this seven-row example; the present calculation does not supply that validation.
# Other checks, counterevidence, and limits

The Appendix C example was recalculated independently. Its four processing times are \(44.05594\), \(35.23810\), \(30.93682\), and \(28.66667\) seconds, supporting the qualitative improvements attributed to the three choices. The second and third time reductions are \(12.21\%\) and \(7.34\%\); the corresponding speedups are approximately \(13.90\%\) and \(7.92\%\). Consequently, wording near \(14\%\) and \(8\%\) can reflect a speedup denominator rather than a time-reduction denominator. This local wording is not used to inflate severity.

Table 3’s Helix comparisons recalculate to \(34.63\%\) and \(24.65\%\), consistent with the rounded \(35\%\) and \(25\%\) labels. All three workload-ratio rows in Table 5 sum to \(100\%\). The throughput and latency experiments, ablations, availability scenarios, multi-model results, and online-replanning discussion were inspected for the claims and assumptions they support. The distinction between a fixed hourly budget and minimum total billed cost matters: the mathematical objective is makespan subject to a rental-rate constraint, and it is reviewed on that definition.

The paper explicitly treats online replanning as an extension and acknowledges a throughput–latency trade-off. These statements limit an inference of a universal online SLO guarantee. No such additional guarantee is attributed to the paper. Raw per-request traces, repeated-run uncertainty, solver inputs, and the assigned implementation were not available in the reviewed package, so the headline aggregate performance gains and the reported less-than-\(1\%\) solver-performance deviation were not independently reproduced. The introductory average throughput figure and Section 5.2 use different summaries; without the raw aggregation definition, this remains a clarification request rather than a further established defect.
No later-version equivalence or author erratum was established from the supplied version-bound materials. A successor implementation is not evidence that this version has been corrected.
# Conclusion and separate decision states

The overall supported assessment is Major, driven by Problem 1. Problem 2 remains individually Minor. These are initial AI scientific assessments awaiting adjudication, not a later independent acceptance or an editorial decision.
Item | Issue assessment | Repair verification | Adoption / remaining work
Problem 1 | Major; derivation defect | Exact model-level repair proved | Not requested; check actual solver formulation and results
Problem 2 | Minor; numerical support | Displayed-value arithmetic verified | Not requested; provide error convention and unrounded data
Empirical gains | Not reproduced here | Not applicable | Raw traces and assigned implementation required

It contains the retained source manifest and identity binding by reference, `initial_checks.py`, `initial_checks.json`, and rendered source pages `initial_source_p7.png`, `p16`, `p18`, and `p19` with the same prefix. The independent script uses Python’s `fractions.Fraction` and standard-library JSON; it executes no released author code. It was run with the existing Anaconda Python 3.13.5 on 24 October 2026 and produced the numerical results cited above. The analytic equivalence proof is separate from those finite computations.

The auxiliary reviewer performed the new paper reading, derivations, arithmetic, and draft preparation. The parent reviewer integrates source evidence, compiles the exact final TeX, and performs final PDF visual inspection. Those steps are recorded when actually performed in provenance, rather than inferred from this source file. Previous recovery metadata is preserved once under `_initial_predecessor`; it is not a new scientific check. No human review is recorded; adjudication remains pending.

report: Abstract: This initial review examines the published dataset, model, evaluation, ablations and embedded supplementary material, together with static inspection of the supplied released source snapshot. A disclosed limitation of the basic-emotion hit rate has a decisive consequence: an input-independent prediction containing every basic label attains its optimum. This materially limits a central part of MER-UniBench and is assessed as Major, without claiming that the reported rankings actually reverse. The supplied later source also selects checkpoints using test scores, but its relationship to the published experiments is unresolved. All scientific decisions and author adoption remain pending.
Date: 24 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of AffectGPT
# Identity, version and inspection scope

The reviewed paper is Zheng Lian, Haoyu Chen, Lan Chen, Haiyang Sun, Licai Sun, Yong Ren, Zebang Cheng, Bin Liu, Rui Liu, Xiaojiang Peng, Jiangyan Yi and Jianhua Tao, AffectGPT: A New Dataset, Model, and Benchmark for Emotion Understanding with Multimodal Large Language Models, ICML 2025, PMLR volume 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assignment is 0196/I25-43565. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbering in the supplied 22-page proceedings PDF. The original PDF and embedded Appendices A–N were read in full through the supplied extracted text; decisive equations and table layout were checked against rendered original pages. The PDF identity is hash-bound in Appendix 7 (#app:evidence).

The static source inspected is the supplied `AffectGPT` subdirectory of `zeroQiaoba/AffectGPT`, commit |95b9257758df29fa6481c138252cdd317cce1735|, dated 13 October 2026 in the acquisition manifest [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. It is later than the paper. It establishes what that snapshot implements, not which implementation generated the 2025 tables. No author code, model inference, training, paid API or downloaded executable was run. Large datasets, weights and intermediate binary predictions are not part of the inspected snapshot. A separate OpenReview attachment remains unresolved in the acquisition record; the embedded supplement is available and inspected.
# Claims checked and methodological context

The paper has three linked contributions. MER-Caption contains 115,595 automatically described samples; MER-Caption+ retains 31,327 after low-level and high-level filtering. The pipeline combines audio and video descriptions, uses human assistance for model selection, and filters examples using signal alignment, description length and classifier agreement. AffectGPT then fine-tunes a multimodal language model, using pre-fusion of audio and visual features. MER-UniBench aggregates nine datasets: four basic-emotion datasets, four sentiment datasets and one fine-grained emotion dataset.

The inspection covered the annotation/filtering pipeline in Sections 2–3 and Appendices E–H; the fusion equations and model configuration; all definitions in Section 4; Tables 2–8 and 10–13; and the sampling-frame ablation in Appendix N. The architecture equations have compatible dimensions: in Eq. (7), \(\widehat Z_{av}^{T}\) is \(d\times2\), \(W\) is \(2\times2d\), and the flattened input is \(2d\)-dimensional. Thus the fused vector is \(d\)-dimensional. The current |encode_multi_attention| implementation pools time, projects modalities, computes two learned weights and forms a weighted combination. These weights are not required by the printed equation to be softmax probabilities, so absence of a softmax is not itself a contradiction. The code uses affine layers, a detail more specific than the bias-free displayed notation.

The reported full audio–video–text scores in Table 2 average to \(74.768888\ldots\), correctly rounded to \(74.77\). The corresponding Emotion-LLaMA row averages to \(64.171111\ldots\). Their difference is about \(10.60\) percentage points. Table 5’s attention pre-fusion result exceeds its no-pre-fusion row by \(1.82\) points; Table 3’s filtered MER-Caption+ result exceeds MER-Caption by \(5.86\) points. These arithmetic checks confirm displayed aggregates, not statistical significance or independent reproduction.

For fine-grained recognition, Eqs. (9)–(12) average per-sample set precision and recall, take their harmonic mean for each wheel, then average over wheels. This is well-defined when denominators are positive and is not the mean of per-sample F-scores; the distinction is explicit in the equations. Empty predicted sets and zero combined precision/recall need conventions. The current code assigns zero precision/recall for an empty prediction but has no explicit guard on the final \(0/0\) F-score. No evaluated all-zero case was established, so this is recorded as a boundary-condition clarification rather than an additional supported scientific defect.
# Problem 1: a basic-emotion optimum without recognition
## Claim, location and necessary assumptions

The conditions relevant to the check are precisely those in the metric: \(\mathcal Y\) is finite; every reference label belongs to it; prediction sets may contain multiple labels; and the same label mapping is applied to prediction and reference. There is no cardinality limit, wrong-label penalty or exclusivity constraint in Eq. [eq:hit] (#eq:hit). The argument operates on the extracted sets supplied to the metric. It does not assume that a particular language-model extraction prompt will always convert an arbitrary caption into a specified set.
## Complete check

Proposition 1.  For every dataset satisfying the preceding conditions, the input-independent prediction \(\widehat Y_i=\mathcal Y\) for every \(i\) attains \(\operatorname{HIT}_k=1\) for every applicable mapping \(G_k\). The result also holds if samples with unmapped reference labels are omitted, provided at least one sample remains.

Proof. Let \(i\) be any retained sample. Since \(y_i\in\mathcal Y\), pointwise mapping gives \(G_k(y_i)\in G_k(\mathcal Y)\). Substituting \(\widehat Y_i=\mathcal Y\) into the indicator in [eq:hit] (#eq:hit) therefore gives one. This holds separately for each retained sample and each wheel, so averaging over samples or wheels preserves one. If the mapping discards some labels, apply the same argument to every sample whose reference has a retained mapped value. No input feature is used. ◻

A finite witness makes all parameters explicit. Take \(\mathcal Y=\{\mathrm{happy},\mathrm{sad},\mathrm{angry},\mathrm{neutral}\}\), four arbitrary inputs, and reference sequence listing those four labels once each. With the identity mapping, a constant four-label prediction gets four hits and score \(1\), exactly the score of four correctly selected singleton predictions. The constant predictor makes no decision about which emotion occurs in which sample. Mapping happy to positive, sad and angry to negative, and retaining neutral changes none of these hits. Removing neutral from both mapped reference and prediction sets leaves three retained hits out of three, again one. The independent check script verifies these and further illustrative mappings. They illustrate a general proof, not a claim to have executed the authors’ wheel files.

The current released metric corroborates the admissible operation. In |my_affectgpt/evaluation/wheel.py|, |func_map_label_to_synonym| maps labels independently; |calculate_openset_onehot_hitrate| maps each reference and prediction and adds the size of their intersection. A single retained reference maps to one label, so that intersection is exactly the indicator above. The function additionally computes a specificity-sensitive auxiliary score, but |evaluation-scoreonly.py| discards it for the basic-emotion primary score. The existence of that auxiliary calculation does not alter Eq. (13) or the Table 2 primary metric.

More generally, for \(\widehat Y_i\subseteq\widehat Y'_i\), pointwise mapping preserves inclusion, and thus \(\operatorname{HIT}_k(\widehat Y')\geq\operatorname{HIT}_k(\widehat Y)\). Adding labels can never hurt the basic score, including when added labels contain no information about the input. This identifies the precise failure: the metric rewards coverage of the reference but does not identify selective recognition.
## Counterevidence, disclosure and scope

The authors explicitly disclose the missing penalty in the paragraph following Eq. (13), p. 7. They explain that labels differing from the single majority-voted reference could be legitimate fine-grained emotions, and leave their evaluation for future work. That is a real annotation limitation; the present review does not accuse the paper of concealing it. Nor does it assume that every extra label is false.

However, uncertainty about additional labels does not make reference coverage a test of choosing the most likely basic emotion. Proposition Proposition 1 (#prop:constant) shows a complete failure of discrimination on this stated task. This is a known limitation reproduced and its consequence quantified, not a new finding that the paper’s formula was implemented contrary to its stated intent. A restricted interpretation as a recall/coverage diagnostic is valid. The broader interpretation as comprehensive basic-emotion recognition evidence is unsupported by this statistic alone.

The four sentiment WAF columns and the fine-grained set F-score are not subject to this particular all-label optimum. The proof does not invalidate the dataset construction, imply that AffectGPT actually emits all labels, establish an erroneous numerical entry, or demonstrate a reversal of the published model ordering. Those would require the saved predictions and a suitable alternative evaluation.
## Core dependency and severity

This issue is Major because the benchmark is a named core contribution, and four of its nine primary components can attain their best possible value without using the input. It directly weakens the basic-emotion comparisons and their contribution to the headline mean. This is material harm to the interpretation of a core evaluation, rather than a demand to refute all empirical gains.

The weighting is concrete. The four basic columns contribute \(4/9\) of the unweighted mean. As a metric stress calculation only, replacing the four full-modality AffectGPT basic scores by their all-label optimum and holding its other five scores fixed changes the mean from \(74.7689\) to \(88.8211\), a \(14.0522\) point increase. This is not a simulated model, an actual improvement, or an estimate of historical bias: it quantifies how the aggregator responds to an input-independent optimum in those columns. No benchmark-score loss, whole-paper collapse or difficult repair is required for this severity.
## Precisely supported correction

For the claim of selecting one basic label, require a single prediction \(\widehat y_i\) from the fixed basic vocabulary and score whether it equals the reference (or use the same explicitly documented canonical grouping on both). Then Eq. [eq:hit] (#eq:hit) reduces to accuracy on that chosen label space. The constant all-label output is no longer admissible. This restores the specific distinction tested by the counterexample, but does not establish completeness of fine-grained annotations or validate all free-form reasoning.

A complementary open-description task can retain coverage as a named diagnostic and use exhaustively annotated reference sets, or an independently specified human evaluation, for additional-label correctness. The report does not assert that a new automatic precision penalty against the original single-label references is ground truth. The proposed singleton restriction is analytically checked; its effect on the actual rankings remains untested.
# Problem 2: test-selected checkpoints in the later release
## Established static behavior

The inspected commit’s README recommends |evaluation-scoreonly.py| for score calculation and shows inference over multiple epochs. In that script, |main_zeroshot_scores| obtains |dataset_cls.get_test_name2gt()|, loops over prediction files, computes the primary score on those labels, and sets
best_index = np.argmax(whole_score1s)

The function returns the scores at that index. The aggregate routine calls this independently for each of the nine datasets with `test_epochs=”`, which does not restrict the candidate epochs. The same pattern occurs in `evaluation.py`. MER2023’s loader explicitly reads `test1_corpus`; the IEMOCAP loader uses Session 5 and asserts 1,241 test samples. Thus these are test-label selections in the inspected call path, not merely a misleading variable name.

Equation reference: eq:oracle. Let \(s_{de}\) be the score of checkpoint \(e\) on dataset \(d\). This routine reports \[
 \frac1D\sum_d \max_e s_{de},\] when multiple checkpoints are present. It need not equal the score of any single checkpoint selected without those test labels. For example, two checkpoints with scores \((0.9,0.1)\) and \((0.1,0.9)\) on two datasets produce [eq:oracle] (#eq:oracle) equal to \(0.9\); each individual checkpoint has mean \(0.5\). The independent script verifies this finite example. It demonstrates a change in estimand, not the amount of bias in the published results.
## What remains unresolved

The source snapshot is dated October 2026. The inspected material does not bind the original 2025 tables to its exact evaluation call, candidate-file set or chosen epochs. A results directory containing only one externally selected checkpoint would have no extra test selection in the maximization. A different historical script or explicit validation-based selection could also alter the inference. No binary predictions were loaded and no experiment was rerun.

Accordingly, the finding’s paper-level judgment is Needs Evidence, while the later-code behavior itself is established by static inspection. It is not counted as a second supported Major defect of the published experiments. A decisive historical check needs the table-generating commit, per-dataset candidate prediction manifest, chosen checkpoint identifiers, and the selection rule and validation data. If the published tables used multiple candidates and the shown routine, their values would measure test-oracle selection; if they used an independently selected single checkpoint, that concern would not apply.

The appropriate correction for future evaluation is to fix checkpoint selection using independent validation data before test evaluation, document whether one common or task-specific checkpoint is intended, and report the resulting held-out scores. Merely retaining the current maximum while calling it a fixed-model score would not restore that interpretation. This protocol change is a precise conditional recommendation, not a verified historical repair.
# Other inspected evidence and limits

Tables 3 and 13 change the training dataset while holding the architecture and settings fixed, providing stronger support for a dataset contribution than the headline comparison alone. Table 4 separates low-level filtering from emotion/sentiment agreement filters; Table 5 separates no fusion, Q-Former fusion and attention fusion. The reported gains remain subject to the metric limitation and the unresolved selection provenance. The paper does not supply seed-level uncertainty for the small ablation differences. Thus differences such as \(74.16\) versus \(74.77\) are descriptive results; this inspection does not establish statistical separation.

The human comparison in Section 5 and Table 7 uses 20 overlapping samples and four annotators. It provides local evidence favoring the new descriptions, particularly over MERR-Coarse, but 80 ratings do not constitute 80 independent sampled videos. Without per-sample ratings, uncertainty or a broader sampling design, this check cannot extend the preference rate to every generated annotation. The paper acknowledges remaining inaccurate descriptions. The wording about guaranteed quality should be understood within this empirical evidence, not as a mathematical guarantee of correct labels.

Appendix F explicitly explains that the description generators were chosen using their individual scores. Table 10 includes a higher-scoring audio–video combination than the chosen pair; because the selection criterion is stated, that observation is not an established selection error. Appendix J defines the basic, sentiment and fine-grained test splits. The supplied IEMOCAP loader agrees with the Session-5 split, but the construction of its label archive was not inspected; the paper’s statement about merging surprise into happiness cannot be verified from this loader alone. It is not promoted to a substantive finding.

No train/test contamination, label fabrication, universal model inferiority or dataset licensing violation is inferred. The downstream scores do not by themselves establish causal explanations for every encoder or LLM choice. They also do not disprove that the proposed dataset and pre-fusion model are useful. The later source configuration broadly agrees with the reported 60 epochs, 5,000 iterations per epoch, batch size 3, learning rate \(10^{-5}\), eight video frames, Qwen2.5, HuBERT-Large and CLIP ViT-Large, but its current dataset pointers are not an exact frozen 2025 training manifest.
# Dependence, repair status and pending decisions

The supported Major judgment concerns the interpretation of a central benchmark component, including its weight in aggregate comparisons. The source snapshot additionally makes a reproducibility question concrete; it does not establish the historical answer. No later erratum or version correcting the metric is supplied in the inspected materials. This is a first scientific review, not independent acceptance.

Every adjudication remains pending. No author adoption has been requested or inferred. There are no human reviews recorded.

report: Abstract: This initial review examines the published proceedings paper, its embedded appendices, and the pinned released evaluation code. A major methodological problem affects the interpretation of TypeCheck: the released procedure checks predicted stub programs separately from original implementations, so the two error counts do not test the same program obligations. An independent, fully typed example passes as a predicted stub yet produces an argument-type error when its predictions are applied to the unchanged implementation. Two local implementation defects concern inherited attributes in TypeSim and an exact-match cache field. The printed model-level arithmetic is reproducible from the supplementary tables. These results establish defects in the evaluated objects and released implementation; they do not determine revised model rankings or identify the code commit used in the historical experiments.
Date: 24 October 2026

Title: Scientific review of TypyBench:
evaluation semantics and implementation checks
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Honghua Dong, Jiacheng Yang, Xun Deng, Yuhe Jiang, Gennady Pekhimenko, Fan Long, and Xujie Si, TypyBench: Evaluating LLM Type Inference for Untyped Python Repositories, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, paper identifier I25-43566 (local number 0197), OpenReview identifier `xl9sv9vEDy` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. All page references below are one-based pages of the 28-page proceedings PDF, including appendices. The original PDF SHA-256 is

cedd43736ab0bfe6fc28e917e93aab07
e1f8aec4353c01f8a0ef7d6aa9c868bc.

The released repository was inspected statically at commit |51feed13381f6bd027caad1f5bf7c4de798bc6a5| [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its acquisition record explicitly does not identify it as the historical experiment commit.

The review covers Sections 1–7, Algorithms 1–4, the metric definitions, data selection and cleaning, Tables 1–4, Appendix A–D, and the evaluation path through `run.py`, `Dockerfile`, |scripts/evaluation.py|, `repo_similarity.py`, `type_similarity.py`, and `helpers.py`. The benchmark’s separate repository dataset and raw model generations were not acquired or executed. Separate OpenReview supplementary attachments remain unavailable in the acquisition record (HTTP 403); the embedded appendices were read. No author code, Docker build, model API, or historical experiment was executed.
# Definitions and positive checks

For two base types the paper defines a Jaccard similarity of supported attribute sets after excluding common `object` operations. Ordered generic arguments are averaged positionwise and normalized by the larger arity; union members use a maximum-weight matching, again normalized by the larger cardinality. The root and argument contributions are averaged. These operations yield scores in \([0,1]\) when the base score does, handle unequal arities as specified, and are symmetric. The published example \[S(\mathrm{List[int]},\mathrm{Sequence[float]})
 =\tfrac12(0.7+0.6)=0.65\] is arithmetically correct. A partial-match score is a similarity heuristic, not a proof of type substitutability; this distinction alone is not counted as a defect.

The supplementary Tables 9–17 contain 50 rows per model, with 47 finite TypeCheck entries. Recomputed TypeCheck means include \(366.0213\) for GPT-4o, \(127.1277\) for Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and \(214.6170\) for DeepSeek-V3; these agree with Table 2 at its printed precision. The corresponding TypeSim means are \(0.80448\), \(0.78762\), and \(0.79468\). This is a check of published arithmetic, not a replication of the measurements. The three unavailable checker runs are disclosed in Table 6, rather than silently treated as zero.

The temporal contamination analysis on pp. 8–9 is presented as a potential explanation. Repository age is confounded with repository characteristics and model training exposure, so the plot is not a causal contamination estimate; the paper’s qualified wording does not establish a separate error. Likewise, the full-repository experiment uses only three eligible repositories, which bounds its generality without falsifying those observations.
# Problem 1: stub-only errors do not measure consistency with implementations
## Claim and operative procedure

Section 4.2 (p. 5) motivates TypeCheck using inconsistencies such as a predicted return type being incompatible with its uses, and interprets counted errors as obstacles to practical use. Section 6.2 (p. 7) compares model error counts with the original repository average of \(141.8\) and interprets a lower count as stronger consistency. The abstract and conclusion make repository-wide consistency a central contribution.

The released dataflow is decisive. `run.py` mounts the prediction directory. The Docker entry point invokes |scripts/evaluation.py| with that directory. Its `evaluate` function calls |get_repo_similarity(original_repo,prediction_directory)|. In `repo_similarity.py`, the original and prediction directories are passed separately to |get_type_dict_from_repo|. In `helpers.py`, that function copies each input program’s own files to a temporary directory and calls Mypy’s builder. No step inserts predicted signatures into the original function bodies or recreates their call sites. The predictions requested on pp. 7 and 14 are `.pyi` stub files. Ordinary stub files contain signatures but elide implementation logic [Retained latex: \cite{mypy}].

Consequently the procedure compares \[E(P_{\mathrm{original}})\quad\hbox{with}\quad
 E(S_{\mathrm{predicted}}),\] where \(E\) is the selected error count and \(S\) is a stub program. To evaluate compatibility of predicted types with the original uses, the required object is instead \[E\!\left(P_{\mathrm{original}}[
       \text{predicted annotations}]\right).\] These quantities need not agree even for complete, syntactically valid predictions.
## Complete counterexample and observed check
Consider this original implementation:
Predict precisely these three signatures:

Code:
def f() -> str: ...
def h(x: int) -> int: ...
def g() -> int: ...

All functions are present; all parameters and returns use ordinary explicit primitive types; there is no `Any`, missing file, syntax error, external dependency, overload, dynamic dispatch, or untyped body. Thus neither missing predictions nor gradual-typing escape hatches explain the discrepancy. This is a counterexample to the metric’s interpretation, not a claimed member of the curated 50-repository dataset.

The predicted stub is internally type-correct. Applying its signatures to the original bodies instead changes only the return annotation of `f`. The literal return value \(1\) is an `int`, contradicting the predicted `str`; moreover `h(f())` supplies a declared `str` to a required `int` argument. The latter is an `arg-type` error, explicitly included in Appendix C.2.

An independently written fixture was checked with the already installed Mypy 1.14.1 and Python 3.13.5. The original implementation produced zero errors; the predicted stub produced zero errors; the reannotated implementation produced two errors, `return-value` and `arg-type`. This is an actual finite diagnostic on new reviewer-written programs, not execution of the authors’ evaluator. The paper reports Mypy 1.11.1/Python 3.12, so this run is not claimed to reproduce that environment. The structural argument does not depend on a version-specific diagnostic: the predicted stub contains none of the original return or call expressions.
## Counterevidence, impact, and correction boundary

Stub checking can detect genuine inconsistencies in declarations, inheritance, and imports. It is useful for interface validation. The paper also reports missing rates, which provide information beyond the raw error count. These facts do not make the stub-only count a test of implementation compatibility: the counterexample has complete signatures and no missing files.

A separate possibility is that historical prediction folders contained transformed implementations in addition to stubs. No supplied raw prediction artifacts establish that, and the released pipeline does not perform such transformation. The report therefore does not assert that every published model score was generated by this commit, or that any ranking reverses. It establishes that the described/released evaluation does not support the broad interpretation placed on TypeCheck, and that the direct model-versus-original comparison changes the set of checked program obligations.

Assessment: Major. Repository-level consistency is a principal benchmark contribution and a central empirical conclusion. Losing the original usage constraints materially affects that measurement, even if TypeSim and the qualitative need for better type inference remain useful. A defensible repair is to apply predictions to a fixed implementation/caller corpus and count the same checks for every model, reporting parse/annotation failures separately. That repair design is logically targeted; its effects on the published benchmark require a fresh evaluation and are not verified here.
# Problem 2: supported operations are replaced by locally declared names

Section 4.1.1 (p. 4) defines base similarity using supported methods and operations. The released |get_type_attributes| returns `TypeInfo.names`, a class’s local symbol table, without traversing its method-resolution order. Consider

An alternative definition based strictly on declarations would make the calculation internally coherent, but would not be the paper’s stated supported-operation definition. Method-name overlap also omits signatures and effects; that separate design limitation is not needed for this counterexample. Assessment: Minor for the demonstrated bounded implementation discrepancy. The extent to which inherited user-defined classes contributed to the historical aggregate scores is not established. Computing effective supported attribute sets would address this specific mismatch; complete semantic similarity and historical numerical recovery are not thereby verified.
# Problem 3: cache reload substitutes TypeSim for exact match

In |scripts/evaluation.py|, `evaluate` saves both |repo_overall_score_wo_missing| and |repo_overall_score_wo_missing_exact|. On a cache hit, however, the variable for the latter is assigned the former dictionary key. The resulting CSV and printed exact-match-without-missing output can change merely because the evaluation is repeated.

For a cache containing TypeSim-without-missing \(u=0.9\) and exact-match-without-missing \(v=0.6\), a cold evaluation correctly stores \(v\), whereas the reload branch assigns \(u\) to the exact field. Its absolute error is \(0.3\). The example needs only a valid cache containing the separately computed fields with \(u\ne v\); the same synthetic score pair is permitted by a partial-credit metric versus exact matching. No author pickle was loaded and no author function was executed.

The cold branch calculates and saves the correct field; the defect is specifically the reload branch. The published main exact-match-by-depth results do not automatically inherit this error, since their depth dictionaries are loaded separately. Assessment: Minor. Replacing the lookup with the exact-match key repairs this local dataflow, but no full author evaluation was rerun and no claim is made that the published tables used the faulty cached scalar.
# Dependence, conclusions, and remaining work

The strongest supported concern is the interpretation and implementation of the core consistency metric. The inherited-attribute and cache findings affect distinct parts of the released evaluation, with narrower demonstrated scope. None of these results justifies fabricating corrected benchmark scores. The basic TypeSim recurrence and the checked supplementary aggregate arithmetic survive these checks.
Issue | Assessment | Repair verification | Remaining work
Stub/implementation mismatch | Major | Targeted design stated; benchmark repair untested | Fixed-program re-evaluation
Inherited attributes | Minor | Counterexample verified; complete repair untested | MRO-aware implementation and score audit
Exact-match cache key | Minor | Local key correction analytically sufficient | Cold/cache regression check
