report: Abstract: This initial review checks the proceedings paper, all embedded appendices, and a pinned released source snapshot. Two problems affect central links in the proposed method: narrowing a policy support does not imply the asserted entropy reduction, and the released tree selector omits ancestor factors required by the stated selection rule. The latter changes the chosen branch on an actual supplied tree. A separate local implementation defect lets evaluation mutate the training environment during PPO rollouts. The appendix’s discrete entropy support bound and its finite-policy identification argument withstand the checks described here. The empirical results support useful strategy-conditioned behavior within their tested settings, but historical code provenance, total interaction costs, and some selection details remain unresolved. No reinforcement-learning experiment or author program was executed.
Date: 24 October 2026

Title: Scientific review of Strategic Planning:
specificity, strategy selection, and rollout integrity
# Identity, version, and review limits

The reviewed work is Max Ruiz Luyten, Antonin Berthon, and Mihaela van der Schaar, Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 52258–52302, local number 0198, paper identifier I25-43567, and OpenReview identifier `xkgQWEj9F2` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page references are one-based pages of the 45-page proceedings PDF, including its appendices. Its SHA-256 is

The 57-file released repository snapshot was inspected at commit |0321ac2cfb1b6a3b407299fc8ce41538b7f24004| [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The acquisition record does not establish this as the commit that generated the published experiments.

The review covers the main paper, Appendix A’s proofs, implementation and prompts in Appendix B, experimental tables and figure descriptions in Appendix C, related-work and illustrative discussions in Appendix D, and limitations in Appendix E. Relevant released code was read statically: tree construction and selection, prompts, reward-score collection and distillation, PPO reward mixing and rollout collection, evaluation callbacks, configurations, and supplied tree JSON. The existing PDF was actually read through Poppler; its path was not treated as evidence of access.

Separate OpenReview attachments remain unavailable in the acquisition record (HTTP 403). The embedded appendices were available and read. Raw seed-level learning curves, model checkpoints, annotation datasets, and the experimental EDE/Dreamer implementations are not present in the supplied source snapshot. Submodule contents were not downloaded. These limits prevent historical numerical reproduction and causal attribution of the published gains. They do not prevent the finite mathematical and static implementation checks below.
# Contribution, definitions, and checked positive results

The paper proposes choosing a distribution \(\delta_\Pi\) over policies before low-level reinforcement learning. Its Strategy Problem trades off specificity, represented by entropy, and retention of a near-optimal policy. The implementation builds a natural-language strategy tree using an LLM, estimates each node’s value and feasibility, and converts a chosen strategy into a distilled state score used for reward shaping. Experiments compare strategy-guided and baseline PPO/EDE agents in original and modified Crafter.

For a discrete prior with policy masses \(p_i\), write \[H(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i,\qquad
 S_\tau=\{\pi_i:p_i\geq\tau\}.\] The appendix explicitly restricts its entropy argument to finite or countable policy collections. It assumes that a near-optimal policy belongs to \(S_\tau\), that candidate policies can be executed, and that episodes are independently sampled from the same initial-state distribution. These are substantive requirements. A natural-language node and a neural policy learner do not automatically provide an enumerable thresholded policy set or the required distribution.
## Entropy support bound

Equation reference: eq:support. Lemma A.1, pp. 14–15, correctly gives \[
 |S_\tau|\leq
 \min\left\{\frac{1}{\tau},
       2+\frac{H_{\max}}{\tau\log(1/\tau)}\right\}.\] The normalization bound follows from \(\tau|S_\tau|\leq1\). For the entropy bound, there are at most two atoms with mass greater than \(1/e\). On the remaining atoms, \(-x\log x\) is increasing up to \(1/e\), so each atom in \(S_\tau\) contributes at least \(\tau\log(1/\tau)\) when that light-atom set is nonempty. The constant two is therefore essential in the stated general bound and is present in the actual appendix. At \(\tau=1\), the appendix supplies the appropriate endpoint convention and at most one policy remains. A criticism that the proof incorrectly assumes all masses are at most \(1/e\) would be unfounded.
## Policy identification

For bounded independent episodic returns in \([0,1]\), Proposition A.2 uses \[m=\left\lceil\frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}
                   \log\frac{4P}{\delta}\right\rceil\] episodes per policy. Hoeffding’s inequality gives simultaneous mean errors at most \(\varepsilon/2\) with failure probability at most \(\delta/2\), which is stronger than the claimed \(\delta\). Comparing the empirical maximizer with the true maximizer then gives an \(\varepsilon\) value gap.

For discounted rewards \(r_t\in[0,1]\), Lemma A.3 explicitly includes the return range \((1-\gamma)^{-1}\) and the truncation tail \(\gamma^T/(1-\gamma)\). Its chosen horizon makes the tail at most \(\varepsilon/2\), while its sampling rule bounds statistical error by another \(\varepsilon/2\). Theorem A.4 then uses value estimates accurate to \(v_{\min}/4\) to obtain algorithmic error \(v_{\min}/2\); adding the prior’s \(v_{\min}\) approximation gap gives the stated \(3v_{\min}/2\) result. This dependency and the discounted \((1-\gamma)^{-2}\) factor are consistent.

The compact main-text Theorem 2.1 must be read with these appendix restrictions, not as a return-scale-free guarantee for arbitrary unnormalized MDPs or a theorem about the implemented neural agent. The paper itself explicitly states on p. 4 that the theoretical bound does not extend to its implementation. No failure of Appendix A is asserted here.
## Empirical and reward checks

Table 1 agrees with Table 5 for the short-schedule Crafter-Medium milestones. Table 2 agrees with Table 8 for long-schedule Crafter-Easy strategy metrics. The reported Crafter-Medium products in Table 9 are \(0.75(0.85)=0.6375\), \(0.9(0.5)=0.45\), and \(0.6(0.7)=0.42\), consistent with the printed ranks after rounding.

The data support a task- and strategy-dependent account, rather than uniform superiority at every milestone. In Tables 3–4, plain PPO reaches the easy hunting threshold at \(0.20\) million steps, before either guided strategy under either schedule. The medium results and the breeding behavior are stronger evidence for the intended difficult-exploration use case. This observation bounds broad prose about consistently faster learning; it does not negate the reported medium gains.

The released direct PPO reward mode computes a convex mixture of environment reward and a scaled distilled state score, consistent with Appendix B.4’s current-state formula and \(\beta=10\) through the configuration’s \(0.1\) scale. Such a score is not generally potential-based reward shaping, but the paper does not claim policy invariance during the shaping phase. Its explicit annealing and discussion of strategy reversion acknowledge that the optimization objective changes. The distinction between the next-state formula in the main text and current-state implementation should be specified in a reproduction, but no unsupported invariance violation is alleged.
# Problem 1: a smaller policy support need not have lower entropy
## Claim and suspect implication

Section 4.1, p. 5, constrains children to increasingly specific policy subsets. Section 4.3 then asserts \[H(\delta_{h_{i,j}})<H(\delta_{h_i})\] as a consequence of the tree’s design. Appendix B.2.1, p. 19, repeats that narrowing subgoals implicitly drives entropy down and explains that neither entropy nor the threshold \(H_{\max}\) is numerically checked. This is the proposed connection between the implementable tree construction and the formal specificity objective.

Support inclusion alone does not imply that Shannon entropy decreases. This remains false under the natural, favorable interpretation that a child distribution is exactly its parent’s conditional distribution on the retained policies, rather than an arbitrarily reweighted new distribution.
## Complete counterexample

Consider a one-step finite MDP. Its initial state has three actions, each deterministically gives reward one and terminates. Fix \(\gamma=0.9\); its value is immaterial after termination. Let \(\pi_0,\pi_1,\pi_2\) be the deterministic policies choosing the respective actions. All policies are implementable, and each has return \(J(\pi_i)=1=J(\pi^\star)\).

Give the parent strategy masses \[p=(0.98,0.01,0.01).\] Let a more restrictive child require choosing either action one or action two. Its support is the proper subset \(\{\pi_1,\pi_2\}\). Condition the parent on that subset: \[q(\pi_1)=q(\pi_2)=\frac{0.01}{0.02}=\frac12.\] Both distributions are normalized, have finite Shannon entropy, and refer to policies in the same MDP. The refinement only removes a permitted policy. It preserves every remaining policy’s optimal value and implementability. Thus no loss of value, infeasibility, unknown dynamics, continuous density, or infinite support explains the example.

With natural logarithms, \[\begin{aligned}
 H(p)&=-0.98\log0.98-2(0.01\log0.01)
       =0.1119020569\ldots,\\
 H(q)&=-2\left(\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)
       =\log2=0.6931471806\ldots.\end{aligned}\] The support shrinks from three policies to two, but entropy increases by approximately \(0.5812451\) nats. Choose \(H_{\max}=0.2\), \(\tau=0.005\), and \(v_{\min}=0.1\). The parent satisfies the entropy budget; the child violates it. Every retained policy lies above the probability threshold and has value one, so both the relative and additive near-optimality requirements hold. Feasibility is one for both strategies, and the child-to-parent optimal-value ratio is one. All the operative value and feasibility conditions therefore survive while the claimed specificity implication fails.

The independent arithmetic check reproduces these numbers in |independent_checks_output.json|. More generally, \(H(p)=h(0.02)+0.02\log2\) here, whereas entropy conditional on the rare two-policy subset is \(\log2\). Conditioning can increase uncertainty for a particular selected branch, even though the average conditional entropy obeys a different inequality.
## Alternative readings and repair scope

If every node were explicitly uniform on its finite support, strict support reduction would imply \(H=\log|\operatorname{supp}|\) decreases. An explicit entropy-contraction constraint would also suffice by assumption. Neither condition is imposed on the paper’s general strategy distributions or implemented by its language prompts. A verbal goal that is more concrete specifies no probability weights.

The assertion may be read as an intended design objective rather than a proven property. Under that reading, the formal inequality should be replaced by a heuristic hypothesis and should not be presented as guaranteed by hierarchy. Appendix B.2.1’s acknowledgment that entropy is not computed is important counterevidence to any claim that the implementation certifies the Strategy Problem; it does not make the displayed implication mathematically true.

A precise repair is to state and enforce an additional distributional condition, or to withdraw the entropy-contraction implication and describe specificity operationally. The uniform-support repair restores this particular implication analytically, but does not prove that natural-language refinements preserve near-optimal policies or accelerate PPO. No implementation of such a repair was tested.
## Dependency and severity

The issue is Major. Specificity is one of the two defining quantities of the Strategy Problem, and automatic entropy reduction is the stated reason that the strategy tree addresses it without calculating entropy. The counterexample invalidates that central derivation. It does not invalidate the conditional PAC theorem or demonstrate that the recorded Crafter improvements disappear. Those surviving results do not remove the direct dependency of the formal-to-algorithm connection on the false implication.
# Problem 2: the released selector omits ancestor factors
## Stated rule and actual dataflow

Equation reference: eq:priority. Appendix B.2, p. 18, selects a leaf using its root-relative feasibility and value. For a path \((h_0,h_1,\ldots,h_m)\), the displayed formulas give \[
 Q(h_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m
         f(h_j\mid h_{j-1})\,V(h_j\mid h_{j-1}).\] This discounts a locally promising subgoal when its ancestors retain little feasibility or value.
In the pinned `strategist/tree.py`, lines 57–83, |find_most_promising_leaf| performs a depth-first search and computes only

Code:
return node["feasibility"] * node["value"]

at each leaf or sequential node. The recursive return passes this score upward unchanged. No ancestor product is accumulated. Both strategy-tree refinement and default final selection call this method in `strategist_agent.py`. The prompts define value relative to the parent, so the omitted factors cannot generally be absorbed into the stored value.
## Check on an actual released tree

The supplied provides a decisive non-synthetic example. Treat sequential nodes as terminal candidates, exactly as the released selector does. Root feasibility and value both equal one. Each relevant field is a finite number in \([0,1]\). Applying the two explicitly specified arithmetic rules to the same JSON gives:
Candidate | Leaf-only score | Root-path score

For example, the survival plan has local \(f=0.6\) and \(V=0.866666\ldots\), giving \(0.52\). Its parent has \(f=0.9\) and \(V=0.7\), so the paper’s score is \(0.9(0.7)(0.52)=0.3276\). Direct hunting is a root child with score \(0.7(0.6)=0.42\).

The released selection arithmetic therefore chooses survival (node 11); the stated root-relative rule chooses hunting (node 2). Both maxima are strict, so neither tie handling nor floating-point rounding explains the difference. The independent script reads only JSON data and computes both formulas; it does not import or execute `Tree`.
## Counterevidence and historical scope

This mismatch does not change every tree’s best candidate. The corresponding reflected easy tree and both supplied medium variants retain the same top candidate under the two rules. Those controls are included in the evidence output. Further, command-line `–branch_i` or `–node` choices can bypass automatic selection during training. The source’s `Config.tree_file` points to `tree.json`; separate reflection files exist, but their role in each historical run is not reconstructed here.

If the stored fields were already root-relative, a leaf-only product could be appropriate. That interpretation conflicts with the parent-relative value description and with Equation [eq:priority] (#eq:priority); it would require a different representation and an explicit conversion. It is not a resolution of the current paper–code discrepancy.

The paper also leaves a related selection provenance question. Section 5.2 says that the top two modified-Crafter strategies are selected by feasibility and value, but Tables 9–10 rank Craft, Hunt, and Breed in that order, while the main medium comparisons emphasize Hunt and Breed. Figure 3 and the post-generation reflection step provide possible evidence of different ranking stages. Without stage-specific run records, the discrepancy is recorded as Needs Evidence about the historical selection procedure, not as proof of post hoc cherry-picking.
## Dependency, severity, and repair

The issue is Major for the released automatic selection implementation. The ranking rule directly determines which strategy branch is refined or chosen for reward shaping, a central algorithmic decision. The actual supplied tree demonstrates a different chosen strategy, not merely a numerically different unused field. The paper’s intended algorithm and its release therefore disagree at a core step.

Multiplying the local factors along each root-to-candidate path restores Equation [eq:priority] (#eq:priority) for a fixed tree and declared parent-relative attributes; the calculation above verifies that specific repair. A log-domain implementation could avoid underflow. This repair does not validate LLM estimates, establish the historical experiment commit, or predict revised learning curves. Those would require separate provenance and experiments.
# Problem 3: evaluation changes the training environment mid-rollout
## Source claim and implementation
The experimental procedure and Appendix B.5 describe ordinary PPO training with periodic evaluation. In |strategist/rl_agent.py|, `RLAgent.train`, lines 229–235, sets

Code:
eval_env = self.env

and supplies that object to the callback. At each logging interval, |WandbCallback._on_step|, lines 93–137, resets this environment and steps it through the evaluation episodes. The provided PPO configurations use a 20,000-step logging interval and ten evaluation episodes.

In `custom_ppo.py`, the training environment step occurs at line 188. The callback runs at lines 193–195. Only afterward does the collector store the transition and assign the saved `new_obs` to `self._last_obs`, at lines 220–229. There is no restoration of the environment’s state or synchronization of the learner’s cached observation after evaluation. Passing the same object creates an actual state mutation, even if a vector wrapper surrounds it for training.
## Complete mechanism check

Let \(s_{t+1}\) be the state just reached by a training step. The collector saves its observation. The callback then resets the same underlying environment and completes evaluation trajectories, leaving its state at \(s_{\rm eval}\). The next training action is chosen using the saved observation of \(s_{t+1}\) but applied to \(s_{\rm eval}\).

An independent four-state deterministic fixture makes the inconsistency explicit. Let the sole action implement \(T(s)=(s+1)\bmod4\). Suppose training has just observed \(0\to1\). An evaluation segment resets to zero and stops at state three. The cached training observation remains one. The next actual transition is \(3\to0\), while the learner can record it as \(1\to0\); the valid transition from one is \(1\to2\). Thus the recorded transition has probability zero under the stated transition kernel. A real environment that forbids stepping after an episode ends can instead raise an error. The exact symptom depends on its wrapper, but the uncoordinated mutation remains.
This fixture checks the object-sharing mechanism only. It is not a Crafter simulation, and no author callback or training loop was run.
## Scope, severity, and repair

The issue is Minor at the supported evidentiary level. It is a concrete local training-integrity defect, but the supplied evidence does not establish its frequency, trajectory consequences, or material impact on the historical learning curves. Both baseline and guided training use the wrapper, so the direction of any comparative bias cannot be inferred. A common defect does not make either trajectory stream valid, yet it also does not demonstrate an unfair advantage for one method.

Constructing an independent evaluation environment prevents evaluation from mutating training state. That separation restores the state-consistency requirement for this mechanism. A proper regression would also check wrapper/reset behavior and evaluation seeds. Such an integrated test was not performed under the no-author-code-execution constraint. No corrected PPO result is claimed.
# Remaining scientific scope and overall dependence
## What the empirical evidence establishes

The paper supplies strategy-specific behavior measurements in addition to scalar returns: saplings supplied to cows, achievement counts, and relevant skill milestones. These are useful checks that guidance affects behavior rather than only a reward label. The medium breeding results are qualified by incomplete success across runs, including three successes in eight PPO runs under the reported schedule. This limitation is visible in the tables and should remain part of the conclusion.

The observed feasibility proxy is a maximum normalized shaped score, while formal feasibility is probability mass on implementable policies. The observed value proxy is an achieved maximum reward, while formal value compares optimal returns within strategy supports. Their plots compare heuristic proxies, not calibrated estimators of the formal quantities. Sections B.2.2–B.2.4 acknowledge heuristic estimates and future feedback updates. No theorem about their calibration is established.

The N=3 EDE and N=8 PPO summaries and displayed confidence bands are descriptive evidence under the authors’ aggregation choices. Without seed-level data, this review cannot reconstruct the confidence-interval computation, check seed independence, or verify every statement of statistical significance. These unresolved checks are not promoted to supported errors.
## Interaction budgets and reproducibility

Appendix B.4 states that the reward model uses 4,000 frames from 200 trajectories of pretrained PPO agents and 1,000 expert-demonstration frames. The released collection code refers to 500,000-step and three-million-step PPO checkpoints. Thus the shaping pipeline uses task-specific offline experience in addition to the plotted online training steps. The experiments can fairly measure downstream online sample efficiency given that prior; they do not by themselves establish a smaller total environment-interaction budget from scratch. Neither the checkpoint creation cost nor its amortization across strategies is resolved here.

The default released configuration also differs from the experimental settings: it contains a 5,000-step training value, 10,000 annotation samples, GPT-4o, a human-data ratio of one, and a short linear schedule. Command-line overrides are supported, so these defaults do not prove that the paper used the wrong settings. They show why exact run configurations and provenance are necessary for replication. The snapshot refers to missing checkpoint paths and an imported |test_reward_function| module not included in the supplied inventory. These are reproduction limits, not evidence that the reported runs never occurred.
## Dependence and surviving conclusions

Problem 1 affects the claimed automatic realization of formal specificity. Problem 2 affects the operative automatic choice of strategy in the released algorithm. Neither refutes the valid conditional finite-policy analysis. Problem 3 concerns a separate local rollout mechanism and has a more limited demonstrated impact.

The experiments may still support the empirical usefulness of their actual strategy-guided reward functions. Determining how they relate to the paper’s selection algorithm requires historical tree stages, selected-node records, exact configurations, and code versions. Determining revised performance after implementation repairs requires new experiments. No later-version comparison or comprehensive erratum search was conducted; no absence of an erratum is asserted. Author adoption and final scientific adjudication remain pending.

report: Abstract: This review checks the published nonparametric construction, retrieval guarantees, capacity argument, and corresponding released implementations. Five substantive problems are established: finite sample constraints are promoted to neighborhood guarantees and a prescribed softmax map is identified with an incompatible regression optimum; the printed retrieval bound is false; the universal sparse-versus-dense comparison is false and its convergence argument does not follow; the radius used in the capacity proof makes its required separation event impossible in the stated spherical setting; and released sparse implementations retain positive weights on excluded memories. The supported overall assessment is Major. These are initial AI-generated scientific findings, with adjudication pending; numerical benchmarks have not been reproduced.
Date: 24 October 2026
Title: Scientific Review of Nonparametric Modern Hopfield Models
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed article is J. Y.-C. Hu, B.-Y. Chen, D. Wu, F. Ruan and H. Liu, Nonparametric Modern Hopfield Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 24232–24269, assigned ID I25-43568 (0199) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the article’s printed pages 1–38. The acquired PDF SHA-256 is

Its embedded appendices were examined, with detailed checks of Sections 3–4 and Appendices D.1–D.8. Sections 1–2, Appendix B, the family and layer constructions in E–F, and the experimental design and reported results in G were also read. The source snapshot is |MAGICS-LAB/NonparametricHopfield|, commit |13ce6a8d9bec319beb8cb7f21ce42fc5eae32489|, dated 8 January 2024 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Relevant kernels, model wiring and retrieval entry points were inspected statically. No author code, training, GPU benchmark or dataset experiment was executed.

The official arXiv record, checked on 24 October 2026, lists v2 of 9 June 2025 as the latest version and identifies it as the camera-ready version [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}]. No separate correction was identified in that record or the inspected repository documentation. This bounded version check does not establish absence of every possible erratum. The acquisition manifest records the separate OpenReview supplement as unavailable because its metadata API returned 403; the complete embedded supplement was available.
# Definitions and assessment

Equation reference: eq:map. Write \(\Xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_M)\), with \(\xi_j\in\mathbb R^d\), \(m=\max_j\left\lVert \xi_j\right\rVert\) and \[R=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}\left\lVert \xi_i-\xi_j\right\rVert,\qquad
 S_\mu=\{x:\left\lVert x-\xi_\mu\right\rVert\le R\}.\] For uncontaminated memories, the displayed sparse map is \[
 T_\mathcal M(x)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal M}p^\mathcal M_j(x)\xi_j,\qquad
 p^\mathcal M_j(x)=\frac{\exp(\beta\langle x,\xi_j\rangle)}
 {\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal M}\exp(\beta\langle x,\xi_\ell\rangle)}.\] The dense map uses all memories. All counterexamples below set the contamination to zero, retain the target memory, use \(\beta>0\), and place the query within the prescribed target ball. Thus they do not exploit the acknowledged failure mode of randomly deleting the target.

Major is used because the demonstrated failures affect the paper’s principal nonparametric identification, sparsity advantages, theoretical guarantees or implementation of the proposed model. This judgment does not require every experiment to fail, or deny that valid efficient attention mechanisms and exponential-capacity Hopfield models exist.
# Problem 1: the regression construction does not provide the stated retrieval map
## Claims and locations

Equation (3.2), Theorem 3.1 and the paragraph crossing pp. 5–6 claim that, for any feature map, fitting the finite query–memory sample gives \(\epsilon\)-retrieval for every \(x\in S_\mu\). Lemma 3.1, Eq. (3.5), further identifies the fitted regressor with the dense softmax map. The decisive proof step is on p. 20, Appendix D.2: the predetermined output memory is set equal to the vector of optimal dual coefficients divided by a feature normalization. Appendix D.3 repeats the identification for the sparse model.
## Complete neighborhood counterexample

Set \(d=1\), \(M=2\), \((\xi_1,\xi_2)=(1,-1)\), zero contamination, \(\Phi(x)=x\), \(C=1\) and \(\epsilon'=\epsilon=1/10\). The linear feature map is legitimate and \(R=1\). In the displayed problem the upper slack constraint forces \(\eta_1=\eta_2=0\). The two upper residual inequalities then give \[1-w\le 1/10,\qquad -1+w\le 1/10,
 \quad\text{hence}\quad 9/10\le w\le11/10 .\] At \(w=9/10\) all slacks may be zero. Since every feasible objective is at least \(w^2/2\), its minimizer is \(w^*=9/10\). The training errors are both exactly \(1/10\).

Now use \(x=1/2\). It lies strictly in \(S_1\) because \(|x-\xi_1|=1/2<1\). Nevertheless, \[T_{\rm SVR}(1/2)=9/20,\qquad
 |T_{\rm SVR}(1/2)-1|=11/20>1/10 .\] A finite set of constraints does not enforce the claimed uniform neighborhood property. This counterexample remains valid if the intended upper bound on both signs of slack is supplied.
## The softmax formula is not the stated optimizer

Use the same memories, \(C=1\) and \(\epsilon'=\epsilon=1/10\), with the exponential-feature construction and \(\beta=1\). Equation (3.5) would give \[T_{\rm Dense}(1)=\tanh(1)=0.7615941559\ldots.\] But the positive training residual is \(1-\tanh(1)=0.2384058440\ldots>1/10\), whereas \(\eta_1=0\). Thus the proposed map is not even feasible for the displayed optimization problem. This is not a difficulty inherent to interpolating the two samples: the exponential kernel Gram matrix on \(\{-1,1\}\) is nonsingular, and positive finite feature normalizations preserve this property.

The representer identity in Theorem 3.1 leaves data-dependent dual coefficients in the solution. It does not allow the labels, which were fixed before optimization, to be redefined afterward as those coefficients. Nor can arbitrary choices of \(C\) and the error tube disappear without an additional argument.
## Counterevidence, impact and bounded repair

The Taylor expansion of the exponential dot-product kernel in Lemmas D.2–D.3 is valid. A normalized kernel smoother with memory values can indeed reproduce Eq. [eq:map] (#eq:map); that useful algebraic construction is not a proof that this smoother minimizes Eq. (3.2). The finite training constraints can support training-point error statements, not a uniform statement on \(S_\mu\) without additional conditions. The natural bounded correction is to retain the learned dual coefficients when describing an SVR solution, and state the normalized kernel smoother as a separately defined model. Establishing a regression optimization that yields the prescribed memory coefficients, and its neighborhood guarantees, requires a new derivation. The present defect is Major because the nonparametric identification is the central construction.
# Problem 2: the printed sparsity-dependent bound is false
## Claim and counterexample

Equation reference: eq:printed. Theorem 4.1, Eq. (4.1), p. 8 bounds the retrieval error by \[
 m(M+k-2)\exp\left\{-\beta\left(
 \langle\xi_\mu,x\rangle-\max_{\nu\ne\mu}\langle\xi_\mu,\xi_\nu\rangle
 \right)\right\}.\] The second inner product was confirmed in the rendered original PDF; it is not an extraction artifact.
## Proof defect and a valid limited replacement

Appendix D.4 instead introduces query-dependent competitor products, but also replaces restricted-support softmax weights by weights with a denominator over all \(M\) memories. Those denominators differ when \(k<M\). A valid elementary bound for Eq. [eq:map] (#eq:map), with \(k\ge2\) and \(\mu\in\mathcal M\), is obtained by defining \[g_\mu(x)=\langle x,\xi_\mu\rangle-
       \max_{j\in\mathcal M\setminus\{\mu\}}\langle x,\xi_j\rangle.\] Indeed, with \(q=(k-1)e^{-\beta g_\mu(x)}\), \[\left\lVert T_\mathcal M(x)-\xi_\mu\right\rVert
 \le 2m(1-p^\mathcal M_\mu(x))
 \le \frac{2mq}{1+q}\le2m(k-1)e^{-\beta g_\mu(x)}.\] The first inequality is the triangle inequality applied to \(\sum_{j\ne\mu}p^\mathcal M_j(\xi_j-\xi_\mu)\); the second follows by bounding the sum of competitor-to-target exponential ratios by \(q\). For \(k=1\) the retrieval error is zero. This repair is proved here only for uncontaminated keys and the displayed restricted softmax. It does not restore the paper’s noisy-key assertions or the other corollaries automatically.
The location of an erroneous inner product may be typographical in origin, but its quantitative consequence is substantive. The main guaranteed bound is false, supporting Major.
# Problem 3: sparse reweighting need not improve the actual retrieval error
## Claim and all assumptions

Corollary 4.1.1, p. 8, asserts \(\left\lVert T_\mathcal M(x)-\xi_\mu\right\rVert\le\left\lVert T_{\rm Dense}(x)-\xi_\mu\right\rVert\) for any \(x\in S_\mu\) and retained target. Use three nonzero, equal-norm memories in \(\mathbb R^2\): \[\xi_1=(1,0),\quad
 \xi_2=(1/2,\sqrt3/2),\quad
 \xi_3=(1/2,-\sqrt3/2).\] Every norm is one, the minimum pair distance is one, \(R=1/2\), and the target separation is \(\Delta_1=1/2>0\). Set \(x=\xi_1\), \(\beta=1\) and \(\mathcal M=\{1,2\}\). The target uniquely has the largest score. This is an admissible generic support in Definition 3.3. The tied example is not the threshold-based top-\(K\) rule of Eq. (3.8), which retains every tied score; the corollary being tested applies to general supports.
## Exact calculation

Put \(a=e^{-1/2}>0\). In the dense update, the vertical components cancel, giving \[\left\lVert T_{\rm Dense}(\xi_1)-\xi_1\right\rVert=\frac{a}{1+2a}
 =0.2740686191\ldots.\] The sparse update deletes one canceling component: \[\left\lVert T_\mathcal M(\xi_1)-\xi_1\right\rVert
 =\frac{a}{1+a}\left\lVert \xi_2-\xi_1\right\rVert
 =\frac{a}{1+a}=0.3775406688\ldots.\] The claimed inequality is reversed. This exact argument avoids zero memories, a negative separation, removal of the target, or a query outside its ball.
## Dependence and counterevidence

The increase of the target’s softmax weight is true. It does not imply a smaller Euclidean error: the direction and cancellation of the other memory vectors also matter. Appendix D.5, pp. 21–22, passes from the target coefficient comparison to the norm comparison without accounting for that geometry. Its Eq. (D.9) also writes unexponentiated scores, but replacing these by the intended exponentials does not repair the counterexample.

The claimed reduction in retrieval iterations, the transfer of one-step accuracy in Corollary 4.1.2, and the proof of Corollary 4.1.3 depend on this comparison. Appendix D.6 additionally invokes convergence to the memory itself, Eq. (D.11). For memories \(\pm1\) and \(\beta=1\), however, the dense map is \(\tanh(x)\) and \(1\) is not a fixed point; continuity precludes an orbit converging to \(1\). A squeeze inequality evaluated at a common input also does not compare two different iterative trajectories. These observations invalidate the supplied convergence proof; they do not establish that a fixed-support, uncontaminated softmax map can never converge to a fixed point.

A sufficient bound can improve with a smaller support under additional controlled gaps. Universal ordering of the actual errors is false. This is Major because guaranteed sparsity advantages are a principal contribution.

Therefore Eq. [eq:separation] (#eq:separation) is impossible. Already two antipodal unit memories give \(\Delta_{\min}=2\), \(R=m=1\), while \( eta=1\) requires \(2\ge2+\log 2\).

Taking the full-support case \(k=M\) makes this contradiction independent of possible ambiguity between a radius over the retained set and a radius over all memories. That case is explicitly included in the paper, which says the result recovers the dense model. For random distinct points on the sphere the same equality applies to each realized configuration; the stipulated event has probability zero, not the advertised positive success probability.
## Impact and possible repair

This does not prove that Hopfield models lack exponential storage capacity. It shows that the paper’s capacity derivation cannot establish it from its specified radius and separation event. A freely chosen smaller local radius may yield a useful sufficient condition, but replacing the radius changes the stated setup and requires rederiving the probability bound. In D.8 the later replacement of the \(2mR\) term by \(1/\beta\) also needs an explicit radius relation, which is not part of the stated definition. No corrected exponential-capacity constant is certified here. This is Major because capacity is one of the principal inherited guarantees claimed by the new construction.
# Problem 5: released top-\(k\) and random masking do not implement restricted support
## Static evidence and finite check

In the pinned snapshot, `layers.py`, |SparseStructured_HopfieldCore.top_k_attn|, lines 95–113, computes the largest scores, scatters them into a tensor initialized to zero, and then applies softmax over the whole score axis. Excluded scores therefore contribute \(\exp(0)=1\), rather than zero probability. In `rand_masked_attn`, lines 116–133, dropout is applied to logits before softmax, with the same zero-logit effect and rescaling of surviving scores. The model path imports this module: `models.py`, line 4, and its sparse model branches instantiate the corresponding layer; the retrieval trainer imports the same layers and models.

For a one-dimensional single-head core with scale one, norm disabled, no external mask, the top-\(k\) branch and `rand_prob=0.5`, query \(1\), keys/values \((1,-1)\) and \(k=1\), the intended restricted map returns \(1\) exactly. The released arithmetic changes logits \((1,-1)\) to \((1,0)\) and returns \[\frac{e-1}{e+1}=\tanh(1/2)=0.4621171573\ldots,\] with target error \(0.5378828427\ldots\). Both memories retain positive weights. The independent script evaluates this formula; it does not import or run the author’s implementation.
## Impact, counterevidence and correction

This establishes a wrong-model implementation in the inspected public snapshot. It does not identify which exact commit or private path produced every published figure. The separately present `layers2.py` includes dense/sparsemax alternatives; its existence does not change the inspected imports of the relevant sparse paths. The paper itself acknowledges practical limitations of random sparse kernels in Appendix G.5. That caveat concerns efficiency, whereas the present defect changes the distribution and retrieved value.

For top-\(k\), assigning excluded logits \(-\infty\) before softmax, or normalizing only the selected logits, implements Eq. [eq:map] (#eq:map) provided at least one element is retained. The two-memory fixture verifies that limited repair. A random-mask repair must retain original selected logits without dropout rescaling if it is to preserve the stated \(\beta\). End-to-end experimental effects remain unmeasured. The supported implementation issue is Major because the central sparse algorithm is replaced by a dense weighted update in these released paths; historical benchmark attribution remains Needs Evidence.
# Overall dependence and empirical assessment

The five problems concern separate links: optimization to dynamics, the error bound, relative error and convergence reasoning, capacity, and implementation. The first four are established from the published mathematical statements and explicit deductions; no empirical score decrease is required to assess them. Valid exponential-kernel expansions, the algebraic attention connection, linear-attention factorization and the possibility of efficient sparse computation survive these findings.

Appendix G reports retrieval, MNIST multiple-instance learning, real-world bag classification, forecasting and efficiency studies. Its single-step experimental restriction (Remark G.1) is material counterevidence against interpreting those experiments as a test of iterative fixed-point convergence. Supervised training curves also measure parameter optimization, not the fixed-memory recurrence of Corollary 4.1.3. The published empirical numbers have not been refuted here. To resolve their relation to the intended sparse method, the exact generating implementation, masks, seeds and raw outputs must be checked, followed by appropriate reruns after correction.

The independent check source is ; its executed output is . It uses only Python’s standard library. The actual command was the existing Anaconda Python executable followed by that script’s full path. report: Abstract: The reviewed paper introduces a common graph-conditioned interface for several prediction, generation, and decision-imitation tasks. The architecture and the reported experiments were examined together with the embedded appendix and a pinned public source snapshot. The principal finding is that the LongBench v2 table cannot represent ordinary accuracies on a common fixed test set under the disclosed protocol: its overall and difficulty-specific results require incompatible test-set compositions, even allowing for rounding. This materially compromises the stated evidence for a central cross-domain comparison and is assessed as Major within that precise scope. A separate Minor finding establishes that the released training path contains missing internal imports and an unconditional dataset-construction failure. The actual experimental code version and the explanation of the table discrepancy remain unresolved. Other numerical results, generalization claims, and the framework itself are not declared false.
Date: 24 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of Graph World Model
# Identity, reviewed version, and scope

This is the initial scientific review for 0200 / I25-43569, Graph World Model, by Tao Feng, Yexin Wu, Guanyu Lin, and Jiaxuan You [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original is the 25-page ICML 2025 proceedings PDF, PMLR volume 267, pages 16931–16955. Page references below are one-based PDF pages; the printed pages coincide with that convention. The embedded supplementary material begins on p. 14. The original PDF has SHA-256

|11ab9a14396a5dbe2a8b51d0cb7f99a3bc3c|
|f96c473d63be8a21e86557a1bb7a|.
The public repository was inspected at commit
|4b9fe29f7e8fb2e7a6162956d86f8eaeffc2516b|.

The source manifest records a complete selected repository snapshot of 63 files, with no excluded files, dated 20 September 2025. This is a released-source version, not an established identifier of the code that produced the published results.

The main paper’s method, tasks, experiment tables, graph-hop and transfer experiments, and the scientific content of Appendices A–E were read. Original PDF pages 7–9 were rendered and actually viewed to verify tables and figures. Relevant released training, model, and input-processing code was examined statically. The only executed scientific check was an independently authored program performing rational arithmetic and parsing source text with Python’s `ast` module. No author code, model, training procedure, or benchmark was executed.

The source-acquisition manifest reports that a separate OpenReview attachment could not be resolved because its metadata request received HTTP 403. The embedded appendix was available and inspected. No inaccessible attachment is claimed to have been read. The findings concern supplied and accessible evidence; they do not assert an exhaustive audit of every dependency, bibliography entry, or experimental artifact.
# The contribution and its dependencies
## Method and mathematical structure

Section 2 represents the state by a graph whose nodes can contain image, text, and table information. An action is represented by a query or instruction selecting relevant state nodes, either directly or by embedding similarity. The output can then be interpreted as a node, edge, or graph update. This is a modeling interface rather than a theorem establishing equivalence to every dynamical world model.

GWM-T first converts modalities into text. Its Eq. (1), p. 4, recursively combines a central node’s textual representation with neighboring representations using a prompt. GWM-E instead forms a concatenated feature vector \[e_v=\operatorname{Concat}(e_v^{\rm image},
                          e_v^{\rm text},
                          e_v^{\rm table}),\] with zero vectors for absent modalities. Sections 4.1–4.2, pp. 5–6, define normalized graph propagation and retain the original features together with features from multiple hops: \[\widetilde A=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2},\qquad
 X^{(\ell)}=\widetilde A^\ell X.\] With a fixed graph and defined degree normalization, multiplication by \(\widetilde A^\ell\) aggregates information along length-\(\ell\) walks. The cross-modal projector maps each retained representation to decoder conditioning tokens. The LLM objective in Eq. (5) is a conditional autoregressive loss; the diffusion objective in Eq. (4) is a conditional denoising loss. Their conditional factorization is coherent. The LLM and diffusion decoders are expressly distinct modules; the presence of two decoders alone is not a contradiction of the framework’s shared-model terminology.

The released `gwm_arch.py` contains per-hop linear projection, layer normalization, and GELU, followed by graph-token insertion. The intended training branch in `train.py`, around lines 1008–1014, freezes the model and re-enables the projector parameters, consistent in purpose with the stated projector-only training. This static correspondence does not establish successful execution, because Problem 2 identifies earlier blocking defects.
## What the experiments actually measure

The six task families contain seven reported groups when multimodal generation and matching are separated. Tables 2–8, pp. 7–8, measure image similarity, modality matching, binary user–item decisions, graph prediction, diagnosis from simulated-agent context, long-context question answering, and expert-decision imitation. These are not all direct measurements of environment rollout success.

In particular, Section 5 and Appendix A.6 expressly use BERTScore for ALFWorld decision text. A higher BERTScore is evidence about the reported imitation metric; it does not by itself certify executable plans, cumulative reward, or completed household tasks. This is a scope clarification, not a claim that the disclosed experiment is invalid merely because it is not a different experiment.

Section 5.2 and Figure 4 compare graph-hop settings with a no-graph variant. Figure 5 and Section 5.3 distinguish single-task training, transfer without target-task training, and subsequent fine-tuning on ten percent of target-task data. Those definitions should remain separate: the fine-tuned bar is not zero-shot. The inspected figure shows that the paper’s favorable zero-shot comparison with single-task training is specifically about RAG; the Agent zero-shot bars are much lower. This qualification is already consistent with the more specific discussion on p. 9.

The central empirical dependencies are therefore identifiable. The cross-domain performance claim relies on comparable evaluation protocols for Tables 2–8. The graph-benefit claim relies on the ablation setup. The transfer claim relies on target-task exclusion and split identities. Problem 1 addresses a direct numerical compatibility requirement of the RAG comparison. Other protocol uncertainties are recorded separately and are not counted as proved defects.
# Problem 1: incompatible RAG accuracies under the disclosed protocol
## Claim and source

Section 5, p. 7, identifies accuracy as the RAG metric. Appendix A.5, pp. 16–17, describes LongBench v2 as 503 multiple-choice questions divided into easy and hard categories, and states an \(8{:}1{:}1\) train/validation/test split. Table 7, p. 8, gives overall, easy, and hard results for seven methods. Its caption and Section 5.1 use these results to claim that GWM with 2k context outperforms long-context baselines and that GWM-E is superior to GWM-T on this task.

The original p. 8 image was inspected. The following are printed percentages, not values inferred from a chart: \[\begin{array}{c|rrr}
 & O & E & H\\ \hline
 \mathrm{BM25}&27.45&41.18&20.59\\
 \mathrm{GWM\text{-}T}&29.40&35.71&21.74\\
 \mathrm{GWM\text{-}E}&33.32&39.16&29.52
\end{array}\] The arXiv v1 HTML also contains these values; no correction is supplied by that version check.
## Required identity and complete check

Equation reference: eq:partition. Suppose, as in the ordinary reading of a single fixed test split and sample accuracy, that the evaluated test set is the same for every method, and that easy and hard partition this set. Let \(n_E,n_H>0\) be the category sizes, and let \(c_{m,E},c_{m,H}\) be a method’s numbers of correct answers. Write \[p=\frac{n_E}{n_E+n_H}.\] The exact percentages must then satisfy \[\begin{aligned}
 E_m&=100\,c_{m,E}/n_E, &
 H_m&=100\,c_{m,H}/n_H,\\
 O_m&=100\,(c_{m,E}+c_{m,H})/(n_E+n_H)
     =pE_m+(1-p)H_m.                     \end{aligned}\] The same \(p\) is required for all methods, regardless of model size, training procedure, answer quality, or stochastic generation.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence
Several explanations are logically possible, and the check does not identify which occurred.

First, some table entries may be transcription or aggregation errors. That would require corrected entries, but the arithmetic alone cannot identify them. Second, rows may use different test subsets. This can explain different implied difficulty proportions, but then their overall accuracies are not measurements on the common fixed test population implied by the comparison.

Third, the authors may have used an undisclosed macro-average over task categories, with different aggregation weights for overall and difficulty-specific results. Such an estimand need not obey [eq:partition] (#eq:partition); it must be defined before these columns can be interpreted. Fourth, the values may average repeated experiments over changing random splits. In that case \[\overline O
 =\overline H+\overline{p(E-H)}\] need not equal \(\overline H+\overline p(\overline E-\overline H)\), because split composition and performance can covary. Repeated stochastic predictions on the same fixed split, by contrast, preserve [eq:partition] (#eq:partition) after averaging and do not resolve the contradiction.

The paper’s inspected methods, appendix, and released files do not provide a macro-aggregation definition, changing-split protocol, per-row test IDs, or prediction records that resolve these alternatives. Therefore the established result is an incompatibility between the numerical table and the ordinary single-split accuracy protocol that is disclosed. The review does not conclude that the data were fabricated, that a particular model’s result is false, or that a corrected comparison must reverse the ranking.
## Impact, severity, and repair status

The finding is assessed as Major for the reported RAG evidence: Table 7 directly supports the central demonstration that a shared graph-conditioned model can outperform specialized and long-context competitors across task families. A comparison that cannot be reconciled with its disclosed evaluation population cannot currently carry that inference in its stated numerical form. This is a core evidence defect; a reversal of the empirical ranking or failure of every other task is not required to recognize it.

The precise corrective requirement is to supply the test example IDs, difficulty labels, generated answers, correctness rule, and aggregation procedure, then recompute all relevant columns on the declared common population or disclose and justify a different estimand. The necessary identity [eq:partition] (#eq:partition) is a verified validation condition for common-test micro-accuracy. It is not a replacement set of experimental results. No numerical repair is adopted or asserted verified. Which entries or protocols need correction, and whether the headline advantage survives, remain Needs Evidence.
# Problem 2: the released training path is not internally executable
## Claim, version, and static evidence

The abstract links the released GWM repository, and its README supplies dataset preparation and training instructions. This finding concerns only commit |4b9fe29f7e8fb2e7a6162956d86f8eaeffc2516b|. The source manifest records the repository tree as complete at acquisition; this is not a case in which the review excluded the missing internal modules.

The package initializer |gwm_e/model/__init__.py|, lines 1–3, imports |language_model.llaga_llama|, |language_model.llaga_mpt|, and |language_model.llaga_opt|. None of the corresponding Python modules or package initializers exists in the acquired tree. The language-model directory contains `gwm_llama.py` instead. Under ordinary Python import semantics, importing this package cannot load the three nonexistent relative modules merely by installing third-party dependencies.

Renaming the first import alone would not establish a working repair. In `gwm_llama.py`, line 27 imports `GWMMetaModel` and `GWMMetaForCausalLM`, but line 35 names the undefined base `GWMMMetaModel`, and line 42 names `LlagaMetaForCausalLM`. Further class references retain other names from the earlier implementation. These are reached during module/class construction, before an experiment can run.
A separate, conclusive control-flow defect occurs in |gwm_e/train/train.py|. The dataset constructor’s loop starts at line 663:

The `else` begins at line 702 and raises at line 703. Static AST inspection confirms that this is the for-loop’s `else` block, not an `if`-branch, and that the loop contains no `break`. Therefore, if all loop iterations finish normally, the constructor unconditionally raises. An exception inside an iteration also prevents successful construction. The subsequent assignment to |self.pretrained_embs| and sample-loading code is located after the unconditional raise within that block. This proof is independent of data content and does not require loading model weights or executing author code.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair

The repository acknowledges that it builds on LLaGA and LLaVA. That explains the naming context but does not make absent relative modules available in the pinned GWM package. A private working tree or a different experiment commit may have contained the intended implementations; the reviewed manifest expressly does not bind this release to the published experimental run. The missing dataset download target in the README and absence of evaluation artifacts further limit reproduction, but are not used to infer a numerical defect in the paper.

This is a supported Minor released-artifact finding. It prevents a reader from following the supplied training path as released. The present evidence does not show that these failing source bytes generated the paper’s tables, that the graph operator itself is mathematically invalid, or that reported performance is lower. Its supported dependency is the usability of the released implementation, rather than a demonstrated failure of a core scientific conclusion; the severity remains Minor even within a report whose separate empirical-evidence finding is Major.

A complete repair would require an internally consistent model package and a corrected, tested dataset constructor. Several independent failures are present, so a one-line rename or indentation change is not certified as sufficient. No author files were modified, no proposed patch was executed, and no repair is marked verified.
# Remaining claims, counterevidence, and overall assessment
## Supported scope and issues not promoted to findings

The paper’s approach provides a plausible common interface: modality encoders, graph propagation, action conditioning, and decoder-specific training are well-defined at the architectural level. The inspected propagation formulas do not contain a theorem comparable to the invalid quantitative claims sometimes encountered in theoretical work; no mathematical theorem failure was established here.

Tables 2–5 and 8 visibly contain both wins and losses. For example, the Goodreads generation and matching tables retain strong specialized baselines, while GWM has favorable entries on Multi-Modal-Paper and several other tasks. The review does not infer universal dominance from the framework description, nor treat a loss on one cell as refuting the broader possibility of a useful shared model.

The graph-hop plots show the claimed qualitative differences. Exact ablation values, seeds, input budgets, and model-capacity matching were not available in the inspected release, so the magnitude and causal attribution of each gain were not independently reproduced. The transfer experiment’s target-task exclusion is a meaningful stated condition, but the released default training list is not evidence of the separate transfer runs. Without their run configurations and checkpoints, neither leakage nor correct exclusion can be established.

The binary recommendation prompt in Table 15 asks whether a user and item should connect. Its recall/F1 table should be understood according to that task and the undisclosed negative-sampling/averaging details, not automatically as an established result on every conventional top-\(k\) ranking protocol. Similarly, the paper explicitly uses accuracy for its HIV experiment; no claim about an unreported ROC-AUC result is inferred.

There is no demonstrated test-target leakage in this review. For link and missing-modality tasks, the precise order of splitting, feature construction, removal of target information, and graph aggregation would matter. The release consumes precomputed graph embeddings rather than exposing all the preprocessing needed to resolve those questions. They remain scope limits and requests for evidence, not additional Problems.
## Versions and unresolved empirical work

The official PMLR record identifies the reviewed proceedings paper. The primary arXiv record [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}] lists v1, submitted 14 July 2025; its HTML repeats the Table 7 values checked above. This is a bounded later-version check, not a claim that every possible erratum location was searched. The later-dated released code is attributed to its own commit and is not silently substituted for a historical experimental implementation.

The reported one-quarter training time and reduced token length in Appendix E are descriptive measurements. No training or profiling was performed here, and their end-to-end inclusion of preprocessing cannot be certified from the inspected artifacts. These efficiency figures do not resolve the RAG aggregate inconsistency or the released package failures.
## Conclusion and decisions

The overall supported issue level is Major, specifically for the incompatibility in the central RAG evidence under the disclosed accuracy protocol. It does not assert failure of the entire graph-world-model framework. The release defect is independently retained as Minor. Under an alternative aggregation protocol substantiated by complete records, Problem 1’s premise and severity must be reassessed; the numerical incompatibility under common-test micro-accuracy remains an exact result.

Title: Technical Verification of ResULIC
# Paper identity, version, and scope

This report concerns Anle Ke, Xu Zhang, Tong Chen, Ming Lu, Chao Zhou, Jiawen Gu, and Zhan Ma, Ultra Lowrate Image Compression with Semantic Residual Coding and Compression-aware Diffusion, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 29626–29650 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assignment is 0201/I25-43570. The reviewed object is the 25-page publisher PDF acquired on 25 October 2026 UTC and fixed by SHA-256; no inference is made from a mutable title or URL alone. Page citations below mean one-based PDF pages, matching the article’s printed pages 1–25, not the proceedings’ continuous pagination.

The inspected scope includes the main method and evaluation descriptions, the embedded Appendix B derivation, Appendix A’s evaluation and index-coding descriptions, and the relevant released coding and inference files. Figures and table text were read for their stated scope; the decisive mathematical pages 16–18 were additionally inspected as rendered images. The empirical results were not rerun. The code is the pinned NJUVISION/ResULIC commit `2aae329852631a1dd2a0f651c3e5791659397aa0`, dated 7 May 2026 [Retained latex: \cite{code}], rather than an established historical experiment-generating commit. Existing source files and archive/member mappings were retained unchanged.
# Definitions and dependencies

Equation reference: eq:forward. Write \(a_n=\bar\alpha_n\), \(\rho=z_c-z_0\), and \[
 z_n=\sqrt{a_n}z_0+\sqrt{1-a_n}(\gamma_n\rho+\epsilon_n).\] Here \(z_0\) is the original latent representation and \(z_c=C_\Theta(z_0)\) is its compressed reconstruction. Definition 5.1 and equation (11), p. 6, specify the forward marginals. The proof of Theorem 5.2 additionally stipulates independence of consecutive standard Gaussian noises after conditioning on \(z_0,z_c\). For any internal timestep of the nondegenerate schedule, \(0<a_n<a_{n-1}<1\).

Equation reference: eq:kernel, eq:coeff. The reverse construction in equation (12) and Appendix B.4 instead writes \[
 q(z_{n-1}\mid z_n,z_0,z_c)
 =\mathcal N(\iota_nz_n+\zeta_nz_0,\sigma_n^2I).\] The default \(\eta=0\) sets \(\sigma_n=0\) and \[
 \iota_n=\sqrt{\frac{1-a_{n-1}}{1-a_n}},
 \qquad
 \zeta_n=\sqrt{a_{n-1}}-\iota_n\sqrt{a_n},
 \qquad
 \gamma_n=\gamma_{n-1}.\] These equations supply the CDM reverse sampler, a principal contribution, and the conditional kernel is reused in the claimed negative-ELBO derivation, equations (37)–(38), p. 18.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Incompatible conditional distributions in the core CDM derivation).  The independent-noise posterior and the deterministic reverse kernel cannot be the same conditional law.
## Source claim and suspect step

Equation reference: eq:independent. Theorem 5.2 and the subsequent paragraph on p. 6, repeated as Theorem B.2 and equation (21) on p. 16, assert \[
 q(z_{n-1}\mid z_n,z_0,z_c)
 =\mathcal N(\mu_{n-1},(1-a_{n-1})I),
 \quad
 \mu_{n-1}=\sqrt{a_{n-1}}z_0+
 \sqrt{1-a_{n-1}}\gamma_{n-1}\rho.\] Appendix B.4 then proposes equation [eq:kernel] (#eq:kernel) as another expression for this conditional. Its coefficient comparison substitutes the random marginal expression for \(z_n\) into the transition and matches the resulting marginal mean and variance. This integrates over \(z_n\); it does not establish the distribution conditional on its observed value.
## Complete check

Conditional-variance contradiction. Choose any internal timestep \(1<n<N_r\) with \(0<a_n<a_{n-1}<1\), and condition on any actual admissible pair \(z_0,z_c\). The residual definition is then automatically satisfied; no special output of the learned compressor is required. The stipulated independent standard Gaussian noises give \[\operatorname{Var}(z_{n-1}\mid z_n,z_0,z_c)
 =(1-a_{n-1})I\succ0.\] The proposed conditional kernel with the paper’s default \(\eta=0\) gives the variance \(0\) for the identical conditioning information. A nondegenerate Gaussian cannot equal a point mass. Equivalently, the independent-noise joint has \[\operatorname{Cov}(z_{n-1},z_n\mid z_0,z_c)=0,\] whereas generating the pair with the proposed deterministic kernel gives \[\operatorname{Cov}(z_{n-1},z_n\mid z_0,z_c)
 =\iota_n(1-a_n)I
 =\sqrt{(1-a_{n-1})(1-a_n)}I\ne0.\] Every condition used here is the one in the paper’s own construction. The contradiction holds for every nondegenerate internal pair of its schedule, rather than requiring a specially chosen schedule. ◻

The independent exact arithmetic in supplies an illustrative scalar calculation: \(a_{n-1}=16/25\), \(a_n=9/25\), \(\iota_n=3/4\), \(\zeta_n=7/20\). The two conditional variances are \(9/25\) and \(0\); the two cross-covariances are \(0\) and \(12/25\), while the marginal variance \(\iota_n^2(1-a_n)=9/25\) still matches. This illustration is not asserted to be a particular Stable Diffusion timestep pair. The general proof above covers the stipulated schedule.
## Alternative interpretation and counterevidence

Theorem B.3 says its coefficient equations must hold for equivalence, which can be read as a necessary-condition statement. The defect is the subsequent use of those marginal conditions to identify the reverse conditional, not merely that wording.

A separate dependent coupling can validate the deterministic transition. Let one shared \(E\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) generate \[z_n=\sqrt{a_n}z_0+\sqrt{1-a_n}(\gamma\rho+E)\] at every timestep, with the deterministic construction’s constant \(\gamma\). Each marginal remains exactly equation [eq:forward] (#eq:forward). Eliminating \(E\) gives \[z_{n-1}=\iota_nz_n+\zeta_nz_0.\] This is an exact marginal-preserving construction. It abandons the conditional independence of Theorem 5.2. The inspected passages do not distinguish such a new joint from the independent-noise joint before identifying their conditionals. Independently sampled training marginals and a different sampling joint can coexist, but their probabilities must be distinguished.
## Impact and supported correction

The assessment is Major: the invalid identification supplies the core CDM reverse derivation and is reused by the ELBO argument. If the stated independent conditional is compared with a zero-variance model kernel, the KL divergence is infinite, not the displayed finite squared-error surrogate. A positive-variance model or a separately defined joint would require its own derivation.

The shared-noise construction above restores exactly the deterministic marginal-preserving transition. It is a partial mathematical repair, not a verification of the complete stochastic construction, ELBO, learned loss, or experiments. The finding does not show that the sampler is unusable or that the reported images and compression gains disappear.

Problem 2 (Uncharged decoding information in the released text coder).  The pinned implementation’s counted text payload is insufficient to reconstruct its encoded token indices without caption-dependent side information.
## Source claim and precise implementation

Equation (2), p. 4, defines total rate as \(R=R_c+R_{z_c}\). Section 4.2, p. 5, and Appendix A.3, p. 13, describe index coding as an efficient way to transmit text conditioning; Figure 16, p. 15, compares its bit costs with zlib. The paper does not itself state that semantic bits are omitted.

In the pinned release, , lines 22–49, constructs a per-input character histogram, sorted alphabet, and cumulative distribution from a decimal representation of token indices. Lines 52–66 pass numeric symbols and the CDF to the arithmetic encoder, then return `encoded_bytes`, `cdf`, and `unique_chars`. Lines 68–76 require all three objects for decoding. In , lines 82–105, the decoder reuses the encoder’s CDF and alphabet in memory, while lines 100–101 charge only \(\operatorname{len}(\texttt{encoded\_data})\times8\). The analogous path occurs in , lines 93–116. These are static source observations, not executed reproduction results.
## Complete ambiguity argument

Consider valid single-index inputs \([333]\) and \([444]\) to the helper on CPU. Both indices lie within the CLIP vocabulary’s integer range. Their decimal strings are `333` and `444`; both have length three, a one-symbol alphabet, CDF \([0,1]\), and numeric symbol sequence \([0,0,0]\). Thus the numerical arguments delivered to the arithmetic encoder are identical, while the alphabets required for reconstruction are respectively \(\{\texttt{3}\}\) and \(\{\texttt{4}\}\). The encoded payload cannot distinguish the two inputs. The exact independent check records these CDFs and sequences without importing Torch, torchac, or author code.

This is an injectivity failure for the payload considered alone, not a claim about a particular byte count returned by torchac. The caption-dependent alphabet is essential in this witness. General inputs also require agreement on the probability model and sequence length. They could be serialized, made fixed and shared, or reconstructed by an explicitly synchronized model; the inspected path does not charge or establish any such mechanism.
## Counterevidence, impact, and remaining work

In-process decoding can succeed because the missing objects are passed directly from the encoder. That does not make them available to a separate decoder at the reported payload length. Conversely, the inspected release is a 2026 commit, and no evidence binds it to the 2025 numerical experiments. The paper’s actual total-rate definition includes text bits.

The supported assessment is Minor for the release-level implementation defect; the magnitude and historical provenance of any error in the paper’s core rate comparisons are Needs Evidence. A larger severity for the historical results would require the actual experiment-generating code, complete serialized streams, and rate–distortion data. No additional-bit estimate or corrected BD-rate is invented. A valid repair must implement and count a complete decoding protocol, then recompute the affected rates; that repair has not been performed.
# Clarifications and empirical boundaries

At \(n=N_r\), the paper chooses \(\gamma_{N_r}=\sqrt{a_{N_r}/(1-a_{N_r})}\). The coefficient of \(z_0\) in equation (35) therefore vanishes, leaving \[z_{N_r}=\sqrt{a_{N_r}}z_c+
 \sqrt{1-a_{N_r}}\epsilon_{N_r}.\] Consequently, the branch \(z_0=z_c\) in equation (36) is not an algebraic recovery of the original latent unless the compression residual is zero. Algorithm 2 explicitly uses the estimator \(\widetilde z_0\leftarrow z_c\), and the text says the endpoint loss is set to zero. These support a legitimate initialization and masking convention. This is recorded as a scope clarification rather than an independent false-algorithm claim.

The empirical text discloses that the principal PerCo comparator is a reproduction and separately compares official PerCo in Appendix D/Table 8. The optional Pfo encoding cost is also explicit: \(0.10+5.77+175.29=181.16\) seconds in Tables 6–7. FID/KID are calculated on \(256\times256\) patches under the stated preprocessing. None of these disclosures establishes a further defect.

Tables 1 and 2 use different BD-rate anchors. Their percentages cannot automatically be composed, because pairwise overlapping quality intervals may differ. Without the raw curves and integration intervals, cross-anchor disagreement is unresolved rather than a demonstrated error. Dataset-wide scores, significance, reconstruction fidelity and latency were not independently measured.
# Overall conclusion

Problem Problem 1 (#prob:posterior) invalidates a derivation closely tied to the principal method, supporting an overall Major assessment. Problem Problem 2 (#prob:rate) is independently established in the released implementation, with its historical empirical effect left unresolved. No later corrected paper or erratum was inspected; absence of a checked correction is not evidence that none exists. Author adoption has not been requested.
