Title: Technical Verification of INN-TD
# Identity and inspected version

The assigned paper is 0202/I25-43571, Interpolating Neural Network-Tensor Decomposition (INN-TD): a scalable and interpretable approach for large-scale physics-based problems, by Jiachen Guo, Xiaoyu Xie, Chanwook Park, Hantao Zhang, Matthew J. Politis, Gino Domel, and Wing Kam Liu [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. This author list is read from the actual PDF; the frozen input repeats Jiachen Guo instead of Wing Kam Liu. That metadata discrepancy does not change the paper identity or constitute a scientific finding.

The reviewed version is the 25-page ICML 2025 publisher PDF, fixed by its preserved SHA-256. All page numbers mean one-based PDF pages, which match the article’s printed numbering. The main formulation, evaluation descriptions, applicable embedded appendices, and selected released sources were inspected. Original pages 13, 21 and 23 were rendered and visually checked before grading their equations.

The paper-linked repository is `hachanook/pyinn`, branch `icml_rev`, commit (21 April 2025) [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its multidimensional data-free INN-TD solver is separately linked as a Docker image and is not present in the staged source. No container or author code was executed. The repository’s reproduction PDF describes an earlier INN article and does not supply the missing manufactured-source implementation.
# Definitions and positive checks

INN-TD represents a multivariate field as a sum of products of univariate interpolated factors: \[Ju(x_1,\ldots,x_D)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\prod_{d=1}^{D}
 \widetilde N_d(x_d)u_d^{(m)}.\] The inspected CP product/sum implementation agrees with equation (7). The nodal Kronecker-delta argument explains enforcement of prescribed nodal values when the relevant coefficients are fixed. It is not, by itself, an error theorem for all trained factorizations.

The additive and product-sinusoid Poisson pairs in Appendix E.2.1 have the stated Laplacians. Their solutions have CP rank at most \(D\) and one, respectively. Thus the high-dimensional results test favorable low-rank cases. The FEM comparison in Appendix E.2.4 measures agreement with the stated discretized FEM reference, rather than separately certified continuum error. These boundaries do not invalidate those comparisons.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Inconsistent manufactured solutions in core validation examples).  The forcing functions in three displayed benchmark specifications do not correspond to their claimed exact solutions.
## Poisson example: source claim and exact derivative

Equation reference: eq:gaussian. For \(R_{ab}=(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2\), direct differentiation gives \[
 \Delta(10e^{-R_{ab}/25})
 =\left(\frac8{125}R_{ab}-\frac85\right)e^{-R_{ab}/25}.\] At the interior point \((60,75)\), the claimed exact solution is smooth and satisfies the prescribed boundary data by definition. Its Laplacian is \[\Delta u_{\rm ex}(60,75)=-1.6+260.8e^{-164}.\] Evaluating all six terms of the printed forcing at that same point gives \[\begin{aligned}
 f_{24}(60,75)
 &=25.6e^{-10.24}+100.8e^{-164}+230.4e^{-23.84}\\
 &\quad+160e^{-146.24}-1.6e^{-32}\\
 &\approx0.000914259157897527.\end{aligned}\] Hence \(\Delta u_{\rm ex}-f_{24}\approx-1.600914259157897527\). This is a violation of the interior PDE, not a boundary-condition discrepancy or an extraction artifact.
## A lower bound on the stated problem’s solution error

Proof. Let \(e=w-u_{\rm ex}\), where \(w\) is the solution of the printed Poisson boundary-value problem. Consider the unit disk centered at \((60,75)\), lying strictly inside \(\Omega\). On this disk, equation [eq:gaussian] (#eq:gaussian) bounds the second Gaussian’s Laplacian above by \(-1.536e^{-0.04}<-1.47\). The distant first Gaussian’s Laplacian is less than \(3\times10^{-66}\) in magnitude: its squared distance is at least \(39^2+49^2=3922\), while its polynomial prefactor is bounded by \(275\).

Equation reference: eq:errorbound. The four positive terms in \(f_{24}\) can be discarded for a lower bound. Its two negative terms together have magnitude at most \[1.6e^{-28.88}+1.6e^{-156.88}<5\times10^{-13}.\] It follows that \(\Delta e=f_{24}-\Delta u_{\rm ex}>1\) on the disk. Since \(\Delta(r^2/4)=1\) in two dimensions, the function \(e-r^2/4\) is subharmonic. Its mean-value inequality yields \[\operatorname{average}_{\partial B_1}e-e(60,75)\ge\frac14.\] Both terms on the left are bounded in absolute value by \(\|e\|_\infty\); consequently \[
 \|w-u_{\rm ex}\|_\infty\ge\frac18.\] ◻
Thus the stated continuous PDE cannot support uniform errors near \(10^{-6}\) against equation (25). This is an analytic bound for the printed benchmark, not a measurement of the plotted run.
## Moving-source example: complete interior check

Equation reference: eq:moving. Appendix E.2.3, pp. 20–22, equations (46), (48)–(49), and Figure 15 concern \[u_t+k\Delta u=b,\qquad
 \Omega_x=[-10,10]^3,\quad 0<t\le0.1.\] Set \(A=1-e^{-15t}\), \(r=x-100t-5\), and \(G=e^{-y^2-r^2}\). The claimed solution is \(u_{\rm ex}=AG\), independent of \(z\). Differentiation gives \[
 u_t=(15e^{-15t}+200rA)G,\qquad
 \Delta u=4(r^2+y^2-1)AG.\] The printed source instead uses \(q=100t-x-5\) and \[b_{48}=\left[
 2(1-2y^2)A+2(1-2q^2)A
 +A(200x+1000-20000t)-15e^{-15t}
 \right]e^{-y^2-q^2}.\]

Choose the admissible conductivity \(k=1\) and the interior point \[t_*=\frac{\log2}{15}\approx0.0462098120,\quad
 x_*=100t_*+5\approx9.62098120,\quad y=z=0.\] Then \(A=1/2\), \(r=0\), \(q=-10\), and \[u_t=\frac{15}{2},\quad \Delta u=-2,\quad
 u_t+\Delta u=\frac{11}{2},
 \qquad b_{48}=\frac{1589}{2}e^{-100}
 \approx2.95560036\times10^{-41}.\] The domain, time and positive-conductivity conditions hold. No boundary interpretation can repair this interior contradiction. The two Gaussian centers differ by ten spatial units, and the time-derivative terms also disagree. Merely changing the diffusion sign does not make the displayed pair compatible.
## Elasticity example: a symmetry contradiction

Appendix E.2.6, p. 23, equations (53)–(55), specifies \[\mu\Delta u+(\mu+\lambda)\nabla(\nabla\!\cdot u)+b=0\] on \([0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,2]\), with constant Lamé parameters and homogeneous boundary data. Take the admissible integer frequencies \(n_1=n_2=n_3=1\). Writing \(c=0.000972354873786749\), the claimed displacement is \[u=c\begin{pmatrix}
 (x^2-x)\sin(\pi y)\sin(\pi z/2)\\
 (y^2-y)\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi z/2)\\
 \sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)(z^2/2-z)
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Every component vanishes on all boundary faces. Exchanging \(x,y\) exchanges the first two components, while preserving the third. The isotropic differential operator has that same symmetry for any constant \(\lambda,\mu\). Therefore its required forcing must satisfy \(b_1=b_2\) on \(x=y\).

At the interior point \(x=y=1/4,z=1\), the printed equation (54) instead gives \[b_1-b_2=-\frac{132176378437499\sqrt2}{10^6}
 \approx-1.869256270116698\times10^8\ne0.\] For example, the corresponding cross-term coefficients are \(58{,}745{,}053.109746\) in \(b_1\) and \(587{,}450{,}563.109746\) in \(b_2\); terms proportional to \(z-1\) vanish at the test point. The independent symbolic calculation verifies that the operator-component difference is exactly zero while the printed forcing difference is not.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and correction

Publication errors in the forcing expressions, with correctly manufactured sources used by the actual solver, are a plausible explanation. The public PINN scripts implement a different moving-laser source; they do not establish the formulas used for Figures 2, 10, 15 or 16. The multidimensional INN-TD solver was not available for static inspection. Consequently, the calculations prove defective benchmark specifications and invalidate their stated exact-reference interpretation; they do not prove that the historical numerical solver produced erroneous fields.

The assessment is Major. The affected examples substantiate central claims of accurate, interpretable and convergent PDE solving. Equation [eq:errorbound] (#eq:errorbound) demonstrates a material incompatibility between one stated problem and its claimed small-error reference. Appendix placement and possible ease of correction do not remove this dependency. Other consistent benchmarks and the representation itself survive.
Problem 2 (Held-out targets enter released preprocessing).  The paper-linked three-file training configuration computes target scaling from training, validation and test labels together.

In , lines 136–152, the three-file branch loads and concatenates all three splits. Lines 213–225 extract the combined targets and compute their minima and maxima; lines 226–232 apply those extrema to every split. The staged selects separate train, validation and test CSV files and sets `bool_normalize: True`.

The resulting transformation is \(T(y)=(y-m)/(M-m)\), where \(m,M\) are computed over all supplied target labels. Keeping training labels \(\{0,1\}\) fixed, replacing a held-out label \(2\) with \(100\) changes the transformed training maximum from \(1/2\) to \(1/100\). Thus the training transformation depends on held-out outcomes. This is a complete algebraic check of the release’s data flow, not an execution of that code.

Fixed physical scaling bounds chosen independently would be a valid alternative; that is not what these statements compute. The inspection does not show that test labels update retained model weights: validation/test helper calls discard prospective optimizer updates. Nor do generic two-file branches describe this three-file configuration.

This is Minor for the released evaluation protocol, with historical effects Needs Evidence. The external CSV files and original run configurations are absent. No accuracy advantage, leakage magnitude or corrected score is inferred. A suitable repair is to fit preprocessing from training labels or predeclared physical bounds and freeze it before evaluation; numerical consequences require rerunning the relevant protocol.
# Overall scope and conclusion

The manufactured-solution finding determines the overall Major assessment. Held-out normalization is a separate supported release issue, with unverified historical consequences. Low-rank scalability demonstrations do not establish arbitrary-dimensional tractability; alternating factor optimization for a general nonlinear PDE would also require a specified nonlinear linearization mechanism. These are declared scope limits, not additional established Problems.

No external interpolation convergence theorem, dataset-wide error, timing, or corrected figure was reproduced. No later erratum or revised paper was inspected, so the report makes no claim that corrections are absent.

Title: Technical Verification of Continuous Semi-Implicit Models
# Identity, version, and scope

This report concerns 0203/I25-43572, Continuous Semi-Implicit Models, by Longlin Yu, Jiajun Zha, Tong Yang, Tianyu Xie, Xiangyu Zhang, S.-H. Gary Chan, and Cheng Zhang [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The inspected source is the 26-page ICML 2025 publisher PDF, including embedded appendices. Pages below are one-based PDF pages. Its SHA-256 is

The main formulation, Algorithms 1–2, Appendix B proofs and Appendix C evaluation descriptions were read. Original pages 4, 13, 18 and 19 were also rendered and visually inspected. The staged manifest records a 404 response for the linked `longinYu/CoSIM` repository and 403 responses for separate OpenReview endpoints. No repository or additional attachment was available, and no new retrieval was attempted. These failures do not establish that no code or attachment exists.
# Definitions and results that survive

For a fixed admissible pair \(0<s<t\), write \(p=p_s\), \(q=q_\phi(\cdot;s,t)\), and \[\delta_\phi=\nabla\log p-\nabla\log q,\qquad
 v_\psi=\nabla\log p-f_\psi.\] Replacing the conditional score by its conditional expectation gives the generator objective \[F(\phi,v)=\mathbb E_q[v^\top\delta_\phi-\alpha\|v\|^2].\] The critic minimizes \(\mathbb E_q[-v^\top\delta_\phi+(1+\lambda)\alpha\|v\|^2]\). For \(\alpha>0,\lambda\geq0\), its exact response is \[v_\phi^*=\beta\delta_\phi,\quad
 \beta=\frac{1}{2\alpha(1+\lambda)},\quad
 F(\phi,v_\phi^*)=
 \frac{1+2\lambda}{4\alpha(1+\lambda)^2}
 \operatorname{FI}(q_\phi\|p).                         \tag{1}\] Equation (1) is a correct profiled-value identity. It does not equate minimization with the critic frozen to minimization after recomputing the critic for every candidate generator.

The distributional consistency argument in Proposition 3.2 is valid if zero Fisher divergence is attained. Equal smoothed marginals have characteristic functions \(\varphi_Y(a_sw)e^{-\sigma_s^2\|w\|^2/2}
=\varphi_{X_0}(a_sw)e^{-\sigma_s^2\|w\|^2/2}\). The nonzero Gaussian factor cancels and \(a_s>0\), yielding \(G_\phi(\cdot,t)_\#p_t=p_0\). Full support alone does not establish a zero minimum for a restricted family. The preceding perfectly trained qualification supports this ideal interpretation. The result is distributional, not samplewise path consistency.

For fixed \((s,t)\), uniform auxiliary error at most \(\varepsilon_f\), and the population argmin stipulated in Appendix B.3, the expansion and Young-inequality argument do yield its equation (43): \[\operatorname{FI}(q_{\hat\phi}\|p)
 \leq(1+\lambda)^2\operatorname{FI}(q_{\phi^*}\|p)
 +2\alpha^2(1+\lambda)^2(2+\lambda)\varepsilon_f^2.\] This does not prove convergence of alternating SGD to that profiled argmin.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The alternating/Nash equivalence is false in general).  Theorem 3.1’s equilibrium claim fails for a smooth admissible misspecified family.
## Claim, assumptions, and dependency

Page 4 describes equation (11) as the Nash equilibrium, says regularization bias does not transfer to \(\phi\), and states that the equilibrium of equation (15) remains consistent with (11). Theorem B.1, p. 14, expressly concerns alternating optimization. Algorithm 2, p. 13, holds critic parameters fixed on generator updates. Neither theorem assumes that the generator family contains the target; Section 3.4 explicitly retains approximation gaps.

The proof on pp. 14–15 substitutes the best-response critic separately for each generator and proves (1). That changes a frozen-opponent comparison into a profiled comparison. The following example verifies the difference with exact scores and a realizable critic.
## Complete counterexample and independent calculation

Use one-dimensional diffusion \(dX_t=dB_t\), with \[p_0=N(0,3/4),\quad a(t)=1,\quad \sigma(t)=\sqrt t,\quad
 s=1/4,\quad t=1/2,\quad T=1.\] Thus \(p_s=N(0,1)\) and \(q_{\rm mix}=p_t=N(0,5/4)\). Choose \[G_m(x_t,t)=m,\quad m\in[19/20,1],\qquad
 q_m(x_s\mid x_t)=N(m,1/4).\] This is an explicit special case of the semi-implicit kernel in equation (18). Its mixing input is unused, which is not excluded. All densities are positive and smooth; all displayed expectations are finite. The theorem allows this compact parameter family and diffusion schedule. Set \(\alpha=1/2,\lambda=1\). Then \[\delta_m(x)=3x-4m,\qquad
 v_m^*(x)=\tfrac32x-2m,\qquad
 \operatorname{FI}(q_m\|p_s)=m^2+\tfrac94.\] The affine critic is its unique best response because \[\mathbb E_{q_m}[-v\delta_m+v^2]
 =\mathbb E_{q_m}(v-\delta_m/2)^2-\tfrac14\operatorname{FI}(q_m\|p_s).\] The Fisher minimizer is therefore \(m_{\rm FI}=19/20\).

The distinction is also present in local gradients. For a frozen response indexed by \(r\), \[F(m,v_r^*)=\tfrac{27}{32}-\tfrac{21}{8}m^2+5mr-2r^2,
\quad
 \left.\partial_m F(m,v_r^*)\right|_{r=m}=-\tfrac14m,
\quad
 \frac{d}{dm}F(m,v_m^*)=\tfrac34m.\] The signs differ. These exact identities were independently recomputed with SymPy 1.13.3 using Gaussian moments; no author code was run.
## Counterevidence, impact, and verified repair

The profiled identity (1) is correct. If \(p\) is representable, \(q=p,v=0\) is a Nash equilibrium. Moreover, any \(q\ne p\) with its exact response has positive profiled loss, whereas switching the generator to \(p\) with that critic fixed gives \(F(p,v_q^*)=-\alpha\mathbb E_p\|v_q^*\|^2\leq0\). Thus the ideal realizable equilibrium result survives when these expectations exist.

The impact is Major: a false general equivalence justifies the central regularized alternating objective, including the approximation setting discussed by the paper. This does not require an observed image-quality loss and does not establish failure of the reported networks or experiments. A verified bounded correction is to state (1) as a theorem about global minimizers of the profiled objective, or add realizability for the equilibrium claim. Neither correction supplies convergence of Algorithm 2.
Problem 2 (Reported regularization lies outside the stated theorem domain).  The main training setting is not covered by the written parameter assumptions.
## Evidence and boundary

Theorem 3.1 requires \(\lambda\geq0\), and Proposition 3.4 uses \(\lambda>0\). Algorithm 2, p. 13, specifies \(\alpha=1.2\) and \(\alpha(1+\lambda)=1\), hence \(\lambda=-1/6\). Appendix C, p. 20, fixes the same \(\alpha\) and varies \(c=\alpha(1+\lambda)\): \[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
c&1/2&3/4&1\\ \hline
\lambda&-7/12&-3/8&-1/6\\
(2c-\alpha)/(4c^2)&-1/5&2/15&1/5
\end{array}\] All three values are outside the nonnegative domain. However, the main \(c=1\) setting retains a positive profiled Fisher coefficient. The quadratic value identity extends positively to \(\lambda>-1/2\). The \(c=1/2\) negative coefficient is consistent with the pathological fused-loss behavior already discussed on p. 4.

This is a Minor theory-to-setting scope discrepancy. State the actual negative parameter and prove any desired extension separately, particularly for error bounds. Failed experiments or reversed main-setting profiled minimizers do not follow from this discrepancy.
Problem 3 (The VE identity-map composition uses the wrong time).  The identity used to motivate the approximation-gap scale is false for the stated VE schedule.
## Exact check and bounded consequence

After equation (44), p. 17, the paper identifies the identity-map output with \(p_{t+s}\). For the VE schedule in equation (56), p. 18, \(a(t)=1,\sigma(t)=t\), identity generation instead gives \[X_s'=X_0+tZ+sZ',\qquad Z,Z'\ \hbox{independent standard Gaussians}.\] Its distribution is \(p_{\sqrt{t^2+s^2}}\), not \(p_{t+s}\). With bounded-support clean data \(p_0=\delta_0\), \(s=1,t=2\), and \(T\geq3\), the actual law is \(N(0,5)\); the claimed law is \(N(0,9)\).

The homogeneous OU/VP schedule does possess the required semigroup identity. Assumption 3.5 is independently imposed, so this does not falsify its inequality or Proposition 3.4. The impact is Minor, confined to the displayed VE justification. Replacing the equality by root-sum-of-squares time is verified; a revised approximation-gap bound needs separate work.
# Remaining checks and limitations

Appendix B.4 was inspected, but the complete clean-output Wasserstein theorem is Needs Evidence. Original equation (49) changes \(W_2\) into expected squared norms without square roots. A valid coupling step is \[W_2(q^{k+1},p_\delta)
 \leq a(\delta)L_G(t_k)W_2(\operatorname{Law}(z_k),p_{t_k})
      +W_2(q_\phi(\cdot;\delta,t_k),p_\delta).\] The OU forward coupling then supplies its time factor. This locally repairs norm bookkeeping, but does not establish the later clean-output conversion or feasibility of \(t_{\rm mid}\leq T\). A generic triangle-inequality conversion, for clean output \(\mu\) and its smoothed law \(\nu_\delta\), is \[W_2(\mu,p_0)\leq a(\delta)^{-1}W_2(\nu_\delta,p_\delta)
                  +2\sigma(\delta)a(\delta)^{-1}\sqrt d.\] It does not verify the smaller bias powers stated in the paper. The external LSI constant estimates were not independently audited. No false final convergence rate is asserted here on that basis.

The empirical review checked Tables 1–6, sampling steps, parameter settings, reference-image counts, training-image budgets and Appendix C. Evaluation uses 50,000 generated images. The CTM downsampling-reference adjustment is disclosed. Three networks are used in training, and only the generator at inference. The smaller L-model training-image budget explains why its listed runtime need not exceed the M model’s. No demonstrated score fabrication or unreported execution was found. A text/table FD discrepancy (56.66 versus 58.66) is local and does not support a material result reversal. No scores, checkpoints or training runs were reproduced.

Title: Technical Verification of SWE-Lancer
# Identity and reviewed materials

The assigned paper is 0204/I25-43573, SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?, by Samuel Miserendino, Michele Wang, Tejal Patwardhan, and Johannes Heidecke, ICML 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed publisher PDF contains 39 pages, including appendices. All page references below are one-based PDF pages.

The paper-linked repository is now a migration notice at commit (18 July 2025). The staged successor source is `openai/frontier-evals`, commit (12 October 2026) [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its README explicitly describes 198 offline-adjusted IC tasks, with 39 of the original 237 dropped. This later version cannot silently stand in for the paper’s historical evaluation.

The main methodology, results and relevant Appendices A.1–A.15 were read. Selected generic harness, prompt and runtime source files were inspected statically. Original pages 7, 13, 20, 22, 25 and 26 were rendered and visually checked. The staged source excludes the task CSV, issue-specific tests, bug patches and replay payloads, including issue #14958. They are also absent from the preserved selective source archive. No author code, containers, models or tests were executed.
# Metric definitions and positive checks

For binary task outcomes \(y_i\), weights \(b_i\), and \(N\) tasks, the benchmark reports \[\operatorname{accuracy}=\frac1N\sum_i y_i,\qquad
 P=\sum_i b_i y_i,\qquad
 \operatorname{earn\ rate}=\frac{P}{\sum_i b_i}.\] Thus payout weighting need not give the same percentage as unweighted accuracy. The reported totals add correctly: \[237+265=502,\quad \$236{,}300+\$264{,}500=\$500{,}800,\] \[764+724=1488,\quad \$414{,}775+\$585{,}225=\$1{,}000{,}000.\] Table 1’s Diamond baseline admits consistent integer counts: \[\begin{array}{c|rrr}
 &\text{IC successes}/237&\text{Manager successes}/265&\text{Combined}/502\\\hline
 \text{GPT-4o}&19&98&117\\
 \text{o1}&39&110&149\\
 \text{Sonnet 3.5}&62&119&181
\end{array}\] Their rounded percentages agree with the main table. The reported evaluated models remain below majority success on these tasks.

The estimator in Section 3.3, \[\widehat{\operatorname{pass@}k}
 =\mathbb E_{\rm tasks}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom nk}\right],\] correctly counts the fraction of \(k\)-subsets containing a successful attempt among \(n\) attempts with \(c\) successes. An independent exhaustive check for \(n=7,c=2,k=3\) gives \(5/7\) by both routes. This measures availability of a successful candidate, not autonomous identification of it.

For total freelancer cost \(B\), API cost \(C\), and successful-task payout \(P\), the fallback analysis gives \[s=1-\frac{C+B-P}{B}=\frac{P-C}{B},\qquad
 R=\frac{P}{C+B-P}.\] The algebra is valid under the stated cost model. The five-run price experiment need not equal Table 1’s single-run payouts. Section 3.6 explicitly discloses historical prices, API-cost accounting, variation across runs, and the verification assumption behind pass@5 savings. Those conditions limit deployment extrapolation without contradicting the conditional calculation.
# Substantive concerns requiring evidence
Problem 1 (Subgroup tables need identifiable run correspondence).  Several subgroup results cannot be partitions of the same outcomes as the main baseline.
## Claim, assumptions, and exact calculation

Table 3 (p. 13) presents Diamond pass rates by nature of work; Table 4 on the same page partitions tasks by creation date. The relevant subgroup sizes sum to the Table 1 populations. Under the interpretation that these are breakdowns of its baseline runs, every group’s integer success counts must sum to the baseline count.
Independent enumeration of all integer counts consistent with the displayed rounding gives:
Breakdown | Implied successes | Table 1 successes
Table 4 Manager, GPT-4o | \(53+30=83\) | 98

For example, Table 4’s GPT-4o entries \(0.373\) on 142 tasks and \(0.244\) on 123 tasks uniquely imply 53 and 30 successes. Their combined rate is \(83/265=31.3208\%\), whereas Table 1 gives \(98/265=36.9811\%\), rounded to \(37.0\%\). o1’s analogous total is \(39.6226\%\), not \(41.5\%\). Ordinary rounding cannot bridge these differences. Sonnet’s corresponding counts do reconcile, providing a useful control for the calculation.
## Counterevidence, impact, and required resolution

Different stochastic runs could explain these tables. The paper acknowledges single-run variability, but the inspected tables do not identify different outcome vectors or run IDs. Accordingly, the assessment is Needs Evidence, not a claim that Table 1 is false.

The affected claims are the category and contamination analyses tied to these breakdowns. Provide task-level outcomes, run identifiers and model/scaffold versions, then regenerate the tables from the intended runs. No corrected baseline is inferred here. Table 4’s GPT-4o manager entries also show a pre-cutoff advantage (37.3% versus 24.4%); that observation alone cannot diagnose training contamination because cohort difficulty and run provenance are unresolved.
Problem 2 (The ZIP-code example does not establish specification–test alignment).  The paper’s own case study leaves the reason for rejecting apparently task-completing patches unresolved.
## Source claims and dependency

The IC prompt contains the issue title, description and codebase (p. 19). Human clarity reviewers are instructed to ignore issue comments and use the issue itself and repository (pp. 16–17). The displayed issue #14958 asks for a validation error when a comma is entered in the home-address ZIP/postcode field (p. 31).

Appendix A.9, p. 20, explicitly says that subsequent discussion expanded the issue to international formats and non-postal countries, and that tests assess this broader scope. On p. 22 the authors say o1’s patch would solve the particular issue, yet failed the end-to-end test because it did not implement other changes in the PR/discussion. Pages 25–26 make an analogous statement about Claude’s patch.

The shown Claude diff retains the branch `countrySpecificZipRegex`, the call to that regex’s `test`, and a format-specific error argument `zipFormat: countryZipFormat`. Page 26 nevertheless attributes failure partly to generic validation without country-specific formats. The displayed diff does not, by itself, substantiate that diagnosis.
## Counterevidence and bounded conclusion

Preserving valid international behavior may be an implicit requirement of the existing repository, and rejecting regression-inducing changes is legitimate. Omitted configuration, missing localization keys, a different historical state, or a different failing assertion could also explain the result. The case description is not a complete executable trace.

The assessment is therefore Needs Evidence for grader validity and the causal failure explanation. The actual historical issue body, repository checkpoint, patch, test assertions and failing outputs must be bound together. In particular, distinguish a failure to fix the stated bug, a regression, and omission of a later requirement. The task-specific bytes and historical rollout evidence are absent from the staged materials, so no false-negative rate, repaired patch, or change to aggregate scores is claimed.
# Release checks, interpretation, and limits

The later generic harness’s manager grader compares the selected proposal ID with the stored reference ID; both task types award stored price times correctness. The IC grader reuses the rollout computer and reruns tests to mitigate nondeterministic failures. This is a static observation about the pinned later source, not verification of historical test behavior or immunity to tampering. The paper’s qualitative claim that end-to-end grading is more robust does not substitute for an adversarial integrity test; none was performed here.

Manager accuracy measures agreement with a historical proposal selection, not proof that every other proposal is technically wrong. The paper acknowledges multiple plausible proposals and reports a separate 99% validation agreement. The annotation records were not available for independent review. Single-repository coverage, text-only input, possible training contamination and preliminary open-model scaffolding are disclosed limitations. The appendix’s isolated screenshot-ingestion wording is inconsistent with its text-only specification, but it does not establish which inputs a historical run actually received.

The $1 million is arithmetically a sum of benchmark task weights. The construction can generate IC and manager tasks from one original issue. Without the task/payment mapping, this review cannot establish either duplication or uniqueness of historical cash transfers. No double-counting defect is asserted, and benchmark awards are not treated as realized autonomous earnings.
# Conclusion
Item | Assessment | Repair/evidence state
Metric and headline arithmetic | No Issue Found | Checked within stated scope
Subgroup run correspondence | Needs Evidence | Historical run records absent
Example grader/failure attribution | Needs Evidence | Task-specific evidence absent
Scientific adjudication | Pending | Human reviews empty
Author adoption | Unknown | Not requested
The unsaturated-benchmark observation survives the checks performed. A stronger claim that these evidence gaps invalidate the main scores is not supported by the accessible material.

The parent independently read the critical evidence, performed calculations, inspected source-page images, compiled the final TeX and visually inspected every final report page. Three native auxiliary agents independently reviewed quantitative, empirical and static-code aspects. They are AI cross-checkers, not human reviewers. The exposed parent model is GPT-6 Astra Pro; auxiliary model identifiers and a conversation URL were not exposed. No new downloads, software installations, paid calls or author-code execution occurred.

Title: Technical Verification of Vector Grimoire
# Identity, version, and scope

The assigned paper is 0205/I25-43574, Vector Grimoire: Codebook-based Shape Generation under Raster Image Supervision, by Marco Cipriano, Moritz Feuerpfeil, and Gerard de Melo, ICML 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed publisher PDF has 28 pages. Page references mean one-based PDF pages.

The staged repository `potpov/VectorGrimoire` is pinned to , dated 12 July 2026 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. It is a later release, not an established publication-time implementation. Its selective source archive and all 82 member mappings were preserved and checked. Datasets, checkpoints and historical experiment outputs were not acquired or executed.

The main method and results, relevant Appendix A.1–A.19 text, Tables 1–12 and selected implementation paths were inspected. Parent image checks covered original pages 4, 8, 9, 15, 17 and 20, including metric tables, the SDS comparison and geometric-loss illustrations. Other qualitative panels were not exhaustively visually audited.
# Representation and objective checks

The finite scalar quantization cardinalities are correct: \[|V|=7\cdot5^4=4375,\qquad |V|+256^2+3=69\,914.\] Sharing consecutive cubic Bézier endpoints gives \(2(3\nu+1)\) coordinates for an open connected path and \(2(3\nu)\) for a closed path. The separation of shape tokens and global positions is explicit. The paper acknowledges quantization displacement, fragmentation and path postprocessing, rather than claiming exact whole-image reconstruction.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Released Fréchet evaluators use incompatible CLIP intensity scales).  The Grimoire and baseline feature pipelines do not apply the same preprocessing under the declared dependency versions.
## Claim, code path, and operative conditions

Sections 5.1–5.2 and Appendix A.12 use CLIP-image features for the reported Fréchet metric. This is a disclosed CLIP-feature distance, not conventional Inception-feature FID. A comparison requires a common feature mapping for all methods.

The release pins `torchmetrics==1.0.1` and `transformers==4.31.0`. Its , lines 66–91, constructs `FrechetInceptionDistance(feature=wrapper, normalize=True)`, but the wrapper calls the CLIP processor with `do_rescale=False`. The same combination appears in , lines 165–189, and , lines 60–85. In contrast, , lines 95–119, uses the same Fréchet normalization flag but leaves CLIP rescaling at its default.

The loaders and raster conversion paths use floating \([0,1]\) tensors. Official TorchMetrics source version 1.0.1 applies \[b=\operatorname{uint8}(255x)\] before passing the tensor to any feature module, including the custom wrapper [Retained latex: \cite{tm}]. No author wrapper divides this value by 255. The official Transformers 4.31.0 CLIP processor defaults to rescaling by \(1/255\) before mean/standard-deviation normalization [Retained latex: \cite{hf}].
## Independent decisive calculation

Consider a spatially constant white RGB image, so resizing and cropping do not alter its values. Float input \(x=1\) becomes byte \(b=255\). With default CLIP red-channel mean \(\mu=0.48145466\) and standard deviation \(\sigma=0.26862954\), \[z_{\rm Grimoire}=\frac{255-\mu}{\sigma}\simeq947.4704,
 \qquad
 z_{\rm default}=\frac{255/255-\mu}{\sigma}\simeq1.9303.\] For float half-intensity, byte conversion gives 127, with red-channel normalized values approximately 470.9778 and 0.06174. The black case agrees, showing why checking only zero pixels would miss the defect. Independent scalar calculations reproduce these values without executing author code or downloaded dependency code.
## Impact, counterevidence, and bounded correction

The evaluators apply different preprocessing maps, so their outputs cannot be interpreted as scores from one common intended CLIP feature pipeline. Both real and generated images pass through each evaluator’s own map; that symmetry does not make cross-evaluator feature definitions identical.

The supported impact is Minor, confined to the acquired release. The historical environment and entrypoints producing the paper’s tables are unbound, so published rankings and numerical changes remain Needs Evidence. No CLIP weights or image features were computed, and no numerical change in Fréchet distance is claimed.

A verified local correction is to restore the processor’s \(1/255\) rescaling after TorchMetrics’ byte conversion, consistently across evaluators. Another option is an explicitly shared floating-input feature pipeline with redundant conversion removed. Only the input-unit correction is established; complete evaluator execution and table recomputation remain outstanding. Author source files were preserved without modification.
Problem 2 (PSNR needs a reference protocol to support the distribution comparison).  The ancillary SDS comparison lacks the correspondence needed to interpret its quantitative evidence.
## Claim and missing information

Section 5.4 and Table 4, p. 8, use PSNR on 20 generated User samples to argue that alternatives fall farther from the target dataset distribution. Values are 45.19 dB for Grimoire, 28.68 for CLIPDraw, 36.62 for VectorFusion, and 34.53 for SVGDreamer. The inspected text and acquired source do not specify reference-image pairing, alignment, pixel range or aggregation. Static searches found no PSNR evaluator.

For reference \(X\) and generated image \(Y\), PSNR depends on a paired error and specified range \(R\): \[\operatorname{PSNR}=10\log_{10}\frac{R^2}{\operatorname{MSE}(X,Y)}.\] Under independent pairing, \[\mathbb E\|X-Y\|^2
 =\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_X+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_Y
  +\|\mu_X-\mu_Y\|^2.\] A generator collapsed to \(\mu_X\) has expected MSE \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_X\); an independent correct generator has \(2\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_X\). This illustrates why paired fidelity alone is not a distributional guarantee. It does not assert that the authors used this pairing or aggregation.
## Assessment and required evidence

The assessment is Needs Evidence. Supply the evaluator, reference/generated sample list, pairing and range definitions, and explain what aspect of distributional matching is measured. Figure 10 visibly illustrates a style difference among its selected samples; it does not determine the missing quantitative protocol. Reconstruction MSE and other comparisons remain separate evidence.
# Empirical boundaries and local clarifications

The paper does not show universal metric dominance. Table 3 reports cases where filled Im2Vec has lower CLIP-feature Fréchet distance, Appendix A.10 gives class-specific exceptions, and Table 7 acknowledges IconShop’s better reported metric values. Tables 1–2 favor VSQ in reconstruction MSE. These support separate judgments about reconstruction, text alignment and generative distribution.

Appendix A.5’s categorical Path Clipping ranking needs narrowing: in Table 6, FIGR-8 reconstruction favors Path Interpolation (FID 0.07 versus 0.10; CLIPScore 32.0 versus 31.97). PC does lead the displayed generation rows. This is a local comparison clarification, not evidence that postprocessing fails.

Full-FIGR-8 scores require checkpoint/cohort correspondence: Tables 3 and 7 give 0.64/29.00, while Tables 6 and 12 give 3.58/27.45 for postprocessed generation. Different configurations or cohorts may explain the difference. The timing description uses both five and 20 samples, and the CLIPDraw speed ratio is \(100.19/2.34\simeq42.8\), so a literal hundredfold advantage does not apply to every comparator.

Raster reconstruction supervision differs from absence of all vector-form preprocessing. The paper openly extracts raster contours, uses positional metadata, and skips contour extraction for vector-origin Fonts. The Fonts split unit is not fully specified, so unseen-font generalization was not independently verified. Small emoji experiments and poorer transfer/completion metrics are disclosed. No dataset leakage, metric-table repair or training result was established by this static review.
# Conclusion

Title: Technical Verification of WMAdapter
# Identity, evidence, and scientific scope

This is initial review 0206/I25-43575 of WMAdapter: Adding WaterMark Control to Latent Diffusion Models, by Hai Ci, Yiren Song, Pei Yang, Jinheng Xie and Mike Zheng Shou, ICML 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The original publisher PDF contains 19 pages, including Appendix A.1–A.8 on pp. 13–19. All page numbers below refer to this PDF.

The paper-linked repository `showlab/WMAdapter` is frozen at , dated 28 May 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its complete tree and 531-byte authoritative ZIP contain only a 60-byte README. The tree is not truncated; no implementation members were omitted by preparation. The README supplies a title and one descriptive sentence, without a migration or checkpoint link. Thus no adapter, training, metric or attack implementation is available in this snapshot. This is a source limitation, not evidence that code never existed elsewhere.

The complete paper text, tables and appendix descriptions were read. The parent also inspected original page images 6–9, 15 and 17–19, including the detection formula, attack curves, ablations and qualitative comparisons. Checks were analytical and static; no author code, model, dataset or neural metric was executed.
# Method and evidence that survive inspection

The six residual fusers in Eq. (1) map image features and a 48-bit message to a feature residual with compatible output dimensions. The embedding, channel concatenation and two pointwise convolutions give a coherent lightweight construction. Equation (2) combines explicitly weighted reconstruction/perceptual and bit-recovery losses; it is an empirical objective, not a claimed optimality theorem.

Hybrid finetuning deliberately trains both the adapter and VAE decoder, then deploys the tuned adapter with the original decoder. Sections 3.1 and 3.4 disclose this procedure. Consequently, the claim of intact diffusion components should be understood at deployment. Training the VAE temporarily is not an undisclosed contradiction. Restoring a different decoder can change watermark accuracy, and Table 5 reports that tradeoff: Adapter-I improves PSNR from 32.8 to 34.8 dB versus the untuned Adapter-B while combined-attack bit accuracy decreases from 0.92 to 0.90. No theorem promises invariant accuracy after restoration.

The contextual versus context-less ablation in Table 4 improves PSNR by \(32.8-28.7=4.1\) dB and bit accuracy by 0.02. Table 2’s nominal 17% PSNR-number increase and 22% FID reduction against Stable Signature are arithmetically consistent: \[100(34.8/29.7-1)=17.17,\qquad 100(1-2.5/3.2)=21.875.\] A percentage of a logarithmic PSNR value is less interpretable than the 5.1 dB difference, corresponding to a factor \(10^{5.1/10}=3.236\) in MSE when the peak and averaging convention agree. This is a reporting clarification, not a demonstrated metric failure.

Appendix A.1 reports three independent trials for each stage, with bit-accuracy standard deviation 0.0006 and PSNR standard deviations 0.03/0.04 dB. This supports limited training stability; it is not an uncertainty estimate for every attack or user pool. Table 3 measures closed-set identification among known enrolled keys, using 1,000 selected users and five images each. It should not be read as an open-set false-attribution guarantee.
# Substantive unresolved findings

Problem 1 (The fixed-key meaning of the advertised false-positive level is unverified).  The paper’s nominal binomial calibration does not identify the actual false-positive rate for each deployed user key without further assumptions or calibration records.
## Claim and exact calculation

Marginally fair decoder bits alone do not imply binomial matches. For a fixed key \(k\), let a hypothetical null decoder output \(Z=k\) or \(Z=\mathbf1-k\), each with probability \(1/2\). Every decoded bit is marginally fair, yet \(M\) is 48 or 0 and \(\Pr(M>40)=1/2\). This example shows the logical need for joint-distribution information. It is not an observed failure of HiDDeN or WMAdapter.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and disposition

There is an important valid alternative: if the target key \(K\) is independent and uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{48}\), then conditional on any natural-image output \(Z\), the matches \(\mathbf1\{K_i=Z_i\}\) are independent fair bits. The binomial tail then holds after averaging over keys even when decoder bits are dependent or biased. The paper’s use of randomly selected keys makes this interpretation plausible.

What remains unidentified is whether Table 2 and the query attack use this key-average interpretation, a fixed-key empirical null, or another implementation, and which integer threshold and preprocessing were used. No null-output sample, fixed-key tail calibration or detection code is available. The dependency matters to the claim that high TPR is achieved at a specified deployment false-alarm level; it does not negate reported bit accuracy or closed-set tracing.

Assessment: Needs Evidence. Supply the detector and cutoff, key-sampling procedure, null image population and calibration by key, or state explicitly that the level is only nominal and averaged over random keys. The counterexample does not warrant asserting an actual false-positive failure or a Major conclusion. A pooled search over many keys would require a separate multiple-comparison calculation; Table 3 does not itself claim otherwise.

Problem 2 (Regeneration robustness is not isolated from unequal initial image quality).  The stated comparison of PSNR drops does not by itself establish a greater absolute distortion cost for removing WMAdapter’s watermark.
## Claim, calculation, and limits

Section 4.3, pp. 6–7, concludes better regeneration robustness from a 4–6 dB PSNR drop for WMAdapter versus approximately 2 dB for Stable Signature. Figure 5 plots bit accuracy against PSNR. However, their un-attacked images begin at different quality levels: Table 2 reports 34.8 dB for Adapter-I and 29.7 dB for Stable Signature. The missing code and raw attack records prevent checking the precise PSNR reference and per-image operating points.

For peak intensity one and MSE \(e\), a drop of \(d\) dB changes MSE to \(e10^{d/10}\). A larger drop need not imply a larger absolute MSE increment when \(e\) differs. Using the reported starting values as an analytical illustration, \[\begin{aligned}
 10^{-30.8/10}-10^{-34.8/10}&=0.00050063
 &&\text{(Adapter-I, hypothetical 4\,dB drop)},\\
 10^{-27.7/10}-10^{-29.7/10}&=0.00062672
 &&\text{(Stable Signature, hypothetical 2\,dB drop)}.
\end{aligned}\] These numbers are a diagnostic identity, not reconstructed attack measurements. An MSE increment relative to a clean reference is also not generally the squared perturbation between the watermarked and attacked images, because cross terms can matter.
## Counterevidence, required evidence, and disposition

The paper’s narrower observation about larger relative PSNR drops can be correct. Its Figure 5 supplies more information than the prose alone, and better un-attacked quality is a real stated design objective. These are reasons not to infer that the architecture or all reported tradeoffs fail.

To establish an intrinsic robustness advantage, provide matched original/watermarked/attacked triples, explicit PSNR references, equal attack budgets or quality operating points, and detection success under the calibrated cutoff. A curve of mean bit accuracy alone does not determine the fraction of images above the detection threshold. Replication should distinguish total delivered quality, extra attack distortion and initial embedding distortion.
Assessment: Needs Evidence. The available comparison does not identify these quantities sufficiently to assert a corrected ranking. No numerical robustness reversal or false plotted value is claimed.
# Boundaries and further checks

The original Figure 8 and Appendix A.3 explicitly show weaknesses under rotation and Gaussian noise. Section 4.3 acknowledges near-lossless white-box removal and a query attack reaching TPR zero at approximately 8 dB PSNR. These disclosures rule out interpreting the paper as a universal attack-resistance guarantee. The claim on p. 4 that having many public decoder choices avoids serious security risk remains an informal threat-model argument, not a demonstrated secrecy mechanism.

Table 6 concerns separately trained adapters for several VAEs, followed by a stated SD2.1-to-SD1.5 transfer example. It does not establish arbitrary zero-shot transfer to unrelated decoders. Figures 6–7 and 10–12 visibly illustrate the claimed artifact differences, but selected visual panels do not establish universal artifact absence. The occasional Adapter-F grid artifacts are expressly listed as a limitation.

The 1.3 MB wording on p. 2 differs from 1.3 million parameters on p. 4; storage depends on dtype. Missing code prevents an exact parameter or latency audit. This unit clarification is not elevated to a scientific Problem. Historical checkpoints, null outputs, attack scripts and per-image metrics remain unavailable; the inaccessible separate OpenReview attachment cannot be assumed not to exist.
# Reproducibility and review provenance

The unchanged source PDF SHA-256 is . The complete source manifest, archive/member hashes, version mappings and parent source checks are retained under the assigned root. Independent standard-library calculations are in and ; original image renders are retained alongside them. No additional download or installation was needed.

The parent independently integrated the scientific conclusions and performed calculations, source-image inspection, compilation and final visual QA. Three native auxiliary agents supplied read-only mathematics, source and empirical checks. The exposed parent model label is GPT-6 Astra Pro; separate auxiliary model identifiers and an actual conversation URL were not exposed. No independent conversation or Space copy is asserted.

The final TeX is compiled twice with the actually available isolated-runtime pdfLaTeX, using the frozen mathematical-journal style. Build commands, exit codes, final TeX/PDF hashes and every-page visual inspection are recorded in the verification package. Scientific status remains `pending`; `human_reviews=[]`. This initial review does not perform acceptance adjudication.

9 H. Ci, Y. Song, P. Yang, J. Xie and M. Z. Shou. WMAdapter: Adding WaterMark Control to Latent Diffusion Models. PMLR 267 (2025), 10901–10919. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/ci25a.html. Show Lab. WMAdapter, frozen repository and member manifest, commit . https://github.com/showlab/WMAdapter.

Title: Technical Verification of ProDistill
# Identity and review scope

The assigned paper is 0207/I25-43576, Scalable Model Merging with Progressive Layer-wise Distillation, by Jing Xu, Jiazheng Li and Jingzhao Zhang, ICML 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The frozen publisher PDF has 27 pages, including proofs, experimental details, ablations and qualitative outputs. One-based PDF pages are used throughout.

The released repository is pinned to , dated 17 February 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its original archive, source hierarchy and member/version/hash mappings were preserved. This revision is not independently bound to the paper’s historical experiment runs. Checkpoints, datasets and raw outputs were not acquired or executed.

The complete paper text and mathematical arguments were read. Parent visual checks covered pages 4–5, 8, 15–16, 18–20 and 22–23. Static source inspection targeted the actual Vision/NLU merging paths, dual activation caches, NLG calibration loaders, generation/exclusion and documented evaluation route. It was not an execution of the release or an exhaustive audit of every dependency.
# Independent verification of the central mathematics
## Fixed-model hardness

Theorem 3.1, pp. 3 and 15, is valid for the constructed linear-regression task. Given a deterministic merged weight \(\widehat w\), choose an expert \(w_i\ne\widehat w\); distinct experts ensure one exists. With \(\delta=\widehat w-w_i\), take \[x_i=\frac{2\sqrt C}{\|\delta\|^2}\delta,\qquad y_i=x_i^\top w_i.\] The expert has zero loss and the merged residual is \(2\sqrt C\). Choose the other input noncollinear with \(x_i\) in dimension at least two and label it by its expert. Both equations can be interpolated by a common weight. Therefore the averaged half-squared loss of the merged model is at least \(C\), while both experts and a joint model have zero relevant loss. Relabeling which expert is attacked does not require the merging rule to be permutation invariant.
## Learned-model hardness

Theorem 3.2, p. 16, explicitly restricts the linear hypothesis class to \(w\ne0\), uses loss \(\max\{-y(w^\top x+b),0\}\), and learns a normalized maximum-margin separator. The two original task pairs on the coordinate axes give experts \(e_1,e_2\). For any nonzero merged direction, an unbounded positive point \((p,q)\) can have merged score below \(-5C\) while \(p>1\) or \(q>1\). Appending it to the corresponding task leaves that expert’s maximum-margin solution unchanged: its original opposite pair already caps the normalized margin at one.

The union remains separable. If \(p>1\), a vector \((1,\eta)\) with sufficiently small \(\eta>0\) separates all five points; the other case is symmetric. As an independent exact check, for merged weight \((1/2,1/2)\), \(C=1\), and new positive point \((2,-14)\), the five merged margins are \[(1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2,-6),\qquad \text{mean loss}=6/5>1.\] The union separator \((1,1/10)\) has margins \((1,1,1/10,1/10,3/5)\), all positive. Strict inequalities permit arbitrarily many nearby damaging points, supporting Remark A.1’s low-accuracy construction.

The nonzero-weight restriction matters: the identically zero predictor would have zero stated margin loss, but is explicitly excluded. These results are worst-case impossibility statements with unbounded inputs/loss, not proofs that each practical task needs data or that a particular few-shot sample size suffices. Remark 3.3 acknowledges the worst-case scope.
## Progressive objective and scope

Algorithm 1 correctly maintains a merged prefix and each expert’s own prefix. It is presented as a surrogate, with empirical comparison to global distillation; no theorem guarantees a global minimizer of the nonconvex objective. If all preceding layer discrepancies vanish, the input paths coincide inductively. Zero discrepancy at a single isolated layer is not enough.

The sum over \(j\) in printed Equations (1)–(2) incorrectly repeats \(\lambda_i\circ\tau_i\); Algorithm 1 and the inspected parameter-merging code correctly use \(\sum_j\lambda_j\circ\tau_j\). This is a local index correction, with direct counterevidence against treating it as the implemented method.

Elementwise scaling increases flexibility relative to scalar coefficients. If every coordinate has a nonzero task-vector entry, it can already reach the full parameter space; the reported prior then acts through initialization/optimization rather than a strict hypothesis-class restriction. This does not refute an empirical advantage.
# Verified release-level Problems

Problem 1 (NLU teacher prefixes are selected from the wrong task).  The released NLU initialization repeatedly loads the final task’s prefix, rather than each teacher’s own prefix required by Algorithm 1.

In , lines 70–71, the loop variable is `dataset`, but the call is `load_fine_tuned_model(args, dataset_name)`. The documented top-level setup leaves the global `dataset_name` equal to `rte`. Thus all eight extractors are built from RTE. The helper in selects `args.load_model_paths_dict[dataset_name]` and captures inputs to the first encoder layer. Subsequent layer loading correctly selects each individual task.

If \(E_i\) is task \(i\)’s embedding prefix and \(B_i\) its first block, the target should be \(B_i(E_i(x))\), but the release uses \(B_i(E_{\rm RTE}(x))\). These expressions need not agree. An independent scalar illustration with \(x=1\), \(E_i(x)=2\), \(E_{\rm RTE}(x)=3\), and \(B_i(z)=5z\) gives 10 versus 15. This is a logical illustration, not a BERT checkpoint measurement.

Assessment: Minor for the released implementation. The defect changes the intended teacher stream when prefixes differ. Identical prefixes on the calibration inputs would neutralize it, and the historical experiment revision and actual feature differences are unavailable. No corrected benchmark score or historical failure is inferred. The local repair is to load the current `dataset` and regenerate the cached features. Full training after that repair was not performed.
Problem 2 (Documented entrypoints do not complete their own file lifecycle).  The released Vision and NLU paths contain independently verifiable execution blockers.

The Vision script constructs a layer directory including the model name, then creates and reloads \[\texttt{layer\_save/ViT-B-32/100/0.01/64/}.\] Its save expression omits the separator between `args.layer_save` and `args.epochs`, producing instead \[\texttt{layer\_save/ViT-B-32100/0.01/64/layer\_0.pt}.\] The ordinary fresh run therefore lacks the save parent; even externally creating it would not align the subsequent reload path. This follows from the actual defaults, README invocation, directory creation and save/load expressions, without executing author code.

Separately, , line 139, evaluates `args.tag` in its cleanup path although the complete parser defines no `–tag` and the setup does not assign it. The ordinary entrypoint therefore raises an attribute error at that point before returning to evaluation. Its saved layer directory also lacks the extra tag component.

Assessment: Minor for reproducibility of this snapshot. Use one common path builder for create/save/read/cleanup, and remove the undefined extra component. These local consistency repairs are verified as path corrections, not as a successful neural training run. An unpublished corrected entrypoint could have produced the historical tables; these release defects do not establish otherwise.

Problem 3 (NLG generation does not consistently exclude calibration prompts).  The documented release path violates the paper’s stated exclusion rule for instruction evaluation and does not reliably implement it for MBPP.

Appendix B.3, p. 18, explicitly samples NLG adaptation data from test sets and excludes those samples during evaluation. The loader , lines 57–60, uses a seed-zero permutation, assigns its first `val_shot` indices to calibration and the remainder to evaluation. The merge script saves those remainder indices.

However, , lines 64–78 and 119, loads the same complete Alpaca JSON and generates every instruction using the default full range. It never consumes `instruct_indices.pt`. The complete simply concatenates the generated batches. The README then sends this combined file directly to the Alpaca evaluator. Hence the documented path retains adaptation prompts in the evaluation-output file whenever instruction adaptation used a nonempty subset of that file.

In , lines 173–179, MBPP filtering removes items from `task_ids` while iterating over that list. For IDs \([11,12,13]\), with only 13 allowed, deleting 11 shifts 12 to index zero; the iterator next visits index one, now 13, leaving excluded 12 behind. This complete iterator-state counterexample proves the filter is not generally correct. It does not assert which actual saved MBPP indices occurred in the paper. Broad fallback on missing index files additionally evaluates all examples.

Assessment: Minor for the released evaluation protocol. Use the saved remainder IDs consistently, construct a fresh filtered list, assert empty intersection with calibration IDs, and fail explicitly when required index files are missing. The calibration procedure consumes inputs, not supervised answer labels; inclusion still violates the stated holdout protocol, but does not prove answer memorization or a measured score increase. Historical generation files, actual IDs and scorer runs are missing, so the published-score impact remains Needs Evidence.
# Empirical conclusions and unresolved support

The headline gains are arithmetically correct: \[86.04-79.90=6.14\text{ percentage points},\qquad
 0.7641-0.6980=0.0661.\] Tables 1–2 support the average vision and RoBERTa comparison, with visible task-level exceptions. Appendix D.3 reports three-seed analyses and acknowledges greater NLU variability with very few samples. Figure 5 also contains a small counterexample to universal progressive superiority: at 32-shot RoBERTa, DistillMerge scores 0.7490 versus ProDistill 0.7473. The broader claim is an overall empirical comparison, not a theorem of per-setting dominance.

NLG cohort comparability: Needs Evidence. Tables 3, 9 and 10 import TIES/WIDEN scores directly from another study, while B.3 evaluates a calibration-excluded remainder. No common sample-ID and denominator binding is supplied. The raw Code+Math gap is \(0.2806-0.2723=0.0083\); the effect of different cohorts cannot be determined without per-example outcomes. In Table 9, ProDistill’s 64-shot raw average 0.2944 is lower than WIDEN’s 0.2968, while its normalized average is higher. Metric and cohort qualification are essential; no corrected ranking is inferred.

Feature versus logit supervision: Needs Evidence. Page 5 attributes this comparison to C.3, but C.3 compares hard-label cross-entropy with teacher-feature matching, not soft teacher-logit distillation. The displayed evidence supports the narrower hard-label comparison. It does not establish that the claimed feature/logit ordering is false.

Resource scope. Section 6.3 expressly excludes preprocessing and evaluation from measured training GPU memory. Layer updates avoid keeping all layers’ optimizer states, but total model storage, loading, cached data and end-to-end cost need separate accounting. The release loads whole checkpoints during some setup operations. The reported depth-independent layer working set is not an end-to-end memory guarantee. Epoch convergence does not by itself certify wall-clock savings. C.2 states equal computational budget, but the exact operational budget and raw profiles are unavailable.
The selected generated examples are final-answer illustrations, not correctness proofs for all intermediate reasoning. No model output, code generation or paid evaluator was executed in this review.
# Evidence, reproducibility, and status

The original PDF SHA-256 is . The complete frozen manifest, archive/member mapping and parent hash checks remain intact. Durable independent checks are and . They bind the critical source hashes and record static AST observations, exact theorem/table arithmetic, path comparisons and an explicitly manual iterator trace. report: Abstract: The original 48-page paper, its appendices and a pinned Audio Flamingo 2 release were inspected. The supported overall assessment is Minor: the printed loader procedures, one ablation aggregate, GPU-hour units, and released conditioning/cache logic contain specific defects. The central contrastive objective and component-level attention arithmetic have no demonstrated mathematical error in the checked scope. LongAudioBench holdout provenance and judge calibration remain Needs Evidence. No historical benchmark failure or empirical score correction was established. Scientific adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Technical Verification of Audio Flamingo 2
# Paper identity and scope

Paper 0208 / I25-43577 is Audio Flamingo 2: An Audio-Language Model with Long-Audio Understanding and Expert Reasoning Abilities, by Sreyan Ghosh, Zhifeng Kong, Sonal Kumar, S Sakshi, Jaehyeon Kim, Wei Ping, Rafael Valle, Dinesh Manocha and Bryan Catanzaro, ICML 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. All page references are to the original PDF; its printed and PDF page numbers coincide. The inspected repository is , ref , commit , dated 3 August 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. This later release is not a verified historical experiment commit. Its README also describes checkpoint update v20250625.

The review covers all paper text, principal tables and algorithms, objective and architecture, curriculum and empirical controls, generation/grading prompts, and relevant released data/model/evaluation paths. All 246 preserved archive members were byte-checked. Semantic inspection concentrates on the main loader, model wrappers, attention helpers, configurations and evaluation logic, not all 146 implementation files. Audio, checkpoints, raw predictions and historical training logs were unavailable. No author code was executed.
# Definitions, dependencies and positive checks

AF2 combines dense AF-CLAP features, three audio transformation layers, gated cross-attention and a frozen Qwen2.5 language model. The 3B designation describes the language model; Table 20 discloses 4.7B total parameters. The three-stage curriculum extends context from 3 to 9 to 30 ten-second windows.

For audio \(x_i\), let \(S(i,i)\) sum exponentiated similarities over its positive captions; \(S(j,i)\) uses another audio’s positives and \(S_{\rm neg}(i)\) uses its compositionally altered negatives. The loss on p. 4 is \[\mathcal{L}=-B^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^B
 \log\frac{S(i,i)}{S_{\rm neg}(i)+\sum_{j=1}^B S(j,i)} .\] For positive temperature and finite embeddings the denominator includes the numerator, so the probability and nonnegative loss are well-defined. The objective encourages the positive group without guaranteeing identical representations for every paraphrase; the paper asserts no such theorem. An inherited CLAP loss in an inference-oriented release does not establish which custom loss trained AF-CLAP.

The p. 4 attention calculation checks out: \(l_1=80\), \(l_2=30\cdot64=1920\) give \((l_1+l_2)^2=4{,}000{,}000\) prefix-attention pairs and \(l_1l_2=153{,}600\) conditioning cross-attention pairs. This component comparison does not remove the quadratic dependence of the three global audio self-attention layers.

Table 4 shows MMAU falling from 69.0 to 48.6 without AudioSkills while AudioCaps stays at 0.58. Tables 8, 16 and 17 test dense features, positional encoding and transformation layers. Table 6 exposes schedule tradeoffs; Table 1 openly contains losses on CochlScene, NSynth instrument classification and UrbanSound8K. These are useful controls and counterevidence to a universal-win interpretation, but their experiments were not reproduced.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Printed sampling and batching do not implement the stated loader).  Minor: verified published-procedure defect.
## Claim, assumptions and location

H.2 (p. 21) attributes proportional sampling, useful length grouping and a padding reduction from 58% to 16% to Algorithms 1–2 (pp. 24–25). Algorithm 1 permits a nonempty bucket of size \(n\), positive weight \(w\), and integer epoch \(e\geq0\). Assume readable files and the displayed ascending loop’s ordinary meaning.
## Analysis and counterevidence

The printed endpoints are \[a=\lfloor enw\rfloor\bmod n,\qquad
 b=\lfloor(e+1)nw\rfloor\bmod n .\] The loop visits \(a,\ldots,b-1\). For \(n=4,e=0,w=1\), all hypotheses hold, yet \(a=b=0\): zero examples instead of four. Weight two likewise gives zero instead of eight. A circular-slice interpretation cannot recover the lost number of full cycles from identical endpoints. For \(e=1,w=3/4\), endpoints 3 and 2 lose the intended three examples. The positive-multiple-of-\(n\) reshuffling branch is unreachable when both range endpoints are reduced modulo \(n\).

Algorithm 2 finalizes whenever batch size is smaller than positive integer `bsz_mult` or divisible by it. Size one always qualifies. If each item individually fits the limits, the first item is finalized and the state resets; induction gives only singleton batches. Eight ten-token items with limits 80 tokens, eight sentences and multiple two yield eight singletons, although a joint batch of eight fits. Singletons are formally allowed by the alignment rule: the defect is compulsory early finalization that defeats useful packing.

Crucial counterevidence is :258–270: the release keeps range endpoints unwrapped and applies modulo only to lookup. Lines 531–538 use a fixed-size DataLoader, not the printed dynamic packer. Table 21 gives total training epochs, not necessarily per-loader-epoch weights; it does not establish integer effective weights in historical training. Exact parent calculations are preserved in .
## Impact and correction

The published loader is not a usable specification of the reported efficiency procedure. The demonstrated dependency is this supporting data-loading utility: the objective, curriculum and benchmark inference do not logically require the defective literal pseudocode, and the released sampler supplies a working alternative to its first defect. This bounded dependency supports Minor; the reason is neither appendix location nor ease of repair.

Unwrapped endpoints with modulo lookup restore the intended count \(\lfloor(e+1)nw\rfloor-\lfloor enw\rfloor\). Packing should retain a feasible partial batch until a budget or chosen boundary actually requires finalization, with oversized-item handling. Only the sampling repair and local singleton diagnosis were checked. A complete repaired packer and the 58%–16% measurement need implementation and profiling records.
Problem 2 (Table 13’s no-LongAudio average does not match its categories).  Minor: verified aggregate inconsistency.

Table 13 (p. 17) displays six no-LongAudio scores: \[46.02,\quad44.15,\quad51.00,\quad35.92,\quad33.61,\quad42.39.\] Their macro-average is \(42.1816667\), not \(50.22\). The full-AF2 entries average to \(64.1916667\), agreeing with its \(64.19\) aggregate. If Table 11’s Complex QA corresponds to Table 13’s Needle QA, its benchmark counts yield a sample-weighted no-LongAudio score of \(43.2311733\), also not \(50.22\). Independent rational arithmetic excludes a rounding explanation.

If the categories are correct and the same macro rule is intended, the corrected gain is \(22.01\) points rather than \(13.97\). All six categories favor finetuning; this correction strengthens that direction and does not show an inflated benefit. Raw predictions are needed to identify whether the aggregate or category entries are wrong. The verified repair is conditional arithmetic, not new measured performance.
Problem 3 (Table 20 labels elapsed cluster time as GPU hours).  Minor: verified unit inconsistency.

H.3 (p. 21) states 128 A100 GPUs for each stage and variant. The 3B durations are approximately four days, five days and twelve hours: \[H_{\rm elapsed}=4(24)+5(24)+12=228,\qquad
 H_{\rm GPU}=128(228)=29{,}184.\] Table 20 labels 228 as GPU Hours. Under the stated allocation it is elapsed cluster hours. Relabel the column, or report aggregate GPU-hours consistently with allocation logs. Neither monetary estimates nor measured durations were independently disproved. The paper already excludes language-model pretraining and failed experiments from these costs.
Problem 4 (Released conditioning paths disagree and the cache predicate tests unset fields).  Minor for the pinned release; historical impact Needs Evidence.
The main-path files are , and under . Source hashes are bound in the independent check output.

For a single `<audio>` marker and supplied `max_window_per_audio: 1`, :375–404 permits direct LM cross-attention only to transformed feature zero. With one allowed key its softmax weight is one, preventing query-dependent selection among audio features at this block. However, :186–198 first concatenates and globally transforms all window features. Feature zero can therefore encode later audio. This is a direct-attention bottleneck, not proof that later audio is inaudible. The pretrained HF helper at lines 368–375 omits this restrictive mask, establishing a released-path discrepancy.

Separately, :29–45 initializes and tests `audio_x`/`audio_x_mask`, but its setter writes `sound_x`/`sound_x_mask`. Static AST inspection confirms the disjoint attributes: the setter cannot make that predicate true. On an incremental call without an audio marker, lines 156–165 consequently cannot reuse media locations; the main helper’s empty-marker path accesses index zero of an empty list. This invalid static path was not executed in a framework. The HF helper lacks the failing mask branch.

No historical checkpoint/code binding establishes an effect on published scores. Aligning the predicate with actual fields and selecting a consistent attention policy are proposed source repairs; full generation, checkpoint compatibility and empirical effects remain untested. The released two-minute context default is configurable and does not establish that five-minute support is impossible.
Problem 5 (LongAudioBench separation across training stages is unbound).  Needs Evidence; no demonstrated contamination.

Sections 3.1.1 and 4.2 use MiraData and Video ReCap for AF-CLAP and LongAudio; LongAudioBench is sampled from LongAudio. Tables 9, 11, 21 and 23 identify these dependencies. A QA-level split alone cannot establish recording- or parent-video-level separation when segments and questions share recordings.

The release requires users to construct manifests and supplies illustrative configurations. It lacks benchmark IDs, parent-video mapping and stage-specific exclusions needed to check encoder training and all three model-training stages. The p. 6 selection statement of 10% (\(\approx3\)k) also needs an intermediate-pool denominator to reconcile with 262,928 LongAudio QA pairs.

Counterevidence is explicit: p. 7 says zero-shot datasets are excluded from all stages. Shared collections alone do not demonstrate overlapping recordings. E.7 describes at least two human annotators per QA pair, complete-recording listening and author review. The unverified object is generalization on a recoverably held-out long-audio cohort. Required evidence comprises immutable recording/parent IDs and exact and segment-overlap checks across stage manifests.
Problem 6 (LongAudioBench’s judge needs an independent calibration binding).  Needs Evidence; no demonstrated aggregate ranking reversal.

Figure 25 (p. 40) gives the evaluator a question, reference and response, but no audio. It requests a 1–10 score without anchored criteria or reported agreement with humans grading model answers while listening. Table 22 (p. 23) gives reference Sad. and a response describing a deep and resonant mood a perfect ten. The latter does not explicitly express sadness; the perfect score needs explanation. This example alone determines neither aggregate bias nor a corrected score without its audio and grading record.

Human validation of reference questions, visual-cue removal (Figure 24), and audio-focused self-verification (Figures 38–39) are meaningful safeguards; they do not independently calibrate output grading. The headline 64.2% is a rescaled judge score, not established exact-answer accuracy. Prediction/reference/score bindings, blinded human agreement, repeated-judge sensitivity and exact-option results where applicable would resolve this concern. No replacement aggregate is claimed.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The local defects warrant correction, while displayed model improvements remain empirically unrefuted within this review. The loss, representation pipeline and curriculum have relevant positive checks and ablations. Attribution to cross-attention alone is limited because the GAMA comparison also changes representations and the LM. Raw recordings as long as 1,797.71 seconds, a five-minute paper context and supplied two-minute defaults require clipping/configuration records to establish actual temporal coverage.
