report: Abstract: The complete original paper and embedded appendix were reviewed. Three Major findings concern core mathematical foundations: an invalid variational decomposition and inconsistent loss signs; a contrastive objective minimized by equal matched-pair scores, including collapsed representations; and a false nuisance-information upper bound under the stated hypotheses. These defects affect the justification of MCVAE and invariant relational learning. Historical benchmark execution is unavailable, so the findings do not establish that corrected implementations lose reported accuracy. Conflicting CompSolv results and incomplete experimental bindings remain Needs Evidence. Adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Technical Verification of Relational Invariant Learning for Robust Solvation Free Energy Prediction
# Paper identity and reviewed scope

Paper 0209 / I25-43578 is Relational Invariant Learning for Robust Solvation Free Energy Prediction, Yeyun Chen, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 72210–72227 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Its original publisher PDF has 18 pages, including Appendices A–D. PDF and printed page numbers coincide and are used below.

The PDF, complete manifest and publisher page were actually inspected. No verified author implementation was identified in the acquired sources; this is not a claim of global nonrelease. OpenReview access returned 403 during preparation, leaving an additional supplement’s existence undetermined. The review tests the published mathematical specification, not a recovered training program. All main sections, proofs, tables, figure captions, dataset/implementation details and limitations were read. Original-page images confirm the decisive signs, indices and numerical entries.
# Model, assumptions and dependencies

Equation reference: eq:joint. RILOOD encodes a solute–solvent graph pair, constructs interaction features, mixes representations in a conditional variational module (MCVAE), refines coarse/fine features through MCAR, and minimizes \[
 L=L_{\rm inv}+\alpha L_{\rm MCVAE}+\beta L_{\rm MI},
 \qquad \alpha,\beta>0.\] This is paper Eq. 13; C.4 also uses positive weights. Proposition 4.2 ties MCVAE optimization to sufficiency and the joint objective to invariance. Validity of the losses and their theoretical support is therefore part of the core contribution.

A.1 explicitly places both mixed representations in \(\mathbb R^d\); C.1 clarifies use of graph-level features. Different atom counts do not establish an unavoidable mixup shape error. Section 3.1’s graph interaction matrix dimensions are consistent. The attention token axis, environment pairing and held-out-solvent conditioning remain incompletely specified, rather than demonstrated runtime failures.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The variational identity and minimized MCVAE loss are inconsistent).  Major. The discrepancy affects a central conditional modeling module and its claimed derivation.
## Claim and location

Equation reference: eq:printed. Equations 5–6 (pp. 5–6), A.2 Equations 21–24 (pp. 12–13), and Proposition 4.2 (p. 7) motivate a conditional evidence objective. Writing \(x=\widetilde H_1\), Eq. 23 claims \[
 \log p_\theta(x\mid e)
 =-\mathrm{KL}\{q(z\mid x,e)\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x)\}
   +\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z,e).\] Equations 6/24 combine negative KL with a positive reconstruction/variance penalty, and enter the minimized loss [eq:joint] (#eq:joint).
## Exact counterexample and alternative interpretation

Equation reference: eq:correct. The prose on p. 13 instead mentions \(p(z\mid e)\). Granting that intended prior still does not justify equality for arbitrary \(q\). In the same joint, \(q=N(0,1)\) gives a proper ELBO of \(-1.4189385332\), below the evidence by \(0.1534264097\). The correct decomposition is \[\begin{aligned}

 \log p_\theta(x\mid e)
 &=\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z,e)
   -\mathrm{KL}\{q\Vert p_\theta(z\mid e)\}\\
 &\quad+\mathrm{KL}\{q\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x,e)\}.\nonumber\end{aligned}\] This refutes the particular asserted marginal-likelihood identity. It does not claim every data-conditioned prior in a different generative model is invalid.
## Optimization direction and finite diagnostic

Negating likelihood-minus-KL for minimization changes both terms, giving negative log likelihood plus KL. Equations 6/24 change the reconstruction sign but retain negative KL. The appendix repeats this discrepancy.

Set \(x=0\), comparison prior \(N(0,1)\), \(q=N(0,v)\) and fixed reconstruction variance parameter \(\sigma^2=1\). This explicitly separates posterior and reconstruction variances; the paper gives no equation binding them. With its reconstruction coefficient, \[K(v)=\tfrac12(v-1-\log v),\quad
 J_-(v)=-K(v)+v,\quad J_+(v)=K(v)+v.\] Independent symbolic calculations give:
\(v\) | \(K(v)\) | Printed \(J_-(v)\) | Corrected \(J_+(v)\)

Both satisfy \(\mathrm{KL}<0.4\), yet the losses order them oppositely. Without a hard KL bound, \(J_-(v)=\frac12(v+1+\log v)\to-\infty\) as \(v\downarrow0\). If \(\sigma^2\) is tied to \(v\), the reconstruction term itself has another degeneracy; that alternative is not used to attribute all unboundedness to the KL sign. The identity and sign findings do not depend on this diagnostic’s variance interpretation.
## Impact and checked repair

The published derivation does not establish its ELBO interpretation or prior-matching regularization, undermining MCVAE’s theoretical justification and Proposition 4.2. This supports Major independently of a benchmark rerun. It does not prove historical training used these signs or diverged.

Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) restores the exact decomposition. A coherent minimized objective is \(-\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z,e)+\gamma\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p_\theta(z\mid e))\), \(\gamma>0\); \(\gamma=1\) gives the usual negative ELBO. Specify decoder, prior and variance roles. These local repairs do not prove predictive sufficiency or OOD invariance and were not tested in a neural implementation.
Problem 2 (The contrastive loss only equalizes matched-pair scores).  Major. Equation 12 does not implement the discrimination used to motivate the central mutual-information mechanism.
## Claim and exact calculation

Equation reference: eq:equalize. Section 4.3 presents Eq. 12 (p. 7) as an approximation to Eq. 11’s mutual-information objective. Original-image inspection confirms that its denominator uses \(\operatorname{sim}(\widehat H_{\rm inv}^{\,j},H_1^j)\) for every \(j\ne i\), rather than anchor \(i\) against sample \(j\). Set \(s_i=\operatorname{sim}(\widehat H_{\rm inv}^{\,i},H_1^i)\). Then \[
 L_{\rm MI}=\log\sum_{j=1}^M e^{s_j}
             -\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M s_i
 \ \geq\ \log M.\] Jensen’s inequality gives equality whenever all matched-pair scores are equal. A common additive score shift leaves the loss unchanged; its score gradient is \(\operatorname{softmax}(s)_i-1/M\), zero at equality.

Take two equally likely inputs \(H_1^1=(1,0)\) and \(H_1^2=(0,1)\), and set both learned representations to the same nonzero unit vector \(u=(1,1)/\sqrt2\). With either dot-product or cosine similarity, both scores equal \(1/\sqrt2\) and the loss attains its global minimum \(\log2\), although the representation is constant and its mutual information with \(H_1\) is zero. The informative choice \(\widehat H_{\rm inv}^{\,i}=H_1^i\) also attains \(\log2\) while retaining \(\log2\) information. For constant \(Y\), the same distinction applies to the conditional information in Eq. 11. No undefined cosine or numerical approximation is involved.
## Counterevidence, impact and repair limits

The supervised term can oppose collapse; this does not prove collapse of the complete predictor. An intended anchor-versus-negative formula is a plausible correction, but no appendix correction or acquired implementation supplies it. The demonstrated failure concerns the contrastive/MI mechanism central to the invariant-learning argument, so Major does not require showing benchmark loss.

A candidate repair compares anchor \(\widehat H_{\rm inv}^{\,i}\) against every \(H_1^j\) in its denominator. A bound on the conditional information of Eq. 11 additionally needs appropriate conditioning and negative sampling. An index change alone does not prove that bound or invariance. For deterministic \(w\), moreover, \(I(w(H_1);H_1\mid Y)=H(w(H_1)\mid Y)\); maximizing it can retain nuisance variation. If \(H_1=(Y,C)\) for independent fair bits, retaining \((Y,C)\) preserves more conditional information than retaining \(Y\) alone, despite equal predictive information. This limits the noise-removal interpretation.
Problem 3 (The mixup nuisance-information upper bound is false).  Major. Appendix A.1 is explicitly invoked as theoretical justification for the proposed mixup conditional modeling.
## Claim and complete admissible counterexample

Equation reference: eq:bound. A.1 (p. 12), Eqs. 14–20, assumes a Lipschitz predictor with constant \(L_f>0\), bounded nonnegative loss \(B\), and \(\widetilde H=\lambda H_1+(1-\lambda)H_2\), \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). It asserts \[
 \mathcal E_{\rm mixup}(\lambda)
 \leq \mathcal E^*+c_2\sqrt{I(\widetilde H;C_{\rm nuisance})},\] where \(\mathcal E^*\) is optimal achievable error and \(c_2>0\) depends on \(L_f,B\).

Let \(Y\) be a fair bit and set \(H_1=H_2=e_1=e_2=Y\). Then \(\widetilde H=e=Y\) for every \(\lambda\), including a Beta-distributed one. Use prediction/target domains \([0,1]\), squared loss, \(B=1\), and \(f(h)\equiv1/2\). This satisfies the displayed Lipschitz inequality with \(L_f=1\). Let \(C_{\rm nuisance}\) be an independent fair bit. Then \[I(\widetilde H;C_{\rm nuisance})=0,\quad
 \mathcal E^*=0,\quad
 \mathcal E_{\rm mixup}=\mathbb E(1/2-Y)^2=1/4.\] The zero optimum is attained by \(f^*(h)=\min(1,\max(0,h))\), also globally 1-Lipschitz. Equation [eq:bound] (#eq:bound) therefore requires \(1/4\leq0\), independently of \(c_2\).

A one-hot version removes any concern about environmental encoding. Let \(Y\) be uniform on the two unit vectors in \(\mathbb R^2\), set all four representations/labels equal to \(Y\), predict \((1/2,1/2)\), and use half squared Euclidean loss on the probability simplex. The loss is bounded by one and the risk is \(1/4\); Euclidean projection onto the simplex is 1-Lipschitz and attains zero risk on the support. Both versions are in the independent calculation record.
## Counterevidence and consequence

A.1 never assumes that the evaluated predictor already minimizes risk. Adding that premise changes the claim; nuisance independence alone cannot remove predictive or optimization error. The qualitative need to preserve task information remains sensible, but Eq. 19 and the two-sided Eq. 20 do not supply the advertised generalization justification. This is a demonstrated invalid derivation tied to a core module, hence Major. It does not refute all mixup applications or the reported scores. No replacement upper bound is verified: substantive assumptions and an excess-risk or approximation term would be required.
Problem 4 (The CompSolv solvent result lacks a consistent experiment binding).  Needs Evidence. A reporting conflict is visible; the correct historical score and ranking remain unresolved.

Table 1 (p. 8) reports RILOOD \(0.3660\pm0.022\), while Table 2 (p. 9) reports full-model Ours \(0.4689\pm0.006\) for CompSolv solvent splitting, a difference of 0.1029. The other three shared full-model cells agree exactly, including their deviations. No protocol difference is identified in the complete appendix.

If comparable, the second value loses to Table 1’s CMRL 0.3777 and CGIB 0.3886, whereas the first wins. Different splits, configurations or a transcription error could explain this; available evidence does not identify which. Figures 8–9 (p. 17) also require binding: their dataset labels/scales and baseline annotations do not reconcile with Table 1, and each plotted hyperparameter grid is shifted by a factor of ten from C.4’s stated grid. Automatically swapping captions or inventing a corrected score would be unjustified.

Supply dataset/split IDs, selected configurations, seeds, units/scaling, individual predictions and run-to-table/figure mappings. The main tables do not specify what their deviations mean or the number of repetitions; formal significance cannot be inferred from means alone. Table 1 nevertheless shows the lowest RILOOD mean in all six settings, positive evidence that is not erased by the unresolved reporting conflict.
# Additional checks and overall impact

The three Major findings independently invalidate mathematical support for central components. No unavailable implementation or score rerun is needed to demonstrate them; conversely, they do not imply every displayed experiment is false.

Proposition 4.2’s bridge to conditional invariance is not supplied by A.3’s marginal conditions. Let \(S,U,E\) be independent fair bits, input \(X=(S,U,E)\), representation \(S\), residual \((U,E)\) and target \(Y=S\oplus E\). Representation–residual independence, within-environment factorization and equal representation marginals hold, yet \[P(Y=1\mid S=0,E=0)=0,\qquad
 P(Y=1\mid S=0,E=1)=1.\] An invariant sufficient alternative \(S\oplus E\) exists, so this does not deny its existence. A.3 explicitly concludes marginal stability and is not silently promoted to a separate false theorem. The implication from optimization to label-conditional invariance remains unproved. Its unrestricted additive-noise definition is also not a substantive sufficiency test.

B.1’s intended scaffold- and solvent-group-disjoint splits are appropriate safeguards. Actual partitions, five-solvent QM9Solv allocation, DDI shift definitions and synthetic spurious-feature interventions remain unavailable. C.2’s dielectric scatter plot does not specify the intervention or establish that a chemically predictive property is spurious. Table 4 explicitly labels its extensions IID. Bounded prose corrections are also needed: removing MCAR is worse than the stated baseline on both scaffold columns of Table 2, and Table 4’s FreeSolv winner is CMRL, not the CGIB named in C.3. These do not create additional core-failure claims. Figure 4 mentions validation-based checkpoint selection; sensitivity plots of test errors alone do not establish test-set tuning.

report: Abstract: The original 38-page paper and its embedded supplement were reviewed. The overall assessment is Major: a stated Theorem 4.1 bound fails on an admissible scalar instance; the SAGA proof uses a false independence step and its unrestricted variance lemma has a counterexample; and the advertised nonmonotone example violates essential assumptions. Restricted repairs and counterevidence are supplied. Two application mappings also need correction. These findings do not establish algorithmic divergence or loss of the headline asymptotic order. Historical experiments remain unverified. Scientific adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Technical Verification of Variance-Reduced Forward-Reflected-Backward Splitting
# Identity, version and coverage

Paper 0210 / I25-43579 is Quoc Tran-Dinh, Variance-Reduced Forward-Reflected-Backward Splitting Methods for Nonmonotone Generalized Equations, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:60034–60071 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original publisher PDF has 38 pages, including Appendices A–E. All locations below use 1-based PDF pages, which coincide with the printed page numbers.

The complete staged manifest, original PDF and publisher metadata were actually read and hash-checked. All main sections, technical proofs, experimental descriptions, figures/captions and references were inspected as text; decisive original equations and plots were checked as images. No verified author implementation was identified in the acquired materials. OpenReview access was blocked during source preparation, so an additional separate attachment’s existence remains undetermined. Neither fact implies global nonrelease. This review contains analytic and finite independent checks, not an empirical reproduction.
# Definitions and core dependencies

The paper solves \(0\in Gx+Tx\), with \(G=n^{-1}\sum_iG_i\). Assumptions 1.1–1.4 require a solution, maximal monotonicity of \(T\), averaged Lipschitz continuity \[\frac1n\sum_i\|G_ix-G_iy\|^2\le L^2\|x-y\|^2,\] and a weak-Minty solution \(x^\star\) satisfying \[\langle Gx+v,x-x^\star\rangle\ge-\kappa\|Gx+v\|^2
 \quad(x\in\operatorname{dom}(G+T),\ v\in Tx).\] For \(\gamma\in(1/2,1)\) the reflected quantity is \(S_\gamma^k=Gx^k-\gamma Gx^{k-1}\). Definition 2.1 requires an unbiased estimator and \[\mathbb E\|\widetilde S_\gamma^k-S_\gamma^k\|^2\le\Delta_k,\qquad
 \Delta_k\le(1-\rho)\Delta_{k-1}+CU_k+\widehat C U_{k-1},\] where \(U_k=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb E\|G_ix^k-G_ix^{k-1}\|^2\). VFR updates \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\eta\widetilde S_\gamma^k\); VFRBS adds the implicit term \(-\eta[\gamma v^{k+1}-(2\gamma-1)v^k]\).

The variance recurrences feed the Lyapunov arguments in Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 and their SVRG/SAGA complexity corollaries. Their quantitative correctness is central to the contribution. A valid proof repair, or survival of an asymptotic rate, does not erase a false published derivation; it does bound its impact.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Theorem 4.1 has a false bound and an incomplete initial-potential calculation).  Major. This directly concerns the stated convergence guarantee for the new inclusion method.
## Claim and admissible counterexample

Equation reference: eq:bad. Theorem 4.1, Eq. 12 and the definition of \(\widehat\Theta_2\) (p. 7), state \[
 \frac1{K+1}\sum_{k=0}^K\mathbb E\|x^k-x^{k-1}\|^2
 \le\frac{\widehat\Theta_2\widehat R_0^2}{K+1},
 \quad
 \widehat\Theta_2=
 \frac{4(3\gamma-1)\widehat R_0^2}
 {(1-\gamma)(1-ML^2\eta^2)}.\] Thus the right side is quartic in initialization scale.

Take any number of identical components \(G_i\equiv0\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(Tx=(8/3)x\), \(L=1\), \(\kappa=0\), \(\gamma=3/4\), \(\eta=1/2\), \(\rho=1\), \(C=\widehat C=0\), and the exact zero estimator with \(\Delta_k=0\). Let \(x^\star=0\), \(x^{-1}=x^0=a=1/100\) and \(y^0=2a\). The zero set is nonempty; \(T\) is continuous, positive linear and maximally monotone; the Lipschitz inequality is \(0\le|x-y|^2\); and weak Minty is \((8/3)x^2\ge0\). Initialization satisfies \(x^0=J_{\gamma\eta T}y^0\). Moreover \[M=9/4,\quad \delta=1/5,\quad
 0<\eta=1/2\le2/3=1/(L\sqrt M).\] Every original hypothesis is satisfied; an upper Lipschitz bound need not be minimal.
## Separate proof defect and bounded repair

Appendix D, Eq. 30 (p. 23), defines \[\mathcal L_k=\|x^k+\gamma\eta(Gx^{k-1}+v^k)-x^\star\|^2
 +\mu\|x^k-x^{k-1}+\gamma\eta(Gx^{k-1}+v^k)\|^2.\] With \(\mu=(1-\gamma)/(3\gamma-1)\), p. 26 drops the positive second term at \(k=0\) when asserting \(\mathbb E\mathcal E_0\le2\widehat R_0^2\). In the same deterministic example, \(\mu=1/5\) and \[\mathcal E_0=21a^2/5>4a^2=2\widehat R_0^2.\] Deleting the extra \(\widehat R_0^2\) in [eq:bad] (#eq:bad) does not fix this independent derivation error.

Problem 2 (The SAGA variance argument and quantitative specialization need correction).  Major. The unrestricted estimator lemma is false as stated, and a core step-size lower bound is false. The batch regime used for the main complexity result has a verified restricted repair.
## Source claim and dependence error

Lemma 2.3 (p. 5) and Appendix B.2, Eq. 20 (p. 18), prescribe \[\Delta_k=\frac1{nb}\sum_i\mathbb E\|G_ix^k-\gamma G_ix^{k-1}
 -(1-\gamma)\widehat G_i^k\|^2\] with \(\rho=b/(2n)\), \(C=[2(n-b)(2n+b)+b^2]/(nb^2)\) and \(\widehat C=2(n-b)(2n+b)\gamma^2/(nb^2)\). The proof replaces the updated table by a probability-weighted mixture of refreshed and unrefreshed expressions while leaving \(x^k\) inside an unconditional expectation. But \(x^k\) and that table update use the same batch \(B_{k-1}\).

This equality fails even on an admissible VFR trajectory. Set \(n=2\), \(b=1\), \(G_1x=x\), \(G_2x=2x\), \(x^0=1\), \(\gamma=3/4\) and \(\eta=1/20\), with the required initial table. Then \(x^1=157/160\) and the two \(x^2\) values are \(3083/3200\) and \(1543/1600\). Exact enumeration yields \[\Delta_2=\frac{4041}{4096000},\qquad
 \text{factorized expression}=\frac{1611}{1638400},
 \qquad \text{difference}=\frac{27}{8192000}>0.\] Here \(x^\star=0\), \(\kappa=0\), \(L^2=5/2\), and \(\eta^2L^2M=2983/3840<1\); all VFR hypotheses hold. Crucially, the recurrence’s right side is \(23823/3276800>\Delta_2\). This check refutes the intermediate equality, not convergence or the recurrence on this trajectory.
## Counterexample to the unrestricted stated recurrence

For Lemma 2.3 itself, take \(n=20\), \(b=19\), \(\gamma=3/4\), \(G_1x=x\) and \(G_ix=0\) for \(i>1\). Initialize \(x^{-2}=x^{-1}=x^0=0\) and the table at zero. Draw independent uniform 19-subsets. Choose the adapted sequence \[x^1=28/3,\qquad
 x^2=\begin{cases}28/3&1\in B_1,\\8&1\notin B_1,\end{cases}\] and let \(x^3=x^2\), except that \(x^3=8+760/99\) if both \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) omit index 1. Use precisely the paper’s table update. These are valid adapted iterates for the generic estimator lemma, which imposes no VFR update. The operators are Lipschitz (\(L^2=1/20\)) and their average is monotone with root zero. This is explicitly not a VFR trajectory.
## Restricted repair and its exact scope

The counterexample uses \(b>n^{2/3}\), outside the complexity corollaries. Their variance recurrence can be proved without the false independence step. Set \(q=b/n\) and let \(I_i\) indicate non-refresh. Writing \(r_i\) for the previous component residual, \(s_i=G_ix^{k-1}-G_ix^{k-2}\) and \(d_i=G_ix^k-G_ix^{k-1}\), the exact identity is \[a_i^k=d_i+I_i(r_i-\gamma s_i).\] Only \(r_i,s_i\) are fixed before the previous draw; \(d_i\) may depend on it. For \(D=Cb=4/q-2-q>1\), Young’s inequality bounds this by \(D\|d_i\|^2+D(D-1)^{-1}I_i\|r_i-\gamma s_i\|^2\). After averaging \(I_i\), its second coefficient is \(A=(4-2q-q^2)/(q+4)\). The required domination \[A\|r-\gamma s\|^2
 \le(1-q/2)\|r\|^2+\gamma^2(4/q-2-2q)\|s\|^2\] has first principal minor \(q(q+2)/[2(q+4)]\) and determinant \(\gamma^2q(8-6q-3q^2)/[2(q+4)]\). It therefore holds for \(0<q\le(\sqrt{33}-3)/3\). Dividing by \(nb\) recovers the printed constants. Every \(b\le n^{2/3}\) with \(n\ge2\) lies in this range; \(n=b=1\) is checked directly. This is a verified repair of the relevant recurrence, not of the unrestricted lemma.
## A separate false step-size specialization

Corollary 3.3 (p. 6) asserts \(\eta=1/(L\sqrt M)\ge0.1494b^{3/2}/(nL)\). For \(n=1000\), \(b=100=n^{2/3}\), \(\gamma=3/4\), all \(G_ix=x\), \(L=1\) and \(\kappa=0\), its own constants give \[\rho=1/20,\quad C=379/1000,\quad
 \widehat C=1701/8000,\quad M=54913/1200.\] Hence \(\eta=0.14782675297<0.1494\), although all assumptions hold. The symbolic \(\sigma\) on pp. 22–23 evaluates to \(0.1341808523\), not \(0.14948\). The symbolic \(\Gamma\) evaluates to \(841.8947368\), not \(2815.8\); the chosen 2816 is nevertheless conservative.

Equation 9 additionally contains \(bp^2\) although the SAGA corollary defines no \(p\). A supported replacement at \(\gamma=3/4\) follows from \[\Lambda=\frac2b+\frac{4(1+\gamma^2)(2n^2-nb-b^2)}{b^3}
 \le\frac{8(1+\gamma^2)n^2}{b^3},
 \quad M\le\frac{1157n^2}{24b^3}.\] Theorem 3.1 then gives the valid rounded bound \[\frac1{K+1}\sum_{k=0}^K\mathbb E\|Gx^k\|^2
 \le\frac{526L^2\|x^0-x^\star\|^2n^2}{b^3(K+1)}\] under its hypotheses and the repaired variance recurrence. The exact intermediate coefficient is \(4724/9\). This preserves the stated asymptotic scaling; no trajectory violating an appropriately repaired residual rate is claimed. Evidence: pp. 5–6, 18, 22–23 and independent , with their exact JSON outputs.

Problem 3 (The advertised admissible nonmonotone example is ineligible).  Major. Appendix A.2 supplies the explicit argument, cited in the main assumption discussion, for the central extension beyond monotonicity.

A.2 (pp. 15–16) proposes, for any \(\epsilon>0\), \[G=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 T=\begin{pmatrix}-\epsilon&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 \kappa=\epsilon.\] It repeatedly asserts \(G\succeq0\) and infers weak Minty and arbitrarily small admissible \(L\kappa\). In fact \(G\) has eigenvalues \(\pm1\), and \(T\) is not monotone, violating Assumption 1.2. With zero affine offset and solution \(x^\star=0\), the matrix that must be PSD is \[S=(G+T)+\epsilon(G+T)^\top(G+T)
 =\begin{pmatrix}\epsilon^3&1-\epsilon^2\\1-\epsilon^2&\epsilon\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det S=2\epsilon^2-1.\] For \(\epsilon=1/100\) and \(x=(1,-1)\), the actual weak-Minty test is \(-2.01\ge-0.020201\), which is false. The paper’s intermediate matrix is PSD; adding the indefinite \(G\) is the invalid inference. These failures concern the claimed eligibility of this example, not a counterexample satisfying the abstract theorem.

A verified replacement shows the class is nonempty: \[T=0,\quad G=-\epsilon I+
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 L=\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2},\quad
 \kappa=\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon^2}.\] The symmetric part is \(-\epsilon I\) and \(G^\top G=(1+\epsilon^2)I\), so weak Minty holds with equality at zero. \(T\) is maximally monotone, zero is a solution, and \(L\kappa\to0\). Replicating \(G_i=G\) supplies a finite sum satisfying the averaged Lipschitz condition. Thus the core illustrative derivation fails, while the broader nonmonotone research claim survives this precise replacement. Evidence: pp. 15–16 and .

Problem 4 (The quadratic objective and its printed saddle operator differ).  Minor. The application mapping is wrong; no historical implementation binding establishes damage to the generic solver conclusions.

The correction above is verified directly. Absorbing a factor of two into differently defined matrices would change the published objective, and the reported equal dimensions do not repair the omitted transpose for nonsymmetric \(L_i\). Actual saved matrices or code could establish a correct implementation; they are absent. The finding does not show that the historical curves came from the wrong operator. Evidence: p. 32 and .
Problem 5 (The logistic reformulation changes the stated uncertainty model).  Minor. A local modeling equivalence fails, while the displayed alternative remains a legitimate optimization problem.

E.3(a), p. 34, defines \(f_i(w)=\max_j\ell(\langle X_{ij},w\rangle,y_i)\), but Eq. 39/main Eq. 16 uses one common \(z\in\Delta_m\) for all observations. Consequently its maximized loss is \[\max_j\frac1N\sum_i\ell_{ij}(w),
 \quad\text{instead of}\quad
 \frac1N\sum_i\max_j\ell_{ij}(w).\] For \(N=m=2\), \(w=1\), \(y_1=y_2=0\) and \(X=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the specified logistic loss gives \(h=\log(1+e^2)\) and \(l=\log(1+e^{-2})\). The intended samplewise worst-case value is \(h=2.1269280110\); the printed shared-scenario value is \((h+l)/2=1.1269280110\). The gap is exactly one, and adding the same \(\tau|w|\) leaves it unchanged. All inputs and binary labels satisfy the model’s definitions.

A precise repair uses separate \(z_i\in\Delta_m\) and \(\max_{z_1,\ldots,z_N}N^{-1}\sum_{ij}(z_i)_j\ell_{ij}\). Alternatively, explicitly assume a shared scenario index across the dataset; that is a different uncertainty model. The generic convergence analysis can apply to a correctly specified problem of either kind. There are no reported classification or robust-accuracy results to refute here, and the historical effect requires a source-bound rerun. Evidence: p. 34 and .
Problem 6 (Experimental nonmonotonicity and oracle-cost comparisons need run bindings).  Needs Evidence. The inspected record does not settle these empirical claims.

Section 5.1 and E.2 (pp. 8, 32–33) assert or motivate nonconvex–nonconcave tests by generating possibly indefinite component matrices. This does not certify indefinite averages or an admissible weak-Minty constant for each actual instance. For example, \(\operatorname{diag}(-0.1,1)\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-0.1)\) are both indefinite but average to \(0.45I\). Actual aggregate spectra, Lipschitz estimates, \(\kappa\) tests, seeds and saved instances are missing. This example does not prove that any historical instance was monotone.

Figures 1–13 use epochs, but the full-snapshot, multiple-minibatch and diagnostic-residual costs lack a recoverable common plotting convention. E.1 describes \(\lfloor n/b\rfloor\) inner iterations per double-loop round, which alone does not make that round cost \(n\) component evaluations. E.3 uses different algorithm step sizes without clearly identifying a common evaluation parameter for the FBS residual \(G_\eta\). The correct empirical cost and residual-comparison bindings require code and logs, not a guessed correction.

Substantial counterevidence limits any allegation of unfairness: synthetic results average ten instances; batch size and refresh probability are varied; enlarged steps and manual tuning are disclosed; the unstable MNIST baseline is explicitly omitted; and some competitive SAGA/VEG behavior is acknowledged. These are optimization-residual demonstrations. The logistic objective is convex–concave on its feasible domain. The synthetic WGAN has component form \(G_i(x)=Ax+c_i\), so same-batch SVRG cancels sampling noise exactly; that valid simple example has limited variance-reduction stress, while the other experiments broaden coverage. No benchmark execution or ranking reversal is established.
# Overall dependence, retained results and remaining work

Theorem 4.1’s false quantitative statement and proof, the SAGA lemma/specialization, and the failed eligibility argument are separately tied to core theoretical claims. Their supported assessment is Major under the assigned standard, even though restricted repairs preserve substantial content. The quadratic and logistic mappings are separately assessed Minor because historical damage to the solver comparison has not been demonstrated. Missing experiments do not raise any supported severity.

The VFR residual proof in Appendix C and the main descent algebra in D were checked without finding a further decisive counterexample. The implementable resolvent form is consistent with the main VFRBS update. Fresh uniform batches, conditioned on the full pre-draw state including memory and \(v^k\), give unbiasedness. The paper’s narrower \(\mathcal F_k=\sigma(x^0,\ldots,x^k)\) does not alone justify every VFRBS product cancellation involving \(v^k\); the broader abstract class remains unverified. Uniform sampling without replacement changes an i.i.d. variance equality to an upper bound, which is sufficient.

Oracle counts \(np+3b\) for loopless SVRG are expected counts; SAGA’s three-minibatch accounting is conservative relative to two fresh evaluations. The replacements of \(b=\lfloor n^{2/3}\rfloor\) by \(n^{2/3}\) are not exact identities, but bounded rounding preserves the order. Constants with \(1-ML^2\eta^2\) in their denominators are not finite at the allowed endpoint; this is not evidence of divergence. No separate current-literature priority audit, later-version comparison or erratum was available in the frozen source set. No known correction has been silently attributed to the original.

report: Abstract: This review checks the task-vector span argument, the interference bound, the implemented surrogate, and selected released-source correspondence. The bound survives a direct rederivation. A two-dimensional construction establishes a precise limit: zero surrogate loss does not imply minimum actual interference. Because the paper explicitly introduces empirical approximations, this is a scope clarification, not a refutation of its theorem. A separate, supported Minor finding concerns the released NLP merging learning rate. Historical experiment provenance and benchmark performance were not reproduced. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of WUDI-Merging
# Paper identity and reviewed scope

Runxi Cheng, Feng Xiong, Yongxian Wei, Wanyun Zhu, and Chun Yuan, Whoever Started the Interference Should End It: Guiding Data-Free Model Merging via Task Vectors, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 10121–10143 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment: 0211 / I25-43580; OpenReview identifier xR9msNaREW. The reviewed version is the frozen publisher PDF, retrieved 25 October 2026 UTC, with 23 PDF pages. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed local page numbers.

The principal inspected material is Sections 3.1–3.3 (pp. 3–5), Lemma 1, Proposition 1, Theorem 1, the normal equations in Appendix A.1, Algorithm 1, the reported optimizer settings, and the corresponding released merging routines. Selected empirical summary arithmetic and appendix tables were checked; experiments were not rerun. The pinned primary repository is commit `dc3cd1204a68d1930a32da11c5cddb0cbd7410bb` (1 October 2025) [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The separately staged PEFT dependency was identity/hash checked, not comprehensively audited. The publisher PDF contains the appendix; an additional OpenReview attachment was inaccessible during source preparation (HTTP 403), so its existence and content remain undetermined.
# Definitions and claims that survive checking

Equation reference: eq:sur. For a linear layer, let \(\tau_i\) be task \(i\)’s weight difference from a common pretrained model and let \(M\) be the merged task vector. The paper defines \(\delta_i=M-\tau_i\) and \[J_i(M)=\mathbb E_{x\sim p_i}\|\delta_i x\|_2^2 .\] Its implemented objective, Eq. (21), is \[
 S(M)=\sum_i \frac{\|(M-\tau_i)\tau_i^\top\|_F^2}{\|\tau_i\|_F^2},
 \qquad \|\tau_i\|_F>0.\] The nonzero-norm condition is necessary for this expression; the review did not establish that any evaluated checkpoint violates it.

Under ordinary gradient descent, each row update is a weighted sum of the corresponding layer inputs. If these inputs are fixed, the row belongs exactly to their span. With bounded drift, the triangle inequality gives the error bound in Proposition 1. Lemma 1’s proof requires Lipschitz continuity in the upstream parameters for fixed sample, not merely Lipschitz continuity in the network input. Reading the statement consistently with its proof supplies this interpretation. Displayed index inconsistencies do not undermine the consistently indexed proof, and are not counted as substantive findings.

For any representation \(x=\tau_i^\top c(x)+r(x)\), set \[A(x)=\|c(x)\|_2^2+1.\] Cauchy–Schwarz and the Frobenius bound give \[\begin{aligned}
 \|\delta_i x\|_2^2
 &\le A(x)\{\|\delta_i\tau_i^\top\|_F^2+
                  \|\delta_i\|_F^2\|r(x)\|_2^2\},\\
 J_i(M)&\le \mathbb E A(x)\|\delta_i\tau_i^\top\|_F^2+
          \mathbb E[A(x)\|r(x)\|_2^2]\|\delta_i\|_F^2 .\end{aligned}\] Thus Theorem 1 has a valid direct derivation when these moments are finite. A signed-coefficient triangle-inequality line in the appendix can be bypassed by this direct calculation; it does not make the final theorem false. The ridge normal equations also agree with Eq. (20), subject to nonzero task norms and invertibility; positive ridge coefficient is sufficient for invertibility.
# Scope clarification: the surrogate does not inherit the full bound
## Source claim and exact boundary

Proposition 1, Eq. (12), describes task-vector rows as approximate combinations of inputs. Equation (13), p. 4, reconstructs inputs from task-vector rows with an explicit residual. Theorem 1, Eq. (15), retains the resulting residual penalty. The transition to Eq. (18) replaces unknown constants by an empirical coefficient, and p. 5 introduces Eq. (21) as an alternative motivated by implicit regularization. There is no theorem asserting equivalence between the minimizers of \(S\) and \(\sum_iJ_i\).
The following construction checks the scope of that motivation. It is not an allegation that Theorem 1 or Proposition 1 is false.
## Construction and verification of assumptions

Take two fixed features \(e_1,e_2\) in \(\mathbb R^2\), each with probability \(1/2\) for both tasks, and a scalar-output layer \(w=(w_1,w_2)\) pretrained at zero. Let \(\phi\) be the unit-threshold Huber loss: \[\phi(u)=
 \begin{cases}u^2/2,&|u|\le1,\\ |u|-1/2,&|u|>1.\end{cases}\] Use \(L_1(w)=\phi(w_1-1)+\phi(w_2)\) and \(L_2(w)=\phi(w_1)+\phi(w_2-1)\). This formulation makes each loss derivative with respect to a sample output globally bounded by one, rather than relying on a local bounded-gradient reading of squared loss. It agrees with squared loss along the single step used here.

One full gradient step of size \(a\in(0,1]\) produces \[\tau_1=(a,0),\qquad \tau_2=(0,a).\] There are \(N=2\) samples and \(T=1\) iteration. The inputs do not depend on trainable upstream parameters, so their drift is exactly zero; the upstream update bound may be taken as \(G_l=0\) and a finite Lipschitz constant as \(C_l=1\). The output-gradient bound is \(\Gamma_l=1\). Proposition 1 holds with zero error, the vectors are nonzero, and all reconstruction moments below are finite. This example meets both a trajectory-wise and a global output-gradient interpretation.
Nevertheless, each task-vector rowspace omits one input direction. Exact forward inclusion of rows in the input span does not reverse that inclusion.
## Complete calculation

For \(M=(m_1,m_2)\), direct substitution into Eq. [eq:sur] (#eq:sur) yields \[S(M)=(m_1-a)^2+(m_2-a)^2.\] Its unique minimizer is \(M_s=(a,a)\), exactly Algorithm 1’s sum initialization. The gradient is zero there, so ordinary gradient descent and Adam with zero initial optimizer state make no update. The actual summed interference is \[\begin{aligned}
 J_1(M)+J_2(M)
 &=\tfrac12\{(m_1-a)^2+m_2^2+m_1^2+(m_2-a)^2\}\\
 &=(m_1-a/2)^2+(m_2-a/2)^2+a^2/2.\end{aligned}\] It is minimized at \(M_j=(a/2,a/2)\). Hence \[S(M_s)=0,\quad J_1(M_s)+J_2(M_s)=a^2,
 \qquad S(M_j)=a^2/2,\quad J_1(M_j)+J_2(M_j)=a^2/2.\] An independently authored exact-rational calculation at \(a=1/100\) returned respectively \(0,1/10000\) and \(1/20000,1/20000\) for surrogate and summed interference; the executable input and output are retained in the verification directory.

Theorem 1 remains valid. For task 1 choose \(c(e_1)=1/a\), \(c(e_2)=0\), \(r(e_1)=0\), \(r(e_2)=e_2\). Then \(\omega^1=1+1/(2a^2)\) and \(\omega^2=1/2\). At \(M_s\), the retained residual term is exactly \(a^2/2=J_1(M_s)\); task 2 is symmetric. The omitted term therefore carries all interference at this zero-surrogate point.
## Interpretation and counterevidence

The construction rules out a distribution-free guarantee that minimizing Eq. (21) minimizes true interference, and it shows that gradient descent does not always replace the discarded residual protection. It does not refute the stated bound or contradict measured benchmark scores. The paper explicitly labels the coefficient substitution and optimizer route as design choices. Those passages are decisive counterevidence against treating the example alone as a Major invalid-theorem finding.

No general repair is claimed. A guarantee would require additional coverage or covariance assumptions and a corresponding analysis. Whether the proposed implicit regularization explains the evaluated models remains Needs Evidence. This item is recorded as scope clarification, separate from the supported issue below.
# Substantive finding
Problem 1 (Released NLP merging learning rate differs from the paper).  The current pinned NLP routine uses twice the learning rate declared in the paper.
## Claim, evidence, and check

The experimental settings on p. 5 and Appendix A.8.3, p. 23, specify Adam with learning rate \(10^{-5}\) and 300 iterations. In the pinned release, `nlp_roberta/lamassu.py`, line 9, constructs Adam with `lr=2e-5`; the default iteration count at line 3 is 300. Its Eq. (21) loss is implemented at lines 16–17. The ViT routine, `vit/wudi_main.py`, uses \(10^{-5}\) at line 49. These are static source observations, not inferred training behavior.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair state

The repository commit postdates the PDF’s June 2025 creation metadata, so the discrepancy does not determine which learning rate generated the published NLP results. Neither a score difference nor a changed conclusion has been measured. The supported assessment is Minor: a local paper-to-release reproducibility mismatch. Resolving it requires identifying the actual experiment configuration and documenting the intended release setting; changing either value without that evidence would be speculative. No repair has been applied to author sources.
# Overall dependence and conclusion

The principal theoretical inequalities remain valid under their stated/interpreted domains. The surrogate has a verified limitation but is explicitly introduced as an approximation. The supported paper-level impact is therefore Minor, arising from the released learning-rate mismatch; pending empirical questions do not raise it. The reported headline gains were arithmetically checked against displayed comparisons, not independently reproduced. A signed-versus-absolute normalization convention in the released weak-baseline evaluation remains an unresolved auxiliary observation, not an additional graded problem.

report: Abstract: This review examines the main optimization and inference-complexity guarantee, its output-layer construction, and concentration dependencies. Two demonstrated derivation defects bear directly on that guarantee: a factor-of-two normalization error in the constructed output layer and a false general weighted-Gaussian concentration lemma. The first has a verified local repair; a complete repair of the second’s applications is not certified. These are Major at the level of the affected core derivations, without establishing that the main theorem is false. A separate rate-comparison overstatement is Minor. The apparent noisy-query contradiction is withdrawn under the text’s clean-query interpretation. Adjudication remains pending.

Date:
Title: Technical Verification of Nonlinear Transformer Feature Learning
# Identity and scope

Naoki Nishikawa, Yujin Song, Kazusato Oko, Denny Wu, and Taiji Suzuki, Nonlinear transformers can perform inference-time feature learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment 0212 / I25-43581; OpenReview xQTSvP57C3. The reviewed publisher PDF, retrieved 25 October 2026 UTC, has 32 pages. All references below use one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed local page numbers. The embedded appendix occupies pp. 13–32.

The inspected scope includes the single-index model, Assumption 4, Algorithm 1 and Theorem 1, the core approximation and concentration dependencies, selected appendix calculations, and the disclosed synthetic-experiment protocol. It is not a line-by-line certification of every Hermite expansion. No author code was identified in the staged sources; the separate OpenReview attachment endpoint returned HTTP 403 during acquisition. Neither observation establishes that code or additional material does not exist. No models were trained or author programs executed.
# Necessary setup

The target is \(f_*(x)=\sigma_*(\langle\beta,x\rangle)\) for \(x\sim N(0,I_d)\), with a fixed mean-zero, variance-one polynomial link. The unit feature \(\beta\) is uniformly sampled in an \(r\)-dimensional subspace, \(1\le r\le d\). Context labels have independent noise \(\zeta_i\in\{-\tau,\tau\}\), where \(\tau=O_d(1)\). The prose on pp. 3–4 describes the query target as \(f_*(x)\); it does not explicitly give the query a fresh noise variable.

Write \(l=\mathrm{ge}(\sigma_*)\in\{1,2\}\). Theorem 1 gives a sufficient inference context length \(\widetilde\Omega(r^{3l/2})\), with corresponding pretraining and width requirements. Its proof first constructs an attention matrix, then a continuous output-layer representation (Lemma 23), discretizes it (Lemma 24), and transfers optimization error to inference error (Lemmas 25–27). The problems below identify specific points in this chain, rather than equating a failed proof step with a false final theorem.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The output-layer density normalization halves the constructed target).  Equation (D.1), p. 26, uses half the coefficient required by its sampling distribution.
## Original claim and hypotheses

Lemma 23, pp. 25–26, assumes \[g(x)=P_1+\alpha\langle\beta,x\rangle^l+n(x),\qquad
 \alpha=P_2r^{-l/2},\] with \(P_1=o_d(1)\), logarithmically scaled positive \(P_2\), and a specified vanishing remainder. It constructs \(\pi(v,b)\) for independent \(v\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{-1,1\}\) and \(b\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]\) so that \[\mathbb E_{v,b}\pi(v,b)\operatorname{ReLU}(vg(x)+b)
 =\sigma_*(\langle\beta,x\rangle)+o_d(1).\] Let \(A=\alpha\log^2d\). Equation (D.1) multiplies its two window-restricted branches by \(1/(2A)\). The windows have length \(2A\), centered at \(P_1\) and \(-P_1\), and each branch additionally requires one sign of \(v\).
## Complete density calculation

Assume the windows lie inside \([-1,1]\), as they do for the admissible specialization below. Each branch has probability \[\Pr(v=\pm1)\Pr(b\text{ in the corresponding window})
 =\tfrac12\cdot \frac{2A}{2}=\frac A2.\] Multiplication by \(1/(2A)\) therefore gives \(1/4\) times each conditional-window expectation. The first equality immediately after (D.1) instead gives \(1/2\) times each. This is an exact discrepancy in normalization, independent of the specific representation coefficients.

For a fully specified specialization, take \(\sigma_*(z)=z\), \(l=1\), \(r=d\), \(P_1=0\), \(P_2=1/\log d\), and \(n(x)=0\). The link has Gaussian mean zero and variance one; the feature and input distributions are exactly those of Assumption 4. Context noise may be zero. Then \(\alpha=1/(\sqrt d\log d)\) and \(A=\log d/\sqrt d<1\) for all sufficiently large \(d\). All remainder and scale hypotheses of Lemma 23 hold. For \(Z=\langle\beta,x\rangle\), \(|Z|\le\log^2d\) holds with probability tending to one.

A parent-authored integral calculation at \(d=100\) returned half the target at \(Z=-1,-1/4,1/2,1\); multiplying the printed construction by two returned the target. This finite check supports the exact calculation, not a general numerical proof.
## Dependency, alternative reading, and verified repair

Lemma 24 defines \(a_j=m^{-1}\pi(v_j,b_j)\) using this same \(\pi\), so its construction inherits the factor. The resulting approximation is then the comparator in the optimization proof on p. 27 and the inference argument of Theorem 1. This makes the defect a Major invalid core derivation under the specified calibration, even though its repair is short.

The interpretation of expectation as integration against an unnormalized measure would not rescue the calculation: Algorithm 1 and the lemma explicitly use uniform sampling. Correcting the prefactor to \(1/A\) doubles \(\pi\) and the associated discrete coefficients, restores the continuous representation, and leaves the stated big-\(O\) coefficient and norm orders unchanged. This local repair is analytically verified. It is not a certification of the entire repaired theorem or a statement about the experimental network’s trained weights.
Problem 2 (High-probability boundedness does not control the weighted tail mean).  Lemma 31, p. 31, is false without a tail-moment condition.
## Original assertion and suspect step

The lemma takes independent Gaussian \(X_i\sim N(0,I_d)\) and i.i.d. scalar weights \(z_i\) that may depend on \(X_i\), with \(|z_i|\le C\) with high probability. It asserts \[\left\|\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N z_iX_i-\mathbb E[z_1X_1]\right\|
 \le \widetilde O(C\sqrt{d/N})\] with high probability. In the truncation proof, \(z_i'=z_i\mathbf1_{\{|z_i|\le C\}}\), the expectation difference must contain \(z_i\). The displayed tail calculation drops that factor.
## Counterexample satisfying every stated condition

For every integer \(d\), choose \(N=d^2\), \(C=1\), independent \(X_i\sim N(0,I_d)\), and \[z_i=\exp(d^2/2)\mathbf1_{\{X_{i1}\ge d\}}.\] The pairs are independent and identically distributed, \(z_i\) depends only on the allowed \(X_i\), and every expectation here is finite. Moreover, \(\Pr(|z_i|>1)=\overline\Phi(d)\) is smaller than every inverse polynomial in \(d\). Thus the stated high-probability boundedness holds, even simultaneously for all \(N\) samples with probability at least \(1-d^2\overline\Phi(d)\).

Let \(\varphi\) be the standard normal density. Gaussian integration gives \[\mathbb E[X_{i1}\mathbf1_{\{X_{i1}\ge d\}}]=\varphi(d),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[z_iX_i]=e^{d^2/2}\varphi(d)e_1
                 =\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e_1 .\] On the event that none of the \(X_{i1}\) exceeds \(d\), every observed weighted vector is zero. Hence the left side is exactly \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\) with probability tending to one, whereas the asserted right side is \(\widetilde O(d^{-1/2})\to0\). Polylogarithmic factors cannot remove this contradiction. The independent diagnostic records the exact mean and Gaussian union bound; it does not simulate rare events.
## Core dependency and counterevidence

Lemma 19 explicitly invokes Lemma 31 for vector concentration, and Corollary 32 invokes it for matrix concentration. The latter is used in Lemma 21 on p. 25 to control \(T_1^{-1}\sum_t m^t(x^t)^\top\), yielding the trained attention matrix in Proposition 22. Proposition 22 feeds Proposition 8 and the output-layer construction underlying Theorem 1. Thus the unsupported general concentration premise is part of the core optimization proof, not an unrelated appendix statement. This is assessed Major for that derivation; the counterexample does not claim that the paper’s actual exponential weights equal the rare-spike weights above.

There is substantial counterevidence against declaring the final theorem false. Lemma 18, pp. 16–17, explicitly controls a scalar weighted tail by Hölder and Gaussian exponential moments; Lemma 19 calls for the same technique. For clipped, bounded-label exponential weights, a vector tail can be bounded through \[\|\mathbb E[zX\mathbf1_E]\|
 \le \{\mathbb E[z^2\|X\|^2]\}^{1/2}\Pr(E)^{1/2}.\] The specific Gaussian-exponential second moment is finite and controlled on the stated typical-query event. This supplies a viable local argument for the Lemma 19 branch. An equivalent complete tail argument for the pretraining-task matrix in Lemma 21 was not verified here. The full theorem therefore remains an open repair-verification item, rather than a refuted empirical or mathematical conclusion.
## Precise local correction

A valid replacement keeps the tail bias explicitly. For i.i.d. pairs, define \(z'=z\mathbf1_{\{|z|\le C\}}\) and \(b_d=\|\mathbb E[zX\mathbf1_{\{|z|>C\}}]\|\). If \(\Pr(\max_i|z_i|>C)\le\eta\), then standard bounded-weight Gaussian concentration and the triangle inequality give, with probability at least \(1-\delta-\eta\), \[\left\|\frac1N\sum_i z_iX_i-\mathbb E[zX]\right\|
 \le K C\sqrt{\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{N}}+b_d\] for a universal constant \(K\). The centered bounded-weight vector is sub-Gaussian up to a universal factor, since each projection is dominated in absolute value by \(C\) times a Gaussian projection. The added \(b_d\) is exactly the quantity absent from the original proof. Recovering its advertised rate requires a separate bound on \(b_d\) for every application.
Problem 3 (Strict sample-complexity superiority is overstated at low degree).  The exponent comparison in Section 4.2(i), p. 6, does not follow from \(\mathrm{ge}\le\deg\) alone.

The displayed sufficient exponent is \(3\mathrm{ge}/2\). The paper’s own kernel comparator has exponent \(\deg\), and its CSQ comparator has exponent \(\max\{\mathrm{ie}/2,1\}\). Strict polynomial separation therefore requires respectively \[\deg>3\mathrm{ge}/2,\qquad
 \max\{\mathrm{ie}/2,1\}>3\mathrm{ge}/2 .\] For the admissible normalized link \((z^2-1)/\sqrt2\), all three indices are two. The sufficient exponent is three, compared with kernel exponent two and CSQ exponent one. The inequality \(\mathrm{ge}\le\deg\) does not establish the claimed strict advantage. For \(\mathrm{He}_3/\sqrt6\), the theorem’s exponent \(3/2\) equals the cited CSQ exponent.

This is a Minor scope overstatement: the advertised all-regime comparison must be restricted, but the high-degree existential separation and the theorem’s explicit sufficient-rate statement are not refuted. An insufficient upper bound also does not prove the algorithm’s optimal complexity is worse. The experiment’s finite-dimensional fitted slope is not an asymptotic replacement for the theorem.
# Noise interpretation and other checked boundaries

An initial candidate compared the vanishing-risk claim with the \(\tau+o_d(1)\) endpoint printed on p. 27 and the subsequent zero-error invocation in Lemma 26, p. 29. The main prose, however, identifies the query target as \(f_*(x)\) and explicitly adds noise only to context labels. With clean query targets, Lemma 24’s approximation, after the factor correction above, gives the stronger \(o_d(1)\) endpoint directly. The noisy-query allegation is therefore not retained as an unconditional finding.

If one instead adds independent query noise, then \(\tfrac12(|u-\tau|+|u+\tau|)=\max\{|u|,\tau\}\ge\tau\) and vanishing absolute risk at fixed \(\tau>0\) is impossible. That conditional fact must not be presented as a counterexample satisfying a query-noise assumption the paper never states. Clarifying \(y\) and removing the extraneous \(\tau\) in the clean-target proof would resolve the notation.

The disclosed experiment uses a six-layer GPT-2 architecture and curriculum, rather than Algorithm 1’s single structured layer; the difference is stated in the paper. Its causal prediction positions and the theory’s fixed query-label embedding do not reveal the held-out query label in the inspected description. No additional empirical defect was established.
# Conclusion and state

The highest supported assessment is Major for the two identified core derivations. The factor-of-two repair is verified locally. The concentration lemma needs a valid replacement and application-specific tail checks. These judgments do not assert whole-paper collapse, failed benchmarks, or impossibility of the proposed inference mechanism.

report: Abstract: This claim-focused review finds four invalid derivations connected to the paper’s core upper and lower bounds: an insufficient known-bound cancellation constant, a false clipping-error lemma, a mismatch between sparse penalty support and its proof, and an inadmissible lower-bound construction. Each is Major at the level of the affected derivation. None of the counterexamples is presented as a disproof of the actual algorithm’s final regret rate. Local repairs are distinguished from complete revised guarantees; an alternative existential lower-bound construction is proved. A generic scalar-solver defect is Minor. Title: Technical Verification of Unconstrained Robust Online Convex Optimization
# Identity, evidence, and scope

Jiujia Zhang and Ashok Cutkosky, Unconstrained Robust Online Convex Optimization, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; assignment 0213 / I25-43582; OpenReview xPzwJznH9S. The reviewed official publisher PDF was acquired on 25 October 2026 UTC and has 31 pages, including appendices on pp. 11–31. Locations below use one-based PDF pages, which equal the printed local page numbers.

The review checks the corruption model, known-\(G\) error cancellation, unknown-\(G\) filtering and error-correction dependencies, lower-bound constructions, and the generic implicit solver. Applications and the illustrative experiment receive narrower checks. No author repository was identified in the staged acquisition; additional OpenReview material was access-blocked (HTTP 403). This does not establish nonrelease or absence. No author code or empirical reproduction was run. Later versions and errata were not independently retrieved.
# Setup and core dependencies

The decision domain is \(\mathbb R^d\). Convex losses have true gradients \(g_t\) with \(\|g_t\|\le G\); feedback \(\widetilde g_t\) may be corrupted. A supplied budget \(k\) satisfies the two conditions on pp. 2–3: \[|\{t:\|g_t-\widetilde g_t\|\ge G\}|\le k,\qquad
 \sum_t\min(\|g_t-\widetilde g_t\|,G)\le kG .\] The analysis clips feedback to the ball of radius \(h_t\). Write \(C_h\) for that projection. Its regret decomposition includes \[\mathrm{ERROR}=\sum_t\langle g_t-C_{h_t}\widetilde g_t,w_t\rangle,\qquad
 \mathrm{CORRECTION}=\sum_t r_t(w_t).\] The aim is to cancel their difference without bounding the decision domain. Theorem 5.1 treats known \(G\), with \(h_t=G\) and regularizer scale \(c=kG\); Theorem 6.1 treats unknown \(G\) through FILTER and TRACKER. Both regimes know a corruption bound \(k\). The lower bounds support the claimed optimal dependence on comparator size, horizon and corruption.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The known-\(G\) error bound misses a factor of two).  The estimate used for cancellation in §5.1, p. 4, and the proof of Theorem 5.1, pp. 14–15, is not valid under the stated corruption budget.
## Claim, admissible check, and consequence

The proof uses \(\mathrm{ERROR}\le kG\max_t\|w_t\|\) and cancels that coefficient with the regularizer at \(c=kG\). Take \(d=1\), \(T=4\), \(G=k=1\), and one round with \(g_t=1\), \(\widetilde g_t=-1\), \(w_t=M>0\). Put all other gradients and iterates at zero. These are gradients of convex linear losses. There is exactly one large corruption and its capped cost is \(\min(2,1)=1\), so both budget conditions hold. Clipping at one leaves the feedback unchanged. Thus \[\mathrm{ERROR}=2M,\qquad kG\max_t|w_t|=M.\] This is a counterexample to the uniform algebraic estimate, not a claim that this iterate history is generated by Algorithm 2. With the single nonzero iterate, the regularizer contribution is at most \(cM\); the displayed cancellation therefore cannot follow from these estimates alone.
## Verified local repair and counterevidence

Projection onto a ball containing \(g_t\) is nonexpansive and cannot increase its distance from \(g_t\). Both points after projection have norm at most \(G\), so \[\|g_t-C_G\widetilde g_t\|
 \le\min(\|g_t-\widetilde g_t\|,2G)
 \le2\min(\|g_t-\widetilde g_t\|,G).\] The correct general sum bound is \(2kG\), attained by the sign-flip example. Replacing \(c=kG\) by \(c=2kG\) gives, using the paper’s regularizer lower bound with \(\alpha=\epsilon/k\), \[\mathrm{ERROR}-\mathrm{CORRECTION}
 \le2kG\max_t\|w_t\|-2kG(\max_t\|w_t\|-\epsilon/k)
 =2\epsilon G.\] This verifies the local cancellation repair; the comparator bias remains of the same asymptotic order. It does not certify all base-learner and implementation dependencies. A sharper analysis of actual iterates could conceivably justify the original parameters, but none is supplied by this step. Because this is the mechanism of the central known-\(G\) guarantee, the invalid derivation is Major, despite the short repair.
Problem 2 (Lemma H.1 charges clipping-created errors to the corruption budget).  Lemma H.1, p. 23, is false when a clipping threshold is below the true gradient norm.
## Every hypothesis and the exact discrepancy

The lemma assumes the original corruption conditions and \(0<h_t\le\tau\), and asserts \[\sum_t\|g_t-C_{h_t}\widetilde g_t\|\le2k\max(\tau,G).\] Choose \(d=1\), \(T=4\), \(G=k=1\), \(h_t=\tau=1/4\), losses \(\ell_t(w)=w\), and \[(g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4)=(1,1,1,1),\qquad
 (\widetilde g_1,\widetilde g_2,\widetilde g_3,\widetilde g_4)=(1/2,1,1,1).\] The true gradients have norm one, the large-corruption count is zero, and the capped corruption budget is \(1/2\le1\). There is exactly one changed feedback. Every clipped value equals \(1/4\), whence \[\text{left side}=4(1-1/4)=3,\qquad
 \text{asserted upper bound}=2.\] The last line of the proof invokes the budget for \(\|g_t-C_{h_t}\widetilde g_t\|\) although the assumption bounds \(\|g_t-\widetilde g_t\|\). Uncorrupted rounds can acquire clipping error.
## Dependence, special case, and limited correction

Lemma H.2 uses H.1 in the unknown-\(G\) error/bias analysis, including a fixed-threshold comparison; that analysis feeds Theorem 6.1. The failure is consequently Major for the presented core derivation. If \(h_t\ge G\), this particular objection disappears, but that is not H.1’s hypothesis and is unavailable throughout unknown-\(G\) adaptation.

A valid general replacement, for the same \(h_t\le\tau\), is \[\sum_t\|g_t-C_{h_t}\widetilde g_t\|
 \le \sum_t(G-h_t)_+ +2k\max(G,\tau).\] Indeed, insert \(C_{h_t}g_t\) by the triangle inequality. The first distance is at most \((G-h_t)_+\); the second is at most \(\min(\|g_t-\widetilde g_t\|,2h_t)\) by nonexpansiveness and the diameter bound. For \(e\ge0\), \(\min(e,2h_t)\le2\max(1,\tau/G)\min(e,G)\). Summation proves the claim. The new truncation term may grow with \(T\); merely inserting this correction does not restore the advertised final rate.
Problem 3 (The sparse penalty is positive on fewer rounds than its proof assumes).  Equation (11), p. 7, and the OFFSET\(_1\) calculation in Lemma H.2, p. 24, use incompatible supports.

The definition is \(\alpha_t=\gamma_\alpha\mathbf1_{\{h_{t+1}\ne h_t\}}\). The proof instead substitutes \(\alpha_t=\gamma_\alpha\) on every clipped round and applies \[(G+h_t)X-\alpha_tX^2\le \frac{(G+h_t)^2}{4\alpha_t}.\] A clipped round need not increase the threshold. Set \(T=4\), \(k=2\), \(G=1\), \(\tau_G=1/4\), \(\epsilon=1\), and consider a first uncorrupted feedback \(g_1=\widetilde g_1=1\). Initialize the clipping counter to zero and grant the conventional unchanged-threshold fallback omitted from the pseudocode. After this round its counter is one, so neither a trigger at \(k\) nor at \(k+1\) doubles the threshold. Consequently \(\alpha_1=0\). All corruption conditions hold with budget at most two.

Lemma H.2 allows arbitrary iterates bounded by \(\epsilon 2^T/2=8\); for example \(w_1=1\) and the others zero satisfy that condition. Other parameters may be chosen \(c=\gamma_\alpha=\gamma_\beta=\tau_D=1\), \(p=\ln4>1\), and the prescribed \(\alpha=\epsilon\tau_G/c=1/4\). The displayed pointwise argument divides by zero in this admissible case. Its supremum over \(X\ge0\) is infinite when \(\alpha_t=0\). This refutes the proof step, without proving H.2’s final aggregate bound or Algorithm 2’s regret false.

There is also a concrete FILTER discrepancy. Algorithm 3, p. 21, doubles at counter \(n=k\), whereas the proof of Lemma F.2, p. 22, requires \(k+1\) exceedances. For \(G=k=1\), initial threshold \(10\), \(g_1=1\), \(\widetilde g_1=11\), the printed rule gives \(h_2=20\), exceeding the claimed \(\max(10,4G)=10\). The capped corruption cost and large-corruption count are both one. Using \(k+1\) removes this example but does not resolve the penalty-support mismatch.

The sparse correction mechanism is essential to Theorem 6.1, so the demonstrated invalid derivation is Major. Defining \(\alpha_t\) on every clipping event makes the displayed completion of the square valid locally; it also changes the algorithm and requires a fresh count and global regret analysis. No complete repair is certified here.

Problem 4 (The logarithmic lower-bound construction has coupled sign and domain errors).  The comparator in Lemma E.4, p. 19, and its use in Theorem E.5, p. 20, do not give the asserted admissible construction.

For the all-\(e_1\) feedback sequence, the proof sets \(f(x)=\epsilon\exp(x^2/T)\) and prints \(f'(-T)=+2\epsilon e^T\). Direct differentiation gives \(f'(-T)=-2\epsilon e^T\). The always-zero learner satisfies its origin-regret requirement \(R_T(0)=0\le\epsilon\), but for the printed positive comparator \(u=Ue_1\) its regret is \(-TU\), not the positive lower bound obtained in (19).

Correcting the sign alone is insufficient. The next proof defines on corrupted rounds \(g_t=\widetilde g_t-u/\|u\|\). With the corrected \(u=-Ue_1\) and \(\widetilde g_t=e_1\), this is \(2e_1\), violating the explicit unit-gradient condition. With the printed positive comparator the gradient is admissible, but the inherited lower bound is not. These are analytic, source-visible failures in the advertised matching-logarithm argument, hence Major under the core-derivation calibration. The existential theorem can nevertheless be recovered as follows.
## A verified replacement with its quantifiers

Suppose a deterministic learner has origin regret at most \(\epsilon>0\) for every received gradient sequence of norm at most one, as in the uniform premise of (17). Its iterates satisfy \(\|w_t\|\le\epsilon2^{t-1}\). To see this directly, at any prefix choose the next gradient aligned with \(w_t\) and the remaining gradients zero. The origin guarantee implies \(\|w_t\|\le\epsilon-\sum_{s<t}\langle\widetilde g_s,w_s\rangle
 \le\epsilon+\sum_{s<t}\|w_s\|\); induction gives the bound.

Let \(T\ge1\) and \(0\le k\le T\) be integers, \(U=2\epsilon e^T\), \(u=-Ue_1\), true gradients \(g_t=e_1\) always, and feedback zero on any exactly \(k\) rounds and \(e_1\) on the others. Both gradient sequences have norm at most one and there are exactly \(k\) corruptions. Then \[R_T(u)\ge UT-\epsilon(2^T-1)\ge UT/2.\] The second inequality follows from \(2^T-1\le Te^T\). Also, \[\log(1+U^2T/(2\epsilon^2))=\log(1+2Te^{2T})\le4T.\] For \(T\ge1\), \(1+2T\le e^{2T}\) gives the latter bound. Since \(\epsilon\le UT\) and \(k\le T\), \[R_T(u)\ge\frac18\left[
 \epsilon+U\sqrt{T\log(1+U^2T/(2\epsilon^2))}+Uk\right].\] This restores an existential logarithmic-form lower bound for this exponentially large comparator under the stated uniform origin guarantee. It does not prove matching logarithmic dependence at every prescribed comparator magnitude, nor a pathwise result from an expectation-only origin premise.

The coarser Theorem 5.2 also survives the checked construction with explicit random tie-breaking: if \(S\) is the sum of the last \(T-k\) Rademachers, use \(\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(S)\) for \(S\ne0\) and an independent fair sign for \(S=0\). The first \(k\) true gradients are \(\sigma e_1\) with zero feedback; choose \(u=-D\sigma e_1\). Expected regret equals \(D(k+\mathbb E|S|)\). For \(m=T-k>0\), the moments \(\mathbb ES^2=m\), \(\mathbb ES^4=3m^2-2m\) give \(\mathbb E|S|\ge\sqrt{m/3}\) by Hölder; \(m=0\) gives \(Dk\). This verifies the coarse order and handles the tie and endpoint cases.
Problem 5 (The generic scalar inverse and bisection bracket are incorrect).  The paragraph after Algorithm 2, p. 14, gives an algebraically incorrect inverse and an unsupported universal bracket.

For \(p>1\), \(c,S>0\) and \(R(x)=cp\,x^{p-1}/(S+x^p)^{1-1/p}\), set \(q=(y/(cp))^{p/(p-1)}\). Solving gives \[R^{-1}(y)=\left(\frac{Sq}{1-q}\right)^{1/p},
 \qquad 0\le y<cp .\] The paper prints \(1+q\) and claims all \(y\ge0\). For \(S=c=1\), \(p=2\), \(y=1\), the printed \(x=1/\sqrt5\) yields \(R(x)=\sqrt{2/3}\ne1\); the correct \(x=1/\sqrt3\) yields one. No finite inverse exists for \(y\ge cp\).

The asserted generic upper bisection endpoint \(S_t^{1/p}\) also fails for parameters allowed by the generic base result. Take \(\epsilon=1\), \(c=10^{-6}\), \(p=2\), \(\alpha=10^{-12}\), \(h_1=h_2=1\), \(w_1=0\), and first gradient \(-1\). The consistent first-order update has target \(\|\theta\|=1\), \(V_2=2\), \(B_2=32\), and \(a_2=1/(\sqrt{32}\log^2 32)\). On its square-root branch, \[L_2(x)=6\sqrt{2\log(1+x/a_2)}
       +\frac{2c x}{\sqrt{\alpha^2+x^2}}.\] At the advertised upper endpoint \(\alpha\), this is \(0.0000713580111<1\); independent bisection gives the root \(0.0002058350167\). These calculations concern the consistent first-order equation, not an exploitation of the pseudocode’s separate \(\theta\) index slip.

A valid local bracket follows from \(L=\Psi'+R\ge\Psi'\): use \([0,x_\Psi]\) where \[x_\Psi=
 \begin{cases}
 a\{\exp(\theta^2/(36V))-1\},&\theta\le6V/h,\\
 a\{\exp(\theta/(3h)-V/h^2)-1\},&\theta>6V/h .
 \end{cases}\] Then \(L(0)=0\) and \(L(x_\Psi)\ge\theta\); continuity and monotonicity permit bisection. This verifies the local solver repair. Failure under the main theorem’s coupled \(c=kG,\alpha=\epsilon/k\) was not established, so this generic implementation/domain defect is Minor, separately from the Major cancellations above.
# Applications, surviving scope, and conclusion

Corollary D.1, p. 15, invokes a pathwise gradient-bound theorem from only \(\mathbb E_t\|g_t\|\le G\). Those hypotheses differ. For \(G=1\), let \(g=3\) with probability \(1/5\) and \(g=-3/10\) with probability \(4/5\). Then \(\mathbb E|g|=21/25\), \(\mathbb Eg=9/25\), and \(\mathbb EC_1g=-1/25\): clipping can reverse the mean without corruption. This establishes that the cited premise is not automatic, but no complete actual-algorithm stochastic counterexample is claimed. Strengthening to an almost-sure bound repairs this invocation conditional on a repaired known-\(G\) theorem. The weighted-gradient invocation in Corollary D.2, p. 16, similarly needs a separate argument when importance weights exceed one; its final validity remains Needs Evidence.

The findings do not negate the goal of robust unconstrained optimization, and the supplied lower-bound replacement preserves an existential optimality statement. Unknown-\(G\) analysis requires more than a constant adjustment. Figure 1’s illustration was inspected as a disclosed protocol, without rerunning simulations; no empirical failure is inferred from proof defects.
