report: Abstract: This review checks the theoretical motivation, regularization objective, released implementations and selected evaluation claims. Two core discrepancies are demonstrated: Theorem 3.3 drops the state expectation from its return bound, and Equation (6) places a margin hinge outside the expectation while Algorithm 1 and the released implementations place it inside. Complete examples show false statewise bounds and different regularizer values and gradients. Both are Major for the affected core derivations/specification. Precise local corrections are verified, without claiming that the reported empirical improvements fail. A deterministic-policy scope clarification and unresolved evaluation provenance are retained separately. Adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of Goal-Conditioned Policy Self-Regularization
# Identity and inspected version

Xudong Gong, Sen Yang, Dawei Feng, Kele Xu, Bo Ding, Huaimin Wang, and Yong Dou, Improving the Continuity of Goal-Achievement Ability via Policy Self-Regularization for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment 0214 / I25-43583; OpenReview xPMDwGL1TT. The frozen publisher PDF, acquired 25 October 2026 UTC, has 20 pages; its appendix is on pp. 11–20. All page references are one-based PDF pages, equal to printed local numbers. The input metadata’s Feng Dawei is rendered here in the author order printed on the original PDF.

The staged source includes the paper-linked `fly-craft-examples` repository at commit and the environment repository `fly-craft` at . These are pinned acquired snapshots, not assertions of publication-time experiment commits. Static inspection only was performed. Separate OpenReview material was access-blocked during acquisition; its existence is undetermined. Later revisions, raw outcomes and trained checkpoints were not independently obtained.
# Definitions and review scope

The goal-conditioned Markov decision process has common transition kernel \(T\), bounded rewards \(|r|\le R_{\max}\), discount \(0\le\gamma<1\), goal map \(\phi\) and success threshold \(\delta\). Write \(\pi_g\) for the policy conditioned on \(g\), and \[d_{\pi}(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\Pr_\pi(s_t=s),
 \quad \rho_\pi(s,a)=d_\pi(s)\pi(a|s).\] Then \(J(\pi_g)=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\mathbb E_{\rho_{\pi_g}}r(s,a,g)\). The theoretical motivation relates goal perturbation, policy KL divergence and return change. The proposed MSR penalty is added to an RL objective with strength \(\lambda\), margin \(\beta\), and \(N\) goal perturbations per transition.

Checked claims include Theorems 3.1, 3.3 and 3.4, the assumptions of Corollary 3.2 and the bounds in Corollaries 3.5–3.6, Equation (6), Algorithm 1, relevant SAC/PPO source, and the disclosed tables and evaluation scope. Training runs and every appendix plot were not reproduced. Neither finite calculations nor source inspection certify the full empirical study.
# Substantive problems
Problem 1 (Theorem 3.3 loses the state average).  The KL terms in Equations (1)–(2), p. 3, contain a free state \(s\) rather than a state expectation or uniform supremum.
## Original assertion and decisive step

Let \(p=\pi_g\), \(q=\pi_{g+\epsilon}\), and \(B=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\mathbb E_{\rho_p}r(s,a,g+\epsilon)\). The theorem displays upper and lower bounds on \(J(q)\) centered at \(B\), with error \[\frac{2\sqrt2R_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^2}
 \sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(\cdot|s),p(\cdot|s))}.\] No quantifier or distribution for the remaining \(s\) is supplied. Appendix A.4, pp. 11–12, has \(\mathbb E_{s\sim d_p}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(q_s,p_s)\) in (15) and (23), then drops that expectation when applying Pinsker in (16) and (24). The rendered main equations confirm this is not a text-extraction artifact.
## Complete admissible statewise counterexample

Take two states \(s_0,s_1\), two actions \(0,1\), initial state \(s_0\), and \(\gamma=1/2\). Either action at \(s_0\) leads to \(s_1\); \(s_1\) is absorbing. Rewards are zero at \(s_0\) and \(r(s_1,a,z)=\mathbf1_{\{a=1\}}\) for all goals \(z\), so \(R_{\max}=1\). Let the goal space be \(\mathbb R\), \(\phi(s_0)=0\), \(\phi(s_1)=1\), \(\delta=1/10\), and take goals \(g=4\), \(g+\epsilon=5\). Neither is reached, so any success termination convention is inactive; Theorem 3.3 does not require either goal to be achieved.

Both policies choose either action with probability \(1/2\) at \(s_0\). At \(s_1\), \(p(1|s_1)=1/4\) and \(q(1|s_1)=3/4\). These are valid stochastic policies with finite KL. Direct summation gives \[B=\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\frac14=\frac14,\qquad
 J(q)=\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\frac34=\frac34.\] At \(s_0\), \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{s_0},p_{s_0})=0\). Thus the printed upper bound, if read statewise, gives \(3/4\le1/4\). At \(s_1\) the divergence is \(\frac12\log3>0\); information at the initial state cannot bound later policy differences.
## Precise correction and counterevidence

For the same hypotheses, a valid replacement is \[|J(q)-B|\le
 \frac{2\sqrt2R_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^2}
 \mathbb E_{s\sim d_p}\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_s,p_s)} .\] Indeed, the reward bound gives \(|J(q)-B|\le2R_{\max}(1-\gamma)^{-1}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\rho_q,\rho_p)\). To verify the occupancy step, write the discounted balance equations for \(d_p,d_q\). Subtract them using \(P_q\) on the difference and bound the remaining kernel difference by the policy total variation. This yields \[D_{\mathrm{TV}}(d_p,d_q)
 \le\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{d_p}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(p_s,q_s),
 \qquad
 D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\rho_p,\rho_q)
 \le\frac1{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{d_p}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(p_s,q_s).\] Pinsker applies at each state; using even the paper’s looser \(D_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{2D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\) gives (3.1). A supremum over states is another valid, generally weaker replacement. In the example the corrected right side is about \(4.19259\), which safely bounds the actual gap \(1/2\).

Theorem 3.4 in the same paper already retains the state expectation, strong evidence for an omitted operator rather than an intended new phenomenon. Nevertheless the printed universal core guarantee and its derivation are invalid as written. This is Major at the affected derivation level. The local repair preserves the qualitative motivation and does not imply empirical failure.
Problem 2 (The defined loss and the implemented loss average different hinges).  Equation (6), Algorithm 1 and released source disagree for positive margins.
## Claims and actual implementation

For \(K=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_g(\cdot|s),\pi_{g+\epsilon}(\cdot|s))\), Equation (6), p. 4, defines \[A=(\mathbb E_{s,\epsilon}K-\beta)_+ .\] Algorithm 1, p. 5, applies \((K-\beta)_+\) separately to each sampled transition/perturbation and averages, thereby estimating \[B_{\mathrm{hinge}}=\mathbb E_{s,\epsilon}(K-\beta)_+ .\] The text claims that increasing \(N\) makes estimation of Equation (6) more accurate. Instead it improves estimation of the second functional. Convexity gives \(B_{\mathrm{hinge}}\ge A\), with strict inequality when divergences straddle the margin.

At the pinned examples-repository commit, , lines 233–245, computes the divergence in the stated direction, subtracts the threshold elementwise, takes the elementwise maximum with zero, and then calls `mean()`. The analogous PPO operation is at lines 262–273 of . The parent read both actual files. Appendix C, p. 14, sets \(\beta=0.1\), \(N=16\) for the reported task configurations; the inspected VVC SAC configuration also has these values. The difference is therefore not automatically removed by setting \(\beta=0\).
## Smooth-policy example using the stated uniform noise

Use one absorbing state, common zero reward, \(R_{\max}=1\), \(\gamma=1/2\), \(\phi=0\), goal space \(\mathbb R\), and \(\delta=2\). Let the real-valued action policy for goal \(z\) be \(\mathcal N(\theta z,1)\), with \(\theta>0\), and choose base goal \(g=0\), uniform perturbation \(\epsilon\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]\), \(\beta=0.1\), \(\theta^2=0.3\). The state occupancy is a point mass, the policies are smooth in goal, and the perturbation radius one is below \(\delta\). Gaussian KL is symmetric for equal variances, so no direction ambiguity enters: \[K(\epsilon)=\frac{\theta^2\epsilon^2}{2}=0.15\epsilon^2,
 \qquad \mathbb EK=\frac{\theta^2}{6}=0.05<0.1 .\] Thus \(A=0\) and its derivative with respect to \(\theta\) is zero in a neighborhood of this point.
## Correction, dependence, and limits

Moving the hinge inside the expectation in Equation (6) exactly aligns the mathematical definition with Algorithm 1 and the inspected code. Conversely, retaining the printed definition requires averaging KL before applying the hinge. These are alternative methods; their equivalence cannot be asserted. At \(\beta=0\) they agree, and they also agree for distributions entirely on one side of the threshold. Neither special case covers the general positive-margin formulation.

This affects the central proposed MSR objective and the stated sampling interpretation, hence is Major. The correction that changes Equation (6) is verified as a specification alignment; it does not establish that MSR’s reported benchmarks would change. The available source snapshot does not identify which exact bytes generated the historical results.
# Scope clarifications and empirical counterevidence

Corollary 3.2, p. 3, is stated in general MDP language, but Appendix A.3, p. 11, explicitly proves it for deterministic transitions and deterministic policies, then assumes a fixed initial state. Under those conditions, zero expected KL forces equality on visited states and induction reuses the same trajectory. Theorem 3.1’s trajectory-level statement follows directly from \(\phi(s_T)=g\) and \(\|\epsilon\|<\delta\).

Those restrictions matter. With a fixed start and an action-independent stochastic transition to terminal achieved goals \(-0.9\) or \(+0.9\), each with probability \(1/2\), let \(\delta=1\) and use identical policies for every goal. Desired goal \(g'=0\) is reached with probability one. A realized trajectory attaining \(g=0.9\), perturbed by \(\epsilon=0.9\), defines a new goal \(1.8\). The same policy reaches it with probability only \(1/2\), although the KL is zero. Thus the broad stochastic guarantee is false. This does not refute the explicitly restricted appendix proof; the outcome is scope clarification, with a valid deterministic reading preserved.

Theorem 3.4 and Corollaries 3.5–3.6 retain a state average. Their return-gap bound follows by adding and subtracting the cross-goal reward under one occupancy, applying the occupancy bound above, and using the reverse triangle inequality for \(r=-\|\phi(s)-g\|\) within the globally bounded-reward setting. No additional substantive issue was established in this reasoning. An upper bound does not make lower KL necessary for a smaller actual return gap. Similarly, the hinge stops penalizing KL below \(\beta\); it does not impose a positive lower bound on KL.

Selected empirical checks supply important counterevidence. All nine mean-return comparisons in Table 1 improve directionally with MSR. The paper explicitly discusses increased KL in the Reach/PPO and VVC/PPO cases, rather than concealing those exceptions. Evaluation around policy-achievable goals and the absence of a worst-case continuity guarantee are disclosed. Table 6’s overhead percentages agree with its times to rounding. These checks do not establish significance, reproduce training, or recover per-goal outcomes.

An auxiliary static check found an evaluation script computing baseline-to-perturbed KL while Table 1 labels the reverse. The main objective itself uses the former direction. Without a binding between that script, checkpoints and the table’s runs, the historical metric provenance is Needs Evidence, not a claimed numerical error. The source evidence records this limitation.

report: Abstract: The checked fourth-root estimator is unbiased, and its released scalar implementation matches the main formula. A substantive limitation arises in the improved block method: balance of the input points does not imply balance of their differences. A fully admissible pair of balanced points has relative distance error at least one with probability one under dimensions satisfying the advertised improved scaling. This invalidates the unrestricted pairwise extension, assessed Major, while leaving the balanced-single-vector theorem intact. A stronger main-text tail formula is already corrected in the appendix and is a local Minor inconsistency. Released experimental settings also differ from the documented settings, with historical figure provenance unresolved. Adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of Complex Sketches for Dynamic-Weight Distances
# Identity and scope

Simone Moretti, Paolo Pellizzoni, and Francesco Silvestri, Dimensionality Reduction on Complex Vector Spaces for Euclidean Distance with Dynamic Weights, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment 0215 / I25-43584; OpenReview xKMMGugUgy. The reviewed publisher PDF, acquired 25 October 2026 UTC, has 20 pages, including appendices on pp. 12–20. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and equal the printed local numbers.

The released repository `aidaLabDEI/complex-dimensionality-reduction` is frozen at commit (28 May 2025). Its complete acquired snapshot contains two files, including the 141-line . The parent read this source without executing it. Source archives and member/version mappings remain unchanged. The acquisition recorded HTTP 403 for separate OpenReview material; no assertion of its absence is made. Later revisions and historical experiment checkpoints were not retrieved.

The review checks unbiasedness, the block estimator, assumptions and application of the near-uniform theorem, selected concentration dependencies, finite-family probability accounting, and experimental source settings. It does not certify every imported sub-Weibull result or every coefficient expansion in the general chaos analysis. No author programs, training runs or dataset downloads were performed.
# Estimator and necessary assumptions

Inputs and weights are real, with nonnegative weights in the intended weighted-distance setting: \(\|x\|_w^2=\sum_jx_j^2w_j^2\). The sketch is complex. For independent uniform fourth roots \(A_{ij}\in\{1,-1,i,-i\}\), \[g(x)=Ax/\sqrt{k},\qquad
 \rho(g(x),w)=\frac1k\sum_{r=1}^k
 \operatorname{Re}\left[
       \left(\sum_jA_{rj}x_j\right)^2
       \left(\sum_j A_{rj}^2w_j^2\right)\right].\] Ordinary squares, not Hermitian squared magnitudes, are intentional. Since \(\mathbb EA=\mathbb EA^2=\mathbb EA^3=0\) and \(\mathbb EA^4=1\), only equal-index terms survive expectation. Hence \(\mathbb E\rho=\sum_jx_j^2w_j^2\). Independent enumeration for \(x=(1,2,-1)\) and \(w=(2,1,3)\) over all \(4^3=64\) root triples returned mean \(17\), equal to the exact target. This is a finite corroboration of the moment proof.

The block method partitions coordinates into \(L\) fixed blocks, applies independent \(k\)-row sketches, and sums their norm estimates. Section 4.4 assumes a fixed constant \(\zeta\) with \[\|x^{(\ell)}\|_2^2\le\zeta\|x\|_2^2/L,\qquad
 \|w^{(\ell)}\|_4^4\le\zeta\|w\|_4^4/L
 \quad(\ell=1,\ldots,L).\] Theorem 4.6 uses, with \(h=\log(8/\delta)\), \[k\ge c\max\left\{\frac{\Delta^2h}{L^2\epsilon^2},
                  \frac{\Delta h^2}{L^{3/2}\epsilon}\right\}.\] It yields additive error \(\epsilon\|x\|_2^2\|w\|_4^2/\Delta\), and relative error when the corresponding norm ratio is at most \(\Delta\). Constants may absorb the fixed balance constant. The theorem is read with the immediately preceding balance assumptions; omitting those assumptions from its repeated statement does not license applying it to arbitrary differences.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Balanced points need not have balanced differences).  The pairwise-distance remark immediately after Theorem 4.6, p. 8, extends the improved guarantee using only a common partition and linearity. Those conditions are insufficient.
## Source claim and fully specified counterexample

The remark asserts that fixing the partition for all \(x\in X\) preserves linearity and that the dimensionality reduction maintains pairwise distances in \(X\). Unlike the general estimator, the improved theorem has an additional input-balance hypothesis. Linearity gives \(\bar g(x)-\bar g(y)=\bar g(x-y)\), but does not transfer that hypothesis.

Let \(L\) be a positive integer, \(d=4L\), and partition coordinates into \(L\) blocks of size four. Set \[k=1,\qquad w=y=\mathbf1_d,\qquad x=\mathbf1_d+e_1,
 \qquad X=\{x,y\}.\] All weights are positive and the partition is common. The \(y\) and \(w\) block bounds hold with \(\zeta=1\). For \(x\), \(\|x\|_2^2=4L+3\); its first block has squared norm seven and the others four. With \(\zeta=2\), \[7\le2(4L+3)/L,\qquad 4\le2(4L+3)/L .\] Thus both original points satisfy (2.1) with a fixed constant independent of \(L\).

Their difference is \(u=x-y=e_1\), with \(\|u\|_w^2=1\) and \(\|u\|_2^2\|w\|_4^2=2\sqrt L\). Choose \(\Delta=2\sqrt L\), any fixed \(0<\epsilon<1\), and, for example, \(\delta=1/4\). Then (2.2) at \(k=1\) is satisfied whenever \[L\ge c\max\{4h/\epsilon^2,\;2h^2/\epsilon\}.\] For any fixed admissible universal constant \(c\), such integers \(L\) exist. The output has \(L\) complex coordinates, or \(2L\) real coordinates, fewer than the input’s \(4L\) real coordinates.

Only the first block contributes to the distance estimate: \[\begin{aligned}
 \bar\rho(\bar g(x)-\bar g(y),w)
 &=\operatorname{Re}\{A_1^2(A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2+A_4^2)\}\\
 &=1+\sum_{j=2}^4 A_1^2A_j^2 .\end{aligned}\] The three products are independent uniform signs (condition on \(A_1^2\)). The estimate therefore takes values \[-2,\ 0,\ 2,\ 4
 \quad\text{with probabilities}\quad
 \tfrac18,\ \tfrac38,\ \tfrac38,\ \tfrac18 .\] Every value is at distance at least one from the true squared distance one. Consequently the claimed relative-error event fails with probability one for \(\epsilon<1\), regardless of how large \(L\) becomes. Parent enumeration of all 256 root quadruples returned counts \(32,96,96,32\) and the same failure probability.
## Impact, counterevidence, and exact scope repair

This is a Major limitation of the improved pairwise conclusion, a central advertised use of linear dimension reduction. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 4.6 applied to a genuinely balanced single vector: \(u=e_1\) has all its energy in one block and fails (2.1) for any fixed \(\zeta\) as \(L\) grows. The general single-vector theorem and its general pairwise application are also not refuted.

A correct pairwise extension requires (2.1) for every relevant nonzero difference \(x-y\), and for each relevant weight vector, together with the norm-ratio bound for those differences. Apply Theorem 4.6 to each such fixed pair and use a union bound for a finite collection. This verifies the extension under strengthened assumptions. Reading those difference assumptions implicitly into the remark gives a valid interpretation; balance of the points alone does not. The appendix experiments estimate single-vector norms and do not test this missing pairwise condition.
Problem 2 (The main \(L^3\) tail display conflicts with the appendix’s correct \(L^2\) version).  Lemma 4.5 has different Gaussian exponents on pp. 8 and 18.

Let \(M=\|x\|_2^2\|w\|_4^2\). The p. 8 display has Gaussian term \(8\exp(-kc_1L^3t^2/M^2)\), whereas the p. 18 restatement has \(8\exp(-kc_1L^2t^2/M^2)\). Both retain the heavy-tail term \(8\exp(-\sqrt{k}c_2 L^{3/4}\sqrt t/\sqrt M)\).

The stronger main display is not generally valid. Use \(d=2L\), blocks of size two, \(k=1\), and \(x=w=\mathbf1_d\), which satisfy exact block balance. One block estimate is eight with probability \(1/4\) and zero with probability \(3/4\). Its centered value \(Z\) is six or minus two, so \(\mathbb EZ^2=12\) and \(\mathbb EZ^4=336\). For independent block errors \(S=\sum_{\ell=1}^L Z_\ell\), \[\mathbb ES^2=12L,\qquad \mathbb ES^4=432L^2-96L .\] Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the truncated second moment, equivalently the Paley–Zygmund inequality for \(S^2\), yields \[\Pr(|S|>\sqrt{6L})\ge
 \frac{(1-1/2)^2(12L)^2}{432L^2-96L}>\frac1{12}.\] But \(M=2\sqrt2L^{3/2}\); at \(t=\sqrt{6L}\) both terms in the p. 8 maximum tend to zero for any fixed positive \(c_1,c_2\). Its purported upper bound contradicts this fixed lower bound.

The supplied appendix itself resolves the discrepancy. Lemma A.5 gives fluctuation scale \[M\left(\frac{c_1\sqrt v}{\sqrt{k}L}
       +\frac{c_2v^2}{kL^{3/2}}\right);\] Lemma 4.5 on p. 18 uses \(L^2\), and the final proof on p. 19 explicitly uses that \(L^2\) exponent. Theorem 4.6’s stated dimension requirement agrees with the appendix. Thus this is Minor as a local inconsistent display: the checked operative derivation already uses the correct version. It is not treated as a failure of the final balanced-vector rate, nor as an uncredited new repair.
Problem 3 (Released experimental settings differ from the stated protocol).  The available source does not reproduce several declared settings without changes.

Appendix B, p. 19, and the figure captions specify 1,000 independent sketch trials. At the pinned commit, sets `N = 50`. Figure 5, p. 20, specifies \(m=100\) nonzero coordinates; line 121 sets `m = 200`. These are direct source/protocol discrepancies. The common dimension \(d=20000\) and the estimator/normalization match the paper.

There is also an internal weight-range discrepancy: Appendix B prose states \([0.1,1.2]\), whereas the captions and source line 48 use \([1.0,1.2]\). Both cannot be the exact specification of the same draw. The latter range is supported by the released generator, but the historical draw is not identified from that observation.

These are Minor reproducibility discrepancies, with no demonstrated failure of the theoretical estimates or core empirical conclusion. The inspected snapshot is complete but contains no plotting script or hash-bound results identifying which settings generated the published figures. It may represent a cheaper test configuration. Matching `N` and `m` would align those two settings, not regenerate the original plots or settle the weight-range provenance. The saved `out[0]` metadata is an unsquared norm, while samples estimate squared norms; without plotting code, a wrong plotted reference line is not established and remains Needs Evidence.
# Other checked scope and remaining work

The main estimator’s real-part quartic expression and the block row averaging agree with the released code. In particular, replacing squares by complex conjugates would alter the moment construction; no such correction is justified. The new concentration results are conditional on fixed inputs and independent sketch randomness. The paper’s finite-weight-set corollary does not assert validity for unlimited adaptively chosen weights; this review makes no such accusation.

For precise finite-family probability bookkeeping, let \(N\) bound the number of pair/weight events and let \(\eta\) be the desired total failure probability. Applying the pointwise theorem at \(\delta=\eta/N\) gives success at least \(1-\eta\). Corollary 4.4’s printed choice \(\delta=1/(|W|n^2)\), p. 7, only gives a failure upper bound of one after the stated crude union bound, not a specified high-probability level. The exact choice above restores a meaningful bound. If \(|W|=O(n)\) and \(\eta=n^{-a}\) for fixed \(a>0\), the logarithmic dimension order remains unchanged. The asymptotic corollary is therefore supported by the already available pointwise result with explicit probability allocation; no false corollary is claimed.

No independent empirical distributions were generated using author code. The finite enumerations here test algebra and furnish counterexamples, not the paper’s large-dimensional experiments. A broader test of pairwise distances would require a dataset whose differences satisfy the strengthened assumption, or a different analysis for unbalanced differences.

Title: Technical Verification of Projection Optimization for Multi-Objective RLHF
# Identity, reviewed version, and scope

Nuoya Xiong and Aarti Singh, Projection Optimization: A General Framework for Multi-Objective and Multi-Group RLHF, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment 0216 / I25-43585; OpenReview xHhURhYmgK. The official publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026 has 42 pages, with supplementary material on pp. 12–42. All locations below use one-based PDF pages, equal to printed local page numbers.

The original PDF and staged source manifest were read and their actual bytes checked. No verified author repository was identified in the prepared sources. The optional OpenReview API and attachment endpoint returned HTTP 403; this does not establish absence of additional material. No later revision, external erratum or historical experimental checkpoint was retrieved. The paper and its embedded appendix are the scientific sources of this review.

The parent independently checked the examples below, their model assumptions and proof dependencies, and inspected source-formula images on pp. 5, 8, 18 and 37. The review covers the objective geometry, selected offline and online guarantees, reward-free identities and documented experiments. It does not certify every imported statistical lemma, every concentration calculation or empirical reproducibility. Three native auxiliary checks informed, but did not replace, the parent’s integration.
# Model and claims being tested

Unattainable target sets are allowed: the guarantees compare against the best achievable distance. Consequently the examples below do not rely on imposing a target-feasibility condition absent from the paper. Where the pseudocode and prose differ in the running-average notation, the examples grant the intended arithmetic average stated in the prose.
# Core findings

Problem 1 (Negative-power target sensitivity is not uniformly Lipschitz).  Lemma C.2, p. 37, asserts \[d_B(W^\alpha_{p,c},W^{\alpha'}_{p,c})
 \le \frac{m^{3/2}B}{|p|}\|\alpha-\alpha'\|_\infty .\] For the paper’s truncated symmetric set distance, \(d_B\) includes the distance to the other full set of every point in either set with \(\ell_\infty\) norm at most \(B\). The assertion fails for allowed negative \(p\).
## Complete counterexample and exact check

Set \(m=2\), \(p=-1\), \(c=1\), \(B=2\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\). Define \[\alpha=(1-\varepsilon^4,\varepsilon^4),\quad
 \alpha'=(1-\varepsilon,\varepsilon),\quad
 x=(1+\varepsilon^2,\varepsilon^2).\] Both weight vectors are strictly inside the simplex and both coordinates of \(x\) are positive. Moreover \(\|x\|_\infty<2\), and \[\frac{1-\varepsilon^4}{1+\varepsilon^2}
 +\frac{\varepsilon^4}{\varepsilon^2}=1,\] so \(x\in W^\alpha_{-1,1}\). No convention about negative powers at zero is needed.
## Dependency, counterevidence, and impact

The proof on p. 37 uses \(\sum_i x_i^p\le mB^p\) from \(x_i\le B\). For \(p<0\) the coordinate inequality reverses. There is no supplied positive lower-coordinate or uniform lower-weight assumption that rescues this step; the example has strictly positive coordinates and weights.

This lemma controls learned target-set changes in the online theory. In the consensus proof it feeds Eq. (31), p. 23, then terms in Eqs. (32)–(35), pp. 24–25, and Eq. (36) supporting Theorem 5.4. In the malfare proof it feeds Eq. (50), p. 28, and Eqs. (51)–(54), pp. 29–31, supporting Theorem 5.5. These are direct core dependencies, so the finding is Major. It is a false intermediate guarantee and a gap in the stated online proofs, not an independently established regret lower bound for every policy sequence.

Restricting coordinates or weights away from zero might yield a different constant or modulus, but no complete repaired theorem is certified here. The square-root behavior of this family alone is not a global replacement continuity theorem.
Problem 2 (The malfare expansion drops a first-order factor \(q\)).  The proof of Theorem 5.2 in Appendix B.3, p. 18, after Eq. (15), uses an invalid expansion for general \(q>1\).

Take one group, \(m=1\), \(q=2\), \(B=1\), \(W=[1,\infty)\) and \(V^t=0\) at every round. Then \(x=-(T-1)\) and \(y=-1\), satisfying the norm bounds used in the proof. At \(T=100\), the left side of [eq:badexp] (#eq:badexp) is \(100000000\) and the right side is \[99^4+2(99)^3+9(100)^2(2)^4=99440199.\] The inequality fails by \(559801\). The omitted term is of order \(T^3\) and cannot be absorbed into the stated order-\(T^2\) remainder.

This is compatible with an actual offline instance, not merely arbitrary vectors: use one prompt, responses \(0,1\), feature \(\phi(y)=\mathbf1\{y=1\}\), parameter space \([0,1]\), true parameter zero, \(B=\beta=1\), uniform reference, and baseline concentrated on response zero with \(C=0\). A balanced preference dataset comparing the distinct responses has feature-difference covariance one and is consistent with true comparison probability \(1/2\). The pessimistic optimization in Eq. (6) selects parameter zero: its maximum regularized reward is nondecreasing in the nonnegative parameter, and the balanced negative log likelihood is minimized at zero. The optimal policy is then the reference and every estimated regularized reward is zero. Choose \(p=1,c=1\) for the target. The true comparator gap is zero in this example; only the proof inequality, not the final regret conclusion on this instance, is contradicted.

The invalid step is used in Eqs. (16)–(20), the main offline malfare guarantee, and reused in the online malfare analysis. It is therefore Major under a core-derivation standard. The correctness of the \(q=1\) first-order coefficient and the existence of a local repair are counterevidence against claiming that the entire approach is impossible.

Problem 3 (The printed weight estimator is inconsistent).  Equation (11), p. 8, maximizes a sum of selection probabilities. Theorem B.4, Eq. (57), p. 32, claims vanishing weight-estimation error, but the invoked Lemma D.1, p. 38, assumes maximization of a sum of log probabilities.
## An identifiable model with no reward-estimation error

Use one prompt, two responses \(0,1\), and two identical objectives \(r_1(y)=r_2(y)=\mathbf1\{y=1\}\). Each has scalar feature \(\phi_i(y)=\mathbf1\{y=1\}\), true parameter one and \(B=1\). Take uniform reference and baseline, \(C=1/2\), and \(\beta=1\). The baseline identification condition fixes each scalar parameter exactly at one, so there is no reward-model estimation error. Choose one group, \(p=1,c=2\) and true weights \(\alpha_*=(3/4,1/4)\). An unattainable threshold is permitted.

Every normalized nonnegative direction produces the same linear reward. Its optimal policy has \(\pi_*(1)=\sigma(1)\). The paper’s Assumption 5.3 holds with \(\gamma=1/2\): \[\mathbb E_{y_1\sim\pi_*,\,y_2\sim\pi_{\rm base}}
 |r_i(y_1)-r_i(y_2)|=\tfrac12.\] The baseline/reference density ratio is one. Unequal response pairs are sampled with strictly positive probability \(2\sigma(1)(1-\sigma(1))\). Their absolute reward gaps are \((1,1)\), while equal pairs provide no weight information.

For \(\alpha=(a,1-a)\), the selection probability of objective one on an unequal pair is \[s(a)=\frac{e^a}{e^a+e^{1-a}}=\sigma(2a-1).\] Thus the true probability is \(s(3/4)=\sigma(1/2)=0.6224593312\). If \(N_1,N_2\) count the two selected objectives on informative pairs, the printed Eq. (11) criterion is \[N_1s(a)+N_2(1-s(a))
 =N_2+(N_1-N_2)s(a).\] Eventually \(N_1>N_2\) almost surely. The unique maximizer is then \(a=1\), not \(3/4\). Both the raw estimates and their running averages converge to \((1,0)\), with \(\ell_\infty\) error \(1/4\). This contradicts the vanishing error in Eq. (57) for the routine as printed. At the population level the probability-sum score is \(0.5299925756\) at the true parameter and \(0.5565905580\) at the boundary.

The example respects positive true weights and an identifiable selection model; it does not exploit unobserved rewards, zero signal or an absent covariance condition. Because the objectives are identical, the policy can nevertheless remain optimal. A failure of the final policy regret rate on this example is not claimed.
## Existing intended interpretation and exact local correction

Algorithm 4 explicitly calls Eq. (11). Its weight-estimation guarantee is a core component of online adaptation, so the printed estimator/proof mismatch is Major, despite a clear intended local fix. Neither the original formula nor the corrected one resolves Problem 1’s target sensitivity gap. No released implementation was available to determine which estimator was actually used.

Problem 4 (The claimed exact linear special case drops an active orthant constraint).  Example 3.1, p. 5, and the direction claim on p. 7 equate the \(p=1\) target-distance objective to ordinary linear MORLHF. The equality requires more than the displayed lower bound on \(c\).

Let there be one prompt and two responses. Use \[r_1=(0,1),\quad r_2=(0,0.01),\quad
 \alpha=(0.9,0.1),\quad \beta=B=1,\quad c=0.901.\] Both scalar features are \(\mathbf1\{y=1\}\); parameters are \(1,0.01\) and meet the stated bounds. The reference is uniform; the baseline is response zero with common \(C=0\). Both objective weights are positive. Moreover \(c=\max_\pi\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbb E_\pi r_i\), satisfying Example 3.1.

For \(q=\pi(1)\), write \(K(q)=q\log(2q)+(1-q)\log(2(1-q))\). Then \(S(q)=(q-K(q),0.01q-K(q))\), while the ordinary linear objective is \(F(q)=0.901q-K(q)\). Its unique maximizer is \[q_*=\sigma(0.901)=0.7111549596,\quad
 S(q_*)=(0.6191220874,-0.0849213226).\] The projection onto the unrestricted halfspace has a negative second coordinate and is not in \(W^\alpha_{1,c}\). The actual projection is the corner \(z=(901/900,0)\). The boundary KKT condition is strict: \[-S_2-\frac{z_1-S_1}{9}=0.0424780977>0.\] Consequently the true distance is \(0.3913147649\), whereas the paper’s hyperplane formula gives \(0.3890306687\).

The strongest counterreading is important. The paragraph immediately preceding Example 3.1 defines a restricted class \(\Pi\) with every \(S_i(\pi)\ge0\) when relating a specially chosen attainable threshold to nonlinear welfare maximization. If this restriction is imposed globally, the present witness is outside that class. However, Eq. (4), Example 3.1 and the stated closed-form linear oracle do not impose it; the oracle in this admissible reward model returns \(q_*\), violating it. The unrestricted classical-RLHF reduction therefore fails as stated. This is Major for that exact core reduction; under an explicitly restricted policy reading it becomes a scope/enforcement issue, not a refutation inside \(\Pi\).

For \(p=1\) alone, removing the orthant constraint makes the halfspace distance formula correct and restores the unrestricted reduction. Alternatively, enforcing \(S_i\ge0\) makes the formula valid on that restricted policy domain, but yields a constrained policy problem. Neither modification is claimed to repair all nonlinear branches or to have been adopted. The target-distance objective itself remains a meaningful separate design.
# Local inconsistencies and inspected empirical scope
Problem 5 (Reward-free formulas have internally supplied corrections).  Two local displayed formulas conflict with derivations already provided in the frozen paper.

On p. 6, the combined policy is written proportional to \(\pi_{\rm ref}\prod_i\pi_{\theta_i}^{d_i}\). For normalized directions and individual policies \(\pi_{\theta_i}\propto\pi_{\rm ref}\exp(r_i/\beta)\), the correct combination is \(\prod_i\pi_{\theta_i}^{d_i}\) without the additional reference factor. The p. 4 description and Appendix E.2, p. 41, already give that correct product.

For example, with one objective, \(d_1=1\), constant reward \(1/2\), \(B=\beta=1\), and reference \((3/4,1/4)\), the exact optimum is the reference. The extra-factor formula gives \((9/10,1/10)\) and strictly loses regularized objective by its positive KL divergence. A constant unit feature and parameter \(1/2\), with the reference also used as baseline, satisfy the reward and common-baseline assumptions.

The practical Algorithm 5 is explicitly distinguished from theoretical Algorithms 3–4 in Table 1. It averages directions and uses estimated expected reward vectors from 100 training prompts; the paper does not assert that it is literally the same guaranteed algorithm. The described experiments use Llama 2 7B, Anthropic HH, and Humor/Helpful/Harmless objectives. Inspection of the reported tables supports the wording that the method is generally better, not universally best: Table 3 has the \(0.3/0.7\) row with distance \(0.578\) versus MOD’s \(0.572\). The max-min comparisons in Table 4 also show mixed outcomes. No uniform-dominance failure is alleged.

No author code, per-seed outputs or historical run manifests were available for this review. The table entries were checked as reported, not independently reproduced; neither statistical significance nor the exact numerical reward computations are recertified.
# Overall assessment and remaining verification

The demonstrated failures affect specific core arguments, with distinct consequences. Problem 1 invalidates the stated uniform target sensitivity used by both online guarantees. Problem 2 invalidates the malfare expansion underlying an offline theorem and later analysis. Problem 3 disproves consistency of the printed weight-learning routine, while identifying the intended proper-likelihood alternative. Problem 4 refutes the unrestricted exact linear-special-case reduction and explicitly preserves a constrained interpretation. None establishes collapse of the whole framework or a loss in the practical benchmark scores.

# Identity, versions, and review boundaries

Giulio Starace, Oliver Jaffe, Dane Sherburn, James Aung, Chan Jun Shern, Leon Maksin, Rachel Dias, Evan Mays, Benjamin Kinsella, Wyatt Thompson, Johannes Heidecke, Amelia Glaese, and Tejal Patwardhan, PaperBench: Evaluating AI’s Ability to Replicate AI Research, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment 0217 / I25-43586; OpenReview xF5PuTLPbn. The frozen publisher PDF retrieved 25 October 2026 has 31 pages; appendices begin on p. 13. Locations below use one-based PDF pages, equal to printed local page numbers.

The available source is the migrated repository `openai/frontier-evals`, commit , dated 12 October 2026 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. This is later than the paper, not a verified publication-time implementation. The selective lossless snapshot preserves 212 source/common files with archive/member/Git-blob mappings. The preparation manifest records 518 benchmark or rubric dataset members as excluded. Those payloads, agent/human run artifacts and JudgeEval gold-label/result payloads were unavailable for this review. Their absence here is not a claim of nonrelease.

The parent read the original, inspected relevant code statically, independently transcribed and recalculated decisive table entries, and viewed source pages 3, 21, 24 and 25. Three native auxiliary reviews provided arithmetic, source and challenge checks. No author code, agent, LLM judge or API was run; no software or dataset was downloaded. The optional OpenReview endpoint was blocked by HTTP 403. Later revisions and external errata were not searched.
# Scoring definition and checks that agree

A rubric is a tree with nonnegative sibling-relative importance weights. Leaves receive binary scores. For an internal node \(v\) whose children have positive total weight, \[s_v=\frac{\sum_c w_c s_c}{\sum_c w_c}.\] Recursion gives root score \(S=\sum_\ell a_\ell y_\ell\), where \(a_\ell\) is the product of normalized edge weights along the leaf’s path and \(\sum_\ell a_\ell=1\). Induction proves this: a parent forms a convex combination of its children’s convex combinations. Thus \(S\) measures weighted partial completion, not the fraction of papers fully replicated or an unweighted count of independent experiments. Static inspection of the recursive scorer agrees.

The paper explicitly awards partial credit for source that appears correct, execution, and matching results. Fresh execution uses a separate environment and `reproduce.sh` as entrypoint. Code-Dev deliberately omits execution and is described as a noisy, less robust proxy (p. 4). No claim that Code-Dev proves empirical replication is found.
# Supported discrepancies
Problem 1 (Reported means are internally inconsistent).  The Claude BasicAgent headline and a Gemini row do not follow from the displayed runs.
## Claude BasicAgent: complete arithmetic and rounding

If each score was rounded to three decimals, its error is at most \(0.0005\), so the mean error is at most \(0.05\) percentage points. The discrepancy is \(1.1833333\) percentage points, far outside this bound even allowing one-decimal headline rounding.
## Gemini: a row contradicted by its own runs

Table 17, p. 25, lists the `fre` scores as \(0^*,0^*,0.007\) but gives mean \(0.061\) and standard error \(0.009\). Asterisks indicate disqualified scores set to zero under Section 2.5. Their mean is \[(0+0+0.007)/3=0.0023333333,\] not \(0.061\). Excluding both disqualifications would give \(0.007\), still not the displayed mean. A stale pre-disqualification summary is possible, but not established.
## Impact and conditional correction

These are Minor numerical inconsistencies. At least one entry in each conflicting set is wrong or belongs to another run collection. Versioned run identifiers and grade records are needed to recover historical truth. If the appendix scores are authoritative, Claude’s mean rounds to \(19.8\%\) and the Gemini row to \(0.002\). These are conditional arithmetic corrections.

The recalculated Claude value remains above o1 BasicAgent’s reported \(13.2\%\), so the main-setup ordering does not reverse. No demonstrated effect on the human comparison or benchmark design follows. Major impact is not inferred solely from the headline location.
Problem 2 (Uncertainty reporting needs an explicit finite-sample convention).  Per-paper errors differ from customary sample SEM; several aggregate errors require unavailable historical details.

For \(n\) independent repeated scores the conventional sample-based SEM is \[{\rm SE}_1=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_j(s_j-\bar s)^2}{n(n-1)}}.\] Using population variance instead yields \[{\rm SE}_0=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_j(s_j-\bar s)^2}{n^2}}
           =\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}}\,{\rm SE}_1.\] For three repeats the factor is \(\sqrt{2/3}=0.8164966\).

The Table 10 adaptive-pruning row, p. 21, has scores \(0,0.027,0.193\), giving \[{\rm SE}_1=0.0603388579,\qquad
 {\rm SE}_0=0.0492664712.\] The reported \(0.049\) matches the latter. Keeping the disqualified zero exact and allowing the other scores their full rounding intervals still gives sample SEM between \(0.0601099\) and \(0.0605684\).

This is a Minor uncertainty-convention concern, not an assertion that every population-variance plug-in estimate is forbidden. The convention should be declared. If customary sample SEM is intended, use denominator \(n(n-1)\). The later uses `ddof=1` for complete-run and per-paper statistics; this does not identify the historical implementation.

Aggregate uncertainty also depends on the replication unit. Treating Table 15 columns as complete benchmark repeats gives sample SEM \(1.0322\) percentage points. Treating papers as fixed strata with independent within-paper repeats gives \[\frac1{20}\sqrt{\sum_{p=1}^{20}\frac{s_p^2}{3}}
 =0.8505\ {\rm percentage\ points}.\] The paper reports \(0.8\). Rounding and undisplayed raw precision could affect this close stratified comparison, so it is not used as a decisive contradiction. Other aggregate errors remain unresolved: for example, o1 BasicAgent’s displayed complete-run columns give \(1.022\) percentage points, versus \(0.3\) in Table 3.

Historical run grouping, revised grades and the exact estimator are needed before deciding which aggregate uncertainty is correct. This is Needs Evidence, not an established significance failure. No confidence interval or ranking reversal is inferred.

Problem 3 (The released grader rejects log-only result evidence).  The pinned 2026 source automatically zeros Result Analysis leaves when genuine results appear only in `reproduce.log`, although the paper permits that evidence channel.

Section 2.4, p. 3, and Table 1, p. 4, allow Result Match grading using `reproduce.sh`, `reproduce.log` and reproduction outputs. Appendix D, p. 15, describes timestamp filtering for additional result files, without requiring every result to be saved separately.
The current implementation calls this category `Result Analysis`. Relative to , the control flow is:
1. creates a timestamp file and pipes runtime output into `reproduce.log`.
2. reads the script and log separately and establishes the reproduction timestamp.
3. filters document/table files. Allowed extensions exclude `.log` and `.creation_time`; the script and log are explicitly handled separately.
4. If all retained files predate reproduction, including when the list is empty, lines 328–334 set `reproduce_touched_files=False`.
5. Lines 557–568 return valid score zero for every Result Analysis leaf without asking the judge to inspect the log.

A complete witness is a submission with preexisting `reproduce.sh` and `method.py`, optionally an old README, that genuinely recomputes results and prints the full numerical evidence to standard output. It creates no new file with an eligible extension; temporary computation may be in memory or outside the submission. The wrapper creates a fresh log and timestamp file, but neither enters the eligible list. With no README the list is empty; with an old README all retained times predate reproduction. Every Result Analysis leaf is therefore zeroed, even for a criterion fully evidenced in the fresh log. Metadata in is written outside the submission and does not rescue the branch.

This is a static control-flow proof, not author-program execution or an API test. It establishes a Minor version-specific protocol discrepancy and a deterministic false-negative mode. It does not establish that a historical run had this form, how much rubric weight was affected, or that the reported F1 is false. An imperfect automatic judge need not be correct on every example to achieve its reported average accuracy.

A bounded correction is to remove the implication that no eligible auxiliary file means no reproduced result and allow fresh log evidence to be assessed. A log must not grant automatic credit; correctness and provenance still require judging. This removes the forced-zero condition only. No source was changed, and no complete accuracy or adversarial-robustness repair is certified.
# Judge validation and comparison scope
## The current JudgeEval aggregation is a different statistic

Section 4.2, p. 6, describes macro-averaging across papers. The pinned instead pools valid leaf labels across examples, and macro-averages F1 across the binary classes. Equal-paper and pooled-class averaging differ.

For example, paper A has 500 positive and 500 negative labels, all correctly classified. Paper B has five of each, all incorrectly classified. Equal-paper F1 is \((1+0)/2=0.5\). After pooling, each class has 500 true positives, five false positives and five false negatives in its one-versus-rest calculation: \[{\rm pooled\ macro\ F1}=\frac{2(500)}{2(500)+5+5}
 =\frac{1000}{1010}=0.990099.\] This illustrates the estimand difference, not actual JudgeEval performance. The code also excludes invalid grades from the classification inputs. Without historical payloads and a publication-time revision, provenance of the original \(0.83\) under the stated paper-level definition is Needs Evidence. Present-source behavior does not prove how the original number was produced.

Unweighted F1 also does not by itself bound weighted score error. If \(y_\ell\) are true labels and \(\widehat y_\ell\) are judged labels, then \[|\widehat S-S|
 \le \sum_\ell a_\ell\mathbf1\{\widehat y_\ell\ne y_\ell\}.\] Effective rubric weights matter. JudgeEval provides useful agreement evidence, not a mathematical guarantee of weighted calibration or model-ranking accuracy. The paper discloses nondeterminism, imperfect judging and the need for adversarial testing.

A further bounded concern is that the frozen judge prompt in Figures 8–9 describes the provided files as complete and treats missing material as failure, while retrieval may omit files under the context limit. Retrieval omission and true submission absence are different events. Historical error from this mechanism was not measured here.
## Human baseline and model ordering

The human comparison is a selected expert baseline: eight ML PhD participants, three initial attempts per paper, continuation of the best after the first week, and a three-paper subset with 48-hour human results versus 36-hour o1 runs. AI assistants are allowed; four attempts used an A100 instead of an A10. These conditions are disclosed on pp. 7–8. The comparison is not a matched-budget effect for randomly sampled humans. No available evidence establishes that matching the conditions would reverse the ordering.

The abstract’s unqualified best-tested-agent wording needs the main-setup qualifier already present in the conclusion, p. 9. Table 4 reports \(24.4\%\) for o1 IterativeAgent and \(26.0\%\) with extended runtime, above the Claude BasicAgent headline. Section 5.3 openly explains scaffold-dependent ranking. This is a scope clarification, not concealment of those results.

Appendix B filters papers for feasible replication and author collaboration; the corpus is not a random sample of all ML research. Appendix F discloses scaffold prompt development using a small subset of the final dataset. These choices restrict external generalization but do not alone prove corrupted evaluation or false in-sample scores.

# Identity and source versions

Deqian Kong, Minglu Zhao, Dehong Xu, Bo Pang, Shu Wang, Edouardo Honig, Zhangzhang Si, Chuan Li, Jianwen Xie, Sirui Xie and Ying Nian Wu, Latent Thought Models with Variational Bayes Inference-Time Computation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment 0218 / I25-43587; OpenReview xCWAcX4pNa. The official publisher PDF retrieved 25 October 2026 has 18 pages, with appendices on pp. 13–18. All source page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with printed local numbers.

The official project page identifies the released repository . The prepared snapshot is commit , dated 30 October 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its nine files were preserved completely, without omitted members, and their staged hashes and archive/Git-blob mappings checked. This commit postdates the conference paper. No historical run manifest or original experiment revision binds it to the published numbers.

The parent inspected the original model and evaluation descriptions, the full posterior optimizer, the relevant decoder/ELBO and training paths, and configuration; independently performed the calculations below; and viewed source pages 4, 5 and 7. Three native auxiliaries independently checked mathematics, source control flow and counterreadings. No author code, dataset, training job, judge or paid API was executed. The snapshot has no separate zero-shot, GSM8K or MAUVE evaluation driver or historical result artifacts. Optional OpenReview access returned HTTP 403, and later revisions/errata were not retrieved.
# Definitions and mathematical checks that survive

The model is \[p_\beta(x)=\int p(z)p_\beta(x\mid z)\,dz,\qquad
 p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I),\qquad
 p_\beta(x\mid z)=\prod_{n=1}^N
 p_\beta(x^{(n)}\mid x^{(<n)},z).\] Each sequence has local diagonal-Gaussian variational parameters \(q_\psi(z\mid x)=\mathcal N(\mu,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma^2))\). The decoder parameters \(\beta\) are shared. Equation (5), p. 4, is \[\mathcal L(\beta,\psi;x)
 =\mathbb E_{q_\psi}\log p_\beta(x\mid z)
  -D_{\rm KL}(q_\psi\|p).\] The identity \[\log p_\beta(x)-\mathcal L(\beta,\psi;x)
 =D_{\rm KL}(q_\psi\|p_\beta(z\mid x))\ge0\] proves the ELBO bound whenever the expectations are well-defined. Optimizing \(\psi\) using the entire observed test sequence is legitimate for density estimation under this identity; it is not itself evidence of answer leakage.

The Fisher identity in Eq. (3), the Langevin noise scaling in Eq. (4), and the conditional predictive integral in Eq. (6) are also consistent under their usual differentiation/integration assumptions. Conditional generation infers \(q(z\mid x)\) from the prefix \(x\), then generates the completion; the formula does not require access to the true completion. Finite-step inference bias is explicitly acknowledged on p. 4.

Importantly, the released charges the full Gaussian KL, \[K=\frac12\sum_j(\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2-1-\log\sigma_j^2),\] with coefficient one. It sums the reconstruction loss over tokens, adds \(K\), divides by sequence length, exponentiates per sequence, and averages the resulting perplexities across the batch. The issue is not omission or arbitrary downweighting of KL. The validation caller records this perplexity separately from a reconstruction-only loss.
# Core implementation findings
Problem 1 (Local inference and validation gradients enter the shared-decoder update).  The pinned training path does not isolate fast local optimization from slow global optimization.
## Source claim and complete control-flow evidence

Algorithm 1, p. 4, separates updating each sequence’s local \((\mu,\sigma^2)\) from a slow update of the shared decoder. During validation, local fitting should leave shared parameters and their training optimizer state unaffected.

In , the inner AdamW optimizer owns only `mu` and `log_var`. Its `zero_grad` at line 117 therefore clears only those variables. The backward calls at lines 122/126 traverse the decoder as well as the local variables. Decoder weights retain their gradient requirements; changing the module to evaluation mode does not freeze them. The code detaches an optional cache, not the full decoder computation.

The validation routine in repeatedly calls this same posterior optimizer on `val` batches. Periodic evaluation at lines 336–338 precedes the training micro-batches. Their inner backward passes and final reconstruction backward pass add more gradients. The global optimizer consumes the accumulated decoder gradients at line 398. Only line 402 clears them, after the step. The inspected source contains no intervening decoder freeze or reset that cancels this path.

The actual default configuration has 16 fast steps, 100 validation batches, evaluation every 1,000 iterations, and a positive global learning rate at iteration 1,000. It uses `bfloat16`, so the gradient scaler is disabled. This ordinary supported path is sufficient; no behavior of a particular multi-GPU execution is assumed.
## Independent calculus check and counterreadings

The mechanism does not depend on a large Transformer. For a scalar decoder logit \(\beta+\mu\) and a validation target one, the negative log likelihood is \(-\log\sigma(\beta+\mu)\). At \(\beta=\mu=0\), \[\partial_\beta\ell_{\rm val}=-\tfrac12.\] An optimizer that clears only \(\mu\) leaves that decoder gradient untouched. Even a subsequent training loss with zero decoder gradient cannot remove it by addition.

Zero global learning rate on the first iteration is not a general rescue. With the supplied Adam coefficients \((0.9,0.95)\), one such gradient creates first/second moments \(-0.05\) and \(0.0125\) even if that step’s learning rate is zero. At the next step, with zero new gradient and learning rate \(4\times10^{-7}\), the bias-corrected Adam update moves an initially zero parameter by approximately \(2.71459\times10^{-7}\). Without the validation gradient it remains zero. This is an independent analytic optimizer calculation, not a run of the author software. Later evaluation steps already have positive learning rates and establish the problem without relying on this moment-state observation.

An evaluation-only script that never makes another global update would not have this training contamination. The finding concerns the released combined training/validation loop. Nor is it an accusation that legitimate local posterior fitting inherently trains the global model on test answers; it is the specific uncancelled global-gradient path that does so here.
## Impact and precise repair boundary

This is Major for the released core learning/evaluation implementation: the slow update differs from the stated dual-rate algorithm, and held-out validation targets can affect shared training. It directly threatens the interpretation of validation perplexity and scaling curves generated by this path. The exact magnitude and whether the historical published runs used this version are Needs Evidence; no published score is declared refuted on provenance alone.

A correct isolation rule is to compute fast-step gradients only for the local variational parameters, or temporarily freeze decoder parameters while retaining differentiation through the decoder to its latent inputs. Restore the decoder’s gradient flags for the slow step. Validation must leave both decoder gradients and global optimizer state unchanged. Deliberate outer micro-batch gradients must be preserved, so indiscriminately clearing all gradients after every inner step is not a general repair. These rules remove the identified paths; implementation testing and retraining would still be needed to validate revised results. No author source was modified.

Problem 2 (Fitting and scoring with the same noise invalidates the fitted-ELBO estimator).  The released optimizer uses one random tensor for posterior fitting and final perplexity, unlike Algorithm 1’s sampling inside the fast loop.
## Actual source and the statistical distinction

draws \(e\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) once, before the loop at line 112. Every ELBO call at line 119 uses that same \(e\). The final latent at line 141 and final metric at line 145 reuse it again. Thus \(\widehat\psi\) depends on \(e\) and the scored point is \[z(e)=\mu_{\widehat\psi(e)}
      +\sigma_{\widehat\psi(e)}\odot e.\] It is not a fresh draw from the fitted Gaussian conditional on \(\widehat\psi\).

Common random numbers can be a legitimate optimization device. Also, even an independent one-sample ELBO estimate need not be a pointwise bound on a particular draw. The decisive issue here is stronger: adaptive reuse can invalidate the bound interpretation even after averaging over the scoring randomness. Table 1, p. 7, explicitly labels LTM perplexities as upper bounds, and the released validation metric is offered as such an ELBO-derived statistic.
## A fully specified Gaussian/categorical counterexample

Consider the probabilistic family in Eqs. (1), (2) and (5), specialized to one binary token: \[z\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad
 p(x=1\mid z)=\sigma(kz),\qquad k=100.\] This is a smooth two-class softmax decoder. Symmetry and \(\sigma(kz)+\sigma(-kz)=1\) give \(p(x=1)=1/2\), hence true perplexity two. Take the observed token to be one and draw the fixed reparameterization noise \(e\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\).

Let \(a=0.1\) and choose the following admissible fitted Gaussian for each noise draw: \[(\mu(e),s(e))=
 \begin{cases}
 (a-e/\sqrt{1+e^2},\,1/\sqrt{1+e^2}),&e<a,\\
 (0,1),&e\ge a,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad q_e=\mathcal N(\mu(e),s(e)^2).\] Every variance is strictly positive and every KL is finite. The reparameterized scoring point is \(z=\mu(e)+s(e)e=\max(e,a)\), so \[-\log p(x=1\mid z)\le
 \epsilon:=\log(1+e^{-ka}).\] For \(e<a\), direct substitution into the full Gaussian KL gives \[K(e)=\tfrac12\left[
 a^2-\frac{2ae}{\sqrt{1+e^2}}+\log(1+e^2)
 \right]
 \le a+\tfrac12a^2+\tfrac12\log(1+e^2).\] For \(e\ge a\), \(K(e)=0\). No KL term is omitted.

The construction extends to any sequence length, including \(N=1024\): use independent prior coordinates, independent binary conditional factors, the observed all-one sequence, and the product of the above Gaussian variational factors. The true marginal is \(2^{-N}\) and true per-token perplexity remains two. The released scoring functional exponentiates summed sampled NLL plus KL divided by \(N\), which is the geometric mean of the one-coordinate perplexities. By the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, its expectation is still at most \(1.292448567\). This also addresses the code’s actual order of operations: it averages per-sequence perplexities rather than exponentiating a batch-averaged loss.

All probabilistic assumptions behind the ELBO argument are satisfied: a normalized standard Gaussian prior, a normalized smooth categorical likelihood, positive diagonal Gaussian variances, and the complete KL. The example is a counterexample to the general estimation rule, not a simulation of the trained Transformer or a claim that its finite AdamW trajectory returns this particular family. An exact optimizer of the sampled objective could do at least as well on that objective as this feasible family, so the defect is not cured merely by longer optimization.
## Independent finite-step numerical corroboration

A separate parent-written scalar calculation uses \(p(x=1\mid z)=\sigma(8z)\) and 16 AdamW steps, with \(\mu_0=0\), \(\log s_0^2=-5+0.1\eta\), independent standard-normal \(\eta,e\), coefficients \((0.9,0.999)\), weight decay \(0.01\), denominator offset \(10^{-8}\), and step sizes \[\gamma_t=0.034+\frac{0.34-0.034}{2}
 [1+\cos(\pi t/16)],\qquad t=0,\ldots,15.\] Only the local Gaussian parameters are updated in this diagnostic. Deterministic Gaussian quadrature of orders 80 and 160 gives reused-noise mean negative ELBOs \(0.6693841\) and \(0.6692426\), respectively, below the true \(-\log p(x)=\log2=0.6931472\). Fresh-noise evaluation of the same fitted distributions gives \(1.0228832\) and \(1.0226480\). An independent auxiliary Monte Carlo calculation is consistent with these values.

These are numerical integrations of an independently written analytic-gradient toy, not rigorous quadrature error bounds or author-code execution. They corroborate the finite-step mechanism but do not reproduce the Transformer or historical scores. The preceding analytic construction remains the decisive general counterexample.
## Impact, repair and preserved counterevidence

This is Major for the released core estimator: the implementation does not justify interpreting its adaptively reused-noise score as the ELBO-based perplexity upper bound used to support sample/parameter efficiency and inference-step scaling. The exact mathematical ELBO in Eq. (5) remains valid. Neither the example nor static inspection establishes the actual corrected value of the published \(3.05\), Table 1 entries, or every scaling curve.

Use independent scoring noise after fitting \(\psi\), or sufficiently accurate integration of the fitted expectation. Conditional on the fitted parameters, fresh Monte Carlo log-likelihood samples then estimate the actual ELBO without this adaptive reuse bias. Resampling within the fast loop also aligns the implementation with Algorithm 1. A finite Monte Carlo estimate is not a deterministic pointwise bound; precision and uncertainty still need reporting. No corrected experimental result is claimed.

More inference can also tighten a valid variational bound for a fixed decoder without changing its true marginal distribution. That ordinary distinction should be retained when discussing inference-step scaling; it is separate from the adaptive-noise defect above.
Problem 3 (The expression labeled per-token compute retains a sequence-length factor).  Section 2.4, p. 5, changes the stated unit without dividing the preceding per-sequence cost by \(N\).

The displayed forward cost for a length-\(N\) sequence is \[O\!\left(L(N^2H+NN_zH+NH^2)+NVH\right).\] Multiplying by the number of fast/slow passes preserves a per-sequence unit. Under that same dense-attention accounting, the per-token expression is \[O\!\left((T_{\rm fast}+1)
 \{L(NH+N_zH+H^2)+VH\}\right),\] obtained by division by \(N\). Here \(N_z\) follows Section 2.4’s explicitly stated per-layer convention, unlike the total-latent convention elsewhere. Efficient fixed-window attention would further change the attention term, but is not needed to identify this unit discrepancy.

This is Minor as a local cost expression. At a fixed training length, an omitted common factor does not by itself reverse configuration rankings, and no evidence binds the actual Table 1 numerical FLOP counts to evaluation of that erroneous symbolic expression. The report does not claim the published FLOP numbers are all inflated by \(1024\) or that the empirical compute comparisons have been numerically refuted.
# Empirical claims: inspected scope and limits

The paper clearly separates the 3B-token pretraining example from Table 1’s equal-total-compute checkpoints, including the 0.9B-token LTM-Large checkpoint. Their different training-token counts are not inherently contradictory. The release configuration, however, uses width 768 and 12 heads, while Appendix A.1 specifies width 512 and eight heads for the reported models. This reinforces the need for a historical configuration binding rather than silently treating the current defaults as the published runs.

Appendix A.3, p. 13, discloses GSM8K pass@5 on a 1K test subset with at most 50 new tokens per candidate. GPT-2 uses beam width five, while LTM uses five posterior fits and multinomial samples. That is a decoding/protocol difference limiting attribution to architecture alone. No released caller establishes access to true test answers, and this review finds no demonstrated GSM8K answer leakage.

Conditional generation uses 1,000 50-token prefixes, five 50-token completions each, and borrowed baseline MAUVE values. The absence of seed-level outputs and confidence intervals limits claims about small score differences. The reported unconditional evaluation uses 64 length-1024 sequences, greedy decoding and GPT-2-XL scoring. Prior sampling for unconditional generation legitimately avoids posterior inference; it would be incorrect to charge all \(T_{\rm fast}\) steps to that task’s generation speed solely by analogy with conditional inference.

Progressive latent-layer inclusion on 200 validation sequences is evidence of reconstruction patterns (pp. 17–18). A causal interpretation as unique semantic synthesis layers would require controls separating layer position from the amount of latent information supplied, such as matched-count or alternative-order interventions. The present review does not disprove the reported reconstruction pattern. The VAE/Langevin comparisons likewise do not receive a new failure judgment without raw diagnostics and evaluation drivers.

None of these unresolved empirical questions is used to inflate the severity of the two demonstrated implementation findings. The original finite-step-bias discussion, correctly normalized KL, valid ideal probabilistic identities and explicit evaluation differences remain counterevidence against broader accusations.
