report: Abstract: This review checks the published latent-diffusion method, its computational evaluation, and a pinned released implementation. The supported assessment is Major, scoped to the release’s default ESM2/transformer decoder-training route under nonidentity normalization: training and noiseless validation apply the inverse normalization twice, while generation applies it once. This invalidates the shared latent-to-token interface on which the trained decoder’s use in generation depends. Three further Minor findings concern inconsistent reported metric values, repeated-sequence weighting in pLDDT, and an optional compressed-length mask. Independent algebra, finite examples, source inspection, and source-page images establish the discrepancies. Historical experiment-to-source bindings and quantitative benchmark effects remain unresolved; no replacement scores are asserted. Exact-sampling, biological-function, and matched-resource interpretations are bounded explicitly below. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of DiMA
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The paper is Diffusion on Language Model Encodings for Protein Sequence Generation, by Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Pavel Strashnov, Andrey Shevtsov, Fedor Nikolaev, Nikita Ivanisenko, Olga Kardymon, and Dmitry Vetrov, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment identifiers are 0219 / I25-43588. All page references below refer to the 42-page publisher PDF; its printed Arabic page numbers agree with these PDF indices. The embedded appendix occupies pp. 15–42. The publisher-linked PDF was acquired on 25 October 2026 and is identified by its actual SHA-256 in Appendix 6 (#app:evidence).

The released source is , commit , dated 17 July 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its acquisition manifest does not assert that this commit generated any paper table. All 68 acquired members retain their archive, Git-tree, byte, and hash mappings. The two omitted members are documented NumPy length-distribution payloads; neither they nor datasets, model weights, normalization statistics, generated sequences, or historical run logs were acquired in this review.

The original parent reviewer read substantive main-text pp. 1–9 and appendix pp. 16–42, checked the equations and numerical comparisons discussed here, and independently inspected the central training, sampling, normalization, decoder, and metric source paths. Source pages 6, 26, 27, 29, 37, 40, and 42 were also inspected as rendered images. Other figure content received the coverage recorded in the ledger, not a claim of raw-data reanalysis. Three native auxiliary agents independently checked mathematics, source correspondence, and alternative interpretations. Their roles and limitations are preserved separately. No author code was executed.
# Method and assumptions needed for the review

Equation reference: eq:schedule. DiMA encodes an amino-acid sequence into pretrained protein-language-model representations, normalizes each coordinate, learns a continuous denoiser, and decodes generated latent vectors. Writing the paper’s variance coefficient as \(A(t)\) to distinguish it from its square root, \[A(t)=\frac{1}{1+d^2\tan^2(\pi t/2)},\quad d=10,\qquad
 z_t=\sqrt{A(t)}z_0+\sqrt{1-A(t)}\epsilon,\quad \epsilon\sim N(0,I).
 \] Equation (2), p. 3, is a squared reconstruction objective with a detached self-conditioning prediction. At generation time the length is sampled separately, so the method need not learn the complete length distribution through padding tokens. The paper explicitly reports a quality–diversity trade-off, rather than simultaneous dominance on every metric.

The pLDDT evaluation in Appendix B.1, p. 16, first describes an average over residues within a predicted structure. Section 3.1, p. 4, describes evaluation over 2,048 generated sequences. These are model-based structural-confidence measurements. They do not, by themselves, certify experimentally measured folding or function. The authors acknowledge intrinsically disordered regions as a reason for low confidence; this caveat is retained rather than counted as an error.

The following findings distinguish a contradiction in published numbers, a deterministic source-level estimator change, and mismatches in released training/inference and compressed-length interfaces. Only the first directly concerns the published numerical presentation. The source-level findings require historical source/run bindings before their quantitative effect on that presentation can be established.
# Supported problems

Problem 1 (Cluster-density definitions and reported values do not agree).  Appendix B.2, p. 17, defines positive clusters as co-clusters containing both generated and dataset sequences and negative clusters as co-clusters containing only generated sequences. It defines PCD and NCD as their respective counts divided by the total number of sequences. Tables 5 and 6, pp. 26–27, report a reference row with \(\mathrm{PCD}=0.990\) and \(\mathrm{NCD}=0.304\). Table 5 reports \(0.214\) and \(0.945\) for flow matching.

Complete check. Let \(G\) be the number of generated sequence instances and let \(P,N\) count the two kinds of clusters in the same clustering. Each counted cluster contains at least one generated instance, and clusters are disjoint. Thus \(P+N\leq G\). If the common denominator \(M\) is the number of generated instances, or the number of all generated-plus-reference instances, then \(M\geq G\), and \[\mathrm{PCD}+\mathrm{NCD}=\frac{P+N}{M}\leq 1.\] This argument does not require any monotonicity property of the clustering algorithm or an assumption that two thresholded clusterings are nested. The printed sums are \(1.294\) and \(1.159\). Even allowing independent rounding errors of \(0.0005\) in both entries, the sums are at least \(1.293\) and \(1.158\). They cannot represent the stated common-denominator quantities. ◻

Counterevidence and bounded impact. Separately normalized conditional densities, a transposed row, or an unstated denominator could explain the numbers, but each would require a corrected definition or table. The available repository lacks the co-clustering evaluation driver and underlying cluster counts, so the review does not choose replacement numbers. The contradiction prevents literal quantitative interpretation of these particular reference/ablation entries; it does not establish that the headline pLDDT or FD comparisons are wrong.

There is a separate, direct cross-table conflict in the ESMc-300M result: Table 3 and its discussion on p. 6 report \(\mathrm{CD}_{0.5}=0.963\), while Table 7 on p. 29 reports \(0.863\) for the corresponding AFDBv4-90 comparison. The difference is \(0.100\), not rounding. Both values remain below ESM2-650M’s \(0.986\), so the direction of that local comparison survives. The record must identify which value and run are authoritative. Likewise, the RFDiffusion unique success rate is described as \(0.06\) on pp. 8 and 36 but appears as \(0.07\), with an external-analysis footnote, in Table 13; either is below DiMA’s reported \(0.10\). These are Minor reporting defects, with exact corrections unverified. Parent arithmetic is in ; source-image anchors are listed in Appendix 6 (#app:evidence).

Problem 2 (Released pLDDT aggregation discards within-rank multiplicity).  The inspected release’s , lines 31–40, stores a predicted score under the protein-sequence string: \(\texttt{result[protein] = score}\). The active caller in , lines 24–27, averages that dictionary’s values. Repeated occurrences on one rank overwrite their earlier entries.

Complete check. Assume a deterministic quality score \(q(u)\in[0,100]\) for each distinct sequence \(u\), and let \(m_u\) be its multiplicity among generated draws. The ordinary mean over draws is \[\bar q_{\rm draws}=\frac{\sum_u m_uq(u)}{\sum_u m_u},
 \qquad
 \bar q_{\rm unique}=\frac{1}{|\{u:m_u>0\}|}\sum_{u:m_u>0}q(u).\] The code computes the second quantity within each rank. Take four valid score-bearing draws \(A,A,A,B\), with hypothetical scores \(q(A)=90\), \(q(B)=30\). Then the generated-draw mean is \(75\), while the one-rank dictionary mean is \(60\). This example uses admissible score values, assumes no score stochasticity, and executes no folding model. If split into equally sized rank lists \((A,A)\) and \((A,B)\), the equal average of rank-local unique means is \((90+60)/2=75\). Thus even with equal shard lengths, the implemented result can depend on the partition. The independently authored finite calculation reproduces these values.

Counterevidence and impact. Quality of distinct outputs is a legitimate estimand when explicitly defined, especially alongside a diversity measure. It is not the same as average quality per generated attempt. A dictionary may also serve as a computation cache, but the final average must then restore each key’s multiplicity if the target is the draw mean. When all predictions are distinct, the present implementation agrees with the draw mean on equal-sized shards. The paper explicitly discusses duplicate generation in some baselines, so this distinction is relevant to comparative evaluation; it does not prove that this release evaluated those historical baselines, or establish the direction of any historical ranking change.

This is a Minor released-evaluator defect in its correspondence to the stated sample evaluation. Its effect on published core comparisons is Needs Evidence. A precise local repair is to retain a score per sample index, or cache by sequence while averaging with occurrence counts, and reduce sums/counts across ranks. Algebra verifies that this restores the intended finite-sample mean. No corrected protein score is claimed.

The same file averages PDB atom B-factors, whereas p. 16 describes residue averaging. These agree if residue weights are equal or appropriate aggregation is used; otherwise atom counts weight residues differently. The exact dependency/PDB convention was not independently run here, so that additional correspondence remains unresolved. A separate unequal-shard indexing issue exists when sample count is not divisible by world size, but the default counts 512/2,048 are divisible by the usual configured multi-GPU counts; it is not used to infer damage to reported runs.

Problem 3 (Decoder training and generation apply different inverse-normalization maps).  The method’s coordinate normalization and token reconstruction are described on pp. 3–4. The release’s documented decoder-training route calls . In its `loss_step`, line 26 denormalizes the latent, then line 29 calls `batch_get_logits`. The ESM2 implementation, , lines 89–95, denormalizes again. In contrast, `batch_decode`, lines 74–86, used by generation, denormalizes once. The training entry point enables the normalizer.

Core dependency. Figure 1, p. 2, identifies the decoder as one of the method’s three core components; the token-reconstruction paragraph, p. 3, describes its finetuning, and Table 5, p. 26, includes the finetuning ablation. The release’s , lines 3–4, selects ESM2 with the transformer decoder. , line 13, configures three new layers. , lines 37–47, constructs this decoder and loads its checkpoint when present; , lines 16–17, constructs the transformer and output projection from configuration. The documented Stage 2 command in , lines 128–142, trains that decoder through the affected route. Finally, , lines 492–532, sends generated normalized latents through `pred_logits` and `batch_decode`, using the single inverse map. The discrepancy therefore crosses the default learned decoder’s training, validation, and deployment boundary.

Equation reference: eq:double. Complete check. For one nondegenerate coordinate let the stored mean and standard deviation be \(\mu\) and \(s>0\), with \(s\geq 10^{-5}\) so the small-variance guard is inactive. Put \[N(x)=(x-\mu)/s,\qquad D(z)=sz+\mu.\] Training therefore presents \(D(D(z_t))\) to the decoder; generation presents \(D(z)\). Their difference at the same normalized input is \[D(D(z))-D(z)=s(s-1)z+s\mu.
 \] Equality for every \(z\) requires \(s=1,\mu=0\). The discrepancy also occurs in the noiseless decoder-validation branch, which bypasses corruption but not either denormalization.

For a valid finite interface example, take equally frequent raw encodings \(-1\) and \(3\). Their population mean is \(1\), variance \(4\), and normalized encodings are \(-1,+1\). The decoder’s training inputs are \(-1,7\), whereas the generation inputs are \(-1,3\). A two-class decoder with logits \(0,u-5\) correctly classifies targets \(0,1\) at the training inputs but assigns both generation inputs to class \(0\). Scaling both logits’ difference makes the training classification arbitrarily confident without repairing the inference mismatch. This establishes that fitting the double-transformed training inputs need not make the single-transformed inference path correct. It is an illustrative interface counterexample, not a claim that ESM2 produces these embeddings or that the released optimizer learns this classifier.

Counterevidence, repair, and impact. The discrepancy vanishes for identity statistics, at particular fixed points, or for a decoder insensitive to the transformed directions. The README also permits skipping decoder training with the pretrained `lm_head` (line 132); that alternative does not establish correctness of the default newly trained transformer path. Other encoders or historically different code are outside this finding’s demonstrated dependency. Actual normalization tensors and trained decoder weights are absent, so the example cannot estimate historical accuracy loss. A model might tolerate some mismatch. These possibilities bound the affected configurations and numerical impact; they do not make the default training and deployment interfaces equal.

Removing the outer denormalization from `loss_step`, while retaining the existing denormalization inside `batch_get_logits`, restores the single map \(D(z_t)\) algebraically for every admitted \(\mu,s,z_t\). This is an interface repair only: it does not validate old checkpoints or prove the paper’s reported finetuning improvement without retraining/evaluation. The supported assessment is Major for the pinned release’s default ESM2/transformer decoder-training route under nonidentity statistics. A core learned component is optimized and validated on a different latent-to-token interface from the one used in generation; the finite example proves that successful fitting and noiseless validation need not transfer through that interface. Quantitative historical effects and the paper’s reported finetuning gain remain Needs Evidence. The scope is this demonstrated core training/deployment inconsistency, without a claim that every encoder, checkpoint, or published protein-generation result fails.

Problem 4 (The optional shorten-two mask applies a second length reduction).  The CHEAP shorten-two component is evaluated in Sections 3.4.2 and E.6. In the pinned release, , lines 74–86, first compresses the batch maximum length by two, then clips each uncompressed sequence length to that already compressed maximum before halving it again.

Complete check. Take the valid interface inputs \(\texttt{lens}=[254]\), \(\texttt{max\_sequence\_len}=254\), and \(\texttt{shorten\_factor}=2\). The allocated latent width is \(\lceil254/2\rceil=127\), but the per-sequence mask receives only \[\left\lceil\frac{\min(254,127)}2\right\rceil=64\] active positions, rather than 127. The decoding path at lines 70–71 explicitly truncates the sequence to twice the mask sum, so the output has at most 128 residues, not the requested 254. The length sampler returns raw sequence lengths and supplies no prior factor-two conversion. This calculation depends only on the explicit mask and output-slice arithmetic, not on the external CHEAP decoder’s behavior.

Counterevidence and impact. The supplied default and supported pretrained configuration use shorten-one, where this particular branch is inactive. No historical shorten-two configuration or generated-length records bind this code to the corresponding paper results. The supported judgment is therefore Minor for the optional released path, with historical impact unresolved. A precise repair is to clamp each raw length to the raw maximum before applying the single compression: \(m_i=\lceil\min(\ell_i,L_{\max})/2\rceil\), bounded by the allocated compressed width. For odd lengths the decoder must also retain the requested raw length if exact truncation is intended. This restores the mask count; it does not validate external decoder integration or old experiments. The parent calculation is recorded in .
# Checks that do not establish additional core failures
## Diffusion coefficients and self-conditioning

The discrepancy is quantified rather than assumed catastrophic. At \(d=10\), \(A(0.95)=6.1935750\times10^{-5}\), \(\beta(0.95)=40.1624805\), and \(\beta(0.99)=200.0324088\). The capped forward process would have \[A_{\rm cap}(1)=A(0.95)\exp[-0.05\beta(0.95)]
 =8.3142718\times10^{-6},\] whereas the uncapped formula tends to zero. For standardized Rademacher data \(z_0=\pm1\) with equal probabilities, both processes retain mean zero and variance one. Their endpoint fourth cumulants are respectively \(-2A_{\rm cap}(1)^2=-1.3825423\times10^{-10}\) and zero. This is a legitimate consistency witness and also strong counterevidence to claiming a large effect from this example. It is neither a general high-dimensional error bound nor an estimate of the reverse sampler’s actual protein error.

The default sampling grid ends at \(t=0.05\) and returns the final solver mean, not its predicted clean \(z_0\); here \(A(0.05)=0.6175142\) and the forward noise standard deviation is \(0.6184543\). Exact clean-latent sampling cannot simply be presumed from this interface. However, Appendix C.5, p. 23, explicitly motivates robustness at \(t=0.05\), reporting near-lossless CHEAP reconstruction. The paper offers an empirical schedule and no exact finite-step sampling theorem. Numerical endpoint regularization and intentional early decoding are therefore credible interpretations. Their effects across encoders remain Needs Evidence, not an additional demonstrated Major problem.

For an exact denoiser, the source conversion \(\widehat{\mathrm{score}}=-(z_t-\sqrt{A(t)}\,\widehat z_0)/(1-A(t))\) has the expected sign and scaling, and the Euler reverse-step noise uses \(\sqrt{-dt}\) for decreasing time. The current training code computes both detached self-conditioned and zero-conditioned losses on each batch. Their sum has twice the expected 50/50 mixture objective in paper Eq. (2). The missing random branch coin alone is not an invalid objective; proportional objectives do not imply identical finite optimizer trajectories under clipping and other settings. The tan-10 rationale is presented as a heuristic, not a theorem that every representation’s loss must be linear in time.
## Empirical comparisons and conditional tasks

The stated Gaussian Fréchet formula and the biased equal-size MMD formula in Appendix B.3 pass the inspected algebraic checks. The released masked-token pseudoperplexity excludes special tokens from its average and follows the stated conditional-log-probability construction. These are scoped checks of formulas and inspected paths, not empirical reproductions.

The 35M comparison counts the denoiser, while DiMA benefits from a pretrained encoder during training. Removing the encoder at deployment can support a smaller generation model; it does not imply equal total pretraining resources. The phrase that all models are trained from scratch in Section 3.3/Table 6 needs this qualification. The paper discloses pretrained encoders, and the no-encoder ablation is useful counterevidence against concealment. A causal claim that only the diffusion paradigm explains the performance gap would require a matched-representation/resource comparison not supplied here.

For motif scaffolding, independently summing the 24 DiMA entries in Table 13 yields 19 positive success-rate tasks and mean success rate \(0.1658333\), agreeing with 19/24 and the printed \(0.17\). This check supports the numerical headline. It does not reproduce structures or unique-success clustering. Table 13 also includes a sequence-mode ESM3 result with 21 solved tasks, so the main-text comparison against named EvoDiff/DPLM/DPLM2 baselines should not be broadened to every sequence-based model.

For fold conditioning, Appendix E.9 explicitly defines the mean as the best TM-score among ten attempts per target, and acknowledges that DiMA receives richer conditioning than RFDiffusion’s secondary-structure/block-adjacency information. The reported \(0.93\) is not an unconditional per-attempt mean or a comparison at equal information. Nonzero RMSD alone cannot exclude copying followed by imperfect reconstruction, but Figure 5’s selected low sequence identities provide counterevidence to a blanket exact-sequence-copy allegation. No such allegation is established.

The family-task evaluation filters to correctly annotated family members before reporting quality/diversity, while reporting fidelity separately. That conditional estimand is disclosed on p. 31. The infilling comparison uses ten attempts on 180 targets; its 42.2% versus 40.0% point estimates do not establish a statistically resolved advantage without per-target outcomes. Biological annotation, predicted disorder, and predicted structures support computational plausibility; no wet-lab functional validation was established or represented as having been performed.
# Dependence, severity, and remaining work

The supported overall impact is Major, scoped to the pinned release’s default ESM2/transformer decoder-training and generation route under nonidentity normalization. Problem Problem 3 (#prob:decoder) establishes an invalid input contract across a core component’s learning, validation, and use. The metric-definition, multiplicity, and optional-mask findings remain Minor for the bounded reasons stated individually. Historical source bindings and corrected benchmark values remain unresolved. This does not lower the demonstrated core-interface error to Minor: severity follows its operative dependency, while the extent of historical numerical harm remains a separate question. The judgment does not depend on appendix placement, repair difficulty, a severity quota, or whole-paper collapse.

No later corrected PDF or author-adopted repair was established from the frozen inputs. The optional OpenReview metadata and separate-supplement endpoint had returned HTTP 403 during acquisition; that does not establish that no additional material exists. The complete available source is sufficient for the static checks but omits conditional-task drivers, several reported metric pipelines, and historical run artifacts. Current defaults also differ from the narrative: a three-layer transformer decoder is configured instead of the described simple decoder, and pLDDT/pseudoperplexity use 512 samples while FD/MMD use 2,048. These are version-correspondence limitations, not proof of the published settings.

Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Initial scientific review of Ex-VAD
# Paper identity, version, and scope

This is the initial review of Ex-VAD: Explainable Fine-grained Video Anomaly Detection Based on Visual-Language Models, by Chao Huang, Yushu Shi, Jie Wen, Wei Wang, Yong Xu, and Xiaochun Cao, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assignment is 0220 / I25-43589. All page references are one-based indices of the 12-page publisher PDF; they agree with its printed Arabic page numbers. The embedded appendix is p. 12. The exact original was acquired on 25 October 2026 and remains unchanged; hashes are in Appendix 6 (#app:provenance).

The parent read the complete PDF text, including equations (1)–(11), Tables 1–7, the model and evaluation descriptions, and the qualitative appendix. Original pages 4–8 and 12 were also rendered and visually inspected, including the actual numerical cells and score-definition sentence. Three native auxiliary agents separately checked mathematics, source/empirical correspondence, and counterinterpretations. The parent independently integrated their findings and performed the calculations and final artifact checks.

The staged source manifest contains the publisher page and original PDF, with no verified author repository. Thus there is no code archive to inspect for this paper. Earlier source preparation encountered HTTP 403 for OpenReview metadata and the possible separate supplement; this establishes an access limit, not absence of additional material. No new download, author-code run, model inference, dataset acquisition, paid API request, or software installation was performed. The supplied evidence supports paper-level checks but cannot resolve the precise implemented graph or reproduce the historical benchmark scores.
# Method and the claims being checked

The anomaly-explanation generation module (AEGM) captions sampled frames using BLIP-2, replaces captions by the highest image–text similarity match within the video’s caption set, and prompts a language model to summarize unusual events. The explanation \(E\) is encoded and fused with temporally adapted visual features. A coarse classifier predicts anomaly confidence. A separate label-augmentation and alignment module (LAAM) compares fused frame features with embeddings of original and expanded class labels.

The stated losses comprise binary cross-entropy on video-level top-\(K\) scores, multiclass cross-entropy on top-\(K\) label similarities, and a nonnegative-cosine penalty between normal and anomalous label embeddings. Under nonzero cosine inputs, positive temperature, and valid probabilities, the cosine, BCE, softmax, and multiclass-cross-entropy algebra is standard in the inspected equations. No formal theorem or exact guarantee of caption correction, causal explanation, or universal detection performance is given.

The evaluation distinguishes coarse frame-level AUC/AP from fine-grained event mAP at IoU thresholds \(0.1,\ldots,0.5\). Fine-grained mAP is explicitly computed only on abnormal test videos, p. 6. Its average therefore should not be interpreted as a comprehensive measure of normal-video false alarms; the separate coarse metrics remain relevant. This disclosed evaluation scope is not itself an error.
# Supported problems

Problem 1 (Reported averages and comparative statements are internally inconsistent).  Section 4.1, p. 6, defines AVG as the average mAP over the five reported IoU thresholds. Table 2’s XD-Violence AVG entries for Ex-VAD and VadCLIP disagree with the arithmetic of those same rows. Section 4.2, p. 7, additionally gives UCF-Crime values and gains inconsistent with Tables 1, 5, and 6.

For UCF-Crime, the Ex-VAD components average \[(16.51+12.35+9.41+7.82+4.65)/5=10.148,\] which is consistent with the tables’ \(10.15\), but not the prose’s \(9.00\). The displayed AVG cells \(10.15\), \(6.68\), and \(6.48\) give improvements \(3.47\) and \(3.67\) over VadCLIP and STPrompt, whereas the prose gives \(1.32\) and \(1.52\). Computing all three means from their threshold cells gives gains \(3.466\) and \(3.668\), the same discrepancy at the relevant precision.

The parent independently audited all 26 AVG rows in Tables 1, 2, 5, and 6. Only the two Table 2 averages exceed the conservative rounding tolerance. In particular, Table 5’s caption mean \(10.874\) versus printed \(10.88\), and Table 2’s STPrompt mean \(23.448\) versus printed \(23.44\), are compatible with unprinted precision and are not counted as errors. The inputs, complete row audit, and results are preserved in and .

Counterevidence and exact impact. The average of Ex-VAD’s displayed XD cells remains greater than every listed baseline’s recomputed average. Its recomputed margin over VadCLIP is \(28.034-24.530=3.504\) points. Its UCF average likewise remains highest among Table 1’s rows. Thus these checks invalidate the exact reported averages/margins as a mutually consistent set; they do not reverse the displayed average ranking.

A different aggregation, stale threshold row, or mismatched experimental run could account for the disagreement. Such an explanation requires a corrected definition or provenance, rather than treating the inconsistent numbers as the same experiment. The arithmetic of displayed cells is not a replacement measurement of the historical model. Raw predictions, evaluation code, and run identifiers are needed to decide which fields should change.

The superiority language also needs scope. At XD IoU \(0.2\), Ex-VAD’s \(32.75\) is below CLIP-TSA’s \(32.88\), so it is not best at every threshold. Table 3 reports VERA’s XD AP as \(88.2\), above Ex-VAD’s \(86.52\), and p. 7 explicitly calls Ex-VAD second best there. Page 8 reports TCVADS UCF AUC \(88.58\), above Ex-VAD’s \(88.29\), and acknowledges the difference; TCVADS is omitted from Table 3. These are the paper’s own numbers, not independently verified external baseline results. The evidence supports leading reported fine-grained AVG among the listed methods, with several disclosed coarse/threshold exceptions. The supported severity is Minor for this bounded numerical and reporting inconsistency.

Problem 2 (The literal normal-similarity rule reverses anomaly ordering).  Section 3.6, p. 6, describes two coarse-score branches. The first is the direct anomaly classifier. The second is stated as the similarity to the normal class minus \(1\). Taken literally, if \(r\) is normal-class similarity, this is \(a=r-1\). Under the paper’s higher-is-anomalous convention, subtracting a constant preserves normality ordering instead of reversing it.

Complete check and assumptions. Let the normal and anomalous class vectors be \(L_N=(1,0)\) and \(L_A=(-1,0)\). Let the fused vectors of a normal frame and anomalous frame be \(f_N=L_N\) and \(f_A=L_A\). All vectors are nonzero and unit norm, so cosine similarity is well defined. Normal-class similarities are \(r_N=1\) and \(r_A=-1\). The class penalty in Eq. (10) is zero, since \(\max(0,L_N^\top L_A)=0\). These are admitted vectors in the described similarity calculation; they are not asserted to be outputs of the historical trained CLIP pipeline.

The literal rule gives \(a_N=0\), \(a_A=-2\). With anomaly as the positive class and larger scores indicating anomaly, the AUC for this positive/negative pair is \(0\). The decreasing transform \(a'=1-r\) gives \(a'_N=0\), \(a'_A=2\), and AUC \(1\). Repeating each vector over any number of frames leaves this ordering unchanged and permits any valid top-\(K\) selection. More generally, \(a'=-a\), so reversing every pair’s order yields \[\operatorname{AUC}(1-r)=1-\operatorname{AUC}(r-1)\] under the usual half-credit convention for ties. The parent independently evaluated the finite example. Equation (7)’s \(y=1\) anomaly convention and Figure 5’s high anomaly curves support the higher-is-anomalous reading.

Counterreading, repair, and bounded severity. The strongest explanation is a wording reversal: the intended rule may be \(1-\)normal similarity. The direct classifier branch remains available, and the paper explicitly chooses between the two branches. Neither the trained outputs nor the implemented scoring code are supplied. Consequently, this example is a defect in the literal written alternative rule, not proof that a reversed score generated any published AUC.

The correction \(a'=1-r\) restores the intended monotone direction algebraically; it does not guarantee accurate detection when similarity itself is poor. The exact score normalization and branch-selection protocol must still be supplied. This is Minor as a localized inference specification problem, with deployed behavior Needs Evidence. It is not an invalidation of the fine-grained alignment objective, the independent classifier branch, or the explanation pathway.
# Core questions that remain unresolved
## Which trainable variables does the contrastive term affect?

The paper describes frozen image and text encoders on p. 6 and label strings generated and selected by semantic similarity on pp. 5–6. Its contrastive loss is \[L_{\rm CTS}=\sum_j\max\left(0,
 \frac{L_N^\top L_{A_j}}{\|L_N\|_2\|L_{A_j}\|_2}\right).\] If the labels are fixed text-encoder outputs with fixed aggregation, and the trained parameters \(\theta\) belong only to the temporal adapter and classifiers, then \(L_N,L_{A_j}\) are independent of \(\theta\). The chain rule gives \[\nabla_\theta L_{\rm CTS}=0\] for every loss weight \(\lambda\). Under that parameterization, this loss cannot pull the fixed class embeddings apart; BCE and multiclass alignment can still train other components.

That conditional derivation is not proof that the actual loss is inactive. A frozen encoder can backpropagate into learnable input/context vectors, and a trainable label projection or aggregation can also provide a gradient path. The paper mentions context length \(l=20\), discusses prompt learning, and includes a learnable-prompt ablation. The final LAAM’s exact parameter graph is not specified sufficiently to exclude these readings. This is Needs Evidence: a trainable-parameter list, label-construction equation, gradient trace, or verified code is needed. No unconditional zero-gradient defect or Major consequence is asserted.
## Fusion and alignment dimensions

On p. 5, the feature equation is \(F_F=F_V+F_T\), while p. 6 explicitly states concatenation and Figure 2 labels the operation as Concat. For streams in \(\mathbb R^d\), addition yields \(\mathbb R^d\), whereas concatenation yields \(\mathbb R^{2d}\). The two operations are not interchangeable: for \(F_V=(1,0)\) and \(F_T=(0,1)\), their outputs are \((1,1)\) and \((1,0,0,1)\). The subsequent cosine alignment also requires compatible label dimensions.

Both architectures can be valid with suitable mappings. For example, a projection \([I\ I]\) after concatenation would recover the sum, but no claim is made that this is the actual projection. The text also leaves the integration of the selected label embeddings underspecified. The implemented fusion, broadcasting of a video-level text vector across frames, and projection into label space therefore remain Needs Evidence. An inconsistent description is established; an impossible running model is not.
## What is established about explanations?

The generated explanation is computed from captions before the learned detector and is subsequently used as a feature. Appendix Figure 5 supplies six selected qualitative examples, including normal and abnormal videos, with predicted curves and textual descriptions. This demonstrates example generation and semantic usefulness; detection ablations provide further evidence that the text can help the predictor.

It does not independently quantify factual accuracy, coverage of anomalous events, causal correctness about why an event occurred, or faithfulness to the trained detector’s decision. Because the explanation is upstream of the classifier, its existence alone does not determine which features the classifier used. Conversely, generation before classification is not proof of unfaithfulness: a useful semantic bottleneck can genuinely influence a decision. No factual error in a specific shown video is established from the sparse frames alone. The stronger explanation/cause claims remain Needs Evidence, requiring a defined evaluation with representative outputs and evidence tying the text to decisions. Generic possible caption failures do not refute a nonexistent universal caption-correction theorem.

Table 5 openly reports that captions achieve higher fine-grained AVG than explanation summaries, \(10.88\) versus \(10.15\). Page 8 explicitly chooses the latter for a performance/interpretation trade-off. Table 4 reports different coarse AUC results: visual-only \(86.76\), with captions \(86.33\), with the explanatory-text configuration \(87.86\), and with LAAM \(88.29\). The different metrics and disclosed trade-off should not be reframed as a concealed regression. The combined ablations do not separately identify every causal contribution of caption cleaning, summarization, or interpretation quality.
## Selection, evaluation, and compute boundaries

Section 3.6’s selection of the better coarse-score branch and the top-\(k\) analysis do not identify the data split used for selection. A validation-based or precommitted choice is possible. No test-label leakage is demonstrated. The disclosed caption/explanation input contains video content, not a documented ground-truth test-label prompt; whole-video context is consistent with an offline benchmark and does not by itself constitute label leakage.

Table 7 reports \(9.97\)M trainable parameters, \(15.37\) ms per frame, and \(12.04\)G MACs. Trainable counts legitimately exclude frozen weights. Captioning and video summarization may be cached or amortized in an offline pipeline. The paper does not supply a full timing boundary, model variants, frame/token counts, or separate BLIP-2, LLM, encoder, and detector costs. End-to-end/online efficiency interpretations are therefore unresolved, but no contradictory runtime measurement or timing fabrication is established.

Exact prompts, decoding settings, generated label phrases, threshold choices, baseline/run identities, raw predictions, and uncertainty estimates are unavailable. Several baseline bibliography associations do not identify their named VAD methods; those citation mismatches are preserved in the source note but are not promoted to standalone scientific Problems. The appendix’s phrase about unused anomaly categories does not supply a held-out-class protocol; no zero-shot generalization result is inferred from it.
# Overall dependence and conclusion

The supported assessment is Minor: the exact numerical presentation needs reconciliation, and one written alternative score rule needs its direction clarified. The core fine-grained average-ranking claim survives the displayed-cell arithmetic. report: Abstract: We check the theoretical argument, attack specification, selected experimental metrics, and a pinned public implementation of AdvMKC. A gradient inconsistent with the defined objective can increase that objective. The stability statement leaves iteration dependence unspecified, the printed reward has the opposite ordering to the released implementation, and the released attack does not enforce its noise cap. Two reported accuracy–purity pairs are also impossible under the stated definitions. The highest supported impact is Major. Historical experimental consequences of code discrepancies remain unresolved; scientific adjudication is pending.

Title: Technical Verification of AdvMKC
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

This report concerns Hao Yu, Weixuan Liang, Ke Liang, Suyuan Liu, Meng Liu, and Xinwang Liu, On the Adversarial Robustness of Multi-Kernel Clustering, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 73175–73196 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assigned identifiers are 0221/I25-43590 and OpenReview `xAGDSXAJgf`. Page references are one-based PDF pages, matching the printed internal pages 1–22, not the proceedings page range. The reviewed publisher PDF was acquired on 25 October 2026 UTC. Its SHA-256 is .

The review covers Sections 2.1 and 4–6 and Appendix A, including the objective, gradient, reduced-gradient update and perturbation bound; the attack-budget specification, metric definitions and selected table consistency; and the actor, critic, environment, main entry point, supplied configurations and relevant metric code at commit [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. All 113 archive members and their checkout bytes were hash-matched. This commit is not established as the version that generated the tables. The embedded appendix is available; access to a possible separate OpenReview supplement was blocked during source preparation. No author program or benchmark experiment was executed.
# Definitions and necessary assumptions
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The stated gradient can be an ascent direction).  Proposition 6.1 (p. 5), repeated in Appendix A.1 (p. 13), gives \(\partial_pf=2\gamma_p\operatorname{tr}[\bar K_p(I-\widehat H\widehat H^\top)]\). This is not the derivative of the linear mixture in Equation (2). It directly affects the MKKM-RG update in Equations (18)–(19).
## Complete check

Take \(N=2\), \(k=1\), \(m=2\), and \[K_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.8\\0.8&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 K_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.2\\0.2&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both matrices are positive definite, have unit diagonal, and are Gram matrices of unit vectors. After division by \(N=2\), their eigenvalues in the common eigenbasis are \((0.9,0.1)\) and \((0.6,0.4)\). For every feasible \(\gamma\), the leading eigengap is \(0.8\gamma_1+0.2\gamma_2\geq0.2\). The minimizing projector is unambiguous and \[f(\gamma)=0.1\gamma_1+0.4\gamma_2,\qquad \nabla f=(0.1,0.4).\] At \(\gamma=(0.9,0.1)\), the printed gradient is instead \((0.18,0.08)\). With \(u=2\), Equation (19) gives \(d=(-0.1,0.1)\). For \(\eta=0.1\), both old and new weights are interior to the simplex, but \[f(0.9,0.1)=0.130,\qquad
 f((0.9,0.1)+0.1d)=f(0.89,0.11)=0.133.\] Indeed \(\nabla f^\top d=0.03>0\); every sufficiently small positive step increases the stated objective. Independent eigenvalue evaluation agrees (`check.py`, `calc.json`). This refutes the proposition for its printed objective without relying on the later globally worded Assumption 6.2.
## Alternative reading, impact, and local correction

Appendix Equation (25) uses \(\alpha_p^2-\beta_p^2\), indicating an intended squared-weight mixture. Under that changed definition and a spectral gap, the factor \(2\gamma_p\) is appropriate. This is substantive counterevidence about intent, but it changes the objective. Appendix A.1 also writes \(f=f_1+f_2\) for \(f_2=\max_H\operatorname{tr}(\bar K_\gamma HH^\top)\); the actual decomposition is \(f=f_1-f_2\). For a linear mixture with a unique optimal projector the local correction is \(\partial_pf=\operatorname{tr}[\bar K_p(I-\widehat H\widehat H^\top)]\). No complete repaired stability theorem is supplied. This is Major because the invalid derivative defines the central theoretical optimization procedure, irrespective of whether empirical attacks survive.

Problem 2 (The stability proof removes iteration dependence).  Theorem 6.3 (p. 6) bounds the difference between weights obtained from original and perturbed kernels by a constant times the largest kernel-noise norm. Appendix A.2, p. 17, Equation (34) and its final chain do not establish an iteration-independent bound.
## Recurrence and a conditional diagnostic

Writing \(e_t=\|\alpha^{(t)}-\beta^{(t)}\|_\infty\) and \(\varepsilon=\max_p\|N_p\|_{\rm op}\), a recurrence \(e_{t+1}\leq C e_t+C\varepsilon\), \(e_0=0\), gives \[e_T\leq C\varepsilon\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}C^j.\] Even \(C=1\) gives \(T\varepsilon\). No contraction argument removes this dependence.

Two interpretation limits are essential. Assumption 6.2 says every \(\gamma\in\mathbb R^m\); at \(\gamma=0\) a homogeneous kernel mixture is zero and its eigengap is zero. That literal premise is infeasible. The following diagnostic deliberately adopts the meaningful simplex domain and the squared-weight mixture suggested by Appendix (25). It is not claimed to satisfy the impossible all-real-weights premise.

Let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\), \(N=2,k=1,m=2\), and \[K_1=K_2=J_2,\qquad
 \widetilde K_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&1-\varepsilon\\1-\varepsilon&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \widetilde K_2=J_2.\] Every kernel is positive semidefinite with unit diagonal, and \(\|\widetilde K_1-K_1\|_{\rm op}=\varepsilon\). The matrices share the leading eigenvector. In the squared mixture normalized by two, the perturbed simplex eigengap is \((1-\varepsilon)\gamma_1^2+\gamma_2^2\geq(1-\varepsilon)/2\geq1/4\). The original objective is identically zero; the perturbed objective is \(\widetilde f(\gamma)=\varepsilon\gamma_1^2/2\). Starting both sequences at \((1/2,1/2)\), choose \(u=2\) and \(\eta=0.1\leq1/4\). Equation (19) leaves the original sequence fixed and gives \[\widetilde\gamma_1^{(t)}=\tfrac12(1-\eta\varepsilon)^t,\qquad
 e_t=\tfrac12[1-(1-\eta\varepsilon)^t].\] Every finite iterate is feasible, the perturbed objective decreases, and \(e_t\to1/2\). With \(T=10/\varepsilon\), independently calculated errors are \(0.316984,0.316152,0.316069\) for \(\varepsilon=0.1,0.01,0.001\).
## Bounded conclusion and counterevidence

A bound \(O_T(\varepsilon)\) at a fixed prescribed finite \(T\) can absorb iteration dependence and is not refuted. The theorem does not specify that restriction, and its proof does not establish stability of optimized weights uniformly over run length. Correcting the mixture and restricting the gap premise to the simplex alone do not recover such a bound. The theorem-level assessment is Needs Evidence / scope clarification: the paper does not explicitly require a constant uniform in the iteration count. A fixed-horizon interpretation remains admissible, so the conditional counterexample does not establish a Major defect in the original theorem. The remaining question is the permitted constant dependence and stopping rule. An upper bound on weight change also does not imply monotone deterioration in external clustering accuracy. The example’s leading eigenspace in fact remains unchanged.

Problem 3 (The printed reward orders the attack objective backwards).  Equation (9), p. 4, is a positive within-original-cluster cosine similarity. Equations (11)–(12), p. 5, maximize its expected return; Equation (16) minimizes the negative policy objective. The release instead uses one minus that similarity.

For original clusters \(\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\), compare \[H_0=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\0&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 H_1=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both have orthonormal columns and are leading embeddings of the positive-semidefinite, unit-diagonal kernels \(2H_iH_i^\top\). For the same original co-occurrence matrix, Equation (9) gives \(r(H_0)=8/16=1/2\) and \(r(H_1)=4/16=1/4\). Maximization favors the preserved grouping over the crossed grouping. This is an objective-ordering calculation, not a full data-perturbation construction at a specified small budget.

Counterevidence about the released intent is clear: and use \(1-r\). The printed sign must not be imputed to historical runs. Replacing the reward by \(1-r\) repairs its local ordering only. The printed core attack specification has a Major directional inconsistency; its historical empirical consequence needs evidence.

Problem 4 (The released RL path fails its central noise constraint).  The threat model requires \(\|\mathcal N\|\leq\epsilon\) (p. 3, Eq. 3); the generator is normalized in Eq. 10 (p. 4). The released RL path does not enforce that bound.

The entry point passes a Gaussian-sampled action directly to `ClusterEnv.step`. The method `perturbed_data`, lines 205–212, accumulates this action and rescales only when the noise norm is smaller than \(b=\texttt{thresh}\sqrt d\). From reset, take one environment, \(d=4\), \(\texttt{thresh}=10\), and cumulative action \((30,0,0,0)\). Its norm is 30, the bound is 20, and the condition \(30<20\) is false. The output remains norm 30. Any action in an open neighborhood of \(2b e_1\) similarly violates the cap; these neighborhoods have positive probability under the released Gaussian policy.

The alternate optimizer calls `normalized_noise`; the RL path does not. The soft penalty is on the actor mean, not sampled cumulative noise, so cannot provide the hard guarantee. The three released configurations also set `thresh: 10`, whereas p. 7 states \(\epsilon=0.1\sqrt d\), a 100-fold nominal RMS difference.

The projection \(v\mapsto v\min\{1,b/\|v\|\}\), with zero handled separately, enforces a local cumulative-vector cap. This algebraic observation is not a tested patch or repaired experiment. The failure is Major for the released bounded-attack procedure. Historical table-generating code is unknown; no published score loss is inferred. Evidence: `code.json`, `calc.json`.

Problem 5 (Two metric pairs violate accuracy–purity ordering).  Table 3 (p. 8), BBCSport, surrogate JMKSC and victim MKSSC-ERC, reports ACC \(71.73\%\), PR \(45.40\%\). Table 5 (p. 19), BBCSport, MVC-LFA with no attack, reports ACC \(81.88\%\), PR \(81.07\%\). Both pairs were visually checked in the original PDF.

For a contingency table \(n_{ij}\), the stated Hungarian-assignment accuracy and per-cluster majority purity satisfy \[\mathrm{ACC}=\frac1N\max_\pi\sum_i n_{i,\pi(i)}
 \leq\frac1N\sum_i\max_j n_{ij}=\mathrm{PR}.\] This holds for each run and paired-run averages. The released implementation and output indices agree with these definitions. Violations of 26.33 and 0.81 percentage points exceed rounding error. At least one value or association in each pair is incorrect. Unmatched aggregations would require an undisclosed comparison protocol. This is a supported Minor reporting defect. Raw predictions are needed to identify the bad cells; no substitute value is guessed.
# Dependence and unresolved provenance

Problems 1–2 concern the theoretical contribution, regardless of appendix placement. Problem 3 concerns the printed attack objective and Problem 4 a central constraint of the release. MKC vulnerability may survive these defects; that does not validate the failed derivations or budget compliance.

The release also selects a final candidate using ground-truth external metrics (`main.py:190–211`), an oracle-selection evaluation protocol. Training reward uses initial predicted clusters, so supervised training-label leakage is not established. Historical use and equal baseline treatment need provenance. The publisher and repository landing pages returned no correction notice in the inspected content; this was not an exhaustive erratum or priority search.

# Identity and inspected evidence

This report concerns Muleilan Pei, Shaoshuai Shi, Lu Zhang, Peiliang Li and Shaojie Shen, GoIRL: Graph-Oriented Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Trajectory Prediction, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 48699–48713 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; assigned 0222/I25-43591, OpenReview `x9LGowGzZu`. The 15-page publisher PDF was acquired on 25 October 2026 UTC. Its SHA-256 is . Page references are one-based PDF pages, matching internal printed numbering.

The inspected scope comprises the main method, Algorithm 1, Equations (1)–(17), benchmark definitions and elementary table consistency, and the implementation and evidentiary statements in embedded Appendices A–D. The source manifest records no located/acquired author repository; this does not prove that none was ever released. Possible separate OpenReview material was inaccessible with HTTP 403. No author code, datasets, weights, raw predictions, or supplementary video were executed or inspected. The absence of code is a coverage limit, not itself a scientific defect.
# Checked reasoning
## Gibbs likelihood and state visitation

For a finite admissible plan set \(\mathcal T\) independent of the reward parameters, with a fixed start/termination convention, write \[p_\theta(\tau)=\frac{\exp R_\theta(\tau)}{Z_\theta},\qquad
 R_\theta(\tau)=\sum_s\mu_\tau(s)R_\theta(s).\] Differentiating the log partition function gives \[\nabla_\theta\overline L_D
 =\sum_s\{\overline\mu_D(s)-\mathbb E_\theta\mu_\tau(s)\}
       \nabla_\theta R_\theta(s).\] This verifies Equation (3), p. 5, provided its expected visitation counts come from the same normalized distribution as Equation (2). Equation (1), p. 4, is the law of total probability over the same plan support.

An independently written three-path diagnostic uses count vectors \((2,0),(1,1),(0,2)\), reward parameters \((0.3,-0.2)\), and the first path as a demonstration. It gives analytic gradient \((0.679843332170,-0.679843332170)\). A centered finite difference with step \(10^{-6}\) differs by \(1.51\times10^{-11}\). This checks a finite instance of the identity, not the unpublished driving implementation.
## Trajectory and probability formulas

Equations (8)–(9), p. 6, use the degree-\(n\) Bernstein basis and \(n+1\) control points. The binomial theorem gives \(\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}t^j(1-t)^{n-j}=1\) for \(0\leq t\leq1\); the proposed curve and timestamp substitution are well defined. Equations (15)–(17), p. 13, define the Huber residual loss and pairwise hinge loss consistently with the stated final-displacement winner selection.

The product fusion in Equation (11) is a normalized probability vector when both inputs are nonnegative and their product has positive total mass. For inputs \((0.2,0.3,0.5)\) and \((0.5,0.25,0.25)\), the output is \((1/3,1/4,5/12)\). This is a valid heuristic fusion rule; neither Bayesian independence nor a calibration theorem is needed to define it. The report does not infer calibrated probabilities solely from normalization.
## Reported numerical relationships

The checked combined Argoverse scores equal the stated Brier component plus minFDE: \(0.6232+1.1725=1.7957\) for the single model and \(0.5684+1.1263=1.6947\) for the ensemble. Table 4’s four ablation rows satisfy the same identity at displayed precision. The nuScenes minima and miss rates decrease when more modes are available, as their definitions permit. These are consistency checks of reported numbers, not reproductions.

Appendix B and Table 5, p. 13, explicitly list stronger overall ranking scores for QCNet and SEPT and call GoIRL competitive. This qualification is counterevidence against turning the main selected-baseline comparison into a fabricated claim of an undisclosed universal leaderboard lead.
# Unresolved implementation and evidence scope
## Finite horizon versus stationary policy

Section 3.1, p. 3, defines a fixed planning horizon and calls the grid-cell policy stationary. Algorithm 1, p. 5, returns one policy after \(N\) soft backups; the setup gives \(H=25\), without specifying \(N\), its relation to \(H\), or the complete end-action and terminal-reward conventions.

This is Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated erroneous implementation. The algorithm is explicitly called approximate value iteration. A stopping-time model, a converged fixed-point construction with suitable terminal treatment, or implicit time augmentation may explain the description. The required evidence is the actual value/occupancy routine, terminal convention, backup count and sampled plan support. No full algorithm counterexample is asserted in their absence.
## Grid specification

The implementation paragraph on p. 7 specifies \(100\times100\), downsampled to \(25\times25\). Appendix A.1, p. 12, explicitly specifies \(H_G=W_G=50\) at 1 m spacing for the feature adaptor, separately from a 100 m drivable-area graph. Both statements were visually confirmed. A radius-versus-side interpretation might explain some prose but does not by itself reconcile the two explicit dimensions. The operative crop and downsampling configuration require clarification; no prediction-score consequence has been demonstrated.
## Generalization and physical feasibility

Section 4.3 and Appendix C provide qualitative drivable-area-change examples. They support the illustrated cases, not a measured success frequency over an independently specified shift population or a universal causal superiority of IRL over behavior cloning. A matched perturbation protocol and quantitative scene-level results would resolve that broader scope.

A polynomial proposal is smooth, but unconstrained control points allow unbounded speed or acceleration; learned refinement offsets need not preserve a derivative bound. The paper’s kinematic-feasibility language therefore should not be read as a proved dynamics guarantee. No actual infeasible prediction is established here, and no formal universal theorem was stated.

Title: Technical Verification of Phase Transitions for Unregularized M-estimators
# Identity, scope and background

This report concerns Takuya Koriyama and Pierre C. Bellec, Phase transitions for the existence of unregularized M-estimators in single index models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 31519–31540 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; 0223/I25-43592, OpenReview `x8S61xscqh`. The preserved 22-page publisher PDF, retrieved 25 October 2026 UTC, is the reviewed version. Page references below use its one-based PDF numbering, which matches the printed page numbers.

The main assumptions, threshold and nonlinear-system claims, conic projection, KKT correspondence, uniqueness strategy and phase-transition dependencies were inspected, including embedded Appendices A–E. No repository was acquired; a possible separate OpenReview supplement returned HTTP 403. No author code ran, and external convex-analysis results were not independently reproved.
# A demonstrated error in the central projection

Problem 1 (Major: the displayed projection violates its defining cone).  The paper explicitly defines \(z_-=\max(-z,0)\) on p. 3. Lemma A.1, p. 9, requires \(tU+p\leq0\) on \(\Omega_\nearrow\), but defines \(p(t)=-tU+(G+tU)_-\) there. It asserts cone membership, \(\varphi(t)=\mathbb E[(G-p(t))^2]\), and at the optimizer \(\mathbb E[p_*^2]=\mathbb E[Gp_*]\). These assertions are incompatible with the stated convention.
## An admissible complete test

Let \(U,G\) be independent standard normals and let \(Y\) be an independent balanced sign. Use \[\ell_y(u)=\log(1+e^{-yu}),\qquad
\Omega_\nearrow=\{Y=-1\},\quad\Omega_\searrow=\{Y=1\}.\] Each loss is \(C^1\), strictly convex and nonconstant. Its infimum is zero and its Gaussian-input expectation is finite, since \(\ell_y(u)\leq\log2+|u|\). There are no coercive losses, so the probability requirement is satisfied. The two positive expectations in Assumption 2.4 each equal \(1/2\): independence gives one half of the second moment of \(U\). The growth condition holds with \(b=1,D(Y)=1\), using \(\log(1+e^u)\geq u\) and \(\log(1+e^{-u})\geq-u\). Both required moments of \(D\) are finite. This is an allowed single-index model with a constant response link, not a noiseless separable exception.

Symmetry and independence give \(\varphi(t)=(1+t^2)/2\), so \(t_*=0,\delta_\infty=2\). The printed candidate is \[p_*=G_-I_{\{Y=-1\}}+G_+I_{\{Y=1\}}.\] On \(\{Y=-1,G<0\}\), of probability \(1/4\), it is positive where the cone requires it to be nonpositive. Exact half-normal moments give \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[p_*^2]&=\tfrac12,&
\mathbb E[Gp_*]&=\tfrac12(-\tfrac12)+\tfrac12(\tfrac12)=0,\\
\mathbb E[(G-p_*)^2]&=\tfrac32\ne\varphi(0)=\tfrac12,&
\mathcal G(p_*)&=1/\sqrt2>0.\end{aligned}\] Thus the asserted direction is infeasible even at the allowed boundary \(\delta=\delta_\infty=2\). An independently written 60-node Gauss–Hermite calculation in `check.py`/`calc.json` confirms respectively \(0.5,\ 2.03\cdot10^{-17},\ 1.5\). The analytical identities, rather than quadrature accuracy, establish the contradiction.
## Dependency and consequence

The proof of Lemma A.1 on p. 10 also uses \(z_-^2=z_-z\), which is false for the defined nonnegative negative part. The finite-dimensional projection on p. 13 repeats the same sign. Lemma E.1, pp. 18–19, uses the false moment identity to certify the nonexistence direction’s feasibility in [eq:constraint] (#eq:constraint). Its claimed bound on the ray loss fails too: at \(Y=-1,G=-1\), \(\ell_{-1}(p_*)=\log(1+e)=1.313262>\ell_{-1}(0)=0.693147\). The strict inequality persists on a positive-probability set.

For the existence branch, Lemma E.2, p. 20, forms \(\widetilde v=-aU+(aU+v)_-\) on increasing losses and asserts \((a,\widetilde v)\in C\). With \(a=0,v=G,\delta=3\), the input is feasible because \(\mathcal G(G)=1-\sqrt{3/2}=-0.224745<0\). Its expected loss is at most \(\log2+\sqrt{2/\pi}<2\), so it lies in an allowed sublevel set. Yet the constructed \(\widetilde v\) again violates the cone on \(\{Y=-1,G<0\}\). The projection inequality (25), followed by (26)–(27) on p. 21, therefore lacks its asserted premise. These steps support both sides of Theorem 3.4 and hence the nonlinear system’s phase transition in Theorem 2.7; the finite-dimensional proof of Theorem 2.6 also uses the projection. This is a consequential invalid core derivation, even though it has an evident local repair.
## Counterevidence and verified local correction

The surrounding formulas evidently intend the signed convention \(z_-=\min(z,0)\). That alternative explains the error and is strong counterevidence against treating the theorem statements as false. The original rendered pages confirm that the conflict is not text extraction.

A global convention swap alone is insufficient to verify every proof line. On p. 19 the final contradiction uses equal positive expectations for \(G_-\) and \(G_+\); signed negative parts instead have opposite expectations. With the nonnegative convention each mean is \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), not the printed \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\). A valid local replacement is to square the asserted zero random variable on the disjoint loss-type events, yielding \[0=\tfrac12\{\mathbb P(\Omega_\nearrow)+\mathbb P(\Omega_\searrow)\}>0,\] a contradiction. These local repairs restore the inspected algebra; they are not a certification of a completely revised proof.
# Other checks and scope boundaries

For a response independent of \(U\), with \(c=\mathbb P(\Omega_\vee)\), symmetry gives \(\varphi(t)=(1+c)(1+t^2)/2\). Thus the critical plotted ratio is \(p/n=\delta_\infty^{-1}=(1+c)/2\). For balanced binomial responses with \(q\) trials it is \(1-2^{-q}\); for Poisson mean one it is \(1-e^{-1}/2=0.8160602794\). The binomial values at \(q=1,2,4,8,16\) are \(0.5,0.75,0.9375,0.99609375,0.9999847412\). Loss classifications and the reciprocal conversion between the theory’s \(n/p\) and plots’ \(p/n\) are coherent.

The KKT-to-proximal-system calculations on pp. 15–16 give \(\|\sigma G-v\|^2=\delta^{-1}\sigma^2\) and \(\mathbb E[G(v+aU)]=\sigma(1-\delta^{-1})\) as stated. No additional substantive defect was established in the inspected nondegeneracy or uniqueness strategy. Theorem 2.6 omits the critical equality case for asymptotic estimator existence, whereas Theorem 2.7 addresses a different infinite-dimensional object and includes equality on its nonexistence side; this is not a contradiction.

Figure 2’s caption states \(n=1500\), while Section 4 states \(n=1000\). The actual simulation configuration and linear-programming tolerance remain unresolved; no change in a numerical conclusion is established. No raw experiments were reproduced.

Title: Technical Verification of Bayesian Coherence Diagnostics in Neural Networks
# Identity, version and scope

This report concerns Gábor Pituk, Vik Shirvaikar and Tom Rainforth, Do Bayesian Neural Networks Actually Behave Like Bayesian Models?, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 49420–49458 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; 0224/I25-43593, OpenReview `x5RQnF7Vw9`. The preserved 39-page publisher PDF was retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. Page references use one-based PDF pages, matching printed numbering.

The main claims, Bayesian identities, sequential and martingale protocols, embedded Appendices A–K and selected released implementations were inspected. Static checks covered both frozen repositories: `bnn-msc` commit and `bnn_seq_vi` commit . All 26 and 54 archived members, respectively, match the preserved checkout. Historical experiment-to-commit correspondence is unknown. No author code, training, checkpoints, datasets or weights were executed. A possible separate OpenReview supplement returned HTTP 403.

Equation reference: eq:tower. For a common prior \(\pi\) and conditionally independent disjoint data batches, likelihood multiplication verifies Proposition 5.1: sequential exact updating equals pooled exact updating. For the matching joint predictive \(p(dy)=\int p(dy\mid\theta)\pi(d\theta)\), the tower property verifies Proposition 6.1: \[
\int \pi(d\theta\mid y)p(dy)=\pi(d\theta),\qquad
\mathbb E_Y\mathbb E[h(\Theta)\mid Y]=\mathbb E_\pi h(\Theta).\] Bounded class probabilities meet the integrability requirement. This finite identity does not require the asymptotic parameter-identifiability conditions discussed with Doob’s theorem. The paper does state those conditions; omitting them would manufacture an unrelated objection.
# Core findings

Problem 1 (Major: an interval for one noisy estimator is used to test equality against another).  Section 6, p. 8, infers failure of Bayesian updating from deviations outside the bootstrapped martingale-posterior interval; Figure 7, p. 9, treats improved performance as falsifying coherence. Appendix E.1, p. 20, resamples only the imputed/retrained posterior groups. It does not include Monte Carlo uncertainty in the initial model average.
## Actual estimator and source correspondence

For VI the reported construction uses \(n=20\) groups and \(k=20\) samples per retrained posterior. The released sets `vi_ensemble_size=20`. The evaluation in averages that many stochastic predictions. The default in `ensemble_checkpoints.py` is also 20; `run_ensemble_retrained_vi.sh` resamples only retrained checkpoints (100 bootstrap replicates). No corresponding initial BMA resampling was found in that path. Thus the actual finite baseline cannot be treated as its exact expectation merely by increasing the number of retrained groups.
## Exact Bayesian null and independent diagnostic

Take \(\Theta\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\). At every pseudo-data input let \(Y\mid\Theta\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) independently of \(\Theta\). At the test input let the success probability be \(h(\Theta)=0.2+0.6\Theta\). All probabilities are valid and bounded; the pseudo-label likelihood is identical at both parameter values, so every exact updated posterior is exactly the original posterior. Joint predictive sampling, normalization and [eq:tower] (#eq:tower) all hold. Independent exact posterior draws are permitted.

Write \(A\) for a 20-draw mean of \(\Theta\), and \(M\) for the mean of 20 groups of 20 exact draws. Then \[\mathbb EA=\mathbb EM=\tfrac12,\quad
\operatorname{Var}(A)=\tfrac1{80},\quad
\operatorname{Var}(M)=\tfrac1{1600},\quad
\operatorname{Var}(A-M)=\tfrac{21}{1600}.\] An interval estimating uncertainty of \(M\) alone omits the dominant term. The normal approximation gives coverage \(2\Phi(1.96/\sqrt{21})-1=0.3311\), rather than 0.95. This is a diagnostic approximation, not an assertion of exact finite coverage.

The independently written `check.py` uses the actual discrete group-resampling rule: 10,000 independent null trials, 20 groups of 20 draws, 1,000 bootstrap replicates per trial, seed 224, percentile endpoints 0.025 and 0.975. It records a false-rejection rate \(0.6775\), with Monte Carlo standard error \(0.00467\). Its bootstrap replicate count differs from the released 100; the analytical missing-variance defect does not depend on that choice. The affine map from \(\Theta\) to \(h\) preserves interval exclusion. For a positive-label test case, the monotone log score does as well.

Improved expected log score can arise under this null without any update error: exact binomial summation gives \(-0.70239651\) for 20-draw integration and \(-0.69359779\) for 400 independent draws. This follows from averaging and concavity, despite identical posteriors.
## Impact, counterevidence and required repair

The error is in the inference from the finite comparison to non-Bayesian updating, not in Proposition 6.1 or in an interval for \(M\) alone. Resampling whole groups correctly preserves within-group dependence. The released classification path averages probabilities after softmax; its pseudo-label generator samples one parameter vector for the entire label vector. Neither operation is a defect.

The null is a calibration counterexample to the diagnostic, not a simulation of CIFAR or a claim that the observed gap is Monte Carlo noise. The experiment may still show a real incoherence or a useful ensemble gain. A corrected comparison must estimate the initial integration error as well, propagate covariance if samples are coupled, and use a confidence interval for the difference, or make the baseline integration error demonstrably negligible. Matched-budget exact-update controls would test the complete procedure. These repairs have not been run on the published experiment.

Problem 2 (Major: the Laplace construction substitutes squared aggregate gradient for curvature).  Appendix G.4, p. 24, calls \(\{(\partial l/\partial\theta_i)^2\}_i\) the diagonal curvature at MAP, then adds \(\lambda\) and inverts it. This quantity is neither the Hessian diagonal nor the usual sum of per-observation score squares.

For a differentiable total loss \(L\) at an interior stationary MAP, \(\nabla L(\widehat\theta)=0\). The specified rule therefore gives \[\Sigma_{\rm rule}=\lambda^{-1}I\] regardless of the local likelihood curvature. Adding shrinkage does not recover the lost information.

For a complete one-dimensional diagnostic, take \(\theta\sim N(0,1)\) and independent \(y_1=-1,y_2=1\) from \(N(\theta,1)\). The negative log posterior is \(L(\theta)=\tfrac32\theta^2+\mathrm{const}\); the MAP is zero, its Hessian is 3, and the summed per-observation likelihood-score squares are 2. The aggregate gradient square is zero. With \(\lambda=1\), the stated rule gives variance 1, while adding the same regularizer to the posterior Hessian gives \(1/4\). The exact unregularized posterior variance is \(1/3\). This illustrates an operator failure, not a measured neural-network score.

The static release corroborates the literal reading: , lines 819–828, passes the full-data `TraceMeanField_ELBO` loss to `optax.fisher_diag` and adds shrinkage; the callback includes the prior and has no per-observation loop. The inspected official current Optax implementation squares the flattened gradient of that entire scalar callback [Retained latex: \cite{optax}]. Its exact bytes and URL are preserved in `ox0.txt`/`deps.json`. The historical dependency version is not established. The paper’s printed formula independently specifies the same erroneous curvature substitution.

This affects the method used to support central claims about Laplace functional variability, information retention and tails (Sections 4–5). A covariance determined by optimizer residuals and arbitrary shrinkage cannot isolate failures of a correctly constructed diagonal curvature approximation. The disclosure of shrinkage and reports of full-rank experiments are relevant counterevidence, but do not make squared total gradient a curvature matrix. The scope is this construction and its evidentiary attribution; it does not invalidate VI/SGLD experiments, prove all historical figures used this commit, or quantify how corrected Laplace results would change. A repair requires a specified Hessian/GGN or per-observation Fisher with proper prior curvature and scaling, followed by the affected comparisons.
# Local findings

Problem 3 (Minor: the printed Langevin score drift has the wrong sign).  Appendix B.5, p. 17, specifies \(-\nabla\log\pi\) in its diffusion and discretizations while claiming stationarity at \(\pi\). For \(\pi=N(0,1)\), even interpreting its noise as the usual Brownian differential, this gives \(d\Theta_t=\Theta_t\,dt+\sqrt2\,dB_t\). Starting in the claimed stationary law yields \[\operatorname{Var}(\Theta_t)=2e^{2t}-1,\] rather than 1. At step size 0.1 the printed Euler step increases variance from 1 to 1.41. The correct score sign is positive; its continuous diffusion preserves variance 1 (Euler still has discretization bias).

The release uses the correct positive score: , lines 98–104, adds the likelihood/prior gradient produced by `utils/train_utils.py`, lines 104–130. Thus the error changes the mathematical sampler description, but is not evidence that the SGLD experiments used an explosive process.

Problem 4 (Minor: the misspecification illustration’s finite quantity is not the stated KL divergence).  Appendix K.2 and Figure 24, pp. 35–36, use truth \(P=(\delta_{-1}+\delta_1)/2\) and continuous Gaussian posterior predictions with fixed \(\sigma>0\), but plot a finite KL divergence.

Every such predictive \(Q\) assigns mass zero to \(\{-1,1\}\), while \(P\) assigns mass one. Hence \(P\not\ll Q\) and \(D_{\rm KL}(P\|Q)=+\infty\). The archived notebook , cells 7–10, instead computes \(\log(1/2)-\tfrac12\{\log q(1)+\log q(-1)\}\): a finite expected log-density score plus a constant, not this KL. It specifies no binning or smoothed true law.

Even under that charitable scoring interpretation, the claimed optimal mixing distribution at \(\mu=\pm1\) is not exact. For equal Gaussian components centered at \(\pm a\), \[\frac{d}{da}\log q_a(1)
=\frac{\tanh(a/\sigma^2)-a}{\sigma^2}<0\quad(a=1).\] At the notebook’s \(\sigma=0.5\), the derivative is \(-0.00268280\); moving to \(a=0.999\) improves the log score from \(-0.91860313\) to \(-0.91860243\). Relabeling the axis and correcting the optimizer would repair these local claims, not prove a general misspecification result. The notebook also uses prior standard deviation \(1/3\) rather than the text’s 1, balanced deterministic observations, and samples observations as the `mu` values for its zero-data baseline; these further limit exact Figure 24 reconstruction. No author notebook was executed. The main coherence identities and classification experiments do not depend on this illustrative KL calculation.

Problem 5 (Minor: the preserved launch settings contradict a required batch divisibility assertion).  The released VI pretraining script requests 4,080 training examples. `utils/data_utils.py` requires that this size divide evenly across devices; `utils/train_utils.py`, lines 62–65, then requires each device’s training count to be divisible by 1,024.

If both assertions held for \(P\) devices, \(4080/P=1024m\) for an integer \(m\), forcing 4080 to be divisible by 1024. It is not (\(4080\bmod1024=1008\)). Thus the preserved configuration cannot pass both setup assertions. This is a static reproducibility defect in this release, not an observed execution or evidence against historical scores. A compatible prediction batching routine would avoid changing the intended data split; no such repair was executed.
# Other inspected evidence and overall impact

Section 5’s pooled-versus-sequential comparisons remain relevant empirical tests, and the paper acknowledges HMC mixing as an alternative explanation. The count-only mean formula on p. 6 is not generally an identity for a nonlinear input-dependent heteroskedastic BNN; however, the pooled HMC control and additional fixed-noise experiments prevent attributing the entire phenomenon to that heuristic alone. Its exact calibration remains Needs Evidence.

For SGLD, Appendix E.1 selects 18 spaced checkpoints from one chain and then invokes between-group independence. Spacing does not establish that assumption; effective sample size or a dependence-aware analysis is needed. No autocorrelation or actual effect-size correction was measured here. The claimed static predictive utility of the methods is not refuted. Nor does the valid population identity require correct specification of the external test-data distribution.
