Title: Technical Verification of Orient Anything
# Identity, version and scope

This report concerns Zehan Wang, Ziang Zhang, Tianyu Pang, Chao Du, Hengshuang Zhao and Zhou Zhao, Orient Anything: Learning Robust Object Orientation Estimation from Rendering 3D Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 65556–65574 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; 0225/I25-43594, OpenReview `x4yTgv2WkJ`. The preserved publisher PDF has 19 pages; page references are one-based PDF pages and match printed numbers. It was retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. All sections and embedded appendices were text-inspected, with parent visual checks of pp. 3, 5, 7, 14 and 16.

The frozen `SpatialVision/Orient-Anything` release [Retained latex: \cite{code}], commit , contains 17 archive members, all byte-verified against the extracted source. It supplies inference and rendering, not the training loss, benchmark evaluation, asset split identifiers or Ori-Bench responses. A possible separate OpenReview supplement returned HTTP 403. No author code, trained weights, datasets or paid VLM calls were executed or acquired. Historical experiment-to-commit correspondence is unknown. The README advertises a later V2 project; its existence does not establish a correction of this frozen ICML version.

The core construction trains a pretrained visual encoder with polar, azimuth and roll classification heads plus an orientation-confidence head. Synthetic views supply angle labels after semantic front-face annotation. Tables 2–3 evaluate real-image 3D orientation; Table 4 also uses a distinct coarse direction-recognition task. The results support transfer within their reported evaluations. This review neither reproduces the training nor certifies every numerical result.
# Demonstrated local problems

Problem 1 (Minor: optional augmentation averages a circular rotation linearly).  In , lines 26–47, `get_3angle_infer_aug` combines six crop predictions. Azimuth uses circular averaging; rotation uses the ordinary IQR-filtered mean defined in , lines 104–119, before subtracting \(180^\circ\).

Take six valid 360-bin rotation predictions \[(1,1,1,359,359,359).\] Every value is in the decoder’s domain. The quartiles are 1 and 359; all six survive the stated \(1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}\) filter. Their mean is 180, hence the returned roll is \(0^\circ\). The individual decoded rolls are instead \(-179^\circ\) and \(179^\circ\): all lie within one degree of the same physical angle at \(180^\circ\). Circular averaging returns that angle, so the implemented rule can create a \(180^\circ\) error from individually accurate predictions. The independent calculation is retained in `calc.json`; `code.json` binds the exact source members and lines.

A circular mean, with a declared rule for a zero resultant, repairs this boundary example; it does not guarantee robust aggregation for arbitrary multimodal predictions. The plain inference function performs no such averaging, and `app.py`, line 60, disables augmentation by default. No evidence binds this optional path to the paper’s benchmark scores. The supported consequence is a released optional-feature failure.

Problem 2 (Minor: the documented head dimension is incompatible with the decoder).  The README example, lines 76–83, constructs \(\texttt{out\_dim}=360+180+180+2=722\). The decoder in `inference.py`, lines 15–22, expects 360 azimuth, 180 polar and 360 rotation logits, followed by two confidence logits.

With 722 outputs, the slice \(540{:}900\) contains only 182 entries. It includes confidence positions 720 and 721. Its argmax minus 180 therefore ranges only from \(-180^\circ\) to \(1^\circ\), while confidence logits compete as rotations. If the linked checkpoint instead has the 902-row head expected by the decoder, loading that head into the documented architecture is dimensionally incompatible. Checkpoint bytes were not inspected, so the actual loading branch is not claimed observed.

The correct architecture size for the stated slices is 902; `app.py`, lines 16–23, already uses that size and a separately named checkpoint. Thus the documentation example is defective, while neither the app’s architecture nor historical experiments are refuted. The dimension repair was checked algebraically, not by loading weights.

Problem 3 (Minor: the published direction template has overlapping sectors).  Appendix E, p. 14, maps \(292.5^\circ<\hat\phi<360^\circ\) to front-facing, but also maps \(292.5^\circ<\hat\phi<337.5^\circ\) to front-and-right-facing.

The admissible integer prediction \(315^\circ\) satisfies both conditions. Independent `if` statements emit two descriptions; a first-match interpretation suppresses the intended diagonal description. The strict bounds additionally omit zero and sector boundaries. Zero can occur in the released argmax decoder.

An unambiguous eight-sector rule is \[s=\left\lfloor\frac{(\hat\phi\bmod360^\circ)+22.5^\circ}{45^\circ}
\right\rfloor\bmod8,\] with sectors ordered front, front-left, left, back-left, back, back-right, right, front-right. It assigns \(315^\circ\) only to sector 7 and zero only to sector 0, and declares half-open boundary ownership. Equivalently, the first printed lower bound should be \(337.5^\circ\), with boundary conventions repaired throughout.

This affects the stated orientation-to-language procedure. Its historical execution is unresolved because the release lacks that template and its evaluation records. The appendix’s illustrated diagonal descriptions also argue against assuming universal execution of a faulty first-match rule. No score change is inferred.

Problem 4 (Minor: Table 1’s two baseline totals conflict with its subgroup counts).  Section 3, p. 3, defines 73 direction, 39 part and 88 relation pairs, each successful only if both the original and mirrored question are correct. Table 1’s rounded subgroup rates uniquely determine the following counts.
Model | Direction | Part | Relation | Derived | Printed

For example, \(36+6+24=66\), and \(66/200=0.33\). Rounding cannot explain the discrepancy; the two baseline totals appear exchanged. Correcting them reverses those baselines’ overall order but leaves the proposed method’s 18.5-percentage-point advantage over the stronger baseline intact. The paired random baseline is not refuted. This is a numerical ranking correction, not evidence that the central orientation method fails.
# Training-target and evaluation questions

Equation (2), p. 5, uses the continuous von Mises density \[q_i=\frac{\exp[\kappa\cos(i-\phi)]}{2\pi I_0(\kappa)},
\qquad \kappa=\sigma_\phi^{-2},\] at 360 one-degree grid points. With the stated \(\sigma_\phi=20^\circ\), converted to \(\pi/9\) radians, and admissible \(\phi=120^\circ\), direct summation gives \(\sum_iq_i=57.2957795131\), not one. Equation (1)’s polar target, by contrast, explicitly uses a finite-grid normalizer. If these raw density values are supplied to soft-target cross entropy, then, writing \(C=\sum_iq_i\), \[-\sum_iq_i\log p_i=C\,H(q/C,p),\qquad
\nabla_{\rm logits}L=C(p-q/C).\] Literal use scales the circular-head terms by about 57.3 relative to the polar and confidence terms. Exact categorical targets use \(q_i^\star=\exp[\kappa\cos(i-\phi)]/
\sum_j\exp[\kappa\cos(j-\phi)]\).

The prose explicitly says that a continuous distribution is subsequently discretized. Bin integration or grid renormalization is therefore a plausible intended reading, and the missing training code prevents resolving the executed objective. A constant scale preserves an isolated head’s unrestricted optimum and argmax, even though shared optimization weights change. This is recorded as Needs Evidence for the actual training objective, not a demonstrated central training failure.

Other bounded questions remain. Training uses 55,000 selected Objaverse assets and testing uses 300 selected assets; absent identifiers prevent verifying object disjointness, but do not establish leakage. Table 4’s random roll accuracy at \(5^\circ\) is 16.67%, whereas full-circle uniform sampling gives \(10/360=2.78\%\). A restricted \(60^\circ\) roll range is a valid alternative; the sampling support is unspecified. Wrap conventions and Cube RCNN coordinate conversions also need the missing evaluation implementation. Visual inspection of p. 16 confirms the displayed axis differences; those pictures alone cannot identify their cause.

Table 7’s 45 oriented categories have mean displayed accuracies \(20.00,31.7778,45.8889,73.6667\%\), compared with Table 4’s \(20.25,31.95,45.78,72.44\%\). Equal per-category denominators would require agreement. Sample exclusions or another aggregation rule could explain the difference; per-example records are needed.

Finally, equal chance rates do not make eight-bin direction accuracy and continuous \(22.5^\circ\) accuracy identical. True/predicted angles \((-22^\circ,22^\circ)\) share a front bin but differ by \(44^\circ\); \((22.4^\circ,22.6^\circ)\) differ in bin but only by \(0.2^\circ\). Thus similar aggregate scores alone cannot establish preservation of continuous accuracy across domains. The separate real-image 3D results in Tables 2–3 remain relevant positive evidence.
# Overall impact and state

The established problems are confined to a released optional inference feature, a usage example, a language template and numerical reporting. No demonstrated dependency makes these a Major failure of the central real-image results. The annotation audit supplies positive, imperfect validation; pretrained real-image encoders and simplified spatial templates are disclosed, so neither is treated as a hidden violation.

Title: Technical Verification of Parallel Control Fine-Tuning
# Identity, version and scope

This report reviews Chi Zhang, Lianhai Ren, Jingpu Cheng and Qianxiao Li, From Weight-Based to State-Based Fine-Tuning: Further Memory Reduction on LoRA with Parallel Control, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 75453–75467 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; 0226/I25-43595, OpenReview `x4qvBVuzzu`. The original PDF’s author ordering is used here; publisher metadata lists the second author’s name as Ren Lianhai. The preserved 15-page publisher version was retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. References below use one-based PDF pages, matching printed numbering.

The main construction, both theorems, Appendix A proofs, experiment protocols and embedded Appendix B were inspected. Source review was static, using `czhang024/ParallelControl`, commit . All 121 archived members match preserved extracted bytes. Selected ViT, RoBERTa and LLaMA forward paths, configurations and existing logs were inspected. The possible separate OpenReview supplement was inaccessible (HTTP 403). No author code, training, datasets or checkpoints were executed or downloaded; measured memory, accuracy and timing were not independently reproduced. Historical source correspondence remains incomplete.

The proposed method places a trainable low-rank additive branch around a frozen residual component. LoRA is recovered on a linear edge. The paper’s theoretical support comprises a deep-linear representability bound and a local nonlinear comparison. These are distinct claims.
# A core nonlinear comparison fails under its stated hypothesis

Equation reference: eq:FG. Problem 1 (Major: Theorem 4.2 uses the activation Jacobian at \(x\) instead of \(Wx\)).  Equations (2)–(3), p. 3, define, for fixed state \(x\), \[
F_x(H)=x+f((W+H)x),\qquad G_x(H)=x+f(Wx)+Hx.\] Theorem 4.2, p. 6, asserts that singularity of \(J_f(x)\) makes the pushforward at \(H=0\) under \(F_x\) a proper subspace of \(\mathbb R^d\), whereas \(G_x\) reaches the whole space when \(x\ne0\). Appendix A.2, p. 12, Eq. (19), repeats \(J_f(x)Hx\) as the first-order term. The correct chain rule gives \(J_f(Wx)Hx\).
Here \(J_f\) denotes the Jacobian. The claim and displayed proof were checked directly in original PDF renders; the discrepancy is not an extraction artifact.
## Counterexample satisfying the printed assumptions

Let \(d=2\), \(x=(-1,-1)^\top\), \(W=-I_2\), and let \(f\) be coordinatewise ReLU, an activation expressly mentioned on p. 3. Then \(x\ne0\), \(J_f(x)=0\) is singular, but \(Wx=(1,1)^\top\) and \(J_f(Wx)=I_2\). Both points are strictly away from the ReLU kink. For sufficiently small \(H\), all coordinates of \((W+H)x\) stay positive, so \[F_x(H)=Hx,\qquad G_x(H)=Hx.\] For any \(v\in\mathbb R^2\), choose \[H_v=\frac{vx^\top}{\|x\|^2}=-\tfrac12v(1,1).\] This has rank at most one and satisfies \(H_vx=v\). The curve \(H=\varepsilon H_v\) remains in the permitted local region for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), and \(DF_x(0)[H_v]=v\). Thus the image is all of \(\mathbb R^2\), contradicting the asserted proper subspace.

Independent finite differences at \(\varepsilon=10^{-6}\) for \(v=e_1,e_2\) give the two coordinate directions with numerical error below \(3\times10^{-11}\); both perturbation matrices have rank one (`check.py`, `calc.json`). These numerical checks supplement the exact argument. If global smoothness is desired, a scalar counterexample is \(x=1\), \(W=2\), \(f(z)=(z-1)^2\). It has \(f'(x)=0\), but \(F_x(h)=2+2h+h^2\), hence \(DF_x(0)=2\), whose image is all of \(\mathbb R\).
## Corrected statement and proof

Equation reference: eq:repair. For \(x\ne0\), \(W\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\), and \(f:\mathbb R^d\to
\mathbb R^d\) differentiable at \(Wx\), \[
\operatorname{im}DF_x(0)=\operatorname{im}J_f(Wx),\qquad
\operatorname{im}DG_x(0)=\mathbb R^d.\] Indeed \(H\mapsto Hx\) is surjective, as the explicit \(H_v\) above shows. Composition with \(J_f(Wx)\) gives the first identity; the second follows directly from [eq:FG] (#eq:FG). Thus singularity of \(J_f(Wx)\), rather than \(J_f(x)\), is the sufficient condition for a proper subspace. A differentiability assumption gives a first-order remainder \(o(\|H\|)\); an \(O(\|H\|^2)\) remainder additionally requires suitable local smoothness. ReLU satisfies the stronger local expansion at the counterexample’s interior points.

The same reachable-direction conclusion holds on the rank-at-most-\(r\) cone for \(r\ge1\), because each \(H_v\) has rank one. The cone is not a manifold tangent space at zero. Nor does this statement automatically describe derivatives with respect to a particular initialized pair of LoRA factors \(A,B\); the theorem explicitly parametrizes by \(H=\Delta W\). These distinctions do not rescue the incorrect evaluation point.
## Dependency and counterevidence

Section 4.4 introduces these theorems to justify preserving expressive capacity while reducing memory and parameters. The paragraph following Theorem 4.2 explicitly uses its singularity condition to assert greater nonlinear adaptability. The counterexample defeats that theoretical comparison under the stated condition, so its impact is central even though the hypothesis can be repaired briefly. One could reinterpret \(f\) as a precomposed function or assume \(Wx=x\), but neither is the function definition or an assumption in Equations (2)–(3); such a reading changes the theorem.

The corrected statement [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) is proved here. It supports a conditional pointwise comparison, not a uniform dataset-level or training-performance guarantee. No measured accuracy or memory result is contradicted. The architecture, state-based viewpoint and deep-linear inclusion remain viable. Author adoption of this correction is unknown.
# Other checked claims and unresolved empirical attribution
## The deep-linear bound is valid
## What the memory explanation does and does not establish

For frozen linear layers, input adjoints need only the weights, so some saved wide states can indeed be eliminated when their LoRA branches are removed. This is valid counterevidence to a blanket objection to Figure 2, p. 5. For a nonlinear frozen block \(f(x)=W_2\sigma(W_1x)\), however, \[D f(x)^\top g=W_1^\top
\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(W_1x))W_2^\top g.\] Earlier trainable controls still require this input adjoint. The activation-derivative information must be retained or recomputed; frozen weights alone do not remove it. For example, the scalar residual \(a+\mathrm{GELU}(a)+\mathrm{GELU}(-a)\) has derivative \(2.1666309412\) at \(a=1\), rather than 1 if the frozen nonlinear branch is incorrectly omitted.

The inspected ViT implementation keeps the nonlinear branch on the graph: , lines 86–94 and 150–159, evaluates GELU, the added identity-initialized linear layers, and the residual plus control. No detached-branch error is alleged. Removing a postactivation needed only by LoRA can still save memory while a preactivation remains. Therefore the general interpretation that every wide nonlinear activation disappears is not established by the schematic. Per-operation allocation and recomputation traces are needed to attribute measured savings. This limitation does not falsify the reported memory reductions.
## Configurations and measurements

The FFN parameter counts \(10rd\) for two LoRA-adapted \(d\)-to-\(4d\) and \(4d\)-to-\(d\) layers, versus \(2rd\) for one parallel controller, are algebraically consistent. Table 4’s caption says rank 32 for all methods, but Appendix B.3 explicitly specifies rank 64 for Control and 32 for LoRA/DoRA. Its DoubleControl count agrees with the appendix: \[4(32)(4096)(64)=33{,}554{,}432.\] The hybrid counts likewise reproduce 41.94304M and 35.651584M. This is a caption clarification, not evidence of concealed parameter inflation. The equal-budget GLUE comparison also declares different ranks.

The toy ViT’s added frozen linear layers make the favorable memory setting explicit. GLUE checkpoint selection by validation performance is disclosed. The main text and Table 3 differ on whether the timed task is CoLA or RTE; the precise run configuration needs clarification. The consumer-GPU table specifies accumulation 2, whereas nearby prose describes one additional step. Existing DoubleControl logs reproduce the rounded Table 5 task scores; the LLaMA2 rank-64 log records 33,554,432 trainable parameters and 72,596.7289 seconds, consistent with its reported 20h09m runtime. These are source-log correspondence checks, not a fresh benchmark reproduction. No matched baseline memory trace or per-run provenance establishes every efficiency comparison in this review.
# Local release reproducibility defects

Problem 2 (Minor: the GLUE driver does not implement the reported regression and dual-MNLI protocol).  The preserved , lines 186–187, unconditionally reads categorical label names; line 287 sets `is_regression=False`; lines 384–386 use class argmax.

The accompanying download script requests standard `nyu-mll/glue`. Its STS-B labels are scalar floating-point similarity scores, not a `ClassLabel` with a `names` attribute [Retained latex: \cite{glue,features}]. Thus the ordinary STS-B input fails the categorical feature assumption. Even bypassing that access would leave classification decoding where the paper reports Pearson correlation of similarity predictions. For MNLI, lines 356–358 select only `validation_matched`; the inspected remaining evaluation path does not evaluate `validation_mismatched`, whereas Table 2 specifies both. A regression-specific model/decoding branch and explicit evaluation of both MNLI splits are needed. These are static defects in the preserved reproduction driver; no dataset was downloaded or author program run. Another historical implementation could have produced the reported numbers, and no preserved GLUE run logs settle that correspondence.

Problem 3 (Minor: the supplied nonquantized LLaMA path does not activate its requested checkpointing).  , lines 139–145, loads with `load_in_8bit=False`, then passes its checkpointing flag to at line 205.

The bundled helper , lines 45–68, calls only if both `loaded_in_8bit` and the flag are true. The first condition is false on the supplied path, so requesting the flag cannot activate that branch. The inspected Trainer arguments supply no independent checkpointing activation. This establishes a local flag-behavior mismatch, not a measured memory regression or a contradiction of nonquantized training. Moving checkpointing activation outside the quantization guard is a candidate repair; its gradient and memory behavior was not executed. Title: Technical Verification of Competitively Consistent Clustering
# Identity, reviewed version and model

This report concerns Niv Buchbinder, Roie Levin and Yue Yang, Competitively Consistent Clustering, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 5793–5810 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]; 0227/I25-43596, OpenReview `x2xZidAK4J`. The preserved publisher PDF has 18 pages, retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. One-based PDF pages agree with printed numbering. Main Sections 1–5 and embedded Appendices A–D were inspected, including the rounding proofs, LP conversion, lower-bound constructions and experimental plots. The cited positive-body-chasing theorem was inspected as stated here, not independently re-proved from its original publication.

The full finite metric and candidate facility set are given in advance. For \(k\)-center and \(k\)-median, footnote 4 on p. 3 specifies \(F=M\). Clients can depart without removing that location from the facility set. Recourse counts center-set edits, \(\sum_t|S^t\mathbin{\triangle}S^{t-1}|\), rather than reassignment of clients. The fractional rounding input counts only \(\sum_t\|x^t-x^{t-1}\|_1\); assignment changes in \(y\) are free. Appendix A uses fractional comparator LPs and the preliminaries define \(\mathrm{OPT}^t\) as a fractional clustering optimum. These conventions must be retained when interpreting the broader introductory language.

No author repository, executable experiment or numeric result files were acquired or located in the checked sources; that does not establish nonrelease. The possible separate OpenReview supplement was blocked by HTTP 403. All appended material is present in the original PDF. No author code, datasets or software were executed or installed.
# The recourse potential lacks a valid small-radius treatment

Equation reference: eq:potential, eq:claimed. Problem 1 (Major: the claimed amortized inequality is false for legal fractional service radii).  The facility-location algorithm on p. 6 assigns a newly selected client radius \(r_j=\gamma R_j\), where \(R_j=\sum_i d_{ij}y_{ij}\). With \(\alpha=11,\gamma=10/9,\delta=2\), Eq. (3.4), p. 7, has the form \[
\Phi=K\sum_{j\in A}\max\{0,1/10-x(B_j)\}
-\eta\sum_{j\in A}\log_2(\Delta/r_j),\] where \[\eta=\frac1{\log_2(69/20)},\qquad
K=110(1+\eta\log_2\Delta).\] Equation (3.5) asserts \[
\Delta N_1+\Delta N_2+\Delta\Phi
\le O(\log\Delta)\|x^t-x^{t-1}\|_1.\] The proof also asserts a lower bound \(\Phi\ge-C\log\Delta\sum_i x_i\). Both assertions fail under the printed assumptions.

The minimum positive distance between distinct points being one does not imply \(R_j\ge1\): \(R_j\) is a fractional weighted average that can include self-distance zero. The following construction keeps \(\Delta,\beta\), the number of points and all opening costs fixed.
## Admissible first insertion

Let \[M=F=\{a=0,b=1,c=2\},\qquad d(u,v)=|u-v|,\qquad f_a=f_b=f_c=1.\] This is a metric with minimum positive distance one and aspect ratio \(\Delta=2\). Set \(\beta=2\), start from the prescribed empty state, and insert the single client \(a\). For any \(0<s<0.1\), choose \[x_a=y_{aa}=1-s,\quad x_b=y_{ba}=s,\quad x_c=y_{ca}=0.\] Assignments sum to one, \(0\le y_{ia}\le x_i\), and the cost is \(1+s\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}^1\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}^1=1\). The fractional optimum is exactly one because coverage requires \(\sum_i x_i\ge1\), all opening costs are one, and opening at \(a\) attains one. Initial fractional movement is one.

Equation reference: eq:firstphi. The algorithm adds \(a\), whose service cost is \(s\), radius is \(r_a=\gamma s<1\), and ball is the singleton \(B_a=\{a\}\). Its mass \(1-s>1/10\) satisfies all mass invariants; separation is vacuous and the sole client is covered by the cheapest facility \(a\). The nonnegative term in [eq:potential] (#eq:potential) vanishes, so \[
\Phi^1=-\eta\log_2\frac{2}{\gamma s}.\] As \(s\downarrow0\), this tends to minus infinity while \(\Delta=2\) and \(\sum_i x_i=1\). Therefore no claimed universal terminal bound of that form holds.
## A legal deletion falsifies the one-step inequality

The same failure can be obtained without an empty second state. Insert \(c\) instead, and set \(x_b=1,\ y_{ba}=y_{bc}=1\). The cost is 3, within the \(\beta=2\) budget \(2\mathrm{OPT}^2=4\). Here \(\mathrm{OPT}^2=2\): opening at both endpoints attains 2, and dual client values \(1,1\) certify the lower bound since \(\sum_j\max\{1-d_{ij},0\}\le f_i=1\) for every facility. The old singleton ball is dropped. Whichever current client is selected next has radius \(\gamma\) and a ball containing \(b\) with mass one. Any cheapest facility chosen there covers the other client within distance \(2<11\), so exactly one replacement ball suffices. The resulting change is \[\Delta N_1+\Delta N_2+\Delta\Phi
=1+\eta\log_2(1/s),\qquad
\|x^2-x^1\|_1=2(1-s)<2.\] This also contradicts a universal bound [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed), independently of tie choices.
## Independent numerical check and proof dependency

For \(s=2^{-400}\), direct reviewer-authored arithmetic gives \(\eta=0.5597235175\), \(\Phi^1=-224.3640508\), whereas even the weaker explicit bound \(-110(1+\eta)\sum_i x_i\) is \(-171.5695869\). The deletion-step left side is 225.3640508, and the insertion-step left side is 224.8894070. The symbolic family \(s=2^{-m}\), rather than any single large value, establishes failure for every universal constant. Exact rational inputs and numerical outputs are retained in `check.py`/`calc.json`.

The faulty potential step is used to prove Theorem 3.4’s principal facility-location recourse guarantee. Theorem 3.7 explicitly inherits the \(k\)-median recourse bound from Theorem 3.4. The error therefore concerns the core competitive-recourse derivation, supporting Major under the specified calibration.
## Related boundaries, counterevidence and repair limits

The \(k\)-center potential (3.2), p. 5, has the same logarithm. For one client and \(k=1\), the allowed \(F=M\) gives \(\mathrm{OPT}=0\), so its created radius is zero and \(\log(\Delta/r)\) is undefined. Exact self-service also produces zero radii in the facility-location and \(k\)-median formulations. This is not fixed by separating distinct metric points.

At the other end, facility-location radii are not capped: \(r=\gamma R\) may exceed \(\Delta\). The p. 8 add-only argument \(-\eta\log_2(\Delta/r)\le0\) then also needs a separate justification. For example, on the same metric a singleton at \(a\) can be fractionally served entirely from \(c\) with opening cost 1 and service cost 2; with \(\beta=3\) this is feasible, and its new radius is \(2\gamma>2\).

These observations do not demonstrate excessive actual recourse. The deletion construction makes just one opening and one closing, total recourse 2, matching its total fractional movement 2. Nor does the review show that the particular positive-body-chasing implementation must produce this fractional path. Theorem 3.4 and its proof purport to round any fractional input satisfying the stated conditions, which the example does.

A bounded scale potential together with a separate singleton-ball argument may repair the proof. Merely replacing \(r\) inside the logarithm is not a verified repair: replacement-event credits and all boundary transitions must be re-established. No complete corrected amortization is claimed. The geometric coverage and approximation arguments may survive independently.
# Checks that survive and remaining scope

Appendix B’s covering–packing conversion is valid. For a fixed client, \[\min_{F'\subseteq F}\left(\sum_{i\in F'}y_{ij}
+\sum_{i\notin F'}x_i\right)=\sum_i\min\{y_{ij},x_i\}.\] Clipping \(y'_{ij}=\min\{y_{ij},x_i\}\) therefore preserves coverage, enforces \(y'\le x\), decreases nonnegative service cost and leaves \(x\)-recourse unchanged. Selecting \(F'=\{i:y_{ij}\le x_i\}\) gives the separation oracle. Finite subset enumeration independently checks illustrative cases; the coordinatewise identity proves the claim.

The geometric arguments in Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6 also check out. For \(k\)-center the exact constants \(\alpha=3+2\sqrt2,\delta=\sqrt2\) give \((2+2\delta)/(\alpha-\delta-1)=\delta\). For facility location the shrink factor is 3.45 and the separation comparison is \(12/6.9<2\). Disjoint balls of mass at least \(1/11\) give the stated \(11k'\) center count for \(k\)-median. These checks do not repair the potential argument.

The HST lower-bound displays on pp. 14–15 incorrectly bound \(\sum_{k=0}^{m}(4c)^k\) by its last term. The correct upper bound is \(\frac{4c}{4c-1}(4c)^m\le\frac43(4c)^m\) for \(c\ge1\). The subsequent separation still exceeds the required comparison by a factor at least \((4c-1)/(2c)\ge3/2\), so that local arithmetic can be repaired without losing the logarithmic order. Counting an opening plus a closing as one recourse instead of two likewise changes only a constant.

Two lower-bound scope questions remain: the facility-location construction uses repeated clients at one node despite the set notation \(C^t\subseteq M\), and the displayed \(k\)-median argument directly uses a 2-approximate offline comparator whereas the theorem is phrased for arbitrary input \(\beta\ge1\). A multiplicity convention or checked distinct-copy construction, and the missing parameter extension, are needed for a literal full-scope proof. These are Needs Evidence, not asserted counterexamples to the existence of the lower bounds. Selecting an adversarial path using a randomized algorithm’s marginal distribution does not by itself require observing its realized random seed.

Appendix D studies 100-step streams on Glass, Wine and Airfoil, with insertion/deletion probabilities \(0.9/0.1\), \(k=4,\beta=3/2,\epsilon=1/4\). The displayed low-recourse traces support those short streams; they do not prove constant recourse for arbitrary long streams. Lower online recourse than the fractional comparator is possible under resource augmentation. The original plots were visually inspected, but not digitized or independently reproduced. Facility costs, preprocessing, random seeds, repetitions, solver details and per-step numeric traces are not supplied in the acquired material. The blue \(\alpha\beta\mathrm{OPT}\) reference also needs parameter clarification: direct composition for facility location and \(k\)-median includes the fractional relaxation’s \(1+\epsilon\) factor.

Title: Scientific review of invariant LLM unlearning
# Identity, scope, and principal result

This report concerns Invariance Makes LLM Unlearning Resilient Even to Unanticipated Downstream Fine-Tuning, by Changsheng Wang, Yihua Zhang, Jinghan Jia, Parikshit Ram, Dennis Wei, Yuguang Yao, Soumyadeep Pal, Nathalie Baracaldo, and Sijia Liu, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 65464–65479 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assignment is 0228/I25-43597, OpenReview identifier `x2lm33kdrZ`. The reviewed object is the staged 16-page publisher PDF, retrieved on 25 October 2026. Page references below use its PDF pages, coinciding with its printed 1–16 numbering.

The complete main paper and appended material were read. Checks cover Eqs. (1)–(5), the task-vector analysis, the definitions of forget quality (FQ), robust accuracy (RA), and fine-tuning accuracy (FA), Tables 1–4/A1–A2, and the experimental qualifications. The preserved repository was inspected statically, including the registered training methods, objective, configuration, and evaluation dispatch. All 58 archived members had verified archive/checkout correspondence. No author code or model was executed; no empirical replication is claimed.

The central empirical comparison remains supported by the printed results within its tested scope. For example, Table 2 reports average RA of 0.65 for RMU+ILU and 0.42 for RMU. RA is explicitly a mean over three training milestones, not a worst-case guarantee. Figures 3/A2 separately give final-epoch FQ and Fig. 5 gives trajectories, so this definition alone does not invalidate the resilience evidence.
# Necessary distinctions

ILU adds a penalty to an unlearning objective: \[\ell_u(\theta)+\lambda\sum_i s_i(\theta)^2,\qquad
 s_i(\theta)=\left.\partial_w\ell_i(w\circ\theta)\right|_{w=1}.\] Here \(w\) is the paper’s virtual scalar predictor. The paper explicitly describes IRMv1 as a relaxation and its stationarity condition as necessary, not sufficient. A stationary scalar direction is distinct from stationarity in all model parameters, and either is distinct from preservation of forgetting under arbitrary future optimization.

In Section 5, let \[u=\theta_u-\theta_o,\quad f=\theta_{ft}-\theta_o,\quad
 d=\theta_{uft}-\theta_u.\] The vectors \(u\) and \(f\) start at the original model; \(d\) starts at the unlearned model. The final displacement from the original model is \(u+d\). Cosines require nonzero vectors. The paper’s sign argument assumes \(\cos(u,f)<0\), not that \(f\) is exactly a negative multiple of \(u\).
# Supported problems

Problem 1 (The two cosine-sign criteria are not opposites; Minor).  Section 5, p. 6, interprets \(\cos(d,u)\geq0\) as preserving the unlearning direction and, conversely, \(\cos(d,f)\geq0\) as misalignment with unlearning. The second implication does not follow from \(\cos(u,f)<0\).

Complete check. Choose \[u=(1,0),\qquad f=(-1/2,\sqrt3/2),\qquad
 d=u+f=(1/2,\sqrt3/2).\] All vectors have norm one and satisfy the stipulated \(\cos(u,f)=-1/2<0\). Nevertheless, \[\cos(d,u)=1/2,\qquad \cos(d,f)=1/2.\] Thus both alleged opposing diagnostics hold simultaneously. This is not an extraction artifact: the paper itself reports the same sign pattern for ILU, namely \(\cos(d,u)=0.09\) and \(\cos(d,f)=0.3554\), while \(\cos(u,f)=-0.64\). ◻

There is also a distinction between an update and the final displacement: \[u^\top(u+d)=\|u\|^2+\|u\|\|d\|\cos(d,u).\] A negative update cosine need not make the final displacement oppose \(u\). For example, \(d=-0.1u\) leaves \(u+d=0.9u\). With the reported NPO cosine \(-0.41\), a negative final projection would additionally require \(\|d\|/\|u\|>1/0.41\approx2.439\). This ratio is not supplied.

The correct local statement is that \(\cos(d,u)\geq0\) increases or preserves the projection of \(u+d\) onto \(u\). It does not establish a forgetting property of the resulting network. Positive alignment with \(f\) implies negative alignment with \(u\) only under stronger conditions, such as exact antiparallel reference vectors with strictly positive alignment. Those conditions are absent here.

The reported cosine triples are geometrically admissible: their Gram determinants are approximately 0.080604 (NPO) and 0.415049 (ILU). No fabricated measurement is inferred. The defect affects the explanatory sign diagnostic and its causal interpretation, rather than a theorem or optimization guarantee on which ILU’s objective depends. This is the reason for Minor calibration; unchanged empirical scores alone would not downgrade a defective core theorem. Evidence: p. 6, `s06.png`, and independent `check.py`/`calc.json`.

Problem 2 (Descriptions overstate uniform forgetting and utility preservation; Minor).  The p. 8 narrative says MUSE-News ILU retains zero VerbMem across all fine-tuning settings, whereas Table A1, p. 15, reports 0.46 after GSM8K and 2.07 after QQP. The p. 7 claim that FA improves relative to either baseline is also not uniform in its own comparisons.

Table 2 gives average FA 82.43 for RMU and 82.32 for RMU+ILU(GSM8K), a decrease of 0.11 percentage point. This small difference, without uncertainty estimates, does not establish a significant degradation. The larger MUSE trade-offs should nevertheless be explicit: before fine-tuning, retained-set KnowMem on MUSE-Books falls from 57.19 for NPO to 45.20 for ILU, a difference of \(-11.99\) points; it remains lower in all six post-fine-tuning settings. MUSE-News WinoGrande FA is 67.40 versus 59.00, a difference of \(-8.40\) points.

Counterevidence bounds this issue. Appendix B.3 already says zero in nearly all settings; the nonzero ILU VerbMem scores remain far below NPO’s 35.38 and 33.46. Other utility comparisons remain favorable or close, so general model collapse has not been established. The defensible description is improved measured robustness with dataset-dependent utility trade-offs and small residual memorization. Utility-matched experiments would be needed to separate robustness gains from capability loss in the affected MUSE comparisons. Evidence: Tables 2/A1 and `calc.json`; the exact tabulated values, not a rerun, support this conclusion.

Problem 3 (The convergence rule is inconsistent; Minor).  Section 6.1, p. 7, specifies less than 1% FA change over three consecutive epochs; Appendix A.2, p. 13, specifies two consecutive epochs and applies that criterion to all six tasks.

These are distinct stopping rules. For a run with two sufficiently small successive changes followed by a larger change, one rule can stop while the other continues. Since RA averages FQ at the first quartile, median, and final epoch, the stopping horizon can change all three checkpoints. This is a reproducibility defect in the stated protocol. The direction or size of any effect on the published RA values is not established. A single documented rule, actual per-run horizons, and checkpoint logs are required; choosing either printed rule without those records would not verify a repair. Evidence: `s07.png`, `s13.png`, and the bound page text.
# Scope clarifications and unresolved evidence
## Scalar stationarity

For the benign binary cross-entropy model \[\ell(w\theta)=\log(1+\exp(-w\theta)),\] at \(\theta=0,w=1\) one has \(\partial_w\ell=0\), hence zero regularization penalty, but \(\partial_\theta\ell=-1/2\). A gradient-descent step of size 0.1 moves \(\theta\) to 0.05. Thus a zero scalar penalty cannot certify full-parameter stationarity. This analytical example addresses an unrestricted interpretation of the mechanism, not the full ILU training objective or its measured performance. In light of the paper’s explicit relaxation language and absence of a universal theorem, stronger guarantees are Needs Evidence, not a manufactured failed theorem.
## Released implementation and historical binding

The preserved release [Retained latex: \cite{repo}] states that code is ongoing. The method registry and command-line entrypoint expose NPO and other baseline methods, but no ILU or RMU implementation. The NPO loss in , lines 114–129, consists of the forget loss plus the retain loss, without the invariance term. A repository-wide textual scan for the relevant invariance terms found hits only in the README; this negative search is corroborated by direct inspection of the registered objective path.

The WMDP configuration specifies NPO+FT, a mask, 500 steps, and WMDPALL for both datasets, whereas Appendix A.1 describes 2000 NPO steps, a biology forget set, and WikiText retain data. This establishes that this current configuration is not an adequate recipe for the paper’s described experiment. It does not establish what generated the historical results.

The actual evaluator calls the external `lm_eval` wrapper for WMDP and MMLU. A separate TOFU forget-quality script and a standalone WMDP scorer are not proof of a metric error in that route. The evaluation harness revision, ILU implementation, downstream stopping/RA code, MUSE results, and timing logs are not bound by the inspected release. These remain Needs Evidence. Source excerpts and member SHA256/Git-blob bindings are in `code.json`; archives and their existing maps are preserved.
## Numerical ambiguities and robustness limits

Table 4, p. 9, prints original-model GSM8K FA as 0.75 alongside other FA percentages. The stated mean 75.02 equals the mean using 0.75. If that cell were intended to be 75, the mean would be 87.40. Different runs are possible, so a label swap is not established.

Table 3 discloses remaining targeted-relearning vulnerability: ILU FQ falls from 0.56 to 0.50 for NPO and from 0.68 to 0.54 for RMU. The stronger SAM comparison and future-work qualification are acknowledged by the authors. Arbitrary-task, adaptive, longer-horizon, or permanent-erasure interpretations exceed the tested scope. report: Abstract: The paper demonstrates useful task elicitation by learned head masks. Two central evidentiary steps need substantive correction: delayed switching under reordered head removal does not establish interactions between contributions, and published translation examples corroborate an undisclosed character-and-space BLEU convention whose comparison can reverse under word tokenization. These are Major findings with bounded scope. Actual task elicitation and the corrected aggregate translation ranking are not refuted. Local metric, expectation, and table inconsistencies are also documented. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Date: Initial review, 25 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of selective attention head masking
# Identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Heads up! Large Language Models Can Perform Tasks Without Your Instruction via Selective Attention Head Masking, by Senyu Han, Hongchuan Zeng, Kai Yu, and Lu Chen, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 21948–21973 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment: 0229/I25-43598; OpenReview identifier `x2Dw9aNbvw`. The frozen object is the 26-page publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026. Locations below use PDF pages, corresponding to printed 1–26.

All main and appendix page texts were read. Checks cover masking, task evaluation, head removal, the pathway interpretation, scaling, and the appendix tables, examples, and overlap calculation. Original pages 3, 4, 6, 12, 14, 21, 22, 23, and 25 were visually inspected. All 19 preserved repository members were hash-verified; relevant training, masking, model-loss, and notebook paths were inspected statically. No author code, model, or dataset evaluation was executed.

The three contributions concern task elicitation without inference-time task instructions, interdependent functional pathways, and improved performance by suppressing other heads. The first can survive the problems below. Major judgments attach to the derivation supporting the second and the scoring evidence supporting the third; neither requires whole-paper failure.
# Problem 1: rank trajectories do not identify interactions

Problem 1 (The independence-to-acceleration premise is false; Major).  Section 4, p. 6, and Appendix C.3.1, p. 23, measure each removed head’s target-rank improvement along an initial trajectory, sort heads by these improvements, and repeat removal from the full model. The stated premise is that independent heads would make this influential ordering accelerate the switch to target-token dominance. The observed delay then supports the interdependent-pathway interpretation.
Fixed additive head contributions must be distinguished from an additionally assumed, context-independent effect on token rank. The latter does not follow from the former.

Complete counterexample. Order logits as target \(T\) and competitors \(A,B\). Let the full logits and fixed head-removal increments be \[z_\varnothing=(0,2,-1),\quad
 \delta_1=(0,-3/2,2),\quad
 \delta_2=(0,-1,-2),\quad
 \delta_3=(0,-1/10,1/10).\] For every removed-head set \(S\), set \[z_S=z_\varnothing+\sum_{i\in S}\delta_i.\] All contributions are nonzero. Equivalently, binary present-head masks give \(z(m)=b+\sum_i m_i a_i\), with \[b=(0,-3/5,-9/10),\quad
 a_1=(0,3/2,-2),\quad a_2=(0,1,2),\quad a_3=(0,1/10,-1/10).\] Every mixed discrete logit difference is identically zero: \[z_{S\cup\{i,j\}}-z_{S\cup\{i\}}-z_{S\cup\{j\}}+z_S=0
 \quad(i,j\notin S).\] Thus no head contribution depends on another head’s presence. The initial order \(1,2,3\) gives:
Removed heads | \(z_A\) | \(z_B\) | Target rank
Signed rank improvements, previous minus new rank, are \((-1,2,0)\). Descending order is \(2,3,1\), giving:
Removed heads | \(z_A\) | \(z_B\) | Target rank

The reordered trajectory has a better early rank, yet persistent top-1 starts at removal three instead of two. There are no target ties, zero contributions, or changed removal sets. This reproduces the qualitative combination reported by the paper without logit interactions. ◻

The source confirms the signed convention: zero-based cell 18 of , lines 4–5, negates successive rank differences and sorts descending. Absolute-change sorting would be a different protocol. Initial learned priorities can be any strictly ascending values for heads \(1,2,3\); the diagnostic supplies no condition excluding this case. Rational trajectory arithmetic and all six mixed-difference checks are in `calc.json`.

Rank effects depend on which competitors cross the target at the current point. An additive logit system can therefore have nonadditive rank effects. If independence instead meant invariant marginal rank gains, the experiment could reject that stronger rank-level assumption, without thereby identifying neural interactions.

Table 6 establishes group importance; Figs. 4–5 establish representational resemblance. Neither identifies interaction edges or excludes this null explanation. Co-movement during joint training also does not identify computational dependence. Actual LLM interactions are not disproved. The invalid inference directly supports the central pathway interpretation, warranting Major. A repair needs an operational interaction null and conditional interventions, such as mixed differences of specified logits across inputs. No repaired empirical mechanism is verified.
# Problem 2: translation scoring changes the evidentiary comparison

Problem 2 (Undisclosed character-and-space BLEU; Major).  Section 5, p. 8, uses improved IWSLT2017 BLEU to substantiate better translation performance, with Table 8 and Table 42 examples on p. 25. The release passes strings to BLEU. Five of six printed example scores agree with character-and-expanded-space calculations; one published comparison reverses under ordinary word tokenization.

In , zero-based cell 18 labels cell 19 as the Table 8 evaluation. Cell 19, lines 18–46, removes punctuation, joins `jieba` output into a string, and calls \[\texttt{sentence\_bleu([target\_str], t, smoothing\_function=smoothing)}.\] NLTK expects token lists and counts \(n\)-grams over the supplied sequences [Retained latex: \cite{nltk}]. Strings produce character \(n\)-grams, including spaces. This is a defined overlap measure but is not equivalent to conventional word-token BLEU. Appendix C.5 describes response cleanup without disclosing this scoring unit.
## Published-example verification
Reference: And I wonder what youd choose because Ive been asking my friends this question a lot lately and they all want to go back
Original: Ive been asking my friends this question a lot lately and they all say go back in time
Scaled mask: Ive been wondering how you would choose and lately Ive asked my friends this question a lot and they all say go back in time
The parent independently scored visually verified transcriptions with existing NLTK 3.9.1, using word lists and, separately, character strings with three spaces between words:
Example | Condition | Printed | Characters/spaces | Words

Five character scores match the printed precision. The sixth fails and is retained as a failed match. Example two changes from \(.616<.813\) to \(.527>.286\). All four word precisions are positive, so smoothing cannot explain that reversal. Full strings/settings/results are in `bleu.py`/`bleu.json`; auxiliary reviewers independently reproduced the second pair with their own \(n\)-gram arithmetic.

This construction corroborates the character-and-whitespace explanation, without claiming execution of the original preprocessing. The existing environment lacks `jieba`; it was not installed or run. The sixth mismatch and missing full generations prevent exact aggregate reconstruction.
## Counterevidence and bounded impact

The paper says BLEU, without explicitly saying word BLEU. Character overlap is not intrinsically invalid, and word BLEU is not semantic ground truth. Nevertheless, the undisclosed unit changes a published comparison and cannot be treated as the standard token comparison implied by the reported metric. Unlike the PPL issue below, this is not a monotone change of scale. It materially compromises the scoring evidence supporting the third contribution, warranting Major. It does not establish decreased average semantic translation quality.

The release additionally chooses the generated paragraph with the highest score against the gold reference. This exceeds reference-free cleanup and can interact with response style, although both branches use it. Cell 19 has a null execution count and no retained outputs. Matching single-paragraph examples do not prove that this oracle selection affected historical Table 8 runs. Its historical effect and the corrected aggregate Table 8 ranking remain Needs Evidence.

The positive controls are retained: scaling was selected on XNLI; IWSLT is an additional dataset; Appendix C.5 acknowledges explanation-style effects and attempts cleanup. A correction must declare tokenization and sentence versus corpus aggregation, use a prespecified reference-free extraction rule, and rescore original generations. No aggregate repair is verified.
# Local supported problems

Problem 3 (PPL values are averaged cross-entropies; Minor).  Tables 1/6/12–21 and Fig. 6 contain purported perplexities below one. The released evaluation averages per-example cross-entropy losses without exponentiation.

Notebook cell 12, lines 64/68 append `output.loss`; lines 69–70 apply `nanmean`. The bound Llama implementation, lines 1275–1297, uses shifted target-token cross-entropy with `-100` exclusion. Retained output 3 has the English instructed row \[1.091267,\ .618853,\ .550162,\ .627102,\ .954034,\ 1.303265,\] rounding to Tables 1/12. This binds the discrepancy to published numbers.

Ordinary perplexity is at least one: \(\exp(.504)=1.655329\) and \(\exp(.552)=1.736723\). Exponentiating this same aggregate preserves ordering, so the local label error does not refute loss improvements. Equal-example averaging differs from token-pooled corpus loss; the latter requires lengths/losses and need not preserve all rankings. Rename the quantity precisely or recompute the intended aggregation. Evidence: `code.json`, `calc.json`, original pages 4/14.

For nonempty sets, \(f''(k)=2(a+b)/(a+b-k)^3>0\). The printed value is therefore a Jensen lower bound, strictly so for nonconstant \(I\). At \(N=2,a=b=1\), the exact expectation is \(1/2\) versus the printed \(1/3\).

The parent evaluated all 154 size pairs in Tables 37–38 with the finite hypergeometric sum, numerically normalized. The maximum correction is \(0.000144775\); all observed similarities still exceed their corrected expectations, by at least \(0.0278059\). For the 12 main Table 5 pairs, corrections range from \(0.0000381\) to \(0.0000804\). The equality fails, but the qualitative above-chance result survives this checked correction. This is a verified formula repair, not a significance analysis. Evidence: `check.py`/`calc.json`, original pages 12/21.

Problem 5 (A duplicated transfer block conflicts with Table 1; Minor).  The final Table 12 block, labelled with a Llama-3.1-8B mask, repeats all 42 cells of the preceding native-mask block. Its English row is \[1.017,\ .552,\ .504,\ .580,\ 1.055,\ 1.322,\] whereas the corresponding main Table 1 transfer row is \[2.269,\ 1.114,\ 1.061,\ 1.612,\ 2.105,\ 2.381.\]

Visual inspection of pages 4/14 confirms the conflict. No fabrication, invalidity of native-mask results, or choice of the correct historical values is inferred. Correct off-English transfer results require their original records.
# Resolved concerns and remaining limits

For \(\tau>0\), Eq. (3)’s hard gate obeys \[{\bf1}\{\sigma((\mathcal M+G)/\tau)\geq1/2\}
 ={\bf1}\{\mathcal M+G\geq0\}.\] For \(G=\log(-\log U)\) its keep probability is \(\exp[-\exp(-\mathcal M)]\), independent of positive temperature. The ordinary derivative is zero almost everywhere. But , lines 40–45, implements `y_hard-y_soft.detach()+y_soft`. Temperature affects the straight-through surrogate gradient and future learned parameters. Actual training is not shown impossible; the custom noise need not be presumed to implement some different Bernoulli law.

Other potential concerns were resolved by actual source inspection. Training withholds the last 100 rows used for evaluation; scripts disable dataset caching; target-only losses mask prompts and padding; the optimizer receives the mask model, not the separate language model. No original-weight update or train/test leakage is demonstrated. Heads are multiplied before output projection, while extra FFN slots are held at multiplier one. Evaluation uses stated final checkpoints. Simple-task substring/prefix matching is explicit and should be interpreted on those terms.

Absence of instructions concerns inference-time task prompts; masks are learned using supervised targets. Some shell defaults differ from manuscript model/temperature settings, but historical choices are unknown. External masks, excluded payloads, complete original generations, and model replications were not acquired. The separate OpenReview supplement returned 403; the complete embedded appendix was inspected. There is no exhaustive later-revision/erratum audit, novelty claim, wall-clock speedup test, or whole-paper correctness certificate.
# Overall impact and state

The additive construction defeats the inference from delayed rank switching to interacting pathways. Published translation examples show non-equivalent scoring and an illustrated ranking reversal. Actual interactions, task elicitation, and the corrected aggregate translation improvement remain separate questions. No author correction or adoption was verified.

report: Abstract: Theorem 4.4’s stated conditions do not ensure its advertised optimal convergence. A finite MDP with a fixed stationary behavior policy satisfies every printed condition, yet the learned greedy policy remains suboptimal forever. This is a Major finding. The exact reachability iteration remains supportable. Additional local issues concern released importance-weight broadcasting, numerical interpretations, the Circle safety specification, and a reproduction command. Historical experiment effects and full repairs are distinguished from the demonstrated results. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Date: Initial review, 25 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of safety-polarized reinforcement learning
# Identity, scope, and necessary background

This report concerns Safety-Polarized and Prioritized Reinforcement Learning, by Ke Fan, Jinpeng Zhang, Xuefeng Zhang, Yunze Wu, Jingyu Cao, Yuan Zhou, and Jianzhu Ma, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 15862–15886 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assignment: 0230/I25-43599; OpenReview `x10ryC8F0C`. The reviewed version is the frozen 25-page publisher PDF, retrieved on 25 October 2026. Page references use PDF pages, matching printed 1–25.

All main and appended page texts were read. Checks cover the MaxSafe objective, Lemmas 3.1/4.2, Theorems 4.3/4.4 and their proofs, Algorithm 1, masking/polarization, prioritized replay, Tables 1–5, experimental interpretations, and appendix figures. Selected original pages were visually checked, including the full theorem conditions and relevant formulas/tables. All 139 preserved archive members and extracted counterparts were hash-verified. Relevant released training, replay, configuration, environment, and evaluation paths were inspected statically; no author code or empirical training was executed.

MaxSafe first minimizes the probability of ever reaching the unsafe set \(S_u\), then maximizes discounted reward among safest policies. The optimal state-action reachability function is denoted \(\psi^*\); the exact safety mask retains actions attaining the minimum risk. The sampled updates change only the currently visited coordinate \((s_t,a_t)\). This distinction from a simultaneous vector update is decisive.
# Problem 1: the sampled convergence theorem fails

Problem 1 (Global step-size conditions are insufficient; Major).  Theorem 4.4, pp. 4–5, asserts convergence of the sampled reachability and Q updates, and of the learned policy to a MaxSafe optimum. It assumes infinite visitation of every state-action pair, global conditions \[0<\beta_t\leq1,\qquad \sum_t\beta_t=\infty,\qquad
 \sum_t\beta_t^2<\infty,\] and a positive mask tolerance \(\kappa\) smaller than half the gap to unsafe actions. These conditions do not ensure sufficient cumulative learning at each updated coordinate.

Parameters and verification of every condition. Take two states \(x,y\) and two actions \(g,b\) at each. Both actions alternate the states deterministically: \(P(y\mid x,a)=P(x\mid y,a)=1\). Set \[S_u=\varnothing,\quad \rho(x)=1,\quad \gamma=1/2,\quad
 r(x,g)=1,\] and set all other rewards and all costs to zero. Use the fixed stationary behavior policy \(\pi_b(g\mid s)=\pi_b(b\mid s)=1/2\), with independent draws. Each of the four state-action pairs is visited infinitely often almost surely, in fact with limiting frequency \(1/4\).

For \(n\geq0\), set the deterministic global step sizes \[\beta_{2n}=2^{-(n+5)},\qquad \beta_{2n+1}=\frac1{n+2}.\] They lie in \((0,1]\), tend to zero, and satisfy both printed sum conditions: the odd subsequence has divergent harmonic sum, while the sum of squares is \(1/768+\pi^2/6-1<\infty\). But all visits to \(x\) occur at even times, and \[\sum_{n\geq0}\beta_{2n}=\frac1{16}.\] Initialize \(\psi_0\equiv0\), \(Q_0(x,b)=1/2\), and every other Q-value at zero. The theorem specifies zero initialization for \(\psi\), not for \(Q\).

All policies are safest with unsafe probability zero, so the stated availability of many safest policies holds. The empty unsafe set is allowed by \(S_u\subseteq S\). Every \(\psi_t\) remains zero and every learned mask is the entire action set. The gap condition (15) is satisfied vacuously because there are no excluded actions, for any \(\kappa>0\). Thus the update reduces exactly to the printed Q-learning update without a masking complication.

The interval \([0,2]\) is invariant for every Q-value, since rewards are in \([0,1]\) and each target is at most \(1+(1/2)2=2\). Therefore, on every sample path, \[Q_t(x,g)\leq2\sum_{n\geq0}\beta_{2n}=\frac18.\] For \(b\), all targets are nonnegative. The product over the times when \(b\) is actually updated is no smaller than the product over all even times, so \[Q_t(x,b)\geq\frac12\prod_{n\geq0}(1-\beta_{2n})
 \geq\frac12\left(1-\sum_{n\geq0}\beta_{2n}\right)
 =\frac{15}{32}.\] The last inequality follows first for finite products of numbers in \([0,1]\) and then by a limit. Consequently the learned greedy policy strictly prefers \(b\) forever.

That policy earns zero reward. A safest policy choosing \(g\) at \(x\) instead earns \[V^*(x)=1+\gamma^2+\gamma^4+\cdots=\frac43.\] The true optimal action values are \(Q^*(x,g)=4/3\), \(Q^*(x,b)=1/3\), and \(Q^*(y,\cdot)=2/3\). Hence both claimed value convergence and claimed policy optimality fail. ◻

This counterexample uses a stationary behavior policy, deterministic step sizes, bounded initialization, and the exact safety mask. It does not depend on nonstationary exploration, rare state visitation, approximation error, or terminal-state interpretation. The step sequence is not nonincreasing, but monotonicity is not a printed assumption; even the stated diminishing-to-zero property holds.

Appendix B.4, pp. 14–16, applies a synchronous vector stochastic-approximation lemma to a coordinate update, then invokes classical Q-learning convergence. The missing local learning condition invalidates that inference. A necessary repair is, for each \((s,a)\), \[\sum_{t:(s_t,a_t)=(s,a)}\beta_t=\infty,
 \qquad
 \sum_{t:(s_t,a_t)=(s,a)}\beta_t^2<\infty.\] An appropriate per-visit schedule would exclude this counterexample. A full repair also requires a valid asynchronous argument identifying the reachability limit; that complete theorem is not certified here.

The parent independently evaluated the bounds and ran a reviewer-owned 2000-step illustration with seed 230. It produced \(Q(x,g)=0.0561212\) and \(Q(x,b)=0.4971123\), with all four coordinates visited 477–523 times. This finite computation illustrates the exact proof; it does not replace the infinite-time argument or reproduce author experiments. Evidence: `check.py`/`calc.json`, original pages 4–5/14–16 and their selected renders. The invalid guarantee is a central advertised contribution, supporting Major regardless of the potential simplicity of a repair.
# Local supported problems

Problem 2 (Classic-control PER loses individual importance weights; Minor).  Section 5.2, Eq. (20)–(21), and Algorithm 1 prescribe transition-specific importance weights. The preserved classic-control SP2/SP3 implementations broadcast those weights across the batch instead.

In , lines 61 and 70–73, weights have shape \((B)\). In , lines 146–150 and 177–187, actions/costs/terminal flags are columns of shape \((B,1)\) and weights retain shape \((B)\). Consequently gathered safety residuals have shape \((B,1)\) in , lines 197–216, and , lines 199–218. Their multiplication broadcasts to \((B,B)\) under the documented semantics [Retained latex: \cite{torch}]: \[L_{\rm actual}=\frac1{B^2}\sum_{i,j}e_i^2w_j
 =\left(\frac1B\sum_i e_i^2\right)\left(\frac1B\sum_jw_j\right),
 \qquad
 L_{\rm intended}=\frac1B\sum_iw_i e_i^2.\] For admissible safety residuals \(e=(1/4,3/4)\) and weights \(w=(1,1/2)\), these are respectively \(15/64\) and \(11/64\). The residual gradients are \((3/16,9/16)\) instead of \((1/4,3/8)\). For example, current safety values \((.30,.80)\) and targets \((.05,.05)\) realize those residuals within \([0,1]\). With exponent \(\theta=.4\), sampling probabilities in ratio \(2^{2.5}\) yield the stated normalized weight ratio; priorities need not equal the current residuals after network updates.

The error removes sample-specific correction while retaining prioritized sampling and a common batch multiplier. The optional SP3 weighted Q loss has the same shape problem. Reshaping weights to \((B,1)\), or squeezing residuals to \((B)\), restores the intended local algebra.

Counterevidence limits the scope: , lines 184/189/191, squeezes highway residuals to \((B)\) and applies weights correctly. Published ACC/Circle runs are not bound to this exact code/configuration. No benchmark impact or historical repair is established. The calculation used reviewer-owned scalar arithmetic; PyTorch was absent in the checked execution runtimes, so no tensor-library execution is claimed. Evidence: hash-bound source excerpts in `code.json`, `calc.json`, and the primary broadcasting documentation.

Problem 3 (Reported dominance and numerical summaries exceed the tables; Minor).  Section 6.2, p. 8, and Appendix C.3.1, p. 20, give overall SWU scores .90/.79 for SPOM_PER/SPOM. Tables 1/4 instead give .98/.74 and .95/.73. The p. 8 prose also interchanges the TwoWay and Merge winners, and p. 20 claims both methods beat SafeQ in both reward and crash rate across all tasks.

Averaging the six displayed Table 1 cells gives .975 and .738333, consistent with its rounded overall scores. Table 1 favors SPOM_PER in TwoWay (.98 versus .88), but SPOM in Merge (.95 versus .94). Table 5 directly contradicts blanket metric-wise dominance: TwoWay rewards are 10.124 and 10.520 versus SafeQ’s 10.636, while Roundabout crash rate for SPOM is .167 versus SafeQ’s .090.

These are local interpretation/reporting errors, not evidence of fabrication or failure of the overall SWU ranking. The tables retain first and second overall places for the proposed methods. Importantly, the Table 1 versus Table 4 Roundabout change is not itself a contradiction: SWU uses the smallest crash rate among included comparators. Adding RESPO changes that reference from approximately .055 to .047, rescaling the scores by about .855. Evidence: `calc.json`, original pages 7–8/20–21 and their renders.

Problem 4 (Circle’s displayed unsafe set reverses the cost classification; Minor).  Appendix C.1, p. 18, says the robot must stay inside \(|x|\leq x_{\max}\), but defines \(S_u=\{s:|x|\leq x_{\max}\}\) and gives the ordinary motion reward only outside \(S_u\).

At \(x=0\), \(x_{\max}=2.5\), the printed formula labels an interior state unsafe; at \(x=3\) it labels an exterior state safe. This reverses the essential safety-cost classification and terminal/reward interpretation if the displayed MDP is implemented literally.

The released , lines 65–70, uses \(|x|>x_{\max}\) for crash/cost, consistent with the prose. Thus the corrected set is \(S_u=\{s:|x|>x_{\max}\}\) for that environment, including the safe boundary. The source is counterevidence against an inversion in the actual experiments. The local specification is wrong; the historical experiments are not thereby invalidated. The current configuration’s crash reward is separately \(-10\), whereas the paper prints \(-1\); historical settings remain unresolved.

Problem 5 (The advertised Circle command selects a different method; Minor).  The README says that bare `python main_classic_control.py` launches SPOM_PER on Circle. Its actual default selects `priorrewsdqn`.

The entrypoint reads , whose line 6 sets that algorithm, and dispatches to `PriorRewsDQN` in lines 137–138. The executed entrypoint has no command-line override parser. This is a distinct reward-shaping baseline, not the advertised SPOM_PER path. The separately documented Merge command explicitly chooses `sp_perdqn` and is consistent. Correct the classic-control instruction/configuration mapping and bind the intended settings; no author execution or complete launch repair was performed. Evidence: `code.json` and the preserved README/entrypoint/default configuration.
# Valid results, clarifications, and unresolved claims
## Exact reachability iteration

The deterministic finite-state update in Theorem 4.3 remains supportable under pointwise minimum reachability. Starting at zero, its iterates are nondecreasing finite-horizon minimum hitting probabilities, bounded by one. Their limit is a fixed point because finite minima and expectations are continuous. A stationary policy greedy for the limiting state risk has each finite-horizon hitting probability bounded by that limit, hence also its eventual hitting probability. Conversely the iterative lower bound is no larger than any policy’s eventual risk. These two inequalities identify the limit with minimum reachability, including a forced initial action.

Lemma 4.2’s probability recursion and the restricted discounted Bellman contraction in Lemma 3.1 are sound. With pointwise minimum reachability, policies restricted to minimizing actions preserve minimum risk. Given actual convergence of \(\psi_t\), the finite safety-gap argument eventually identifies the correct mask. These valid steps do not supply the missing sampled convergence.

Appendix B.3’s literal undiscounted cost conversion requires a terminal convention. It sets reward \(-1\) at absorbing unsafe states and writes an infinite sum, which gives \(Q_N(u,a)=-N\) at an absorbing unsafe state, instead of minus a hitting probability. But p. 3 explicitly terminates episodes on entry. A one-time charge with zero terminal continuation repairs that representation. This is a clarified boundary convention, not a claim that Theorem 4.3 is false. Also, an arbitrary policy optimal only from \(\rho\) need not be optimal at unreachable states; the pointwise statements should choose a uniformly optimal policy or define \(\psi^*\) pointwise.
## Practical algorithms and metric scope

Algorithm 1 and Section 5.3 disclose discounted safety targets; Eq. (17) also discloses finite soft polarization. These are useful heuristics whose objective differs from exact lexicographic MaxSafe. For \(\gamma=.99\), risk .5 at time 1 gives discounted value .495, while certain failure at time 100 gives \(.99^{100}=.3660323\). The latter is lower despite larger actual risk. With exact risks zero and .01 and Q-values zero and one, \(10\log(1-\psi)\) gives the riskier action score \(.899497>0\). Thus neither change automatically inherits the undiscounted hard-mask guarantee. These are analytical limits of disclosed choices, not reproduced failures of the experimental curves.

The six-seed results, confidence intervals, baseline adaptations, and ablations are positive evidence within the reported tasks. They do not independently certify a global safety optimum. Figure 9 additionally compares PPOBarrier, without a full numeric SWU row in Table 4. The exact optimum and fully bound comparison/aggregation protocol remain Needs Evidence.

Recomputing SWU directly from Table 5 means also leaves an unresolved discrepancy. Circle SPOM_PER has the lowest printed crash rate, so the corresponding mean-based reward ratio is \(279.432/270.404=1.03339\), rather than .96. Rounding of the reward means changes this only to approximately \([1.033383,1.033391]\). But averaging nonlinear per-seed scores need not equal scoring the aggregated means. No SWU script or raw run records were located in the preserved snapshot, so no corrected aggregate result or definite cause is asserted.

Other current configurations differ from the paper’s unified settings: classic-control SP3 uses reciprocal rather than \(10\log\) polarization and a different Q learning rate; ACC’s released reward includes a factor .1. These establish reproduction limits, not historical settings. Training versus optional held-out logging, termination versus time-limit truncation, and the highway safety-target/priority route were inspected. The paper labels its curves as training statistics; no evaluation leakage is inferred from a logger prefix.
# Dependence, corrections, and state

Theorem 4.4 fails under its printed assumptions. Its failure is independent of the implementation and reporting issues, and the empirical average SWU advantage may survive. The exact reachability proof can be expressed with a correct terminal convention. The PER reshape fixes a local expression; its effect on learning requires bound runs. Historical configurations, aggregation records, and author adoption are unknown. No exhaustive later-revision/erratum audit or first-discovery claim is made.

Title: Technical Verification of
Sparse Autoencoders, Again?
# Identity, version, and checked scope

This report concerns Yin Lu, Xuening Zhu, Tong He, and David Wipf, Sparse Autoencoders, Again?, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 40952–40976 (OpenReview identifier `wxU2LuTE74`; local identifier 0231/I25-43600). The reviewed object is the 25-page publisher PDF preserved in the supplied source manifest, retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. Page references below refer to the PDF’s printed pages, which equal its one-based PDF page indices. The frozen PDF’s SHA-256 is recorded in Appendix 5 (#sec:prov). The released VAEase repository was inspected at commit `acdcf2bfb9bcd50f64139c9aca9cc75c357da99d`; this is not established to be the code that generated the published tables.

The review focused on the model objective (Sections 2–3), the theoretical comparison in Section 4, the reconstruction/active-dimension evaluations in Section 5, and the proof of Theorem 4.7 in Appendix E.3. A core local-minima claim is false, as the exact counterexample below demonstrates. A separate released-code defect affects the active-dimension threshold calculation when a code contains zeros. Empirical training was not reproduced. Theorem 4.5, the other appendix proofs, and the complete repository are not certified by this report. Embedded appendices are available; the preparation manifest records HTTP 403 access failures for a possible separate OpenReview attachment. No inference of nonexistence is made.
# Model and assumptions

The VAEase encoder is Gaussian with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma>0\), and its latent sample is gated by \(1-\sigma\) before decoding. Theorem 4.7 permits \(d=\kappa\), a fixed orthonormal matrix \(U\), the decoder \(U\operatorname{diag}(w)\widetilde z\), arbitrary encoder functions, and an arbitrary single data point. It claims uniqueness of the minimum, local or global, apart from the sign symmetry identified in its footnote. There is no stated exclusion of \(\sigma=1\) or \(\mu=0\). We take \(\gamma\) fixed, as in the displayed optimization in Appendix E.3. On a one-point input, constant encoders realize every scalar parameter choice below and are Lipschitz even if that condition is additionally imposed.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The fixed-variance argument discards a suboptimal dormant local minimum).  The uniqueness claim on p. 6 is contradicted by an admissible local minimum of the full three-variable scalar objective. The omitted branch is removed by the division by \(1-\sigma\) on p. 22 of Appendix E.3.
## Complete check

Equation reference: eq:f, eq:local. Set \(d=\kappa=1\), \(U=[1]\), \(x=2\), and \(\gamma=1\). The decoder is exactly the theorem’s linear decoder and its coefficient \(w\) is unconstrained. Subtracting the irrelevant normalizing constant \(\tfrac12\log(2\pi)\) from the loss on p. 21 yields \[
F(w,\mu,\sigma)=\frac12\left[
 (2-w(1-\sigma)\mu)^2+w^2\sigma^2(1-\sigma)^2
 +\sigma^2-2\log\sigma+\mu^2-1\right].\] At \((w,\mu,\sigma)=(0,0,1)\), \(F=2\). This is a local minimum in all its variables, not only on a selected slice. For \(\sigma>0\), \(\log\sigma\leq \sigma-1\) implies \[\sigma^2-1-2\log\sigma\geq(\sigma-1)^2.\] Writing \(t=1-\sigma\) and dropping only the nonnegative term \(w^2t^2(\mu^2+\sigma^2)\) gives \[\begin{aligned}
2(F-2)&\geq \mu^2+t^2-4|w|\,|\mu|\,|t|\\
&\geq(1-2|w|)(\mu^2+t^2)\geq0
       \qquad (|w|<1/2).\end{aligned}\] The region \(|w|<1/2,\sigma>0\) contains a neighborhood of the specified point, so this proves local minimality. Flatness along part of the dormant branch does not disqualify it as a local minimum.

Now use the equally admissible point \[w=2\sqrt3,\qquad \mu=\sqrt3/2,\qquad \sigma=1/2.\] Its reconstruction bias squared is \(1/4\) and its reconstruction variance is \(3/4\). The remaining contribution inside the brackets in [eq:f] (#eq:f) is \(\log4\), so \[F(2\sqrt3,\sqrt3/2,1/2)=\frac{1+\log4}{2}
 \simeq1.19314718056<2.\] The dormant local minimum is therefore suboptimal. The independent standard-library calculation `c.py`, with results in `calc.json`, reproduces these values. Its 10,000 finite neighborhood evaluations are only a diagnostic; the proof is inequality [eq:local] (#eq:local).
## Suspect step and counterevidence

The first stationary-point elimination on p. 22 writes \(w=\mu x/[(1-\sigma)(\sigma^2+\mu^2)]\) and the next elimination also cancels \(\mu\). Neither operation covers the dormant branch. Direct visual inspection of p. 22 confirms that this is in the typeset source rather than an extraction artifact. The paper’s active stationary point remains a valid lower-loss point in this example. Its footnote allows multiple sign-equivalent global minima, whereas the new point has a strictly larger loss. Optimizing out \(w\) changes local geometry: leaving the dormant neighborhood can require a large change in \(w\). No strict-minimum qualifier is present.

There is a separate ambiguity about \(\gamma\). Section 2.2 permits learning it, whereas Appendix E.3 differentiates only with respect to \(w,\mu,\sigma\). The counterexample above addresses precisely that fixed-\(\gamma\) argument. If \(\gamma\) is jointly optimized, the same dormant point has \(\partial L/\partial\gamma=-3/2\) and is not a local minimum. It must not be used to claim joint-optimization spurious minima.

Joint optimization also has a non-sign continuum of global minimizers, a different failure of literal uniqueness. For \(x\ne0\), write \(a=w(1-\sigma)\) and \(r=\mu^2+\sigma^2\). Minimizing the reconstruction error over \(a\) gives \(R=x^2\sigma^2/r\), and minimizing over \(\gamma>0\) sets \(\gamma=R\). The resulting lower bound is \[L\geq \tfrac12\{\log(2\pi x^2)-\log r+r\}
 \geq \tfrac12\{\log(2\pi x^2)+1\}.\] For each \(s\in(0,1)\), equality is attained by \(\sigma^2=s\), \(\mu^2=1-s\), \(\gamma=x^2s\) and \(w=x\mu/(1-\sqrt{s})\). Thus the joint reading does not restore literal uniqueness, but this continuum is global, not suboptimal.
## Dependency, severity, and correction

The invalid fixed-variance derivation is Major: Section 4.3 and p. 7 explicitly use Theorem 4.7 as the unique-minimum half of their exponential SAE/VAEase local-minima comparison. The claimed elimination of suboptimal minima in that setting fails. The VAEase architecture, empirical comparisons, and the separate manifold-recovery claim are not refuted by this example. No replacement uniqueness theorem or full correction is established here.
Problem 2 (Released threshold calculation becomes nonfinite at zero codes).  The inspected release does not implement a finite minimum-variance partition for inputs containing a zero activation.

Section 5.1 (p. 7) describes partitioning active and inactive dimensions by minimizing within-group variance. In the pinned release, `activation_sae.py`, lines 121–124, and the corresponding block in `activation_sae_log.py` pass \(\log |z_j|\) into `utils.py:find_optimal_threshold_torch`, lines 211–245. The utility initializes the threshold to the sorted minimum and constructs variances using cumulative sums and squared sums.

For example, let \(|z|=(0,0.01,1,2)\). The logarithmic input includes \(-\infty\). Every candidate lower partition contains it, so its variance includes \(\infty-\infty\); the upper calculation also subtracts nonfinite cumulative sums. These comparisons with the initial best variance cannot succeed. The threshold remains \(-\infty\) and the final strict comparison counts all three positive entries. The result is a positivity count, with no successful variance minimization. This follows from the displayed source and floating-point arithmetic, not from running author code.

Zero activations are admissible with ReLU encoders. A strictly positive input would avoid this particular failure, and an undocumented preprocessing floor could also alter the behavior, but none appears at these call sites. The defect is Minor at release scope: its dependency on the published Table 3 values is unestablished. No numerical change to a published result is claimed. A choice of zero-handling policy would need to be specified and checked before a corrected empirical comparison could be assessed.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The decisive outcome is an established counterexample to a central optimization guarantee, independent of experiments or assumptions about which code produced the tables. The threshold defect is separately bounded to the reviewed release. No later erratum search was performed; the source record supplies no correction resolving these findings. Re-estimating active dimensions or benchmark differences would require the original evaluation data, exact experimental provenance, and new authorized runs. They are outside this review.
