Title: Technical Verification of
Relational Conformal Prediction for Correlated Time Series
# Identity and scope

The paper is by Andrea Cini, Alexander Jenkins, Danilo Mandic, Cesare Alippi, and Filippo Maria Bianchi, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 (OpenReview `wwYDQ1vXcZ`; 0232/I25-43601). We reviewed the staged 17-page publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC, including the main method and experiments (pp. 1–9), Proposition 3.1 and Appendix A (p. 14), and selected implementation/metric details in Appendices C–E (pp. 14–16). Printed page numbers equal one-based PDF page indices. Released code was inspected at commit `4504c4edf76128bfe657762a41ec9eb043038ca2` of `andreacini/corel`. The code’s correspondence to historical experimental runs is not established.
# Checked reasoning

Fix a target series, forecast time, conditioning history, and fitted model. Write \(P\) for the true conditional target law and \(Q\) for the law whose quantiles define the predicted interval \(C\). By the definition of total variation, \[P(C)\geq Q(C)-\operatorname{TV}(P,Q).\] For quantile endpoints of \(Q\) at levels \(a\) and \(a+1-\alpha\), with both levels in \([0,1]\), the closed interval satisfies \(Q(C)\geq1-\alpha\). Consequently, \[P(C)\geq1-\alpha-\operatorname{TV}(P,Q),\] which is Proposition 3.1. For continuous distributions the probability identity used in Appendix A, Eq. (22), holds in the usual regular case; with atoms it can be an inequality in the favorable direction. That distinction does not invalidate the final lower bound. A width-minimizing choice among valid shifted quantile pairs in Eqs. (15)–(16) preserves this argument for each fixed conditioning history.

The premise is a coherent learned distribution and its approximation error, not exchangeability of arbitrary time series. The paper explicitly states approximate coverage on p. 5, acknowledges arbitrarily large coverage gaps under shifts on p. 6, and describes local-embedding adaptation as an empirical mitigation. Thus this theorem is not an unconditional finite-sample coverage guarantee. No failure of such a stronger claim is attributed to the authors.

For the independent Gaussian innovations in the GPVAR example (Section 5.2, p. 8), \(\sigma=0.4\) and \(\alpha=0.1\) give the central noise-only width \[2\sigma\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)=1.31588290156.\] This independently calculated value is consistent with Table 2’s widths near 1.32 when the point predictor captures the conditional mean. It does not reproduce the fitted model or prove that any particular predictor attains the theoretical conditional distribution.
# Implementation correspondence and limits

The inspected code uses 39 quantile levels from 0.025 to 0.975, pinball loss, and the stated lower/upper interval endpoints. Selected parsing routines remove overlapping calibration/test indices, and the inspected metric definitions correspond to coverage difference, interval width, and Winkler score. No leakage or metric-sign defect was demonstrated in these inspected paths.

The decoder in `lib/nn/decoder/multiquantile_readout.py`, lines 44–61, has unconstrained linear quantile outputs and no monotonicity enforcement in that module. The parent directly inspected this source. The conditional theorem presumes a distribution associated with the estimated quantile function. Arbitrary crossed outputs would not satisfy that premise. No fitted outputs were available to establish that crossing occurred in the reported experiments, so this remains an applicability question, not a demonstrated error in the total-variation inequality. Likewise, the adaptive experiment’s actual chronological execution was not reproduced. No claim is made about complete repository correctness, all hyperparameter choices, or later revisions.
# Conclusion

The outcome is a scope clarification with No Issue Found in the checked probability argument and selected method/source correspondence. The unverified behavior of fitted quantiles and adaptation remains Needs Evidence; it does not raise supported severity. No correction is proposed because no substantive defect has been established.

Title: Technical Verification of
Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models
# Identity and scope

Song Bian, Minghao Yan, and Shivaram Venkataraman, Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 (OpenReview `wslytZ28Ms`; 0233/I25-43602). The reviewed source is the staged 21-page publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. Printed pages equal one-based PDF indices. The main formulation, fitting/evaluation description, Tables 1–4, Figure 8, and selected appendices and source paths were checked. The reviewed `open-lm-morph` snapshot is commit `1872be3750a16c7d5827874d8ab60cde10927358`; the accompanying `dclm-morph` archive is pinned to `07d247239e9cacda75375961171034aebd72e2eb`. Neither snapshot is assumed to identify every historical experimental run.
# Formulation and numerical checks

Equation (4), p. 5, fits \[L(N,D,R)=(E+AN^{-a}+BD^{-a})(1+\varepsilon R^a),
\qquad R=d_{\rm model}/n_{\rm layers},\] after the exponent tying described in Section 3.2. The inspected source implements this expression; its local variable named `gamma` denotes the multiplicative coefficient \(\varepsilon\), not a distinct exponent. Latency is separately profiled for candidate architectures, and downstream scores are measured after candidate training. The procedure therefore does not claim that training loss uniquely determines downstream accuracy or that this fitted expression is a hardware-independent latency theorem.

The parent checked Table 2 (p. 7), including its typeset rendering: \(3.61/1.96=1.8418367\), supporting the rounded \(1.8\times\) speed ratio between Morph-1B-v1 and Morph-1B in the specified timing setting. Both listed mean downstream accuracies are 0.52. This arithmetic confirms the table’s internal comparison, not equality of taskwise performance or statistical equivalence. An auxiliary independently reimplemented the fitted equations using literal data extracted statically from the released fitting scripts, without executing those scripts. The main fit contains 27 observations; the pooled evaluation contains 76, including those 27 fitting points. Figure 8 explicitly distinguishes fitting dots from test crosses. The independent pooled results reproduce its rounded metrics: Chinchilla MSE \(0.0032962\) and \(R^2=0.9895123\), versus shape-law MSE \(0.00055356\) and \(R^2=0.9982387\). Removing the 27 fitting observations leaves 49 held-out observations:
Model | Held-out MSE | Held-out \(R^2\)

Thus the approximately \(6.36\)-fold MSE improvement survives that separation. The four larger-model points yield maximum relative prediction errors of about 1.146% and 4.096%, respectively, consistent with the stated main comparison. These are calculations from released numeric records, not fresh language-model training or proof that those records match the original run logs.
# Scope clarifications

The no-overtraining ablation deserves a precise interpretation. If \(D=cN\) exactly and the exponents are tied, then \[AN^{-a}+B(cN)^{-a}=(A+Bc^{-a})N^{-a}.\] Only the combined coefficient is identifiable on that design: \((A,B)\) and \((A+\delta,B-\delta c^a)\) give the same values. The parent verified this identity analytically and with a small independent finite calculation. Actual released counts vary within nominal size groups, so exact degeneracy is not asserted for that concrete dataset; the calculation explains the nearby confounding. The main fit includes longer training runs, and the paper explicitly reports deterioration when they are removed. This observation therefore does not refute the main fitted comparison.

Selected source checks also revealed that nominal size labels are approximate and that profiling scripts and their defaults cover different timing tasks. Consequently, current default commands cannot be equated automatically with every historical plot. No measured timing bias was established from the inspected source.
# Conclusion and outstanding work

The outcome is No Issue Found in the declared formulation, released-record calculations, and selected static-source checks. The empirical claims remain bounded to their reported hardware, data, model scales, and evaluation procedure. No correction is proposed.

Title: Technical Verification of
Mixed-Curvature Decision Trees and Random Forests
# Identity and checked scope

Philippe Chlenski, Quentin Chu, Raiyan R. Khan, Kaizhu Du, Antonio Khalil Moretti, and Itsik Pe’er, Mixed-Curvature Decision Trees and Random Forests, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 (OpenReview `wptlUkP48t`; 0234/I25-43603). The reviewed publisher PDF has 30 pages and was retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. References use printed pages, equal to one-based PDF indices. We inspected the central definitions, Algorithm 1, midpoint rules, stated geometric desiderata, selected appendices and benchmark descriptions, and relevant released midpoint/split code.

Two `manify` versions are distinguished: the supplied HEAD snapshot `` and the supplied `notebook_archive` snapshot ``. Neither is asserted to prove the provenance of every published experiment. The original files and member/version maps were preserved unchanged.
# Claims and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:boundary. Page 2 states five desiderata, including equal distance from the split to the nearest points on either side, and claims the proposed construction guarantees them across the considered manifolds. The midpoint discussion on p. 5 explicitly refers to geodesic equidistance. For a selected coordinate pair \((x_0,x_d)\), the paper uses the angle \(\theta_x=\operatorname{atan2}(x_0,x_d)\) and the homogeneous boundary \[
x_0\cos\theta-x_d\sin\theta=0.\] Algorithm 1 uses the manifold-specific midpoint rules to generate candidate splits. The examples below have two samples, so the points considered are also the nearest samples on their respective sides. Their projections are nonzero, and no antipodal or wraparound convention is needed.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Spherical angular averaging loses original-space equidistance).  Equation (22), p. 6, and Table 5 prescribe \(m_S(u,v)=(\theta_u+\theta_v)/2\). This does not generally satisfy the equidistance desideratum in dimension two or higher.
## Admissible example and exact calculation

Work on the unit sphere \(S^{2,1}\) and choose \[u=(1,0,0),\qquad v=(0,1/2,\sqrt3/2).\] Both have norm one. Select \(d=1\). Their angles are \(\pi/2\) and \(0\), so Eq. (22) chooses \(\theta=\pi/4\). The resulting great-circle boundary \(B\) has unit normal \(n=(1,-1,0)/\sqrt2\). The two points are strictly on opposite sides because \(n^\top u=1/\sqrt2\) and \(n^\top v=-1/(2\sqrt2)\).

Equation reference: eq:dist. For a point \(x\) on the unit sphere, the shortest distance to \(B=\{y:\|y\|=1,\ n^\top y=0\}\) is \[
d_S(x,B)=\arcsin|n^\top x|.\] Indeed, normalizing the orthogonal projection of \(x\) onto \(n^\perp\) maximizes its dot product with a unit point on \(B\), giving cosine \(\sqrt{1-(n^\top x)^2}\) and hence [eq:dist] (#eq:dist). It follows that \[d_S(u,B)=\frac{\pi}{4}\simeq0.785398,\qquad
d_S(v,B)=\arcsin\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\simeq0.361367.\] The asserted equality fails. The independent script `c.py` checks norms, angles, and both distances in `calc.json`; the analytic argument does not depend on floating-point tolerance.
## Counterevidence and bounded impact

The projected radii are \(1\) and \(1/2\). Equal angular deviations would imply equal distances on a normalized projected circle, but do not imply equal distances in the original sphere. Neither the main statement nor Appendices B–C restricts all samples to equal projection radii. Both inspected code snapshots implement arithmetic spherical averaging. Thus this is a Major failure of an explicit central geometric guarantee, not an observation that a benchmark score must decrease. The resulting great-circle split may still be useful and convex in the usual non-antipodal sense.

A limited pairwise repair is available. For unit-norm, non-antipodal sphere points with nonzero projected sum, take \(\theta_*=\operatorname{atan2}(u_0+v_0,u_d+v_d)\). The boundary then has \(n_*^\top(u+v)=0\), so \(|n_*^\top u|=|n_*^\top v|\) and their distances in [eq:dist] (#eq:dist) are equal. This verifies only the specified pairwise property; degenerate cases, candidate ordering, and the entire tree algorithm are not certified by this repair.
Problem 2 (The printed hyperbolic midpoint can miss the manifold).  Equations (20)–(21), p. 5, produce a non-intersecting boundary for an ordinary pair on the positive unit hyperboloid.
## Admissible example and failed result
The curve \(x(t)=(\cosh t,\sinh t)\) has unit intrinsic speed. Consequently the genuine midpoint is \(x(1/2)\) and its angle satisfies \(\cot\theta_{\rm true}=\tanh(1/2)\simeq0.462117\).
## Source-version counterevidence and severity

Both supplied snapshots use a different expression, whose relevant branch is \[\cot\theta_{\rm code}=\frac{-V-\sqrt{V^2-4}}{2}.\] For this example it equals \(\coth1-\operatorname{csch}1=\tanh(1/2)\). The parent inspected the actual source and typeset p. 5, excluding an extraction artifact. The code is therefore important counterevidence to any claim that the erroneous printed formula generated the benchmarks.

The published formula nevertheless directly drives the stated candidate construction in Algorithm 1 and the hyperbolic specialization in Section 3.2. This supported derivation defect is Major. A correct value for this example does not certify the code generally: its intermediate formula has a singularity when the two angles sum to \(\pi\), and dtype-specific behavior was not tested by running author code. No full replacement algorithm is claimed.
# Overall dependence and conclusion

The two findings independently invalidate advertised midpoint properties. They do not refute the utility of product-space forests or establish damage to the published accuracy/RMSE values. The historical snapshot also contains a training-mask/prediction-mask discrepancy which the newer snapshot recomputes correctly; that auxiliary observation is preserved as version history, not labeled a current defect. No later formal erratum search or experimental reproduction was performed.

# Identity, version, and inspected scope

This report concerns Yongqiang Chen, Quanming Yao, Juzheng Zhang, James Cheng, and Yatao Bian, Hierarchical Graph Tokenization for Molecule-Language Alignment, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, publisher record `chen25cf` (OpenReview identifier `wpbNczwAwV`; local identifier 0235/I25-43604). The reviewed object is the staged 27-page publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. Printed page numbers equal one-based PDF page indices. The preserved release is `LFhase/HIGHT`, commit `a5567c1c98bc274d7059e9f022df737f9b7facf1`; it is not established as the historical experiment commit.

The parent read the main contribution, architecture, benchmark construction, evaluation and conclusions on pp. 1–9, and implementation details on p. 22. Auxiliary checks covered selected dataset, split and implementation material and relevant released files. The decisive table was visually inspected in the source PDF. We independently reconstructed the metric consequences without executing author code. Training, raw prediction regeneration, chemistry-label validation and the other task scores were not reproduced. # Method and the claim under examination

HIGHT adds atom-, motif- and molecule-level representations, separate adapters, and enriched hierarchical instruction data. MotifHallu asks whether specified functional groups occur in a molecule. Section 3.2 and Table 1 describe 23,924 binary questions: \(P=4,124\) positive and \(Q=19,800\) negative. Table 1 reports HIGHT macro-F1 \(66.8\), compared with \(50.0\) for GIMLET, \(56.6\) for Galactica and \(52.6\) for InstructMol. Section 5.2, continuing onto p. 7, explicitly interprets macro-F1 as averaged across classes and claims an improvement of up to 14 percentage points. Figure 1 also uses macro-F1 for its hallucination overview. This is a direct dependency of a principal contribution, not an incidental logging statistic.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (Class filtering changes the metric and the central ranking).  The class F1 and macro-F1 labels in Tables 1–2 do not describe conventional binary classification F1. The corresponding released scoring procedure removes the opposite true class before evaluating each class.
#### Definitions and exact discrepancy.

For a single binary prediction on every question, write \(TP,FN,FP,TN\) for the confusion counts, with \(TP+FN=P\) and \(TN+FP=Q\). Conventional scores are \[\begin{aligned}
 F_+&=\frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN},&
 F_-&=\frac{2TN}{2TN+FP+FN},\\
 F_{\rm macro}&=\frac{F_++F_-}{2},&
 F_{\rm micro}&=\frac{TP+TN}{P+Q}.\end{aligned}\] The last identity follows because, when both classes are pooled, each wrong single-label prediction contributes one false positive and one false negative.

In , lines 181–191 calculate ordinary positive binary F1 from confusion counts. Lines 388–408 then partition predictions by ground-truth class, invert the predictions in the negative group, and call that evaluator separately against all-positive labels. For nonzero correct counts the resulting quantities are \[S_+=\frac{2TP}{P+TP}=\frac{2r}{1+r},\qquad
 S_-=\frac{2TN}{Q+TN}=\frac{2s}{1+s},\] where \(r=TP/P\) and \(s=TN/Q\). False positives from the other true class have been deleted. Therefore \((S_++S_-)/2\) is a transformed-recall balance score, not \(F_{\rm macro}\).

The published table is independently inconsistent with conventional F1 even without historical code attribution. HIGHT’s reported Micro F1 is \(29.7\%\), whereas its accuracy is \(39.1\%\). Its positive F1 is printed as \(85.5\%\) despite a \(69.4\%\) yes-prediction rate and only \(17.24\%\) positive prevalence. Even perfect recall would bound conventional positive F1 by \(2P/(P+0.694(P+Q))<40\%\).
#### Independent quantitative check.

Inverting \(S_+\) and \(S_-\), using \(r=S_+/(2-S_+)\) and \(s=S_-/(2-S_-)\), gives HIGHT \(r\approx0.7467\) and \(s\approx0.3175\). The resulting ordinary positive F1 is about \(29.73\%\), consistent with the table’s number called micro-F1, and macro-F1 is about \(38.04\%\).

To avoid treating rounded class scores as exact, the parent separately enumerated every integer confusion matrix consistent with each row’s reported accuracy and yes ratio, each rounded to 0.1 percentage point. For every feasible \((TP,TN)\) we computed the full-data definitions above. The actual independent script `c.py` and results `calc.json` give:
Model | Published macro-F1 | Feasible conventional macro-F1

There are respectively 239, 276, 288 and 288 feasible matrices. The intervals are logical reconstructions from the stated supports and rounded aggregate measurements, not new model measurements or recovered exact prediction counts. They establish that HIGHT ranks below GIMLET and Galactica under conventional macro-F1, while remaining above InstructMol.
#### Counterevidence and severity.

The restricted scores are legitimate monotone transforms of class recall if explicitly named and motivated as such. A new name alone, however, does not preserve the paper’s standard macro-F1 comparison. HIGHT’s accuracy and conventional macro-F1 gains over InstructMol survive; its reported AUROC and downstream property, caption and reaction results are outside this refutation. A newer repository snapshot might differ from the historical code, but the source-independent table identities and ranking bounds remain.

The finding is Major: it demonstrates material harm to the core MotifHallu macro-F1 conclusion. It does not require the full architecture or all experiments to fail. The abstract’s numerical \(40\%\) hallucination interpretation also requires reconsideration because the affected class scores are transformed recalls; this review does not replace it with an unverified universal percentage.
#### Correction and remaining verification.

Evaluate both class F1 scores on the complete prediction vector, compute their mean, and use micro-F1 equal to accuracy for this single-label task. If retaining positive binary F1, label it accordingly. Publish the confusion counts and revise the affected cross-model statement and figure. These formulas and the conditional rank consequence have been verified here. A corrected historical table still requires the original saved predictions and their experiment provenance. No author adoption or completed empirical repair is asserted.
# Other checks and limits

The static source contains hierarchical nodes and three adapter branches. Disabling codebook lookup at downstream inference agrees with Appendix D’s explicit use of continuous GNN encoder embeddings; it is not evidence that the proposed hierarchy was absent. Distinct training and test paths were found, but the underlying identities were not audited, so neither leakage nor its absence is established.

An auxiliary check found that the released positional-encoding conversion discards computed Laplacian edge weights. This is retained as a source-level discrepancy requiring historical-use and impact evidence, without adding a second core failure here. Chemistry-label concerns were not independently established and are not findings of this report. Full training-data provenance, all ablations and every repository member were not scientifically verified.
# Overall assessment

The supported assessment is Major, confined to the demonstrated metric error and its core ranking consequence. Scientific adjudication is pending, human reviews are empty, repair adoption is unknown, and empirical reproduction was not performed. The hierarchy’s broader usefulness remains an empirical question beyond the established issue.

Title: Technical Verification of
MixMin: Finding Data Mixtures via Convex Minimization
# Identity, version, and scope

This report concerns Anvith Thudi, Evianne Rovers, Yangjun Ruan, Tristan Thrush, and Chris J. Maddison, MixMin: Finding Data Mixtures via Convex Minimization, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, publisher record `thudi25a` (OpenReview `wpaxYGgp2n`; local identifier 0236/I25-43605). The staged publisher PDF has 17 pages and was retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. Page references use printed numbers, equal to one-based PDF indices. The inspected source is `Anvith-Thudi/MixMin`, commit `7212abef3b6e62d2a6164675a46f2ab143d305ca`. Its identity is preserved; it is not independently established as the exact historical experiment revision.

The parent read the main paper, both proofs on p. 12, and supplementary result tables and captions on pp. 13–17; relevant released files were inspected statically with auxiliary assistance. Source p. 4 was rendered and visually checked. Own scalar calculations were run, but author code, model inference, training and dataset evaluation were not. The main findings concern mathematical specification and released source, not a reproduced benchmark. A possible separate OpenReview attachment remained inaccessible in source preparation (HTTP 403); embedded appendices were available.
# Verified reduction and limits

For Lemma 3.2, let \(F_H\) be the finite-class target risk and \(F_*\) the Bayes version. Its uniform approximation and Lipschitz assumptions give \(|F_H(\lambda)-F_*(\lambda)|\le C\epsilon\) for every mixture. If \(\lambda^*\) minimizes \(F_*\) and \(\bar\lambda\) minimizes \(F_H\), then \[F_H(\lambda^*)-F_H(\bar\lambda)
 \le C\epsilon+[F_*(\lambda^*)-F_*(\bar\lambda)]+C\epsilon
 \le 2C\epsilon.\] This verifies the stated argument. Merely enlarging a model class does not by itself establish the uniform approximation assumption or target-risk regularity; the paper states these conditions rather than proving them for the experimental neural networks or bioassays. Source-support extrapolation and empirical Bayes proximity are not certified here.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The printed minimization algorithm moves toward the worse source).  Algorithm 1, p. 4, defines \(g=\nabla_\lambda l\) but updates \(\lambda_p\leftarrow\lambda_p e^{+\eta g_p}/\sum_q\lambda_q e^{+\eta g_q}\). For positive step size this has the opposite sign to entropic descent.
#### Exact admissible check.

Source visual inspection also confirms that line 3 has an extra \(\lambda_p\) prefactor outside the empirical average, with \(p\) unbound at that step. The counterexample above charitably removes that prefactor to use the intended objective displayed in Section 4. Consequently the sign defect remains even after this separate specification ambiguity is resolved.
#### Dependency, counterevidence, and severity.

Section 4 identifies Algorithm 1 as the gradient method that solves the paper’s central convex objective. Its failure on exact Bayes sources invalidates that core printed algorithm as a minimizer. The supported severity is Major, bounded to this algorithmic claim; easy repair does not make the demonstrated optimization failure inconsequential.

There is decisive counterevidence against extending this finding to experimental failure: , in `update_with_stop`, uses `exp(-lr*grad)` and normalizes the weights. The chemistry update also has the negative exponent. Neither Theorem 3.1 nor Lemma 3.2 depends on the erroneous printed sign. The supplied release therefore already embodies the natural sign correction, although its exact relationship to historical runs remains unverified.
#### Verified correction.

Problem 2 (A released likelihood-generation entry point reads an undefined argument).  The checked `logprobs.py` script cannot reach its intended likelihood computation under its ordinary command-line entry point, even if its imports succeed.

In , the parser registers `tokens`, `output_dir`, `task` and `model_size`, then calls `parse_args()` and immediately reads `args.mixture`. No such argument, parser default or prior namespace assignment is present in the complete script. The namespace attribute is therefore absent. This is a Minor static release reproducibility defect; no author program was executed to demonstrate it, and it does not establish that the historical experiments failed. The apparently unused assignment could be removed or an intended parameter explicitly registered, but a complete repaired author run was not performed or authorized.
# Source mapping, empirical scope, and conclusion

The language-model objective in the inspected release mixes sequence probabilities: `logprobs.py` multiplies mean token loss by the number of scored causal tokens; `mixmin_gen.py` applies log-sum-exp across source sequence scores, then length normalization. It is not the unsupported alternative of averaging source next-token probabilities with fixed weights independently at every position. Initial-token conditioning and document-length weighting remain implementation conventions rather than a new theorem guarantee.

The chemistry source excludes the target assay when assembling surrogate models and uses the target training split to fit weights; released example weights are proportional to mixture weight divided by source sample count. These static mappings do not establish absence of molecular overlap or verify AP gains. The auxiliary record also notes that long OpenWebMath documents in one branch reuse preceding likelihood values; the measured frequency and historical effect are unresolved. No numerical damage to a reported figure is inferred from that release observation. Supplementary p-values include nonsignificant comparisons, so descriptive improvement is not treated as uniform statistical significance.

Overall assessment: Major for the demonstrated core printed algorithm error, with a separate Minor release entry-point defect. The reduction and approximation proof survive the inspected checks. Scientific adjudication remains pending, `human_reviews` is empty, and neither empirical repair completion nor author acceptance is claimed.

Title: Technical Verification of
Oracle-MoE: Locality-preserving Routing in the Oracle Space
# Identity, source, and scope

The reviewed paper is Jixian Zhou et al., Oracle-MoE: Locality-preserving Routing in the Oracle Space for Memory-constrained Large Language Model Inference, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 78633–78650, publisher record `zhou25b`, OpenReview `wn6WHREK9k` (0237/I25-43606). We used the staged 18-page publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC; printed page numbers equal PDF page indices. The full source manifest and publisher identity were checked. No author repository was acquired in preparation; this does not establish that no release exists. A possible separate OpenReview attachment was blocked by HTTP 403, while the embedded appendices were available.

The parent read the main analysis, method, experiments and conclusions on pp. 1–9 and mathematical/experimental appendix material on pp. 13–18. Source pp. 13–14 were rendered and visually inspected. Native auxiliaries independently checked mathematics and experimental/source provenance. The parent rederived the decisive counterexamples and ran an independent scalar/Gaussian diagnostic. No author program, trained model, latency benchmark or dataset was executed.
# Claim and dependency

The paper decomposes a token embedding as \(t_i=s_i+u_i\), separates semantic and identity subspaces, groups tokens by thresholded attention, averages each growing group, and routes the mean to a nearest oracle-space cluster. Theorem 1 on p. 5 claims a high-probability reduction in consecutive embedding variation at sufficiently large identity dimension and then concludes \(\mathrm{CSD}_{\rm token}>\mathrm{CSD}_{\rm oracle}\) through its approximate CSD framework. For one active expert, actual CSD is a count of changes of expert index. Appendix A.4 explicitly invokes Lemma 5 with \(K=C(W_g,k)\) and its additive threshold identified with \(2r\). Appendix A.1 is separately cited on pp. 3–4 to justify attention as an indicator of high-level semantic similarity. Both derivations therefore support central contributions.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The norm-comparison lemma used by the main theorem is false).  Lemma 5, pp. 14–15, asserts that \(\|Y\|+m<K\|Z\|\) has probability tending to one as dimension increases for any fixed \(m>0,K>0\) and \(n<m\). Its stated Gaussian construction admits an exact zero-probability counterexample.
#### Complete check.

Let \(n=1\), \(m=2\), \(K=1/4\), and let \(x_1,x_2\) be independent \(N(0,I_d)\) vectors for any \(d\). Select the singleton subset \(S\) uniformly from \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\), exactly as required. In the paper’s notation, \[Z=x_1-x_2,\qquad
 Y=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}-x_S=
 \begin{cases}-Z/2,&S=\{1\},\\ Z/2,&S=\{2\}.\end{cases}\] Hence \(\|Y\|=\|Z\|/2\) identically. The claimed event becomes \[\frac12\|Z\|+2<\frac14\|Z\|,\] which is impossible, including when \(Z=0\). Its probability is zero for every dimension, not asymptotically one. The example satisfies isotropic Gaussianity, independence of the \(x_i\), random subset selection, positive fixed constants and \(n<m\).

The proof’s comparison of \(\mathbb E\|Y\|^2\) with \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2\) cannot justify an arbitrary factor \(K\). In addition, its variance calculation assumes independence of the two squared norms, although here one is exactly one quarter of the other. The claimed Chebyshev conclusion therefore cannot repair the counterexample.
#### Why a norm repair alone is insufficient.

The passage from a smaller continuous displacement to fewer discrete assignments is an approximation on pp. 3, 5 and 14, not a proved error bound. The explicit routing model permits the following check. Let \(H=\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R^d\), let \(s_1,s_2\) be independent uniform variables on \([1,2]\), and let \(u_1,u_2\) be independent \(N(0,I_d)\), independent of the semantic variables. These satisfy Assumptions 1–4 with semantic center \(1.5\) and radius \(0.5\). Take \(W_Q=P\), \(W_K=2P\), where \(P\) projects onto the semantic coordinate. The two tokens belong to one thresholded group with \(\epsilon=0.01\): even including self-attention, the second token’s attention to the first is at least \(1/(1+e^4)>0.01\).

A raw top-one gate with rows \(P\) and zero assigns both tokens to expert 1. For oracle routing, the permitted nearest-center rule with centers \(c_\pm=(1.5,\pm a,0,\ldots,0)\), \(a>0\), assigns by the sign of the first identity coordinate. The growing means are \(z_1=t_1\) and \(z_2=(t_1+t_2)/2\). If \(X=u_{1,1}\) and \(Y=u_{2,1}\), the oracle changes expert precisely when \(X\) and \(X+Y\) have opposite signs. Rotational symmetry of \((X,Y)\) gives probability \(1/4\), independently of \(d\). Thus token CSD is zero for the pair, while oracle CSD is one with probability \(1/4\).

This does not set the raw router to a globally constant dense model: negative-semantic groups elsewhere use its other expert. Nor does it claim these centers were observed in a trained run. It shows that the explicit distribution and nearest-centroid assumptions do not supply the claimed routing guarantee; a further restriction connecting learned centers, semantic directions and boundary margins would be needed. The appendix’s informal cluster-density approximation does not provide such a bound. The independent 100,000-pair sign diagnostic gave \(0.24843\), consistent with the exact \(1/4\); the proof does not depend on this simulation.
#### Severity and counterevidence.

This is Major: a demonstrated false lemma is used directly in the core theorem, and its claimed discrete-routing consequence needs additional control. Averaging independent noise can still reduce variance, and actual learned centers may be favorable. Those facts neither establish the stated universal high-dimensional result nor refute the reported empirical improvements. The threshold condition above is a partial lemma repair, not a verified replacement for the full CSD theorem.

Problem 2 (The attention-semantic argument uses an invalid inner-product bound).  Appendix A.1, p. 13, claims for unit \(X,Y\) and full-rank maps on the shared semantic subspace that \[|\langle M_QX,M_KY\rangle|
 \le \|M_Q^\top M_K\|\,|\langle X,Y\rangle|.\] This is false under the stated assumptions.

Take the two-dimensional shared semantic subspace and \[M_Q=I_2,\quad
 M_K=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 X=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 Y=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both transformations are full rank, are different as allowed, and operate on exactly the same subspace. Both input vectors are unit. The left side equals \(1\) and the right side equals \(0\), since \(\langle X,Y\rangle=0\). Equal subspaces and equal effective ranks therefore do not imply the proposed preservation of input inner products. The correct general inequality is \[|\langle M_QX,M_KY\rangle|
 \le\|M_Q^\top M_K\|\,\|X\|\,\|Y\|.\] It does not infer high original semantic alignment from a large transformed attention product. A stronger condition such as \(M_Q^\top M_K\) being a scalar multiple of the identity would be sufficient for the disputed form, but is not among the assumptions.

This finding is Major: pp. 3–4 explicitly rely on this analysis to connect attention-defined groups with high-level semantic similarity, which is the motivation for oracle-space routing. The counterexample invalidates that mathematical justification. It does not show that empirical attention groups are useless, and the later semantic-distribution assumptions can still be posited independently. The valid spectral bound is a verified algebraic replacement, but not a repair of the claimed semantic implication.
# Empirical evidence and scope of the conclusion

The reported first-token latencies in Table 2 imply speed ratios of approximately \(4.56\), \(4.77\) and \(2.60\) relative to FIFO, LRU and SwapMoE, respectively. These are arithmetic checks of reported measurements, not reproduced timings. Table 1 supports similar or slightly higher aggregate task scores while several individual task scores decrease; no statistical performance-loss conclusion is possible without uncertainty and matched evaluation details. The appendix reports further examples, including fine-grained experts, which remain empirical counterevidence against assuming the method cannot work.

Some experimental identities require clarification: Table 2 names a 765M model while the main configuration is 729M, and the largest-model expert count differs between the main text and Table 3. No particular configuration is inferred to have run. Exact memory accounting, caching traces, timing methodology, model artifacts and source-to-result provenance are unavailable in the staged material. These are Needs Evidence items rather than additional established Major defects.

The overall initial assessment is Major for both demonstrated mathematical problems. Practical latency and accuracy results are not invalidated by assertion. Scientific adjudication remains pending; `human_reviews` is empty. No full corrected theorem, author adoption, code reproduction or subsequent erratum resolution is claimed.

report: Abstract: An explicit two-client, two-layer GCN construction contradicts the central graph-distribution divergence bound: the actual \(H\Delta H\) distance is 2 while the stated upper bound is approximately 1.006. The proof also uses an invalid entrywise-norm inequality. This is a Major flaw in the theoretical justification for improved generalization. A separate HSIC normalization inconsistency is Minor. The reported predictive gains are not refuted, and causal identification remains unverified rather than assumed. Scientific adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:

Title: Technical Verification of
Less is More: Federated Graph Learning with Alleviating Topology Heterogeneity from A Causal Perspective
# Identity, version, and scope

This report concerns Lele Fu, Bowen Deng, Sheng Huang, Tianchi Liao, Shirui Pan, and Chuan Chen, Less is More: Federated Graph Learning with Alleviating Topology Heterogeneity from A Causal Perspective, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, publisher record `fu25a`, OpenReview `wleRTUQj07` (0238/I25-43607). We reviewed the staged 19-page publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026 UTC. Printed page numbers equal PDF indices. Its original bytes and source manifest are preserved.

The parent read the main method and experiments, Algorithm 1, supplementary tables and the proof on pp. 13–18. Source pp. 6, 16 and 18 were visually inspected. Native auxiliary agents independently checked mathematics and experimental/source evidence. The parent separately derived and calculated the counterexample below. No author implementation was acquired in source preparation; this is not a claim that no public release exists. Embedded appendices were available, while access to a possible separate OpenReview supplement was blocked by HTTP 403. No author code, model training, benchmark rerun or dataset download was performed.
# Method and theoretical dependency

FedATH assigns complementary sigmoid edge weights to causal and biased graph branches, trains two GNNs with prediction, entropy-related and dependence losses, and aggregates only the causal GNN. For finite evaluator logits, both masks are strictly between zero and one: the displayed method reweights the existing edges rather than specifying a hard deletion threshold.

Theorem 5.1 expresses a generalization bound through local empirical risks, cross-client \(H\Delta H\) divergences and additional terms. Corollary 5.2, Eq. (14), bounds those divergences using graph and feature norms. The prose immediately after it, repeated after Eq. (40) on p. 18, argues that reducing edge weights shrinks the bound and hence improves generalization. This corollary is therefore a direct theoretical justification for the central topology-reduction strategy.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The central graph-divergence bound fails for bounded GCNs).  Corollary 5.2 and its Appendix D derivation admit a concrete pair of equal-sized graphs for which the stated upper bound is strictly below the actual divergence.
#### Complete construction.

Use two clients with \(m=100\) nodes each and identical complete-graph adjacency matrices \(A_k=A_l=J-I\), where \(J\) is the all-ones matrix. Every degree is 99. Adding self-loops as specified on p. 15 gives \[P=(D+I)^{-1/2}(A+I)(D+I)^{-1/2}=J/100.\] Let \(X_k=0.01\mathbf1\) and \(X_l=-0.01\mathbf1\). Then \[\|A_k\|_F=\|A_l\|_F=\sqrt{9900},\quad
 \|X_k\|_F=\|X_l\|_F=0.1,\quad
 \|X_k-X_l\|_F=0.2.\] Use the paper’s two-layer form \(f(A,X)=\operatorname{sigmoid}(P\operatorname{ReLU}(PXW_1)W_2)\), with \[W_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1),\quad
 W_{2,a}=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1)^\top,\quad
 W_{2,b}=\frac1{\sqrt2}(-1,-1)^\top.\] Each weight matrix has Frobenius norm 1, so \(B_W=1\) and \(B_X=0.1\) are valid bounds. All features are constant within each graph, hence multiplication by \(P\) preserves them. For scalar node feature \(x\), the two pre-sigmoid outputs are \(x/2\) and \(-|x|/2\).

Threshold both sigmoid outputs at \(1/2\). Classifier \(h_a\) predicts 1 on every node of client \(k\) and 0 on every node of client \(l\); \(h_b\) predicts 0 on both clients. The probabilities are approximately \(0.501250\) and \(0.498750\), so there are no threshold ties. Both classifiers belong to the stated bounded two-layer class. Their disagreement probability is 1 on \(\widetilde D_k\) and 0 on \(\widetilde D_l\). Consequently \[d_{H\Delta H}(\widetilde D_k,\widetilde D_l)
 =2\sup_{h,h'}|\Pr_k(h\ne h')-\Pr_l(h\ne h')|=2.\]

The right side printed in Corollary 5.2 is bounded, for this hypothesis class, by \[\begin{aligned}
 B&=1+B_W^2B_X
 \left(\frac1{D_{\min}m}+\frac1{D_{\min}^2}\right)
 (\|A_k\|_F+\|A_l\|_F)
 +\frac{B_W^2}{m}\|X_k-X_l\|_F\\
 &=1+0.1\left(\frac1{9900}+\frac1{9801}\right)
       2\sqrt{9900}+0.002
 \approx1.006040455<2.\end{aligned}\] The supremum cannot enlarge these uniform norm constants. If \(D_{\min}\) instead denotes augmented degree 100, the value is approximately \(1.005980\); using augmented adjacency norms as well gives \(1.006\). Thus the discrepancy is not resolved by the proof’s inconsistent self-loop notation. Independent arithmetic is saved in `c.py`/`calc.json`.
#### Invalid steps and core consequence.

Equation (23) on p. 16 converts binary disagreement divergence into a bound based on small differences of sigmoid scores. Thresholded predictions can differ completely even when scores lie arbitrarily close on opposite sides of \(1/2\), as the construction demonstrates. The displayed soft-score inequalities do not imply that conversion without additional margin/distribution control.

Equation (25) also asserts \(\|M\|_{1,\mathrm{ele}}\le\sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(M)}\|M\|_F\). For the \(2\times2\) all-ones matrix, the left side is 4 while rank is 1 and Frobenius norm is 2. The asserted inequality would require \(4\le2\). The rank-based inequality pertains to the nuclear norm, not the entrywise one-norm. The general entrywise estimate uses the square root of the number of entries instead. This error is used in Eq. (24), not merely mentioned in passing.

The finding is Major: the core graph-divergence corollary itself is false under its supplied model and norm constraints, and it is used to justify enhanced generalization. It is not necessary to show that the empirical classifier loses accuracy. The triangle-inequality manipulation connecting local and global divergences in Eqs. (18)–(20) is not refuted by this counterexample; applicability of the imported FL generalization bound to dependent graph data remains outside this verification.
#### Repair limits and counterevidence.

Correcting the norm inequality alone does not repair the hard-prediction/soft-score step. A valid alternative would need a clearly defined smooth discrepancy or explicit classifier-margin assumptions, followed by a fresh derivation. No replacement theorem is certified here. Moreover, edge reweighting changes minimum degrees as well as adjacency norms, so their coefficients cannot generally be held fixed when claiming a monotone bound decrease. Even a smaller valid upper bound would not by itself prove that actual risk decreases. The reported gains and loss ablations remain empirical evidence of usefulness, independent of this invalid derivation.

Problem 2 (The dependence loss changes the stated HSIC normalization).  Definition 4.1, Eq. (10), uses \((N-1)^{-2}\operatorname{Tr}(K_1CK_2C)\), while Eq. (11) uses \((N-1)^2\) multiplying the same trace and calls it the same HSIC quantity.

The two quantities differ by \((N-1)^4\), which equals \(96{,}059{,}601\) for \(N=100\). Actual inspection of p. 6 confirms the positive exponent in Eq. (11). This is a Minor mathematical specification inconsistency. At a fixed sample size, a positive rescaling can be absorbed into the trade-off coefficient, so it does not independently establish a wrong optimum or harmful result. Across client sizes it changes the effective regularization differently. The implementation is unavailable, so the formula used in the historical runs is unknown. Making Eq. (11) consistent with Eq. (10), or explicitly defining a different scaling and its coefficient, is required; no executed implementation repair is claimed.
# Causal interpretation and empirical checks

The paper describes a causal-inspired method rather than proving a causal-identification theorem. Its selected linear Gram matrices give \(\operatorname{Tr}(H^cH^{c\top}CH^bH^{b\top}C)
=\|H^{c\top}CH^b\|_F^2\), which measures cross-covariance. Zero does not imply general independence: for equally weighted values \(Z\in\{-1,0,1\}\) and \(B=Z^2\), the centered cross-product is zero although \(B\) is a nonconstant deterministic function of \(Z\). A constant biased encoder also gives zero HSIC and a uniform softmax for any graph partition. These observations limit identification of causal edges by the auxiliary objectives alone; they do not negate the method’s predictive regularization effect. Causal identification is recorded as Needs Evidence, not as a separately demonstrated Major claim.

The displayed accuracy tables favor FedATH in all 18 settings. An auxiliary arithmetic check found one exception to the appendix’s universal F1 ranking: Photo with 20 clients has FedATH \(82.88\) versus FedSage+ \(82.94\). This small difference does not establish material damage to overall performance. Both added losses are best in the 12 displayed loss-ablation settings. Sending only the causal GNN avoids communication of the other two modules, but does not demonstrate reduced bytes relative to a same-sized FedAvg GNN.

Algorithm 1 does not explicitly update the edge evaluator, does not carry the trade-off coefficient into its displayed gradients, and leaves training/communication-round nesting unclear. These are implementation-specification questions; no unpublished execution behavior is inferred. Missing seed/uncertainty details, exact evaluated artifacts and source-to-table mappings also prevent reproduction claims.
# Overall assessment

The initial assessment is Major, based on the exact counterexample to the core corollary, with the separate normalization inconsistency assessed Minor. The broader empirical improvements are not disproved. Scientific adjudication is pending, `human_reviews` is empty, and author adoption or completed repair is unknown.

Date: Initial review, 25 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of paper 0239
# Identity, scope, and definitions

The reviewed work is Eric Zhao, Pranjal Awasthi, and Sreenivas Gollapudi, Sample, Scrutinize and Scale: Effective Inference-Time Search by Scaling Verification, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, publisher entry `zhao25a`, OpenReview `wl3eI4wiE5`; assigned identifier I25-43608. The staged 38-page publisher PDF was retrieved on 25 October 2026 at 04:11:21 UTC. Page references mean the printed PDF pages, which coincide with physical pages. Main text and embedded Appendices A–F were read; selected original figures and Table 6 were visually checked. Released code was inspected statically at commit `1caa3137ca5b6d86be001f2595f91db0fb6cae2f`. This retrieval snapshot is not certified as the experiment-time commit.

For a question, \(\operatorname{Pass}@k\) denotes the probability that at least one of \(k\) responses has a correct final answer. Consistency chooses the most frequent extracted final-answer string. Verification scores each candidate by repeated natural-language checks and selects using those scores, with optional comparison-based tie-breaking. The scaling plots omit tie-breaking and subsample one primary pool of 200 candidates and 50 checks per candidate; the 20 subsampling seeds are not 20 independent original experiments. Final-answer correctness and correctness of intermediate reasoning are different targets, explicitly separated in the paper.
# Problem 1: the claimed control does not identify response quality
Judgment: Major for the core identifying argument; Needs Evidence for the proposed mechanism in the actual data.
## Claim, dependency, and suspect step

Section 2.2 (p. 3), supported by Figures 2–3 (pp. 4, 6), conditions accuracy on at least one correct candidate. It presents this as isolating the burden of discriminating among more candidates after accounting for the increased chance of finding a correct answer. The ensuing increase is taken to demonstrate that the larger pool contains higher-quality correct responses, where quality means rigor or freedom from reasoning flaws. This is one of the three principal explanatory factors introduced on p. 3 and contributes to the abstract’s interpretation of scalability.

The condition fixes existence of a correct candidate, not their number or the opportunities for a fixed stochastic verifier to assign a high score. Thus the reported conditional trend does not distinguish improved objective response quality from repeated chances to verify equally good responses.
## A complete countermodel for the identifying inference

Consider independent candidates, each correct with probability \(p=0.1\), with all correct candidates of identical reasoning quality. All correct candidates share one correct final answer and all incorrect candidates one wrong final answer. Each candidate receives 50 independent binary checks, approving a correct candidate with probability \(0.7\) and an incorrect one with probability \(0.6\). These laws do not change with \(k\). Retain the maximum score within each final-answer group, then select the higher-scoring group, breaking a tied maximum uniformly between groups. This is the no-comparison selection rule in the inspected , lines 633–684; selection uses no answer key.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair boundary

This is a counterexample to the sufficiency of the proposed identifying argument, not a claim that the synthetic score distributions reproduce Gemini’s measured errors, question filters, or curves. The authors may be right that larger pools contain better proofs. The empirical rise in conditional accuracy, the headline benchmark gains, and the usefulness of comparison/rewrite interventions all remain possible. The abstract’s partial attribution is cautious, but the more specific isolation and demonstration language in Section 2.2 requires evidence that this control does not supply. No direct candidate-quality measurement or analysis fixing the number of correct candidates was located in the inspected release or relevant appendix.

The Major judgment is tied to a demonstrated invalid inference explaining a principal scientific result; it does not require refuting the method or decreasing its reported scores. The supported immediate correction is to describe the curves as conditional selection accuracy and the quality explanation as a hypothesis. Establishing that explanation would require distinguishing objective response quality, the count of correct candidates, question composition, and verification-score noise. No replacement mechanism is asserted as the empirically established one. Evidence: original pp. 3–6; `grouped_tie_check.py`, `calc.json`, and the pinned selection source. The earlier uniform-candidate-tie calculation is retained as predecessor evidence; the group-tie calculation above matches the inspected release.
# Problem 2: smaller-model superiority has explicit exceptions

Judgment: Minor, local comparative interpretation. Table 6’s caption (p. 15) and Appendix B.1’s continuation (p. 16) say that Pro+Flash verification matches or exceeds Pro consistency, while verification strictly exceeds consistency for all model choices. The displayed MATH comparison is \[\frac{456}{500}=91.2\% < \frac{460}{500}=92.0\% ,\] so Pro+Flash trails Pro consistency by four answers, or 0.8 percentage points. Flash verification and Flash consistency also tie on LiveBench Reasoning at \(84/140\). These are direct comparisons of the stated results, without assumptions about statistical significance.

The other three Pro+Flash columns improve over Pro consistency, by 3, 1, and 9 answers, respectively. Flash improves on its other three tasks. Consequently a precise repair is to acknowledge the MATH exception and Reasoning tie. This leaves the principal Pro-only Table 1 results and the broader feasibility of cheaper verification intact. The numerical repair is verified; historical outcomes were not rerun and author adoption has not been requested. Evidence: source image `s15.png`, printed tables, `calc.json`, and `a_code.json`.
# Checks supporting the remaining inspected claims
## Rare-answer and reference examples

For Table 2 (p. 7), the constraint \(a+b+c=300\) and the stated symmetric cubic equal to \(6{,}000{,}000\) give \[300(ab+bc+ca)-3abc=6{,}000{,}000
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(a-100)(b-100)(c-100)=0 .\] For ordered nonnegative integers, each of the three coordinate-100 sets has 201 elements; their pairwise and triple intersections are the single triple \((100,100,100)\). Inclusion–exclusion gives \(3(201)-3+1=601\). Parent enumeration of all 45,451 admissible triples confirms this and the displayed multiplicities sum to 200.

The dodecagon reference answer 315 in Appendix F.1 was independently checked by enumerating the intersections of perpendicular chord segments: the six orientation-pair counts are \(51,54,51,54,51,54\). Parent floating-point checks at three tolerances agree with the auxiliary’s exact symbolic enumeration. Appendix E’s truth-puzzle, square-count, and unit-conversion answers also check out. In the coin example, \(n\equiv5\pmod8\), \(7n+53>200\), and divisibility by eight give minimum original count \(203\). The displayed reasoning is deliberately flawed while its final answer is correct. Appendix F’s false named theorems are explicitly model-generated rewrites of incorrect responses; they are not scientific theorems asserted by the authors.
## Released procedure and scoring

The static source maps the main settings to 200 candidates, 50 checks, and up to three distinct final answers within 0.05 of the best score for comparison. Ground truth enters final grading after selection in the minimal driver. A notebook shortcut skips verification for already graded homogeneous all-correct/all-wrong sets; any candidate then gives the same accuracy, although such oracle-dependent compute savings cannot be assumed at deployment.

The relevant prompt-tuning cell uses the stated equal-error-rate denominators. A different diagnostic cell has different denominators; attributing that diagnostic to Table 4 would be unsupported. The source’s documented training/validation split logic does not itself demonstrate leakage. The stated \(200\times50\times13{,}000=130\) million output-token arithmetic checks out; the 8192-token limit is per query, whereas a verification thread contains several queries. Historical cost totals were not reproduced.

Table 3 uses AIME denominator 14, while Tables 1 and 6 use 15. In , lines 120–178, the default excludes question 2024-II-9 but explicitly instructs that it still count as an unanswered question. The notebooks retain that default, whereas the minimal scripts request all 15. This explains the discrepancy and supports the conservative headline denominator; it does not establish score inflation. The denominator convention should be stated consistently.
## Limits and unresolved empirical claims

The staged release lacks historical query outputs, pinned dataset revisions/row IDs, and experiment-time configuration evidence. Cross-model protocol matching for the disclosed public o1 scores remains unverified. The manual grading audit was not repeated. Power-law descriptions concern the tested regime. Separate OpenReview access was blocked, not evidence of nonexistence. No later erratum search, author-code execution, paid query, installation, or new download was performed.
# Conclusion and disposition
Item | Judgment | Repair, adoption, and remaining work
Section 2.2 identifying inference | Major | Non-identification proved; actual quality mechanism needs evidence.
Table 6 universal comparison | Minor | Exceptions numerically verified; adoption not requested.
Examples and inspected procedure | No Issue Found | Scoped arithmetic/static checks; no historical inference rerun.
Historical data and external protocol | Needs Evidence | Exact artifacts and matched evaluation remain unavailable.
All scientific decisions are pending. No human review has been entered and no author adoption or independent acceptance has been claimed.

report: Abstract: Three Major concerns are supported in the core convergence/geometry analysis: the stated stationarity bound uses the wrong direction of an asymmetric divergence and has an admissible counterexample; the relative-smoothness proof uses a false zero-entropy premise; and the missing-information matrix need not be symmetric as claimed. Explicit corrections recover the reverse-divergence bound, the smoothness argument, and the spectral criterion, respectively. The principal EM–mirror-descent correspondence survives these checks. Local-rate hypotheses and experimental optimizer comparisons remain incompletely verified. Scientific decisions are pending.
Date: Initial review, 25 October 2026
Title: Scientific review of paper 0240
# Identity, model, and scope

The reviewed paper is Quentin Fruytier, Aryan Mokhtari, and Sujay Sanghavi, Learning Mixtures of Experts with EM: A Mirror Descent Perspective, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 17690–17726, publisher entry `fruytier25a`, OpenReview `wjZcCbTvrU`; assigned identifier I25-43609. The exact staged publisher PDF has 37 pages and was retrieved on 25 October 2026 at 04:11:22 UTC. References below use its printed page numbers, equal to physical PDF pages. The main text and embedded Appendices A–D were read. Critical equations and experimental figures were also checked on rendered original pages. No author implementation was acquired; this does not establish that none exists.

Equation reference: eq:model, eq:mirror. Write \(\sigma(u)=(1+e^{-u})^{-1}\) and \(\theta=(w,\beta)\). In the paper’s one-dimensional symmetric mixture of logistic experts (SymMoLogE), \[X\sim N(0,1),\quad P_\theta(Z=1\mid x)=\sigma(wx),\quad
 P_\theta(Y=y\mid x,z)=\sigma(yz\beta x),\qquad y,z\in\{-1,1\}.
 \] The observed population loss is \(L(\theta)=-\mathbb E_{X,Y;\theta^*}\log p_\theta(Y\mid X)\). For this model the specified mirror map and its divergence are \[A(\theta)=\mathbb E\{\log(1+e^{wX})+\log(1+e^{\beta X})\},\qquad
 D_A(u,v)=A(u)-A(v)-\langle\nabla A(v),u-v\rangle .
 \] At every finite parameter the Hessian of \(A\) is positive definite. All calculations below use population expectations or independently authored finite calculations; none execute author code or reproduce training experiments.
# Problem 1: the advertised stationarity bound is false
Judgment: Major, a false core convergence guarantee.
## Source claim and dependency

Equation reference: eq:claimed. Corollary B.1(1), Eq. (48), p. 23, asserts without additional convexity conditions that \[\min_{1\le t\le T}D_A(\theta^{t+1},\theta^t)
 \le \frac{L(\theta^1)-L(\theta^*)}{T}.
 \] Its proof instead establishes \(D_A(\theta^t,\theta^{t+1})\) in Eq. (52), p. 24. These are different quantities: by Theorem 5.1, their associated complete-data KL divergences have opposite directions. The corollary is the symmetric-model convergence result emphasized in Section 5, so the mismatch affects an explicit principal guarantee, not merely notation in an ancillary calculation.
## An admissible exact EM step

Equation reference: eq:step. Use [eq:model] (#eq:model) with \(\theta^*=(20,20)\), \(\theta^1=(0,20)\), and \(\Omega=\mathbb R^2\). Define \[c=\mathbb E|X|=\sqrt{2/\pi},\qquad
 m(a)=\mathbb E[X\tanh(aX/2)] .\] At the initial parameter, \(\mathbb E_{\theta^1}[Z\mid x,y]=y\tanh(10x)\). Under the true model, \(\mathbb E_{\theta^*}[Y\mid x]=\tanh(10x)^2\). The two exact M-step moment equations therefore give \[\beta^2=20,\qquad
 m(w^2)=\mathbb E[X\tanh(10X)^3].
 \] The function \(m\) is strictly increasing, since \(m'(a)=\tfrac12\mathbb E[X^2\operatorname{sech}^2(aX/2)]>0\). Its right-hand side in [eq:step] (#eq:step) lies strictly between \(0\) and \(m(20)\), so \(w^2\) is a unique finite point in \((0,20)\).

These parameters satisfy the Gaussian-feature and symmetric-logistic assumptions exactly. The complete conditional model is a regular minimal finite-support exponential family; \(A\) is strictly convex. The loss is finite and bounded below. Each block of the population \(Q\) objective is a logistic cross-entropy with nondegenerate soft targets, hence is coercive: along either parameter tail, a positive-measure interval of \(X\) contributes a positive linear growth coefficient. Its sublevel sets are compact and the M-step exists uniquely. Observed-loss strong convexity or identifiability is not assumed in part (1) of the corollary and is not needed here.
## Analytic contradiction

For \(u\ge0\), \(1-\tanh(10u)^3\le6e^{-20u}\). Bounding the Gaussian density by its value at zero gives \[\mathbb E[|X|\tanh(10|X|)^3]\ge
 c-\frac{12}{400\sqrt{2\pi}}=0.985c .\] On \(0\le |X|\le\tfrac12\), \(1-\tanh(2|X|)\ge1-\tanh1\), so \[m(4)\le c\{1-(1-\tanh1)(1-e^{-1/8})\}<0.972c .\] Thus \(w^2>4\). Since the expert parameter stays fixed and \(w^1=0\), [eq:mirror] (#eq:mirror) yields \[D_A(\theta^2,\theta^1)
 =\mathbb E\log\cosh(w^2X/2)
 >2c-\log2=0.9026219410\ldots .\] The initial observed distribution is uniform on \(Y=\pm1\), hence \(L(\theta^1)=\log2\). Moreover \(L(\theta^*)\ge0\), so \[L(\theta^1)-L(\theta^*)\le\log2=0.6931471806\ldots .\] This contradicts [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) for \(T=1\), independently of numerical integration. The distinction is not an iteration-index convention.

Parent Gaussian integration with 24,000 and 48,000 Simpson panels on \([-12,12]\) gives the same displayed values: \[\begin{array}{l|r}
 w^2&13.3796422672\\
 D_A(\theta^2,\theta^1)&4.6932948710\\
 L(\theta^1)-L(\theta^*)&0.6095153680\\
 D_A(\theta^1,\theta^2)&0.5962829095\\
 L(\theta^1)-L(\theta^2)&0.6063297660
\end{array}\] Independent auxiliary quadrature agrees. Numerical checks corroborate the analytic contradiction rather than supply its logical basis.
## Verified correction and limits
# Problem 2: a zero-entropy premise invalidates the smoothness proof
Judgment: Major for the printed core derivation; the corrected result is verified.

Section 3 (p. 4) defines \(H(\theta\mid\phi)=-\mathbb E_{X,Y}\mathbb E_{Z\mid X,Y;\phi}\log p_\theta(Z\mid X,Y)\), then asserts \(H(\theta\mid\theta)=0\). This premise is reused in the proof of Theorem 5.1, Appendix B.2(c), p. 20, Eq. (43), to equate the loss with its unshifted \(Q\) surrogate. Appendix B.3 applies that proof to the logistic case. Part (b) on p. 20 also uses an invalid Jensen chain purporting to make complete-data entropy zero.

Set true and current \(w=\beta=0\) in [eq:model] (#eq:model). Given \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) are independent uniform signs. Therefore, writing \(C_X=-\mathbb E\log p(X)=\tfrac12\log(2\pi e)\) and \(\bar Q=Q-C_X\), \[H(\theta\mid\theta)=\log2,\qquad
 L(\theta)=\log2,\qquad
 \bar Q(\theta\mid\theta)=2\log2 .\] All quantities are finite, the mirror Hessian is \(\tfrac14 I_2\), and the zero parameter is allowed by the symmetric model. The analogous zero-parameter linear model has \(H=\log2\) as well; its full complete-data entropy is \(2C_X+\log2>0\). Thus neither the posterior zero-entropy premise nor the displayed complete-entropy conclusion holds. The omission of the fixed \(C_X\) constant does not account for the nonzero posterior entropy.

Equation reference: eq:qdiff. Here is a precise repair. Let \(r_\phi(z\mid x,y)=p_\phi(z\mid x,y)\). Then \[H(\theta\mid\phi)-H(\phi\mid\phi)
 =\mathbb E_{X,Y}\operatorname{KL}(r_\phi\Vert r_\theta)\ge0 .\] Using \(L=\bar Q-H\), it follows that \[L(\theta)-L(\phi)\le \bar Q(\theta\mid\phi)-\bar Q(\phi\mid\phi).\] The independently checked \(Q\)-difference identity is \[\bar Q(\theta\mid\phi)-\bar Q(\phi\mid\phi)
 =\langle\nabla L(\phi),\theta-\phi\rangle+D_A(\theta,\phi).
 \] These two relations prove the claimed 1-relative smoothness, with the tangent upper surrogate \(\bar Q(\theta\mid\phi)-H(\phi\mid\phi)\). The KL/Bregman identity can likewise use the normalized score identity \(\mathbb E_\theta\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(X,Y,Z)=0\), without the false Jensen chain.

Interpreting the intended surrogate as implicitly shifted is a charitable reading, but it changes the explicitly supplied definitions and Eq. (43); the correction must be stated. The defect is tied directly to the unit-step justification and convergence analysis. The repair verifies those particular identities, not every local-rate claim. Evidence: pp. 4, 20–22, image `s20.png`, and both mathematical check records.
# Problem 3: the missing-information matrix is not symmetric
Judgment: Major for a false lemma used in the core spectral derivation; the criterion itself is repairable.

Theorem B.2, p. 26, converts relative strong convexity into a bound on the eigenvalues of \(M=C^{-1}K\), where \(C=\nabla^2 A(\theta)\succ0\) and \(K=\nabla^2_1 H(\phi\mid\theta)|_{\phi=\theta}\succeq0\). Its proof invokes Lemma B.3 (pp. 26–27), which asserts \(M=M^\top\). The proof diagonalizes \(C^{-1}\), then commutes that diagonal matrix with the transformed \(K\). A diagonal matrix need not commute with an arbitrary symmetric matrix. Likewise, left multiplication by \(C^{-1}\) alone is not a valid symmetric-matrix congruence for the displayed Loewner inequality.

For an exact model counterexample, use \(d=1\), true and current \(w=2,\beta=1\). Define \(f(u)=\sigma'(u)\) and \(a_v=\mathbb E[X^2f(vX)]\). Then \[C=\operatorname{diag}(a_2,a_1),\qquad
 K=\begin{pmatrix}h&b\\b&h\end{pmatrix}.\] Because \(f\) is even and strictly decreasing in \(|u|>0\), \(0<a_2<a_1\). Let \(U=wX/2,V=\beta X/2\) and \(P_\pm=P_{\theta}(Y=\pm1\mid X)\). The exact model gives \[P_\pm=\frac{\cosh(U\pm V)}{2\cosh U\cosh V},\qquad
 b=\mathbb E\!\left[
 \frac{X^2\{\operatorname{sech}(U+V)-\operatorname{sech}(U-V)\}}
 {8\cosh U\cosh V}\right]<0 .\] The inequality is strict because \(w\beta>0\) implies \(|U+V|>|U-V|\) for \(X\ne0\), an event of probability one. Hence \(M_{12}=b/a_2\ne b/a_1=M_{21}\). This proves nonsymmetry analytically within the Gaussian symmetric-model assumptions.

Parent integration gives \[C\simeq
 \begin{pmatrix}.0605275333&0\\0&.1442244802\end{pmatrix},\quad
 K\simeq
 \begin{pmatrix}.0552795015&-.0198487611\\-.0198487611&.0552795015\end{pmatrix},\] \[M\simeq
 \begin{pmatrix}
 .9132951315&-.3279294565\\
 -.1376240780&.3832879234
 \end{pmatrix}.\] The auxiliary’s swapped-parameter example independently gives the corresponding permuted matrix.

Verified repair. Use the symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix \(S=C^{-1/2}KC^{-1/2}\). Since \(M=C^{-1/2}SC^{1/2}\), its eigenvalues are real, nonnegative, and equal to those of \(S\). The correct equivalence is \[C-K\succeq\alpha C
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\preceq(1-\alpha)I
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \lambda_{\max}(M)\le1-\alpha .\] For the example, both matrices have eigenvalues approximately \(0.3086477446\) and \(0.9879353104\). Thus the intended spectral criterion survives, while the claimed Euclidean symmetry and printed proof do not. The Major judgment follows the invalid derivation’s direct role in the principal convergence characterization; it does not assert that Theorem B.2’s conclusion is false. Evidence: pp. 25–27, `s26.png`, `s27.png`, `calc.json`, `a_code.json`.
# Verified scope and unresolved claims
## Correspondence and convergence assumptions

For a conditionally exponential complete-data model, direct expansion gives the natural-space \(Q\)-difference used in Theorem 4.1. If the pointwise mirror step exists, its moment equation makes the constrained \(Q\) minimization equivalent to the stated expected KL projection. For the two symmetric models, [eq:qdiff] (#eq:qdiff) and the complete-data KL identity follow directly with the specified mirror maps. The Gaussian-feature Hessians are positive definite at finite parameters; uniform strong convexity requires a bounded region. These checks support the principal correspondence after the corrections above.

Theorem 4.2 explicitly assumes the projection inequality (25); the paper acknowledges that a nonlinear natural-parameter image need not be convex. That extra condition should not be silently dropped. Separately, its local-rate proof and Corollary B.1 apply local convexity at every iterate without establishing that iterates stay in the specified local set. A suitable invariant-region argument is still needed. Eq. (50) also states an initial objective-gap prefactor, while p. 25 derives a Bregman-distance prefactor. Neither a model counterexample to that stronger prefactor nor a complete proof of it was established here. These remain Needs Evidence, rather than additional claimed counterexamples.
## Norm-based interpretations

Theorem B.4’s literal description of a missing-information integrand as decreasing with \(\|\theta\|\) needs a directional qualification. In the logistic model its scalar factor is \(f(x(w+y\beta))\). For \(x=1,y=-1\), increasing \(\theta\) from \((4,2)\) to \((5,5)\) increases the norm from \(\sqrt{20}\) to \(\sqrt{50}\) while the factor rises from \(f(2)=0.1049936\) to \(f(0)=0.25\). The same inequality persists on a positive-measure interval of \(X\). Along a fixed ray and fixed observed data, the factor is nonincreasing; norm alone does not control changing directions.

This does not refute the conditional spectral criterion. Appendix B.7 explicitly retains \(|w-\beta|\) and \(|w+\beta|\) in its scalar bound, so it is not a uniform high-norm contraction theorem. Indeed, at true/current \(w=\beta=r\), the observed probability \(\tfrac12[1+\tanh(wx/2)\tanh(\beta x/2)]\) has equal \(w,\beta\) derivatives; the observed information has null direction \((1,-1)\) and \(M\) has eigenvalue 1, even for large finite \(r\). This is a scope boundary, not a counterexample to a claimed strict bound at those parameters. The high-norm eigenvalue orders in Lemma B.5, \(r^{-3}\) parallel to the parameter and \(r^{-1}\) transversely, were independently recovered by substituting \(t=rX\) in the Gaussian integrals.
## Optimizer and experimental interpretation

Algorithms 2–3 (p. 36) freeze the same responsibilities at \(\theta^t\). The score identity gives \[\nabla_\theta Q(\theta\mid\theta^t)|_{\theta=\theta^t}=\nabla L(\theta^t).\] Consequently printed Gradient EM is block-scaled GD, with preconditioner \(\operatorname{diag}(\gamma_2 I_w,\gamma_1 I_\beta)\); equal block rates make it exactly GD with that rate. Parent finite-data algebra checks both gradients to numerical precision. Different rates can explain different curves, so a historical implementation error is not established. Numerical learning rates, inner-loop budgets/tolerances, code, and raw trial data were not available to resolve the reported advantage.

The original figures use iteration axes, not wall-clock time; EM performs multiple inner gradient steps. The reported iteration advantage therefore does not establish an equal-compute timing advantage. Approximate M-steps and the greedy sparse extension are disclosed, and their exact-EM convergence is not claimed here. The FashionMNIST reference changes from 83.2% in Table 1 to 79.2% in later prose, altering the comparison with 78.5%; this local reporting discrepancy is recorded without attributing a different Table 2 result. Paired-test results and accuracy values were not independently reproduced.
# Disposition
Concern | Judgment | Repair and remaining scope
Eq. (48) divergence direction | Major | Explicit counterexample; reversed bound verified.
Zero-entropy proof premise | Major | Shifted-surrogate proof verified; original derivation invalid.
Lemma B.3 symmetry | Major | Similar symmetric matrix repairs the spectral criterion.
EM–MD correspondence | No Issue Found | Verified identities with normalization/regularity qualifications.
Local rates and empirical comparison | Needs Evidence | Region invariance, prefactor, optimizer settings, and run data unresolved.

No conclusion of whole-paper failure is made. Each supported Major concerns a core guarantee or its actual derivation. Repairs are analytically checked only within their stated scope. Adoption was not requested; scientific decisions remain pending and the human-review list is empty.
