Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of FlashTP
# Identity, version, and scope

This report concerns paper 0241, I25-43610: Seung Yul Lee, Hojoon Kim, Yutack Park, Dawoon Jeong, Seungwu Han, Yeonhong Park, and Jae W. Lee, FlashTP: Fused, Sparsity-Aware Tensor Product for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed proceedings PDF has 14 pages, retrieved on 25 October 2026. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with printed numbers.

The inspection covers the contraction/fusion argument in Sections 2–5, the arithmetic and interpretation of selected results in Section 6, and Appendices A–B. Relevant released wrapper, metadata, and FP64 CUDA source were inspected statically at commit `d52e41454afc9636cd51757b65df44e7bcdca178` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. This later snapshot is not established as the software used for the paper. The separate SevenNet integration snapshot was preserved and hash-checked, not comprehensively audited. Raw timing traces, training outcomes, MD trajectories, and hardware behavior were not reproduced. Separate OpenReview attachments were inaccessible during source preparation; their absence is not inferred.
# Checked mathematical and numerical claims

For fixed Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, one path computes \[y_k=\alpha w\sum_{i,j} C_{ijk}h_i e_j.\] Here \(\alpha\) is its fixed positive normalization. Traversing only nonzero \(C_{ijk}\) leaves the real-arithmetic contraction unchanged. Grouping paths for input reuse also preserves this expression; summing messages with the same destination commutes with the final linear reduction. Floating-point reassociation is a separate issue, acknowledged in the paper. The inspected backward and double-backward source has the expected product-rule terms within its specialized path layout; this is static evidence, not execution of the kernels.

The headline maxima in Table 2 are supported by \[2566.10/61.72=41.57647,\qquad 1822.67/29.99=60.77593.\] They round to \(41.6\times\) over e3nn and \(60.8\times\) over cuEquivariance, respectively. They need not occur in the same configuration. The l3i5 training and memory ratios in Table 3 are \(76/22=3.45455\) and \(8.52/1.37=6.21898\). Table 12’s eight displayed errors average to \(5.63614875\,10^{-6}\) and \(4.60173975\,10^{-6}\), matching the reported rounded summaries. These are checks of reported arithmetic, not independent latency or accuracy measurements. Numerical evidence based on uniform synthetic inputs does not by itself establish stability of all possible molecular trajectories.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Incompatible l4i5 tensor-product dimensions).  Table 11 (Appendix A.6, p. 14) gives hidden multiplicity 128 at each degree \(0,\ldots,4\) in layers 2–5, but gives output multiplicities \((288,576,704,736,640)\) for layers 2–4.
## Claim, conditions, and complete check

Equation reference: eq:counts. Sections 2.3 and 4 describe channel-preserving tensor products whose valid paths satisfy \(|h-e|\le j\le h+e\), followed by path concatenation and destination reduction. For hidden multiplicities \(m_h\) and one edge channel at each degree \(e=0,\ldots,4\), the displayed full-path convention implies \[
o_j=\sum_{h=0}^4 m_h\sum_{e=0}^4
\mathbf1_{\{|h-e|\le j\le h+e\}} .\] The table displays even parity for these irreps, so parity does not remove the paths in this stated convention. With all \(m_h=128\), direct enumeration gives \[(o_0,o_1,o_2,o_3,o_4)=(640,1536,2048,2176,1920).\] For example, scalar output requires \(h=e\) and therefore has five contributions of 128, totaling 640, rather than 288. More generally, even an omitted subset of full channel-preserving paths would produce multiples of 128, whereas 288 is not one.

For the tapered multiplicities, the same calculation gives \[(m_0,\ldots,m_4)=(128,64,32,32,32)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(o_0,\ldots,o_4)=(288,576,704,736,640).\] Both calculations are preserved in and `calc.json`. The original table was visually inspected in the rendered PDF; this mismatch is not introduced by text extraction.
## Counterevidence, impact, and correction status

An additional learned channel-mixing projection could change output dimensions, but Table 11 labels the tensor-product layer, and the depicted architecture places the subsequent equivariant linear layer after reduction. No such projection explains the published table as written. The tapered multiplicities strongly suggest a hidden-column transcription error, but the actual training configuration is not established by this arithmetic.

This is a local reproducibility/specification defect, graded Minor: a reader cannot reconstruct the stated l4i5 workload consistently. It does not demonstrate false timing ratios, nor a failure of sparse tensor-product algebra. Replacing the hidden column by the tapered multiplicities restores this dimensional identity; it is not a verified correction of the historical experiment.

Problem 2 (Released interface conflates instruction and output indices).  The pinned README describes a drop-in channelwise `uvu` replacement. The selected metadata implementation assumes that every instruction has a unique output-irrep index, without enforcing that restriction.
## Exact source and dataflow

In `flashTP_e3nn/flashTP.py`, lines 59–67 first construct an e3nn tensor product. Lines 94–107 route the ordinary, at-most-256-coefficient case to the large kernel. In , lines 824–832 construct one weight slice per instruction; lines 864–868 index CG fibers by output index, and lines 887–888 select the weight slice using that same output index. The source comment explicitly presumes unique output indices. In the corresponding FP64 forward CUDA file, lines 131–144 use this selected weight offset in the contraction, and lines 150–155 accumulate into the destination output.

The e3nn interface permits separate instructions to contribute to the same output block [Retained latex: \cite{e3nn}]. A specific admissible example is: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{in}_1&=32\times0e+32\times0e,&
\mathrm{in}_2&=1\times0e,&
\mathrm{out}&=32\times0e,\\
\mathcal I&=\{(0,0,0,\texttt{uvu},\mathrm{True}),
(1,0,0,\texttt{uvu},\mathrm{True})\}.
\end{aligned}\] Use two nodes and one directed edge \(0\to1\), source features all equal to one, edge scalar one, and 64 edge weights comprising 32 zeros then 32 ones. All values are finite. The scalar triangle and parity conditions hold; both input multiplicities satisfy the implementation’s multiple-of-32 assertion. Input-2 multiplicity is one, the scalar CG coefficient is one, and there is only one unique coefficient, so the public wrapper selects the inspected branch.

Let \(\alpha>0\) denote the common path normalization. Correct evaluation in every output channel is \(\alpha(0+1)=\alpha\). Both instruction output indices are zero, so the implementation assigns both the same weight block. If the tied sort chooses the first block, its static arithmetic is zero; if it chooses the second, it is \(2\alpha\). Neither equals \(\alpha\). Thus the discrepancy does not depend on the ordering of tied indices. An independent translation of the metadata arithmetic, with both tie orders, is included in `calc.py`; no author program was executed.
## Alternative interpretation and bounded consequence

The paper’s Figure 3 gives each path a separate output block. That specialized convention satisfies the implementation assumption and is important counterevidence to any allegation about the reported SevenNet benchmarks. The concrete defect concerns the broader released interface claim. There is no evidence here that the repeated-output example occurred in the published workloads, and the reviewed commit postdates publication.

The supported impact is therefore Minor, with historical experimental provenance unresolved. A documented and enforced unique-output restriction would narrow the API claim. Supporting arbitrary repeated-output instructions instead requires retaining instruction identities in both weight and coefficient metadata. Neither a complete implementation repair nor its GPU behavior has been verified.
# Overall dependence and conclusion

The core algebra of sparse contraction survives the checks, and selected reported speedup calculations agree with the tables. The two established issues affect a workload specification and a later public interface. New raw records or controlled reruns would be needed to determine any historical performance or training impact. A limited public issue search did not establish an author correction for these two issues; it is not an exhaustive erratum search.

Title: Technical Verification of Bayesian Optimization from Human Feedback
# Identity and inspected scope

Paper 0242, I25-43611, is Aya Kayal, Sattar Vakili, Laura Toni, Da-shan Shiu, and Alberto Bernacchia, Bayesian Optimization from Human Feedback: Near-Optimal Regret Bounds, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed proceedings PDF contains 20 pages. One-based PDF and printed page numbers coincide. The exact input hash is recorded in Appendix 5 (#app:evidence).

The review inspected the model, estimator, roundwise algorithm, Theorems 4.1 and 4.7, their main dependency chain in Appendix B, the proof in Appendix C, and the experimental specification. Released estimator code was read statically at commit . All 17 manifest-mapped source files were hash-checked. Numerical experiments, full external proof dependencies, every round-bound constant, and actual optimization execution were not independently reproduced.

The source-preparation manifest records unavailable separate OpenReview attachments. The embedded appendices are present. An arXiv metadata check on 25 October 2026 showed only version 1 of arXiv:2505.23673, dated 29 May 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}]. No author correction for the findings below was established by the limited search; no priority claim is made.
# Definitions and dependencies

Write \(\mu(s)=(1+e^{-s})^{-1}\) and \(\bar k\) for the dueling kernel induced by the normalized base kernel \(k\). For \(z=(x,x')\), \(h(z)=f(x)-f(x')\) and \(Y\mid z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mu(h(z)))\). Assumption 2.1 requires \(f\in\mathcal H_k\) with norm at most \(B>0\). Theorem 4.7 additionally requires observation locations independent of their labels.

Equation reference: eq:kappa. Equation (7) defines the unconstrained minimizer of the summed logistic loss plus \(\lambda\|h\|_{\mathcal H_{\bar k}}^2/2\), with \(\lambda>0\). Equation (2) defines \[
\kappa=\sup_{x,x'\in X}\frac1{\mu'(f(x)-f(x'))}.\] This is curvature at the true utility differences, not a uniform bound over fitted functions.

Theorem 4.7 supplies confidence intervals used in Appendix B to retain the optimum, eliminate inferior actions, and establish Theorem 4.1. That theorem and Corollaries 4.4–4.5 carry the central near-optimal regret and sample-complexity claims. Thus defects in this confidence argument have a direct core dependency.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The representer expansion changes the regularizer).  Equations (8)–(9), p. 5, and (36)–(37), p. 16, identify the RKHS estimator with an objective penalizing the Euclidean norm of its kernel coefficients. Those objectives are generally different.
## Original step and exact calculation

For \(h=\sum_i\theta_i\bar k(\cdot,z_i)\) and \(K_{ij}=\bar k(z_i,z_j)\), the reproducing identity gives \[\|h\|_{\mathcal H_{\bar k}}^2
=\sum_{i,j}\theta_i\theta_j
\langle\bar k(\cdot,z_i),\bar k(\cdot,z_j)\rangle
=\theta^\top K\theta.\] It does not give \(\theta^\top\theta\), as used in (9) and (36).

Take \(X=\{-1,1\}\), \(k(x,x')=xx'\), \(f=0\), \(B=1\), one deterministic duel \(z=(1,-1)\), and \(\lambda=1\). The base kernel is normalized by \(k(x,x)\le1\); the linear RKHS and deterministic design satisfy the assumptions. Under the BTL model, \(Y=1\) is an allowed event of probability \(1/2\). The dueling Gram matrix is \(K=[4]\). Setting \(s=h(z)=4\theta\), the correct objective is \[\log(1+e^{-s})+\frac{s^2}{8},\] whereas (9) gives \(\log(1+e^{-s})+s^2/32\). Their strictly convex first-order equations are, respectively, \[\mu(s)-1+s/4=0,\qquad \mu(s)-1+s/16=0.\] Both roots are positive and cannot coincide: subtracting the equations would require \(3s/16=0\). Independent scalar bisection gives \(s=1.0425969140\) and \(s=1.9656720992\), with predicted probabilities \(0.7393507715\) and \(0.8771454938\). This finite calculation confirms the analytically established distinction.
## Implementation, alternatives, and consequence

The pinned CPU source , lines 263–298, forms logits \(K\alpha\) and penalizes \(\sum_i\alpha_i^2\). Its gradient likewise uses \(\lambda\alpha\). The synthetic GPU and Yelp files use the same penalty. The CPU objective also averages the likelihood by the number of observations; at fixed \(\lambda\) this introduces a sample-size-dependent regularization rescaling relative to the paper’s summed loss. The one-observation example avoids that additional distinction.

Euclidean regularization is valid in an orthonormal RKHS feature coordinate system, but (8) explicitly uses kernel sections, which are not generally orthonormal. Whitening would require changing both coordinates and the prediction expression. Appendix C’s later switch to RKHS feature parameters therefore does not justify the displayed finite-coefficient objective.

This is a Major estimator/proof consistency problem: the estimator specified in (7), the claimed equivalent finite problem, and the implemented fit are not generally identical. The valid local correction is to use \(\lambda\theta^\top K\theta/2\) in the coefficient expansion, with consistent likelihood scaling. That identity repairs the conversion only; it does not repair the confidence proof below. The available repository’s README associates its CPU variant with the paper, but the inspected commit is not cryptographic evidence of the exact historical run.

Problem 2 (The central confidence-bound proof uses invalid curvature and concentration steps).  Equation (41), Appendix C, p. 17, states \(G_t(\theta^\star,\theta_t)\succeq\kappa^{-1}V_t\). The stated \(\kappa\) does not control the estimator segment. Moreover, the subsequent independent-noise argument treats fitted, outcome-dependent coefficients as fixed.
## Exact counterexample to the curvature inequality

Use \(X=\{0,1\}\), \(k(x,x')=xx'\), \(f=0\), \(B=1\), one deterministic duel \((1,0)\), and \[\lambda=\frac1{1+e}>0.\] The dueling feature is one and \(K=[1]\), so the two regularizers in Problem 1 coincide in this example. The true RKHS norm is zero, the base kernel is normalized, the observation point is independent of its label, and \(Y\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) is precisely the assumed model. Linear kernels are explicitly included in the paper.

For \(Y=1\), the derivative of the strictly convex penalized objective is \(\mu(a)-1+\lambda a\). Its unique zero is exactly \(a=1\). For \(Y=0\), symmetry gives \(a=-1\). In either case the integrated sigmoid derivative between the true parameter zero and the fitted parameter is \(\mu(1)-1/2\). Equation [eq:kappa] (#eq:kappa) gives \(\kappa=4\), and therefore \[\begin{aligned}
G_t&=\lambda+\mu(1)-\tfrac12=\tfrac12,\\
\kappa^{-1}V_t&=\tfrac14+\lambda
=\tfrac14+\frac1{1+e}>\tfrac12 ,\end{aligned}\] because \(e<3\). Thus (41) fails for both labels, hence with probability one. Numerically the two sides are \(0.5\) and \(0.51894142137\).

This does not depend on allowing a singular linear Gram matrix on the original domain. With the strictly positive-definite delta kernel on \(\{0,1\}\), take \(\lambda=2/(1+e)\). Along the dueling-feature direction, whose squared norm is two, the corresponding eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(1/2+2/(1+e)>1\), again contradicting (41). The fitted difference is still \(\pm1\).

A curvature bound uniform over the entire true-to-estimated segment would imply an appropriate related inequality. That is an additional condition, different from (2). Even bounded fitted parameters do not make the true-function curvature bound uniform over that segment. Shrinking true preference differences in later rounds similarly does not by itself control fitted differences.
## A separate obstacle to the concentration argument

For a concrete diagnostic, use \(X=\{0,1\}\), \(k(x,x')=xx'\), \(f(x)=x\), \(B=1\), the same fixed duel, and \(\lambda=1\). Let \(p=\mu(1)\). The fits are \(\pm a\), where \(\mu(a)+a=1\). Direct scalar evaluation gives \[a=0.4010581375,\quad G_1=1.2205835398,\quad G_0=1.2355365793.\] Consequently \[\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{Y-p}{G_Y}\right]
=p(1-p)\left(\frac1{G_1}-\frac1{G_0}\right)
=0.00194946856\ne0 .\] Conditioning on the design does not restore centering; conditioning on the two distinct \(G_Y\) values reveals the label. This numerical diagnostic illustrates the invalid inference about fixed weights. It is not a numerical counterexample to the final confidence interval itself.

The roundwise reset of observations in the released algorithm supports design independence conditional on previous rounds. Cross-round adaptation is therefore not the objection. The remaining dependence arises within the fitted estimator.
## Core impact and repair status

The proof explicitly uses (41) in both (42) and (43), which combine into (45) and Theorem 4.7. The latter feeds Appendix B and the main regret and sample-complexity statements. This demonstrated invalid derivation supports Major without requiring the whole algorithm or every empirical result to fail. Correcting the curvature step alone would leave the concentration obstacle. No complete replacement confidence proof, corrected regret guarantee, or verified implementation repair is supplied by this review.
# Overall assessment

The reported proof does not establish the central guarantee as written. Its ultimate truth under some alternative argument remains unresolved. The variance-based sampling and elimination idea, and the recorded experimental curves, are not refuted by these checks. The paper explicitly qualifies its scalar-feedback lower-bound comparison as informal because of the noise-model difference; this report does not mischaracterize that qualification as a missing formal proof.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Rethinking Addressing in Language Models via Contextualized Equivariant Positional Encoding
# Identity, scope, and evidence
The reviewed original is the 32-page PMLR version of Zhu et al. [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], including Appendices A–E. PDF and printed page numbers coincide. Its SHA-256 is

All 69 preserved source-file hashes match the staged manifest. Static inspection uses VITA-Group/TAPE commit ; its constructed pinned-source archive and member mappings remain preserved. The arithmetic submodule at commit was unavailable in staged material. No author code, training, or benchmark was executed.

The core chains audited are Eqs. 4–8 through Appendix B.1.1 to Theorem B.1/Theorem 4.1, and Eqs. 4–5 to Proposition B.9/4.2. The parent independently checked original mathematical pages, the counterexamples below, and relevant static code. Reviewer-written calculations are preserved in and . Original pages 22 and 24 were rendered and visually checked; final-report compilation and page inspection are separately recorded.
# Problem 1: The expressivity construction fails on legal inputs

Assessment: Major. Theorem 4.1 (p. 7), formalized as Theorem B.1 (pp. 18–20), claims a constant-depth, constant-width construction solving the \(\Pi(5)\) group word problem exactly. It explicitly depends on Lemma B.7 (p. 22), which defines \(M_{ij}=1\) for \(j\leq i\), including the diagonal, and asserts \[\prod_{j=1}^{i}(I-\xi_j\xi_j^\top)
 =I-\sum_{j=1}^{i}\big[(I+M\odot\Xi\Xi^\top)^{-1}\Xi\big]_j\xi_j^\top.\] Here \(\Xi\) has rows \(\xi_j^\top\); the right side is interpreted as outer products.
## A counterexample satisfying the construction

Use the permitted sequence \([\mathrm{bos}],[1\leftrightarrow2]\). The proof’s embedding has \[\xi_1=0,\qquad \xi_2=v=(1,-1,0,0,0,0)^\top,\qquad
 \Xi\Xi^\top=\operatorname{diag}(0,2).\] The printed inverse gives \(\eta_2=v/3\). After the third layer, \[E_{\mathrm{printed}}=I-\tfrac13 vv^\top,\quad
 E_{\mathrm{required}}=I-vv^\top,\quad
 E_{\mathrm{printed}}v=\tfrac13v\ne -v=E_{\mathrm{required}}v.\] Thus it is not the transposition matrix. This is an exact identity failure independent of precision, optimization, or a difficult input distribution.

The second layer uses this inverse (pp. 18–19), and the third invokes Lemma B.7 to identify Eq. 12 with the cumulative permutation (p. 20). The fourth-layer query and key give the score \(a^\top E b\), where \[a=(1,2,3,4,5,54.5)^\top,\qquad b=(1,2,3,4,5,-1)^\top.\] For the actual transposition the score is \(54-54.5=-1/2\); for the printed construction it is \(55-1/3-54.5=1/6\). The sign test in the proof changes on this legal nonidentity word.
## The exact decoder also fails

The final step on p. 20 uses \(h(z)=\min(1,\max(0,z))\) and asserts that a positive input becomes label 1. Even with repaired permutation matrices, an identity prefix of length \(i=3\) (bos followed by the same swap twice) has score \(1/2\) and decoder input \[z=\frac{e^{1/2}}{e^{1/2}+2}-\frac13\approx0.11852943,\qquad h(z)=z\ne1.\] The bos-only prefix gives input zero and output 0 instead of the stipulated identity label 1. The specification requires precise Boolean outputs at every prefix (pp. 17–18); an unstated threshold is not the printed construction.
## Counterevidence, repair, and impact

The recurrence in Lemma B.7 sums only over \(j<i\). Replacing the mask inside the inverse by its strictly lower-triangular part repairs this WY identity; our check verifies the repair on the legal example. Removing the diagonal from the causal attention mask elsewhere would be a different change. A decoder repair and a full uniform exact complexity construction still need proof.

These defects invalidate the supplied derivation of a headline expressivity result and warrant Major even if individual steps are readily repairable. They do not establish that no architecture in the family can solve the problem or that practical arithmetic accuracy is wrong. The broad family permits operations beyond the experimental parameterization; not all computational-precision and architectural-realizability questions are settled here.
# Problem 2: Shared orthogonal equivariance does not imply phase invariance

Assessment: Major. Proposition 4.2 (p. 7) and Proposition B.9 (pp. 23–24) assert invariance to uniform shifts of positional indices for RoPE or reweighted random Fourier features, assuming Eqs. 4–5. Those equations apply one common \(O\in O(R)\) to the last coordinate of every block. A shift produces block-dependent rotations \(O_{\Delta,m}\). The proof displays that dependence and then substitutes a single \(O\) in its induction. General left mixing of the \(ML\) rows in Eq. 8 does not commute with different block rotations.
## Explicit permitted two-layer counterexample

Set \(N=C=M=2\), \(L=B=1\), \(R=2\), \(x_1=(1,0)\), \(x_2=(1,1)\), and causal mask \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Use unit-weight Fourier features \[e_{i,1}=(1,0),\qquad e_{i,2}=(\cos(\pi i/2),\sin(\pi i/2)).\] Layer 1 has zero queries/keys and zero token value map with a token residual. Tokens remain unchanged while Eq. 7 averages the available positional rows. In Eq. 8 take \(W_1=I\), \(\psi(x)=I\), and \[W_2=S=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] The first positional block becomes \(F_1=(1,1)\), \(F_2=(1/2,1/2)\), and the second block is zero. Shifting all indices by \(\Delta=1\) before these operations instead gives \(F'_1=(0,0)\), \(F'_2=(1/2,-1/2)\).

In layer 2 take \(W_Q=W_K=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), \(\phi\) the scalar identity on the within-block dot product, and \(W_V=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Token 2 has logits \((1,1/2)\) before the shift and \((0,1/2)\) afterwards. The scalar values are 0 and 1, so its first output coordinate changes from \[\frac{1}{1+e^{1/2}}=0.3775406688
 \quad\hbox{to}\quad
 \frac{e^{1/2}}{1+e^{1/2}}=0.6224593312.\] A token residual adds the same quantity in both cases.

All parameters are finite. Zero queries/keys and the residual are admitted by the paper’s identity/averaging lemmas. The first positional operation is left multiplication and commutes with every shared right rotation. The second attention uses within-block inner products. Permuting tokens and mask together permutes both operations. Hence Eqs. 4–5 hold, but shift invariance fails. The theorem does not exclude zero frequency or require identical frequencies across blocks.
## Counterevidence and bounded repair

Appendix C (p. 24) uses a smaller experimental parameterization: learned matrices mix attention heads and share weights across \(M,L\). With matched frequency schedules across heads this avoids the cross-frequency mixing above. Table 8’s small shift-ID differences are meaningful evidence for that tested architecture, but cannot prove the unrestricted proposition. No failure of that table is claimed.

A sufficient corrected hypothesis requires invariance/equivariance under the actual blockwise shift subgroup, or the stronger product group \(\prod_m O(R)\). Restricting contextualization maps to commute with those rotations makes the induction valid. This repairs the symmetry implication under changed assumptions, without proving generalization or repairing Problem 1. The original false proposition supports a central claimed stability property, so Major is appropriate.
# Problem 3: Released fine-tuning freezes a stated trainable map

Assessment: Minor; released-version scope. Section 3.3 (p. 6) says the post-attention positional linear map is trained. In the pinned source, defines singular ; initialization at lines 848–852 zeros its weights. But freezes parameters unless names contain or plural . The additional default whitelist is (lines 65–67).

The actual name matches none of these strings. In the documented base-model fine-tuning route it remains frozen. At , the zero projection is added to the positional residual, so this direct attention-derived positional update stays zero. The distinct positional MLP remains trainable.

An explicit whitelist override or a nonzero loaded checkpoint changes part of this scenario; the documented launch supplies no such override. Correcting the singular/plural whitelist addresses this static discrepancy, but no training repair was run. Historical experiment/checkpoint identity is unestablished, so this supports a local implementation finding without invalidating benchmark tables.
# Coverage, positive checks, and unresolved items

Main definitions, both central proof chains, experimental descriptions, and Appendix C–E interpretation were inspected. Common-rotation invariance of left positional maps and inner-product attention is consistent with Eqs. 4–5. The fusion speedup is \(5.63/2.56=2.1992\), consistent with \(2.2\times\). The YaRN relative gain is \(33.92/32.82-1=3.35\%\), consistent with \(3.4\%\). Table 3’s FLOP increase is about \(13.87\%\); calling it negligible is a qualitative judgment, not an independently reproduced performance result.

Missing arithmetic code, the unavailable separate attachment route, historical checkpoint identity, full precision/complexity accounting, and empirical reproduction remain unresolved. A limited primary metadata check found arXiv v2 dated 21 August 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{arxiv}]; that is not a byte-level comparison or verified correction. No claim that no erratum exists is made.

The overall assessment is Major, based on Problems 1–2; Problem 3 is Minor. These are initial scientific judgments pending human review, with no acceptance decision. report: Abstract: The practical information-bottleneck-inspired objective is presented as a heuristic, not a proved mutual-information identity. Three implementation/specification concerns are established in the pinned public source: reference answers enter validation-mask construction, training never clears accumulated gradients, and matrix norms implement different penalties from entrywise sparsity and anisotropic total variation. Title: Initial Scientific Review of
DocVXQA: Context-Aware Visual Explanations for Document Question Answering
# Paper, source version, and scope

The original is Souibgui, Choi, Barsky, Jung, Valveny, and Karatzas, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 56549–56569 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Its 21 PDF pages include Appendices A–B; PDF and printed page numbers coincide. All 27 preserved file hashes match the supplied source manifest. The public source audited is commit of , distinct from an authenticated historical run.

The parent inspected the original method and evaluation text, principal tables, Appendix A implementation, Appendix B result descriptions, and the relevant source dataflow and training paths. Original p. 8 was rendered to check the ablation table and human-study description. Static archive-member comparison was independently assisted by a native auxiliary agent. No author code, training, weights, dataset or participant-level raw data was executed or acquired. Qualitative figure captions were read, but the full set of image explanations was not independently reproduced or exhaustively visually judged.
# Checked reasoning and necessary interpretation

Let \(T=X\odot M\). Equation (2), p. 4, uses \(I(T;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y\mid T)\) with fixed target distribution. For a predictor \(q_\theta\), \[\mathbb E[-\log q_\theta(Y\mid T)]
 =H(Y\mid T)+\mathbb E_T D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p(Y\mid T)\Vert q_\theta(Y\mid T)).\] Cross entropy is therefore an upper surrogate, with a model/optimization gap. The paper uses an approximation sign. Section 3.3 explicitly says the attempted direct mutual-information estimator did not work as expected and substitutes L1 plus continuity regularization. It would be incorrect to attribute to the paper an exact equality between that penalty and \(I(X;T)\).

These losses encourage compact masks and predictive utility; they do not prove global minimal sufficiency or causal faithfulness. Section 4.1 measures the answer model’s performance on masked images. The authors themselves recognize (p. 8) that retaining a number can permit an answer while omitting the context identifying it as the requested total. Human ratings add a separate perceptual criterion. This bounded interpretation is supported; a theorem of faithful recovery of internal reasoning is not supplied.
# Problem 1: Validation masks receive reference-answer information

Assessment: Minor for the evaluator/protocol mismatch under an annotation-free reading; the intended conditioning and historical impact need evidence. Figure 2 and Section 3.1 (pp. 3–4) describe a question/document input that produces a mask and then an answer. Section 4.1 (p. 6) describes comparing the subsequent predicted answer with ground truth. The pinned validation route instead admits ground truth before constructing the mask.
## Static evidence and dependency

In , the dataset’s reference answer is assigned to ; lines 174–177 tokenize it into . In , shifts those labels into decoder input IDs, obtains cross attentions, aggregates them into mask-head features, thresholds the mask, and only then generates a masked-image answer. The evaluator is called after each epoch and its ANLS selects the best checkpoint (lines 247–260).

Thus the validation mask is a function \(M_\theta(X,Q,Y_{\rm ref})\), whereas an annotation-free deployment mask must be obtainable from \(X,Q\) and model-generated information. For a multi-token reference, the shifted decoder input contains reference tokens after the start symbol. The aggregation includes those later positions whenever its selected length exceeds one; reference-conditioned decoder features can therefore affect the mask. This is a traced dependency, not a measured estimate of score inflation.

The standalone has the same reference-conditioned route, but also a misspelled keyword. We do not claim that file executes unchanged. The training evaluator uses the correctly spelled keyword, so the dataflow finding does not depend on repairing the standalone typo.
## Counterevidence and impact

The demo notebook first generates a full-image answer and then tokenizes that prediction to construct the mask (code cells 11 and 13). It supplies an intended annotation-free route and demonstrates that reference conditioning is not unavoidable. If a prediction equals the reference, the token sequences can coincide; no strict score inflation on every example is claimed. Explaining an explicitly supplied answer is also a legitimate conditional task, but its results must be identified as such rather than substituted for question/document-only performance.

Section 4.2 (p. 6) explicitly feeds ColPali a concatenated question and answer. It does not identify that answer here as ground truth or a first-pass prediction. This is material counterevidence to treating every evaluated explanation as necessarily answer-free. The static data dependency is established, but a stronger accusation that all answer conditioning violates the intended task is unsupported. The public validation implementation therefore does not by itself establish annotation-free masked-answer sufficiency. No archived run configuration or checkpoint-to-table mapping establishes that Table 1 used these exact bytes. Re-evaluation with generated first-pass answers, retained raw outputs, and a bound historical version is necessary to resolve that question. Replacing reference decoder inputs with generated ones is a candidate repair; no empirical repair has been verified.
# Problem 2: Training accumulates stale gradients across optimizer steps

Assessment: Minor; released training source. The method optimizes the combined loss in Eq. (3); Appendix A.3 specifies AdamW. In , AdamW is constructed at line 46, and each minibatch calls then at lines 133–134. The loop and epoch driver never call , assign cleared gradients, or invoke a clearing hook. The separate backbone fine-tuning script does clear gradients, but is not called by this training routine.

PyTorch backward adds to gradient buffers; optimizer stepping does not perform that reset [Retained latex: \cite{grad}]. Consequently, after initially empty gradients, the second step receives \(g_1+g_2\) rather than \(g_2\), and subsequent buffers retain still older gradients evaluated at earlier parameter values. This is not ordinary deliberate accumulation over a fixed microbatch group with one later step: the code steps every minibatch and never resets.

For a scalar initialized at zero, take two minibatch losses \(L_1(w)=w\), \(L_2(w)=-w\). With Adam moments initially zero, \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.999\), and \(\epsilon=10^{-8}\), the independent calculation gives
Second step | Gradient supplied | Adaptive update / learning rate
Reset for each minibatch | \(-1\) | \(+0.0526315784\)
Released no-reset pattern | \(0\) | \(-0.6700582447\)

Both have the same first-step weight, so the second-step decoupled weight-decay contribution is identical and cannot remove the discrepancy. This diagnostic demonstrates a changed optimization update, not a prediction of DocVQA accuracy.

An undocumented intention to use cumulative gradients would define a different optimizer and require justification; none was found in the inspected route. Resetting at the intended accumulation boundary restores ordinary minibatch semantics locally. Historical use, retraining effects and repaired metrics remain unverified.
# Problem 3: The released minimality loss uses induced matrix norms

Assessment: Minor; released objective implementation. Section 3.3 (p. 5) describes mask sparsity and anisotropic total variation: entrywise absolute mask values and horizontal/vertical differences. But calls with , and line 199 applies to a two-dimensional token-by-batch matrix. These are induced matrix 1-norms, namely maximum absolute column sums [Retained latex: \cite{norm}].

For a fully valid batch with \(B\) masks and \(N\) unpadded tokens, the sparsity term is \[L_{\rm released}=\frac{10}{BN}\max_b\sum_{n=1}^{N}|M_{bn}|,
 \qquad
 L_{\rm entrywise}=\frac{10}{BN}\sum_b\sum_n|M_{bn}|.\] Use \(B=N=2\), with masks \((0.8,0.8)\) and \((0.1,0.1)\). All entries are strictly inside the sigmoid range. The released term is 4, versus 4.5 for the scaled entrywise mean. Since the first sample uniquely maximizes the sum, the released sparsity gradient for both coordinates of the second sample is zero, versus 2.5 for each under the entrywise expression.

Likewise, take a batch of \(B=2\) identical, fully valid, unpadded \(2\times3\) masks, each equal to \[M=\begin{pmatrix}0.1&0.9&0.1\\0.1&0.9&0.1\end{pmatrix},\] horizontal absolute differences have entrywise sum 3.2 but maximum column sum 1.6; vertical differences vanish. With the code’s common denominator \(6-1\), the per-mask terms and their batch means are 0.64 and 0.32 respectively. Taking two masks is necessary here: the implementation’s unqualified would remove the batch axis for \(B=1\), so this witness uses \(B=2\) to retain the required three-dimensional tensor. The discrepancy does not depend on padding or a boundary mask value.

Both losses can still encourage some regularity; this is not proof of failed learning. A deliberately chosen matrix norm is a possible alternative regularizer, but is not the described entrywise penalty, and it changes which samples/edges receive gradients. Explicit absolute sums with a documented normalization would implement that intended penalty. Only the identities and finite examples were verified; no repaired training run or historical-table effect is established.
# Empirical checks, overall impact, and state

The 42-participant study uses ten images and shows ground-truth answers before ratings (pp. 8–9). It measures perceived context and clarity with answers disclosed; it does not directly measure unaided answering or a causal change in calibrated trust. The separate preference study reports \(163/252=64.6825\%\), consistent with 64.7%. Under independent Bernoulli trials, the two-sided exact binomial value is \(3.65\times10^{-6}\); under independent participants, all 12 favoring the method gives a sign-test value \(2/2^{12}=0.0004883\). These are conditional diagnostics, not a validation of independence. The participant-by-item response matrix and interval construction are unavailable, so uncertainty under repeated judgments remains Needs Evidence.

Table 1 openly shows a PFL-DocVQA unmasked accuracy change from 0.80 to 0.57: 23 percentage points, or 28.75% relative. This should accompany the prose description of a slight decrease. On DocVQA the proposed masked setting and ColPali baseline tie at accuracy 0.38 and pixel ratio 0.23, with ANLS 0.54 versus 0.50. No hidden arithmetic contradiction or universal strict dominance is established. Appendix A says postprocessing is applied to all compared methods.

The supported overall assessment is Minor. The established results are a conditional evaluator/protocol mismatch and local discrepancies in heuristic optimizer and regularizer definitions; no invalid core derivation or material failure of the paper’s core explanation claim is demonstrated by these checks. This scope, rather than a requirement to measure benchmark loss or authenticate a historical commit, determines the severity. The intended answer-conditioning protocol and historical empirical impact remain unresolved.

A related coefficient-only gradient-ranking argument requires additional kernel geometry. Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Nonparametric Teaching for Graph Property Learners
# Paper, version, and review scope

The original is Chen Zhang, Weixin Bu, Zeyi Ren, Zhengwu Liu, Yik-Chung Wu, and Ngai Wong, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 74515–74539 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. It has 25 pages, with printed and PDF page numbers coincident and Appendices A–C embedded. All 132 preserved source-file hashes match the staged manifest. Static code inspection uses commit ; this is a public acquisition version, not a proven submission-time commit.

The parent checked the RKHS/GCN assumptions, the kernel and loss-reduction proofs, the greedy criterion, original rendered pages 6 and 19, selected training/selection/metric code, and released log excerpts. Experimental design, displayed table arithmetic, and appendix result descriptions were inspected; training, timing and prediction-level metrics were not reproduced. Auxiliary agents supplied independent read-only checks, integrated and independently checked by the parent.
# Problem 1: Convergent training does not identify an arbitrary RKHS kernel

Assessment: Major. Theorem 5 and Eq. (20), p. 6, state that for convex loss and a given training set the dynamic GNTK satisfies \[\lim_{t\to\infty}K_{\theta_t}(G_i,\cdot)=K(G_i,\cdot).\] Section 3 defines an RKHS from a symmetric positive definite graph kernel. It does not impose an equality between that fixed kernel and the parameter-induced tangent metric.
## An admissible GCN with successful convergence

Let the graph domain contain a single one-node graph with \(X=[1]\), \(A=[0]\), and convolutional orders \(\kappa_1=\kappa_2=1\). This order is explicitly permitted in Section 4.1. A two-layer, width-one GCN with sum pooling is \[f_{a,b}(G)=b\,\operatorname{ReLU}(a).\] Choose the RKHS kernel \(K(G,G)=1\), which is strictly positive definite on this singleton domain. All scalar functions on the domain, including every network output and \(f^\star(G)=1\), belong to this RKHS. Use \(\ell(f,1)=\tfrac12(f-1)^2\), \(a_0=b_0=1/2\), and \(0<\eta\leq1/4\).

Gradient descent preserves \(a_t=b_t=c_t>0\), with \[c_{t+1}=c_t+\eta c_t(1-c_t^2),\qquad
 1-c_{t+1}=(1-c_t)[1-\eta c_t(1+c_t)].\] For \(0<c_t<1\), the sequence increases and stays below 1. Its limit is therefore 1. The loss and residual tend to zero, and the trajectory never reaches a ReLU kink. Nevertheless, \[K_{\theta_t}(G,G)
 =(\partial_a f)^2+(\partial_b f)^2
 =a_t^2+b_t^2=2c_t^2\longrightarrow2\ne1=K(G,G).\] This is a counterexample with genuine successful training, not a failure to optimize a nonconvex parameter objective. It also works for arbitrarily small positive learning rates in the interval above. The corresponding continuous flow \(\dot c=\eta c(1-c^2)\) has the same limiting contradiction.
## Invalid proof step and surviving statement

Appendix B, Eq. (33), p. 17, equates parameter-gradient evolution with functional gradient descent in the independently chosen RKHS metric. Membership \(f_\theta\in\mathcal H\) does not justify that equality. For differentiable parameter gradient flow, the chain rule gives exactly \[\frac{d}{dt}f_{\theta_t}(G)
 =-\frac{\eta}{N}\sum_i
 K_{\theta_t}(G,G_i)\,\partial_f\ell(f_{\theta_t}(G_i),y_i).\] A finite discrete step has a Taylor remainder; a time derivative does not need the additional remainder used in Eq. (16). Neither form identifies an arbitrary fixed canonical kernel.

Equations (36)–(37) further infer convergence of individual kernel sections from a residual-weighted sum as the residual vanishes. Vanishing coefficients or cancellation cannot establish that conclusion. Defining the canonical kernel retrospectively to equal an existing limiting tangent kernel changes the theorem’s setup; it does not prove convergence to the originally specified RKHS kernel.

The false theorem supplies the paper’s central bridge between finite-width GCN learning and canonical-kernel nonparametric teaching. Its failure is Major. Ordinary tangent-kernel dynamics and practical subset training remain meaningful; no replacement universal kernel-convergence theorem is verified here.
# Problem 2: Kernel upper bounds cannot provide the claimed minimum decrease
## Counterexample with identical tangent and canonical kernels

Use two one-node, edgeless graphs with features \(x_a=(1/2,0)\) and \(x_b=(0,1)\). A one-layer \(\kappa=1\) GCN is \(f_\theta(G)=x_G^\top\theta\). Choose its actual tangent kernel as the canonical kernel: \[K(G,G')=x_G^\top x_{G'},\qquad
 K_{\{G_a,G_b\}}=\begin{pmatrix}1/4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The kernel is strictly positive definite, with tight global upper bound \(\gamma=1\). Train on the one observation \((G_a,1)\), starting at \(\theta=0\), with squared loss, \(\tau=1\) and \(\eta=1/4\). The smoothness and step-size conditions hold; the tangent/canonical kernels agree throughout.

At time zero the actual flow gives \[\dot{\mathcal L}(0)=-\eta K(G_a,G_a)=-1/16,
 \qquad\hbox{whereas Eq.~\text{(eq:claimed)} requires }\dot{\mathcal L}(0)\leq-1/8.\] The inequality is false. Under a discrete-step reading, \(\theta_1=(1/8,0)\) and \(f_{\theta_1}(G_a)=1/16\), so \[\mathcal L_1-\mathcal L_0
 =\tfrac12(15/16)^2-\tfrac12=-31/512>-1/8,\] also contradicting the asserted reduction. This issue is independent of Problem 1.

Appendix B, Eq. (44), p. 19, upper-bounds a positive quadratic form. Equation (46) substitutes that bound into a negatively weighted term, which reverses the valid inequality direction. Even the scalar case above suffices, without any ambiguity about entrywise versus positive-semidefinite matrix bounds.

For canonical-kernel gradient flow the valid identity is \[\dot{\mathcal L}=-\frac{\eta}{N^2}d^\top Kd,\qquad
 d_i=\partial_f\ell(f(G_i),y_i).\] If additionally \(K\succeq\mu I\), this implies \(\dot{\mathcal L}\leq-\eta\mu\|d\|_2^2/N^2\). This changed-assumption flow statement is verified algebraically; it is not a repair of the published finite-step theorem or a proof of improved teaching speed.
## The related coefficient-only greedy argument

Section 4.3, p. 6, claims that gradient size can be increased by maximizing projection coefficients without computing kernel-section norms. In fact, \[\|d_i K(G_i,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal H}
 =|d_i|\sqrt{K(G_i,G_i)}.\] Consider the same linear graph family with \(x_1=(0.1,0)\), \(x_2=(0,1)\), targets \((2,1)\) and \(\theta_0=0\). The target is realizable by \(\theta^\star=(20,1)\). The largest-residual rule chooses graph 1, although its sample-gradient norm is \(0.2\), versus 1 for graph 2. For one selected example and \(\eta=0.1\), full empirical squared loss changes from 1.25 to 1.248001 if graph 1 is selected, or to 1.2025 if graph 2 is selected.

Thus coefficient ordering alone does not provide the claimed gradient-size justification. Equal kernel diagonals would repair the single-example norm ordering; multiple-example correlations and full-loss descent still require analysis. This does not assert that the heuristic must always choose an optimal step or cannot help empirically. Together with the false sufficient-reduction proposition, it undermines the core analytic justification, while leaving empirical time savings to separate evidence.
# Problem 3: The released sampler loses graph identity after shuffling

Assessment: Major, scoped to the pinned implementation of core GraNT selection. Algorithm 1 (p. 7) selects the graphs or batches with the largest stated discrepancies. In , the relevant training loaders use ; lines 265–267 pass that loader to . The sampler scores traversal order, then turns selected positions into ranges (batch variants) or (single variants). At these offsets index the underlying, unshuffled dataset. No original dataset IDs are retained.

Take dataset discrepancies \((1,2,30,40)\), batch size 2, ratio \(1/2\), and admissible shuffled order \((3,0,2,1)\), using zero-based IDs. The observed batch means are 20.5 and 16. GraNT(B) should retain IDs \((3,0)\) but returns \((0,1)\). Selecting one graph from each scored batch, GraNT(S) should retain \((3,2)\) but returns \((0,2)\). The supplied selection operation therefore need not return the graphs it scored highest. Largest-discrepancy teaching is the defining selection operation in Algorithm 1 and Eq. (23), not an incidental utility. Selecting unrelated dataset IDs directly invalidates that operation in the released route and supports Major independently of a measured change in accuracy or speed.

Identity traversal and accidental overlaps are valid special cases; the examples are not claims about an observed random seed. Making only the returned subset loader unshuffled does not repair the lost mapping. Carrying original IDs through scoring or using a separate unshuffled scoring loader would fix the index correspondence locally. Actual training outcomes and historical correspondence are unverified, so no measured loss of speedup is asserted.
# Problem 4: Released metrics have incompatible aggregation
Assessment: Major, scoped to the pinned core evaluation/comparison route; historical corrected values remain Needs Evidence.
## MAE is divided by the batch size again

The released QM9(B) log contains test MAE 0.005005646; the ZINC(B) log contains 0.004855736, corroborating the reported scale. They do not authenticate every table run. A common factor can preserve ordering among GraNT variants and their same-batch baseline. With a partial final batch, multiplying a published aggregate by 256 is not an exact correction: per-example or per-batch errors are required.
## Average precision is computed within batches

For ogbg-molpcba, evaluates AP per batch and averages it. AP is a ranking statistic and is not batch-additive. Consider batches of \((\text{label},\text{score})\) pairs \[,\qquad[(1,0.9),(0,0.8)].\] Each batch has AP 1, whereas global ranked labels \((1,0,1,0)\) give AP \((1+2/3)/2=5/6\). This finite discrepancy also applies to a task within a multitask evaluation. The released full-training molpcba log records 0.326976432, rounding to Table 1’s 0.3270; this supports result correspondence but supplies no predictions from which to compute a corrected AP.

The molhiv graph-level ROC-AUC branch concatenates predictions correctly; this finding should not be generalized to it. The noncommon MAE normalization and replacement of whole-dataset AP by a different statistic directly invalidate the released route as a faithful implementation of the paper’s central metric comparisons. This material evaluation defect supports Major without requiring a demonstrated ranking reversal. Neither the corrected historical MAE/AP values nor their comparative ordering are established. Reaggregation from bound prediction files is the necessary repair check.
# Overall impact, positive checks, and state

The kernel-convergence and sufficient-decrease statements are false as stated, so the overall assessment is Major. The released selection and evaluation paths independently contain Major defects tied to their core roles, with historical experimental attribution kept separate. The routine RKHS evaluation-functional derivative and tangent-kernel chain rule remain valid. The percentages calculated from Table 1’s displayed times are 36.6248%, 38.1947%, 30.9680%, and 47.3025%, consistent with the four headline rounded reductions. Their underlying timings were not reproduced.

The supplied cumulative timer includes selection overhead; there is no basis here for alleging that all teacher costs are omitted. Its epoch timestamp is sampled before the current epoch’s work, a narrower plotting limitation whose material effect was not quantified. Released ZINC validation losses round to the table’s loss entries while test losses differ; exact table/run provenance remains Needs Evidence rather than a definitive attribution.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Bayesian Active Learning for Bivariate Causal Discovery
# Identity, contribution, and scope

The original is Yuxuan Wang, Mingzhou Liu, Xinwei Sun, Wei Wang, and Yizhou Wang, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 63734–63754 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The preserved publisher PDF has 21 pages, with printed and PDF page numbers coincident; the embedded appendix occupies pp. 12–21. The source manifest and all three bound source files passed byte-hash verification. No verified public author implementation, commit, or standalone supplement is available in the staged material. A bounded primary-source lookup found the publisher and institutional entries, but no verified correction or newer implementation; this is not an absence proof.

The paper treats bivariate causal direction as a comparison of \(H_0:X\leftarrow Y\) and \(H_1:X\to Y\), under the stated causal assumptions. Its intervention objective is the prior-weighted probability of decisive and correct evidence, denoted \(r=P_{\rm DC}\). It proposes multistep planning, a count-based dynamic program for categorical interventions, and a smooth approximation for continuous interventions. Applications include binary systems, causal trees, and switch–light simulation.

This review checks the core probability definitions, posterior update, dynamic program and Appendix B derivations, the main experimental specification, and Appendix D’s continuous distribution. Original pages 5, 14, and 20 were rendered and inspected. The review does not reproduce experiments, digitize all curves, or authenticate unavailable run histories. The claimed complexity is polynomial in budget for a fixed intervention alphabet; this does not imply polynomial dependence on every problem dimension.
# Mathematical findings

Problem 1 (Major: the dynamic program optimizes a different objective).  Equation (7), p. 5, defines \[J(x_{1:K})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\gamma^k r(n_k),\qquad 0<\gamma<1,\] where \(n_k\) counts interventions in the first \(k\) positions. Equation (8), used by Algorithm 2 lines 10 and 16, instead applies \[J_k(n)=r(n)+\gamma\max_{a:n_a>0}J_{k-1}(n-e_a).\] Starting from zero, this weights the final reward most strongly and the first reward by \(\gamma^{K-1}\). It is not a constant rescaling of the stated objective.

Admissible finite witness. Take actions \(A,B\), binary outcomes, \(K=2\), \(\gamma=1/5\), equal hypothesis priors, and the paper’s thresholds \(k_0=10\), \(k_1=1/10\). Under \(H_0\), let \(Y\mid\theta_0\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\theta_0)\) independently of the action, with \(\theta_0\sim\operatorname{Beta}(57,1083)\). Under \(H_1\), use conditionally independent Bernoulli outcomes with independent action parameters \[\theta_A\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,999),\qquad
 \theta_B\sim\operatorname{Beta}(56,84).\] All prior parameters are positive. The means match one possible observational table: one success in 1,000 observations at \(A\) and 56 successes in 140 at \(B\). The conditional means are \(0.001,0.4\) and the marginal mean is \(57/1140=0.05\). The paper does not specify enough of its categorical fitting procedure to claim that it would return these exact concentrations; the witness satisfies the stated Beta-prior family.

Use precisely the shared-parameter integrated likelihood in Appendix B.1, equations (14)–(15). If an action-specific Beta\((a,b)\) parameter produces \(s\) successes and \(f\) failures, the probability of that ordered outcome subsequence is \[E[\theta^s(1-\theta)^f]
 =\frac{(a)_s(b)_f}{(a+b)_{s+f}},\] where \((a)_s=a(a+1)\cdots(a+s-1)\). Under \(H_0\) there is one shared factor over all observations; under \(H_1\) the factors for \(A\) and \(B\) multiply. Enumerating the two or four possible outcomes yields \[r(A)=\frac1{40},\quad r(B)=0,\quad
 r(AA)=\frac{278}{5705},\quad
 r(AB)=r(BA)=\frac{1083}{45640},\quad
 r(BB)=\frac{19}{235}.\] For \(AA\), at least one success gives decisive correct evidence under \(H_0\); for \(AB\), only \((Y_A,Y_B)=(1,0)\) does so; for \(BB\), only two successes give decisive correct evidence under \(H_1\). The strict threshold tests have no boundary ties.
Sequence | Equation (7) | Equation (8)’s value

The unique maximizers are \(AA\) and \(BB\). Algorithm 1 executes the first intervention of the optimized sequence, so the disagreement changes its immediate action. This is a concrete core dependency, without requiring a demonstrated loss of benchmark accuracy.

Counterevidence and repair scope. Proposition 4.1’s symmetry of each individual \(r(n_k)\) is valid under the joint likelihood. However, \(AB\) and \(BA\) have the same terminal counts and different Equation (7) values. The claim that the whole \(J(x_{1:K})\) is merely \(J(n_K)\) is therefore false. Count states still suffice if they store the best prefix value: \[V_0(0)=0,\qquad
 V_k(n)=\gamma^k r(n)+\max_{a:n_a>0}V_{k-1}(n-e_a).\] This is consistent with Appendix B.2, equation (16). Parent-written rational enumeration verifies that it recovers \(AA\) in the witness. Thus a local recurrence correction is available; adoption, actual implementation, and experimental consequences remain unverified. Replanning after each observation does not remove the first-action discrepancy.

Problem 2 (Major: the hypothesis update and joint Bayes factor disagree).  Section 4.2, p. 4, explicitly freezes parameter priors fitted from observational data. Its posterior recursion then multiplies the previous hypothesis posterior by the fixed one-observation predictive from equations (2)–(3). Appendix B.1, equation (14), instead places a single shared latent parameter outside the product of all observations. These define different evidence accumulations for nondegenerate priors.

For a fully specified categorical example, take equal hypothesis priors, \(\theta_0\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\) under \(H_0\), and independent \(\theta_A,\theta_B\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) under \(H_1\). Intervene repeatedly at \(A\) and observe successes. Every frozen single-observation predictive is \(1/2\), so \(B^{\rm fixed}_{01}=1\) after any number of observations. But after two successes, \[L_0=E[\theta_0^2]=\frac3{10},\qquad
 L_1=E[\theta_A^2]=\frac13,\qquad
 B^{\rm joint}_{01}=\frac9{10}.\] The corresponding posterior probability of \(H_0\) is \(9/19\), not \(1/2\). In general, for \(n\) successes, \[B^{\rm joint}_{01}=\frac{6(n+1)}{(n+2)(n+3)}.\] At \(n=56\) this is \(171/1711<1/10\), crossing the paper’s decisive threshold within its budget of 100, while the printed frozen-predictive update still reports no preference. This is evidence-model inconsistency, not an assertion about the true causal direction in a particular realized dataset.

Core consequence and counterevidence. The discrepancy directly affects posterior causal belief, stopping/evidence interpretation, and the probabilities used to plan future interventions. The deliberate decision not to refit parameter priors is disclosed, so this is not alleged to be an accidental missing code update. One can retain the original prior and recompute the integrated joint likelihood correctly; equivalently, sequential predictive probabilities must condition on previous outcomes.

A fresh independent parameter draw on every observation would make the fixed-predictive multiplication coherent, but changes Appendix B’s shared-parameter model. The empirical-Bayes point-mass alternative explicitly allowed in Appendix B.5 also makes the two products agree. The finding is therefore restricted to the nondegenerate shared-parameter formulation. No claim is made that a point-estimate implementation has this defect, or that the observed curves use one particular variant. The necessary full repair is a consistent probabilistic specification and its verified implementation.

Problem 3 (Minor: the continuous noise mixture is not normalized as printed).  Appendix D.4, equation (29), p. 20, specifies four components with \[\pi=\tfrac18\mathbf1+\tfrac34\operatorname{Softmax}(z),\qquad z\in\mathbb R^4.\] Since softmax sums to one, \(\sum_i\pi_i=4/8+3/4=5/4\). Consequently the displayed mixture of normalized Gaussian densities integrates to \(5/4\), not one.

The local distribution specification is invalid. Explicit renormalization, or corrected coefficients satisfying \(4a+b=1\), restores a valid mixture. Neither is verified as the author’s intended repair. An omitted normalization in a sampler could remove the practical problem; inaccessible code prevents checking it. No change to the published continuous results is demonstrated.
# Impact, positive checks, and conclusion state

The overall assessment is Major, because Problems 1 and 2 invalidate central derivations or connect incompatible mathematical objects in the proposed intervention method. This conclusion does not require the whole approach to fail. Count-based dynamic programming remains viable, the single-stage decisive-evidence objective is a well-defined utility under a specified model, and empirical superiority remains a separate question.

Appendix B.6’s equation (22) has a negative-argument exponential sign inconsistent with equation (23); the operative expressions (24)–(26) contain the bounded, correctly signed ReLU form. This nearby correction is counterevidence against treating it as an established continuous optimizer failure. The multivariate identifiability limitation is expressly acknowledged. Table 2 does not show uniform superiority over multistep information gain: its second setting is 9.88 versus 9.66 interventions, while the other three displayed means favor the proposed method slightly. Without paired raw results, uncertainty in these differences is unresolved.

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Ensemble Distribution Distillation via Flow Matching
# Paper, version, contribution, and scope

The original is Jonggeon Park, Giung Nam, Hyunsu Kim, Jongmin Yoon, and Juho Lee, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 48170–48191 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The preserved publisher PDF has 22 pages, with printed and PDF page numbers coincident. The staged release [Retained latex: \cite{code}] is pinned to

Its metadata date is 19 August 2025; it is not authenticated as the historical experimental commit. All 44 manifest-bound source files passed hash checks. The auxiliary member check matched all 33 included archive members against extracted bytes, manifest SHA-256 and Git blob identities; 22 payload entries were excluded during preparation. Existing archives and identities remain unchanged.

EDFM learns a conditional distribution of teacher logits by flow matching, using a fixed teacher feature extractor and a lightweight vector-field network. Samples of logits are transformed by softmax and their probabilities averaged. The main scientific questions are whether this preserves teacher diversity and fidelity while reducing inference cost. The inspected evidence covers the main flow construction, Algorithms 1–2, the preconditioning derivation, image-evaluation claims, metric definitions and relevant released image-model paths. Original pages 5, 16, 17 and 22 were visually inspected. Full language-model implementations, historical predictions, timing traces and a complete fidelity-analysis driver are unavailable in the staged release. No model training or author-code execution was performed. A bounded primary-source lookup did not identify a verified author correction of the findings below.
# Problems and independent checks

Problem 1 (Major: the printed sampler runs the forward field backward).  Equations (11)–(13), p. 4, use \(Z_t=tZ_1+(1-t)Z_0\), Gaussian noise at \(t=0\), teacher logits at \(t=1\), and regression target \(Z_1-Z_0\). Algorithm 2, p. 5, instead initializes that noise at \(t_N=1\), integrates to decreasing times, and finishes with \(z\leftarrow z-(t_1-t_0)u_\phi(t_1,z,x)\). This does not sample the target specified by the training path.

Fix \(x\), take independent \(Z_0\sim N(0,16I)\) and \(Z_1\sim N(\mu,I)\), with \(\mu=(1,-1)\) in a two-logit example. Define \[S(t)=t^2+16(1-t)^2>0.\] The population minimizer of the conditional squared-velocity regression is \[v^*(t,z)=E[Z_1-Z_0\mid Z_t=z]
 =\mu+\frac{17t-16}{S(t)}(z-t\mu).\] The exact solution from an arbitrary time \(s\) is \[z(t)=t\mu+\sqrt{\frac{S(t)}{S(s)}}\,[z(s)-s\mu].\] Differentiation verifies the identity directly, since \(S'(t)=2(17t-16)\). Correct forward integration from \(s=0\) transports \(N(0,16I)\) to \(N(\mu,I)\). Starting \(N(0,16I)\) at \(s=1\), as printed, instead gives \[Z_\epsilon\sim N\!\left(
 [\epsilon-\sqrt{S(\epsilon)}]\mu,\;16S(\epsilon)I\right).\] For \(\epsilon=0.001\), the mean is approximately \(-3.995000125\,\mu\) and the covariance is \(255.488272I\). The desired mean and covariance are \(\mu\) and \(I\). This smooth, nonsingular example rules out an explanation based only on endpoint instability or numerical solver error. The effect is not an irrelevant common logit offset.

Core dependency and counterevidence. The training-to-sampling connection is necessary to the paper’s principal distribution-distillation method, so an invalid sampling derivation warrants Major even if easily repaired. However, constructs increasing times from 0 to 1 and uses positive Euler/Heun increments. trains the matching forward target. Thus the available sampler already has the correct direction; there is no evidence here that Algorithm 2’s defect generated the published scores. A corrected paper algorithm should follow that increasing-time convention, or explicitly transform both time and velocity for a reversed convention.

Problem 2 (Major: the preconditioning loss rearrangement is false).  Appendix A.3, equations (14)–(24), pp. 16–17, claims to derive the time weight used by the training scheme in Section 4.3. Equation (15) is not equal to its purported rearrangement (16). The resulting condition \(\lambda/c_{\rm out}^2=1\) reverses the factor needed for a unit-coefficient normalized regression target.

Let \(V=Z_1-Z_0\) and \(D=c_{\rm skip}Z_t+c_{\rm out}F\). Exact algebra gives \[\lambda\|D-V\|^2
 =\lambda c_{\rm out}^2
 \left\|F-\frac{V-c_{\rm skip}Z_t}{c_{\rm out}}\right\|^2.\] For independent centered endpoint coordinates with variances \(a,b>0\), write \(S=t^2a+(1-t)^2b\). Minimizing the residual variance gives \[c_{\rm skip}=\frac{ta-(1-t)b}{S},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(V-c_{\rm skip}Z_t)=\frac{ab}{S}
 =c_{\rm out}^2.\] Thus the normalized target has unit variance when \(c_{\rm out}=\sqrt{ab/S}\), and its loss coefficient is one when \[\lambda=\frac1{c_{\rm out}^2}=\frac{S}{ab}.\] The paper instead obtains \(\lambda=ab/S=c_{\rm out}^2\). It also writes \(c_{\rm out}\) equal to a variance in equation (19), although equation (22) is its square root.

A direct identity check avoids any interpretation of training dynamics. At \(t=1/2\), \(a=1\), \(b=16\), \(Z_1=1\), \(Z_0=0\) and \(F=0\), the printed coefficients give \[c_{\rm skip}=-\frac{30}{17},\qquad
 c_{\rm out}^2=\lambda=\frac{64}{17}.\] The integrand of equation (15) evaluates to \(65536/4913=13.3393038876\) at this realization, whereas that of the printed equation (16) evaluates to \(1024/289=3.5432525952\). This pointwise inequality also persists after expectation: at fixed \(t=1/2\), independent centered Gaussian endpoints of variances 1 and 16 give \(E[(V-c_{\rm skip}Z_t)^2]=64/17\), so the two conditional expected integrands are \(4096/289\) and \(64/17\), respectively. More generally, for \(F=0\) let \(r(t)=16/[t^2+16(1-t)^2]\). These expectations are \(r(t)^2\) and \(r(t)\); since \(r(t)>1\) for \(t>0\), integrating over the paper’s time distribution cannot cancel the difference. The claimed equality of losses fails. Under the actual factorization, the printed normalized-target coefficient is \(4096/289\approx14.1730\) at this time and 256 at \(t=1\), rather than one.

Impact and limits. This is an invalid derivation of the loss specification explicitly used to justify the proposed training preconditioning. Its core methodological role supports Major; the classification does not depend on the proof’s appendix location or on benchmark deterioration. The correctly derived \(c_{\rm in}\) and \(c_{\rm skip}\), and the final expression for \(c_{\rm out}\), remain useful. Positive time-only weights preserve the unrestricted pointwise population flow minimizer, so generic flow-matching consistency is not refuted. Finite-capacity optimization may differ, but its empirical magnitude was not measured.

The release implements the printed MLP coefficients in , but minimizes plain squared velocity error, \(\lambda=1\). It implements neither the printed weight nor the unit-coefficient corrected weight. The local algebraic repair is verified; the intended historical training choice and any corrected experiments are not.

Problem 3 (Major for the pinned official EnDD comparison route; historical effects Needs Evidence).  The released EnDD baseline mixes teacher precision across minibatch examples. In , the entropy-like has shape \((B,)\), but division by produces a \((B,B)\) matrix. The final mean therefore replaces a mean of matched example terms by a product of means. This is a demonstrated objective error, not merely a possible shape concern.

Write \(A_i\) for the student Dirichlet KL penalty, ignoring constants independent of student parameters, and \(\tau_i\) for the corresponding teacher precision. Holding the code’s unshifted precision convention fixed to isolate broadcasting, the intended and actual terms are respectively \[\frac1B\sum_i\frac{A_i}{\tau_i},
 \qquad
 \left(\frac1B\sum_iA_i\right)
 \left(\frac1B\sum_j\frac1{\tau_j}\right).\] For \(B=2\), take student Dirichlets \((2,2)\) and \((3,3)\), whose KL penalties to the uniform Dirichlet are approximately \(0.125092803\) and \(0.267864048\). With \(\tau=(1,9)\), the paired penalty is \(0.0774277373\), while broadcasting gives \(0.109154681\).

The error can change learned diversity even at an ideal optimum. Let both teacher means be \((1/2,1/2)\), with precisions 1 and 9. These values are realizable by symmetric teacher predictions \((q_\tau,1-q_\tau)\) and \((1-q_\tau,q_\tau)\), where \[q_\tau=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-e^{-1/\tau}}}{2}.\] Substitution into the released precision formula yields \(\tau\). For a per-example coefficient \(c\), the proxy objective \[E_Q[-\tfrac12\log q_1-\tfrac12\log q_2]
   +c\,D_{\rm KL}(Q\|\operatorname{Dir}(1,1))\] is minimized by \(\operatorname{Dir}(1+1/(2c),1+1/(2c))\). Correct unshifted pairing gives \((1.5,1.5)\) and \((5.5,5.5)\). Broadcasting makes both coefficients \((1+1/9)/2=5/9\), so both optima become \((1.9,1.9)\). The distinction in teacher uncertainty is lost. These closed-form values use the ideal zero-epsilon objective and the unshifted convention solely to isolate broadcasting. For \(K\) uniform teacher classes the same variational identity gives the unique optimum \(Q_c^*=\operatorname{Dir}((1+1/(Kc))\mathbf1)\): the objective equals \(cD_{\rm KL}(Q\Vert Q_c^*)\) plus a constant. At the configured \(K=10\), precisions 1 and 9 give symmetric concentrations 1.1 and 1.9 when paired, but 1.18 for both inputs after broadcasting. Repeating the two types 128 times gives batch size 256. Uniform means with either precision are realizable using the ten cyclic permutations of \((p,(1-p)/9,\ldots,(1-p)/9)\), each repeated three times: the precision formula gives \(\tau=4.5/\Delta(p)\) with \(\Delta(p)=\log(0.1)-[\log p+9\log((1-p)/9)]/10\), which ranges from zero to infinity for \(0.1<p<1\). The configured epsilon perturbs these closed-form numbers but leaves the erroneous shared coefficient and identical per-input objectives intact.

Reachability and counterevidence. The official README’s EnDD command invokes with ; that configuration selects , ten classes, batch size 256, thirty teachers and offsets 1. Lines 211–215 of the driver call this loss. Sections 5.2–5.3 and Figures 1 and 3 (pp. 1,6–7) make teacher-diversity transfer and full-distribution Wasserstein fidelity central comparisons; Appendix B, equation (39), specifies the per-example teacher-precision objective. The witness destroys precisely the conditional uncertainty that this baseline should preserve. It therefore supports Major for the official released comparison/reproduction route. Batch size one or equal teacher precisions remove this particular cross-example error, but general configured batches need not meet those conditions. The historical commit, predictions and corrected comparisons are not supplied; the direction and magnitude of changes to the published figures remain Needs Evidence.

There are two related specification distinctions. First, equation (39) divides by the shifted teacher precision \(\sum_k\widehat\beta_k=\tau+K\,t_{\rm offset}\), whereas the code constructs shifted but uses unshifted . Second, the statement that the shifted Dirichlet mean equals raw-logit softmax is false: for ten raw exponential logits \((9,1,\ldots,1)\), the shifted mean’s first probability is \(5/14\), while softmax gives \(1/2\). Nevertheless, removing the training offset at prediction can intentionally recover the original ensemble mean when \(\widehat\alpha=\beta+1\). This counterinterpretation prevents inferring an unfair baseline solely from the use of softmax. The broadcasting defect is independent of that convention.
# Overall impact, positive checks, and state

The overall assessment is Major: the printed inference and training derivations contain demonstrated errors tied to the core method. The released EnDD objective also has a Major error that materially changes the input-specific predictive distributions used by the official baseline route. The available implementation provides important counterevidence about the printed sampler and is not treated as an execution of every printed equation. The forward interpolation and conditional-expectation regression are coherent; no issue was found with those identities within the checked scope. Feature extraction is reused once per input in , supporting the stated architecture-level efficiency mechanism.

The ambiguity decomposition uses a disclosed geometric/logit centroid, not arithmetic probability pooling; it should be assessed under that convention. The released equal-sample Wasserstein calculation uses squared pair costs and assignment followed by a square root, consistent with uniform equal-size empirical measures; the solver was not executed or exhaustively certified. Table 2 supports improved displayed NLL for EDFM relative to the listed students, but does not show uniformly best accuracy or calibration. No significance or runtime claims are independently reproduced.

The release’s sampler uses \(s-1\) Heun intervals and one final Euler interval, hence \(2s-1\) function evaluations. Its configuration \(s=7\) implies 13 NFEs, whereas Appendix A.3 describes seven NFEs for the main setting. This remains a configuration/run correspondence gap, not proof that measured timings are false.
