Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of TtBA
# Identity and inspected scope

Feiyang Wang, Xingquan Zuo, Hai Huang and Gang Chen, TtBA: Two-third Bridge Approach for Decision-Based Adversarial Attack, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43631 (local 0262), is reviewed in its 18-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Physical PDF and printed page numbers agree. The embedded appendices and relevant released code at commit `ea6d1649fccda0eb8392c9171e43cc9e0974acf9` were inspected [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. This snapshot is not established as the publication-time executable.

The central geometric interpretation has a demonstrated invalid derivation. Separate local errors concern a Taylor coefficient, a query-count bound and the released evaluator. The empirical two-thirds rule remains an empirical choice; this review neither proves it optimal nor refutes its observed benchmark performance.
# Definitions and the central geometric problem

For a correctly classified source image \(x\), let \(g(d)\) be the radial distance to the first adversarial boundary along \(\hat d=d/\|d\|_2\). Given current unit direction \(d\) and unit boundary normal \(N\), the paper defines \[u(k)=\frac{(1-k)d+kN}{\|(1-k)d+kN\|},\quad G(k)=g((1-k)d+kN).\] The actual boundary curve in image space is \(z(k)=x+G(k)u(k)\); it is not the Cartesian graph \((k,G(k))\).

Problem 1 (Curvature of the wrong geometric object: Major).  Appendix B.3, p. 13, Eq. (9), identifies the decision boundary’s curvature in the physical two-dimensional plane with \(b/(1+a^2)^{3/2}\), where \(a=G'(0)<0\), \(b=G''(0)>0\). This is the graph-curvature formula for \((k,G(k))\), not for \(z(k)\).
## A counterexample with a valid bridge

Take a two-pixel image space \([0,1]^2\), source \(x=(1/2,1/2)\), and the smooth radial boundary about \(x\) \[\rho(\theta)=r[1-\sqrt3\sin\theta+v(1-\cos\theta)],
\qquad r=1/100,\quad v=22.\] Assign the original class to the interior and the adversarial class to the boundary and exterior. Its radial extrema are \(r(23\pm\sqrt{487})\), approximately \(0.00931924\) and \(0.450681\). Thus every radius is positive, the entire curve is inside the pixel square, and every ray from \(x\) has exactly one boundary intersection. The curve is smooth and regular because \(\rho^2+(\rho')^2>0\).

Equation reference: eq:G. At \(\theta=0\), the current boundary point is \(p=x+r(1,0)\), with \(d=(1,0)\). Since \(\rho'(0)=-\sqrt3 r\), the actual outward unit normal is \[N=\frac{(\rho(0),-\rho'(0))}{\sqrt{\rho(0)^2+\rho'(0)^2}}=(1/2,\sqrt3/2).\] Consequently the paper’s exact interpolation gives \[
G(k)=r\left[23-\frac{22-(19/2)k}{\sqrt{1-k+k^2}}\right].\] Direct differentiation yields \(a=-3r/2=-0.015\) and \(b=15r=0.15\), satisfying the stated derivative signs. Solving \(G(k)=G(0)=r\) gives the nonzero bridge \[k_{\rm bridge}=\frac{88}{525}=0.167619\ldots\in(0,1).\] Squaring is legitimate because \(22-(19/2)k\) is positive throughout \([0,1]\); the other root is \(k=0\). Moreover \(G(k)<r\) between these roots. This example therefore also has the bridge required by the method, rather than exploiting a missing-ray or missing-bridge pathology.
## Alternative reading and core dependence

If the intended object is the auxiliary graph \((k,G(k))\), Eq. (9) is valid for that graph. It then cannot be used as a derivation of the physical decision-boundary curvature. Page 3 identifies detecting varied boundary curvatures as the first contribution; pp. 5–6 use the bridge threshold to characterize narrow high-curvature regions and motivate the escape rule. The missing geometric correspondence therefore affects a central explanatory contribution and supports Major.

This witness tests the exact Eq. (9), not the separate higher-order-neglect step in Eq. (10). No assumption that its cubic remainder is negligible is used. The example does not show the attack fails or loses benchmark accuracy. The correct general plane-curve formula is \[\kappa=\frac{|\det(z',z'')|}{\|z'\|^3},\qquad
z'=G'u+Gu',\quad z''=G''u+2G'u'+Gu''.\] It restores the curvature calculation, but a full revised relation between this curvature and \(k_{\rm bridge}\) remains unproved. Even for graph curvature, an inverse proportionality inferred from \(-2a/k_{\rm bridge}\) requires controlling \(a\) across the comparison.
# Independent local findings
Problem 2 (The cubic correction has the opposite sign: Minor).  Appendix B.4, p. 14, Eq. (19), expands the stationary point of \(a+bk+(c/2)k^2=0\) with a positive correction \(a^2c/(2b^3)\).

For \(b>0\) the branch continuous at \(c=0\) is \[k(c)=\frac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-2ac}}{c}
=-\frac ab-\frac{a^2c}{2b^3}+O(c^2).\] Substitution \(k=-a/b+tc\) gives \(bt+a^2/(2b^2)=0\), independently confirming the negative sign. With \(a=-0.1\), \(b=1\), \(c=0.02\), the exact root is \(0.0999001995\), the printed first-order expression is \(0.1001\), and the corrected expression is \(0.0999\). The root is inside \((0,1)\), the discriminant is positive, and \(G''=b+ck>0\). The quadratic relation \(k_{\min}=k_{\rm bridge}/2\) survives. The paper uses two-thirds empirically (p. 5 and Appendix G), so this local sign error is not inflated into a disproof of that heuristic.

Problem 3 (The claimed query upper bound is below the sum: Minor).  Appendix C, p. 15, Eqs. (21)–(22), sets \(q_i=24+\lceil30\sqrt i\rceil\) and claims \[Q_n=10+\sum_{i=1}^{n}q_i\leq24n+20n^{3/2}-34.\]

At \(n=1\), the exact left side is \(64\) and the claimed upper bound is \(10\). At \(n=57\) they are \(10115\) and \(9940.811256\), respectively. An increasing-function sum was replaced by an integral over \([1,n]\) in the wrong direction, and the ceiling contribution was dropped. For every integer \(n\geq1\), a valid conservative replacement is \[Q_n\leq10+25n+20[(n+1)^{3/2}-1],\] using \(\lceil t\rceil\leq t+1\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt i\leq\int_1^{n+1}\sqrt x\,dx\). In the paper’s modeled count, \(Q_{56}=9864\) and \(Q_{57}=10115\). The \(O(n^{3/2})\) order and qualitative small overhead survive. Actual boundary-search costs were stated approximately, so the empirical mean of 57 iterations is not refuted by this model-level correction.

Problem 4 (Released distortion is capped by the source-image norm: Minor).  Section 3 Eq. (1) and Section 5.2 use \(\|\tilde x-x\|_2\). The release, `TtBA.py`, lines 232–241, instead stores \(\min(\|x\|_2,\|\tilde x-x\|_2)\) in the distortion curve and uses it for the success threshold.

Let \(x=1/5\), classify \(z<4/5\) as the original class and \(z\geq4/5\) as adversarial, and set \(\epsilon=3/10\). The source is correctly classified, both source and boundary are legal pixels, and the true boundary distance is \(3/5>\epsilon\). The recorded value is \(1/5<\epsilon\), falsely satisfying the threshold. Clipping and the stated \(10^{-4}\) search tolerance do not erase this margin. Removing the cap and measuring the actual clamped adversarial perturbation corrects this metric definition, but no full release patch was executed. The source norm can exceed all encountered perturbations in other runs, so the cap may be inactive there. Publication-time logs are needed to determine historical impact; no published table is declared wrong from this snapshot alone.

Problem 5 (Normal-estimation settings differ from the stated recipe: Minor).  Algorithm 3, p. 16, uses normalized Gaussian directions with radius \(r_N=0.0003\). In `TtBA.py`, lines 117–122, the actual nonzero noise norm is \(\sigma\sqrt D/s\), and the full-dimensional branch samples uniform-cube rather than Gaussian noise.

Thus a 784-pixel input with \(s=1\) uses radius \(0.0084\), while a \(3\times224\times224\) input with \(s=4\) uses \(0.02909845\). These are direct algebraic consequences of the normalization, not estimated attack effects. Additionally, `dataset.py`, lines 255–262, resizes CIFAR100-ViT to width 224; the constructor’s width rule leaves its default \(s=4\), whereas p. 6 states \(s=1\) for datasets other than ImageNet. These changes may be intentional in the release, but correspondence with the published recipe is unresolved. No conclusion about which settings improve performance follows.

Problem 6 (Initialization fallback lacks a budget exit: Minor).  In `TtBA.py`, lines 271–287, once the initialization counter reaches \(Q/10\), the fallback tries all-white and all-black inputs without incrementing that counter or checking the total budget inside the loop.

If both fallback images retain the source class, the loop repeats them forever. These conditions are compatible with other adversarial images existing: in one dimension, take source \(x=0.2\) and an adversarial interval \((0.4,0.6)\). Both 0 and 1 are non-adversarial. A finite sequence of sufficiently negative Gaussian draws in the initial random phase misses the interval and has positive probability; after the fallback is reached, repeated 0/1 queries cannot escape it. This is a conditional release control-flow failure, not evidence that published runs followed that path. A bounded failure return or budget-aware restart is necessary; neither was implemented or benchmarked here.
# Scope, counterchecks and outcome

The parent checked the original method, main experimental claims, Appendix B–G and the relevant released attack code; auxiliary static checks covered the data/model wrappers. Normal queries were found to be counted, with no established double counting. A completed iteration can cross a budget, but the summary code uses the preceding completed checkpoint for fixed-budget curves; this was not labeled a demonstrated budget-leakage error. The release also supplies radius scaling omitted from the literal Algorithm 2 call convention, so a pseudocode bracketing concern is not asserted as that particular implementation failure.

Original pages 13–15 were visually inspected to confirm the curvature expression, correction sign and inequality direction. Benchmark images, trained weights and datasets were not executed or regenerated; many figure panels were read only through captions and reported values. Four boundary-visualization PDFs in the source archive were preserved but not independently analyzed. Later revisions/errata were not surveyed; separate attachments remain unenumerated after acquisition-time HTTP 403.

Title: Technical Verification of Submission-Limit Fairness
# Identity, scope and definitions

Yuefan Cao, Xiaoyu Li, Yingyu Liang, Zhizhou Sha, Zhenmei Shi, Zhao Song and Jiahao Zhang, Dissecting Submission Limit in Desk-Rejections: A Mathematical Analysis of Fairness in AI Conference Policies, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43632 (0263), is reviewed in its 23-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Physical and printed page numbers agree. The parent read the main argument and experimental description (pp. 1–9), proofs (pp. 13–20), case studies and policy-link appendix (pp. 21–23). Bibliography entries were not independently audited against their original works.

There are \(n\) authors, \(m\) papers and a positive integer cap \(x\). The binary incidence matrix \(W\) has \(W_{ij}=1\) when author \(i\) coauthors paper \(j\). Write \(d_i=\sum_jW_{ij}>0\), \(D=\operatorname{Diag}(d_i)\), and let \(r_j=1\) mean retaining paper \(j\). Feasibility is \(Wr\le x\mathbf1\), \(r\in\{0,1\}^m\). Individual rejection cost is \(c_i=1-(Wr)_i/d_i\). Average and worst-case costs are \(\zeta_{\rm avg}=n^{-1}\sum_i c_i\) and \(\zeta_{\rm worst}=\max_i c_i\). Every witness below has positive degrees.
# The exact LP guarantee

Problem 1 (Fractional extreme points invalidate the core guarantee: Major).  Theorem 5.16, p. 7, and Theorem B.9, p. 20, claim that maximizing \(\mathbf1^\top D^{-1}Wr\) over \(0\le r\le1\), \(Wr\le x\mathbf1\) is equivalent to the binary problem. The proof infers that an LP extreme point must have binary coordinates. Algorithm 1 then retains only papers with \(r_j=1\).
## A fully admissible counterexample

Use the paper’s own Lemma A.6 (p. 15): three papers have author sets \(\{a_1,a_2\}\), \(\{a_1,a_3\}\), \(\{a_2,a_3\}\), with \(x=1\). Thus \[W=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix},
\quad D=2I,\quad \mathbf1^\top D^{-1}W=(1,1,1).\] Every paper has authors and every author has two submissions. The relaxed constraints are \[r_1+r_2\le1,\quad r_1+r_3\le1,\quad r_2+r_3\le1.\] Adding them gives \(r_1+r_2+r_3\le3/2\). The vector \(r=(1/2,1/2,1/2)\) attains this bound. Equality in the sum forces equality in all three constraints, whose unique solution is that vector. It is the unique LP optimum, not an avoidable fractional choice among tied integral optima.

Any two retained papers share an author, so any binary feasible solution retains at most one paper. Keeping one is feasible, hence the integer objective optimum is \(1\), strictly below \(3/2\). Since \(\zeta_{\rm avg}=1-\mathbf1^\top D^{-1}Wr/3\), the LP value is \(1/2\) while the best actual retained set has cost \(2/3\). Algorithm 1, lines 19–24, extracts no paper from its unique LP optimum; its returned cost is \(1\). Parent exact enumeration independently confirms all four binary feasible vectors (`check.json`).
## Generality, alternatives and impact

This is not peculiar to cap one. Lemma A.7 supplies \(n=m=x+2\) and \(W=J-I\). Then \(D=(x+1)I\), all objective coefficients are one, and the unique LP optimum is \(r_j=x/(x+1)\). Its average cost is \(1/(x+1)\). Any binary feasible solution retains at most \(x\) papers: retaining \(x+1\) leaves an omitted author present on all of them, violating the cap. Retaining \(x\) is feasible, giving integer average cost \(2/(x+2)\). At cap four these values are \(1/5\) and \(1/3\); the extraction rule still retains nothing.

The linear-programming theorem ensures existence of an optimal extreme point for this bounded feasible polytope; it does not make that point a vertex of the unconstrained cube. Intersecting the cube with incidence inequalities creates new fractional vertices. Reading the contradictory binary-vector description below Definition 5.15 as an extra binary constraint would instead produce an integer program and remove the asserted LP efficiency guarantee. Independent random rounding does not restore a deterministic cap or exact optimality.

This falsifies a central theorem, the general exactness of Algorithm 1 and its claimed LP-based complexity guarantee (Remarks 5.17–5.18), supporting Major. The relaxation remains a lower bound on achievable average rejection cost. Integer optimization or rounding with a proved guarantee could replace the invalid step, but neither was established or executed here. The repository was unavailable in the staged acquisition, so the actual PuLP variable categories and extraction used for Table 3 remain unknown. This counterexample does not establish that every reported experimental number is wrong.
# The published hardness proof

Problem 2 (The reduction solves a different problem: Major).  Theorem 5.11, p. 6, is a core distinction motivating the switch from worst-case to average fairness. Its proof, Theorem B.7 on p. 19, sets \(x=m\) and adds \(\|r\|_1\le K\), although that cardinality constraint is absent from the target problem.

With \(x=m\), the actual target always permits \(r=\mathbf1\), giving cost zero. The displayed construction without its extra constraint therefore cannot encode a nontrivial Set Cover decision. Calling the additionally constrained optimization easier does not provide an oracle reduction from the stated target.

A second error occurs in Lemma B.6 (pp. 18–19): retaining at least one paper for every author is claimed equivalent to \[\| \mathbf1-D^{-1}Wr\|_\infty\le1-\frac1{\min_i d_i}.\] Take \(W=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(r=(1,0)^\top\). Both authors retain one paper, but the worst cost is \(1/2\), greater than the printed threshold \(0\). The reverse argument correctly reaches a bound using \(\max_i d_i\) before incorrectly replacing it by \(\min_i d_i\). These are substantive failures in the published derivation of a central complexity result, supporting Major even though the theorem can be repaired.
## A complete replacement reduction

Consider a Set Cover instance with \(m\ge1\) sets and \(1\le K\le m\). Empty-universe cases, elements appearing in no set, and \(K>m\) can be decided or normalized directly; nontrivial instances have positive element degrees. Create one author per universe element and one paper per set, with the corresponding incidence. Add one further author who coauthors every paper. Set the common cap to \(x=K\) and the decision threshold to \(\tau=1-1/m\).

The added author’s constraint is exactly \(\sum_j r_j\le K\). Its degree is \(m\), while every other degree is in \([1,m]\). If a cover of at most \(K\) sets exists, retain those papers. Every author retains at least one, all counts are at most \(K\), and \(c_i\le1-1/d_i\le\tau\). Conversely, a binary feasible set with \(\zeta_{\rm worst}\le\tau\) satisfies \((Wr)_i\ge d_i/m>0\) for every original author. Integer counts are at least one, so it covers every element; the added author enforces at most \(K\) selected sets. The construction has polynomial size and proves NP-hardness by comparing the target optimum with \(\tau\).
This analytically checked replacement preserves the worst-case hardness conclusion; it does not validate the published proof or repair the false average-fairness theorem.
# Illustrative arithmetic and evidentiary limits

Problem 3 (Two local numerical statements disagree with their definitions: Minor).  Example C.2 (p. 21) sets \(n=5\) but averages four entries using \(1/4\). Example 6.1 (p. 8) reverses one inequality for the roulette method’s expected worst cost.

In C.2, retaining \(p_3,p_4\) gives all five author costs \((1/2,1,0,0,0)\), so \(\zeta_{\rm avg}=3/10\), not \(3/8\), and \(\zeta_{\rm worst}=1\). Retaining one paper from each pair gives five costs equal to \(1/2\), so both costs are \(1/2\). Parent enumeration confirms both optima. The qualitative conflict between average and worst-case fairness survives; the paper explicitly acknowledges that average optimization can eliminate an individual’s entire portfolio.

In Example 6.1, the roulette expected worst cost is \[\frac{25}{26}\frac1{26}+\frac1{26}
=\frac{51}{676}>\frac1{26},\] not the printed \(\le1/26\). Expected average cost is \(1/26\), above the ideal \(1/52\). This correction agrees with the prose that roulette is suboptimal and creates no further core contradiction.

Algorithm 2 increments counts only for retained papers. For cap one and ordered author sets \(\{A\},\{A,B\},\{B\}\), it retains the first and third papers. A rule counting all original submissions would reject the third. The rule descriptions are not interchangeable. Which rule a specific historical conference actually enforced was not independently checked; policy correspondence remains Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated historical misdescription.

Table 3 concerns simulated caps on public ICLR 2021–2023 submissions; the authors explicitly distinguish these from actual conference desk-rejection outcomes. Improvement factors were read, but datasets, solver runs, raw retained sets and timing were not reproduced. Unavailable code prevents binding the theoretical algorithm to those results. No real-conference experiment is invented as a prerequisite for the normative argument’s mathematical validity.
# Surviving results and conclusion

The small-author feasibility arguments and explicit impossible ideal-retention instances were checked. Theorem 4.3’s negative statement is existential for \(n\ge3\), not failure of every instance or a theorem about each paper having three authors. Binary matrix formulations and \(\zeta_{\rm avg}\le\zeta_{\rm worst}\) survive. Optimizing that lower bound alone cannot guarantee individual protection; the authors already discuss this limitation.

Title: Technical Verification of Optimized DP Noise
# Identity and scope

Atefeh Gilani, Juan Felipe Gomez, Shahab Asoodeh, Flavio P. Calmon, Oliver Kosut and Lalitha Sankar, Optimizing Noise Distributions for Differential Privacy, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43633 (0264), is reviewed in its 18-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Physical and printed page numbers agree. The parent read pp. 1–9 and the complete mathematical/experimental appendix, pp. 12–18. Relevant released optimizer and sampler text was statically inspected at commit `6912f5012a02db1e2307eb78f379c3cd31e70d5b` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]; this is a retrieval-time snapshot, not established as the executable behind every published experiment.

For order \(\alpha>1\), the objective before the logarithm is \[g_\alpha(P,t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}P(j+t)^\alpha P(j)^{1-\alpha},
\qquad g_\alpha(P)=\max_{|t|\le s}g_\alpha(P,t).\] The continuous version replaces the sum by an integral. Minimizing \(g_\alpha\) is equivalent to minimizing RDP at fixed order. The paper’s optimization (11), and finite version (22), impose \(\mathbb E[c(Z)]\le C\). Its symmetric discrete family has probabilities \(p_i\) for \(0\le i\le N\) and \(p_Nr^{|i|-N}\) in the tails, with \(0<r<1\). All counterexamples below have strictly positive mass, finite variance and finite RDP.
# The budget constraint is not necessarily active

Problem 1 (Enforcing cost equality excludes better feasible noise: Major).  Page 7 asserts that the cost constraint is active and places both cost and normalization in \(Ap=b\). Algorithm 3, p. 6, projects every update into this equality space while claiming to solve the inequality-constrained convex problem (22).

Equation reference: eq:gsmall. Take the discrete family with \(N=1\), \(r=1/2\), \(s=1\), \(\alpha=2\) and quadratic budget \(C=\sigma^2=5\). Write \(a=p_0\), \(b=p_1\). Normalization and variance are \[a+4b=1,\qquad \mathbb E[Z^2]=24b.\] Direct summation over the center and two geometric tails yields \[
g_2(a,b)=\frac92b+\frac{a^2}{b}+\frac{b^2}{a}.\] The negative shift has the same value by symmetry, and shift zero gives one, so this is the worst-shift objective.

Cost equality forces \((a,b)=(1/6,5/24)\) and gives \(g_2=213/160=1.33125\). The legal alternative \((a,b)=(1/5,1/5)\) has cost \(24/5=4.8<5\) and \(g_2=13/10=1.3\). Both are normalized, positive on every integer, symmetric and in exactly the same fixed family. Their order-two RDP values are \(\log(213/160)=0.2861183505\) and \(\log(13/10)=0.2623642645\). The improvement does not use a different tail parameter, a truncated distribution or an infeasible utility budget.

This is also not an artifact of an unreachable variance target: Algorithm 2’s Gaussian-parameter bracket has limiting variance zero at its lower end and variance approximately \(5.24620237>5\) at its upper end \(\widehat C=10\). The decisive result concerns the constrained optimization, not a claimed executed return value. For \(N=1\), two equalities leave zero tangent dimension and the pseudocode also needs a zero-gradient stopping convention.
## Changing the RDP order does not repair the witness

For any finite \(\alpha>1\), put \[A_\alpha=2^\alpha+2^{1-\alpha},\qquad
B_\alpha=(4/5)^\alpha+(4/5)^{1-\alpha}.\] Direct geometric summation gives the difference between the equality-cost distribution’s objective and the alternative’s: \[g_\alpha(1/6,5/24)-g_\alpha(1/5,1/5)
=\frac{A_\alpha}{120}+\frac5{24}B_\alpha-\frac25.\] It is zero at \(\alpha=1\) and strictly increasing for \(\alpha>1\), because both \(A_\alpha\) and \(B_\alpha\) are strictly increasing there. Thus the lower-cost alternative improves every finite-order RDP value, not just the selected order. This compares the RDP objectives; it does not assert a strict improvement of every exact composed DP curve.
## A nonzero-dimensional counterexample

For \(N=2\), \(r=1/2\), \(s=1\), \(\alpha=2\), write \((a,b,c)=(p_0,p_1,p_2)\) and choose \(C=39/5\). Then \[a+2b+4c=1,\quad \mathbb E[Z^2]=2b+44c,\quad
g_2=\frac92c+\frac{a^2}{b}+\frac{b^2}{a}
                  +\frac{b^2}{c}+\frac{c^2}{b}.\] At cost equality, nonnegativity of \(a\) implies \(b\le4/25\) and hence \(c\ge17/100\). Since \(u^2/v+v^2/u\ge u+v\) for positive \(u,v\), \[g_2\ge a+2b+\frac{11}{2}c
=1+\frac32c\ge\frac{251}{200}.\] Zero masses give infinite divergence and cannot improve this bound. The strictly positive point \(a=b=c=1/7\) is normalized, has cost \(46/7<39/5\), and objective \(17/14<251/200\). Thus every equality-cost point is worse than a legal inequality-feasible point even when the equality manifold has a free dimension.
## Dependency and repair boundary

This refutes the asserted activity of the constraint and the resulting general solution guarantee for the central finite optimization. Convexity of the original problem does not justify deleting its interior. Adding independent noise can preserve privacy in an unrestricted distribution class, but need not remain in this fixed geometric-tail family. Requiring exactly a given variance is a coherent different problem; Eqs. (11) and (22) explicitly use an upper bound.

The released primary notebook corroborates equality preservation: zero-based cell 1, source lines 38–73, builds cost/normalization rows; lines 186–196 project with \(A\operatorname{diag}(p)\). Parent and auxiliary static reads agree. Keeping the inequality in the optimizer, or proving activity under additional valid assumptions, is necessary. No full repaired optimizer was implemented or certified. The published numerical gains at other parameter settings are not refuted.
# A domain failure of the finite divergence formula

Problem 2 (Overlapping summation ranges in Theorem 3.6: Major).  Theorem 3.6, p. 5, states Eq. (23) with no restriction relating \(s/\Delta\) to \(N\). Its derivation, p. 16, Eqs. (70)–(75), splits a sum into ranges that overlap when the shift exceeds \(2N+1\).

Use the discrete case \(\Delta=1\), \(N=1\), \(r=1/2\), \(p_0=1/2\), \(p_1=1/8\), \(s=t=4\), \(\alpha=2\), and budget \(C=3\). Normalization is \(p_0+4p_1=1\) and variance is \(24p_1=3\), so every stated condition holds. Extend \(p_i\) by the prescribed geometric tail. Exact summation gives \[g_2(P,4)=\frac{42131}{2048}=20.57177734375,\] whereas Eq. (23) gives \[\frac{42259}{2048}=20.63427734375.\] The excess is \(1/16\): the last two ranges both include \(j=-2\), whose term is \(p_2^2/p_2=p_2=1/16\). If the \(p_i\) symbols in (23) are interpreted only as the finite vector, the expression instead refers to undefined \(p_2\); extending them as the proof does still leaves the numerical error.

Equation reference: eq:correctsum. A valid finite expression, already available before the faulty split, is \[
g_\alpha(P,t)=\frac{p_Nr}{1-r}
 \left(r^{(1-\alpha)t}+r^{\alpha t}\right)
 +\sum_{j=-N-t}^{N}p_{|j+t|}^{\alpha}p_{|j|}^{1-\alpha},
\quad t\in\mathbb N,\] where all outside indices use the geometric extension. Alternatively, restricting every candidate shift to \(t\le2N+1\) prevents this overlap in the published split. The parent checked the exact rational discrepancy and the corrected partition.

This is an invalid derivation of the central objective under its stated parameter domain, supporting Major under the claim-level review standard. The error is bounded to the missing large-shift restriction; the illustrated settings with \(N\gg s/\Delta\) avoid it. The example overestimates divergence, so it does not demonstrate an unsafe understated privacy bound or wrong benchmark ranking.
# Local pseudocode and release findings

Problem 3 (Line search keeps the last improvement, not the best: Minor).  Algorithm 3, lines 12–18, compares each candidate to a fixed \(g_{\min}\) initialized before the loop, but never updates \(g_{\min}\). Page 9 says it chooses the largest reduction.

An independent evaluation of the stated formulas at the legal iterate \(N=2\), \(r=1/2\), \(s=1\), \(\alpha=2\), \(p=(0.4,0.2,0.05)\), cost \(2.6\), gives initial objective \(1.9375\). Among the eleven listed candidate steps, index 5 gives \(1.9331317453\), while the last index 10 gives \(1.9372084608\). Both improve on the fixed initial value, so the printed loop overwrites the better point with the worse one. This is a conditional legal-iterate calculation, not an executed author-code trajectory. Updating \(g_{\min}\) on acceptance restores the stated selection rule. The released notebook already uses a minimum and argmin over candidate values (cell 1, lines 164–178), so the defect is not attributed to that implementation.

Problem 4 (Released example samplers omit the geometric tails: Minor).  The paper requires full-support geometric tails and explains on p. 8 why support mismatch makes finite-order RDP infinite. Released ML helpers sample only a finite array of bins and bounded uniform jitter.

In `jax_optimization.py`, lines 297–299 and 319–335, the bin support is finite and jitter lies in \([-1/(2k),1/(2k)]\). In `rdp_mnist.py`, lines 105–116 and 383–392, the same bounded construction is used while a saved finite RDP parameter is reported. No geometric-tail branch is present in these inspected paths.

A nondegenerate bounded-support additive noise law and any nonzero shift fail mutual absolute continuity: near an essential support endpoint, one shifted law assigns positive mass where the other assigns zero. Thus an order-\(\alpha>1\) divergence in the required neighboring direction is infinite. This exact support argument does not depend on how small the omitted tail mass is. Approximate DP might tolerate a quantified support-loss event, but that requires new accounting.

These are released MNIST/coordinate-optimization examples, not established as the programs behind the final paper’s Table 1. No pickle was loaded, no actual saved tail mass was measured and no author code ran. The finding is therefore bounded to the source-level sampling mismatch; published numerical privacy claims are not declared false on this evidence.
# Surviving results and unresolved evidence

Theorem 3.1’s fixed-order convexity and reflection argument survive: the power perspective is jointly convex and averaging a distribution with its reflection preserves the symmetric cost bound. Proposition 3.5’s geometric second-moment sum was checked. The continuous objective is piecewise linear in the shift between aligned grid boundaries, so the reduction of the shift maximization to grid points is valid; Problem 2 concerns the subsequent range split.

Figures 5 and 7 explicitly plot a pointwise envelope of different optimized distributions. They are not misrepresented here as a single mechanism’s full privacy curve. Table 1 excludes the common privately released quantile-preprocessing cost by explicit design; total end-to-end privacy would need that cost, but the declared comparison is conditional on it. Subgroup sensitivity choices and raw accounting outputs are unavailable for independent numerical validation.

Fixed-order convexity does not itself prove global convergence of the joint \((p,\alpha)\) Newton procedure, nor equivalence of the moments-accountant upper-bound optimum to exact composed DP optimality. These broader assurances remain Needs Evidence. Theoretical counterexamples above do not estimate the empirical size of an effect.

# Identity and coverage

Binchi Zhang, Zaiyi Zheng, Zhengzhang Chen and Jundong Li, Beyond the Permutation Symmetry of Transformers: The Role of Rotation for Model Fusion, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43634 (0265), is reviewed in its 17-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Original pages 3, 5, 8 and 15 were rendered to verify equations, proof and the loss/runtime figure page. Page 8’s extracted text contains duplicated background material; the rendered original was used as the authority.

The release at commit `b89d081429d6e6351f3449d60df5562dfa146664` was examined statically [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The parent read the complete NLP matching utilities and merger, relevant averaging/dispatch code, README and configurations. Auxiliary checks also covered the ViT path. No trained model, dataset or author program was executed.
# Core derivation: no issue found in the declared scope
## Attention invariance

For one head let \(Q=XW_Q^\top+b_Q\), \(K=XW_K^\top+b_K\), \(V=XW_V^\top+b_V\), with biases broadcast by token. Under Eq. (5), p. 3, orthogonal \(R_{qk}\) gives \(Q'=QR_{qk}\) and \(K'=KR_{qk}\). Consequently \[Q'(K')^\top=QR_{qk}R_{qk}^\top K^\top=QK^\top.\] Thus the softmax attention matrix is unchanged. Independently, with \(V'=VR_{vo}\) and \(W_O'=W_OR_{vo}\), \[V'(W_O')^\top=VR_{vo}R_{vo}^\top W_O^\top=VW_O^\top.\] Headwise sums, the unchanged output bias and residual therefore agree exactly before LayerNorm is applied. No commutation of a general rotation through LayerNorm or a coordinatewise nonlinearity is required. The FFN argument uses permutations, which do commute with its coordinatewise activation.

The paper defines its rotation set by \(RR^\top=I\) and does not impose \(\det R=1\). The derived solution is therefore assessed on the orthogonal group, including reflections. This is consistent with its inclusion of permutation matrices. A special-orthogonal determinant objection would change the stated domain.
## Two-model matching

Stack the transposed Q/K weights and bias rows into matrices \(A_1,A_2\). Theorem 4.1 minimizes \[\|A_1R_1-A_2R_2\|_F^2,\qquad R_1,R_2\in O(d_h).\] Right multiplication by \(R_2^\top\) reduces this to \(\|A_1R-A_2\|_F^2\), where \(R=R_1R_2^\top\). For \(C=A_1^\top A_2=U\Sigma V^\top\), \[\|A_1R-A_2\|_F^2
=\|A_1\|_F^2+\|A_2\|_F^2-2\operatorname{tr}(R^\top C).\] Because \(U^\top RV\) is orthogonal and each diagonal entry is at most one, \(\operatorname{tr}(R^\top C)\le\sum_i\sigma_i\). Equality is attained by \(R=UV^\top\). This proves the stated solution and permits \(R_2=I\) without loss. Rank deficiency can produce additional optima but does not invalidate this one. The VO case has the same stacked least-squares form. The proof explicitly uses an SVD; the occasional word eigendecomposition does not change the derivation.

The rescaling objective has the form \(Aa^2-2Ba+D/a^2-2C/a+\mathrm{const}\), with \(a\ne0\). Its stationary condition is \(Aa^4-Ba^3+Ca-D=0\), matching Eq. (12). Choosing a global rescaling optimum still requires comparing admissible stationary candidates. Appendix D explicitly limits optimality to binary rotation matching, acknowledges larger symmetry classes, and disclaims global optimality for sequential rotation/rescaling and arbitrary multi-model fusion. Those disclosed limits are not relabeled as defects.

A parent-written NumPy calculation, seed 5265, corroborates the algebra with two attention heads, nonzero biases, residual and fixed affine LayerNorm: maximum final difference \(2.22\times10^{-16}\). A separate Procrustes calculation agrees with the analytic optimum within \(2.14\times10^{-14}\). These are finite checks accompanying the proof, not substitutes for it or tests of pretrained models.
# Released NLP implementation defects

Problem 1 (Full-width bias products are added to headwise matrices: Minor).  The release’s `src/model_merge/pi_utils/utils.py`, lines 52–54 and 76–78, computes head-local weight products but uses unsliced full-width bias outer products in `Chunk_SVD_QK` and `Chunk_SVD_VO`.

Let the full hidden width be \(D=Hd_h\) with \(H>1\). The sliced Q/K weight blocks have shape \(d_h\times D\), so their cross-products are \(d_h\times d_h\). The unsliced biases have length \(D\), so their outer products are \(D\times D\). Adding these is dimensionally invalid. For a concrete legal two-head layer with \(d_h=64\), the requested sum adds a \(64\times64\) matrix to a \(128\times128\) matrix. The parent’s independent NumPy shape calculation raises the expected incompatible-broadcast error. Zero bias values do not cure their incompatible dimensions.

This is on the released caller path: `pi_merger.py`, lines 92–97, obtains full projection tensors and calls both utilities with the default head size 64; `get_QKVO` returns full biases. The README’s `–use_pi` example and DeBERTa configuration select that pipeline. Although correctly sliced variables ending in an underscore already exist, they are not used in these sums.

Using the corresponding head-local bias slices restores the intended matrix dimensions and matches Algorithm 1’s per-head cross-products. A full source patch was not applied or executed. The separate ViT implementation already uses sliced bias products, providing counterevidence to a repository-wide failure claim. The defect obstructs this released multi-head NLP path, but does not falsify the mathematical theorem or establish which version produced Table 1. Its supported scope is a release-level Minor finding; historical empirical impact is Needs Evidence.

Problem 2 (RegMean statistics are silently ignored by the default NLP dispatch: Minor).  The NLP pipeline sends the collected Gram matrices under keyword `grams`, but the averaging routine consumes `all_grams`.

In `src/model_merge/base.py`, lines 377–384, the RegMean flag collects Gram matrices under the dictionary key `grams`. It forwards this dictionary to `merge_to_global`. The baseline forwarder (`avg_merger.py`, lines 40–43) and matching forwarder (`pi_merger.py`, lines 40–50) preserve this keyword. The callee’s signature, `avg_merger.py`, lines 45–53, instead declares `all_grams=None` plus `**kwargs`.

For the normal call without separately supplied `all_grams`, Python binds `grams` to the unused extra-keyword dictionary. The test `if all_grams` at lines 65–69 is false. With Fisher weighting disabled, the routine reaches ordinary averaging at lines 81–87. These conditions are concrete: the default configuration disables Fisher weighting, while the DeBERTa NER RegMean configuration enables `regmean_mean`. This static argument establishes the branch without executing the author pipeline.

Renaming or explicitly forwarding the argument restores this dispatch connection, but does not by itself certify all downstream statistics or matching behavior. The ViT entry point passes `all_grams` correctly and computes statistics after matching. Similarities between published simple-averaging and RegMean scores are not evidence that this release defect caused the historical numbers. The problem remains a supported release-level Minor defect.
# Experimental scope and alternative readings

The parent read the reported language/vision metrics, ablations, parameter distances, loss barriers, runtimes and subset-layer experiments. The displayed comparisons do not establish a theorem that reducing weight distance always improves test utility; the Procrustes theorem guarantees its specified parameter-distance optimum. No loss/accuracy curve or timing was regenerated, and no significance assessment from raw seeds was possible.

The exact symmetry proof applies to the explicitly modeled original attention architecture (p. 3, footnote 1). Architecture-specific relative-position operations require separate correspondence checks. Relative attention alone does not establish failure: when positional Q/K vectors use the same projection modules, they may rotate automatically and preserve their dot products. Separately parameterized positional projections would require corresponding transformations. The acquired model configuration/forward implementation was not sufficient here to decide the actual DeBERTa setting; this remains Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated symmetry violation.

Auxiliary static inspection of the ViT data helper found a validation split drawn from training data and a separate official test set. No test-selection leakage was established in that path. The precise historical checkpoints, outputs and environment remain unbound to the inspected commit. The two release findings therefore cannot support a claim that the reported fusion improvements are false.

Title: Technical Verification of Feedforward Computational Graph Metrics
# Identity, scope and mathematical setting

Alex Vitvitskyi, João Guilherme Madeira Araújo, Marc Lackenby and Petar Veličković, What Makes a Good Feedforward Computational Graph?, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43635 (0266), is reviewed in its 17-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Physical and printed page numbers agree. The parent read the main argument and experimental description, pp. 1–9, and Appendices A–E, pp. 13–17. Original pages 4, 6, 8 and 13 were rendered to check the mathematical expressions, Figure 3 and proof layout. The frozen source manifest was read and its source identity preserved.

The graph has vertices \(0,\ldots,n-1\), a loop at every vertex, forward edges and a unique terminal vertex \(\tau=n-1\). With \(A_{ij}=1\) for \(j\to i\), the paper uses two different normalizations. The walk matrix \(W\) is column-stochastic, dividing by the source outdegree; the feature diffusion matrix \(\Delta\) is row-stochastic, dividing by the target indegree. Their roles cannot be interchanged. The stationary distribution for \(W\) is \(e_\tau\). Under the stated \(L^1\) convention, averaged mixing uses the first integer time at which \[L_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_i\|W^te_i-e_\tau\|_1<\frac14.\] The notation on pp. 3–4 sometimes calls the distance itself a mixing time; this report uses the threshold-time interpretation adopted by the subsequent arguments.
# Two local line-graph corrections

Problem 1 (The line-graph mixing calculation uses the wrong normalization: Minor).  Section 4.3.1, p. 4, derives an average non-absorption probability and concludes that the averaged mixing time is \(3n/2\).

Use the legal line graph with loops and edges \(i\to i+1\). Until absorption, a step advances with probability \(1/2\). If \(B_t\sim\operatorname{Bin}(t,1/2)\), averaging over the initial distance to \(\tau\) gives exactly \[S_n(t)=\frac1n\mathbb E[(n-1-B_t)_+]
=\frac{1}{n2^t}\sum_{j=0}^{\min(t,n-2)}(n-1-j)\binom tj .\] For any probability vector \(q\), \(\|q-e_\tau\|_1=2(1-q_\tau)\). Therefore the paper’s averaged distance is \(L_n(t)=2S_n(t)\), not \(S_n(t)\).

There is a separate range issue in the displayed simplification. The formula \(S_n(t)=1-(t+2)/(2n)\) is exact while \(t\le n-1\), since then the positive-part truncation changes nothing. It cannot be extrapolated as an exact identity to the claimed \(t\approx3n/2\). For larger \(t\), the omitted truncation correction is nonnegative.
The parent’s exact rational calculation in `check.py`/`check.json` yields:
\(n\) | Claimed \(3n/2\) | Correct threshold time | \(L_n(3n/2)\)

Both displayed distances exceed \(1/4\). At \(n=16\), the distances at times 26 and 27 are respectively \(19346383/67108864>1/4\) and \(8160303/33554432<1/4\). Every graph hypothesis is satisfied; this is not a disagreement about a disconnected graph or a different normalization.

The corrected leading coefficient also follows directly. For \(t/n\to c<2\), \(B_t/n\to c/2\) in probability and bounded convergence gives \(L_n(t)\to2-c\). Hence the threshold time divided by \(n\) tends to \(7/4\). A total-variation threshold would explain a leading coefficient \(3/2\), but p. 3 explicitly defines the unhalved \(L^1\) norm. That alternative therefore requires changing the convention.

The defect affects the exact calibration of an illustrative baseline. The line family’s linear-order mixing, the distinction from a rapidly mixing dense graph, and the conditional FS theorem do not depend on the printed coefficient. No dependency of the FS construction or empirical accuracy conclusions on that exact number has been established. This supports a local Minor assessment, rather than treating a correction to this example as a false central guarantee.

Problem 2 (The line-fidelity formula treats the source as a transient interior node: Minor).  Equation (6), p. 6, gives \(\max_a\binom{a}{n-1}/2^a\) for the line graph’s minimax fidelity. It conflicts with the row-normalized diffusion matrix.

For the same line, \(\Delta_{00}=1\), while \(\Delta_{ii}=\Delta_{i,i-1}=1/2\) for \(i\ge1\). The source is consequently different from the other nodes. For \(i\ge1\), writing \(d=n-1-i\) gives \[(\Delta^t)_{\tau i}=\binom td2^{-t}.\] By contrast, \((\Delta^t)_{\tau0}\) accumulates the mass reaching the absorbing source in the reversed walk and tends to one. It is not the transient coefficient with distance \(n-1\).

For \(n=3\), the exact matrix is \[\Delta=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\[1pt]1/2&1/2&0\\[1pt]0&1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}.\] The source-column supremum is one, the sink-column maximum is one at \(t=0\), and the middle-column maximum is \(1/2\) at \(t=1,2\). Thus the minimax value is \(1/2\), whereas Eq. (6) gives \(3/8\).

More generally, for \(n\ge3\) the worst column is \(i=1\), of distance \(n-2\). The exact corrected statement is \[\min_i\sup_{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}(\Delta^t)_{\tau i}
=\frac{\binom{2n-4}{n-2}}{4^{n-2}}.\] Indeed, for a positive integer \(d\), the ratio of consecutive coefficients is \((t+1)/(2(t+1-d))\); the maxima occur at \(t=2d-1,2d\). Their value \(\binom{2d}{d}/4^d\) decreases with \(d\), so the largest interior distance is worst. Direct exact matrix powers independently reproduce the formula for \(n=3,4,8,16\).

The replacement of max by sup is also necessary for the infinite-time definition: already for \(n=2\), the source coefficient is \(1-2^{-t}\), which never attains one. A declared finite horizon is another possible definition, but would be a different metric. The \(n=2\) line’s supremum-based minimax value is one, and is a separate boundary case.

Appendix B correctly maximizes a binomial coefficient with a fixed distance and applies Stirling’s formula. Its input distance is the part that does not match the graph’s worst column. Using \(n-2\) restores the exact calibration and still gives unnormalized fidelity asymptotic to \(1/\sqrt{\pi n}\) and normalized fidelity asymptotic to \(\sqrt{n/\pi}\). The paper’s qualitative line-versus-dense interpretation therefore survives. No released metric implementation was available to establish whether Figure 1 used Eq. (6), direct matrix powers or another horizon. A plotted-data error is not inferred from the algebra alone.
# Other inspected theory and its boundaries
## Stationarity and loss of long-time fidelity

Lemma 4.1’s stationary distribution proof is valid: any nonterminal mass at the smallest occupied vertex must decrease because its outdegree exceeds one. Proposition 5.1’s recurrence for the penultimate column gives a bound of the form \(t2^{-t}\), hence decay to zero, under its stated indegree assumption. These facts support examining transient fidelity rather than only its long-time limit.

The fully connected calculation on p. 4 contains a related local arithmetic clarification. With uniform initialization on the relabeled vertices \(0,\ldots,n\), the initial expected label is \(n/2\), and each step halves it; the expectation after \(t\) steps is \(n/2^{t+1}\). The printed \(n/2^t\) is still an upper bound, so the claimed logarithmic upper order remains valid. This is not evidence against fast mixing.
## Path-count proposition

The first-hit argument in Appendix A is sound for starts \(i<\tau\). Its averaging step silently includes the sink, where the bound needs an endpoint correction if \(s=1,\ldots,t\). Let \(P\) denote average absorption by \(t\). The weighted path sum is at least \(P-2^{-t}/n\), since the sink’s loop paths contribute \(1-2^{-t}\) rather than one. At the stated \(L^1\) mixing threshold, \(P>7/8\). For these nontrivial graphs the threshold cannot occur at \(t=1\), so \(t\ge2\) and \(2^{-t}/n\le1/8\). The sum still exceeds \(3/4\), and pigeonholing yields the stated factor \(3/(4t)\). Thus the endpoint omission does not refute Proposition 4.2.
## Conditional FS mixing bound

Theorem 6.1 assumes a fixed positive lower bound \(\alpha\) on the probability of crossing to the next block at each relevant level. Terminal blocks descend to the next recursive level rather than needing a nonexistent outward crossing. In the proof’s fixed-block-count model, with \(b=\lceil\log n\rceil\) blocks and \(D=O(\log n/\log\log n)\) levels, at most \(Db\) successful crossings are required. Conditional success probability at least \(\alpha\) gives \[\mathbb E H\le Db/\alpha,\qquad
L_n(t)\le2\Pr(H>t)\le \frac{2Db}{\alpha t}.\] Choosing \(t>8Db/\alpha\) proves the same polylogarithmic upper order and makes the \(L^1\) factor explicit. This argument concerns the pessimistic traversal bound; a lower bound on that comparison process does not automatically lower-bound the actual graph’s mixing time.

Remark C.1 explicitly acknowledges that equal edge allocations at all levels need not satisfy a constant \(\alpha\), and proposes a geometric allocation. The upper theorem remains conditional on the stated ratio and the construction details. It is not a theorem that every unqualified implementation or every sampled finite graph has that ratio. No substantive counterexample to the inspected conditional upper bound was established.
# Empirical evidence and unresolved correspondence

The inspected Figure 3 compares maximum retrieval, second-maximum retrieval and parity, with training lengths up to 256 and test lengths up to 1,024. Appendix E gives task-specific architectures, shared parameters for repeated maximum-retrieval blocks, an eight-layer parity model, optimizers and training budgets. Learning rate and weight decay were tuned on the fully connected graph and reused for the other masks. Those are relevant controls; the available text does not demonstrate test-set selection leakage.

The reported metric/performance alignment is empirical evidence, not a necessity or sufficiency theorem for learned computation. Exact edge budgets, random graph draws, seeds, metric horizon and raw score arrays were not available in a located official repository. The FS \(4\log n\) variant has a different nominal expander degree from a \(\log n\) variant, but the latter is also displayed. Without the recursive allocation and total-edge counts, an asserted unfair comparison would go beyond the evidence.

The Poisson generator accepts when a uniform draw exceeds \(p\), while some captions use \(0.2\) and Figure 3 uses \(0.8\). Acceptance versus rejection probability is an admissible explanation. The implemented convention remains Needs Evidence. The short Gemma experiment in Appendix E lacks the data needed for a separate reproducibility assessment. No model, training run or plotted curve was regenerated.
# Assessment and state

The highest supported assessment is Minor for two local analytical calibrations. The exact line formulas require correction, while the inspected structural propositions and conditional FS upper bound remain supported. Missing implementation details do not become empirical falsification claims.

Title: Technical Assessment of LIFT-GS Render-Supervised Distillation
# Paper identity and review scope

Ang Cao, Sergio Arnaud, Oleksandr Maksymets, Jianing Yang, Ayush Jain, Ada Martin, Vincent-Pierre Berges, Paul McVay, Ruslan Partsey, Aravind Rajeswaran, Franziska Meier, Justin Johnson, Jeong Joon Park and Alexander Sax, From Thousands to Billions: 3D Visual Language Grounding via Render-Supervised Distillation from 2D VLMs, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43636 (0267), is reviewed in its 17-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The running header uses a shortened, reversed-order title; the first-page title and frozen official metadata establish identity. Physical and printed page numbers agree.

The parent inspected the main text, pp. 1–9, and Appendices A–B, pp. 15–17, including the training formulation, Tables 1–8, scaling claims and limitations. Original pages 5, 8, 9, 16 and 17 were rendered to check equations, numerical tables, plots and the captioning example. The frozen manifest and staged official project page were read. The project snapshot’s code link is empty and labeled Code(coming soon) [Retained latex: \cite{project}]. No implementation, model weights, raw predictions or training runs were available for this review.
# Training logic and distinctions that matter

LIFT-GS takes a point cloud and query embeddings, predicts Gaussian primitives and candidate 3D masks, renders those masks to posed image views, and trains against SAM-derived 2D pseudo masks and CLIP-derived query features. Equations (1)–(3) distinguish the mask matrix from the proposal-to-query correspondence matrix. The decoder jointly processes visual and query tokens; its final dot products are therefore not the same operation as independently encoding both modalities without interaction.

The headline without 3D annotations concerns pretraining. Section 4, p. 7, explicitly says that the main quantitative experiments fine-tune with 3D labels. Table 1 uses 500 fine-tuning epochs. Figure 6 illustrates zero-shot behavior; p. 6 acknowledges low zero-shot accuracy and difficulty with complex expressions. Appendix B further acknowledges that CLIP image and text embeddings need not coincide despite sharing a nominal space. Accordingly, the supervised Tables 1–2 cannot be treated as a claim of those same scores without 3D supervision.

The SAM-CLIP construction uses image-region embeddings as pseudo queries; the LLaMA-caption variant instead encodes generated captions with CLIP. Appendix A.1 specifies random sampling of up to eight regions and exclusion of masks below 1,024 pixels. These are relevant controls against presenting every target feature to the decoder. They do not alone prove freedom from shortcuts, but they are counterevidence to a claim that the method simply receives all of its desired output features unconditionally.
# Independent checks of the reported comparisons
The parent’s decimal-arithmetic script, `check.py`, transcribes the reported numbers and saves its results in `check.json`. It does not execute author code or regenerate any prediction.

Table 1’s pretraining increment is \(25.7-22.5=3.2\) percentage points of mAP, while the difference from the listed PQ3D result is \(25.7-20.2=5.5\) points. These are distinct comparisons. Table 2’s six pretraining gains relative to the same architecture trained from scratch are:
Benchmark / threshold | Absolute points | Relative gain
These support the stated approximate 10–30% range. No arithmetic inconsistency was found in those claims.

The comparison scope is important. Table 2 separates mesh point clouds, sensor point clouds with mesh-derived proposals, and sensor point clouds. The authors report retraining 3D-VisTA and BUTD-DETR for the sensor setting and disclose that they could not reproduce PQ3D in that setting. Appendix B acknowledges that LIFT-GS remains below two-stage 3D-VisTA at IoU 0.5. Thus an unqualified claim of superiority across all listed settings would exceed the evidence, but the table itself exposes these distinctions.

Table 3 includes PonderV2 retrained with the same SAM-CLIP pseudo features, a relevant control for attributing the difference only to pseudo-label quality. Table 4 compares loss combinations. Adding grounding to the RGB-plus-feature condition changes Acc@0.25, Acc@0.5 and Acc@0.75 by \(-0.16\), \(+2.40\) and \(+2.13\) points respectively. The low-threshold result does not improve, whereas the higher-threshold gains match the text’s more specific emphasis. Without independent seeds and uncertainty estimates, these differences establish reported point estimates rather than a new significance calculation.

Appendix A.2’s Table 8 uses a more expressive decoder and explicitly says so. Its higher scores therefore should not be conflated with the main-table configuration. The inspected evidence does not establish a concealed architecture mismatch.
# Clarifications and Needs Evidence items
## Assignment and feature dimensions

A second implementation detail concerns the feature loss. Section 3.1.2 states 512 feature-loss channels, while Appendix A.1 gives CLIP-L feature dimension 768. Equation (7)’s dot product requires matching dimensions. A projection or a differently sized output head could reconcile them; Figure 5 also indicates embedding transformations for decoder tokens, though it does not fully specify the feature-loss branch. The exact head/projection definition is Needs Evidence. An actual tensor-shape failure cannot be inferred from the available descriptions alone.
## Data efficiency versus an identified scaling law
Table 5 provides meaningful observed-range evidence of transfer benefit:
Comparison | Pretrained score | Scratch score | Difference

The phrase approximately \(2\times\) is a rough description, not an exactly estimated constant: the middle comparison is closer to a sampled \(2.5\times\) equivalence, and the last pretrained value exceeds the full-data scratch result. This does not contradict the existence of substantial data-efficiency gains. It does mean that an exactly constant multiplier, its confidence interval or its extension beyond the measured range has not been established by these four data fractions.

Similarly, the footnoted quantitative definition of a severe low-data regime refers to the data needed to approach an infinite-data performance limit. Neither that limit nor the required data amount is identified by the displayed curves. Positive gains over the observed range are consistent with data scarcity but do not uniquely determine its asymptotic severity. The paper’s broader interpretation remains plausible; its quantitative extrapolation is Needs Evidence rather than a demonstrated false benchmark result.

Table 6’s ScanNet++ increments are \(0.76\), \(0.60\) and \(0.57\) points at the three thresholds. The statement that about 30% additional pretraining data substitutes for about 15% more annotated fine-tuning data depends on a curve conversion and assumptions about the comparable data unit. The displayed fine-tuning curve stops at 100%, and no fitted model or uncertainty for that conversion is supplied. The exact 1:2 transfer ratio and resulting cost comparison cannot be independently confirmed here. No annotation-cost measurement was reconstructed.
## Historical experiment correspondence

The staged project page states that the illustrated pretraining and fine-tuning use the same scenes. Sharing training scenes across unsupervised pretraining and supervised fine-tuning is not, by itself, evaluation leakage. The available source does not provide scene-level split files or raw runs sufficient to test evaluation overlap. The fine-tuning subsampling unit, category protocol, repeated-seed variability, exact graph of preprocessing operations and pretrained-teacher data overlap remain unverified. No leakage finding is asserted.

The reported inference-speed contrast also lacks an independently reproduced hardware and timing comparison. The project page’s external assets and linked later paper versions were not downloaded or treated as inspected evidence. The scientific assessment is bound to the staged proceedings PDF and its actual acquired project snapshot.
# Assessment and state

No demonstrated substantive problem is numbered in this report. The inspected formulation is coherent under its stated Hungarian-matching interpretation, and the principal tabulated improvement arithmetic checks out. This outcome is restricted to the reviewed reasoning and source descriptions. It does not certify empirical correctness, universal scaling behavior or an unavailable implementation.

Title: Technical Verification of Semi-Clipped and PEA
# Identity, coverage and setting

Ihab Bendidi, Yassir El Mesbahi, Alisandra K. Denton, Karush Suri, Kian Kenyon-Dean, Auguste Genovesio and Emmanuel Noutahi, A Cross Modal Knowledge Distillation & Data Augmentation Recipe for Improving Transcriptomics Representations through Morphological Features, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43637 (0268), is reviewed in its 19-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Main-text physical and printed pages agree; physical pages 14–19 are printed appendix pages 1–6. All page references below are physical unless explicitly stated otherwise.

The parent inspected the main argument and results, pp. 1–9, and Appendices A–D, pp. 14–19, with actual rendered-page checks of pp. 4, 8, 9, 16 and 19. These resolve the algorithm, tables, Venn diagram, TVN formula and enrichment source sets against the original PDF. The complete staged manifest was read. No official repository was identified in the acquired source preparation; this is an availability limit, not proof that no release exists.

Semi-Clipped trains a transcriptomic adapter against frozen morphological embeddings using a contrastive loss. Biological metadata define weak pairing, while inference uses transcriptomics. PEA randomizes batch-correction transforms, retained correction steps and the control samples used to estimate the transform. The paper admits at least two controls per biological batch, and its student representation has dimension 256 in Appendix A.2. Its principal downstream outcomes are known-relationship retrieval and an expression-reconstruction/structure preservation metric.
# Enrichment evidence does not establish the stated synergy

Problem 1 (The pathway evidence uses the wrong significance threshold and source set: Major).  Section 5.3, pp. 8–9, analyzes relationships unique to distillation, states a filter \(p<0.01\), and uses cell-cycle and post-translational enrichment to argue for biological insights absent from either unimodal source. Table 3, p. 19, does not supply that evidence.

Let \(S\) be the relationships retrieved by Semi-Clipped, \(T\) those retrieved by the transcriptomic baseline, and \(I\) those retrieved by the microscopy baseline. The stated emergence test concerns \[U=S\setminus(T\cup I).\] This is different from morphology-specific transfer, \[V=(S\cap I)\setminus T.\] Indeed \(U\cap V=\varnothing\): every element of \(V\) belongs to \(I\), whereas every element of \(U\) lies outside \(I\).
The original table explicitly gives the following decisive rows:
Pathway | Source set | Reported \(p\)
REACTOME cell cycle checkpoints | \(U\) | 0.0323
REACTOME post-translational protein modification | \(V\) | 0.0002

The cell-cycle-checkpoints row is the only displayed row sourced from \(U\). Its \(p\)-value is 3.23 times the stated cutoff and does not meet \(p<0.01\). All other displayed rows are sourced from \(V\). The post-translational row meets the cutoff, but concerns relationships already retrieved by microscopy and cannot witness emergence beyond the union of the two baselines.

Thus, among the displayed enrichment results, zero pathways simultaneously have the required unique source set and satisfy the stated significance filter. This conclusion uses the actual source-set labels and reported \(p\)-values; it does not require recreating GSEA or making assumptions about unreported gene lists. The parent’s `check.py`/`check.json` records the threshold arithmetic and set distinction.
## Alternatives and counterevidence

Changing the cutoff to 0.05 would admit the cell-cycle-checkpoints result at a nominal level. It would not change the post-translational result’s membership in \(V\), and it would not establish correction for searching many pathways. A raw-versus-adjusted \(p\)-value distinction could in principle explain different thresholds, but the table labels only P-value and supplies no such distinction. Additional unreported qualifying rows would require their actual source sets, statistics and analysis records. These possibilities are Needs Evidence, not verified corrections.

The Venn diagram in Figure 4 still supports substantial overlap and some newly retrieved relationships. For Semi-Clipped the displayed regions give \(|S|=19+21+17+35=92\) and \(|S\cap T|=21+35=56\) out of \(|T|=61\). The 19 relationships in \(U\) are newly retrieved relative to these baselines. Their existence alone does not establish significant pathway enrichment, causal synergy or previously unknown biology; the retrieval task uses known database relationships.
## Dependency and correction

The dependency is direct: Section 5.3 invokes this enrichment analysis to distinguish emergent synergy from ordinary transfer, and Section 6 repeats the conclusion about cell-cycle and post-translational synergies. The supplied evidence fails the very source-set and threshold test used for that distinction. This is a Major defect in a central biological interpretation, even if all recall improvements remain numerically correct.

A supported narrower statement is that Semi-Clipped retrieves additional known relationships and retains morphology-associated pathway information. The stronger unique-pathway claim must be withdrawn or supported by a corrected analysis with explicit background, gene/ranking construction, source sets, threshold and multiplicity handling. No replacement enrichment result is claimed here.
# The declared TVN recipe is not defined on its allowed control sets

Problem 2 (Random-control PEA lacks the rank condition required by its inverse: Major).  Appendix C.3, p. 16 (printed p. 3), defines the full-dimensional TVN map \(T=WD^{-1/2}W^\top\) from the control covariance eigenvalues. The formulation requires only at least two controls and randomizes their number, without a full-rank condition or a stated regularization rule.

Let \(c\) be the number of selected controls and \(m\) the feature dimension. After centering, their data matrix has rank at most \(c-1\). Consequently its \(m\times m\) covariance satisfies \[\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)\le\min(m,c-1).\] When \(c\le m\), at least one covariance eigenvalue is zero, regardless of numerical precision. Positive variance in each individual coordinate does not ensure a full-rank covariance.

A complete two-dimensional witness is \[X_{\rm control}=
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] There are two controls, the mean is zero, and both coordinate standard deviations are one under Appendix C.2’s convention. Centering and scaling are therefore well-defined and leave this matrix unchanged. Its covariance is \[\Sigma=\tfrac12X_{\rm control}^{\top}X_{\rm control}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{spec}(\Sigma)=\{2,0\}.\] The prescribed \(D^{-1/2}\) requires \(0^{-1/2}\) and has no finite real value. This example isolates the inverse failure from any zero-coordinate-variance problem. Using an unbiased covariance changes the positive eigenvalue, not the zero.

For the actual 256-dimensional student setting, take the two controls \(\mathbf1_{256}\) and \(-\mathbf1_{256}\). Every coordinate again has positive variance, but the covariance has rank one and nullity 255. More generally, any centered control set with \(c\le256\) has singular covariance. No extra constraint in the inspected formulation excludes these counts or requires affine spanning. Selecting the full TVN sequence is an allowed branch of the augmentation recipe; dropping random steps does not define that branch when it is retained.

The parent independently constructed the two-dimensional covariance and verified its rank and eigenvalues numerically alongside the exact calculation. The defect is mathematical definedness of the supplied normalization, not a claim that the author implementation was observed producing an error.
## What a repair must specify

One option is to restrict every relevant control draw to \(c\ge m+1\), require full column rank after centering and positive feature variance, and reject or handle failing draws. The sample-count condition is necessary, not sufficient: even many controls can be collinear.

Another option is an explicit regularized transformation \[T_\varepsilon=W(D+\varepsilon I)^{-1/2}W^\top,\qquad \varepsilon>0,\] together with a rule for zero coordinate scales, consistent centering/scaling of all embeddings, and a stated row/column convention. This produces a finite covariance inverse square root, but changes the whitening property: \[T_\varepsilon\Sigma T_\varepsilon^\top
=W\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j+\varepsilon}\right)W^\top,\] which is not generally \(I\). For the witness at \(\varepsilon=0.1\), its covariance eigenvalues are exactly \(0\) and \(20/21\); the finite parent diagnostic corroborates this. A pseudoinverse or rank truncation is another possible method, but must specify how null directions are handled. No transformation can turn a rank-one covariance into a full-rank identity by deterministic linear multiplication.
## Impact and uncertainty

This is tied to PEA’s central mechanism: control sampling determines the augmentation delivered to the student, and TVN is also used in the teacher/inference/evaluation description. The stated mapping is undefined for admitted inputs, so its operational assumptions must be strengthened or its formula changed. Under the core-contribution calibration, this supports Major for the described method’s definedness.

There is a substantive counterargument: the appendix could be shorthand for a regularized implementation, making this a missing specification rather than an executed failure. No source code, regularizer, retained-rank parameter or control-count distribution was available to verify that reading. The exact implemented normalization and any effect on the published scores remain Needs Evidence. The assessment does not rely on a difficult repair or claim that all PEA runs fail.
# Checks retained and empirical limitations
## Reported performance and evaluation units

Table 1 reports improved relationship recall for every listed method with PEA across the three datasets. For Semi-Clipped, the parent recalculated relative increases of \(16.95\%\), \(54.81\%\) and \(22.02\%\) from the table’s 15-seed means. Figure 2 and its nearby discussion use five seeds, so their approximately 20% SC-RPE1 figure should not automatically be treated as an arithmetic contradiction with the 15-seed table.

PEA does not improve every preservation entry: SHAKE on SC-RPE1 decreases from 36.95 to 36.15, and VICReg from 36.75 to 36.33. The table itself marks these decreases. Semi-Clipped’s corresponding change is 37.54 to 37.56. These exceptions bound broad preservation rhetoric; they do not negate the reported relationship-recall increases. Table 2’s displayed successive ablation means are monotone for all four methods.

The reported Wilcoxon tests use 15 training seeds. Those seeds measure variation across model-training runs, not 15 independent biological populations or the much larger sample count as independent replicate experiments. The raw paired scores, exact \(p\)-values, test sidedness and multiple-comparison treatment were unavailable. It would be invalid to reconstruct a signed-rank test from marginal means and dispersions alone. No such reconstruction is claimed.

Known-relationship recall first aggregates by perturbed gene, takes top/bottom similarity tails and averages recall over five biological databases. The approximately 10% random baseline is compatible with selecting both 5% tails. This metric measures recovery of curated relationships, not precision of all predicted edges or direct validation of new biological mechanisms. The expression-preservation metric requires a reconstruction probe and structural-distance normalization; its fitting split and original normalization derivation were not independently reproduced.
## Controls, tuning and transfer scope

The teacher is frozen, so the stated update cannot change the teacher representation through the student’s gradient. Metadata-based pairing is explicitly acknowledged even for methods termed label-free; that term refers to the learning objective, not absence of all metadata. Control samples are excluded from the paired distillation data and used for correction. These are meaningful disclosed controls.

The paper describes chemical-perturbation training and genetic-perturbation/out-of-domain evaluation, with a different assay and cell type in additional datasets. Exact sample identifiers, encoder-pretraining overlap, gene-feature harmonization and reconstruction-probe partitions were not available. The hyperparameter study refers to HUVEC-KO while the general protocol mentions a validation split; this is not sufficient evidence to assert test-set leakage.

Appendix A.2 lists different training budgets: 10 epochs for several baselines, 30 for C2KD and 50 for DCCA, versus 150 for Semi-Clipped in the main setup. Validation grid search is stated. Without its search space and convergence records, unequal budgets are a comparison limitation, not proof that baselines were intentionally or materially undertrained.

Inference uses batch controls, and relationship evaluation applies TVN to all output embeddings, while preservation uses raw embeddings. These disclosed choices matter for the practical meaning of unimodal out-of-domain inference. They do not by themselves constitute label leakage. No biological dataset, model, enrichment library or author training program was executed.
# Overall assessment and state

The supported highest assessment is Major. One problem defeats the supplied evidence for emergence beyond the two modalities; the other leaves a central normalization branch undefined under the stated control-count domain. The reported recall gains and evidence of transfer remain separate and are not disproved by these findings.
