Title: Technical Verification of No-Regret is not enough!
# Identity, materials, and scope

M. Bernasconi, M. Castiglioni, and A. Celli, No-Regret is not enough! Bandits with General Constraints through Adaptive Regret Minimization, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], 0277/I25-43646. The frozen proceedings PDF has 22 pages, with Appendices A–D on pages 12–22. Printed and physical page numbers agree. The parent read the complete paper and embedded proofs, independently checked the decisive arguments below, and visually confirmed source pages 3, 5, 8, 9, 13, and 22.

The complete staged source manifest was read and its listed original hashes were checked. No official repository was located in the prepared sources; this does not establish that no release exists. The manifest records an OpenReview access failure (HTTP 403). External imported theorems and any unavailable attachments were not independently rederived or acquired. No author code or empirical experiment was run. All calculations here are reviewer-authored.
# Major: realized hindsight policies can memorize reward noise

Problem 1 (Major; Lemma 8.4 and Corollary 8.5).  Section 3.1 defines the adversarial comparator using realized rewards, \[\operatorname{Opt}_{\rm Adv}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}
 \sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x).\] Section 8.2 sets \(\mathcal X=\Pi=\{\pi:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal A\}\), the set of all deterministic policies, and explicitly retains realized utilities. Lemma 8.4 then claims sublinear interval regret against this entire class from a small error in predicting conditional means. That implication fails.
## A complete admissible instance

Let \(K=3\), \(m=1\), \(\mathcal Z=\mathbb N\), and take the oblivious context sequence \(z_t=t\). Draw \(B_t\) independently and uniformly from \(\{1,2,3\}\), and define the random functions \[f_t(z,a)=\mathbf1\{a=B_t\},\qquad g_t(z,a)=-1
 \quad\hbox{for every }z,a.\] Rewards and costs satisfy the required bounds. Their conditional means are \(\bar f=1/3\) and \(\bar g=-1\); a class containing these constant functions is realizable. Exact mean regressors have zero squared prediction error. Apply the claimed theorem with the valid positive upper bound \(\mathrm{Err}=1\), so the argument does not depend on a missing additive term at zero error.

Every action is strictly feasible, with \(\rho_{\rm Adv}=1\). Zero-initialized projected OGD remains at \(\lambda_t=0\), since \([0-\eta]_+=0\). Hence the utility scale is \(L=1\). Algorithm 3 assigns equal predicted scores, so \(\mu_t=3\) and it samples uniformly. In fact, every nonanticipating learner has conditional success probability \(1/3\), regardless of its selected action.

For each realized sequence, there exists a single fixed policy with \(\pi(t)=B_t\). The policy is selected by the hindsight supremum; it is not an online learner. Distinct contexts permit these assignments without conflict. Consequently \[\operatorname{Opt}_{\rm Adv}=T,\qquad
 \operatorname{Rew}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(T,1/3),\qquad
 R^P_{[T]}(\Pi)=T-\operatorname{Rew}.\] The full-horizon regret is therefore \(2T/3+O_{\mathbb P}(\sqrt T)\), whereas Lemma 8.4 asserts \(\widetilde O(\sqrt T)\).

The parent independently enumerated all \(3^8=6561\) joint action and reward-label sequences at \(T=4\). The reward probabilities for \(0,1,2,3,4\) successes are \[(16,32,24,8,1)/81.\] Every hindsight optimum equals four, expected reward is \(4/3\), and expected regret is \(8/3\). This finite check complements the general analytical contradiction; it is not a simulation of author code.
## Direct damage to the stated core conclusion

The invalid dependency is visible on page 22: an analysis based on conditional-mean regression is applied directly to the supremum of realized utility differences over all policies. A union bound over time intervals does not control this additional hindsight selection. The demonstrated failure reaches both a core lemma and the resulting contextual guarantee, supporting Major.
## Counterevidence and correction scope

With a comparator defined using conditional mean rewards, every policy in this example earns mean \(T/3\), and this contradiction disappears. Restricting the policy class and paying an appropriate complexity term is another possible change. These are substantive qualifications to the printed comparison. No repaired general contextual theorem is certified here. The witness does not refute the finite-action noncontextual framework, its competitive coefficient, or Lemma 8.3.
# Major: the literal quadratic scale bound also fails

Problem 2 (Major, scoped to the core primal instantiation).  Definition 6.1 and Lemma 8.4 define \(L\) as the actual supremum of absolute utilities, without a floor at one. Even with a single repeated context and deterministic rewards, Algorithm 3 does not satisfy the stated \(L^2\) bound for arbitrarily small \(L\).

Take two actions, one constraint \(g=-1\), and deterministic rewards \((\varepsilon,0)\), where \(\varepsilon=T^{-1/2}\). Again \(\rho=1,\lambda_t=0\), exact regressors are available, and \(\mathrm{Err}=1\) is a valid bound. With the prescribed \(\eta_P=\sqrt{2T}\), Algorithm 3 has constant suboptimal-action probability \[\mu=\frac{2-\sqrt2+\sqrt6}{2},\qquad
 p_{\rm bad}=\frac1{\mu+\sqrt2}\simeq0.341081.\] Indeed \(1/\mu+1/(\mu+\sqrt2)=1\). Its regret is \(\varepsilon N_{\rm bad}\), with \(N_{\rm bad}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(T,p_{\rm bad})\). Expected regret is \(p_{\rm bad}\sqrt T\), and with probability at least \(1-e^{-p_{\rm bad}T/8}\) it is at least \(p_{\rm bad}\sqrt T/2\).

The claimed scale term is instead \[504\,L^2\log(T^2/\delta)\sqrt{2T}
 =504\sqrt2\,\log(T^2/\delta)/\sqrt T.\] At \(T=10^{12},\delta=.05\), the lower regret threshold is \(170540.689\), whereas the printed bound is \(0.041524\). These values and the normalization equation were independently checked.

Appendix D retains additive exploration terms before its last line; those terms cannot be absorbed uniformly into \(L^2\) as \(L\to0\). Also, its error bound in Equation (12) uses \(1+\sup_t\|\lambda_t\|_1^2\); the inequality \(L\le1+\sup_t\|\lambda_t\|_1\) has the wrong direction to justify the needed replacement by \(O(L^2)\).

This invalidates another essential property of the stated contextual primal algorithm. The severity concerns that core derivation, not an assertion that the self-bounding phenomenon is false. An explicit envelope at least \(1+\sup_t\|\lambda_t\|_1\), with appropriate localization, could address this scale issue. The first Problem uses \(L=1\) and survives such an adjustment. An envelope-based proof has not been completed here.
# Minor: the no-regret counterexample has inconsistent costs

Problem 3 (Minor; Example 5.2 and Proposition 5.3).  Example 5.2, page 5, sets the final-third costs of \(a_2,a_3\) to one. Figure 1 and the proof on page 13 instead use \(\rho\). The displayed proof also concludes \((2M\rho-2)T/3\le0\) from \(M\ge1/\rho\), which only gives the opposite sign, except at equality.

Using the example’s printed cost one, the proposed sequence \(a_3,a_2,a_2\) across the three phases, and multipliers \(0,0,M\), the exact primal regret for \(M\ge1/\rho\) is \[R_T^P=\frac T3\bigl[M(1+\rho)-2\bigr].\] At \(\rho=1/2,M=2\), this equals \(T/3>0\), so that sequence does not satisfy the claimed nonpositive primal-regret premise. Its dual regret is zero and violation is \(T/3\), not \(\rho T/3\).

The parent recomputed all three comparator utilities. Crucially, \(\rho=1,M=1\) gives both regrets zero and violation \(T/3\). Thus the existential conclusion that ordinary no-regret guarantees alone are insufficient survives in a valid special case. This is a local worked-example correction, assessed Minor.
# Checks that support narrower conclusions
## Competitive coefficient and noncontextual reward argument

Theorem 4.2’s two-instance construction obeys the bounded-cost and strict-feasibility requirements. Its limit establishes the asymptotic competitive constant. Independently, the constant instance \[f(a_1)=1,\ f(a_2)=0,\qquad
 g(a_1)=1,\ g(a_2)=-\rho\] gives \(V=(1+\rho)N-\rho T\), \(\operatorname{Rew}=N\), and \(\operatorname{Opt}_{\rm Adv}=T\). Sublinear expected violation forces asymptotic reward fraction at most \(\rho/(1+\rho)\).
## Self-bounding mechanism and remaining proof conditions

The full stochastic proof still needs explicit stopping or clipping to replace a whole-horizon random payoff/multiplier maximum by a deterministic pre-crossing envelope. Lemma B.3’s displayed invocation of Azuma with a future-dependent random maximum is not sufficient by itself. Confidence-event allocation and endpoint indexing also need consistent treatment. No counterexample to the properly localized self-bounding statement is established here.

The stochastic model should specify conditional means given history, or fresh independent draws. Mere common marginal means would not suffice. Theorem 7.3 also mixes per-round and cumulative \(\operatorname{Opt}_{\rm Stoc}\); writing \(B_T=T\sup_{\xi:\mathbb E_\xi\bar g\le0}\mathbb E_\xi\bar f\) resolves that notation. Under the usual stochastic interpretation and a valid self-bound, its intended reward argument is recoverable. These are Needs Evidence/proof-scope qualifications, not additional demonstrated Major conclusions.
# State and evidence

Highest supported impact is Major, scoped to the contextual regret and reward guarantees as written. Conditional support for the noncontextual framework is preserved. The review does not claim exhaustive external-theorem verification or a repaired full framework. Author adoption is unknown; scientific decision is pending and the human-review list is empty.

The durable files `verification/0277/c.py` and `c.json` contain the exact finite enumeration, analytical probability bounds, small-scale calculation, and corrected worked-example utilities. Coverage, findings, provenance, compiler logs, and rendered-page bindings accompany this report. Original sources and mappings remain unchanged. report: Abstract: Two demonstrated defects affect the central theoretical justification of P-I2SB. Stochastic one-to-many degradation does not preclude a unique optimal Schrödinger bridge, and a reversible residual hash does not ensure that supplied training pairs yield the marginal Schrödinger optimum. Smooth Gaussian examples establish both points, including an ideal-predictor check. Graphical counterevidence resolves the intended residual inverse despite conflicting equations. Reported controlled perceptual gains remain relevant. A repeated real-world comparison column requires source evidence. Adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of Feature out!
# Identity and actual scope

X. Qiu, G. Chen, B. Li, C. Han, T. Guo, and Z. Zhang, Feature out! Let Raw Image as Your Condition for Blind Face Restoration, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], 0278/I25-43647. The original 24-page proceedings PDF includes Appendices A–J beginning on physical page 13; printed and physical numbering agree. The parent read the complete text and captions, checked the mathematical dependencies, and visually inspected pages 1, 4–6, 8–9, 14–16, 20, and 24. Qualitative image-panel inspection was selective, not an exhaustive identity or fidelity audit.

The complete staged manifest and listed file hashes were checked. No official repository was located in the prepared sources, and the preprocessing Python file mentioned on page 15 was not supplied. OpenReview attachment discovery was blocked by HTTP 403. These are access limits, not claims that no release or supplement exists. No author code, model, dataset, or restoration run was executed. Independent symbolic and rational calculations are preserved.
# Major: stochastic branching is not SB infeasibility

Problem 1 (Major; application of Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2).  The paper argues that a single HQ image with multiple LQ outcomes prevents a unified Schrödinger bridge (SB), invoking uniqueness of an SDE solution from an initial value. This argument motivates PHM as a correction guaranteeing feasible, optimal, reversible solutions (pages 1–2, 5, 9, and 16). The inference confuses a unique stochastic law with deterministic endpoint transport.

Consider the allowed reference process \[dX_t=dW_t,\qquad X_0\sim N(0,1),
 \quad X_0\ \hbox{independent of }W.\] Its marginals are \(p_t=N(0,1+t)\). Prescribe \(\nu_0=N(0,1)\) and \(\nu_1=N(0,2)\) in Equation (3). The reference law \(R\) is feasible and \[H(R\mid R)=0.\] Nonnegativity and the zero condition for relative entropy imply that \(P^\star=R\) is the unique optimum. Nevertheless, \[X_1\mid X_0=x\sim N(x,1).\] Every fixed starting value has a nondegenerate distribution of degraded endpoints. Thus a unique optimal SB coexists with exactly the one-to-many stochastic relation declared problematic.

All densities are smooth and positive, with finite second moments. The forward drift energy is zero. Under the backward-time convention, the reverse drift is \(x/(1+t)\), whose expected energy is \[\int_0^1\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{X_t^2}{(1+t)^2}\right]dt
 =\log2<\infty.\] The parent symbolically verified \(\partial_t p_t=\tfrac12\partial_{xx}p_t\), the endpoint covariance, and this energy. This example avoids singular Dirac endpoint or infinite-energy objections.
## The narrow statement that does survive

If a law is already pinned to \(X_0=x,X_1=y\) almost surely, then \(P^{xy}=P\). Theorem 4.1 can be read as this valid conditional statement. Likewise, one already-pinned law cannot simultaneously have two different terminal Dirac marginals. Appendix C’s choice of a Dirac endpoint measure is consistent with that narrow reading.

It does not establish the application’s general infeasibility claim. In the example above, conditioning additionally on \(X_1=y\) produces a Brownian bridge with drift \((y-X_t)/(1-t)\). Different conditional drifts can belong to one valid unconditional Markov law. Pathwise uniqueness fixes the driving Wiener path as well as the initial state; it does not remove random terminal outcomes.
The defect directly concerns why the paper claims PHM is necessary and theoretically justified, supporting Major. It does not show that empirical PHM improvements are absent.
# Major: a reversible hash need not yield the marginal optimum

Problem 2 (Major; PHM optimality claim and Equations (3), (13), (15)–(17)).  Even granting the intended, exactly reversible residual convention, the transformed supervised coupling need not minimize the SB objective with only endpoint marginals constrained.

Use a legitimate additive-noise degradation, \[X\sim N(0,4),\quad E\sim N(0,1),\quad X\perp E,\qquad
 Y=X+E,\qquad U=Y-X=E.\] Here \(U\) is the pseudo-image and the inverse \(X=Y-U\) is exact. The transformed endpoint marginals are \(N(0,1)\) and \(N(0,5)\), while their data coupling has covariance one.

Choose unit Brownian reference diffusion starting from \(N(0,1)\). This is Equation (15)’s schedule \(\sigma_t^2=t,\bar\sigma_t^2=1-t\). The reference endpoint covariance and alternative coupling covariances are \[\Sigma_R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \Sigma_c=\begin{pmatrix}1&c\\c&5\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad |c|<\sqrt5.\] Every \(\pi_c=N(0,\Sigma_c)\) has the same prescribed marginals.

For the path law \(P_c\) obtained by mixing reference bridges with endpoint coupling \(\pi_c\), disintegration gives \[H(P_c\mid R)=H(\pi_c\mid R_{01})
 =\frac12\{5-2c-\log(5-c^2)\}.\] The parent independently derived this expression from the Gaussian trace and determinant formula and checked: \[\begin{array}{c|c}
 c& H(P_c\mid R)\\ \hline
 1\quad\hbox{(hashed data)}&0.8068528194\\
 3/2&0.4941995442\\
 c_\star=(\sqrt{21}-1)/2&0.4172447380
 \end{array}\] The supplied paired coupling is therefore strictly suboptimal. At \(c_\star\), the off-diagonal precision entry equals the reference’s value \(-1\); the density ratio factorizes as \(f(U)g(Y)\). The resulting path law is Markov. For any competing law with the same marginals, the expectation of \(\log f(U)+\log g(Y)\) is constant, so relative-entropy decomposition proves this law is the marginal SB optimum. The comparison is not an artifact of allowing a non-Markov optimum.
## Ideal-score learning does not remove the discrepancy
An unconditioned network need not reproduce the entire supplied bridge mixture. The corresponding ideal-predictor interpretation also fails to attain the marginal optimum in this example.

Equation (15) samples \[Z_t=(1-t)U+tY+\sqrt{t(1-t)}\,\xi,\qquad
 S(t):=\operatorname{Var}(Z_t)=1+t+3t^2,\] with independent standard Gaussian \(\xi\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(U,Z_t)=1\). Thus the ideal endpoint predictor is \(\widehat U(z,t)=z/S(t)\). The one-dimensional Gaussian conditional mean and median coincide, so this result does not require inserting a square into the printed loss norm.

The continuum reverse Brownian-posterior update has drift \[b_{\rm rev}(t,z)=\frac{z-\widehat U(z,t)}t
 =\frac{1+3t}{S(t)}z.\] Starting at terminal variance five, its variance remains \(S(t)\): \(S'=2(1+3t)-1=1+6t\). Equivalently, its forward drift is \(3tz/S(t)\). The parent verified both variance equations symbolically. At \(t=1/2\), this construction has variance \[\frac94=2.25,
 \qquad\hbox{whereas the SB optimum has}\qquad
 \frac{6+\sqrt{21}}4\simeq2.645644.\] Hence even exact prediction in the continuous-time limit gives a different interior marginal. If instead the model conditions on the LQ endpoint and preserves the supervised pairing, the preceding endpoint-KL comparison applies directly.
## Impact and counterevidence

A paired restoration objective may intentionally preserve the data coupling rather than optimize over all marginal couplings. That is a meaningful alternative objective. The result here concerns the claimed identification with Equation (3), not usefulness of supervised restoration. Reversible preprocessing alone does not supply the missing optimal-coupling condition. Indeed, \(Y\mid U=u\sim N(u,4)\), so this residual hash does not even eliminate all one-source/multiple-target relations.

The conditional Gaussian formula in Equation (15) itself checks: for independent increment variances \(a,b>0\), the bridge mean is \((bU+aY)/(a+b)\) and variance is \(ab/(a+b)\). The invalid step is promoting correct conditional bridges and reversible hashing to the asserted global optimality guarantee. This is another Major issue tied directly to the core theoretical contribution. No complete repaired optimality theorem or experimental score failure is claimed.
# Minor: conflicting residual equations have a graphical repair

Problem 3 (Minor; Equations (11), (13), and (18)).  Equation (11) defines the residual as \(x-y\); Equation (13) defines it as \(y-x\); Equation (18) decodes it as \(\hat x-y\). The last expression inverts neither preceding definition.
For \(x=4/5,y=1/5\), the two printed forward targets are \(3/5\) and \(-3/5\); the printed decoder returns \(2/5\) and \(-4/5\), respectively.

Crucially, actual inspection of the Figure 2 inverse-PHM box on page 4 finds \(\bar x=y-\hat x\). Figure 3’s vector labels agree with \(\hat x=y-x\). Together with Equation (13), these provide the coherent inverse \[J(H(x,y),y)=y-(y-x)=x.\] That counterevidence limits the finding to a local equation inconsistency. It does not establish that the historical implementation used an incorrect inverse. The corrected composition was independently verified.

Noise-I2SB has an analogous specification ambiguity: Equation (11) and the prose describe HQ plus noise, but the expression introducing Equation (14) writes LQ plus noise. Its exact implementation is unavailable. Moreover, statistical reversal must be distinguished from samplewise inversion. For independent \(X,N,\epsilon\sim N(0,1)\), \(Y=X+N\), and \(Z=X+\sigma\epsilon\), \[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y,Z)=\frac{\sigma^2}{1+2\sigma^2}>0.\] At \(\sigma=1/10\), this is \(1/102\), independently checked. A denoiser cannot recover the original sample exactly from these inputs, although a reverse stochastic kernel remains legitimate. The intended meaning and implementation of the unqualified reversibility claim require clarification.
# Empirical checks, local reporting error, and unresolved evidence

Problem 4 (Minor; Table 3, page 9).  The first two ablation columns are headed NIQE and FID, but their values appear in the opposite order. The baseline entries \(25.6026,6.5709\) are explicitly FID and NIQE in Table 1. The Cat entries \(13.9109,5.3300\) corroborate the same swap.

The parent visually checked both tables. Relabeling the columns preserves the reported improvement. With both LQ and degradation-aware guidance held present, row (c) versus Cat row (e) yields \[\begin{array}{c|rrr}
 &\mathrm{FID}&\mathrm{NIQE}&\mathrm{LPIPS}\\ \hline
 \text{Guided, no PHM}&25.4932&6.3898&0.2945\\
 \text{Guided, Cat PHM}&13.9109&5.3300&0.2395\\
 \text{Reduction}&45.43\%&16.59\%&18.68\%
 \end{array}\] Noise and residual hashing also improve all three listed metrics relative to row (c). These controlled reported results support a PHM contribution. There is no PHM-only row without degradation-aware guidance, so the feature-free configuration’s performance remains Needs Evidence. Guidance alone is not uniformly better: row (c)’s LPIPS \(0.2945\) exceeds baseline \(0.2851\).

Table 1 reports the best FID \(13.910\), NIQE \(5.3300\), and LPIPS \(0.2395\), with margins \(0.338,0.0140,0.0018\) over the best other listed values. PSNR and SSIM are lower than Vanilla-I2SB: \(25.405\) versus \(26.174\), and \(0.6581\) versus \(0.7047\). This is a reported perceptual/fidelity tradeoff, not universal dominance. No repeated-run significance or raw-score reproduction was established.
## Wider FID: a specific unresolved comparison

In Table 2, the parent visually confirmed that all twelve input/baseline FID values repeat exactly from WebPhoto-Test to Wider: \[\begin{gathered}
 174.52,\ 97.42,\ 104.63,\ 88.52,\ 87.49,\ 97.60,\\
 91.95,\ 116.40,\ 89.69,\ 83.76,\ 92.94,\ 108.03.
 \end{gathered}\] They correspond, in order, to LQ, GPEN, GFPGAN, VQFR, CodeFormer, DifFace, DiffBIR, DR2, PGDiff, PMRF, FlowIE, and Vanilla-I2SB. Only P-I2SB changes, from \(84.68\) to \(69.62\). The NIQE columns do change.

The claimed Wider FID lead therefore needs dataset-specific evaluation records or a corrected comparison column. Repetition does not determine the true Wider scores or prove misconduct. The displayed margin over PMRF is \(14.14\), but its empirical provenance is unresolved. The best reported Wider NIQE \(4.9056\) is a separate observation. Other real-world metrics are mixed: P-I2SB does not lead either LFW metric, and PMRF has better WebPhoto FID and CelebChild NIQE.

Comparative timing evidence is also missing, despite speed claims. Figure 4’s caption names Res-I2SB while adjacent text names Cat-I2SB; the plotted variant is unresolved. Selected qualitative and failure panels were actually viewed, but visual plausibility does not establish identity preservation or SB feasibility. Appendix F’s loss curves cannot prove nonexistence of an SB.
# State, repair scope, and provenance

Highest supported impact: Major, for the theoretical feasibility and optimality claims. The narrower empirical benefits remain supported by reported point estimates. Residual signs and ablation labels have local, verified corrections; no complete revised theory or implementation is certified. Author adoption is unknown. Scientific adjudication is pending; the human-review list is empty.

The reviewer-authored `verification/0278/c.py` and `c.json` preserve the Gaussian PDE, covariance, entropy, ideal-predictor, inverse, and table calculations. Title: Technical Verification of EraseAnything
# Identity, source version, and inspection

D. Gao et al., EraseAnything: Enabling Concept Erasure in Rectified Flow Transformers, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], 0279/I25-43648. The frozen proceedings PDF has 25 pages, with Appendices A–F beginning on page 13. Printed and physical page numbers agree. The parent read the complete text and captions and visually checked pages 4–7, 9, 13, 17–18, 21, and 25. Qualitative panel inspection was selective.

The complete source manifest was parsed and source hashes checked. Repository [Retained latex: \cite{repo}] is pinned to `67d8c0bd5b153ff0e394b45e893b6671bc40e30b`, 28 September 2025. It is a retrieval-time release, not independently established as the exact version used for the paper’s experiments. The parent read the complete active training entry point, loss, sampling, dataset, token-index, and custom-scheduler files, the configuration and README, and relevant attention-forward sections. The remaining vendored dependency tree was not exhaustively audited. No author code was imported or executed, and no model, dataset, paid API, or installation was used. All computations below are reviewer-authored.
# Major: the claimed contrastive reversal does not reverse

Problem 1 (Major; Equation (5) and Appendix D).  Page 6 states that Reverse Self-Contrastive (RSC) learning aligns the unlearned feature \(F^{un}\) with irrelevant features \(F^{k_i}\), while separating it from the synonym feature \(F^{syn}\). The printed loss, minimized in Algorithm 1 and Equation (6), has the opposite similarity derivatives.

Appendix D makes this an exact algebraic defect rather than an inference from a verbal label. Its Equation (8) is \[L_{\rm sc}=-\log\frac{e^{s_{\rm syn}}}{\sum_i e^{s_i}}.\] The proposed reversal swaps the ratio and also removes the minus, giving Equation (9): \[L_{\rm rsc}=\log\frac{\sum_i e^{s_i}}{e^{s_{\rm syn}}}
 =L_{\rm sc}.\] The parent independently verified this identity symbolically and visually confirmed the signs on original pages 6, 17, and 18. There is no maximization or negative outer coefficient in the printed algorithm that repairs it.
## A realizable nonnegative attention-feature check

To avoid relying solely on independently varied abstract logits, use \[F^{un}(r)=(r,1-r),\quad
 F^{syn}=(4/5,1/5),\quad
 F^{k_i}=(1/5,4/5),\quad i=1,2,3.\] All entries are positive for \(0<r<1\). Each vector can be a column of a row-stochastic attention matrix whose other column is its complement; finite softmax logits realize such matrices. The printed objective reduces to \[L(r)=\log3+\frac{3/5-6r/5}{\tau},
 \qquad L'(r)=-\frac6{5\tau}.\] At the specified \(\tau=.07\), moving from \(r=.5\) to \(r=.6\) lowers the loss from \(1.098612\) to \(-0.615673\), while synonym similarity rises from \(.50\) to \(.56\) and irrelevant similarity falls from \(.50\) to \(.44\). This independent calculation realizes the reversed scientific effect within the intended nonnegative feature setting.

Page 2 describes penalizing closeness to irrelevant concepts, which agrees with the printed sign but conflicts with page 6’s claimed reversal. This is internal inconsistency, not a resolution of Appendix D’s equality.
## Core dependency and appropriate severity

RSC is presented as a principal mechanism for selective erasure with preservation, and Appendix D is explicitly its derivation. The invalid identity and contrary descent direction therefore support Major, without requiring that the entire method or every reported benchmark fail. Negating the displayed loss would reverse these similarity derivatives, but that local correction alone does not establish the intended neural-network behavior or reproduce the reported experiments.
# Released source: decisive counterevidence and a different objective

The pinned implementation does not minimize the printed Equation (5). In `utils/infoNCE.py`, lines 37–58, the features are cosine-normalized, the synonym is the query, and the keys are the center and irrelevant features. The returned loss is \[L_{\rm code}
 =a-\log\left(e^a+\sum_i e^{b_i}\right),\qquad
 a=\frac{\cos(F^{syn},F^{un})}{\tau},\quad
 b_i=\frac{\cos(F^{syn},F^{k_i})}{\tau}.\] The training configuration has positive `lamb4=0.1`; `train_flux_lora.py`, lines 401–411, adds this loss and calls ordinary backward propagation and an optimizer step.

Consequently \[\frac{\partial L_{\rm code}}{\partial a}
 =1-\frac{e^a}{e^a+\sum_i e^{b_i}}>0,\] so minimizing this expression repels the center from the synonym. Independent evaluation of the formula on the preceding two-dimensional features gives derivative \(+0.1733194\) with respect to \(r\) at \(r=.5\), unlike the printed loss’s negative derivative. No repository function was executed for this check.

The differentiation paths matter. The decorator at `utils/esd_utils.py`, lines 39–40, places every `latent_sample` call under `no_grad`. The synonym and irrelevant maps produced in `utils/calc_loss.py`, lines 544–605, are therefore detached. The center map at lines 508–520 and 608 is differentiable. For this center, \[\nabla_{F^{un}}L_{\rm code}
 =(1-p_a)\nabla_{F^{un}}a.\] The irrelevant maps change the scalar factor, but provide no direct attraction vector toward themselves. Thus the release supports synonym repulsion while differing from the printed objective, its query/keys, and its asserted two-sided alignment mechanism.

This is material counterevidence: the review does not conclude that the released code attracts erased concepts toward synonyms, or that historical scores were obtained with the erroneous printed formula. The paper, derivation, implementation description, and empirical version should be reconciled. No later correction was found in the staged README; no separate later-version search is claimed.
# Formulation and implementation limits
## Alternating updates and the displayed nested program

Equation (6) supplies no separate outer decision variable on which the lower problem depends. Even replacing its inner \(\min\) by \(\arg\min\), the literal program selects among minimizers of a fixed erasure objective. Algorithm 1 instead alternates erasure and preservation steps on the same LoRA parameters. The release performs these on successive global steps with one optimizer (`train_flux_lora.py`, lines 384–412).

These operations are not generally equivalent. For \(f(\theta)=\theta^2/2\) and \(g(\theta)=(\theta-1)^2/2\), the fixed-inner-minimum program permits only \(\theta=0\). Alternating gradient steps give \[\theta_{n+1}=(1-\beta)(1-\alpha)\theta_n+\beta,
 \qquad
 \theta_\star=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta-\alpha\beta}>0.\] At \(\alpha=1/1000,\beta=1/2000\), the fixed point is \(1000/2999\), independently checked. This demonstrates a formulation/algorithm distinction. The paper provides no convergence theorem that this review claims to disprove. A precise nested formulation, approximation statement, or an explicit alternating-optimization interpretation is Needs Evidence.
## Token alignment and sampler state

The source finds target indices in the full shuffled prompt (`lora_dataset.py`, lines 180–187), then may replace the keyword without recomputing the indices. The preservation loss embeds standalone synonym and irrelevant words (`calc_loss.py`, lines 544–546 and 577–579), yet selects their columns using the original full-prompt indices (lines 601, 605, 608). The paper instead describes replacements inside the same sentence.

If a full-prompt target lies at index five while a standalone comparison consists of a word, EOS, then padding, index five selects padding rather than that concept. This is a conditional tokenized diagnostic, not a claim to have run the actual T5 tokenizer. The missing remapping is statically visible; its actual frequency, historical execution, and numerical effect remain unresolved.

The active custom scheduler setter (`tools/scheduler_process.py`, lines 93–111) changes only `self.timesteps`; the same scheduler copy is reused. The inherited `scheduling_flow_match_euler_discrete.py` is absent from the staged repository and member manifest. Without that base implementation, no definite inherited-state crash or timestep failure is certified. This specific dependency gap is preserved as Needs Evidence; nothing was installed or acquired to fill it.
## Checks that rule out broader allegations

The relevant attention code concatenates text and image tokens on the sequence axis and uses \(QK^\top/\sqrt d\) with key-axis softmax. Selected-column mass is not a constant under row normalization, so the attention regularizer is not invalidated by a constant-sum argument. This correct implementation provides counterevidence to reading Equation (1)’s schematic axis notation literally.

The path \(u_t=(1-t)u_{\rm pix}+tx_T\) has derivative \(x_T-u_{\rm pix}\), agreeing with the flow-matching target. Printed Equation (2) is dimensionally malformed as a velocity vector minus a squared-norm scalar, whereas the source uses a proper MSE against \(e_0-\eta(e_p-e_0)\). However, the inspected path evaluates those targets using the same adapter-bearing transformer under no-gradient evaluation; no adapter-disable or separate fixed original teacher appears in that path. The intended teacher convention should therefore be specified alongside the corrected equation. No complete historical ESD-equivalence claim is made here.
# Empirical evidence and what it can establish

Table 2’s detection totals sum correctly. The proposed method reduces the reported detected-content quantity from \(605\) to \(199\), approximately \(67.11\%\), while UCE reports \(173\). The paper explicitly acknowledges this tradeoff. On MS-COCO, proposed FID \(21.75\) and CLIP \(30.24\) are best among the listed edited models, but worse than the original Flux values \(21.32\) and \(30.87\). These are favorable reported tradeoffs, not exact preservation or complete erasure. The detection counting unit is not sufficiently specified to convert \(199\) into an image-level rate over 4,703 prompts.

Table 4 reports lower attack success than ESD and CA on its tested protocols, with proposed rates \(2.46\%\), \(8.77\%\), and \(11.93\%\). The 285 Ring-A-Bell prompts were already processed; the authors explicitly did not rerun that attack. These results do not establish unrestricted adaptive robustness or zero residual generation.

The ablation does not independently verify the disputed RSC mechanism. Table 5’s full model has erased/retained accuracies \(14.9/88.5\), versus \(15.3/82.1\) for ESD plus attention. That comparison adds both LoRA reconstruction and RSC. There is no full-minus-RSC row, nor full-minus-LoRA or full-minus-attention row. Thus the chosen package’s point estimates are supported; attribution of preservation gains specifically to the intended RSC mechanism remains unresolved.

Appendix F.1 also needs a clearer evaluation boundary: it describes a recognizer trained on 5,000 collected images and statistics on a 1,000-image test split, without clearly identifying the generated-image sets producing Table 5. This ambiguity does not prove that generator scores were computed on unchanged real images. Generated counts, recognizer validation, and aggregation across adapters are needed for reconstruction.

Table 3’s category comparisons favor the proposed method over CA, but do not include an original-Flux classification baseline. Held-out status of evaluation synonyms is unspecified. The authors disclose altered Q/K baseline adaptations, a small human study, and dilution of erasure when combining roughly ten or more adapters. Those limits should accompany broad preservation and scalability language. No raw outputs, user-response matrix, or uncertainty estimates were independently reproduced.
# State and evidence

Highest supported impact: Major, scoped to the core RSC derivation and stated mechanism. Released-code counterevidence and reported empirical tradeoffs are retained. Repair verification covers the algebraic sign and formula derivatives; a complete reconciled method or rerun is not certified. Author adoption is unknown. Scientific decision is pending and the human-review list is empty.

The durable `verification/0279/c.py` and `c.json` contain the symbolic identity, admissible feature example, independent source-formula derivative, alternating-update diagnostic, table arithmetic, and source-file hash bindings. report: Abstract: The released normalized-relative Mahalanobis evaluator can mix normalized class statistics with unnormalized global statistics under its prescribed evaluation order. A fully specified example with positive-definite covariances reverses two sample rankings, establishing a Major implementation defect for that reported variant. The primary Mahalanobis++ path and the separate CIFAR relative implementation avoid this defect; historical table effects remain unverified. A Gaussian-moment basis omission and limited numerical summary errors are Minor. The principal 41/44 improvement count, variance-deviation identity, and selected aggregate arithmetic check out within the inspected scope. Scientific adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of Mahalanobis++
# Identity, version, and inspection

M. Müller and M. Hein, Mahalanobis++: Improving OOD Detection via Feature Normalization, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], 0280/I25-43649. The frozen proceedings PDF contains 34 pages; printed and physical page numbers agree. The parent read the complete main text, references, and Appendices A–G. Original pages 4, 7–8, 13–14, 17–18, 20, 26–27, and 31 were also visually inspected, including the principal formulas and selected plots/tables.

The complete source manifest and its integrity records were read. The public repository [Retained latex: \cite{repo}] is pinned to `53de550be7f88acad959f5fdd8f2430fb9a8b6ea`, 30 May 2025. This is the acquired release, not independently established as the historical experimental implementation. The parent inspected the relevant ImageNet evaluator, primary and relative scoring functions, README, metric code, and complete normalized CIFAR postprocessors; auxiliary static review also covered the surrounding evaluator and feature-extraction paths. The remaining repository was not exhaustively audited. No author code, model, dataset, or serialized author cache was executed. All finite computations below use original reviewer code.
# Definitions and the checked scientific dependency

Equation reference: eq:relative. For training features \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), labels \(c_i\), and nonempty classes, the paper estimates \[\mu_c=N_c^{-1}\sum_{i:c_i=c}x_i,\qquad
 C=N^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\mu_{c_i})(x_i-\mu_{c_i})^\top .\] The primary score is \[s_M(z)=-\min_c(z-\mu_c)^\top C^{-1}(z-\mu_c).\] Larger scores indicate more ID-like inputs. The evaluation uses a threshold at 95% ID true-positive rate. Mahalanobis++ applies \(x\mapsto x/\|x\|_2\) to both fitting and test features (Section 4, Equation (6)). The relative version additionally fits global mean \(g\) and covariance \(G\), without class centering, and uses \[
 s_R(z)=-\min_c(z-\mu_c)^\top C^{-1}(z-\mu_c)
            +(z-g)^\top G^{-1}(z-g).\] This is Appendix G’s definition on page 34. Page 7 introduces relative Mahalanobis++ by applying feature normalization to that construction. Its columns recur throughout the main and appendix results. The implementation issue below concerns that specific normalization-dependent score.
# Problem 1: cache order changes the normalized-relative method

Problem 1 (Major; released ImageNet normalized-relative evaluator).  In `NINCO/detection_methods.py`, `evaluate_Relative_Mahalanobis_norm`, lines 548–662, training normalization is conditional on missing class-statistic caches. A later, separately conditioned global fit can consequently use raw features while the class fit and test features are normalized.
## A reachable branch, not a hypothetical cache corruption

Test features are normalized at lines 569–570. Lines 572–580 load `mean_norm.npy` and `prec_norm.npy`. Training normalization at line 585 lies inside the branch at line 583 that runs only if these class statistics are incomplete. Global caches are checked separately at lines 607–617; on a miss, lines 623–629 estimate their mean and covariance directly from the current training array.

This state occurs in the documented workflow. README line 100 recommends `–method all`. `NINCO/evaluate.py`, lines 28–37, places `Mahalanobis_norm` before `Relative_Mahalanobis_norm`; line 416 selects this list. The loop at line 244 passes the same stored raw training array (assigned at line 109) and per-model cache path (line 217) to the two functions at lines 274–287. The first function normalizes by local rebinding at `detection_methods.py`:453 and saves the class caches at lines 468–469. It does not modify the caller’s raw array in place. The relative call then skips training normalization and, if its global caches are absent, fits a raw global Gaussian under normalized-cache filenames.
## Complete positive-definite ranking-reversal example

Take 1,000 classes with three raw training features each. In 500 classes use \[A=\{(2,0),(0,2),(-2,0)\};\] in the other 500 use \[B=\{(2,0),(0,-2),(-2,0)\}.\] All 3,000 vectors are nonzero, every class is nonempty, and the construction respects the source’s hard-coded 1,000-class loop. It tests the finite-feature estimator, which is defined without requiring the empirical features to be exactly Gaussian.

After normalization, the two distinct class means are \[\mu_A=(0,1/3),\qquad \mu_B=(0,-1/3),\] and direct centered sums give \[C=\operatorname{diag}(2/3,2/9),\qquad
 g=0,\qquad G=\operatorname{diag}(2/3,1/3).\] The raw global covariance is \(G_{\rm raw}=4G\), with the same zero mean. All three covariance matrices are positive definite. Let \(u=(0,1)\) and \(v=(4/5,3/5)\); both already have unit norm. Exact arithmetic yields:
Quantity | \(u\) | \(v\)
Minimum normalized class distance | \(2\) | \(32/25\)
Correct normalized global distance | \(3\) | \(51/25\)
Raw-global distance at normalized test point | \(3/4\) | \(51/100\)
Correct relative score | \(1\) | \(19/25\)
Mixed-coordinate relative score | \(-5/4\) | \(-77/100\)

Thus the correct method ranks \(u\) above \(v\), but the mixed fit ranks \(u\) below \(v\). The discrepancy is not a common additive offset or an increasing transformation that would leave ranking metrics unchanged. The parent verified these fractions symbolically and separately fitted the covariance matrices from the explicit 3,000-row synthetic array. Neither computation called author code.
## Counterevidence, impact, and supported correction

An empty-cache relative-first call normalizes the training array before both fits and avoids this branch. Correct pre-existing global caches also avoid it. The primary Mahalanobis++ function never uses the global Gaussian and is coherent on the inspected path. The separate CIFAR implementation, `OpenOOD/openood/postprocessors/rmdsn_postprocessor.py`, normalizes all training features at line 39 before both fits (lines 46–71), so this particular defect does not apply there.

The confirmed result is nevertheless Major for the released normalized-relative variant: a routine cache state changes its stated mathematical estimator and can reverse OOD rankings. That dependency is substantive without requiring failure of the primary method or all empirical conclusions. The retrieved source does not identify the historical cache state or prove that any published FPR value is wrong.

A precise correction is to normalize training features unconditionally before either fit, and to rebuild affected global statistics and dependent cached scores after distinguishing their provenance. This restores the specified estimator algebraically on the example. A repaired author implementation and benchmark rerun were not executed; historical numerical impact remains Needs Evidence.
# Problem 2: the Gaussian variance formula needs eigenbasis means

Problem 2 (Minor; Lemma 3.1, page 4, and Appendix B).  The printed variance numerator uses eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) of \(\Sigma\) paired with coordinates \(\mu_i\), without specifying that the mean is expressed in the covariance eigenbasis.

For \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\), the coordinate-invariant formulas are \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\|X\|_2^2&=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma+\|\mu\|_2^2,\\
 \operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)
 &=2\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^2)+4\mu^\top\Sigma\mu\\
 &=\sum_i\{2\lambda_i^2+4\lambda_i(U^\top\mu)_i^2\},
 \quad \Sigma=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)U^\top .\end{aligned}\] These follow by expanding independent Gaussian coordinates after orthogonal rotation. The lemma instead prints \(\sum_i(2\lambda_i^2+4\lambda_i\mu_i^2)\). For \[\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mu=(1,0),\] the actual variance is \(28\). Pairing the original mean coordinates with eigenvalues \(1,3\) gives \(24\), or \(32\) after reversing their order. An invariant variance cannot depend on that ordering.

Appendix B explicitly states the correct rotated mean \(U^\top\mu\) before later writing \(\mu_i\). This is decisive counterevidence: reading those later coordinates in the eigenbasis restores the moment calculation and Chebyshev argument. The supported defect is a local mathematical statement/notation omission, not a failure of Gaussian norm analysis or a demonstrated violation of the claimed probability bound for a particular threshold. Replacing the numerator by the invariant expression above is analytically verified. No empirical result was shown to depend on the erroneous coordinate reading.
# Problem 3: limited overstatements in numerical summaries
Problem 3 (Minor; Sections 4–5 and Table 4).  Some universal comparator wording and one model-win count disagree with the paper’s own numerical tables.

Page 6 says the method outperforms KNN and cosine similarity in all considered cases. Table 12, page 26, gives EffNetV2-S FPR \(59.9\) for Maha++ versus \(58.8\) for cosine, and ResNet50-supcon \(59.6\) versus \(58.9\) for cosine and \(58.4\) for NNguide. On CIFAR100 RN34, Tables 3 and 16 give Maha++ \(74.51\) versus KNN \(74.44\). Lower FPR is better. Likewise, page 7’s claim that relative normalization improves across models and datasets has exceptions in Table 2: iNaturalist \(2.0\to2.2\) for ConvNeXtV2-B and \(3.5\to3.9\) for SwinV2-B.

Independent enumeration of the 44 displayed Table 4 rows gives 29 Maha++ winners, 6 relative-Maha++ winners, 5 ViM winners, 3 unnormalized-Maha winners, and 1 Ash winner, with no displayed minimum ties. Page 7 instead states 30/44 for Maha++. The full row-wise count is retained in the calculation evidence.

The appendix openly acknowledges comparator exceptions, and the main text acknowledges the three failures to improve ordinary Maha. The correction is therefore to qualify the universal wording and reconcile the 29-versus-30 summary, not to reject the demonstrated average advantage. Original unrounded measurements were not available; rounding of aggregate means is not treated as an additional error.
# Checks that support the primary contribution, and remaining limits
## The variance-deviation identity

Equation (5) and Appendix C are valid for symmetric \(A=C^{-1/2}(C_i-C)C^{-1/2}\), usable whitening covariance \(C\), and uniform \(u\) on the unit sphere: \[\mathbb E(u^\top A u)^2
 =\frac{2\operatorname{tr}(A^2)+(\operatorname{tr}A)^2}{d(d+2)}.\] The stated spherical moments \(3/[d(d+2)]\) and \(1/[d(d+2)]\) produce this result. A separate \(d=2\) check with \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) gives \(15/8\) by both the trace formula and direct fourth moments.
## Primary source correspondence and domain conditions

The primary ImageNet score normalizes fit and test features and uses pooled class-centered covariance (`NINCO/detection_methods.py`:422–485). The complete normalized CIFAR primary postprocessor follows the same construction. `NINCO/utils.py`:548–549 sets the lower 5% ID quantile and counts OOD scores above it. No OOD test features enter the inspected mean/covariance fits.

Normalization requires nonzero features. An ordinary covariance inverse additionally requires sufficient rank; unit-sphere support alone neither ensures nor forbids nonsingular covariance (the uniform sphere has covariance \(I/d\)). The code delegates precision estimation to `EmpiricalCovariance`; actual benchmark spectra and zero-vector incidence were not measured. The paper’s directional QQ plots show improved approximation for selected models, not an exact full-dimensional Gaussian law on a sphere. Radial invariance can discard useful information in other distributions. These qualifications do not contradict the paper’s bounded empirical evidence.
## Result arithmetic and experimental scope

The parent reproduced the displayed Table 4 improvement counts: 41/44 for Maha++ and 39/44 for relative Maha++. Means of the displayed rows are \(42.46591\to34.94545\) for ordinary versus normalized Maha, with ViM at \(41.92955\). Thus the approximately seven-percentage-point average improvement over ViM is supported by the printed data. CIFAR100 average FPR recomputes as \(52.5175\to44.135\); CIFAR10 as \(33.818\to24.510\). These are arithmetic checks, not experimental reproductions.

Table 17 covers 39 models: failed noise tests fall from 354 to 129; 33 models improve, 3 tie, and 3 worsen. Nineteen models have no remaining failures, while some retain 15/17. This supports broad mitigation, not universal elimination, of noise brittleness.

The paper acknowledges ID contamination in several OpenOOD datasets and reports NINCO separately. Full pretraining-corpus overlap was not audited. The within-backbone comparisons control the representation more directly than Table 18’s SSD+ versus larger pretrained models, whose differing architectures and training are disclosed. Formal significance tests, raw feature arrays, historical caches, and complete experiment-version bindings were not verified. Checkpoint descriptions in Tables 19–20 include repeated labels and broad source references, so exact historical checkpoint recovery also requires additional provenance.
# Conclusion and disposition
Item | Judgment | Repair verification | Remaining work
Relative cache fit | Major, release scope | Consistent-fit algebra checked | Historical caches; repaired benchmark evaluation
Gaussian basis | Minor | Invariant moment formula checked | Clarify coordinate notation
Result summaries | Minor | Table contradictions/count checked | Reconcile summary with source measurements
Primary score and checked identity | No Issue Found in scope | No repair required by these checks | No claim of whole-paper correctness

Overall supported assessment: Major, driven by Problem 1’s specific implementation dependency. Author adoption is unknown and was not requested. Scientific decisions remain pending; `human_reviews=[]`. Separate batch acceptance is not part of this initial review.

report: Abstract: The reviewed proceedings version contains two false comparisons of probability-mass updates and an invalid limiting inference from parameter gradients to logit gradients. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of ABKD
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

This report concerns Guanghui Wang, Zhiyong Yang, Zitai Wang, Shi Wang, Qianqian Xu, and Qingming Huang, ABKD: Pursuing a Proper Allocation of the Probability Mass in Knowledge Distillation via \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\)-Divergence, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The assigned identities are 0281 and I25-43650; the OpenReview identifier is `vt65VjJakt`. The reviewed original is the staged 46-page official proceedings PDF, with embedded appendices. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, matching the printed numbers at the cited locations.

The review covers the main argument, divergence definitions, logit-update derivations, the relevant proofs in Appendices C–G, reported experimental settings, and selected released loss implementations. The staged repository is commit `027ec2621aad678b94587bb36cab9a16b8a05fed`; it is not established as the historical experimental commit. Complete source-member hashes and inspected-versus-unexamined coverage are retained separately. No training, author program, dataset, or checkpoint was executed.
# Definitions and update convention

Equation reference: eq:delta. Let \(p,q\) be strictly positive probability vectors, \(q=\operatorname{softmax}(f)\), and \(\eta>0\). For a loss \(D(p,q)\), the Appendix C.1 update is gradient descent in the logits: \[f_i^+=f_i-\eta g_i,\qquad g_i=\partial D/\partial f_i.\] The exact log mass ratio is \(L_i=\log(q_i^+/q_i)=-\eta g_i-\log Z\), where \(Z=\sum_jq_j e^{-\eta g_j}\). Consequently \[
\Delta(1,2)=L_1-L_2=\eta(g_2-g_1).\] This is a finite-step equality. It requires no small-step approximation. It is not automatically the dynamics induced by gradient descent on neural-network weights.

Equation reference: eq:alpha. Writing \(K=D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)\), direct differentiation gives \[g_i^{F}=q_i-p_i,\qquad
g_i^{R}=q_i\{\log(q_i/p_i)-K\}.\] For \(0<\alpha<1\), the paper’s \(\alpha\)-divergence is \[D_\alpha(p\|q)=\frac{\sum_i p_i^\alpha q_i^{1-\alpha}-1}{\alpha(\alpha-1)}.\] With \(w_i=q_i(p_i/q_i)^\alpha\) and \(S=\sum_iw_i\), \[
-g_i^\alpha=\frac{w_i-q_iS}{\alpha},\qquad
\Delta_\alpha=\frac{\eta}{\alpha}\{w_1-w_2-(q_1-q_2)S\}.\] These identities also identify the common normalization term that must cancel when comparing two classes.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Theorem 3.2(4) reverses the forward–reverse comparison).  The formal Theorem 3.2 in Appendix G.2, p. 21, case 4, asserts \(\Delta^R>\Delta^F\) if \(q_2+\zeta\le q_1\le1-\delta_2\) and \(c_0q_2<p_1=p_2<c_1q_1\), where \(c_0>1\) and \(c_1<1\). Its proof is on p. 22, equations (30)–(35). The conclusion supports the main paper’s comparison of the two concentration effects.

Choose \[p=(0.01,0.01,0.98),\quad q=(0.4,10^{-6},0.599999),\quad \eta=1,\] and \(c_0=2\), \(c_1=1/2\), \(\zeta=0.1\), \(\delta_2=0.2\). Both vectors are positive and normalized. Moreover, \[0.100001\le0.4\le0.8,\qquad
0.000002<0.01<0.2.\] Thus every operative case-4 inequality holds. Finite logits \(f_i=\log q_i\) realize the required starting distribution.

The independent calculation gives \[K=1.1811683120598697,\quad
g^R=(1.00308445682,-0.000010391508684,-1.00307406531).\] Equation [eq:delta] (#eq:delta) therefore yields \[\Delta^F=-0.399999,\qquad
\Delta^R=-1.00309484833031,\] so \(\Delta^R-\Delta^F=-0.60309584833031<0\), opposite to the claimed strict inequality. The script and actual output are `kl.py` and `kl.json` in the matching verification directory.

Equation reference: eq:identric. The failure can be expressed without relying on a numerical approximation. For \(p_1=p_2=p_0\), let \[I=\exp\!\left(\frac{q_1\log q_1-q_2\log q_2}{q_1-q_2}-1\right).\] Then the exact identity is \[
\Delta^R-\Delta^F=\eta(q_1-q_2)\{\log(p_0/I)+K\}.\] The stated inequalities do not force this bracket to be positive. In the example \(I=0.147156521915\), much larger than \(p_0\).
#### Proof gap and counterevidence.

The proof concludes that one can choose a sufficiently large \(p_0\) so that equation (35) holds. This establishes a restricted sufficient condition; it does not establish the claimed implication from the listed hypotheses. Equations (31)–(35) also print \(D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)\) where differentiation requires \(D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)\). The counterexample uses the correct gradient, so correcting that notation does not remove the failure.

Nor can arbitrary fixed ratio constants rescue the general implication: fix an admissible \(a\in(\zeta,1-\delta_2)\) and let \(q=(a,\varepsilon,1-a-\varepsilon)\) and \(p=(\sqrt{\varepsilon},\sqrt{\varepsilon},1-2\sqrt{\varepsilon})\). For small positive \(\varepsilon\), both vectors are positive and normalized and the ratio inequalities hold for any fixed finite \(c_0>1\) and \(0<c_1<1\). Yet the bracket in [eq:identric] (#eq:identric) equals \(1+(1-a)\log(\sqrt{\varepsilon}(1-a)/a)+o(1)\) and tends to \(-\infty\).
#### Impact and bounded correction.

This is Major because it invalidates a theorem-level comparison used in the central explanation of confidence concentration, including the discussion on pp. 4 and 23. Other cases of Theorem 3.2 are not refuted by this example. Equation [eq:identric] (#eq:identric) supplies an exact conditional replacement: the comparison holds if and only if \(p_0>Ie^{-K}\). The stronger condition \(p_0>I\) suffices. This adds a restriction and does not restore the original broad statement or prove an empirical performance change.

Problem 2 (Theorem F.3(3) has a false monotonicity claim).  Theorem F.3 on p. 20, restated on p. 30, claims \(\Delta_{\alpha_1}\ge\Delta_{\alpha_2}\) for any \(0\le\alpha_1<\alpha_2\le1\) in case 3, where \(q_2+\zeta\le q_1\le1-\delta_2\) and \(p_1=p_2>c_0q_1\) with \(c_0>1\). Its proof is on p. 32, equations (117)–(120).

Take \[p=\frac{(256,256,33)}{545},\quad
q=\frac{(16,1,528)}{545},\quad
\alpha_1=\frac14,\quad\alpha_2=\frac12,\quad\eta=1.\] Choose \(c_0=2\), \(\zeta=1/100\), and \(\delta_2=1/2\); the unused \(\delta_1\) can be any positive number. Both distributions are strictly positive and normalized, \(q_2+\zeta<q_1<1/2\), and \(p_1=p_2=16q_1>2q_1\). Thus the two compared classes are both underestimated and all case-3 conditions hold.

The ratios \(p/q=(16,256,1/16)\) have fourth roots \((2,4,1/2)\) and square roots \((4,16,1/4)\). Substitution into [eq:alpha] (#eq:alpha), using exact rational arithmetic, gives \[S(1/4)=\frac{60}{109},\quad S(1/2)=\frac{212}{545},\qquad
\Delta_{1/4}=\frac{8608}{59405},\quad
\Delta_{1/2}=\frac{9192}{59405}.\] Hence \[\Delta_{1/4}-\Delta_{1/2}=-\frac{584}{59405}<0.\] A separately evaluated normalized softmax update reproduces the respective values \(0.144903627641\) and \(0.154734449962\). The contradiction is exact and independent of rounding; any positive \(\eta\) simply scales it.
#### Proof gap and counterevidence.

Equation (118) factors a term into two factors with opposed monotonicities. The proof does not establish the required sign for the derivative of their product. Its positive-factor branch compares with the endpoint \(\alpha=1\), which is insufficient for the asserted ordering of every pair \(\alpha_1<\alpha_2\). An optional family in Appendix 6 (#sec:family) also rules out repair merely by increasing the lower teacher/student ratio threshold.

The fixed-\(\beta\) comparison in Theorem D.1 is different. For equal student probabilities it reduces to \(\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}=\eta q^\beta\int_{p_2}^{p_1}t^{\alpha-1}\,dt\). Its derivative in \(\alpha\) is nonpositive because \(\log t\le0\) on \((0,1]\). That valid argument does not extend to the coupled choice \(\beta=1-\alpha\) and unequal \(q_1,q_2\) used here.
#### Impact.

This is Major. The main text on p. 6 explicitly invokes Appendix F to support the claimed inflexible balance of \(\alpha\)-divergence relative to independent \(\alpha,\beta\) tuning. A false supporting theorem remains substantive despite its appendix location. The inclusion of the coupled family within the two-parameter family remains true, and no benchmark ranking is disproved. No general monotonicity repair has been verified.

Problem 3 (Full row rank does not justify the limiting gradient inference).  Appendix C.2, p. 17, equations (12)–(13), claims that full row rank of the logit Jacobian \(J\) makes \(\nabla_W\ell\to0\) imply \(\nabla_f\ell\to0\). Section 3.1, p. 3, uses this implication to connect parameter optimization with shrinking class-wise log mass updates.

Use two logits \(f(W)=(a\tanh w_1,a\tanh w_2)\) with \(a=0.1\), teacher \(p=(3/4,1/4)\), forward KL loss, and gradient descent from \(W_0=(0,0)\) with any fixed \(\eta>0\). Symmetry preserves \(W_k=(t_k,-t_k)\). Writing \(\sigma(u)=(1+e^{-u})^{-1}\), \[t_{k+1}-t_k
=\eta a\,\operatorname{sech}^2(t_k)
 \{3/4-\sigma(2a\tanh t_k)\}>0.\] Because \(\sigma(0.2)<3/4\), a finite limit for \(t_k\) would leave a strictly positive limiting increment. Therefore \(t_k\to\infty\). At every finite iterate, \[J_k=\operatorname{diag}(a\operatorname{sech}^2t_k,
                       a\operatorname{sech}^2t_k)\] has full row rank. Arbitrarily many unused parameters can be appended if \(M\gg C\) is required. Nevertheless, \[\nabla_f\ell\longrightarrow
(\sigma(0.2)-3/4,\;3/4-\sigma(0.2))\ne0,\qquad
\nabla_W\ell=J_k^\top\nabla_f\ell\longrightarrow0.\] This is an actual admissible gradient-descent trajectory, not merely an arbitrary sequence of matrices. A finite 100,000-step diagnostic gives \(t=4.84016192625\), first logit gradient \(-0.200172190347\), and first parameter gradient \(-5.00378008538\cdot10^{-6}\), consistent with the analytic limits.
#### Impact, counterevidence, and correction.

The missing assumption invalidates the paper’s stated bridge from weight stationarity to its core logit-based explanation; this derivation is assessed Major. It does not invalidate Appendix C.1 under its explicit logit-update convention. At a fixed finite stationary point with full-rank \(J\), the corresponding non-asymptotic implication is valid. Likewise, if \(\inf_k\sigma_{\min}(J_k)\ge c>0\), then \(\|\nabla_f\ell\|\le c^{-1}\|\nabla_W\ell\|\), which restores precisely the limiting implication. Some architectures with independent output biases satisfy a suitable bound for a single-example loss. This report does not assert that the paper’s experimental models follow the counterexample trajectory.

Problem 4 (Released vision loss omits boundary normalization factors).  Appendix B, equation (8), p. 16, specifies squared denominators in the continuous extension. The staged `standard_classification/distiller_zoo/abkl.py` instead uses \(1/\beta\) at line 37, \(1/\alpha\) at line 47, and \(1/\alpha\) at line 58 in the \(\alpha=0\), \(\beta=0\), and \(\alpha+\beta=0\) branches, respectively [Retained latex: \cite{code}].

For example, the correct \(\alpha=0\) branch is \[D^{(0,\beta)}=\frac1{\beta^2}
\sum_i\{q_i^\beta\log(q_i^\beta/p_i^\beta)-q_i^\beta+p_i^\beta\}.\] Thus the released scalar expression is \(\beta D^{(0,\beta)}\). With \(p=(1/4,3/4)\) and \(q=(1/2,1/2)\), all probabilities are positive and normalized and finite softmax logits realize them at any positive temperature. At \(\beta=1/2\), the paper’s value is \(0.214091254158\) and the released formula gives \(0.107045627079\). At \(\beta=-1\), the values are \(+0.757969188430\) and \(-0.757969188430\). Negative parameters can therefore reverse the loss contribution, rather than merely change a positive loss weight. Analogous independently calculated checks of the other two branches are in `check.json`.

This is a Minor released-code defect: no dependence of the core reported experiments on the faulty branches is established. The general branch agrees with Definition 4.1; the language-model implementation in `distillation_llm/distillm/losses.py`, lines 15–41, uses the correct squared denominators. The FKLD/RKLD endpoints are unaffected, and the reported primary ABKD parameters in Table 4, p. 40, use nonsingular branches. Squaring the three denominators restores the scalar formulas algebraically; no patched PyTorch execution or numerical-stability claim is made.
# Overall impact and remaining evidence

The highest supported impact is Major because the core theoretical comparisons have explicit counterexamples and the parameter-gradient justification is incomplete. The generic divergence definition, its family inclusions, several fixed-parameter gradient identities, and the existence of the reported experiments survive these findings.

The empirical tables were inspected for their stated task, baseline, seed, and parameter scope, not reproduced. A static auxiliary inspection also identified test-loader checkpoint selection and mismatched example launch settings in the current release. These are retained as provenance questions; the exact historical configurations and an empirical effect are unestablished. They do not increase the supported severity.

No later correction or historical experimental commit was established from the staged sources. This is not a claim that no erratum exists or that these findings are first discoveries. Public OpenReview attachment discovery was unavailable in the supplied preparation record; the embedded appendix was available. These are initial findings, not post-batch acceptance.

Title: Technical Verification of Consistency-Model Convergence
# Identity and scope

The reviewed paper is Yiding Chen, Yiyi Zhang, Owen Oertell, and Wen Sun, Convergence of Consistency Model with Multistep Sampling under General Data Assumptions, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 9764–9782 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assigned identifiers are 0282/I25-43651 and OpenReview `vsJsR3ieCx`. This review uses the staged 19-page proceedings PDF, including Appendices A–I. All locations are one-based PDF pages, matching the printed numbers.

The main statements, KL recursion, consistency-error induction, smoothing lemma, schedule calculations, and simulation construction were inspected. The staged acquisition record contains no attributable released repository; additional OpenReview attachment discovery was blocked by HTTP 403. The saved author page links arXiv:2505.03194, but its versions were not independently compared. Absence of a staged repository is not evidence that no code exists.
# Definitions and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:loss. The forward process has conditional law \(X_t\mid X_0\sim N(\alpha_tX_0,\sigma_t^2I)\). The probability-flow ODE defines a trajectory \(\varphi(u;x,t)\) and a proposed consistency function \(f^\star(x,t)=\varphi(0;x,t)\). Assumption 1, p. 4, requires \(\widehat f(x,0)=x\) for every \(x\) and, on the uniform training grid \(\tau_i=i\Delta\tau\), \[
\mathbb E_{X\sim P_{\tau_i}}
\|\widehat f(X,\tau_i)-
\widehat f(\varphi(\tau_{i+1};X,\tau_i),\tau_{i+1})\|^2
\le\epsilon_{\rm cm}^2 .\] Sampling alternates denoising and fresh Gaussian perturbation, starting from \(N(0,\sigma_T^2I)\). Theorem 3 assumes an \(L\)-smooth log density, meaning that its gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz. It does not impose Theorem 2’s bounded-output assumption.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Theorem 3’s smoothing bias has a false scale dependence).  Lemma 4, p. 17, states \(\operatorname{TV}(P,P*N(0,\sigma^2I))\le2dL\sigma\) for an \(L\)-smooth log density. Appendix E, pp. 15–16, inserts this bound directly into Theorem 3, pp. 5–6.
## Elementary violation of the lemma

Equation reference: eq:tv. Let \(d=1\), \(P=N(0,s^2)\), \(L=s^{-2}\), and \(\sigma=s\). The log-density Hessian is \(-s^{-2}\), so the smoothness hypothesis holds exactly. Gaussian convolution gives \(P*N(0,s^2)=N(0,2s^2)\). Their density-crossing point is \(s\sqrt{2\log2}\), hence \[
\operatorname{TV}(N(0,s^2),N(0,2s^2))
=2\{\Phi(\sqrt{2\log2})-\Phi(\sqrt{\log2})\}
\approx0.166064074984 .\] This distance is invariant under rescaling. The claimed upper bound is \(2/s\), which equals \(0.02\) for \(s=100\). Thus the lemma is false. No restriction \(L\ge1\) or small-noise restriction appears in the stated claim.
## A counterexample satisfying the full main theorem

To show that other terms in Theorem 3 do not conceal this defect, use the admitted Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process \[dX_t=-X_t\,dt+\sqrt2\,dW_t,\qquad P_{\rm data}=N(0,10000).\] Set \[s=100,\quad L=10^{-4},\quad T=20,\quad
\Delta\tau=1,\quad M=20,\quad N=1,\quad
\epsilon_{\rm cm}=10^{-8},\quad \sigma_\epsilon=100.\] For \(v_t=e^{-2t}s^2+1-e^{-2t}\), choose the exact consistency estimator \[\widehat f(x,t)=f^\star(x,t)=\frac{sx}{\sqrt{v_t}}.\] Every assumption can be checked explicitly. The target has a positive smooth density and finite second moment \(s^2\). The boundary identity holds because \(v_0=s^2\). The PF-ODE trajectory is \(\varphi(u;x,t)=\sqrt{v_u/v_t}\,x\), and therefore \(\widehat f(\varphi(u;x,t),u)=\widehat f(x,t)\) pointwise. Every loss in [eq:loss] (#eq:loss) is exactly zero, hence below the specified positive tolerance. The grid is \(0,1,\ldots,20\), and \(t_1=T\) is an admissible sampling time. The linear, unbounded estimator is permitted by Theorem 3.

The sampler starts with variance \(1-e^{-2T}\), so the denoised and smoothed variances are \[\widehat v=\frac{s^2(1-e^{-2T})}{e^{-2T}s^2+1-e^{-2T}},
\qquad v_{\rm smooth}=\widehat v+\sigma_\epsilon^2.\] Here \(\widehat v=9999.999999999576\) and \(v_{\rm smooth}=19999.999999999578\). For centered Gaussian variances \(v_1<v_2\), their crossing point satisfies \(c^2=v_1v_2\log(v_2/v_1)/(v_2-v_1)\), and their TV is \(2\{\Phi(c/\sqrt{v_1})-\Phi(c/\sqrt{v_2})\}\). Thus the actual TV in the theorem is \(0.166064074983508\).
## Impact, counterevidence, and repair scope

This is Major: Theorem 3 is a principal convergence guarantee, and its smoothing optimization on p. 6 depends on the false bias term. The counterexample has exact consistency and a smooth target, so neither estimation error nor the singular endpoint discussed below causes it. Increasing the number of sampling steps is unnecessary to expose the failure because the theorem includes \(N=1\).

A different definition of the smoothness parameter or an added scale restriction would change the statement. Neither is supplied. The external lemma cited by the authors was not independently retrieved here; the counterexample refutes the printed inequality regardless of its attribution. A valid replacement smoothing bound must be proved and propagated through the optimized rate. No general repair is certified by this report.

Problem 2 (The general-data induction uses an impossible deterministic endpoint coupling).  Lemma 2, p. 14, equation (19), states that \(\varphi(\tau_{j+1};X,\tau_j)\sim P_{\tau_{j+1}}\) when \(X\sim P_{\tau_j}\). Its application at \(j=0\) is invalid for atomic targets included in the advertised bounded-support data class.

Take \(d=1\), \(P_0=\delta_0\), and the variance-exploding SDE from Section 3.3: \[dX_t=\sqrt{2t}\,dW_t,\qquad P_t=N(0,t^2).\] For \(t>0\), its score is \(-x/t^2\) and the PF-ODE is \(\dot x=x/t\). Every curve \(x(t)=ct\) solves this positive-time ODE and extends to \(x(0)=0\). Thus the time-zero initial-value problem is nonunique. More fundamentally, a deterministic function of the almost-sure constant \(X_0=0\) has a point-mass law. It cannot have the nondegenerate law \(N(0,\tau_1^2)\) required by equation (19), regardless of the selected branch.

The first training pair in [eq:loss] (#eq:loss) consequently does not control the positive-time marginal used in Lemma 2’s change of variables. That lemma supplies the evaluation-error estimate in Lemma 1 and Theorems 2–4. This is a demonstrated invalid proof step in the core general-data argument, assessed Major; it is not a numerical-instability complaint. The paper’s Bernoulli simulation makes the atomic domain relevant rather than hypothetical.
#### Alternative formulation and boundaries.

A backward endpoint map can still exist: for this example every positive-time trajectory ends at zero. One can instead impose the first consistency loss under \(X_{\tau_1}\sim P_{\tau_1}\) paired with its backward endpoint, or supply a random entrance law at zero. Either changes the stated deterministic forward-pairing assumption. This report does not certify a complete repaired theorem.

The literal assumptions of Theorems 2 and 4 also combine \(\widehat f(x,0)=x\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) with a finite global output bound at every \(t\in[0,T]\). These are incompatible outside the radius-\(R\) ball at zero. Restricting the output bound to positive times is a natural domain correction; it does not repair equation (19). No counterexample satisfying that contradictory literal boundedness pair is asserted. Problem 1, by contrast, satisfies every assumption of the separately stated Theorem 3.
# Surviving reasoning and interpretation

The Gaussian-channel KL inequality of Lemma 3 follows correctly from coupling, conditional Gaussian KL, and data processing. Conditional on a valid reference trajectory coupling, Lemma 1’s KL recursion and Lemma 2’s Minkowski argument have the stated algebraic structure. The conversion \(W_2\le2R\sqrt{\operatorname{TV}}\), followed by Pinsker, explains the fourth root in Theorem 2. These arguments are not refuted by the smoothing example.

The p. 7 variance-exploding schedule was checked in the rendered original: the radical covers only \(1/e\), so \(t_1=e^{-1/2}R\Delta\tau/\epsilon_{\rm cm}\), consistent with the derivative of the displayed objective. An extraction-only suspicion about this formula was rejected.

Corollary 1 supplies upper bounds. The subsequent approximate factors \(2/3\) and \(1/2\) for actual Wasserstein errors do not follow from comparing those bounds; no matching lower bound is supplied. This is a scope clarification, not a refutation of the displayed upper bounds.

Appendix I constructs a threshold estimator with evaluation MSE \(t^2\); it is not a trained-model experiment. An independent calculation of its disclosed two-step Bernoulli mechanism gives \(W_2=13.8227195146\) and \(9.25161843145\) at \(t=\log(10^6)\) and \(\log(10^4)\). This supports that particular qualitative improvement. It is not a reproduction of the unavailable plotting implementation or every baseline in Figure 2.
# Conclusion
Claim | Assessment | Repair and remaining work
Theorem 3 / Lemma 4 | Major | False bound; replacement and rate unverified
Atomic endpoint induction | Major | Invalid step; changed coupling required
Boundedness and error ratios | Clarification | Restrict domains and interpretation
Adjudication | Pending | Initial review; separate acceptance outstanding
Author adoption | Unknown | No contact or adoption requested

No later correction was established from the staged materials. Exact source-code availability, unavailable attachments, external proof hypotheses in Appendix F, and later arXiv revisions remain unverified. No empirical claim of first discovery or whole-paper invalidity is made.

report: Abstract: The principal quantitative approximation theorem is false under its stated Wasserstein regularity assumption. An exact transformer disproves the claimed scaling with domain diameter, and an independent zero-transformer construction on a fixed cube disproves the advertised dimension-independent rate. The conditional flow-stability conclusion survives after explicit repairs to its proof. Static inspection also establishes erroneous evaluation reductions in the released notebooks, without establishing which historical executions produced the published numbers. The assessment is Major; scientific adjudication remains pending.
