Title: Technical Verification of Mean-Field Transformer Approximation
# Identity and review scope

This report concerns Shiba Biswal, Karthik Elamvazhuthi, and Rishi Sonthalia, Universal Approximation of Mean-Field Models via Transformers, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assigned identifiers are 0283/I25-43652. The reviewed proceedings PDF has 16 pages; all locations below use one-based PDF pages, matching the printed numbers.

The complete paper text, the main theorem and appendix derivations, and the staged six-member source release were inspected. The parent independently checked the decisive formulas in rendered original pages, derived and replayed the calculations below, and integrated three native auxiliary checks. Released notebooks were parsed as data and read statically; no author code, training, dataset, or checkpoint was executed. Hash verification covered all 12 staged manifest entries without mismatch.
# Mathematical setting

Equation reference: lip. For a compact \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) containing zero, write \[
u_z^m= rac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\delta_{z_j},\qquad
 (F_m(z))_i=F(z_i,
u_z^m).\] The expected transformer is \[T_n(x,\mu)=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu^{\otimes n}}(T([x;z]))_1.\] Assumption 4.3(a), p. 6, requires \[
 \|F(x,\mu)-F(y,
u)\|_2
 \le L igl(\|x-y\|_2+W_1(\mu,
u) igr).\] The error \(\mathcal E=\sup_{z\in\Omega^{n+1}}\|T(z)-F_{n+1}(z)\|_2\) is a uniform finite-sequence error, and \(\|H\|_*=\sup_{x,\mu}\|H(x,\mu)\|_2\). On compact \(\Omega\), membership in \(\mathcal P_p(\Omega)\) imposes no additional restriction as finite \(p\) increases.
# Substantive findings

Equation reference: bad. Problem 1 (The principal quantitative approximation bound is false).  Theorem 4.7, pp. 7 and 11, asserts \[
 \|T_n-F\|_*\le\mathcal E+
 L D^p\left(\frac1{n+1}+C(p,q,d)G(n,p,q)\right),
 \qquad D=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega),\] where \(C\) depends only on \(p,q,d\), and \(G=n^{-1/2}\) when \(p>d/2\), \(q>p\), and \(q\ne2p\).
#### A directly false proof inequality.

Appendix A, p. 12, equation (21), uses \[W_1(\nu_z^n,\nu_{(x,z)}^{n+1})\le\frac{D^p}{n+1}.\] Take \(\Omega=[0,\tfrac12]\), \(p=2\), \(n=1\), \(z_1=0\), and \(x=\tfrac12\). The left side is \[W_1\left(\delta_0,\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_{1/2}\right)
 =\frac14,\] whereas the claimed upper bound is \(1/8\). The correct general augmentation bound is \(D/(n+1)\): keep \(n/(n+1)\) of the empirical mass fixed and transport the remaining mass to \(x\). The displayed example attains this linear bound.
#### An exact transformer disproves the full uniform-constant statement.

Fix \(d=1\), \(p=2\), \(q=3\), \(n=1\), and \(\Omega=[0,a]\). Define \[F(x,\mu)=2x+\int y\,d\mu(y).\] The mean is 1-Lipschitz in \(W_1\), so [lip] (#lip) holds with \(L=2\). Every required moment exists.

This field has an exact implementation in the paper’s own architecture. Appendix D, p. 16, defines \[\operatorname{Block}(X)=X+\operatorname{FC}(X+\operatorname{Att}(X)).\] Use one attention head with \(W_Q=W_K=0\) and \(W_V=W_0=1\). Its attention is the broadcast arithmetic mean \(\bar X\). Choose both positionwise networks as the identity on the nonnegative inputs; ReLU realizes these identities on the required domain. Then \[T_i(X)=2X_i+\bar X=(F_{n+1}(X))_i,
 \qquad \mathcal E=0.\] Consequently, with \(m_\mu=\int y\,d\mu(y)\), \[T_n(x,\mu)=2x+\frac{x+n m_\mu}{n+1},\qquad
 \|T_n-F\|_*=\frac{a}{n+1}.\] The supremum is attained at \(x=a,\mu=\delta_0\).

For any alleged finite nonnegative \(C=C(2,3,1)\), choose \[a=\frac1{4(1+2C)}.\] At \(n=1\), the actual error is \(a/2\), but [bad] (#bad) gives \[2a^2\left(\frac12+C\right)=\frac a4.\] Thus no constant with the declared dependencies can make the theorem true over its stated domains. This is an analytic family indexed by the proposed constant, not an assumption that the unknown constant equals a chosen numerical value. The saved rational-arithmetic check verifies illustrative family members exactly.
#### A fixed-domain counterexample to the dimension-independent rate.

The defect cannot be repaired by changing only \(D^p\) to \(D\). Fix \(\Omega=[0,1]^3\), \(d=3\), \(p=2\), \(q=5\), and put \(m=n+1\). Let \(D_m(\Omega)\) be the set of equally weighted \(m\)-point empirical measures and define \[F^{(m)}(x,\mu)=\operatorname{dist}_{W_1}(\mu,D_m(\Omega))e_1.\] The set \(D_m(\Omega)\) is compact, because it is the continuous image of \(\Omega^m\). Distance to a nonempty subset of a metric space is 1-Lipschitz. Hence every field in this family satisfies [lip] (#lip) with the same \(L=1\), independently of \(x\).

For every \(m\)-token input, its empirical measure belongs to \(D_m(\Omega)\), so the corresponding finite target is identically zero. Choose the exact zero transformer by setting its output network to zero. Then \(\mathcal E=0\) and \(T_n=0\), with no appeal to an external universality theorem.

Equation reference: quant. Let \(U\) be uniform measure on the cube, \(v_3=4\pi/3\), and \(c=(16v_3)^{-1/3}\). Every measure \(\nu\) supported on at most \(m\) points satisfies \[
 W_1(U,\nu)\ge c m^{-1/3}.\] Indeed, balls of radius \(r=(2m v_3)^{-1/3}\) about the support points cover at most half the cube’s volume. At least half of its mass must travel distance at least \(r\), proving [quant] (#quant). This lower bound also applies to the smaller class \(D_m(\Omega)\).

It follows that \[\|T_n-F^{(m)}\|_*\ge c(n+1)^{-1/3},\] while [bad] (#bad) requires \[\|T_n-F^{(m)}\|_*\le
 3\left(\frac1{n+1}+C(2,5,3)n^{-1/2}\right).\] For any finite declared \(C\), the lower bound eventually exceeds the upper bound. The field varies across members of this family, which is legitimate because the stated constant excludes dependence on the field, and all members have identical domain, \(L\), dimension, and moment exponents.
#### Dependency, counterevidence, and correction scope.

This is Major: Theorem 4.7 is a principal contribution, Remark 4.8 explicitly advertises improved regularity and dimension-independent rates from choosing larger \(p\), and Corollaries 4.10 and 4.16 reuse its bound. Assumption [lip] (#lip) supplies no such \(p\)-dependent regularity. Appendix A, p. 11, moves from the \(W_1\) assumption to a rate written for an expected \(W_p\) with \(p\)-power homogeneity; the elementary counterexamples above suffice without resolving the external citation’s conventions.

Problem 2 (The core dynamics proof uses unjustified coupling and support bounds).  The derivations supporting Theorems 4.12 and 4.14 contain invalid intermediate steps, although their conditional conclusions admit the explicit repairs below.
#### Synchronous transport is not necessarily optimal.

Appendix C, p. 15, integrates the displacement of the two flow maps \(X,Y\) over their common initial law, then replaces \[D(t)=\int\|Y(t,x)-X(t,x)\|_2\,d\mu_0(x)\] by \(W(t)=W_1(\mu_F(t),\mu_{T_n}(t))\) inside a right-hand-side upper bound. The pushforward coupling proves only \(W(t)\le D(t)\). It does not permit that replacement.

For a concrete diagnostic, let \(\mu_0\) be uniform on a circle of radius \(r\) in \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(F=0\), and let \(T_n(x,\mu)=\omega Jx\), where \(J\) generates planar rotation. This linear map is representable by positionwise networks. Both marginal laws remain the same uniform circle measure, so \(W(t)=0\), while \[D(t)=2r|\sin(\omega t/2)|>0\] at nontrivial times. The fields are locally Lipschitz with linear growth. On a fixed ball the approximation error can be made arbitrarily small by reducing \(|\omega|\). This disproves the implicit optimal-coupling identification; it is not a counterexample to the final stability bound.
#### A verified replacement argument.

Keep \(D\) throughout the source’s valid pointwise displacement estimate. For trajectories remaining in the approximation ball, \[D(t)\le\varepsilon t+
 L\int_0^tW(s)\,ds+L\int_0^tD(s)\,ds
 \le\varepsilon t+2L\int_0^tD(s)\,ds.\] Gronwall gives \(D(t)\le\varepsilon t e^{2Lt}\), and therefore \[W_1(\mu_F(t),\mu_{T_n}(t))\le\varepsilon t e^{2Lt}.\] Thus the stated conditional conclusion of Theorem 4.14 survives this repair.
#### The companion support calculation.

Proposition B.1, p. 13, drops the initial \(\|x\|_2\) when adding a trajectory bound to a first-moment bound. At \(t=0\), \(\mu_0=\delta_R\) with \(R>0\), its intermediate inequality becomes \(2R\le R\). This calculation is invalid.

The required support estimate can instead be obtained from the support radius \(r(t)\): \[r(t)\le R+M\int_0^t(1+2r(s))\,ds,
 \qquad
 r(t)\le(R+\tfrac12)e^{2Mt}-\tfrac12
 \le(R+2Mt)e^{3Mt}.\] A first-exit argument applies this bound while the support lies inside \(B_K\). The strict condition \(K>(R+2M\tau)e^{3M\tau}\) prevents an exit before \(\tau\). For the approximating field replace \(M\) by \(M+\varepsilon\) and choose \(\varepsilon\) small enough to preserve the strict inequality. Local Lipschitz continuity and a compact cutoff supply the usual local existence and uniqueness step on that region.
#### Assessment and boundary.

These are demonstrated invalid steps in the proof of the paper’s central dynamical approximation claim, assessed Major under the requested core-derivation standard. The repairs above preserve the conditional support and stability bounds; no false-conclusion claim is made for those bounds. They do not repair Problem 1 or its propagated rate. The needed domain evaluations on \(B_K\) are understood to be defined, as required by the source’s own hypotheses.

Problem 3 (Released evaluation paths do not compute their stated metrics).  The pinned notebook release has definite reduction and metric defects. The historical dependency of the published scores is unresolved, so the demonstrated release defects are assessed Minor and the published numerical consequences remain Needs Evidence.
All cell indices below are zero-based. Exact cell text, source paths and hashes are saved in `e.txt` and the source audit.
#### Test MSE and selection.

In `Cucker_Smale_using_Transformer.ipynb`, cell 27 initializes a four-element zero loss vector and \(i=0\), but never increments \(i\) inside the batch loop. Cell 35 averages that vector. Therefore it reports \(L_{\rm last}/4\), not the test-set MSE. If every target coordinate has squared error one, the correct MSE is one and the released path returns \(1/4\). This diagnostic is independent of model or dataset.

The GNN evaluator in cell 36 increments its index and retains all batch losses, making the reduction asymmetric across the compared methods. Cell 34 also overwrites its validation statistic on each of five trials and selects using the last trial; the GNN selector in cell 37 accumulates a trial average. Correct evaluation must sum squared errors over all coordinates and divide by their total count, rather than merely average unequal-sized batch means.
#### Trajectory errors.

In `Simulating_CS_Dynamics.ipynb`, cell 27 stores a separate error array for every trial but divides each trial’s particle-averaged absolute coordinate error by 100. Cell 30 takes medians and quartiles without undoing that factor. The quantity is \[\frac1{100N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}|e_j|,\] whereas p. 5 describes a 2-norm. If every \(e_j=1\), the released value is \(0.01\), the MAE is one, and the 2-norm is \(\sqrt N\). Removing the factor alone does not resolve the metric mismatch.
#### Parameter errors and baseline range.

In `Mean_Field_Two_Layer_Transformers.ipynb`, cell 20 stores the coordinate mean of squared parameter errors; cell 26 labels it as a squared norm, while p. 5 describes a Frobenius norm. For the specified \(11\times100\) parameter array, a saved value \(v\) corresponds to Frobenius norm \(\sqrt{1100v}\).

The CS notebook’s `Cylindrical_FNN` in cell 12 applies ReLU after every layer, including the final output. Its enclosing cylindrical baseline therefore cannot produce negative accelerations. Two co-located particles with velocities \(1\) and \(0\) and the paper’s unit CS parameters require acceleration \(-1/2\) for the first particle. This is an explicit representational restriction of the released baseline for the signed target.
#### Counterevidence and remaining evidence.

These formulas are statically established, but the current commit is not certified as the conference-time experiment version. Its stored CS score differs from Table 1, its trajectory cell uses 20 particles and a time horizon of 20 rather than the reported 30-particle setting, and the current two-layer evaluation cell specifies one trial rather than 100. Checkpoints and the private/local tensors loaded by these notebooks are unavailable. No corrected score, changed ranking, or exact error factor for the published plots is asserted. Fish-milling evaluators were separately inspected by an auxiliary and do not share the missing-index bug.
# Conclusion and verification boundaries
Claim | Assessment | Verified consequence
Theorem 4.7 and inherited rate | Major | Two exact counterexample families; rate requires revision
Core dynamics derivation | Major | Invalid intermediate steps; conditional conclusion repaired
Current notebook evaluation | Minor | Wrong metrics/reductions; published numerical effect unresolved
Scientific adjudication | Pending | Initial review only; human reviews empty
Author adoption | Unknown | No contact or adoption request

The report does not claim whole-paper invalidity. The expectation construction, permutation-equivariant design, and conditional flow-stability mechanism retain meaningful content. The paper’s empirical phenomena were not reproduced or refuted. A finite grid or stored notebook plot does not certify the supremum over all measures in the theoretical norm.

No later correction was established from the staged materials. Separate OpenReview attachment discovery was unavailable in the preparation record (HTTP 403); the embedded appendices were fully available. External cited-paper proofs, precise historical experiment provenance, raw data and trained checkpoints remain unverified.

Title: Technical Verification of Sliding Puzzles Gym
# Identity, sources, and scope

This report reviews B. L. M. de Oliveira, L. G. B. Martins, B. Brandao, M. L. da Luz, T. W. de L. Soares, and L. C. Melo, Sliding Puzzles Gym: A Scalable Benchmark for State Representation in Visual Reinforcement Learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Assigned identifiers are 0284/I25-43653. The original proceedings PDF has 29 pages. Locations below are one-based PDF pages, matching printed numbers; code locations use one-based file lines.

The complete paper text, decisive original table images, benchmark environment, and selected experiment/evaluation sources were inspected. All 194 staged manifest entries passed hash checks. The environment release is pinned to
the experiment release is pinned to
ce0be1b3c6bf849219be629b9c9cb4fc25d1b116.

Both are current public commits recorded by source preparation, not certified conference-time versions. Their source-only archives and member/version/hash mappings were preserved. The parent independently checked source control flow, performed the calculations below, and integrated three native auxiliary reviews. No author code or training was executed.
# Definitions and positive checks

The principal experiments fix a \(3\times3\) puzzle, four directional actions, and a pool of images used to render tile identities. Increasing the image pool leaves the underlying numbered-tile transition and distance-reward rules unchanged. The separate grid-size experiment explicitly changes the state space and search difficulty.

The printed counts, p. 4, are correct: \[|S_{3\times3}|=\frac{9!}{2}=181440,\qquad
 |S_{4\times4}|=\frac{16!}{2}=10461394944000.\] A reviewer-written breadth-first search over all legal blank-neighbor swaps independently found 181440 reachable states, maximum distance 31, and uniform mean shortest-path distance \[\frac{249167}{11340}=21.972398589065257.\] This supports the approximately 22-step reference on p. 9. The current fast initializer moves an accidentally sampled goal to a random one-step neighbor, changing that mean by only \(1/181440\), to \(21.9724041005291\). The nominal exact uniform distribution and this release detail should be distinguished, but the 22-step approximation is unaffected.

The paper’s primary outcome is environment steps to 80% success. It also uses success flags for early stopping and final evaluation. The integrity of those flags and their aggregation is therefore central to its comparative claims.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Central sample-efficiency results are reported incompatibly).  Main Table 1, p. 6, and Appendix Tables 10 and 12, pp. 24 and 27, give different values for the same method, pool size, and stated outcome: million environment steps to 80% success.
Method | Pool | Main Table 1 | Tables 10/12

The parent verified the original images and row alignment. These are not extraction errors. The DBC pool-10 conflict is particularly consequential: Table 1 suggests threshold attainment near 2.13M steps, while Table 12 records the 10M cap and only \(2\pm1\)% final ID success. The displayed uncertainty intervals cannot reconcile these values as two renderings of the same summary. Table 10 repeats the appendix efficiency values.
#### Impact and counterevidence.

This is Major because the inconsistency affects the core comparison of representation-learning methods and whether a configuration successfully learned. It does not identify which table is authoritative. A different historical run, configuration or statistic might explain the discrepancy, but no such distinction is stated at the compared entries. The staged sources do not supply the SPGym numerical run traces or table-generation inputs needed to resolve it. A corrected table must be bound to exact runs and a defined censoring rule; merely choosing the preferred value is not a verified repair.

The same results discussion, p. 6 and Appendix C.2.1, p. 25, overstates DreamerV3’s sample-efficiency dominance. RAD’s reported means are 0.24, 0.42 and 0.82M at pools 1, 5 and 10, versus DreamerV3’s 0.42, 1.23 and 1.44M. Lower is better, so RAD is faster at every shared pool. Standard SAC is also faster at pools 1 and 5. This does not contradict the separate observation that standard Dreamer handles larger pools more successfully, or eventually finds shorter solutions. Those outcomes should not be substituted for universal sample-efficiency superiority.

Problem 2 (The released environment can terminate an unsolved reset state as a success).  The environment retains a prior episode’s terminal flag through reset and reuses it on an invalid action. This violates the benchmark’s basic success semantics.
#### Exact control flow.

The file initializes the cached flag only in its constructor (lines 158–164), setting `last_terminated` to `False`. Valid actions recompute reward and termination, but lines 229–234 reuse `self.last_terminated` on invalid actions. Lines 236–242 store the result and set `info["is_success"]=terminated`. The reset method, lines 249–278, resets the step counter and puzzle state without resetting that cached terminal flag.
#### A legal, complete trace.

Use the default blank value \(-1\) and the states \[A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&-1&8\end{bmatrix},
 \quad
 G=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&-1\end{bmatrix},
 \quad
 B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\-1&7&8\end{bmatrix}.\] Starting at \(A\), action 2 moves the blank right and produces \(G\). The goal test sets `last_terminated=True`. Reset to \(B\). This state passes the release’s explicit-state validation, is solvable, and has positive probability under its ordinary fast shuffle. It is two valid moves from \(G\), as the independent graph calculation confirms.

Now take action 0, whose blank displacement is downward. Since the blank is already in the bottom row, this action is invalid. The code leaves the state equal to \(B\) and returns \[\text{reward}=-1,\qquad
 \text{terminated}=\texttt{True},\qquad
 \text{is\_success}=\texttt{True}.\] No puzzle was solved in the new episode. The negative reward does not correct the false success flag.
#### Core dependency and limits.

The PPO/SAC utility `r02/ppo_sac/src/utils.py`, lines 323–343 and 379–398, consumes terminal success flags for rolling statistics, early stopping and evaluation. Dreamer’s adapter, `r02/dreamerv3/embodied/envs/spgym.py`, lines 63–105, passes them into terminal observations and `log_success`. Thus this is a demonstrated defect in the released benchmark’s core outcome, assessed Major.

A valid first action after reset recalculates termination and clears the stale flag when the new puzzle remains unsolved. The finding therefore does not imply every episode is affected. A shuffle that happens to generate the solved state also executes a valid move, which can clear the cache; the explicit non-goal \(B\) avoids that branch. No empirical frequency or historical score inflation is inferred.

Resetting episode-specific cached fields and making invalid-action termination depend on the current state would repair this trace. The source was not modified and a patched environment was not executed. The saved check validates the independent state transitions and statically confirms that reset does not assign `last_terminated`; it does not import or run the author environment.

Problem 3 (The released Dreamer success statistic has the wrong denominator).  The supplied Dreamer training path counts successes in a 100-episode rolling window but divides by the number of parallel environments, 64.
#### Configuration and implementation.

In `r02/dreamerv3/embodied/run/train.py`, lines 33–34 construct deques with `maxlen=args.rolling_window`. Lines 65–70 append each completed episode’s success and compute \[\texttt{success\_rate}
 =\frac{\texttt{sum(success\_deque)}}{\texttt{args.num\_envs}}.\] The supplied `dreamerv3/configs.yaml`, relative to the experiment’s Dreamer directory, sets `rolling_window:100` in its defaults and `num_envs:64` in the SPGym preset. The image preset inherits SPGym; the experiment launcher selects that preset. Episode `log_success` is aggregated by maximum, making each correctly classified episode’s contribution zero or one.
At a full window, let \(k\) be the number of successful episodes. The true success rate is \(k/100\), but the release logs \(k/64\):
Successes in 100 episodes | True rate | Released logged rate
An 80% threshold on this logged quantity can therefore be crossed at only 52% true success. This calculation assumes genuine episode labels and is independent of Problem 2.
#### Early stopping and comparison.

Lines 75–78 increment the early-stop counter when the logged value equals one; lines 154–157 stop after sufficient increments. A periodic sequence containing 64 successes and 36 failures per 100 episodes has exactly 64 successes in every full 100-episode window. It can satisfy the code’s 100% test continuously despite persistent failures. A truly perfect full window instead gives 1.5625 and resets that counter.

PPO/SAC’s utility divides its success count by the deque length correctly; Dreamer’s return average also uses the deque length. The denominator error is therefore specific and makes the released success statistics incomparable. This is Major for the core released metric and dependent stopping behavior.
#### Historical attribution and repair.

The paper’s Table 7, p. 16, lists 16 Dreamer environments, whereas the current SPGym preset uses 64. This is additional evidence that the current release must not be silently identified with the historical run configuration. No staged raw SPGym logs or aggregation code establish whether the published tables used this erroneous field unchanged. A particular published numerical correction is therefore not asserted.

The local correction is division by the number of episodes actually represented, with a clearly defined full-window requirement and early stopping based on the corrected fraction. The independent arithmetic and periodic-window diagnostic verify the intended normalization; no patched Dreamer training was executed.
# Claims that still need evidence
#### Dreamer Hard-OOD coverage.

Section 5.3, p. 8, states that all five seeds of PPO, SAC and Dreamer were tested on Hard OOD. Appendix C.2, p. 23, says those OOD metrics were not computed for Dreamer because of codebase complexities, and Table 13 has no OOD columns. The observed manuscript conflict is definite; Dreamer’s actual OOD result is unknown. Extending the measured near-zero PPO/SAC result to Dreamer, including the 100-image training-pool regime, needs run-level evidence. No missing Dreamer score is invented.
#### Linear-probe correlation and analysis unit.

The parent transcribed all 37 displayed mean pairs in Table 10 and independently recomputed Pearson correlation: \[r=-0.7729793020026258,\qquad
 p_{\mathrm{iid}}=2.0630148456076282\times10^{-8}.\] The paper reports \(r=-0.81\), \(p=1.1\times10^{-13}\). Replacing the seven disputed efficiency means by their Table 1 values gives \[r=-0.7279571991017988,\qquad
 p_{\mathrm{iid}}=3.294554605371535\times10^{-7}.\] The substantial negative association survives. These reference calculations do not prove the published statistic false: unrounded run-level inputs, a different subset or another analysis unit may have been used. The exact paired data, method/pool clustering and treatment of budget-censored observations are required to assess its inferential meaning. The reference \(p\)-values assume independent pairs; that assumption is not certified for this experiment.
#### Censoring, budgets, units, and interpretation.

Values of \(10.00\pm0.00\) alongside very low final success should not be treated as demonstrated threshold attainment at 10M steps; the censoring convention must be explicit. The 4-by-4 PPO result of \(24.46\pm7.58\)M, p. 9, needs the stated 10M budget’s extended-run exception documented. Easy-OOD values such as 0.49 are repeated under percentage headings in Tables 11–12, while the released evaluator emits a fraction; exact table aggregation is needed to resolve the display units.

The manuscript acknowledges, p. 23, that end-to-end representation and policy learning are not perfectly separable. Pool-size control is useful, but correlations and degradation curves do not uniquely identify memorization or architectural mismatch as their cause. These are interpretation boundaries, not proofs that the benchmark idea or every empirical trend is invalid.
# Conclusion
Item | Assessment | Established scope
Efficiency-table conflict | Major | Same stated metric has incompatible reported results
Reset success leakage | Major | Concrete false success in current release
Dreamer normalization | Major | Wrong success rate and stopping condition in current release
Historical numerical impact | Needs Evidence | Exact runs and metric inputs unavailable
State counts and optimal distance | No Issue Found | Independently checked finite puzzle graph
Adjudication / adoption | Pending / Unknown | Human reviews empty; no author contact

The core benchmark idea and the verified combinatorics remain useful. The source record demonstrates outcome-semantic defects and inconsistent reporting, but does not establish revised historical rankings or a whole-paper failure. Initial scientific review is complete within the stated scope; separate acceptance is outstanding.

Title: Technical Verification of VTGaussian-SLAM
# Identity, evidence, and contribution

This report concerns P. Hu and Z. Han, VTGaussian-SLAM: RGBD SLAM for Large Scale Scenes with Splatting View-Tied 3D Gaussians, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], assigned 0285/I25-43654. The reviewed original PDF has 24 pages. Locations use one-based PDF pages and source lines. The complete text, decisive original pages, source manifest and selected released implementation paths were inspected. All 74 staged manifest entries matched their hashes. The preserved source archive contains 67 selected members; preparation separately records 23 excluded compiled cache members. No author program was executed.
The release [Retained latex: \cite{code}] is pinned to

This is the available public identity, not a certified historical experiment commit. The method groups neighboring RGBD frames into sections, fixes Gaussian centers to depth-derived locations, uses isotropic Gaussians, and optimizes color, radius and opacity while tracking camera poses. Section selection and offloading limit the active working set. Eqs. 1–2 define empirical objectives, not a convergence theorem. Three native auxiliaries supplied mathematical, source and empirical challenges. The parent independently integrated evidence, calculated witnesses, inspected source pages and performed compilation and visual checks.
# Demonstrated problems

Problem 1 (Major: the released tracking evaluator does not compute its stated RMSE).  The tracking metric is specified as root mean square absolute trajectory error on p. 5 and in Tables 1, 4–6, 10–11, 13, 15 and 20. In `utils/eval_helpers.py`, lines 29–63 align estimated and ground-truth positions and form per-position Euclidean errors. Lines 66–83 return their arithmetic mean; lines 544–550 call the result `ate_rmse` and report it as ATE RMSE.

For aligned errors \(e_i=\|R\hat t_i+t-t_i^{\rm GT}\|_2\), these quantities are \[M=\frac1n\sum_i e_i,\qquad Q=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_i e_i^2}.\] They satisfy \(M\le Q\), with equality exactly when all magnitudes agree. The prior square root constructs each Euclidean distance; it does not make the subsequent arithmetic mean an RMSE.
#### A valid ranking reversal.

Take all eight ground-truth positions \(g=(x,y,z)\in\{-1,1\}^3\), in metres, and estimates \[\hat g_A=g+0.01yz(1+x)e_1,\qquad
 \hat g_B=g+0.012yz e_1,\qquad e_1=(1,0,0).\] Both error fields have zero mean and zero cross moment with \(g\). The centered cross-covariance is \(8I_3\), positive definite and full rank. Identity is the unique optimal rigid rotation and translation is zero. The construction therefore does not exploit degenerate alignment. A has four zero errors and four errors of \(2\) cm; B has eight errors of \(1.2\) cm:
Trajectory | Returned mean (cm) | Correct RMSE (cm)

The ranking reverses. Imposing a common first-pose convention by subtracting each trajectory’s first center adds only translations removed by alignment. A parent-written SVD calculation verifies both conventions, covariance and residuals; a mathematical auxiliary independently verified the construction.
#### Core dependency and counterevidence.

This is an active path: `src/vtgaussian_slam.py` imports the evaluator at line 28, invokes it for saved evaluation around lines 1389–1396, and for final evaluation around lines 2880–2886. The released Replica configuration enables the latter through `use_wandb=True`. Tracking accuracy is a core contribution, so a mathematically different statistic capable of reversing its ordering supports Major without requiring a demonstrated benchmark-score loss. However, historical trajectories, logs and code-to-table bindings are absent. No particular published score correction is established.
#### Correction and verification.

Compute \(\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(e_i^2)}\) after alignment, preserve frame correspondence and regenerate affected tables from original runs. Correct arithmetic is verified on the witness, but no author-code patch or experiment was run. A similar square-root-before-mean expression occurs in the released depth RMSE calculation; the paper’s reconstruction tables explicitly use depth L1, so that naming defect does not itself invalidate those tables.

Problem 2 (Major: retained attributes contradict the released storage account).  Section 3.2, p. 3, explicitly removes location, rotation and two scale components, retaining three color scalars, one radius and one opacity. It claims \((14-5)/14=64.3\%\) storage savings; Table 7, p. 9, gives five parameters per Gaussian. The available implementation persistently retains twelve scalar attributes.
In `src/vtgaussian_slam.py`, initialization at lines 132–170 stores:
Array | Scalars per Gaussian
`means3D` | 3
`rgb_colors` | 3
`unnorm_rotations` | 4
`logit_opacities` | 1
`log_scales`, isotropic case | 1
Total | 12

Additional Gaussians use the same structure at lines 692–726. Selected sections copy all five arrays to CUDA at lines 900–928; updates retain them at lines 980–996. Lines 2832–2835 move their values to CPU rather than delete them. Lines 2870–2876 serialize the entire parameter-list dictionaries to `params_ls.npy`. These are active and persistent arrays, not dead initialization state.

At float32 precision, this attribute payload is \(48N\) bytes for \(N\) Gaussians, versus \(20N\) for five scalars. Relative to the manuscript’s fourteen-scalar reference, \[(14-12)/14=1/7\approx14.3\%,\] not \(64.3\%\). This calculation excludes images, camera state, optimizer buffers, scratch arrays and indexing metadata. It is not a measurement of total or peak memory.
#### Counterevidence and bounded impact.

The abstract \(9/14\) arithmetic is correct. Zero learning rates for centers and rotations in `configs/replica/room0.py` support five optimized attributes, but do not eliminate stored arrays. View tying is partly implemented: lines 2705–2727 move stored centers with an updated head-frame pose. CPU offloading genuinely limits GPU residency. Broader scalability is therefore not disproved.

The available release nevertheless contradicts an explicit central storage mechanism. Major concerns that demonstrated representation/claim mismatch. A different historical implementation could resolve it, but none is bound to the paper’s tables; historical memory totals remain Needs Evidence.
#### Correction and verification.

Either reconstruct centers from retained depth/pixel/frame references and omit redundant isotropic rotations, accounting for that metadata and transient renderer buffers, or describe the twelve-attribute representation. Report optimized, retained, GPU-resident and peak allocations separately. Static persistence and arithmetic were verified; no profiler or modified renderer was run.

Problem 3 (Minor: comparative prose and displayed averages require correction).  The ScanNet statement on p. 7 claims the best average tracking accuracy. Table 5, p. 8, and Table 13, p. 18, give Ours \(11.3\) cm and unstarred NICE-SLAM \(10.7\) cm. Excluding pretrained-prior methods cannot remove this contradiction.

The six displayed scene values give \(68/6=11.3333\ldots\) for Ours and \(64.4/6=10.7333\ldots\) for NICE-SLAM. Restricting the claim to displayed Gaussian-splatting methods without marked pretrained priors resolves it. Two other simple means disagree:
Quantity | Recomputed | Printed
LoopSplat ScanNet++ ATE, Table 15 | 2.01 | 2.05
Point-SLAM Replica PSNR, Table 18 | 35.045 | 35.17

The first inputs are 1.14, 3.16, 3.16, 1.68, 0.91. The second inputs are 32.40, 34.08, 35.50, 38.26, 39.16, 33.99, 33.48, 33.49. Discrepancies exceed two-decimal rounding uncertainty. A different weighting rule would need disclosure. Neither correction reverses the proposed method’s corresponding ranking. Correct the prose and aggregates or document the intended weighting. Raw-run reconciliation remains unavailable.
# Surviving checks and unresolved claims
#### Bounded No Issue Found.

Inspected backprojection uses inverse world-to-camera pose on depth-scaled camera rays; forward transformation applies world-to-camera pose. Isotropic covariance obeys \(R(r^2I)R^\top=r^2I\). Initialization logs the square root of squared projected radius, and rendering exponentiates it to recover \(r=D_{\rm GT}/f\), consistent with Eq. 3. The manuscript’s loose radius/variance terminology did not establish a substantive covariance error. Eqs. 1–2 define objectives, not a proven convergence or drift-elimination guarantee.

The method’s ScanNet++ mean \(1.548\to1.55\) and novel-view PSNR \(21.456\to21.46\) agree with the displayed scene values. Appendix C discloses refinement on all training views and testing on held-out views; novel-view evaluation is present. Table 3’s reconstruction superlative also needs a comparison scope, but pp. 6 and 14 explicitly acknowledge extra inputs for Point-SLAM and marked-prior systems.
#### Needs Evidence.

Tables 20–21 provide selected KITTI accuracy and rendering results: large-scene experiments are not absent. Appendix B gives only parts of sequences, without exact frame ranges or spatial extents. Those details and run identities are needed to interpret the city-scale claim. Table 21 reports peak GPU use \(4.79\) GiB for Ours, \(2.74\) for Gaussian-SLAM, \(3.56\) for LoopSplat and \(22.37\) for SplaTAM. The text acknowledges a quality/capacity tradeoff; these values neither prove universal memory superiority nor refute useful offloading.

Table 9’s total and maximum counts lack precise retained/resident definitions. They cannot alone establish prior methods’ architectures. Table 22 gives depth-noise tests without the corruption distribution or amplitude; robustness is bounded to that unspecified experiment. Historical contamination of tracking tables, actual memory allocations, selected KITTI scope and general robustness remain unresolved.
# Disposition and evidence

The assessment is Major, based on Problems 1–2; Problem 3 is Minor. This is initial scientific review, not acceptance. Adjudication is pending, author adoption unknown and human reviews empty. No whole-paper correctness or collapse is claimed.

Title: Technical Verification of Certification for Differentially Private Prediction
# Identity and scope

This review concerns M. Wicker, P. Sosnin, I. Shilov, A. Janik, M. N. Mueller, Y.-A. de Montjoye, A. Weller and C. Tsay, Certification for Differentially Private Prediction in Gradient-Based Training, ICML 2025, PMLR 267 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}], assigned 0286/I25-43655. All 20 original PDF pages were read as text; decisive equations and proofs were additionally inspected in rendered original pages. Page references are one-based PDF pages. Source references use one-based file lines.
All 98 staged manifest entries matched their recorded hashes; the preserved source archive contains 91 members. The public repository [Retained latex: \cite{code}] is pinned to

This identity is not asserted to be the historical experiment commit. Static inspection covered active privacy training, gradient accumulation, clipping, interval SGD, certificate selection and prediction mechanisms. No author code was executed. Native mathematical, source and challenge auxiliaries worked independently; the parent recomputed the decisive examples, checked original pixels, integrated findings and compiled and inspected this report.

The method first encloses parameters reachable after bounded dataset edits, then certifies a constant binary prediction on that enclosure. It uses a certified stability radius \(k_c(D)\) to obtain the pointwise bound \[SS_\beta(f_x,D)\le B(D):=e^{-\beta k_c(D)}.\] The final step uses \(B(D)\) as a noise scale. These logically distinct stages must be checked separately.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Major: a pointwise upper bound is not a smooth noise scale).  Theorem 5.1 and Eq. 9, p. 6, establish a pointwise sensitivity upper bound. Corollary 5.2, p. 7, substitutes it into Cauchy noise and claims pure \((\epsilon,0)\)-DP. Appendix D.6, p. 17, justifies this by saying that any upper bound can replace smooth sensitivity because increasing noise cannot reduce privacy. That assertion is false for dataset-dependent increases.

A suitable scale must control variation between neighboring datasets. Pointwise domination \(B(D)\ge SS_\beta(f_x,D)\) does not imply \[B(D)\le e^\beta B(D')\quad\text{whenever }d(D,D')=1.\] Appendix C, pp. 14–15, explicitly selects the largest certified value from an affordable grid. A sound but incomplete or grid-rounded certificate can jump between neighbors.
## A counterexample using sound AGT bounds

Use a scalar logistic model with logit \(\theta x\), label \(1\{\theta x>0\}\), binary cross-entropy loss, public initialization \(\tau=1/10000\), learning rate \(1\), one epoch, coordinate clipping \(\gamma=1/2\), and a public maximum batch size of 121. Let the public dataset domain contain labeled multisets with sizes between 61 and 121. Thus every permissible dataset has exactly one batch and all selected radii below are smaller than the batch size. This restriction makes the example independent of the batch-count defect in Problem 2.

Let \(D_{121}\) contain 121 individuals with \((x,y)=(1,0)\), and obtain adjacent \(D_{120}\) by deleting one. Query \(x=1\). The original gradients at initialization are \(\sigma(\tau)>1/2\), hence clip exactly to \(1/2\). Both nominal trained parameters are \[\theta_{\rm nom}=\tau-\tfrac12=-0.4999,\qquad f_x(D_{121})=f_x(D_{120})=0.\] Theorem 4.6 and Algorithm 1 give, for \(n=120,121\), \[\Delta\Theta_k=[\tfrac12-k/n,\tfrac12],
 \qquad
 \Theta_k(D_n)=[\tau-\tfrac12,\;\tau-\tfrac12+k/n].\] These are sound bounds: arbitrary added gradients are clipped to \([-1/2,1/2]\), and the formula even covers independently up to \(k\) removals and \(k\) additions, a larger perturbation set than a total edit budget \(k\).
Take the permissible grid \(\mathcal K=\{0,50,60\}\). Its 50-to-60 gap also occurs in both released OCT and IMDB grids; the example is not a reproduction of those datasets or hyperparameters.
Dataset | Upper endpoint, \(k=50\) | Upper endpoint, \(k=60\) | Selected \(k_c\)

The first interval at \(k=60\) is strictly negative; the second contains negative and positive logits. There is no floating-point tie. All certificates that succeed are sound. The released loader also accepts each sole batch: it infers the full size from the first observed batch, so the 120-record neighbor is processed.
## Violation for the actual released binary event

At \(\epsilon=1\), Eq. 10 uses \(s_k=6e^{-k/6}\). Since both nominal labels are zero, the event \(R=1\) has probability \[p_k=\Pr\{\operatorname{Cauchy}(s_k)>1/2\}
     =\frac{\arctan(2s_k)}{\pi}.\] Independent calculation yields \[p_{60}=0.00017341494055,\qquad
 p_{50}=0.00091814122188,\qquad
 \frac{p_{50}}{p_{60}}=5.294475891>e.\] Equivalently, \(p_{50}-e\,p_{60}=0.0004467505402>0\). This violates the pure-DP inequality for neighboring datasets after binary postprocessing. Adding the released helper’s \(10^{-8}\) scale floor leaves the ratio \(5.294318243>e\).
#### Implementation and core dependency.

In , lines 82–123 choose the largest available certified \(k\), and lines 149–150 exponentiate it. In , lines 134–160 add Cauchy noise with scale \(6e^{-\epsilon k/6}/\epsilon+10^{-8}\) and threshold the binary prediction. The OCT script line 49 and IMDB script line 36 contain consecutive candidates 50 and 60. The independent calculation models these formulas without importing them.

Corollary 5.2 supplies the principal privacy guarantee, its ensemble application and subsequent composition. Its failure therefore supports Major directly. Theorem 5.1’s pointwise inequality remains valid; the counterexample uses valid enclosures. No claim that historical experiment records instantiate the example is needed to refute the theorem.
#### Possible repairs and their limits.

The exact maximal true stable radius is 1-Lipschitz across neighboring datasets: for equal predicted labels, distances to the opposite-label set differ by at most one; opposite-label neighbors both have radius zero. A certified lower bound need not inherit that property. One mathematical repair is a global smooth majorant \[\overline B(D)=\sup_Z e^{-\beta d(D,Z)}B(Z).\] It dominates \(B\), and the triangle inequality proves its neighbor ratio is at most \(e^\beta\). But this may reintroduce the intractable dataset-space optimization the paper avoids. A practical replacement must prove smoothness or supply a different valid mechanism, then revisit utility at the claimed privacy levels. No efficient repair or revised benchmark curve is verified here.

Problem 2 (Major: changed update counts can invalidate parameter enclosures).  Theorem 4.5, p. 5, and Appendix D.3, pp. 15–16, claim valid parameter bounds for gradient training with fixed hyperparameters. The induction encloses a common sequence of updates but does not ensure that neighboring datasets have the same number or correspondence of updates. Fixed data ordering does not establish that property. The released incomplete-batch policy gives an explicit false prediction-stability certificate.

Use a scalar bias logit \(\theta\), binary prediction \(1\{\theta>0\}\), BCE loss, 20 identical zero-input/zero-label records, and \[\theta_0=3/20,\quad \gamma=1/10,\quad
 \alpha=1,\quad b=10,\quad E=1,\quad k=1.\] All original gradients over the relevant pre-update parameter intervals exceed \(1/10\), so clipping gives exactly \(1/10\). Each nominal full batch has certified gradient bounds \[g_L=\frac{9(1/10)-1/10}{10}=\frac{2}{25},
 \qquad g_U=\frac{9(1/10)+1/10}{10}=\frac1{10}.\] Interval SGD therefore gives \[[0.15,0.15]\longrightarrow[0.05,0.07]
                 \longrightarrow[-0.05,-0.01].\] The nominal parameter is \(-0.05\), and the entire final interval predicts zero. The method therefore certifies stability at distance one.

Delete one individual. The neighbor has 19 records. The released wrapper processes ten, then skips the final batch of nine, leaving the actual parameter \[\theta(D')=0.15-0.10=0.05>0.\] This lies outside the certified enclosure and predicts one. Identical records remove any dependence on shuffle order, and the sign margins avoid numerical boundary cases.
#### Source binding.

The active loop in calls ; the latter in `training_utils.py`, lines 168–223, sets full batch size from the first batch and skips subsequent unequal sizes. The experiment training helper, lines 135–146, uses an ordinary shuffled DataLoader. Coordinate clipping is at `training_utils.py` lines 255–259. The private accumulator’s lines 253–317 implement the trimmed sums and nominal-batch denominator. Bounded SGD lines 102–104 apply the interval update. These static paths yield the exact arithmetic above.
#### Impact, counterevidence, and correction.

The counterexample invalidates Definition 4.3’s enclosure and the prediction certificate inferred from it. It is independent of Problem 1: there, the enclosure is sound and the noise scale is wrong; here, the enclosure itself fails for the released training schedule. The main experiments use maximum/full batches, so this example does not prove their reported certificates encountered this particular multi-batch boundary.

A repair must specify and enforce a neighboring-dataset-consistent update schedule and batch coupling, or enclose changes in both membership and update count. Removing the skip alone is insufficient: including a new last partial batch can instead introduce an extra update. The per-batch theorem can support a correctly coupled training definition; the unqualified minibatch claim and accessible implementation need correction. No patched training implementation was run.
# Surviving mathematics and evidence limits
#### Bounded No Issue Found.

Lemma 4.2 follows from the dataset-distance triangle inequality; Lemma 4.4 is valid conditional on a genuine parameter enclosure. Theorem 5.1’s pointwise bound survives. For \(0\le k<b\) and nonempty batches, Theorem 4.6’s final clipped-gradient bound is independently recoverable: maximizing a scalar mean permits adding \(k\) copies of \(+\gamma\) and removing the \(k\) smallest originals, producing the top-\((b-k)\) sum plus \(k\gamma\), divided by \(b\). Each operation increases the mean. Coordinatewise interval extension is sound. The parent checked 20,250 finite exact-rational cases as a supplementary diagnostic; that finite check is not the proof.

Appendix D.4’s intermediate all-\(b\) summation indices do not match the final trimmed sum, and Appendix B repeats a lower-bound label where the upper-bound expression is intended. These local notation defects do not supply another false final theorem. The inspected IBP/BCE/clipping formulas pass bounded algebraic checks.

For positive vote margin and a public partition in which one record edit affects one teacher, the main ensemble radius \(\sum_{i\in S_n}k_i+n-1\) follows because flipping teacher \(i\) costs at least \(k_i+1\) edits. Appendix D.7 omits that additive term in its proof. Exact vote ties yield the undefined displayed \(K=-1\); they require a nonnegative fallback or corrected flip count. No additional implemented ensemble counterexample is asserted. A valid ensemble stability bound would still need a repaired privacy mechanism.
#### Experimental scope and Needs Evidence.

The OCT claim concerns private dense-layer fine-tuning with assumed-public pretraining. IMDB uses fixed assumed-public GPT-2 embeddings and a trained small classifier, not a certificate for updating all GPT-2 parameters. The paper candidly discusses loose bounds for deeper models, many iterations, small batches and multiclass losses. These limits are not treated as scientific errors.

Accuracy plots and Table 1 were read, but raw experiment outputs and historical model/configuration bindings were unavailable. Surprising student values in Table 1 do not alone prove a numerical defect. The empirical noise/accuracy observations can remain real, while their interpretation at the claimed DP level is unsupported by the invalid mechanism. No dataset, checkpoint, author training run, GPU benchmark, external proof or later correction was independently reproduced.
# Disposition

Both demonstrated Problems are Major and concern core guarantees. Conditional lemmas and useful per-batch machinery survive. This is initial review only: adjudication pending, author adoption unknown, human reviews empty. No whole-paper correctness claim or post-batch acceptance is made.

report: Abstract: This review checks the published architecture, forecasting procedure, computational arguments, numerical tables, experimental scope, and all 25 pages of the supplied paper. Three local defects are supported: an incomplete full-cost expression, an incomplete forecasting pseudocode listing, and an incorrect ablation percentage. The highest supported assessment is Minor. The displayed main performance rankings survive the checks performed. Implementation, historical run provenance, practical computational advantage, and resolution-consistency claims require additional evidence. No author code or experiments were executed; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of SCENT
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is SCENT: Robust Spatiotemporal Learning for Continuous Scientific Data via Scalable Conditioned Neural Fields, by David Keetae Park, Xihaier Luo, Guang Zhao, Seungjun Lee, Miruna Oprescu, and Shinjae Yoo, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, identifier I25-43656, local number 0287 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed version is the staged 25-page PMLR PDF, including Appendices A–L. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, which match printed page numbers.

All extracted pages were read; architecture, algorithm, ablation, hyperparameter, and cost pages were also inspected as original rendered pages. The staged PMLR and author-page entries were read and their exact paper links checked. They supply the paper and OpenReview entry, but no implementation archive was staged. The recorded OpenReview discovery attempt returned 403; supplement availability beyond the embedded appendices is therefore unresolved. A neighboring arXiv link on the author page belongs to another paper and is not evidence for this one. This review makes no claim that code is absent everywhere.
# Definitions and dependencies

SCENT encodes irregular observations into latent tokens, evolves those representations, and decodes requested coordinates. Sparse attention limits each of \(N\) observation or query tokens to \(S\) attended tokens. The cost discussion uses \(L_s\) sparse-attention layers, \(M\) latent tokens, \(L_m\) latent self-attention layers, latent width \(d\), and \(W\) forecasting calls. The Warp-Unrolling Forecasting (WUF) description advances by at most the trained horizon \(t_h\), feeding the predicted state into the next call. Its call-count claim is distinct from any claim about accumulated forecasting error.

The evidence distinguishes a mathematical operation count, a literal algorithm listing, a rounded table calculation, and empirical performance. No proof in this review establishes correctness of the complete learned model. The model-width study changes several hyperparameters, so it does not isolate a single width variable experimentally.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The full computational-cost expression omits dense-layer costs).  Assessment: Minor; practical cost comparisons need evidence.
## Original claim and location

Equation reference: eq:published. Appendix L, pp. 23–25, presents a computational-complexity analysis and labels the sum of sparse, cross, and latent self-attention costs as the final Big-O complexity: \[
O\bigl(WL_sNSd+WNMd+WL_mM^2d\bigr).\] Appendix F, p. 19, specifies a feed-forward multiplier of four and varies latent dimension from 128 to 1024. The suspect step is treating attention-interaction costs alone as all contributions without stating a bounded-width or attention-dominated regime.
## Calculation and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:ff. For the conventional dense feed-forward block indicated by the multiplier, a token passes through matrices of dimensions \(d\times4d\) and \(4d\times d\). At \(M\) latent tokens, the two matrix products require \(8Md^2\) multiply-accumulate operations per block. Thus the latent processor alone contributes \[
8WL_mMd^2,\] before biases, nonlinearities, or query/key/value and output projections. With \(W,L_s,N,S,M,L_m\) fixed and positive, [eq:published] (#eq:published) is \(O(d)\) whereas [eq:ff] (#eq:ff) is \(\Theta(d^2)\). An unrestricted full-cost statement cannot omit this dependence. For \(L_m=2\), \(M=128\), one call gives 33,554,432 such operations at \(d=128\), and 2,147,483,648 at \(d=1024\). These are analytic counts, independently evaluated in and , not measurements of a released implementation.

This argument assumes ordinary dense feed-forward matrices, as suggested by the stated multiplier. An undocumented structured implementation could change the count; no code is available here to verify that alternative. Encoder and decoder widths need not equal latent width, and this calculation does not conflate them.

Substituting Table 6 into the paper’s own interaction proxies independently reproduces Table 7. Writing \(A\) for one SCENT call and \(B\) for one FNO step gives \[\begin{aligned}
A&=6(2000)(500)(128)+(2000)(128)^2+2(128)^3\\
 &=804{,}962{,}304,\nonumber\\
B&=4(2000)\log_2(2000)(60)+4(2000)(16)^2(60)\\
 &\simeq128{,}143{,}576.46.\nonumber\end{aligned}\] Here FNO’s Fourier-mode symbol is 16, whereas SCENT’s latent-width symbol is 128; the two uses of \(d\) in the source are not identified. With \(t_h=3\) and \(W=\lceil T/3\rceil\), these proxies give \[\frac{WA}{TB}\geq\frac{A}{3B}\simeq2.09391.\] At \(T=1\) the ratio is 6.28172; at \(T=20\) it is 2.19860. The shrinking gap in Table 7 is reproduced. These proxies do not demonstrate a crossover to a cheaper SCENT model, nor are Big-O expressions with unspecified constants numerical runtime measurements.
## Counterevidence, impact, and correction

Appendix L explicitly acknowledges that SCENT is the most expensive of its three listed models at the selected training scale and that the gap shrinks with unrolling. Its long-horizon efficiency wording can reasonably refer to fewer model calls. This review does not attribute a categorical FNO crossover claim to the authors.

The expression remains a valid description of attention interactions. With widths and \(S\) fixed, adding dense-layer terms still permits linear scaling in \(N\). Figure 4 reports empirical error versus parameter count; no dependency of that curve on the incomplete cost derivation was established. Consequently the verified defect is an insufficiently qualified cost model, rather than a demonstrated invalid central accuracy or fixed-width scalability result. That dependency analysis, not appendix location or repair difficulty, supports Minor.

A correction should either label [eq:published] (#eq:published) as an interaction-only proxy and specify its regime, or include all layer costs with their respective widths. Hardware timing, memory, and measured operations are needed to establish practical relative cost. This review does not certify the baseline architectures’ complete cost formulas.
Problem 2 (The WUF listing does not implement its described state recurrence).  Assessment: Minor.
## Original claim and location

Algorithm 1 in Appendix B, p. 15, is intended to implement the WUF procedure described on p. 4 and in Figure 3. It computes a prediction at \(t_c\) and advances \(t_i\) to \(t_c\), but never assigns the predicted state as the next input state. It defines a remainder \(t_r\) but tests \(r>0\). Its final call uses \(U^{t_i+t_r}\), which is a state at the target time, rather than the currently available predicted state. For an exact multiple of the horizon, the final output variable is not explicitly assigned. These are literal listing defects confirmed in the rendered original.
## Analysis, alternative reading, and bounded correction

The main text explicitly says the predicted horizon state becomes the next reference; Figure 3 supports the same intended recurrence. Thus the most defensible interpretation is an incomplete or erroneous listing. It is not evidence that the experiments actually used unavailable future targets or teacher forcing.

A self-contained recurrence is as follows. Initialize \(v=U^{t_i}\) and \(t=t_i\). While \(t<t_o\), set \(\Delta=\min(t_h,t_o-t)\), predict \[v\leftarrow F_\theta(v,\text{coordinates},t,t+\Delta),\qquad
t\leftarrow t+\Delta,\] then return \(v\). For \(t_o=t_i\) it returns the input. This handles remainders and exact multiples without a future-state input. Under the stated restriction that each call advances at most \(t_h\), any rollout over \(H=t_o-t_i\geq0\) needs at least \(\lceil H/t_h\rceil\) calls; this recurrence attains that bound. That proof establishes minimal call count, not smaller forecasting error.

The reviewer-authored toy flow \(du/dt=1\), \(t_h=3\), checked horizons \(0,1,3,6,7,20\), including both boundary cases and remainders. Its outputs and call counts match the corrected recurrence (). No author implementation was run or repaired. The manuscript’s unambiguous prose supplies counterevidence against a central algorithmic failure; the supported problem is local reproducibility of the listing. Actual rollout semantics and historical results remain unverified.
Problem 3 (The CN ablation percentage is inconsistent with its displayed errors).  Assessment: Minor.
## Original claim and decisive arithmetic

Table 3, p. 8, reports relative MSE 0.326 for the full model and 0.364 without CN, with a stated degradation of \(11.0\%\). On the table’s relative-change convention, the calculation is \[100\left(\frac{0.364}{0.326}-1\right)=\frac{1900}{163}\%
\simeq11.65644\%.\] Even allowing each displayed error to have been rounded to three decimals, the possible percentage lies between \[100\left(\frac{0.3635}{0.3265}-1\right)\simeq11.3323\%
\quad\text{and}\quad
100\left(\frac{0.3645}{0.3255}-1\right)\simeq11.9816\%.\] Thus ordinary rounding cannot explain \(11.0\%\). The numbers were checked against the original image, excluding extraction ambiguity. The natural correction from displayed values is approximately \(11.7\%\). The direction of the ablation and the ranking remain unchanged; no larger empirical consequence is established.
# Surviving checks and unresolved scope

The displayed main results support the reported favorable rankings on S1–S5 and AD-T/F. AD-B lists AROMA at 40.78 versus SCENT at 44.20, and the main text acknowledges SCENT’s second place. The displayed NS-3/4/5 results also support the stated rankings, with NS-4/5 described as comparable. Small gains, such as about \(0.95\%\) on S2 and \(1.90\%\) on NS-4, do not by themselves establish statistical significance; none is certified here. The relative-MSE definition is coherent when target energy is nonzero. No formal theorem or proof of universally superior error is claimed by this review.
Several issues remain Needs Evidence, without increasing severity.

First, query tokens interact through decoder self-attention. In a diagnostic attention layer with uniform weights and identity scalar values, query value zero outputs zero alone but \(1/2\) when a second query of value one is added. This demonstrates why pointwise query-set consistency needs examination, but is not a counterexample to the complete SCENT network: its learned projections, normalization, and residual pathways were not instantiated. Arbitrary-resolution evaluation need not mean exact query-set invariance. Shared-coordinate tests under different query batches, densities, and seeds would settle the relevant behavior.

Second, the main text states 50,000 training steps for S1–S5, whereas Appendix D lists 100,000 for S1/S2 and 50,000 for S3–S5. Actual run configurations are needed to resolve the discrepancy and compare budgets. Appendix F varies width, latent count, depth, heads, and learning rate together. Appendix G’s batches 76, 128, 256 over 50,000 steps expose 3.8, 6.4, and 12.8 million examples. These experiments do not isolate width alone or dataset diversity at fixed processed-example count; their joint scaling experiments are not thereby invalid.

Third, AD-T’s random time shuffle is disclosed and deliberately removes distribution shift. It supports its specified random-split setting, not an unseen-future distribution guarantee. No actual label leakage or overlapping-window contamination was established. Kuroshio and rainfall use chronological splits, so the AD-T limitation must not be generalized to every task. The stated NS-3 test count and appendix validation count could denote different splits and are not treated as a proven contradiction. The interpolation protocol and differing RBF endpoint access are disclosed. Historical run files, checkpoints, baseline bindings, and measured computational data are unavailable here.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The evidence supports three local corrections and leaves the central displayed prediction results unrebutted within the inspected scope. It does not certify complete experimental reproducibility or practical efficiency. No later revision or erratum was available in the staged evidence, and no author adoption is known. Fresh runs would be needed to quantify query-set sensitivity, measured cost, budget comparability, and any implementation consequence.

report: Abstract: The supplied paper and public source are reviewed for metric validity, training-regime semantics, evaluation, and numerical conclusions. A dimensional error in the released mutual-information estimator invalidates a core component of the proposed explanatory framework: constant representations receive nonzero or negative scores, and adding an unused coordinate changes the score. This supports Major for that released metric, with historical Figure 5 provenance unresolved. A separate Minor finding corrects overbroad comparisons of alternative regimes. The displayed main accuracy results substantially support the paper’s qualified medium/high-budget recommendation. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of
How to Train Your Multi-Exit Model?
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is How to Train Your Multi-Exit Model? Analyzing the Impact of Training Strategies, Piotr Kubaty, Bartosz Wójcik, Bartłomiej Krzepkowski, Monika Michaluk, Tomasz Trzcinski, Jary Pomponi, and Kamil Adamczewski, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43657, local number 0288 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied proceedings PDF has 20 pages, including Appendices A–E. Page references are one-based PDF pages.
The released repository is `kamadforge/early-exit-benchmark`, frozen at commit

It is the public revision observed at source preparation, not a proven conference-time revision. All 71 staged entries and 65 source-only archive members passed the parent hash audit. Every paper page was read as extracted text; decisive metric, plot, table, and training pages were inspected visually. Relevant code was read statically; no author code, training, or checkpoint was executed. Historical raw runs and exact figure-producing configurations are not supplied. OpenReview supplement discovery returned 403; the embedded appendix is available.
# Background and evidentiary distinctions

Disjoint training first trains the backbone and then freezes it while training internal classifiers (ICs). Joint training optimizes backbone and ICs together from initialization. Mixed training first trains the backbone and then jointly optimizes the complete multi-exit model. The paper proposes gradient alignment, mode connectivity, numerical rank, and mutual information as explanatory tools in addition to accuracy–cost comparisons.

A defect in the released metric is distinct from proof that its current bytes generated a historical figure. Likewise, a counterexample to a causal interpretation does not refute the measured accuracy. These distinctions matter here: the inspected basic regime and offline routing implementations are consistent with their declared roles, while the information calculation has an exact mathematical defect.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The released mutual-information score mixes scalar and vector densities).  Assessment: Major for the released core framework metric; historical figure impact needs evidence.
## Claim, location, and dependency

Section 3.4, pp. 3–4, defines \(I(X;Z)\) and says it is estimated by Monte Carlo sampling. Figure 5 and pp. 5–6 use the layerwise values to explain information retention, compression, and which training regime is suitable for easy or difficult data. This is an explicit component of the paper’s proposed analytical contribution.

In , line 217 computes a one-dimensional Gaussian log density at zero; line 302 sums feature log densities to obtain a \(d\)-dimensional joint density; line 239 subtracts the latter from the former. Lines 255 and 273 repeat the mismatch for the conditional calculation. The logged unconditional score at line 187 averages values over 14 bandwidths. These are source statements at the pinned revision [Retained latex: \cite{code}]; numbered excerpts and hashes are preserved in .
## Complete counterexample and invariant failure

Let every sampled representation be the same vector \(z_0\in\mathbb R^d\), with \(d=2\), and let the positive kernel standard deviation be \(\sigma=1\), one of the released bandwidths. Any number of source samples and either sampling seed are admissible: every reference and evaluation vector is \(z_0\). The true information is \[I(X;Z)=0,\qquad Z=z_0.\] It is also zero if independent Gaussian observation noise is added to this constant vector.

Equation reference: eq:mi. Write \(c_\sigma=\log\phi_\sigma(0)=-\log(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})\). In the released Monte Carlo branch, the mixture of identical \(d\)-dimensional kernels has log density \(dc_\sigma\) at every evaluation vector. The scalar conditional-density term is only \(c_\sigma\). Thus the returned score is exactly \[
\widehat I_{\rm release}=(1-d)c_\sigma
=(d-1)\log(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}).\] For \(d=2,\sigma=1\), this is \(0.9189385332\) nats instead of zero. At the also-supported \(\sigma=0.01\), it is \(-3.6862316528\) nats. The Jensen branch has the same values because all components coincide. Random sampling cannot explain the discrepancy: the result is identical for every draw.

The actual bandwidth list is \[.01,\ .1,\ .25,\ .5,\ .75,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 6,\ 9,\ 12,\ 15,\ 18,\ 21.\] Averaging [eq:mi] (#eq:mi) over that list gives \(1.4642039381\) for a constant two-dimensional representation and \(2926.9436723553\) for a constant 2000-dimensional representation. These are independent scalar calculations in /, not author-code execution.

More generally, append an identically zero coordinate to any representation. The true information obeys \[I(X;(Z,0))=I(X;Z).\] The released joint log density acquires \(c_\sigma\), while its scalar numerator is unchanged, so the reported score increases by \(-c_\sigma\). This holds for arbitrary source vectors and either log-mixture branch. Averaged over the released bandwidths, each unused coordinate adds \(1.4642039381\) to the score. If the appended coordinate instead carries independent Gaussian noise in a noisy-channel interpretation, it likewise adds no true information. Thus an apparent layerwise change can be manufactured by adding or removing unused coordinates, without changing predictions or information content.
## Counterevidence and historical boundary

A kernel-based surrogate can be useful, and finite-sample estimates need not obey every population inequality exactly. Neither observation excuses this deterministic dimension mismatch. Calling the output a bound also requires a valid derivation: the displayed score is not justified as the paper’s \(I(X;Z)\), and the invariant failure is not sampling uncertainty.

However, the current standard early-exit entry point comments out `setup_mi` at :654. Default MI flags and even the named MI example’s flags are false; enabling them without setup would access uninitialized analysis objects. No Figure 5 run file binds the figure to the current revision. The report therefore does not claim that the historical plotted values equal the defective current output. The plot’s exact provenance and estimator must be supplied.
## Impact and precise repair scope

The invalid computation directly affects a core analytical metric and its proposed evidentiary use for choosing training regimes. Major applies to that demonstrated released computation, not to an inferred change in the accuracy tables. Establishing that those tables lose their advantage is unnecessary to establish the metric defect.

Equation reference: eq:repair. Multiplying the scalar term by \(d\) removes this dimension mismatch but does not by itself make evaluation at noiseless feature centers an estimator of the specified mutual information. A complete repair must declare the random variable. For example, for an empirical uniform input distribution and the changed, noisy representation \(\widetilde Z=f(X)+\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2I_d)\), the valid target is \[
\mathbb E_{i,\varepsilon}\left[
\log\phi_{\sigma,d}(\varepsilon)-
\log\left\{\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
\phi_{\sigma,d}(f(x_i)+\varepsilon-f(x_j))\right\}\right].\] This definition gives zero for a constant map, and an additional independent noise coordinate cancels in the likelihood ratio. It is not the unsmoothed deterministic estimand. Its statistical implementation, bandwidth choice, and any repaired Figure 5 have not been verified. The associated compression-based interpretation requires re-evaluation.
Problem 2 (Alternative-regime comparisons overstate the displayed results).  Assessment: Minor.
## Original comparison and exact contrary cases

Appendix A, p. 13, says alternating training consistently falls short of both mixed and joint training, then says mixed-gradual outperforms mixed. The paper’s own results contradict these unqualified comparisons.

Table 10, p. 14, reports ViT-T/CIFAR-100 accuracy at the 100% budget of \(68.39\pm0.78\) for alternating and \(66.49\pm1.08\) for joint; mixed is \(70.25\pm0.56\). At 75%, alternating is \(67.81\) versus joint’s \(66.22\). More directly, Table 14, p. 15, gives STS-B MSE at 100% of \(0.50\) for alternating, \(0.52\) for joint, and \(0.51\) for mixed: lower is better. At 75%, alternating is \(0.51\) versus \(0.53\) for each comparator. These are comparisons of reported means, not newly claimed significance tests.

Mixed-gradual also fails to dominate mixed: Table 13 gives 20-Newsgroups accuracy \(81.35\pm1.24\) versus \(85.25\pm0.64\) at each of 50%, 75%, and 100%. Lower-budget ResNet-34 results provide further exceptions. Original page images verify the signs, labels, and metric directions.
## Correction, counterevidence, and effect

The defensible comparison is task- and budget-dependent. Alternating trails mixed in the cited CIFAR-100 cases but can exceed joint; it also has lower displayed STS-B MSE than both at high budgets. Mixed-gradual improves several high-budget vision/regression results but performs worse on the cited classification setting. The tables disclose these exceptions, and the main paper’s more qualified recommendation remains well supported. The flaw is a local comparative conclusion, with no demonstrated reversal of the central mixed-versus-joint empirical trend.
# Positive checks and issues requiring evidence
## Regimes, routing, and the central empirical trend

Static inspection verifies that the main regime configuration distinguishes backbone pretraining, joint optimization, and frozen-backbone IC training. The frozen-backbone path disables its gradients and places its core modules in evaluation mode. Early stopping uses the designated validation loader, with per-head patience tracking.

The offline evaluator obtains all head predictions, chooses the first head exceeding a confidence threshold, falls back to the final head, and averages cumulative head FLOPs using exit counts. The table generator selects the last threshold before averaged cost exceeds the specified budget; it does not maximize accuracy over all feasible thresholds. Consequently occasional lower accuracy at a larger budget is possible. Labels enter scoring, not the inspected confidence-routing or cost choice. No test-label threshold optimization was demonstrated.

The parent independently recomputed Table 1: mixed exceeds joint in 19 of 24 displayed means, including 17 of 18 at 50–100% budgets and only two of six at 25%. This supports the paper’s qualified medium/high-budget recommendation. The one medium/high exception is MSDNet at 50%, \(72.01\) versus \(72.02\). Standard deviations in the appendix and explicit exceptions for disjoint at high budgets provide important counterevidence to universal-superiority readings.
## Gradient alignment and causal explanation

The defined gradient-dominance score is a cosine, and the released implementation calculates that cosine. It need not rank influence by magnitude or projected contribution. For a concrete realizable diagnostic, use shared representation \(\theta=0\in\mathbb R^2\), three bias-free binary-logit heads \(w_i^\top\theta\), label zero, and cross-entropy loss. Set \(w_i=2g_i\) with \[g_1=(.001,0),\quad g_2=(1,100),\quad g_3=(1,-100).\] At \(\theta=0\), each backbone gradient is \(g_i\) and every head-weight gradient is zero. The total is \(G=(2.001,0)\). Cosines are \(1\) for \(g_1\) and approximately \(0.0099995\) for the others, yet \(g_2\cdot G=g_3\cdot G=2.001\), a thousand times \(g_1\cdot G=0.002001\). Common averaging of losses does not change this ordering. Identity intermediate layers can realize the early-exit depths without changing this check.

This establishes that alignment alone cannot identify the largest causal update contribution. Section 3.1 says potentially dominates, and scaling ablations provide additional qualitative evidence. No reversal of the actual Figure 2 influence ranking was established. The causal explanation therefore needs norm/contribution measurements or a more targeted intervention; it is not an additional demonstrated Major.
## Other bounded reproducibility and interpretation limits

The current scaling code deserves clarification. Its SDN coefficient is \[\min\left(c_i,\ .01+(t+1)\frac{c_i}{t+1}\right)=c_i\] at every step. The active GE branch gives internal-head coefficients \(1/(K+1)\) and final-head coefficient \(2/(K+1)\) on the shared backbone for \(K\) total heads, before common loss normalization. The parent independently derived and checked these coefficients. The commented earlier branch differs. Whether these are the intended reference methods, and whether Table 5 used them, needs exact version/configuration evidence; the present ablation script names CIFAR-100 whereas Table 5 concerns TinyImageNet. No historical table corruption is inferred.

Equation (5)’s rank of an activation matrix differs from the released rank of its centered covariance with a relative eigenvalue threshold. A constant nonzero representation has activation rank one and covariance rank zero. This needs an explicit metric convention before interpreting capacity. Likewise, a high-loss straight interpolation does not rule out a low-loss curved connection: \((x^2+y^2-1)^2\) has a zero-loss semicircle between \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\) but a straight-line midpoint loss of one. This is a logical diagnostic, not a counterexample instantiated in the paper’s networks. Figure 3 establishes its inspected section of the landscape, not global disconnectedness.

Table 11 labels as 35% the same ResNet-50 means labeled 25% in Tables 1 and 19. The correct budget needs run binding. Table 6’s broad head-size caption also needs a budget qualification: at 25%, mixed increases from 44.03 with one layer to 44.92 or 44.61 with larger heads, although the higher-budget degradation is displayed. The reported 1166 versus 1610 epochs is 27.58% fewer epochs; total training compute and wall-clock savings require full phase accounting.

A one-survivor threshold-deployment mask is squeezed to a scalar in :124, raising a concrete indexing concern downstream. This path is separate from the paper’s offline evaluator. An independent tensor-shape probe could not run because `torch` is absent in both available Python environments; no package was installed. The concern is retained as static, unverified runtime evidence. The table generator also leaves `result_valid` uninitialized or stale when no threshold crosses a budget; no effect on the published finite-budget columns was established.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The released information estimator cannot support the information-theoretic interpretation as written. Its connection to historical figures, the intended estimand, and a corrected analysis need evidence. The alternative-regime discussion needs a local scope correction. The main accuracy comparisons, basic regime semantics, and offline threshold routing survive the bounded checks performed; no complete experimental replication is claimed. No later erratum or author adoption was supplied.
