Title: Technical Verification of
Latent Diffusion Planning for Imitation Learning
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The paper is Latent Diffusion Planning for Imitation Learning, Amber Xie, Oleh Rybkin, Dorsa Sadigh, and Chelsea Finn, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43658, local number 0289 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied proceedings PDF has 15 pages including references and Appendix A; all page numbers below are one-based PDF pages. All extracted pages were read. The decisive equations, tables, and implementation details were also checked on original page images.
The public repository is `amberxie88/latent_diffusion_planning`, pinned to

The complete manifest was parsed, and all 110 staged entries were hash-checked. The two preserved archives contain 88 and 14 members; the latter includes robot mesh assets. This is the released revision observed at source preparation, not a demonstrated record of the code used for each published table. No historical checkpoints, run configurations, or corrected results were supplied. Member/version mappings and source hashes remain in ; unchanged originals were reused.
# Background and checks that survive

LDP encodes observations into a low-dimensional VAE representation, diffuses future latent states conditional on recent observations, and uses an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to infer actions between planned states. Action-free expert observations can train the planner; additional action-labeled suboptimal transitions can train the IDM. The central empirical claims concern these heterogeneous sources and the value of dense, closed-loop forecasting.

The inspected dense implementation consistently aligns adjacent state pairs with the corresponding actions. Its planner predicts future observations after the observation horizon and prepends the current latent state at inference. The latent loader removes past actions consistently when the observation horizon exceeds one. The mixed-data loss sends the main expert/action-free observation batch to the planner and mixed action-labeled transitions to the IDM. The supplied action-free and suboptimal configurations preserve this separation and the stated 50/50 mixed sampling.

The VAE objective in equation (1) is a maximized ELBO; the released MSE plus weighted KL loss is consistent with minimizing its negative under a fixed-variance Gaussian decoder. No sign error was established. Offline and online latent paths use the same frozen encoder parameters and posterior means, with consistent normalization in the inspected single-camera setting. The noise-prediction objective and reverse time-index order were checked statically. The imported external `FlaxDDPMScheduler` implementation was not staged, so its numerical correctness was not independently verified.
# Substantive problems

Problem 1 (Hierarchical planner and IDM use incompatible endpoint times).  Assessment: Major for the released hierarchical ablation; historical Table 4 binding Needs Evidence. Section 5.5 and Table 4 (p. 8) describe subgoals four steps apart, with four actions extracted between consecutive subgoals. The resulting comparison is used to support dense forecasting as an important contribution. The released hierarchical planner instead learns its first target one step ahead, while its IDM is trained on endpoints four steps apart.
#### Exact source correspondence.

In , line 115 selects planner targets using \[\texttt{obs\_emb[:, obs\_horizon::idm\_horizon]}.\] Lines 126–128 pair states beginning at `obs_horizon-1` with states `idm_horizon` steps later and associate each pair with that many actions. At inference, lines 431–441 prepend the current state to the planner output and pair consecutive entries; lines 444–459 generate and flatten four actions per pair. The YAML selects this class, and the public `sample` method calls this inference path. The evaluation entry point resolves the configured class through `create`. No intervening offset correction was found. These are static source statements, not an author-code execution claim.

Let the observation horizon be one, the subgoal spacing be four, and the supplied sequence be \((z_0,\ldots,z_{16})\). These agree with the paper’s observation horizon and four-step ablation. This is an explicit horizon-17 override, not an unchanged default launch. The four-subgoal sequence is statically compatible with the selected U-Net depths; no author runtime was executed. Direct evaluation of the slices gives
Object | Temporal indices
Planner training targets | \(1,5,9,13\)
IDM training endpoint pairs | \((0,4),(4,8),(8,12),(12,16)\)
Oracle-plan inference pairs | \((0,1),(1,5),(5,9),(9,13)\)
Aligned planner targets | \(4,8,12,16\)
The first pair has a different duration from the IDM’s training task, and the entire plan ends three steps earlier than the intended endpoint grid.
#### Independent, assumption-checked calculation.

Consider physical dynamics \(s_{t+1}=s_t+a_t\), \(s_0=0\), with expert actions \(a_t=1\). Represent the states by \(z_t=s_t/16\), keeping all planned latents in \([0,1]\). Let an exact four-action inverse for physical endpoints \((u,v)\) return \[\mathcal{I}_4(u,v)=\left((v-u)/4,(v-u)/4,(v-u)/4,(v-u)/4\right).\] It is sufficient that the inverse-data distribution include the corresponding constant-velocity segments of speeds one and one quarter. Such action-labeled additional transitions are allowed by the method; thus the first query need not be unsupported in the IDM data. The expert planner is exact at its own training targets.

Composing these ideal components using the released indices produces \[\underbrace{\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14}_{0\ \mathrm{to}\ 1},
 \underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{12\ \mathrm{actions}},\] so the physical state after four actions is \(1\), whereas the expert’s four-step endpoint is \(4\). After sixteen actions it is \(13\), whereas the aligned plan reaches \(16\). The corrected indices yield sixteen unit actions. This discrepancy is exact; it is neither sampling noise nor a failed training assumption. The reviewer-authored rational calculation and all indices are recorded in and , with source excerpts in .
#### Execution horizon and counterevidence.

The released constructor requires `action_horizon` to be divisible by `idm_horizon`. We therefore use the supported value four, not one. The hierarchical inference slice treats that value as a number of subgoals, returning sixteen primitive actions in this example; the environment loop executes the entire returned chunk. Dense LDP with action horizon four returns four actions. Consequently, the diagnostic does not establish a persistent quarter-speed closed-loop rollout or the effect size in Table 4. It establishes misaligned temporal composition under supported horizon values. Padding does not repair the first target, and increasing sequence length preserves the offset.

The dense implementation is correctly aligned. A historical corrected branch, learned compensation, or different run configuration could change empirical outcomes. None is established by the supplied artifacts. The hierarchy also changes the IDM architecture from an MLP to a diffusion U-Net (p. 15), so a pure causal attribution to temporal density requires controlling architecture and replanning frequency.
#### Impact and bounded repair.

The released object does not implement the stated four-step hierarchical comparator. This directly affects the implementation supplied for the paper’s core dense-forecasting argument, supporting Major at that scope without requiring a demonstrated benchmark-score decrease. It does not prove that the historical Table 4 scores were produced by this revision, that their ranking reverses after repair, or that the heterogeneous-data results fail.

For this alignment defect, start planner targets at \[\texttt{obs\_horizon-1+idm\_horizon}\] and retain the same stride. The exact diagnostic then recovers the IDM endpoint grid and the intended physical endpoints. This verifies only the indexing repair. A full repaired comparison still requires explicit primitive-action horizon semantics, compatible initialization and shapes, matched execution schedules, training, and result provenance. No repaired author model was executed.

Problem 2 (The base LDP average is inconsistent with its task results).  Assessment: Minor. Tables 1 and 2 (pp. 6–7) report base LDP task means \(0.69,0.70,0.46,0.64\) with an average of \(0.65\). The stated task-average calculation gives instead \[\frac{0.69+0.70+0.46+0.64}{4}=\frac{249}{400}=0.6225.\]

If each displayed task mean is rounded within \(0.005\), the underlying unweighted average lies between \(0.6175\) and \(0.6275\); rounding cannot explain \(0.65\). The DP pretrain-and-finetune row averages \(0.635\). Thus base LDP is below that row on this aggregate, whereas the printed averages suggest the reverse. Source page images and exact rational arithmetic independently confirm the discrepancy.

This is a local comparison defect. LDP with suboptimal data averages \(0.695\), and LDP with both additional sources averages \(0.945\); both exceed \(0.635\). The main claim that combining heterogeneous sources improves these low-demonstration tasks survives. The prose comparing LDP’s suboptimal-data use can reasonably refer to the explicit LDP + Subopt row, so it should not be read as a separate universal false claim about the base row. Correct the base average to approximately \(0.62\) and qualify the local ranking. The arithmetic correction is verified; raw-run aggregation and author adoption are unknown.
# Remaining empirical questions and overall impact
#### Data and comparison scope.

Appendix A (p. 15) explicitly states that even nominal LDP uses a VAE trained on the additional action-free and suboptimal data. The representation baseline shares that VAE. Accordingly, base LDP versus DP is not an equal-data, expert-demonstrations-only comparison; this is disclosed, not hidden leakage. The tested action-free data are robot demonstrations with actions removed and compatible observation/proprioception information. General transfer from arbitrary human video or other embodiments is future work.

Simulation uses few expert demonstrations, 50 evaluation trials for each of two seeds, and the real task uses 45 trials across three seeds. These are useful bounded experiments, not broad coverage guarantees. The real-world mean improvements and simulation combined-data gains were checked as reported, but raw trajectories and uncertainty computations were unavailable. The text selects the best of the last five checkpoints; the independence of checkpoint-selection and final reporting trials needs run-level evidence.
#### Evaluation details requiring evidence.

The Robomimic loop checks success after each returned action chunk. If success can be transient, sampling it at different chunk boundaries can change measured success: a trajectory successful at step four but not step eight is detected with stride four and missed with stride eight. records this conditional diagnostic. The inspected wrapper reports current success rather than latching it, and the released dense LDP/DP defaults use different chunk lengths. Whether actual task success persists, or whether any published score is affected, remains unverified. ALOHA checks success per step.

The UniPi appendix uses task-specific rollout horizons; the released LDP configuration can inherit dataset metadata. Exact historical horizons require the absent dataset/run configurations. Some main and appendix UniPi means differ and could represent separate reruns; no data fabrication inference follows. ALOHA planner widths and representation-baseline choices also differ as disclosed. Stronger causal comparisons would require matched capacity and documented run identities. No measured latency result establishes a general speed claim; the paper itself acknowledges the overhead of state diffusion.
#### Surviving conclusions and limits.

The central heterogeneous-data loss separation, dense state–action alignment, and the displayed advantage of the combined-data variant survive the checks performed. A VAE can omit control-relevant information, but the paper acknowledges this limitation and asserts no universal sufficiency theorem. No issue was established for that qualified statement. The hierarchical release requires correction and provenance resolution before it can substantiate a clean dense-versus-hierarchical explanation. These assessments do not certify all numerical experiments or every repository member.

report: Abstract: The supplied proceedings paper and released implementation were checked for forward equivalence, training derivatives, expert placement, communication accounting, and empirical comparisons. The released training path discards task-loss gradients to routing weights even without collaboration pruning. An exact softmax counterexample establishes a Major defect in that core training path, independently of historical benchmark provenance. Two Minor findings concern a capacity error in the printed placement algorithm and an overstatement of similarity-based pruning’s comparative quality. Fixed-routing aggregation, the balanced-capacity communication bound, and several reported tradeoffs survive the bounded checks. Historical run identities and corrected training results remain unresolved; scientific adjudication is pending.

Title: Technical Verification of Occult:
Optimizing Collaborative Communications across Experts
for Accelerated Parallel MoE Training and Inference
# Paper identity and reviewed version

The reviewed paper is Occult: Optimizing Collaborative Communications across Experts for Accelerated Parallel MoE Training and Inference, Shuqing Luo, Pingzhi Li, Jie Peng, Yang (Katie) Zhao, Yu (Kevin) Cao, Yu Cheng, and Tianlong Chen, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43659, local number 0290 [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The supplied proceedings PDF has 19 pages, including Appendices A and B. All extracted pages were read; references below use one-based PDF pages.
The released repository `UNITES-Lab/Occult` is pinned to

This is the public revision observed at source preparation, not a certified historical training revision. The complete manifest was parsed; all 58 staged entries and all 51 source-archive members matched their recorded identities. The two preserved source archives contain 47 and four members. No author code, model, or GPU kernel was executed. Static source checks and reviewer-authored calculations are distinguished throughout.
# Background and positive checks

Equation reference: eq:moe. For selected experts \(S(x)\) and routing weights \(p_e(x)\), the paper’s equation (1) is \[y(x)=\sum_{e\in S(x)}p_e(x)E_e(x).
 \] Occult sends one copy of a token to each destination device that contains a selected expert. Local expert outputs are weighted and summed before the return collective, then device-level contributions are summed at the origin. For fixed routes and weights, this is an algebraically valid regrouping of [eq:moe] (#eq:moe). The inspected dispatch, expert-index mapping, weighted down-projection, and combine operations follow this design. The source applies the GLU nonlinearity before the weighted down-projection; the omitted activation in schematic Algorithm 2 is not evidence of an executed nonlinear commutation error.

Equation reference: eq:packing. With \(N_e\) experts evenly divided among \(N_d\) devices, capacity \(q=N_e/N_d\), and \(k\) distinct selected experts, the number \(D(x)\) of touched devices satisfies \[\left\lceil k/q\right\rceil\le D(x)\le\min(k,N_d).
 \] This follows by packing at most \(q\) experts into each device. It verifies the intended simplified-replica bound in equation (5), under balanced placement. A device-local copy is included in this count, so it is a communication proxy rather than an exact count of off-device bytes or a universal latency law.

For activation gradients, the inspected all-to-all wrapper reverses its input/output split sizes, and combine’s backward scatters the gradient to contributing copies. These are positive static checks, not a complete GPU-kernel certification. Finite-precision summation order, race safety, and measured latency were not tested.
# Substantive problems

Problem 1 (Released training drops task-loss derivatives of routing weights).  Assessment: Major, scoped to the released core training implementation. Sections 3.1 and A.1 describe equivalent MoE computation with a backward pipeline; Figure 6 explicitly includes backward operations. Page 8 states that timing experiments tune all MoE modules and freeze other parameters. The released weighted forward function depends on the router, but its backward path omits the task-loss derivative through the routing weights.
#### Active source path.

The trainable router in produces softmax scores and selected weights. The active `dMoE` path passes these through dispatch to the condensed GLU implementation. The forward kernel multiplies expert outputs by the transmitted weights. The task-gradient connections are nevertheless removed at several points:
Source location | Implemented behavior
| Backward returns `None` for routing-weight input `ew`.
| Weight communication and post-dispatch run inside `torch.no_grad()`.
| Weight condensation runs inside `torch.no_grad()`.
| Condensed merge backward returns `None` for `tiles_list_w`.

These are on the selected condensed implementation, not merely an unused legacy wrapper. Explicitly returning no gradient for a differentiable weight input cannot be repaired by the fact that its value was used in the forward kernel. The relevant source bytes and excerpts are bound in and .
#### Complete differentiable counterexample.

Equation reference: eq:gategrad. Take two experts and two devices, one expert per device, with \(k=2\), no pruning, and no jitter. Both experts are selected, so there is no top-\(k\) selection-boundary issue. At a fixed nonzero input, let expert outputs be \(E_0=1\), \(E_1=3\), and router logits be \((\log 3,0)\). Such fixed-input expert values are realizable by choosing the down-projection weights of bias-free experts. The softmax weights and output are \[p=(3/4,1/4),\qquad y=3/2.\] Use the differentiable task loss \(L=y^2/2\). For softmax logits \(z_i\), \[\frac{\partial y}{\partial z_i}=p_i(E_i-y),\qquad
 \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i}=y\,p_i(E_i-y),\] and therefore \[\nabla_z L=(-9/16,\;9/16).
 \] The released task graph supplies no gradient through these weights. This is a discrepancy between the derivative of the computed function and its specified backward pass.

The calculation uses exact rational weights. Independent central differences in reviewer-authored scalar code, with step \(10^{-6}\), give \((-0.562500000134,\;0.562500000023)\), within \(1.35\times10^{-10}\) of [eq:gategrad] (#eq:gategrad). This is an analytical/finite-difference check, not an executed PyTorch, BF16, or CUDA test. The structural omission remains for any nonzero task derivative; rounding does not supply a missing autograd edge.
#### Counterevidence and dependency.

Expert-parameter and direct activation gradients have implemented backward paths. Auxiliary losses can also reach router parameters: the supplied DeepSeek example creates a trainable gate and attaches `AddAuxiliaryLoss`. It would therefore be incorrect to say that the router receives no gradients at all. An auxiliary balancing or logit penalty cannot generally replace the omitted task term, which depends on expert outputs and the downstream loss.

The paper supplies no premise that routing weights are constant during training. Freezing router parameters alone would also not generally remove the router-dependent contribution to gradients of upstream trainable activations. The missing term is part of the core training function, so this is Major without requiring proof that the entire system fails or that a particular accuracy score falls. Forward inference with fixed routing weights is not refuted.
#### Correction and verification boundary.

For upstream vector \(g=\partial L/\partial y\), an exact local backward must supply \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial p_e}=\langle g,E_e(x)\rangle\] and propagate it through weight condensation, index remapping, communication, dispatch, and the router. Removing a `no_grad` block alone is insufficient while custom backward functions still return `None`. This formula restores the missing analytical term and yields [eq:gategrad] (#eq:gategrad); no complete repaired distributed implementation was produced or run. Historical training/quality figures are not bound to the retrieved revision, so their quantitative effect remains Needs Evidence.

Problem 2 (Printed placement loop exceeds the stated device capacity).  Assessment: Minor. Algorithm 1 (p. 5) constructs an even expert partition but continues its insertion loop while \(\operatorname{len}(L_d)\le N_e/N_d\). A group already at capacity receives one more expert.

Take \(N_e=8\), \(N_d=2\), and capacity four. A valid profiling batch contains one top-two token for each unordered expert pair, giving equal positive off-diagonal collaboration entries and zero diagonal under the source’s intended distinct-expert convention. Choose lexicographic tie breaking. The first group starts with experts \(0,1\), then the printed loop appends \(2,3,4\), giving size five. The second starts with \(5\) and adds \(6,7\), then attempts to maximize an empty candidate dictionary. The trace is saved in . The overfill is independent of which tied eligible IDs are chosen.

Changing the insertion condition to strict \(<\) gives \((0,1,2,3)\) and \((4,5,6,7)\) in this case. General capacity-one use also needs a one-expert initialization, and initial pairs should explicitly exclude equal IDs. The released graph builder already excludes self-pairs, so the diagonal omission in the printed equation is resolved by source intent.

The decisive counterevidence is that all 265 supplied layer/parallelism placement maps pass complete-permutation, local/global agreement, device-count, and exact-capacity checks: 32 Mixtral, 32 OLMoE, 120 Qwen, and 81 DeepSeek maps. The release loads these precomputed maps; the generating clustering workflow was not found. Thus the demonstrated defect is in the printed algorithm, not in the supplied placements or the historical speedup. Minor reflects that bounded dependency, not the ease of changing one symbol. The repaired capacity trace does not establish optimal placement.

Problem 3 (Similarity-based pruning is not consistently superior).  Assessment: Minor. Section 4.2 (p. 7) states that similarity-based pruning consistently outperforms router-based pruning. At the same two-device budget, Tables 3–5 directly contradict that unqualified comparison.

For OLMoE, WSC is \(83.52\) for similarity versus \(86.45\) for routing, and RACE is \(38.28\) versus \(39.62\). Qwen PIQA is \(79.87\) versus \(80.25\); DeepSeek SST-2 is \(73.05\) versus \(76.72\). These are reported point estimates, not new statistical-significance claims.
An independent tally of all 75 metric rows gives:
Model | Similarity versus routing | Similarity versus standard SFT
| wins / ties / losses | wins / ties / losses

These count 25 metric rows per model, not independent benchmarks: MRPC and COQA each have two metrics. Even among the six showcased tasks, similarity wins four and loses two for each model. The source values and tallies are preserved in and were checked against original page images.

Similarity also has substantial successes: Qwen RTE reaches \(75.45\) versus routing’s \(69.68\) and SFT’s \(71.12\); DeepSeek MMLU reaches \(41.91\) versus SFT’s \(38.66\). Therefore the weaker claim that two-device pruning can achieve comparable or superior quality has supporting examples. Correct the systematic preference to a task-dependent conclusion and report uncertainty. This local comparative overstatement does not independently invalidate the communication/quality tradeoff. Author adoption and repeated-run significance remain unknown.
# Remaining scope, counterevidence, and overall impact
#### Pairwise collaboration is a proxy.

Pairwise intra-collaboration is not an order-preserving substitute for the number of touched devices. With the OLMoE-compatible values \(N_e=64\), \(N_d=4\), capacity 16, and \(k=8\), distribute one token’s selected experts as \((4,4,0,0)\) or \((6,1,1,0)\); fill unused slots with other experts. The first arrangement has 12 unordered intra-pairs and touches two devices. The second has 15 intra-pairs, fewer inter-pairs, and touches three devices. Equal group sizes also preserve this ordering for the paper’s normalized pair averages. Thus improved pairwise objective value alone does not guarantee lower \(C_T\). This bounds the heuristic interpretation; it does not prove that the actual greedy method selects the worse placement or refute the reported gain.

Table 1’s rescheduling numbers support the approximate 20% claim: expected replica count falls from \(3.68\) to \(3.02\) (17.93%) and latency from \(15.93\) to \(12.53\) seconds (21.34%). No near-optimality guarantee was verified beyond the empirical comparison.
#### Pruning semantics.

Appendix A.3 explicitly changes signed cosine similarity to squared cosine. These can rank candidates differently: relative to \((1,0)\), candidates \((-1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) have cosines \(-1\) and \(1/\sqrt2\), but squares \(1\) and \(1/2\). This is a changed heuristic, not an established universal quality guarantee. The exact historical profiling/normalization procedure was unavailable. The released DeepSeek integration replaces expert IDs while retaining rank-associated weights; helper functions also construct a permuted score distribution. The intended weight-transfer convention needs clarification, rather than an assumption that all replacements use their original gate scores.
#### Timing and environment provenance.

Table 1’s \(24.50/9.22=2.657\) is a conventional latency-ratio speedup. The prefilling prose’s approximately \(1.70\) times faster may instead express the ratio minus one. Original Figure 9 shows the relevant Occult curves below the baseline; the sub-unit expressions for other models must not be interpreted as demonstrated slowdowns. Exact denominators and a consistent convention require raw measurements.

The paper describes all experiments as single-node PCIe A6000 runs, whereas the current README describes eight-way runs on one node and sixteen-way runs on two nodes, using A6000 Ada devices. Because communication depends on the interconnect, this discrepancy needs historical run/environment binding; it does not show that competing methods used different hardware. Timing is reported for tuning MoE modules, not arbitrary full-model training. Small-batch acceleration limits, framework-reference scope, and unresolved load balancing are acknowledged by the authors.
#### Unavailable evidence and surviving conclusions.

The release lacks complete published-run drivers, checkpoints, raw latency and seed-level quality records, and the historical configuration mapping. Several example configuration references point to absent model implementation files, recorded in . External supplement discovery was blocked by the recorded OpenReview access error; the embedded appendices were available. No later erratum or author adoption was established.

The fixed-routing forward principle and packing bound survive; pruning’s changed-routing nature and several quality improvements are disclosed. The released missing task derivative is a direct correctness defect in the training path. Corrected training and matched timing must be established before using this revision to reproduce an equivalent-training claim. Historical empirical impact remains separate.
# Conclusion and state
Item | Assessment | Repair verification | Adoption / remaining work
Task-loss gate derivative | Major | Exact derivative and finite differences | Unknown; distributed repair and reruns
Placement pseudocode | Minor | Capacity trace; 265 valid maps | Unknown; specify generator
Quality comparison | Minor | Fixed-budget table tally | Unknown; qualify by task
Historical timings and runs | Needs Evidence | Published/static scope | Exact run artifacts required

Title: Technical Verification of HVR
# Identity, version and inspected scope

This report concerns Flavio Petruzzellis, Cristina Cornelio and Pietro Liò, Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, OpenReview `vfqdJy12Kk` (local identity 0291/I25-43660) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original is the staged 23-page proceedings PDF. Page references are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with its printed 1–23 numbering. The separately versioned released repository is `corneliocristina/HVR`, commit `eeb267932657a2c23bc57e2bb0412f9a0178303f` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. This commit is not assumed to be the version that produced the conference experiments.

The review inspected the method and metrics in Sections 2–4, the relevant implementation details and limitations in Appendix B, and the numerical results in Appendices C–D. Static inspection targeted atomic-action definitions, action admissibility, the precondition checker and its validation caller. The principal issue is a failure of that checker to enforce its own declared Boolean formula. It is not a claim that every generated plan fails. No simulator, model, author script, training run or historical experiment was executed. Other predicate and effect implementations were not exhaustively verified. The original PDF and source manifest are preserved unchanged.
# Necessary definitions and dependence

HVR combines hierarchical generation, knowledge-graph retrieval and symbolic verification. Section 2.4 (pp. 4–5) describes checking plan feasibility and feeding violated conditions back for correction. Section 3.3 (p. 6) specifies a custom Python validator supporting conjunction, disjunction and conditional PDDL statements. Section 4.1 (p. 7) separately defines plan correctness (PC) against reference plans and expanded plan verification (EPV) against symbolic conditions. These are distinct quantities: symbolic feasibility does not by itself establish completion of the natural-language goal.

In the inspected implementation, a state is the union of three lists of property, state and relational assertions. For an action to be feasible its ordinary preconditions and each required disjunction must hold. The `pour` action in `planner/planner_funcs.py`, lines 64–75, requires the source to be held and picked up, the robot to be at the destination, the destination to be empty and suitable for liquid, and the source to contain coffee, wine or water.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (Pouring is accepted without liquid in the source).  The released validator’s disjunction parsing removes the source-liquid requirement from the effective test. This invalidates the precondition soundness of a core verification component.
## Original claim and suspect operation

The source implementation is the concrete counterpart of the custom Boolean validator described on p. 6. Its source-liquid condition is \[(\texttt{filled\_with\_coffee}\;s)
\;\lor\;(\texttt{filled\_with\_wine}\;s)
\;\lor\;(\texttt{filled\_with\_water}\;s).\] In `check_action_preconditions_object_state` (lines 146–192), every precondition containing `OR` is excluded from the ordinary conjunct list. Instead it is processed with
`re.findall(r"\([a-z0-9 ]*\)", precondition[4:-1])`.

The allowed character set contains no underscore. Consequently none of the three source-liquid atoms matches. Each encountered disjunction also overwrites the previous alternative list rather than retaining a list of separate disjunctions. The last disjunction for `pour` therefore leaves an empty list, whose subsequent checking loop executes zero times.
## Complete counterexample and hypothesis check

Take the distinct instances \(s=\texttt{Bottle-1}\) and \(d=\texttt{Cup-1}\). Let the relevant assertions be \[\begin{aligned}
S=\{&
 \texttt{inside(Bottle-1,RobotGripper-1)},\
 \texttt{pickedUp(Bottle-1)},\\
&\texttt{at(Robot,Cup-1)},\
 \texttt{non\_filled\_with\_liquid(Cup-1)},\\
&\texttt{non\_filled\_with\_liquid(Bottle-1)},\\
&\texttt{fillable\_with\_liquid(Cup-1)},\\
&\texttt{fillable\_with\_liquid(Bottle-1)}\}.\end{aligned}\] Use the implementation’s parenthesized string notation when storing these assertions, partitioning them into property, state and relational lists. There are no source-liquid assertions. The source has an ordinary empty state, rather than missing state metadata. The instance names are already normalized and neither belongs to the sliced/cracked-object substitution cases. All four ordinary conjuncts are explicitly true. The destination disjunction is true because the cup is fillable; the source-liquid disjunction is false because the bottle is empty. Being held and being empty are compatible conditions. Additional irrelevant type or visibility assertions do not alter the argument.
## Counterevidence and the actual caller

A possible rescue would be an earlier action mapper rejecting empty sources. However, `main/utils.py`, lines 231–243, constructs admissible `pour` actions from fillable object types without imposing a source-liquid-state test. Another possible rescue would be a later pre-execution check. The caller `validate_execution_steps`, lines 801–828 of `planner/planner_funcs.py`, obtains the Boolean from this checker and records a validation failure only when it is false. The pouring effect helper (lines 267–299) reports missing liquid but does not reject the action when the source has ordinary empty-state metadata; it retains the uninstantiated liquid placeholder.

Execution in a simulator could still fail, and a goal-based PC evaluation could still penalize the plan. Neither possibility restores the preceding symbolic precondition decision. The conclusion is confined to the inspected release and the specified state. The construction does not establish how often this state occurred in the paper’s runs.
## Supported impact and repair status

The dependence is direct: \[\text{precondition parser}\longrightarrow
\text{atomic feasibility decision}\longrightarrow
\text{plan validation and correction feedback}.\] This is the verification component named in the paper’s core contribution, not a display-only utility. The inspected implementation’s claimed Boolean validation is unsound, supporting Major under the supplied calibration. The historical PC/EPV values, improvement over baselines and simulator success rates are not disproved by this counterexample; their dependence on this precise commit requires experiment provenance.

A proper implementation would retain every disjunction, instantiate its arguments and require at least one true atom in each group. Merely extending the character class is insufficient: overwriting groups, lack of instantiation and the current early-return structure must also be addressed. No implementation repair or general validator proof has been verified here.
# Other checked evidence and unresolved questions

Independent arithmetic recovers the HVR mean PC values in Tables 6 and 12: \(59.6567\%\) and \(94.1925\%\), agreeing with the rounded main-table values \(59.66\%\) and \(94.19\%\). The eleven displayed LD values in Tables 8 and 14 average to \(203.3918\%\) and \(109.1264\%\), reproducing Table 2. These LD tables omit T12 although their captions refer to twelve tasks; a twelve-task LD mean cannot be reconstructed from the displayed entries.

There is also an unresolved task-level correspondence: Table 4 gives T5 HVR EPV as \(6.76\%\) for Phi3 and \(34.55\%\) for Gemini, whereas the same numbers appear under T2 in Tables 9 and 15; their T5 entries are \(56.06\%\) and \(100\%\). These are incompatible as same-run, same-task entries. Task-keyed run records are needed to identify the correct mapping. No change in aggregate ranking is inferred, and this unresolved correspondence does not raise the supported severity.

Appendix B.3 explicitly permits maximizing PC over valid partial-order linearizations. Therefore this review does not treat PC as requiring one arbitrary action ordering. Appendix B.2 also describes run-dependent references for open-ended tasks. Independent replication, uncertainty across repeated model calls, the task-keyed EPV mapping and conference-time code correspondence remain outside the completed checks. No later revision or erratum was supplied or independently adjudicated.

report: Abstract: Three defects affect the stated theoretical guarantees: a purported linear spline construction is quadratic, a clipping threshold depending on the current response invalidates a conditional expectation identity, and the stated rate vanishes on a permitted zero-variation signal. Explicit counterexamples establish these claims. They support Major assessments of the affected derivations and theorem statements, without establishing that the intended positive-variation rate or the empirical advantages are false.

Title: Technical Verification of AKORN
# Identity and scope

The reviewed paper is Sunil Madhow, Dheeraj Baby and Yu-Xiang Wang, AKORN: Adaptive Knots generated Online for RegressioN splines, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, OpenReview `vfRmp9RPV7` (0292/I25-43661) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The source is the frozen proceedings PDF; one-based PDF pages coincide with printed page numbers in the cited locations. Released code was inspected separately at `SunilMadhow/AKORN`, commit `13bb80f30c1e212b4c6c2a0d7453aba87a70bcc6` [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its conference-time provenance is not established.

The checks cover the principal algorithm definitions, Theorems 6.1–6.2, the projection argument in Lemma C.2, the knot-count/projection proof chain in Appendix C, and the conditional-noise step in Appendix D. They include selected static code correspondence and exact independently written calculations. Appendix E’s full approximation analysis, Appendix F’s nonuniform-design extension, external cited proofs and empirical reproduction were not exhaustively verified. No author code was executed.
# Definitions and the core dependencies

The observations are \(Y_i=f(x_i)+\epsilon_i\), with \(x_i=i/n\), independent \(\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), bounded \(|f|\le1\), and \[C=\sum_{i=3}^n\left|
 \frac{f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})}{x_i-x_{i-1}}-
 \frac{f(x_{i-1})-f(x_{i-2})}{x_{i-1}-x_{i-2}}\right|<\infty .\] The paper permits \(C=0\). Let \(S(K)\) be continuous linear splines evaluated on the design, with knots \(K\), and \(F(K)\) the larger piecewise-linear space permitting discontinuities. AKORN outputs the least-squares projection \(P_{S(K)}Y\). Lemma C.7 supplies a spline sandwiched between forward and backward fits to control approximation error. Lemma D.6 supplies the noise identity used in the martingale argument for ADDLE; ADDLE’s guarantee in turn supports knot detection. Both dependencies are central to Theorem 6.2.
# Substantive findings

Equation reference: eq:bad. Problem 1 (The constructed function in Lemma C.7 is not a linear spline).  Lemma C.7, Case 2 (p. 18), sets \[
 s(z)=g(z)+(h(z)-g(z))\frac{z-a}{b-a},
 \qquad a=k_{i-1},\ b=k_i,\] and asserts membership in the linear-spline space. The claimed implication from noncrossing to linearity is false.
## Complete check

Use \(n=8\), \(K_f=\{1/2\}\), \(K_b=\{1/4\}\), and, on \([0,1]\), \[g(z)=\max\{0,z-1/2\},\qquad h(z)=\max\{5/4,1+z\}.\] These are in \(F(K_f)\) and \(F(K_b)\), respectively; continuous piecewise-linear functions are allowed members. The knot sets are disjoint, and \(g\le1/2<5/4\le h\), so there are no crossover points, regardless of whether crossings are tested on the grid or continuously. The first knot \(1/4\) belongs to \(K_b\), so the proof’s base case gives \(s=g=0\) up to that knot. The next knot \(1/2\) belongs to \(K_f\), satisfying precisely the hypotheses of Case 2.

On \([1/4,1/2]\), Equation [eq:bad] (#eq:bad) becomes \[s(z)=4z^2+3z-1,\qquad s''(z)=8.\] All three of \(1/4,3/8,1/2\) are design points, but \[s(1/4)=0,\qquad s(3/8)=11/16,\qquad s(1/2)=3/2.\] An affine segment with these endpoints must have midpoint \(3/4\). The discrepancy is \(-1/16\). Thus membership fails even if \(S(K)\) is interpreted only as vectors of evaluations on the finite design. Exact rational arithmetic reproduces these values in `verification/0292/check.json`. The original p. 18 was rendered and inspected to exclude extraction error.
## Counterevidence, correction and impact

The pointwise convex combination in Equation [eq:bad] (#eq:bad) does stay between \(g\) and \(h\); that fact does not make it affine. Equal slopes would be a valid special case, but equal slopes are not a lemma hypothesis. The lemma’s existence conclusion is not disproved by this example. Indeed, the local endpoint interpolant \[s_*(z)=6z-\tfrac32\quad (1/4\le z\le1/2)\] works here: \(s_*\ge g=0\) and \(h-s_*=5/2-5z\ge0\). More generally, endpoint interpolation stays in an ordered strip between two affine functions because the relevant differences are affine and nonnegative at both endpoints. This verifies a local repair, not all jump, crossover and collision cases in the full construction.

Theorem C.9 (pp. 18–19), hence Theorem 6.2, invokes Lemma C.7 to produce a member of \(S(K)\) with controlled error. The written construction fails at that exact required membership step. This is a Major defect in a core derivation even if a corrected construction can restore the lemma; it is not a proof that the desired rate is unattainable.

Problem 2 (The clipping threshold destroys the conditional-noise identity).  Algorithm 5 (p. 13) uses \[B=\max_{1\le i\le n}|Y_i|+
 \max\{\sigma\sqrt{2\log(4n/\delta)},1\}\] to clip the linear experts. Lemma D.6(1) (p. 20), with \(\mathcal F_j=\sigma(Y_1,\ldots,Y_{j-1})\), asserts \[E[(Y_j-z_j)^2-(Y_j-\theta_j)^2\mid\mathcal F_j,V]
 =E[(z_j-\theta_j)^2\mid\mathcal F_j,V].\] The identity fails because \(B\), and consequently \(z_j\), depends on the current response.
## Parameters, hypotheses and calculation

Take \(n=3\), \(\sigma=0.1\), \(\delta=0.1\), and \((\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)=(-1,1,1)\). A permissible underlying function equals \(-1\) up to \(x_1\), rises linearly with slope \(6\) to \(x_2\), and then equals \(1\). Thus it is bounded by one, has the required design values and \(C=6\).

Equation reference: eq:noise. Write \(a=\sigma\sqrt{2\log120}=0.3094347<1\) and \(V=\{|\epsilon_i|\le a\text{ for all }i\}\). First evaluate the conditional law at past responses \(Y_1=-1,Y_2=1\); their noise values satisfy \(V\). The linear expert starting at the first observation extrapolates to \(3\) at \(x_3\). Conditional on the past and \(V\), \(e=\epsilon_3\) has a symmetric normal law truncated to \([-a,a]\), and \[B=2+\max(e,0)<3,\qquad z_3=B.\] All clipping operations are therefore in the stated clipped branch. Subtracting the right side of Lemma D.6(1) from its left side gives \[\begin{aligned}
 -2E[e(z_3-\theta_3)\mid V,Y_1=-1,Y_2=1]
 &=-2E[e(1+\max(e,0))\mid |e|\le a]\notag\\
 &=-E[e^2\mid |e|\le a]<0. \end{aligned}\] The exact conditional moment has the analytic form \[v=\sigma^2\left(1-\frac{2c\phi(c)}{2\Phi(c)-1}\right),
 \qquad c=a/\sigma,\] and independent evaluation gives \(v=0.0097938491\). Thus the claimed zero difference is approximately \(-0.0097938491\).

The exact past point has probability zero, so it is not itself asserted to be a positive-probability counterevent. Conditional moments and this clipped prediction vary continuously with the two past responses in a small neighborhood of \((-1,1)\), while \(V\) has a positive-density interior there. The strictly negative difference in Equation [eq:noise] (#eq:noise) therefore persists on a neighborhood of positive probability. This establishes failure of the asserted conditional identity as an almost-sure statement.
## Alternatives and dependence

Conditioning on \(V\) alone preserves the symmetric truncated law of each independent noise variable. The failure comes from the response-dependent threshold, not from an automatic claim that every conditioning argument is invalid. The counterexample follows Equation (1)’s Gaussian model and Section 3.1’s \(|f|\le1\) bound. Algorithm 3’s \([0,1]\) history annotation conflicts with that model; imposing it would exclude theorem-covered data. A deterministic bound or a threshold measurable with respect to the past would remove this particular dependence, but would change the algorithm or its assumptions and require a fresh proof. The released code’s omission of this clipping step is additional evidence that its guarantees cannot simply be equated with the printed algorithm.

Lemma D.8 (p. 21) uses Lemma D.6 to declare the corresponding noise term a martingale difference and apply a Freedman-type inequality. The counterexample invalidates that justification. This is Major for the ADDLE error proof and the dependent AKORN guarantee. No failure rate of the empirical estimator is inferred; no complete replacement concentration argument has been verified.

Problem 3 (The stated bounds incorrectly vanish on affine signals).  Theorems 6.1 and 6.2 (p. 7) quantify over \(C<\infty\), but give total error \(\widetilde O(n^{1/5}C^{2/5})\) and mean squared error \(\widetilde O(n^{-4/5}C^{2/5})\), respectively, without a parametric baseline.

For Theorem 6.2 choose \(f=0\), any \(n\ge3\) and \(\sigma>0\). All stated assumptions hold and \(C=0\). For every selected knot set, \(S(K)\) contains constants. Least-squares orthogonality consequently gives, pathwise, \(\overline{\widehat f}=\overline Y=\overline\epsilon\), even though \(K\) is data-dependent. Therefore \[\frac1n\|\widehat f\|_2^2\ge\overline\epsilon^{\,2}>0
 \quad\text{almost surely},\qquad
 \frac{n\overline\epsilon^{\,2}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_1.\] The displayed upper bound equals zero; it cannot hold with probability \(1-\delta>0\). For the online claim, the constant signal \(f=1/2\) also has \(C=0\), whereas the empty-history first prediction is zero, already giving total error at least \(1/4\).

Multiplicative constants and logarithms cannot turn zero into a positive upper bound. There is no stated lower bound on \(C\). Counterevidence for the intended interpretation is explicit: Lemma C.1 retains \(\max\{n^{1/5}C^{2/5},1\}\), and Section 5 discusses an \(n^{-1}\) parametric rate. Thus a parametric term was plausibly intended. Nevertheless, it disappears in the theorem statements and later Corollary C.6/C.9 bounds. Retaining a baseline such as \(\widetilde O(n^{-1}+n^{-4/5}C^{2/5})\) is necessary for a uniform offline statement. This report does not certify that amended bound, because Problems 1 and 2 leave other proof obligations open. The assessment is Major for the stated central uniform guarantee; the positive-\(C\) leading exponent is not refuted by this check.
# Source correspondence and surviving results

Lemma C.2’s nested-projection argument is sound: since \(S\subset F\), \(\|P_SY-P_S\theta\|\le\|P_FY-\theta\|\), and the triangle inequality gives the displayed factor-two bound after squaring. This deterministic statement remains valid for a selected random \(K\). The interval-uniform strategy in Lemma C.3 also avoids simply treating adaptive knots as independent of the responses; that idea is not the source of Problem 2.

The released `akorn.py`, lines 71–81, uses continuous `RegressionSpline` preliminary fits rather than the \(F(K)\) fits in Algorithm 2; `splines.py`, lines 25–29, confirms the basis \(1,x,(x-k)_+\). It also omits collision-repair knots, a proof requirement acknowledged in Remark 4.2, and uses a pseudoinverse. The historical-indexed predictions in `flh.py` agree with Appendix C’s intended stopping statistic rather than a literal repeated latest-prediction subscript in Algorithm 1. These counterexamples are therefore not attributed indiscriminately to every release branch. The exact theoretical coverage of this different released estimator and its connection to the reported runs remain Needs Evidence.

The reported simulations, visual fit quality and possible existence of an optimal repaired estimator can survive the demonstrated proof defects. No empirical scores were rerun or revised. Later versions and author errata were not supplied or separately adjudicated.
# Conclusion

C.7 construction | Major: written function leaves the required spline space
D.6 noise identity | Major: explicit nonzero conditional cross term
Zero-variation theorem domain | Major: stated zero error contradicts permissible signals
Repair verification | Local interpolation checked; no complete repaired theorem
Released estimator’s rate | Needs Evidence
Scientific adjudication | Pending

Title: Technical Verification of
Canonical Rank Adaptation
# Identity, reviewed versions, and scope

The paper is Canonical Rank Adaptation: An Efficient Fine-Tuning Strategy for Vision Transformers, by Lokesh Veeramacheneni, Moritz Wolter, Hilde Kuehne, and Juergen Gall, ICML 2025, PMLR 267; assigned identifier I25-43662, display number 0293, OpenReview `vexHifrbJg` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed original is the staged 18-page proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are PDF page numbers, which agree with printed numbering.

The review examined the main construction and experiments, especially Sections 3.1–3.4, Equations (8)–(20), Tables 2, 4, and 5, the complete gradient derivation in Appendix A, and implementation details in Appendices B–C. Appendices D–E were read for scope; their experiments and attribution maps were not reproduced. The inspected public source is commit , acquired during source preparation on 25 October 2026 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. It is not established as the commit used for the conference experiments. Available source files and retained archive members were checked without executing author code. No training data, model weights, or new software were downloaded.
# Necessary background and checked components

Equation reference: eq:forward. CaRA tensorizes attention and feed-forward updates and represents each as a CP sum. Writing either update uniformly, with tensor order \(m=3\) or \(4\), \[
 W_{\rm eff}=W_0+\alpha\sum_{r=1}^{R}\lambda_r
       a_r^{(1)}\circ\cdots\circ a_r^{(m)},\] the factors and \(\lambda_r\) are learned; \(W_0\) is frozen and \(\alpha\) is the external scale. The feed-forward tensor has dimensions \(9l\times d_{\rm model}\times d_{\rm model}\). Equation [eq:forward] (#eq:forward) is a valid parameterization.

The released initialization sets one factor in each CP sum to zero, retaining nonzero other factors and nonzero scaling coefficients. Consequently the initial update is zero but its derivative with respect to the zero factor need not vanish. No dead-gradient initialization was established for the supplied configurations. The ViT-B adaptation parameter count also reconciles: the factors and two coefficient vectors use \(2526R\) parameters and shared biases use \(4608\), yielding \(85440\) at \(R=32\), as in Table 5. The classifier head is trained but excluded from this adaptation count.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The stated scalar-loss gradients omit the chain rule).  Assessment: Major; outcome: issue found.
## Original claim and location

Section 3.3, pp. 5–6, explicitly introduces a loss function \(L\) and states its gradients with respect to \(\lambda_r\) and individual factor vectors in Equations (12)–(20). For example, the coefficient gradient is given as the outer product of the factors. This is an order-\(m\) tensor, although the derivative of a scalar loss with respect to scalar \(\lambda_r\) must be scalar. Factor derivatives are similarly given as outer products involving an identity matrix, which are Jacobians of the tensor update, not factor-shaped gradients of \(L\).
## Complete check and independent calculation

For an explicit example satisfying the paper’s dimensions, take the feed-forward formulation with \(l=1\), \(d_{\rm model}=2\), \(R=1\), and hence shape \(9\times2\times2\). Let all three factors be their first standard basis vectors, \(\alpha=3\), \(\lambda_1=2\), and \[L=\tfrac12\|W_{\rm eff}-W_0\|_F^2.\] No paper assumption excludes this differentiable loss or these parameter values. Only update entry \((1,1,1)\) is nonzero, equal to \(6\). Therefore \(L=18\), \(\partial L/\partial\lambda_1=18\), and \(\nabla_{a_1^{(k)}}L=36e_1\) for each factor. The corresponding entry of the printed outer product or uncontracted Jacobian is \(1\); it also has the wrong output shape. Exact rational central differences of this quadratic loss reproduce 18 and 36, without author-code execution (`verification/0293/check.py` and `check.json`).
## Alternative reading, impact, and repair

Appendix A, pp. 13–14, differentiates the tensor-valued update \(\mathcal F_z\) rather than scalar \(L\), and explicitly absorbs \(\lambda_z\) into the first factor after Equation (23). Those statements supply a valid Jacobian interpretation and explain the origin of the displayed objects. They do not make the main-text equations gradients of an arbitrary scalar loss in the original coordinates, where the coefficient is separately learned. The source retains a separate trainable coefficient. Source-page images `s05.png` and `s13.png` were inspected to exclude an extraction error.

The invalid derivation directly concerns optimization of the paper’s principal parameterization and supports Major under the specified calibration. Equations [eq:lambda] (#eq:lambda)–[eq:factor] (#eq:factor) are a locally verified correction by the chain rule, with no changed parameter domain. This does not establish an erroneous benchmark computation: Section 3.3 says autograd is used, and the inspected source reconstructs CP tensors with TensorLy’s PyTorch backend, applies the scale in the forward pass, and calls `loss.backward()`. It does not implement the erroneous displayed expressions as a custom backward rule. The CP construction and empirical results may survive this derivation error.
Problem 2 (The released training entry point selects checkpoints on the test split).  Assessment: Major for the frozen release’s core evaluation protocol; historical empirical impact: Needs Evidence.
## Original claim, assumptions, and source path

Section 4.1, p. 6, describes the VTAB-1k protocol with 800 training and 200 validation samples. The released training route in `image_classification/vit_cp.py`, around lines 152–198, calls `get_data(evaluate=True)` and passes its second loader into `train`. In `image_classification/vtab.py`, lines 83–94, this choice maps the first loader to `train800val200.txt` and the second to `test.txt`. The finding assumes those named lists have their advertised split meanings and the ordinary training branch is used. No dataset bytes were inspected.
## Decisive trace and counterevidence

Inside `train`, lines 57–68, epochs 10, 20, …, 90 trigger evaluation on that second loader; a higher score updates `args.best_acc` and saves the associated checkpoint. Final evaluation also participates in the comparison, and the reported accuracy is the retained best value. Thus the procedure both chooses a checkpoint and reports a maximum using labels from `test.txt`. For evaluated accuracies \(\widehat a_1,\ldots,\widehat a_J\), the reported statistic is \(\max_j\widehat a_j\), which is pathwise at least each individual score. It is not an untouched evaluation of a checkpoint selected independently of test labels.

Combining the 800 and 200 samples for a final fit can be legitimate after model selection; that fact alone is not the defect. The available `evaluate=False` branch provides a validation loader, but this training entry point does not select it. These observations come from reading the complete training and loader files, with archive correspondence independently checked in `a1.json`.
## Bounded impact and correction status

This is a Major defect in the frozen release’s core evaluation protocol: test labels determine both checkpoint selection and the reported maximum. The direct dependency is test-loader labels to checkpoint choice to the reported VTAB accuracy, so the procedure no longer supplies an independent held-out evaluation. The magnitude of selection bias cannot be determined without predictions or reruns. The present commit is not bound to the historical runs underlying Table 2, so those scores are not declared contaminated. This provenance limitation bounds attribution to historical experiments; it does not remove the demonstrated failure of the inspected core evaluation procedure. A protocol using validation scores for selection and one final held-out test evaluation would remove this selection path; a corrected end-to-end training run has not been verified.
Problem 3 (Intermediate evaluation leaves later training in evaluation mode).  Assessment: Minor; outcome: issue found in the release.

In `vit_cp.py`, `model.train()` is called before the epoch loop. The first intermediate `test()` calls `model.eval()`, and neither its return path nor subsequent epochs restore training mode. The next optimizer updates therefore run in evaluation mode. The inspected CaRA forward path contains dropout, so this changes the training-time stochastic behavior after the first intermediate evaluation. Gradients continue to run: evaluation mode does not itself disable autograd.

This trace is independent of which split the evaluation loader contains. The source does not document such a schedule as intentional. Its numerical effect and connection to historical experiments remain unknown. Restoring the prior training state after evaluation is the local proposed correction, but no author code was edited or executed and no training outcome is certified.
# Other checked claims and remaining evidence

The 19 printed CaRA accuracies in Table 2 average to \(74.1421\%\), agreeing with the reported overall \(74.14\%\). Averaging the three group means from those rounded entries gives \(76.4274\%\); the reported \(76.46\%\) is within what one-decimal input rounding can explain. No arithmetic defect is asserted there.

The ViT-L parameter count is unresolved. Appendix C.4 reports rank 32, while Table 4 gives \(0.076\)M parameters. Applying the stated full-tensor formula to \(l=24\), \(d_{\rm model}=1024\), \(h=16\), \(d_h=64\) yields \(110144\) CP parameters, or \(116288\) with analogous shared biases. The inspected release hardcodes ViT-B dimensions; no ViT-L branch or reduced adaptation rule was located. The relevant implementation and counting convention are needed before assigning a defect.

At fixed per-projection rank \(R\), a CP tensor unfolding has matrix rank at most \(R\) and is representable by matrix LoRA of rank \(R\). Tensorization therefore introduces structural sharing and inductive bias, rather than proving a strict expressive-power increase over unconstrained matrix updates of the same rank. Equal parameter budgets and cross-layer sharing are different comparisons. Since the paper acknowledges fewer degrees of freedom, this is a scope clarification, not a further substantive finding.

No empirical retraining, significance analysis of baseline comparisons, historical checkpoint provenance check, complete Swin/GLUE reproduction, or saliency-map validation was performed. Appendix D tables were read but not comprehensively recalculated. External supplementary discovery was blocked during source preparation; the embedded appendices were available.
# Overall impact and state

The supported overall assessment is Major, based on the central loss-gradient derivation and the frozen release’s test-dependent core evaluation protocol. The locally corrected derivatives leave the forward CP model intact. Ordinary autograd provides concrete counterevidence against concluding that this mathematical presentation error was used in training. The test-selection defect is separately Major at the release level; the training-mode inconsistency remains Minor. Historical run records and a corrected training procedure are needed to determine consequences for the reported benchmarks.

Title: Technical Verification of
Sparse-Comparison Matrix Factorization
# Identity, versions, and scope

The reviewed paper is Recommendations with Sparse Comparison Data: Provably Fast Convergence for Nonconvex Matrix Factorization, by Suryanarayana Sankagiri, Jalal Etesami, and Matthias Grossglauser, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, identifier I25-43663, display 0294, OpenReview `vcNJgiEGdz` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The staged proceedings PDF has 35 pages. All page references below are PDF pages, agreeing with printed numbering.

The review covers the model and Algorithm 1; Theorem 4.1 and its dependency on Lemmas 5.1–5.7; the projection, score, expectation, and concentration arguments in Appendices A–E at the scope recorded in the coverage ledger; and the descriptions of Figures 1–2. The primary assistant read the decisive main and appendix steps and performed independent calculations. Native auxiliaries challenged the mathematical arguments and statically inspected source. Every external cited proof was not rederived, particularly the imported regularizer inequality in Appendix E.1. This is not an exhaustive certification of the theorem.

The frozen author source is `indy-lab/matrix-factorization-comparisons`, commit [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The Figure 1 notebook and Figure 2 training/data-generation source were inspected as text. Retained archive members and source hashes were verified. Historical figure-producing runs were not established by executing or reproducing the release.
# Assumptions and valid scope

There are \(n_1\) users, \(n_2\) items, \(n=n_1+n_2\), and a rank-\(r\) utility matrix \(X^*=U^*\Sigma^*V^{*T}\). The balanced factor is \[Z^*=\begin{bmatrix}U^*\\V^*\end{bmatrix}\Sigma^{*1/2},
 \qquad
 \mu=\frac{n\|Z^*\|_{2,\infty}^2}{\|Z^*\|_F^2}.\] The centered item factors satisfy \(1^TV^*=0\). Comparisons sample a user and an ordered pair of distinct items uniformly and independently across observations. The theorem uses the exact probabilities \(g(x^*_{u,i}-x^*_{u,j})\), not Bernoulli outcomes, and assumes a warm start. These restrictions are explicit in the paper and are not treated as defects.

The objective is the average cross-entropy plus \((\lambda/4)\|Z^TDZ\|_F^2\), with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(I_{n_1},-I_{n_2})\). Algorithm 1 applies row clipping and then item-centering. Its error is distance to the rotational orbit \(\Phi\) of \(Z^*\), written \(\Delta=Z-\Phi(Z)\). The theorem requires positive link curvature \(\xi\), with \(\tau=\xi/\Xi\) and \(\alpha=\xi\gamma\sigma_r^*\), where \(\gamma=2/[n_1(n_2-1)]\).
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The Bernoulli tail bound supporting smoothness is false).  Assessment: Major; outcome: issue found.
## Claim and precise dependency
## Counterexample, including the used specialization

This is supported by exact rational certificates, not only floating-point tails: the rational number in [eq:atom] (#eq:atom) exceeds \(10^{-19}\), while \(\sum_{j=0}^{100}50^j/j!>10^{21}\) implies \(e^{-50}<10^{-21}\). The reviewer-written `check2.py` verifies both comparisons and also evaluates the displayed values to 60-digit precision. No author code is involved. The original p. 28 was visually inspected (`s28.png`); the denominator is indeed \(2p(1-p)\).
## Verified local repair and bounded impact
Problem 2 (The stated curvature lemma omits the singular-value scale).  Assessment: Minor; outcome: issue found, with downstream counterevidence.

Lemma 5.1 on p. 7 and its restatement on p. 31 use \((\xi\gamma/4)\|\Delta\|_F^2\) as the first lower-bound term. The derivation on p. 32 and the final theorem proof on p. 34 instead use the necessary factor \(\sigma_r^*\).

Here is an admissible quantitative counterexample to the statement. Set \(n_1=1\), \(n_2=2\), \(r=1\), \(s_0=0.01\), \[X^*=(s_0/\sqrt2,-s_0/\sqrt2),\quad
 Z^*=\sqrt{s_0}(1,1/\sqrt2,-1/\sqrt2)^T,\quad
 Z=1.01Z^*.\] Use the sigmoid link. Then \(\sigma_r^*=s_0\), \(\mu=1.5\), \(\kappa=1\), \(\gamma=2\), \(\xi=g'(24s_0)=0.24643428\ldots\), and \(\tau=0.98573712\ldots\). The item factors are centered; the factors are balanced, so the regularizer gradient and \(\Delta^TD\Phi\) vanish. Also \(\|\Delta\|_F^2=2\times10^{-6}<\tau s_0/50\) and the largest row norm \(0.101\) is below the allowed \(\overline C\) radius \(0.34641\ldots\). Thus the proximity, centering, and incoherence hypotheses all hold.

The correction is to insert \(\sigma_r^*\) in the first term. The paper’s own derivation and final proof already retain it. Hence this is a false quantitative lemma statement with a locally verified correction, but no additional failure of the theorem’s final contraction calculation is established. That counterevidence bounds its assessment to Minor.
Problem 3 (The reported incoherence is impossible for the stated balanced factors).  Assessment: Minor; outcome: issue found.

Section 6, p. 8, reports \(\mu\approx1.01\) for dimensions \((200,300)\) and \((2000,3000)\). Equation (2) gives equal squared Frobenius energy \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma^*\) in the user and item blocks. In the smaller block, at least one row therefore has squared norm at least \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma^*/\min(n_1,n_2)\). Substitution into Equation (10) yields the deterministic lower bound \[\mu\ge\frac{n_1+n_2}{2\min(n_1,n_2)}=1.25\] in both reported settings. Rank is positive, so the energy denominator is nonzero. This argument holds regardless of the random distribution used to generate the matrix.

The released Figure 1 notebook assigns `mu=1.01`; it does not recompute Equation (10) after balancing its matrix. A user-chosen tuning constant with that name is possible, but it is not the defined ground-truth incoherence. The stated value and its connection to sample-size and projection formulas require correction. This does not establish that the plotted errors or qualitative convergence observations are false. The actual incoherence of historical matrices was not recovered.
# Additional checks, implementation scope, and limits

The identity in Lemma C.1 follows from \(\mathbb E(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^T=2J/(n_2-1)\) and user sampling; an independent exact enumeration for a \(2\times3\) matrix gives \(14/3\) on both sides. The vectorized quadratic-form statement of C.4 and the uniform operator-norm argument of C.6 were checked. The two projection steps are nonexpansive relative to a ground truth lying in both constraint sets, and centering expands the row bound by at most two, as used in A.3. The final step-size algebra with \(a=\xi\gamma\sigma_r^*/4\) agrees with E.3.

A link-domain qualification is needed. Smooth strict monotonicity and symmetry alone do not imply \(\xi>0\): \(g(x)=1/(1+e^{-x^3})\) has all those properties but \(g'(0)=0\), making \(\xi=0\) on the interval used by the paper. The theorem’s finite sample threshold and positive rate require \(\xi>0\). This is an effective-domain clarification; no finite-threshold counterexample to Theorem 4.1 is claimed from a case where its constants are undefined.

Static source inspection identifies further differences requiring historical run evidence. The Figure 1 notebook generates normalized feature rows and balances their product rather than truncating an iid Gaussian utility matrix as described. It clips rows without the subsequent centering projection of Algorithm 1, uses a different clipping radius, and supplies different regularization and step-size formulas. A later singular-value rescaling is not applied to the already built \(Z^*\). Its actual optimization gradient uses noiseless probabilities, despite an unused Bernoulli data helper. Figure 2 openly uses Adam without projection, as Appendix F permits; its implemented error centers the residual. Neither an unused helper nor a disclosed algorithm variant is promoted into a defect. Full release traces are retained in `a1.json`. Their effects on the historical plotted curves remain Needs Evidence.

No author notebook, training code, tests, or original simulation was executed. No real recommendation dataset was required by the paper’s claimed simulation scope. Separate external supplementary discovery was unavailable; the complete embedded appendices were available. The imported external regularizer inequality and every concentration constant were not exhaustively independently certified.
# Overall impact and state

The highest supported assessment is Major, confined to an invalid concentration step used in the main convergence proof. A complete local replacement restores D.7 with its original statement. The curvature-scale omission is already corrected in the paper’s downstream algebra. The impossible incoherence value limits the accuracy of the reported experimental setup, while numerical effects remain unmeasured.
