Title: Technical Verification of
Clone-Robust AI Alignment
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The paper is Clone-Robust AI Alignment, by Ariel D. Procaccia, Benjamin Schiffer, and Shirley Zhang, ICML 2025, PMLR 267; identifier I25-43664, display 0295, OpenReview `vbw9hSlOaG` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed version is the staged 24-page proceedings PDF. Page references are PDF pages, agreeing with printed numbering.

The review examined the definitions and results in Sections 2–4, the main robustness proof in Appendix G, its convexity dependency in Appendix E, the normalization proof in Appendix F, the supporting impossibility and clone-reversal arguments, and the case-study design in Section 5 and Appendix I. The primary assistant independently derived the decisive examples below and inspected original source-page renderings. Auxiliary agents supplied mathematical challenges and checks of the supporting results. No attributable author repository was located in the completed source preparation; this is an availability limitation, not a claim that none exists. Embedded appendices were available, while external OpenReview attachment discovery was blocked.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

The alternative space \(S\subset\mathbb R^d\) is assumed to have finite volume, and the observed set \(M\) is finite. Annotator rewards are \(K\)-Lipschitz in context distance; pairwise probabilities are population averages of Bradley–Terry–Luce probabilities. A representative dataset has exactly those pairwise probabilities. The clone-robustness definition asks for qualitative continuity when a new alternative approaches an existing one.

Equation reference: eq:weighted. Let \(\sigma(t)=(1+e^{-t})^{-1}\). Write the unweighted ordered-pair negative log likelihood as \[L_M(r)=-\sum_{x,y\in M}p_{xy}\log\sigma(r_x-r_y).\] Equation (1) minimizes \(F_\lambda(r)=L_M(r)+(\lambda/2)\sum_xr_x^2\). The weighted objective in Equation (2) is \[
 f_w(r)=-\sum_{x,y\in M}w_xw_yp_{xy}\log\sigma(r_x-r_y)
       +\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_xw_xr_x^2,\] where \(w_x\) is the normalized volume of the Voronoi cell, splitting ties. The examples in Problems 1–3 all have positive cell weights, positive \(\lambda\), and valid representative probabilities. Thus none relies on a zero-weight ambiguity.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Finite volume does not give the rate asserted in Lemma G.2).  Assessment: Major; outcome: issue found.
## Claim and dependency

Lemma G.2, p. 18, states \(|\widehat r_w^D(y)-r_1(y)|=O(\sqrt\epsilon)\) when a clone is within \(\epsilon\) of its original. Its Equation (13) first asserts that merged Voronoi weights change by \(O(\epsilon)\). Here \(r_1\) is the weighted optimizer after replacing the old weight of the cloned alternative by the combined weights of it and its clone, while retaining the old alternatives and probabilities. Theorem 4.2’s proof on pp. 16–18 uses this rate to choose \(\epsilon=c\delta^2\). The model on p. 3 assumes finite volume, not boundedness of \(S\).
## Admissible domain and actual weight movement

Consider the fixed two-dimensional domain \[\begin{aligned}
 S&=([0,1]\times[-1,1])\cup T,\\
 T&=\left\{(u,v):v\ge e^2,\quad
       \frac34\le u\le\frac34+\frac1{v(\log v)^2}\right\}.\end{aligned}\] It is measurable with positive finite volume \(V=2+\int_{e^2}^{\infty}[v(\log v)^2]^{-1}dv=5/2\). Let \(M=\{a=(0,0),b=(1,0)\}\) and add \(a'=(0,\epsilon)\), where \(0<\epsilon<e^{-2}\). All three Voronoi cells have positive area within the rectangle. The distance between \(a'\) and \(a\) is exactly \(\epsilon\).
## Reward calculation, not merely a geometric objection

Use one annotator with reward \(r^*(u,v)=(\log3)u\), globally Lipschitz with \(K=\log3\), and set \(\lambda=1\). Then \(p_{ab}=1/4\) and the clone has exactly the same preferences as \(a\). All comparison probabilities are \(1/4\), \(3/4\), or \(1/2\), so finite representative datasets exist.

For any two positive weights \(w_a+w_b=1\), the first-order conditions for [eq:weighted] (#eq:weighted) give a fixed reward gap \(d=r_a-r_b\) satisfying \[d+\sigma(d)=\tfrac14,\qquad
 r_a=w_b d,\quad r_b=-w_a d.\] The unique root is \(d=-0.2001330666939489\ldots\ne0\). Increasing \(w_a\) by \(q\) therefore shifts both original rewards by \(-qd\). By [eq:q] (#eq:q), \[|r_1(y)-\widehat r_w^D(y)|
 \ge\frac{|d|}{V\log(1/\epsilon)},\qquad y\in M.\] Dividing by \(\sqrt\epsilon\) diverges as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). This directly falsifies Lemma G.2, with every relevant original assumption and positivity condition satisfied. The geometry and algebra are exact; `check.json` records supporting root and rate evaluations.
## Counterevidence and bounded conclusion

The lower bound still tends to zero. The example refutes the asserted rate and the proof’s quadratic choice of neighborhood size, not the qualitative continuity in Definition 3.1. For finite-volume measurable domains, dominated convergence can support qualitative continuity of merged cells away from the null tie hyperplanes. A bounded-domain restriction would also change the geometry behind the claimed rate, but would be an additional assumption. No unconditional repaired version of Theorem 4.2 is certified here. The demonstrated false lemma is directly used in its central proof, supporting Major.
Problem 2 (Lemma G.4 uses the wrong weights in its curvature bound).  Assessment: Major; outcome: issue found.
## Claim and complete bounded-domain check

On p. 21, Lemma G.4 invokes Lemma E.1 with \(\lambda\min_{z\in M}w_M(z)\) to convert an objective gap for \(f_2\) into a reward bound. But \(f_2\), defined on p. 17, uses the enlarged-set weights \(w_{M'}\). Those weights may approach zero even when the original minimum weight is fixed.

Take \(S=[0,1]\), \(M=\{0,1\}\), and clone \(x'=\epsilon=0.01\). The new weights in the order \((0,\epsilon,1)\) are \((0.005,0.5,0.495)\); the original minimum weight is \(0.5\). Let all annotator rewards be zero, all pair probabilities be \(1/2\), and \(\lambda=1\). Constant rewards satisfy Assumption 2.1 for any positive Lipschitz upper bound; finite representative datasets exist. The unique optimizer of \(f_2\) is \(r_2=0\).
## Verified local replacement

The original invocation is invalid in a step directly proving Theorem 4.2, hence Major. Equation [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) locally repairs this part for positive weights; it does not repair Problem 1’s asserted rate or settle all domain issues.
Problem 3 (The moment identity and uniform-weight equivalence use inconsistent normalization).  Assessment: Major; outcome: issue found.
## Original statements and independent derivation

Theorem 2.5, p. 4, claims \(\operatorname{AWR}_D(x)=\lambda\widehat r_x+\widehat{\operatorname{AWR}}(x)\) for Equation (1), with average win rate defined using \(1/m\). The paragraph on p. 6 also claims that uniform weights make Equation (2) a scaled version of Equation (1), with the same optimizer.

For Equation (1), differentiation instead gives \[0=\lambda r_x+\sum_y\{\sigma(r_x-r_y)-p_{xy}\},\] and hence \[\operatorname{AWR}_D(x)=\frac{\lambda}{m}r_x+
                  \widehat{\operatorname{AWR}}(x).\] The one-sentence proof in Appendix F substitutes weights 1 into the weighted identity, but does not divide the regularizer term when converting sums into averages. With uniform \(w_x=1/m\), Equation (2) is \[f_w(r)=\frac1{m^2}L_M(r)+\frac{\lambda}{2m}\sum_xr_x^2
       =\frac1{m^2}F_{m\lambda}(r),\] so it matches the standard optimizer at regularization \(m\lambda\), not \(\lambda\).
## Explicit legitimate discrepancy

Let \(S=[0,1]\), \(M=\{0,1\}\), \(p_{ab}=3/4\), and \(\lambda=1\). The Voronoi weights are both \(1/2\). A single Lipschitz annotator with reward gap \(\log3\) generates the representative probabilities. Strict convexity and symmetry imply optimizers \((a,-a)\) and \((b,-b)\), where \[\sigma(2a)+a=\tfrac34,\qquad
 \sigma(2b)+2b=\tfrac34.\] Independent bisection gives \(a=0.1671800993781829\) and \(b=0.10006653334697452\). Theorem 2.5’s residual for alternative \(a\) is \(-0.08359004968909145\); the corrected \(\lambda/m\) identity has residual zero to the recorded precision. The analytic stationarity equations establish the error independently of the numerical solver.

These false statements concern the claimed preservation of the baseline’s interpretation and its equality to the new method in uniform instances. This supports Major for the affected mathematical relationship, without claiming empirical score loss. Retuning \(\lambda_{\rm standard}=m\lambda_{\rm weighted}\) restores the comparison. Alternatively, replacing Equation (1)’s loss by \(L_M/m\) would make the printed moment coefficient and same-\(\lambda\) uniform comparison consistent, but changes the defined baseline. Only this algebraic correction is verified; historical experiments were not rerun.

The ranking relationship survives a positive coefficient \(\lambda/m\), so this problem does not invalidate the Borda-based clone reversal in Theorem 3.2. The weighted identity of Theorem 4.4 itself is valid for positive weights.
# Surviving results, domain qualifications, and empirical limits

The two-population indistinguishability argument in Theorem 2.3 was checked within its variable reward-scale setting. The Borda example in Appendix D was independently recalculated: the original scores are approximately \((1.589919,1.5,1.410081)\) and the cloned scores \((2.040504,2.139334,1.910081,1.910081)\), retaining the winner reversal from \(a\) to \(b\). Theorem 4.6’s finite-sum/integral substitution was checked under measurable positive finite-volume conditions.

The domain also needs a rule for zero-volume cells. For example, \(S=[0,1]\cup\{2\}\) and \(M=\{0,1,2\}\) satisfy finite positive volume but assign weight zero to 2. The objective then leaves its reward unconstrained. An accumulating measure-zero sequence of potential clones has the same issue. This establishes nonuniqueness under the bare domain assumptions, not failure of every possible tie-breaking rule. Positive-cell assumptions or a specified extension are required before the proposed local repairs become a fully defined global algorithm. The intended restriction or rule remains unresolved.

The case study is explicitly synthetic and departs from complete representative comparisons. Appendix I describes 1000 comparisons per dataset, separately fitted 1500-component PCA, a small neural network, 20 training runs, and Monte Carlo weight estimation. No released dataset, implementation, regularization value, seeds, or historical model configuration was available for verification. Response-level standard-deviation bars and dataset size alone do not establish that a shift cannot be due to generation/training variability. Run-level uncertainty and the relationship between separate PCA coordinates and one fixed \(S\) remain Needs Evidence. No paid API calls, model training, or empirical reproduction was attempted.
# Overall impact and state

The overall assessment is Major. Two independent flaws affect the proof of the central robustness theorem, and a further normalization error changes a claimed exact relationship between the proposed and baseline objectives. The report distinguishes these from a refutation of qualitative clone robustness: the rate counterexample still converges, and a valid local replacement is given for G.4. A complete repaired theorem requires explicit domain conditions and a revised continuity argument.

Title: Technical Verification of
Objective Drives Similarity Consistency
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Objective drives the consistency of representational similarity across datasets, by Laure Ciernik, Lorenz Linhardt, Marco Morik, Jonas Dippel, Simon Kornblith, and Lukas Muttenthaler, ICML 2025, PMLR 267; I25-43665, display 0296, OpenReview `va3zmBXPat` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The source is the staged 29-page proceedings PDF, including Appendices A–J. Page references are PDF pages and agree with printed numbering.

The review covers Section 3’s definitions, the principal claims in Sections 4–5, sampling and downstream evaluation, alternative metrics, bounded-scale transformations, anchors, training-domain controls, and relevant released aggregation and plotting code. The repository `lciernik/similarity_consistency` was inspected at commit [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The selected source archive and member mappings remain unchanged. This release does not establish historical figure-generation provenance. External OpenReview attachment discovery was unavailable; embedded appendices were read.
# Checked definitions and surviving reasoning

For model sets \(\Theta,\Phi\), the paper forms a vector \(s_{A,\Theta,\Phi}\) of CKA values on dataset \(A\), using distinct model pairs and excluding a model’s comparison with itself. It defines consistency as \[r_{AB}=\operatorname{corr}(s_{A,\Theta,\Phi},s_{B,\Theta,\Phi}),\] and summarizes these values over distinct dataset pairs. There are \(\binom{23}{2}=253\) unordered pairs per model-set comparison.

The released aggregation uses an upper triangle with offset one for within-group comparisons and unordered combinations for dataset pairs. Anchor aggregation removes the anchor from its peer set. The similarity computation fills a symmetric matrix with unit diagonal; its subsequent exclusion is material and correctly present. No diagonal-inflation defect was established. CKA computation is delegated to `thingsvision==2.6.10`; that dependency was not executed or downloaded.

Pearson correlation measures linear agreement, not equality of absolute scales: \(\operatorname{corr}(s,a+bs)=1\) for \(b>0\). This supports the paper’s distinction between direct transfer and relative consistency. A high coefficient does not guarantee every pairwise ordering, so the ranking language on p. 4 is an aggregate indication, not an exact ranking theorem.

The overall mean 0.756 and standard deviation 0.124, subgroup orderings, and accuracy-gap correlations are reported descriptive results. Their arithmetic was not independently reproduced without underlying matrices. Static inspection verifies aggregation structure, not those historical values.
# Substantive release finding
Problem 1 (A plotted significance threshold ignores the computed probability).  Assessment: Minor; outcome: issue found in the inspected release.
## Claim, location, and suspect step

Figure 15, p. 22, prints \(p<0.001\) for comparisons of consistency values obtained with different metrics. In , code cell 7 (zero-based), the released plotting path computes \[(r,p)=\texttt{stats.pearsonr}(\texttt{r coeff sm1},\texttt{r coeff sm2}),\] but its annotation interpolates only \(r\) and always appends the literal `p-value < 0.001`. It neither uses \(p\) nor checks the threshold. The inspected cell produces two panels; the proceedings figure has four. Its exact historical relationship to that figure is not presumed.
## Complete finite check

Consider 23-by-23 symmetric correlation matrices \(A,B\) with unit diagonals, all off-diagonal entries zero except these three pairs: \[(A_{12},A_{13},A_{23})=(-1/2,0,1/2),\qquad
 (B_{12},B_{13},B_{23})=(1/4,-1/2,1/4).\] Their smallest eigenvalues are respectively \(0.2928932188\ldots\) and \(0.3169872981\ldots\), so both are positive definite correlation matrices. The 253-element upper-triangle vectors have zero means, nonzero norms, and zero dot product. Their Pearson coefficient is exactly zero. The ordinary two-sided Pearson test then has probability one, whereas the annotation would still state \(p<0.001\).

These are reviewer-generated valid coefficient inputs to the plotting logic, not claimed outputs of the paper’s features. No author code was run. Reviewer-written `check.py`/`check.json` confirms eigenvalues, coefficient, and sample count; the contradiction follows algebraically from the literal string.
## Counterevidence, impact, and correction

The actual probabilities might all be below 0.001. Then the displayed threshold would happen to be correct despite the defective path. The release cannot alone establish a false published threshold or changed objective ordering. The supported defect is local reporting, without established dependence of the central descriptive conclusion on it; its severity is Minor.

Rendering the computed \(p\), or conditioning a threshold label on its value, restores correspondence with the numerical result. This local correction does not validate the probability’s statistical model. Historical data, plotting provenance, and a justified analysis of dependence remain necessary to verify published significance.
# Statistical and methodological boundaries
## Overlapping pairs and inferential calibration

Figure 15 pools coefficients across dataset pairs and model-set pairs. Many observations reuse datasets and models. The descriptive coefficient is well-defined, but the ordinary independent-observation null calibration does not follow merely from counting plotted points.

For an explicit diagnostic, let \(Z_i\) be \(K\) independent dataset effects with variance \(\sigma^2\), and set \(T_{ij}=Z_i+Z_j\), \(i<j\). Then \[\overline T=\frac2K\sum_i Z_i,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(\overline T)=\frac{4\sigma^2}{K}.\] Treating all \(\binom K2\) pair values as independent instead gives \(4\sigma^2/[K(K-1)]\). At \(K=23\), the variance ratio is 22. Choosing \(Z_i\) uniform on \([-1/2,1/2]\) keeps pair statistics in \([-1,1]\). This demonstrates the need to address shared endpoints, not Figure 15’s actual distortion or a replacement probability.

The anchor notebook contains rank-sum calculations on pair vectors and Bonferroni correction. Its final plotting call, however, sets `add_significances=False`; the original Figure 18 on p. 24 has no significance labels. Those unused diagnostics are not evidence of an invalid published anchor test. Dataset-level resampling or an explicit probabilistic model could address uncertainty, but no complete correction is certified without actual data and the target sampling population.
## Objective attribution and controls

The model pool is observational: objective, corpus, architecture, size, and extraction layer are correlated. The paper acknowledges these dependencies in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 and extraction-layer alternatives in Section 5. Appendix G fixes one anchor while comparing it to heterogeneous peer groups; it does not independently change objective while holding all other choices fixed at both endpoints. Appendix I changes training domain within a small supervised CNN subset and supplies useful domain-dependence evidence.

The evidence supports associations in the selected pool. It does not identify an objective-specific causal effect or guarantee that changing objective alone yields the reported ordering. That stronger reading of the title remains Needs Evidence, rather than a demonstrated false causal conclusion, particularly given the paper’s qualifications.
## Scale, sampling, and downstream claims

Appendix E applies \(\arccos\) and \(\tan\) and observes a similar mean–standard-deviation shape. Under its stated \([0,1]\) domain, both transformed ranges remain bounded: \([0,\pi/2]\) and \([0,\tan(1)]\). For any empirical distribution on \([a,b]\), \[\operatorname{Var}(X)\le (b-\mathbb EX)(\mathbb EX-a),\] as \(\mathbb E[(X-a)(b-X)]\ge0\). Persistence after these transformations therefore does not isolate a mechanism independent of range constraints. It remains a descriptive robustness check. The release requests unbiased CKA; its finite-sample range and delegated implementation were not fully verified, so no separate range defect is asserted.

Appendix C’s ImageNet sample-size and bootstrap studies support empirical stabilization for that dataset and selected anchors, rather than a uniform accuracy theorem. Appendix B specifies validation-based hyperparameter selection and full-training-set refitting before test evaluation. No test-selection leakage was established in the inspected path. Accuracy-gap pairs also share models and require care for uncertainty, while their plotted correlations remain valid summaries. Raw outputs, seed-level results, and a frozen full dependency environment are unavailable for numerical reproduction.
# Conclusion and state

The highest supported impact is Minor, restricted to the release annotation defect. No failure of the central descriptive objective ordering was established. Objective-specific causality and published nominal significance require additional evidence.

Title: Technical Verification of
Gradient-Free Cutting-Plane Active Learning
# Identity, version, and review scope

The paper is Active Learning of Deep Neural Networks via Gradient-Free Cutting Planes, by Erica Zhang, Fangzhao Zhang, and Mert Pilanci, ICML 2025, PMLR 267; I25-43666, display 0297, OpenReview `vZhdXRnfPU` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed source is the staged 49-page proceedings PDF with embedded Appendices A–H. Page numbers below are PDF pages and agree with printed numbering.

The review checked the two-layer equivalence, the three-layer construction, the definitions and algorithms underlying Sections 5–6, the centroid and inexact-cut convergence arguments, experimental design and reported scalar comparisons, and released core/source application paths. The general-depth indexing and all external approximation results were not independently certified. Exact raw historical query logs and results were unavailable.

The released repository `pilancilab/cpal` was inspected at commit [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Its README identifies it as preliminary. Forty selected source members were checked against archive bytes and Git blob identities. No author program was executed. This version uses analytic centers rather than the center of gravity used in the principal theorem, treats a zero prediction differently from the printed pseudocode, and uses zero-margin classification cuts. Those differences are material counterevidence against equating written-algorithm failures with historical experimental failures.
# Necessary definitions and valid components

With fixed activation patterns \(D_i\) and variables \(\theta=(u'_1,u_1,\ldots,u'_P,u_P)\), the lifted two-layer score is linear: \[f_\theta(X)=\sum_iD_iX(u'_i-u_i).\] The signs of the primed and unprimed variables are interchanged between some earlier and later displays; the examples use the Section 6 convention and are invariant to consistently swapping these roles. Activation constraints require \((2D_i-I)Xu'_i\ge0\) and \((2D_i-I)Xu_i\ge0\).

Theorem 4.1’s splitting of positive and negative output weights, merging inside each activation cone, and reconstruction with at most \(2P\) neurons were checked. The three-layer construction similarly duplicates signed branches under the stated ample-width condition. These are feasibility reformulations; they do not by themselves supply an initial radius, a statistically meaningful label budget, or prediction identification.

For a full-dimensional convex body, an active valid linear cut excluding its centroid retains at most \(1-1/e\) of the volume. Adding activation constraints cannot increase that retained volume. This portion of Theorem 6.3 is sound within its assumptions. It is a per-active-cut statement, not a guarantee for arbitrary queries, arbitrary analytic centers, or convergence to one prescribed real-valued prediction.
# Problems in the central guarantees and algorithms
Problem 1 (Volume decay is incorrectly promoted to prediction identification).  Assessment: Major.

Appendix G.1, p. 30, asserts that nestedness, nonemptiness, and vanishing volume imply \(\bigcap_tT^{(t)}=\{\theta^*\}\). Appendix G.2, pp. 30–31, then uses the purported implication \(\theta^{(k)}\to\theta^*\) to prove Corollary 6.4’s convergence of real-valued scores on every fixed \(X\).

The geometric implication is false even for active homogeneous cuts. Let \(T_k\) be the closed unit-disk sector with angles \(0\le\phi\le\alpha_k\), where \(\alpha_k=(\pi/2)3^{-k}\). Each is a compact convex body with nonempty interior. Cutting at angle \(\alpha_k/3\) retains \(T_{k+1}\), removes the old centroid (whose angle is \(\alpha_k/2\)), and reduces area by exactly \(1/3\). Nevertheless, \[\bigcap_kT_k=[0,1]\times\{0\},\qquad
 \operatorname{CG}(T_k)=
 \left(\frac{2\sin\alpha_k}{3\alpha_k},
       \frac{2(1-\cos\alpha_k)}{3\alpha_k}\right)
 \longrightarrow(2/3,0).\] The retained feasible point \((1/3,0)\) is not the limit, and the linear output equal to the first coordinate differs by \(1/3\) in the limit. This is an exact counterexample to the geometric inference used by the proof; it is not asserted to be a complete network-query trajectory.

The network setting also preserves scale ambiguity: zero-margin classification and activation constraints are homogeneous, so a feasible nonzero ray segment can remain inside the initial ball. Correct classification does not fix score amplitude. The finite-intersection property guarantees a nonempty intersection, not a singleton. Corollary 6.4 is therefore unproved by the supplied argument, directly affecting a central prediction-convergence claim. No failure of the conditional volume inequality itself is alleged.

A precise sufficient additional assumption would be \(\operatorname{diam}(T_k)\to0\) with \(\theta^*\in T_k\). For a fixed lifted matrix \(A_X\), it then gives \(\|A_X\theta^{(k)}-A_X\theta^*\|\le
\|A_X\|\operatorname{diam}(T_k)\to0\). This conditional repair is valid; the proposed algorithm has not been shown to enforce its new premise.
Problem 2 (The inexact-cut bounds fail on admissible ReLU domains).  Assessment: Major.
## Theorem G.2: explicit counterexample for every proposed dimension constant

Theorem G.2, pp. 32–34, claims \[\frac{\operatorname{vol}(T_1)}{\operatorname{vol}(T)}
 <1-e^{-1}(1-\widetilde\lambda)^d,\qquad
 \widetilde\lambda=
 -\frac{R^dH_{T^-}}{\Theta_d\operatorname{vol}(T)H_{T^+}}h,\] where \(h\) is the centroid’s distance to the cut, \(R\) is the radius of a \((d-1)\)-ball with the cross-section’s volume, and \(\Theta_d>0\) depends only on dimension.

Use input dimension one, \(X=[1]\), label \(+1\), and the complete pattern set \(\{1,0\}\). The lifted parameter dimension is four. In orthogonal coordinates set \[q=(u'_1-u_1)/\sqrt2,\qquad s=(u'_1+u_1)/\sqrt2,\] and define the rectangular body \[-\epsilon\le q\le1,\quad 2\le s\le3,\quad
 -2\le u'_0,u_0\le-1,\qquad 0<\epsilon\le0.1.\] It is compact and full-dimensional. Both active-pattern variables are positive because \(s>|q|\), and both inactive variables are negative. Thus every activation constraint is satisfied strictly throughout \(T\). The classification cut is exactly \(q\ge0\) and removes no additional volume through activation constraints.

Its volume is \(1+\epsilon\), its cross-section at \(q=0\) has three-volume one, and \[R=(3/(4\pi))^{1/3},\quad
 h=(1-\epsilon)/2,\quad
 H_{T^-}/H_{T^+}=-\epsilon.\] Writing \(K=R^4/(2\Theta_4)>0\), the printed expression gives \(\widetilde\lambda=K\epsilon(1-\epsilon)/(1+\epsilon)\). For any positive \(\Theta_4\), choose \(\epsilon=\min\{0.1,1/(10K)\}\). Then \[\frac{\operatorname{vol}(T_1)}{\operatorname{vol}(T)}
   =\frac1{1+\epsilon}\ge\frac{10}{11},
 \qquad
 1-e^{-1}(1-\widetilde\lambda)^4
   \le1-e^{-1}(0.9)^4=0.7586343\ldots .\] The claimed upper bound is contradicted. All quantities are well-defined, both half-spaces meet \(T\), and \(0<\widetilde\lambda\le0.1\). Uniformly scaling \(T\) by \(1/5\) places it inside the unit ball, preserves all signs and the retained fraction, and multiplies \(\widetilde\lambda\) by \(1/5\), strengthening the contradiction. This refutes the theorem’s stated universal convex-body bound; the box is not claimed to be a particular recorded historical iterate.
## Corollary G.3: failure from the algorithm’s actual initialization

Corollary G.3, p. 35, claims that uniform, increasingly dense input data and minimum raw margin recover the \((1-1/e)^t\) volume bound for Algorithm 5. Take independent inputs uniform on \((0,1)\) and give every input label \(+1\). Both labels being represented is not assumed. The full activation-pattern set remains \(\{1,0\}\); a strictly correct four-neuron representation exists.

Starting at \(B_2\subset\mathbb R^4\), every positive input induces the identical constraints \[u'_1\ge u_1\ge0,\qquad u'_0\le0,\quad u_0\le0.\] The first cut retains one orthant, with half of its active-coordinate ordering, so \(\operatorname{vol}(T^{(1)})/\operatorname{vol}(T^{(0)})=1/32\). All later distinct queries add redundant copies of the same constraints. Hence the ratio remains \(1/32\) for every \(t\ge1\), independently of dataset size or minimum-margin selection. Already at \(t=8\), \[(1-1/e)^8=0.02549173\ldots < 1/32=0.03125.\] This is a direct counterexample to the claimed asymptotic bound using the specified initialization and valid ReLU cuts.

The proof also confuses raw margin with normalized distance: \(h=|f_\theta(x)|/\|a(x)\|\). Here \(a(x)=x(1,-1,0,0)\). Small positive \(x\) makes the raw margin small but leaves the hyperplane and its distance unchanged. Dense inputs do not guarantee informative cuts. Theorem 6.3 survives because these later cuts are not active. No complete corrected inexact-cut theorem is certified.
Problem 3 (The fixed unit margin is incompatible with a universal unit-ball radius).  Assessment: Major.

Section 5, p. 5, claims the unit ball contains optimal parameters by scale invariance, while Algorithm 1’s cut enforces margin at least one, as in Equation (3). Scaling preserves the sign, but not that fixed margin.

The incompatibility persists with explicit bias augmentation and both classes. Let \(x_+=(0.1,1)\), \(x_-=(-0.1,1)\) and labels \(+1,-1\). These independent rows realize all four first-layer patterns, so \(P=4\) and the stated ample-width condition is met by \(m=8\). The original network \[f(z)=10(z_1)_+-10(-z_1)_+\] (padded with zero neurons) has both margins exactly one.

For any lifted parameter with \(\|\theta\|_2\le1\), the reconstructed ReLU function is Lipschitz with constant at most \[\sum_{i=1}^{P}(\|u_i\|_2+\|u'_i\|_2)
 \le\sqrt{2P}\|\theta\|_2\le\sqrt8.\] The two outputs can therefore differ by at most \(0.2\sqrt8=0.565685\ldots\), whereas the two unit margins require a difference of at least two. Thus the radius excludes every solution of a feasible original instance.

This invalidates the initialization argument for the central fixed-margin training scheme. A data-dependent adequate radius, or an explicitly changed margin/domain, is required. The zero-margin cuts in Algorithms 2/4 and in the release avoid this particular contradiction; that distinction is not a repair of Algorithm 1 as printed.
Problem 4 (The printed strict-mistake rule stalls at the initial center).  Assessment: Major; written algorithm, with different released behavior.

Algorithms 1, 2, and 4 (pp. 4, 6, 16) start from the unit ball and cut only if \(y f_{\theta_c}(x)<0\). Its centroid and symmetric barrier center are zero, and \(f_0(x)=0\) for every input. Therefore no label, including either binary class, can trigger the strict inequality. The localization set and center remain unchanged by induction. In Algorithms 2/4, \(D_{\rm AL}\) stays empty, so a positive budget is never reached. Algorithm 1’s cut counter also stays zero.

This is a complete execution argument for the printed rule, not a rounding issue or an assumption about data separability. It prevents the proposed starting procedure from producing its first cut. The conditional theorem assuming active cuts does not make a zero score negative.

Counterevidence is decisive: the release uses \(\texttt{np.sign(pred)}\ne y\), which treats zero as a mistake for labels \(\pm1\), and therefore can leave zero. Treating zero margins as eligible cuts restores this initial step; a cut through the centroid has a non-strict \(1-1/e\) bound. Neither full termination nor all other guarantees follows from this local change. Historical runs are not alleged to have stalled.
Problem 5 (Accepted cuts are counted instead of acquired labels).  Assessment: Major for the stated query-budget interpretation.

Algorithms 2/4 query a label before testing correctness, but add the point to \(D_{\rm AL}\) only if the cut is accepted. Their stopping condition counts \(|D_{\rm AL}|\). Algorithm 9’s baselines instead add every newly queried label. This matters directly to Section 7’s comparisons at a fixed number of queries.

The same accounting appears in : the routine reads both `y[i_mini]` and `y[i_maxi]`, records tried indices, but increments `data_used` only on mistakes. The sentiment application likewise plots and budgets `len(data_used)`. Correctly classified queried labels have already been acquired, although they do not change the feasible set.

A complete local trace uses inputs \(1,2,3,4,5\), all labels \(+1\), both scalar patterns, and requested budget three. At the exact zero center, minimum and maximum scores tie at index zero. Both stale-center tests append that same index, giving `data_used` length two but one distinct label. After these positive cuts, any strict barrier center has positive score on every remaining positive input. The next candidate pairs are indices \((1,4)\) and \((2,3)\); all four labels are inspected and all predictions are correct. Five distinct labels have now been acquired while the counter remains two, below the requested budget three. No numerical solver value is needed beyond the strictly positive cut slack.

The list also allows duplicate initial entries, so it is neither a distinct-label counter nor a reliable oracle-call counter. Fixing only the duplicate does not fix the uncharged correct labels. This demonstrates a core mismatch between the advertised label budget and the proposed accounting. It does not determine the actual number of labels behind the published curves or prove their ranking would reverse. A separate ledger of all queried distinct indices, with each label charged when requested, restores budget semantics; historical comparisons require those logs or fresh experiments. There is no certified numerical correction to the reported curves.
# Additional released-code findings
Problem 6 (Three-layer prediction reuses the inner-loop index).  Assessment: Major for the frozen release’s core implementation; historical impact unresolved.

In , `predict` iterates over outer index \(l\) and inner index \(j\), then multiplies both outer sums by `Di[i,j]` instead of `Di[i,l]`. The three-layer query and mistake tests call this routine, while the cut uses the intended outer pattern.

Take \(d=P_1=1\), \(P_2=2\), \(x=1\), \(Q=[1]\), and the generator-compatible sorted outer row \(D=[0,1]\). In the routine’s four parameter blocks choose \[c_1=(.1,.3),\ c_2=(.4,.1),\
 c_3=(.1,.2),\ c_4=(.2,.1).\] Their squared norm is \(.37<1\). All inner weights are positive; the outer preactivations are \((-.3,.2)\) and \((-.1,.1)\), strictly matching \(D\). The intended score is \(.2-.1=.1\). The released expression instead uses \(D_0=0\) for both outer terms and returns zero. This is an admissible sampled-pattern instance, not a violation of an activation constraint. Changing the selected index to \(l\) restores this displayed score and the corresponding general sum. The mathematical reformulation itself is not refuted; historical three-layer figures are not bound to this preliminary implementation.

This is Major for the frozen implementation’s core three-layer algorithm. In , line 55 uses this predictor to rank query candidates, and lines 78–83 use it to decide whether to cut and count a sample. The cut in lines 40–43 uses the intended outer pattern, so these central decisions use a different score from the constraint. The preliminary label and missing historical run binding limit attribution to the paper’s figures; they do not remove this demonstrated core implementation failure. A historical benchmark loss is not required to establish the defect in the inspected algorithm.
Problem 7 (Sentiment evaluation decodes the lifted vector in the wrong order).  Assessment: Major for the frozen release’s application evaluation; historical impact unresolved.

The sentiment application’s query and cut use interleaved pattern-major blocks through a Kronecker product. Its evaluation instead applies default row-major \(\texttt{c.reshape((2*d,m))}\). The required matrix layout has these blocks as columns.

For \(d=m=2\), take data rows \((-1,0)\) and \((1,0)\) with sorted pattern columns \[D=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 c=(.3,0,.1,0,-.1,.8,-.2,0).\] Its squared norm is \(.79<1\). The intended positive and negative weight matrices are \[U_+=\begin{pmatrix}.3&-.1\\0&.8\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 U_-=\begin{pmatrix}.1&-.2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] All signed preactivations on both data rows are strictly positive. At \((1,0)\), the correctly decoded ReLU score is \(.3-.1=.2\). The default reshape yields positive-block rows \((.3,0),(.1,0)\) and negative-block rows \((-.1,.8),(-.2,0)\), producing \(.3-.8=-.5\). Thus evaluation reverses the sign of a valid parameter vector. Column-major decoding restores the specified block correspondence.

The release also crops embeddings to 200 dimensions, whereas the paper reports 2560, and uses a different fixed data seed. These differences further prevent attributing Figure 4’s historical values to this exact code. The demonstrated evaluation defect remains; its historical score effect requires provenance and reruns.

This is Major for the frozen sentiment application’s evaluation path. Lines 168–172 compute and display train/test predictions with the incorrect layout, and lines 175–181 append that accuracy to the returned `score` sequence. The reversed classifier sign therefore reaches the application’s actual evaluation output. Query and cut calculations continue to use the separate Kronecker layout; they are not claimed to share this reshape defect. Historical uncertainty does not repair the demonstrated failure of this core evaluation path.
# Overall dependence, surviving results, and empirical limits

Problems 1–2 directly affect the advertised convergence theory. Problems 3–4 affect the specified training/active-learning algorithms, and Problem 5 affects the label-efficiency interpretation. They support Major without requiring a collapse of the convex reformulation or observed prediction scores. Problems 6–7 are also Major for the frozen release’s core three-layer decisions and sentiment evaluation, respectively. Their effect on historical paper figures remains unresolved because the exact release is not bound to those runs.

The reported quadratic-regression reductions in Table 5 are arithmetically consistent: \(1-.0111/.0568=80.4577\%\) for training and \(1-.0100/.0408=75.4902\%\) for test RMSE. These checks do not validate equal label costs. The spiral and regression studies use 100 points with an 80/20 split and five seeds for error bars. The IMDB experiment uses 50 training and 20 test examples, explicitly disclosed in Appendix H.1. It demonstrates a small selected experiment, not full-dataset validation.

The paper discloses sampled activation patterns, analytic-center optimization, and choosing whether to use a final regularized solve. Those choices must remain distinct from exact all-pattern and centroid theory. Baseline tuning, complete seed-level outputs, actual oracle histories, and the relationship between the preliminary code and the frozen figures remain unverified. No empirical rerun or external theorem reproduction was performed. No later correction was established from the available sources.

Title: Technical Verification of
Avoiding Spurious Sharpness Minimization
# Identity, version, and inspected material

The paper is Avoiding spurious sharpness minimization broadens applicability of SAM, by Sidak Pal Singh, Hossein Mobahi, Atish Agarwala, and Yann Dauphin, ICML 2025, PMLR 267; I25-43667, display 0298, OpenReview `vYMuAcbdIE` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed source is the staged 18-page proceedings PDF, including Appendices A–D. PDF and printed page numbers agree.

The review examined the Hessian decomposition, first-order updates, normalized diagnostics, preconditioning argument, reported experimental design and tables, and Appendix C’s JAX illustration. No standalone official repository was available in the completed source preparation; the embedded listing was available. Its helper, loss/auxiliary construction, complete preconditioned implementation, configurations, and raw runs were not supplied. External OpenReview attachment discovery was blocked.
# Definitions and checked central derivation

Write \(g=\nabla_\theta L\), \(u=g/\|g\|\), and let \(J=\partial F/\partial\theta\) have outputs as rows. For a smooth loss composed with \(F\), \[H_L=H_G+H_F,\qquad
 H_G=J^\top H_\ell J,\qquad
 H_F=\sum_a(\partial_{F_a}L)\nabla_\theta^2F_a,\] including the paper’s sample averaging. At nonzero \(g\) and under the smoothness needed for Taylor expansion, \[\nabla L(\theta+\rho u)
 =g+\rho(H_G+H_F)u+O(\rho^2).\] Holding the output-loss cotangent \(v=\nabla_F L(\theta)\) fixed while perturbing only the Jacobian gives \[J(\theta+\rho u)^\top v
 =g+\rho H_Fu+O(\rho^2),\] which verifies the first-order interpretation of Equation (11). These are positive gradient conventions; an optimizer applies descent.

A direct smooth binary cross-entropy check with logits \((\theta^2,0)\), first-class target, and \(\theta=1\) gives \(g=-0.53788284\), \(H_G=0.78644773\), and \(H_F=-0.53788284\). For this example the displayed Functional-SAM expansion is exact because the Jacobian is affine in \(\theta\). This confirms the intended isolation of the functional term locally, without claiming that it always decreases total sharpness or improves generalization.

Equations (4) and (7) omit a common \(\rho\) relative to \(\mathrm{SP}=\rho\|g\|\); the correct derivative is \(\nabla\mathrm{SP}=\rho H_Lu\). This is treated as a scaling clarification: it cancels from Equation (9)’s normalized composition if used consistently and does not invalidate the explicit-\(\rho\) update above. Also, the squared-norm terms in Equation (9) sum to one only together with the cross term; individual terms need not be probabilities or fractions bounded by one.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The preconditioning ratio uses inconsistent trace normalization).  Assessment: Major; a core motivating derivation is invalid.
## Original claim and dependency

Section 4.2, p. 5, cites Appendix B.1 to argue that inverse-GGN preconditioning amplifies the functional path relative to the logit path, motivating preconditioned SAM and its combination with Functional-SAM. Appendix B.1, p. 16, assumes symmetric invertible, freely independent matrices \(A,B\) and a random unit vector \(v\). It defines \(w=A^{-1}v\) and compares \[r_1=\frac{\mathbb E\|Bv\|^2}{\mathbb E\|Av\|^2},
 \qquad
 r_2=\frac{\mathbb E\|Bw\|^2}{\mathbb E\|Aw\|^2}.\] Equation (14)’s factor \(1/N\) uses ordinary trace. But Equation (13) factors ordinary traces without \(1/N\), Equation (16) sets \(\mathbb E\|Aw\|^2=1/N\), and Equation (17) gives an incompatible product of trace moments, followed by a strict \(r_2>r_1\) conclusion.
## All-assumptions certificate

Take \(N=2\), \(A=B=I_2\), and \(v\) uniformly distributed on the unit circle. These matrices are symmetric and invertible, are valid degenerate random matrices, and their scalar algebras satisfy freeness: every centered scalar polynomial is zero. The same construction works as a sequence for every \(N\), so it is not a finite-size approximation issue.

Here \(w=v\) exactly and \[\mathbb E\|Av\|^2=\mathbb E\|Bv\|^2
 =\mathbb E\|Aw\|^2=\mathbb E\|Bw\|^2=1.\] Thus \(r_1=r_2=1\). Equation (13), at powers one, instead gives \(2=4\); Equation (16) gives \(1=1/2\); and Equation (17)’s middle trace equals two while its final factorized expression equals four. Most directly, \(Aw=v\) proves that the printed \(1/N\) norm is wrong for every invertible \(A\) and unit \(v\).

This is not only an equality-edge case for the numerical ratio. With \(A=Q\operatorname{diag}(1,2)Q^\top\), \(Q\) an independent uniform random rotation, and \(B=I_2\), scalar \(B\) is still free from \(A\). For independent uniform \(v\), \[r_1=\frac1{(1+4)/2}=\frac25,\qquad
 r_2=\frac{1+1/4}{2}=\frac58.\] The middle and final expressions printed in Equation (17) give \(5/4\) and \(5/2\), respectively, instead of \(5/8\). The calculations are recorded in `check.json` and follow exactly from isotropy.
## Verified corrected statement

Assume \(v\) is independent and isotropic on the unit sphere, the necessary moments are finite, and the stated free mixed-moment factorization holds with normalized trace \(\tau(C)=\operatorname{tr}(C)/N\). Set \[\alpha=\mathbb E\tau(A^2),\quad
 \beta=\mathbb E\tau(B^2),\quad
 \gamma=\mathbb E\tau(A^{-2}).\] Then \[\mathbb E\|Aw\|^2=1,\qquad
 r_1=\frac{\beta}{\alpha},\qquad
 r_2=\beta\gamma,\qquad
 \frac{r_2}{r_1}=\alpha\gamma\ge1.\] Indeed, cyclicity and normalized factorization give \(\mathbb E\tau(A^{-1}B^2A^{-1})=\beta\gamma\). Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the absolute eigenvalue and its reciprocal, with an eigenvalue drawn uniformly and averaged over matrix randomness, gives \(\alpha\gamma\ge1\). Equality is possible, including \(A=aI\); strict inequality needs nonconstant squared spectral scale.

With ordinary trace, the corrected ratio is \[r_2=\frac{\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(B^2)\,
                \mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(A^{-2})}{N^2}.\] Interpreting every printed trace as normalized does not reconcile all equations, because Equation (14) and the unit-vector norm in Equation (16) then remain wrong.
## Impact and counterevidence

The wrong quantitative derivation is directly invoked for a core proposed method, supporting Major under the assigned calibration. The correction preserves nondecrease in the idealized model; it does not establish failure of preconditioning in Transformers. The paper explicitly acknowledges that actual gradients and Hessian components do not satisfy its toy calculation exactly. Adam’s diagonal second-moment preconditioner, normalized perturbations, and coupled training dynamics require additional justification or measurements. This report neither transfers the corrected theorem to those settings automatically nor claims that the empirical improvements disappear.
Problem 2 (The illustrative implementation reverses gradient and auxiliary outputs).  Assessment: Minor; implementation illustration only.

Listing 1, p. 17, calls `grad(loss_fn,hax_aux=True)` and binds the result as \[\texttt{dL\_dlogits,\ dL\_dtheta = grad(...)(params)}.\] The consulted official JAX API uses `has_aux` and returns the parameter gradient before auxiliary data [Retained latex: \cite{jax}]. Thus correcting the keyword alone still reverses the two spaces: the logit cotangent is used to perturb parameters, and the parameter gradient is supplied to the output VJP.

A finite calculation shows that this is substantive even when shapes happen to agree. Take scalar \(F(\theta)=\theta^2\), loss \(\ell(z)=z^2/2\), and \(\theta=2\), with the auxiliary value defined as \(\partial\ell/\partial z\). The correct pair is \((16,4)\). Both entries normalize to positive one, so the perturbed parameter is \(2+\rho\) even after the mistaken swap. The intended VJP is \[4\cdot2(2+\rho)=16+8\rho,\] whereas the swapped cotangent yields \(16\cdot2(2+\rho)=64+32\rho\). At \(\rho=0.1\) these are 16.8 and 67.2. This uses a smooth generic loss accepted by the illustration and tests the return-order issue without author-code execution. With unequal logit and parameter structures the mismatch can instead prevent evaluation.

The local correction is \[\texttt{dL\_dtheta,\ dL\_dlogits =
 grad(loss\_fn,has\_aux=True)(params)},\] provided the auxiliary value is explicitly the unperturbed logit-loss cotangent. The remaining VJP then matches Equation (11). This API/formula correspondence is verified statically; a complete runnable implementation is not certified. JAX was absent from both checked runtimes, and the helper and loss wrapper were missing. The illustration is not proven to be the code that produced historical runs, and the mathematical update itself survives.
Problem 3 (Angle-SAM requires a radius rescaling to recover SAM).  Assessment: Minor; optional extension.

Appendix D, p. 18, states that \(\phi=\pi/4\) recovers SAM to first order in \(\rho\). Equation (20) instead gives \[G_{\rm angle}=g+\frac{\rho}{\sqrt2}(H_G+H_F)u+O(\rho^2),\] whereas standard SAM has coefficient \(\rho\). Their difference is generally order \(\rho\), not order \(\rho^2\).

For an admissible binary cross-entropy example with logits \((\theta,0)\), first-class target, and \(\theta=0\), one has \(g=-1/2\), \(u=-1\), \(H_G=1/4\), \(H_F=0\). Writing \(\sigma\) for the logistic function, \[G_{\rm SAM}=-\sigma(\rho),\qquad
 G_{\rm angle}=-\frac12+
       \frac{-\sigma(\rho)+1/2}{\sqrt2}.\] At \(\rho=0.1\) these equal \(-0.5249791875\) and \(-0.5176629529\). Moreover, \[\lim_{\rho\to0}\frac{G_{\rm angle}-G_{\rm SAM}}{\rho}
 =\frac{1-1/\sqrt2}{4}\ne0.\] The corrected statement is that Angle-SAM at radius \(\rho\) matches SAM at radius \(\rho/\sqrt2\) to first order; equivalently use Angle-SAM radius \(\sqrt2\rho\) to match SAM radius \(\rho\). This does not assert exact finite-radius equality. The \(\phi=0\) Functional-SAM endpoint is unaffected. The paper presents this interpolation as future work rather than the method used in its main experiments, so the supported impact is local.
# Empirical scope and unresolved interpretation

The first-order decomposition does not alone identify the cause of a cross-domain performance difference. The paper measures Hessian-vector composition during AdamW training and uses its imbalance as a hypothesis motivating interventions. Those interventions and the reported loss improvements are useful evidence, but normalized composition does not establish an optimizer-independent causal mechanism. The paper itself allows that Functional-SAM may be inappropriate in other settings.

Tables 2–3 report improvements of preconditioned Functional-SAM over AdamW across the listed scales. The five-seed standard deviations and the single-seed exception for the largest Chinchilla-style run are disclosed. The 10,000-step token count is consistent with \(256\cdot512\cdot10{,}000=1{,}310{,}720{,}000\) tokens. The principal comparisons use equal steps; Section 8 explicitly acknowledges roughly twice AdamW’s gradient computation. This is not an undisclosed equal-compute claim.

Table 4 also shows that ordinary SAM can have the smallest maximum Hessian eigenvalue while worse validation loss, so lower scalar sharpness alone is not sufficient to rank generalization. No direct measured loss or Hessian value was reproduced here. Smaller untested SAM radii, the exact norm/second-moment convention, warm-up handling, and seed-paired uncertainty remain outside the available record.

A concrete reproducibility ambiguity remains: Section 5.3 says the common learning rate for Tables 6–7 is \(10^{-4}\), whereas both appendix captions state \(10^{-3}\). Without configurations, neither value can be selected as the true historical one. The preconditioned variant used in the principal tables is not fully implemented in the embedded listing. These are Needs Evidence items and do not independently establish a false experimental ranking. No later correction was established from the available frozen sources.
# Conclusion and state

The overall assessment is Major, confined to the invalid core preconditioning derivation, with its corrected toy-model result explicitly preserved. The two Minor findings affect an implementation illustration and an optional interpolation claim. Functional-SAM’s checked first-order decomposition remains intact; empirical performance and broader causal explanations are not certified by this review.

report: Abstract: The assessment is Major. The printed curvature estimator has the wrong orientation and scaling behavior; the central hyperbolic transport formula fails to preserve the metric; and the written isometry proof drops necessary second derivatives. Exact, assumption-valid checks and precise local repairs are given. A separate Major defect in released masked transport breaks the linear parameter-sharing operation. A further Major defect affects the released core \(H^1\) evaluation path. These results establish defects in specified mathematics and current source, without identifying which implementation generated the reported experiments. The source’s use of external geometry preprocessing and several valid underlying geometric principles are retained as counterevidence.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: Initial review, 25 October 2026

Title: Technical Verification of
Curvature-aware Graph Attention for PDEs on Manifolds
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The paper is Curvature-aware Graph Attention for PDEs on Manifolds, by Yunfeng Liao, Jiawen Guan, and Xiucheng Li, ICML 2025, PMLR 267; I25-43668, display 0299, OpenReview vWYLQ0VPJx [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The staged proceedings PDF has 19 pages. PDF and printed page numbers agree; Appendix A begins on p. 12, despite the source manifest’s supplementary heading range beginning at p. 13. The entire main argument and Appendices A–D were read. Original pages 3, 5, 6, and 13–15 were additionally rendered and inspected.

The released source is `Supradax/CurvGT`, commit . Five selected source members and their archive/member mappings are preserved. This is the current public commit at acquisition, not a demonstrated conference-time commit. Static inspection included the complete main implementation and README; auxiliary review covered the remaining selected files. Dataset, weight, and serialized geometry files were excluded during source preparation. No author code was run. External OpenReview attachment discovery was blocked; absence of an additional supplement is not inferred.
# Definitions and dependence

The proposed layer transports a neighbor’s tangent feature \(h_v\) to \(T_uM\), applies learned tensors, and aggregates. A rank-one map \(w_1\otimes w_2^*\) acts by \(h\mapsto w_1\langle w_2,h\rangle_{g_u}\); this algebra is valid if the parameters and arguments belong to the specified tangent spaces. Parallel transport for the Levi–Civita connection preserves \(g\) and is linear in its initial vector. The paper uses these facts both for attention, Equations (7)–(10), and subtree parameter sharing, Equations (17)–(19).

Its fast procedure selects a sphere, plane, or hyperbolic model from the estimated Gaussian curvature, Equation (12), and applies closed forms in Section 4.3. Consequently the estimator and transport formulas are central dependencies. The use of constant-curvature local approximations is disclosed; it does not excuse a formula that fails on the constant-curvature model itself. No error bound for transfer from these models to an arbitrary mesh was established in the inspected record.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The stated Gaussian-curvature estimator has incorrect geometric invariances).  Assessment: Major; the quantity used to select the core geometric branch is not a valid intrinsic Gaussian-curvature expression as written.

Equation (1), p. 3, defines \[\widehat K_i=\frac12\sum_{j\in N(i)}
\frac{v_j-v_i}{\|v_i-v_j\|_2}\,\varphi_{ij}\cdot n_i.\] Visual inspection confirms that the denominator is the Euclidean norm, with subscript \(2\), not its square. Figure 2 defines \(\varphi\) as the arccosine of the dot product of adjacent unit face normals. Thus \(\varphi\) is unchanged by reversing all normals.

Complete finite check. Use the regular octahedron inscribed in the unit sphere. At \(v_i=(0,0,1)\) the four neighbors are \((\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0)\), and the consistent outward vertex normal is \(n_i=(0,0,1)\). Adjacent outward face normals have dot product \(1/3\), so every edge has \(\varphi=\arccos(1/3)>0\). Every unit edge from \(v_i\) has normal component \(-1/\sqrt2\). Therefore \[\widehat K_i=-\sqrt2\arccos(1/3)\simeq-1.74083950.\] The intrinsic angle defect at that convex vertex is \(2\pi-4(\pi/3)=2\pi/3>0\), and the underlying unit sphere has positive Gaussian curvature. Reversing the orientation makes the printed estimate positive, even though intrinsic Gaussian curvature is orientation independent.

Uniformly scaling all coordinates by \(s>0\) leaves every unit edge, normal, and dihedral angle unchanged. Hence \(\widehat K_i\) stays fixed, whereas the underlying sphere has \(K=s^{-2}\), and an angle-defect estimator divided by area also scales as \(s^{-2}\). This is an exact invariance failure, rather than an assertion that a coarse-mesh estimator must equal smooth curvature exactly. With the paper’s \(\epsilon=10^{-3}\), the outward-oriented example is assigned the negative-curvature branch of Equation (12).

Counterevidence and consequence. The current README explicitly says Gaussian estimates and principal directions come from `libigl`; `CURVGT.py` loads precomputed curvature and branch masks. Their generating source is absent. It is therefore not established that the experiments used Equation (1). The Major finding is the invalid printed geometric quantity directly feeding the central construction. An angle-defect-over-area expression is a possible discrete replacement, but its exact area convention, convergence assumptions, and correspondence to the historical preprocessing were not verified. No complete pipeline repair is claimed.
Problem 2 (The fast hyperbolic transport formula does not preserve the metric).  Assessment: Major; a central closed-form transport theorem is false on its own model space.

Assumption-valid certificate. Take the upper-half-plane metric \(g=(dx^2+dy^2)/y^2\) and the semicircle of radius one centered at \((1,0)\). Set \[v=1+i,\qquad u=\frac85+\frac45i,\qquad h_v=(1,0).\] Both points lie strictly in the upper half-plane on this geodesic; all tangent coordinate vectors are admissible. The left endpoint is zero, so the paper’s translation parameter is \(a=0\). Inversion sends \[\widetilde v=-\frac12+\frac12i,\qquad
\widetilde u=-\frac12+\frac14i,\] which are on the same vertical line. Thus the vertical scaling ratio in Equation (16) is \(1/2\). Substitution gives \[P_{\rm paper}h_v=\frac12J_{\rm paper}(\widetilde u)
J_{\rm paper}(v)h_v=(2/5,-3/10).\] Its target metric norm squared is \[\frac{(2/5)^2+(3/10)^2}{(4/5)^2}=\frac{25}{64},\] although \(\|h_v\|_{g_v}^2=1\). This contradicts the isometry property used by Equation (17). It is not a mesh-approximation error.

Verified local repair. Replacing each \(J_{\rm paper}\) with \(D\phi\) gives \[Ph_v=(16/25,-12/25),\qquad \|Ph_v\|_{g_u}^2=1.\] The full corrected formula \(P=(\widetilde y_u/\widetilde y_v)
D\phi(\widetilde u)D\phi(v+a)\) follows from the true isometry commutation property and vertical transport, with the inverse translation’s identity derivative. It is valid in the stated Euclidean coordinate frames. Calling \(J_{\rm paper}\) an orthonormal-frame rotation does not repair the printed calculation: the explicit vertical coordinate scaling must then also change.

Lemma 4.3 also wrongly identifies arbitrary complex Möbius transformations with hyperbolic isometries and states that \(1/z\) is a self-isometry of the upper half-plane. But \(1/i=-i\) is outside that domain. The usual real-coefficient fractional maps with positive determinant preserve it; \(-1/z\) and real translations used in the corrected construction are valid. Thus the intended strategy survives, while the printed group statement and matrix calculation do not.

Spherical scope check. Theorem 4.1, pp. 5–6, sets \(e_1=u\), \(e_2=(u\times v)/\|u\times v\|\), \(e_3=e_1\times e_2\). For \(0<\theta<\pi\), \(v=\cos\theta\,e_1-\sin\theta\,e_3\), not the plus-sign endpoint printed for its path. Moreover, \(h_v=a e_3+b e_2\in T_vS^2\) forces \(a=0\). Its advertised source representation therefore does not cover a generic tangent vector. We do not present an \(a\ne0\) vector violating that hypothesis as a theorem counterexample. A correct generic, non-antipodal formula is \[P_{v\to u}h=h-\frac{\langle h,u\rangle}{1+\langle u,v\rangle}(u+v),
\quad h\perp v.\] For \(u=(1,0,0)\), \(v=(1/2,\sqrt3/2,0)\), and \(h=(-\sqrt3/2,1/2,0)\) it returns \((0,1,0)\). Decomposing \(h\) into the geodesic tangent and fixed perpendicular direction proves the formula. These coordinate and endpoint issues need correction, but the decisive false theorem in this Problem is the all-assumptions hyperbolic certificate.

The released geometry matrices and spherical frames are precomputed and unavailable for inspection; the README describes a more explicit exponential-map embedding. Neither the wrong printed matrix nor the spherical convention is attributed to historical runs without that evidence.

Problem 3 (The isometry proof drops the Hessian of the coordinate map).  Assessment: Major for an invalid derivation directly supporting the central transport construction; the lemma’s conclusion remains true.

Lemma 4.4 is the commutation principle used in Theorem 4.5. In its proof, Appendix A.4, steps (50)–(51) and (56)–(57) discard derivatives of coordinate Jacobians, leading to Equation (54): \[\Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k\phi^m
=\partial_i\phi^l\,\partial_j\phi^k\,\widetilde\Gamma^m_{lk}.\] This transforms connection coefficients as if they were a tensor.

Take \(M=\mathbb R^2\) with \(dx^2+dy^2\) and \(N=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\) with \(dX^2/X^2+dY^2\). The global diffeomorphism \(\phi(x,y)=(e^x,y)\) is an exact isometry, because its pullback metric is \(dx^2+dy^2\). At \((x,y)=(0,0)\), its Jacobian is the identity, source Christoffel symbols vanish, and \(\widetilde\Gamma^X_{XX}=-1\). Equation (54), with \(i=j=x,m=X\), says \(0=-1\).

The correct identity includes the missing term: \[\Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k\phi^m
=\partial_i\partial_j\phi^m+
\partial_i\phi^l\,\partial_j\phi^k\,\widetilde\Gamma^m_{lk}.\] Here the omitted Hessian is \(1\), giving \(0=1-1\). The correct connection transformation already appears in the paper’s Equation (40); its later elimination is invalid.

Repair and counterevidence. Lemma 4.4 itself is valid. Pulling back the target Levi–Civita connection by an isometry yields a torsion-free, metric-compatible connection. Uniqueness makes it the source Levi–Civita connection. Thus \(\phi_*(\nabla_XY)=\widetilde\nabla_{\phi_*X}\phi_*Y\); a parallel field maps to a parallel field with the pushed-forward initial value. Uniqueness of the parallel-field ODE proves the desired commutation identity. This restores exactly the lemma, but it does not fix Problem 2’s incorrect differentiation. Major is supported by the invalid written core derivation, without claiming a counterexample to the valid geometric principle.
Problem 4 (Released masked transport applies remainder to feature values).  Assessment: Major within the released core parameter-sharing implementation; historical benchmark impact is unbound.

In the pinned `CURVGT.py`, line 292 contains \[\texttt{x\_j*(cur\_tree\_mask+1)\%2 + pt\_ed2*cur\_tree\_mask}.\] The comment says a masked edge should use the identity. The negative-curvature branch selects this expression at lines 295–297, and repeated tensor broadcasts call it at lines 313–315, 326–334, and 389–391. Ordinary operator precedence applies the remainder to the scaled feature, not to the mask.

For a binary mask \(m\) and intended linear transport \(T\), the actual scalar-coordinate operation is \[R_m(x)=\bigl((m+1)x\bmod 2\bigr)+mT(x).\] At \(m=0\), \(R_0(-1/2)=3/2\) instead of \(-1/2\); it is neither the identity nor an odd linear map. At \(m=1\), even a positive \(x=1/4\) adds an unintended \(1/2\) to \(T(x)\). With \(T\) equal to the identity this gives \(3/4\) instead of \(1/4\). The latter example is not needed to assume that every actual edge has identity transport: the erroneous additive term occurs for any \(T\).

The precise binary-mask correction is \((1-m)x+mT(x)\), or applying remainder to the integer mask before multiplying \(x\). Its two cases are verified algebraically. This repairs only the mask selection, conditional on correct frames and \(T\); it is not a certified repair of the entire source. The defect directly breaks the claimed linear, inner-product-preserving parameter transport used throughout the core subtree mechanism. Actual activation frequency, stored tensors, and effects on published scores remain unknown, since those artifacts were not inspected and this commit is not bound to the experimental version.
Problem 5 (Released gradient evaluation includes padding as a real face).  Assessment: Major for the frozen release’s core \(H^1\) evaluation; historical table values remain unverified.

The source builds a padded vertex-to-face incidence array using \(-1\) at lines 95–99. Both `H1Criterion` definitions, lines 674–691 and 829–846, index the face field with this array and average all slots without masking the padding. In this indexing convention \(-1\) means the last face.

For a vertex with incidence row \([0,-1]\), let the valid face gradient be \((1,0,0)\) and the unrelated final face gradient be \((3,0,0)\). Such different gradients are realizable by piecewise affine scalar fields on separate mesh triangles. The computed average is \((2,0,0)\) instead of \((1,0,0)\); with unit mass the gradient contribution is \(4\) instead of \(1\). Altering a nonincident face changes this vertex’s loss. The batch offset also uses the number of vertices rather than the number of face rows, although \(G\) produces face gradients; their equality is not guaranteed on the meshes in Table 4.

A correct padded average sums only valid incident faces and divides by their count, and each batch must offset by the actual face count. These statements are verified as indexing/aggregation identities; complete execution on the excluded meshes was not performed. Counterevidence is important: the feature-construction path does mask its face averages, and the training loss is the separate \(L^2\) routine. The demonstrated evaluation defect does not, by itself, identify errors in the paper’s historical \(H^1\) values.

The dependency is a core evaluation path. Equations (22)–(23) and Table 1 report \(H^1\) alongside \(L^2\) for all three PDE benchmarks. In the frozen source, lines 744–750 aggregate this faulty \(H^1\) loss; lines 801–809 use it during training evaluation and after loading the selected model. The second evaluation path calls the same defective aggregation at line 870 and prints and returns it at lines 877–885. Thus the admissible aggregation counterexample changes an actual primary evaluation output, not merely an unused helper. This supports Major for the frozen implementation. The separate \(L^2\) training objective remains unaffected, and the absent historical run binding limits attribution to published scores rather than the severity of this demonstrated evaluation failure.
# Other checked claims and unresolved evidence

The planar identity transport and the vertical hyperbolic scaling \(h\mapsto(y_u/y_v)h\) agree with the metric and connection. The rank-one tensor formulas are valid under their tangent-space assumptions. A generic ambient componentwise activation need not preserve a tangent plane: at normal \((1,1,0)/\sqrt2\), ReLU maps the tangent vector \((1,-1,0)\) outside it. Accordingly Remark 1 needs a tangent-preserving activation or a local-coordinate implementation. The released update instead includes projections and scalar feature conversion, so a historical ambient-activation failure is not established.

Several correspondence questions remain Needs Evidence. The release uses an affine combination of the two inner-product scalars (lines 345–346), rather than the bilinear product of Equations (9)–(10); no fixed affine form can equal \(st\) on all four pairs \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\). It normalizes attention over source indices at line 348, while the written formula normalizes the neighbors of each receiving vertex. On edges \(a\to b,a\to c,b\to c\) with zero logits, these rules give weights \((1/2,1/2,1)\) and \((1,1/2,1/2)\), respectively. Their incoming sum at \(c\) is \(3/2\) versus \(1\). These are concrete semantic differences, but the historical method-to-code binding is absent.

Appendix C specifies a validation split and validation-selected checkpoint. The release has train/test loaders and selects minimum training loss (lines 797–800), not test loss. No test-label selection is demonstrated. Its evaluator returns raw mass-weighted squared errors without the persistence-baseline denominator described on p. 8. Table 2 labels the GNOT baseline \(L^2=4.39\pm1.92\), matching Table 1’s rounded \(H^1\) entry rather than its \(L^2=2.466\pm1.453\). A metric/configuration clarification is needed before interpreting the ablation magnitude.

The paper describes manufactured time-dependent fields and source terms, a random train/test split, and additional Bunny experiments; the generation functions, trajectory-level split identities, raw repetitions, geometry preprocessing, and complete baseline runs were unavailable. Future forcing, initial-state sufficiency, Equation (71)’s second time derivative versus the stated single-time input, and held-out trajectory independence therefore remain unresolved. Table 5 does not show universal dominance, and the paper itself says best performance in most cases. Neither the empirical ranking nor a full numerical PDE solver was reproduced. Runtime concerns about cached parameter tensors were noted statically but not promoted to a verified execution finding.
# Conclusion and state

The overall Major assessment is supported by explicit central mathematical failures and the released core transport and \(H^1\) evaluation defects. Valid geometric principles and possible different historical preprocessing do not erase those bounded findings; they do prevent an unsupported conclusion that all reported gains disappear.
