Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification: MetaAgent: Automatically Constructing Multi-Agent Systems Based on Finite State Machines
# Paper identity and reviewed version

This report concerns MetaAgent: Automatically Constructing Multi-Agent Systems Based on Finite State Machines, by Yaolun Zhang et al., ICML 2025, PMLR volume 267; identifier `I25-43677`, OpenReview `vOxaD3hhPt`. The reviewed object is the frozen published proceedings PDF, retrieved on 25 October 2026. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the internal page numbers. They are not the continuous PMLR volume pagination.
# Review scope and interpretation

MetaAgent generates agents, a finite control graph, natural-language transition conditions and listener lists, then asks an LLM to merge states. The contribution is an empirical framework, not a proved theorem about formal automata. Main Sections 1–5, Algorithms 1–2, the merging prompt, software criteria, example software FSM and selected ML deployment trace were inspected. Core execution and optimization source was read statically at commit , dated 2 December 2025. That later public snapshot is not assumed identical to the historical experimental implementation. No author code, LLM calls or generated tool actions were executed.

The finite graph is a useful control abstraction. Agent memories, tool outputs and environment state are additional execution state; graph expressiveness alone does not prove generalization or correctness. In particular, role similarity and overlapping tools do not establish behavioral equivalence of states. The Section 3.2.3 assertion that merging preserves functionality should be treated as an empirical objective unless transition guards, memory effects and observable outputs are checked.

There is a positive invariant: if every accepted merge replaces two distinct states by one, Algorithm 1 terminates after at most \(n-1\) merges. Under finite-time LLM calls, at most \[\sum_{k=2}^{n}\binom{k}{2}=\binom{n+1}{3}\] pair tests suffice, including repeated scans. This is a termination and call-count bound, not a quality guarantee or a token-cost bound. The independent script verifies the combinatorial identity for several sizes.
# Concrete failures of graph preservation in the pinned optimizer

Problem 1 (State merging can collide with an existing identifier and discard a guard).  The inspected optimizer does not preserve two basic graph invariants after an accepted merge: uniqueness of state IDs and preservation of distinct transition conditions.

In , lines 470–475 remove two states and then choose the new ID as the length of the remaining list. Consider IDs \(1,2,3,4,5\), with state 1 initial, state 5 final, and states 2, 3 and 4 ordinary. If an allowed pair 2 and 4, assigned to different agents, is approved for merging, the surviving IDs are \(1,3,5\) and the new ID is also 3. The flags check at lines 119–121 does not exclude this case. The later renumbering dictionary at lines 515–533 maps the duplicated old ID 3 to the last new value, 4; edges to the original surviving state 3 are consequently redirected to the merged state rather than its own new ID 2. Renumbering after a collision cannot recover the lost distinction.

Independently, lines 332–340 deduplicate transitions using only \((\text{from},\text{to})\), ignoring their conditions. If merging produces two edges \(m\to f\) with guards \(A\) and \(B\), retaining only the first implements \(A\) rather than \(A\lor B\). The four-row Boolean enumeration finds a lost transition when \(A\) is false and \(B\) true. This failure can occur even if the state ID is chosen correctly and even when the LLM’s intended merged instruction is otherwise reasonable.

These are Major implementation defects in the pinned optimizer, conditional on the corresponding merge being chosen. The independent calculation operates on a five-label list and a two-guard toy graph; it neither imports the author module nor claims that the actual LLM selects this pair on a benchmark. A repair is to allocate a fresh ID before editing, assert uniqueness and valid edge endpoints, and preserve each condition or combine same-endpoint guards by a well-defined logical disjunction. The independent repaired examples retain both the surviving state and all four guard truth-table outcomes. They are not a general validation of semantic state merging. Original benchmark impact and a full patched implementation remain unverified.
# Deployment algorithm and implementation do not describe the same trace

Problem 2 (Algorithm 2 routes output using the destination state’s listeners).  Algorithm 2, page 16, assigns \(s\leftarrow s_{\mathrm{target}}\) at line 10, then inserts the old state’s output into \(s.\mathrm{Lis}\) at lines 12–13. Sections 3.2–3.3 specify the originating state’s listeners instead.

Take \(A\to B\to C\) with listeners \(L(A)=\{B\}\) and \(L(B)=\{C\}\). After \(A\) generates its result and transitions to \(B\), the displayed algorithm sends that result to \(C\) and leaves \(B\) without it. A deterministic listener-map calculation verifies the discrepancy. Saving the source state before assignment and broadcasting through its listener list repairs this example.

Algorithm 2 also contains no final-state termination test despite the definition in Section 3.1. Its null-transition branch calls the agent a second time but does not verify that second output before the next iteration begins. These are material omissions for a literal implementation, although they may be pseudocode mistakes. The pinned , lines 140–148 and 173–177, already checks submission/final state and broadcasts through the source state’s listener list. Thus the listener issue is Minor for the paper’s pseudocode, with an observed implementation-level correction; it is not evidence of that particular runtime failure in the released code.

The same source implements transition choice by parsing a marker in the task agent’s own output (lines 101–105, 131 and 149), whereas the paper describes a separately queried condition verifier. It also uses a local four-conversation cap and a separate count of graph transitions. These distinctions require version-specific documentation; the paper’s algorithm cannot alone establish the behavior of this later release. No historical version reconciliation was performed.
# Numerical claims and execution evidence

Problem 3 (Several reported summary statistics cannot be reconstructed from their displayed inputs).  Table 5 uses inconsistent averages for its foundation-model ablation, and Table 6 overstates one optimization reduction.
The five displayed dataset scores in Table 5 give the following arithmetic means:
Designer / executor | Printed | Mean of five entries

The first three printed values are consistent with dividing by six instead of five, up to rounding. The row labels and accompanying text also disagree: the paragraph attributes .26 and .35 to designer/executor replacement, respectively, while those are not the table’s corresponding two values. Correcting the means still supports the qualitative ordering that the weaker executor loses more than the weaker designer, but changes the magnitudes.

For software optimization, \((.85-.65)/.85=23.53\%\), not the stated \(35.3\%\) decrease. Likewise software checkpoint success rising from .35 to .85 is a 50 percentage-point increase, or \(142.86\%\) relative improvement, not literally “50% more” checkpoints. These are Minor numerical/reporting errors: the main ordering survives. Table 3’s claim of roughly 97% of Data Interpreter performance is consistent with \(.83/.86=96.51\%\). Table 7’s displayed design-plus-deployment totals also add correctly. Its software cost coverage is six tasks, however, while Table 4 and Appendix B name five; the sixth case and its relationship to the performance aggregate are unresolved.

Problem 4 (The provided ML example does not support its final model-selection narrative).  Appendix H.1 displays a random-forest run with accuracy .8324, followed by a report naming gradient boosting as best and listing several additional unshown models and features.

Pages 24–26 show preprocessing that drops the passenger-name column and trains a random-forest classifier. The recorded execution result on page 26 is .8324. The reporting agent then claims title extraction, five evaluated model families, random forest at .82 and gradient boosting best at .83. The displayed trace contains no execution evidence for these additions. This is a Major gap in using the example as evidence of reliable execution-grounded reporting; it is not evidence that all table scores were fabricated or that the random-forest .8324 result itself is wrong. The correct action is to bind reported metrics to saved predictions, evaluation outputs and model identities, and to disclose whether Table 3 came from those outputs or unconstrained generated summaries. The small wrapper only returns the system result and supplies no independent ML scorer. Other benchmark-specific evaluators or logs may exist outside this snapshot; their absence here is retained as an uncertainty.
# Strengths, remaining tests and conclusion

The framework integrates practical tools and backtracking into a reusable task-level graph, publishes code, and supplies ablations and explicit software checkpoints. These are useful contributions. The reported advantages are package-level empirical comparisons: Table 6 gives tool-free GPQA performance .52 versus full-system .60, while Table 2 lists .55 for Self-Refine. Without equal tools and budgets, the headline gain cannot be attributed solely to the FSM or its verifier. The table entries alone do not establish paired statistical significance, and a zero sampling temperature does not establish identical service behavior across runs. Five software cases with four criteria each give coarse scores; one criterion, aesthetically displaying weather data, still requires judgment.

The supported findings concern graph-integrity failures in a specific later source commit, correctable pseudocode routing, reproducible arithmetic discrepancies, and a concrete mismatch between an execution trace and its narrative. Finite calculations validate the local counterexamples and repairs. They do not replace LLM deployment tests, evaluation-set isolation checks, comprehensive tool audits, independent scoring or a search for later corrections. The main empirical ordering is not overturned by the arithmetic corrections alone. Focused independent AI acceptance is complete. Adjudication, original-run impact and author adoption remain pending or unknown; there has been no human review.

1 Yaolun Zhang et al., MetaAgent: Automatically Constructing Multi-Agent Systems Based on Finite State Machines, PMLR 267 (2025), published proceedings version. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/zhang25bc.html.

report: Abstract: A stationary conditional-softmax counterexample refutes the printed directional-improvement theorem, and a norm-ratio inversion identifies a repair to its sufficient condition. A separate finite example exposes a support and fallback gap in the claimed DPO connection. Selected continual-editing averages materially exaggerate local gains. The locality argument remains defensible as a first-order result under isotropy. These findings do not establish failure of the empirical method as a whole; adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification: Mitigating Heterogeneous Token Overfitting in LLM Knowledge Editing
# Paper identity and reviewed version

This report concerns Mitigating Heterogeneous Token Overfitting in LLM Knowledge Editing, by Tianci Liu et al., ICML 2025, PMLR volume 267; identifier `I25-43678`, OpenReview `vOu5K93z4f`. The reviewed object is the frozen published proceedings PDF, retrieved on 25 October 2026. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the internal page numbers. They are not the continuous PMLR volume pagination.
# Scope, contribution and assumptions

OVERTONE replaces a hard token target with a mixture of that target and a filtered current prediction, with a fallback to the hard target if the mixture changes the most probable token. A lower loss threshold suppresses updates on already fitted tokens. The paper studies four editing methods and several benchmarks. Main Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–D were read, including the proofs, implementation choices and continual-editing tables. The frozen source search did not locate an author implementation; this is a bounded availability result, not a claim that no implementation exists. No author code or LLM training was executed.

The method is a plausible regularizer and the component ablations are useful. The reduction to ordinary cross-entropy at \(\epsilon=0,\lambda=1\) is sound. Its additional per-token filtering cost is linear in vocabulary size, apart from the model forward/backward pass. These observations do not imply the stronger directional or preference-optimization guarantees. The following calculations distinguish a false theorem under its listed assumptions from limits on an empirical explanation.
# A realizable counterexample to the directional theorem

Problem 1 (Assumption A.7 does not imply Theorem A.10).  The strict directional improvement claimed in Theorem A.10 fails even when the pretrained loss is stationary and the filtered target is locally constant.

Use the paper’s notation \(a=
abla\ell_{m CE}(z^{m new})\), \(b=-
abla\ell_{m CE}(z^{m old})\), and \(c=
abla\operatorname{CE}(\pi_{m flt},\pi_	heta)\). Set \[a=c=(1,0),\qquad b=(-1,1/10),\qquad a+b=(0,1/10).\] Assumption A.6 makes \(G=(a+b)/N\). Then \(\cos(a,G)=0\), whereas Assumption A.7 only requires \[\cos(b,c)>1- rac{\|b\|^2}{8\|a+b\|^2}
                  (1-\cos(a,a+b))^2=-11.625.\] The actual cosine is \(-1/\sqrt{1.01}\simeq-.995037\), so the assumption holds. Nevertheless \(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)c=a\) for every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Its cosine remains zero: no strict improvement exists. The negative threshold also shows why the verbal description of A.7 as requiring close directions is not generally valid.

This is realizable by a small conditional softmax model, rather than an unattached vector construction. At \(\theta=0\), choose new-context probabilities \(p=(.5,.3,.2)\), preferred token 0, and logits \(\log p+J\theta\), where \[J=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] With the published filter parameter \(n=.5\), only token 0 survives, giving \(q=\pi_{\rm flt}=(1,0,0)\). Thus \(J^T(p-e_0)=a=c\), and every mixture passes the most-probable-token check. For the old context use uniform probabilities and logit Jacobian \[J_o=\begin{pmatrix}-1.5&.15\\0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad -J_o^T((1/3,1/3,1/3)-e_0)=b.\] A pretraining set with one old-context example of each label and new-context label counts \((5,3,2)\) has zero gradient. Its summed-loss Hessian eigenvalues are approximately \(.0130413\) and \(11.502\), so this is a strict local minimum. Distinct old/new teacher-forced contexts can be formed by different first tokens after the same input, with fixed first-token probabilities \((.6,.3,.1)\) independent of \(\theta\); their filters are defined and their gradients vanish. The two-token sequences therefore realize the context change in the paper’s setup. The independent script checks stationarity, curvature, filtering and a finite-difference CE gradient \((1.00000000008,0)\). This finite model addresses the stated gradient assumptions, not the measured behavior of a particular LLM.

The error is visible on page 17. With \(A=\|a+b\|\), \(B=\|b\|\), \(k=\cos(a,a+b)\) and \(d=\|c/\|c\|-b/\|b\|\|\), solving \((A-Bd)/(A+Bd)>k\) gives \(d<(A/B)(1-k)/(1+k)\) when \(k>-1\). The proof instead uses \(B/A\). A sufficient repaired assumption, for nonzero vectors and a locally fixed target, is \[\cos(b,c)>1-\frac{\|a+b\|^2}{8\|b\|^2}
                       (1-\cos(a,a+b))^2.\] Indeed it gives \(r=Bd/A<(1-k)/2\leq1\), hence a positive numerator and cosine at least \((1-r)/(1+r)\geq1-2r>k\), at the proof’s chosen \(\lambda=\|c\|/(B+\|c\|)\). The repaired condition rejects the counterexample: its threshold is \(.998762\). It is substantially stronger in this example and has not been verified empirically. The original theorem is Major; changing the ratio repairs this sufficient vector argument when the selected mixture is actually used, not the full fallback algorithm or its assumptions.
# Target dependence and the preference interpretation

Problem 2 (The DPO connection does not cover the stated algorithm’s support and fallback).  Theorem A.16 and Equation (17) use a filtered reference probability in a logarithmic ratio, although Algorithm 1 deliberately assigns exact zeros and Equation (3) can fall back to a label outside that support.

For current probabilities \((.8,.15,.05)\), \(n=.5\) retains only the first token. If the desired token is the third and \(\lambda=.1\), the proposed mixture is \((.9,0,.1)\) and fails the argmax check. The actual target becomes \(e_2\), with finite loss \(-\log(.05)=2.995732\) at \(\epsilon=0\). But the reference probability of the preferred token in Equation (17) is zero, so its log-ratio is undefined or infinite. The independent calculation reproduces this exact algorithmic branch. The theorem’s unconditional interpretation therefore needs support restrictions and explicit treatment of fallback cases. This is a Major gap in the theoretical connection, not a counterexample to finite OVERTONE training loss.

The derivation also treats the target entropy and reference as constants while Algorithm 1 recomputes them from the current logits. Equation (6)’s displayed KL expansion has the wrong entropy sign: \(D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)=\operatorname{CE}(q,p)-H(q)\). Omitting that entropy in a gradient calculation requires a detached, fixed target for the current update. The clipping constant can likewise be dropped for gradients only within a fixed active set. These conventions, and the dependence of the argmax fallback on \(\lambda\), should be explicit. The counterexample above does not rely on this ambiguity because its target is locally a fixed point mass.

On pages 19–20 the proposed preference probability is a clipped exponential. At zero margin it assigns \(1/e\) to each direction, totaling \(2/e\simeq.73576\), rather than complementary probabilities for an exhaustive binary comparison. A tie or abstention model could account for leftover mass, but none is specified in that derivation. A valid repair must define the pairwise probability model, positive reference support, update-time detachment and fallback objective; merely calling the algebra DPO is insufficient. Those repairs have not been implemented or validated here. Finally, equal logits have standard deviation zero, so the literal filter removes all tokens. A deterministic keep-at-least-one rule is a small necessary boundary repair.
# What the locality argument does establish

The absolute values in Theorem A.15 are essential and are present in the rendered PDF. Under the stated isotropic gradient-direction assumption, with radius independent of direction, \(\mathbb E|v^TW|=C\|v\|\). Consequently, if \(\|c\|<\|a\|\) and \(\lambda<1\), the triangle inequality proves a smaller expected absolute first-order probability perturbation for the mixture. A 20,000-angle deterministic quadrature on the unit circle, with \(a=(2,0)\), \(c=(0,.5)\) and \(\lambda=.1\), gives respectively \(1.273240\), \(.318310\) and \(.313499\) for the two directions and their mixture. The ratio for \(c\) versus \(a\) is exactly \(.25\) to numerical precision, agreeing with the norm ratio.

This supports the local linearized calculation. It does not establish a finite-step inequality without a sufficiently small learning rate and control of higher-order terms; \(\lambda=1\) gives equality. Nor does lack of prior knowledge about gradient directions establish isotropy in an LLM. The empirical locality gains remain relevant evidence, but are distinct from verifying those distributional assumptions.
# Continual-editing aggregates and empirical scope

Problem 3 (Incorrect table averages inflate some continual-editing gains).  Several displayed averages in Tables 4–5 cannot be obtained from their component scores. Their corrections materially change individual claimed improvements.

For \(T=100\), Table 4’s LLaMA 2 MELO WikiBio row gives reliability \(48.88\) and locality \(97.61\), but average \(48.88\). The arithmetic mean is \(73.245\). Its OVERTONE row averages \(74.805\), so the gain is \(1.56\) percentage points, rather than the displayed \(25.93\). In Table 5, LLaMA 3 MELO on Wikicounterfact lists \((22.2,22.9,97.85)\) and average \(22.55\); the correct mean is \(47.65\). The corresponding OVERTONE mean is \(47.7333\), making the gain approximately \(.0833\) rather than \(25.18\) points. Table 5’s FT-M plus OVERTONE WikiBio row similarly averages \((94.23+85.83)/2=90.03\), not \(94.23\).

These are directly checked numerical discrepancies, also verified in the rendered source tables. They are Major for those local improvement magnitudes; they do not erase the many larger LoRA gains elsewhere. Recomputing every aggregate from saved per-example outputs is needed to establish the table as a whole. This review corrects the named cells and does not certify every other entry.

Claims of preserving reliability or uniformly improving portability also need qualifications already visible in Table 1. LLaMA 2 LoRA on WikiBio changes reliability from \(100\) to \(97.68\), while locality improves from \(48.84\) to \(68.45\). LLaMA 3 WISE portability changes from \(49.27\) to \(47.54\), despite a better overall average. These are tradeoffs, not universal dominance. Appendix B additionally shrinks WISE’s activation threshold by a factor \(.6\) under OVERTONE. A matched-threshold ablation is needed before attributing the whole WISE difference to the loss alone.

Figure 1’s rising portability loss and Figure 2’s token-wise heterogeneity motivate the method. The proposed underfitting-degree statistic compares an edited target’s confidence with a pre-edit greedy confidence; a negative value by itself is not a held-out generalization error or a causal identification of heterogeneous overfitting. The paper itself proposes repeated runs and acknowledges unresolved knowledge conflicts. These uncertainties should remain in the empirical interpretation rather than being filled by the invalid directional theorem.
# Conclusion

The contribution remains a useful empirical editing regularizer with informative ablations. The direction guarantee is false under its printed assumptions; the preference connection omits operative algorithm branches; and selected continual-editing averages substantially exaggerate local gains. The locality result has a defensible first-order interpretation. Independent finite calculations and source-page inspection establish the specific findings and the limited vector repair. Training replication, gradient-assumption measurements, implementation detachment, raw-score verification, later corrections and author adoption remain unverified. Scientific adjudication is pending.
1 Tianci Liu et al., Mitigating Heterogeneous Token Overfitting in LLM Knowledge Editing, PMLR 267 (2025), published proceedings version. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/liu25ae.html.

Title: Technical Verification: Neural Encoding and Decoding at Scale
# Paper identity and reviewed version

This report concerns Neural Encoding and Decoding at Scale, by Yizi Zhang et al., ICML 2025, PMLR volume 267; identifier `I25-43679`, OpenReview `vOdz3zhSCj`. The reviewed object is the frozen published proceedings PDF, retrieved on 25 October 2026. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with the internal page numbers. They are not the continuous PMLR volume pagination.
# Scope and what the objective supports

NEDS trains a shared transformer with neural, behavioral, within-modality and cross-modal reconstruction tasks, then adapts session-specific components to new animals. Main Sections 1–7 and Appendices A–H were read. Relevant architecture, masking, optimizer, checkpoint, data-split and metric paths were statically traced in the frozen public NEDS source at commit , dated 20 March 2026. This later release is not presumed identical to the code that generated the 2025 results. No author module, training program or model checkpoint was executed. Independent calculations use only small arrays and a newly written CPU PyTorch example.

The core statistical motivation is sound. If a Poisson prediction has rate \(r>0\) and target conditional mean \(\mu\), its expected negative log-likelihood, apart from a constant, is \[r-\mu\log r,\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial r}(r-\mu\log r)=1-\mu/r.\] For \(\mu>0\) it is minimized at \(r=\mu\), even when the true count distribution is not Poisson. MSE similarly targets a conditional mean; categorical cross-entropy targets class probabilities. A finite check with equally likely counts \(0,0,6\) confirms the Poisson quasi-loss minimum at mean 2 among the tested rates. The code uses log-rate Poisson loss and exponentiates predictions for evaluation, resolving the positive-rate link only implicit in Equation (1).

These objectives justify conditional prediction under the actual input masks. They do not by themselves establish a mutually compatible joint generative distribution, causal influence of behavior, or transfer without fine-tuning. The animal-level pretraining holdout is a meaningful strength. The reported evaluation then adapts on 70% of each held-out animal’s trials, selects settings on 10% and tests on 20%. The inspected main data-preparation path implements this random trial partition and excludes listed test sessions from multi-session pretraining. Exact identifiers and sample membership were not independently compared with raw data.
# The released within-modality task uses additional information

Problem 1 (The source implements a different conditional reconstruction task).  Section 3.2 and Figure 1 define within-modality reconstruction as \(\mathbb E[X_{\rm masked}\mid X_{\rm visible}]\) or its behavioral counterpart, with the other modality absent. The pinned implementation leaves the other modality visible.

In , lines 100–106 set a random neural mask for `self-spike` and zero masks for all behavioral modalities; `self-behavior` analogously leaves spikes unmasked. Zero means visible, as confirmed by , lines 152–160. All multimodal inputs are concatenated and attend to one another. Hence neural reconstruction can use \(\mathbb E[X_{\rm masked}\mid X_{\rm visible},Y]\). The mixed-batch path at lines 301–315 of the same model file has the same information exposure.

This changes the task mathematically. Let a masked neural value \(X\) be a uniform bit, let visible same-modality information be constant, and let behavior satisfy \(Y=X\). The intended within-modality optimal MSE is \(1/4\); with visible behavior it is zero. The independent two-outcome calculation verifies both values. Thus the two masks cannot be treated as equivalent regularizers or as identifying the same conditional expectation. This is a Major method-to-source discrepancy, particularly for interpreting the masking ablation in Table 2. It is not test-set leakage: it concerns information supplied during an explicitly multimodal training task.

The source also uniformly samples five named tasks, separating the two within-modality variants, rather than the four categories drawn uniformly in Equation (1). Their aggregate probability is consequently \(2/5\), not \(1/4\), while encoding and decoding each receive \(1/5\). To implement the paper literally, input visibility must be separated from the loss-selection mask: hide the other modality completely but compute reconstruction loss only for the selected within-modality targets. The source already distinguishes these concepts for selected-variable encoding. Alternatively, revise the stated conditionals and report the actual sampling weights. The finite example verifies the information-set distinction; neither a patched training run nor a historical mask reconstruction was performed.
# Unimodal output heads are not registered model components

Problem 2 (The pinned unimodal baseline omits its output modules from optimization and checkpoints).  The unimodal setup stores session-specific output decoders and temporal pooling weights inside ordinary Python dictionaries. They are not discovered by the model’s parameter and state traversal.

In , lines 114–124 create ordinary dictionaries for the output decoders and temporal pooling weights, then insert decoder modules and nested parameter dictionaries. These components are used in the forward path at lines 253–277. But , lines 297–302 constructs AdamW solely from `model.parameters()`, and , lines 544–561 saves `model.state_dict()`. No manual addition of those dictionary-held components was found along these paths. By contrast, multimodal encoders are in a registered module dictionary, and their output modules and pooling parameters are registered attributes.

An independent PyTorch model reproduces the container mechanism without importing any NEDS code. Its dictionary-held output head has gradient norm \(129\), yet a real AdamW step changes its weight by exactly zero. Its pooling parameter also remains unchanged, and the checkpoint contains only the registered feature layer. Reloading that state into an otherwise identical model initialized with different fixed weights changes predictions by as much as \(21.89\) in this toy. Using registered module dictionaries instead gives nonzero head and pooling updates, includes all relevant keys in the checkpoint, and reproduces predictions exactly after reload. These are actual CPU results, not predicted test outcomes.

The issue is Major for reproducing a trained unimodal comparator. An upstream encoder can still learn through a fixed random output projection, so the code is not necessarily unable to fit any task. Nor must a fresh reload differ if the same initialization happens to be recreated. The stronger, supported point is that the declared output heads are neither optimizer-managed nor preserved by the inspected checkpoint path, unlike the multimodal counterpart. This compromises attribution of a reproduced multimodal advantage to the training objective alone. Registration and checkpoint-roundtrip checks repair the toy mechanism; original checkpoints, benchmark effects and historical implementation remain unverified.
# The returned continuous-behavior metric retains the trial average

Problem 3 (Reported single-trial interpretation and metric implementation differ).  Section 4.1 says continuous decoding \(R^2\) accounts for the trial average, but gives no separate residual-metric equation. If this means removing the mean time course, the pinned evaluation does not implement it: it returns ordinary \(R^2\) after flattening all trial/time values.

, line 762 passes raw `y` and `y_pred` into the flattening metric. The wrapper at lines 917–943 returns this value. Its `subtract_psth` option affects a separate plotting routine and never changes the returned scalar. The main evaluation passes `subtract="task"`, so that option’s presence does not resolve the mismatch. Training-validation selection likewise uses flattened raw values in , lines 214–221.

For a concrete example take two observed trials \((-1,9)\) and \((1,11)\) and predict their shared average \((0,10)\) in both trials. Ordinary flattened \(R^2\) is \[1-\frac{4}{104}=\frac{25}{26}\simeq .961538.\] After subtracting the average time course, the true residuals are \((-1,-1)\) and \((1,1)\) while the predicted residuals are zero, yielding \(R^2=0\). A model can therefore score highly under the implemented metric while explaining none of this trial-to-trial variation. This does not make raw \(R^2\) an invalid metric; it makes the stronger stated interpretation unsupported by that computation. The distinction is Major for claims about residual single-trial variability. If the wording instead meant ordinary centering about one grand mean, it needs clarification rather than a change to that raw metric. The intended residual interpretation and whether the published scores used this release remain Needs Evidence.

A repair should specify both metrics explicitly, state how any condition-specific mean is estimated, and use the same definition across models and checkpoint selection. The example verifies the corrected residual calculation, not the paper’s scores. The test helper also places the final model call outside the batch loop in its behavioral path (lines 400–447); it retains only the last batch. Its current loader requests 10,000 examples per batch, which can conceal the issue on small sessions. This is a conditional scalability defect, not evidence that the stated IBL sessions actually crossed that limit.
# Additional boundaries and reporting corrections

Singleton session groups are mishandled in several routines: `argwhere(...).squeeze()` produces a scalar when a session has exactly one example. The subsequent positive-dimension guard skips session embeddings and temporal pooling weights in , and drops such groups during validation in , lines 333–358. An independent array-shape check confirms this case; a flat index array preserves the group. In the pooling path, skipped weights remain zero, leaving only the subsequent decoder bias for that group. This is a Minor but concrete boundary defect whose prevalence depends on batching; full-batch single-session evaluation with many trials avoids it.

Table 11 does not support improvement from embeddings across all five tasks. Removing temporal embeddings raises encoding from \(.20\) to \(.24\) bps, and removing both temporal and modality embeddings raises it to \(.25\); choice accuracy also rises from \(.84\) to \(.86\) in the latter row. Wheel and whisker decoding decline. The correct description is a task-dependent tradeoff, with paired session-level uncertainty needed before making significance claims. Table 2 similarly shows unchanged rounded choice accuracy when within-modality masking is removed. These are Minor reporting qualifications, not a finding that the measurements are false.

The roughly 400,000 neuron-hours stated on page 14 needs an exposure ledger. For session \(s\) with \(N_s\) neurons recorded for \(h_s\) hours, exposure is \(\sum_s N_s h_s\), not \((\sum_s N_s)(\sum_s h_s)\). The latter product of the headline counts, \(27{,}380\times14=383{,}320\), includes cross-session terms. A two-session check with \((N_1,N_2)=(100,200)\) and \((h_1,h_2)=(1,2)\) gives 500 neuron-hours, versus the incorrect product 900. The resemblance to the reported headline warrants reconciliation; an exact corrected dataset exposure cannot be obtained without per-session durations and neuron counts. No specific replacement total is asserted.

The 83% brain-region classification result uses five-fold cross-validation over neurons from the ten already adapted animals, as Section 5.3 discloses. It measures discrimination within that pooled population, not a classifier’s generalization to a new animal excluded from all classifier folds. A leave-animal-out evaluation and controls for firing rate, session identity and embedding dimension would clarify the emergent representation claim. In particular the multimodal feature concatenates input and output weights, whereas each unimodal feature uses only one of them. Neither the confusion matrix nor predictive encoding from a single behavior identifies a causal influence or functional equivalence of brain regions. These are limits on interpretation, not demonstrated contamination of the reported classifier.
# Evidence that survives and conclusion

The study provides animal-level pretraining separation, several linear and transformer comparisons, extensive validation-based searches, and useful ablations. Appendix D explicitly checks a larger single-session model and reports worse performance, so the pretraining gain cannot simply be dismissed as an unexamined capacity increase. Appendix F also openly states that the POYO+ comparison uses trial-aligned windows without temporal jitter, and that NDT2 is reimplemented. The ranking is therefore for those specified adaptations and budgets. Table 10’s point estimates favor NEDS, but marginal standard errors alone do not establish paired statistical significance across ten sessions. Appendix H provides a useful separately trained monkey example, not evidence of mouse-to-monkey zero-shot transfer.

The supported concerns are different input conditionals for within-modality masking, unregistered unimodal output components, and a raw returned metric whose stronger residual interpretation needs clarification. Smaller batching and reporting issues also require correction. Independent toy computations establish the local mechanisms and limited repairs. They do not establish the magnitude of any historical score change or refute the value of a unified multimodal model. Original-run reconstruction, patched benchmark evaluation, raw data audits, brain-region classifier replication and author adoption remain unverified; scientific adjudication is pending.
1 Yizi Zhang et al., Neural Encoding and Decoding at Scale, PMLR 267 (2025), published proceedings version. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/zhang25bw.html.
# Evidence and reproducibility
The exact source PDF has SHA-256

The matching `verification/0310` directory contains the source text extraction, independently written calculation script and actual output, inspected page images, coverage ledger, findings and provenance. Source code supplied by the authors was not executed. The calculation is an independent finite or analytic diagnostic, not a reproduction of the original training experiments. The final PDF is compiled from this TeX; the compiler log and visual receipt identify the exact bytes inspected. This initial review was performed by the delegated AI unit with GPT-6 Astra / Max formally selected. A separate AI unit subsequently checked the stated Problems against the frozen original source, assumptions, decisive arguments, counterevidence and impact boundaries. Its fresh evidence and exact artifact bindings are retained in the same verification directory. No human review has occurred; scientific adjudication is pending and author adoption is unknown.

Title: Technical Verification: CLARIFY: Contrastive Preference Reinforcement Learning for Untangling Ambiguous Queries
# Identity and scope

CLARIFY: Contrastive Preference Reinforcement Learning for Untangling Ambiguous Queries. Ni Mu; Hao Hu; Xiao Hu; Yiqin Yang; Bo Xu; Qing-Shan Jia. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43680. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main text (pp. 1–8), Appendix A (pp. 11–13), and experimental/architecture appendices C–E (pp. 13–19) were read. The decisive checks concern the convex-separation proof and the released rejection sampler. Published performance values were read as reported evidence; no training, human experiment or statistical reanalysis was performed. Figures 2 and 3 were inspected in the actual PDF. Their colored embedding plots illustrate particular learned representations and do not prove a universal separation property.
# The checked objects

In Section 4.1, a pair \((\sigma_+,\sigma_-)\) identifies relatively preferred and non-preferred trajectories. The encoder maps trajectories to vectors \(z\). The paper uses Euclidean distance \(\ell\) and trains a combination of ambiguity, quadrilateral, reconstruction and norm losses, Eq. (11). Its main quadrilateral objective, Eq. (6), contains two within-query cross-class distances minus two within-class distances. Proposition 5.2 claims a separating hyperplane for convex positive and negative embedding sets when the quadrilateral loss is minimized “with a margin.” Appendix A.2 purports to supply the proof and defines the margin as half the distance between class means.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The core convex-separation argument does not follow from its premises).  The proof of Proposition 5.2, Appendix A.2, p. 12, Eqs. (28)–(35), is invalid. The appendix statement with its printed loss also admits an explicit counterexample. This is a Major concern about the theoretical justification of the central representation-learning mechanism.
## Original claim and suspect step

Let \(C^+,C^-\subset\mathbb R^d\) be convex, \(\mu^\pm=\mathbb E z^\pm\), \(w=\mu^+-\mu^-\), \(b=-(\|\mu^+\|^2-\|\mu^-\|^2)/2\) and \(\eta=\|\mu^+-\mu^-\|/2\). The appendix concludes, at a global minimum of its displayed objective, that every point of \(C^+\) has signed distance at least \(\eta\) and every point of \(C^-\) at most \(-\eta\). Equation (34) computes these distances only at the two means. The next sentence uses affinity and convexity to extend the bounds to all points of the sets.

An affine function takes the average of its values at a mean; its value at that mean is not a lower bound on every value in a convex set. No extreme-point or radius restriction is supplied. In fact, a random variable bounded below by its own expectation must equal that expectation almost surely, so the proposed positive-class conclusion would require zero variation in the normal direction.
## Complete counterexample to the printed Appendix A.2 statement

Take dimension one, independent draws \(z^+,z^{+\prime}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,2]\) and \(z^-,z^{-\prime}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[-1,1]\). The two compact intervals are convex and are the full distributional supports. All distances are Euclidean and expectations finite. The printed Eq. (29) is \[L_A=-\mathbb E\bigl[|z^+-z^{-\prime}|+|z^{+\prime}-z^-|-|z^+-z^-|-|z^{+\prime}-z^{-\prime}|\bigr].\] All four terms have the same expectation because all positive and negative draws are independent with their respective common marginals. Hence \(L_A=0\) for every encoder with finite expectations under this independent-pair distribution. This is a global minimum, not merely a stationary point. One may realize the encoder on two disjoint compact trajectory domains as \(f(+,u)=u+1\) and \(f(-,u)=u\), with \(u\sim\mathrm{Unif}[-1,1]\); sources can have consistently ordered preference labels while their embeddings overlap. The result does not impose disjoint embedding sets.

Here \(\mu^+=1\), \(\mu^-=0\), \(w=1\), \(b=-1/2\), \(\eta=1/2\), and \(\widetilde d(z)=z-1/2\). At \(z^+=0\in C^+\) the asserted \(\widetilde d(z^+)\ge1/2\) instead gives \(-1/2\); at \(z^-=1\in C^-\) the asserted upper bound \(-1/2\) instead gives \(1/2\). Failure also occurs on positive-measure neighborhoods, so it is not an endpoint convention. The two sets overlap; no strictly separating hyperplane exists. The independent rational enumeration in `independent_output.json` checks the same expectation cancellation on a finite grid and the signed-distance values. The continuous argument above supplies the convex-support example.
## Alternative readings and impact boundary

Equation (29) is visibly different from Eq. (6), verified against the rendered page. Replacing it with Eq. (6) removes the cancellation argument: this counterexample is therefore not presented as a global-minimum counterexample for the main-text objective. Nevertheless, the convexity inference is invalid regardless of that replacement. The derivatives with respect to \(w,b\) in Eq. (31) are also not derived from the displayed distance loss, which introduces no freely optimized classifier parameters. The phrase “with a margin” in Proposition 5.2 has no quantitative loss-side definition establishing the required pointwise premise. If it is meant to assume the very separation claimed, it does not derive that separation from minimizing the loss.

The main text (p. 6) uses the theorem to justify linear separability, a safety gap and reliable avoidance of ambiguous queries. The invalid argument therefore concerns a central stated guarantee even if empirical utility survives. Figure 3 and Table 1 do not repair a universal proof; conversely this analysis does not invalidate their observed scores. The public trainer uses negative mean squared distances, sigmoid transformations and a norm penalty, further preventing an automatic identification of its optimized objective with Appendix A.2.
## Precisely limited repair

For fixed noncoincident means, if one separately assumes \(\|z-\mu^\pm\|\le r_\pm\) on each class, then \[\widetilde d(z^+)\ge\eta-r_+,\qquad \widetilde d(z^-)\le-\eta+r_-.\] This follows from \(\widetilde d(z)-\widetilde d(\mu^\pm)=w^\top(z-\mu^\pm)/\|w\|\) and Cauchy–Schwarz. Radii strictly smaller than \(\eta\) give a positive separation margin. The paper has not shown that its loss enforces these added assumptions; this is a valid conditional geometric statement, not a verified repair of the complete algorithm or original theorem.

Problem 2 (The released rejection routine does not generally sample its target).  In the frozen released `reward_model.py`, lines 62–69, the acceptance probability is the target/proposal ratio clipped at one. This is a supported Minor implementation discrepancy; its effect on the historical experiments is unestablished.

For proposal masses \(p_i\) and target masses \(q_i\), the routine’s idealized output masses are proportional to \(p_i\min(q_i/p_i,1)=\min(p_i,q_i)\). For \(p=(1/2,1/2)\) and \(q=(9/10,1/10)\) it yields \((5/6,1/6)\) instead of \((9/10,1/10)\). The independent exact-arithmetic check reports this result. The code additionally uses interpolation and an \(10^{-6}\) denominator; neither supplies the missing envelope constant. Calling this a heuristic filter is consistent with its behavior, but it is not exact sampling from the designated target in Section 4.2. The following maximum-disagreement stage (lines 643–647) intentionally changes the distribution further; the concern here is only the preceding claimed rejection-sampling step. A standard exact discrete rejection step with \(M\ge\max_i q_i/p_i\) and acceptance \(q_i/(Mp_i)\) would restore the target on common support. This statement does not validate the paper’s density estimates or overall empirical procedure.
# Overall dependence and remaining evidence

The highest supported impact is Major because Appendix A.2 is the proof for a main theoretical guarantee, not because every component of CLARIFY fails. Title: Technical Verification: Doubly Protected Estimation for Survival Outcomes Utilizing External Controls for Randomized Clinical Trials
# Identity and scope

Doubly Protected Estimation for Survival Outcomes Utilizing External Controls for Randomized Clinical Trials. Chenyin Gao; Shu Yang; Mingyang Shan; Wenyu Ye; Ilya Lipkovich; Douglas Faries. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43681. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main paper, pp. 1–9, and mathematical Appendix A, pp. 12–25, were read, with a focused check of identification and its censoring assumptions. Appendix B and Figures 1–4 were inspected as reported simulations, not reproduced. Static inspection covered the released survival-estimation routine at the lines recorded in the coverage ledger. The study-specific clinical conclusions and original patient data were not independently validated.
# Definitions and conditions

The target is the trial-population restricted mean survival-time (RMST) difference \(\theta_\tau=\int_0^\tau(S_1(t\mid R=1)-S_0(t\mid R=1))\,dt\). The observed data contain \(Y=\min(T,C)\) and \(\Delta=1(T<C)\); \(R=1\) denotes trial enrollment and \(A\) treatment. Assumption 3.1 requires internal treatment exchangeability and positive treatment/source probabilities. Assumption 3.2 requires \(T^{(a)}\perp C\mid X,A=a,R=r\). It does not require censoring to have the same distribution in the two randomized arms. Assumption 3.3 requires equality of control survival curves across sources, conditional on \(X\).
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The stated identification formula omits treatment in the censoring probability).  Theorem 3.4(a), p. 3, defines \(\pi_1^C(t,X)=P(C\ge t\mid X,R=1)\) and uses this same denominator for both treatment arms. Under its stated Assumptions 3.1–3.3 this formula is false. This is a Major concern about a core identification result as stated; it does not establish failure in the narrower simulation designs.
## Exact counterexample

Take \(X\) constant, \(P(R=1)=1/2\), and randomized \(P(A=1\mid R=1)=1/2\). In the external study \(A=0\). Let both potential event times have the exponential distribution with rate one, independently of assignment and source. Given \(R=1,A=0\), let \(C\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)\); given \(R=1,A=1\), let \(C\sim\mathrm{Exp}(3)\). External censoring may be \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\). In every arm draw censoring independently of the potential event times. Set, for example, \(\tau=1\) and check \(t=1/2\).

Consistency holds by construction. Treatment exchangeability holds because assignment is independent of potential outcomes. Both positivity probabilities equal \(1/2\). Conditional independent censoring holds in every observed arm. Control event-time distributions agree across sources for every \(t\). There are no ties, and every relevant censoring probability is positive at finite times. Theorem 3.4 does not invoke the additional asymptotic rate conditions of Assumption A.1.

Give the theorem the favorable interpretation that its treatment propensity is conditional on trial participation. Its marginal trial censoring survival is \[G(y)=\tfrac12e^{-y}+\tfrac12e^{-3y}.\] After cancellation of the source and treatment weights, the proposed formula for \(S_1(t\mid R=1)\) equals \[\begin{aligned}
I(t)&=\int_t^\infty\frac{e^{-y}e^{-3y}}{(e^{-y}+e^{-3y})/2}\,dy\\
&=2\int_0^{e^{-t}}\frac{u^2}{1+u^2}\,du
=2\{e^{-t}-\arctan(e^{-t})\}.\end{aligned}\] The correct survival is \(e^{-t}\). At \(t=1/2\), the claimed expression is \(0.1226460717641\) and the true value is \(0.6065306597126\). Their difference is a population-level discrepancy, with no estimation or finite-sample nuisance error. The independent script checks the integral and closed form with SciPy quadrature; both agree to the reported digits. Even at \(t=0\) the proposed expression is \(2-\pi/2\), not one.
## Counterevidence and narrower interpretation

Appendix A.1, p. 12, ends with a denominator \(S^C(Y\mid X,A=0,R=1)\) for the control arm. This is the appropriately arm-conditional quantity, and is material evidence that an omitted conditioning variable may have been intended in the main theorem. It is not the explicitly defined marginal quantity on p. 3. The appendix also conditions \(T^{(0)}>t\) on \(C>T\) in an intermediate equality; independent event and censoring times do not justify conditioning on the event \(C>T\), which selects longer or shorter event times unequally. The corrected weighting identity below avoids that step.

The simulation censoring hazard in Section 4 depends on \(X\) and the study but not treatment. Those experiments lie in a special case where the present distinction vanishes. Static code inspection found that `srEC_Surv.R`, lines 27–34 and 62–71, defaults `X.pred.c` to the three \(X\) variables and uses that list in the censoring model, while `X.pred.f` includes \(A\) and is used in the event model. The argument documentation names those two lists in the opposite order. Thus defaults do not silently impose an arm-specific censoring fit, though a caller could explicitly add \(A\) to the list actually used for censoring. No claim is made about the exact call used for historical results.
## Verified repair of the identification identity

Define \(G_{a,1}(y,X)=P(C\ge y\mid X,A=a,R=1)\) and use the trial treatment propensity \(p_a(X)=P(A=a\mid X,R=1)\). Then \[S_a(t\mid R=1)=\frac1{P(R=1)}\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{R1(A=a)\Delta1(Y>t)}{p_a(X)G_{a,1}(Y,X)}\right]\] under the stated conditional independence, consistency, treatment exchangeability and positive denominators. Conditional on \(T,X,A=a,R=1\), the expectation of \(1(C>T)/G_{a,1}(T,X)\) is one (for continuous times). Iterated expectation then gives the result. In the example this replaces \(G(y)\) by \(e^{-3y}\) and yields \(\int_t^\infty e^{-y}\,dy=e^{-t}\), independently verified numerically. Alternatively, adding \(C\perp A\mid X,R=1\) restores the marginal denominator. These are different repairs: the former changes the formula, the latter narrows the assumptions. This report does not certify all efficiency projections or asymptotic claims after either change.
# Other checked reasoning and limitations

The source/source-odds identity in Theorem 3.4(b) follows by iterated expectation for the external controls on common support once appropriate censoring weights are used. Theorem 3.5 then uses survival-curve identification as the foundation for the integrative influence functions, establishing the core dependency of Problem 1. The nuisance-product expression in Theorem 3.6 must be interpreted as a remainder bound rather than a bound on the entire random estimation error: even known nuisances leave the empirical influence-function term. Appendix A.3 mixes these objects, so this review does not certify its exact rate statement.

The selective procedure on pp. 5–6 detects zero integrated RMST drift whereas Appendix A.5 invokes equality of the survival curves for all times in the selected set. These are distinct restrictions. As a bounded diagnostic, \(S_T(t)=e^{-t}\) and \(S_E(t)=a e^{-t/2}+(1-a)e^{-2t}\) have equal RMST at \(\tau=1\) for \[a=\frac{(1-e^{-1})-(1-e^{-2})/2}{2(1-e^{-1/2})-(1-e^{-2})/2}=0.5634084559\ldots,\] while the curves differ. This does not satisfy Assumption 3.3 and is not offered as a counterexample to a theorem requiring that assumption. It identifies remaining work in extending the adaptive claim beyond homogeneous data: zero RMST drift alone cannot establish the curve-level tangent-space restriction. The optional oracle-weighted-curve calculation in the evidence is only a finite diagnostic of this distinction, not an empirical reproduction or a second adjudicated theorem counterexample.

Figures 1 and 3 show simulation trends for the specified settings, with some finite-sample type-I-error and efficiency limitations acknowledged in the Discussion. Figure 2 is an application analysis rather than independent evidence of transportability assumptions. None of these plots tests the arm-dependent-censoring counterexample. The original clinical estimates can survive this concern; determining their sensitivity requires actual censoring models, call configurations and patient-level data. The highest supported assessment concerns the false identification formula under its stated domain. No later erratum was established from the frozen packet.

Title: Technical Verification: Adversarial Robustness via Deformable Convolution with Stochasticity
# Identity and scope

Adversarial Robustness via Deformable Convolution with Stochasticity. Yanxiang Ma; Zixuan Huang; Minjing Dong; Shan You; Chang Xu. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43682. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main paper (pp. 1–9) and Appendices A–B (pp. 13–16) were read. The central check concerns Lemma 1 and the use of its receptive-field bound as a sufficient guarantee. Attack scores and ablations were inspected as reported observations; neither adversarial training nor evaluation of released checkpoints was executed. The frozen code is a later public snapshot, not established as the historical experimental implementation.
# Scope and mathematical setting

DCS samples a binary mask with \(n\) retained points in a \(k\times k\) convolutional boundary, with stride \(S\). Equations (6)–(8), p. 4, relate the input-gradient cosine similarity of two independently sampled paths to the retained points. Lemma 1 gives \(n\le S^2\epsilon_c\), and the surrounding text says this guarantees small expected gradient similarity. The combined interval in Eq. (12) is subsequently used as a guarantee governing the robustness/natural-accuracy trade-off. The counterexample below concerns this sufficiency claim, with uniformly sampled, spatially shared convolution masks.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The receptive-field upper bound does not guarantee the stated gradient similarity).  For \(k=5\), \(S=2\), \(n=1\) and \(\epsilon_c=1/4\), the claimed condition holds, but a valid masked convolution has expected gradient cosine \(4096/15625=0.262144>1/4\). The failure affects the core data-independent guarantee and supports Major impact.
## Construction and verification of conditions

Use a single-channel \(103\times103\) input, a \(5\times5\) kernel, stride two, zero padding of width zero (valid convolution), and weights all equal to one. There are \(50\times50\) output locations. At each forward pass choose one of the 25 offsets \((a,b)\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}^2\) uniformly and independently of the preceding pass; apply that same one-point mask across all spatial positions. Thus \(n=1<S^2=4\), and \(n\le S^2\epsilon_c=1\). This is a shared-weight convolution of the form in Definition 1. There is no circular padding, asymptotic image limit or nonuniform mask sampling.

Let the scalar logit be the sum of all convolution outputs, with a second logit zero. Evaluate cross-entropy for class zero of the zero-logit class at the all-zero input. Its derivative with respect to the summed logit is \(1/2\). Consequently, apart from this common positive scalar, the input gradient for mask \((a,b)\) is the indicator of \[G_{a,b}=\{(2i+a,2j+b):0\le i,j<50\}.\] Each set has 2500 distinct entries, so both gradient norms are nonzero and the cosine for a mask pair is exactly \(|G_{a,b}\cap G_{c,d}|/2500\). This supplies a legitimate classifier loss, not merely an artificial unnormalized dot product.
## Exact expectation

In one dimension write \(H_a=\{2i+a:0\le i<m\}\) with \(m=50\). Odd differences in offsets give zero intersection; equal offsets give \(m\); differences two and four give \(m-1\) and \(m-2\). Among the 25 ordered one-dimensional offset pairs there are five equal pairs, six pairs with difference two, and two pairs with difference four. Hence \[\sum_{a,c=0}^4 |H_a\cap H_c|=5m+6(m-1)+2(m-2)=13m-10.\] The two coordinate dimensions factor independently, giving \[\mathbb E\cos(\nabla_X L,\nabla_X L')=
\left(\frac{13m-10}{25m}\right)^2
=\left(\frac{64}{125}\right)^2=\frac{4096}{15625}>\frac14.\] The reviewer-written script constructs all 25 two-dimensional support sets, enumerates all 625 ordered pairs using rational arithmetic, checks their common size and independently matches this closed form. It imports no author code. The excess \(0.012144\) is exact, not Monte Carlo noise.
## Defective implication in the source proof

Appendix A.1, p. 13, Eq. (20), obtains the stricter expression \[n\le \frac{k^2(\epsilon_c-1)}{\lfloor k/S\rfloor^2}+S^2.\] It then relaxes it to \(n\le S^2\epsilon_c\) in Eq. (21). For the example, the former right-hand side is \(-11/16\) and the latter is one. A weaker necessary restriction on \(n\) does not retain a sufficient guarantee obtained from the earlier worst-case inequality. The proof therefore cannot justify using every point in the enlarged interval as safe. The exact convolution calculation demonstrates that this is a real failure of the asserted sufficiency, not just an unproved implication.
## Alternative readings, counterevidence and impact

If Lemma 1 is interpreted only as a necessary upper restriction, the counterexample does not refute that one-way reading. The main text, however, explicitly uses it to guarantee small similarity and Eq. (12) to guarantee the trade-off. That interpretation is what fails. The public `MaskedConv2d` in `model/randpos_resnet.py`, lines 321–359, multiplies one weight tensor by a mask and calls `conv2d`; the mask is spatially shared. Lines 685–733 also form a spatial mask and tile it across channels. This supports the shared-mask interpretation used here. Some released calls choose three points rather than one; the universal lemma and Table 5 explicitly include \(n=1\), so the counterexample is not a claim to reproduce the default experiment. If a different formulation independently resamples a separate mask at every spatial location, it would be a different stochastic operator requiring its own proof; no such independence assumption repairs the published shared-convolution guarantee.

The method’s introductory contribution and Section 4 explicitly rely on this bound to claim data-independent control of gradient similarity. This is a central theoretical dependency even though the empirical method may remain useful. Figures 3–4 and the grid-search heatmaps in Figure 6 are finite observations and do not establish the universal claim. The counterexample does not show a drop in CIFAR or ImageNet robustness, and it is not an attack on the trained networks. No general corrected bound is claimed: keeping an intermediate inequality is not sufficient until the earlier probability and gradient decompositions are also verified.
# Other inspected claims and limitations

Appendix A.2 was read through its normalization and probability bounds. An additional issue requiring careful rederivation is the expectation/absolute-value interchange around Eqs. (9)–(10); the present report does not assign a separate theorem finding without a fully specified normalization convention. The lower bound is therefore not independently certified.

The source reports PGD, AutoAttack, EOTPGD, transfer and adaptive attacks. The inspected `BPDA.run` in `evaluate_nonrepeated_eotbpda.py`, lines 258–323, averages independently optimized perturbations after each run rather than accumulating transformation-averaged gradients before each update. This does not by itself establish the provenance of Table 6 or quantify any robustness overestimate. A fresh appropriately adaptive evaluation, with exact checkpoints and stochastic attack settings, would be needed; no new adversarial accuracy is asserted here. Reading these code paths statically is not an execution or reproduction. The report’s supported severity rests solely on the fully checked core-bound counterexample.

Title: Technical Verification: S2-Track: A Simple yet Strong Approach for End-to-End 3D Multi-Object Tracking
# Identity and scope

S2-Track: A Simple yet Strong Approach for End-to-End 3D Multi-Object Tracking. Tao Tang; Lijun Zhou; Pengkun Hao; Zihang He; Kalok Ho; Shuo Gu; Zhihui Hao; Haiyang Sun; Kun Zhan; Peng Jia; Xianpeng Lang; Xiaodan Liang. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43683. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main text, pp. 1–9, and embedded Appendices A–D, pp. 12–17, were read. The focused technical check concerns the probabilistic decoder’s objective, its integration into the full loss, and arithmetic in the comparison and ablation tables. No public author implementation was available in the frozen packet. The supplementary video was unavailable. Thus the implemented historical loss and benchmark scores cannot be established independently here.
# Definitions and the affected objective

Section 3.3 models each attention value by a Gaussian and gives the reparameterization \(\alpha=\mu+\sigma\epsilon\), \(\epsilon\sim N(0,1)\), where \(\sigma>0\) is a standard deviation. Write \(m=q_i k_j/\sqrt d\) and \(r=\alpha-m\). The description calls Eq. (6), p. 5, a negative log-likelihood. The actual printed summand, confirmed in the original page image, is \[\ell_{\rm print}(r,\sigma)=\log\left(\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\] There is no leading minus sign, and the logarithm closes before the exponential. Section 3.5 explicitly incorporates this loss into Eq. (10) with a positive coefficient, default one; Appendix A.2.3 repeats that choice.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The specified UPD loss reverses the Gaussian scale incentive).  The printed loss is not the claimed Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The difference changes the optimization direction even in a single admissible scalar attention entry. It affects the mathematical specification of one of the paper’s three core modules.
#### Complete calculation.

Equation reference: eq:nll. For an observation \(\alpha\) from the stated Gaussian centered at \(m\), the negative logarithm of its density is \[
 \ell_{\rm NLL}(r,\sigma)=\log(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)+\frac{r^2}{2\sigma^2}.\] Take \(m=\mu=0\), allowed by zero query/key dot product and an MLP output of zero mean, and any positive \(\sigma\). At the fixed residual \(r=0\), the printed expression is \(-\log(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)\), with derivative \(-1/\sigma\); the genuine NLL has derivative \(+1/\sigma\). This is not merely an additive constant or harmless normalization.

The distinction also survives the reparameterization in the paper, so it is not dependent on a probability-zero draw. With \(\alpha=\sigma\epsilon\), direct Gaussian integration gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\ell_{\rm print}(\sigma\epsilon,\sigma)
 &=-\frac{\log(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)}{\sqrt2},\\
 \mathbb E\ell_{\rm NLL}(\sigma\epsilon,\sigma)
 &=\log(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)+\frac12.\end{aligned}\] Indeed, \(\mathbb E e^{-\epsilon^2/2}=1/\sqrt2\) and \(\mathbb E\epsilon^2=1\). Thus the printed expected loss decreases without bound as \(\sigma\to\infty\), whereas the stated NLL increases. The reviewer-written script independently integrates the former for \(\sigma=0.1,1,10,100\) and agrees with the closed form within \(10^{-10}\). This proves an error in the specified component objective; it does not prove that the full tracking loss is unbounded, because the other terms can depend on the sampled attention.
#### Counterevidence and alternative readings.

The words “negative log-likelihood” suggest that the authors may have intended Eq. [eq:nll] (#eq:nll). Enlarging the logarithm’s parentheses alone would still give a log-likelihood with the wrong sign for minimization. A full correction must change both sign and scope. A variance output \(\sigma^2\) versus standard-deviation output \(\sigma\) does not resolve this issue. A bounded positive scale does not restore the NLL identity either, though it can remove the unbounded limit. No bound is stated in the inspected specification. Reported positive ablation results are compatible with a correct implementation despite an incorrect equation. With no implementation in the packet, that possibility remains unresolved.
#### Impact and repair scope.

The assessment is Major for the invalid likelihood-based specification of the core uncertainty module: Eq. (6) defines its regularizer and Eq. (10) directly consumes it. This is not an assertion that the reported tracker fails. Replacing the summand by Eq. [eq:nll] (#eq:nll) restores the Gaussian negative-log-density identity, by taking the logarithm explicitly. It does not establish calibrated predictive uncertainty or reproduce the 4.4-point UPD gain. Moreover, the corrected NLL with freely learned scale can itself collapse at zero residual; practical scale constraints and the intended statistical target must be specified. No complete algorithmic repair or author adoption has been verified.
# Other checks and surviving evidence

Table 2’s headline difference is arithmetically correct: \(100(0.663-0.574)=8.9\) percentage points. It compares ViT-L with V2-99, explicitly shown in the table. The same-backbone V2-99 difference is 3.4 points; the larger headline difference cannot isolate the three modules from backbone effects. The controlled small-resolution ablations in Table 3 give UPD, PQI and HQD improvements of 4.4, 2.4 and 2.9 points, respectively, and a combined 6.4 points. Those are internally consistent and need not be additive.

The denoising partition is well-defined for \(0\leq\beta_{\rm lower}<\beta_{\rm upper}\leq1\): positive and negative strict inequalities are disjoint and intermediate values are ignored. Equality at a threshold can naturally join the ignored set, but the implementation is not available to check it. The backprojection formula in Section 3.2 is consistent with pinhole depth backprojection when depth means optical-axis depth and the rigid transform includes the usual homogeneous coordinate. These conditional observations do not validate the detector or its training.

Figures 4, 6 and 7 were viewed as source images. They illustrate selected occlusion examples, initial query locations, boxes and attention concentration; they do not supply calibration curves or a measured coverage guarantee for predictive uncertainty. Appendix B.2 offers a qualitative rationale, while Table 3 reports entropy and standard deviation. Lower uncertainty alone is not proof of better calibration. This is a limit of the evidence, not a second demonstrated error. Raw predictions, training seeds, evaluator configuration and the unavailable video were not inspected. No issue is asserted about the benchmark arithmetic or the PQI/HQD modules beyond the stated scope.

Title: Technical Verification: unMORE: Unsupervised Multi-Object Segmentation via Center-Boundary Reasoning
# Identity and scope

unMORE: Unsupervised Multi-Object Segmentation via Center-Boundary Reasoning. Yafei Yang; Zihui Zhang; Bo Yang. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43684. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main text, pp. 1–10, and embedded Appendix A, pp. 13–26, were read, with focused verification of distance-field normalization, boundary updates and the distinction between direct discovery and detector training. Pages 5–6 contain extraneous text in extraction; their visible original pages were read directly. The current public source snapshot was inspected statically at the recorded lines. No author code was executed and no dataset, model weights or benchmark predictions were loaded.
# Distance-field reasoning

For an object mask, Section 3.2 defines a signed distance \(S\) to the nearest boundary, positive inside. Let \(D=\max(SM)>0\) and \(f=S/D\) on the foreground. Equation (4), p. 4, asserts that \(D=1/\|
abla f\|\) at any pixel with \(f>0\). This is used to motivate the boundary displacement \(f/\|
abla f\|\) in Eq. (6), p. 6. The intended continuum calculation is straightforward: at a differentiable point of a true Euclidean distance field with unit gradient, \(
abla f=
abla S/D\) and hence \(1/\|
abla f\|=D\). The universal pixel-level wording needs more conditions.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The inverse-gradient identity does not hold at every interior pixel).  Equation (4)’s condition \(f>0\) alone neither ensures differentiability nor gives the claimed identity for a discrete gradient. This is a local mathematical overstatement, assessed Minor; no central algorithmic failure is established.
#### Exact example.

Consider the single connected square object \([-2,2]^2\) with Euclidean boundary distance \[S(x,y)=2-\max(|x|,|y|),\qquad f(x,y)=\tfrac12S(x,y)\] on its interior. Its maximum distance is \(D=2\). At its center \(f(0,0)=1>0\), so the printed condition is satisfied, but the gradient does not exist: along the \(x\) axis the left and right derivatives are \(+1/2\) and \(-1/2\). If “gradient” instead means the common central difference on unit-spaced pixels, the two components at the center are both zero, so the reciprocal norm is undefined/infinite, not two. Forward differences both equal \(-1/2\), giving \(1/\|\nabla_+f\|=\sqrt2\), again not two. The samples are also obtained exactly from the nearest boundary pixels of this square; no learned-field error is required. The independent script uses rational arithmetic for these samples and separately checks the valid regular point \((1,0)\), where the gradient is \((-1/2,0)\) and the reciprocal equals two.
#### Valid interpretation and bounded repair.

The identity is valid in the continuum at points where the signed distance is differentiable and has gradient norm one, with a positive fixed normalization constant and the same spatial metric. In a neighborhood with a unique smooth nearest-boundary projection, this follows by differentiating the Euclidean distance. Stating this restricted identity, then describing finite-difference and learned-field updates as approximations, repairs the mathematical assertion. It does not prove convergence, safe step sizes, or accuracy of the trained network. The square example does not show that the border pixel actually selected by every proposal lies on its medial ridge.
#### Material counterevidence and impact.

Appendix A.3, p. 14, explicitly replaces pointwise gradients with foreground/background averages and changes the step size, with at most 50 iterations. The public `object_reasoning.py`, lines 140–174, computes image gradients, adds numerical stabilizers to averages and reciprocals, and uses weighted reciprocal averages. Lines 441–471 apply the stopping rule, expansion/contraction adjustment, coordinate rescaling and image bounds. Thus the actual released algorithm is not the singular pointwise rule alone. These provisions are relevant counterevidence against inferring a catastrophic implementation failure from Eq. (4). No benchmark damage has been demonstrated, and the empirical contribution may survive this correction.
# Source correspondence and other checks

There are useful specification distinctions that prevent stronger conclusions. First, the released averaging is \(w/a+(1-w)/b\), whereas a literal reciprocal of the combined gradient average in Appendix Eqs. (7)–(8) is \(1/(wa+(1-w)b)\). For positive \(a,b\), these need not agree: at \(a=1,b=2,w=\operatorname{sigmoid}(0.5)\) they are approximately \(0.81123\) and \(0.72593\). This is an algebraic correspondence check, not an estimate of the actual gradient averages or benchmark error. The exact historical implementation is not established by the current commit.

Second, Eq. (1) and `datasets.py`, lines 200–208, define outward center vectors, while the surrounding prose describes inward directions. Appendix A.3 instead describes an inward kernel, whereas the main text describes an outward one. Simultaneously reversing field and kernel preserves their dot products; this sign discrepancy does not alone demonstrate that the released splitting procedure is wrong. Third, Table 4 lists a final ReLU for signed outputs, but the inspected prediction heads end with a linear convolution (or an explicitly selected signed activation); the `relu` branch has ReLU only in hidden layers. A literal terminal ReLU cannot represent negative distances, but the static source supplies a plausible corrected reading. These observations are retained as correspondence limitations, not inflated into independent empirical failures.

Training uses pseudo masks from ImageNet and distinguishes a frozen objectness network from an optional additional class-agnostic detector. Consequently, “network-free reasoning” cannot mean that inference never queries a neural network; Section 3.3 explicitly does so. Human/SAM-assisted additions to COCO* are evaluation annotations as described in A.16, not demonstrated supervision leakage into objectness training. The reported counts satisfy \(36{,}781+10{,}336=47{,}117\). Table 1’s full-method mask AP improvement over CuVLER is \(15.5-12.6=2.9\) points; Table 7’s original-COCO improvement is \(11.7-10.4=1.3\). These verify table arithmetic only. Label quality, split overlap, setting selection and uncertainty of the empirical comparisons were not independently measured.

Figures 3–4 and 10 show the intended proposal-splitting and boundary-update behavior; Figure 11 explicitly shows failures on overlapping objects, consistent with A.14’s limitation. Figure 17’s average update magnitude falls to a nonzero plateau near four pixels. This supports a practical tolerance-based stopping interpretation, not a mathematical claim of zero update or universal convergence. No such general convergence theorem is established by this review. The remaining result tables and feature visualizations were read as reported evidence, with the visual coverage limited to pages recorded in the ledger.
