Title: Technical Verification: An Error Analysis of Flow Matching for Deep Generative Modeling
# Identity and scope

An Error Analysis of Flow Matching for Deep Generative Modeling. Zhengyu Zhou; Weiwei Liu. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43685. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main paper, pp. 1–8, and proof Appendices A–D, pp. 12–30, were read. The detailed checks below cover the covariance argument underlying the improved rate, the approximation construction, and the discretization balance. Generalization and coupling arguments were traced, but the external approximation and covering-number references were not independently audited. No author repository was available in the frozen source packet. This is a mathematical review, with no training experiment or author program executed.
# Setup and proof dependencies

The prior is \(X_0\sim N(0,I_d)\), independent of the target \(X_1\). The interpolant is \(X_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1\) and \(v^*(x,t)=\mathbb E[X_1-X_0\mid X_t=x]\). Assumption 1.1 confines the target to \([0,1]^d\). Assumption 1.2 writes its density as \(e^{-V}\) and requires a twice continuously differentiable potential with \(-\alpha I\preceq\nabla^2 V\preceq\alpha I\), \(\alpha>1\). Lemma 1.4 asserts a spatial Lipschitz constant uniform over \(\mathbb R^d\times[0,1]\). Theorem 1.7 inserts that constant into the approximation, generalization and sampling bounds to claim rate \(\widetilde O(n^{-1/[3(d+5)]})\). The bounded-support consistency theorem, Theorem 1.6, uses the weaker time-dependent Lipschitz bound instead.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The bounded-support covariance lower bound is false).  Lemma D.8, p. 28, asserts \(\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(X)\succeq(\mathbb E_\mu\nabla^2U)^{-1}\) for a density \(e^{-U}\) on an arbitrary convex set, assuming only twice continuous differentiability. This statement is false on a bounded interval. It is used explicitly in Eq. (69), p. 29, and therefore invalidates the supplied derivation of the core uniform Lipschitz lemma.
#### Counterexample satisfying the lemma’s conditions.

Take \(d=1\), \(\Omega=[0,1]\), \(Z=\int_0^1e^{-y^2/2}\,dy\) and \[U(y)=\tfrac12y^2+\log Z,\qquad \mu(dy)=Z^{-1}e^{-y^2/2}\,dy\quad\hbox{on }\Omega.\] The set is convex; \(U\) is smooth and even strictly convex; the density integrates to one; and \(U''=1\), so the asserted lower bound is one. But any random variable in \([0,1]\) satisfies \[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E(Y-\tfrac12)^2-(\mathbb EY-\tfrac12)^2\leq\tfrac14<1.\] This is an exact contradiction independent of numerical precision. Reviewer quadrature additionally evaluates the variance as approximately \(0.07965\). The usual boundary-free integration-by-parts reasoning cannot simply be applied on this interval; the boundary density is nonzero.
#### The two readings of the target assumption.

If \(V\) is finite and \(C^2\) on all of \(\mathbb R^d\), \(e^{-V}\) is everywhere positive, contradicting bounded support. Then the simultaneous assumptions of the improved-rate theorem have no examples. If smoothness is intended only on the support, the truncated Gaussian above satisfies Assumptions 1.1–1.2 in that interpretation with \(\alpha=2\). It nevertheless defeats the uniform Lipschitz conclusion, as follows.

Equation reference: eq:jac. For \(d=1\), write \(s=1-t\). At \(x=0\), the conditional target density is proportional to \(\exp(-Ay^2/2)\) on \([0,1]\), with \(A=1+t^2/s^2\). Direct differentiation of the conditional-mean formula gives the valid identity from Lemma D.5: \[
 \partial_xv^*(0,t)=\frac{t}{s^3}\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X_t=0)-\frac1s.\] After setting \(z=\sqrt A\,y\), the conditional variance is \(A^{-1}\) times that of a standard Gaussian restricted to \([0,\sqrt A]\). As \(t\uparrow1\), this latter variance tends to \(1-2/\pi\). Consequently, \[\lim_{t\uparrow1}(1-t)\partial_xv^*(0,t)=-2/\pi,\] so the derivative is unbounded. At \(t=0.99\) independent quadrature already gives magnitude above 63, whereas the printed \(\zeta(2,1)=\frac12(2+\sqrt{2+2})^2=8\). The conditioning is legitimate: for every \(t<1\) the Gaussian convolution has a positive smooth density at \(x=0\). This is not a counterexample to the logically empty global-potential interpretation; it shows why restricting the potential to the cube does not repair the result.
#### Impact and possible correction.

The assessment is Major because the false lower bound supplies the essential cancellation in Eq. (69) and Lemmas D.9/1.4, which Theorem C.5/1.7 uses explicitly. The weaker Lemma D.6 does not use this lower bound. Extending the target to full support with suitable integrability and boundary conditions may support a different argument, but also removes Assumption 1.1 and requires new approximation/tail analysis. No such complete repair is verified here; the improved rate is not established by its present proof.

Problem 2 (The approximation proof cannot combine sharp zero extension with uniform boundary approximation).  Appendix A.1, pp. 12–13, uniformly approximates \(v^*\) on \(K=[-R,R]^d\) and says that the constructed ReLU network is identically zero outside \(K\), from which global Lipschitz continuity is asserted. Those simultaneous construction properties are impossible for admissible targets whose velocity is nonzero on the boundary.
#### Exact check.

Let \(d=1\) and \(X_1=0\) almost surely. This satisfies Assumption 1.1 and gives \(v^*(x,t)=-x/(1-t)\), which is spatially Lipschitz on every \([0,T]\) with \(T<1\). At \(t=0\) its value at \(R\) is \(-R\). Every finite ReLU network is continuous; if it is zero for all \(x>R\), it must also be zero at \(x=R\). Its uniform approximation error on \(K\) is therefore at least \(R\), contradicting the claimed arbitrary tolerance \(\epsilon<R\). This is a counterexample to the stated construction properties, not to the existential \(L^2\) approximation theorem.

The explicit partition has a separate visible endpoint defect. The notation \([N]=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\) is defined on p. 3. At \(x'=1\) all terms \(\psi(3N(x'-m/N))\) vanish, because \(3(N-m)\geq3\) and \(\psi\) vanishes beyond two. Thus the proposed sum is zero, not a partition of unity. At \(x'=-1/(6N)\) its \(m=0\) term equals one, so the factors do not vanish immediately outside the cube either. Both facts are checked exactly for \(N=1,2,4,10\) by a reviewer-written rational calculation.
#### Counterevidence, impact and scope.

Adding endpoint nodes and tapering on an enlarged cube are plausible ways to change the construction, and the cited approximation literature may contain suitable constructions. They were not established by the displayed proof. A taper needs a new Lipschitz bound and tail estimate; merely imposing a hard cutoff is discontinuous. This is a Major gap in the construction used by Theorems 3.1 and 4.4 and hence both main guarantees. No impossibility of learning bounded-support targets is claimed, and no full network-class repair is certified.

Problem 3 (The stated mesh exponent does not yield the claimed rate from the supplied discretization bound).  Even conditionally granting the preceding lemmas, the last substitution in Theorem C.5, pp. 24–25, does not establish its asserted rate using the parameters in Theorem 3.1.
#### Exponent calculation.

Let \(a=1/[3(d+5)]\), \(s=1-T=n^{-a}\) and \(h=\max_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)\). The theorem chooses \(h=O(n^{-4a})\). Its network class allows \(K=\widetilde O(s^{-1})\) and \(\gamma_2=\widetilde O(s^{-4})\). On a uniform mesh, \(\sqrt{\sum_k(\Delta t_k)^3}=h\sqrt T\). Thus the displayed discretization estimate yields only \[\widetilde O((K+\gamma_2)h)=\widetilde O(n^{4a}n^{-4a})=\widetilde O(1),\] whereas the early-stopping term is \(n^{-a}\) and the estimation term is \(s^{-2}n^{-1/(d+5)}=n^{-a}\). Exact fraction arithmetic in the script confirms these exponents for several dimensions; the symbolic expression holds for every \(d\geq1\).

This is failure of the given upper-bound argument, not a lower bound on actual Euler error. A smaller mesh \(h=O(n^{-5a})\) makes that same discretization upper bound \(\widetilde O(n^{-a})\), conditional on the other lemmas. Such a smaller mesh also belongs to \(O(n^{-4a})\), so an existential interpretation of “choose” can accommodate it. The printed condition alone and the claimed direct substitution do not ensure it. The impact is Major for the supplied core rate derivation, separately from Problems 1–2. The stronger mesh repairs this algebraic step only; it does not restore the false covariance argument or complete the approximation proof.
# Checked steps that do survive and remaining limits

Lemma 4.1’s least-squares orthogonality is valid: conditioning on \(X_t\) makes the residual \(X_1-X_0-v^*(X_t,t)\) orthogonal to any square-integrable function of \(X_t\). Its \(1/T\) normalization must be retained (Eq. (5) omits that factor). The early-stopping coupling gives \(W_2(\pi_T,\pi_1)\leq(1-T)\sqrt{\mathbb E\|X_1-X_0\|^2}\leq(1-T)\sqrt{2d}\) under the stated bounded support and Gaussian prior. The flow stability and Euler error arguments have the usual Gronwall structure conditional on a network with the required bounds. These valid conditional steps do not fill the construction gaps.

The generalization section uses empirical risk minimization; an exact minimizer is an assumption of the analysis, not a computational guarantee for gradient training. No numerical experiment is supplied in the paper, and no such validation is manufactured here. The report does not assert that all final theorems are false: it distinguishes a false covariance lemma, vacuity versus an invalid on-support extension, and two incomplete core proof steps. Scientific adjudication remains pending and no author correction was established from the frozen packet.

Title: Technical Verification: DCTdiff: Intriguing Properties of Image Generative Modeling in the DCT Space
# Identity and scope

DCTdiff: Intriguing Properties of Image Generative Modeling in the DCT Space. Mang Ning; Mingxiao Li; Jianlin Su; Jia Haozhe; Lanmiao Liu; Martin Benes; Wenshuo Chen; Albert Ali Salah; Itir Onal Ertugrul. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43686. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main text, pp. 1–9, and Appendix A–C, pp. 13–27, were read. Verification concentrates on the two spectral statements, the SNR rescaling, token counts and the correspondence of selected released source routines. Tables and sample captions were read, but generated images, FID statistics and training costs were not reproduced. The source commit is dated April 2026; its identity with the code used for the published experiments is not established. No author program was run or imported.
# Model and checked algebra

DCTdiff converts RGB to YCbCr, subsamples the two chroma channels, applies an orthonormal block DCT and groups four luminance blocks with two chroma blocks. With \(N=hw/(4B^2)\) tokens and \(6(B^2-m)\) retained coefficients per token, the dimension relative to \(3hw\) RGB values is \((B^2-m)/(2B^2)\). Thus the compression factors in Table 1 are \(4\) for \((B,m)=(4,8)\) and \(64/9\simeq7.11\) for \((8,46)\). These are coefficient-count ratios; chroma reduction and coefficient deletion are lossy operations. Section 5.2 explicitly uses “lossless” operationally to mean reconstruction FID below \(0.5\), not exact invertibility. A small FID does not prove preservation of every image detail.

The SNR rescaling in Appendix A.2 is algebraically sound when \(c>0\) and the intended schedule is \(\beta(t)=a+bt\). Write \(y(t)=at+bt^2/2\) and \[F(t)=y(t)-\log c+\log(1+(c-1)e^{-y(t)}).\] Then \(e^{-F}/(1-e^{-F})=c/(e^y-1)\) and \(F'(t)=\beta(t)/(1+(c-1)e^{-y(t)})\). This proves Eq. (19), including recovery of the original schedule at \(c=1\). Solving \(\lambda=\frac12\log\operatorname{SNR}'\) gives \(y=\log(1+ce^{-2\lambda})\) and Eq. (30). The independent calculation checks the ratio and inverse at four times for \(c=4\). The introductory expression \(at+b\) on p. 14 swaps the constants relative to the subsequent derivation and code; the latter consistently use \(a+bt\).
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The spectral power identity omits the drift restriction).  Theorem 5.1, p. 6, states \(\mathbb E|\widehat x_t(k)|^2=|\widehat x_0(k)|^2+\int_0^t g(s)^2ds\) for an SDE with a general drift \(f\). The proof immediately assumes \(f=0\). The unrestricted statement is false, including for the VP family actually used in Section 4.4.
#### Exact check and correction.

Use a finite orthonormal transform and a deterministic initial image with one transform coefficient equal to one. Let each pixel solve \(dx=-x\,dt/2+dW\) independently. The transformed coefficient satisfies the same Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation, so \[\mathbb E|\widehat x_t(k)|^2=e^{-t}|\widehat x_0(k)|^2+1-e^{-t}=1.\] The printed expression gives \(1+t\), hence two at \(t=1\). All coefficients of this SDE are smooth, and there is no transform-normalization ambiguity. More generally, for the VP kernel in Eq. (7), with \(a_t=\exp(-\int_0^t\beta)\), the correct identity is \[\mathbb E|\widehat x_t(k)|^2=a_t|\widehat x_0(k)|^2+(1-a_t).\] It follows directly by linearity and covariance preservation of a unitary transform; for zero drift the paper’s formula is valid under that normalization. The main proof’s \(\mathbb E|\widehat\epsilon|=0\) should be the zero mean of \(\widehat\epsilon\), as correctly used in Appendix A.3.
#### Impact and counterevidence.

This is assessed Minor because the intended restricted claim is explicit in both proofs and the VP correction preserves the frequency-order argument: if the initial spectrum decreases with frequency, \(a_t|\widehat x_0(k)|^2/(1-a_t)\) crosses a fixed SNR threshold earlier at higher frequencies. This is an SNR ordering, not an exact factorization into a frequency-autoregressive generator. Appendix A.4 and the released implementation already use the VP kernel. The evidence does not invalidate the training method or its reported FIDs. The finite orthonormal formulation also avoids Appendix A.3’s formal integral over the infinite spatial line, which would need a spectral-density normalization.

Problem 2 (The upsampling approximation has no stated aliasing-error condition).  Theorem 5.2 and Appendix A.5 replace a parity-selected cosine by an average of two cosines, yielding Eq. (12) with an approximation sign. No error bound or small-high-frequency assumption is part of the theorem. The approximation can miss the entire low-resolution coefficient for an admissible image.
#### Exact finite-dimensional derivation.

Let \(C_N\) be the orthonormal DCT-II matrix and let \(P\) average adjacent pairs. For \(0<k<B\), the only nonzero entries in row \(k\) of \(C_BP C_{2B}^{\top}\) are \[M_{k,k}=\frac{\cos\theta_k}{\sqrt2},\qquad
 M_{k,2B-k}=-\frac{\sin\theta_k}{\sqrt2},\qquad \theta_k=\frac{k\pi}{4B}.\] The row \(k=0\) has only \(M_{0,0}=1/\sqrt2\). These identities follow by averaging the two neighboring inverse-DCT cosines and using discrete cosine orthogonality. Hence the exact two-dimensional transformation is \(\overline D=MDM^{\top}\). In particular, \[\overline D(k,0)=\tfrac12\cos\theta_kD(k,0)-\tfrac12\sin\theta_kD(2B-k,0).\] The second term is missing from Eq. (12). Set \(B=2\), add a constant pixel background of 128, and set the sole non-DC coefficient to \(D(3,0)=64\). The resulting \(4\times4\) pixels lie inside \([0,255]\), so this is also a valid bounded grayscale image. Its \(D(1,0)=0\), while \(\overline D(1,0)=-32\sin(\pi/8)\simeq-12.246\). Equation (12)’s retained term is zero. Reviewer-written matrices verify the exact alias identities for \(B=2,4,8\) to floating-point precision; the trigonometric derivation explains the discrepancy independently of rounding.
#### Repair and scope.

If every high-frequency coefficient having either index at least \(B\) vanishes, the claimed approximation becomes exact. More generally, the error is exactly the sum of the omitted two cross-alias terms and one double-alias term of \(MDM^{\top}\), so their absolute values give an immediate bound. This is a verified conditional repair, not a guarantee that arbitrary natural images satisfy a numerical tolerance. Since the paper explicitly marks the relation approximate and motivates zero filling by small high-frequency energy, the finding is assessed Minor: the theorem needs a stated approximation regime, but no falsification of the selected FID comparison follows. The source upsampling routine implements the low-frequency inverse and zero fill; its FID helper downsamples with bicubic interpolation, whereas the theorem assumes average pooling. That empirical comparison therefore does not directly test the theorem’s exact operator assumptions. Appendix A.10 candidly reports that substituting DCT upsampling into an existing super-resolution model worsens FID from 10.71 to 14.53; superiority is not universal.
# Source and empirical boundaries

Static reading confirms common-\(\eta\) scaling, zigzag deletion, six-block token layout and coefficientwise squared-error weighting. The named entropy is computed by 100-bin histograms on \([-1,1]\) after percentile filtering; it is not differential entropy. A common rescaling does not literally preserve differential entropy (\(h(X/\eta)=h(X)-\log\eta\)), so the entropy-consistent wording is best read as retaining relative spectral scale. The reported positive histogram weights avoid the unbounded objective that negative differential-entropy weights would create.

The released `squared_diffusion_integral(s,t)` applies the nonlinear rescaling to \(y(t)-y(s)\), rather than returning \(F(t)-F(s)\). These differ for \(s>0,c\ne1\); the independent arithmetic records a discrepancy at \((s,t)=(0.2,0.7),c=4\). The inspected call sites use \(s=0\) for marginals, where they agree, while the Euler sampler uses drift and diffusion directly. Thus this is a bounded API correspondence observation, not demonstrated damage to published training or sampling.

Table 2 explicitly has CelebA/DPM-Solver exceptions to the broad performance claim. Table 5’s 2.5-fold step-count improvement is \(750/300\), and its AFHQ per-forward-pass ratio is \(133/575\simeq0.231\). These do not by themselves establish a wall-clock training ratio including all backward passes and preprocessing. Table 6 reports a high-NFE inference disadvantage, while Appendix A.9 compares different NFEs at better FID. Table 14 is a progressive ablation rather than a full factorial experiment. Figure 6 visibly shows high-frequency power approaching the noise floor earlier; Figures 7 and 10 illustrate selected perturbation and upsampling behavior. These images do not measure uncertainty, prove universal sharpness, or reproduce FID. The later sample grids were read through their captions; only the source pages recorded in the coverage ledger received image-level inspection.

Title: Technical Verification: Unlocking the Capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models for Generalizable and Explainable Deepfake Detection
# Identity and scope

Unlocking the Capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models for Generalizable and Explainable Deepfake Detection. Peipeng Yu; Jianwei Fei; Hui Gao; Xuan Feng; Zhihua Xia; Chip Hong Chang. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43687. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The main text, pp. 1–9, and the embedded appendix, pp. 13–19, were read, including the video-level evaluation rule and failure-case discussion. The dialogue screenshots on pp. 17–19 and the relevant main-text visualizations were examined as images. Static source review covers the current inference example, KFD-to-language input path and selected architecture routines. There is no benchmark rerun, author-code execution, weight inspection, or patient/person-specific inference in this review. The February 2026 source snapshot is later than the publication and is not assumed identical to the experimental implementation.
# What the reported evaluation measures

KFD produces a localization map and a continuous forgery score. The language model receives visual embeddings, forgery embeddings and an explicit textual KFD score. Appendix A.1 resolves an ambiguity in the main text: the language-model score for video \(v\) is \[s_v=\frac1{32}\sum_{j=1}^{32}\mathbf{1}\{\text{frame }j\text{ is parsed as fake}\}.\] This has 33 possible values. Its empirical AUC is the fraction of positive-negative video pairs correctly ranked, with half credit for ties. It is a legitimate, albeit quantized, ranking statistic; it is not necessarily the balanced accuracy of a single binary response. An exact reviewer calculation with positive scores \(16/32,24/32\) and negative scores \(1/32,8/32\) gives AUC one. Calling the paper’s use of AUC invalid merely because frame outputs are binary would therefore be incorrect. This score is a vote fraction, not a demonstrated calibrated posterior probability.

The KFD and full LVLM scores should also remain distinct. Table 3 reports KFD AUCs \(99.53,94.71,99.64,97.62,91.81\) and LVLM AUCs \(97.11,89.90,92.26,95.97,86.70\) on the same five listed datasets. The latter are lower throughout. The contribution is an interactive system with strong reported cross-dataset detection, not an established increase in detection accuracy caused by the language decoder. Appendix A.4 explicitly acknowledges this tradeoff.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The released response parser can inherit a previous image’s label).  In `inference.py`, lines 94–112, the loop sets `pred` only inside a sequence of substring conditions. There is no per-image initialization or unmatched-response branch. This conflicts with Appendix A.1’s rule that an unmatched response is labeled real.
#### Independent logical check.

Take the response “The image is a genuine photograph.” It contains none of the tested strings: `pristine`, `deepfake`, capitalized `Yes` or `No`. If the previous image set `pred=1`, the current printed judgment remains fake; if the previous value was zero, it remains real. On the first image the name has not been assigned. This follows from the visible module-level control flow and does not depend on any model weights. A reviewer-written transition model of the six ordered conditions confirms outputs \((\text{unassigned},0,1)\) for previous states \((\text{unassigned},0,1)\). It does not import or execute the author script. The case-sensitive tests and order of overrides also differ from the prose’s lowercase keyword specification.
#### Impact and bounded repair.

This is Minor and limited to the released inference helper: its printed judgment is not a function of the current image response alone for unmatched text. Initializing the label to zero at each iteration implements the documented default and removes this state carryover. It does not solve every linguistic ambiguity; an explicit case-normalized parser with a documented negation/precedence rule and an unmatched-response count is needed for a reproducible evaluator. No author file was changed. The frozen source does not provide the 32-frame video AUC evaluation loop, so neither the frequency of unmatched benchmark outputs nor any resulting change to published AUC is established. The observed helper error must not be silently extrapolated to the historical evaluation.

Problem 2 (The dataset attribution in the timing table is inconsistent with the main tables).  Appendix Table 10, p. 14, is titled as a CDF2 comparison. Its AUC vector for CADDM, Ours-KFD, FAK-Owl and Ours-LVLM is \((85.68,97.62,69.84,95.97)\). Every entry instead matches that method’s CDF1 value in Tables 1 or 3.

For comparison, the corresponding CDF2 entries in those tables are \((93.88,94.71,60.85,89.90)\). The matching CDF1 vector and mismatching CDF2 vector are independently transcribed and compared in the check output, and the original Table 10 was visually checked. A caption error is a plausible explanation, but raw evaluation records are absent, so this review cannot determine which dataset was actually timed or replace the published entries. This is a Minor reporting defect: the claimed joint speed/AUC operating point has ambiguous dataset identity. Correcting the caption or the AUC column must be tied to the original run; no correction is certified here.

Related numerical differences need provenance rather than invented explanations. Table 7 gives Vicuna-7B DFD AUC \(84.26\), whereas Table 3 gives \(92.26\), an eight-point difference. Table 7’s mean \(86.25\) agrees with its own four entries to rounding, so this is not simply a bad mean. Table 6 also uses results different from the main FF++ training row. Different checkpoints or settings could explain these differences, but those distinctions are not stated sufficiently to reconcile them. They remain unresolved correspondence questions, not proof that the underlying measurements are false.
# Knowledge, localization and explanation: bounded evidence

The method’s external descriptions and reference-based training are scientifically relevant but not fully validated by the available release. Appendix A.1 lists rich pristine/fake descriptors and says their feature dimension is 4096. The inspected source constructs only the literal “real” and “fake” text inputs before combining each with a shared learned context; its image decoder maps 1280-dimensional patch features to 1024, while 4096 is the language-model embedding width. This is a concrete correspondence difference, not evidence that the historical model never used the listed descriptions. The acquired subset contains the inference path but not the full two-stage data-generation/training/evaluation pipeline. Historical configuration, descriptor selection and ROP training effects remain unverified.

The explicit KFD score is present in the published prompt and in the source generation path. Supplying a model prediction is not ground-truth leakage. However, the language model can obtain authenticity information from that scalar independently of fine-grained spatial embeddings. Table 5’s FPL ablation shows substantial reported gains, but does not separately quantify a score-only prompt, maps with the scalar removed, and all inputs together. Consequently, it supports the combined interface more directly than a causal claim that localized prompt features alone explain the classification gain. Such controlled comparisons would clarify the attribution; no outcome of those missing experiments is predicted here.

Figures 4–5 show attention/localization maps and selected textual descriptions. They support the ability to emit regional descriptions but provide no measured localization IoU, explanation faithfulness score or population-level dialogue accuracy. Figure 6 explicitly contains classification errors and unsupported descriptions despite its asserted correct locations. The multi-turn screenshots include repetition of a supplied forgery score and general facial-content statements. These are useful examples of interaction, but neither a highlighted face nor a repeated score establishes faithful reasoning about the artifact. No ground-truth masks or independent annotations were available for quantitative verification of the selected examples.

The real/fake mixture in Eq. (6) is an alpha-mask blend as written, whereas the prose calls the simulation Poisson blending. The full data-generation routine is not in the acquired subset, so this wording cannot identify which procedure generated the training pairs. Likewise, use of real FF++ images to synthesize training forgeries is disclosed; it does not mean that all training examples remain pristine. The paper’s DF40 description shares an FF++ source domain, so that experiment is principally cross-manipulation, distinct from the separate cross-dataset tests. No identity leakage is established without the actual split manifests.
# Checked comparisons and remaining limits

The independent script verifies Table 3 means \(96.662\) (KFD) and \(92.388\) (LVLM), Table 8 means \(89.9975\) without ROP and \(90.815\) with ROP, and selected ablation differences. Table 8’s ROP effect is not positive in every dataset: DFDC changes from \(79.31\) to \(79.12\). Table 1 likewise does not support universal superiority: CDF2 AUC is below LAANet, DFDC below UDD/RepDFD, and DFDCP below RepDFD. Table 2 contains InSwapper and FS-vid2vid exceptions. The results can support competitive or selected-dataset improvements without an across-all-methods, across-all-datasets claim.

Some baselines have missing columns or different fine-tuning protocols, as their captions disclose; averages across different available datasets are not a matched comparison. No independent split audit, seed variability, evaluator validation, raw-score audit or pretrained-data-overlap check was performed. These limitations leave empirical strength and explanation faithfulness open for further evidence, while the two verified local defects justify the Minor assessment. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

problems.source_location: p5 Eqs7-10 and p6 opening conclusion
claim: Periodic polarity stimulation yields chaos by the given analysis
analysis: Check: Recurrence substitution, unique positive equilibrium proof and contracting alternating-input example

Independent verification. Original claim and assumptions: Read and visually checked physical p.5 Eqs.(4),(7)-(10), and p.6 opening assertion of periodic-input chaos. Title: Technical Verification: A Chaotic Dynamics Framework Inspired by Dorsal Stream for Event Signal Processing
# Identity and scope

A Chaotic Dynamics Framework Inspired by Dorsal Stream for Event Signal Processing. Yu Chen; Jing Lian; Zhaofei Yu; Jizhao Liu; Jisheng Dang; Gang Wang. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43688. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The full scientific text, pp. 1–8, was read, including the recurrence derivation, Gaussian transform, threshold rule and all three result tables. The ten-page published PDF contains no appendix; separate OpenReview material was unavailable during source preparation. Relevant dataset conversion, network and evaluation source files were read statically. No author code, data conversion, training or inference was executed. Independent calculations below implement only mathematical checks written by the reviewer.
# Core mechanism and dependency

The method groups events by spatial coordinate, feeds the polarity sequence to an uncoupled recurrence, transforms its output, sums transform coefficients and thresholds their signs to form an event image. With \(a=e^{-\alpha_f}\), \(q=e^{-\alpha_e}\) and \(\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}\), Eq. (4) reads \[U_k=aU_{k-1}+V_k,\quad E_k=qE_{k-1}+V_EY_{k-1},\quad Y_k=\sigma(U_k-E_k).\] The central explanation is that changing polarity yields chaos, constant polarity yields periodicity, and the transform coefficient sign separates the two. Neither this explanation nor its literal transform specification is established by the displayed derivation.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The printed transform cannot produce the signs needed by the core representation).  Equation (12), p. 6, integrates \(Y(t)\) against a strictly positive Gaussian with a positive normalization. Equation (4) makes \(0<Y_k<1\) for all finite states. Thus the claimed negative transform coefficients, used by Eqs. (13)–(14), are impossible under the printed transform.

For \(a,\sigma_0>0\) and a nonzero observation interval, the displayed quantity is \[C(a,b)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi a}\,\sigma_0}\int_0^K
 Y(t)\exp\!\left(-\frac{(t-b)^2}{2a^2\sigma_0^2}\right)dt>0.\] Here any positive interpolation of the sigmoid samples gives the strict inequality; a positive-weight discrete quadrature has the same property. It is independent of whether the signal is periodic, chaotic or neither. Consequently, every nonempty coefficient sum in Eq. (13) is positive. Interpreting the threshold input \(f\) as that sum, as the surrounding prose says, Eq. (14) returns zero at every such location. A literal implementation therefore cannot produce Figure 8’s nonblank event frames or the proposed sign-based separation. Reviewer quadrature of constant- and alternating-polarity trajectories checks positive coefficients at several scales and shifts, but the pointwise sign proof is the decisive evidence.
#### Counterevidence and correction limits.

The released conversion routines instead specify `wavename="gaus1"` and scales `arange(1,4)`. The official PyWavelets documentation defines this family as derivatives of a normalized Gaussian; `gaus1` is the first derivative. [Footnote: PyWavelets, Continuous Wavelet Transform, Gaussian Derivative Wavelets, consulted 25 October 2026: https://pywavelets.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ref/cwt.html.] That signed, zero-mean kernel can produce negative coefficients and is materially different from Eq. (12). This supports a plausible kernel-specification error rather than a claim that all released outputs are zero. Correcting the kernel can remove the positivity contradiction, but does not prove that the sum of its finite-window coefficients separates chaotic and periodic dynamics. The source also uses three scales, while the text describes ten. The assessment is Major because the written operator defeats the central representation mechanism; no conclusion that the reported benchmark measurements are fabricated or that every corrected implementation fails is warranted.

Equation (14) is additionally a nonlinear sign threshold, not a linear low-pass filter: for \(h(s)=255\mathbf{1}_{s<0}\), \(h(-2)=255\ne2h(-1)=510\). This is a terminology/operator distinction within the same finding. Its behavior at zero and the spatial indexing in Eq. (15) should also be specified, but they do not cause the positivity contradiction.

Problem 2 (The recurrence and equilibrium calculations do not establish periodic-input chaos).  Equations (7)–(10), pp. 5–6, contain incorrect recurrence and fixed-point reasoning. The concluding “therefore” that periodic stimulation generates chaos does not follow.
#### The input filter.

The exact solution is \[U_k=a^kU_0+\sum_{j=1}^k a^{k-j}V_j.\] For a persistent periodic input it approaches a periodic response, rather than decaying to zero. The proposed Eq. (7) is a decaying sinusoid. Even taking its own initial value and the paper’s sinusoidal input \(V_k=\sin(k\pi/2)\), substitution fails the recurrence: at \(\alpha_f=0.1,k=101\), the independent residual \(U_k-aU_{k-1}-V_k\) is approximately \(-1\). No initial condition can repair this asymptotic mismatch. The text also identifies \((0,1,0,1,\ldots)\) with \(\sin(k\pi/2)\), although the latter includes negative values. These are different inputs.
#### The equilibrium.

For a fixed \(U\) and \(0<q<1\), Eq. (8) is \[E(1+e^{E-U})=c,\qquad c=V_E/(1-q)>0.\] There is exactly one solution: a nonpositive \(E\) cannot solve it, and on \(E>0\) the left side has derivative \(1+e^{E-U}(1+E)>0\), starts at zero and diverges. Replacing the exponential by a first-order Taylor polynomial without a remainder bound changes the equation. The resulting quadratic’s negative root is not an equilibrium of Eq. (8). Its actual discriminant is \((U-2)^2+4V_E/(1-q)\), whereas Eq. (10) uses \(4V_E(1-q)\). Under nonconstant periodic forcing, \(U\) itself is not fixed; the appropriate object is a periodically forced orbit, not two time-dependent expressions labeled equilibria. Even a valid count of equilibria would not by itself establish chaos.
#### A fully admissible nonchaotic periodic-input example.

The derivation supplies only positive parameters, without a specified chaotic parameter domain. Choose \(a=q=1/2\) and \(V_E=1\), and alternate polarities \(+1,-1\). On its limiting two-cycle \(U\) alternates between \(2/3\) and \(-2/3\). For each fixed value of \(U\), the threshold-state map is \[G_U(E)=\tfrac12E+\sigma(U-E),\qquad
 \tfrac14\le G_U'(E)=\tfrac12-\sigma(U-E)(1-\sigma(U-E))\le\tfrac12.\] Thus the two-step map is a contraction with constant at most \(1/4\). It has a unique attracting two-cycle, and its output cannot be chaotic. The interval \([0,2]\) is invariant; the same derivative bound gives global attraction. Taking \(U\) initially on the two-cycle satisfies the original recurrence exactly. Independent iteration from two different threshold states confirms convergence, but the contraction proof establishes the result. The release’s different parameters \((\alpha_f,\alpha_e,V_E)=(0.1,1,50)\) are not covered by this counterexample; their behavior has not been certified here.
#### Impact.

This is Major because the invalid derivation underlies the central dynamical rationale, independently of the transform defect. It shows that the parameter-free implication is false and that the supplied proof does not validate the selected regime. It does not prove that chaotic behavior is impossible for other parameter choices. A repair needs the correct forced recurrence, explicit parameters/initialization and defensible dynamical diagnostics or analysis, then a separate demonstration linking that behavior to the event representation. Neither waveform irregularity nor a finite phase portrait in Figures 4–5 supplies that full repair.
# Static-source correspondence and experimental limits

Several concrete release differences prevent treating it as a faithful executable specification of the paper. The N-CARS routine uses a negative-sum test (lines 222–225), whereas N-Caltech101 uses a nonzero-sum test (lines 123–126), retaining positive as well as negative values. Both keep neuron states outside the per-pixel and per-file loops, so different pixels share an evolving state despite the stated uncoupled, coordinate-wise design. For example, at the released initialization and parameters, two identical one-event positive-polarity pixels processed consecutively have different sigmoid outputs; independently resetting their states would make them identical. The reviewer calculation records this state-dependence without executing either converter. No benchmark impact is inferred from this tiny diagnostic.

The supplied `ResNet34` constructor returns four stages with \([2,2,2,2]\) basic blocks and width 32; the shown constructor contains no pretrained-weight loading or dropout. The training/testing files refer to externally undefined loaders and optimizer variables. These observations do not identify the full historical classifier or reproduce the claimed 21.9M parameters. The IoU script selects a timestamp window via `ts < first_ts + frame_length`, whereas Table 3 labels the conditions by event counts. Its box-area formula is ordinary intersection-over-union for positive-area, axis-aligned boxes; no complete annotation/matching or empty-contour audit was performed. The available script has visibly incomplete code, so no runnable-reproduction claim is made.

The text uses a 3:1:1 random split for each dataset and compares published baseline accuracies, without sufficient split/run records to establish matched protocols. Results from separately trained dataset-specific classifiers do not alone measure transfer to an unseen task or robustness to altered sampling, noise or event rates. Table 1 gives N-Caltech101 \(84.4\) versus the abstract’s \(84.3\); its advantage over HATS is \(84.4-64.2=20.2\) percentage points, not the prose’s \(17.5\). The N-CARS gain over TOKEN is correctly \(4.5\) points. The stated throughput follows arithmetically from \(1000/2.12\simeq471.7\) samples per second, but preprocessing inclusion is not established by a timing harness. Table 3’s gains over time surfaces are \(0.0034,0.0111,0.0268,0.0252\). Raw predictions, repeated seeds, data splits and original timing records were not available for verification.

Figure 6 visibly contains signed color scales; it therefore cannot be the output of the positive operator as printed. Figure 8 shows selected nonblank frames and enclosing boxes, which is consistent with some alternate implementation but cannot adjudicate its quantitative accuracy or causal mechanism. Poppler emitted a missing Symbol-display-font warning while rendering these source pages; the equations and relevant graphs were visible in the inspected images. The assessment concerns two demonstrated core derivation defects and preserves the distinction between these defects and unreplicated empirical outcomes.

problems.title: Incorrect quantization scaling and invalid subgroup PSD inference in the PTQ bound
problems.source_location: p4 Eq4/Theorem4.1 Eq8; AppendixA.1-A.2 pp12-13; Lemma4.4/A.5 pp6,14
claim: Quantization norm is at most sqrt(n)*smax^2/2 and subgroup excess risk admits the stated gradient/trace bound
analysis: Check: Exact rational quantization at even bit-widths; symbolic global/group Hessians; nonnegative polynomial counterexamples; local corrected norm/Taylor bound
Counterevidence: Scale typo is locally repairable, but curvature and regularity assumptions need separate correction; aggregate Hessian PSD and convex subgroup special cases remain valid

Independent verification. Original claim and assumptions: Independently read physical pp.3-4 Eq.(3)-(8), pp.12-13 Appendix A.1-A.2, and pp.6,14 Lemma 4.4/A.5. Visually inspected pp.12-13 to confirm the double scale multiplication and subgroup-PSD assertion are printed, not extraction artifacts. Assumptions are a nonnegative twice-differentiable loss, aggregate ERM minimizer, symmetric nearest quantizer with no clipping and 0<s<1; subgroup optimality is not assumed.

Independent verification. Decisive independent check: Rounding w/s has error <=1/2, so dequantized error <=s/2 and norm <=sqrt(sum s_i^2)/2. Fresh exact rational checks for even b=4,6,8,10,12 with fixed w*=(1,-1,1/3), identical risks (w3-1/3)^2/2, recover delta=-s/3, G=s^2/18 > 3s^4/8. At b=4 these are 1/882 versus 3/19208; the Taylor remainder is zero. With risks (z^2-1)^2+u^2 and 3z^2+u^2, their average is z^4/2+z^2/2+u^2+1/2, globally minimized at zero, yet subgroup A Hessian is diag(-4,2) with trace -2. Quantizing only u gives positive s^2/9 versus negative trace bounds. Separately risks (z^2-5)^2 and 11z^2 have traces -20,22 and aggregate maximal eigenvalue 1; Lemma 4.4 with n=3 predicts 22<=6 after dropping a negative trace. These derivatives and expansions were independently recalculated.

Independent verification. Alternative readings and counterevidence: A single scale-exponent typo can be repaired locally but does not justify the separate subgroup PSD inference. Title: Technical Verification: Understanding the Unfairness in Network Quantization
# Identity and scope

Understanding the Unfairness in Network Quantization. Bing Liu; Wenjun Miao; Boyu Zhang; Qiankun Zhang; Bin Yuan; Jing Wang; Shenghao Liu; Xianjun Deng. PMLR 267 (2025), paper I25-43689. The reviewed source is the published PMLR PDF frozen for B004. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages (also the article page labels), not volume pagination. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication remains pending.

The scientific main text, pp. 1–9, and Appendices A–C, pp. 12–20, were read. This review traces the quantization-error bound into the PTQ and QAT theorems, checks the subgroup-size arguments, and inspects Figures 1–9 and the reported experimental settings. The frozen packet contains no verified author repository; the bounded source search’s non-discovery is not proof that no code exists. Separate OpenReview attachments were inaccessible. No author program, training or benchmark evaluation was executed. The independent calculations use exact rational arithmetic and symbolic differentiation of explicitly specified examples.
# Definitions and dependence of the conclusions

For a symmetric range \([-w_{\max},w_{\max}]\), the paper uses \[s=\frac{w_{\max}}{2^{b-1}-1},\quad 0<s<1,\qquad
 q(w)=s\,\mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\mathrm{round}(w/s),-2^{b-1},2^{b-1}-1\right).\] There is no clipping within this range. The empirical minimizer \(w^*\) minimizes the aggregate risk, not necessarily each subgroup risk \(L_a\). The paper defines \(G_a=L_a(q(w^*))-L_a(w^*)\) and \(\varphi=\max_{a,a'}|G_a-G_{a'}|\). A subgroup’s \(G_a\) can be negative. This loss-based metric is distinct from accuracy disparity.

The central theoretical explanation uses Eq. (4) to bound each \(G_a\) by a gradient norm and Hessian trace, then argues that subgroup sizes order these quantities and hence order quantization harm. The QAT comparison relies on an additional Taylor-expansion bound. The three concerns below affect these links individually; the empirical observations need not be false for the theoretical claims to fail.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The quantization scale and subgroup-curvature assumptions invalidate the core PTQ bound).  Equation (4), p. 4, asserts \(\|\Delta w\|\le\frac12\sqrt n\,s_{\max}^2\). Appendix A.1, p. 12, explicitly derives \(|\Delta w_i|\le s_i(s_i/2)\). These are the printed powers, confirmed in the page images. Theorem 4.1 consequently uses \(s_{\max}^2\) in its linear term and \(s_{\max}^4\) in its quadratic term.

Rounding \(w_i/s_i\) has error at most \(1/2\) in integer units. Multiplication by \(s_i\) therefore gives \(|\Delta w_i|\le s_i/2\), with only one scale factor. The correct norm bound is \(\frac12\sqrt{\sum_i s_i^2}\le\frac12\sqrt n\,s_{\max}\). The proof double-counts dequantization. This is not an extraction ambiguity: Appendix A.1 displays both factors and the resulting fourth powers.
#### A fixed admissible counterexample.

Take three parameters, \(w^*=(1,-1,1/3)\), and identical subgroup risks \[L_a(w)=\tfrac12(w_3-1/3)^2.\] This is a nonnegative, infinitely differentiable, convex risk, realizable by a linear prediction \(f_w(x)=3w_3\), class label \(1\), and squared loss \((f_w(x)-1)^2/18\). The first two coordinates are unused model weights setting the symmetric range; nonunique minimizers are allowed. Any positive group sizes give this same aggregate risk and \(w^*\) is a global minimizer. Its gradient is zero and Hessian trace is one.

For every even \(b\ge4\), put \(m=2^{b-1}-1\) and \(s=1/m\). Since \(m\equiv1\pmod3\), ordinary nearest rounding gives \(q(w_3^*)-w_3^*=-s/3\), without a tie or clipping. The other coordinates are exactly represented. Hence \[\|\Delta w^*\|=s/3,\qquad G_a=s^2/18,
 \qquad\hbox{Theorem 4.1's explicit bound}=3s^4/8.\] At \(b=4\), the actual norm is \(1/21\simeq0.04762\), versus the claimed \(\sqrt3/98\simeq0.01767\). The actual loss increase is \(1/882\), versus \(3/19208\). The quadratic Taylor remainder is identically zero. More generally, the actual \(s^2\) term cannot be absorbed into an \(O(s^3)\) remainder as even \(b\to\infty\) for this fixed problem. The executed rational check verifies the same mismatch at \(b=4,6,8,10,12\).
#### Fixing the powers alone is insufficient.

Appendix A.2, p. 13, additionally asserts that every subgroup Hessian is positive semidefinite because \(w^*\) is a local optimum. Only the aggregate risk has that optimality guarantee. For an explicit counterexample, take \(w^*=(1,-1,0,1/3)\), \(z=w_3\), \(u=w_4-1/3\), two equally sized groups, and \[L_A=(z^2-1)^2+u^2,\qquad L_B=3z^2+u^2.\] Both risks are nonnegative and smooth. Their average is \(z^4/2+z^2/2+u^2+1/2\), globally minimized at \(z=u=0\). Such risks can be realized with a group-dependent model and a common squared output loss. At the minimum, \(g_A=0\) and the active Hessian of \(L_A\) is \(\mathrm{diag}(-4,2)\), with trace \(-2\), although the aggregate Hessian is positive semidefinite. Quantization changes only \(u\) by \(-s/3\), giving \(G_A=s^2/9>0\) with zero remainder along this path. Both the printed trace bound \(-s^4\) and the power-corrected trace bound \(-s^2\) are negative. Thus the trace substitution fails independently of the scale error.

The same unstated sign condition appears when Appendix A.5 drops a subgroup trace in Lemma 4.4. For three parameters with only \(z=w_3\) active, equal-sized risks \((z^2-5)^2\) and \(11z^2\) have subgroup traces \(-20,22\), while the aggregate Hessian has maximum eigenvalue \(1\) at its global minimum. Lemma 4.4 bounds the second trace by \(n|D|\lambda_{\max}/|D_B|=6\), although it equals \(22\).
#### Repair and impact.

A valid local bound follows if each subgroup risk has a Hessian with Lipschitz constant \(M_a\) on the relevant segment. With \(r=\frac12\sqrt n\,s_{\max}\), Taylor’s theorem and norm inequalities give \[G_a\le r\|g_a\|+\tfrac12r^2\|H_a\|_{\mathrm{op}}+M_ar^3/6.\] The operator norm may be replaced by the trace if the subgroup Hessian is explicitly assumed positive semidefinite. Twice differentiability alone, as stated in Theorem 4.1, does not ensure a cubic Taylor remainder; the counterexamples above are smoother and do not depend on that additional deficiency. This establishes a bounded repair of the local inequality, not the paper’s subsequent fairness ordering. The defect is Major because the incorrect estimate and curvature step underlie the principal PTQ guarantee and are reused in QAT. A short correction to one exponent does not repair all these dependencies.

Problem 2 (Subgroup-size bounds do not establish the claimed ordering of fairness damage).  The discussion following Theorem 4.1, pp. 4–6, and Takeaways 1–2 infer greater quantization harm from larger gradient norms and Hessian traces, and infer these quantities’ inverse ordering by subgroup size. Valid upper bounds alone do not establish those orderings.

The weighted stationarity identity \(\sum_a |D_a|g_a=0\) and the triangle-inequality proof of Lemma 4.2 are valid. When exactly two groups exhaust the dataset, the gradient-norm ratio in Corollary 4.3 is also valid. The surrounding prose explicitly acknowledges this two-group condition; its omission from the corollary’s standalone wording should not obscure that valid special case. It does not extend to the five-, seven- or ten-group settings by selecting an arbitrary pair.

For a fully convex three-group example, let sizes be \((1,2,3)\) and let \(z=w_3-c\) with unused range-setting weights \((w_1,w_2)=(1,-1)\). Set \[L_A=\tfrac12z^2,\qquad L_B=(z-1)^2,\qquad
 L_C=\tfrac32(z+4/9)^2.\] At \(z=0\), the gradients are \((0,-2,4/3)\), so their size-weighted sum is zero. The aggregate curvature is \(7/3>0\), making this a global minimum. Subgroup Hessian traces are \((1,2,3)\): they increase with group size. The smallest group has gradient norm zero, less than the larger second group’s norm two. All risks are nonnegative quadratics. Thus neither generic inverse ordering follows from the stated ERM assumptions, even with positive semidefinite subgroup Hessians.
#### Loss direction and bit-width.

Even when the smaller group has both a larger gradient norm and larger curvature, its loss need not deteriorate more. With group sizes \((1,2)\), take \[L_A=\tfrac32(z+2/3)^2,\qquad L_B=\tfrac12(z-1)^2.\] At \(z=0\) the gradients are \(2,-1\), the Hessian traces are \(3,1\), and the aggregate risk is minimized there. For \(c=1/3\) and \(b=4\), quantization gives \(\delta=-1/21\), and \[G_A=2\delta+\tfrac32\delta^2=-9/98<0,
 \qquad G_B=-\delta+\tfrac12\delta^2=43/882>0.\] The supposedly more vulnerable group improves. The signed inner product \(\delta^{\top}g_a\) and directional curvature cannot be recovered from separate magnitudes. Nor is worsening \(\varphi\) with lower bit-width universal: for the same two risk shapes with \(c=1/7\), four-bit quantization is exact and \(\varphi_4=0\). Eight-bit quantization gives \(\delta=-1/889\) and \(\varphi_8=2666/790321>0\). These use the paper’s actual range and scale, not arbitrary perturbations.
#### Scope of the concern.

These examples refute the purported general implications about \(G_a\) and \(\varphi\); they do not estimate accuracy changes in the reported image datasets. Figures 1–2 and the artificial-imbalance experiments are empirical evidence for associations in those runs. They may survive after the theoretical claims are narrowed. This is Major because the missing implications are central to the advertised explanation of unfairness, independently of the incorrect numerical bound. A repair needs additional directional/distributional conditions or an explicitly empirical scope. The valid two-group stationarity relation alone is insufficient.

Problem 3 (The QAT theorem drops quantization remainders that do not vanish with the learning rate).  Theorem 5.1, Eq. (13), pp. 6–7, gives explicit gradient/trace terms plus only \(O(\eta^2)\). Appendix A.6 expands in both quantization errors and the learning rate, but does not retain the independent quantization remainder. This fails even for a convex, infinitely differentiable risk and identical batches/groups.

Take the same range-setting weights and \(w_t=(1,-1,c)\) with \(c=1/3\), all subgroup risks \(L_a=(w_3-c)^4\), and \(b=4\). These are nonnegative convex risks, realizable with a linear score and a fourth-power loss. The aggregate minimizer is \(w_t\); every group gradient and Hessian there is zero. Let \(r=s/3=1/21\). Initial quantization gives \(q(w_t)_3=c-r\). Under the paper’s Eq. (11), the next unquantized QAT coordinate is \[c-r+4\eta r^3.\] Appendix A.6 then requantizes it. For \(0<\eta<27/(8s^2)\), its displacement from \(c-r\) is less than half a quantization step, so it rounds back to \(c-r\). The unquantized comparator starts at the minimizer and remains at \(c\). Consequently, \[G_{t+1}(a)=r^4=1/194481>0\] for arbitrarily small positive \(\eta\), while every explicit term of Eq. (13) is zero. For fixed bit-width this positive constant is not \(O(\eta^2)\). The exact independently executed update/requantization checks confirm it for four decreasing learning rates; the analytic interval proves the limiting discrepancy. Correcting the powers of \(s\) does not change the zero gradient/trace terms.
#### Other proof limitations.

Equation (21d), p. 16, replaces batch gradients and Hessians by subgroup quantities using an approximation, although the preceding training setup selects a batch from the full dataset. Even sampling within a group does not give a deterministic norm identity: two sample gradients \(+1,-1\) have zero mean gradient but mean single-sample gradient norm one. No fluctuation bound is included. Moreover, the stated individual error bounds yield \(\frac12\|\Delta w_t+\Delta w_{t+1}\|^2\le\frac12ns_{\max}^4\) under the paper’s own erroneous scale convention, not the \(\frac18ns_{\max}^4\) substituted in Eq. (21e). These are additional derivation gaps, not separate empirical-failure claims.

If Eq. (13) is intended merely as a heuristic second-order approximation, the quartic example identifies a discarded term rather than an unexpected training failure; it still defeats the theorem as an upper bound with the displayed remainder. A corrected result must state a joint quantization/learning-rate regime or retain all mixed remainders and batch-control terms. No such general correction is verified here. This is Major because the invalid bound supplies the theoretical QAT/PTQ comparison. Even a valid larger upper bound for QAT would not itself prove larger realized subgroup disparities or larger \(\varphi\).
# Experimental checks, counterevidence and limits

All nine figures were inspected as rendered source pages; plot trends and labels were checked, without pretending to recover underlying arrays. Figure 1 shows the stated deterioration of the small Others group; Figure 2 shows the reported inverse association; Figure 3 and Tables 2–3 show improvements under augmentation in the prominent low-bit settings. Table 2’s ResNet50 UTK-Face four-bit \(\varphi\) values change from \(18.8\) to \(2.6/1.7\) under PTQ and from \(25.4\) to \(2.7/2.0\) under QAT for GT/RE. These are internally reported empirical outcomes, not invalidated measurements by the counterexamples.

The improvements are not universal even within the tables: Table 5’s VGG19 FER2013 sixteen-bit PTQ values increase from \(0.6\) to \(1.4/1.7\) under GT/RE. This qualifies the scope of the mitigation claim. Augmentation also changes the full-precision reference model substantially, so comparing excess-loss gaps against each new reference is not by itself an isolated measurement of quantization’s causal effect.

The appendix reports ten repeated runs and average results; it should not be described as reporting no replication. Raw runs, seeds, loss values, an error-bar definition and a Hessian-trace estimation procedure were unavailable for checking. The settings do not specify enough of the loss computation and quantization/training configuration to reconstruct the tabulated loss-based \(\varphi\) from the accuracy plots. No actual fairness metric was recomputed from model predictions.

Several local documentation inconsistencies remain: Appendix C.2 says ResNet50 while B.2 and figure captions identify ResNet18 for the imbalanced datasets; Table 4 lists 23,782 imbalanced MNIST training images while C.2 states 23,250. The listed FER2013 class counts sum to 28,706, versus the stated 28,708. The UTK-Face class counts do sum correctly to 18,964. Captions for Figures 5–9 repeatedly refer to gender classification and four groups despite the described object/digit/ethnicity/expression tasks; Figure 6(c) uses object-class labels on its MNIST bar chart. These may be copied labels or reporting mistakes, and no measured consequence is inferred without the underlying runs. They are not additional Major findings.
# Overall impact and calculation record

The Major assessment concerns demonstrated failures in the central theoretical chain: the scale/curvature bound, the inference from magnitudes and group sizes to actual harm, and the QAT remainder. Empirical associations and the practical usefulness of some augmentation settings may remain valid. No fabricated-data allegation, full empirical refutation, verified author correction or author adoption is asserted.

The accompanying `independent_check.py` and `independent_check_output.json` record every explicit example above, the exact quantizer, rational outputs, symbolic Hessians, parameter values and runtime. The proofs specify why the hypotheses hold and why finite calculations support, rather than replace, the universal counterarguments. The norm repair is established only under its newly stated regularity/curvature assumptions; no repaired universal fairness-ordering theorem is claimed.

analysis: Check: At tau=1 every hitting time must equal 1 almost surely. More than one state would require a row of the transition matrix to contain two entries equal to 1. Thus the sole state gives an exact gradient oracle. Gradient descent from zero is zero-respecting and achieves min gradient norm squared <=2LDelta/T. Fixing L=Delta=sigma=tau=1 contradicts the epsilon^-4 term as epsilon tends to zero. Splitting gives rare-state mass q*pi_v and positive return mean 1/(q*pi_v)>=1/q, violating fixed tau for small q.

Title: Technical Verification of Markov-Sampling Lower Bounds
# Identity and inspected scope

Zhenyu Sun and Ermin Wei, Improved Lower Bounds for First-order Stochastic Non-convex Optimization under Markov Sampling, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 57754–57772; identifier I25-43690 (0321), OpenReview `vBYRG3p21R`. The reviewed version is the frozen 19-page publisher PDF. Page numbers below are PDF pages, which equal its printed pages. All main-paper and appendix text was read. Claim-level checks concentrated on Definitions 2.1 and (6), Theorem 3.1, the construction in Appendix A.4, Algorithm 1, the decomposition in Theorem B.5, and Section 2.1. Figures 1–2 and the relevant equation pages were visually inspected. There are no reproduced experiments. No released code was available in the packet; the separate OpenReview attachment inventory was inaccessible. The remaining lemmas have been read but not independently proved in full.
# Definitions that matter

Equation reference: eq:hit. The oracle returns \(g(x;s)=\nabla f(x;s)\) with stationary expectation \(\nabla F(x)\) and stationary variance at most \(\sigma^2\). The function class has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(F(0)-\inf F\leq\Delta\). The chain class in (6) imposes \[
 \tau_{\rm hit}=\max_{v,w}E_v\inf\{t\geq1:s_t=w\}\leq\tau.\] In particular, the maximum includes return times (\(v=w\)), not just mixing times. Zero-respecting algorithms can use gradient descent from zero, including selection of a previously queried iterate.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Theorem 3.1 is incompatible with its hitting-time class).  This is a major defect in the principal stochastic lower bound.
## Source claim and decisive check

For every admissible \(F\), deterministic gradient descent with step \(1/L\) satisfies the smoothness descent inequality \[F(x_{t+1})\leq F(x_t)-\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla F(x_t)\|^2,
 \qquad
 \min_{t<T}\|\nabla F(x_t)\|^2\leq\frac{2L\Delta}{T}.\] It is zero-respecting and uses one query per step. Selecting the queried iterate with smallest observed gradient therefore gives \(N_s^\epsilon=O(L\Delta\epsilon^{-2})\) at \(\tau=1\). Fix \(L=\Delta=\sigma=1\) and let \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). This contradicts the positive \(\epsilon^{-4}\) term in [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed). No special choice of objective, variance lower bound, or hidden regularity assumption is needed: the upper bound holds for the entire displayed class at this parameter.
## Why the construction does not resolve this

Appendix A.4 (pp. 13–15, Fig. 2) splits \(v^*\) into states with stationary masses \(q\pi_{v^*}\) and \((1-q)\pi_{v^*}\), and chooses \(q^{-1}=1+\sigma^2/(8a_2\epsilon^2)\). For a recurrent irreducible chain, the expected positive return time to a state of mass \(p\) is \(1/p\): successive return cycles have mean length \(m\), and their stationary visit frequency is \(1/m=p\). Hence the new chain obeys \[\widetilde\tau_{\rm hit}\geq\frac{1}{q\pi_{v^*}}\geq\frac1q.\] For fixed \(\tau\), sufficiently small \(\epsilon\) puts it outside (6). For example, \(q=0.01\) forces a return time at least \(100\), inconsistent with \(\tau=10\). This necessary condition does not depend on how the unpictured transition probabilities are completed. More generally, a finite uniform return-time bound forces every stationary mass to be at least \(1/\tau\), so the irreducible state space has at most \(\lfloor\tau\rfloor\) states. Allowing a countable state space does not remove the obstruction.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair scope

An i.i.d. chain on several states has mixing time one, but hitting time \(\max_w1/\pi_w\), not one. Interpreting \(\tau\) as mixing time could avoid the singleton argument, but contradicts Definition 2.1 and (6), and requires a new proof and parameter accounting. The stated core theorem is false in its explicit parameter range; the supplied construction also fails for small \(q\) at fixed hitting bound. This does not refute stochastic lower bounds under other oracle classes. No repaired lower bound is certified here. The separate weighted-gradient lower bound in Lemma A.1 also requires normalization scrutiny; it is not needed for this verdict.
Problem 2 (Algorithm 1 does not maintain the gradient sum used in Theorem B.5).  This is a major invalid derivation in the core MaC-SAGE guarantee.
## Claim and fully admissible calculation

Equation reference: eq:actual. On p. 6, line 5 sets \[
 G_t=G_{t-1}-y_{t-1}^i h_{t-1}^i+y_t^i
abla f_i(x_t),
 \quad s_t=i.\] The prose then claims \(G_t=\sum_jy_t^jh_t^j\). This equality is used to bound \(\|
abla F(x_t)-G_t\|^2\) in Theorem B.5 (p. 18). Consider two states sampled independently with probabilities \(1/2,1/2\), \(f_1(x)=x^2/2+x\) and \(f_2(x)=x^2/2-x\). Then \(F(x)=x^2/2\), \(L=1\), the initial gap at \(x_0=0\) is zero (thus at most \(\Delta=1\)), and \(|
abla f_i(x)-
abla F(x)|=1\) for every \(x\). Assumption 4.1 holds with \(\sigma=1\) and the hitting bound is \(	au=2\).
## Repair and bounded consequence

Equation reference: eq:repair. For the intended invariant \(G_t=\sum_jy_t^jh_t^j\), a correct update is \[
 G_t=\frac{t}{t+1}G_{t-1}
 -\frac{t}{t+1}y_{t-1}^i h_{t-1}^i
 +y_t^i\nabla f_i(x_t).\] To verify it, use \(y_t^j=t y_{t-1}^j/(t+1)\) and \(h_t^j=h_{t-1}^j\) for \(j\ne i\), then replace just the \(i\)th term. The zero initialization also makes this valid at \(t=0\). This repairs the invariant only. It does not validate the rest of Appendix B, including the application of a fixed-function moment bound to iterate-dependent gradients. Alternatively, one could analyze the printed algorithm with its extra accumulated error, but that analysis is absent. The finite-path example refutes the claimed equivalence and its use in the proof; it does not by itself prove asymptotic divergence or rule out the stated rate after repair. Because the defect invalidates the derivation of the proposed algorithm’s central guarantee, its impact is major.
Problem 3 (The TD line integral is not a potential for the TD vector field).  This is a minor defect in the motivating application, without a shown dependency in the abstract lower-bound theorems.

Section 2.1 (p. 3) defines \(f(\theta;\bar s)=\int_0^1g(\theta_0+u(\theta-\theta_0);s,s')^T
(\theta-\theta_0)\,du\) and concludes \(\nabla f=g\). Take \(\theta_0=0\), \(\gamma=1/2\), reward zero, \(\phi(s)=e_1\), \(\phi(s')=e_2\). These features can be assigned to the two states of the preceding i.i.d. chain. The true discounted value is identically zero, so the assumed exact linear representation holds with \(\theta^*=0\). The transition \(s\to s'\) has positive probability. For \(\theta=(x,y)\) the specified formulas give \[g(\theta;s,s')=(x-y/2,0)^T,\quad
 f=x^2/2-xy/4,\quad
 \nabla f=(x-y/4,-x/4)^T.\] At \((0,1)\) these are \((-1/2,0)^T\) and \((-1/4,0)^T\). The Jacobian of \(g\) is nonsymmetric, so no differentiable scalar potential with this gradient exists on \(\mathbb R^2\). A conservative vector field would make the line-integral argument valid, but that condition is neither assumed nor supplied by linear value representation. Even if the expected TD field is conservative in a special chain, that does not establish the asserted per-sample identity. The proposed reformulation of ordinary TD updates is therefore invalid in general.
# Overall impact and state

Theorem 3.1 fails as stated, and the MaC-SAGE convergence proof does not apply to its displayed recurrence. These concern two central contributions, irrespective of whether related results can be recovered. Theorem 4.2 and all remaining proof steps are not certified by this review. No experimental scores are challenged, since the paper is theoretical. No later correction was present in the frozen packet; a later-version/erratum comparison was not performed and author adoption is unknown.

Title: Technical Verification of Latent-View Black–Litterman Models
# Identity and scope

Thomas Y.L. Lin, Jerry Yao-Chieh Hu, Paul W. Chiou, and Peter Lin, Latent Variable Estimation in Bayesian Black-Litterman Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, 37846–37873; I25-43691 (0322), OpenReview `v8ipdsBPEx`. This review uses the frozen publisher PDF and repository commit `185f30154940b5114d01a7a754a5dce6fcf7ce83` dated 5 October 2025. The actual PDF has 28 pages, with identical printed and PDF numbering. The source-preparation manifest’s count of 52 came from control characters in extracted graph labels; page-wise extraction and `pdfinfo` establish 28, without changing the PDF bytes.

The main text and applicable appendices A–F were read. Detailed checks cover the Gaussian posteriors, the normal–inverse-Wishart integral, the predictive limit, reported summary arithmetic, and the released mean calculation. The model, optimizer and strategy files were inspected statically, as were lines 183–239 of `old_version/main.py`. No author code, optimizer or backtest was run. Historical data and transaction-cost robustness were not reproduced. Separate OpenReview attachments were unavailable. The graph and allocation figures were viewed as recorded in the coverage ledger, not regenerated.
# Background and positive checks

Equation reference: eq:slp. For Gaussian prior \(N(\theta_0,\Sigma_0)\) and a Gaussian feature measurement centered at \(a=\alpha^F+F\beta^F\), completing the square gives \[
 V=(\Sigma_0^{-1}+(\Omega^F)^{-1})^{-1},\quad
 b=\Sigma_0^{-1}\theta_0+(\Omega^F)^{-1}a,\quad
 E[\theta\mid F]=Vb.\] If \(r\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,\Sigma)\) with conditionally independent return noise, then \(r\mid F\sim N(Vb,\Sigma+V)\). These are the formulas in Theorem 3.2 and Appendix E.3. The law of total variance justifies the addition of \(\Sigma\) to covariance, not to the mean multiplier. Theorem 3.1’s Gaussian quadratic calculation similarly requires \(\gamma^2 P^T\Omega^{-1}P\) in its precision.

The ten paired Sharpe ratios in Tables 1–2 yield a mean relative improvement of \(49.7545\%\); the ten paired turnover rates in Table 6 yield a mean reduction of \(55.0528\%\). Thus the abstract’s rounded \(49.8\%\) and \(55.1\%\) summaries are arithmetically supported. This check does not validate the underlying backtests or establish performance on new data.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The FIV-BL Student-\(t\) approximation has incorrect degrees of freedom).  The affected core approximation is Corollaries 3.3.1–3.3.2 (p. 8), supported by Lemma D.3 (p. 18) and Appendix E.5 (p. 23).

Equation reference: eq:tcorrect. The paper assumes \(	heta\mid S\sim N(\mu',S)\) and \(S\sim IW(\Psi',
u')\), using in (D.8) the density proportional to \(|S|^{-(
u'+m+1)/2}\exp[-\operatorname{tr}(\Psi'S^{-1})/2]\). Take \(\Psi'\) positive definite, \(
u'>m-1\), and \(\mu'\) fixed, exactly as required for this approximate model. Integration gives, for \(u=	heta-\mu'\), \[ egin{aligned}
 p(	heta)&\propto\int |S|^{-(
u'+m+2)/2}
 \exp[-\operatorname{tr}((\Psi'+uu^T)S^{-1})/2]\,dS\
 &\propto|\Psi'+uu^T|^{-(
u'+1)/2}
 \propto(1+u^T(\Psi')^{-1}u)^{-(
u'+1)/2}.\end{aligned}\] The kernel of an \(m\)-variate \(t_\kappa(\mu',C)\) is \((1+u^TC^{-1}u/\kappa)^{-(\kappa+m)/2}\). Matching both factors forces \[
 \kappa=
u'-m+1,\qquad C= rac{\Psi'}{
u'-m+1}.\] The paper instead specifies degrees of freedom \(
u'\) explicitly and writes \(t_{
u'}\) with the same scale matrix. Its intermediate \(
u=
u'-m+1\) does not justify changing the final subscript back to \(
u'\). This is not an unspecified alternative \(t\) convention: both the density of \(IW\) and the claimed degrees of freedom are explicit.

For a concrete admissible example, set \(m=2,\nu'=5,\Psi'=I_2,\mu'=0\). The correct distribution is \(t_4(0,I_2/4)\) with covariance \(I_2/2\). The printed \(t_5(0,I_2/4)\) has covariance \(5I_2/12\). Their densities at \((1,0)\) are respectively \(0.07957747\) and \(0.08136289\), checked independently. Both distributions are well-defined; their inequality is substantive for uncertainty and tails.

Appendix A (p. 14) also calls \(\Psi'/(
u'-m+1)\) the inverse-Wishart mean, with existence threshold \(
u'>m-1\). Under its stated density, the mean is \(\Psi'/(
u'-m-1)\) and requires \(
u'>m+1\). This follows from the same mixture: \(E[S]=\operatorname{Var}(	heta)
=\kappa C/(\kappa-2)\). The displayed denominator is the \(t\) scale, not \(E[S]\). Equation [eq:tcorrect] (#eq:tcorrect) repairs the marginal law of the stipulated approximate hierarchy, and the corrected mean repairs that moment only. Neither proves the hierarchy is a faithful approximation of the original \(\Omega\) mixture. The empirical study uses SLP-BL, so these errors do not directly invalidate its reported scores. They do invalidate a core FIV-BL predictive derivation, supporting Major.

Problem 2 (Perfect views do not force the stated predictive point mass).  Remark 3.3 (p. 5), repeated in the conclusion (p. 9), states that \(\Omega\to0\), \(q\to Pr^*\) and \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(0,0,1)\) imply \(\widetilde r\Rightarrow\delta_{r^*}\).

Use \(m=k=1\), \(P=1\), \(\Sigma=\Sigma_0=\Omega^F=1\), \(\theta_0=0\), feature center \(\alpha^F+F\beta^F=0\), \(r^*=q=2\), and \(\Omega=\varepsilon>0\). Every covariance is positive definite, the stated regression parameters are classical, views are accurate, and their uncertainty tends to zero. Theorem 3.1 gives \[\mu_\varepsilon=\frac2{1+2\varepsilon},\qquad
 V_\varepsilon=\frac{\varepsilon}{1+2\varepsilon},\qquad
 \widetilde r\sim N(\mu_\varepsilon,1+V_\varepsilon).\] Consequently \(\widetilde r\Rightarrow N(2,1)\), not \(\delta_2\). For example, its limiting characteristic function at frequency one is \(e^{2i-1/2}\) rather than \(e^{2i}\), directly ruling out the claimed weak limit without relying on convergence of moments. The latent mean \(\theta\) does collapse in this scalar example; the future noisy return \(r\) does not.

The mean claim also needs an identifiability condition on \(P\). For \(m=2,k=1,P=(1,0)\), prior and feature precision both \(I_2\), their centers zero, and \(r^*=(0,1)^T,q=0\), the second posterior coordinate remains \(N(0,1/2)\) as \(\Omega\to0\). The theorem allows this rectangular \(P\). Appendix A’s practical choice \(P=I\) avoids this second obstruction but not the intrinsic-noise obstruction above.

Under full-column-rank \(P\) with \(\Omega=\varepsilon\Omega_1\), \(\Omega_1\succ0\), accurate views and bounded prior/feature terms, the repaired conclusion is \(\theta\Rightarrow\delta_{r^*}\) and \(\widetilde r\Rightarrow N(r^*,\Sigma)\). This follows because the posterior precision diverges in every parameter direction and its covariance tends to zero. A predictive point mass additionally requires \(\Sigma\to0\). This is a major defect in the asserted general recovery property; it does not refute ordinary Bayesian shrinkage or the separate empirical SLP-BL comparisons.
Problem 3 (Released code uses the predictive covariance to form the mean).  The supported release-level discrepancy is Minor; its effect on the historical paper results Needs Evidence.

At the pinned commit, `models/black_litterman.py` computes `middle_inv` \(=V\) and `adjusted_cov`\(=\Sigma+V\), then `adjusted_mean = adjusted_cov @ rhs`. The same expression occurs in `old_version/main.py`, lines 237–238. It therefore returns \((\Sigma+V)b\) rather than [eq:slp] (#eq:slp)’s \(Vb\).

For \(\Sigma=\Sigma_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)\), \(\Omega^F=I\), \(\theta_0=0\), and \(a=(1,1)^T\), all matrices are positive definite and \(V=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,4/5)\). The correct mean is \((1/2,4/5)\); the released expression gives \((3/2,24/5)\). With predictive covariance \(C=\operatorname{diag}(3/2,24/5)\), the unconstrained positive Sharpe direction is \(C^{-1}\mu\); its normalized entries are already long-only. Thus the theoretical weights are \((2/3,1/3)\), versus \((1/2,1/2)\) for the released expression. This is an independent matrix calculation, not execution of the author’s program or a historical backtest.

Replacing the multiplier of `rhs` by `middle_inv` repairs this algebraic discrepancy. The repository describes itself as a refactor and includes an older file, but neither proves which exact code and inputs generated Tables 1–2. In addition, the code uses linear SVR while Appendix A derives Gaussian-regression estimators. A new documented backtest and parameter correspondence are needed to determine historical empirical consequences. No score degradation is inferred here.

Problem 4 (Two predictive corollaries are inconsistent with their antecedent posteriors).  These local formula defects are Minor, given the correct adjacent derivations and no demonstrated additional empirical dependency.

Corollary 3.1.1 omits \(\gamma^2\) from the precision retained by Theorem 3.1 and its proof; Corollary 3.2.1 prints \(G^F\) rather than \((G^F)^{-1}\) in the mean. For the first, take scalar \(P=\Sigma_0=\Omega^F=\Omega=1\), zero prior and feature centers, \(\alpha=\beta=0\), \(q=1\), and \(\gamma=2\). The correct precision is \(6\), giving mean \(1/3\) and latent variance \(1/6\); the corollary’s precision \(3\) gives mean \(2/3\) and latent variance \(1/3\). For the second, take \(\Sigma_0=\Omega^F=1\), \(\theta_0=0\) and feature center \(a=1\): \(G^F=2\) and \(b=1\), so the printed mean is \(2\) instead of \(1/2\). All variances are positive. Restoring the squared coefficient and inverse, respectively, recovers the completed-square identities. The first discrepancy disappears when \(\gamma=1\); neither formula alone establishes which implementation produced the experiments.
# Remaining qualifications and conclusion

The FIV mixture’s conditional-independence interpretation also needs a more explicit joint model: Figure 3 draws \(\theta\to q\leftarrow F\), while Appendix E.4 assumes \(\theta\perp F\mid(q,\Omega)\). That independence does not follow from the displayed graph. This remains a scoped Needs Evidence item; the explicit mixture can itself be adopted as a different model. No later erratum comparison was performed.
