report: Abstract: CUPS improves several reported pose-estimation metrics, but three mathematical steps used for its uncertainty guarantees fail under their stated assumptions. Label-dependent calibration weights can destroy coverage even for independent identically distributed observations. Ranking these weights does not give the claimed temporal-decay bound. A separate Beta-distance bound is numerically and analytically false. These are major defects in core theoretical derivations; they do not establish that the reported empirical improvements are false. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of CUPS Coverage Guarantees
# Identity and inspected scope

Harry Zhang and Luca Carlone, CUPS: Improving Human Pose-Shape Estimators with Conformalized Deep Uncertainty, ICML 2025, I25-43692 (0323), OpenReview `v7ebdKPTnG`. The frozen publisher PDF has 19 pages; PDF and printed page numbering agree. The main text and Appendices A–H were read. Detailed verification concerns Definitions 1–3, the weighted quantile, Theorems 1–3 and their proofs, and the interpretation of Table 3. Original architecture, pose and coverage figures on pp. 4, 6–8 and the decisive proof pages 14 and 16 were viewed. The acquired packet contains no author repository; a separate OpenReview attachment inventory was inaccessible. No author program, pose estimator, dataset or training run was executed.

The relevant cited conformal paper was consulted at the authors’ public preprint, specifically Sections 3.1 and 5.5. Its fixed-weight requirement and its conditional-total-variation alternative matter here. Other cited literature was not independently audited. No later CUPS erratum comparison was performed.
# Method and checks that survive

CUPS uses a learned nonconformity score \(S(X,Y)=\sigma(\phi(X,Y))\), a sigmoid applied to an MLP embedding, and a set \(\{Y:S(X,Y)\le\tau\}\). The adversarial losses push scores of ground-truth poses toward zero and those of predictions toward one; the predictor receives the opposing score loss. This is consistent with using lower scores as greater conformity. Training does not impose a deterministic mathematical constraint on the score’s distribution.

The independent arithmetic check of Table 1 agrees with the stated 3DPW improvements over GLoT: PA-MPJPE improves by \(1.9\) mm, MPJPE by \(4.5\) mm, and MPVPE by \(4.6\) mm. Acceleration error increases from \(6.6\) to \(6.9\), as the text acknowledges. These checks concern printed numbers, not benchmark reproduction. Appendix F’s finite proposal aggregation is a practical heuristic; no guarantee of sampling uniformly from the entire conformal set is inferred.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Theorem 1 does not cover the proposed label-dependent weights).  This is a major defect in the core coverage justification. Theorem 1 (p. 6 and Appendix B, pp. 12–13), combined with Definition 3 (pp. 6, 14), uses an unconditional swap-distance correction for weights computed from each calibration response.

Equation reference: eq:weight. Definition 3 specifies \[
 w_i=\exp(-\|\phi(X_i,\widehat Y_i)-\phi(X_i,Y_i)\|^2/T).\] These depend on the ground-truth calibration label \(Y_i\). The borrowed fixed-weight theorem does not automatically apply. This is more than a missing citation condition: the coverage assertion can fail under exchangeability, where every unconditional swap distance is zero.

To see this, fix \(X\) and a predictor \(\widehat Y=0\), and let a scalar pose coordinate \(U\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), independently across the calibration and test records. Keep other coordinates fixed. Choose a fixed MLP projection \(\phi(X,Y)=U\), so \(S=\sigma(U)\) and \(\phi(X,\widehat Y)=0\). A linear projection is within the specified MLP score family. Set \(T=0.01\) and \(\alpha=0.1\). This realizes [eq:weight] (#eq:weight) exactly with \(w_i=e^{-U_i^2/T}\in(0,1]\). It is a counterexample to the distribution-free mathematical claim, not an assertion about a particular trained CUPS checkpoint.

Because \(\sigma\) is strictly increasing, the weighted \(0.9\) quantile of scores is the sigmoid of the weighted \(0.9\) quantile of \(U\). The law of large numbers gives its limit \(q\) uniquely by \[\int_0^q e^{-u^2/T}\,du
 =0.9\int_0^1e^{-u^2/T}\,du,
 \qquad
 q=\sqrt T\,\operatorname{erf}^{-1}
       (0.9\operatorname{erf}(1/\sqrt T))=0.1163087154.\] Strict positivity of the density gives quantile convergence. Conditional test coverage equals the realized threshold in \(U\) coordinates; bounded convergence therefore gives limiting marginal coverage \(q\), far below \(0.9\). The sample and its coordinate-swapped version have identical joint laws, so the unconditional total-variation terms in Theorem 1 are all zero. Consequently the claimed bound cannot hold for all finite calibration sizes under these assumptions.

Equation (5) omits the extra atom at \(+\infty\) that appears in the Appendix B proof and the cited method. Including an atom of mass \(1/(1+\sum_iw_i)\) repairs that finite-sample convention, but does not repair this example: the atom vanishes as \(n\to\infty\), leaving the same limit. An original diagnostic calculation with 500 independent calibration sets of size 1500 gives mean conditional coverage \(0.11618\) without this atom and \(0.11855\) with it. The decisive argument is the limit above, not the Monte Carlo estimate.

The cited conformal analysis explicitly fixes weights before observing the calibration records. It also describes a different bound using total variation conditional on random weights, averaged over those weights; this does not reduce to zero merely because the unconditional records are exchangeable. Treating training as fixed does not fix weights that depend on new calibration labels. A defensible repair is to specify weights in advance and include the test atom, or to prove and control the appropriate conditional distances. Neither repair is established for the current feature-distance procedure. This invalidates the advertised calibration guarantee without refuting the empirical effectiveness of the adversarial score.

Problem 2 (Feature-weight rank is substituted for chronological order).  Theorem 2, equation (11), and its Appendix C.1 proof (p. 14) assert a \(\rho^k\) bound after a changepoint, using \(w'_i=\rho^{n+1-\pi(w_i)}\), where \(\pi(w_i)\) is the ranked position of feature weight \(w_i\), rather than time index \(i\).

Take \(n=4,k=3,\rho=1/2\). Let the sole old observation have the largest feature weight, with ranks \((4,1,2,3)\). Then \[(w'_1,w'_2,w'_3,w'_4)=(1/2,1/16,1/8,1/4).\] Let the old score be deterministically \(0.2\), and the recent and test scores be deterministically \(0.8\). Recent full observations can be i.i.d., with continuous feature weights below the old weight; their ordering is immaterial because the sum of geometric rank weights is fixed. For example the old weight can be \(0.9\) and recent weights lie in \((0.1,0.3)\), all realizable in Definition 3 by squared embedding distances \(-\log w_i\) at \(T=1\). Fixed ground-truth embeddings \(\operatorname{logit}(0.2)\) and \(\operatorname{logit}(0.8)\) give these scores; predicted embeddings can differ by \(\sqrt{-\log w_i}\). The recent records and the test record may have identical distributions, as the changepoint assumption requires.

Swapping a recent score with the test score leaves the score vector unchanged, so its total variation is zero. Swapping the old score with the test score changes a deterministic vector, so its total variation is one. Thus the asserted left side is \[\frac{1/2}{1/2+1/16+1/8+1/4}=\frac8{15}
 >\frac18=\rho^k.\] Even if the proof’s denominator \(1+\sum_iw'_i\) replaces the theorem’s \(\sum_iw'_i\), it equals \(8/31>1/8\). Ties among recent ranks are avoided by continuous weights. The construction satisfies even the stronger condition that recent score-vector swaps have distance zero; it does not rely on confusing marginal and joint exchangeability.

Problem 3 (The Beta-distance bound is false near a parameter boundary).  Theorem 3, equations (12) and (28), and Appendix C (pp. 15–17) assert a bound depending only on \(n\) and \(|a_1-a_2|\le k\) for \(\mathrm{Beta}(a_1,n-a_1)\) and \(\mathrm{Beta}(a_2,n-a_2)\).

Even granting the charitable scalar interpretation of the notation \(S_\theta(Z)\), take \(n=100,k=1,a_1=1,a_2=2\). These are positive integer Beta parameters satisfying every stated parameter constraint. For \(P=\mathrm{Beta}(1,99)\) and \(Q=\mathrm{Beta}(2,98)\) the density ratio is \(f_Q/f_P=98x/(1-x)\), so there is exactly one crossing at \(x_*=1/99\). Integration gives \[d_{\rm TV}(P,Q)=F_P(x_*)-F_Q(x_*)
 =\left(\frac{98}{99}\right)^{98}=0.3697484374.\] The paper’s bound is \[\sqrt{2-2(1-2/101)^{1/2}}=0.1410708778,\] strictly smaller. This refutes the pairwise inequality from which the weighted result is derived; no assumption on weights can make that pairwise inequality valid. The notation also alternates between a score vector and a univariate Beta variable, but resolving that ambiguity cannot fix the false scalar inequality.

The decisive error is visible in (27). The quadratic \(D(a_1)=a_1n-a_1^2-a_1k+kn\) is maximized at \((n-k)/2\). The function \(1-kn/D\) increases in positive \(D\). Substituting this maximum therefore gives an upper bound, whereas the proof uses it as a lower bound. In fact with \(a_1=1,a_2=2,k=1\) and \(n\to\infty\), the exact variation tends to \(e^{-1}\), while the claimed bound tends to zero. A restriction that keeps Beta parameters away from the boundary would need a new proof and is absent here.
# Impact, limitations, and disposition

Table 3 reports weighted empirical coverage \(86.2\%\), \(87.3\%\) and \(89.0\%\) for nominal \(90\%\). These observed quantities are separate from the disputed claimed lower bounds. The counterexamples do not change the recorded percentages or establish a benchmark fabrication. They establish that the present derivations cannot certify the proposed coverage behavior. Labels/activity changes used to estimate \(k\) in Remark 2 also do not by themselves establish a bound on fitted Beta parameters; no empirical identification of that link was reproduced.

Title: Technical Verification of Outlier Gradient Analysis
# Identity and scope

Anshuman Chhabra, Bo Li, Jian Chen, Prasant Mohapatra and Hongfu Liu, Outlier Gradient Analysis: Efficiently Identifying Detrimental Training Samples for Deep Learning Models, ICML 2025, I25-43693 (0324), OpenReview `v77ZMzbsBA`. The frozen publisher PDF has 20 pages; PDF and printed numbering agree. The main scientific text and Appendices A–D were read, including the experiment and implementation details. The bibliography was not independently audited. Original Figures 1, 3 and 4, and relevant formula/table pages, were viewed.

The pinned repository commit is `a62c3807bed227efffa57ac7f0b1473efbb742f3`, dated 3 May 2025. The README, synthetic logistic plotting file, CIFAR-10N experiment, RoBERTa selection script, LLM identification scripts and influence engine were inspected statically. Selected logistic-model and ResNet definitions were also read. The precise file hashes and line ranges are in the coverage record. No author program, model training, downloaded checkpoint or dataset was executed. Separate OpenReview attachments were inaccessible; later revisions and errata were not checked.
# The proposal and supported positive checks

Algorithm 1 constructs per-sample gradients and detects outliers with Isolation Forest or gradient norms, then retrains after removing a specified budget. This is a well-defined empirical data-trimming procedure without an explicit Hessian inversion. Appendix B.2.6 qualifies the implementation: it generally uses last-layer gradients, with sparse random projection for high-dimensional cases.

The displayed Table 2 gains over cross entropy check arithmetically: the best proposed variants improve Aggregate, Random, Worst and Noisy100 accuracies by \(1.34\), \(1.49\), \(1.93\) and \(4.04\) percentage points, respectively. Table 4 supplies standard deviations omitted in the main table. These observations support a favorable descriptive comparison in the reported experiments, not a causal or distribution-free identification guarantee. Figure 1’s synthetic noisy samples are visibly separated in the gradient plots, but this alone does not prove the equivalence asserted in Section 3.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The influence-sign bridge is invalid as stated).  Equations (1)–(2), Observation 3.1 and Sections 3.2–3.3 (pp. 2–4) are affected. The sign error is directly correctable; the asserted general conversion from gradient outliers to detrimental samples needs substantially more assumptions.

Equation reference: eq:correct. Write \(L_T(\theta)=\sum_i\ell_i(\theta)\), \(H=\nabla^2L_T(\widehat\theta)\succ0\) and \(v=\nabla L_V(\widehat\theta)\). For the paper’s downweighting objective \(L_T(\theta)-\varepsilon\ell_j(\theta)\), differentiation of its first-order condition gives \[
 \left.\frac{d\widehat\theta_{-\varepsilon,j}}{d\varepsilon}\right|_0
 =H^{-1}g_j,
 \qquad
 \left.\frac{dL_V(\widehat\theta_{-\varepsilon,j})}{d\varepsilon}\right|_0
 =v^TH^{-1}g_j,
 \quad g_j=\nabla\ell_j(\widehat\theta).\] Multiplying the whole training objective by \(1/n\) does not change this calculation. Equation (1) defines \(I_j=-v^TH^{-1}g_j\), whereas (2) calls \(I_j<0\) detrimental. With lower loss as better utility, that inequality says that downweighting increases loss, which describes a beneficial sample. One can either remove the minus sign or reverse the harmful/beneficial inequality.

This discrepancy is not merely a limitation of infinitesimal approximations. Consider binary logistic regression with a scalar constant input \(x=1\), no regularizer, four labels \(1\) and two labels \(0\), and cross-entropy loss. The finite optimum is \(\widehat\theta=\log2\), \(p=2/3\), with \(g_j=p-y_j\) and \(H=6p(1-p)=4/3>0\). The objective is strictly convex and smooth, and the model is exactly converged. Use a validation record with label \(1\), so \(v=-1/3\). The resulting quantities are
Removed label | Paper’s \(I_j\) | Refit probability | Exact validation loss change
Thus both printed classifications are reversed even for exact leave-one-out retraining in this admissible convex example.

There are two separate obstacles to the proposed equivalence even after correcting the sign. First, if the evaluation set in (1) is the training set, as the paper explicitly permits and uses in several comparisons, an unregularized interior ERM optimum obeys \(v=\sum_i g_i=0\). Every first-order aggregate influence in (1) is then zero, although the individual gradients need not be zero or have similar norms. In the example they are four copies of \(-1/3\) and two copies of \(2/3\). A gradient-outlier ranking can still be nontrivial, but is not the discrete sign classification of (1). This exact-zero argument does not apply unchanged to an incompletely optimized or separately regularized objective; those require their own analysis and cannot justify the stated ERM observation.

Second, the common factor \(v^TH^{-1}\) remains decisive for signs, even though it is shared across samples. Keep the identical six training records, model and gradient cloud, but change the validation label to \(0\). Removing any of the four positive-label records now reduces validation loss by \(\log(5/6)\), while removing a negative-label record increases it by \(\log(5/3)\). The detrimental fraction is \(4/6\), contradicting Observation 3.1’s conclusion that a much smaller minority is detrimental. An algorithm receiving only the unchanged gradient cloud and budget cannot produce correct sign labels for both validation targets. This does not depend on Hessian approximation or nonconvexity.

Counterevidence and scope. The paper calls statement 3.2 a hypothesis, rather than a formal theorem, and acknowledges distribution adaptation with OneClassSVM in Section 8. No universal failure of outlier removal follows from this review. The demonstrated defect is the claimed logical transformation and Observation 3.1, including the statement that average empirical loss makes it clear. The synthetic and noisy-label experiments can validate a useful heuristic on their distributions without validating that general transformation. A repair should correct the sign, state the target utility, distinguish aggregate training influence from self-influence, and present gradient outlyingness as a conditional empirical hypothesis unless assumptions connecting the target direction and outliers are proved. These restricted repairs do not establish a general equivalence. The impact is Major because this bridge is an explicit principal contribution, even if the practical method and some empirical gains survive.

Problem 2 (Released evaluation differs from its mathematical and experimental descriptions).  The confirmed release-level discrepancies are Minor; their effects on the historical published numbers remain Needs Evidence.

The repository provides concrete counterevidence to reading every formula literally. In `synthetic/PLOT_TOY_LR.py`, line 108 uses \(+g_j^TH^{-1}v\), and line 277 selects validation-based influence. That positive sign is consistent with the loss-change interpretation in [eq:correct] (#eq:correct); it differs from (1) and the main text’s training-only description of the synthetic comparison. By contrast, `nlp/src/influence.py`, lines 116–125, returns the negative inner product, and `ROBERTA_SELECTION_1_LATEST.py`, lines 69–72 and 185–195, removes the lowest values. Different code paths therefore do not establish a single common convention.

Section 7 says the LLM class-detection AUC compares absolute influence values with pseudo-labels. However, `LLM_INFL_ID_1.py`, lines 81–87, passes signed scores directly to AUC; only recall uses absolute values at lines 93–101. The distinction can reverse a result: one positive example with score \(-2\) and one negative with score \(-1\) yield signed AUC \(0\) and absolute-score AUC \(1\). This small rank calculation proves a metric mismatch, not a change in Table 3, whose historical score arrays were not available or recomputed.

Appendix B.2.1 describes ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-34 fine-tuning. The inspected CIFAR entry point instead constructs a fresh local `ResNet34` at lines 240 and 318; its class builds new layers, and no weight loading occurs along that inspected entry point. Lines 335–336 report maxima over all 100 test-accuracy observations, so the release summary uses test-set checkpoint selection. This is not the same estimand as a prespecified final checkpoint or checkpoint selected on separate validation data. The correct repair requires documenting the actual initialization, checkpoint criterion and score convention, then recomputing matched comparisons if necessary. No numerical degradation or deliberate leakage is inferred without historical execution records.
Problem 3 (Some comparison summaries exceed the displayed evidence).  These local reporting defects are Minor and do not erase the reported gains.

Appendix C.2 claims that a proposed variant is in the top two for every trimming budget. In Table 5, Aggregate at \(2.5\%\) has DataInf \(92.34\), Gradient Tracing \(92.11\), and the best proposed method, L2, \(92.10\). Thus the proposed method ranks third. The largest Worst value across that table is LiSSA’s \(84.51\), not L2’s \(84.48\) claimed in the accompanying summary. Correcting the prose to a qualified competitive-performance statement suffices for these examples; no significance ranking is justified from these means alone.

Table 7 writes the exact Hessian method’s cost as \(O(nv^3)\) while defining \(v\) as the number of validation/test records and \(p\) as the parameter dimension. A dense Hessian is \(p\times p\); its explicit storage alone is \(\Omega(p^2)\) and ordinary dense factorization costs \(O(p^3)\). The displayed expression cannot be an exact dense-Hessian cost uniformly in \(p\). For logistic losses and the aggregate target in (1), a direct implementation can form \(H\) in \(O(np^2)\), factor it in \(O(p^3)\), sum validation gradients in \(O(vp)\), solve once and score the training gradients in \(O(np)\). This illustrates the missing parameter dependence without claiming a universal cost for all neural-network gradient computations. The algorithm can still avoid a dense factorization; the correction does not reverse that practical advantage. Runtime tables compare specific measured stages and are not end-to-end training guarantees.
# LLM interpretation and remaining limits

The LLM extension explicitly trains one detector per known training class. Its code assigns each class score to all 90 training examples in that class (`LLM_INFL_ID_2.py`, lines 48–62). Consequently it cannot rank samples within a class. Perfect AUC and recall can reflect correct category recognition, as the task definition states, without demonstrating causal sample influence or identifying a unique most influential example. This is a scope limitation, not an allegation of concealed supervision: the class-conditioned construction is disclosed on p. 8. Comparing these perfect values to other methods does not establish their causal-attribution accuracy.

Title: Technical Verification of Modified K-means Algorithm with Local Optimality Guarantees
# Identity and scope

Mingyi Li, Michael R. Metel and Akiko Takeda, Modified K-means Algorithm with Local Optimality Guarantees, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:35656–35684, I25-43694 (0325), OpenReview `v68wPjgEQ8`. The frozen publisher PDF has 29 pages; all page references use its printed/PDF numbering. The main text and Appendices A–F were read. The bibliography was not independently audited. Figures 1–3, Table 1 and Tables 10–11, together with decisive theorem/proof pages, were visually inspected.

The available repository is pinned at commit `7493c390670da6071b2d56bb937a4812a3ef8549`, dated 13 February 2026. The complete Python and C++ algorithm files, README, C++ settings/statistics helper and real-world experiment driver were read statically. The two other run entry points were not read. No author program, dataset experiment or benchmark was run. Separate OpenReview attachments were inaccessible; later errata were not surveyed. This later repository is not proof of which program produced the 2025 tables.
# Definitions and supported derivations

The data are distinct points in the interior of the convex domain of a strictly convex differentiable generator \(\phi\), with positive weights, \(N>K\), and Bregman divergence \(D_\phi(x,c)\). The hard assignment set \(S_1\) consists of vertices of the product-simplex relaxation \(S_2\). For \(F(P)=\min_C f(P,C)\), nonempty clusters have unique weighted-mean centers. \(A(C)\) is the set of minimizing assignments for fixed centers, while \(T(P)\) contains the hard assignments obtained by changing one point’s cluster. D-local optimality compares \(F(P)\) with all of \(T(P)\); C-local optimality is local optimality of \(F\) on \(S_2\). These are different from global optimality.

The concavity of \(F\), as an infimum of linear functions of \(P\), supports the D-local to C-local implication: near a vertex, feasible directions lie in the cone generated by its one-point neighbors, and concavity bounds the objective below by convex combinations of their values and \(F(P)\). The nonempty-cluster condition is essential when using continuous dependence of the weighted means on \(P\).

The paper’s example \(X=(-4,-2,0,1.5,2.5)\), unit weights and \(K=2\) also checks. At centers \((-2,2)\) and the indicated \(3+2\) partition, \[F(\alpha)=\frac{57}{2}-\frac{36}{3-\alpha}-\frac{16}{2+\alpha},\qquad
 F'(\alpha)=\frac{-20\alpha(\alpha+12)}{(\alpha-3)^2(\alpha+2)^2}<0
 \quad(0<\alpha\leq1).\] Thus \(F(0)=17/2\) and \(F(1)=31/6\), validating this failure of ordinary K-means to reach a C-local solution under the paper’s definition.

For Theorem 4.2, a partial optimum with all masses positive and a unique nearest assignment has strictly positive assignment gaps. They persist for centers in a neighborhood. The weighted means \(C(P')\) are continuous there, so \(f(P',C(P'))\geq f(P,C(P'))\geq F(P)\) for nearby \(P'\). This independently supports C-local optimality. Lemma D.4 establishes the partial-optimality and distinct-center premises at the algorithm’s special branch; strict descent through a finite set of hard assignments then supports Theorem 4.4’s finite termination. The complexity result concerns each iteration, not an equal total runtime or a polynomial iteration bound.
# Findings

Problem 1 (Theorem 4.3’s second assertion lacks a premise).  The statement on p. 5 and its proof on p. 18 assert that nonsingleton \(A(C_P^*)\) implies \(A(C_P^*)\cap T(P)\ne\varnothing\), assuming only distinct centers for a solution \((P,C_P^*)\). Partial optimality is also necessary for this assertion as written. This is a Minor, local statement defect.

Take \(\phi(x)=x^2\), six distinct real points \((-5,0,2,-2,1,4)\), unit positive weights and \(K=2\). Assign \(\{-5,0,2\}\) to the first cluster and \(\{-2,1,4\}\) to the second. Both clusters are nonempty, their unique optimal centers are \(-1\) and \(1\), and \(F(P)=44\). The point \(0\) ties between these centers, so \(A(C_P^*)\) has two elements. However, point \(2\) is assigned to the wrong nearest center, as is point \(-2\). Every member of \(A(C_P^*)\) must change both assignments, and hence differs from \(P\) in at least two coordinates. The intersection with \(T(P)\) is empty. Exact enumeration of the \(2^6\) assignments gives Hamming distances \(2\) and \(3\) for the two minimizers.

Adding \(P\in A(C_P^*)\), equivalently partial optimality here, repairs the second assertion. A tied point can then be moved alone while every other assignment stays minimizing. Distinct centers ensure that this tied point differs from each center, and Lemma 4.1 gives strict decrease through the positive center-shift terms. The first assertion, that a C-local solution with distinct centers has singleton \(A(C_P^*)\), is not refuted by this example. The text immediately below the theorem discusses converged K-means, which supplies the missing premise. Lemma D.4 likewise supplies it at the actual invocation in Theorem 4.4. Thus this counterexample does not invalidate the main algorithm’s convergence proof. Reading the word “solution” as implicitly meaning “partial optimal solution” would also avoid the defect, but that qualification is explicit in Theorem 4.2 and absent in 4.3; stating it removes the ambiguity.

Problem 2 (Released C-LO can terminate outside the proved conditions).  The pinned Python and C++ implementations omit Algorithm 1’s \(x_g\ne c_b\) requirement when repairing an empty cluster. Their random initialization samples with replacement. Together with the tie handler, this admits non-C-local output. This is a confirmed release-level defect; its historical experimental effect is Needs Evidence.

For the C++ file `cpp/LO_K_means.hpp`, random initialization at lines 81–84 draws independently, empty-cluster repair at 222–229 checks only that the donor has more than one point, and lines 242–244 assign a tied point to the second minimizing index without ensuring a change. The corresponding Python paths are at 79–83, 165–170 and 173–180. The public API permits ordered distinct data \(X=(0,-1,1)\), unit weights, \(K=2\), squared divergence and random initialization. Both sampled centers equal \(0\) with probability \(1/9\) under independent uniform draws.

At these centers all points tie, so nearest assignment sends all three to cluster 0. The empty-cluster repair takes the first point, \(0\), into cluster 1. Both resulting centers remain \(0\) and the labels are \((1,0,0)\). The next iteration repeats those assignments and repair. The tie handler examines point \(0\), sets its label to 1, which is already its label, and breaks. The unchanged-assignment stopping condition terminates with loss \(2\). This is a static state trace of the inspected code, not an execution of the authors’ program.

Move an \(\alpha\) fraction of point \(-1\) from cluster 0 to cluster 1. The cluster masses are \(2-\alpha\) and \(1+\alpha\), both positive, with centers \(\alpha/(2-\alpha)\) and \(-\alpha/(1+\alpha)\). Exact recomputation gives \[F(\alpha)=2-\frac{\alpha^2}{2-\alpha}-\frac{\alpha^2}{1+\alpha}<2
 \qquad(0<\alpha\leq1).\] Assignments and centers converge to the returned state as \(\alpha\downarrow0\); it is therefore neither C-local nor CJ-local. At \(\alpha=1\) the loss is \(1/2\), so it is not D-local either. The supplied input satisfies the data, weight and divergence assumptions; the failure comes from implementation choices that differ from the paper’s algorithm.

The paper samples without replacement and explicitly requires \(x_g\ne c_b\) in the empty-cluster repair. Its proof relies on the resulting strict decrease. These conditions exclude this trace and are material counterevidence against treating it as a false theoretical guarantee. The real-world driver selects random initialization, but its helper sorts and deduplicates data; that driver does not preserve the particular input ordering above. No assertion is made that a reported benchmark encountered this state. Aligning initialization and repair with the pseudocode, and requiring a genuine tie move, addresses the exhibited mechanism. A fully verified finite-precision implementation and historical rerun remain open. The shared \(10^{-10}\) tolerances and positive-mass thresholds also mean the release is not an exact-arithmetic implementation for arbitrarily small positive weights.
# Impact and empirical limits

These findings leave the principal descent/convergence argument intact under its intended partial-optimality premises and exact pseudocode. The later release requires repair before its output can be given the same unqualified guarantee. Figures 1–3 and the real-data tables give descriptive comparisons; raw runs and their uncertainty were not reproduced. The released implementation stores an \(N\times K\) distance array, whereas the paper says an \(O((N+K)d)\)-space implementation is possible. This release choice does not disprove that existence claim.

report: Abstract: The finite-level telescoping estimator is unbiased when its endpoint is exact, and the adaptive residual-norm probabilities minimize its conditional second moment. However, an explicit quadratic example disproves the stated numerical nonconvex convergence bound, and two quantization constructions do not satisfy their own unbiasedness/variance derivations. These are Major issues in the theoretical claims; they do not refute the general estimator or prove that the reported training gains disappear. A separate optimality statement needs a worst-case-bound qualification. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of the Multilevel Monte Carlo Compression Method
# Identity and coverage

Ze’ev Zukerman, Bassel Hamoud and Kfir Y. Levy, Beyond Communication Overhead: A Multilevel Monte Carlo Approach for Mitigating Compression Bias in Distributed Learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:80933–80960, I25-43695 (0326), OpenReview `v4mcWhN0Sf`. The frozen publisher PDF contains 28 pages; references use PDF/printed page numbers. All main scientific text and Appendices A–G were read, with Figures 1–6 and decisive formula pages visually inspected. The bibliography was not independently audited. No released repository was found in the bounded source acquisition, and OpenReview attachments were inaccessible. This does not imply that code does not exist. No author code or training experiment was executed, and no later errata survey was performed.
# Supported core calculations

For a fixed stochastic gradient \(v\), let \(r_l=C^l(v)-C^{l-1}(v)\), \(C^0(v)=0\), \(C^L(v)=v\), and let \(p_l>0\) sum to one. The estimator \(Y=r_J/p_J\), with \(J\sim p\), obeys \[\mathbb E[Y\mid v]=\sum_l r_l=v,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(Y\mid v)=\sum_l\frac{\|r_l\|^2}{p_l}-\|v\|^2.\] Conditioning first on \(v\) makes the argument valid even when \(p_l=p_l(v)\). For randomized compressors, the coupling must preserve the intended marginal levels; deterministic examples used here require no additional randomness. Independent sampling across workers is needed for the \(1/M\) variance reduction.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\sum_l\|r_l\|^2/p_l\geq(\sum_l\|r_l\|)^2\), with equality at \(p_l\propto\|r_l\|\). Zero residual levels can be omitted; the zero vector needs an explicit zero-output convention. This supports Lemma 3.4’s conditional optimization, with that boundary convention. For Top-k, residuals are disjoint coordinates or segments. An independent check with \(v=(3,-1,2)\) and coordinate probabilities \((1/2,1/6,1/3)\) gives mean \(v\), second moment \(36\) and variance \(22\) exactly.
# Problems

Problem 1 (The nonconvex convergence calculation drops initial suboptimality).  Appendix F.1, the step from (92) to (93), is invalid even for identity compression. It supplies the nonconvex bound in Theorem 4.1 and is repeated in Appendix F.4, (122)–(124). This is a Major error in a core derivation.

Consider one worker, \(f(x)=x^2/2\), stochastic loss \(f(x,z)=x^2/2+zx\), and independent equiprobable \(z=\pm1\). Then \(L=1\), \(\sigma^2=1\), \(x^*=0\), and the stochastic gradient is \(x+z\), unbiased with uniformly bounded variance. All smoothness, homogeneity and finite-optimum assumptions hold. Use the single-level identity compressor, so \(\widehat\omega=0\), \(x_1=\sqrt{200}\), \(\Delta_1=100\), and \(T=10{,}000\). The displayed step-size choice before (93), with its inactive compression cap omitted, permits equality \(\eta=T^{-1/2}=0.01\).

Writing \(\rho=(1-\eta)^2\), the exact recursion is \[x_{t+1}=(1-\eta)x_t-\eta z_t,\qquad
 \mathbb E x_t^2=200\rho^{t-1}+\eta^2\frac{1-\rho^{t-1}}{1-\rho}.\] Thus, with \(S_T=(1-\rho^T)/(1-\rho)\), \[\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E|\nabla f(x_t)|^2
 =\frac{200S_T+\eta^2(T-S_T)/(1-\rho)}{T}
 =1.010025\ldots.\] Equation (93) instead bounds this quantity by \(4\Delta_1/T+4/\sqrt T=0.08\). Independent direct iteration of the moment recursion agrees with the closed form to \(10^{-12}\). This is a calculation of exact expectations, not a noisy Monte Carlo or author-code run.

The issue is already visible in (92): minimizing \(4\Delta_1/(T\eta)+4(2\widehat\omega^2+1)\sigma^2 L\eta/M\) requires a \(\sqrt{\Delta_1}\) factor in the balancing step size. A supported repair, using \(q=\widehat\omega^2\) as the relative-variance coefficient, is \[\eta=\min\left\{\frac1L,\frac{M}{8qL},
 \sqrt{\frac{\Delta_1 M}{(2q+1)\sigma^2 LT}}\right\},\] omitting inactive zero-denominator caps. This yields, up to numerical constants, \(\Delta_1 L/T+q\Delta_1 L/(MT)+
\sigma\sqrt{(2q+1)L\Delta_1/(MT)}\). Alternatively, keeping the paper’s step size requires retaining its actual \(\Delta_1\) dependence in the noise term. The word “\(\leq\)” in the final step-size prescription should not be read as allowing arbitrarily tiny step sizes with an unchanged final bound.

Scope and counterevidence. The preceding descent bound (92) and the telescoping unbiasedness argument remain useful. If \(\Delta_1\) is fixed and hidden in a big-O constant, the advertised \(T,M\) exponents can survive. That reading does not rescue explicit (93), nor a bound displaying dependence on \(\Delta_1\) but dropping it from its variance term. The counterexample uses the stated step size at equality, so it does not rest on the “\(\leq\)” wording alone. It establishes neither nonconvergence nor loss of the repaired parallelization order. The paper also alternates between \(\widehat\omega\) and \(\widehat\omega^2\) as the coefficient in (3); defining \(q\) explicitly avoids that ambiguity, and the identity example is unaffected by it.

Problem 2 (The quantization extensions violate the conditions used to remove bias).  The floating-point derivation in Appendix B and the RTN construction in Section 3.2/Appendix G.2 are incompatible with the endpoint/base conditions of Lemma 3.2. This is Major for these claimed unbiased-compression extensions, with historical experimental effects unresolved.

Floating-point base. Write a positive normal floating-point number as \(e=b(1+\sum_{j=1}^{52}m_j2^{-j})\), \(b=2^{E-1023}\). Appendix B states \(e^0=0\), but (22) subtracts the truncated expression with leading \(b\) also when \(l=1\). The cancellation leading to (23)–(24) therefore omits \(b\) from the first residual. For \(e=1\), all mantissa bits vanish. Equations (29)–(31) give second moment zero, and (33) gives variance \(-1\), an impossibility. This input is a normal, finite, exactly represented number, so subnormal or rounding conventions do not explain the result.

With the declared zero base, the correct first residual is \(b(1+m_1/2)\), not \(bm_1/2\). For \(e=1\) and \(p_1=2^{-1}/(1-2^{-52})\), the correct estimator is \(1/p_1\) with probability \(p_1\) and zero otherwise. Its mean is one, second moment \(1/p_1=2(1-2^{-52})\), and variance \(1/p_1-1\). If instead one uses only the mantissa residuals in the derivation with zero base, the mean is zero. A different valid construction sets \(e^0=b\) and transmits/reconstructs that base, retaining the \(e^0\) term in (6); its variance on this example is zero. Either repair requires recomputing the stated second moment, variance and optimal probabilities under the chosen construction. The known leading bit can be reconstructed from sign/exponent metadata, so this review does not assert that the nominal bit budget must increase; the published calculation is nevertheless invalid.

RTN endpoint. Equation (125) writes \(C^l(v)=\delta_l\operatorname{clip}(\operatorname{round}(v/\delta_l),-c,c)\), with \(\delta_l=2c/(2^l-1)\). For fixed \(c\), its output range shrinks to zero as \(l\) increases, instead of approaching an identity map. Take the scalar \(c=1\) and \(v=3/4\), safely inside the stated clipping range. At levels \(2,4,8,16\) the printed map returns respectively \(2/3,2/15,2/255,2/65535\). If the highest level is 16, the telescoping estimator has expectation \(2/65535\), not \(3/4\), for every choice of positive level probabilities. No finite level of the printed family equals the identity on all inputs. A gradient-dependent distribution does not fix that endpoint bias.

One can correct the clipping indices to match a fixed physical range, but finite quantization still needs an exact terminal correction, a suitably unbiased terminal map, or an explicit residual-bias analysis. Simply correcting the clipping scale does not establish Definition 3.1. Figure 6 reports good MLMC-RTN performance and provides counterevidence to assuming the plotted implementation used the formula literally. With no available implementation or raw trace, the review cannot determine which correction it used or how its communication cost was accounted for. The general MLMC lemma remains correct for families that actually satisfy its premises; these examples fail to instantiate those premises or the associated variance derivation.

Problem 3 (Fixed-point optimality is optimality of a surrogate bound).  Lemma 3.3, p. 6 and Appendix C, states that \(p_l\propto2^{-l}\) minimizes the fixed-point estimator’s variance. Its proof minimizes an upper bound obtained by replacing each input bit by one. The literal instancewise optimality claim is false; this narrower issue is Minor.

For the exactly representable scalar \(e=1/2\), only the first bit is nonzero. For any positive probability vector, its variance is \(1/(4p_1)-1/4\). The proposed \(p_1=1/[2(1-2^{-63})]\) gives variance approximately \(1/4\). Choosing \(p_1=3/4\) and distributing the remaining \(1/4\) positively over the other 62 levels gives variance \(1/12\), strictly smaller, with the same single-residual communication format. Thus even requiring every probability to be nonzero does not rescue the pointwise claim. The geometric probabilities do minimize the bit-independent second-moment upper bound \(\sum_l 2^{-2l}/p_l\), by Cauchy–Schwarz. That is a defensible replacement statement, explicitly consistent with the proof’s instruction to bound the bits. It is not a proof of minimizing the true worst-case variance, because the subtracted \(e^2\) also depends on the bit pattern. Lemma 3.4 already supplies the instance-adaptive alternative. Likewise, Lemma 3.6’s scale must be qualified as in [eq:exp] (#eq:exp).
# Empirical interpretation and dependence

The six figures were inspected and show favorable descriptive curves in several settings. They do not establish the false algebraic identities above. The text equates epochs with iterations, while changing worker counts and sometimes batch sizes; raw step definitions and communication accounting are needed for a controlled scaling comparison. The sparse-vector cost must also encode original coordinate indices unless the receiver already knows the gradient-dependent ordering. No alternative numerical ranking is asserted without such records. The comparisons are communication/epoch plots, not wall-clock speedup measurements.

The corrected generic moment argument can still support useful convergence bounds and the stated asymptotic parallelization exponents with fixed problem/compression constants. The present Major assessment follows from demonstrably invalid core quantitative derivations and unsupported unbiased quantization instances, rather than from a claim that all conclusions fail.

Title: Technical Verification of Mean-Field Langevin Stochastic Descent-Ascent
# Identity, scope and conventions

Zhangyi Liu, Feng Liu, Rui Gao and Shuang Li, ICML 2025, I25-43696 (0327), OpenReview `v4DWXM93VV`. The frozen publisher metadata title is Convergence of Mean-Field Langevin Stochastic Descent-Ascent for Distributional Minimax Optimization; the actual PDF title inserts the word Gradient before “Descent-Ascent.” Both titles refer to the same frozen source recorded in the manifest; no ID or input title is changed.

The reviewed publisher PDF has 25 pages. All main scientific text (pp. 1–8) and Appendices A–D (pp. 11–25) were read. Page references are PDF/printed numbers. The decisive algorithm, theorem, constants and proof pages were visually inspected; the paper has no empirical figure or results table. No relevant released repository was identified by the bounded source acquisition. Separate OpenReview attachments were inaccessible. The bibliography and later errata were not independently audited. No author program or finite-particle experiment was run.
# Framework and a fully admissible test family

The paper studies \(E(\mu,
u)=J(\mu,
u)+	au\mathrm{KL}(\mu\midho)-
	au\mathrm{KL}(
u\midho)\) for a standard Gaussian reference \(ho\), with convex-concave \(J\). Its assumptions bound spatial derivatives of first variations through order four and derivatives of second variations, assume LSI for the associated Gibbs measures, and require finite initial energy and fourth moments. Algorithm 1 uses alternating Euler updates with independent Gaussian noises. The stochastic extension adds unbiased oracle noise with a bounded fourth moment. These are distribution-level statements; the paper explicitly leaves finite-particle error analysis for future work.

Equation reference: eq:params. Set \(d=1\), \(J\equiv0\), and \(\rho=N(0,1)\). Every Gibbs operator and both equilibrium distributions equal \(\rho\), with LSI constant \(\alpha=1\). All derivatives of \(J\) vanish, so one may take \(M_i=0\) and the valid upper bounds \(C_1=C_2=1/2\) (also any nonnegative \(C_0\)). Choose \[
 \tau=\tfrac12,\quad\lambda=\tfrac1{10},\quad
 \eta_2=\tfrac1{100},\quad\eta_1=\tfrac1{2000}.\] Then \(\tau<1/(2C_1^2)=2\), \(\eta_1<1/C_1=2\), \(\eta_2<1/(2\tau\alpha)=1\). The time-scale relation holds exactly: \[\eta_1=\min\{\lambda,0.2,1/(\tau\alpha)\}\tau\alpha\eta_2.\] Exact gradients are a permissible stochastic oracle with \(\zeta=0\). Every Gaussian initial law below has finite entropy, KL divergence and fourth moment. The requirements are thus checked without relying on nonsmooth densities or unbounded functional derivatives.

Equation reference: eq:OU. For \(a_i=\eta_i\tau\), each marginal follows the elementary Gaussian update \[
 \begin{gathered}
 X_{k+1}=(1-a_i)X_k+\sqrt{2a_i}\,\xi_k,\\
 m_{k+1}=(1-a_i)m_k,\qquad s_{k+1}=(1-a_i)^2s_k+2a_i,
 \end{gathered}\] where \(s_k\) denotes variance. The exact KL is \(\mathrm{KL}(N(m,s)\mid\rho)=(m^2+s-1-\log s)/2\). Also \(L_1=\tau\mathrm{KL}(\mu\mid\rho)\), \(L_2=\tau\mathrm{KL}(\nu\mid\rho)\). These identities support all checks below.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The stated main contraction bound is false).  Theorems 1–2, pp. 6–7, assert contraction \((1-2\eta_1\tau\alpha)^K\) with the explicit remainders in Appendix A.3. The following counterexample disproves that quantitative statement. This is Major because it directly concerns the main last-iterate theorem.

Let \(q_i=(1-a_i)^2\). After \(K\) updates, \(m_{\mu,K}=(1-a_1)^K10^5\) and \(s_{i,K}=q_i^K+2a_i(1-q_i^K)/(1-q_i)\). Substituting these values in the Gaussian KL formula gives the exact Lyapunov value. Already after one update its excess over the enlarged claimed bound exceeds \(152\); after ten updates the excess exceeds \(1500\). The independent 60-digit calculation records both complete values. This is not particle simulation and contains no sampling error.

The mechanism is explicit. The mean contribution contracts by \((1-a_1)^2=1-2a_1+a_1^2\), strictly slower than \(1-2a_1\). The extra \(a_1^2L_1(\mu_0)\) cannot be bounded uniformly by a remainder that omits arbitrary finite initial moments. Appendix C, p. 22, actually concludes the weaker factor \(1-\eta_1\tau\alpha\), not the displayed factor in the theorem. Lemma 10, pp. 15–16, keeps initial moments in its moment estimate, but A.3 drops them when defining the final constants. These are concrete sources of the mismatch.

Using the weaker factor eliminates this particular Gaussian mean counterexample, and retaining appropriate initial-moment dependence is another necessary accounting repair if a sharper factor is pursued. Neither observation verifies the general repaired theorem, because the next problem affects its one-step entropy estimate independently. With \(\zeta=0\), the same example applies to Theorem 2’s stated bound. There is no implication here that the algorithm fails to approach a small discretization neighborhood in this example: [eq:OU] (#eq:OU) shows that it does.

Problem 2 (The required uniform one-step estimates do not follow from the assumptions).  Lemma 1, Proposition 1 and the entropy argument in Lemmas 6–7 are affected. These are Major defects in the core elementary discretization proof.

Lemma 6 introduces a uniform log-density Hessian bound that Assumptions 1–3 do not provide. Its convexity observation about heat-flow entropy does not by itself give a quadratic Taylor upper remainder. For a Gaussian of variance \(s\), heat-flow entropy has second derivative \(1/[2(s+\epsilon)^2]\) in the negative-entropy convention, so its Taylor constants necessarily depend on the density scale. In addition, the equality in (26) omits the inverse transpose Jacobian: \[

u)(T(x))

u(x)-
abla_x\log|\det DT(x)|\}.\] Even for \(T(x)=a x\), Fisher information scales as \(a^{-2}\), not as the expression in (26). An elementary proof may still be possible, but the present uniform remainder and transport identity require replacement.

Second, Proposition 1 uses \(f_k+
abla\log\mu_k\), whereas the energy’s Wasserstein gradient is \(f_k+	au
abla\log\mu_k\). At \(\mu_0=
u_0=ho\), \(f_0=g_0=	au x\). The true next \(L_1\) is positive, since the Euler step changes its variance to \(1+(\eta_1	au)^2\). The proposition’s right side is at most \(-\eta_1(	au-1)^2/2+100\eta_1^2=-0.0000375\). Thus the missing temperature factor is not harmless under the theorem’s arbitrary \(	au\) convention. The LSI identity at the top of p. 22 repeats the same missing factor. Correcting it to \(	au
abla\log\mu_k\) resolves this equilibrium contradiction, but does not resolve [eq:badlemma] (#eq:badlemma).

The smooth Gaussian examples avoid all integration-by-parts boundary and initial-singularity ambiguities. A defensible repair must either prove the needed density regularity uniformly, state stronger initial/iterate assumptions with their constants, or use a different discretization estimate that does not require such uniform Fisher/Taylor control. No corrected general complexity theorem is claimed by this review.

Problem 3 (The Wasserstein coefficient is inverted).  Corollary 1, p. 7, writes \((2	au/\alpha_1)(W_2^2(\mu,\mu^*)+
W_2^2(
u,
u^*))\leq	au(\mathrm{KL}(\mu\mid\mu^*)+
\mathrm{KL}(
u\mid
u^*))\). This local conversion error is Minor.

For \(\mu=N(1,1)\), \(\nu=\rho\) and both targets \(\rho\), the distance sum is \(1\) and the KL sum is \(1/2\). With \(\alpha_1=1\), the displayed inequality requires \(2\tau\leq\tau/2\), which fails. The correct coefficient is \(\tau\alpha_1/2\). Appendix C, p. 23, states the correct underlying Talagrand inequality \(W_2^2\leq(2/\alpha_1)\mathrm{KL}\), providing direct counterevidence to an alternative LSI convention. The local coefficient repair is verified. The corollary also invokes the stochastic setup while retaining \(R_1\) rather than its noise-dependent analogue; a complete repaired corollary must inherit whatever valid stochastic remainder is ultimately established.

Problem 4 (Continuous-time noise uses the wrong time-scale factor).  Equation (4), p. 3, multiplies both drift and Brownian increment for \(\omega\) by \(\eta\). This is Minor relative to the discrete-time contribution.

For \(J=0\) the printed equation is \(d\omega=-\eta\tau\omega\,dt+\eta\sqrt{2\tau}\,dB\), whose invariant variance is \(\eta\), rather than the target Gaussian variance \(1\). For example \(\eta=2\) gives \(N(0,2)\). Scaling the noise by \(\sqrt{\eta}\), giving \(\sqrt{2\eta\tau}\,dB\), restores the target. Algorithm 1 uses the correct square-root dependence on its own ascent step size, so this observation does not itself refute that algorithm.
# Positive checks, dependence and remaining work

For the uncoupled Gaussian family, the best-response operators, nonnegative Lyapunov terms and their KL identities are exact. The bounded-perturbation LSI reasoning in Propositions 3–4 has the expected form: a perturbation bounded in oscillation by \(2G_0/\tau\) or \(2F_1m_0/\tau\) gives the stated exponentially reduced Gaussian LSI constant. The nonlinear best-response dependence and its smoothness must still be controlled in a repaired proof; the finite computations here do not certify all those steps.

The core contribution is the discrete-time last-iterate convergence analysis. Both a final stated theorem and its foundational one-step estimates fail on admissible cases, supporting Major independently of typographical defects. A weaker rate statement might survive after substantive proof repair; it is not established merely by replacing the factor two in Theorem 1. The application discussion supplies formulations and regularity examples, not empirical validation or a finite-particle convergence theorem.

Title: Technical Verification of Knowledge-Guided Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization
# Identity and scope

Zitao Wang, Ziyuan Wang, Molei Liu and Nian Si, ICML 2025, I25-43697 (0328), Knowledge-Guided Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization. The frozen publisher PDF contains 23 pages. All main scientific text, pp. 1–9, and Appendices A–F, pp. 11–23, were read. The bibliography was not independently audited. Both original figures and Tables 2–5 were visually checked, along with decisive formulas. No relevant repository was identified in the bounded source acquisition; separate OpenReview attachments were inaccessible. Later errata and raw experimental results were unavailable to this review. Page numbers below are one-based PDF numbers, equal to printed numbers.
# Core contribution and independent checks

Equation reference: eq:dual. Strong transfer constrains perturbations \(\Delta\) to \(S=\{\Delta:\theta_m^T\Delta=0\ \forall m\}=\Theta^\perp\), where \(\Theta\) is the span of the prior predictors. The restricted support function is \[
 a(\beta)=\sup_{u\in S,\,\|u\|_q\leq1}|\beta^Tu|
 =\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta}\|\beta-\vartheta\|_p.\] This is the dual norm on the quotient by \(\Theta\), including \(p=1,\infty\). For squared loss and average transport cost at most \(\delta\), Minkowski and [eq:dual] (#eq:dual) bound root risk by \(\sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}_N}+\sqrt\delta\,a(\beta)\). For nonzero empirical residual vector \(r\), choose an attaining unit \(u\in S\) with \(\beta^Tu=a\) and \(\Delta_i=-\sqrt\delta\,r_i u/\sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}_N}\). This attains the bound and uses exactly budget \(\delta\). When every residual is zero, a shift of length \(\sqrt\delta\) attains \(\delta a^2\); \(a=0\) is immediate. Thus the fixed-\(\beta\) identity, and hence Theorem 3.3, hold without the appendix’s singular divisions.

For logistic and hinge losses, the Lipschitz upper bound gives empirical loss plus \(\delta a\). A mass of order \(\delta/t\) sent distance \(t\) along an adverse unit direction approaches that bound as \(t\to\infty\), because both losses have asymptotic adverse slope one. This verifies the supremum formula behind Theorem 3.6, including the endpoint norms. It need not produce an attained worst-case distribution.

For weak transfer, \(A=I+\lambda\theta\theta^T\) and the correct penalty is \[\sqrt{\beta^TA^{-1}\beta},\qquad
 A^{-1}=I-\frac{\theta\theta^T}{\|\theta\|_2^2+\lambda^{-1}}.\] This equals \(\|\beta\|_{\Psi_{\lambda^{-1}}}\) under the main-text definition of \(\Psi\). It establishes Theorem 3.5 by the same argument. Replacing \(I\) by positive definite \(\Lambda\) verifies Corollaries 3.7 and D.1. The full-rank prior span reduces to ERM, as the authors explicitly note. Independent numerical checks use \(\theta=(1,2)\), \(\beta=(3,-1)\): \(a=3.5,7/\sqrt5,7/3\) for \(p=1,2,\infty\). A three-residual example also checks exact transport budget and attained risk. These are checks of identities, not reruns of reported learning experiments.
# Localized findings and repairs

Problem 1 (The sample-outside-the-ambiguity-set interpretation is unsupported).  The sentence following Proposition 3.1, p. 5, describes its minimax bound as out-of-sample performance at least as good as the empirical domain adapter. This is false without a condition placing the target law in the ambiguity set. Severity: Minor, a necessary scope correction.

Let \(d=2\), \(\theta=e_1\), \(N=1\), and observe \((x,y)=(e_1,1)\). For any \(\delta>0\), the root robust objective is \(|1-\beta_1|+\sqrt\delta|\beta_2|\), with unique minimizer \(\beta=e_1\) and value zero. Let the true target distribution give equal probability to \((e_1,1)\) and \((e_2,1)\). The observed sample has probability \(1/2\), but this predictor has target squared risk \(1/2\), while the empirical adapter risk is zero. The target law cannot belong to the ambiguity set: its \(\theta^TX\) marginal differs from the frozen empirical marginal.

Proposition 3.1 itself is valid: choose \(\beta=\alpha\theta\) and use the preserved joint law of \((Y,\theta^TX)\). No minimax interchange is needed. Its guarantee is for laws in that restricted set. For a continuous \((Y,\theta^TX)\) population, the exact preservation of the empirical discrete marginal generally precludes population membership for every radius. Increasing \(\delta\) does not cure that obstruction. The text should state this scope, distinguish the limit \(\beta\in\Theta\) from \(\beta\to\theta\), and avoid a general no-negative-transfer interpretation. The conclusion’s explicit deferral of statistical guarantees is important counterevidence to treating this as a failed central statistical theorem.

Problem 2 (Several displayed proof formulas require local corrections).  Appendix B, pp. 17–18, Appendix C, pp. 18–19, and Proposition E.2(4), p. 22, contain algebraic errors. Severity: Minor; the main equivalences have independent derivations above.

In the weak-transfer proof, write \(r=y-\beta^Tx\) and \(b=\sqrt{\beta^TA^{-1}\beta}\). The correct radial maximization is \[\sup_{t\geq0}\{(b^2-\gamma)t^2+2|r|bt\}
 =\frac{r^2b^2}{\gamma-b^2}\quad(\gamma>b^2).\] The printed negative linear term is wrong, the next line drops the square on \(b\), and the finiteness threshold must compare \(\gamma\) with \(b^2\). The residual is also inadvertently defined as squared on p. 17. For \(\theta=e_1\), \(\beta=e_2\), \(r=1\), \(\gamma=2\), the actual inner supremum is \(1\), attained at \(\Delta=-e_2\), whereas the printed radial expression \(-t^2-2t\) has supremum zero. For \(b>0\), at \(\gamma=b^2\) a nonzero residual gives infinity; zero-residual and \(b=0\) cases require separate limits, also in the proof of Theorem 3.3.

For \(h(x)=\log(1+e^{-x})\), the correct conjugate has domain \([-1,0]\): \[h^*(z)=(-z)\log(-z)+(1+z)\log(1+z),\quad -1\leq z\leq0.\] The printed \([0,1]\) formula belongs to \(\log(1+e^x)\). At \(z=1/2\), \(zx-h(x)\to\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\), contradicting the finite printed value. Lemma C.1 must use \(-\alpha\beta\) in its biconjugate expression, or redefine \(h\) consistently. The final distance to the linear span is unchanged by this sign, so its conclusion survives.

The signed linear “weighted penalty” in Section 3.4, p. 7, must instead be the square root of \(\min_\kappa\{(\beta_1-\kappa\theta_1)^2/d_1+
(\beta_2-\kappa\theta_2)^2/d_2\}\). As printed the linear minimization can equal \(-\infty\). Theorem E.5’s unrestricted sum-conjugacy statement generally needs closure or a qualification; the finite continuous norm functions used here supply the needed qualification. The rank-one difference between the weak metric and the strong projection is positive semidefinite, not positive definite: equality holds for \(\beta\perp\theta\), contrary to the strict comparison on p. 6. The ellipse and the non-strict inclusion remain correct.

Problem 3 (Empirical prose and plotting do not consistently match the tables).  Section 4.1, Figure 2 and Tables 3–5 need reconciliation. Severity: Minor; the reported improvements in several regimes remain supported.

At \(N=80,s=1,\rho=0.3\), Table 3 gives KG-WDRO accuracy \(0.583\) versus WDRO \(0.654\), a loss of \(7.1\) percentage points. At \(N=50,s=1\) and the same correlation it gives \(0.586\) versus \(0.619\). Thus the unqualified claim that both transfer methods significantly outperform target-only WDRO is contradicted by the paper’s own averages. Tables give no dispersion or paired confidence intervals, so statistical significance cannot be inferred from their rounded means. This does not negate the clear favorable regimes at high correlation or the low-sample comparisons.

The two lower panels of Figure 2 label \(N=70\) but draw the WDRO dashed baseline near \(0.49\), whereas Table 5 gives \(0.375\) and \(0.354\) for the displayed settings. The latter values are below the plotted vertical minimum \(0.4\). This is a visible inconsistency, not a claim about which underlying experiment is correct. The generating scheme is described clearly enough to understand the comparisons, but Appendix A.2.3 lists a correlation grid beginning at \(0.3\), while Section 4.3 and Table 5 start at \(0.7\) and include \(0.75,0.85\); the actual grid needs identification. By contrast, the real-data table does support five wins in eight states and a \(7.587\%\) reduction in aggregate log loss, rounding to \(7.6\%\). Its evaluation split and uncertainty remain insufficiently specified for independent reproduction without code/data-processing details.
# Assessment, evidence and limits

The central transport-to-regularization mechanism is sound under its stated finite-sample ambiguity sets. Its handling of collinearity permits scalar rescaling and sign changes, but does not by itself guarantee invariance to arbitrary feature-specific transformations or eliminate negative transfer. The mathematical repairs above are local and do not establish a new population generalization theorem. Accordingly the overall assessment is Minor, with no demonstrated Major defect in the principal reformulations. All judgments remain pending; author adoption is unknown and no human review is recorded. Focused independent acceptance is documented in the existing verification files.
1 Z. Wang, Z. Wang, M. Liu and N. Si, Knowledge-Guided Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization, ICML 2025, frozen publisher PDF. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wang25df.html.

Source SHA-256: `4ee170ac69376b3133a4b4a790342b5c194c249be02af44e579aba38974ca10b`. The independent Python script uses NumPy and SciPy for the low-dimensional dual-norm, inverse-matrix, transport, conjugate and table checks. Inputs, outputs, exact source-page hashes and initial visual observations accompany this report. No author modules were imported or executed. The final TeX is actually compiled and its PDF pages inspected, with build and page-image records saved separately. Title: Technical Verification of RIFLEx: A Free Lunch for Length Extrapolation in Video Diffusion Transformers
# Identity, evidence and contribution

Min Zhao, Guande He, Yixiao Chen, Hongzhou Zhu, Chongxuan Li and Jun Zhu, ICML 2025, I25-43698 (0329), RIFLEx: A Free Lunch for Length Extrapolation in Video Diffusion Transformers. The frozen PDF has 19 pages. Main scientific text (pp. 1–9) and Appendices A–F (pp. 13–19) were read. All thirteen original figures, including the contact sheets, and the tables were visually inspected. Bibliographic claims were not independently audited. Static pictures do not establish actual playback speed, temporal smoothness, or full-video non-repetition; no video playback is claimed.

The source snapshot is commit `18e0bc34d5a68cae5753a6e33e35313bec89c1db`, dated 13 May 2025, in the repository now named DiT-Extrapolation. Complete static reads covered the three Python source files, README, requirements, and four demo prompt files. These are not proved to be the bytes used for the paper experiments. No author program, model, training run or evaluation was executed. The private 20,000-video training set, raw results, evaluation implementation, multi-GPU branch and separate OpenReview attachments were unavailable within the acquired material. The prompt files contain 38 demo entries, not the stated 100-prompt Hunyuan evaluation set.

RIFLEx measures a repeated-frame lag, selects the nearest RoPE component period, and reduces that frequency to \(2\pi/(sL)\). Other components are retained. The principal contribution is empirical training-free twofold extrapolation on CogVideoX-5B and HunyuanVideo, with additional short-video fine-tuning for improved quality and threefold extrapolation. The paper does not supply a convergence or generalization theorem. It explicitly acknowledges that intrinsic-frequency identification lacks a theoretical foundation and that fourfold extrapolation degrades.
# Frequency analysis and limits of the inference

Problem 1 (A component period is not a content non-repetition guarantee).  Sections 3.2–3.4, pp. 5–6, infer repetition of generated content from individual RoPE periods and call (8) a non-repetition condition. That inference is invalid as a general implication. Severity: Minor as a scope correction to this empirical contribution, not a refuted formal theorem.

For a rotary pair \(R(p\theta)x\), the relative attention term is \(q_p^TR((q-p)\theta)k_q\). Periodicity of \(R\) does not make the content-dependent vectors \(q_p,k_q\) or the value vectors equal. With multiple components, a period of one component is not even a period of the full positional representation. In the Hunyuan example documented in `identify_k`, \(b=256,d'=16\), hence \[(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_8)=(1,1/2,\ldots,1/128).\] At \(N_4=2\pi/(1/8)=16\pi\), component four returns to phase one, but component five has phase \(-1\), with encoding distance \(2\) from its initial value. Thus the full embedding has not repeated. In discrete time, \(2\pi/\theta_j\) is generally noninteger; a continuous period also does not imply an exact collision at an integer frame. A model ignoring the edited component can still produce repetitive values, even while its remaining position codes are distinct. These observations invalidate the implication, not the possibility that a learned component strongly influences repetition.

Equation (8) correctly ensures at most one continuous cycle for the chosen component over the target interval. With positions \(0,\ldots,L'-1\) and \(\theta'=2\pi/L'\), its first and last phases are nevertheless very close: \[\|e^{i(L'-1)\theta'}-1\|=2\sin(\pi/L').\] For \(L'=66\), this distance is about \(0.0952\). Absence of an exact phase collision therefore does not yield robust separation, much less non-repetition of semantic content. A defensible replacement is a stated empirical hypothesis, with controlled frequency interventions, unchanged seeds and model weights, complete lag statistics, and held-out prompts.

Equation (6) uses a signed cosine difference, which is neither positive nor pointwise monotone in frequency. For the complete sine/cosine pair, the norm of the one-step change is instead \(2|\sin(\theta/2)|\), independent of position and increasing on the frequencies \(0\leq\theta\leq1\) used here. That supports an encoding-scale intuition, but no formula given connects it quantitatively to generated optical motion. Moreover, isolating one frequency and fine-tuning changes model weights; it cannot alone identify causal dominance inside the original multi-frequency network.

As a positive consistency check, the Hunyuan NTK formula gives intrinsic period \(16\pi s^{3/7}\). It exceeds the approximate target latent length \(33s\) for \(s=2\) and falls below it for \(s=2.3\), matching the reported change of behavior. This is support for the heuristic on those settings, not independent verification of the generated videos.
# Implementation and evaluation findings

Problem 2 (The released frequency differs from Algorithm 1).  Algorithm 1 uses \(2\pi/L'\), whereas `riflex_utils.py`, lines 43–48, uses \(0.9(2\pi/L')\). Severity: Minor; the historical experimental setting needs evidence before attributing published scores to either variant.

The source and README explicitly say the extra factor addresses occasional tail-frame repetition. It changes the period to \(L'/0.9\), an increase of \(11.11\%\), and changes the first/last phase separation for \(L'=66\) from about \(0.0952\) to about \(0.699\). This is a substantive specification difference for a method whose defining operation is one frequency edit. It remains within the inequality (8), so it is not a violation of that inequality; it is different from the claimed minimal equality choice. Report which setting produced each result and ablate the safety factor.

Both entry points correctly convert output frames to latent frames through \((F-1)/4+1\) and apply the edit only to the temporal axis in their default branches. Hunyuan uses \(k=4\), CogVideoX uses \(k=2\), and normal-length training-free generation is left unchanged when its latent length does not exceed the supplied period. The fine-tuned branches deliberately use a checkpoint frequency length passed as `N_k`, rather than the current output length; callers must match that value to the checkpoint. The CogVideoX 1.5 branch at lines 175–183 omits \(k\) and \(L\_test\), so its helper receives the defaults and applies no edit. This is a local release limitation, not evidence against the paper’s default CogVideoX-5B 1.0 results. The Hunyuan script uses 8-bit quantization; the README already warns that it may alter quality and directs demo reproduction to the unacquired multi-GPU branch.

Problem 3 (Metric specification and broad quality claims need qualification).  Table 1, Section 4.2 and Appendix D do not establish universal non-repetition or preservation of all quality measures. Severity: Minor, with raw-data-dependent conclusions explicitly unresolved.

The NoRepeat Score searches near a frequency-derived lag, selects the closest first-frame match, and thresholds an average \(L_2\) distance at \(100\). The search window, pixel scaling, resizing, aggregation and whether the lag is from the original or modified frequency are not specified. A restricted-lag score can miss a different period: an independent sequence cycling through four orthogonal vectors of norm \(200\) repeats exactly at lag \(4\), yet all paired distances at lags \(9,10,11\) equal \(200\sqrt2>100\). This is a sensitivity example for the stated kind of metric, not a rerun or claimed bug in the unavailable evaluator. An all-lag check and blinded human validation would separate method-specific search assumptions from actual repeat detection. Threshold units and all settings must be released.

On Hunyuan twofold training-free extrapolation, RIFLEx has NoRepeat \(72\) versus NTK \(81\), motion rank \(1.6\) versus \(1.5\) (lower is better), and imaging quality \(65.2\) versus \(65.3\). Its overall rank improves from \(1.6\) to \(1.4\) and dynamics from \(55\) to \(57\). This is a trade-off, not dominance on every measure. On CogVideoX twofold training-free generation, relative to normal length, dynamics fall \(67.5\to59.4\), imaging \(64.4\to56.9\), and overall consistency \(25.8\to23.5\). The \(70.2\%\) normal-length preference further precludes interpreting “free lunch” as no quality cost. It can reasonably mean no added training requirement for that setting, while longer inference still costs resources.

Conversely, the table does support RIFLEx’s best overall average user rank in each listed extrapolation group, a \(34\)-point NoRepeat improvement over NTK at Hunyuan \(2.3\times\), and a \(48.1\)-point improvement over fine-tuned PE at CogVideoX \(2\times\). Those positive comparisons should be retained. Ten participants and aggregate ranks do not supply paired uncertainty or the effective number of independent judgments. Prompt counts, repeated seeds, ranking/tie rules, randomization and respondent-level results are needed before interpreting small differences as statistically established. Appendix D does specify that ties are allowed for training-free comparisons and disallowed after fine-tuning; the remaining gap concerns aggregation and respondent-level uncertainty. The stated \(1/50{,}000\) training-compute ratio also lacks a reproducible denominator and FLOP/time accounting in the available setup table.
# Assessment and verification boundary

The static source confirms an inexpensive frequency modification, and the published aggregates show useful regimes. The mathematical limitation is that a phase-period constraint is not a sufficient condition on generated content. The authors’ empirical framing, explicit theoretical limitation, and reported less-than-perfect NoRepeat scores argue for correcting scope and reproducibility rather than declaring the method disproved. The overall assessment is Minor. Scientific judgments remain pending, adoption is unknown and human reviews are empty. Focused independent acceptance is recorded in the existing verification files.

Source SHA-256: `c70ed2570ce325854bab61156bff175d8516930054dbf01fc64cdda8823097a7`. An independent NumPy script evaluates rotary phases, endpoint separation, NTK periods, a restricted-lag score example and table differences. It imports no author code and loads no model. Full static file coverage and hashes, original-page observations, calculations, compilation and actual report-page inspection are recorded in the verification directory.
