report: Abstract: Daily Oracle supplies a useful, densely sampled retrospective benchmark, and the reported figures support date-related differences in accuracy. The central inference that residual decline identifies outdated internal representations, and consequently the necessity of continuous pre-training, is not established by the design. Gold-context truncation in the pinned release further weakens the claim that all relevant information was supplied. Expanding regression slopes do not identify accelerating local decline; chronology validation and several aggregation conventions also require repair. The overall assessment is Major because a central explanatory conclusion is unsupported, while the descriptive benchmark contribution remains intact.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of Are LLMs Prescient? A Continuous Evaluation using Daily News as the Oracle
# Identity, contribution and inspected evidence

Hui Dai, Ryan Teehan and Mengye Ren, ICML 2025, I25-43699 (0330), Are LLMs Prescient? A Continuous Evaluation using Daily News as the Oracle. The frozen original has 35 pages. All main scientific text (pp. 1–10) and Appendices A–D (pp. 13–35), including all prompt text, were read. All Figures 1–22 were visually inspected, together with selected prompt figures. Tables 2–4 were checked against the rendered pages. Bibliography entries were not independently audited.

The acquired Daily Oracle repository is commit `9166ceb7b4badc3ac198077b0f030e9bd400ee5a`, dated 27 July 2025. Complete static reads covered seven Python files, README and requirements. No author program, API evaluation, training, dataset-generation pipeline or model was executed. The full news/QA datasets, response records, scoring/plotting implementation and separate prompt files were not in the acquired source-only mirror. The paper supplies prompt text, but byte identity with deployed prompts is unverified. Separate OpenReview material was unavailable behind an API 403/browser challenge. Code-level observations below concern this pinned release, not a proven reconstruction of the historical experiments.

The pipeline selects six articles per day, generates two true/false (TF) and two multiple-choice (MC) questions per article, then applies seven quality criteria with a threshold of 13 out of 14. The evaluated collection contains 16,783 TF and 14,727 MC questions from 2020–2024. Eight models are compared in closed-book, temporally restricted retrieval, and gold-article settings. There is no formal forecasting/generalization theorem. The reported beginning/end TF drop, \(64.68\%\to50.74\%\), is \(13.94\) percentage points or \(21.55\%\) relatively. For MC, \(58.30\%\to51.69\%\) gives \(6.61\) points, about \(11.34\%\) relatively; the stated \(11.33\%\) can reflect underlying unrounded values. These are descriptive summaries, not independently recomputed model results.
# The central explanatory inference

Problem 1 (A date trend does not identify representation obsolescence).  The abstract, Section 4.2 (p. 7) and Section 4.3 (p. 8) attribute residual gold-article decline to outdated representations and infer that continuous pre-training is still needed. Severity: Major. The experimental controls do not identify this mechanism or necessity, materially weakening a central scientific conclusion without invalidating the benchmark or its reported accuracy differences.

For a fixed model \(g\), let \(D_t\) be the distribution of generated questions, choices and supplied contexts at date \(t\). Observed accuracy is \[A_t=\mathbb{E}_{D_t}[\mathbf1\{g(X)=Y\}]
     =\sum_z\pi_t(z)a_t(z).\] A change in \(A_t\) does not distinguish changed mixture weights \(\pi_t\) from changed conditional accuracies \(a_t\). For example, keep accuracy on remembered outcomes at \(0.9\) and on unseen forecast questions at \(0.5\). Reducing the remembered fraction from \(0.8\) to \(0.2\) changes accuracy from \(0.82\) to \(0.58\) with unchanged forecasting ability. The paper itself explicitly distinguishes pre-cutoff historical questions from post-cutoff future questions (Section 4.1); combining them does not measure a single invariant ability. This example does not assert the actual memorization fractions or erase the practical cost of stale knowledge.

Even complete gold articles do not remove question difficulty, changing entities, distracting content, answer extraction or generator effects. Hold gold-context accuracy fixed at \(0.95\) for easy questions and \(0.70\) for hard questions. Reducing the easy fraction from \(0.8\) to \(0.2\) changes aggregate accuracy from \(0.90\) to \(0.75\) without any change in either conditional ability. This is an explicit nonidentification example, not an estimated decomposition of Figure 5. The generator/filter models also change from GPT-4/GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini around October 2024 (p. 4, footnote 6). That creates a design change near the end of the time axis; it cannot explain the entire earlier decline, but it must be controlled when interpreting the final months. A roughly stable category histogram in Figure 8 does not establish stable within-category difficulty.

There is also a concrete implementation obstacle to the claimed full-context control. In `evaluation/eval.py`, lines 127–128, gold articles pass through `get_first_k_words`, whose default at lines 183–187 is 512 words. The generation code in `qa-generation/utils.py` passes the whole article to prompts after accepting texts between 800 and 10,000 characters. A 5,644-character synthetic article with its answer at word 513 is therefore admitted by that length rule but loses the answer under the released gold preprocessing. This independent construction proves that the implementation does not guarantee answer-containing gold context. It does not prove any particular dataset item was affected, nor that this code version generated Figure 5. Historical configuration and per-question answer-span coverage are necessary to settle those questions.

The authors provide relevant counterevidence: Figures 9–11 show that declines remain after excluding refusals, and gold accuracy is often near \(0.9\). Thus refusal alone is not a sufficient alternative explanation, and many questions are answerable. The limitation section acknowledges generator and event-selection bias and the short post-cutoff horizon. Those concessions do not turn the gold experiment into a causal isolation of internal representations. Calling gold retrieval an “upper bound” also requires an operational assumption: additional or differently arranged context can change an LLM’s answers, so correctness is not monotone in context inclusion.

Repair requires freezing the generator and evaluator, auditing answer coverage, comparing full versus truncated gold text, controlling item difficulty/topic/source and separating historical recall from genuine post-cutoff forecasts. To establish a benefit of continued pre-training, compare matched models with and without that intervention on the same held-out future items, alongside retrieval/adaptation alternatives. Without these controls, the defensible conclusion is descriptive decline on this retrospectively constructed distribution; the proposed mechanism remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated necessity.
# Temporal statistics and chronology

Problem 2 (The expanding slope is not a local rate of deterioration).  Section 4.3 and Figure 6 use increasingly negative expanding-window coefficients as evidence of faster decline near and after the cutoff. Severity: Minor for the statistic itself; it reinforces the identification problem above. An expanding-window slope does not estimate the derivative at its last month.

For the specified monthly decay \(\lambda=0.995\), an observation 59 months old retains relative weight \(0.995^{59}=0.744\), and the weight half-life is \(\log(1/2)/\log(0.995)=138.28\) months. The fit therefore remains strongly influenced by earlier levels. As an independent check, let raw accuracy be \(0.8\) for months 1–36 and \(0.6\) for months 37–60. After a trailing five-month mean, expanding weighted slopes are approximately \(-0.000225\), \(-0.003078\), \(-0.004954\) and \(-0.005197\) at months 37, 42, 48 and 60. They become more negative although the post-change raw series is exactly constant. These are accuracy fractions per month; they are illustrative values, not digitizations of Figure 6. The paper’s moving-average alignment is not specified, so the calculation declares its own trailing alignment.

An expanding fit is a valid descriptive summary of accumulated data, but its coefficient cannot by itself establish ongoing local acceleration or a cutoff-induced change. Report unsmoothed monthly denominators and uncertainty, specify smoothing/alignment, and compare segmented or local models with separate level and slope changes. Multiple QA pairs share an article and event, so treating every question as independent understates uncertainty; article/event or date blocks are appropriate for sensitivity analysis. No significance calculation was reproduced without the raw data.

Table 3 also needs an explicit definition of the YoY observations, weights and cutoff masks. If Pre and Post exhaustively partition the same nonnegatively weighted observations, their combined mean must satisfy \[\min(\bar y_{\rm pre},\bar y_{\rm post})\leq\bar y_{\rm all}
 \leq\max(\bar y_{\rm pre},\bar y_{\rm post}).\] TF GPT-3.5 reports \((-4.33,-3.43,-2.84)\), and MC Claude reports \((-6.26,-11.78,-5.03)\), in Pre/Post/Avg order; both violate that interpretation. Excluding cutoff-straddling intervals or using different masks can explain the numbers. Consequently this is an unresolved definition/reproducibility problem, not a proved arithmetic error. Annual means are insufficient to reconstruct monthly YoY changes.

Problem 3 (Publication time does not certify earliest answerability).  Section 3.1 equates article publication with resolution time; Appendix A.3 requires that the answer was unavailable earlier. The prompts and quality audit do not establish that requirement. Severity: Minor with potentially material unknown prevalence; a dataset-wide invalid-question rate has not been measured in this review.

Figure 23 requires an event newly occurring on publication day, yet its second example accepts a May 28 temperature record for a May 29 article. That demonstrates a mismatch between the instruction and its own example; it does not establish the first public disclosure time of that record. Table 2 asks how many US states the April 8, 2024 eclipse path would cross, as reported by February 2024. NASA’s resource dated April 12, 2023 already describes the mapped April 2024 path [Retained latex: \cite{nasa}]. This raises a specific prior-answerability problem for the example, rather than a speculative claim about all news questions. The exact 15-state answer in an archived 2023 source and the original news item’s first publication were not independently recovered, so no stronger historical count claim is made. The audit must establish earliest answer availability, not merely the date of the chosen reporting article. Retrospective question wording and distractors can also condition on outcomes already observed; the authors explicitly acknowledge that events never occurring may be absent.

The human sample is informative but limited. Table 4 reports Fleiss’ \(\kappa=0.02\) for non-answerability before publication and mean \(\kappa=0.26\). These values flag disputed labeling; they are not direct error rates. Sampling 60 questions from the already accepted dataset and obtaining \(85\%\) agreement on acceptance corresponds to 51/60 on the described frame. A binomial Wilson interval is approximately \([0.739,0.919]\), conditional on independent items and fixed consensus labels; shared events and label uncertainty can add uncertainty. This sample cannot measure rejection sensitivity or specificity because rejected candidates were not sampled. The reported \(89.52\%\) mean criterion agreement is also not a demonstrated forecast-validity rate. Audit both retained and rejected items with dated primary evidence, stratify by date and generator, and distinguish calculable/scheduled facts, retrospective recall and genuinely unresolved outcomes.
# Released protocol and assessment

Problem 4 (Date boundaries and released configuration need reconciliation).  Section 4.1 says retrieval reaches the day before resolution, while its half-open interval and the release exclude that day. Severity: Minor; the direction is less recent context, not demonstrated future leakage.

In `evaluation/rag.py`, lines 34–36, the bound is `article_date < yesterday`. For resolution on 10 January, an article dated 8 January passes and one dated 9 January does not. The fixed-cutoff branch similarly uses a strict inequality. This agrees with the printed half-open formula but differs from an inclusive reading of the accompanying prose. State an unambiguous timestamp/timezone rule and recompute boundary-sensitive comparisons if the intended interval differs. The retrieval script obtains ten candidates, but `eval.py` selects the first five; that is consistent with the paper’s top-five evaluation and is not a ten-versus-five defect.

Table 5 specifies `gpt-3.5-turbo-0125`, whereas the released model mapping uses the unversioned `gpt-3.5-turbo` alias. Exact endpoint versions, run dates, response parsing/refusal rules, random seeds and historical prompts are required to reproduce the aggregates. The release’s random distractor-ordering and article-selection paths are not all seeded. No observed score change is attributed to those differences without runs.

The original figures support real benchmark differences, heterogeneous benefits from newer retrieval, and remaining errors with gold context. The forecasting-market comparison also supports the practical advantage of denser, more uniform sampling; smoother plots do not prove a more valid forecasting construct. The authors appropriately avoid claiming that all LLM-generated questions are inherently higher quality. Overall assessment: Major, driven by the unsupported central explanatory inference in Problem 1. The other issues warrant specification and validation repairs rather than a claim that the reported accuracies are fabricated or the entire dataset is unusable. Scientific adjudication remains pending, human reviews are empty and adoption is unknown. Focused independent acceptance is recorded in the existing verification files.

report: Abstract: The printed contact splitting update, the contact-flow variational formulation, and the energy evolution law are checked against the paper’s own coordinate equations. The kinetic update fails the defining contact condition, and a stated latent model does not satisfy the proposed unconstrained action principle or its action reparameterization. These invalidate derivations supporting two central geometric claims. A separate sign error affects the displayed energy law. These are findings about the published formulas; unavailable implementation code prevents attributing them to the reported experiments. Adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Contact preservation and the variational claims in Geometric Contact Flows
# Paper identity and inspected scope

This report concerns Andrea Testa, Soren Hauberg, Tamim Asfour and Leonel Rozo, Geometric Contact Flows: Contactomorphisms for Dynamics and Control (ICML 2025, PMLR 267; OpenReview identifier `v2nQ1e78Rc`), in its 26-page published proceedings version. Pages below mean physical PDF pages. The central review covers Sections 3–5, Appendix A, and Appendices B.1–B.4; Sections 1–2 and 6–7 and the implementation and experimental descriptions in Appendices C–D supply context. The experiments were read as reported evidence, not replicated. The extended empirical material was only partially inspected. The saved author project page says that code will be released soon; no relevant implementation was available in the frozen packet.
# Coordinate conventions and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:field. We use the paper’s canonical coordinates \(z=(q,p,s)\) and its equation (31), on page 16: \[
 \dot q=H_p,\qquad \dot p=-H_q-pH_s,\qquad \dot s=pH_p-H.\] In one degree of freedom the associated standard contact form is \(\eta=ds-p\,dq\). A contact transformation \(\Phi\) must satisfy \(\Phi^*\eta=a\eta\) for a nowhere-zero scalar function \(a\); allowing \(a\) to depend on position is more permissive than the paper’s constant notation. Equation (11), page 5, uses \(H=\tfrac12 p^\top M(p)p+V(q)+F(q)s\). The constant smooth choice \(M=1\), \(V=F=0\) is within this displayed mechanical class and within the scalar bounds \([-2,2]\) stated on page 19. No positivity or damping assumption excludes this choice. The calculations are local, so no global compactness or long-time completeness is needed.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The printed kinetic update is not a contact transformation).
## Claim and location

Equation reference: eq:printed. Appendix B.2, page 16, describes (33a)–(33c) as a contact splitting integrator preserving the contact structure. Section 4, page 5, explicitly uses this integrator to construct the learned contactomorphisms. For the admissible constant choice above, (33a) and (33b) are identity maps, and the displayed (33c) becomes \[
 \Phi(q,p,s)=(q+\tau p,\ p,\ s+\tau p^2).\] The \(s\) update is the suspect step.
## Complete check

Equation reference: eq:correct. The map is smooth and invertible for every \(\tau\), but invertibility alone does not make it contact. Direct differentiation gives \[\Phi^*\eta=d(s+\tau p^2)-p\,d(q+\tau p)
             =ds-p\,dq+\tau p\,dp.\] The coefficient of \(ds\) forces \(a=1\); the extra \(dp\) coefficient then forbids \(\Phi^*\eta=a\eta\) whenever \(\tau p\ne0\). In particular \(\tau=0.2\), the duration reported in Appendix D.1, and \((q,p,s)=(0,1,0)\) give a contact-condition residual of \(0.2\) in the \(dp\) coefficient. Equation [eq:field] (#eq:field) instead gives \((\dot q,\dot p,\dot s)=(p,0,p^2/2)\), whose exact flow is \[
 \Phi_{\rm kin}(q,p,s)=(q+\tau p,\ p,\ s+\tfrac12\tau p^2).\] At the stated test input, the printed and correct outputs are \((0.2,1,0.2)\) and \((0.2,1,0.1)\), respectively. The latter has exactly zero contact residual. The independent SymPy calculation in `check_contact.py` reproduces both identities symbolically, rather than merely testing one floating-point point.
## Counterevidence, impact and bounded repair

The actual source page was visually checked, including the absence of a \(1/2\) in the \(s\) line; this is not an extraction artifact. Redefining the kinetic Hamiltonian as \(p^2\) would not rescue the pair of updates, because it would require \(q'=q+2\tau p\). Appendix B.3 reports empirical contact residuals below \(10^{-5}\), which is pertinent counterevidence about the authors’ implementation. It cannot make the displayed universal update contact, and the unreleased code prevents deciding whether that implementation used a different formula or tested a restricted numerical regime. This is a Major defect in the printed construction: the core architectural claim that the learned maps preserve contact structure depends on it, as do the physical-interpretability arguments in B.4. The conclusion does not assert that the experiments used (33c), or that their performance is false. Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) repairs this constant-kinetic substep exactly; it does not by itself certify all the general variable-\(M\) updates or a corrected implementation.
Problem 2 (The stated action minimization does not generate the contact flow).
## Claim and location

Equation reference: eq:action. Section 3, page 4, presents equation (4), \[
 \min_{q,p,s}\int_0^1[p\dot q-H(q,p,s)]\,dt,\] as a variational description of the contact flow, followed by the reparameterization \(ds=\sqrt{H-H_V}\,dt\) and the geodesic problem (5). Appendix A.3, page 15, repeats the identification of the contact action with geodesic length. Section 5, page 6, invokes this correspondence to interpret (16)–(18) as uncertainty-aware geodesics and metric reshaping.
## Complete counterexample within the proposed latent model

Take the paper’s own (7b), \(H_B=(p^2+q^2)/2+s\), with \(q(0)=p(0)=0\) and \(s(0)=1\). Equation [eq:field] (#eq:field) gives the valid smooth contact trajectory \(q(t)=p(t)=0\), \(s(t)=e^{-t}\). Fix even both endpoints of every variable, which is a more restrictive admissible variation than the unconstrained display. The perturbation \(s_\epsilon(t)=e^{-t}+\epsilon t(1-t)\) preserves these endpoints and remains positive for sufficiently small \(\epsilon\). Its first variation of [eq:action] (#eq:action) is \[\left.\frac{dJ}{d\epsilon}\right|_{0}
 =-\int_0^1t(1-t)\,dt=-\frac16\ne0.\] Thus this contact trajectory is not even stationary for the stated functional. More generally, free variation of \(s\) imposes \(H_s=0\), in conflict with the very dissipative model \(H_s=1\) being advocated. There is also a direct incompatibility in the identification of \(s\): at \(t=0\) the true action derivative is \(\dot s=-1\), whereas the proposed reparameterization, with \(H_V=q^2/2\), gives \(ds/dt=\sqrt{1}=1\). Throughout this example the expression under the root is positive. The discrepancy is therefore not caused by a forbidden square root or a turning point.
## Alternative reading and consequences

An additional differential constraint \(\dot s=p\dot q-H\) and a terminal-action variational principle would change the admissible variations and hence define a different problem; it is not the unconstrained minimization written in (4). Using a separate length parameter would likewise remove the immediate same-variable contradiction but would require a fresh derivation of the claimed metric, parameter mapping and control equivalence. Appendix A does not supply these missing conditions: (29) is an implicit action expression followed by the same length identification. The Major impact is restricted to the central geometric justification for converting contact dynamics into the geodesic objectives (5), (16) and (18), a stated contribution of the method. It does not establish that the optimal-control objective (18) is unusable as a heuristic, or invalidate every possible geometric formulation of contact mechanics. Figure 4 was inspected: its trajectory illustration is consistent with a control modification but cannot establish the claimed variational equivalence. No general repair is verified here; a corrected constrained formulation and its claimed equivalence need a separate proof.
Problem 3 (The displayed energy evolution has the opposite sign).

Section 4, equation (8), page 4, prints \(H(t)=H(0)\exp(\int_0^t H_s\,d\tau)\) while explaining on page 5 that \(H_s>0\) dissipates energy. For an autonomous differentiable \(H\), substitution of [eq:field] (#eq:field) gives exactly \[\dot H=H_qH_p+H_p(-H_q-pH_s)+H_s(pH_p-H)=-H_sH.\] Consequently the exponent must carry a minus sign. The preceding trajectory has \(H(0)=1\) and \(H(1)=e^{-1}\); (8) instead yields \(e\). The source image confirms the positive sign. The negative sign already appears in equation (40), page 20, and the accompanying stability discussion is consistent with decay. This counterevidence supports classifying the displayed discrepancy as Minor: a local but substantive energy calculation error, without evidence that the algorithms or experiments used the wrong sign. Replacing the exponent by \(-\int H_s\) repairs this autonomous-energy identity exactly. It does not repair either of the preceding Major derivations.
# Overall dependence and conclusion

The geometric-contact premise and the uncertainty-based control heuristic remain intelligible proposals. What fails is the published exact-contact construction and a derivation used to justify its geodesic interpretation. Neither argument needs an empirical score decrease or whole-paper failure to be central. Static formula analysis cannot identify the software that generated the empirical tables. Code release, the contact-condition diagnostic used in B.3, and a corrected variational derivation are needed to resolve the implementation and downstream scope. No later revision or erratum was acquired in this packet; this is not a claim that none exists.
Item | Impact | Repair checked | Remaining work
Kinetic step | Major | Constant-\(M\) exact substep only | General scheme and code
Action/geodesic derivation | Major | None | Correct constrained proof
Energy exponent | Minor | Negative exponent identity | Implementation provenance
All three issue judgments await independent acceptance and scientific adjudication. Author adoption is unknown; no human reviews are present.
# Evidence and review limits
The source is the frozen PMLR proceedings PDF, identified by SHA-256

Physical PDF page numbers are one based and coincide with the paper’s printed page numbers in this version. The companion verification directory contains the page-indexed text extraction, the independent check program and its actual output, the coverage ledger, source and report hashes, and execution provenance. The check program was written for this review; no author program was executed. Published training runs, data collection and reported performance were not reproduced. This is an initial AI technical review with GPT-6 Astra / Max selected through the platform control. It is not independent acceptance. No human review or author adoption is recorded. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025). Title: The diffusion objective and released reconstruction path in TimeDART
# Identity and scope

Daoyu Wang, Mingyue Cheng, Zhiding Liu and Qi Liu, TimeDART: A Diffusion Autoregressive Transformer for Self-Supervised Time Series Representation, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, OpenReview `v2G9HML7ep`, is reviewed in its 25-page proceedings version. Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–C were read; the empirical discussion in D–G was sampled to understand scope, without reproducing training or checking every full-results cell. Figure 2 and the derivation page were inspected as images. The relevant release is https://github.com/Melmaphother/TimeDART, commit `e658a648cf6b04612ca643d10a634b45e136194c`. The README identifies it as the official code and also notes refactoring and a later v2 extension. This report checks the original `TimeDART` path, not the v2 implementation.
# Diffusion assumptions and checked valid steps

Write \(\alpha_s=1-\beta_s\) and \(\bar\alpha_s=\prod_{r=1}^s\alpha_r\), with \(0<\alpha_s<1\). The forward noising formula is \(x_s=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_s}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_s}\epsilon\), \(\epsilon\sim N(0,I)\). The clean encoder inputs are shifted right by one patch using an SOS token; the triangular encoder mask and diagonal decoder mask correctly impose the described positional attention restrictions. These restrictions are statements about the normalized patch representations. Whole-window instance normalization is not itself a causal transformation of raw data: its mean and variance depend on the entire look-back sequence. Consequently those masks alone are not a proof of a raw-data autoregressive factorization. This distinction does not imply leakage from the downstream forecasting target: the inspected forecasting path normalizes its observed input window, and pre-training uses `batch_x`, not `batch_y`.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The clean-data objective is not the stated ELBO without weights).
## Claim and suspect step

Section 3.2, equation (11), page 5, calls its unweighted denoising loss formally equivalent to the ELBO. Appendix C.3, equations (27)–(31), page 17, derives this by assuming Gaussian reverse distributions with the same variance as the forward posterior and then replacing the reverse-mean error by clean-data error. The linear relation mentioned between (29) and (30) carries a time-dependent slope; it cannot in general be dropped.
## Complete calculation

The independent calculation uses the release’s cosine schedule with \(T=1000\), offset \(0.008\), and beta clipping at \(0.999\), matching the inspected `ETTh2.sh` setting and schedule construction. It obtains \[w_2=6391.9150350,\qquad w_{500}=0.0030509888932.\] Both steps have positive forward and posterior variances. Their ratio is approximately \(2.0950\times10^6\), rather than one. These numbers are not training measurements. To illustrate the algebraic consequence for shared parameters, the two-term loss \(w_2\theta^2+w_{500}(1-\theta)^2\) is minimized at \(4.7732\times10^{-7}\), while the unweighted version is minimized at \(1/2\). This toy calculation does not purport to be the optimum of the published network; it shows why nonconstant relative weights are not a harmless common scaling.
## Alternative readings, impact and repair scope

An intentionally simplified diffusion loss is a valid optimization choice. Likewise one could choose different reverse variances or a nonuniform sampling law to account for weights. Neither resolves the stated derivation, which invokes equal covariances and writes equality without compensating weights. The frozen source samples time steps uniformly (`layers/TimeDART_EncDec.py`, lines 149–163) and uses ordinary MSE (`exp/exp_timedart.py`, lines 68–75 and 165–190), so it does not silently supply the displayed missing factors. The time step is sampled and returned but is not passed as an explicit decoder argument in the inspected model path; that observation is not needed for the weight counterexample.

The supported impact is Major for the invalid derivation of the core objective’s claimed exact probabilistic justification. The paper explicitly uses this justification to distinguish its denoising objective from ordinary autoregressive MSE. This classification does not assert that unweighted denoising is invalid or that representation quality decreases. Equation [eq:weight] (#eq:weight) repairs the intermediate Gaussian KL identity under the specified parameterization; a full ELBO additionally needs the endpoint terms and a fully specified reverse model. Alternatively, the manuscript could describe its actual loss as a reweighted surrogate, without claiming exact ELBO equivalence. Neither alternative has been experimentally evaluated here.
Problem 2 (The frozen release mixes patch positions in the reconstruction head).
## Source correspondence and explicit dependency

Equation (8), page 4, projects each \(z_j^{\rm out}\) separately to \(x_j^{\rm out}\). In contrast, `models/TimeDART.py`, lines 20–42, defines `FlattenHead` with `Linear(seq_len*d_model,pred_len)`. Lines 123–128 select it for pre-training, and lines 194–197 apply it to the entire denoised sequence. Writing the flattened output features as \([z_1;\ldots;z_N]\), the first reconstruction can therefore be \(y_1=W_{1,2}z_2\) with \(W_{1,2}\ne0\). For two scalar features, \(W=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) maps \((2,3)\) to \((3,0)\) and \((2,4)\) to \((4,0)\): changing a later feature changes the earlier output despite any preceding attention mask. The same off-block weight is allowed in the full-dimensional dense layer; the two-dimensional example is its submatrix, not an execution of the model.
## Counterevidence and bounded consequence

The code contains a patch-local `ARFlattenHead`, but its selection is commented out at lines 129–133. A fitted dense matrix could happen to have the relevant off-block entries zero; the implementation does not enforce it. The masks themselves are not defective. This is a Minor, release-specific correspondence defect, because it changes the advertised pre-training dependency structure while historical experiment provenance has not been established. It is not evidence of held-out test-target leakage or a basis for withdrawing the performance tables. A patch-local head is a structurally sufficient fix for this output-mixing path, but does not make global normalization causal in raw coordinates. A corrected release and new runs are required to measure effects.
# Conclusion and evidence limits

The report distinguishes a demonstrated derivation failure from an independently observed release discrepancy. The finite diagnostics establish mathematical dependencies, not performance or experiment provenance. The pre-training benefits in the published tables remain empirical claims not reproduced here. The later v2 implementation and any subsequent correction are outside this review.

Title: Selected evidence and evaluation checks for EMMA
# Identity and reviewed material

This report reviews Yunzhuo Hao, Jiawei Gu, Huichen Will Wang, Linjie Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Lijuan Wang and Yu Cheng, Can MLLMs Reason in Multimodality? EMMA: An Enhanced MultiModal ReAsoning Benchmark, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, OpenReview `v26vwjxOEz`. The frozen proceedings PDF has 47 pages. The main text and the applicable benchmark/protocol appendices B–C were read, with selected breakdown tables. The extensive case-study appendix was not exhaustively solved or visually inspected. The release at https://github.com/EMMA-Bench/EMMA, commit `47259952dd8e95bc1e3855a4164ccd3634f8eb1e`, was inspected statically for query construction, answer extraction, equality testing and aggregation. The acquired snapshot excludes large data/result JSON files; it does not permit an item-level reproduction of the historical scores.
# Concrete checks and their outcomes
## Composition and score weighting

Table 2, page 6, uses subject counts \((892,156,1176,564)\), summing to 2,788. Overall full-benchmark accuracy is an item-weighted quantity, \[A=\frac{892A_{\rm math}+156A_{\rm phys}+1176A_{\rm chem}
                 +564A_{\rm code}}{2788},\] not the unweighted average of four subject percentages. Using the printed subject rates gives \(35.0788\%\) for direct Claude 3.5 Sonnet, \(32.4247\%\) for direct GPT-4o, and \(42.5039\%\) for Gemini Thinking-0121. These agree with the corresponding printed \(35.08\%\), \(32.42\%\) and \(42.50\%\) at the precision justified by rounded inputs. EMMA-mini has 100 questions per subject, so its overall score is instead the equally weighted subject average. The human values \((75,64.5,86,85.5)\) average to \(77.75\%\). The gap to \(48\%\) is 29.75 percentage points, as stated.

The coding construction in B.2, pages 16–17, yields \(47(4+4+2+2)=564\) questions, agreeing with the task counts \((188,188,94,94)\). It also explains why coding category membership is nonexclusive. Summing category scores as if they partitioned the dataset would be inappropriate, but the inspected accumulator adds each question only once to the overall and subject totals while allowing multiple coding category memberships.
## Scaling results and error taxonomy

Table 3, page 7, distinguishes actual selection methods from Pass@\(N\) oracle coverage. The best reported selection score, \(50.75\%\), remains 27 percentage points below the human average; Pass@16 of \(81.5\%\) is an upper bound requiring knowledge of which response is correct. These statements are consistent: high oracle coverage does not establish that the tested selector can identify a correct response. The results support the bounded statement that the evaluated methods, models and budgets did not close the gap. They do not rule out larger budgets or different selectors. The paper reports different decoding temperatures for one-sample and multi-sample experiments in Table 6, page 20; this prevents reading the comparison as a controlled estimate of sampling count alone.

For the 106 incorrect o1 answers in the selected math/coding analysis, the displayed percentages in Figure 5, page 8, correspond to counts \((32,56,10,8)\): perceptual, visual-reasoning, textual-reasoning and knowledge errors. The resulting percentages are \((30.1887,52.8302,9.4340,7.5472)\%\), agreeing with the figure. This validates the arithmetic, not the annotators’ attribution of each individual error. The two-expert-per-subject average is a reported human baseline, not a population-level estimate established by this review.
## An independently solved source image

Figure 1, page 1, depicts charges \(+Q,-2Q,+3Q\) at the vertices of an equilateral triangle and asks for the force on the top \(+Q\). Taking side length one and positions \[r_+=(0,\sqrt3/2),\quad r_-=(-1/2,0),\quad r_3=(1/2,0),\] with the common factor \(kQ^2\) suppressed, the two forces are \((-1,-\sqrt3)\) and \((-3/2,3\sqrt3/2)\). Hence \[F=(-5/2,\sqrt3/2),\] pointing \(19.1066\) degrees above the leftward horizontal, consistent with the figure’s answer b and its correction of the model’s repulsion direction. The relevant source image was actually viewed. Figure 6 and its current-loop diagram on page 8 were also visually inspected for the error-analysis context, but no separate quantitative magnetic-field validation is claimed.
# Interpretive and reproducibility limits

The filtering protocol in Section 3.2, page 4, removes an item if one of three models solves its text-plus-caption version at least five times out of ten. This is an operational, model- and caption-dependent selection rule. It is not a proof that no sufficiently detailed textual description or future text reasoner can solve a retained problem. For perspective, under an illustrative independent four-option guessing model, the chance of at least five successes in ten trials is \[\sum_{k=5}^{10}\binom{10}{k}(1/4)^k(3/4)^{10-k}=0.0781269.\] This is a property of the toy binomial model, not an estimate of the actual filter’s error rate; correlations, nonuniform option counts and open-ended questions preclude such an extrapolation. Manual review and the observed performance gap provide additional evidence, but do not turn the filtering rule into a theorem about modality necessity.

The inspected evaluator accepts direct letters, boxed answers and selected final-answer phrases, then tests strings, number words and mathematical equivalence, including a numerical two-decimal comparison. It also offers an optional model-based evaluation mode. These are real released-code behaviors; the exact mode and output files used for each historical result have not been established. No API calls or author scripts were executed. Corpus-level answer-key validity, chemical structures, parsing failure rates, contamination, expert labeling agreement and the independence of generated candidates remain outside the inspected evidence. The main text’s retained-chemistry count of 42 differs from the appendix’s 20; the appendix’s \(892+80+20=992\) retained total reconciles the headline figure. This is a provenance clarification requiring the actual curation manifest, not evidence here of an incorrect scored answer or material result change.
# Conclusion

No substantive issue is established in the checked aggregation, selected scaling comparisons, source logic and electrostatics example. The conclusion is deliberately narrower than full-benchmark validation.

Title: Hamiltonian and implementation checks for gradient-based QHD
# Source and scope

This report concerns Jiaqi Leng and Bin Shi, Quantum Optimization via Gradient-Based Hamiltonian Descent, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, OpenReview `v14jD1ankb`. The 19-page proceedings PDF was read through the main technical development and Appendices A–E, including the commutator and Lyapunov proofs. References were not independently audited. The public release https://github.com/jiaqileng/Gradient-Based-QHD, commit `1d9ed3241bd50df4d37ba6d69a8e032aef13a092`, was inspected statically: `GradBasedQHD.py`, `convex_optim.py`, `nonconvex_optim.py` and README. Legacy notebooks and the separate Styblinski–Tang driver were not examined. Source pages 4, 8 and 16 were actually viewed, including Figure 3. The independent SymPy check uses a one-dimensional quartic test function, not the authors’ simulator.
# Problem 1: experimental implementation differs from the stated model

Severity: Minor. Scope: released implementation and experimental attribution; historical numerical outcomes remain unverified. Equations (13)–(14), the splitting in Section 5.1, and Appendix E.1 specify \[H=- rac{\Delta}{2t^3}+ rac{\alpha}{2}\{-i
abla,
abla f\}
   + rac{\alpha^2+ eta}{2}t^3\|
abla f\|^2+(t^3+\gamma t^2)f.\] The convex experiment sets \(\alpha=-0.1, eta=0,\gamma=5\) and the nonconvex experiments set \(\alpha=-0.05, eta=0,\gamma=5\) (page 8). The release drivers call `high_res_qhd_simulator` with the default `use_new_helper=False`, reaching `high_res_qhd_helper`. Its `a1=1/t**3` is used in two Fourier factors, each with duration \(\Delta t/2\). Their combined generator is \(-\Delta/t^3\), twice the stated kinetic term. The code’s `a3=0` removes the gradient-square potential, although the required coefficient is \(0.005t^3\) in the convex experiment and \(0.00125t^3\) in the nonconvex experiments. The variable named `beta` in the release supplies the anticommutator coefficient and thus corresponds to paper \(\alpha\); a variable-name reinterpretation does not restore the missing term. The baseline `qhd_simulator` also uses the doubled kinetic coefficient.

The helper approximates the anticommutator subflow with explicit Euler updates. A skew-Hermitian generator eigenvalue \(i\lambda\) gives squared norm multiplier \(|1+i\lambda\Delta t|^2=1+\lambda^2\Delta t^2\), rather than one. This is a finite-step consistency concern, not a claim about the actual error size. The code renormalizes probabilities for objective and success statistics, but `convex_optim.py` computes gradient moments from the returned, unnormalized wavefunction. Hence those two metrics need not use the same probability normalization.

In addition, Appendix E.1 describes unbiased Gaussian noise in SGDM, whereas the released SGDM routine uses `np.random.rand(2)`. Each coordinate has mean \(1/2\), so the expected estimator is \(\nabla f+(1/2,1/2)\), not \(\nabla f\). This changes a principal comparator. The independent check records the coefficient ratios, missing potential coefficient and elementary norm/noise calculations. It does not execute the release or reproduce Figure 3.

These discrepancies affect what method and baseline the public evidence implements. They cannot establish that the paper’s actual historical figures are wrong: the authors could have used a different revision. The needed resolution is a pinned historical implementation, correct Hamiltonian coefficients and noise, normalized observables, and a time/space discretization check. Merely increasing the inner Euler count cannot fix the doubled kinetic or omitted potential. The supported assessment is Minor for the released implementation. The missing and doubled terms alter the stated algorithm, but the available evidence does not connect this commit to the historical figures or demonstrate material damage to the paper’s core empirical conclusion. Historical experimental impact remains Needs Evidence. This boundary is based on the missing provenance link, not on whether every result fails or a repair is difficult.

The paper explicitly leaves the detailed classical comparison to future work, limiting the impact of this defect.
# Problem 3: a false Lyapunov identity with a valid sign repair

Crucially, the corrected expression remains nonpositive for convex \(f\ge0\), minimizer zero, and \(\omega\ge0\). Thus this calculation repairs the monotonicity argument instead of refuting its convergence rate. It does not independently certify the stated initial-energy bound, operator domains for merely \(C^1\) objectives, or all of Theorem 4’s parameter conditions. Those require further checking. In particular, the printed \(T_0\le1/\alpha\) condition excludes negative \(\alpha\) despite the negative values used in experiments, and Lemma 5 lists different conditions from Theorem 4; these are unresolved statement-level scope issues, not additional claimed counterexamples.
# Disposition and limits

The core continuous-time monotonicity mechanism survives the checked local repair. The code-to-model discrepancy is substantive for empirical attribution. The spatial smoothness assumptions and complexity argument in Appendix D were read but no rigorous end-to-end quantum gate or discretization-error bound was established. Nonconvex performance, hardware advantage, and the complete experimental ranking were not reproduced. Title: Scoring and protocol checks for AGAV-Rater
# Identity and evidence

Yuqin Cao, Xiongkuo Min, Yixuan Gao, Wei Sun and Guangtao Zhai, AGAV-Rater: Adapting Large Multimodal Model for AI-Generated Audio-Visual Quality Assessment, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, is reviewed from the 19-page proceedings PDF. Main Sections 1–6 and Appendices A–C were read, with particular attention to scoring, pretraining construction and evaluation. Figures 2 and 4 and the original equation (1) were actually viewed on pages 3, 15 and 8. No audio clip was listened to and no source video was evaluated for perceptual quality.

The acquired repository https://github.com/charlotte9524/AGAV-Rater is pinned at `36a30b016e8bd91a8667f0a562c9be9aaf7408ee`. Static reading covered README, the top-level inference driver, package inference helpers and the modified Qwen2 model. No model weights or large dataset archives were acquired for this check. The README still lists release of the training script as a TODO. This snapshot therefore cannot establish the historical folds, baseline token mappings, or training settings used for the tables.
# Problem 1: level weights reverse the intended ordering

Severity: Minor for the confirmed specification defect; empirical impact Needs Evidence. Equation (1), page 8, orders levels as \((\text{excellent},\text{good},\text{fair},\text{poor},\text{bad})\) and weights their normalized exponentials by \((1,2,3,4,5)\). Section 5.4 then selects the AGAV with the highest score. Appendix B.1 instead defines higher scores as higher quality, with excellent at 4–5 and bad at 0–1. These conventions conflict. For illustrative logits \(z_A=(8,0,0,0,0)\) and \(z_B=(0,0,0,0,8)\), the printed mapping gives \[S_A=1.0033501,\qquad S_B=4.9966499.\] Thus a confidently bad candidate defeats a confidently excellent one. For this level order the corrected weights are \((5,4,3,2,1)\), or any positive affine equivalent. Equivalently \(S_{\rm corrected}=6-S_{\rm printed}\). This reverses every strict ordering and the sign of rank correlation with a nonconstant quality target. The issue is not a small rounding difference. The text also calls \(X\) a probability distribution before exponentiating it; whether \(X\) means logits or probabilities should be made explicit, although either reading retains the direction defect.

Crucial counterevidence is present in the release: `wa5` in `videollama2_qwen2.py` uses \((1,0.75,0.5,0.25,0)\) for the same excellent-to-bad order, giving \(0.9991625\) and \(0.0008375\) in this example. It therefore has the correct direction. The top-level AGAV-Rater inference uses a regression head, not this helper; the code does not establish what every comparison model used historically. The defensible conclusion is a confirmed paper-formula error with a verified local repair. A claim that Tables 1–3 actually used reversed scores would require the missing baseline evaluation paths and raw outputs. No ranking reversal of the published methods is asserted.
# Problem 2: the released loss differs from equation (3)

Severity: Minor; release-to-description discrepancy, not a demonstrated failure of training. Appendix C.2 defines \(L=(1-\rho)/2\). The inspected Qwen2 `plcc_loss` instead standardizes prediction and target with population standard deviations, computes two mean-square losses divided by four, and averages them. Ignoring its \(10^{-8}\) numerical stabilizers and assuming nonconstant vectors, the first term is \((1-\rho)/2\) and the second is \((1-\rho^2)/4\). Hence the returned loss is \[L_{\rm release}=\frac{3-2\rho-\rho^2}{8}.\] At \(\rho=0\) the paper loss is \(0.5\) and the release loss is \(0.375\); their derivatives with respect to \(\rho\) are \(-1/2\) and \(-(1+\rho)/4\). Both favor \(\rho=1\), so the discrepancy alone does not refute the method. It changes optimization gradients and should be documented or corrected against the actual training revision. The released call reduces the tensor globally rather than specifying a dimension-wise reduction, which also needs historical clarification.

Both losses are invariant to a positive affine transformation of a single prediction vector, so correlation supervision alone does not determine calibration on the 0–100 MOS scale. For example, \(s=(10,20,30)\) and \(\hat s=2s+100\) have \(\rho=1\) and zero paper loss but RMSE \(120.2775\). This is a diagnostic of the objective, not a measurement of the model’s actual predictions. The normalization or calibration used for reported RMSE should be stated and tied to training/validation data. The inspected source uses a three-output linear head on the final hidden state; it does not by itself establish a numerical score-to-score causal chain among the three predictions.
# Arithmetic and interpretation checks

The dataset construction counts reconcile: \(386\times8=3088\), \(3088\times3=9264\) scalar MOS values and \(3088+294=3382\) AGAVs. The 9,264 figure is not the number of individual subject ratings. Fifteen subjects rating all 3,088 items in three dimensions would yield 138,960 raw scalar ratings before any exclusions. At most 60 videos per subject per day requires at least 52 rating days, consistent with the approximately two-month schedule stated in B.4.

The pretraining components printed in Section 4.1 do not reconcile with the total: \[25,592+19,000+6,000=50,592\ne50,952.\] The 360-pair difference is a Minor numerical/provenance defect. Either a component or the total should be corrected from the construction manifest; the acquired source does not resolve which. No particular missing training example is inferred.

Against the largest printed comparison SRCC for content consistency, the relative improvements are \(10.8941\%\), \(6.5562\%\) and \(3.2780\%\) for AGAVQA-MOS, TTA and TTM, agreeing with the rounded 11%, 7% and 3% claims. These are relative changes, not percentage-point changes or independently demonstrated statistical significance. Table 10 category counts sum to 230. Weighting its rounded accuracies gives \(0.8044783\); integer successes \((32,13,17,17,25,15,16,9,12,20,9)\) are compatible with those cells and sum to 185, or \(0.8043478\). This supports the table’s rounded 0.80, but is only a compatible reconstruction, not access to raw preference labels. It does not establish the distinct wording that 80% of ten people prefer the selected videos. The aggregation unit and tie rules need to be specified. Latency/throughput values in Table 9 agree approximately with reciprocal times; no hardware measurement was performed.
# Remaining limits and disposition

The 75 selection questions originate in demonstration pages where each source promotes its own VTA method. Manual verification is reported, but the raw judgments are unavailable here; third-party origin alone is not proof of an impartial sampling frame. The paper reports fivefold validation without sufficient information here to verify whether all audio variants of the same video stay in one fold. This is a need for a content-grouped split manifest, not an assertion that leakage occurred. Likewise an observed SRCC of 0.6860 between two quality dimensions (B.5) does not establish statistical independence. It can support discussing distinct, correlated constructs; it cannot prove their independence.

The three confirmed local defects are the reversed printed score mapping, the loss-description mismatch and the pretraining arithmetic discrepancy. No Major empirical failure is established in the available evidence. The score-map repair and loss algebra are verified by independent small calculations; retraining, benchmark regeneration and author adoption were not performed. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending, with no human review recorded.

Title: Exact counterexamples to two A-PSRO guarantees
# Identity, scope and notation

This is an initial review of Yudong Hu, Haoran Li, Congying Han, Tiande Guo, Mingqiang Li and Bonan Li, A-PSRO: A Unified Strategy Learning Method with Advantage Metric for Normal-form Games, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. The frozen proceedings PDF has 27 pages. The main definitions and results, Appendix A proofs, Appendix B algorithms and Appendix C experimental settings were read. Some dense plot-label text was recovered separately with whitespace compression. Figures 4–5 on page 7 and the statements and proof passages on pages 4, 5 and 16 were actually viewed. Other figures were not exhaustively inspected.

Optional supplementary code remains unavailable: the source inventory records an OpenReview verification barrier. No workaround was attempted, no author code was run and no historical experiment was reproduced. The independent `check_counterexamples.py` uses exact rational arithmetic. For a row strategy \(x\) and payoff matrix \(A\) in a zero-sum game, the paper’s advantage is \(V(x)=\min_j(x^\top A)_j\).
# Problem 1: no improving pure direction in Theorem 4.2

Severity: Major. Theorem 4.2 is false under its stated hypotheses. The theorem, page 4, requires that whenever a current meta-equilibrium \(\theta\) has \(V(\theta)<0\), some pure action \(e_j\) satisfies \(V((1-d)\theta+de_j)>V(\theta)\) for all sufficiently small positive \(d\). Consider the symmetric zero-sum game with row matrix \[A=\begin{pmatrix}
0&-1&-1&-1\\
1&0&-2&2\\
1&2&0&-2\\
1&-2&2&0
\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=-A^\top,\] and column payoff \(-A\). Take both populations to be the singleton \(P_i=P_j=\{\theta\}\), where \[\theta=(3/4,1/12,1/12,1/12),\qquad
 \theta^\top A=(1/4,-3/4,-3/4,-3/4).\] This is a legitimate meta-equilibrium: the restricted game has one action per player and payoff \(\theta^\top A\theta=0\). The underlying strategy is strictly interior to the full simplex, and \(V(\theta)=-3/4<0\). Direct multiplication gives, for every \(0<d\le1\), \[\begin{aligned}
 V((1-d)\theta+de_1)&=-3/4-d/4,\\
 V((1-d)\theta+de_j)&=-3/4-5d/4,\quad j=2,3,4.\end{aligned}\] Thus all pure directions strictly worsen advantage. Reducing the step size, or selecting the best of these directions, cannot produce the claimed improvement. At \(d=1/100\), the four values are \((-301/400,-61/80,-61/80,-61/80)\), all below \(-3/4\).

In contrast, the mixed direction \(m=(0,1/3,1/3,1/3)\) satisfies \(m^\top A=(1,0,0,0)\) and \[V((1-d)\theta+dm)=-3/4+3d/4>V(\theta).\] The independent script confirms the displayed formulas at exact rational steps, including \(10^{-6}\), \(10^{-2}\), \(1/2\) and \(1\). The formulas themselves establish the full interval, not just those four tests.

The proof fails between Appendix A.5 equations (18) and (19), pages 15–16. Existence of an improving mixed direction and a pure component with positive inner product do not imply that the pure component improves a nonsmooth concave objective. Here the three active worst-case payoffs are improved by different components; every individual component harms another active payoff. This is consistent with concavity of \(V\) and does not challenge the valid min-of-linear representation in Theorem 3.4.

The effect is central: the pure-action LookAhead search in Section 4.1 and Algorithm 2 cannot inherit deterministic improvement or a sublinear rate from Theorem 4.2. Random population expansion and diversity may escape this example; the counterexample does not claim the complete stochastic algorithm can never converge. A possible mathematical repair is to allow a genuinely mixed direction with larger \(V\), since concavity then proves improvement along its segment. That changes the oracle and does not supply the paper’s claimed rate or efficiency automatically.
# Problem 2: optimistic advantage need not be continuous

Severity: Major. The Lipschitz assertion in Theorem 4.6 is false. Let the two payoff matrices, with the same row/column ordering, be \[A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.\] This game is simplified under Definition 4.3, including its stated quantifier order. Every action of either player is uniquely optimal against one opposing pure action. Thus no action satisfies the paper’s dominated action criterion. No deletion or dominated-action ambiguity is involved.

For row strategy \(x=(p,1-p)\) the column player’s payoffs are \(p\) for column 1 and \(2(1-p)\) for column 2. Therefore column 2 is uniquely best for \(p<2/3\), column 1 for \(p>2/3\), and both are best at \(p=2/3\). Definition 4.5 chooses the best response giving the row player the larger payoff at a tie, so \[V(p)=\begin{cases}
 1-p,&p<2/3,\\
 4/3,&p=2/3,\\
 2p,&p>2/3.
 \end{cases}\] In particular, \[V(2/3)-V(2/3-\varepsilon)=1-\varepsilon,
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon<2/3.\] The strategy displacement in Euclidean norm is \(\sqrt2\varepsilon\), so no finite Lipschitz constant exists. The scalar-parameter difference ratios at \(\varepsilon=10^{-2},10^{-4},10^{-6}\) are exactly \(99,9999,999999\). The left and right limiting values differ, so changing only the value assigned at the tie cannot restore continuity.

Appendix A.7, page 16, asserts that the zero-sum continuity proof does not require zero-sumness. It does: in zero-sum games, opponent best responses minimize the reviewed player’s own payoff, making \(V\) a minimum of finitely many continuous linear functions. In general-sum games, equal opponent utility does not imply equal own utility. The example gives equal column utility \(2/3\) at the switch but row utilities \(4/3\) and \(1/3\). Simplification and locally unique best responses on either side do not eliminate the jump.

The claim that nearby strategies have nearby advantage, used in the interpretation following Theorems 4.6–4.7, is therefore unsupported. Continuity on an individual strict-best-response region is a valid restricted statement, but cannot replace the global theorem. Neither this counterexample nor the first one negates all empirical gains. A repaired general-sum theory must explicitly handle best-response boundaries or add assumptions ensuring compatible payoffs there.
# Other inspected claims and limits

For zero-sum games the advantage really is a finite minimum of linear payoffs, hence concave and Lipschitz, and exploitability decomposes as \(E(x,y)=-V_i(x)-V_j(y)\). These properties survive both findings. The phrase “unique maximum” should distinguish a maximum value of zero from uniqueness of its maximizing strategy. Multiple equilibrium strategies are possible. No uniqueness claim is needed for either counterexample.

Theorem 4.8 and Appendix A.9 were read, but their approximation-rate proof was not accepted: convexity of \(-V\) does not establish a smooth quadratic remainder for the generally piecewise-linear \(V\), and the printed proof takes a descent step on \(f=V\) despite seeking its maximum. A projected nonsmooth or suitably regularized ascent analysis, with precise error conditions, would be needed. This is an additional unresolved proof obligation, not a third independent claimed counterexample here.

Figure 4’s plotted rewards and Figure 5’s embedded advantage landscapes were inspected as reported empirical evidence. They do not certify a universal convergence theorem. The t-SNE pictures do not prove continuity of the original function. Reported repeat counts and implementation parameters were read, but raw game matrices, trajectories, seeds and supplementary code were unavailable for reproduction. The multiplayer coalition-response approximation was read as an approximation, not treated as an exact equilibrium oracle.
# Disposition

Both Major findings directly contradict central mathematical assertions under the paper’s hypotheses. Their exact payoff calculations are verified by the initial reviewer. The suggested restrictions/oracle changes are not a verified replacement algorithm. Experimental performance, author adoption and independent acceptance remain unverified; scientific adjudication is pending and no human review is recorded.

Title: Structured-map and normalization checks for Monarch circuits
# Identity and inspected material

This report reviews Honghua Zhang, Meihua Dang, Benjie Wang, Stefano Ermon, Nanyun Peng and Guy Van den Broeck, Scaling Probabilistic Circuits via Monarch Matrices, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. The 15-page proceedings PDF was read through Sections 1–7 and Appendices A–B. Static source inspection used https://github.com/wangben88/MonarchCircuits, commit `6d7c47f2a50d1c7ec97cfe069a001680eaec61cc`. It covered the HMM multiplication initializer, selected forward/parameter routines, Monarch PC layer construction, image driver/training path, color transforms, quantization and patch extraction. No training, GPU kernel, author script, or dataset download was executed. Figures 1–4 and Appendix B.3 formulas were actually viewed on pages 3, 5, 6 and 15.
# Checks supporting the construction

For row-major vectorization of \(x\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\), direct index contraction verifies equation (1): \[_{kl}
 =\sum_{ij}A_{ki}B_{lj}x_{ij}=[(B(Ax)^\top)^\top]_{kl}.\] An independent seeded NumPy example with rectangular matrices gives maximum difference \(2.22\cdot10^{-16}\). For the untied tensors in Definition 3.1, building the dense matrix \(M_{kl,ij}=A_{kij}B_{ljk}\) and comparing it with the two contractions gives error \(1.11\cdot10^{-16}\).

If all entries are nonnegative, \(\sum_iA_{kij}=1\) for each \((k,j)\), and \(\sum_jB_{ljk}=1\) for each \((l,k)\), then \[\sum_{ij}M_{kl,ij}=\sum_jB_{ljk}\sum_iA_{kij}=1.\] Thus a normalized sum map can be implemented with normalized factors. The independently constructed example has row-sum error \(2.22\cdot10^{-16}\). Sum/permutation stages on a common scope preserve smoothness, and do not alter the disjoint-scope requirement at product nodes. General arbitrary signed matrices would not be probability weights; nonnegativity and normalization remain necessary.

For equal dimensions \(h=c^d\), the factor representation uses \(dhc\) entries/elementary weighted edges. This yields \(2h^{3/2}\) for two equal factors and \(h\sum_t c_t\) for unequal factors with \(\prod_tc_t=h\). Selected Table 6 entries agree: \(h=4096,c_t=(64,64)\) gives 524,288; \(h=8192,c_t=(64,128)\) gives 1,572,864; and \(h=4096,c_t=(16,16,16)\) gives 196,608. These use the paper’s operation counting convention, not an independent hardware profiler. The memory argument correctly retains activation storage proportional to \(dnhB\); fewer parameters need not imply less total training memory.

Appendix A’s bit-factor sparsity discussion was read, but the exact input/output permutation and factor-order conventions in the fully indexed butterfly equivalence were not exhaustively certified. The numerical tests above establish the stated local two-factor identities, not every index formula in that appendix.
# Problem 1: local emission normalization changes the product model

Severity: Minor; initialization semantics in the public release. Sections 3.1–3.2 motivate initialization by a circuit satisfying \(p_C(x)\propto p_A(x)p_B(x)\). The release initializer adds log-emission tables and applies a per-state `log_softmax`; it forms initial state weights from the product of the original weights without including the state-dependent emission normalizers. These operations generally produce a valid normalized model that is different from the globally normalized product.

Consider a single-observation HMM, equivalently a two-component categorical mixture, with uniform initial weights for each source model: \[E_A=\begin{pmatrix}9/10&1/10\\1/5&4/5\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 E_B=\begin{pmatrix}4/5&1/5\\2/5&3/5\end{pmatrix}.\] The source observed distributions are \((11/20,9/20)\) and \((3/5,2/5)\). Their normalized product is \[p_C=(11/17,6/17).\] The four componentwise emission products have sums \(Z=(37/50,21/50,8/25,14/25)\). Normalizing each product separately, then averaging them with unchanged pair weights \(1/4\), instead gives \[\widetilde p_C=(183/296,113/296)\ne p_C.\] These are exact rational values from independent enumeration of the documented operations. The test does not load or execute the initializer. In the one-observation example, multiplying each pair’s prior weight by its \(Z_{ij}\) before global normalization restores \((11/17,6/17)\) exactly. For longer sequences, corresponding partition contributions must propagate through the circuit; local leaf normalization alone is insufficient.

This does not refute the linear Kronecker identity or existence of a properly normalized product PC. Nor does it show that the implemented initialization is poor: it may be an effective heuristic, and subsequent EM can change the distribution. The needed repair is to describe the release as a locally normalized product-parameter initializer, or implement and verify the partition-weight corrections. Historical initialization ablation results were not regenerated, and no claim is made that their reported improvement disappears.
# Problem 2: the printed color specification differs from the code

Severity: Minor; reproducibility-level formula errors with direct counterevidence against assuming the same bug affected experiments. Appendix B.3, page 15, defines normalized RGB values in \([0,1]\) and then prints \(y=2\,tmp+cg+1\), claiming \(y\in[-1,1]\). Since \(tmp=(r+b)/2\) and \(cg=g-tmp\), the printed expression is \(y=(r+b)/2+g+1\in[1,3]\). Black gives 1 and white gives 3. With the stated clipping quantizer for \([-1,1]\), this would collapse the luminance channel to the highest bin. The inspected source instead uses \[Y_0=tmp+cg/2,\qquad y=2Y_0-1=2\,tmp+cg-1,\] which sends black and white to \(-1\) and \(1\). Thus a sign correction in the paper reproduces the source, and no luminance-collapse defect in the actual released transform is established.

The lossless transform itself has the valid inverse \[tmp=Y-\lfloor Cg/2\rfloor,\quad
 G=Cg+tmp,\quad B=tmp-\lfloor Co/2\rfloor,\quad R=B+Co.\] But the printed range \(Cg\in[0,255]\) is false before an offset: RGB \((255,0,255)\) gives \((Y,Co,Cg)=(127,0,-255)\). Both chroma channels can range from \(-255\) to \(255\). The source correctly offsets both by 256, using a larger categorical support. Independent integer arithmetic checks black, white, two saturated colors and a small nontrivial RGB triple, recovering the inputs exactly. This supports losslessness on those cases and the displayed algebra, not a complete audit of the image dataset pipeline.
# Evaluation scope and disposition

A shared normalized patch model \(q\) on disjoint 8-by-8 patches defines a normalized full-image model \(Q(I)=\prod_bq(I_b)\). Its full-image BPD equals the average patch BPD when each image contributes the same number of equal-sized patches. Thus patchwise scoring need not invalidate likelihood comparison; it explicitly assumes independence across patches. This derivation does not certify that every reported loader and aggregate uses identical weighting or color conventions. Lossy YCoCg scores remain incomparable with original-RGB likelihoods; the paper appropriately separates lossy and lossless columns.

Figure 4’s x-axis says inference FLOPs/character while its caption says training FLOPs. Under identical token/pass counts these are proportional, but total training comparisons also require backward/EM and initialization cost accounting. The study’s plotted quality-versus-budget trend was viewed, not independently benchmarked. The approximately 200-fold sampling-time comparison agrees arithmetically with \(3.60/0.017\), but is specific to the listed diffusion baseline and timing setup.

The two confirmed discrepancies admit local repairs and do not establish a Major failure of the core structured sum-block method. Initial checks of the local mathematics are complete; historical outcomes, end-to-end repairs, author adoption and independent acceptance are unverified. Scientific adjudication remains pending with no human review recorded.

Title: Scope and quantitative checks for in-context time-series fine-tuning
# Identity, scope, and method

This report reviews Matthew Faw, Rajat Sen, Yichen Zhou and Abhimanyu Das, In-Context Fine-Tuning for Time-Series Foundation Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. The frozen 20-page proceedings PDF was read through Sections 1–7 and Appendix A.1–A.9, focusing on model construction, temporal information restrictions, metrics, aggregates and timing. Original source figures on pages 4, 6, 8, 11 and 19 were viewed. Individual trajectories in Figure 8 and every entry of the wide WQL/baseline tables were not independently verified. The source manifest records no located release of this specific method; the upstream TimesFM implementation was not treated as its substitute. No author code, training, forecast or raw dataset was run.

The model embeds length-32 input patches, predicts length-128 output patches, inserts a learned separator between examples, and permits causal attention to preceding examples. Section 3’s inclusion of the target horizon in training notation does not itself expose that horizon to an earlier prediction: the specified causal computation of output \(o_j^{(i)}\) uses the target’s tokens only through \(j\). Its validity also requires masking padded and unavailable values in the actual loader. The paper explicitly defines zero-shot as no gradient update on the unseen task; using observed target-domain histories is consistent with that definition. It is not a claim of having no target-domain information.

Appendix A.9 restricts random context selection to the past history of other series. Under synchronized forecast cutoffs, this is an admissible information set. The absent release prevents checking exact timestamps, asynchronous series, all padding cases and split implementation. No test leakage is demonstrated. Overlapping training windows alone do not prove test leakage. Likewise, the paper’s caveat that unaligned examples are outside Moirai-MV’s intended use is explicit; this auxiliary comparison cannot establish a general superiority over correctly aligned multivariate forecasting.
# Independent numerical checks

For \(L>S\), positive seasonal-naive scale, and forecast horizon \(H\), the stated MASE is the usual ratio \[\frac{H^{-1}\sum_{t=L+1}^{L+H}|\widehat y_t-y_t|}
 {(L-S)^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{L-S}|y_{t+S}-y_t|}.\] An independent check with history \((1,2,4,7)\), future \((11,16)\), forecast \((10,14)\) and \(S=1\) gives \(1.5/2=0.75\). The formula requires an explicit convention for zero denominators and histories shorter than the seasonal period; no evidence here establishes that an evaluated series violates those conditions. At quantile \(1/2\), twice the stated pinball loss is absolute error, so the WQL formula reduces to normalized absolute error as expected.

The script `check_aggregates.py` parses all 27 Table 6 rows and removes the four named in-pretraining datasets, leaving 23. It computes the geometric mean of the printed dataset MASE values divided by each dataset’s seasonal-naive value:
Model | Reconstructed | Printed aggregate
TimesFM base | 0.833999 | 0.834

The first four columns broadly reconcile at printed precision (Table 2 uses 0.811 for LH). The ICF reconstruction differs by 0.00231. This does not establish erroneous aggregation: the paper says it averages seed-wise geometric means, whereas the calculation above takes a geometric mean of rounded per-dataset means. These operations do not commute, and the geometric mean is concave. Raw paired seed results are needed to resolve the exact difference.

The advertised improvements follow from the aggregate entries: \(100(1-0.777/0.834)=6.8345\%\) and \(100(1-0.777/0.818)=5.0122\%\). The prose’s 2.4% LH improvement does not follow exactly from Table 2, which yields 2.7578%; this small arithmetic discrepancy does not change the ordering and is not treated as a substantive methodological failure. Independently averaging the four ICF horizons in Table 9 yields 0.4045, 0.37825, 0.378 and 0.30725, consistent with the rounded Table 1 rows.
# Unresolved uncertainty and controlled-comparison details

Section 6.2, page 7, describes ten runs and standard-error bars. Appendix A.6, page 14, explicitly describes five evaluations, each averaged over ten random seeds, and labels the Table 6 intervals one standard deviation of the five evaluations. Its final paragraph averages five geometric means. Figure 10 separately calls its bars one standard deviation of evaluations averaged over ten seeds. Thus the appendix does supply a nested arrangement; the remaining uncertainty is which replication level and SD/SE convention apply to the main-figure and table comparisons. Different experiment sets could reconcile the wording, and no particular interval is shown to be wrong. Standard deviation and standard error are not interchangeable: for independent replicate units their ratio is \(\sqrt n\), or 2.236 for \(n=5\) and 3.162 for \(n=10\). Those factors apply at the chosen replication level and cannot be used to convert a nested design without its aggregation details.

Consequently the small ICF–FT difference, 0.001 in Table 6, supports a descriptive statement of similar point estimates, not a verified statistical equivalence claim. Table 1 also bolds entries said to lie within one standard error without printing those errors. This review does not infer that any specific interval or bold entry is wrong. The needed evidence is the experimental unit, seed grouping, SD/SE definition, paired outputs and the precise aggregation operation. This is recorded as Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated false forecasting result.

Section 6.4.2 describes at most five length-512 examples against a length-2048 single-series baseline. Five complete examples contain 2560 observed values, 25% more than 2048, before separators; actual short examples may use less. Thus this is a useful cross-series versus single-series comparison, but is not strictly token- or information-budget matched. Moreover, Table 2 repeats ICF’s 0.777 aggregate while the main experiment and Figure 10 use 50 examples. Equal rounded outcomes are possible; they do not prove the five-example run was omitted. A distinct five-example result and length-matched ablation would resolve this issue. No controlled causal attribution to the separator alone is certified.
# Timing interpretation and disposition

Table 8 compares one sequential pass over the benchmark including fine-tuning. Its 418 minutes versus 25 minutes gives a ratio of 16.72, consistent with the stated approximately 16-fold advantage. Inference alone instead takes 1500 versus 28 seconds, a factor of 53.57 favoring the already fine-tuned model. If the same fine-tuned models are reused for \(K\) equally sized forecast batches without retraining, the reported costs imply \[T_{\rm ICF}=25K,\quad T_{\rm FT}=418+\frac{28}{60}K
 \quad\hbox{minutes},\] with crossover at \(K\simeq17.04\). This conditional calculation is not a new benchmark and does not contradict the paper’s explicitly one-pass timing. The 334-minute row already achieves the same rounded 0.776 score; the reported speed ratio is tied to the selected training budget.

The viewed qualitative forecasts demonstrate the intended ambiguity resolution on selected examples, not population-wide guarantees. The main arithmetic supports a positive average effect and similar ICF/FT point estimates in the reported setup. No substantive defect is established in the inspected architecture or metric definitions. Uncertainty, context budgets and implementation provenance remain open.
