Title: Oracle-guided loss bounds and metric consistency in MOGIC
# Paper and inspected scope

This report concerns Suchith Chidananda Prabhu and coauthors, MOGIC: Metadata-infused Oracle Guidance for Improved Extreme Classification, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. The 28-page proceedings PDF was read through the main method and experiments and Appendices A–H, with detailed independent checks of Appendix E’s bounds and selected numerical and metric claims. Bibliographic sources cited by the paper were not individually re-reviewed. Source pages 5, 7, 19, 20, 23 and 25 were actually viewed to check the architecture, plots, formulas and tables.

The public repository https://github.com/suchith720/mogic was inspected at commit `d244dff86cc4f4d18a8106b2c597a188ee278a68`. This covered its README, the full selected 001 MOGIC training entry point, the relevant configuration/import/evaluation portions of variants 002–004, a selected input-concatenation entry point and the minimal `core.py`. The actual model/loss/metric classes are imported from `xcai`; their implementation is not in this frozen repository snapshot. No author program, dependency installer, dataset or model was executed. The independently written `check_bounds.py` uses exact rational arithmetic for the counterexample.
# Problem 1: a false perturbation bound in the core guarantee

Equation reference: eq:printed. Severity: Major; the theoretical derivation of oracle-guided accuracy is invalid at its stated label-side inequality. Appendix E, Lemma 2 and equations (6), (13)–(16), assert that replacing label embeddings by oracle embeddings changes the averaged triplet loss by at most \[
 \frac{2KB}{L}\sum_{l=1}^L\|z_l-z_l^*\|_2.\] Here \(g\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz, the embeddings have norm at most \(B\), and the triplet loss averages over all positive–negative pairs. The proof replaces the two class-specific incidence weights by a uniform label weight in equation (14). Those weights need not agree.

Counterexample satisfying the stated conditions. Take one query, four labels, one positive label (label 1), and three negative labels. Let \(e_1=(1,0)\), \(e_2=(0,1)\), \(K=B=1\), and \(g(t)=[t+3/10]_+\), using the experimental margin 0.3. Set \[x=x^*=e_1,\quad z_1^*=e_1,\quad z_1=-e_1,
 \quad z_l=z_l^*=e_2\quad(l=2,3,4).\] Every embedding has norm exactly one, and \(g\) is globally 1-Lipschitz. The oracle positive score is 1 and all negative scores are zero, so its three triplet losses are zero. With the disciple labels, the positive score is \(-1\) and each triplet loss is \(1+0.3=1.3\). Averaging three identical losses leaves \(13/10\). Only label 1 changes, by Euclidean distance 2. The paper’s claimed upper bound is therefore \[\frac{13}{10}\ \leq\ 0+\frac{2}{4}\,2=1,\] which is false. Repeating the query any number of times preserves the same averaged violation. This failure is independent of sample noise, optimization error and the omitted summation notation elsewhere in the proof. A hypothesis class can contain both displayed configurations, so restricting to oracle-realizable classes does not repair Lemma 2. ◻

Equation reference: eq:correct. For a query \(i\) with positive set \(S_i\) of size \(P_i\), define \(e_l=\|z_l-z_l^*\|_2\). The direct Lipschitz calculation instead gives \[
 |\ell(Z^\top x_i,y_i)-\ell(Z^{*\top}x_i,y_i)|
 \leq KB\left(\frac{\sum_{l\in S_i}e_l}{P_i}
 +\frac{\sum_{l\notin S_i}e_l}{L-P_i}\right).\] Each positive label occurs in \(L-P_i\) pairs and each negative label in \(P_i\) pairs; dividing by \(P_i(L-P_i)\) yields these coefficients. The example’s corrected upper bound is 2, which is valid. Uniform \(2/L\) coefficients agree in the balanced case \(P_i=L/2\), not for general extreme classification, where positives may be sparse.

Lemma 3 explicitly averages Lemma 2’s inequalities to obtain equation (23); Theorem 5 then combines Lemmas 3 and 4, and Section 3.4 presents Theorem 1 as the central justification. Thus a false supporting lemma invalidates the supplied proof of that guarantee. This is not a claim that no suitably qualified alternative theorem exists, nor that the benchmark improvements disappear.
## Realizability and the scope of the main theorem

Appendix Lemma 3 also assumes exact oracle realizability by the disciple. Section 3.4’s standalone theorem lists boundedness, Lipschitzness and complexity control but does not state that assumption. Without it, the oracle-comparison bound is false even for binary loss. Consider a point-mass distribution with positive label \(y=1\), query embedding 1 for both models, oracle label embedding 1, and a singleton disciple label class containing only \(-1\). Use \(\ell(s,y)=(1-ys)/2\) on \([-1,1]\), so \(K=1/2\), \(B=1\) and the loss is bounded in \([0,1]\). The only disciple is an empirical minimizer of any objective over its singleton class, but its risk is 1 versus oracle risk 0. Under the usual signed empirical Rademacher definition both singleton complexities are zero. With \(N=100\) and \(\delta=0.05\), the displayed right side is \(2\sqrt{\log(20)/100}=0.346164\), and the bound fails with probability one.

This second example deliberately does not meet Lemma 3’s realizability assumption. It refutes only the unqualified main statement; reading that assumption into the theorem blocks this example, but leaves the independent Lemma 2 defect above. An approximation term or explicit realizability restriction is needed. Lemma 4’s brief appeal to standard Rademacher arguments does not supply a checked uniform bound for the combined loss; its constants and normalization remain unverified. The unsquared norms in equations (2)/(5), MSE terminology in Appendix C, and the experimental weights also need reconciliation before transferring an analysis to the implemented objective.
# Problem 2: metric formulas and repeated table columns conflict

For the identical MOGIC(OAK)/DistilBERT row, Tables 2 and 4 report N@5=27.44 and Table 4 gives PSP@1=35.70. Table 3 labels these two numbers in the opposite columns: N@5=35.70, PSP@1=27.44. The same pattern appears in Tables 11/12 and the first dataset of Table 20. The internal conflict and original PDF layout were checked directly. It is consistent with transposed reporting columns, but raw metric outputs are needed to identify every affected row. P@1/P@5 entries are not changed by this swap. The external metric implementation was not available in the inspected snapshot, so no historical scoring bug or reversed performance ranking is asserted.
# Empirical and source-code limits

The six Table 2/16 P@1 gains over OAK are 0.91, 2.46, 0.59, 1.05, 0.11 and 1.69 percentage points, all positive. The headline “1–2%” is therefore a rough characterization, not a per-dataset guarantee. Table 5’s oracle P@1 loss from ground-truth to predicted metadata is 22.54 points; its caption’s 17 differs, while the body says approximately 22. The oracle–disciple gaps in that table are 13.01 and 10.69 points, not the prose’s 8 and 6. These do not reverse the visible robustness trend. Its random replacement/removal experiments do not establish robustness to every structured corruption.

A training-only regularizer can leave an otherwise identical deployed architecture unchanged. Table 14, however, compares an OAK encoder at 10.30 ms against MOGIC at 14.95 ms, not a clearly matched end-to-end OAK system; that is a 45.15% mean-latency increase for the listed objects. This cannot verify equal system latency, but neither does it disprove a zero incremental cost of guidance relative to the same complete disciple pipeline. Table 13 separately compares oracle and disciple stages; total two-stage training must include the oracle.

The selected released MOGIC entry points freeze teacher embeddings, supporting the stated frozen-oracle design, but pass zero weights for one cross-loss direction and label matching. They also pass `block.test.dset` as the evaluation dataset while configuring best-P@1 checkpoint selection. These are concrete release settings requiring historical run mapping and a clarified held-out selection protocol. They may be exploratory variants; imported learner semantics, original experiment commits and logs are unavailable. No claim is made that published test scores were selected by this exact code or that the full method was rerun.
# Disposition

P1 Major | Weighted local bound derived | Unknown | Revised theorem and objective
P2 Minor | Perfect-rank normalization checked | Unknown | Metric code and table mapping
Source concerns: Needs Evidence | No rerun | Unknown | Historical configs and split logs

The core theoretical derivation needs correction. Empirical positive gains and the architectural idea of metadata-guided training survive these checks as reported observations, without independent reproduction. Scientific adjudication remains pending, with no human review recorded.

Title: Evaluation and representation checks for the few-shot image detector
# Identity and scope

This report reviews Shiyu Wu, Jing Liu, Jing Li and Yequan Wang, Few-Shot Learner Generalizes Across AI-Generated Image Detection, ICML 2025, PMLR 267. The technical body on pages 1–8 of the 12-page proceedings PDF was read, together with the available public source at https://github.com/teheperinko541/Few-Shot-AIGI-Detector, commit `b545c05f3c927ef67c1b00f9a8badf3b68c5f4b3`. The remaining PDF pages contain acknowledgments, impact and references; there is no technical appendix in this version. Static inspection covered the prototype utility, train/test drivers, dataset loaders, argument parser, model/save utilities, train/evaluation/rebuild shell scripts, requirements, README and visualization driver. Logger internals were not reviewed. No repository program, model, checkpoint, image dataset, GPU training or t-SNE computation was run. Original Figures 2–6 and Algorithm 1 on source pages 3, 4, 7 and 8 were actually viewed.
# Checks supporting the local method

An independently written NumPy check uses real supports \((-2,-1)\), fake supports \((1,2)\) and queries \((-0.4,0.4)\). The centers are \(-1.5,1.5\); squared distances are \((1.21,3.61)\) and \((3.61,1.21)\). The correct-class probabilities are both 0.916827, and the affine logit differences are \(-2.4,2.4\), agreeing with direct distances. An independent identity-index example also checks the train driver’s class-major flattening followed by task/sample/class reshaping. The resulting query labels alternate in the same order as its repeated class labels, and the first-\(K\) support IDs do not overlap the remaining query IDs. The release’s evaluation mode disables training-mode batch-statistic updates. No within-episode support/query self-inclusion is established. Actual file duplicates and dataset splits were not audited.

The six Table 1 entries average to 84.0667% for 10-shot FSD, 77.0500% for zero-shot FSD, and 72.4833% for LARE2. They agree with the rounded 84.1, 77.1 and 72.5. The reported 11.6 improvement is in percentage points, corresponding to a relative increase of 16.0% over 72.5; the additional few-shot gain over the reported zero-shot FSD value is 7.0 points. These calculations validate table arithmetic, not independent model accuracy.
# Problem 1: the released test transform omits the stated resize

Severity: Minor; a supported reproduction discrepancy with unmeasured historical effect. Section 4.2, page 5, says that test images are resized and then center-cropped to \(224\times224\). In `datasets/__init__.py`, the validation/test loader instead applies only `CenterCrop(224)` and `ToTensor()`; `test.py` directly uses this loader on each class’s validation directory. The training loader has a resize, so this is not merely a shared omitted description of preprocessing.

For a \(1024\times1024\) input, the release’s native \(224\times224\) crop retains 4.7852% of the original area. Resizing to \(256\times256\) before the same crop covers approximately \(896\times896\) original coordinates, or 76.5625%, a sixteenfold geometric area difference. This is a coordinate-footprint calculation, not a claim that all benchmark images have that resolution or that either transformed image was run through the detector. Spatial scale and retained image content are different inputs to the detector, so these pipelines are not interchangeable in general.

If every supplied file was already resized to the required size by an unrecorded preprocessing step, the discrepancy could disappear. The included rebuild script creates symlinks and does not perform that resize, and the README does not specify such a step. The historical dataset/preprocessing chain is therefore needed. A reproduction should explicitly choose the documented resize-and-crop path or revise the method description to match the intended native crop, then rerun the affected comparison. No performance repair has been tested.
# Problem 2: visualization uses a different representation

Severity: Minor; release-level mismatch in the evidence for the learned metric space. Figure 2 specifies 1024-dimensional features, and the train/test drivers instantiate a ResNet-50 with a 1024-output head. Figure 4 and Section 4.5 describe visualizing the final-layer features of the model. However, `visualization/tsne_script.py` loads that model and then replaces `model.fc` with `torch.nn.Identity()` before feature extraction. This removes the trained projection used by the actual prototype classifier, producing backbone features instead.

A learned projection need not preserve neighbors: take backbone points \(a=(0,100)\), \(b=(1,0)\), \(c=(2,100)\) and projection \(W=(1,0)\). Then \(\|a-c\|=2<\|a-b\|\simeq100.005\), but \(|Wa-Wb|=1<|Wa-Wc|=2\). The independent calculation verifies this reversal. Thus a visualization of pre-head features cannot directly certify the geometry of the post-head metric representation. This does not prove that the displayed historical figures used the current script, or that their qualitative clusters would disappear. The repair is to retain the classifier’s projection when studying its metric space, or accurately label the plotted features as backbone features and provide a separate post-head analysis. Neither actual visualization was regenerated here. Even correctly sourced t-SNE plots are qualitative two-dimensional evidence, not quantitative guarantees of generalization.
# Protocol clarifications and unresolved comparisons

The source and Algorithm 1 use \(K\) support images per class. A binary 10-shot episode therefore uses ten fake and ten real supports; only the ten fake images may be new acquisitions if the real pool is already available. In the released evaluator, each new shuffled batch receives a fresh support subset, and all query predictions are then aggregated. Across \(m\) such episodes, up to \(mK\) distinct labeled fake images are used, not one fixed global set of \(K\). An independent two-episode ID example with \(K=2\) consumes four distinct fake supports without any query overlap. This is valid episodic few-shot evaluation, but does not by itself measure deployment with ten total fake labels reused for an entire generator’s test stream. The fixed 1:3 support/query ratio in Section 4.6 is compatible with this episodic interpretation. A fixed-support evaluation and uncertainty over repeated support draws would establish the stronger acquisition-budget claim.

Other concrete release settings also need an explicit run mapping. The supplied evaluation shell script does not override parser defaults of five supports and fifteen queries, hence it requests 5-shot evaluation. It passes a seed, but `test.py` never calls the seed-setting helper; a static syntax-tree inspection confirms that absence. The test loader shuffles. The training example requests 50,000 steps instead of the paper’s 200,000, though it can be configured to that value. The README/train comment describes real images from SD v1.4/v1.5, whereas the paper says the real subsets are aggregated. None of these defaults proves which configuration produced a published checkpoint. The zero-shot training-prototype procedure is described in the paper but not implemented by the inspected test driver.

Section 4.3 reports FSD trained jointly on the non-test generator classes, while its baseline comparison averages separate models trained on individual non-test subsets. FSD also receives labeled target-generator supports in the few-shot condition; the paper explicitly acknowledges that difference. Consequently the 11.6-point comparison combines a different training information regime with target support adaptation. It does not isolate the causal effect of the prototype method. A joint-data baseline, equally budgeted target adaptation and quantitative multiclass versus binary ablation would resolve that attribution. No matched rerun is available, so this is Needs Evidence, not a claim that FSD would lose its advantage.

The release requests a multiclass average-precision metric with ten thresholds; the paper also states a coarse threshold step. The exact library version, averaging convention and output scores were not available for reproducing AP. No exact rank-based AP equivalence is assumed, and no incorrect historical AP value is established.
# Disposition
Assessment | Repair verification | Author adoption | Remaining work
P1 Minor | Geometry difference checked | Unknown | Historical transforms; rerun
P2 Minor | Projection counterexample checked | Unknown | Exact feature provenance
Protocol: Needs Evidence | No empirical repair | Unknown | Fixed-support, matched baselines

The local prototype algebra and disclosed accuracy arithmetic survive the checks. No Major failure of the detection method has been demonstrated. The two concrete release discrepancies and remaining protocol questions limit reproduction and interpretation. Scientific adjudication remains pending, and no human review is recorded.

Title: Technical Verification of MFRNet
# Identity, version, and scope

The paper is Yingying Feng, Jie Li, Chi Xie, Lei Tan, and Jiayi Ji, Multi-Modal Object Re-identification via Sparse Mixture-of-Experts, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:16796–16807, identifier I25-43710 (0341) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed proceedings PDF has twelve pages; page references below mean PDF pages, which equal the local printed page numbers 1–12. All main sections, the conclusion, and the reference list were read. There is no appendix in this PDF. A separate OpenReview supplement was unavailable in the acquired packet; its absence is not proof that none exists.

Static inspection used the official MFRNet repository at commit , dated 21 July 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The training/evaluation entry points, configured CLIP path, fusion and expert modules, relevant preprocessing, losses, and retrieval metric were inspected. No author program, model checkpoint, training, or evaluation was executed. The independent checks below evaluate elementary arithmetic and branch conditions only. Figures 1–3 and the relevant equations and tables on pages 3–8 were visually inspected.
# Method and checks that survived

The inputs are aligned RGB, NIR, and TIR image triples. With modality features \(I_R,I_N,I_T\), the feature fusion module (FFM), equations (2)–(5), adds a retained feature \(\lambda I_M\) to a normalized weighted sum of generated features from other modalities. The feature representation module (FRM), equations (7)–(10), routes tokens through adapter experts. The intended model uses FFM before the transformer and FRM in its final block (Tables 7 and 10). Equations (11)–(15) define routing balance penalties and the total objective; no formal performance guarantee is claimed.

The two source-feature weights in ordinary fusion are normalized jointly in , lines 795–804, agreeing with the text after equation (3). The internal adapter residual in equation (8) is also present in the released expert, lines 239–245; its presence alone is not an accidental double-residual defect. Six adapter experts and top-1 routing match the described configuration. Table 5 gives mAP increases \(75.1-69.2=5.9\) and \(77.8-69.2=8.6\) percentage points for the individual modules. Table 3 gives mean mAP \(49.0833\) and mean Rank-1 \(49.6167\) for MFRNet, compatible with the printed 49.1 and 49.6. These are checks of reported numbers, not replications of measurements.

The retrieval implementation removes same-identity/same-camera gallery items before computing CMC and average precision. On a retained relevance sequence \((0,1,0,1)\), the standard precision-at-relevant-ranks calculation gives \(\mathrm{AP}=((1/2)+(2/4))/2=1/2\), consistent with the inspected expression. Identical test directories used for query and gallery therefore do not by themselves demonstrate self-match leakage: the exclusion rule matters.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (A single input triple bypasses FFM and FRM).  The published architecture and released profiling method do not describe the same computation for the profiler’s input batch.
## Source claim and assumptions

Sections 3.1–3.2 and Figure 2 describe FFM and FRM as the proposed model’s two components. Table 4 and section 4.4 report computational cost for that model. The concrete released path uses `ViT-B-16`, `GEN=True`, `ADA=True`, with the separate `PROMPT` and `ADAPTER` switches false, as in the supplied RGBNT201 configuration and defaults. Let \(b\geq1\) be the number of complete RGB/NIR/TIR triples, and consider evaluation mode.
## Decisive check

The wrapper concatenates the three modalities on the batch axis (, lines 137–164). The visual transformer therefore sets \(B=3b\) (, line 687). Its FFM branch at line 773 requires \(B>3\). After permutation to sequence–batch–channel order, the FRM guard at line 353 likewise requires `x.shape[1] > 3`; the final block uses the ordinary MLP when that condition fails (lines 351–361). Hence \[b=1\ \Longrightarrow\ B=3\ \Longrightarrow\
  \text{FFM bypassed and final-block FRM bypassed}.\] For \(b=2\), \(B=6\) and both guards permit the proposed modules. This is a change of computational path, not merely a different amount of parallel work. The independently written branch check records both cases in `independent_results.json`.

The released `MFRNet.flops`, lines 72–92, constructs each modality tensor with leading dimension one and passes them to an evaluation-mode copy. Thus, if that profiling call completes, it traces precisely the bypass path. It cannot certify the FLOP count of the ordinary FFM/FRM-enabled path. This conclusion does not require executing the profiler or knowing how an external FLOP library counts individual operators.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair scope

The distributed configuration normally evaluates batches of 128 triples, so it usually takes the enabled path. This limits the demonstrated inference defect to singleton triples and any singleton remainder; a batch remainder was not established for the published data. Sparse routing can itself introduce batch effects, but that does not account for an explicit guard selecting a different architecture. A profiling-only special case could explain the guard’s origin, yet there is no restriction at the public forward interface requiring \(b>1\).

The supported assessment is Minor for this release. Singleton deployment and the released profiling recipe are affected. The evidence does not show that Table 4’s 22.1G value came from this exact call, does not provide a replacement FLOP count, and does not invalidate reported retrieval scores. Determining the paper’s actual efficiency requires historical profiling provenance and a fresh count on a path with the proposed modules active. Removing batch-size-dependent architecture selection is a plausible repair direction; compatibility with Tutel’s singleton behavior and the complete corrected model has not been tested.
Problem 2 (The RGB-only branch uses unnormalized signed weights).  One missing-modality case uses raw linear outputs where the described reconstruction normalizes available-source weights.
## Source claim and assumptions

The end of section 3.1 on page 3 and its continuation on page 4 specify Softmax normalization of reconstructed-modality weights. Equation (6) restricts reconstruction to available modalities. For one available source, a normalized source weight is one. In the release, `Gen_lack_weight` is average pooling followed by an unconstrained linear layer (lines 577–585), and `MISS=’nt’` denotes missing NIR and TIR. Take \(b\geq2\) so Problem 1 does not suppress FFM.
## Decisive check

For missing RGB+NIR and RGB+TIR, lines 852–863 apply Softmax to each single-source weight. For missing NIR+TIR, however, lines 864–869 instead calculate \[\widehat I_N=q_{R\to N}(I_R)g_{R\to N}(I_R),\qquad
  \widehat I_T=q_{R\to T}(I_R)g_{R\to T}(I_R),\] without Softmax. Set the linear weight vector to zero and its bias to \(-1\), a permitted parameter choice. For any nonzero generated feature \(g\), the released result is \(-g\), whereas the normalized single-source result is \[\operatorname{softmax}([-1])g
   =\frac{e^{-1}}{e^{-1}}g=g.\] The independent scalar check uses \(g=(1,2)\) and obtains \((-1,-2)\) versus \((1,2)\). The feature is an intermediate algebraic example, not a claimed output of a trained checkpoint. No constraint on the linear layer forces its output to one. For a nonconstant feature, a negative scale also need not disappear under a subsequent normalization; in particular, centered normalization reverses its sign.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair scope

Equation (6) is not completely explicit about renormalizing after restricting the available set. Nevertheless, the preceding normalization rule and the two symmetric released cases support the normalized interpretation. Treating equation (3)’s unnormalized \(q\) as the final coefficient instead would make the missing-`nt` branch an intentional special case, requiring documentation and leaving the other two cases asymmetric. Equality is possible for a particular learned raw weight of one, but is not an identity of the implemented function.

This is Minor, confined to the supplied RGB-only reconstruction branch. The evidence does not establish the sign or size of learned weights or an error in Table 3’s M(NIR+TIR) measurements. Applying the same one-element Softmax used in the other two single-source cases restores the normalized intermediate expression; only that algebraic repair is verified. Accuracy after correction needs a fresh evaluation with the relevant historical checkpoint.
# Overall dependence and limitations

The reported retrieval improvements are empirical claims. The numerical differences and average calculations are broadly consistent, and the displayed expert assignments in Figure 3 provide qualitative examples rather than a statistical proof of semantic specialization. No formal theorem was refuted. The code findings concern implementations of core modules, but the demonstrated damage is bounded to released execution paths; the missing historical link prevents promoting them into claims that the paper’s benchmark results are false.

The inspected preprocessing applies its stochastic transform separately to each modality; the paper’s pixel-alignment rationale therefore warrants a provenance check of synchronized training augmentation. This review did not recover the exact dependency implementation, random draws, or training trace and does not assign an additional defect or empirical effect. Equation (13)’s load-probability convention and its exact correspondence to the external Tutel dependency were not independently verified. Total parameter counts, baseline fairness, seed variability, the unshown CLIP TOP-ReID rerun, raw datasets, and checkpoints were not reproduced. No later revision or erratum was acquired, so current correction/adoption status is unknown.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Issue judgment | Two Minor release-specific findings; historical experimental effect unresolved.
Repair verification | Single-source Softmax identity checked; full repairs and revised performance untested.
Author adoption | Unknown; no author response requested.
Remaining work | Trace profiling provenance; validate singleton execution and corrected RGB-only reconstruction.
Scientific adjudication | Pending; independent acceptance not yet performed.

report: Abstract: The main paper, all appendices, and relevant released inference code were inspected. The finite-mixture limit proof contains a false finite-dimensional Dirichlet-process assertion, demonstrated by an exact variance counterexample. This is a Major defect in that central derivation, not a counterexample to the stated limiting conclusion. A separate dependence error in the truncation proof is repairable without weakening its bound. The printed Gibbs concentration update and its inspected implementation both include all Dirichlet factors; no omission is established. Two additional Minor release-specific defects affect the local variational stick update and the ELBO entropy terms. No historical experiment is shown to be affected. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of the Global–Local Dirichlet Process
# Identity and scope

This review concerns Arhit Chakrabarti, Yang Ni, Debdeep Pati, and Bani K. Mallick, Global-Local Dirichlet Processes for Clustering Grouped Data in the Presence of Group-Specific Idiosyncratic Variables, ICML 2025, identifier I25-43711 (0342) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. All 36 PDF pages were read, including appendices A–H and the final acronym and notation tables. Locations below use one-based PDF pages; printed pagination restarts near the end. The original PDF SHA-256 is

Static code inspection used GLocalVI commit , dated 17 December 2024 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. The main VI loop, its update and ELBO functions, simulation generator and restart selection, the Gibbs sampler’s inference loop, and relevant real-data preprocessing were inspected. Author code was not executed. The calculations here are independently written scalar probability calculations, not simulation replications. The original figures 1–17 were actually viewed, together with the decisive proof and algorithm pages.
# Model and distinct approximations

The model uses group-specific local variables and shared global variables. Its random measures satisfy \[V\sim\operatorname{DP}(\gamma,H),\qquad
 G_j\mid V\sim\operatorname{DP}(\alpha,U_j\otimes V).\] A local table \(t\) has a local atom \(\psi^L_{jt}\) and a global label \(k_{jt}\); all observations at that table share \(k_{jt}\). This distinction matters for the probability calculation below. The finite symmetric-Dirichlet approximation in equation (10) and appendix C uses \(\pi_j\sim\operatorname{Dir}(\alpha/T,\ldots,\alpha/T)\) and \(\beta\sim\operatorname{Dir}(\gamma/K,\ldots,\gamma/K)\), with \(T\geq K\). It is different from the lumped-tail stick-breaking truncation used in section 3 and appendix D. The following findings do not conflate them.
# Mathematical findings

Problem 1 (The finite-limit proof identifies a finite mixture with an exact DP).  Appendix C, PDF pages 14–15, equations (C.28)–(C.29), contains two false equalities that are used to conclude the finite-mixture limit.

Equation reference: falseDP. In (C.28), the second line replaces the sampled atom \(\psi^G_{jt}=\phi_{k_{jt}}\) by a sum over all \(k\), without an indicator \(\mathbf1\{k_{jt}=k\}\). On the whole parameter space the first line is \(\sum_t\pi_{jt}=1\), whereas the printed second line is \(\sum_t\sum_k\pi_{jt}=K\). Thus \(T=K=2\) already contradicts the equality for every realization. Restoring the missing indicator fixes this normalization, but does not imply (C.29), which states, at finite \(T,K\), \[
 G_j^{T,K}\sim\operatorname{DP}(\alpha,U_j\otimes V^K).\]

Counterevidence and consequence. The extra factor \(1+\alpha/T\) tends to one; the counterexample does not disprove convergence as \(T,K\to\infty\). Nor does it invalidate the separate infinite stick-breaking construction. Reading (C.29) as an asymptotic rather than exact assertion would require an actual joint convergence argument and a stated topology; the displayed proof supplies neither at this step. The paper’s advertised finite-mixture connection and the theoretical justification for that approximation depend on this derivation. The assessment is Major: an invalid central proof, even though the limiting claim may be correct and a replacement proof may be available. A complete replacement convergence proof has not been certified here. There is no inference about the accuracy of the published clustering experiments.

Problem 2 (A dependence factorization in the truncation proof is not an equality).  The probability factorization leading to (D.4), PDF pages 16–17, treats shared global labels as independently resampled per observation and separates expectations involving the shared global stick.

For a concrete check, use the stick-breaking model with \(J=1\), \(n_1=2\), \(T=K=2\), and \(\alpha=\gamma=1\). The first local and global sticks \(u_1,v_1\) are independent uniforms. The event that both observations have \(t_i<T\) and \(k_{t_i}<K\) requires both to use table 1, whose one shared label must be 1. Its probability is \[\mathbb E[u_1^2]\mathbb E[v_1]=\frac16,
 \qquad\text{rather than the printed }\mathbb E[u_1^2]\mathbb E[v_1^2]=\frac19.\] This is a dependence error; it is not a counterexample to Proposition 3.1’s final bound.

Indeed, write \(A_j=\sum_{t<T}\pi_{jt}\), \(S=\sum_{k<K}\beta_k\), and \(N=\sum_jn_j\). Conditional on selected local tables, there are \(M\leq N\) distinct group–table pairs requiring global labels. Given \(\beta\), the probability that all their labels are below \(K\) is \(S^M\geq S^N\). The global stick is independent of the local selection. Jensen’s inequality and independence of the group-local sticks then give \[\begin{aligned}
 P(\text{good})
 &\geq\mathbb E\Big[\prod_j A_j^{n_j}\Big]\mathbb E[S^N]\\
 &\geq\left[1-\left(\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}\right)^{T-1}\right]^N
       \left[1-\left(\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma}\right)^{K-1}\right]^N.\end{aligned}\] Couple the truncated and infinite models identically on this event. Their total variation distance is at most \(P(\text{bad})\), and their \(L^1\) distance at most \(2P(\text{bad})\). Consequently the paper’s looser factor-four bound remains valid. The posterior argument likewise yields at most twice the prior \(L^1\) bound, wherever conditional distributions are defined. These statements condition on fixed positive \(\alpha,\gamma\); averaging over hyperpriors requires averaging the bound, not substituting posterior means. The assessment is Minor: the asserted equality is false, but the inequality actually needed by this truncation argument is valid in the same direction under the original assumptions, as established above. No change of model, truncation rate, or theorem conclusion is required; this distinction, rather than repair effort, bounds the defect to the local equality.
## Checked Gibbs concentration update

Algorithm 1, appendix E, physical PDF page 19, step 8 prints the product \[\frac{\Gamma(\gamma)}{\Gamma(\gamma/K)^K}
 \prod_{k=1}^{K}\beta_k^{\gamma/K-1}p(\gamma).\] The upper limit in the original rendered formula is \(K\), so the last simplex factor is present. This is the correct conditional form for the finite symmetric Dirichlet model. The inspected , lines 44–64, likewise uses `sum(log(beta))` over the full vector. No missing-factor issue is supported. The earlier report’s reading of this upper limit as \(K-1\) was incorrect and has been withdrawn; the preserved predecessor records that correction.
# Release-specific inference findings
Problem 3 (The local variational stick update drops \(\mathbb E_q\alpha\)).  The printed coordinate update is correct, but the released C++ function does not implement its second Beta parameter.

Appendix F, PDF page 21, step 3 gives, for \(t<T\), \[\bar a_{jt}=1+\sum_i\xi_{jit},\qquad
 \bar b_{jt}=s_1/s_2+\sum_{\ell>t}\sum_i\xi_{ji\ell}.\] In , lines 146–186, `Update_Ujt_cpp` receives `b_bar`, but line 167 assigns only `reverse_cumsum_cpp(N_jt.row(j).t())`. The helper at lines 17–19 is the sum strictly beyond the current entry. The supplied mean concentration is unused. The R loop passes and updates that mean at lines 83–102 of ; it is not supplied elsewhere in this update.

Take one group, two sticks, one observation with responsibilities \((1/2,1/2)\), and \(s_1/s_2=1\). These are normalized, strictly positive responsibilities and an admissible proper concentration factor. For the first stick the release yields Beta(\(3/2,1/2\)), whereas the printed coordinate optimum is Beta(\(3/2,3/2\)). Their means are \(3/4\) and \(1/2\). Independently, their KL divergence in the direction release-to-optimum is exactly one nat, confirming that they are different coordinate solutions. This uses the non-final stick; setting the final stick to one does not explain the discrepancy. Positive Gamma parameters also preclude interpreting \(s_1/s_2\) as zero.

The assessment is Minor, release-specific: this routine is not coordinate ascent for the stated prior. The printed update survives, and no historical execution trace connects this commit to the reported scores. Adding the mean concentration to non-final tail counts restores this one coordinate formula; the complete revised algorithm has not been run or validated.
Problem 4 (The released ELBO adds expected log densities instead of their negatives).  The Normal–Wishart variational factors enter the released objective with the wrong entropy sign.

Equation reference: eqlogq. The ELBO is \(\mathbb E_q\log p-\mathbb E_q\log q\). The function `elbo_q_Phi_k` in , lines 539–561, returns, summed over components, \[
 \frac12\mathbb E\log|\Lambda|+
 \frac p2\{\log(\lambda/(2\pi))-1\}-H(q_\Lambda).\] This is \(\mathbb E\log q(\mu,\Lambda)\), because its first two terms are the conditional Gaussian expected log density. The Wishart helper, lines 62–68, returns the entropy \(H(q_\Lambda)\). The local-atom function at lines 565–596 returns the same expression for each local factor. The R loop assigns these to `elbo7` and `elbo8`, then adds both at lines 262–263, alongside the prior and likelihood terms. There is no subsequent negation.

For an explicit proper factor, let \(p=1\), \(\Lambda\sim\operatorname{Wishart}(2,1/2)=\operatorname{Gamma}(1,1)\), and \(\mu\mid\Lambda\sim N(0,(\lambda\Lambda)^{-1})\). Then \(H(q_\Lambda)=1\) and \(\mathbb E\log\Lambda=-\gamma_E\). Expression [eqlogq] (#eqlogq) is \(-2.707546\ldots\) at \(\lambda=1\) and \(-1.707546\ldots\) at \(\lambda=e^2\). The released contribution increases by one, whereas the required entropy contribution decreases by one. Thus the error is parameter-dependent and cannot be dismissed as a dropped constant. Beta normalizer helpers were also checked: they return \(-\log B(a,b)\), so no additional Beta-normalization sign defect is alleged.

The release uses the objective for stopping and chooses the largest final value across restarts (, lines 18–25; the real-data script, lines 290–298). These code paths establish relevance, not an observed change in a winning run or a paper result. The assessment is Minor, release-specific. Negating the two expected-log-\(q\) terms repairs these contributions only; this review does not certify the entire ELBO implementation, numerical convergence, or published experiments.
# Coverage, surviving results, and limits

The product-space prior and infinite stick-breaking construction remain coherent under the stated general model. Problems 1 and 2 concern different approximations. The repaired coupling calculation preserves Propositions 3.1–3.2 for fixed concentrations. The printed VI responsibility, Normal–Wishart, and concentration updates were traced against their likelihood and prior dependencies; this was an algebraic audit rather than a full convergence proof. The finite Gibbs concentration update includes all \(K\) factors in both the paper and the inspected implementation.

The simulation designs, all displayed ARI/NMI/purity comparisons, timing and memory plots, and pan-cancer example were read. Figures 1 and 6–14 show distributions or illustrative realizations, not proofs of uniform superiority. The real-data pipeline uses ten joint expression principal components, selected local variables, and complete cases; appendix H changes the local feature set for the comparator and discloses that restriction. The displayed survival curves are descriptive. No survival effect, biological mechanism, adjusted significance, raw cluster assignment, or external validity was independently established. The published plots were visually checked, but no data were reverse-engineered from their pixels.

Code coverage is deliberately bounded: the principal VI files were read in full; the Gibbs driver and selected real-data branches were traced; unused alternative C++ likelihood variants, the entire HDP baseline implementation, plotting-only code, raw TCGA data, dependency internals, and historical outputs were not comprehensively verified. No benchmark or author code was executed. Later errata and author adoption of the suggested repairs are unknown. These limits prevent converting release defects into claims about historical experimental accuracy.
# Conclusion

The overall assessment is Major, resting on the explicit failure of the central finite-mixture-limit derivation. The limit theorem itself has not been refuted. The truncation result survives a supplied dependence-aware proof, while two released VI computations need the bounded corrections described above. The original claim of a missing Gibbs factor was withdrawn after independent inspection of physical page 19. This report includes focused independent AI verification; scientific adjudication remains pending and no human review is asserted.

Title: Technical Verification of RULEBREAKERS
# Paper, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Jason Chan, Robert Gaizauskas, and Zhixue Zhao, RULEBREAKERS: Challenging LLMs at the Crossroads between Formal Logic and Human-like Reasoning, ICML 2025, identifier I25-43712 (0343) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. All 30 PDF pages, including appendices A–N, were read. Page references are one-based PDF pages. The original PDF SHA-256 is

All eight figures were visually inspected, together with the relevant template and numerical tables. The public author repository at commit , dated 10 December 2025, contains a README and a CSV dataset, with no experimental implementation source in that tree. The README was read; the CSV was excluded from the acquired packet by its source-selection scope. The absence of code in this snapshot is not evidence about earlier or private code. Tokenization, actual model outputs, test implementation, and per-instance labels were consequently not reproduced.
# Design and independent checks

The benchmark pairs a knowledge-inconsistent scenario with a minimally changed counterpart. Its specified target behavior rejects a conclusion in a rulebreaker and accepts it in a non-rulebreaker. The main templates have forms \(P	o
eg Q,Q\vdash
eg P\) and \(P\lor Q,
eg Q\vdash P\). These are valid classical forms. In the rulebreaker interpretation, background knowledge relates the predicates and makes the stated premises jointly inconsistent. The authors explicitly distinguish their intended knowledge-informed response from classical entailment, including explosion (appendix I, page 25). Thus classical validity alone is not a counterexample to their operational labels. It also does not establish that every generated item has the stated human response; no representative human evaluation on this full benchmark is supplied.

The construction counts check: \[2(183)(6)(5)+2(91)(2)(5)=10{,}980+1{,}820=12{,}800.\] Adding one non-rulebreaker per rulebreaker gives 25,600 instances. If the reported 20-city exclusion removes precisely the stated geographical instances, there remain 11,600 instance pairs, or 232,000 individual prompts after ten phrasings. These are deductions from the described design, not a count of the unacquired CSV.

Equation reference: bounds. Let \(R,N\) denote correctness indicators on the two members of a pair. The paired score is \(\tau=\Pr(R=N=1)\); hence \[
 \max(0,\tau_R+\tau_N-1)\leq\tau\leq\min(\tau_R,\tau_N).\] All 28 condition/model triplets in Table 8 and the six complete triplets in Table 10 satisfy these bounds, allowing two-decimal rounding. A constant positive or negative answer gives paired accuracy zero; independent fair binary guesses give \(1/4\), as stated. More generally, independent guesses with positive-answer probability \(q\) give \(q(1-q)\leq1/4\). These properties substantiate the metric’s intended protection against a constant answer preference, not against all possible confounding.

Table 8’s reported Gemma gain is \(31.27-7.14=24.13\) percentage points. Table 10 shows CoT increasing GPT-3.5 paired accuracy from 50.80 to 65.36, a 14.56-point gain, whereas the two evaluated symbolic pipelines reduce it. Accordingly, the evidence should remain specific to those methods and configurations; it does not establish that every reasoning enhancement lowers paired accuracy. The paper does acknowledge heterogeneous responses and several counterexamples to its familiarity and attention hypotheses.
# Confirmed local findings
Problem 1 (The symbolic conclusion in Figure 1 has the wrong polarity).  The upper example on PDF page 1 shows “A or B” and “Not B” on the left, with “Not A” on the right.

Under the propositional interpretation used in the caption and surrounding text, set \(A\) true and \(B\) false. Both premises are true and the displayed conclusion \(\neg A\) is false. In fact, the only truth assignment satisfying the premises has \(A\) true, so the correct symbolic conclusion is \(A\). This calculation was independently enumerated. The lower natural-language panel’s conclusion, “Anne is in Stockholm”, also corresponds to \(A\), not \(\neg A\).

The body text on page 1 and the formal rule in Table 1/page 4 give the correct disjunctive syllogism. This counterevidence strongly favors an isolated diagram-label mistake over a mistaken experimental rule. The caption presents the top panel as rule application; if it were intended as a deliberately erroneous model output, that distinction would need to be stated. The supported assessment is Minor, confined to Figure 1. Changing the green conclusion bubble to “A” aligns it with the valid rule and the surrounding explanation. No dataset or model-result error follows from this label error.

Problem 2 (The reported minimum accuracy in appendix H disagrees with Table 8).  On page 23, the alternative-phrasing-plus-prefixed-premises result is described as ranging from 31.27 (Gemma) to 69.12 (Llama-3-8B).

The paired-accuracy column for that condition in Table 8, page 24, is \[(28.72,44.66,69.12,56.19,40.09,31.27,31.92)\%.\] Its minimum is 28.72% for Phi-3-mini, not 31.27%. The correct range is therefore 28.72–69.12%, assuming the table is authoritative. The prose refers to all models and gives no restriction excluding Phi-3-mini. The error is Minor: it misidentifies the lowest-scoring model under this condition, while preserving the broader observation that the prompt change does not yield uniformly high performance. The raw observations were unavailable, so this is an internal prose–table inconsistency, not proof of which original measurement is correct.
# Unresolved inferential checks
## The city, rather than each duplicated score, is an essential dependence unit

Section 6, Table 3, page 8, defines familiarity by one first-country-token probability per city, then compares familiarity between correctly and incorrectly answered prompt pairs and reports Welch-test significance. Footnote 19 states that each city occurs in 600 pairs. Thus, if \(f_c\) is its familiarity and \(z_{cj}\) is correctness of pair \(j\), the reported means have the form \[\overline f_{+}=\frac{\sum_c\sum_j z_{cj} f_c}{\sum_c\sum_j z_{cj}},\qquad
 \overline f_{-}=\frac{\sum_c\sum_j (1-z_{cj}) f_c}{\sum_c\sum_j(1-z_{cj})}.\] These are valid descriptive, prompt-weighted means. They are not two samples of independent city-familiarity observations: identical \(f_c\) values recur, and a city can contribute to both groups. Unequal-variance Welch formulas alone do not address that dependence.

An independent synthetic calculation isolates the problem without claiming to recreate the authors’ data. Four city scores \((0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0)\) in one group and four \((0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9)\) in the other give Welch \(t=1.0954\) and two-sided \(p=0.3153\). Repeating every value 600 times leaves the mean difference at 0.1 but makes a naive observation-level Welch calculation give \(t=30.9774\) and \(p\simeq3.12\times10^{-192}\). No new independent information was added. This demonstrates the failure of treating repeats as independent, not that Table 3’s actual association is absent.

The paper does not provide test sample sizes, degrees of freedom, or a city-cluster procedure, and the inspected public tree supplies no analysis implementation. An unreported city-level or cluster-aware calculation could resolve the concern. Consequently this remains an unresolved evidence gap, not a confirmed claim that the authors executed the naive test or that their corrected \(p\) values would be nonsignificant. A suitable reanalysis would preserve all variants of a city together, state the target population and weighting, and use an appropriate city-level model or cluster resampling. The same audit is needed before interpreting the accuracy confidence intervals as generalization uncertainty; their construction is not specified here.
## Other limits on interpretation

The confidence means in equations (5)–(6) condition on the model giving a positive answer, selecting different subsets. They are not an unconditional within-pair discrimination statistic. The first-token familiarity score is a proxy for full country knowledge, not the probability of the full country name. Without token mappings and probabilities, neither proxy’s calibration was verified. Attention ratios and neuron activation counts are observational, model-aggregated summaries; the available analysis does not isolate a causal mechanism. Appendix N sums positive activations over token positions, so differing prompt lengths can affect the counts. No claim that this explains the observed curves was established.

Appendix A reports an informal annotation and cites small prior human studies (Table 5); it does not provide a human baseline for this dataset’s full range of verbs and phrasings. This restricts generalizations about actual human behavior but does not by itself falsify the defined task. The prompt variants, generated-conclusion task, and explicit knowledge reminders in appendices H–I are useful counterevidence against attributing all behavior merely to one wording. The unparsed response categories are disclosed rather than silently labeled as correct. Parser behavior, output-length effects, labels for every generated example, symbolic-solver execution, and the cited studies themselves remain unverified at the raw-data level.
# Conclusion

The two established defects warrant a Minor assessment and bounded corrections. The main score definitions and checked numerical relationships survive. The familiarity significance requires clarification or grouped reanalysis, but the evidence available here does not support a Major scientific allegation or a claim that historical experiments were corrupted. Later corrections and author adoption are unknown. This initial review is pending adjudication and is not independent acceptance.

report: Abstract: The paper’s finite-penalty stochastic optimal controller and its training distribution do not describe the same stochastic process. A one-dimensional example gives true variance \(3/8\) where the stated marginal has variance \(1/4\); a second admissible example makes the claimed transition innovation variance negative. This invalidates a central derivation of the finite-penalty framework and warrants Major revision. The deterministic mean and the infinite-penalty bridge limit survive these checks. A separate printed reverse-update sign and scale inconsistency is Minor because the inspected implementation uses the consistent noise convention. Empirical image-quality results were not reproduced. This is an initial review; adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of UniDB
# Paper and evidence scope

The reviewed work is Kaizhen Zhu, Mokai Pan, Yuexin Ma, Yanwei Fu, Jingyi Yu, Jingya Wang, and Ye Shi, UniDB: A Unified Diffusion Bridge Framework via Stochastic Optimal Control, ICML 2025, I25-43713 (0344) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. All 28 proceedings-PDF pages, including appendices A.1–A.9, B and C, were read. All ten original figures and relevant equation/table pages were visually inspected. Page numbers below refer to one-based PDF pages. The original SHA-256 is

The author repository was inspected at commit (14 August 2026). Static reading covered the complete SDE utility, denoising model, matching loss, super-resolution train/test scripts, corresponding differences for deraining/inpainting, selected configuration files, paired-data loading, image conversion and PSNR/SSIM routines. The README supplies a GOU implementation; no released VE/VP implementation was inspected. The acquired source packet contains 45 files, all verified against its manifest. No author code, model, data download, training or inference was run. Independent computations use only reviewer-written scalar formulas and symbolic identities.
# What survives the mathematical checks

Write \(y\) for the prescribed target, \(F_t=\int_0^t f_s\,ds\), \(G_t^2=\int_0^t e^{-2F_s}g_s^2\,ds\), and \[d_t=\gamma^{-1}+e^{2F_T}(G_T^2-G_t^2).\] For deterministic scalar coefficients, positive finite \(\gamma\), and the additive linear diffusion in (11), the feedback in (13) is the usual linear-quadratic control. Its deterministic trajectory (14) also gives the controlled stochastic mean. Certainty equivalence justifies this feedback relation; it does not remove the covariance generated by the Brownian forcing.

As \(\gamma\to\infty\) and for \(t<T\) with nondegenerate remaining noise, the Gaussian transition-density gradient gives the controller in Theorem 4.2. The reviewed counterexamples below do not refute that limit. Proposition 4.3 concerns the deterministic objective (12). A lower optimized objective with a softer terminal penalty is compatible with nonzero terminal mismatch. For example, \(f=h=0\), \(g=T=1\), \(x_0=0\), \(y=1\) gives constant optimal deterministic control \(u=\gamma/(1+\gamma)\) and cost \(\gamma/[2(1+\gamma)]\), compared with hard-constraint energy \(1/2\). This cost comparison by itself does not prove superior perceptual image quality.
# Major issue: finite-penalty marginals and transitions

Problem 1 (The training variance is incompatible with the controlled SDE).  Section 4.3, equation (18), and appendix A.4 (pages 5 and 17) combine the finite-\(\gamma\) mean with a hard-bridge variance that does not depend on \(\gamma\).

Equation reference: case, actual. Take a scalar instance satisfying the stated linear, additive-noise and positive-penalty setting: \[
 f=h=0,\qquad g=1,\quad T=\gamma=1,\quad x_0=0,\quad y=1.\] Substitution into (13) and (11) yields \[dX_t=\frac{1-X_t}{2-t}\,dt+dW_t,\qquad X_0=0.\] Its mean and variance satisfy \[\mu'_t=\frac{1-\mu_t}{2-t},\qquad
 v'_t=-\frac{2v_t}{2-t}+1,\qquad \mu_0=v_0=0,\] and hence \[
 \mu_t=t/2,\qquad v_t=t(2-t)/2.\] Equation (18) has this same mean, but \(v_t^{\rm paper}=t(1-t)\). At \(t=1/2\) these variances are \(3/8\) and \(1/4\), respectively. At \(T=1\) the true variance is \(1/2\) while the printed variance is zero. The disagreement therefore exists in the interior and is not solely a convention at a singular endpoint. Symbolic substitution verifies both moment ODEs in [actual] (#actual); substituting the printed variance into the variance ODE gives a nonzero residual.

Equation reference: cov. More generally, integrating the fundamental solution \(e^{F_t}d_t/d_0\) gives the actual conditional-on-\(x_0,y\) covariance \[
 \operatorname{Var}(X_t\mid x_0,y)
 =e^{2F_t}G_t^2\frac{d_t}{d_0}\,I.\] The target \(y\) here is a fixed parameter of the feedback, not an additional hard conditioning event \(X_T=y\). At infinite penalty [cov] (#cov) reduces to the hard-bridge expression. At finite penalty it generally does not.

Appendix A.4 applies Bayes’ formula to the uncontrolled Gaussian transitions (57). That computes a process conditioned to hit its endpoint exactly. Its mean must then also be the hard-conditioned mean. Keeping the soft-control mean while importing the hard-conditioned variance is not a derivation of the law of (11)/(13). The paper explicitly invokes stochastic interpolants to introduce a vanishing-endpoint noise term. Such an interpolant can be defined in its own right, but its compatible drift and joint transitions must be derived; it is not automatically the controlled SDE or its reverse (15).
## The claimed transition can have negative variance

Appendix A.5, equation (63), further assumes that the marginal construction admits a Gaussian Markov transition with innovation variance \[q_{s,t}=v_t^{\rm paper}-v_s^{\rm paper}(a_t/a_s)^2,
 \qquad a_t=e^{F_t}d_t.\] Choose \(f=h=0\), \(g=1\), \(T=10\), \(\gamma=1/10\), \(s=8\) and \(t=9\). These are ordinary interior, unit-spaced times with a strictly positive finite penalty. Here \[a_t/a_s=11/12,\quad v_s^{\rm paper}=8/5,\quad
 v_t^{\rm paper}=9/10,
 \qquad q_{s,t}=\frac9{10}-\frac85\left(\frac{11}{12}\right)^2=-\frac49.\] No real Gaussian innovation has this variance. Thus interpreting (18) as an arbitrary interpolant alone does not rescue the specific joint construction and posterior mean used in (19). The issue is a failed central training derivation, not merely a small error in a terminal approximation.
## Terminal-distribution interpretation and scope

For the GOU specialization, let \(S=\lambda^2(1-e^{-2\bar\theta_T})\). The finite-control terminal variance is \(S/(1+\gamma S)\). Proposition 4.5, equation (23), accounts only for squared mean displacement. Under \(\theta=\lambda=\gamma=T=1\) and \(x_0=y=0\), its right-hand side is zero, whereas the actual stochastic terminal mean-square error is \[\mathbb E|X_T-y|^2=\frac{1-e^{-2}}{2-e^{-2}}\simeq0.46371.\] For this point target the same quantity is the squared \(W_2\) distance. Equation (23) remains a valid statement about the deterministic mean. Its use in Figure 4 as a full controlled-terminal distribution distance requires correction. This is a downstream manifestation of the same covariance problem, not a separate Major finding.

The released uses a \(\gamma\)-independent standard deviation at lines 143–146 and 227–228, a \(\gamma\)-dependent mean at 190–194, the innovation square root at 202–203, and these together to generate training states at 363–375. The code therefore corroborates the hybrid construction in the inspected version. However, training samples \(t\in\{1,\ldots,99\}\), and the supplied configurations use \(\gamma^{-1}=10^{-7}\) or \(10^{-8}\). An independent evaluation of their scalar schedule gives strictly positive innovations at those sampled times (minimum about \(4.88\times10^{-6}\)). The negative endpoint innovation is excluded from training; sampling also special-cases \(t=100\). Consequently, the broad counterexample is not evidence that these default runs produced NaNs or that reported image scores are wrong. No historical-run correspondence is established.

The assessment is Major: the connection from finite-penalty SOC to the training process is a central contribution, and the claimed transition derivation fails under its own admissible parameters. Repair requires choosing a consistent process: use [cov] (#cov) and rederive transition targets, endpoint initialization and reverse sampling, or explicitly develop a different interpolant with a compatible drift and joint law. Either repair needs new analysis; empirical performance of a repaired implementation remains untested.
# Minor issue: printed reverse-noise convention

Problem 2 (Equations and pseudocode disagree with the declared score parametrization).  Equation (19) and appendix A.5 use a positive noise-prediction term after specifying the score as \(-\epsilon_\theta/\bar\sigma'_t\). Algorithms 1 and 2 additionally divide by \((\bar\sigma'_t)^2\).

Let \(b_t=f_tx_t+h_tm+g_tu^*_{t,\gamma}\). Equation (15) and a backward time step \(\Delta>0\) give \[\mathbb E[X_{t-\Delta}\mid X_t=x]
 \simeq x-\Delta b_t+\Delta g_t^2\nabla_x\log p_t(x)
 =x-\Delta b_t-\Delta\frac{g_t^2}{\bar\sigma'_t}\epsilon_\theta.\] At unit step, the printed equation (19) instead adds \(g_t^2\epsilon_\theta/\bar\sigma'_t\). Equation (66), page 19, exhibits the sign change when substituting the declared score. Algorithms 1 and 2, page 6, visibly use \(+g_t^2\epsilon_\theta/(\bar\sigma'_t)^2\). For \(g=1\), \(\bar\sigma'=1/2\), \(\epsilon_\theta=1\), the score contributions are respectively \(-2\), \(+2\), and \(+4\). A reversed definition of predicted noise could change a sign, but it would contradict the explicit score parametrization and would not by itself repair the extra denominator power.

The released implementation is important counterevidence. Lines 274–276 set ; lines 254–269 subtract \(g^2\) times that score inside the drift; lines 37–38 subtract that drift. Sampling follows the same sign and standard-deviation convention (322–345). The denoising model calls these functions at 134–140. Hence this verified defect is Minor, confined to the printed equations/pseudocode relative to their declared convention. Correct the sign, divide by the standard deviation, and state the time-step factors consistently. It is not a demonstrated wrong-sign implementation or an explanation of historical results.
# Empirical evidence and remaining limits

Tables 1–6, the hyperparameter study, implementation details and all qualitative panels were examined. Table 1’s super-resolution SDE comparison improves LPIPS from 0.220 to 0.179 and FID from 20.85 to 16.21 while reducing PSNR from 26.89 to 25.46 and SSIM from 0.7478 to 0.6856. The paper explicitly prioritizes perceptual scores in section 5.3. These data support a reported tradeoff rather than uniform metric dominance. The observed panels show the claimed local texture/sharpness differences, but visual inspection cannot certify the benchmark values or the causal SOC explanation.

The released configurations specify 900,000 iterations while appendix B says 1.2 million, and the shared matching loss is unweighted L1. These release-versus-description differences are recorded as reproducibility limits, not evidence that the published experiments used the wrong budget or objective. Training logs, checkpoints, raw results, FID feature computation and sampling variability were not available in the reviewed packet. Network internals and data utilities beyond the listed paths were not exhaustively audited. The review does not establish statistical significance or reproduce any image metric.

The two confirmed findings require different responses: a coherent replacement derivation for the finite-penalty stochastic process, and local corrections to the printed reverse-update convention. The hard-bridge limit, the deterministic mean calculation, and the reported empirical measurements are not refuted by the supplied counterexamples. Final scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.

report: Abstract: The proposed demonstration score has encouraging reported empirical results, but its claimed theoretical guarantee is not established for the stated in-context-learning setting. The proof requires an unstated cross-sample gradient condition, and its identification of an additive attention update with loss minimization has the wrong direction under the declared gradient convention. Exact scalar examples expose both gaps. These are central theoretical defects and warrant Major revision. Three bounded Minor findings concern a released matrix transpose, contradictory ranking prose, and an inaccurate case-study summary. All 14 physical PDF pages and six figures were inspected, with complete static reading of the two-file public release. No author code or LLM inference was run. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of LMS3
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Jiayu Liu, Zhenya Huang, Chaokun Wang, Xunpeng Huang, ChengXiang Zhai, and Enhong Chen, What Makes In-context Learning Effective for Mathematical Reasoning, ICML 2025, I25-43714 (0345) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The source PDF SHA-256 is

All 14 pages, including appendices A–E, were read; references use physical PDF page numbers, which match the printed numbering. All six original figures, the theorem pages, algorithm and numerical tables were visually inspected. An initial text extraction incorrectly treated embedded chart-font form-feed characters as page boundaries. This was detected, preserved in the evidence record, and corrected by extracting each physical PDF page explicitly.

The pinned author repository [Retained latex: \cite{code}] at commit , dated 26 May 2025, contains and ; both were read completely. Seven acquired packet files were hash-verified. The released script constructs prompts; experimental generations, evaluation scripts, run logs, full model configurations and outputs were not provided in this packet. No correspondence between this snapshot and any historical run is assumed.
# The theoretical claim and its dependency

Equation reference: plus, influence. The paper replaces softmax attention with the linearized expression (3), writes its self contribution as \(W_0h_{\rm test}\), and identifies the demonstration contribution with \[
 \Delta W=\nabla_F L(z_0,W_0)z_0^\top,
 \qquad \nabla_F L(z_0,W_0)=\frac{W_Vh}{\sqrt d}.\] It then studies a different object: the minimizer \(\widehat W_{\epsilon,z_0}\) of pretraining loss plus \(\epsilon L(z_0,W)\), where \(\widehat W=W_0\). For a differentiable local minimizer and positive-definite Hessian \(H\), the influence identity \[
 \left.\frac{d\widehat W_{\epsilon,z_0}}{d\epsilon}\right|_0
 =-H^{-1}\nabla_W L(z_0,W_0)\] has the familiar negative sign. Positive alignment of test and demonstration gradients under \(H^{-1}\) gives a negative derivative of the surrogate retrained test loss. Transferring this fact to the additive update [plus] (#plus), and to a full LLM, requires additional reasoning that is not supplied.

Problem 1 (The central loss-decrease guarantee is not justified in the stated setting).  Theorem 1 and its proof, equations (11)–(12) on page 4 and (33)–(34) on page 12, use within-loss smoothness as a bound between gradients from different labeled samples. Equations (3)–(9) also identify incompatible parameter updates.
## An explicit supervised-loss counterexample

Equation reference: missing. The notation section says that labels are omitted for brevity. Under this ordinary supervised reading, Lipschitz continuity of \(
abla_F\ell_y(F)\) in \(F\), for each label \(y\), does not imply \[
 \|
abla_F\ell_{y_t}(Wh_t)-
abla_F\ell_{y_0}(Wz_0)\|
 \leq\mu\|W(h_t-z_0)\|.\] There is an uncontrolled label-dependent term. Take scalar squared loss \(\ell_y(F)=	frac12(F-y)^2\) and \[d=d'=1,\quad h_t=h=W_K=W_V=1,\quad z_0=1,
 \quad y_0=0,\quad y_t=2.\] Let the pretraining set have \(n\) copies of input \(2\) and label \(2\). Its average loss is \(	frac12(2W-2)^2\), so \(\widehat W=1=W_0\) as required by (4), and \(H=4>0\). Each output-loss gradient is globally 1-Lipschitz. The demonstration satisfies (5), since \(
abla_F\ell_0(1)=1=W_Vh/\sqrt d\).

The two gradients with respect to \(W\) are \(g_t=-1\) and \(g_0=1\). The eigenvalue ratio in (7) is one. Its left side is \(1\), while its right side is zero because \(h_t=z_0\). Thus its strict sufficient condition holds. Nevertheless, \[\widehat W_{\epsilon,z_0}=\frac4{4+\epsilon}<1,
 \qquad \ell_2(\widehat W_{\epsilon,z_0})>\ell_2(1)=\frac12
 \quad(\epsilon>0).\] For \(n=1000\), \(\epsilon=1/n\), the exact new loss is \(8008002/16008001\), an increase of approximately \(0.00024997\). The derivative at zero is \(+1/4\), so making the upweighting arbitrarily small does not help. The failed step [missing] (#missing) tries to bound \(2\) by zero.

Distinct labeled problems are not assumed to have injective representations in the paper. This example uses the permitted coincidence of representations, not contradictory labels for one stipulated deterministic mathematical problem. If the intended theorem instead assumes one common, label-independent loss function or explicitly assumes the cross-sample bound [missing] (#missing), this particular example is excluded. That would be a materially narrower hypothesis than ordinary per-label smoothness and must be stated and justified for the reasoning task.
## A separate failure even with identical test and demonstration labels

Set the test label to zero in the preceding construction and leave everything else unchanged. The theorem condition still holds. The surrogate minimizer now does reduce the test loss, so this variant is not a counterexample to that surrogate conclusion. However, equation (3) has zero-shot output \(1\) and one-shot linear-attention output \(1+1=2\). Its squared test loss rises from \(1/2\) to \(2\).

This directly refutes the claimed identification of the two procedures inside the paper’s own linearized model. Under (5), the attention increment is a positive gradient outer product; [influence] (#influence) is a negative Hessian-preconditioned increment. Calling the former a conceptual analogy does not make their loss changes equal. Reversing the loss-gradient convention would also require changing (5) and the influence calculation. Moreover, no approximation error bound connects softmax attention (2), linear attention (3), contextual representations and the final answer loss.

The proof’s first-order Taylor step (9)/(30) also supplies no remainder bound ensuring that the particular finite choice \(\epsilon=1/|D_{\rm pre}|\) stays in a loss-decreasing neighborhood. A valid negative derivative establishes a sufficiently small neighborhood under regularity, not an unquantified universal finite-step guarantee. This is an additional proof-scope limitation; the two exact examples above do not rely on it.
## Rejection does not follow from a sufficient condition

Page 5 states that examples failing the condition will have a negative effect. Theorems 1 and 2 are presented as sufficient conditions, not necessary ones. Even in the retraining surrogate with a shared zero-label squared loss, put \(h=3\), \(h_t=W_K=W_V=1\) and keep the same pretraining objective. Equation (5) holds, \(C_1=1\), and (7) reads \(1>8\), which fails. Yet \(\widehat W_\epsilon=4/(4+9\epsilon)\) reduces test loss for every \(\epsilon>0\). Failure of the bound therefore cannot establish harmfulness. Replacing unknown absolute quantities by a percentile threshold, as LMS3 does, is a practical heuristic that needs empirical validation.

The assessment of Problem 1 is Major. It affects the advertised theoretical explanation and guarantee, not a peripheral presentation detail. A defensible repair must state the required loss/label regularity, derive the loss change for the actual attention update or explicitly limit the theorem to retraining, control finite-step/approximation errors where a guarantee is claimed, and describe rejection as a heuristic unless a separate necessity result is established. This review does not supply or certify such a replacement theorem. The empirical success of the score is not refuted by these examples.
# Bounded implementation and presentation findings
Problem 2 (The released selection transform has an extra transpose).  Equation (21) uses \(W_K^\top W_Qh\), but the inspected script computes a different matrix product.

Let \(K\) denote the square key-projection matrix after the head expansion at , and let \(Q\) denote . Line 52 assigns \(=K^\top\). Line 101 then evaluates , which is \(KQh\), rather than \(K^\top Qh\). This is a literal discrepancy with (21), independent of whether (21) itself is an adequate attention-derived score.

For an independent two-dimensional illustration, take \[K=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad Q=V=I,
 \quad h_t=(1,2)^\top,\quad h_1=(1,0)^\top,\ h_2=(0,1)^\top.\] The intended distances are \((0,\sqrt2)\) and the released-product distances are \((2,\sqrt2)\). The stability factors are equal, so the selected candidate reverses. A symmetric \(K\) would hide the defect, but no symmetry constraint is specified. This is Minor, scoped to the pinned release and its agreement with the written algorithm; the local repair removes one transpose after confirming the projection convention. No real Llama activations, weights or experiments were executed, and the amount or direction of benchmark impact is unknown.

The same static read identifies additional scope differences: lines 124–129 encode only the question field, while the paper says the whole demonstration reasoning path is included. Solutions are added to the final prompt at lines 170, 194 and 218, after selection. The representation routine truncates to 128 tokens (76–77). Thus the release does not implement a selection score over the full question-and-solution text as described. These observations should be reconciled with the exact experimental version; they do not establish what historical runs encoded.
Problem 3 (The ranking direction in section 4 contradicts the algorithm).  Page 5 twice describes selecting the highest product scores, although the score is a product of quantities to minimize.

Algorithm 1, page 13, selects the smallest scores. The release likewise uses ascending and takes its first \(k\) indices (134–136). For two candidate scores 1 and 2, these two instructions choose different candidates. The surrounding minimization discussion, pseudocode and code agree on the smaller value. The correction is to replace “highest” by “smallest” in the prose. This is Minor; no reversed ranking in the inspected implementation is alleged.

Problem 4 (Appendix D incorrectly summarizes the first two cases).  Page 13 says both OpenAI and Best-validate made errors in cases 1 and 2. Figure 6 explicitly shows one of these baselines correct in each case.

In case 1, the line through \((7,8)\) and \((9,0)\) has slope \(-4\) and intercept \(36\), giving sum \(32\). Best-validate and LMS3 both return \(32\) and both have green check marks. In case 2, \((x-y)(x+y)=-2y^2+1\) simplifies to \(x^2+y^2=1\). OpenAI and LMS3 both return the correct circle label C, again with green checks. Thus this is a confirmed error in the textual summary, not in those figure labels. Case 3’s total \(8+16+19+8=51\) and depicted rejection remain consistent. The correction is local and Minor; it weakens the particular case-study contrast, not the aggregate tables.
# Empirical checks and limits

The six LMS3-versus-zero-shot gains in Table 2 are 1.9, 3.3, 2.8, 1.5, 1.7 and 2.9 percentage points. All 30 paired entries in Table 3 improve after adding the rejection mechanism, by 0.1–2.0 points. These arithmetic checks support the reported directions. Table 4 explicitly shows GPT-4/MATH dropping from 0.758 to 0.752, which the paper acknowledges; a universal improvement claim should remain limited to the specified main backbones/settings.

Figure 3’s few-shot trends, Figure 5’s threshold dependence, and all case-study panels were actually viewed. Table 2 marks five of six LMS3 entries with significance stars, while the prose speaks broadly of significance; the Llama3/MAWPS entry has no star. The number of repetitions, precise statistical test, paired observations and meaning of the uncertainty terms are not specified sufficiently here to recalculate the stated \(p\) values. This is an unresolved validation limit, not a finding of a particular failed significance test.

Figure 4 is described as z-score-normalized while displaying distributions on a 0–1 axis and comparing variances. Per-distribution z-scoring fixes variance, whereas a shared normalization or another transform could preserve relative variance. The precise plotting transform and raw scores are unavailable, so no specific normalization implementation is inferred. The claim of \(O(M+N)\) complexity is explicitly measured in LLM calls; it should not be read as total pairwise scoring time, which the released script computes over \(MN\) pairs.

The full static release, all mathematical arguments in the packet, and selected exact arithmetic were checked. No LLM prediction, tokenizer-specific truncation rate, benchmark replication, significance analysis, contamination audit or historical-run reconstruction was performed. The theoretical guarantee requires substantial repair, while the reported empirical improvements remain evidence to be independently evaluated. Human review and independent acceptance are pending.
