report: Abstract: The hierarchical matching approach has a plausible repair path preserving its headline asymptotic tradeoff, but the published augmentation construction, its local complexity, and several update instructions require correction. The released implementation supplies useful counterevidence to a claim of a broken matching engine: it uses directed residual transitions and records actual point distances. Its deletion timing, however, is stale. The augmentation specification and the update invariant are Major defects in the published proof of the main dynamic theorem. The crossing calculation and released timing instrumentation remain bounded Minor findings. A repair may preserve the headline theorem, but it is not supplied by the published argument. The lower bound must state the representation and recourse model it needs. All 25 physical PDF pages and all five original figures were inspected, together with the complete small source release. Only reviewer-written finite checks were executed. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of Fully Dynamic Euclidean Bi-Chromatic Matching in Sublinear Update Time
# Identity, sources, and coverage

The reviewed paper is Gramoz Goranci, Peter Kiss, Neel Patel, Martin P. Seybold, Eva Szilagyi, and David Zheng, Fully Dynamic Euclidean Bi-Chromatic Matching in Sublinear Update Time, ICML 2025, I25-43715 (0346) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The frozen PDF SHA-256 is

The complete 25-page paper, including appendices A–F, was read. Locations below are physical PDF pages. Figures 1–5 and the relevant proof and pseudocode pages were actually viewed. All 14 acquired packet files passed their frozen manifest hashes.

The author repository [Retained latex: \cite{code}] was read at commit , dated 21 November 2025: all 747 lines of , the three input-generator scripts, README, build script and CMake file. This later public snapshot is not assumed to be the version that produced the paper’s experiments. No author program, build, benchmark, or data generator was run.
# The algorithmic argument and checks that survive

Each cell matches a balanced subset of the points forwarded by its children and forwards a monochromatic excess set. At leaves the matching is exact. Internal cells aggregate excess points to at most \(p^2\) child centers, solve transportation there, and expand the assignment to actual points. The random-shift analysis charges cross-cell edges of an optimal matching at each level; \(\log_p U=O(1/\epsilon)\) for polynomial spread and the chosen \(p\).

The static theorem’s high-probability wording is not, by itself, an error. Appendix C, page 14, explicitly repeats independent shifts \(O(\log n)\) times and selects a minimum-cost solution. The exponent slack in \(p=n^{\epsilon/10}\) can absorb this amplification for fixed \(\epsilon\). The dynamic theorem states an expectation. A guarantee against an adaptive adversary that observes the shift or output is not established by the fixed-instance crossing calculation; this scope should be explicit.

Claims E.1–E.2 contain the standard optimal-matching extension idea. For an optimal old matching, a shortest alternating augmenting path produces an optimal extension: the other components of the symmetric difference are nonnegative-cost alternating cycles. Deleting matched pairs leaves an optimal restriction on the remaining endpoints, so the proposed removal-and-reinsertion reduction is reasonable when its distinct-endpoint cases are handled. Independent enumeration of 100 instances with zero to four old pairs confirmed the cost identity for the corrected directed residual network, to numerical error below \(10^{-9}\). These small tests support that repair; they do not prove all dynamic invariants or runtime bounds.
# Confirmed corrections

Problem 1 (The written augmentation graph and its complexity are incorrect).  Appendix E.1, page 21 (the lemma heading prints A.4, while the surrounding text and page 22 refer to E.4), does not specify a valid residual network as written, and its \(O(p^3)\) bound in Lemma E.4 does not follow from the graph it constructs.

First, the new vertices \(x',y'\) are connected only to old opposite-color centers. Their direct edge is missing. With an empty old matching, two newly inserted opposite-color points must be matched to each other, but the specified graph has no \(x'\)–\(y'\) path. This case is allowed by the lemma and arises naturally when a cell first obtains both colors.

Second, a single undirected signed edge per pair of centers does not enforce alternating paths. A transportation residual network needs forward red-to-blue arcs of positive distance and reverse blue-to-red arcs, of negative distance, wherever positive flow can be removed. The forward capacity is not lost merely because the same center pair already carries some flow. The text instead assigns either a positive or negative weight according to whether the pair is used. Interpreting an undirected negative edge as two directed arcs also creates a negative two-cycle. The endpoint paragraph additionally copies \(x'\) where \(y'\) is intended.

Third, with \(k=p^2\) centers and half of each color, the constructed complete bipartite graph has \[|V|=\Theta(p^2),\qquad |E|=\Theta(p^4).\] Explicit construction alone can take \(\Theta(p^4)\), and the quoted Bellman–Ford bound is \(O(p^6)\), not \(O(p^3)\). For example, \(p=16\) gives 256 centers and 16,384 old bipartite edges, already exceeding \(p^3=4096\).

These defects are Major because the proof of Theorem 1.1 on physical page 22 explicitly invokes this augmentation routine for its update time and correctness. The empty-state example invalidates the specified subroutine on an admitted state, and the stated graph counts invalidate its cited runtime derivation. The intended directed residual algorithm is a credible repair, and the headline exponent might survive: \(p^6=n^{0.6\epsilon}\) for the stated \(p\), while even an \(O(p^2)\)-node rebuild has exponent below the reserved \(p^{10}\) scale. That slack does not validate the present lemma. A replacement network, proof of its augmentation property, and complete update/rebuild accounting are required. Neither the existence of an algorithm with the headline tradeoff nor the inspected implementation is refuted by this finding.

The inspected C++ is counterevidence to a broader accusation. Lines 313–350 use directed positive forward transitions and negative backward transitions along matched edges. An opposite-color exposed point is a candidate destination, including the direct new-pair case. Lines 357–408 recover the alternating path. Thus the literal missing-edge/direction defect in the paper is not established in this implementation.
Problem 2 (The printed update pseudocode violates its excess invariant).  Algorithms 1, 3 and 5 on pages 18–19 and 23 require coordinated corrections, rather than literal implementation.

For Algorithm 5, take a non-marginal leaf containing one blue point and no red points. Insert one red point. Line 41 recomputes the imbalance as zero; the \(\eta\geq0\) branch then adds the red point to the old blue excess set without matching them. A balanced leaf is left with a bichromatic excess set and no match. This contradicts the invariant used in Appendix D.2. If the intended branch uses the old imbalance, the other branch still uses \(E_v\leftarrow E_v\cup\{b\}\) at line 47, where removal is needed after matching \(b\).

Algorithm 1 decreases the imbalance after inserting red into a blue-excess cell, although \(|A|-|B|\) increases by one. Algorithm 3 recursively calls Insert-Update during deletion. Its leaf case can add the deleted point itself to the excess set. These are explicit specification failures. The repair is to state pre/post-update imbalance consistently, remove points when they are consumed, forward only remaining endpoints, and recurse with the correct operation. The release’s , lines 511–552, follows endpoint changes and calls removal functions instead; no identical implementation failure is inferred. The finding is Major for the published algorithm: the correctness proof of Theorem 1.1 on page 22 assumes precisely the post-update monochromatic-excess property violated by this trace. A local example can be embedded in a globally balanced pair update by placing the other new point in a separate cell. The invariant prose and later code are useful evidence for an intended repair, but they do not prove that the printed procedures preserve the claimed state. Corrected procedures and a case-complete invariant proof are required; this does not establish failure of the later implementation.
Problem 3 (The crossing estimate has the wrong scale factor).  Claim C.6, page 16, divides expected crossings by cell width; the subsequent cost proof needs multiplication.

For a fixed horizontal edge of length \(L\leq\lambda\) under a uniform grid shift of width \(\lambda\), the crossing probability is exactly \(L/\lambda\). Thus its contribution satisfies \[\lambda\,\mathbb E[\operatorname{Cross}]=L,
 \qquad \mathbb E[\operatorname{Cross}]/\lambda=L/\lambda^2.\] The correct upper bound is \(\lambda_\ell\mathbb E[\operatorname{Cross}(\mu^*,\ell)]=O(c(\mu^*))\), using an upper crossing-probability bound. The printed proof instead writes an \(\Omega(L/\lambda)\) probability and says it contributes \(L\). Long edges also require truncating a probability bound at one. Equation (5), page 17, is consistent with the corrected identity.

The bad-point counting in Claim C.3 also needs care: if half of \(B_\ell\) bad points are incident to crossing edges, an edge may have two such endpoints, giving \(B_\ell\leq4\operatorname{Cross}\) from that argument. Each swap eliminates at least two bad points and costs at most \(4\lambda_\ell\), which recovers the stated constant 8. The displayed \(B_\ell\leq\operatorname{Cross}/2\) on page 16 has its relationship reversed. These are Minor local proof errors: the exact uniform-shift upper bound and endpoint accounting above establish the inequality actually used in equation (5), under the same fixed-instance assumptions, with the same expected \(O(1/\epsilon)\) approximation bound. The classification rests on this verified surviving argument, not on the ease of editing the formulas.
Problem 4 (Deletion rows in the released logger reuse an old runtime).  The public snapshot does not measure deletion update time in its reported column.

Insertion assigns inside lines 561–565. Deletion, lines 570–576, never assigns it. The per-operation reset at lines 64–67 resets only changed-edge and iteration counters, and each operation then prints the statistics at line 723. Symbolically, an insertion assigning time 123 followed by any deletion produces another row with time 123, regardless of the deletion duration. If no insertion has set it, the initial value is \(-1\). Also, insertion’s timer starts after point storage and tree traversal in , which is called at line 557 before the timer at line 561, so it measures the recursive matching modification, not the complete exposed insertion operation.

This is a confirmed Minor measurement defect in the release, relevant to reconstructing the fully dynamic benchmark of Figure 5. It does not establish that the historical figure used this logger or has a particular error size. Full-operation timing should bracket both insertion and deletion consistently, and the historical experimental version and raw logs should be supplied. The exact-baseline branch at lines 711–713 is only a TODO in this snapshot; that is a reproduction limit, not evidence that the paper’s separately reported exact baseline was never computed.
# Scope questions and empirical limits

The lower bound in Theorem F.1, pages 24–25, converts \(o(n)\) update time into \(o(n)\) changed edges on some update. That conversion needs an explicit-maintenance or charged-recourse model. On its alternating-line construction, the exact matching can instead be represented by the left endpoint, right endpoint, and the rule “pair consecutive positions from the left.” Each insertion changes two stored endpoints; the exact cost is \(n+i\), and enumerating the full matching later costs \(O(n+i)\). The independent check confirms this rule for the displayed sequence. This does not disprove a general two-dimensional lower bound. It shows why the given proof does not cover unrestricted implicit representations or cost-only queries. Under explicit edge maintenance, the recourse argument is persuasive; the theorem and introductory claim should state that restriction. This is recorded as a model-scope question rather than an unconditional refutation.

Figures 2–5 were checked against their captions and prose. Figure 3 includes exact comparisons only through roughly 2000 samples; Figure 4 extends approximate curves to one million but has no exact comparator. Consequently the less-than-two empirical approximation claim is directly supported only where an exact comparator is available, not certified by visual convergence at a million points. Figure 5 depicts distribution drift and update times, but no repeated-run uncertainty is supplied. The source packet lacks the historical taxi preprocessing, raw benchmark outputs, complete exact-baseline implementation and plotting pipeline. These numerical results were not independently reproduced.

The program’s point manager adds and subtracts actual point distances when matching and unmatching (138–156). Thus the basic algorithm’s center-cost estimate should not be confused with the implementation’s reported total matching cost. The basic prose explicitly describes an estimate on page 6; equality between center cost and expanded matching cost is not assumed in this review.
# Disposition and evidence

Recommendation: Major revision, driven by the invalid augmentation specification and post-update invariant on which the main dynamic theorem relies. The crossing calculation, timing instrumentation, and theorem-scope qualifications also require the bounded corrections stated above. No quota was applied. No conclusion about historical experiment contamination, universal correctness of the implementation, or an adaptive-adversary guarantee is made.

The companion evidence includes physical-page text, source hashes, original-page render hashes, reviewer-written and , claim-level findings and coverage, isolated compilation logs, and actual final-PDF inspection records. Task , token ; selected model , effort . The predecessor is preserved. Focused independent AI verification corrected severity using the actual theorem dependencies and checked the counterevidence; it does not certify a replacement algorithm or historical experiments. Scientific adjudication is pending and human reviews are empty.

report: Abstract: The proposed representation and prototype heuristics may be useful, but their principal causal and generalization guarantees do not follow. The probability-of-sufficiency risk is replaced by a different quantity; the target-risk bound fails by explicit finite counterexamples; the variance-only generalization bound can be negative when the generalization gap is zero; and mutual-information maximization does not imply the claimed exogeneity. These are Major theoretical findings. Separate, version-bounded source defects affect a distributed training path, benchmark defaults, and regularization accounting. They do not establish that the published experiments used these defects. All 22 physical PDF pages, all original figures, and the complete acquired Python release were read or viewed as appropriate. Only reviewer-written checks were run. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of COSDA: Counterfactual-based Susceptibility Risk Framework for Open-Set Domain Adaptation
# Identity and scope

This report concerns Wenxu Wang et al., COSDA: Counterfactual-based Susceptibility Risk Framework for Open-Set Domain Adaptation, ICML 2025, I25-43716 (0347) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The frozen PDF SHA-256 is

All 22 physical pages, including appendices A–D, were read. Page numbers below are physical PDF pages. All eleven original figures and five released t-SNE PDFs were actually viewed. All 28 acquired packet files passed their frozen hashes. The complete 13 Python files and accompanying documentation/configuration were statically read at repository commit , dated 2 October 2026 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. This later snapshot is not presumed to reproduce the historical experimental version. No author code was imported or executed.

COSDA combines a learned feature intervention, Gaussian representations, target pseudo-labels from known and virtual unknown prototypes, and contrastive alignment. The support decomposition in Theorem 1 is a legitimate partition once its risk is defined consistently. The concerns below concern the stronger identification and upper-bound claims, rather than that partition or the existence of a useful empirical classifier.
# The causal risk and target bound

Problem 1 (Major: the risk identity and Theorem 2 are invalid).  Proposition 1, equation (8), and Appendix B.1 replace a ratio by a difference. Theorem 2, equation (10), and Appendix B.3 then give an invalid upper bound even if that difference is adopted as a new surrogate risk.

Let \(p=P(Y=y\mid C=c)\), \(q=P(Y=y\mid C'=c')\), \(a=1-p\), and \(b=1-q\). Under the identification assumptions used by the paper, \(\mathrm{PS}=(p-q)/(1-q)\), so \[1-\mathrm{PS}=\frac{a}{b},\qquad\text{whereas equation (8) uses }D=a-b.\] For \(a=1/5,b=4/5\), these are \(1/4\) and \(-3/5\). Both probabilities are realizable by monotone potential outcomes: take independent uniform \(U\), let correctness under \(c\) be \(\mathbf1\{U<1-a\}\) and under \(c'\) be \(\mathbf1\{U<1-b\}\), and randomize the treatment independently of \(U\). Thus this is not a violation of exogeneity or monotonicity.

There is useful counterevidence to an overly broad objection. For \(0<a\le b\le1\), the weaker inequality \[a/b\le \exp(a-b)\] does hold, since \(\log a-\log b\le a-b\). It could justify a limited surrogate interpretation. However, Appendix B.1’s intermediate bound \(a/b<\exp(a-b-2)\) fails in the example above: \(0.25>0.07427\). More importantly, minimizing the difference need not minimize the true risk. The feasible pairs \((a,b)=(.01,.2)\) and \((.4,.9)\) have differences \(-.19,-.5\) but true risks \(.05,4/9\) respectively. The smaller difference chooses the larger true risk. A corrected statement must distinguish the risk from a surrogate and its possible upper bound.
## Subtracting upper bounds does not upper-bound their difference

Equations (36)–(38), pages 15–16, subtract two upper bounds on joint errors. From \(u\le U\) and \(v\le V\) one cannot infer \(u-v\le U-V\). The sign is central because the intervention error is deliberately subtracted.

For a binary counterexample, let the source have two nuisance states with masses \((1/2,1/2)\) and the target have masses \((.9,.1)\), all with the same known label. Let a deterministic classifier be correct on the observed representation and wrong on the intervened representation at both states. The representation can ignore the nuisance state, so its invariance and monotonic correctness are preserved. Then both disagreements vanish, \(e_S(c)=0\), \(e_S(c')=1\), and \(\beta_\infty=1.8\). Equation (10) claims \(-1\le-1.8\), which is false even after replacing its strict inequality by a weak one.

This is not solely a closed-set boundary issue. Add target-only unknown mass \(.2\) on a new support point, with equal errors before and after intervention; give the old target states masses \(.72,.08\). The unknown difference term is zero, \(\beta_\infty=1.44\), and the claimed inequality becomes \(-.8\le-1.44\). This extension uses the paper’s support-restricted density ratio. A convention making the divergence infinite for every open-set problem would instead render the advertised bound uninformative.
## The Gibbs decomposition is binary-specific

Equation (35) also applies \(R=\tfrac12d+e\) to a multiclass problem. When two voters predict distinct wrong classes, the two error indicators sum to 2, while disagreement plus twice joint error is 3.

The failure can reverse the final inequality without any domain shift. Set \(S=T\), fix true label 0, and choose four equiprobable voters with outputs \[(h_1(c),\ldots,h_4(c))=(0,1,1,1),\qquad
 (h_1(c'),\ldots,h_4(c'))=(1,1,2,2).\] Every voter’s correctness is monotone under this intervention. Direct enumeration gives \[(R,d,e)_c=(3/4,3/8,9/16),\qquad
 (R,d,e)_{c'}=(1,1/2,1).\] The true difference is \(-1/4\), but the right side of equation (10), with \(\beta_\infty=1\) and no unsupported mass, is \(-1/2\). Replicating this construction under cyclic class relabeling supplies all three true classes if desired. A new multiclass decomposition and a valid bound for a signed error difference are needed. The advertised source/target loss justification materially depends on both missing steps; the findings do not by themselves refute measured accuracy.
# The generalization bound and causal assumptions
Problem 2 (Major: Corollary 1 is not a valid high-probability bound).  Equation (14), pages 4–5, asserts a uniform bound by \(-\log\sigma_C+\log\sigma_{C'}\). Appendix B.4 does not establish it.

Take Gaussian representations with standard deviations \(\sigma_C=2\), \(\sigma_{C'}=1\), one fixed true label, and a constant wrong classifier. Observed and intervened errors are both 1; correct-class probabilities are both 0. Consequently the difference risk in equation (8) and its empirical difference in equation (13) are both zero for every sample. Nevertheless the alleged bound is \(-\log2<0\). It fails with probability one, independently of sample size. Monotonicity holds with equality. This also avoids relying on the opposite sign conventions of equations (8) and (13), which must themselves be reconciled.

In the proof, upper bounds are again subtracted. Equation (42), page 17, then replaces \(-\mathrm{KL}(\rho\|\gamma_{C'})\) by \(+\mathrm{KL}(\gamma_{C'}\|\rho)\) as an equality. These are not equal: for \(\rho=N(0,1)\) and \(\gamma_{C'}=N(0,4)\), the forward and reverse KL divergences are approximately \(.318147\) and \(.806853\). Nor does taking the prior variance to infinity yield a finite PAC-Bayes bound: the KL diverges. Dropping a parameter-independent divergent term may motivate an optimization heuristic, but cannot preserve a finite probability guarantee. A repaired result needs a proper prior, correct signs, and sample-size/confidence dependence.

Problem 3 (Major: the stated mutual-information equivalence and monotonicity enforcement do not follow).  Proposition 2, equation (16), and Appendix B.5 identify domain-invariant conditional labels with maximized cross-domain mutual information. Equation (15) is also presented as satisfaction of monotonicity. Neither implication is established.

Let \(Z\) be a fair binary label, and pair source and target features from that label as \(C_s=Z\) and \(C_t=1-Z\). Their mutual information is the maximum possible, one bit. In a pooled population with independent fair domain \(E\), let \(C=Z\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}E\) and \(Y=Z\). Then \(C\perp E\), but \[I(Y;E\mid C)=1\text{ bit},\qquad
 P(Y\mid C,E)\ne P(Y\mid C).\] Thus maximal shared information, even with domain-independent feature marginals and same-label pairing, does not ensure the required conditional invariance. Mutual information is unchanged by invertible domain-specific permutations. This does not show that COSDA’s particular cosine alignment necessarily selects such a permutation; it disproves the claimed equivalence used to justify it.

There is a further definitional issue: conditional on a fixed class and fixed training set, the source centroid \(C_s^k\) is constant, so its literal mutual information with a random target feature is zero. The variables and joint sampling law need to be specified before the displayed expectation of mutual information is meaningful. Equation (44) writes a single event’s log term in place of a full KL/conditional-MI sum, and equation (46)’s claimed “transmissibility” supplies no missing implication.

Likewise, a positive average correctness difference does not exclude individual defiers. A population with \(.6\) responders \((Y_c,Y_{c'})=(1,0)\), \(.1\) defiers \((0,1)\), and \(.3\) never-correct units has \(p-q=.5\), yet violates monotonicity on ten percent of units. With randomized intervention, true sufficiency is \((.6)/(.9)=2/3\), while the formula assuming monotonicity gives \((.6-.1)/(.9)=5/9\). An average objective is not an enforcement mechanism for the pointwise assumption. CFA and VMP can remain useful heuristics; claims that they establish causal identification require additional conditions or weaker wording.
# Static implementation findings and empirical checks
## A conditional target-label leak in the distributed path

In , lines 157–185, the loop runs for the maximum of source and target loader lengths. When the source iterator is exhausted, lines 163–165 reset it to the target loader. Its third output becomes and enters source cross-entropy at line 185 and lines 94–98. The dataset returns the annotation-derived label at , mapping unknown labels to the unknown index.

If the source loader is shorter and the run reaches that branch, target annotations therefore enter the supervised gradient. An independent three-step iterator example, with two source batches and three target batches, confirms the last supervised batch comes from target data. This is a Major protocol defect for an affected distributed experiment. It is conditional on this path and does not prove that any published result is affected. In particular, the README’s adaptation command uses , whose line 142 correctly resets the source loader. The optional true-label contrastive branch defaults off; its existence is not evidence of label leakage in normal non-distributed adaptation. The repair is to reset the source iterator correctly and document the historical command and revision.
## Minor release mismatches requiring reproducibility corrections

The current DomainNet configuration fixes 150 shared and 172 unknown classes at , while Tables 4–5 specify 173/172. Dataset filtering thus retains target class IDs 0–321 rather than all 345 classes, omitting 322–344 and moving the known/unknown boundary. Office-31’s default 10 unknown classes at line 130, combined with the offset in , selects 20–29 rather than the paper’s 20–30; an explicit override to 11 repairs that default. These are confirmed current-configuration differences, not evidence that the historical tables used the wrong split.

Both domains’ loss dictionaries use the same keys and . In the non-distributed loop, source update at line 169 is overwritten by target update at line 207, so the total at line 209 retains only target values, rather than both domains’ regularizers. Distinct keys or explicit summation are needed if Algorithm 1 is intended. Moreover, applies a positive-part entropy threshold to both representations, not equation (14)’s signed log-standard-deviation difference. The implemented cross-entropy surrogate is also not a literal estimator of the disagreement/joint-error expressions. These discrepancies need an explicit algorithm-to-code mapping; replacing the false theorem alone does not document the implemented objective.
## Minor arithmetic and limits of visual evidence

Table 3, page 7, reports an average OS* of 64.6 without \(L_s\), whereas its four entries \(72.9,71.1,51.5,49.8\) average to \(61.325\), or 61.3 at the displayed precision. In Table 8, page 22, the C\(\to\)A OS* improvement over ANNA is \(71.2-48.6=22.6\) percentage points, not the prose’s 20.6. The corresponding UNK and HOS differences, 40.5 and 38.9, agree. These corrections do not reverse those individual improvements.

Figures 1–11, including both Figure 5 sensitivity surfaces and the five released embeddings, were visually inspected. The t-SNE separation is descriptive evidence, not proof of exogeneity. The synthetic graph in Figure 8 is \(Y\to C\to S\); its distance-correlation measurements demonstrate retention of label-associated factors in that generative model, not identification of an intervention effect \(C\to Y\). This is a limit of the proposed causal validation, not an allegation that its plotted measurements are fabricated. The packet does not provide raw run-level uncertainty, a complete historical benchmark record, or synthetic-generation code sufficient to reproduce all these claims. Best-checkpoint selection and correspondence between current training paths and reported tables remain unresolved.
# Disposition and reproducible evidence

Major revision is warranted because the central target-risk, generalization, and causal-identification arguments require replacement. Empirical usefulness can survive these theoretical failures and must be evaluated on its own evidence. The distributed code defect needs correction before that path can support an unsupervised adaptation experiment. Version provenance is essential before attributing it to published results.

The reviewer-owned records exact Gibbs enumeration, density-ratio examples, Gaussian/KL arithmetic, binary conditional mutual information, monotonicity probabilities, a plain-iterator model, loss-dictionary accounting, and table arithmetic in . binds quoted source lines to their file hashes. Source integrity, physical-page coverage, render manifests, actual visual inspection, isolated cached compilation, and report hashes are retained beside this report. No independent acceptance or human review is claimed.

report: Abstract: CED’s conditional statement about an interior stationary point has a sound indifference argument. Its claimed last-iterate convergence proof, however, replaces nonzero response and evaluation errors by exact gradient identities without controlling those errors. An explicit one-state example disproves the asserted gradient/local-maximum argument while leaving convergence itself unresolved. Uniform coverage alone also does not ensure the interior condition. In the pinned public release, the neural trainer lacks the advertised opponent-response update, and the reachable evaluator never applies actions to the environment. These are substantial version-bounded reproduction defects; they do not establish that historical experiments used the same code. All 18 physical pages and nine original figures were examined, with relevant static source and independent calculations. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of Constrained Exploitability Descent: An Offline Reinforcement Learning Method for Finding Mixed-Strategy Nash Equilibrium
# Identity, scope, and positive checks

The paper is Runyu Lu, Yuanheng Zhu, and Dongbin Zhao, Constrained Exploitability Descent: An Offline Reinforcement Learning Method for Finding Mixed-Strategy Nash Equilibrium, ICML 2025, I25-43717 (0348) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The frozen PDF SHA-256 is

All 18 physical pages, including appendices A–D, were read. All nine original figures and relevant algorithm/proof pages were actually viewed. The 22 acquired packet files passed their frozen hashes. Static source inspection used commit , dated 15 July 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. No author program, simulator, network, or training script was executed.

The method evaluates a moving joint policy by Bellman updates, ascends in a constrained max-player policy \(\mu\), and obtains a regularized min-player response \(\nu\) using a fixed behavior-policy value \(Q^{\mu_\beta,\nu_\beta}\). The soft response in Lemma 4.1 is the correct unique solution when the behavior policy has positive support. The policy-gradient identity in Lemma 5.1 and the simplex-tangent subtraction in Lemma 5.5 are consistent with their usual interpretations. Lemma A.1’s ratio bound yields the stated \(L^1\) bound; the ratio should retain its action index inside the final sum, but this does not invalidate the inequality.

Independent exact arithmetic confirms the matrix equilibria \((\mu(1),\nu(1))=(6/7,4/7)\) and \((5/6,1/2)\), the five-action equalizer \((1/9,1/9,1/9,1/3,1/3)\), and the undiscounted tree-root equilibrium \((13/16,9/16)\). The displayed learning curves are compatible with these reference values. None of these checks establishes a general convergence theorem.
# The convergence argument needs replacement

Problem 1 (Major: Theorem 5.2 does not establish the claimed convergence).  The proof on page 5 and Appendix A.3 on page 14 replace a limiting approximation by an exact gradient statement, then conclude convergence to a local maximum of the composed utility.

For \(F(\mu)=u(\mu,
u(\mu))\), the exact derivative contains \[
abla F=\partial_\mu u+(D_\mu
u)^	op\partial_
u u.\] Appendix A.3 correctly shows \(D_\mu
u	o0\) as \(1/\epsilon	o0\), for fixed finite behavior values. For any finite \(\epsilon\), this term generally remains nonzero. A small learning rate multiplies both the retained and omitted terms; it does not make the update an exact gradient. The proof also uses approximate state visitation and a single Bellman update as if they gave exact policy evaluation, without quantitative tracking bounds, a vanishing-error schedule, or a Lyapunov argument for the actual joint recursion.

This is a substantive failure of the given argument, not merely missing notation. Consider a deterministic one-state self-loop game with \(\gamma=1/2\) and reward matrix \[M=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] It respects the stated reward range. State visitation is independent of policy, and any normalization difference is a fixed learning-rate factor. The common continuation offset in \(Q\) cancels from both the soft response and the projected action difference, so this example eliminates value-tracking ambiguity from the update direction.

This example does not prove that CED fails to converge: its scalar dynamics can converge to the indicated fixed point. It disproves the argument offered for general last-iterate convergence. A valid proof may use a different objective in matrix games; for example, a regularized minimax value has an envelope derivative there. That does not automatically extend to a Markov game whose response uses fixed \(Q^\beta\) while its policy update uses changing \(Q\). A new proof must analyze that actual coupled system and state quantitative assumptions. The convergence theorem is a principal contribution, so this gap is Major even though the conditional stationary-point result below survives.
# The interior condition is essential, and a conditional result survives

Theorem 5.6, page 6, properly requires an interior fixed point in the constrained simplex. With positive state weights and an exact stationary Bellman value, projection stationarity implies all max-player action values are equal. This argument is valid when interior means interior within the simplex’s affine hull and the constraint permits a neighborhood there.

Uniform coverage does not imply that condition. In the same normalized matrix, take uniform behavior, the full simplex as the feasible set, and \(\epsilon=100\). The required interior probability would be \[p=\frac67\left(1-\epsilon\log(4/3)\right)<0.\] The CED update instead moves to the boundary \(p=0\), where \(q=\operatorname{logistic}(.01)\simeq.502500\). The min-player’s discounted exploitability is \[\frac{(1-q)-3/7}{1-\gamma}\simeq .137857>0.\] All actions have full-support data, and the original game has a completely mixed equilibrium. In this example an interior equalizer requires \(\epsilon<1/\log(4/3)\simeq3.47606\). Consequently the abstract’s “as long as” uniform-coverage wording and the conclusion on page 9 need qualification. This is a Minor scope correction relative to the explicitly conditional Theorem 5.6, not a counterexample to that theorem. Appendix D already acknowledges the conflict between a large penalty and the interior condition, which is important counterevidence against claiming the authors overlooked it everywhere.

There is also a stronger exact repair to the paragraph combining the two runs. Suppose one run produces \(\hat
u\) and \(v=V^{ ar\mu,\hat
u}\) with every max action’s \(Q\) average equal to \(v(s)\). Then \(T_{\mu,\hat
u}v=v\) for every \(\mu\), so discounted Bellman uniqueness gives \(V^{\mu,\hat
u}=v\) for every \(\mu\). The symmetric run supplies \(\hat\mu\) whose value is independent of the min-player policy. At their intersection the two values coincide, proving that \((\hat\mu,\hat
u)\) is a Nash pair. Thus two exact, everywhere-indifferent outputs can be combined without the paper’s unquantified approximate-\(Q\) closeness argument. This preserves a useful conditional conclusion; it does not establish that the algorithm reaches those outputs.
# Pinned implementation and reproducibility findings
Problem 2 (Major for the released evaluation path: actions are never executed).  The reachable calls in . That loop samples actions for both teams but does not apply them.

Lines 72–76 and 91–95 comment out the environment movement, attack, and associated updates. The active statements record actions, refresh features, and call ; the movement-conflict handler and alternative scripted enemy that do contain action calls are not invoked by this path. All robots start alive with full HP. If the path completes, no robot loses HP, all 128 iterations expire, and lines 135–137 set both scores to \(.5\), regardless of policy quality. Static AST inspection confirms no reachable or call in the work loop, observation routine, or action selector. This is not a missing plotting update: the physical transition calls themselves are absent.

The shipped test drivers instantiate this worker. Consequently that public path cannot reproduce nonconstant win-rate curves or the nontrivial pairwise outcomes in Figures 5–6. This conclusion is limited to commit ; it is not an allegation that the paper’s reported results were obtained with this evaluator. The experiment-producing version and raw evaluation records are needed, and the current path needs actual action application and transition-level checks.

Problem 3 (Major reproducibility gap: the neural trainer does not implement the stated two-policy CED update).  The advertised optimizes one actor with a soft actor-critic style loss and a KL penalty to a fixed reference, rather than the max-policy update followed by the regularized min-response in Algorithm 2.

Its policy optimizer at line 101 owns only . Lines 310–316 optimize \[\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi}[\alpha\log\pi(a)-Q(s,a)]+\mathrm{BETA}\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\pi_{\rm ref}).\] The critic is trained on self actions and reward/next-state transitions, with entropy-augmented bootstrapping at lines 318–357. No training forward call uses , and no optimizer performs the negative-value regularized response against fixed \(Q^\beta\). Instead, line 393 copies the self actor into the enemy actor every 100 iterations. Because the buffer is fixed, copying an unused opponent network does not change the opponent response represented by those transitions. The otherwise closely matching OSP driver removes the KL term; the saved source diff makes this comparison inspectable.

An approximate neural implementation need not reproduce every tabular operation, but the absent adversarial response and joint-action value cannot be justified as merely finite optimization error in the stated update. Either provide the experiment-producing CED implementation or explicitly define and evaluate the different neural algorithm. This is a current-release reproduction defect, not proof of an incorrect historical comparison.

The tabular C++ example also uses the current \(Q\) in , whereas Algorithm 2 and Appendix C explicitly freeze \(Q^{\mu_\beta,\nu_\beta}\) for that response. This is a narrower implementation mismatch. It does not necessarily change the final answer in the supplied tree: the behavior continuation values at its two leaves are \(.5\) and \(0\), matching their equilibrium values. Transient dynamics can still differ, and the example additionally documents a state-weight convention different from the plotted one. The exact variant used for each figure should be recorded.
# Empirical interpretation, coverage, and disposition

All nine original figures were actually examined, including logarithmic NashConv curves, both neural initialization panels, and the pairwise score tables. The soccer curves provide evidence about those particular experiments; they do not repair the proof. Near-50% performance against one equilibrium opponent is not generally a bound on a policy’s worst-case exploitability, and neural win rates against selected opponents are not a Nash certificate. The small 51–52% comparisons require match counts and uncertainty before a statistical superiority claim can be assessed. Such raw counts/seeds and the soccer implementation are not available in this source packet. No experimental rerun or historical-version attribution was attempted.

Static coverage included the complete C++ algorithm, complete CED trainer and network model, OSP comparison diff, the BC loss section, data-generation and runner entry paths, complete test worker and test drivers, and the relevant environment/worker observation, transition, reward, and replay paths. Unused legacy worker branches and rendering helpers were not exhaustively audited. The current generator stops at 10,000 stored transitions; correspondence with the paper’s 2,000-trajectory dataset remains unverified. Large data, base checkpoints, and external attachment contents were unavailable or excluded by the source-acquisition scope.

Major revision is recommended for the unsupported convergence guarantee and the released implementation’s inability to substantiate the claimed neural/evaluation pipeline. The interior stationary-point result, exact matrix reference solutions, and possible practical utility remain intact within their stated limits. Reviewer-owned and preserve the analytic calculations and static AST checks. and bind source claims to bytes. Coverage, rendering, actual inspection, isolated cached compilation, and provenance are recorded alongside the report. Scientific adjudication is pending, with no human review or independent acceptance claimed.

Title: Technical Verification of Non-asymptotic Error Bounds in \(\mathcal W_2\)-Distance with Sqrt(d) Dimension Dependence and First Order Convergence for Langevin Monte Carlo beyond Log-Concavity
# Identity, scope, and positive checks
The paper is by Bin Yang and Xiaojie Wang, ICML 2025, I25-43718 (0349) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Its frozen PDF SHA-256 is

All 25 physical pages, including Appendices A–G, were read. The acquired publisher metadata and PDF passed their frozen hashes. Physical pages 3, 5, 8, 17, 19, 21, and 23–25 were actually viewed; page 8 contains all four panels of the original numerical figure. No author release was located in the source search recorded in the frozen manifest. That is a bounded availability statement, not a claim that no implementation exists anywhere. Separate OpenReview attachments remained unresolved after the source phase’s access barrier.

The key recurrence in Appendix D is sound in its intended homogeneous Markov setting. If a block of length \(T=mh\) gives a uniform discretization error \(A h^q\), and \(K e^{-\eta T}\le e^{-1}\), then \[W_2(\nu\widetilde P_n,\pi)\le A h^q+e^{-1}W_2(\nu\widetilde P_{n-m},\pi).\] Iterating the recurrence gives a geometric transient and an \(O(h^q)\) error floor. Pairwise contraction between arbitrary initial laws is unnecessary; the assumed contraction toward \(\pi\) suffices. Uniform numerical moments control the random initial point at each restart. The ceiling in the block length is correctly included in (114) and (119).

For \(U(x)=|x|^2/2\), the Euler chain has invariant covariance \((1-h/2)^{-1}I_d\) for \(0<h<2\). Therefore \[W_2\!\left(N(0,(1-h/2)^{-1}I_d),N(0,I_d)\right)
 =\sqrt d\bigl((1-h/2)^{-1/2}-1\bigr)
 =\tfrac14\sqrt d\,h+O(\sqrt d\,h^2).\] Independent arithmetic at \(d=1,10,100\) and \(h=0.1,0.01,0.001\) confirms this scaling. This validates a nontrivial special case, not the full nonconvex theorem. Dimension-independent log-Sobolev and growth constants remain essential hypotheses of the general claim.
# Corrections required in the mathematical argument

Problem 1 (Minor: the last inequality of (169) is false).  On physical page 24, the weighted increment integral is bounded by \(C(d^{2\gamma+1}+|x|^{4\gamma+2})^{1/2}h^2\). The square root cannot hold uniformly in \(x\) under the stated assumptions.

Take the one-dimensional Ornstein–Uhlenbeck potential \(U(x)=x^2/2\) and use the admissible polynomial upper-growth exponent \(\gamma=2\). This smooth potential satisfies dissipativity, the one-sided condition, log-Sobolev, and the required third-derivative bound (its third derivative vanishes). For deterministic \(X_0=x>0\), \[\mathbb E|X_s-x|^2=x^2(e^{-s}-1)^2+1-e^{-2s}.\] Since \((1+x^2+X_s^2)^2\ge x^4\), the left side of (169), with \(t=0\), is at least \[x^4\{x^2 A(h)+B(h)\},\quad
 A(h)=h-2(1-e^{-h})+\tfrac12(1-e^{-2h}),\quad
 B(h)=h-\tfrac12(1-e^{-2h}).\] For fixed \(h=1/2\), \(A(h)>0\), so this grows as \(x^6\), whereas the printed right side is \(O(x^5)\). No constant independent of \(x\) repairs that inequality. The required constant’s rigorous lower bound grows from approximately \(1.24\) at \(x=10\) to \(1164.86\) at \(x=10000\); the unbounded asymptotic ratio, rather than these samples, proves failure.
Problem 2 (Minor: Appendix G does not verify the example with its stated constants).  The double-well derivatives in (188)–(189), and the parameters asserted on page 8, are incorrect.

For the verification’s \(\alpha=\beta=1\) potential \(U(x)=|x|^4/4-|x|^2/2\), direct differentiation gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \nabla^2U&=(|x|^2-1)I+2xx^\top,\\
 \Delta U&=(d+2)|x|^2-d,\qquad
 \nabla\Delta U=2(d+2)x.\end{aligned}\] The printed Hessian omits a factor two; the Laplacian and its derivative then have further coefficient/sign errors. In particular, the proposed \(4d|x|\) bound fails at \(d=1\). With \(\gamma=2\), the page-8 choice \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2=1\) also violates the explicit condition \(\gamma_1+\gamma_2=\gamma+1\) and would only supply a \(\sqrt d|x|\) term in Assumption 2.14. A valid repair is \(\gamma_1=2\), \(\gamma_2=1\), and \(L_0=6\) for all \(d\ge1\). The stated \(L_1=1\) in Assumption 2.12 fails already in one dimension as \(y\to x\to\infty\), where the derivative is \(3x^2-1\) but the bound is \(1+2x^2\). Taking \(L_1=2\) is sufficient.

The Gaussian-mixture expression (186) also changes the denominator’s last coefficient from one to three in its second equality. Its intended linear bound nonetheless survives: writing \(z=\langle x,a\rangle\) gives \(\nabla\Delta U_1=2|a|^2\operatorname{sech}^2(z)\tanh(z)a\), whose norm is at most \(2|a|^4|x|\), tighter than (187). These corrections establish admissibility with modified constants; they do not overturn the examples or establish any defect in the historical simulations. The actual numerical double well uses \(\beta=16\), so its constants should be documented separately from the \(\beta=1\) illustration.

Problem 3 (Major: the general-SDE proof uses an unprovided moment range).  The proof of Theorem 3.3 uses exact-solution moments beyond the range guaranteed by its stated Condition (A1) and Lemma 3.1. The remaining indexing and identity corrections listed below are Minor and should be distinguished from this hypothesis gap.

Condition (A1), physical page 6, provides one \(p^*\ge1\); Lemma 3.1, page 7, only bounds exact-solution moments of order \(2p\) for \(p\le p^*\). Yet (79) and (94)–(103) use orders \(2r_0\) and \(2r+r_0\) without relating \(p^*\) to \(r_0\) or \(r\). Condition (A2) supplies numerical-solution moments; the published argument does not derive the required exact-solution bounds from it. This is not resolved by changing the argument of a moment constant.

The gap is Major for the general framework: Theorem 3.4 explicitly invokes Theorem 3.3 in (112), so the unprovided bound is used in a principal result, not an isolated example. A sufficient repair for this proof is to assume \[p^*\ge\max\{r_0,r+r_0/2\}\] and the corresponding finite initial moment, or provide a different proof deriving all needed exact moments under the original assumptions. This review establishes a gap in the supplied proof, not a counterexample to the fully stated theorem with (A2). The additive-noise dissipative Langevin applications explicitly admit arbitrary finite moment orders from deterministic starts, as (172) confirms, and their prescribed initial moments cover the application. Their survival does not validate the broader published proof.
The following associated corrections can be checked without executing a sampler.

- In (94)–(103), a moment of order \(2r+r_0\) calls for \(\widehat C_i^*(r+r_0/2)\) under (37)/(39), not \(\widehat C_i^*(2r+r_0)\). The latter would give a larger dimension power than (177). The generic theorem must also require enough exact-solution moments: \(p^*\ge\max\{r_0,r+r_0/2\}\) suffices for the moments used in this proof. Condition (A1) as printed only states \(p^*\ge1\). This is the Major proof-range issue above; the corrected index itself is a Minor bookkeeping change. The Langevin applications admit the needed moments, so their rates are not refuted by this issue.

- The gradient Itô identity (128) should have drift \(-
abla^2U
abla U+
abla\Delta U\). The printed exterior minus applies to both terms. Subsequent triangle-norm bounds can use the same sum of norms after correcting the sign; the same issue occurs in (159).
- Equation (19) follows from (17) with \(1+2|x|^\gamma\), not \(1+|x|^\gamma\), unless the Lipschitz constant is enlarged. This is a constant change, not an exponent change.

- In (141) and (176), \(K_2^*\) is assigned the hatted quantity although it should be the unhatted coefficient multiplying the power of \(|x|\). Equation (144)’s expanded second line contains an extra factor \(d\) inside a bracket already multiplied by \(d\). Its first line has the intended \(O(d)\) size. The \(r_0=0\) case of (103) should be stated separately to avoid a formal division by zero and to use only second moments.

- The supremum in (24) cannot coexist with a right-hand side decreasing in the free index \(n\) for arbitrary large initial data. State a pointwise decaying bound, or replace the decaying initial term by its value at zero. The argument in Appendix A already has the appropriate pointwise form for ordinary LMC. The constants in (149) exchange the transient and bias labels; selecting \(h\) with the corrected labels preserves the asserted complexity order.

These are version-bounded claims about the published equations. Some are plainly compatible with transcription errors. The corrected moment indexing reproduces the power \(d^{11\gamma/2+1}\) before taking the square root in the projected bound; the literal printed indexing does not. A revised proof should state these repairs explicitly rather than asking the reader to silently change constants and indices.
# Evidence limits and assessment

The four panels on page 8 are compatible with qualitative density approximation and finite-time strong order one. The error study uses \(T=6\), a reference discretization \(h_{\rm ref}=2^{-13}\), and 3000 samples. Such a coupled finite-time experiment is not a direct empirical measurement of invariant-distribution \(W_2\) error or a dimension-asymptotic validation. No raw trajectories, seeds, implementation, or uncertainty analysis was available for independent numerical reproduction. No historical computational failure is alleged.

The recommendation is Major revision for the unprovided moment range in the general-SDE proof and its dependent uniform theorem. The local pLMC repair, derivative corrections, and bookkeeping findings remain Minor for the reasons demonstrated above. The nonconvex restart mechanism and the main LMC rate have not been refuted by these checks. The false bound (169) is an actual mathematical error, but its explicit weaker replacement fits the downstream polynomial target, which limits its severity. The projected local-error gap has been closed here by the explicit weaker estimate; the original simplified increment claim is bypassed. The generic moment-range issue still requires a stated qualification or a replacement derivation. Focused independent AI verification is recorded with the preserved predecessor; adjudication is pending and there are no human reviews.

report: Abstract: DEFAME combines multimodal evidence retrieval with iterative planning and produces inspectable fact-checking reports. The comparisons with its own GPT-4o baselines are promising. However, a principal literature comparison substitutes a baseline F-score for accuracy, and the published implementation does not enforce its claimed temporal restriction for reverse image search. Its accuracy calculation also excludes refusals and can finalize incomplete runs without an explicit full-population score. These are substantive defects in the comparison and reproduction contracts, although they do not establish that historical runs used contaminated evidence or produced inflated accuracy scores. Additional configuration, dataset-count, and human-study details need reconciliation. All 35 physical pages, applicable appendices, relevant original figures, and the available central implementation paths were examined. No author program was executed. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification of DEFAME: Dynamic Evidence-based FAct-checking with Multimodal Experts
# Identity, scope, and checks that survive
This report concerns Tobias Braun, Mark Rothermel, Marcus Rohrbach, and Anna Rohrbach, ICML 2025, I25-43719 (0350) [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The frozen proceedings PDF has SHA-256
All 35 physical pages, including Appendices A–O, were read. The acquired source packet’s 218 files passed their frozen hashes. Code claims below concern only the released `icml` branch at commit

That release is presented as the ICML version; nevertheless, the actual historical run commit, prediction files, retrieved pages, and rating data were not established. Current code defects are not evidence that those defects affected reported experiments.

The main dynamic procedure does implement repeated planning, execution, evidence summarization, development, and judgment, with continuation on NEI and a bounded iteration count. The GPT formatter includes both image references and image data. The MOCHEG loader explicitly deduplicates claim identifiers and removes missing rulings, consistent with the declared restricted evaluation population. The text-search backend carries a date restriction into its query. These positive checks constrain the concerns below.

Appendix J’s identity is valid for a single-label classifier evaluated on the same complete population: if \(N\) decisions contain \(C\) correct predictions, then aggregated \(TP=C\) and \(FP=FN=N-C\), so \[F_{1,\mathrm{micro}}=\frac{2C}{2C+2(N-C)}=\frac CN.\] It does not convert an arbitrary reported F-score into accuracy, or equate metrics computed on different subsets.
# Substantive comparison and reproducibility problems

Problem 1 (Major: the MOCHEG literature comparison mixes metrics).  Table 3 (physical page 7) places MetaSum’s 48.6 in an accuracy column and compares it with DEFAME’s 59.2. Appendix J does not justify that substitution.

The cited MetaSumPerceiver primary paper [Retained latex: \cite{msp}], physically inspected at pages 6–7, labels 48.6 as an F-score in Table 4. Its Table 3 separately reports 55.6 accuracy for the same named setting: both critics, text-plus-image evidence, and Llama 2. Thus the source itself distinguishes these quantities. No assumption about whether its F-score is macro, weighted, or another aggregation is needed to identify the unsupported relabeling.

The subtraction \(59.2-48.6=10.6\) percentage points therefore does not establish an accuracy improvement. Subtracting the two published accuracy values instead gives \(3.6\) points, but this is not a repaired matched-population estimate: DEFAME evaluates 1,689 retained claims, and equivalent baseline filtering and evidence conditions have not been demonstrated. A source-table error is another possible explanation, but then the comparator is unresolved rather than established by the micro-F1 identity. Release aligned sample identifiers and recompute both methods under a common metric and evidence protocol, or label the comparison as non-comparable. This finding materially affects a principal benchmark improvement; it neither refutes DEFAME’s own baseline comparison nor establishes that its measured accuracy is wrong.

Problem 2 (Major: reverse image search lacks the stated temporal restriction).  Page 4 states that all web tools restrict sources to dates preceding the claim when its date is known. The pinned implementation does not enforce this for reverse image search (RIS).
The complete inspected path is
`FactChecker` \(\to\) `Actor` \(\to\) `Searcher` \(\to\) `GoogleVisionAPI`.

The first stages preserve the claim date and set `ImageQuery.end_date`. But , lines 28–78, sends only the image to `web_detection`, then scrapes matching pages after domain filtering. It neither reads the date constraint nor assigns publication dates to its `WebSource` objects. The inspected cache/API wrappers and `Searcher.search` remove known URLs and truncate results; they do not supply a missing date filter. An independent AST inspection confirms that this backend never accesses `end_date` or `start_date`.

This is a conditional but direct implementation counterexample: an allowed matching page newer than a known claim date, if returned by the service and successfully scraped, is admitted by the inspected path. In contrast, `query_serper.py` does send a date-limited text/image-search query. Therefore the finding is specific to RIS, not an assertion that all date handling is absent. Search-provider behavior or an occasional date-aware summary is not a software guarantee of exclusion. The inspected publication-date query also does not by itself archive the earlier contents of subsequently edited pages.

The defect concerns the temporal evaluation premise, a central motivation of the work. Repair RIS with recorded publication-time validation and an explicit unknown-date policy; preserve evidence snapshots and query/run timestamps. Historical impact remains unknown without the actual retrieved pages. I do not claim that any particular reported prediction used future information.

The benchmark’s stronger “leakage-free” characterization also needs qualification. Selecting fact-check articles after the backbone’s cutoff does not establish that their claims, images, or semantic contents were absent before it. Page 5 expressly allows earlier events to be revisited, and substitutes the review date when the claim date is missing. This is a reasonable post-cutoff article collection, but verified novelty or a quantified overlap audit is needed for the stronger interpretation. This logical limitation is not evidence of actual training contamination.

Problem 3 (Major: released accuracy is conditional on accepted, completed outputs).  The evaluation code’s denominator differs from ordinary accuracy over all selected benchmark claims when a refusal or worker failure occurs.

In , `compute_metrics` counts refusals and returns \[\widehat A_{\rm release}=\frac{C}{M-R},\] where \(M\) is the number of saved predictions and \(R\) the number marked `REFUSED_TO_ANSWER`. `compute_accuracy` uses the same exclusion. This path is reachable: `Judge._generate_verdict` returns that label when verdict extraction fails, and the logger saves the enum name used by the metric. Separately, a worker exception sends an error message without a prediction; the main loop can terminate after all workers finish and finalize the saved CSV. It does not enforce one terminal outcome for every requested claim before reporting this score.

An independent ten-claim example with eight correct decisions, one wrong decision, and one refusal yields \(8/9=88.89\%\) under the release formula, compared with \(8/10=80\%\) over all attempts. This is an exact denominator effect, not a reconstruction of the paper’s runs. Selective accuracy is legitimate if explicitly named and accompanied by coverage and a common abstention policy. Here it must not silently stand in for the ordinary accuracy and micro-F1 population discussed in the paper. Save a complete claim ledger, distinguish refusal from operational failure, report \(C/N\) and coverage alongside selective accuracy, and make incomplete runs visibly incomplete. If all historical runs had full coverage and no refusals, their accuracy values would be unaffected; that remains a plausible alternative requiring the run artifacts.

The original plots reveal small but concrete population discrepancies worth reconciling independently of the code. Figure 8(f)’s MOCHEG matrix totals 1,688 rather than the declared 1,689; its NEI row totals 521 rather than 522. Figure 8(i)’s VERITE matrix totals 1,000 rather than 1,001. These do not prove that refusal exclusion caused either omission. In Figure 4, all three ClaimReview matrices sum to 300, but their supported/refuted/misleading/NEI row totals are \((89,136,55,20)\), whereas page 5 gives \((89,129,61,21)\). A dataset revision could explain this, and should be versioned. By contrast, the actual AVERITEC diagonal is \(84+4+259+6=353\), giving \(70.6\%\), compatible with Table 3’s \(70.5\pm0.6\); an apparent discrepancy from text extraction was rejected after inspecting the image.
# Method specification and inferential qualifications

Problem 4 (Minor: the released ablation and model configurations disagree with the description).  Several explicit release settings do not reproduce the named experiment without clarification or repair.

Page 8 defines “w/o Planning” as a fixed schedule executing each tool exactly once without the planner. The released `no_planning.yaml` files instead select `summary/static`, whose `apply_to` calls the planner once and executes its chosen actions. The alternative `summary/all_actions` still calls the planner and can repeat while the verdict is NEI. Neither inspected implementation is the stated fixed schedule. The ClaimReview configuration also names the unregistered benchmark `claimreview2024q`. Moreover, MOCHEG’s main configuration selects `test`, whereas its no-planning and all-actions configurations select `dev`; the loader actually uses this string in the dataset path. These are present-release reproduction discrepancies, not proof that the historical ablation used those configurations.

The geolocator defaults to `geolocal/StreetCLIP`, with image–country-text scoring, whereas page 4 and Figure 2 name GeoCLIP. The inspected main configurations leave that default in place. Appendix H (page 21) also says MOCHEG has no extra judgment rules and assigns the warning against argument from ignorance to AVERITEC. In the release, MOCHEG carries that warning; AVERITEC instead permits absence-of-expected-evidence reasoning, and ClaimReview adds a rule always suggesting geolocation. Release the exact run-specific model, prompts, split identifiers, and ablation schedules. This finding is conservatively Minor because the observed discrepancies establish an inadequate released specification, while their relation to the historical experiments is unverified.

Problem 5 (Minor: the human-study significance needs a stated analysis unit).  The reported \(p\approx9.1\times10^{-9}\) does not come with enough design information to assess generalization across claims and raters.

Pages 9 and 25 report 185 ratings over 36 claims, at least five ratings per claim, split into 154 DEFAME and 31 CoT ratings, and a Mann–Whitney test. Repeated ratings of the same claim/report share an item; the number of raters, assignment, pairing, and repeated-rater structure are not supplied. A pooled independent-observation analysis is not automatically a valid test of an effect over new claims. For illustration only, an exchangeable cluster of five ratings with within-claim correlation \(\rho\) has variance inflation factor \(1+4\rho\); the actual correlation is unknown.

Provide anonymized claim/report/rater identifiers, group assignment, and the exact tested units. Use an item-aware paired/permutation analysis or a suitable crossed/clustered model for the intended population. A test on already aggregated independent units could resolve this concern, but the paper does not establish that this was done. The descriptive completeness advantage can survive such a correction; the present record does not establish that the reported \(p\) is numerically false. The release’s study helper selects successful cases by default and targets a different sample layout; this is not enough to allege that the published 36-claim study used that selection.

Two further wording corrections are warranted. Appendix M says the one-shot variant improves all metrics even against fine-tuned systems, but Table 8 gives BLEU \(7.31<11.40\) and BERTScore \(87.42<88.10\), although its ROUGE-L is larger. Improvement over DEFAME’s own zero-shot row is supported; superiority on every metric over the fine-tuned row is not. Also, an updated real-world fact does not alone invalidate a time-indexed historical label. Appendix K’s proposed timestamped evaluation is therefore preferable to treating all old labels as currently wrong. The claimed individual annotation errors in Appendix I were viewed, but their full external source histories were not independently adjudicated.
# Assessment and evidence limits

Recommendation: Major revision. The metric substitution affects a principal performance comparison, and the current release lacks an important temporal safeguard and a complete-population scoring contract. Correcting these issues may preserve substantial benefits from multimodal retrieval; the evidence here does not show a collapse of the entire approach.

The review read the whole proceedings paper and relevant core code, traced queries, judgment, logging, scoring, benchmark loaders, model formatting, prompts, and ablations, and performed independent integer and denominator calculations. All Figures 1–18 were actually inspected on their physical pages, together with relevant tables; the cited comparator’s two metric tables were separately viewed. The accompanying coverage record distinguishes these checks from unperformed work. No LLM inference, search-provider call from author code, model download, benchmark rerun, raw-rating reanalysis, or historical artifact reconstruction was performed. Separate OpenReview attachments remained unavailable in the acquired packet. Utility-only and unrelated benchmark paths were not exhaustively audited. Evidence files bind calculations, line anchors, original images, and the exact final report to their hashes. This is an initial review, not independent acceptance; adjudication is pending and the human-review list is empty.

report: Abstract: The published spectral formula and the condition-number decrease guarantee are checked by exact two-dimensional calculations. Proposition 3.2 mistakes diagonal entries for eigenvalues; Theorem 4.3(1) permits a step that increases the condition number from 4 to 9. Both affect core theoretical arguments and support Major findings. A separate transpose inconsistency in the released preconditioner is Minor because its effect on the published experiments is unknown. These findings do not invalidate the reported empirical observations. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:

Title: Technical Verification of
Model Immunization from a Condition Number Perspective
# Identity and reviewed scope

Amber Yijia Zheng, Cedar Site Bai, Brian Bullins and Raymond A. Yeh, Model Immunization from a Condition Number Perspective, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 78041–78066, OpenReview `uitj69FqD5` [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The reviewed artifact is the 26-page publisher PDF retrieved on 25 October 2026. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with its printed page numbers. The publisher metadata shortens the second author’s name to Site Bai; the PDF uses Cedar Site Bai.

The review reads the main mathematical development and experiment descriptions, Appendix A, the relevant proofs in B.1–B.4, and Appendix C. It checks Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 4.3(1) decisively, and checks the chain rule underlying Theorem 4.2. The general rank-changing domain of \(R_{\rm ill}\) and every detail of the increase proof are not certified. Figures 1–4 were actually viewed; no underlying training run was reproduced. The current released code snapshot , dated 8 June 2025, was inspected statically in the files listed in the verification record. Its relation to the historical experiment executable is unestablished.
# Definitions and checked dependencies

The model uses a square linear feature map \(x^\top\theta\) and \(K=X^\top X\succeq0\), with \(H(\theta)=\theta^\top K\theta\). The paper defines \(\kappa(S)=\|S\|_2\|S^+\|_2\); all counterexamples below have full rank, so zero-singular-value conventions are immaterial. The least-squares Hessian has an inessential factor of two under the unhalved loss in (8); we use the paper’s exact \(H\) convention. The minimizing regularizer is \[R_{\rm well}(H)=\tfrac12\|H\|_2^2-\tfrac1{2d}\|H\|_F^2.\] At a unique largest eigenvalue \(a\) with eigenvector \(v\), its feature gradient is \[\nabla_\theta R_{\rm well}=2K\theta(avv^\top-H/d),\] which follows directly by \(dH=(d\theta)^\top K\theta+\theta^\top Kd\theta\). This validates the gradient used in the second counterexample independently of the disputed step-size argument. Section 4.4 explicitly says separate regularizer guarantees do not automatically combine for the full objective; the review respects that limitation.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The spectrum in Proposition 3.2 is not given by row norms).

Source and assumptions. Proposition 3.2, (10), p. 3, and B.1, pp. 13–14, purport to give every singular value of \(H\) as \[\sigma_i=\sum_j[\sigma_{\theta,i}(u_{\theta,i}^\top q_j)\gamma_j]^2.\] The text calls \(\gamma_j\) the singular values of \(K\), whereas B.1 writes \(K=Q\Gamma^2Q^\top\). We first use the more favorable latter interpretation, so \(\gamma_j^2\) are the eigenvalues of \(K\).

Exact check. Set \(d=N=2\), \(\theta=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\) and \[K=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=K^{1/2},\qquad
H=\begin{pmatrix}8&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}.\] \(K\) is positive definite with eigenvalues 3 and 1; \(\theta\) is invertible with distinct singular values. This is an admissible square linear feature extractor with a genuine data Gram matrix. Labels may be zero, as they do not affect \(H\). Choosing \(U_\theta=I\) and \(q_1=(1,1)^\top/\sqrt2\), \(q_2=(1,-1)^\top/\sqrt2\), the formula gives 8 and 2. But \[\det(tI-H)=t^2-10t+12,\qquad
\operatorname{spec}(H)=\{5+\sqrt{13},5-\sqrt{13}\},\] approximately \(\{8.605551,1.394449\}\). Both predicted eigenvalues are wrong. If the statement is instead read literally with \(\gamma_j=3,1\), it gives 20 and 5 and remains false.

Failed step and counterevidence. With \(M=\Sigma_\theta U_\theta^\top Q\Gamma\), B.1 correctly obtains \(H=V_\theta MM^\top V_\theta^\top\). It then calls the row-normalized \(M\) an orthonormal matrix and treats row norms as singular values. In this example the normalized row inner product is \(1/2\), not zero. Normalizing lengths does not remove correlations. The proposed factorization also places the row scaling on the wrong side. The expression is valid in aligned cases where \(U_\theta^\top KU_\theta\) is diagonal; alignment is not a hypothesis of Proposition 3.2.

Impact and supported correction. This is Major for the spectral derivation used in Section 3.1 to explain the role of singular-vector angles. The exact general replacement is the eigenvalue list of \(\Sigma_\theta U_\theta^\top KU_\theta\Sigma_\theta\), equivalently the squared singular values of \(K^{1/2}\theta\). It is not the list of its diagonal entries. This identity is proved by orthogonal similarity and restores the spectrum, but does not establish every subsequent qualitative existence claim. The independent numerical output is `check_output.json`, entry `proposition_3_2`.
Problem 2 (Theorem 4.3(1) admits a condition-number increase).

Source. Theorem 4.3(1), pp. 4–5, repeated in B.4, pp. 20–22, asserts strict decrease after \(\theta'=\theta-\eta K^{-1}\nabla_\theta R_{\rm well}\) when the largest eigenvalue \(a>b\) is unique and \[0<\eta<\min\left\{\frac1{(1-1/d)a},\frac{\sqrt{ab}-b}{(2/d^2)b^2}\right\}.\] Exact check of every condition. Take \(d=2\), \(X=K=I_2\), \(\theta=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), \(H=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), rank two, and \(\eta=1/5\). The maximum 4 is unique, \(K^{-1}\) exists, and the displayed upper bound is \(\min\{1/2,2\}=1/2\), strictly exceeding \(1/5\). If a harmful-task covariance is needed to instantiate the common notation, set \(K_H=I_2\) also; no constraint from part (2) is needed for part (1). The valid gradient above gives \[\nabla_\theta R_{\rm well}=\operatorname{diag}(8,-1),\quad
\theta'=\operatorname{diag}(2/5,6/5),\quad
H'=\operatorname{diag}(4/25,36/25).\] Thus \(\kappa(H')=9>4=\kappa(H)\). Both old and new matrices are positive definite, and even the feature diagonal entries stay positive. No singular limit, sign ambiguity, stochasticity or combined-loss interaction is used.

Proof diagnosis and alternatives. The expansion on p. 21 is correct: the old largest mode becomes \(a[1-2\eta(1-1/d)a]^2\) and the other modes become \(b_i(1+2\eta b_i/d)^2\). Page 22 then claims the stated bound preserves their order. Here the old largest mode is \(4/25\) and the other is \(36/25\), so that step fails. A smaller step can work: for this example \(0<\eta<3/17\) yields strict decrease, excluding the singular step \(1/4\) automatically. This example-specific interval is not offered as a universal repaired theorem.

Impact. Major: monotone regularizer updates are an explicit contribution in the introduction, and Section 4.3 provides the theoretical justification of Algorithm 1. The invalidity is already present in the isolated regularizer step, beyond the acknowledged caveat about combining gradients. It neither disproves empirical effectiveness nor proves that the published learning rates caused the failure. Evidence: `check_output.json`, `theorem_4_3_1`.
Problem 3 (The dummy-layer preconditioner acts on the transposed axis).

Figure 4, p. 26, and released `models/linear.py`, lines 15 and 31–38, use \(Y=XW^\top\) and compute the weight gradient \(G_W\) as the upstream gradient transposed times \(X\). They return \((K+\lambda I)^{-1}G_W\). Since \(\theta=W^\top\), Algorithm 1’s left multiplication in \(\theta\) corresponds instead to \(G_W(K+\lambda I)^{-1}\) in \(W\). For a square, full-rank example, take \(X=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt2,1)\), \(\lambda=1\) and \(G_W=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Such an upstream gradient is attainable because \(X\) is invertible. The two returns are \[\begin{pmatrix}0&1/3\\1/2&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\hbox{and}\quad
\begin{pmatrix}0&1/2\\1/3&0\end{pmatrix},\] with Frobenius difference \(\sqrt2/6\). They coincide in commuting special cases, but not generally. `models/model.py` activates this path for linear regularization; the relevant forward convention rules out silently treating \(W\) as \(\theta\). A right solve, equivalently solving against \(G_W^\top\) and transposing, repairs this local transpose mismatch. The ridge approximation still differs from the theorem’s exact inverse. This is a Minor implementation/pseudocode discrepancy: the operator mismatch is established, but its effect on reported experiments and the identity of their historical code remain Needs Evidence. No author program was executed. The unused `S2_gradients` helper was also read; its formula is not used to infer an experimental defect.
# Overall impact and conclusion

The two Major findings concern separate core mathematical derivations. The gradient chain rule and the exact spectral congruence remain valid. Figures 1 and 3 visually show the reported slower harmful-task probing trends, and Figure 2 shows the authors’ success coloring; these observations cannot rescue the false universal claims or be rejected by the synthetic counterexamples. Tables 1–4 and the experimental settings were read, but seed-level statistics, data processing, checkpoint selection and the 20-group Hessian estimates were not reproduced. The Appendix C statement about early stopping with test accuracy requires clarification before interpreting reported generalization without selection bias; no quantitative bias is established here. No later correction or historical code provenance has been independently verified.
