Title: Technical Verification of
High-Dimensional Tensor Regression with Oracle Properties
# Identity, scope and assumptions

Wenbin Wang, Yu Shi and Ziping Zhao, High-Dimensional Tensor Regression With Oracle Properties, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp.64302–64342, OpenReview `ue1ptN4kSS`. The reviewed publisher PDF has 41 pages; all locations below use one-based PDF pages, matching printed numbers. Main definitions, Theorems 5–6, the relevant Appendix B.1/B.4 arguments, the algorithm and experimental descriptions were read. Appendix A/B extensions and Appendix C were inspected only to the extent recorded in coverage; the full suite of rates and concentration lemmas is not certified.

The model contracts tensor predictors with a coefficient tensor and minimizes a squared loss plus a separable or singular-value penalty. SCAD and MCP satisfy bounded concavity assumptions, and the theory assumes loss curvature \(\mu\) greater than the penalty concavity \(\zeta\). The low-rank definitions use the compact singular spaces \(U,V\) of the true unfolding. We preserve that definition rather than silently replacing it with the usual tangent space.

Two available repositories were read statically: `dsailab/TensorReg_ncvx` at (16 April 2025), and at (20 August 2026). Both READMEs identify the paper. Neither snapshot is established as the exact executable used for the published tables.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The low-rank proof omits two cross blocks).

Section 4.2.2, p.5, defines \(F=\{W:\operatorname{col}(W)\subseteq U,\operatorname{row}(W)\subseteq V\}\) and labels the space with both column and row spaces perpendicular to \(U,V\) as \(F^\perp\). Its projections are written \[P_F(W)=UU^\top WVV^\top,\qquad P_N(W)=(I-UU^\top)W(I-VV^\top).\] Both displayed maps are genuine orthogonal projections, but their ranges do not exhaust the matrix space. The first equality after (23) in Lemma 14, p.25, nevertheless decomposes an arbitrary inner product using only these two projections. Equation (35), p.27, repeats this decomposition in the deterministic error bound; pp.34–35 use it to identify the oracle estimator with the penalized estimator.

Complete algebraic check. Let the true unfolding be \(A^*=\operatorname{diag}(4,0)\), hence \(U=V=e_1\), and set \[W=e_1e_2^\top=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This is a legitimate two-mode tensor/matrix; no high-order restriction excludes it. Then \(P_FW=P_NW=0\) while \(W\ne0\). With the other inner-product factor also \(W\), the unprojected product is \(\langle W,W\rangle_F=1\), whereas the asserted two-term decomposition gives zero. This refutes the universal algebraic identity used by the proof, not merely a bound’s constant. It is independent of distributional, curvature and signal-strength assumptions: those assumptions do not imply vanishing cross components of arbitrary gradients or estimation errors. Indeed, \(A^*+\epsilon W\) remains rank one for every \(\epsilon\), so a low-rank restriction alone does not eliminate this direction.

Correct identity and limits of repair. With \(P=UU^\top\) and \(Q=VV^\top\), the full identity is \[W=PWQ+PW(I-Q)+(I-P)WQ+(I-P)W(I-Q).\] The true complement of \(F\) has projector \(W-PWQ\). Alternatively, the tangent-space projector is \(PW+WQ-PWQ\), whose complement is the paper’s \(P_N\). Substituting that tangent space changes dimension, rank and projected-noise bounds; it does not by itself prove the stated oracle rate. The example does not claim to instantiate every assumption of Theorem 6 as a stochastic counterexample. It is a decisive counterexample to a universal proof identity on which that theorem’s derivation depends.

Impact. Major for the central low-rank oracle argument. The abstract and Theorem 6 rely on this derivation, and Appendix B.5 refers back to it for slice-wise low rank. The sparse case does not use the same matrix decomposition and is not refuted by this calculation. Evidence: `check_output.json`, `projection`; source pp.5,25,27,34–35.
Problem 2 (Full-ball strong convexity cannot cover underdetermined designs).

Section 4.1, p.4, defines the sparse-case neighborhood as the full Frobenius ball \(C=\{B:\|B-A^*\|_F\le r\}\) and Assumption 2 demands, for all \(A,B\in C\), a positive \(\mu\) such that \[L(B)\ge L(A)+\langle\nabla L(A),B-A\rangle+\tfrac\mu2\|B-A\|_F^2.\] The following text asserts that the curvature conditions can be proved with high probability. For scalar responses (\(M=N\), explicitly allowed in Section 3.1), vectorize the coefficient to \(p\) coordinates and write the design as \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\). If \(p>n\), choose a nonzero \(h\in\ker Z\). For any \(r>0\) choose \(0<t<r/\|h\|\). Taking \(A=A^*\), \(B=A^*+th\) gives \(L(B)=L(A)\) and \(\langle\nabla L(A),th\rangle=0\), while the final term is strictly positive. The assumed inequality is impossible.

This holds for every underdetermined design, including every realization of independent standard Gaussian entries satisfying Assumption 4 with population covariance \(I\). Increasing signal size to satisfy the minimum-signal assumption does not change the kernel. The script also checks \(Z=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(h=(-1,-1,1)^\top\), for which \(Zh=0\) and at \(\mu=1/2\) the unsatisfied quadratic term is \(3/4\) before rescaling.

Interpretation and impact. This does not refute Theorem 5 as an implication conditional on Assumption 2: in the stated regime its antecedent is unavailable. It does invalidate the advertised application of that full-ball hypothesis to high-dimensional scalar regression with \(p>n\). This is Major for that core scope claim. A sparsity-restricted cone or a tolerance-bearing curvature inequality could be suitable, but would require changed assumptions, an argument that the error lies in the admissible set, and a new proof. The actual full-ball definition cannot be replaced silently. Overdetermined designs and other restricted formulations remain possible.
Problem 3 (Released routines do not take a SCAD proximal step).

The paper’s Section 5 calls for a proximal step for the nonconvex penalty, and Section 6 says SCAD is used in the experiments. In both inspected `codes/func/niAPG.m` snapshots, `prox_operator` instead replaces each singular value \(z\) by \(\max(z-\lambda\eta,0)\). The earlier version also uses entrywise soft thresholding for its sparsity branch. These are the convex nuclear/\(\ell_1\) shrinkages, not a general SCAD proximal map. The later repository’s `codes/test.m` calls the inspected routine; its separate experiment runners also call distinct solvers, so the discrepancy is not automatically attributable to all published results.

For the paper’s SCAD definition, set \(a=3.7\), \(\lambda=1\), \(\eta=1/2\), and scalar input \(z=5\). On \(u>3.7\), \(p_\lambda(u)=(a+1)/2=2.35\). The proximal objective \(\tfrac12(u-z)^2+\eta p_\lambda(u)\) is 1.175 at \(u=5\) and 1.300 at the released shrinkage \(u=4.5\). The released answer is therefore not a minimizer; even a local move to 5 improves it. Additionally, both files’ local SCAD helper uses the plateau \((a^2-1)\lambda^2/2=6.345\) rather than 2.35, creating a jump at \(a\lambda\). These are exact scalar discrepancies, not a MATLAB execution result.

The current-source inconsistency is Minor because historical provenance and effects on the comparative tables remain Needs Evidence. A correct proximal implementation and continuous SCAD plateau are necessary local repairs, but the other solvers and complete experiment pipeline require separate audit. The nonmonotone selection branch is present in both code versions; this is counterevidence against treating the overwritten selection in the printed Algorithm 1 as proof that every executable omitted the safeguard.
# Overall conclusion and remaining evidence

The supported outcome is Major for a central low-rank proof defect and the impossible full-ball application in underdetermined scalar regression, with a separate Minor release discrepancy. No claim is made that nonconvex tensor regression cannot work or that the experimental scores are fabricated. Figures 1–4 were actually viewed and show the stated comparative patterns; they neither supply missing mathematical assumptions nor establish code provenance. The 100-realization aggregate statistics, cross-validation choices, data processing and all supplementary figures were not reproduced. Later repository dates are recorded separately; no later theorem correction or author adoption was verified.

Title: Technical verification of SIMPLEMIX
# Paper identity, scope and summary

Tianjian Li and Daniel Khashabi, SIMPLEMIX: Frustratingly Simple Mixing of Off- and On-policy Data in Language Model Preference Learning, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:35081–35100, OpenReview . The reviewed PMLR PDF has 20 pages; all page references below count PDF pages from one. The main text (pp. 1–9) and substantive appendices A–I (pp. 16–20) were read. Figures 2–11 and Tables 2–5 were inspected on rendered pages. Bibliographic entries were not independently verified.

The inspected evidence establishes no failure of the mixing objective or reversal of the published aggregate ranking. One headline aggregation needs its scope specified: the two abstract gains are exactly recovered from the Tulu subset, whereas pooling both evaluated models produces smaller gains. The assessment is Needs Evidence, with outcome scope clarification, rather than a demonstrated false experiment. The absence of an identified author repository and run-level outputs prevents implementation and significance verification.
# Checked objective and empirical comparisons

Equation (1) maximizes the expected DPO log-sigmoid objective. With \(z=(x,y_w,y_l)\) and loss \(\ell_\theta(z)\), sampling a whole pair from the two sources with probability \(1/2\) gives \[\mathbb E_{z\sim (P_{\rm on}+P_{\rm off})/2}\ell_\theta(z)
 =\tfrac12\mathbb E_{P_{\rm on}}\ell_\theta(z)+\tfrac12\mathbb E_{P_{\rm off}}\ell_\theta(z).\] This is an identity for the objective, not a claim that fitted policies or test scores average linearly. Section 4.1 fixes the number of training pairs and one epoch; it explicitly acknowledges unequal generation cost. Its on-policy definition includes initial-SFT samples; footnote 1 acknowledges its difference from strict current-policy RL terminology. Neither is treated as an undisclosed error.

Independent decimal arithmetic confirms that SIMPLEMIX exceeds all four baseline LC entries in every model–dataset cell of Table 2. Recomputing the eight-task SIMPLEMIX means from Tables 4–5 gives \(63.0575\), \(62.12375\), \(61.13625\), and \(61.22125\) for Llama–UltraFeedback, Llama–HelpSteer2, Tulu–UltraFeedback, and Tulu–HelpSteer2. These round to the reported scores. Individual tasks do not all improve, but the main claim is about aggregate metrics.
# Clarification: denominator of the abstract gains

The abstract on p. 1 states average improvements of \(6.03\%\) over on/off-policy DPO and \(3.05\%\) over HyPO/DPO-Mix-P, without naming a model subset. For each cell \(c\), let \(s_c\) be SIMPLEMIX LC in percentage units and \(b_{cj}\) one of the two relevant baselines. Define the equally weighted percentage-point difference \[\Delta(C)=\frac{1}{2|C|}\sum_{c\in C}\sum_{j=1}^2(s_c-b_{cj}).\] Table 2 supplies all operands. The actual independent script yields:
Model scope | Versus on/off DPO | Versus hybrids
Tulu, both datasets | 6.025 | 3.050
Llama, both datasets | 3.0025 | 1.775
Both models, both datasets | 4.51375 | 2.4125

Thus the printed headline values are reproducible after rounding under a Tulu-only interpretation. This admissible reading is decisive counterevidence against declaring them fabricated or numerically false. They are not the pooled two-model gains, and they are absolute percentage-point differences rather than relative percentage increases. The clarification needed is to state the aggregation population and unit. Specifying “Tulu across both datasets” preserves the headline numbers; reporting the equally weighted full grid instead gives \(4.51\) and \(2.41\) percentage points. The calculation verifies these two alternatives, not which one the authors intended. No author correction was available in the frozen source set.
# Statistical and reproducibility limits

Figure 7 and Appendix B imply approximately 35 math and 57 coding prompts among 805 judged examples, compared with 122 creative-writing and 146 recommendation prompts. Figure 2’s subgroup directions and Figure 8’s mixed-data tradeoffs are visible, but paired judgments, category assignments, LC fitting details and training seeds were not available. Treating the LC values as independent binomial win counts would be unjustified; no such significance test was performed. Figure 3’s bootstrapped bars do not by themselves establish a causal task-type mechanism. The paper explicitly limits generalization in Section 7, which should accompany its broader verbal conclusions.

Figures 4–6 show the reported mixture and filtering trends, including overlapping uncertainty bands. The selected half-and-half ratio is the largest plotted point estimate, not a verified uniformly optimal ratio. Appendix A specifies a hyperparameter sweep but does not supply its selection traces. Appendix D specifies greedy evaluation and a 2048-token cap. Figures 10–11 support the reported reward-distribution shift under the same reward model; they are not independent human-quality measurements. None of these limitations alone proves the original results wrong.

The frozen source preparation did not identify an associated author repository after bounded title/link checks. Generic OpenRLHF and evaluation-harness links do not establish the authors’ exact executable version. No author program was run, and historical training, benchmark contamination, paired uncertainty and later revisions remain unverified.
# Conclusion and state
No substantive objective error or aggregate-ranking contradiction was found within the inspected scope. The headline denominator and empirical uncertainty remain open.

Title: Technical verification of FourierMamba
# Identity and inspected scope

Dong Li, Yidi Liu, Xueyang Fu, Jie Huang, Senyan Xu, Qi Zhu and Zheng-Jun Zha, FourierMamba: Fourier Learning Integration with State Space Models for Image Deraining, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:35342–35365, OpenReview . This review uses the frozen 24-page publisher PDF; references below are one-based PDF pages. The main text and Appendix A.1–A.18 were read, with selected architecture, restoration and ablation figures actually viewed. The source preparation did not identify an associated public author repository after bounded discovery. No exact implementation or training logs were available, and no author code was executed.

Two local mathematical equivalences are false as written: the stated global-pooling/amplitude equality omits scale and sign, and the frequency-loss equality changes the loss. Both are assessed Minor: their demonstrated consequences concern the interpretation and reproducibility of particular components; no invalidation of the central architecture comparison is established. Literal phase extraction and exact scan indexing require implementation evidence.
# Definitions and surviving observations

Equation (1) uses a unitary spatial DFT, with scale \(1/\sqrt{HW}\); Equation (2) defines amplitude as the complex modulus. The channel transform in Equation (3) uses \(1/C\), a different but permissible normalization. The Fourier spatial module processes amplitude and phase separately and reconstructs with an inverse transform. The channel module first pools the input feature \(F_r\) and then applies a channel DFT. There is no restriction that every feature entry or channel mean is nonnegative.

Table 1 supports best PSNR/SSIM on three of its four datasets, not on Test2800; the main text says “most”, so that is consistent. Tables 3–4 support the printed ablation rankings. Appendix A.5 supplies approximate computation-matched comparisons, so an unqualified allegation that all ablations merely add capacity would be unsupported. The five-task mean of the final row of Table 11 recomputes to \(39.046\) dB and \(0.96984\), agreeing with its rounded entries. These checks concern reported values, not their experimental provenance.
# Problem 1: pooling is not the stated DC amplitude

Problem 1 (Missing normalization and modulus in Appendix A.7).  Appendix A.7 (p. 15) claims that global average pooling equals \(\mathcal A(0,0)\) and treats Equation (14) as an average. Section 3.3.3 (p. 7) invokes this correspondence to interpret the pooled channel feature.

For any real feature \(x\in\mathbb R^{H\times W}\), put \(g=(HW)^{-1}\sum x(h,w)\). Direct substitution into the printed DFT gives \[\mathcal F(x)(0,0)=\sqrt{HW}\,g,
 \qquad \mathcal A(x)(0,0)=\sqrt{HW}\,|g|.\] These equalities follow for every real input, without an approximation. A constant \(2\times2\) feature of value \(1\) has GAP \(1\) and DC amplitude \(2\). A constant feature of value \(-1\), also allowed by the feature domain, has GAP \(-1\) and amplitude \(2\). The independent FFT diagnostic reproduces both cases. Thus the discrepancy persists for nonnegative inputs through scale alone and for signed inputs through the modulus as well.

An alternative forward normalization \(1/(HW)\) would give DC coefficient \(g\) but amplitude \(|g|\); it repairs the claimed equality only with the additional assumption \(g\geq0\). Neither change is stated in A.7. If “corresponds” on p. 7 means only that both encode a DC statistic, the weaker interpretation is valid. The exact assertion of equality in the appendix is not. The correction is to retain the displayed scaled signed-coefficient relation above. It does not require replacing GAP in the architecture, and no effect on the reported PSNR is inferred.
# Problem 2: the frequency loss changes under polar decomposition

Problem 2 (Equation (15) is not an identity for a complex \(L^1\) loss).  Equation (12), p. 7, penalizes \(\|\mathcal F(Y_{\rm out})-\mathcal F(Y_{\rm gt})\|_1\). Appendix A.16 (p. 22), Equation (15), equates this to the sum of the amplitude-difference and phase-difference \(L^1\) norms.

Appendix A.16 may be read as defining a different polar-coordinate training objective and using the left side as shorthand. Under that reading, the right side is a valid chosen loss, but it must not be described as the same complex \(L^1\) norm. Correct reproduction requires naming which objective was actually used, its phase wrapping convention, and its reductions/normalization. Table 16 shows similar printed results for several other losses and explicitly places the focus on architecture; this is counterevidence to claiming a collapse of the main empirical contribution. Without code or run provenance, no historical training error or numerical score change is established.
# Open implementation questions and visual scope

Equation (2) and the corresponding channel formula use \(\arctan(I/R)\). Taken literally, \(z=-1+i\) is assigned \(-\pi/4\) instead of \(3\pi/4\), so \(|z|e^{i\phi}\) reconstructs \(-z\). A quadrant-aware argument resolves this local definition, but the notation may stand for an actual `atan2`/angle operation. Implementation impact therefore remains Needs Evidence.

The half-spectrum description is compatible with real-valued reconstruction only when Hermitian pairing, self-conjugate DC/Nyquist bins and phase modulo \(2\pi\) are handled correctly. The schematic scan in Figure 2 is insufficient to certify every discrete index and boundary case; no failure is inferred from it. Exact frequency-radius ordering also was not certified from the schematic. The source images on pp. 2–4, 7–9, 15, 17, 20, 22–24 were viewed. The presented restoration examples and error maps provide qualitative support, while raw pixels, selection procedures, confidence intervals and independent reruns are unavailable. Other image panels were read through captions but not individually visually certified.
# Overall impact and state

The two false equivalences require local mathematical and specification corrections. The proposed architecture, its measured benchmark rankings and the usefulness of Fourier-domain interactions are not refuted by these checks. No later author correction was reviewed.

Abstract: The reported simulated magnetization improvements are not refuted by this review. Exact Bloch and noise calculations distinguish those proxies from equilibrium recovery and concentration precision. The reduction of total measurement time at matched abundance error remains unverified from the supplied evidence.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical verification of policy-based NMR sequencing
# Identity, scope and outcome

Rohan Shenoy, Evan A. Coleman, Hans Gaensbauer and Elsa A. Olivetti, Counting atoms faster: policy-based nuclear magnetic resonance pulse sequencing for atomic abundance measurement, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:54810–54824, OpenReview . This review covers the frozen 15-page publisher PDF, main Sections 1–4, Appendix A’s Bloch equations and Appendix B’s policy and PPO descriptions. All four result figures were actually viewed; page numbers below refer to PDF pages. An associated author repository was not identified in the frozen bounded source search. Author code was not executed.

The assessment is Needs Evidence. No specific numerical experiment is shown false. The results support improved simulated magnetization proxies, but do not establish a concentration-error-versus-total-time comparison at matched precision. Independent analytic checks explain why transverse suppression, peak signal and faster cycles are insufficient by themselves for that stronger inference. The paper’s own partial-observation and non-equilibrium qualifications are preserved.
# What the paper demonstrates

Section 2.2 fits effective spin frequencies and weights to laboratory caffeine spectra and samples longitudinal relaxation parameters. Section 3 uses PPO to maximize the running peak of \(M_x^2+M_y^2\), minimize transverse magnetization, and toggle the two policies. Figure 1 reports peak magnetization against concentration with errors across five training seeds and five environments. The learned curves increase more strongly than the baseline in the plotted concentration range. Figure 2 shows a lower transverse-magnetization trace for a spoiling policy in one environment. Figures 3–4 show state-action structure and repeated magnetization cycles.

Section 3.1 reports approximately \(16\%\) of baseline time to attain a peak. At face value this is a time-to-peak statement, not a matched-error metrological speedup. The plotted curves and text do not specify an inverse concentration estimator, held-out concentration prediction errors, detection limits, or a total-time curve at a fixed concentration confidence interval. Five seeds and multiple simulated scans are useful evidence; they are not absent. However, their plotted uncertainty does not directly provide the required calibration error after inversion or dependence across repeated toggled scans.
# Analytic checks that bound the interpretation
## Transverse spoiling versus equilibrium recovery

With the paper’s Bloch equations, \(B=(b,0,B_0)\) and fixed parameters, the states \[M^+=(0,0,M_0),\qquad M^-=(0,0,-M_0)\] have identical observed transverse magnetization and identical spoiling reward zero. Nevertheless, their distances from equilibrium are \(0\) and \(2|M_0|\), and \[\dot M_y^+=\gamma bM_0,\qquad
 \dot M_y^-=-\gamma bM_0.\] For the dimensionless diagnostic \(M_0=\gamma=T_1=T_2=B_0=1\), \(b=0.2\), the derivatives are \((0,0.2,0)\) and \((0,-0.2,2)\). Thus suppressing the observed transverse component alone does not determine longitudinal recovery or the next response. This is a check of the printed equations, not a claim that the learned policy reaches \(M^-\). It identifies the unmeasured variable needed to justify accelerated equilibrium recovery.

Crucially, p. 6 explicitly states that the shortened spoiling interval does not reset the system to equilibrium and considers partial resets; Appendix B, p. 13, explicitly says \(M_z,M_0,T_1,T_2,\gamma\) are masked and a non-recurrent policy need not reconstruct the dynamics. Consequently, partial observability is an acknowledged scope condition, not a newly discovered fatal flaw. A stable non-equilibrium measurement cycle may be useful if calibrated. The unresolved question is its accuracy and repeatability, not whether partial-reset control is categorically invalid.
## A peak reward is not a noise-free abundance statistic

In the stated Gaussian readout model, consider a simple special case with zero true transverse signal and independent noise components \(\epsilon_x,\epsilon_y\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) at each readout. Then \(Z=\epsilon_x^2+\epsilon_y^2\) is exponential with mean \(2\sigma^2\). For \(N\) independent readouts, \[\mathbb E\max_{1\leq j\leq N} Z_j=2\sigma^2 H_N,
 \qquad H_N=\sum_{j=1}^N j^{-1}.\] This follows by integrating \(1-(1-e^{-z/(2\sigma^2)})^N\), or by exponential order-statistic spacings. The independent calculation gives \(10.3748\sigma^2\) for \(N=100\) and \(14.9709\sigma^2\) for \(N=1000\), although abundance is unchanged. The paper’s nonzero, temporally dependent, changing-temperature trajectories need not obey this special-case formula. It is not an estimate of bias in Figure 1 and does not establish that PPO exploits noise. It shows why the actual peak acquisition window and a calibrated error estimate must accompany a peak-based precision claim. If all methods use fixed matched windows and calibration absorbs the noise, this concern may be resolved.
## Repeated scans and the square-root rule

Section 3.2 motivates repetitions through \(1/\sqrt n\) noise reduction. For equal-variance readouts \(X_i\), \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}
 +\frac{2}{n^2}\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).\] Independent measurements recover the stated rule. Equicorrelation \(\rho\) instead gives \(\sigma^2[\rho+(1-\rho)/n]\). For \(n=100\), \(\rho=0.1\) this is \(0.109\sigma^2\) rather than \(0.01\sigma^2\). This illustrative valid covariance model does not assert that the experimental covariance is positive or that electronic noise must become dependent after partial reset. Persistent physical state and independently sampled electronic noise are distinct. Actual scan covariance and estimator bias are needed to determine whether the accelerated cycle maintains the same precision per unit time.
# Algorithm and source limits

The printed PPO clipped surrogate, GAE recursion and actor/critic roles are consistent at their stated abstract level. The simulator observes fewer variables than its full Markov state; it is best interpreted as partially observed control. At \(0.2\) ms per control step, the 200-step toggle restriction corresponds to \(40\) ms. The source does not expose the exact ODE integrator, internal tolerances/substeps, fitted spin sets, pulse implementations or historical library commit. A claim of numerical instability from the control step alone would be unsupported, since an integrator may use smaller internal steps. Hardware cost and thermal feasibility, quantum footnote details, independent laboratory validation and external baseline provenance were not certified.
# Conclusion and evidence needed

The simulation results justify further study of the three-policy design. A stronger abundance-measurement claim needs an explicit concentration estimator evaluated on held-out concentrations, errors or confidence coverage against total acquisition time, and repeated-cycle calibration/covariance. Full-state recovery measurements are needed only for the stronger equilibrium-recovery interpretation; a calibrated partial-reset method need not restore equilibrium. No correction or failed experiment is asserted, and no later author revision was inspected.

Abstract: A connected seven-node counterexample disproves the general multi-cluster surrogate upper bound under the stated covariance condition. Static source inspection also identifies a relative-weight discrepancy and clipped propensities that change robustness to outcome-model misspecification. The overall initial assessment is Major; empirical performance and historical implementation impact remain unverified.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical review of Causal Graph Cut
# Identity, scope and outcome

Jin Zhu, Jingyi Li, Hongyi Zhou, Yinan Lin, Zhenhua Lin and Chengchun Shi, Balancing Interference and Correlation in Spatial Experimental Designs: A Causal Graph Cut Approach, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:79918–79937, OpenReview . The running PDF title places “Causal Graph Cut” first. This review covers the frozen 20-page PDF, main text and Appendices A–D, and selected static source files from , commit (26 May 2025). No author program was executed.

The assessment is Major: the multi-cluster extension’s claimed upper bound is false for an admissible connected spatial graph and positive definite covariance. This invalidates a central theoretical justification for the general algorithm, without disproving its empirical usefulness or the two-cluster proposition. Two additional version-specific implementation differences require clarification. No claim is made that this repository revision generated the published figures.
# P1: the general multi-cluster upper bound fails

Take the path graph \(1-2-3-4-5-6-7\), the partition \[C_1=\{1,2,3\},\quad C_2=\{4,5,6\},\quad C_3=\{7\},
 \qquad \Sigma=\tfrac12 I_7+\tfrac12\mathbf1\mathbf1^T.\] Its covariance eigenvalues are \(1/2\) (six times) and \(4\). Every distinct-pair covariance is \(\rho=1/2\), so Assumption 2 holds with equality, including a stronger interpretation comparing every neighboring pair with every nonneighbor. All clusters and the whole graph are connected. Take independent Bernoulli-\(1/2\) cluster treatments, constant covariates, a Gaussian residual vector with this covariance, independent of the treatments, and, for example, \(g_i(A)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}A_j\). Assumption 1 and the oracle-nuisance premise of Appendix B.1 then hold. No estimated covariance, negative weight assumption or asymptotic approximation is needed.

The boundaries are \(\partial C_1=\{3\}\), \(\partial C_2=\{4,6\}\) and \(\partial C_3=\{7\}\). The nonzero ordered contributions to \(J\) are \[(j,k)=(1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2):\qquad 3\rho,3\rho,3\rho,\rho.\] Thus \(J=10\rho=5\). The only cut edges are \((3,4)\) and \((6,7)\), giving \[U=\frac{14}{3}(2\rho)=\frac{14}{3}<5=J.\] At \(N=1\), the purported bound is \(112/3\), whereas \(I_1=40\). The independent script verifies the adjacency, boundaries, covariance eigenvalues and all 40 ordered triples satisfying the literal premise of Assumption 2. As a separate consistency check, enumerating all eight treatment assignments gives oracle variance \(112\), identical to Appendix B.1’s overlap-count formula. Here \(SC=52\) and the remaining \(I_2=20\); the bound failure concerns \(I_1\) itself and is not caused by omitting \(I_2\).

The two-cluster proof on p. 17 naturally produces the factor \(|C_j|+|C_k|\). It equals \(R\) when there are two clusters, but need not equal or be bounded by \(2R/m\) for arbitrary partitions. Equal-size clusters would remove this particular counterexample; neither the general definition nor the described unconstrained clustering imposes that condition. The example even satisfies \(m=3\le 7^{2/3}\), the stated search limit. “Balanced design” on p. 15 explicitly refers to treatment probability \(p=1/2\), not equal cluster cardinalities.

Impact and repair. Section 3.2 explicitly delegates the general surrogate to Appendix A, so this is a failure of the algorithm’s stated theoretical derivation. Restricting admissible cluster sizes or proving another valid bound would require a corresponding algorithmic change or a narrower claim. No general replacement theorem is certified here. The subsequent selection by the exact oracle MSE may still choose a useful candidate; it does not make the candidate-generation bound true. The reported numerical comparisons remain unreproduced, rather than refuted.
# P2: the public cut weights differ from the printed weights

In , `compute_similarity` constructs \[S=(R/m)\max(V,0)\odot(W+I)-V,\qquad L=\operatorname{diag}(S\mathbf1)-S.\] For cross-cluster off-diagonal pairs this uses \((R/m)V^+_{ii'}W_{ii'}-V_{ii'}\), while Appendix A uses \((2R/m)V^+_{ii'}W_{ii'}-V_{ii'}\). At \(m=2\), the discrepancy is likewise \(R/2\) versus the main text’s \(R\). Diagonal self-weights cancel from \(L\); they cannot supply the missing factor. Uniformly scaling the Laplacian cannot repair the relative coefficient, since the negative \(V\) term is unchanged. The active `graph_cut_algo` calls this function and `multi_graph_cut` calls that routine for each \(m>1\).

This is a Minor, version-specific implementation discrepancy. It changes the optimized relaxation, but the code also ranks candidates with the exact overlap-count objective in . That downstream step is favorable counterevidence against automatically inferring failed experiments. The inspected revision and published experimental runs are not linked by executable provenance. Clarifying the intended coefficient and releasing the actual run configuration are necessary before assigning historical impact.
# P3: clipped propensities alter the advertised unbiasedness

The active pooled and local branches of `SemiEstimator.compute_tau` in call `propensity_score_smooth`, rather than the adjacent commented-out exact score. In `ClusterDesign`, the indexed branch floors the known exposure probability at \(0.125\). Equation (1), by contrast, uses the exact probability. The distinction matters when the regression function is misspecified, even with independent training data.

For a region whose neighborhood touches four independently assigned clusters, let \(Y=\prod_{j=1}^4 A_j\) and let the fitted nuisance function be identically zero. The all-treated exposure probability is \(1/16\), the all-control outcome is zero, and the true all-treated versus all-control effect is one. Direct enumeration of the sixteen assignments yields \[\mathbb E\widehat\tau_{\rm exact}=\frac{1/16}{1/16}=1,
 \qquad \mathbb E\widehat\tau_{\rm clipped}=\frac{1/16}{1/8}=\tfrac12.\] Thus the version’s clipped estimator does not inherit unbiasedness under arbitrary regression misspecification from a known randomization probability. This is a Minor implementation/theory mismatch, not a counterexample to the paper’s exact-probability oracle estimator. Correct nuisance regression can remove this particular bias; clipping may deliberately trade bias for variance. Its frequency and effect in the historical runs are unknown. A documented unclipped analysis or an explicit clipped-estimator analysis would resolve the mismatch.
# Preserved qualifications and coverage limits

The main text expressly treats negative eigenvalues when choosing eigenvectors (p. 8); that issue was not ignored. Appendix D expressly acknowledges potentially non-negligible \(I_2\). Appendix B.1 assumes known \(g_i\), whereas p. 9 discusses empirical results without cross-fitting and Appendix C.3 describes an optional cross-fitted construction. Those distinctions prevent treating the oracle variance identity as a universal finite-sample identity for every fitted implementation. The public estimator does use folds; the pooled branch splits concatenated rows. Independent replicate-level separation and the adaptive history procedure have not been certified here.

Figures 1, 3–9 were actually inspected on pages 5, 7–9 and 20. Their plotted MSE trends support the reported simulated comparisons qualitatively; no digitized confidence-interval reconstruction was attempted. Figure 2’s caption and discussion were read, but its pixels are outside the visual coverage. The real-data-based experiment is a simulator calibrated from historical data; Appendix C.2 estimates its reference ATE by 1,000 Monte Carlo days. Raw trajectories, seeds, uncertainty of that reference and historical code correspondence were not established. External cited proofs and later revisions were not certified. The counterexample and diagnostic expectations are independent small calculations, not reruns of author experiments.
# Reproducibility and roles

The matching directory contains the independent check script and its actual output, source and code hashes, coverage, findings, compiler logs and page-level visual records. Author programs were not executed. The source PDF SHA-256 is . Separate assigned GPT-6 Astra / Max units performed the initial review and the subsequent independent source-based check recorded in the verification files. Scientific adjudication remains pending; human reviews are empty.

Abstract: The Kronecker transform and inverse-transpose implementation pass independent algebraic checks, and the main accuracy averages are internally consistent. The historical basis for the advertised end-to-end latency remains unresolved: the recommended timing script measures one layer, while full-model dense FP16 cache storage at the headline batch size exceeds the stated device capacity. The initial assessment is Needs Evidence.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical review of FlatQuant
# Identity, scope and outcome

Yuxuan Sun, Ruikang Liu, Haoli Bai and colleagues, FlatQuant: Flatness Matters for LLM Quantization, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:57587–57613, OpenReview . The frozen 27-page PDF and its embedded appendices were read for the transformation, calibration, accuracy and latency claims. Relevant code was statically inspected at , commit (25 November 2025). No author code, calibration or GPU benchmark was executed.

The assessment is Needs Evidence, principally for the interpretation of the reported end-to-end speedups. The README-recommended timing program measures one Transformer layer, and a dense full-model FP16 cache at the headline batch size exceeds the stated GPU’s memory. The historical measurement configuration has not been established. The central Kronecker equivalence passes independent numerical checks, and the main accuracy advantage is supported by the printed tables within their stated evaluation scope.
# Checks of the mathematical construction

With row-major vectorization, the printed identity is correct: \[\operatorname{vec}_r(V)(P_1\otimes P_2)
 =\operatorname{vec}_r(P_1^TVP_2).\] Consequently, applying \(P=P_1\otimes P_2\) to an activation row and \(P^{-T}\) to a weight row preserves \(XW^T\) before quantization. An independent NumPy calculation used nonsymmetric invertible factors of sizes \(2\) and \(3\), three activation rows and four weight rows. Maximum absolute errors were \(8.9\times10^{-16}\) for the forward reshape identity, \(5.6\times10^{-17}\) for the inverse-transpose weight identity, and \(1.8\times10^{-15}\) for the resulting linear output. These checks test the transpose convention rather than relying only on orthogonal matrices, where mistakes can be hidden.

Static inspection agrees: `kronecker_matmul` in right-multiplies by the second factor and left-multiplies by the first factor’s transpose after reshaping. The SVD parameterization returns \(U D V^T\) or \(U D^{-1}V^T\) for the inverse-transpose weight path, as required. Its diagonal is trained directly; invertibility requires nonzero entries. Neither the paper nor this inspection establishes uniform conditioning during training, and no singular training trajectory was observed or claimed.

The attention code applies the query/key pair of inverse-transpose and forward transforms after RoPE, preserving dot products in exact arithmetic. It merges value transforms with output weights and folds down-projection scaling into the up projection. Targeted static inspection therefore did not establish an algebraic failure in these mechanisms. The fused Triton kernel’s main path performs two matrix products followed by scale computation, rounding, clamping and INT4 packing. This confirms the presence of a fused implementation, not its numerical accuracy on all shapes or a measured speedup.

For \(n=n_1n_2\), factor storage is \(n_1^2+n_2^2\ge2n\), and transform arithmetic is proportional to \(n(n_1+n_2)\). The square-factor bounds in Section 3.1 follow. Exhaustive divisor checks give \((64,64)\) for \(4096\) and \((64,128)\) for \(8192\). For \(11008\) the unrestricted closest pair is \((86,128)\); Appendix C.6 instead states \((64,172)\) for its intermediate dimension. This is a configuration distinction to preserve when reproducing Figure 5, not evidence that its measured timing is false.
# Accuracy and scope of the flatness evidence

Recomputing the six LLaMA-3-70B task scores in Table 2 gives \(79.945\) for FP16, \(79.0133\) for FlatQuant–RTN, \(71.6567\) for SpinQuant–GPTQ and \(65.6633\) for SpinQuant–RTN. The displayed averages are consistent with rounding of underlying scores. The stated \(0.94\%\) loss is a difference of percentage points between displayed averages; the relative drop is about \(1.18\%\). FlatQuant–RTN exceeds the displayed SpinQuant–GPTQ average by \(7.35\) points and SpinQuant–RTN by \(13.35\) points. Thus the abstract’s approximate \(7.5\%\) comparison should be tied to a specified baseline and unit, but the sizeable table advantage survives this clarification. No paired significance test or benchmark rerun was performed.

The paper supplies useful ablations, including learnable transforms, scaling, clipping, calibration data and lower-bit settings. In particular, Appendix C.5 compares three calibration datasets, so a claim that calibration sensitivity was wholly unexamined would be incorrect. Conversely, Appendix C.6 explicitly says that Figure 5’s perplexity experiment quantizes only the last Transformer block. Its weak sensitivity to factor size is not a whole-model ablation across factor sizes. This also limits the broad expressivity interpretation in Appendix C.9: general invertible matrices are not all single Kronecker products. For example, \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,2)\) cannot be a \(2\times2\) by \(2\times2\) Kronecker product, because its two nonzero diagonal blocks are not proportional.

The flatness metric \(f(d)=\|d-\|d\|_2\mathbf1/\sqrt n\|_2\) is scale-sensitive under positive rescaling: \(f(cd)=c f(d)\) for \(c>0\). For \(d=(1,2,4)\) it equals \(2.22699\), while \(f(d/10)=0.222699\) without changing relative channel imbalance. Figure 7’s co-decline with training loss is therefore descriptive evidence, not an isolated causal test of distribution shape. No universal theorem equating flatness with quantization quality is assumed. The actual accuracy and calibration-loss results remain relevant independent evidence. Appendix B.1’s displayed memory values imply a \(22.13\%\) reduction from FP32 inverse training to AMP–SVD, while the displayed times imply \(59.09\%\); the prose’s joint “50%” characterization should not replace those measured quantities.
# P1: the end-to-end latency interpretation needs provenance

Section 4.3 and Appendix C.8 call the measurements end-to-end speedups on an RTX 3090, with 2,048 prompt tokens, 256 decoding tokens and batch size up to 64. Figure 4 reports \(2.30\times\) prefill and \(1.76\times\) decoding at batch 64. In the inspected release, the README directs the user to . That file extracts `model.model.layers[0]`, deletes the rest of the model and times that layer on random hidden states. Its cache constructor fixes `n_layers=1`. Its function named `run_e2e` runs prefill plus decoding for the same single layer. Embeddings, remaining layers and the output head are outside that timing.

An independent capacity calculation provides a second reason to request the exact measurement protocol. For ordinary dense independent-sequence FP16 KV storage, with \(L=32\) layers, \(32\) KV heads of dimension \(128\), batch \(B=64\) and context \(S\), storage is \[M_{\rm KV}=2\,LBS(32)(128)(2\,\text{bytes}).\] This is \(64\) GiB at \(S=2048\) and \(72\) GiB at \(S=2304\), before model weights and temporary buffers. The official Meta implementation’s default architecture has width 4096, 32 layers and 32 heads, with KV heads defaulting to attention heads. NVIDIA lists 24 GB for RTX 3090. These primary-source checks are cited below. For one layer the final cache is only \(2.25\) GiB, consistent with the recommended benchmark’s scope. This is a capacity argument under explicitly stated storage assumptions, not a measured out-of-memory event.

Alternatives and limiting evidence. Layerwise extrapolation, microbatching, offloading or shared-prefix storage could change memory requirements and timing. None can be assumed from the reported batch number alone. A later does contain whole-model calls, and describes real-quantization additions and points to an earlier revision for closer original-paper results. That earlier revision was not in the frozen source subset and was not retrieved. These facts rule out claiming that the authors had no whole-model implementation or that the currently inspected layer script necessarily generated the historical figures. Table 20 separately and explicitly labels its memory experiment as single-layer; that experiment is not misrepresented here.

Impact and resolution. The public layer measurement supports an operator/layer speed comparison. It does not by itself establish the claimed full-model latency at batch 64 on the stated device. This remains Needs Evidence, with historical provenance unresolved, rather than a fabricated benchmark allegation or a demonstrated failure of quantization. The useful resolution is the exact commit, command, number of resident layers, batching/offload/cache policy and raw per-stage timings for Figure 4. Alternatively, the claim can be labeled as a layer benchmark or a stated extrapolation. The accuracy tables and Kronecker algebra do not depend on this missing timing evidence.
# Coverage and sources

Main Sections 1–5 and the mathematical, implementation, experiment and limitation discussions in Appendices A–E were inspected. Relevant source images on pages 3–4, 7–9, 14–15, 21–22, 24, 26–27 were actually viewed, including Figures 1–11 and 16–21 where present. Figure panels on p. 25 and all raw plotting arrays were not visually/digitally certified. Table 6 was sampled for the profiling context rather than recomputed row by row. Code inspection was targeted to transformation, calibration, integration, fusion and timing paths; it does not cover all 97 acquired files, every architecture, low-level CUDA correctness or deployment checkpoints. Raw logits, calibration randomness and historical timing logs remain unverified.

The two supplementary read-only web checks on 25 October 2026 were NVIDIA’s official RTX 3090 specifications (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/graphics-cards/30-series/rtx-3090-3090ti/) and Meta’s official Llama model source (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/meta-llama/llama/main/llama/model.py), specifically `ModelArgs` and the attention cache shapes. These support the hardware limit and architectural diagnostic, not the author’s historical run configuration. The gated Hugging Face configuration could not be read and was not bypassed.
# Reproducibility and roles

The matching directory contains the independent check script and its actual output, source and code hashes, coverage, findings, compiler logs and page-level visual records. report: Abstract: The displayed experiments favor AoT-O3 in both accuracy and average reasoning steps. Independent arithmetic identifies incorrect summary ranges and a local environmental-figure inconsistency. The headline 80 percent reduction and translation from steps to tokens or runtime need additional evidence. Reward and small-sample checks clarify the conclusions without alleging a failed historical implementation.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical review of AoT-O3
# Identity, scope and outcome

Bilgehan Sel, Lifu Huang, Naren Ramakrishnan, Ruoxi Jia and Ming Jin, LLMs Can Reason Faster Only If We Let Them, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:53827–53842, OpenReview . The frozen 16-page publisher PDF was read for Sections 1–6 and Appendices A–B. All three figures and the two tables were actually viewed. Page anchors below are physical PDF pages, checked against individual-page extraction. No associated author repository was identified by the supplied bounded source search; the custom trainer was unavailable and no author code was executed.

The initial assessment is Minor, with unresolved evidence requests. Table 2 supports the direction of improvement in all nine AoT-O3 versus AoT-SFT comparisons. Its arithmetic does not match several numerical summaries, and the headline \(80\%\) cannot be reconstructed from the supplied aggregate results. Steps, tokens, latency and energy must be kept distinct. The reward construction has a coherent trajectory-average interpretation, but the implementation of that objective and the statistical precision of the claimed improvements remain unverified.
# P1: Correct the quantitative summaries and identify the headline comparison
Table 2 on p. 8 labels solution length as the average number of reasoning steps. For each model and task, computing \(100(1-\ell_{\rm O3}/\ell_{\rm SFT})\) gives:
Task | Gemma2-2B | Llama3-1B | Llama3-3B

Thus the Game of X range is \(51.3\)–\(69.6\%\), not the printed \(51.3\)–\(62.4\%\); N-Puzzle is \(27.8\)–\(52.6\%\), not \(27.8\)–\(46.0\%\). Game of X accuracy gains are \(15\), \(17\) and \(16\) percentage points, not the stated range of \(11\)–\(17\). These discrepancies are too large to be explained by rounding one-decimal step counts. The displayed Word-Ladder example \(26.1\to13.8\) correctly gives \(47.1\%\).

The maximum displayed reduction is \(69.5925\%\), from \(31.9\) to \(9.7\) steps. Neither the main results nor the experimental appendix supplies an aggregate comparison yielding the abstract and conclusion’s “up to \(80\%\)”. It could refer to an unreported subgroup, an individual instance, another baseline, or a token metric; none should be guessed. This is an unresolved numerical provenance request rather than proof that every possible \(80\%\) comparison is false. Either provide its baseline, denominator and measurements or tie the headline explicitly to the displayed maximum. Correcting the prose leaves all nine lower step means and higher accuracy point estimates intact, so this is not a demonstrated failure of the main empirical direction.
# Reward and algorithm checks

Let a correct generated trajectory have \(n\) transitions, of which \(k\) belong to the extracted successful path. Under the natural uniform interpretation of \(\mathbb E_{T_i\in y}\) in Eq. (5), Eq. (2) yields the trajectory objective \[\overline V(y)=\max(1-\alpha n,\beta)+\kappa k/n,
 \qquad \overline V(y)=-1\ \text{for incorrect }y.\] Appendix B.3.2 gives \(\alpha=0.02\), \(\beta=-0.5\), \(\kappa=0.2\). Every correct trajectory therefore receives more than \(-1\). For fixed \(k\), the objective decreases with \(n\) before the cutoff; the base term is flat from \(n=75\) onward. With \(\kappa=0\), it supplies no further length discrimination in that region. This checks the intended incentives, rather than assuming an erroneous sum of positive step rewards: p. 6 explicitly warns against that sum and Eq. (5) uses an expectation.

Per-trajectory ordering is not a theorem that the optimized policy must preserve accuracy. For example, a certain correct trajectory with \((n,k)=(75,4)\) has reward \(-0.48933\), while a policy correct with probability \(0.8\) and \((n,k)=(4,4)\) on success has expected reward \(0.8(1.12)+0.2(-1)=0.696\). This is a diagnostic of the unregularized objective, not a claim about the trained models; the KL penalty can alter policy preferences, and Table 2 actually reports higher accuracy. The useful interpretation is a tradeoff whose empirical accuracy needs evaluation, as the paper does, rather than a mathematical guarantee.

Equation (3) relates \(\alpha\) to context size \(w\), while \(n\) is measured in transitions. The implemented limit should therefore be expressed in transitions or accompanied by a token-to-transition conversion. Treating 2048 tokens as 2048 transitions would yield \((1-\beta)/2048=0.0007324\), very different from \(0.02\); this conditional calculation does not show that the authors made that substitution.

Appendix B specifies a custom TRL RLOO trainer with “minor but crucial differences”, four samples per problem, KL coefficient \(0.1\), and a value-loss coefficient \(0.5\). It gives no executable version or complete gradient pseudocode. For a trajectory-average objective, the score-function estimator uses \(\overline V(y)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\), with a suitable baseline. A different per-transition weighting requires its own derivation. The available description does not establish which estimator was used. The value-loss entry, transition/token masking, normalization, reward parser and stopping rules need the actual trainer or precise pseudocode; no incorrect implementation is inferred from its absence. The printed 50 total RL steps and 50 warmup steps also warrant the exact scheduler configuration, without assuming it is impossible to train.
# What the experimental evidence establishes

Appendix B.2 reports 100 test examples per benchmark. Differences of \(2\)–\(5\) percentage points correspond to only \(2\)–\(5\) net successes if each reported percentage is one deterministic evaluation. The paired outcomes are unavailable. Enumerating all overlap counts compatible with Table 2 gives a two-sided exact McNemar \(p\) range of \(0.5\)–\(0.9111\) for Word-Ladder \(59\to61\), and \(0.015625\)–\(0.4426\) for N-Puzzle \(66\to73\). These are feasible ranges, not computed significance tests on the original outcomes. They illustrate why the margins alone do not establish statistical precision; neither pooled task independence nor repeated training seeds is assumed. The directional results remain valid descriptive comparisons.

The denominator of the length average needs clarification. Appendix B.2 imposes Manhattan distance at least 15 for N-Puzzle. If one reported step is one legal tile move, any successful solution requires at least 15 moves, whereas the Llama3-1B AoT-O3 mean is 14.2. This is compatible with averaging all attempts, including short failures: at a \(68\%\) success rate the elementary unconditional lower bound is only \(0.68(15)=10.2\). It would be incompatible with an average restricted to valid single-move paths. Hence this is a request for the averaging and truncation rules, not an allegation of impossible trajectories. Report lengths for all attempts and for matched successes, alongside generated token counts.

The table measures steps, not measured tokens or elapsed time. A transition includes textual state descriptions and thinking; its token count need not remain constant. No latency benchmark or energy measurement is given. Figure 2 demonstrates a shift of the generated-step distribution with demonstration length, but does not isolate a causal token-to-time relationship. Section 3.1’s random-demonstration comparison also lacks a matched gold-demonstration row in Table 1; the cited literature and original prompting/training runs were not independently reproduced. These limits do not erase the presented table improvements.
# P2: A local inconsistency in the environmental illustration

The arithmetic in Appendix A is consistent with its stated illustrative assumptions: \(400\times10^9\) tokens per day at \(9.72\times10^{-7}\) kWh/token gives \(141.912\) GWh/year, and \(30\%\) and \(50\%\) reductions give \(42.5736\) and \(70.956\) GWh/year. These are conditional calculations, not measurements of actual deployment consumption. Appendix A explicitly discusses fixed overhead, training cost and rebound effects; those qualifications should be retained.

Figure 3 on p. 14 lists coal equivalents \(17{,}366{,}480\) and \(2{,}932{,}036\) pounds for carbon savings \(15{,}634\) and \(26{,}057\) tonnes. Under a common conversion factor, the second should be about \(1.66669\) times the first, not \(0.16883\) times it. Holding the first value fixed would give approximately \(28{,}944{,}504\) pounds. That is a consistency diagnostic, not an independently verified EPA conversion. The original calculator inputs should determine the corrected figure. This local apparent transcription/conversion error has no bearing on the RL accuracy results.
# Resolution and remaining coverage

P1’s numerical ranges can be repaired directly from Table 2; the \(80\%\) statement, token/latency interpretation and length denominator require additional evidence. P2 needs the source calculator values. Author adoption and independent repair verification are unknown. The most useful reproducibility additions are exact model identifiers, data split and generator seeds, valid-plan checks, trajectory-level outcomes and the custom trainer revision. None of the missing artifacts is evidence of fabrication or historical implementation failure.

Main pp. 1–8, impact text p. 9, and Appendices A–B pp. 13–16 were read. Source pages 1, 2, 4–8 and 13–16 were visually checked. External reference claims, prior-art priority, original GPT-4 experiments, dataset overlap, learned checkpoints and later author revisions were not independently certified. OpenReview’s separately hosted attachments remained unavailable in source preparation; the embedded appendix was available and inspected.

Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical review of BRIDGE
# Identity, scope and outcome

Hao Li, Yu-Hao Huang, Chang Xu, Viktor Schlegel, Renhe Jiang, Riza Batista-Navarro, Goran Nenadic and Jiang Bian, BRIDGE: Bootstrapping Text to Control Time-Series Generation via Multi-Agent Iterative Optimization and Diffusion Modeling, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:34742–34773, OpenReview . Main pp. 1–9 and the applicable appendices on pp. 14–32 were read; all seventeen figures were inspected as rendered source pages. References were not independently certified. Anchors use physical PDF pages.

The independently checked assessment is Major for the invalid published core inference algorithm, with additional Minor findings and unresolved protocol and historical-version evidence. The paper supplies useful positive generation results, but the printed sampler, metric definitions and bootstrap significance procedure require corrections. Inspection of the public repository is substantial counterevidence to treating the sampler’s documentation error as an implemented historical failure. Neither the original experiment outputs nor their exact execution revision was available; no author program was run.
# P1: Algorithm 2 repeatedly assigns an estimate of the clean sample to the next noisy state

Equation reference: eq:printed. Algorithm 1 on p. 20 defines the standard cumulative-noise forward process \[x_n=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_n}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_n}\epsilon.\] Algorithm 2, line 6 on that page, assigns \[
 \widehat x_{n-1}=\frac{\widehat x_n-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_n}\widetilde\epsilon_n}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_n}}.\] This is the usual reconstruction of \(x_0\), not a complete transition to noise level \(n-1\). The loop then treats it as the latter. This is a substantive pseudocode error, rather than an extraction artifact: the formula was checked in the rendered PDF.

A small analytic diagnostic takes \(x_0\sim N(0,1)\), a fixed uninformative condition, and the exact square-loss noise predictor \(\epsilon^*(x_n,n)=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_n}x_n\). All forward marginals are \(N(0,1)\). Equation [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) multiplies \(x_n\) by \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_n}\). Starting from unit Gaussian noise, its final variance is therefore \(\prod_{n=1}^N\bar\alpha_n\). With \(\alpha_n=0.99\) and \(N=100\), it is \(0.99^{5050}=9.07\times10^{-23}\), rather than one. An exact Gaussian reverse transition \(x_{n-1}=\sqrt{\alpha_n}x_n+\sqrt{1-\alpha_n}z\) preserves unit variance. This counterexample concerns the literal printed algorithm under its own noise-prediction interpretation; it is not a simulation of the trained BRIDGE network.

The pinned public implementation materially limits the implication. At repository revision dated 2026-10-19, , lines 187–194, computes the clean estimate and then adds the previous-level coefficient, direction term and stochastic term. The DDPM path in , including lines 220–256 and 714–767, also has posterior coefficients and noise. The main generation test helpers (lines 80, 127, 254 and 333) request DDPM sampling; the plot helper at line 200 requests DDIM. Thus the missing transition is present in current code; there is no basis to claim it was absent in the historical runs. Replace Algorithm 2 with the actual sampler, specify the noise schedule and variance choice, and identify the experiment revision. The printed core inference specification is therefore assessed as Major: a necessary generation algorithm fails even with the exact noise predictor. A standard repair and survival of other results do not validate that algorithm. Current-code counterevidence prevents extending this conclusion to the historical implementation or all reported experiments; that separate question remains unresolved.
# P2: The documented MDD and the implemented histogram scores are different quantities

Appendix G, pp. 23–24, defines \(\mathrm{MDD}(P,Q)=\sum_x|P(x)-Q(x)|\) for probability distributions. On a discrete probability interpretation, it is bounded by two, whereas Table 1 includes values such as Solar \(375.531\). This does not make the table impossible: the pinned code implements a different, unbounded density-based quantity.

In , `HistoLoss` (lines 107–148) forms per-time histograms and averages absolute differences of bin densities, without multiplying by bin width. For two bins with probabilities \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((1,0)\), the probability \(L^1\) distance is one, but the mean density difference for width \(0.001\) is 500. The result depends on units, preprocessing, bins and the aggregation convention. The numerical table can be consistent with this definition. Publish the actual formula and preprocessing, or recompute a probability-distance metric; do not compare the reported magnitude with a theoretical probability-distance bound.

There is also a concrete limitation in the current KL estimator. Lines 10–16 construct real-data bin edges, then call `numpy.histogram` with `density=True` for generated samples on those edges and pass the result to `scipy.stats.entropy`. Generated values outside the real range are discarded and the in-range histogram is renormalized. An independent calculation with one percent matching in-range samples and 99 percent samples at 100, while the real data lie in \([0,1]\), gives KL \(8.7\times10^{-17}\). The score can consequently miss arbitrarily large out-of-range mass. This is a property of the inspected estimator, not evidence that the paper’s generated samples actually have those outliers. The MDD implementation need not have the same blind spot because its generated counts use the total sample count.

Retain overflow bins or a declared common support, report the excluded fraction, and specify smoothing and normalization. Re-evaluate original outputs to determine whether rankings change. Current-code metric behavior is verified; identity with the historical evaluator and any effect on the paper’s rankings remain unresolved.
# P3: Bootstrap replicates are not additional independent experimental units

Appendix M, p. 27, states that OWA is resampled 1000 times and a \(t\)-test is conducted on the resulting subset. If the resampled OWA values are treated as independent observations in an ordinary \(t\)-test, the procedure divides uncertainty by approximately \(\sqrt{1000}\) a second time. Bootstrap replication estimates a sampling distribution; increasing its Monte Carlo resolution does not increase the original number of test series.

An independent diagnostic uses 20 paired differences, ten each of \(-0.9\) and \(1.1\). The original paired \(t\)-test has \(p=0.668\). With seed 359, 1000 bootstrap means have percentile interval \([-0.3,0.5]\), while a one-sample \(t\)-test treating those means as the sample gives \(p=7.70\times10^{-38}\). This is a deliberately constructed example, not a reconstruction of Table 14 or a claim that its true conclusions reverse. It shows why the stated procedure cannot by itself validate those significance marks.

For OWA, resample the appropriate original series units jointly across methods, recompute the full statistic and its normalizing reference within the declared protocol, and use a valid interval or null-calibrated test. Account for dependence where series are not independent and state the multiple-comparison policy. If the actual test instead used a valid bootstrap tail probability or another correction, provide the implementation and amend the description. The direct SMAPE/MASE tests mentioned on the same page are a separate procedure and are not invalidated by this bootstrap argument. Original paired errors and the test script are required to verify the significance claims.
# Current text-conditioning code and unresolved evaluation details

The available exposes a `description` argument, but both `_predict_llmtime` (lines 102–140) and `_predict_promptcast` (143–182) never read it. Static AST inspection independently confirms zero loads in either function. Thus this wrapper, with all other inputs fixed, cannot measure a prediction change caused by changing that text argument. This is a verified local implementation limitation; it does not establish that this wrapper produced Table 5. The inspected entry point also permits a different predictor arrangement. Supply the original text-conditioning call path before attributing the reported refinement improvements to this public wrapper; wire the argument into the model request if that wrapper is intended to reproduce them.

The paper explicitly distinguishes optimizing description templates on AirPassengers/Sunspots from filling the frozen templates with per-instance statistics in other domains. Conditioning a time-series generator on statistics of the desired target is part of the stated task. It is not, by itself, forecasting leakage. However, the separately described zero-shot forecasting evaluation and its future-statistic examples on pp. 15–16 require an information-cutoff account: which target-window statistics were available to the prediction prompt, and which windows were reserved for evaluation after template refinement. The current confirms per-window statistic filling, but cannot establish the historical split or the causal source of Table 5 gains. Conditional generation, held-out-domain transfer and forecasting must each state their information sets.

Human ranking also needs its exact candidate pool. Table 3 gives HE-Rank 4.2 for the no-text variant on Traffic and Taxi. If the pool is the three displayed variants plus ground truth, a mean ordinal rank cannot exceed four. Appendix H says “different model settings” and does not enumerate the pool, so additional unlisted candidates or a score-versus-rank convention could explain 4.2. This is an evidence request, not proof of invalid annotations. Provide candidate counts, rubric, number of annotators and items, raw rankings and aggregation; distinguish HE-Rank from HE-Mixed, which adds three distractors. The prose claim of an improvement over three points for Traffic and Pedestrian also does not follow from the displayed HE-Rank differences of 2.8 and 1.1.
# Positive checks, coverage and resolution

The full model improves JFTSD over the no-text variant in all twelve displayed domains, and beats both ablations in eleven; Rain has a slightly better no-prototype value. Against external baselines, Table 1 gives the best MDD in ten domains and best KL in eleven, so a count of eleven must identify the metric. Table 5’s four initial-to-refined relative improvements are \(17.06\%\), \(18.06\%\), \(18.77\%\) and \(14.77\%\); these support the general improvement direction, with the last slightly below the prose’s \(15\%\). These arithmetic checks neither substitute for uncertainty estimates nor imply that domain averages are independent replicates.

All source figures, including the prototype panels on pp. 28–32, were viewed. They illustrate conditional sample behavior but cannot establish distributional calibration from selected examples. Main text, Algorithms 1–2, description construction, model and dataset specifications, metrics, human evaluation, ablations and downstream evaluation were inspected. The selected public files cover text construction and refinement, evaluation metrics, the prototype module and the relevant diffusion sampling/loss paths. Eight additional files were retrieved through the authorized repository connector at the same pinned revision, with exact Git-blob and SHA-256 checks recorded. Large diffusion and utility files were inspected at the relevant functions, not certified in full. No original model training, author code execution, external literature replication, complete dataset audit, annotation audit or historical checkpoint verification occurred. Separately hosted OpenReview attachments were unavailable during source preparation; embedded appendices were available.

Correct the printed algorithm and metric specification, replace or clarify the OWA significance procedure, and connect the reproduction package to the historical run. The latter evidence requests are unresolved. Author adoption is unknown, and repairs beyond the demonstrated algebra and diagnostic examples have not been independently verified.
