Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical review of high-dimensional sequential prediction
# Identity, scope and outcome

Georgy Noarov, Ramya Ramalingam, Aaron Roth and Stephan Xie, High-Dimensional Prediction for Sequential Decision Making, ICML 2025, PMLR 267:46762–46783, OpenReview . The reviewed artifact is the frozen 22-page publisher PDF. Main pp. 1–9 and Appendices A–D, pp. 13–22, were read. The decisive formulas and algorithms were inspected in rendered physical pages. The paper is theoretical: there are no experimental figures, tables or reported training runs to replicate. The supplied bounded search did not identify author code; this is a scoped non-discovery.

The independently checked assessment is Major for the invalid core reductions in P1 and P2, with additional Minor corrections and evidence requests about exact rates and computational assumptions. A counterexample disproves the Appendix D candidate-set reduction under its stated disjointness assumption. That accelerated variant is separate from the general inner-loop algorithm. Main-text proofs also contain an invalid expectation identity and missing factors, but their principal bounds up to logarithms admit the explicit repairs below. Repairability and survival of other results do not validate those core derivations or lower their severity. These checks do not establish that all qualitative high-dimensional prediction and decision-making conclusions are false, nor do they certify every claimed optimal rate or priority claim.
# P1: Disjoint events need not cover the prediction space

Appendix D, p. 19, assumes binary events with \(\sum_E E(x,\widehat s)\leq1\). It retains one minimizer \(\widehat s^{*,E}\) from each active region and claims in Lemma D.4 that restricting to these points preserves the minimax problem. This omits the case in which no event is active.

Take \(S=[0,1]\), one event \(E(\widehat s)=\mathbf1[\widehat s\geq1/2]\), and positive weights \(q_+=3/4\), \(q_-=1/4\). The event is binary and disjoint, and its active region \([1/2,1]\) is nonempty, closed and convex, with an elementary separation oracle. The surrogate is \[u(\widehat s,s)=\tfrac12\mathbf1[\widehat s\geq1/2](\widehat s-s).\] Definition D.1 returns the unique active-region minimizer \(\widehat s^{*,E}=1/2\), so Algorithm 3 is restricted to \(P=\{1/2\}\). Its minimax value is \(\max_{s\in[0,1]}u(1/2,s)=1/4\). In the full problem, the point prediction \(\widehat s=0\) has payoff zero for every \(s\). Conversely \(s=0\) makes every payoff nonnegative, proving that the full minimax value is exactly zero. The gap is \(1/4\); a solution supported only on \(P\) cannot be \(\epsilon\)-optimal for \(\epsilon<1/4\). Any positive imbalance \(q_+>q_-\) gives the same obstruction, scaled accordingly.

An independently written linear program reproduces values \(0\), \(0.25\) and \(0\) for the full candidate set, the printed restricted set, and the set repaired by adding the null point. The analytic argument proves the continuum result, so the conclusion does not depend on discretization. Lemma D.4’s proposed mass transfer on p. 22 maps the full optimum \(\delta_0\) to total mass zero, exposing the precise failure: it is not a probability distribution. Its printed dominance inequality also has the minimization direction reversed.

One repair is to assume a genuine exhaustive partition. Another is to include an accessible representative of the region on which all original events vanish; its original surrogate payoff is identically zero. Finding such a representative and handling empty event regions require a stated oracle or additional geometric assumptions. Merely adding a new positively weighted event would change the game. Requiring a cover also narrows the theorem’s stated scope.

Remark D.2 needs a separate boundary qualification: lexicographic best-response cells need not be closed polytopes. On \([0,1]\), utilities \(u_1(s)=0\), \(u_2(s)=s\), with ties assigned to action 1, give the action-2 cell \((0,1]\). Minimizing a positive linear function on this cell has an unattained infimum. Closed-cell optimization, approximate feasible representatives and tie-breaking must be reconciled before claiming exact solutions to Definition D.1. The general Algorithm 1 allows discontinuous events and does not require this Appendix D reduction; therefore the counterexample is localized to the accelerated method, rather than a refutation of the main prediction algorithm. The broader repair and its bit-complexity guarantee remain unverified. P1 is Major because the accelerated contribution relies on a false minimax equivalence and an algorithm that fails its stated approximation guarantee; localization to an appendix does not reduce that defect to a minor one.
# P2: Repair the expectation and comparator steps in the decision reductions

Definition 2.2 defines \(\mathrm{Bias}_T(E)=\max_i\mathbb E|Z_{E,i}|\), where \[Z_{E,i}=\sum_{t=1}^T E(x_t,\widehat s_t)(\widehat s_{t,i}-s_{t,i}).\] The displayed calculation on p. 7 instead identifies this with \(\mathbb E\|Z_E\|_\infty\). These are different. If \(Z\) equals \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) with probability \(1/2\) each, then \(\max_i\mathbb E|Z_i|=1/2\), while \(\mathbb E\|Z\|_\infty=1\). This example is realizable with one round, \(S=[0,1]^2\), a fixed zero outcome and a randomized prediction; it refutes the identity, not the final theorem. Also, bounding expected regret to every fixed swap does not alone bound the expectation of the hindsight maximum over swaps.

Equation reference: eq:joint. The available proof structure permits a stronger, valid argument. Let \(Q_E=\sum_t E(x_t,\widehat s_t)^2\), \(\Lambda=\log(2d|\mathcal E|T)\) and \(U_T=\sum_t u_t(\widehat s_t,s_t)\). Keeping the realized \(Q_E\) until taking expectations, the outer-regret step gives, simultaneously over coordinates, \[
 |Z_{E,i}|\leq C\bigl(\Lambda+\sqrt{\Lambda Q_E}\bigr)+U_T.\] The residual \(U_T\) is common to every coordinate and event. Taking a maximum over coordinates before expectation is consequently valid on the right-hand side. Jensen’s inequality and the inner-game bound then yield \[\mathbb E\|Z_E\|_\infty
 \leq C\bigl(\Lambda+\sqrt{\Lambda n_T(E)}\bigr)+\mathbb E U_T.\] This argument supplies the missing stronger statement; it does not replace a maximum and expectation by an equality.

For a best-response action event \(E_a\), linearity and \(L\)-Lipschitzness give the pathwise inequality \[\mathrm{SwapReg}_T(u)\leq 2L\sum_{a=1}^K\|Z_{E_a}\|_\infty.\] It holds uniformly over all swaps, including the hindsight maximizing swap. Applying Lipschitzness to the event-weighted averages keeps arguments within the convex state space; homogeneity then gives the displayed cumulative expression. Since the action events partition rounds, \(\sum_a n_T(E_a)=T\). Thus, with the corrected inner-loop conventions, the proof yields \(O\bigl(L[K\Lambda+\sqrt{KT\Lambda}]\bigr)\). The factor two is also missing from the original two-term comparison, but has no effect on the asymptotic order.

Theorem 4.1’s proof on p. 9 similarly bounds the comparator’s utility error by one coordinate bias, omitting a factor of up to \(d\). With one round, all subsets available, true reward \(\mathbf1\in\mathbb R^d\), prediction zero and event always one, the difference between the two best fixed-action utility totals is \(d\), whereas the coordinate bias is one. A valid pathwise bound for a fixed conditioning function \(\xi\) is \[\mathrm{CReg}_T(\xi,i)\leq
 \sum_{e=1}^d|Z_{E_\xi,e}|+
 \sum_{e=1}^d|Z_{E_{e,\xi},e}|.\] Using [eq:joint] (#eq:joint) uniformly, with \(Q_E\leq T\), also handles the maximum over the finite conditioning collection. The corrected bound still has order \(\widetilde O(d\sqrt T)\). Thus the local intermediate inequality is false, but its repair preserves the advertised dimension order. These are proof repairs, not empirical tests or counterexamples to the final regret rates with logarithms retained. P2 is Major because the original main decision-making derivations contain invalid expectation and comparator steps. The stronger pathwise argument is a substantive replacement proof, not evidence that the printed proof was valid.
# P3: The displayed derivations retain logarithmic factors

Section 2.2 and Theorem 3.7 drop both the additive logarithm and the square-root logarithm from Theorem 2.4 while using ordinary \(O\), not \(\widetilde O\). The underlying experts theorem indeed contains these terms: the statement of Chen, Luo and Wei’s Theorem 2 was checked in the primary publisher PDF [Retained latex: \cite{chen}]; its full proof was not independently audited.

For multicalibration with \(m\) bins, summing the stated bounds and using Cauchy–Schwarz gives, for a fixed group, \[\mathbb E\mathrm{ECE}(G)
 =O\bigl(T/m+m\Lambda+\sqrt{mT\Lambda}\bigr),
 \qquad \Lambda=\log(2m|\mathcal G|T).\] The printed choice \(m=T^{1/3}\) therefore retains logarithms. Balancing with \(m\) of order \((T/\Lambda)^{1/3}\), using a suitable upper bound for \(\Lambda\), gives \[O\bigl(T^{2/3}\Lambda^{1/3}+T^{1/3}\Lambda^{2/3}\bigr).\] This establishes the exponent up to logarithmic factors, but does not establish the literal log-free headline rate from the supplied derivation. Likewise the swap calculation above retains \(K\Lambda\) and \(\sqrt{KT\Lambda}\). Amend the claims to state the retained factors or supply a sharper argument. No lower bound ruling out log-free rates is asserted here, and the general usefulness of polynomial-time event-unbiased prediction is not negated by this accounting issue. The rounding procedure should also be stated operationally: the adversary must commit before the current private draw is revealed, and the released discretized prediction and its corresponding event calculation need a consistent definition.
# Main algorithm checks and smaller corrections

The copycat inner-game idea is sound under the nonanticipating protocol of p. 4: for a fixed surrogate, \(u_t(s,s)=0\), and the payoff is linear in the adversary’s state. For \(M\) pre-update inner plays \(z_0,\ldots,z_{M-1}\) with respective gradients \(g_0,\ldots,g_{M-1}\), the valid identity is \[\max_{s\in S}\frac1M\sum_{\tau=0}^{M-1}u_t(z_\tau,s)
 =\frac1M\max_{s\in S}\sum_{\tau=0}^{M-1}\langle g_\tau,z_\tau-s\rangle.\] An independent scalar projected-gradient calculation with two threshold events and \(M=10{,}000\) gave both sides \(0.000689125\). It is an illustrative check of the identity, not author-code execution or a general algorithm benchmark.

Algorithm 1 samples \(t^2+1\) points including the initial point, but the proof averages \(t^2\) terms and mixes pre- and post-update indices. Make these indices consistent. The additional bounded-payoff point costs only \(O(t^{-2})\) when properly compared, so this is not evidence of a linear-bias failure. Also normalize the outer losses: \(E(\widehat s)(s_i-\widehat s_i)\) can lie in \([-2,2]\), whereas the stated experts primitive assumes \([-1,1]\); dividing by two and restoring the constant suffices. Replace a realized sum of squared events by its expectation only after applying Jensen.

The dimension dependence of the inner primitive can be made explicit. At a fixed outer round, put \(a_i=\sum_{\sigma,j}w_{\sigma,i,j}\), so \(\sum_i a_i=1\) and \(|g_i|\leq a_i\). The weighted norm \(\|z\|_a^2=\sum_i a_i z_i^2\) has state-space diameter at most two and dual gradient norm squared at most \(\sum_i g_i^2/a_i\leq1\). Weighted projected gradient descent therefore gives a dimension-independent \(O(\sqrt M)\) regret constant when that projection is available. Zero-weight coordinates can be removed from the norm after projecting the feasible set onto the positive-weight coordinates; a feasible lift must still be supplied for a general state space. On a box, any admissible values in those zero-weight coordinates suffice. With \(M=t^2\), this supplies \(\mathbb E U_T=O(\log T)\), as needed above. An unspecified generic OLO routine can instead have geometry-dependent constants; the implementable projection/optimization access to a general \(S\) should be declared. The simple box state space used for combinatorial rewards supports this construction directly.

Two small notation corrections were also verified. Footnote 1 on p. 4 says \(n_T(E)\) is at most the count of rounds where \(E=1\). For \(E\equiv1/2\), \(n_T(E)=T/4\) while that count is zero. The valid statements are \(n_T(E)\leq\mathbb E\sum_t E_t\) and \(n_T(E)\leq\mathbb E\#\{t:E_t>0\}\), with equality to the usual count for binary events. In Theorem C.3 on p. 17 the calibration condition should range over predicted values. As printed over true values, the one-round pair \(s_1=0\), \(\widehat s_1=1\) vacuously satisfies the written equality, but fails transparency for \(u(s)=s\). The surrounding term “fully calibrated” and the proof make the intended correction clear. Under the corrected calibration condition and the standing linear-utility assumption, the partition/coarsening arguments of C.3–C.8 are consistent.
# Information timing, repair scope and limitations

Section 2 explicitly lets the adversary see the prediction distribution before committing the state, and only then samples the realized prediction. This restriction is essential. Section 4 lists action commitment before reward production; specify that the current private action or realized public prediction is not revealed to the adversary before that commitment. If an adversary could see a realized singleton action, it could assign that action reward zero and the other reward one. The learner would get zero while the best fixed action gets at least \(T/2\), precluding the claimed no-regret guarantee. Exhaustive enumeration of all \(2^8\) action sequences verifies this diagnostic for \(T=8\). This stronger observation model is excluded by Section 2, so it is an interpretation warning, not a counterexample under the intended model.

Appendix D additionally needs an optimization-access and representation statement, including treatment of lower-dimensional feasible sets and precision. Bounded coefficient magnitude alone does not bound rational encoding length; an explicit rounding-error budget is required. These computational details were not independently completed. The null-event counterexample and core proof defects above are established; a fully repaired accelerated implementation and its general oracle runtime remain evidence requests.

All principal displayed proofs and relevant appendix algorithms were read. Source pp. 3–9 and 17–22 were actually viewed at legible resolution; the paper contains no source plots. Appendix A’s related-work discussion and the bibliography were not verified for priority or completeness. No source repository, executable implementation, experimental data or historical run was available to inspect. Author adoption is unknown. Independent checking is recorded in the verification files. The demonstrated corrections preserve the main reductions up to logarithmic factors under the stated primitive and timing assumptions; exact-rate and accelerated-method claims require the identified amendments.

Title: Verification of Joint Learning of EBMs and their Partition Function
# Paper and reviewed scope

This report concerns M. E. Sander, V. Roulet, T. Liu and M. Blondel, Joint Learning of Energy-based Models and their Partition Function, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 52778–52797, paper I25-43730 (0361). The reviewed publisher PDF has 20 pages; all page references below are one-based PDF pages, equal to its printed page numbers. The main formulation, Propositions 1–5, their Appendix C arguments, Algorithm 1, and the empirical interpretation in Sections 4–5 and Appendix A were read. Figures 1–3 and the relevant theorem pages were viewed. No relevant released implementation was available in the acquired packet. Separate OpenReview attachments were inaccessible during source preparation.
# Checked central reasoning

For a finite output set, let \(q_y>0\), \(Q=\sum_yq_y\) and \(Z=\sum_yq_y e^{g_y}\). The scalar objective in (13) is \[H(t)=t+Ze^{-t}-Q,\qquad H'(t)=1-Ze^{-t},\quad H''(t)=Ze^{-t}>0.\] Consequently \(t_* =\log Z\) and \(H(t_*)=\log Z+1-Q\). For the probability reference used in Algorithm 1, \(Q=1\), so eliminating \(t\) gives exactly the reduced MLE objective. More generally it changes only a term independent of the learned parameters. Moreover, \[H(t_*+d)-H(t_*)=d+e^{-d}-1\geq0.\] This verifies the decisive scalar step in Propositions 1–2. Continuity of \(g_y(x)\) and \(q_y(x)>0\), with finite \(Y\), makes this particular \(\log Z(x)\) continuous. In the finite-sum case each free \(v_i\) can be eliminated independently, even if \(g_w\) is nonlinear in \(w\). For linear \(g_w\), the Hessian of each exponential term is a nonnegative multiple of an outer product, confirming Proposition 5’s convexity claim. Unbiased sample averages in Algorithm 1 follow directly for finite \(Y\); interchanging differentiation with an unrestricted population expectation still requires integrability.

The finite check with \(q=(.2,.3,.5)\) and \(g=(-.7,.2,1.1)\) gives \(t_*=0.6769267884824374\), \(H(t_*)=t_*\) and total mass \(1\). It checks the formula, not stochastic-training convergence. The continuity argument in Appendix C.5 was traced through the root bracket, strict monotonicity and the bounded-subsequence argument. The sparsemax case \(f(u)=(u^2-1)/2\) has \((f_+^*)'(v)=[v]_+\), as required for the probability formula. The general statement is read with its stated strictly convex generator; it does not imply the broader auxiliary lemma below.
# Local finding
Problem 1 (Convexity alone does not justify the gradients in Lemma 1).

Claim and assumptions. Appendix C.1, p. 16, assumes only that \(\Omega_+\) is convex with domain in the positive-measure cone, sets \(\Omega_1=\Omega_++\iota_{\mathcal P_1(Y)}\), and asserts, for every \(h\), \(\nabla\Omega_1^*(h)=\nabla\Omega_+^*(h-\tau_*)\). Its proof cites Danskin’s theorem without a uniqueness condition.

Complete check. Let \(Y=\{1,2\}\) and \(\Omega_+(p)=0\) on \(\mathbb R_+^2\) and \(+\infty\) elsewhere. This is a proper convex function whose domain is exactly the nonnegative-measure cone used with the simplex. Direct conjugacy gives \[\Omega_1^*(h)=\max(h_1,h_2),\qquad
 \Omega_+^*(z)=\begin{cases}0&z_1,z_2\leq0,\\+\infty&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] The scalar minimum still exists: its feasible set is \(\tau\geq\max(h_1,h_2)\) and its optimizer is \(\tau_* =\max(h_1,h_2)\). At \(h=(0,0)\) it equals zero. But \(s\mapsto\Omega_1^*(s,0)=\max(s,0)\) has left derivative \(0\) and right derivative \(1\). Thus the asserted gradient does not exist. The independent finite-difference check at \(10^{-6}\) returns those same one-sided slopes; the displayed exact calculation is the proof. If “positive” is interpreted strictly, taking zero on the open positive orthant yields the same conjugates and the same failure at \(h=0\).

Counterevidence, correction and impact. This is a defect in the breadth of the lemma, assessed Minor. The paper’s central KL and quadratic generators are strictly convex; their relevant maximizing probability vector is unique, and the scalar calculations above support their formulas. The example does not refute Propositions 1–4 under those stronger conditions. A defensible local repair is to limit the gradient assertion to points where both conjugates are differentiable and a common maximizer exists; the gradients then equal that unique maximizer. This does not purport to repair every possible duality pathology allowed by the very broad first sentence of Lemma 1. No experimental consequence is inferred.
# Normalization and interpretation limits

Equation (17), p. 7, is the counting-reference formula \(\sum_j\log(1+e^{\theta_j})\). For the uniform probability reference used by Algorithm 1 it instead equals \[\log Z=\sum_{j=1}^k\log(1+e^{\theta_j})-k\log2.\] For \(k=2,\theta=0\), direct enumeration gives \(\log Z=0\), whereas the counting-reference expression gives \(2\log2\). These are valid alternative conventions, and probabilities and derivatives with respect to \(\theta\) agree. Figure 2 includes negative values, consistent with the normalized convention. Without source code or raw plot data, this observation cannot identify the actual experimental implementation. This is recorded as a scope clarification, not a second proven experimental defect.

The population argument constructs a pointwise optimal continuous \(\tau\); risk minimization alone identifies arbitrary optimizers only on the support of the input law. Finite minimizers of unregularized MLE need not exist, so the value equivalence is also meaningful with infima. Neither issue is used here to allege failure of the constructed pointwise solution. The SGD-rate statement on p. 5 was not independently established under unbounded exponential gradients. Figures 1 and 3 show finite training trajectories, not a proof of a rate or eventual convergence; Figure 2 illustrates a particular test sample. Tables 1–7 and the training protocol were read for claim correspondence but neither data splits nor scores were reproduced. No later revision or erratum was included in the packet or independently compared in this review.
# Conclusion
The inspected scalar equivalence and finite-sum construction survive the local lemma defect. Scope is limited to the stated checks.

Title: Verification of Granularity-Adaptive Geographical Embeddings
# Identity and scope

The reviewed paper is Z. Wang, Y. Sun and H. Zhu, Unifying Knowledge from Diverse Datasets to Enhance Spatial-Temporal Modeling: A Granularity-Adaptive Geographical Embedding Approach, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43731 (0362). The publisher PDF contains 15 pages; references below use its one-based PDF/printed page numbers. Sections 1–7 and Appendix A.1–A.7 were read, with detailed checks of the quadtree query and the complexity/generalization argument. Figure 2 and the relevant mathematical pages were visually checked. The acquired packet contains no accessible author implementation; the OpenReview attachment inventory was blocked during source acquisition.
# Definitions and decisive dependency

Section 3.1 divides each square node into four equal quadrants. Section 3.3 represents an entity by selected nodes, and (5) aggregates their embeddings with weight \(2^{-i}\) at depth \(i\). Section 4, pp. 5–6, and Appendix A.5, pp. 13–14, use \(m=O(\log k)\) selected nodes for an entity containing \(k\) grid cells. They substitute this into an MLP input dimension \(md\) and a parameter count \(p'\propto md\), contrasting \(kd\) and \(p\propto kd\) for the grid method. Appendix A.7, p. 15, also asserts \(O(\log N)\) query time on \(N\) cells, based on at most four visited nodes per level. These are substantive theoretical explanations for the proposed representation.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (A rectangular strip needs linearly many quadtree nodes).

Take an \(M\times M\) grid with \(M=2^h\), \(h\geq1\), and the connected entity \[E=\{(0,j):0\leq j<M\},\qquad k=M,\qquad N=M^2.\] This is a rectangle, so it satisfies even the Cartesian-product entity description in Definition 2, p. 2. It is also a binary mask permitted by Section 3.3 and an axis-aligned query of the form used in Appendix A.7. No irregular, disconnected or non-dyadic boundary is required.

First use the favorable intended interpretation: a selected node is wholly contained in the entity, partial overlap causes recursion, and disjoint nodes are pruned. Every non-leaf square has height at least two and therefore contains cells outside \(E\). No such node can be part of an exact cover. Exactly the \(M\) unit leaves must be selected. Consequently \[m=M=k,\qquad \frac{m}{\log_2 k}=\frac{2^h}{h}\longrightarrow\infty.\] At depth \(\ell\), \(2^\ell\) nodes overlap the strip. A traversal testing all four children of every overlapping internal node visits \[1+4\sum_{\ell=0}^{h-1}2^\ell=4M-3\] nodes, including disjoint nodes immediately pruned. Even counting only overlapping nodes gives \(2M-1\). Merely outputting the \(M\) selected nodes takes \(\Omega(M)=\Omega(\sqrt N)\) time. Thus the claimed logarithmic representation and query bounds fail for this admissible family. The independent traversal returns \((m,\text{visits})=(16,61),(256,1021),
(1024,4093)\) for those three side lengths, matching the exact proof.

Counterevidence and interpretation. A perfectly aligned square entity can indeed use one node; favorable geometries can be compact. A one-dimensional segment tree or a different range-search structure has other guarantees, but the paper defines quadrant subdivision and does not impose a shape restriction that excludes the strip. Replacing exact coverage by an approximation could reduce the node count but would change the entity representation and require an error criterion absent from this bound.

Further defect in the comparison. Even granting the two displayed upper bounds \(R_g\leq U_g\) and \(R_s\leq U_s\), \(U_s<U_g\) does not imply \(R_s<R_g\), as claimed in Appendix A.5.4. For example \(R_g=.01,U_g=.2,R_s=.03,U_s=.1\) obey both bounds but reverse the asserted ordering. This is a logical countermodel, not a simulated value for the paper’s hypothesis classes. A comparison of valid bound expressions must be stated as such, and comparison of complete risk bounds must also retain their different empirical-error terms.

Impact and supported correction. Assessment: Major. The false \(m=O(\log k)\) premise directly removes the asserted strict size reduction in the generalization argument, and the same family refutes the query scalability claim. For exact disjoint covers, the safe combinatorial bound is \(m\leq k\), since every selected node contains at least one distinct entity cell; the example attains equality. General queries can always be bounded by \(O(N)\) total tree nodes. These corrections restore simple worst-case counting statements, not a strict generalization advantage. The linear storage geometric series and the per-level quadratic graph-cost series remain valid under the paper’s fixed-width, fixed-time accounting. Published forecast scores are not refuted by this analysis.
Problem 2 (The written stopping rule and intended query disagree).

Section 3.3, p. 5, says to add a node when it overlaps any occupied mask cell and then halt traversal of its children. Literally the root overlaps every nonempty entity, so \(Q_E=\{T_{0,0}\}\) for all such entities. Equation (5) then gives \(e_E=e_{0,0}\), independent of the entity. For a nonzero root embedding all pairwise cosine similarities in (2) equal one. This follows for any two distinct nonempty masks; the independent strip check selects exactly the root under the literal rule.

Figure 2 instead shows a selection from several depths, and the discussion repeatedly calls for boundary-sensitive representations. Those are strong counterevidence to interpreting root-only selection as the intended method. Full containment, rather than any overlap, as a stopping condition resolves this particular collapse, but still has the nonlogarithmic behavior in Problem 1. Because the implementation is unavailable, this is recorded as Needs Evidence concerning the implemented traversal, not a claim that the reported experiments used identical embeddings. The specification should state all containment, partial-overlap and disjoint cases explicitly.
# Empirical and version limits

Section 3.4.2 and Appendix A.6 clarify that “unseen” refers to pretraining: the downstream model and graph are fitted using target-entity histories. This is not a claim of prediction without any target history. Table 2’s China City regressions for MTGNN and GWNet are acknowledged in the text; no universal improvement claim is inferred. Table 3’s AGCRN row improves when GE is removed, so the sentence claiming a decrease for all methods is too broad, but this local observation does not establish a general failure of the component. No raw data, temporal splits or reported scores were reproduced. The cosine graph in (2) and dot-product/softmax graph in Appendix A.3 leave an implementation detail unresolved. Figures 3–5 were read through their accompanying text only; no quantitative visual validation of those plots is claimed. The publisher version is the only scientific version compared; later errata and inaccessible attachments remain outside scope.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Supported impact | Major: invalid logarithmic-node and query-complexity premise central to the theoretical comparison.
Implementation question | Needs Evidence: literal stopping rule versus intended boundary-sensitive traversal.
Repair verification | \(m\leq k\) and total-node bounds proved; no repaired strict risk comparison certified.
Adoption | Unknown; not requested.
Remaining work | Actual query implementation, precise learning-class assumptions, temporal split and empirical reproduction.
Adjudication | Pending; human reviews empty; initial review only.

Title: Verification of REG Guidance Theory and Released Implementation
# Identity, version and scope

This report reviews Z. Gao, K. Zha, T. Zhang, Z. Xue and D. S. Boning, REG: Rectified Gradient Guidance for Conditional Diffusion Models, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43732 (0363). The 20-page publisher PDF is the reviewed scientific version; page numbers below are PDF/printed numbers. Sections 2–5, Appendices A–D and the experimental settings in E.1–E.2 were read, with particular attention to the claims that marginal scaling is invalid and joint scaling constructs a new DDPM. Figures 1–4 and the relevant theorem/proof pages were viewed. The released REG repository was inspected statically at commit `b9c867cff57a3e2e0146f0bc8395eed5e009b6e4` (13 August 2025); its connection to the historical experiments is unverified.
# What the path-space calculation does establish

Equation reference: eq:tilt. For a positive reward with \(0<Z=\mathbb E_pR_0(X_0)<\infty\), define \(E_t(x)=\mathbb E_p[R_0(X_0)\mid X_t=x]\). The change of measure \[
 \bar p(x_{0:T})=p(x_{0:T})R_0(x_0)/Z\] has transitions \(\bar K_t(dx\mid z)=K_t(dx\mid z)E_t(x)/E_{t+1}(z)\) and marginals \(\bar p_t=p_tE_t/Z\). Conditional expectation proves that each kernel integrates to one, and the factors telescope to [eq:tilt] (#eq:tilt). This verifies the central Markov change-of-measure calculation in (15)–(16) and Appendix C. The conditional kernels are unique on the support of the conditioning marginal. The issues below concern additional conclusions drawn from this calculation.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (A terminal marginal constraint does not fix the other marginals).

Section 3, pp. 3–4, argues that the endpoint target (5), \(\bar p_0\propto p_0R_0\), implicitly leaves every \(p_t\), \(t>0\), unchanged, and therefore declares the target itself invalid. That implication is absent from (5): specifying one marginal leaves the joint law unspecified. Indeed, marginalizing the paper’s own (13) gives exactly (5), as Section 4 explicitly observes. When \(E_t\) is nonconstant, other marginals change.

An explicit finite example removes any normalization ambiguity. Set \(T=1\), \(a=1/2\), \(X_1\sim N(0,1)\), and \(X_0\mid X_1=z\sim N(\sqrt a z,1-a)\); hence \(X_0\sim N(0,1)\). Take \(R_0(x)=e^{bx}\), \(b=1\). This is positive and integrable, with \(Z=e^{b^2/2}\). Completing squares gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \bar X_1&\sim N(\sqrt a b,1),\\
 \bar X_0\mid\bar X_1=z&\sim N(\sqrt a z+(1-a)b,1-a),\\
 \bar X_0&\sim N(b,1).\end{aligned}\] The last line is exactly \(p_0(x)e^{bx}/Z\). The new initial mean is \(1/\sqrt2\), the transition intercept is \(1/2\), and their combined endpoint mean is \(1\). Both joint scaling and terminal marginal scaling are satisfied; the latter never required an identity reward at \(t=1\).

Counterevidence and impact. Prescribing incompatible scaled marginals at every time can be inconsistent, and fixing a particular initial law and transition ansatz introduces additional restrictions. The example does not assert that a fixed original start with every original score/noising identity unchanged automatically realizes the target. It shows that those restrictions cannot be inferred from the terminal-marginal equation alone. Assessment: Major, because the claimed invalidity of marginal objectives is a central theoretical contribution. A precise correction is that joint tilting selects one path-space extension of a valid terminal target, whereas an arbitrary timewise score modification need not sample that target.
Problem 2 (The tilted Markov kernels need not be Gaussian DDPM kernels).

Immediately before Theorem 4.1, p. 4, the paper says that a new DDPM can be constructed to realize (13). Yet the DDPM in (2) has Gaussian transitions, while (15) multiplies such a Gaussian by a generally nonquadratic reward factor. Normalization does not prove closure in that family.

Use the same one-step base chain but take the smooth bounded reward \[R_0(x)=\frac{2+\cos x}{3}\in[1/3,1].\] It satisfies positivity and finite normalization, and can itself be a valid auxiliary class probability with CG strength one. Direct Gaussian integration gives \[E_1(z)=\frac{2+e^{-(1-a)/2}\cos(\sqrt a z)}3,
 \quad \bar K_0(x\mid z)=\frac{R_0(x)\phi(x;\sqrt a z,1-a)}{E_1(z)}.\] For \(z=0\), the second derivative of its log density is \[\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\log\bar K_0(x\mid0)
 =-2+\frac{-2\cos x-1}{(2+\cos x)^2}.\] It equals \(-7/3\) at zero and \(-1\) at \(\pi\). Every nondegenerate Gaussian log density has constant second derivative. Thus (15) is a valid non-Gaussian kernel, even if a learned Gaussian variance is allowed. Independent quadrature gives \(E_1(0)=0.9262669276904681\) and kernel integral \(0.9999999999999998\), agreeing with the exact calculation.

Counterevidence, correction and impact. Theorem 4.1’s abstract transition and marginal formulas survive. The marginal score identity in (17) follows algebraically where differentiable, but inserting that score into a finite Gaussian update does not establish equality with these non-Gaussian kernels. A continuous-time diffusion limit is a distinct possibility requiring its own assumptions; it does not make the finite-step kernel Gaussian. Assessment: Major for the claimed exact DDPM realization. The defensible repaired statement is a Markov change-of-measure theorem with positive integrable reward, without Gaussian-transition closure. No repaired exact finite-step REG sampler is certified, and no benchmark effect is inferred.
Problem 3 (Released text-to-image REG labels do not reach a valid update).

This is a Minor, release-specific defect. In `t2i_diffusers/sample_ddp.py`, lines 30–46, the constructor accepts `gradoriginal`, `gradlinear` and `gradcosine`. The supplied replacement `call_method.py`, lines 262–293, computes gradients only when the type string contains `grad`. However, its REG update branches, lines 322–334, recognize `reg_original`, `reg_linear` and `reg_cosine`. The former names pass construction and gradient calculation but fall through to `NotImplementedError`; the latter names are rejected by construction. If passed directly to the replacement call, they skip the gradient branch and refer to unassigned local `coeff1`, `coeff2` and `grad` at the update. The independent string truth table confirms that no listed REG name passes all three gates. It executes no author function. The README directs users to install this replacement method, so a hidden adapter cannot be assumed. A consistent naming scheme fixes this dispatch contradiction; full pipeline compatibility remains untested. This snapshot does not establish which implementation generated Table 4.
# Additional checks and unresolved scope

The inspected DiT, EDM2 and text-to-image gradient blocks compute gradients of summed model outputs and multiply the guidance vector elementwise, consistent with the stated heuristic in (21) and Appendix E.2. This operation is a column-sum Jacobian surrogate; it becomes the desired diagonal multiplication if the Jacobian is diagonal, an approximation the paper explicitly acknowledges. No universal improvement is inferred. The toy script uses 100 stochastic rollouts and a separate deterministic rollout to estimate its reference gradients; these are estimates, not an exact oracle. Appendix E.1 also discloses removal of unusually large 2D reference gradients when plotting Figure 2.

Theorem 4.2 remains unresolved here: Appendix D substitutes time-zero noise predictions using (33) while retaining \(\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\). The score-to-noise scale depends on time, and its zero-time limit requires separate control; bounded noise predictions alone do not justify that substitution. No full counterexample satisfying every regularity premise or complete repaired bound is claimed. Theorem 4.3 is consistent with integration by parts when the density times log reward ratio has vanishing boundary terms; Appendix D’s informal differentiation-under-the-integral explanation does not state those conditions.

Figures 1–4 show particular finite comparisons. Table 3’s DiT cosine row changes IS from \(300.73\) to \(287.48\) despite an upward arrow; the FID improves. Thus simultaneous improvement at each reported optimum is not universal. This does not refute a Pareto-front improvement, which compares different operating points. No images, weights, FID, IS or CLIP scores were reproduced. Figures 5–10 were not visually checked. No later paper revision or erratum was compared; separate OpenReview attachments were unavailable in the packet.
# Conclusion

Supported impact | Major: invalid endpoint-marginal inference and unjustified finite Gaussian DDPM realization.
Local release finding | Minor: inconsistent text-to-image dispatch labels.
What survives | Positive-reward Markov tilt, telescoping normalization and its marginals.
Repair verification | Restricted Markov statement and dispatch consistency only; no revised full algorithm tested.
Remaining work | Approximation theorem, implementation provenance and empirical reproduction.
Adoption / adjudication | Adoption unknown; adjudication pending; human reviews empty.

Title: Technical review: FP4 language-model training
# Scope and result

This review concerns I25-43733, the 21-page PMLR version of Optimizing Large Language Model Training Using FP4 Quantization. The principal contribution is an empirical training recipe: E2M1 weights and activations, a surrogate weight derivative (DGE), and activation outlier clamping with residual compensation (OCC). The actual experiments emulate FP4 using FP8 hardware; a native FP4 end-to-end speedup is not measured. The inspected evidence supports several local corrections and an unresolved implementation-to-experiment linkage, rather than a demonstrated failure of the reported learning curves. Assessment: Minor; scientific adjudication remains pending.
# DGE mathematics

Problem 1 (Minor: the scaling derivative requires a frozen-scale convention).  Appendix C.2, equations (18)–(22), describes its result as the true weight gradient, but omits derivatives through the weight-dependent absmax scale in equation (1).

Writing \(s=s(w)\) and \(F_i(w)=Q(sw_i)/s\), direct differentiation of a smooth surrogate gives \[dF_i=Q'(sw_i)\,dw_i+
 \left\{w_iQ'(sw_i)/s-Q(sw_i)/s^2\right\}ds.\] The second term couples a column through its maximum. For a positive, unique maximum \(w_1\) and E2M1 maximum 6, \(s=6/w_1\) and \(Q(6)=6\), so \(F_1=w_1\) exactly and its total derivative is 1. At \(k=5\), the paper’s interval surrogate has endpoint derivative \(1/k=0.2\); the frozen-scale formula instead gives 0.2. This is a counterexample to the unconditional chain-rule claim, not to using 0.2 as a chosen surrogate update. Explicitly stopping differentiation through \(s\) repairs the derivation’s intended scope. The acquired code uses a power-of-two scale, piecewise constant away from scale transitions, and a custom backward pass; this is relevant counterevidence against imputing a historical training error from the paper’s absmax formula.

Problem 2 (Minor: bounded smoothing and clipping are not mathematically equivalent).  Appendix C.3, equation (28) and its following paragraph, infers equivalence from equal peak bounds. This does not establish equality of the gradient functions.

Let \(u=2x/\delta-1\), \(g_c(u)=\min\{k^{-1}|u|^{1/k-1},c\}\), and \(g_\epsilon(u)=k^{-1}(u^2+\epsilon^2)^{(1/k-1)/2}\). Setting \(\epsilon=(kc)^{-k/(k-1)}\) makes both peaks equal \(c\). Nevertheless, at \(|u|=\epsilon\), \(g_c=c\) whereas \(g_\epsilon=c\,2^{(1/k-1)/2}\). For \(k=5,c=3\), these values are \(3\) and \(2.273575\). Their agreement at a single point cannot prove equivalence in a neighborhood. Both are bounded positive surrogate gradients, so the practical cap remains well defined. Equation (7) itself has an infinite derivative at the midpoint; it is continuous but not differentiable there. A precise repair is to call the implemented update a clipped surrogate and state its boundedness directly, without a smoothing-equivalence claim. No convergence or superior gradient-accuracy guarantee follows merely from boundedness.
# Performance calculation

Problem 3 (Minor: two numerical substitutions in Appendix B are incorrect).  With \(h=4096,s=2048,\alpha=0.99\), the displayed adjusted-speedup formula on page 15 evaluates to \(3.027292\), not \(2.95\). Its OCC overhead ratio is \(0.028206\), not \(5.6\%\).

The unadjusted ratio is \(3.115460\) and the stated DGE ratio is \(0.000918\), consistent with the rounded \(3.12\) and \(0.1\%\). These are arithmetic checks of the printed model, not hardware benchmarks. Moreover, the DGE operation applies to weight entries (equations (6), (22) and the inspected backward code), whereas its overhead is counted as \(96bsh\) activation-shaped elements. For the standard dense block counted in Table 5, the corresponding six weight matrices contain \(12h^2\) entries, giving \(96h^2\) scalar-operation units under the paper’s eight-operation assumption. This assumption itself treats nonlinear operations as equal-cost FLOPs. Clarify the counted objects, precision throughput baseline, quantile-sort and memory costs before interpreting the estimate as runtime. The paper explicitly excludes native FP4 measurements, which substantially limits the consequence of this issue.
# Static implementation and empirical scope

The acquired Azure/MS-AMP commit is `9746ea85289f8e6233646e73ace35f730d1245d5` (1 December 2025), later than the conference proceedings. Static inspection covered `msamp/operators/fp4_quantize/fp4_quantize.py` lines 1–186, its CUDA kernel lines 1–140, `msamp/megatron/layers.py` lines 1–218, and `msamp/common/tensor/meta.py` lines 37–56. No author program or test was executed.

The CUDA lookup thresholds agree with Appendix A, including upward ties. The piecewise DGE derivative is capped at 3 and evaluated on saved scaled weights. The API correctly interprets the clamping parameters as empirical quantiles, resolving the ambiguity in equation (9), whose literal bounds \(1-\alpha,\alpha\) would otherwise clip negative activations incorrectly.

Needs Evidence: OCC reproduction path. The Megatron activation call (line 67) enables clipping but omits `residual_compensation`; the callee defaults that argument to false (line 114). The forward function then passes the quantized input to one FP8 GEMM and adds only bias (lines 108–116). Thus this inspected entry point discards the clipped residual and does not realize the sparse residual multiplication described in Section 3.2. The optional API can add a residual back before casting, but that is not selected here, and is not by itself the stated high-precision sparse GEMM. A paper-matched configuration/commit and compensation implementation are needed to connect this release to Tables 1–3. This is an observed release limitation; the historical runs may have used different code, and no effect on their scores is inferred.

Figures 3–6 were inspected as images. Figure 5 supports a small positive FP4 loss gap, with transient spikes, rather than exact equality. Table 2’s mean accuracy is sometimes higher under FP4; Table 3’s average perplexity is worse for 7B and 13B, so “comparable” is more defensible than uniform superiority. The ablations separate weight and activation mechanisms and vary \(k\), \(\alpha\), and quantization granularity. Their lack of run-level uncertainty and raw checkpoints prevents a significance or reproducibility conclusion. Figures 11–14 visibly support heterogeneous activation tails and channel outliers; they do not alone establish a distribution-wide optimal clipping quantile.
# Coverage, falsification, and provenance

The review read the central methodology and experiment sections (pages 1–7), relevant related-work/conclusion portions, Appendix A–C (pages 13–18), and Appendix D’s explanation and displayed activation distributions (pages 20–21). The dense weight histograms on page 19 were not visually audited in full; references and external cited work were not exhaustively checked. Independent scalar calculations tested the scale derivative, clipping/smoothing counterexample, and speedup arithmetic. The positive alternative interpretations—frozen scales, bounded surrogate gradients, explicitly hypothetical hardware throughput, and a later public code release—are included above to prevent stronger unsupported conclusions.

Publisher PDF SHA-256: `ad874f1297ae67fb3d84af51f6a76ebd765aff4b595479e09a79c571980c4245`. Evidence consists of the hash-checked source mirror, saved code excerpts, independent calculation script/output, source-image inspection record, exact TeX build record, and final-PDF page inspection record. Other revisions, inaccessible separate OpenReview attachments, full training reproduction, and hardware timing remain outside this review. The selected reviewer configuration is Astra Max; this is an initial review, with no human decision or independent acceptance claimed.

Title: Technical review: trust fusion under conflicting views
# Scope and assessment

The reviewed source is the 25-page PMLR version of I25-43734, Navigating Conflicting Views: Harnessing Trust for Learning. The method learns a referral network to discount each view’s belief before Dempster–Shafer-style belief constraint fusion (BCF), with alternating functional/referral training. Assessment: Major. The stated conflict-resolution guarantee has a concrete counterexample. The acquired release also uses its final test labels for checkpoint selection and creates artificial samples to make an otherwise undefined AUROC computable. Those implementation findings are restricted to the inspected commit; their use in historical experiments is not established. Scientific adjudication is pending.
# Core guarantee and its missing assumptions

Problem 1 (Major: Proposition 3.5 does not follow from one correct view).  Proposition 3.5 (page 5) claims that trust discounting maximizes the ground-truth belief after BCF when at least one view predicts correctly. Appendix C.4 replaces learned trust by perfect oracle gates and then treats optimizing a loss as a guarantee of the desired ordering.

Take two classes, ground truth \(g=1\), and valid finite-evidence opinions \[b^1=(0.0009,0.0001),\quad u^1=0.999,
 \qquad b^2=(0,0.99),\quad u^2=0.01.\] View 1 predicts \(g\) strictly correctly. Use trust probabilities \(p_1=0.95\), \(p_2=0.05\), exactly the two target probabilities induced by the paper’s label smoothing \(\eta=0.9\). These are realizable by finite Beta parameters \((1,19)\) and \((19,1)\) under the stated distrust/trust ordering. Discounting gives \[\breve b^1=(0.000855,0.000095),\quad \breve u^1=0.99905,
 \quad \breve b^2=(0,0.0495),\quad \breve u^2=0.9505.\] Substitution in equation (2) gives approximately \[\bar b=(0.000813,0.049550),\qquad \bar u=0.949637,\] so the fused prediction is incorrect despite the correct view and correctly ordered, near-oracle trust. The strict gap survives small perturbations to all entries; zero evidence is not essential. This does not assume a failed optimizer: even matching the smoothed correctness targets does not yield the claimed classification guarantee.

There are two possible meanings of “maximizes.” If it means \(\bar b_g\geq\bar b_k\), the example above disproves it under the stated assumptions. If it means maximizing the numerical value of \(\bar b_g\) over trust choices, even the ideal binary oracle need not do that. For \(b^1=(0.6,0.01),u^1=0.39\) and \(b^2=(0.4,0.41),u^2=0.19\), discarding the incorrectly predicting second view gives \(\bar b_g=0.6\), while keeping it gives \(\bar b_g=0.68\).

The strongest favorable interpretation is narrower and valid: exact oracle gates set all incorrect views to zero trust and retain correctly predicting views; if the remaining views strictly prefer \(g\), their BCF product also prefers \(g\). Indeed, \[e_k^{\mathrm{fused}}=K\left[\prod_v(1+e_k^v/K)-1\right]\] is coordinatewise increasing. But neither finite learned referral probabilities, one warm-up epoch, later cross-entropy minimization, nor test-time generalization establishes exact oracle gates. Appendix F.1 itself acknowledges imperfect warm-up. A repair requires an explicit oracle theorem or quantitative trust/margin conditions, with the practical algorithm treated as empirical. This is a failure of a central theoretical justification, not a claim that all measured gains disappear.
# Verified identities and uncertainty limits

Corollaries 3.1 and 3.4 were independently rederived: \(e_k^{12}=e_k^1+e_k^2+e_k^1e_k^2/K\) and \(e'_k=pu\,e_k/(1-p+pu)\) follow from \(e_k=Kb_k/u\) for finite evidence. A separate 1,000-case arithmetic check confirms the BCF identity to floating-point precision. For \(0\leq p\leq1\), the multiplier is in \([0,1]\), so every discounted evidence coordinate decreases. The product identity then proves fused uncertainty \(K/(K+\sum_k e_k)\) is nondecreasing. This proves the weak version of Proposition 3.6 without requiring conflicting views; strictness needs a nonzero contribution actually discounted.

An increase in uncertainty is not, by itself, improved calibration or error ranking. Appendix E.2’s inference of more accurate, unbiased uncertainty is therefore unsupported by Proposition 3.6 alone. Appendix E.6 appropriately discusses AUROC decreases and gives a corrected-yet-uncertain example; this is important counterevidence to reading the empirical claim as universal. Likewise, positive scalar trust discounting preserves a fixed view’s argmax, so agreement changes must arise through retraining. Section 4.2 explicitly recognizes that distinction.
# Acquired implementation: evaluation boundary

The inspected source is Trust4Conflict commit `e2a3dc9faa8553d0ad9bae530c4853e617fba464`, dated 22 August 2025. This is a released snapshot, not an attested record of the paper’s runs. Static inspection covered `Trust/models/tf.py` (1–122), `Trust/models/util.py` (32–65, 139–171), `Trust/train.py` (30–164), `Trust/data.py` (1–146), and `Trust/util.py` (140–232). The discount, BCF and smoothed-loss implementations match the inspected formulas. No author code was executed.

Problem 2 (Major, release-scoped: test labels select the reported checkpoint).  The standard training path constructs `test_dl` from `test_idx` (train.py 48–53), evaluates it after every epoch, saves the checkpoint with highest test accuracy (84–95), reloads it, and repeats the same selection in subsequent training stages (109–125, 134–150). Final metrics use that same loader (152).

The evaluator compares predictions with these labels (util.py 156), so this is adaptive use of final-test outcomes, not harmless logging. Later stages are initialized with test-selected models. Consequently, executing this release’s standard path cannot produce an untouched holdout estimate. The loader also fits MinMaxScaler on all \(X_v\) before selecting train/test subsets (data.py 129–136), allowing held-out feature extrema into preprocessing. This latter behavior could be a declared transductive convention; it cannot remove the label-based selection issue. Use a training-derived validation split for preprocessing and checkpoint selection, then evaluate the test set once. Historical scripts, split indices and run logs are needed before attributing this defect to Tables 4–5 or estimating its magnitude. The separate Food101 end-to-end branch, which the paper says has a validation set, was not traced and is not covered by this finding.

Problem 3 (Minor, release-scoped: AUROC is manufactured in single-class cases).  In `Trust/util.py` 223–229, when every prediction has the same correctness label, the evaluator appends a synthetic sample of the opposite correctness with uncertainty equal to that synthetic label before calling AUROC.

For three correctly classified real samples with uncertainties \(0.2,0.4,0.8\), error-detection AUROC is undefined because there is no error case. Appending an invented error with score 1 yields AUROC 1. This score measures a constructed comparison, not discrimination among observed errors. Report undefined AUROC and the error count, or aggregate real out-of-fold predictions using a specified protocol. The near-perfect Handwritten setting makes the branch relevant to inspect, but the original run-level outputs are unavailable and no claim is made that this branch produced Table 13.
# Empirical and visual checks

Original images of Figures 2–7 were inspected. The framework diagram is consistent with referral conditioning; the conflict heatmaps show reduced disagreements on Scene15, while the uncertainty case study visibly illustrates changed correctness rather than a universal uncertainty theorem. Noise curves include small crossovers, so absolute superiority at every noise level is too strong. Table 4 supports ETF’s average advantage, but TF does not beat every non-pseudo baseline: MGP and TMNR exceed it on Handwritten, and CCML exceeds it on CUB. In Table 5, TF’s average \(0.57\) is below CCML’s \(0.58\); ETF’s \(0.66\) is highest. These are scope corrections, not refutations of ETF’s overall trend. MVAGT is strict-majority per-view correctness, so for two original views it requires both correct; including a pseudo-view changes the electorate. It is not fused accuracy or a theorem about reliability. The ablation separates TD from the altered training schedule, a useful control. Reported repeated-seed summaries are not an independent replication.
# Coverage and evidence

Main sections 1–5, Appendix A–G, proof dependencies, experiment setup and the relevant released vector-data implementation were read; external bibliography, all baseline code, raw datasets, end-to-end training branches and other revisions were not exhaustively audited. The independent script records both counterexamples, algebraic checks, uncertainty monotonicity, and the AUROC edge case. Source PDF SHA-256: `9dfd6faa1532fca1166ee803b3cccf7a66a32988ef82b6a7f0d58b23fbf34215`. Saved excerpts, source-image observations, exact TeX build and final-PDF inspection are linked by provenance hashes. Separate OpenReview attachments remained inaccessible. This Astra Max initial review has no human review or independent acceptance; all scientific decisions remain pending.

Title: Technical review: patchification scaling
# Scope and outcome

This is a review of I25-43735, Scaling Laws in Patchification: An Image Is Worth 50,176 Tokens And More, in its PMLR version. The source has 13 physical PDF pages, with Appendix A on pages 12–13. An inherited source-manifest count of 25 arose from embedded form-feed characters in figure text, not extra PDF pages; the frozen source was preserved and physical-page extraction was used. Assessment: Minor, with substantive causal and reproducibility questions marked Needs Evidence. The measured monotone trends are internally consistent with the displayed tables; this review does not establish a failure of those experiments or a general performance theorem.
# Patchification and information loss

Problem 1 (Needs Evidence: information loss in the trained patch embeddings).  Sections 1, 4.2 and 4.3 repeatedly interpret smaller-patch gains as recovery of visual information irreversibly compressed by patchification. For the base models used in central experiments, patchification need not lose any input information.

A patch has \(3p^2\) scalar coordinates and its embedding is \(z=Wx+b\in\mathbb R^D\). If \(D\geq3p^2\) and \(W\) has full column rank, a left inverse recovers \(x\). For \(p=16,D=768\), the base-model projection is square. With \(W=I\), patch flattening and rearrangement are exactly invertible. At \(224\times224\), \(196\cdot768=224\cdot224\cdot3=150{,}528\): fewer spatial positions do not imply fewer scalar coordinates. For \(p\leq8\) the same \(D\) is already an expansion. An independently constructed integer image was patchified at \(p=16\) and reconstructed exactly with zero error. The inspected code’s patch layer is a strided convolution followed by flattening, with identity normalization, so this counterexample lies within the described layer class.

The introduction qualifies its claim as patchification “often” incurring irreversible loss; it does not state that every patch projection destroys information. The invertible construction therefore does not refute that empirical claim or establish that the trained embeddings are lossless. It rejects only a deduction of necessary information destruction from fewer spatial tokens. Accordingly, this item is Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated error in the actual learned representations.

This does not prove that the trained matrices are full rank, numerically well conditioned, or sufficient for the downstream task. Tiny and small models at large patches can have genuine dimensional bottlenecks. Finite-precision effects and learned rank collapse are also possible. A justified clarification is to distinguish spatial granularity and computational access to coordinates from irreversible input loss. A rank/singular-value study or reconstruction experiment on the actual learned embeddings is needed before assigning the observed gains primarily to lost information.

Needs Evidence: causal interpretation of Table 5. The token-interpolation control shows that simply interpolating coarse tokens gives much smaller gains than reducing patch size. It is useful evidence against that particular sequence-extension method. It does not equalize local token geometry, receptive fields, the learned projection, positional parameterization, or the ease with which mixers access fine structure. Even an invertible patch embedding and a pixel embedding can differ in all these properties while containing identical information. Thus the control does not identify information recovery as the principal cause. An invertible space-to-depth baseline, fixed/invertible projection controls and matched parameter/compute experiments would separate these explanations more directly.
# Empirical scaling and its limits

Tables 1 and 4 show increasing ImageNet accuracy at each tested patch size. The headline sequence length is correct: \(224^2=50{,}176\) image tokens (plus the separate class token in the inspected model), and the displayed Adventurer-Base accuracy improves from \(82.6\%\) to \(84.6\%\). The longest ViT experiment is restricted to 4,096 image tokens; the 50,176-token result uses Adventurer, so it should not be attributed to a full-resolution pixel ViT experiment.

Figures 1–4 were actually inspected. Figure 1 contains approximately straight trends over a handful of log-scaled points, but the paper supplies neither a fitted exponent with uncertainty nor an out-of-range predictive test. The claim on page 6 that smaller patches guarantee performance gains is stronger than a finite empirical sweep. Successive base-model gains at \(224^2\) are \(1.3,0.4,0.2,0.1\) percentage points. Without seed-level variation, the last increment cannot be assigned statistical certainty. “Observed scaling trend” is supported; a universal guarantee or theoretical scaling law is not established.

The compute cost is disclosed rather than hidden: Table 6 reports \(27.45\) versus \(115.08\) normalized A100 GPU-hours per ImageNet epoch for Adventurer at \(p=2\) and \(p=1\), a factor of about \(4.19\) for the final \(0.1\)-point gain. The runs are not equal-training-compute comparisons. The appendix correctly describes the GPU-hour numbers as multi-node measurements/estimates normalized by GPU count, with memory excluding model and optimizer storage. This supports feasibility, not compute optimality. The multi-stage recipe reuses \(128^2\) pretraining before 120 additional epochs at \(224^2\); those are not 120 total epochs from scratch.

For ADE20k, Figure 2’s decoder advantage declines from 1.7 to 0.1 mIoU across the tested patch sizes. A linear classification head remains; “decoder-free” means omitting UperNet. Detection and instance segmentation still use Cascade Mask R-CNN. Table 3’s finest tested base model uses \(p=4\), while the tiny model reaches \(p=2\); the text’s shared \(p=2\) hardware-limit description should be narrowed accordingly. These observations support reduced decoder benefit on the tested segmentation setting, not elimination of all task heads across dense tasks.
# Static source checks

The acquired release is Patch_Scaling commit `fb8cce8c015d4d9ac04b73d2521751e10e0f5af3` (25 February 2025). Static reading covered `models_mamba.py` lines 32–55, 160–216 and 254–332, `main.py` lines 298–351, and the README’s evaluation/training instructions. The code has an explicit non-overlapping patch convolution, appends the class token at the end, and uses learned absolute positional embeddings. Only this release is characterized; no author program, checkpoint or training job was executed.

Needs Evidence: parameter-count convention. In the inspected base model, the learned positional tensor has \((L+1)D\) parameters. At \(224^2\), changing \(p=16\) to \(p=1\) increases it from \(151{,}296\) to \(38{,}535{,}936\) parameters. The convolution decreases from \(590{,}592\) to \(3{,}072\). With other blocks fixed, their net change is therefore \(37{,}797{,}120\) parameters, much more than the roughly 1M difference between the paper’s 99M baseline and 100M pixel-model descriptions. The paper may count only core blocks, use a different positional scheme, or use a different checkpoint; none is established here. Specify the parameter inventory and paper-matched code. This is also a possible additional capacity change that should be accounted for in causal comparisons; no impact on historical accuracies is inferred.

Problem 2 (Minor, release-scoped: position transfer assumes the wrong class-token end).  The model appends its class token after image tokens (models_mamba.py 260–262), whereas the resolution-transfer routine preserves the first positional entry as the extra token and interpolates the remaining entries (main.py 332–345).

For a symbolic stored sequence \([p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3,c]\), the correct image grid is \([p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3]\) and the retained class position is \(c\). The routine instead retains \(p_0\) and interpolates \([p_1,p_2,p_3,c]\), then concatenates the preserved entry first. Changing grid size thus mixes the old class position into the image grid and does not preserve it as the new last class position. At unchanged grid size the identity interpolation can conceal the issue. Preserve the last entry and interpolate the preceding image entries for this model convention. The multi-resolution recipe makes this path relevant, but its historical invocation and accuracy consequences remain unknown.
# Coverage and provenance

The complete scientific main text (physical pages 1–9) and Appendix A (12–13) were read. References on pages 9–11 were not exhaustively verified; separate downstream-task code, interpolation-ablation implementation, raw losses, model checkpoints, repetitions and other paper versions were not available for full verification. Source figures were read visually because their embedded text encoding is malformed. The independent calculations cover invertibility, token counts, parameter differences, cost ratio and the symbolic positional-transfer mismatch. Source SHA-256: `c7dfa3bc59533fb0c4c42ce0a5af165827c84ec1630ebca81d3b6651f734edc0`. Physical-page diagnostics, saved excerpts, calculations, source-page views, exact TeX compilation and final-PDF inspection are recorded. The initial review and focused independent acceptance were performed by separate Astra Max AI units. The latter narrowed the information-loss finding after checking the original claim and rebuilt this report. Scientific adjudication remains pending and human reviews are empty.

Title: Technical review: complexity trade-offs in unlearning
# Scope and assessment

This review concerns I25-43736, When to Forget? Complexity Trade-offs in Machine Unlearning, in the 17-page PMLR version. Assessment: Major. A private one-step algorithm contradicts the principal indistinguishability lemma used for the lower bound. Separately, the local regularity hypothesis does not justify the unprojected Gaussian-noise upper bounds. These are defects in central derivations; they do not establish that every proposed regime is false under a repaired formulation. The retained-data-only oracle model, exact pretrained optimum and nonatomic-distribution assumption substantially delimit the conclusions.
# A counterexample to Lemma B.2

Take \(d=1\), \(L=2\), \(\mu=1\), so \(R=1\). Let \(D_r,D_f,D_f'\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), \([2,3]\), \([4,5]\), respectively. They meet Assumption 2. Use the lemma’s functions \(g^\gamma\), with \(A_\gamma=[0,(1+\gamma)/2]\) on the retain support, and the quadratic loss \(\ell^\gamma(\theta,\xi)=\theta^2/2-g^\gamma(\xi)\theta\). Its derivative has magnitude at most 2 on \([-1,1]\), and it is globally 1-strongly convex. For \(\gamma>r_f/(1-r_f)\) the full optimum is \(\theta^*_\gamma=(1-r_f)\gamma-r_f>0\), while \(\theta^*_0=0\).

At the first update, an algorithm may ignore its sampled gradient and output a bit \(Y\in\{0,1\}\). Set \[\Pr(Y=1\mid\theta_0>0)=p_+=\frac{e^\epsilon}{1+e^\epsilon},\qquad
 \Pr(Y=1\mid\theta_0\leq0)=p_-=\frac1{1+e^\epsilon}.\] This is a measurable update of Algorithm 1, using its random seed. For any two initial values and either output atom, the likelihood ratio is at most \(e^\epsilon\). Consequently it satisfies Definition 2 for every loss and every change in the forget distribution, with \(\delta=0\), hence also for the positive \(\delta\) below. It uses neither forget data nor extra oracle information. For longer horizons it can retain the sampled bit in memory; only \(T=1\) is needed here.

Choose \(r_f=0.01\), \(\gamma=r_f/(1-r_f)+10^{-6}\), \(\epsilon=1\), \(\delta=10^{-8}\) and \(T=1\). The two output laws are Bernoulli\((p_+)\) and Bernoulli\((p_-)\), with \[d_{\rm TV}=p_+-p_-=\tanh(1/2)\simeq0.462117.\] The claimed bound [eq:b2] (#eq:b2) is approximately \(0.00802\). The independent scalar calculation records the exact parameters, optimum signs and both probabilities. No simulation or author program is required.

The algorithm is not intended to attain small excess risk. That is irrelevant: Lemma B.2 claims an indistinguishability bound for the admissible unlearning algorithms before any utility restriction is applied. The proof’s final equation (32) retains a ceiling \(K'=\lceil((1-r_f)\gamma-r_f)_+/(2r_f)\rceil\), whereas (29) replaces it by the unrounded quantity. An arbitrarily small positive change of the initial optimum can change a private randomized-response distribution by a fixed amount; privacy alone does not provide the fractional-step continuity assumed by that replacement. Other displayed equalities in (31) should also be inequalities with an absolute telescoping difference.

Dependency and repair. Theorem 2 explicitly combines Lemmas B.1 and B.2 in (33)–(35); Corollary 1 and the claimed inefficient-region boundary inherit this gap. Restoring a ceiling changes the subsequent condition and does not, by itself, rederive the printed threshold. A new argument, an appropriately restricted algorithm class, or a revised lower-bound range is needed. This counterexample refutes the lemma and the supplied proof, not the theorem independently.
# Local assumptions do not control the noised iterates

Problem 2 (Major: the upper-bound argument uses regularity outside its domain).  Assumption 1 imposes \(L\)-Lipschitzness and \(\mu\)-strong convexity only on \(B(0,L/(2\mu))\). Optimization is nevertheless over \(\mathbb R^d\), and Appendix A adds Gaussian noise without projection and applies a bounded-gradient SGD estimate. Neither the noised point nor subsequent iterates are guaranteed to remain in that ball.

Even imposing a unique global minimizer does not fix this. With \(L=2\), \(\mu=1\), \(R=1\), consider a data-independent loss \[f_C(\theta)=\tfrac12\theta^2+C(|\theta|-1)_+^4,\qquad C>0.\] It is differentiable and globally 1-strongly convex, is 2-Lipschitz on \([-1,1]\), and has unique minimizer zero for every distribution. Thus it satisfies the paper’s hypothesis, with even stronger convexity. The Appendix A noising rule still has a positive variance \(\sigma^2\) for \(r_f,\kappa>0\). Its excess risk is exactly \[\mathbb E f_C(G)=\sigma^2/2+C\mathbb E(|G|-1)_+^4,\quad G\sim N(0,\sigma^2).\] The last expectation is strictly positive, so the risk is unbounded as \(C\) increases although all prescribed constants remain fixed. For \(r_f=0.1\), \(\epsilon=1\), \(\delta=0.1\) and \(C=100\), independent Gaussian quadrature gives risk \(0.204016\), exceeding Theorem 1’s lower endpoint \(e=0.131036<e_0=0.5\). The failure is of the proposed universal risk estimate, even when the full and retain minimizers are both inside the ball. A data-aware method could observe that this example needs no noise; that does not rescue the specific universal construction used in the proof.

The same domain issue affects (22)’s \(\gamma L^2/2\) term and the scratch-SGD argument (39). Restricting the optimization domain and projecting the initial noise and every update would be a plausible repair: projection is postprocessing for privacy, and keeps the regularity hypotheses applicable. Its details, sensitivity calibration and complexity constants must actually be proved. Global strong convexity plus global Lipschitzness on all of \(\mathbb R^d\) cannot simply be substituted.

Additional exact-formula discrepancies. With \(q=r_f/(1-r_f)\), Lipschitzness, if valid at the required points, would give a bound proportional to \((\sqrt d\,\kappa q+q^2)L^2/\mu\). The powers of \(q\) in printed (17) are interchanged; (18) also removes denominators and introduces \(e_0=L^2/(8\mu)\) without a valid equality or inequality. At the parameters above (17) is about \(0.555\), whereas (18) is about \(0.117\), so their displayed ordering fails. Equation (25)’s equality drops a factor 64 upon expressing \(L^2R_1^2/e^2\) in terms of \((e_0/e)^2\). The latter factor does not change a big-\(O\) rate, but Theorem 1 states an explicit threshold. Repair of the local-domain issue should include a fresh constant audit.
# Definitions, algorithms and empirical interpretation

There is also a formal zero-query inconsistency. Under Algorithm 1 and (5), \(T=0\) returns \(\theta^*\) unchanged, for every update rule; for neighboring forget distributions with distinct full optima this deterministic map cannot be \((\epsilon,\delta)\)-private when \(\delta<1\). Yet Theorem 1 uses free randomized initialization and returns a noised model with zero gradient queries. The cost interpretation reasonably allows this, but the algorithm class must explicitly allow zero-cost initial/final processing. This is a repairable definition mismatch, not an argument against counting only gradient queries.

Algorithm 2 also initializes \(\theta_0\) but first accesses \(\theta_1\), uses a decreasing step size and weighted iterates, whereas the proof of Theorem 3 chooses a constant step size optimized for \(T\) in (22)–(24). The proof may support an existence result with a corrected algorithm; it does not establish the displayed algorithm’s bound as written. The experiment’s oracle sensitivity \(\|\theta^*-\theta_r^*\|\) (page 9) uses the retain optimum, and the experiment averages realized threshold-crossing times. Equations (6)–(7) instead take the first deterministic time at which expected risk is small. These quantities need not coincide. Figure 2 is illustrative evidence for chosen procedures, not a measurement of the minimax ratio over all procedures and losses.

The non-atomic condition in Assumption 2 is essential for the continuum of Bernoulli biases in the proof. It excludes a fixed finite empirical distribution, despite the motivating finite-dataset example. First-order retain-only access, exact initial training and absence of retained pretraining state beyond the optimum are further substantive scope restrictions. The discussion acknowledges some of these and the unmatched dimension dependence. In particular the asserted exact-unlearning consequence \(\kappa=+\infty\) is outside Theorem 2’s stated \(\delta\geq10^{-8}\) range; a limiting or separate proof is needed.
# Checks and remaining coverage

Main pages 1–9 and Appendices A–D (12–17) were read, and Figures 1 and 2 were actually viewed. Lemma B.1’s coupling argument gives the stated two-point squared-distance constant. Lemma C.5’s binomial bound follows from a score-variance bound and integration of \((1-\gamma^2)^{-1/2}\) (with ordering/absolute-value conventions). The expected squared distance in (21) correctly splits into the independent centered-noise variance and squared bias. These valid components do not imply the invalid Lemma B.2 or supply missing domain control. No relevant author repository was acquired; no raw experiment, external citation theorem, historical version or separate inaccessible supplement was independently reproduced. Figure 2’s qualitative regions cannot adjudicate the proof defects.

The source SHA-256 is `ec459fbbd69c48ee4ffcecb690deb640a918d797f6872f0aae93169d3a4c2898`. Saved physical-page extracts, independent numerical checks, viewed-page hashes and exact-TeX build records accompany this initial Astra Max review. Scientific adjudication remains pending; human reviews are empty and this is not independent acceptance.
