Title: Technical Verification of
GMAIL: Generative Modality Alignment for generated Image Learning
# Identity and available evidence

Mo and Yun, GMAIL: Generative Modality Alignment for generated Image Learning, ICML 2025, I25-43745, is reviewed in its 23-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. The main article and Appendices A–E were read. All numbered figures were actually viewed, including the qualitative images on pp. 18–23. The author-linked repository at commit `c1114abe50104176679786050877e07d4645ea98`, dated 10 July 2025, contains only a README saying code will be released [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Thus no implementation is available in the acquired evidence. No author program, generated dataset or model was run.
# Checked objective

For a batch of \(m\) paired generated/real examples, define \(s_{ij}=\operatorname{sim}(f_g(x_{g,i}),f_r(x_{r,j}))\) and \(p_{ij}=\exp(s_{ij}/\tau)/\sum_k\exp(s_{ik}/\tau)\), with \(\tau>0\). Equation (1) is \(L=-m^{-1}\sum_i\log p_{ii}\). Each row of \(p\) sums to one and \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial s_{ij}}=\frac{p_{ij}-\mathbf1[i=j]}{m\tau}.\] The reviewer-authored four-example finite-difference check at the appendix’s \(\tau=0.07\) agrees with this derivative. With a frozen \(f_r\), this is a well-defined teacher-target contrastive objective, assuming nonzero vectors for cosine similarity. It does not require differentiating the frozen real branch. The check establishes only local objective mechanics, not a universal collapse-prevention or downstream-generalization guarantee.
# P1: prose gains and method attribution differ from tables

Location and classification. Section 4.2, p. 6, and Section 4.3, p. 8, against Tables 1, 3 and 6. Minor reporting error; table entries are used as the reference, without assuming they are verified raw results.

The text on p. 6 assigns Flickr30k text-to-image values \((39.3,61.5,71.8)\) to CLIP+GMAIL. In Table 3 those values belong to Long-CLIP+GMAIL. The CLIP+GMAIL row is \((30.2,50.3,60.5)\), versus the CLIP baseline \((24.7,45.1,54.6)\). Its corresponding percentage-point improvements are therefore \((5.5,5.2,5.9)\), not the stated \((14.6,16.0,17.2)\). The higher figures mix different backbone rows; even that cross-row R@5 subtraction is \(61.5-45.1=16.4\), not the stated \(16.0\). Correcting the label/comparison preserves the direction of the table’s improvements but reduces the attributed CLIP gain substantially.

Table 6’s alignment deltas, in the order B@4, METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE, ROUGE-L and WMD, are \[(1.97,\ 1.35,\ 4.18,\ 0.80,\ 1.15,\ 1.08).\] The paragraph below gives B@4 as 3.56 and METEOR as 1.13 (and WMD as 1.09). Likewise Table 1’s Llama3 gains are \((2.85,3.38,10.40,4.23)\) for B@4, METEOR, CIDEr and SPICE, whereas the paragraph gives \((2.85,2.46,10.35,4.30)\). The independent calculation retains the exact input numbers and differences. These discrepancies cannot all be explained by rounding to two decimals. They might reflect stale narrative from another run; that possibility requires versioned raw outputs. The local repair is to regenerate narrative deltas and model labels from the final verified tables. No author adoption is established.
# Inference-path and training-data questions: Needs Evidence

Section 3.2 and Figure 1 say the original real-image encoder is unchanged and used at inference. Algorithm 1, p. 14, updates only \(f_g\) in the alignment phase and explicitly uses \(f_r(x_r)\) instead of \(f_g(x_r)\) at inference. However, the final sentence of the inference paragraph on p. 4 says that the encoder fine-tuned with LoRA and the real projection are used on real images. Appendix A further states that both real and generated projections are fine-tuned for 50,000 steps. These descriptions do not uniquely specify the tensor path for the CLIP retrieval/classification results, which have no caption decoder to absorb an adaptation.

The distinction is consequential. If real encoder \(f_r\), text encoder \(h\), both scoring projections, preprocessing and similarity are all unchanged, then real-image/text score matrices are identical before and after updating \(f_g\), so rankings and top-1 predictions must remain unchanged. The independent toy calculation verifies that simple invariance. It is a conditional diagnostic, not a counterexample to the reported implementation. Training the real projection, the text branch, or using the LoRA-adapted encoder can change the scores; the appendix explicitly makes at least the projection alternative plausible. Captioning can also improve through a fine-tuned decoder with an unchanged image encoder. Accordingly, this review does not label the reported gains impossible. A per-task module/freeze table, forward equations and checkpoint/configuration mapping are needed to resolve the ambiguity.

Similarly, Algorithm 1 line 12 uses both real and generated embeddings for downstream LLM fine-tuning, while the introductory descriptions emphasize generated-image training. Equation (1) explicitly consumes paired real targets, which is compatible with training only the generated encoder but not with a literal claim that no real-image information is used. The real-data contribution in each comparison should be stated separately from which branch is trainable. Table 9 labels its second fine-tuning row “Synthetic,” while the accompanying paragraph calls it mixed real/generated data; the exact training mixture remains unclear. No data-leakage claim is inferred from these ambiguities.
# Experiment and visual checks

The appendix does include equal-training-step controls (Table 13), a second generator (Table 17), cosine-similarity results (Table 14) and real-only comparisons (Table 9); these counterbalance an interpretation that the work lacks any controls. They do not supply the unavailable raw samples, scripts, train/test image identifiers or inference modules. Table 4 explicitly marks its SynCLR ImageNet numbers “ft,” so those entries should not be interpreted as an unqualified zero-shot comparison. The WMD column is marked higher-is-better, but the transformation from raw Word Mover’s Distance to that reported score is not specified in the inspected material. A similarity transformation could explain it; without metric code, it is an unresolved convention rather than a confirmed reversed comparison.

The original Figure 1 diagram and Algorithm 1 were inspected in pixels. All Figure 2 and Appendix E image grids were also viewed: many examples share broad objects/scene semantics but differ in attributes, composition and object counts. This supports the motivation for a modality gap, while not proving artifact suppression or generalization. Figure 3’s t-SNE panel shows increased red/blue overlap after alignment, with remaining spatial separation. A two-dimensional projection does not by itself establish quantitative high-dimensional alignment; Table 14 provides a separate reported cosine measure that was not recomputed. No inference of image manipulation or experimental misconduct is made.

The reported scaling comparison changes dataset source as well as sample count (COCO, CC3M, CC12M), so it demonstrates improvement across those reported settings rather than isolating a pure sample-count effect. Paired outputs, seed variation, confidence intervals and prompt/test split details sufficient for reproduction were not verified. The acquired OpenReview metadata attempt returned 403. No later erratum or released implementation is established beyond the pinned README.
# Conclusion and verification states

The confirmed overall finding is Minor: narrative arithmetic and backbone attribution require correction. The inference architecture, real-data contribution, WMD convention and exact empirical effects remain Needs Evidence. The contrastive derivative and numerical deltas are independently checked; an implemented repair and benchmark replication are not. Scientific adjudication is pending, human reviews are empty, and author adoption is unknown.

Title: Technical Verification of
Optimal Information Retention for Time-Series Explanations
# Identity and scope

Yue et al., Optimal Information Retention for Time-Series Explanations, ICML 2025, I25-43746, is reviewed in its 26-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Main Sections 1–5 and the embedded Appendices A–H were read, with focused derivation checks in B.1/B.2 and Algorithm 1. The repository at `bb3df70b00f51102293079cd3e2d42c54b190de9`, dated 6 June 2025, contains two Python files and a README promising the complete code later [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Both files were read statically, without import or execution. Their imported model/data infrastructure is absent from the snapshot, and the precise experimental invocation was not authenticated.
# P1: retained values and selection masks are different information variables
Location and classification. Section 2.2, Eqs. (3)–(5), and Appendix B.1, Eqs. (19)–(21), pp. 4 and 13–14. Major: a central derivation of the optimization objective is invalid.

The identity \(I(X;X^m\mid Y)=\mathbb E_{X,Y}D_{\rm KL}(p(X^m\mid X,Y)\Vert p(X^m\mid Y))\) is valid. It does not permit replacing \(X^m=X\odot M\) by \(M\). The map from \(M\) to \(X^m\) depends on the very random variable \(X\) whose information is being measured; it is not a fixed invertible transformation of one variable. Equality of conditional distributions cannot be obtained by merely renaming the argument.

Take a length-two univariate sequence \(X=(Y,Z)\) where \(Y,Z\) are independent uniform signs, and let the black-box classifier read the first coordinate. All quantities are finite and discrete, so no differential-entropy singularity is involved. Two admissible fixed masks give
\(M\) | \(I(X;X^m\mid Y)\) | \(I(X;M\mid Y)\) | \(I(X;Y\mid X^m)\)

Both masks preserve the classifier’s predictions exactly, so the semantic JS constraint in Appendix B.1 cannot remove this counterexample. The full mask retains one bit of independent nuisance information; the mask itself is constant and conveys none. With the reported prior \(r=1/2\), both deterministic mask laws have the same finite prior penalty \(2\log 2\), so the proposed mask penalty does not distinguish their different nuisance retention.

The same mismatch can be exhibited with strictly interior mask probabilities. Compare masks independent of \(X\) with retention probabilities \((3/4,1/4)\) and \((3/4,3/4)\) under prior \(r=1/2\). Both have mask penalty \(2[(3/4)\log(3/2)+(1/4)\log(1/2)]\), while their retained nuisance information is respectively \(1/4\) and \(3/4\) bit, by the erasure channel on \(Z\). The first-coordinate mask distribution is identical, so the expected semantic penalty for a classifier of that coordinate is also identical. This pair has equal semantic penalty, rather than the perfect fidelity of the deterministic pair.

The issue is not confined to deterministic endpoints. If both mask entries are independent Bernoulli\((1/2)\) variables independent of \(X\), then \(p(M\mid X)=q(M)\) and \(L_{\rm mask}=0\), while \(I(X;X^m\mid Y)=1/2\) bit. The nonzero signs make an erased coordinate distinguishable from an observed coordinate. The independent script enumerates all 16 equally likely joint outcomes to verify these values. This second case isolates the regularizer; unlike the fixed-mask pair, it is not claimed to satisfy perfect semantic fidelity.

A valid variational identity would instead be \[\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p(M\mid X,Y)\Vert q(M\mid Y))
=I(X;M\mid Y)+\mathbb E_YD_{\rm KL}(p(M\mid Y)\Vert q(M\mid Y)).\] It concerns the mask, not the retained values. An actual derivation for the criterion must keep \(X^m\) in the conditional distribution, or add and justify assumptions linking its information to the mask. An alternative honest repair is to call \(L_{\rm mask}\) a mask-prior regularizer and withdraw the asserted derivation/equivalence. Sparsity and fidelity penalties may still improve the practical model, but empirical usefulness does not restore the missing identity. No complete replacement guarantee is verified here.
# Completeness and contrastive interpretation

Equation (6), \(I(X;Y\mid X^m)=0\), expresses sufficiency of the retained signal for \(Y\) under the assumed channel; it does not generally imply that the physically deleted complement is uninformative. For \(X=(Y,Y)\) with \(M=(1,0)\), the conditional mutual information is zero but \(I(X\odot(1-M);Y)=H(Y)=1\) bit. Repeated task-relevant temporal information is not excluded by the paper’s setting. Thus the narrative that removal necessarily destroys label information requires an additional condition or a direct residual criterion. This example does not deny that retaining one duplicate can already be information-sufficient.

The chain rule in Appendix B.2 Eq. (31) is valid. Treating \(I(X;Y,\widehat X)\) as constant requires the separately assumed condition \(I(X;\widehat X\mid Y)=0\); this is precisely a no-nuisance condition, not a consequence of reconstruction or marginal distribution matching. Also, equality or similarity of marginals does not by itself preserve conditional mutual information. The jump to Eq. (33) does not state a contrastive mutual-information bound or the needed negative-sampling distribution. Here negatives are produced from the same input through inverse masking and Gaussian filling, rather than established independent draws from the positive marginal. The loss is a plausible pair-separation surrogate, but an InfoNCE-style label alone would not prove the claimed criterion is optimized under that sampling scheme. The empirical ablations remain relevant evidence of usefulness; they are not a replacement for the missing probabilistic derivation.
# P2: the released gradient hook differs from the stated relaxation
Location and classification. Appendix C Algorithm 1 versus :67–100. Minor confirmed release/specification discrepancy; applicability to the reported runs is Needs Evidence.

Algorithm 1 forms a backward softmax using the backward temperature. In the released function, the lines constructing that softmax are commented out; a hook instead multiplies the gradient at the forward logits by \(\tau_f/\tau_b\). Freeze the temperatures by taking the permitted adaptation rate zero, let \(l=(1,-1)\), \(g=(0,0)\), \(\tau_f=1\), and \(\tau_b=3\). If \(J(p)=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\), the source then yields \(J(p_f)/\tau_b\), where \(p_f=\operatorname{softmax}(l/\tau_f)\), whereas Algorithm 1 yields \(J(p_b)/\tau_b\). Their first diagonal entries are approximately 0.0350 and 0.0747. Scaling the forward Jacobian cannot generally substitute the differently shaped backward softmax Jacobian. The independent calculation verifies the discrepancy; it does not execute autograd or the author program. With equal temperatures the two coincide, which limits the affected scope.

There is also a noise-scaling difference. The source uses \((l+g)/\tau_f\), so its hard argmax is unchanged by any positive forward temperature for fixed \(l,g\). The paper uses \(l/\tau_f+g\). For \(l=(1,-1)\), \(g=(-0.4,0.4)\), the latter changes its chosen index between temperatures 1 and 3, while the source does not. These strict comparisons persist in a neighborhood of the noise values. The reference implementation therefore cannot be assumed to validate the written two-temperature algorithm. A repair needs one specified estimator and a matching forward/backward implementation, followed by new gradient and empirical checks. No such author-code repair was run.
# Experimental provenance and visual limits

The released :320–339 has a consequential conditional evaluation path: when its argument named `test` is supplied, ground-truth explanation AUPRC on that argument becomes the checkpoint selection score. If this argument is the held-out test set, selection leaks test explanation labels; if it actually contains an independent validation set, that concern does not apply. The invocation and split provenance are absent, so this is Needs Evidence, not a finding that the published experiments leaked test data. The file also includes Gaussian KL and configurable raw/latent contrastive terms beyond the short displayed objective, underscoring the need for the exact run configuration.

The source prints uncertainty as sample standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of evaluated explanations; this does not by itself establish run-to-run uncertainty. Neither seed-level results nor raw saliency maps were reconstructed. Synthetic truth masks, ECG interval heuristics and perturbation AUROC evaluate different notions and should not be read as direct empirical estimates of the conditional information criteria. The paper does provide CNN/LSTM checks, multiple loss ablations and explicit hyperparameters; these were considered, not ignored.

Figures 1–5 and 7–10 were actually viewed, together with the original B.1/B.2 equations and Algorithm 1 typography. Figure 4’s insertion experiment retains bottom-ranked features; lower AUROC at a small retained fraction can support attribution selectivity, despite the generic caption saying higher is better. The accompanying prose recognizes this distinction. In the qualitative panels each heatmap has its own color scale, so visual darkness alone cannot quantitatively compare methods. The supplied plots can illustrate localization but do not authenticate the numerical tables. Figure 6 was read through its text/caption but not separately image-inspected. OpenReview metadata access was unavailable with a recorded 403; no later correction or complete implementation was established.
# Conclusion

The overall assessment is Major because the claimed derivation of nuisance-information minimization substitutes non-equivalent random variables. Exact finite counterexamples survive the semantic fidelity constraint. The method can still be a useful empirical regularized explainer. The code estimator discrepancy is separately confirmed within the pinned release, while historical protocol impact remains unresolved. Algebraic and finite checks are complete; a corrected objective theorem, implemented repair and benchmark rerun are not. Scientific adjudication is pending, human reviews are empty, and adoption is unknown.

Title: Technical Verification of
Cross-City Latent Space Alignment for Consistency Region Embedding
# Scope and provenance

Chen et al., Cross-City Latent Space Alignment for Consistency Region Embedding, ICML 2025, I25-43747, is reviewed in its 14-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Main Sections 1–5, the impact statement, and Appendix A.1–A.6 were read. All nine numbered figures were actually viewed. The acquired public source is pinned to `68725173eaf6579ef7fccaca9dae95df7f05c37d`, dated 7 November 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]; its date is later than the proceedings, and it is not authenticated as the experimental version. The complete model, training, data loader and evaluator files, plus the small helper and evaluation scripts, were read statically. No author program, dataset or checkpoint was executed.
# P1: the objective cannot fix relative orientation

Location and classification. Eqs. (3)–(13), especially the alignment interpretation following Eq. (12) and the last paragraph of Section 3.4. Major for the central claim that optimizing these losses ensures directly compatible semantic coordinates.
Hold the source embeddings \(Z^X\), anchors \(A\), and linear query/key matrices fixed, and replace only \(Z^Y\) by \(-Z^Y\). Each objective term remains unchanged:
1. Intra-city dot products \(Z^Y(Z^Y)^\top\) do not change, so every destination probability and the mobility loss are identical.

2. The first relative matrix \(A_{\rm rel}^Y\) changes sign, under either the stated cosine similarities or Eq. (7)’s dot products. Row normalization preserves this sign change. The second Gram matrix \(A_{\rm rel}^Y(A_{\rm rel}^Y)^\top\) is identical, including its final normalization. Hence \(L^{\rm LMA}\) is unchanged for every common anchor realization.
3. Both cross-city attention matrices in Eq. (11) change sign. Their cycle products and both intra-city correlation targets in Eq. (10) are unchanged. Hence \(L^{\rm LIA}\) is unchanged.

Consequently Eq. (13) has exactly the same value for the two orientations, for any weights \(\alpha,\beta\). This is not a simultaneous global rotation, which a source predictor could absorb: the source coordinates and trained predictor stay fixed while the target reverses. No final nonnegative embedding constraint or nonnegative/softmax attention constraint appears in the stated equations. The actual PDF was checked to exclude an OCR omission. The two cities have separate encoders. A sign-reversed output is compatible with the final linear-valued attention aggregation; it is not excluded by an identified assumption.

For a concrete nonzero example take two regions per city, \(d=2\), \(Z^X=I_2\), and \(Z^Y=\pm I_2\). Use any anchors with nonzero rows and set \(W_q=W_k=2^{1/4}I_2\). Both alignment losses are zero in both orientations: cross-attention is \(\pm I_2\), its cycles are \(I_2\), and the anchor Gram matrices agree. The mobility losses agree for any given counts. With identity trip counts each city has \(L^{\rm RE}=\log(1+e^{-1})\simeq0.31326\). A source ridge regressor with intercept, regularization one and labels \((1,3)\) predicts \((1.5,2.5)\) on \(I_2\) and \((2.5,1.5)\) on \(-I_2\). Against the same target labels its MAE changes from 0.5 to 1.5. The script independently calculates the losses and solves the centered ridge system; it also verifies sign invariance on unequal-size random matrices.

This directly limits the claim that cycle consistency and manifold matching establish individual semantic alignment. Increasing the number of random anchors cannot break this exact symmetry. It does not show that all trained runs reverse orientation, nor does it refute the six reported city-transfer results. Optimization biases, city structure or additional undocumented implementation choices could favor useful orientations empirically. A repair needs an explicit orientation-identifying cross-city constraint/assumption, or a narrower empirical claim with an acknowledged identifiability limit. A sign-flip diagnostic on saved embeddings would help distinguish the objective from favorable optimization behavior. No such historical diagnostic or repaired method was run.
# P2: public alignment losses differ from the paper

Location and classification. , functions `cross_align` and `cross_rec`, compared with Eqs. (8)–(12). Minor confirmed release/specification discrepancy; impact on original experiments is Needs Evidence.

The release constructs the intra-city reconstruction targets from projected query/key products, not the raw embedding Gram matrices specified in Eq. (10). Setting both linear projections and their biases to zero then makes all released targets and cycle products zero regardless of the embeddings. Its pairwise-distance default epsilon leaves only a tiny numerical floor (approximately \(4\times10^{-12}\) for two regions in each city). For \(Z^X=Z^Y=I_2\), the written Eq. (12) instead equals one at these zero projections. Thus the release permits a trivial projection collapse that does not correspond to the displayed objective. This shows an objective discrepancy, not that training actually converged there.

The release also omits the second relative matrix normalization described after Eq. (8), and computes a mean of squared row distances rather than a mean over all entries. Ignoring the numerical epsilon, the latter is a factor \(N_a\) for the manifold matrix and factors \(N_X,N_Y\) for the respective individual terms. With weights all set to one these differences are not a single harmless global rescaling of the whole objective. The constant one in the code’s distance-to-Gram transformation cancels when taking differences; it is not itself an error. The mobility loader globally normalizes trip counts, so the weighted reconstruction sum agrees with averaging over trips in Eq. (4), and no missing-normalization finding is assigned to that term. The source needs reconciliation with the reported loss definitions and actual run configuration before it can serve as a reproduction of the paper.
# P3: masking after division does not handle zero labels
Location and classification. , `MAPE` and `metrics_local`. Minor conditional implementation defect.

The code first divides by \(|y|\) and only then multiplies by a nonzero-label mask. IEEE floating-point \(0/0\) or \(\infty\cdot0\) remains NaN. For labels \((0,2)\) and predictions \((0,2.2)\), its formula returns NaN, whereas restricting to the nonzero-label subset before division gives MAPE \(0.1\). The independent NumPy calculation confirms this without importing the evaluator. If every evaluated label is strictly positive, this path is unaffected. The excluded raw arrays were not inspected, so occurrence in the published experiments is unknown. A repair should subset before division and explicitly define the all-zero case, followed by a check of the actual data.
# Empirical and visual checks

All twelve Table 1 improvement percentages recompute from the displayed runner-up and CoRE values to the printed rounding (maximum discrepancy below 0.0051 percentage points). The comparative means in Tables 1–2 favor CoRE as stated. The paper reports five runs and paired \(t\)-tests with \(p<0.01\), but paired run-level values, pairing details and multiplicity handling are unavailable here; significance cannot be independently reconstructed from means alone. Source evaluation uses a source-only ridge fit, which supports the claimed prediction direction. The training script periodically evaluates target labels but contains no explicit best-score selection; evaluation alone is not evidence of training leakage. The actual checkpoint and hyperparameter selection protocol remains Needs Evidence, particularly for the target-error sensitivity plots.

Figures 1, 3 and 4 illustrate the intended pipeline. Figures 2 and 8 show city mixing in t-SNE, but neither supplies ground-truth cross-city correspondence or proves high-dimensional semantic orientation. Figure 8 colors city identity, not socioeconomic class. Figures 5–7 and 9 show ablations/sensitivity with no displayed run-level uncertainty; their qualitative trends do not resolve the sign symmetry. Appendix A.5 discusses within-city trade-offs but does not fully specify a held-out split here. Regional targets are raster sums and the mobility evidence is one month of taxi trips; extrapolation to other sampling regimes is not established by these three cities. Raw results, saved embeddings and baseline execution were outside the acquired source-only scope. OpenReview metadata was unavailable with a recorded 403; no bypass or later correction was established.
# Conclusion

The assessment is Major, limited to the central alignment justification: the full objective has an exact relative-orientation ambiguity that changes the reused predictor. Empirical improvements may remain valid. Separate release discrepancies and a conditional metric defect are confirmed but not attributed to the historical experiments without provenance. Repairs are proposed rather than adopted or empirically verified. Scientific adjudication is pending and human reviews remain empty.

All fourteen numbered figures were actually viewed, including original equation typography on pp. 6, 15 and 16.

The public source and supplementary files are pinned to `8c051a255913b068692ed50d6252bb2684a8f1ad`, dated 26 November 2024 [Retained latex: \cite{code}], predating the final paper. The eight-page was read for its substantive prose and definitions; its older architecture and diagonal definition were compared with the final version. The four-page visualization supplement’s captions were read, and the four supplied PNGs were viewed; the architecture PDF was also rendered and viewed because the transparent PNG obscured some text. Duplicated visualization PDF pages were not all separately image-inspected. No author program or native extension was executed.
# P1: invalid steps in the uniqueness proof
Location and classification. Theorem 3.4 on p. 6 and Appendix C on p. 16. Major: the stated ground-truth uniqueness guarantee is not established by the supplied proof.

The theorem assumes that the oracle rationale is smaller than its complement and is minimal for the label: every proper subgraph of that oracle loses label information. Minimality within the oracle does not imply the opening proof assertion that every predictive-optimal candidate contains it; another informative subgraph or redundant copy is not excluded by this condition. A stronger global identifiability assumption would be needed for that reduction. The architecture also feeds complementary topological features to the classifier, so prediction sufficiency cannot simply be identified with the selected-edge set without accounting for that channel.

Even granting the proof’s containment reduction, its subsequent graph identities fail. For a finite graph, \[\beta_0=|V|-|E|+\beta_1,\] not the edge-count relation used in the proof. On the common vertex set \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), let the rationale edges be \(\{01\}\) and the noise edges be \(\{12,23\}\). Then \(|E_\epsilon|>|E_X|\), yet \(\beta_0^\epsilon-\beta_0^X=2-3=-1\), while \(|E_\epsilon|-|E_X|=1\). If isolated vertices are discarded, both subgraphs are connected and the component difference is instead zero, still not one. Thus neither conventional vertex treatment supports the printed equality. This counterexample already uses an acyclic connected full graph, so excluding cycles would not repair the displayed sign/count identity.

Nor does a larger edge count imply more finite zero-dimensional bars: use rationale edges \(\{03,13\}\) and noise edges \(\{01,12,02\}\) on four common vertices. The noise has three edges versus two, but both have exactly two component-merging events. The extra noise edge creates a cycle rather than another \(H_0\) death. The independent union-find calculation records these counts.

The proof additionally asserts a bottleneck distance proportional to a difference of Betti numbers. Bottleneck distance minimizes a maximum matching cost and does not add up multiplicity differences. Let \(P_n\) contain \(n\) copies of \((0,1)\) and let \(Q\) be empty. Every copy can match the diagonal at cost \(1/2\), hence \(d_B(P_n,Q)=1/2\) for all \(n\geq1\). The independently enumerated partial matchings give exactly 0.5 for \(n=1,2,4\). A positive constant times the number of unmatched bars cannot represent this distance. These finite examples avoid complications from essential bars; if essential bars are retained at infinity, the convention must also be stated before the proof’s finite bound is meaningful.

Finally, Definition 3.2 is Wasserstein distance between distributions of diagrams, whereas the proof concludes from per-graph counts and an asserted weighted sum of homology-degree distances. The later finite-function lower bound need not preserve the maximizers of the original distance. An arbitrarily large learned scale is not automatically compatible with the one-Lipschitz requirement. None of these bridges is supplied. Consequently repairing a sign or bounding the first Betti number alone is insufficient. A valid replacement theorem would need explicit identifiability, diagram conventions, a justified objective and a proof for its actual surrogate. Such a theorem has not been established in this review; the finding concerns the proof, not a claim that every empirical fit must fail.
# P2: the stated kernel does not supply the required Lipschitz bound
Location and classification. Proposition 3.3 and the Rational Hat construction in Section 3.1, p. 6. Major for the claimed tractable lower bound.

Proposition 3.3 itself is valid when its functions really are one-Lipschitz under \(d_B\): for any coupling, the difference of expectations is bounded by the expected distance, and taking the infimum yields the result. The problem is the proposed realization. Set the allowed learnable parameters \(c=(0,0)\), \(r=1\), take \(P_\varepsilon=\{(0,\varepsilon)\}\) and \(Q=\varnothing\). The printed kernel gives \[\varphi(P_\varepsilon;c,1)-\varphi(Q;c,1)
 =\frac1{1+\varepsilon}-\frac1{2-\varepsilon}
 \longrightarrow\frac12,
 \qquad d_B(P_\varepsilon,Q)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\longrightarrow0.\] Its ratio to \(d_B\) diverges. For \(\varepsilon=10^{-6}\) the ratio is approximately \(999997.5\). No finite constant \(C\) makes this displayed map \(C\)-Lipschitz over the stated diagram space; multiplying by \(1/C\) therefore does not fix it. The problem is sensitivity to creation/deletion of a near-diagonal bar, not differentiability of the pointwise kernel. A common persistent component can be added to both diagrams without changing this argument. The variable-cardinality diagram setting is relevant to the paper’s variable-size graph rationale setting.

A restricted diagram domain, a diagonal-vanishing construction with proven cardinality control, and explicit norm constraints could support a different guarantee. Those conditions are not stated here. The sum of two individual maximizers also need not remain a lower bound with constant one: even two identical valid witnesses can yield twice the distance. An average or a separately justified Lipschitz bound would be required; learned attention does not establish this automatically. These are limitations of the asserted theoretical approximation, not evidence against the possibility of using the feature map as an empirical regularizer.
# P3: incorrect projection onto the diagonal
Location and classification. Appendix B Definition B.1, p. 15. Minor local mathematical error.

For \(p=(b,d)\) the closest diagonal point under the infinity norm is \(((b+d)/2,(b+d)/2)\), with cost \(|d-b|/2\). The paper prints \((d-b,d-b)\). For \(p=(0.1,0.7)\), the printed point is \((0.6,0.6)\) with cost 0.5; the correct point is \((0.4,0.4)\) with cost 0.3. Both the final PDF and the older supplement show this text, so it is not an extraction artifact. Replace the projection and use the standard diagonal cost. This local repair was checked algebraically and numerically, but does not repair P1 or P2.
# Implementation and empirical qualifications

The complete , the relevant readout, Gaussian mixture and attention classes in , the Rational Hat class, and selected training/checkpoint/C++ sections were read. The native backend uses extended vertex-filtration persistence; its \(H_0\) routine performs union-find merges rather than counting all edges. This does not certify the full extension. The released readout uses cycle-length features, sixteen structure elements, graph-dependent attention, and a negative sum of squared paired differences. This differs from the paper’s maximum absolute difference of expectations with eight functions. As a simple diagnostic, paired values \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\) have identical empirical distributions and zero difference of means, but the sum of squared paired differences is two. The early code is therefore not, on its face, an implementation of the stated discrepancy; historical applicability remains Needs Evidence.

The source uses an \(\ell_1\) point norm in its hat class, omits an identified bottleneck-Lipschitz normalization, and applies min–max normalization to node/edge attention. The paper’s later visualization prose says such normalization is unnecessary. These are version-specific observations, not a claim of concealed processing in the final experiments. The checkpoint helper selects validation prediction AUC (with a loss tie-break), whereas Appendix E.2 describes accuracy; it does not select by test performance in the inspected branch. Exact final configurations and correspondence to the paper remain unknown.

The empirical evidence is substantial but scoped: five-seed means and standard deviations, multiple backbones, ablations, varying motif counts, and synthetic spurious-correlation tests. Mean-minus-one-standard-deviation shading is descriptive, not a calibrated significance test. Tables 1–2 show that TopInG is not uniformly best on MUTAG; Appendix E.4 and Table 6 explicitly acknowledge this and report the degree-zero variant’s improved AUC/accuracy. That response was considered. Table 2 gives GIN TopInG SPMotif0.5 accuracy \(52.22\pm2.07\), whereas Table 5’s nominal Topo./Gauss row gives \(50.22\pm2.07\); the CINpp SPMotif0.5 AUC deviation is 1.84 in Table 1 and 0.82 in Table 5. Different configurations or transcription can explain this, so run-level reconciliation is requested rather than presumed fabrication.

All original figure panels were visually inspected. The rationale diagrams provide qualitative localization evidence but cannot establish population uniqueness or causal validity. The single/average edge-weight histograms in the older supplement illustrate separated empirical modes without proving universal two-cluster behavior of a Gaussian-mixture penalty. Runtime statements are reported measurements on one RTX 4090 and were not reproduced. The other 221-file snapshot contents, notebooks’ full execution histories, baseline implementations, raw arrays and checkpoints were not exhaustively audited. OpenReview metadata was unavailable with a recorded 403, and no later correction was authenticated.
# Conclusion

The assessment is Major: central uniqueness and computable-bound justifications contain demonstrable mathematical gaps. The local diagonal formula has a verified correction. The practical method may remain useful, and its empirical results are not invalidated solely by these findings. A full replacement theorem, repaired implementation and benchmark reproduction remain unverified. Scientific adjudication is pending, human reviews are empty, and author adoption is unknown.

report: Abstract: The central vector-space construction is invalid because addition depends on the representative of a decision-equivalence class. Exact examples using normalized nonnegative densities and signed valid logits demonstrate the problem. The zero-density limit and the alternative appendix do not establish a uniform probability distribution over the whole feature space. These theoretical objections do not invalidate finite-box noise training as an empirical method. Static inspection also finds bounded issues in one released classifier-combination variant and in training-mode restoration, together with a local noise-contrastive density formula error. Title: Technical Verification of
Discovering a Zero (Zero-Vector Class of Machine Learning)
# Scope, identity and assessment

Metta and Radhakrishnan, Discovering a Zero (Zero-Vector Class of Machine Learning), ICML 2025, I25-43749, is reviewed in the 30-page proceedings version [Retained latex: \cite{paper}]. Main text pp. 1–9 and all embedded Appendices A–F on pp. 11–30 were read, including the alternative explanation on pp. 29–30. All 44 numbered figures were actually image-inspected on their original PDF pages. Physical page count was verified independently with a PDF parser; references were not individually verified.

The retained source is revision , dated 13 May 2025 [Retained latex: \cite{code}]. Sixteen relevant Python files and the extracted code cells of two notebooks were read, covering image and synthetic noise generation, data separation, training, metrics, architectures, unary and grouped repositories, and the polynomial model. No author program or notebook was executed. Independent checks use exact fractions, small NumPy calculations, static syntax inspection, and a separately constructed two-layer public PyTorch probe. The overall assessment is Major, driven by P1’s failure of the central mathematical construction. The evidence does not refute the reported empirical curves.
# P1: decision equivalence does not define the claimed vector space

Location and classification. Sections 2–3, Eqs. (1), (6)–(12), pp. 2–5; dependent zero and basis claims in Section 4 and Appendices C/F. Major: the purported vector structure and its derived zero-class interpretation are not established.

For an operation on equivalence classes, changing a representative must not change the result. Section 3 verifies familiar identities of functions but never verifies this prerequisite. Consider two unit-volume bins and normalized piecewise-constant densities, written as two-entry vectors: \[p=(0.7,0.3),\quad p'=(0.9,0.1),\quad q=(0.15,0.85),
 \qquad \tau=0.5.\] All three densities are nonnegative and integrate to one. Both \(p\) and \(p'\) classify just the first bin; moreover \(p'=2(p-\tau)+\tau\), precisely an allowed transformation in Eq. (1), with normalization constant one. Nevertheless the equal-mixture construction in Eq. (6) gives \[(p+q)/2=(0.425,0.575),\qquad (p'+q)/2=(0.525,0.475).\] At the same threshold \(0.5\), these classify opposite bins. Equivalently the unnormalized sums at threshold one classify opposite bins. Thus even restricting inputs to normalized genuine densities does not make the asserted class operation independent of the representative. The mixture identity in Appendix A is correct for specified component densities and equal mixing weights; it is not a well-defined union operation on their decision-equivalence classes.

The direct Eq. (11) failure is equally explicit at zero threshold. Let \(h=(1,-1)\), \(h'=2h\), and \(g=(-1.5,1.5)\). Then \([h]=[h']\), but \(h+g=(-0.5,0.5)\) and \(h'+g=(0.5,-0.5)\) induce opposite decisions. Signed functions are permitted by the valid-logit set \(S\) in Section 2; they can also be obtained by centering and scaling nonnegative densities and their thresholds. They are unavoidable if the claimed negative scalar multiplication is retained. There are no equality-boundary cases in these examples. More abstractly, at zero threshold the proposed scalar rule gives \(2[h]=[2h]=[h]\) for every such nontrivial decision class. In a real vector space subtraction would force \([h]=0\), contradicting the claimed distinct class-vectors.

Alternatives considered. Page 3 explicitly acknowledges that arbitrary representative logits cannot be merged. Passing to their equivalence sets does not remove the problem when addition is then defined through those same representatives. Picking a distinguished density would require additional information and a different construction, rather than prove the present quotient well-defined. Applying Boolean union/complement to already computed indicators is legitimate (the four rows of Table 1 were checked); it does not identify union with vector addition. In particular, union is idempotent whereas real-vector addition is not, except at zero.

Appendix F introduces threshold tuples and monotone transforms, but retains the same representative addition in Eq. (44). Strictly increasing transforms already include the rescaling counterexample. As literally written, allowing non-decreasing constant transforms also destroys decision preservation by collapsing both the logit and its threshold to the same constant. The appendix expressly calls its argument intuition and omits constraints; restricting these transforms would remove that latter degeneracy but would not repair the additive counterexample.

Dependent zero and basis interpretations. The ordinary zero function has integral zero, so normalization is undefined. A sequence \(\varepsilon r(x)\to0\) normalizes to any chosen probability density \(r\), not uniquely to a uniform one. Independently checking \(r=(0.8,0.2)\) at three positive \(\varepsilon\) values gives the same nonuniform normalized result. The constant-path choice in Eqs. (19)–(20) does give a uniform law on each fixed finite box. However, \(q_R=(2R)^{-1}\mathbf1_{[-R,R]}\) has total mass one and converges pointwise to zero, with \(q_R([-1,1])=1/R\to0\). It has no probability limit that is uniform on the whole real line. The same obstruction holds in higher dimensions. Section 4 itself labels the derivation an indication, and Appendix F also disclaims a formal proof; those qualifications must be preserved. They do not support the stronger discovery claim in the conclusion.

Appendix C’s independence assertion is also unsupported. In particular, Appendix F’s monotone decision equivalence gives \([x]=[x^3]\) at zero threshold, since cubing and its inverse preserve the threshold decisions. Even before quotienting, its ordered multivariate tensor coefficients are redundant: nonzero coefficients \(m_{12}=1\), \(m_{21}=-1\) give \(x^\top m x=0\) for every \(x\). The stored exact/finite checks include this cancellation. Symmetric multi-index coefficients and explicit approximation/domain conditions would be needed for a different polynomial parameterization; a learned quadratic separator remains usable without the claimed universal basis.

Consequence and repair scope. The proposed real vector space, its additive-identity distribution, and the associated basis theorem require replacement. A finite-domain noise classifier and ordinary Boolean operations remain coherent empirical constructions. This review verifies the counterexamples, not a replacement theory or a claim that noise training cannot help.
# P2: a released unary combiner compares non-identifiable raw logits

Location and classification. and , especially lines 26–30 of the latter. Minor, restricted to the two-output cross-entropy variant in the inspected revision; the exact historical experiment route is unverified.

That variant trains two output logits for each unary model. The combiner selects the largest last-column raw logit across models, without subtracting the corresponding noise logit. Let two models output \(A=(0,2)\) and \(B=(0,1)\) for one input. The combiner selects \(A\). Adding 10 to both outputs of \(B\) gives \((10,11)\), so it selects \(B\), although every probability, cross-entropy loss and within-model prediction of \(B\) is unchanged. The independent calculation obtains the same \(B\) class probability \(0.7310586\) and loss \(0.3132617\) before and after the shift. Adding a common final-layer bias realizes this invariance for all inputs. Uniform noise in the loss does not fix this free offset.

Compare a log-odds margin or probabilities with explicit prior/noise calibration, and authenticate the executed configuration. This suggested local change removes the additive-offset ambiguity but does not prove general cross-model calibration. Crucially, the separately inspected specifies a single-output BCE variant, to which this two-logit invariance does not apply. Its configuration also differs from the current helper’s binary-branch selector, so execution provenance is needed. The grouped route uses softmax probabilities and masks a model’s noise-class win; it likewise is not subject to the raw-offset example. The finding therefore is not assigned indiscriminately to Figures 41–44 or their reported accuracies.
# P3: evaluation mode persists into later training epochs
Location and classification. , lines 69–107, 127–159; . Minor implementation issue, with unmeasured historical effect.

Each epoch invokes training followed by three evaluation routines. Those routines call , but the training routine and surrounding loop never restore . Static syntax inspection finds evaluation calls at lines 107, 129 and 159 and no model-training-mode call. Consequently, after the first evaluation a newly constructed model stays in evaluation mode for subsequent optimization epochs. The CIFAR architectures contain both batch normalization and dropout, so dropout is disabled and running batch-normalization statistics cease to update. Gradients and optimizer updates still occur; this is not a claim that training stops.

The installed framework’s actual mode implementation was read and hashed. A separately created BatchNorm/Dropout probe confirms the behavior: the batch counter is 1 after the training forward, remains 1 after an evaluation-mode forward, and becomes 2 after explicitly restoring training mode. Restore the mode at the start of each training epoch and then compare affected runs. Both compared CIFAR models share the helper; the direction and magnitude of any benchmark effect cannot be inferred. The inspected notebook uses 100 epochs while the script and Figure 29 use 50, further limiting historical attribution. Pure linear/ReLU MNIST models do not acquire the same dropout/normalization consequence.
# P4: constant in the noise-contrastive density formula
Location and classification. Section 6, Eqs. (26)–(29), pp. 8–9. Minor algebraic error in density normalization.

With the paper’s definition \(p_n(u)=k\), substituting in Eq. (26) gives \(G=\log p_d-\log k\), not \(\log p_d-k\). Hence \(p_d=k e^G\), not \(e^{G+k}\). For \(p_d=0.4\) and \(k=0.25\), \(G=0.4700036\) gives the correct density 0.4, while the printed expression gives 2.0544407. One could instead define a new symbol \(k=\log p_n\), but that is not its definition in the text. The score identity is unchanged because the missing term is constant in \(u\).

More generally, the Bayes binary log-odds is \(\log p_d-\log p_n+\log(\pi_d/\pi_n)\) when the sampling priors differ. For equal priors and uniform noise on a finite box, the positive region is a density superlevel set \(p_d>1/V\); it is not automatically the full distributional support or an arbitrary future class’s complement. This does not contradict the paper’s conditional mode-seeking generation discussion, but does not establish exact recovery of a true manifold either.
# What the experiments and code do support

The image generator samples independent pixel values uniformly on \([0,1]\), and the data loaders create separate training, test and occupancy-noise draws. The inspected MNIST/CIFAR preprocessing uses official training/test splits. Their accuracy test loader excludes noise whereas purity includes separately generated test noise, consistent with the figure captions. Thus the source does not justify a training/test-noise reuse allegation. Synthetic noise instead uses a data-dependent bounding box with ten-percent padding; its test-noise box is calculated from test data, so its evaluation distribution should be explicitly documented.

Figures 6–7 and 17 show finite synthetic rejection regions. Figures 18, 29 and 40 display low uniform-noise occupancy with broadly comparable closed-set accuracy; this is useful empirical evidence for rejecting that chosen noise. An exclusive classifier with no reject output has occupancy one by construction. Purity is sample precision, and both quantities depend on the noise population and region. Appendix D.2.2 explicitly acknowledges this dependence and requests its disclosure. These metrics alone do not certify rejection of semantically novel classes or coverage of all empty space.

The unary plots (Figures 19–28 and 30–39) show high individual accuracy against uniform noise, while the actual repository diagrams report 81.65% on MNIST and 25.39% on CIFAR10. The grouped repository falls from 97% to 85% to 73% as datasets are added. The main text and conclusion acknowledge poor scaling; these failures are not hidden and should not be mistaken for evidence of universally compatible class boundaries. The generated-digit panel is qualitative mode-seeking evidence; no new image-quality statistic was inferred from it.

Raw predictions, repeated-seed uncertainty, historical configurations/checkpoints, the ImageNet embedding pipeline and the remaining source tree were not reproduced or exhaustively audited. Stored notebook outputs were not treated as new execution. OpenReview access remains unavailable under the recorded 403 response. The review establishes a mathematical counterexample and bounded source defects; empirical repair effects and scientific adjudication remain pending.

Title: Technical Verification: Theoretical guarantees on the best-of-n alignment policy
# Paper identity and scope

Theoretical guarantees on the best-of-n alignment policy. Ahmad Beirami; Alekh Agarwal; Jonathan Berant; Alexander D’Amour; Jacob Eisenstein; Chirag Nagpal; Ananda Theertha Suresh. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43750. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

Sections 2–7 and Appendix A were read with attention to assumptions and parameter domains. Figures 1–3 and 7–9 were visually inspected. Appendix B was read for the chain-rule argument and Appendix C for experimental scope. Language-model experiments were not reproduced. No author implementation is available in this packet.
# Definitions and surviving checks

Fix one prompt, finite support with distinct rewards, and ordered masses \(p_i>0\). Set \(F_i=\sum_{j\le i}p_j\). Lemma 2.3 gives \(q_i=F_i^n-F_{i-1}^n\), by the distribution of the maximum of independent uniform variables. Write \(S=\sum_i p_i^2=e^{-H_2(p)}\) and \(B_n=\log n-(n-1)/n\). Theorem 3.1 follows from the integral log-sum inequality on each interval \([F_{i-1},F_i]\) for density \(nv^{n-1}\), followed by integration over \([0,1]\). Its gap is a sum of nonnegative conditional KL divergences (Lemma A.1, p. 12). The two cases in Lemma A.3 yield the collision upper bound for \(n\ge2\); \(n=1\) is identically zero.

The win rate equals \(\sum_iq_i(F_i+F_{i-1})/2\); the interval inequality in Lemma A.4 gives \(n/(n+1)\) as its upper bound. For rewind-and-repeat with \(0<w\le1\), \(\mathbb E H_{M-1}=\sum_{k\ge1}(1-w)^k/k=-\log w\). These arguments do not use the defective steps below.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Theorem A.7 does not define the claimed universal upper bound).  Theorem A.7 (physical p. 19) claims an upper-bound function for any reference distribution, parameterized for \(\tau\ge1\) by \[W_U(\tau)=\frac{\tau}{\tau+1},\qquad
 D_U(\tau)=\log\tau-\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}-2\tau(\tau-1)S.\] Definition 7.1 (p. 8) requires a function of nonnegative KL that is evaluable at every actual \(D_n\).

Admissible example. Use one prompt, two outcomes with rewards \(0<1\) and \(p=(1/2,1/2)\). Finite support and unique rewards satisfy Assumptions 2.1–2.2, and \(S=1/2\). At \(n=2\), \(q=(1/4,3/4)\), hence \[D_2=\tfrac14\log(1/2)+\tfrac34\log(3/2)=0.1308120359>0,\qquad
 W_2=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14+\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac58.\] Yet \(D_U(1)=0\), and for every \(\tau>1\), \[D_U(\tau)\le(\tau-1)\left(1-\frac1\tau-\tau\right)<0,\] using \(\log\tau\le\tau-1\). No parameter supplies the positive abscissa \(D_2\). In particular, \(D_U(2)=-1.8068528194\). ◻

The suspect step is converting two sample-count bounds to a function of KL without establishing an invertible domain or completing the range. This is a failure of the specified universal function, not a counterexample to Theorems 3.4 or 5.3. More generally \(D_U'(1)=-2S<0\) and \(D_U(\tau)\to-\infty\) for any finite distribution.

An interpretation on a suitable increasing branch for sufficiently small \(S\) would change the statement; the binary example has no positive branch. Defining a trivial value \(1\) outside a justified domain also requires a new statement. Figures 8–9 use a conjectured bound, distinct from A.7. They neither validate A.7 nor become invalid from this example. This is Major for the general theoretical tradeoff guarantee advertised in Section 7; the foundational KL and win-rate inequalities survive. No global repair is asserted.

Problem 2 (The precision dependence of averaging is incorrect).  The paragraph after Lemma 4.5 (p. 5, left column) claims that \(M=O(\log n\,\log(1/\delta))\) independent estimator draws suffice to make the mean’s standard deviation smaller than \(\delta\).

Set \(n=2\), rewards \(0<1\), and \(p=(0.9,0.1)\), satisfying finite support and uniqueness. Selected masses are \(0.9,0.1\) with probabilities \(0.81,0.19\). Substitution in equation (24) gives \[d_2(0.9)=0.07326269888,\qquad d_2(0.1)=0.19305943694,\] and therefore \[\sigma^2=0.81(0.19)\{d_2(0.9)-d_2(0.1)\}^2
 =0.002208658675>0.\] The mean’s standard deviation is exactly \(\sigma/\sqrt M\). At fixed \(n\), no constant multiple of \(\log(1/\delta)\) suffices as \(\delta\downarrow0\). At \(\delta=0.001\) at least \(2209\) draws are needed.

A supported correction follows from \(0\le d_n\le B_n\): \(\operatorname{Var}(d_n)\le B_n^2/4\), so \(M\ge B_n^2/(4\delta^2)\) ensures standard deviation at most \(\delta\); strict inequality gives a strict bound. This is not a bias or tail-probability guarantee. Reading \(\delta\) as a failure probability does not rescue the printed standard-deviation claim. Uniform reference distributions have zero variance, but the explicit nonuniform example avoids that exception. The impact is Minor: an ancillary precision claim fails, while the estimator definition, boundedness and conjectured expectation inequality remain separate.
# Dependence and limitations

The primary KL upper-bound proof uses neither issue. Conjectures 4.4 and 7.2 remain unresolved; the source explicitly distinguishes them from proved results. Strict positivity of the gap at \(n=1\) needs an endpoint qualification but is not treated as another substantive finding. No supplied later revision or erratum resolves the concerns. No benchmark degradation is inferred.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | Major
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | Variance bound checked; A.7 unrepaired
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded
One universally specified tradeoff bound fails, and a local precision claim needs correction. These findings do not establish failure of best-of-\(n\) or of all theoretical guarantees.

Title: Technical Verification: LADA: Scalable Label-Specific CLIP Adapter for Continual Learning
# Paper identity and scope

LADA: Scalable Label-Specific CLIP Adapter for Continual Learning. Mao-Lin Luo; Zi-Hao Zhou; Tong Wei; Min-Ling Zhang. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43751. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

The focus is Section 3, Sections 4.1–4.5 and Appendix A–D. Figures 1–3 and Tables 1, 7–8 were actually viewed. The published-source snapshot is commit `c74806cd8ebe50f51dc6b448d3abe404ff4b41cb` of https://github.com/MaolinLuo/LADA. Static inspection covered `models/lada.py`, `models/models.py`, `utils/sampler.py`, optimizer and replay passages of `trainer.py`, and the README. No author code was executed.
# Checked mechanism and assumptions

For a frozen feature vector \(i\in\mathbb R^d\), each class has \(\lambda_1\) memory vectors. The class score in equation (6) is \[s_c(i)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\lambda_1}\exp\{-\beta(1-w_{c\ell}^{\top}i)\}.\] The matrix multiplication and one-hot aggregation in `LADA.forward` implement this expression. The block-diagonal classifier construction associates newly appended centers with the new classes. The optimizer includes the current memory vectors and text tuner, while preceding memory is stored as a buffer. Thus old adapter logits remain fixed for fixed image features; new class logits can still defeat them. Section 3.2 explicitly acknowledges this distinction and introduces old-class replay. It would be incorrect to infer a universal no-forgetting theorem from parameter freezing.

For isotropic noise \(e\sim N(0,I_d)\), equation (11) has covariance \[\operatorname{Cov}(\widetilde p)=\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{d}I_d.\] This is not an arbitrary full-covariance GMM sampler. However, the release fits `GaussianMixture` with spherical covariance. For \(\Sigma=s^2I_d\), the displayed scale is exactly \(s\), matching `sample_from_prototypes`. Taking one independent sample per component and weighting by \(\pi_\ell\) has expectation \(\sum_\ell\pi_\ell\mathbb E\mathcal L(X_\ell)\), the fitted mixture loss in equation (10). This verifies consistency with the chosen spherical approximation, not exact recovery of the original feature distribution.

The inference branch in `models/models.py` first finds the text-logit maximum. It adds adapter logits only when this label is seen, with a large negative padding for unseen classes. This matches the conditional rule at the end of Section 3. It is distinct from an external vanilla-CLIP task selector; Figure 3’s comparison does not mean that no conditional decision occurs anywhere.
# Independent arithmetic and visual checks

The six principal aggregate rows in Tables 1–2 were transcribed into an independent script. Their unrounded means are \[(61.5333,\ 72.7000,\ 83.1200),\qquad
 (61.9000,\ 75.1600,\ 86.9100),\] for Transfer, Average and Last in the 16-shot and full-shot settings. They round to the printed values. Transfer averages nine tasks because the first has no preceding training step; Average and Last use ten. Appendix A’s definitions agree with this convention. At \(1100\) classes, \(\lambda_1=16\) and \(d=512\), the nominal memory count is \(1100\cdot16\cdot512=9{,}011{,}200\), consistent with Table 4’s \(9.01\) million (classes with fewer centers can reduce this).

The visible learning-step curves in Figure 2 are consistent with the broad pattern of Tables 7–8: jumps when tasks are learned and approximately stable later performance. This is a visual consistency check, not a recreation of predictions or raw measurements. Table 3’s improvements are empirical observations, not statistical significance tests.
# Impact boundary

No numbered defect is supported by these checks. The method assumes access to names of unseen classes, as Section 3.1 states, and should be interpreted under that X-TAIL protocol. Its spherical replay, aggregate point estimates and tested task sequences do not establish exact distribution preservation, arbitrary-sequence immunity to forgetting, or universal scaling performance. These limits do not contradict a formal guarantee: none was proved in the inspected sections. A causal assessment of each component and a historical experiment-to-code correspondence would need run records and fresh experiments.

Title: Technical Verification: In-Context Adaptation to Concept Drift for Learned Database Operations
# Paper identity and scope

In-Context Adaptation to Concept Drift for Learned Database Operations. Jiaqi Zhu; Shaofeng Cai; Yanyan Shen; Gang Chen; Fang Deng; Beng Chin Ooi. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43752. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

The review concentrates on Section 3.4 and Appendix E, with Sections 2–3 and Algorithms 1–2 used to determine the data, query and context assumptions. Table 1 and Figures 4–5 were visually inspected, together with the theorem and proof pages. The pinned release is `cfea0dc47bfd04de6b2c74c609ce2206ed56907c` at https://github.com/zjiaqi725/FLAIR. Selected attention and prediction-interface source passages were read statically; no implementation was run.
# Problem 1: the universal stale-model lower bound is false

Theorem 3.1 (physical p. 6) considers an initially trained, frozen \(\widehat f_i\), followed by \(s\) insertions and \(r\) deletions, \(k=s+r>1\), with final data iid from any continuous distribution. It asserts \[\sup_x\mathbb E|\widehat f_i(x)-f_{D_j}(x)|\ge k-1.\] Appendix E.1 (p. 19) defines \(f_D(x)\) as the count of data points in an axis-parallel query rectangle.

Take one-dimensional data, \(i=j=2\), and independent initial points \(X_1,X_2\sim U(0,1)\). Train an exact counting model \(\widehat f_i(x)=f_{D_i}(x)\) and freeze it. No capacity or approximation restriction in the theorem excludes this finite step-function model. Delete the two initial records and insert two independent \(U(0,1)\) records \(Z_1,Z_2\). Then \(s=r=2\), \(k=4>1\), \(|j-i|=|s-r|=0\), and the final points are iid from a continuous distribution. The database actually changes almost surely; no insertion is canceled by deleting that same new point.

For every interval \(x\) and every realization, both old and new counts lie in \(\{0,1,2\}\). Therefore \[|\widehat f_i(x)-f_{D_j}(x)|\le2,\qquad
 \sup_x\mathbb E|\widehat f_i(x)-f_{D_j}(x)|\le2<3=k-1.\] This pathwise bound holds whether the expectation also averages the initial data or conditions on it. Even changing the order of supremum and expectation cannot repair this example.

The proof’s median minimization principle is valid, but the next step is not: having possible extreme outcomes of a random variable does not force its median to be \(\pm1\) or its expected absolute deviation to be \(k-1\). In the present mixed stream the net count difference lies in \([-2,2]\), not at the asserted extremal \(\pm4\). For a purely one-sided stream the probability of an extreme outcome would still not provide the claimed expectation lower bound.

A reading restricted to a separate adversarial operation class would require changing the quantifiers and proof. As written, a supremum over queries does not remove the mixed-operation counterexample. This is Major: Section 3.4 uses the lower bound to infer mandatory retraining frequency and compare FLAIR’s accuracy with all static models. Neither inference follows from a false lower bound. The example does not say stale models always remain accurate.
# Problem 2: the adaptive upper-bound derivation is invalid

Theorem 3.2 (p. 6; Appendix E.2, p. 20) claims an absolute-error bound uniform in the query, of order \(\varrho^{-1/2}\), for a FIFO context of size \(\varrho\). Its proof decomposes error into an approximation term \(\mathcal E_M\) and a context term \(\mathcal E_C\). The triangle inequality is correct. The next inference, \[\mathcal E_M\le\sqrt{\{\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)+\log(1/\delta)\}/(2\varrho)},\] has no empirical-error term, bounded-loss specification, or established relation between parameter KL and approximation to the context-optimal predictor.

Small parameter KL alone cannot imply this absolute-error conclusion. As a diagnostic of that inference, take identical prior and posterior point masses on a predictor whose loss is constantly one. Then \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)=0\), the empirical and population losses are one, but at \(\varrho=1000\) and \(\delta=0.05\) the displayed term is \(0.0387023\). The contradiction concerns the invoked general implication; it is not an executed counterexample to a particular trained FLAIR checkpoint. A valid concentration bound for a generalization gap would be consistent with this example because the gap is zero. Calling training adequate and then asserting a bounded KL does not supply the missing approximation-error condition.

The context term also identifies prediction discrepancy with deviation of a sample average and invokes \(2e^{-2\varrho\epsilon^2}\). The unnormalized cardinalities of E.1 are not unit-range variables. Moreover, iid records in the current database do not make recent query-result pairs iid from the current target distribution: the stated FIFO mechanism explicitly spans a changing database. Independence, range scaling, representativeness, and the identity connecting performance averages to query-specific counts are not established. A pointwise high-probability statement is also changed to a supremum over all queries without a uniform event argument.

These are invalid steps in a core guarantee, graded Major under the claim-level standard. They show that the stated theorem has not been established by this derivation; they do not by themselves prove that no suitably restricted FLAIR guarantee is possible. A repair would require explicit loss normalization, sampling/drift conditions, approximation or empirical risk, and uniformity control. No complete repaired theorem is offered.
# Surviving observations and dependence

Algorithm 2 predicts before adding the current result to memory, so the described protocol itself does not require current-label leakage. The Bayesian predictive integral and Gaussian negative log-likelihood in equations (8)–(12) are consistent as modeling formulas; they do not imply the universal finite-sample guarantees.

Independent arithmetic gives \((5.79-4.49)/5.79=22.4525\%\), \(6.8/1.3=5.23077\) and \(40.4/21.4=1.88785\), matching the rounded headline examples. Inspection of Table 1 confirms that the 29-of-32 quantile comparison excludes the separately listed fine-tuning row, and has three exceptions: the two severe-STATS P-error tail entries and the severe JOB-light 95th-percentile Q-error. Title: Technical Verification: Feedforward Few-shot Species Range Estimation
# Paper identity and scope

Feedforward Few-shot Species Range Estimation. Christian Lange; Max Hamilton; Elijah Cole; Alexander Shepard; Samuel Heinrich; Angela Zhu; Subhransu Maji; Grant Van Horn; Oisin Mac Aodha. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43753. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

Sections 1–6 were read for the architecture and empirical claims. Appendix A.1, A.2–A.3 in part, Tables A1–A4, and selected training and baseline descriptions in C.1–C.2 were examined. Original pages 4, 6, 8, 19 and 25 were visually inspected. The source snapshot is `09bf7a79bbe2ae3c696559aaf3bdf69f9ba67d6d`, https://github.com/Chris-lange/fs-sinr. This is a static inspection, with no training, evaluation or author-code execution.
# Checked structure and scope of prediction

For a token matrix \(X\) and a permutation \(P\) that fixes the class token, row-wise softmax satisfies \[\operatorname{softmax}(PAP^\top)=P\operatorname{softmax}(A)P^\top.\] Consequently a self-attention layer without positional embeddings is permutation equivariant. Shared row-wise feedforward layers, normalization and residual connections preserve this property; the fixed class-token output is invariant under reordering context tokens, with masks permuted correspondingly. This establishes the ordering claim in Section 3.2 at deterministic inference. The independently implemented attention diagnostic gives agreement to floating-point precision; it is not a test of the authors’ trained network.

The inspected `models.py` passages assemble typed context tokens, extract the first token after the Transformer and compute the sigmoid of the query/species-embedding inner product. The inspected `datasets.py` branch excludes listed evaluation taxa when zero-shot mode is enabled and excludes the selected query location from its context sample. The actual dataset list and historical run configuration were not available for verification. The loss code masks off-diagonal same-species negatives, avoiding a spurious assumption that distinct examples must be distinct species. These observations support the described mechanism but do not certify every source branch.

Presence-only pseudo-absence training supplies a discriminative score, not by itself a calibrated ecological probability. Appendix A.1’s sparsification exercise assesses whether ensemble variance ranks errors usefully; it does not establish probability calibration. The paper itself acknowledges geographic and taxonomic bias and cautions against unvalidated biodiversity assessments. No additional claim of ecological validity is inferred here.
# Problem 1: exceptions to the empirical dominance statement

Section 4.2 (p. 5) states, in paraphrase, that FS-SINR outperforms existing methods in every instance with the same available metadata. Table A4 (p. 19) gives a direct counterexample within the one-to-fifty-context range plotted in Figure 3: \[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
\text{S\&T, locations only} &\text{FS-SINR}&\text{Prototype}&\text{Active}&\text{LE-SINR}\\
\hline
1&0.50&0.54&0.53&0.52\\
50&0.71&0.66&0.64&0.72
\end{array}\] At fifty contexts SINR also reports \(0.72\). Thus both strict dominance and weak dominance fail in some matched-information comparisons. The four-point gap at one context cannot be eliminated by rounding these entries to two decimals. The original Figure 3 also shows the location-only curves crossing; this is not an extraction artifact.

Text-conditioned FS-SINR remains strong: at ten contexts, the printed gains over text-conditioned LE-SINR are \(0.04/0.62=6.45\%\) on IUCN and \(0.03/0.69=4.35\%\) on S&T. The paper’s main observation of useful few-shot predictions therefore survives. The defect is Minor: qualify the universal sentence and identify the exceptions. These are comparisons of reported means, not independent significance tests or reproductions.
# Problem 2: the stated prototype probability has the wrong distance direction

Appendix C.2.3 (p. 25), equation (5), defines \[p_+(x)=\frac{\exp(d(f_\theta(x),r_+))}
 {\exp(d(f_\theta(x),r_+))+\exp(d(f_\theta(x),r_-))}\] and explicitly calls \(d\) cosine distance. With the usual \(d(a,b)=1-\langle a,b\rangle/(\|a\|\|b\|)\), choose nonzero unit query \(f_\theta(x)=r_+=(1,0)\) and absent prototype \(r_-=(0,1)\). Such prototypes are means of singleton support sets and meet equation (4). Then \(d_+=0\), \(d_-=1\), and \[p_+(x)=\frac{1}{1+e}=0.268941.\] The classifier favors the orthogonal absent prototype even at the presence prototype. More generally, its presence probability increases with presence distance, contradicting the stated distance-based interpretation.

Replacing both exponents by \(-d\) yields \(1/(1+e^{-1})=0.731059\) in this example. Alternatively, keeping the signs but defining \(d\) as cosine similarity gives that same corrected probability, since the shared constant in \(-d=\text{similarity}-1\) cancels. This is the strongest admissible benign reading. The available snapshot did not expose a prototype-baseline implementation in the searched Python sources, so no claim is made that the published baseline runs used the reversed rule. The supported defect is the local mathematical specification, graded Minor; historical benchmark impact needs further evidence.
# Dependence and proposed clarification

Problem 1 is repaired at the statement level by describing the gains as typical, with the explicit S&T exceptions. Problem 2 requires stating whether the implemented score was negative distance or positive similarity. The analytic sign repair restores nearest-prototype preference but does not validate a rerun or establish author adoption. Neither finding changes the feedforward computation of FS-SINR. Speed measurements and raw per-species accuracy remain outside the independent checks.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | Minor
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | Local algebra checked; historical use unknown
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded

Two local defects are supported. The highest demonstrated impact is Minor. A failure of the central FS-SINR method, systematic data leakage, or corruption of the historical benchmark results is not established.
