Title: Technical Verification: PieClam: A Universal Graph Autoencoder Based on Overlapping Inclusive and Exclusive Communities
# Paper identity and scope

PieClam: A Universal Graph Autoencoder Based on Overlapping Inclusive and Exclusive Communities. Daniel Zilberg; Ron Levie. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43754. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

Sections 2–3 and Appendix A.1–A.4 were examined in detail, with the main empirical discussion and selected Appendix D material read to bound the consequences. Original pages 5–7 and 13–16 were visually inspected. The reviewed code snapshot is `948cf7f87b572d0cd09886648074cd7198f9d7ce`, https://github.com/danizil/PieClam. Only selected likelihood, message-passing, probability and distance routines were read statically. No author code was executed.
# Definitions and the affected claim

Write \(f=(t,s)\), \(L=\operatorname{diag}(I,-I)\), and \[T^C=\{(t,s): |s_c|\le t_c\text{ for all }c\}.\] The decoder \(p_{nm}=1-\exp(-f_n^\top Lf_m)\) is a probability on this cone because \(t_{nc}t_{mc}-s_{nc}s_{mc}\ge0\) coordinate by coordinate. Theorem 3.8 claims that every target graph can be approximated in the regularized log-cut distance by a cone-constrained code whose dimension depends only on the error tolerance.

The proof first approximates \(\widetilde A=-\log(1-(1-\delta)A)\) by a symmetric nonnegative block matrix \(B\), with block values \(b_{ij}\). The essential next assertion (p. 16) is that its prescribed features satisfy \(f_n^\top Lf_m=b_{k_nk_m}\). Without this equality the weak-regularity approximation does not transfer to the probability decoder.
# Problem 1: the block representation cancels the required edges

For cross-class channels, Appendix A.4 assigns \(t=\sqrt{b_{ij}/4}\) and \(s=-\sqrt{b_{ij}/4}\) at both channel indices \((K-1)i+j\) and \((K-1)j+i\). Consider \(K=2\) singleton classes and \[B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This is a nonnegative symmetric block matrix as required by Definition A.4. The diagonal channel values vanish. Both cross-channel indices equal \(3\), and the displayed rule gives both nodes the same nonzero pair \((t_3,s_3)=(1/2,-1/2)\). Both features lie in \(T^{K^2}\). Nevertheless, \[f_1^\top Lf_2=\frac14-\frac14=0\ne1=b_{12}.\] All decoded probabilities are zero, whereas the claimed representation would have cross probability \(1-e^{-1}\). The cut-norm error in the block matrix is \(2/2^2=1/2\), despite starting from an exact block target.

This is not restricted to a particular value of the weak-regularity class-count bound. For any \(K\ge2\), a zero-diagonal target with nonzero off-diagonal blocks makes every assigned feature satisfy \(s_n=-t_n\), and hence makes the entire Lorentz Gram matrix zero. The independent \(K=4\) calculation with off-diagonal entries one gives cut error \(3/4\). Thus the failure remains for larger permitted class counts. The index map also collides, but correcting only the indexing does not correct the same-sign cancellation.

The original page image confirms the two negative signs; the adjacent bipartite example on p. 4, which uses opposite exclusive signs, provides clear counterevidence to interpreting this as a necessary limitation of IeClam. The error is in the printed construction, not in the cone’s expressive capacity.

The dimension and tolerance bookkeeping cannot be used literally either. Theorems 3.7–3.8 print a minus sign before \(\log(\epsilon/2)^2\). At \(\epsilon=1/2\), these expressions give \(K=-69.1852\) and \(C=2^{-28}\), neither a code dimension. A charitable reading is to square \(-\log(\epsilon/2)\) instead. Even then, A.4 requests only \(\|\widetilde A-B\|_\square\le\epsilon\) and subsequently adds \(\epsilon/2\), which yields at best \(3\epsilon/2\), not the stated \(\epsilon\). The strict bound also needs slack. These are not used as isolated typographical complaints: the displayed expressions do not establish the central quantitative guarantee.

This is Major under the claim-level standard. Theorem 3.8 is the proof supporting the paper’s probability-valued universality contribution. A repairable invalid construction remains an invalid core derivation. The counterexample does not disprove the existence of another encoding, and the benchmark results do not depend on implementing this proof construction.
# An explicit repair with a changed quantitative bound

Every nonnegative symmetric \(K\)-block matrix has a valid cone representation using \(C=K(K+1)/2\) inclusive/exclusive coordinate pairs. Give each diagonal block \(i\) one coordinate, with \(t=\sqrt{b_{ii}}\), \(s=0\) on class \(i\) and zero elsewhere. Give every unordered pair \(i<j\) a distinct coordinate, writing \(a_{ij}=\sqrt{b_{ij}/2}\). On class \(i\) put \((t,s)=(a_{ij},a_{ij})\), on class \(j\) put \((t,s)=(a_{ij},-a_{ij})\), and put zero elsewhere.

Every feature belongs to \(T^C\). A pair coordinate contributes zero within either class, \(2a_{ij}^2=b_{ij}\) between its two classes, and zero otherwise. A diagonal coordinate contributes exactly \(b_{ii}\) within class \(i\). Summing proves \(f_n^\top Lf_m=B_{nm}\) for every pair, including self-pairs. The finite checks for \(K=2,4,6\) agree within \(4.45\cdot10^{-16}\); the preceding argument is the general verification.

For precision, a repaired qualitative statement is: for every \(0<\epsilon<1\) and every symmetric binary adjacency matrix \(A\), there is a code in \(T^C\) with \(D_\square(P\|A)<\epsilon\) and a dimension bound independent of the number of nodes. One sufficient bound follows by setting \[\delta=\eta=\epsilon/3,\quad R=\log(3/\epsilon),\quad
 K\le 4^{\lceil R^2/\eta^2\rceil},\quad C=K(K+1)/2.\] Use the nonnegative block approximation to \(\widetilde A=-\log(1-(1-\delta)A)\) with cut error at most \(\eta\), then the exact encoding above. The decoded \(P=1-e^{-B}\) has entries in \([0,1)\) and \[D_\square(P\|A)\le\delta+\|\widetilde A-B\|_\square
 \le 2\epsilon/3<\epsilon.\] Smaller actual partitions can be padded by unused code coordinates. Tolerances at least one are covered by applying the construction at a smaller tolerance. This restores qualitative universality, with an explicitly changed dimension bound; it does not validate the printed bound or claim author adoption.
# Other checks and boundaries

The unrestricted construction in A.3 represents a signed matrix as a difference of two Gram matrices. That algebra is valid. A negative entry can, however, give \(1-e^{-c}<0\), which is outside the probability-valued decoder definition. Section 3.5 explicitly discloses this possibility. Thus the first theorem should be read as a signed approximation result; it cannot replace the cone argument when a probabilistic decoder is required.

For Claim 3.6, averaging the four bipartite blocks and using \(|a^2-\langle q,y\rangle|\ge a^2-\langle q,y\rangle\) supports the claimed lower bound under its self-pair convention. The no-self-loop setting is distinguished in Appendix A.2; the bound is not silently transferred to a different convention here.

An independent finite-difference calculation verifies equation (11)’s likelihood gradient at an interior cone point, with maximum discrepancy \(1.62\cdot10^{-10}\) at step \(10^{-5}\). The inspected probability routine uses \(1-\exp(-f_n^\top Lf_m)\) and explicitly zeros its diagonal. The inspected log-cut routine estimates a cut norm at a supplied regularizer using rounded/SDP outputs. Figure 1 itself labels a fixed \(d=0.01\); it does not prove convergence in the infimum-based distance or global likelihood optimization. Main Figures 2–3 visually illustrate prior and block reconstruction, without independently verifying data provenance or accuracy.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | Major
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | Qualitative theorem repaired; bound changed
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded

The highest supported impact is Major because the central cone-universality derivation is invalid as printed. A verified alternative construction restores the qualitative result with a changed dimension bound. No empirical failure or impossibility of the proposed decoder is established.

1 Daniel Zilberg; Ron Levie. PieClam: A Universal Graph Autoencoder Based on Overlapping Inclusive and Exclusive Communities. PMLR 267 (2025), published PDF. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/zilberg25a.html.
# Reproducibility and limits

`independent_check.py` implements only the printed and repaired finite constructions, dimension arithmetic and an independent likelihood-gradient diagnostic. It imports no author modules. Source reads included `clamiter.py` lines 142–219 and 1539–1604, and `utils/utils.py` lines 50–109 and 407–438. Their presence does not establish the provenance of historical runs. Other source branches, prior optimization, raw datasets, downstream results and external references were not exhaustively audited.

For completeness, the block approximation used in the repair can be justified by the usual finite energy argument. Normalize the matrix inner product by \(N^2\). Let \(B\) be the blockwise average of a matrix in \([0,R]^{N\times N}\) on a common row/column partition. If its cut error exceeds \(\eta\), refine every part by a witnessing pair of subsets \(U,V\), multiplying the number of classes by at most four. The refined projection \(B'\) satisfies \(\langle B'-B,1_U1_V^\top\rangle
=\langle A-B,1_U1_V^\top\rangle\). Since the normalized norm of the indicator is at most one, \(\|B'-B\|_2>\eta\). Orthogonality of the projections increases \(\|B\|_2^2\) by more than \(\eta^2\). This energy is at most \(R^2\), so fewer than \(R^2/\eta^2\) unsuccessful refinement steps are possible, giving the stated conservative class bound. Block averages remain nonnegative and symmetric. This argument verifies the repaired qualitative result without assuming that the published coordinate formula is correct.

Title: Technical Verification: Does learning the right latent variables necessarily improve in-context learning?
# Paper identity and scope

Does learning the right latent variables necessarily improve in-context learning?. Sarthak Mittal; Eric Elmoznino; Leo Gagnon; Sangnie Bhardwaj; Guillaume Lajoie; Dhanya Sridhar. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43755. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

Sections 1–5, Appendices B–C and the prose of D–E were read. Original Figures 2–4, 6–8, 10 and 12, and Tables 7–8 were visually inspected on physical pages 3–5, 7–8, 17, 19 and 27. The frozen packet contains the published PDF with its appendices but no located author-code release. No code or checkpoint behavior is asserted.
# What the factorization establishes

The explicit model uses \(h=z_\psi(D)\) and \(p_\gamma(y\mid x,h)\); the implicit model uses \(p_\phi(y\mid x,D)\). Since \(h\) is computed without the query, the stated architecture removes direct query-to-context attention. It does not mathematically force \(h\) to equal a particular generative parameter. An invertible reparameterization of a sufficient latent is equally usable if the predictor inverts it. Conversely, a bottleneck can contain the right information while a learned predictor uses it poorly. The paper addresses this distinction empirically, through probing, auxiliary latent losses, a known prediction function and intervention tests.

The auxiliary loss \(\|z-Wh\|^2\) supervises a linear decoding of \(h\), while the prediction network still consumes \(h\). Figure 8 additionally tests direct supervision \(\|z-h\|^2\); its similar reported error limits the explanation that the linear readout alone created the failure. The known-decoder experiment retrains an explicit model with the prescribed \(g\) and is a privileged control, not merely an intervention that swaps one layer of an otherwise unchanged trained model. Its favorable result supports the usefulness of the correct prediction rule, without uniquely identifying a cause in every trained model.

Appendix E’s implicit proxy \(p_\gamma(y\mid x,z_\psi(D,x))\) retains the bottleneck while allowing query-dependent aggregation. This is an appropriate structural contrast to the explicit factorization. Appendix C confirms that the prediction target is masked and that the setting is fixed-context supervised prediction with bidirectional attention, rather than ordinary causal next-token training.
# Independent checks and interpretation of error

For linear prediction with a latent estimate independent of a fresh query, write \(e=\widehat z-z\). If \(x\sim N(0,\sigma^2I)\) independently of \(e\), then \[\mathbb E[(x^\top e)^2\mid e]=\sigma^2\|e\|^2.\] Tripling query standard deviation therefore multiplies prediction risk by nine even without worsening latent inference. An independent paired calculation with a fixed three-dimensional error vector confirms the factor exactly to numerical precision. This does not explain away the comparisons: all models in an OOD panel face the same query distribution, and the nearly perfect known-decoder linear result is a separate control. It does mean that a larger raw OOD MSE alone is not evidence that latent inference deteriorated.

A finite context can also leave genuine latent uncertainty. In noiseless Gaussian linear regression, when the design matrix has rank below the parameter dimension, the unobserved null-space component is not identifiable from the context. Thus the high-dimensional scaling experiments cannot demand perfect latent recovery without a context-rank qualification. The paper acknowledges this uncertainty when discussing Figure 6.

The described distributed-alignment intervention can be written \[h'=h+QQ^\top(h_{\rm source}-h),\qquad Q^\top Q=I.\] It replaces the selected source coordinates while preserving the orthogonal complement. An independent \(20\)-dimensional calculation with a \(10\)-dimensional subspace verifies both properties. The normalized intervention score in C.4, \((a-b)/(1-b)\) for baseline \(b<1\), maps baseline performance to zero and perfect performance to one. It is not raw classification accuracy. The text states that evaluation uses held-out latent pairs; actual split membership could not be checked.

The task-count arithmetic is consistent: the modular MoE has \(5^5=3125\) latent combinations, and Alchemy has \(109\cdot48\cdot32=167424\) environments, leaving \(67424\) after holding out \(100000\).
# Figure evidence and scope of the negative result

Figures 2–3 show substantial regression degradation and a pronounced benefit from the known decoder for linear and sinusoidal tasks. They do not show universal equality of all methods: for example, the MLP explicit variant has lower mean OOD linear-regression error than the implicit model in Figure 2. Figure 4 also has latent- and architecture-specific differences; the implicit stone-map intervention result is stronger than its graph/potion-map results. These are reasons to retain the paper’s qualified, aggregate interpretation rather than turn it into an all-tasks dominance claim.

Figure 7 explicitly reports a case where a stronger shortcut-generating training distribution makes the implicit model perform worse, and the explicit Transformer benefits. Figure 12 supplies an enlarged context-aggregator control, so a simple objection based only on splitting the original model’s depth is not unaddressed. Tables 7–8 likewise show variation across configurations. These controls and exceptions are consistent with the title’s question about necessary improvement.

The checked evidence does not establish that every Transformer intrinsically fails at structured ICL, that the implicit model never represents task latents, or that bottlenecks are useless. In particular, failure of a restricted intervention search is not an exhaustive absence proof over all representations. The paper’s stronger explanatory language should be read within its tested tasks, model families and training procedures. No independent numerical effect size, significance test or population-wide claim is certified here.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | No Issue Found
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | No repair proposed
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded

No substantive defect is established within the declared scope. The result is best read as an empirical counterweight to the expectation of automatic gains from explicit latent recovery, with the reported exceptions preserved. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification: FactTest: Factuality Testing in Large Language Models with Finite-Sample and Distribution-Free Guarantees
# Paper identity and scope

FactTest: Factuality Testing in Large Language Models with Finite-Sample and Distribution-Free Guarantees. Fan Nie; Xiaotian Hou; Shuhang Lin; James Zou; Huaxiu Yao; Linjun Zhang. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43756. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

The main statistical construction, Theorems 2.1–2.2 and 3.1, their Appendix A proofs, the conformal connection, and the experimental definitions were examined. Original pages 3, 4, 7, 8, 14, 17 and 19 were visually inspected. The frozen repository https://github.com/fannie1208/FactTest, commit `2f7bb87530d8321423304330964b70e50b621307`, was read selectively, including the HotpotQA vanilla calibration, score generation and evaluation scripts. Author code was not executed.
# The finite-sample guarantee and its scope

Let \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) be the distributions of question–answer pairs conditional on incorrect and correct answers. The classifier accepts a pair when \(\widehat\eta>T_{(\widehat k)}\), where the incorrect calibration scores are ordered and \[v(k)=\sum_{j=k}^{n_0}{n_0\choose j}(1-\alpha)^j\alpha^{n_0-j},
 \qquad \widehat k=\min\{k:v(k)\le\delta\}.\] The sentinel \(T_{(n_0+1)}=\infty\) is essential. The order-statistic argument gives Theorem 2.1’s high-probability control of \(R_0=P_0(\text{accept})\), including discrete scores when the comparison is strict. For example, with \(n_0=100,\alpha=.05,\delta=.01\), direct summation gives \(v(100)=.00592053\), \(v(99)=.0370812\), and \(\widehat k=100\).

This controls acceptance among incorrect examples. It is not the same quantity as the error proportion among accepted answers. The paper defines selective accuracy and answer rate separately, and Appendix D.3 reports the latter. Finite test-set FPR values exceeding \(\alpha\) do not by themselves contradict a calibration-probability statement.
# Problem 1: the optimal posterior threshold need not exist

Section 2.3 (p. 3) asserts that an optimizer over deterministic measurable classifiers has the form \[f_\alpha^*(x)=\mathbf1\{\eta(x)>\tau_\alpha\},
 \qquad \eta(x)=P(Y=1\mid X=x).\] Theorem 2.2 assumes a continuous estimated score \(\widehat\eta(X)\) under \(P_0\). This does not imply that \(\eta(X)\) has no atoms. The proof on p. 14 subsequently uses the exact equalities \(P_0(\eta>\tau_\alpha)=\alpha\) and \(P_0(\eta>\tau_{\alpha'})=\alpha'\).

Here is a counterexample to this characterization. Take \(X\) uniform on \([0,1]\), with \(Y\) an independent fair Bernoulli variable. Thus \(P_0=P_1\) is uniform and \(\eta\equiv1/2\). For any \(0<\alpha<1\), every strict threshold of \(\eta\) either accepts everyone, violating the constraint, or accepts nobody, with \(R_1=1\). Yet \[f(x)=\mathbf1\{x\le\alpha\},\qquad
 R_0(f)=\alpha,\quad R_1(f)=1-\alpha\] is admissible and strictly better. In fact every admissible rule has power at most \(\alpha\), so this rule is optimal. Taking \(H\) to be the identity and \(\widehat\eta(x)=1/2+\epsilon_\eta(2x-1)\) supplies a continuous score and the required uniform approximation for arbitrarily small positive \(\epsilon_\eta\).

The difficulty occurs before the bound can be evaluated: the stated optimal-threshold parameters are not defined as claimed for this distribution. This is not presented as a numerical counterexample satisfying an additional, implicit assumption that those exact posterior quantiles already exist. Rather, it disproves the asserted general characterization and identifies the missing hypothesis in the power theorem and proof. Sample-size conditions and continuity of the estimated score do not remove the posterior atom.

A restriction ensuring exact posterior tail probabilities at \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha'\) would eliminate this particular obstruction. Alternatively, a boundary-selection or randomized NP rule needs an explicit definition and a new excess-risk argument. The full repaired power bound is not certified here. The finding is Major because the defective step supports the paper’s central Type II guarantee. The Type I theorem, which uses arbitrary scores rather than posterior optimality, remains intact.
# Qualification: the practical shift procedure lacks the theorem’s envelope

Theorem 3.1 (p. 4) explicitly assumes the exact conditional density ratio \(w=dP_0/d\widetilde P_0\) and a global upper bound \(B\). Under those assumptions, accepting each source sample with probability \(w/B\) indeed gives the target conditional law; the proof is sound. Section 5.4 (p. 8) instead estimates \(w\) and takes a 90th-percentile envelope. Appendix C.4 specifies logistic-regression estimation, without an error bound. These are disclosed practical choices, but they do not retain the theorem’s guarantee.

Even with an oracle ratio, clipping at a quantile changes the accepted law to a density proportional to \(\min(w,B)\) relative to \(\widetilde P_0\). For a two-stratum example, set \[\widetilde P_0(E)=.001,\quad P_0(E)=.09,\quad
 w(E)=90,\quad w(E^c)=.91/.999.\] The 90th percentile under either source or target is \(B=.91/.999\). Every source point is then accepted because both ratios are at least \(B\), so the retained distribution is the source, not the target. Choose score \(\mathbf1_E\) and \(n_0=100,\alpha=.05,\delta=.01\). With probability \(.999^{100}=.904792\), the calibration sample contains no point of \(E\) and the calibrated threshold is zero. The target FPR is then \(.09>.05\). This obeys covariate shift by taking \(Y\) independent of the stratum in both domains. If points above \(B\) are discarded instead of clipped, the rare target stratum is also lost.

This example refutes transfer of the exact guarantee to that quantile-envelope rule, not Theorem 3.1. It does not reproduce ParaRel-OOD or establish that its observed curve is incorrect. Section 5.4 explicitly presents these choices and conclusions as an experimental evaluation. Its wording can therefore reasonably be read as a statement about the displayed empirical curves, rather than a claim that the estimated/truncated implementation satisfies Theorem 3.1. The counterexample establishes a limit on transferring that theorem; it does not establish a false empirical claim in the paper. This is a scope clarification, with any stronger practical guarantee or historical violation requiring further evidence. A general guarantee for this implementation would need a ratio-error and truncation correction.
# Problems 3 and 4: two local release discrepancies

The stored-score branch in `calibration/HotpotQA/calculate_vanilla_threshold.py`, lines 85–101, accumulates the binomial upper tail downward and reads `certainties[k]` when the sum first exceeds \(\delta\). In the ordinary interior case this indexing corresponds correctly to \(T_{(k+1)}\). But for \(n_0=10,\alpha=.05,\delta=.01\), the first term is \(.95^{10}=.598737>\delta\): the branch immediately requests index \(10\) of a ten-element array. The paper instead prescribes the sentinel \(\infty\). The loop also excludes \(k=1,0\), so it is not a complete implementation for all parameter regimes. This is a static control-flow demonstration, not an executed author-code failure. An explicit full-domain selection with the sentinel repairs the identified boundary case; no full implementation certification is claimed. This release-only finding is Minor.

The final two print statements in `evaluation/HotpotQA/eval.py` label \(\mathrm{FP}/(\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{TN})\) as `fnr`, and \(\mathrm{FN}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN})\) as `fpr`. For \((\mathrm{TP},\mathrm{FP},\mathrm{TN},\mathrm{FN})=(3,1,4,2)\), the true rates are \(.2\) and \(.4\), respectively, but those labels are interchanged. Relabeling the outputs is a local correction. The inspected comparator itself is correctly strict, preserving tie conservatism. This is Minor; the frozen release alone does not prove which script or post-processing generated the published tables.
# Empirical and alternative-reading checks

Figures 1 and 4 display empirical FPR curves, not repeated-calibration confidence experiments. Figure 2 correctly acknowledges that selective accuracy need not be monotone in threshold, although FPR and FNR move in opposite directions. Table 7 makes the accuracy–coverage tradeoff visible: its high accuracy is not unconditional accuracy on every question. Discrete entropy scores are permitted by Theorem 2.1, while the separate continuity assumption in Theorem 2.2 must not be silently attributed to them. These distinctions are preserved as counterevidence against a blanket rejection of the method.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | Major
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | Local corrections identified; full power repair open
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded

The highest supported impact is Major, confined to the missing posterior-boundary condition in a core power derivation. The basic finite-sample Type I construction and the exact-ratio shift theorem remain supported within their assumptions. Practical shift guarantees and released-code outputs require the qualifications above; historical benchmark provenance remains unresolved.

# Reproducibility and limits

`independent_checks.py` uses elementary binomial sums and analytic finite examples only; its JSON output records every numeric value cited above. No LLM, dataset generation, author script, API or training procedure was run. The repository review is selective and no complete historical pipeline or checkpoint was available for reproduction. Bibliography claims and the novelty priority of the conformal correspondence were not independently adjudicated.

Title: Technical Verification: Efficient Source-free Unlearning via Energy-Guided Data Synthesis and Discrimination-Aware Multitask Optimization
# Paper identity and scope

Efficient Source-free Unlearning via Energy-Guided Data Synthesis and Discrimination-Aware Multitask Optimization. Xiuyuan Wang; Chaochao Chen; Weiming Liu; Xinting Liao; Fan Wang; Xiaolin Zheng. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43757. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

Sections 3–4, all three theorem statements, Algorithm 1, and the numerical tables and figures were examined. Physical pages 3–9 were actually viewed, including a high-resolution crop of Algorithm 1 to resolve the square-root extent in its noise term. The frozen source package contains the eleven-page proceedings paper and no available author implementation or separate supplement. No historical code execution or empirical reproduction is claimed.
# Problem 1: a translation gradient step is not its optimizer

Theorem 3.1 (pp. 3–4) minimizes \(\mathrm{KL}(q_T\|p)\) over translations \(T(x)=x+\epsilon\) and calls \[T(x)=x+\alpha\,\mathbb E_q[\nabla_x\log p(x)]\] the resulting optimal transformation. Take \(q=N(1,1)\) and \(p=N(0,1)\), both smooth positive densities, and choose the permitted step size \(\alpha=.1\). Then \[\mathrm{KL}(q_T\|p)=\tfrac12(1+\epsilon)^2.\] The exact optimum is \(\epsilon=-1\), with KL zero. The stated transformation gives \(\epsilon=-.1\), with KL \(.405\). Even interpreting the gradient equation implicitly at the updated translation yields \(\epsilon=-\alpha(1+\epsilon)\), whose solution is \(-\alpha/(1+\alpha)\), still not the minimizer.

The derivative at zero is a legitimate descent direction. Relabeling the formula as one gradient step, with appropriate smoothness and step-size conditions for descent, removes the false optimization claim. It does not prove a distribution-matching theorem: a common translation cannot alter the covariance of \(q\). Nor does the expectation-valued translation itself derive the samplewise noisy update in equation (3). The finding is Major because this theorem is presented as the derivation motivating the first central stage. It does not show that a separately justified Langevin sampler cannot be useful.
# Problem 2: the accelerated update changes the diffusion

Equation (4), called an exact solution on p. 4, contains only a drift integral. A Langevin diffusion with drift \(\alpha s(X)\) also contains a Brownian increment, with variance \(2\alpha\Delta t\) for a frozen coefficient. Equation (5) uses noise \(\sqrt{2\alpha}\,\varepsilon\), while Algorithm 1, lines 9 and 13, uses \(\sqrt{2\alpha}\,\Delta t\,\varepsilon\). The original page and enlarged crop confirm that \(\Delta t\) lies outside the radical. These formulas define different samplers for nonunit intervals.

A scalar target exposes the consequence without an author implementation. Set \(E(x)=x^2/2\), \(s(x)=-x\), \(\alpha=1\), momentum decay \(\gamma=0\), and all time intervals \(\Delta t=h\), with \(0<h<1\). These are valid inputs to the printed sampler; the normalized energy law is \(N(0,1)\). The energy can also be obtained from a class probability \(M_y(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\) in equation (1). The remaining class probability is \(1-M_y(x)\).

Using the same fresh standard normal \(\varepsilon_i\) in the predictor and corrector, exactly as Algorithm 1 states, gives \[X'=(1-h)X_i+\sqrt2h\varepsilon_i,\qquad
 X_{i+1}=a_hX_i+b_h\varepsilon_i,\] \[a_h=1-h+h^2/2,\qquad b_h=\sqrt2h(1-h/2).\] Since \(|a_h|<1\), the stationary variance is \[V_h=\frac{2h^2(1-h/2)^2}{1-(1-h+h^2/2)^2},
 \qquad V_h\sim h\quad(h\downarrow0).\] Thus reducing the mesh collapses the variance to zero rather than approaching the target variance one. Direct values are \(V_{.1}=.0997375\) and \(V_{.01}=.00999975\). Starting from the prescribed \(N(0,1)\) initialization also immediately changes the variance; at \(h=.1\) it becomes \(.837075\).

A deterministic Runge–Kutta accuracy statement does not repair this missing diffusion scaling. For the zero-momentum, unit-coefficient diagnostic, replacing the noise by \(\sqrt{2h}\,\varepsilon_i\) in both stages gives the usual stochastic Heun scaling and restores the correct small-mesh variance limit. This is only a local diagnostic repair; the full momentum algorithm and its invariant law still require specification and analysis. Special unit intervals hide the disagreement between the printed formulas, but do not justify the general time sequence. No code is available to identify the historical implementation. The defect is Major because it invalidates the claimed sampling-accuracy rationale for AEGDS, not because an empirical speedup has been disproved.

There is a further scope boundary: the normalized density proportional to \(M(y\mid x)\) need not equal the original \(p(x\mid y)\), which is proportional to \(M(y\mid x)p(x)\) even for a perfect classifier. The paper supplies no universal recovery theorem for the missing marginal. The feature plots are therefore empirical support, not an identification proof.
# Problem 3: the dual substitution does not yield equation (13)

Write \(\phi=c^2\|g_T\|^2\). The correct inner maximization in equation (10), for \(\lambda>0\), is \[\max_d\left[g_w^\top d-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|d-g_T\|^2+
 \frac{\lambda\phi}{2}\right]
 =g_w^\top g_T+\frac{\|g_w\|^2}{2\lambda}+
 \frac{\lambda\phi}{2}.\] Substitution of \(d=g_T+g_w/\lambda\) shows this directly. Equation (13) on p. 7 incorrectly retains an extra \(-\lambda\|g_T\|^2/2\), and equation (14) differentiates that erroneous expression.

For an admissible one-dimensional example, take all three gradients equal to one, with initial loss weights summing to one. Then \(g_T=g_w=1\) for every simplex weight, and set \(c=1/2\), so \(\phi=1/4\). The primal feasible interval is \([1/2,3/2]\) and its optimal value is \(3/2\). The printed dual becomes \[1+\frac{1}{2\lambda}-\frac{3\lambda}{8},\] which tends to \(-\infty\). Its derivative at the claimed \(\lambda^*=2\) is \(-1/2\), not zero. This cannot be the dual of the bounded primal problem. The error is an invalid core derivation, hence Major even though it is repairable.

The corrected dual above gives \(\lambda^*=\|g_w\|/\sqrt\phi\) when \(\phi>0\) and \(g_w\ne0\), and the minimized expression \(g_w^\top g_T+\sqrt\phi\,\|g_w\|\). This recovers the paper’s final weight objective and, at a regular saddle point, its direction \(d^*=g_T+\sqrt\phi\,g_{w^*}/\|g_{w^*}\|\). Indeed the scalar example has corrected dual value \(1.5\) at \(\lambda=2\), agreeing with the primal. The objective is the support function of the compact feasible ball; minimax interchange with the compact weight simplex gives the optimal value directly. This supplies a general algebraic repair for the regular case, rather than validating the printed equations.

The theorem also permits \(c=0\). That case has the unique feasible direction \(d=g_T\) and must be handled directly; the displayed division by \(\sqrt\phi\) is undefined. If \(g_{w^*}=0\) at positive radius, the normalized expression is likewise undefined and an optimal primal direction must be recovered separately. The repaired statement here explicitly excludes that degeneracy. Optimizing the worst inner product also does not promise strictly positive improvement for every task when their gradients oppose one another.
# Problem 4: empirical diagnostics do not certify complete erasure

Section 4.2 (p. 8) infers complete removal of forget information from \(A_f=0\), and Section 4.4 (p. 9) asserts no privacy risk because synthetic samples are visually unintelligible. Neither implication follows from its diagnostic. A model can retain an unchanged data-dependent hidden representation while a modified head always suppresses the forget label; it then has zero forget-class accuracy without erasing that representation. A visually noise-like vector can likewise encode an input through a known invertible permutation or mask.

These examples invalidate the inference, not the measured DSDA accuracy or a demonstrated attack against its actual output. The paper does include a logistic-regression membership attack, which is relevant positive evidence and must not be ignored. It is one specified attack, however, not a proof against all recovery. Table 1 itself gives PinsFaceRecognition MIA \(18.39\) for DSDA versus \(.82\) for retraining, a \(17.57\) percentage-point difference. The local absolute language should be replaced with the achieved accuracy and tested attack results. This finding is Minor: actual residual information in the unavailable trained models remains unresolved.
# Checks that support surviving conclusions

The retain/forget loss signs in Section 3.3 agree with cross-entropy minimization on retained examples and maximization on forgotten ones. The discrimination objective compares normalized feature directions and includes adaptive nonnegative weights; its visual motivation is distinct from a quantitative distribution-equality guarantee. Figures 2 and 5 do show the reported projected cluster structure and noisy synthetic samples, but a low-dimensional projection cannot establish equality of full data laws.

The tables support substantial reductions in elapsed time against GKT and ISPF. Averaging the twelve per-cell relative reductions \(1-\mathrm{ET}_{DSDA}/\mathrm{ET}_{baseline}\) over Tables 1–2 gives \(68.4146\%\), close to the stated \(68.50\%\); a different aggregation or unrounded timings could explain the small difference, so it is not elevated to a finding. The reported source-free accuracy gains and ablations are not negated by the mathematical examples. Timing includes evaluation according to Section 4.1; it is not pure optimization time.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | Major
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | Regular dual repaired; sampling repair incomplete
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded

The highest supported impact is Major because central sampling and optimization derivations fail explicit checks. A corrected dual recovers the regular-case multitask expression, while the sampler needs an unambiguous stochastic update and new justification. The available record does not establish that DSDA’s measured accuracy or speed comparisons are false.

# Reproducibility and limits

`independent_checks.py` evaluates analytic Gaussian moments, the scalar primal and dual, and table arithmetic. It imports no author code and performs no model training. No implementation was present in the frozen source packet, so the connection between the conflicting published update formulas and the historical experiments is unknown. report: Abstract: The theoretical bound used to justify prototype retrieval confuses geometric covering with transport of probability mass. An exact k-center example with distinct points violates the displayed Wasserstein bound by a wide margin. A weighted prototype measure restores the bound, but changes the retrieval rule. Selective static inspection also finds an unmasked cross-sequence attention path in the released training implementation. Local numerical summaries need correction. The original adaptation results and retrieval ablations remain empirical evidence; their historical execution has not been reproduced.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date:
Title: Technical Verification: World Model Implanting for Test-time Adaptation of Embodied Agents
# Paper identity and scope

World Model Implanting for Test-time Adaptation of Embodied Agents. Minjong Yoo; Jinwoo Jang; Sihyung Yoon; Honguk Woo. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43758. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

Sections 3–4, Appendix A.1, implementation details in Appendix C, and the additional analyses in Appendix D were read. Original pages 4–8, 11, 16 and 18 were visually inspected. The frozen source is https://github.com/mjyoo2/WorMI, commit `96a2375ad7e96e75073f478bd37462f931dc39bc`. The retrieval, tensor-distance, attention-hook, model-forward, dataset and selected training routines were inspected statically. No author module was imported or executed.
# Problem 1: covering radius does not control equal-mass transport

Equation (4) (p. 4), proved in Appendix A.1 (p. 11), claims \[W(p_i,p_j)\le W(E_i,E_j)+2\rho,\] where \(p_i,p_j\) are optimal \(k\)-center subsets and \(\rho\) bounds the distance of every embedding to a nearest center. The proof uses \(W(E_i,p_i)\le\rho\). That inference needs the prototype mass at each center to equal the mass assigned to it. It does not hold for uniform empirical measures on the center sets.

A finite counterexample avoids repeated-point conventions. Put \[S=\{0,.0001,.0002,\ldots,.0100\},\quad
 E_1=S\cup\{1\},\quad E_2=S\cup\{2\},\quad k=2.\] Each set contains 102 distinct real points. The unique optimal center sets are \(p_1=\{.005,1\}\) and \(p_2=\{.005,2\}\), with \(\rho=.005\). To verify optimality, an isolated outlier must have its own center for any radius below \(.005\); the remaining center must cover both endpoints of \(S\), requiring radius at least \(.005\), attained only at \(.005\). Independent enumeration of all center pairs confirms this argument.

For uniform empirical measures, ordered one-dimensional transport gives \[W_1(E_1,E_2)=1/102,\qquad W_1(p_1,p_2)=1/2.\] Thus the asserted inequality would require \[.5\le 1/102+.01=.0198039,\] which is false. This uses exact centers, so an approximation algorithm cannot explain it away. The example also extends to the reported \(k=15\): append the common isolated points \(4,5,\ldots,16\) to both full sets and center sets. Then there are 115 data points and 15 centers, still with radius \(.005\), but the two sides are \(1/15=.0666667\) and \(1/115+.01=.0186957\).

The frozen `TensorSet.dist` in `wormi/modules/utils.py` calls `scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance_nd` without mass weights. This supports the equal-mass reading rather than supplying the missing cluster masses. `ModelStore` in `wormi/model_store.py` uses KMeans centers rather than the paper’s subset-constrained \(k\)-center optimization. This is an additional source-to-description discrepancy, but it is not needed for the counterexample. The inspected scripts do not establish that this release generated the original retrieval experiments.
## A precise weighted repair

Let \(\mu_i\) be the empirical data measure, let \(Q_i\) assign each point to a center within \(ho_i\), and set \(
u_i=(Q_i)_\#\mu_i\). The coupling \((X,Q_i(X))\) proves \(W_1(\mu_i,
u_i)\leho_i\). The triangle inequality then yields the stronger two-sided statement \[ ig|W_1(
u_i,
u_j)-W_1(\mu_i,\mu_j) ig|
 \leho_i+ho_j.\] In the two-center example the masses are \((101/102,1/102)\), and the repaired prototype distance is exactly \(1/102\). The same argument works for finite-order Wasserstein distances under the corresponding moment assumptions because every transported point moves by at most its radius.

This repair requires retaining cluster masses. It does not validate uniform-center distances, and it changes the intentional suppression of frequent objects described on p. 4. If equal weighting is a desired modeling choice, its relationship to full empirical transport needs a different statement. Even the repaired bound alone does not ensure identical top-\(K\) retrieval without separation between candidate distances.

This is Major: the false bound is the theoretical justification for substituting prototypes in a central retrieval component. Its failure does not imply that the prototypes select poor models on VirtualHome or invalidate the attention mechanism. Table A.11’s near-equal success rates for full and prototype retrieval are useful empirical counterevidence, but cannot prove the universal inequality.
# Problem 2: the released attention path is not causal over training tokens

In `wormi/modules/hooks.py`, lines 150–187, the base hook calls its reasoning-level cross-attention with query, key and value but no `attn_mask`, `key_padding_mask`, or causal flag. The stored `world_mask` is converted to floating point but not passed into the call. In the world-wise subclass, lines 423–459, world representations are combined separately at each sequence position, then returned as a full sequence for this outer attention.

The model’s forward path supplies the same token sequence to the world models and the main model. The training wrapper uses completion-only causal-LM collation, and the VirtualHome chat conversion includes the assistant action in that sequence. Consequently a hidden state at an earlier prediction position can attend through the implanted path to a later world-model state that already includes a target action token. A causal mask inside each frozen language model does not prevent this new cross-position path.

The mechanism can be checked without a language model: with two scalar values \((0,z)\) and equal unmasked attention logits at the first query, the first output is \(z/2\). Changing only the future value from zero to two changes that output from zero to one; a causal first-position output remains zero. This illustrates the dependence permitted by the code, not the numerical behavior of a trained WorMI checkpoint.

The defect is assessed as Minor at the released-source level because the historical training implementation and effect size are unknown. It warrants a causal mask aligned to token positions, together with padding treatment and a future-token invariance check on the actual training path. Such a check was not run here, and no repaired training system is certified. Prefix-only autoregressive inference does not supply unavailable future tokens; the issue is the mismatch with full-sequence teacher forcing, not a claim that evaluation directly reads unseen answers.
# Problem 3: local performance summaries do not match their tables

Several discrepancies can be resolved using the printed numbers alone. In Table 1, the VirtualHome unseen-task/unseen-scene success-rate difference is \(66.12-45.71=20.41\) percentage points. The introduction calls this an average zero-shot improvement, whereas the equal-weight mean over all three reported VirtualHome conditions is \(17.2767\) points. The \(20.41\) value should be tied to the stated hard condition rather than an unspecified average.

The ALFWorld pending-step reduction in Section 4.1 is \(23.86-20.18=3.68\), or \(15.42\%\) relative to the baseline, rather than the stated \(18.23\%\) (which uses the new method as denominator). In the compound-attention ablation, Table 3(b) gives a reduction versus WorMI-ADD of \(17.43-15.17=2.26\) steps, not \(1.79\). The long-horizon goal-conditioned success difference in Table 6 is \(49.35-39.22=10.13\) points, not \(13.13\).

These are Minor reporting errors: all corrected comparisons retain the direction of advantage. The few-shot mean gain is \(26.5867\) points from the rounded per-shot values, consistent with approximately \(26.58\) using reported aggregate rounding; that comparison is not challenged. The intervals in Table 2 cannot be independently validated from aggregate means alone.
# Additional checks and limits on interpretation

The zero-shot protocol explicitly excludes target-domain demonstrations during training, while few-shot adaptation supplies 1, 5 or 10 such demonstrations. World models and the composition module undergo substantial source-domain training. Thus zero-shot refers to target-domain data, not to an entirely untrained policy. No split leakage was established by the materials inspected.

The two-level attention shapes are coherent when world models use aligned token positions: world-wise weighting yields one value vector per position, and the summed keys have the same sequence length. The temporal masking issue is separate from this dimensional compatibility. The apparent training callback that sets exposed parameters trainable is not evidence of unfreezing the entire LLM: `WorMI.named_parameters` filters internally stored model parameters, which were separately frozen.

Figures 4 and A.6 show changing world-attention weights. They support examples of selective attention, not causal identification of every model’s knowledge. Figure 5 intentionally adds pertinent models; it is not evidence that arbitrary additions always help. Table 5 and the adverse-model results expressly show degradation in other regimes. Removing a module demonstrates behavioral dependence; it does not certify erasure of all domain information from the learned composer or base model. The paper’s deployment and unlearning language is kept within those experimental limits here.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | Major
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | Weighted transport bound verified; rule changed
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded

The highest supported impact is Major for the invalid uniform-prototype transport guarantee. A proof is supplied for a changed, mass-weighted construction. The code and arithmetic findings are local and do not establish historical benchmark failure. The empirical adaptation results remain distinct from the failed universal bound.

# Reproducibility and limits

`independent_checks.py` records exact center enumeration, one-dimensional transport calculations, a two-token attention diagnostic and table arithmetic. These are independently written calculations, not author-code execution. The source review is selective; no LLM, simulator, checkpoint, split-generation process or historical confidence-interval calculation was reproduced. Runtime magnitude and historical provenance of the causal-attention issue remain open.

Title: Technical Verification: One Leaf Reveals the Season: Occlusion-Based Contrastive Learning with Semantic-Aware Views for Efficient Visual Representation
# Paper identity and scope

One Leaf Reveals the Season: Occlusion-Based Contrastive Learning with Semantic-Aware Views for Efficient Visual Representation. Xiaoyu Yang; Lijian Xu; Hongsheng Li; Shaoting Zhang. ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43759. The reviewed source is the frozen published proceedings PDF. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages.

The main text, Tables 1–12 and Appendices A–B were read; Figures 1–3 and source pages 2–9 and 16 were actually viewed. The selected author source is https://github.com/XiaoyuYoung/OCL, commit `fd2cbdbfa430edc3059a1f3555929bada172ac50`. Static tracing covered masking, encoding, the loss, the pre-training entry point and loop, the launcher and documented recipe, with a targeted check of linear-probe freezing. Author code was neither imported nor executed. This is a method and source-consistency review, not an ImageNet reproduction.
# Problem 1: the displayed denominator is not the implemented objective

Equation reference: eq:correct. Section 2.3 (p. 4) defines \(B\) image pairs, one normalized vector \(u_i\) and \(v_i\) from each image, and \(B^2-B\) cross-view negatives. Algorithm 1 forms a \(B\times B\) similarity matrix and applies cross-entropy in both directions. Its row loss is \[
 \ell_i=-\tau s(u_i,v_i)+\log\sum_{k=1}^{B}\exp\{\tau s(u_i,v_k)\},\] with the positive term included in the denominator. Equation (3), however, sums to \(2B\) while retaining a lower-branch vector \(y_k^L\), and excludes \(k=i\). There are only \(B\) such lower-branch vectors. With the pair ordering used in Algorithm 1, \(k=i\) is the positive rather than the anchor’s self-comparison.

These differences affect the calculation. For \(B=2\), let \(u_1=v_1=e_1\) and \(u_2=v_2=e_2\), choose the paper’s \(\kappa=64\) and an admissible positive scale \(\tau=1\). Both vectors have unit norm. The positive and negative similarities are \(1\) and \(1/130\). Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) gives \[\ell_i=\log(1+e^{-129/130})=0.3153363.\] Merely changing the upper limit to \(B\) while retaining the exclusion gives \(-129/130=-0.9923077\), a different objective; if the scale grows, this latter expression tends to \(-\infty\) rather than zero. The expression with the original upper limit is undefined under branch-local indexing.

A charitable global-index interpretation would concatenate both branches and exclude the anchor itself. That produces an ordinary all-view contrastive objective, but also introduces same-branch negatives absent from Algorithm 1. It requires changing the vector notation and still does not describe the supplied \(B\times B\) computation. The frozen `models_mae.py`, lines 167–189, agrees with Algorithm 1 and includes the diagonal positives. The supported correction is Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) and its transpose average. This is a Minor formula defect: the paper itself contains the coherent intended algorithm, and no loss error in the historical experiments is established.
# Problem 2: the concentration explanation has its direction reversed

Section 3.2.4 (p. 7) instead describes increasing \(\kappa\) as making the task more demanding; this is useful counterevidence to a systematic conceptual error. The mathematical correction is local: reverse the direction in the p. 4 explanation. Positive-pair labels remain assigned by image identity rather than by a similarity threshold. Neither this derivative nor the half-height criterion proves the proposed semantic interpretation or predicts the optimum in Table 6. Assessment: Minor.
# Problem 3: the frozen release does not specify the reported model recipe

The paper specifies a fixed Xavier-initialized patch projection (Section 2.1, p. 2), a trainable scale in the loss (p. 4), and \(\kappa=64\) by default (p. 5). In the frozen `models_mae.py`, lines 26–68 and 162–164, the default is \(\kappa=1/64\) and the temperature is the ordinary scalar \(0.07\). Similarities use the same rational formula as Equation (2), followed by division by that scalar. The pre-training constructor in `main_pretrain.py`, line 157, passes no concentration override, and the argument parser exposes none.

This is not a harmless reciprocal notation for \(\kappa\): the formula multiplies by the stored value in both sources. For orthogonal vectors, \[s_{64}(0)=1/130=0.0076923,\qquad
 s_{1/64}(0)=32/65=0.4923077.\] At \(c=.5\) the values are \(0.0227273\) and \(0.7441860\). Their relation is not a single global rescaling or additive shift that a softmax temperature could absorb. The fixed reciprocal temperature could represent the numerical value \(\tau=1/.07\), but it does not implement training of \(\tau\).

The projection weights are initialized and then used directly in the forward path; only the positional embedding is explicitly frozen. The pre-training optimizer receives the model’s ordinary trainable parameters, with no projection exclusion or detachment. Under the ordinary `timm.PatchEmbed` behavior, the projection therefore remains trainable. This contradicts the fixed-projection recipe; it does not assert that its resulting gradients are nonzero on every input.

There is a separate immediate recipe inconsistency: `PRETRAIN.md` passes `mae_vit_large_patch16`, while the frozen model namespace defines the `sae_vit_large_patch16` family. The entry point indexes that namespace directly, so the documented name cannot resolve if execution reaches model construction. This conclusion is static; the launcher was not run. The appendix also lists a ViT-L pre-training batch of 2,400 (Table 10, p. 16), whereas the main-text default is 2,048.

These are Minor release and specification defects with unresolved historical provenance. An exact benchmark configuration, including the concentration, scale parameterization, projection freeze and actual batch layout, is needed to choose a faithful repair. Simply replacing defaults here would not establish reproduction of 85.8% accuracy. No author adoption or repaired training run is claimed.
# Qualification 4: optimizer batch size and the contrastive negative pool

The discussion around Table 3 (p. 6) attributes batch-size gains to a larger negative pool. `PRETRAIN.md` recommends gradient accumulation to retain an effective batch size when memory or GPU count is reduced. The entry point calculates this size as \(bAR\), where \(b\) is the per-device microbatch, \(A\) is the accumulation count and \(R\) is the number of devices.

The release’s loss, however, constructs similarities only from the current local input. No cross-device feature gathering appears in this path. `engine_pretrain.py`, lines 45–60, computes the loss separately for each microbatch, divides by \(A\), and accumulates its gradients. Distributed gradient synchronization and later scalar logging do not add feature vectors to a loss denominator. Each anchor therefore has \(b-1\) negative candidates, not \(bAR-1\).

The distinction is exact, not merely a potential optimization difference. In the two-image example of Problem 1, processing both images together gives loss \(0.3153363\). Processing two singleton microbatches with \(A=2\) gives zero in each: the sole class has probability one. Its gradient is identically zero. For a nonstationary comparison, keep \(u_1=e_1,u_2=e_2,v_2=e_2\) and set \(v_1=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) at \(\theta=.3\). The full symmetric loss is \(0.4477130\), with central-difference derivative \(0.2866228\) in \(\theta\) (step \(10^{-6}\)); the accumulated singleton derivative remains exactly zero. All vectors are normalized and both procedures have optimizer effective batch two.

Accumulation still increases the number of images contributing to an optimizer step, so that conventional meaning of effective batch is valid. It cannot be used to infer an equivalent contrastive pool. Nor is a local-negative objective intrinsically invalid. The documented recommendation does not explicitly promise an identical negative pool. Moreover, varying the local microbatch at fixed accumulation and device counts would enlarge both the effective batch and the local pool, a reading compatible with the Table 3 explanation. The available evidence therefore establishes a scope clarification, not a demonstrated batch-semantics error or a falsification of Table 3. An assertion that the historical runs held the pool fixed while attributing gains to a larger pool would need additional run configuration evidence. Faithful comparisons must report both microbatch/pool size and optimizer batch size; a changed global-pool implementation would require feature aggregation with appropriate gradients and its own validation.
# Checks that survive and boundaries of the evidence

The masking path samples a random permutation and retains an even number of tokens before splitting it. For \(196\) patches, global masking ratios \(.3\) and \(.4\) retain 136 and 116 tokens, or 68 and 58 per branch. The sets are disjoint and the visible fractions \(.34694\) and \(.29592\) agree with the rounded \(.35\) and \(.30\) descriptions. Positional embeddings are attached before shuffling. Figures 1–2 illustrate the intended pairing but do not independently establish semantic diversity for every masked image.

The arithmetic behind several headline summaries is consistent: the FLOP reduction from \(15.6\) to \(12.0\) is \(23.08\%\); the COCO AP-box gain over the listed MoCo-v3 baseline is \(3.6\) percentage points; the ADE20K Base-to-Large gain is \(7.1\) points. The abstract’s \(133\times4=532\) GPU-hours is compatible with a rounded 533 GPU-hours in Table 3. Figure 3 supports a reported efficiency tradeoff, not an independently standardized hardware measurement. Table 3 also shows a slight decline from 2,048 to 4,096, so a general monotonic batch-size claim would be too strong.

The release applies a shared random crop and flip before masking. The paper’s narrower statement about not generating separate augmented views is compatible with that path; it should not be read as absence of all preprocessing. The targeted linear-probe check freezes the backbone and trains the head. Tables 7–9 include outcomes below competing methods, so the supported empirical claim is a tradeoff rather than universal accuracy dominance. Masking and batch size co-vary in some ablations; the tables do not isolate every claimed semantic cause. No measured accuracy, runtime or robustness result is independently refuted by this review.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Highest supported impact | Minor
Scientific adjudication | Pending
Repair verification | Loss and concentration identities verified
Author adoption | Not established
Human reviews | None recorded

The highest supported impact is Minor. The displayed objective and concentration explanation need local correction, and the release needs an unambiguous configuration and batch-pool specification for faithful replication. Algorithm 1 remains coherent. The available evidence does not establish a central benchmark failure or determine the historical implementation.

1 Xiaoyu Yang; Lijian Xu; Hongsheng Li; Shaoting Zhang. One Leaf Reveals the Season: Occlusion-Based Contrastive Learning with Semantic-Aware Views for Efficient Visual Representation. PMLR 267 (2025), published PDF. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/yang25ao.html.
# Reproducibility and limits

The independently written `independent_checks.py` evaluates the normalized-vector examples, concentration derivatives and thresholds, random-mask set properties and table arithmetic; outputs are in `independent_check.json`. Selected source excerpts are retained in `code_evidence.txt`. No dependency installation, author-code execution, checkpoint loading or training was performed. The source inspection is selective; full fine-tuning, detection, segmentation and robustness pipelines were not audited or reproduced. Original benchmark logs and matched historical configurations are unavailable in this packet.

The initial review was performed by the assigned AI review unit. Independent acceptance rechecked the original loss, concentration calculation, release recipe and batch-pool argument, and narrowed the last item to a scope clarification. Scientific adjudication remains pending and no human review is recorded. The matching verification directory contains physical-page extracts, source checks, independent calculations, compilation records, visual inspection and provenance. Title: Technical Verification of Quantum Algorithms for Finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes
# Identity and scope

This report concerns Bin Luo, Yuwen Huang, Jonathan Allcock, Xiaojun Lin, Shengyu Zhang and John C. S. Lui, Quantum Algorithms for Finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, pp. 41200–41234, paper I25-43760 (0391), OpenReview identifier `toTYcYf4qI`. The reviewed object is the 35-page published PMLR PDF in the supplied frozen packet. Page references below mean one-based physical PDF pages, which agree with its printed numbering.

All main text and embedded Appendices A–B were read. Detailed checks concentrated on the Bellman error propagation, QMEBO normalization, probability accounting, and the lower-bound reduction. Tables 1–2 and the decisive mathematical pages were inspected as rendered source pages. No author repository was available in the packet; separate OpenReview attachments could not be acquired in source preparation. External cited proofs, later revisions and errata were not independently retrieved. A fresh independent acceptance check revisited both reported Problems, their assumptions, counterevidence and repair boundaries.
# Necessary definitions

The finite model has \(S\) states, \(A\) actions, \(H\) stages, rewards \(r_h(s,a)\in[0,1]\), stochastic transition kernels \(P_h\), and terminal value \(V_H=0\). Definition 2.3 requires \(\epsilon\) accuracy uniformly over states and all stages. The generative oracle in Definition 4.1 returns transition samples in coherent superposition; rewards are separately supplied. In Appendix B.3 the discounted model has discount \(\gamma\in[0.9,1)\) and effective horizon \(\Gamma=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\). Its lower-bound theorem assumes at least two states and two actions.
# Substantive findings

Equation reference: eq:wrong. Problem 1 (The truncation length does not establish the lower-bound reduction).  Equations (127) and (135), pp. 32 and 34, use \[
-\log(1-\gamma)\leq\gamma\] to claim that \(H=\lceil2\Gamma\log(2/\epsilon)\rceil\) makes the finite and infinite values differ by at most \(\epsilon\). This step is false: \(-\log(1-\gamma)\geq\gamma\), strictly for \(0<\gamma<1\). The displayed inequality and its stated justification were checked against the actual PDF images.
## A complete admissible calculation

Let the discounted model have states \(\{x,y\}\), actions \(\{a,b\}\), reward one at both states under both actions, and identity transitions under either action. Set \(\gamma=99/100\) and \(\epsilon=1/10\). These give two states, two actions, stochastic transitions, rewards in \([0,1]\), \(\gamma\geq0.9\), \(\Gamma=100\), and \(2\epsilon<\Gamma/4\). Thus the domains used by the proposed reduction and its quoted infinite-horizon theorem are respected.

Apply exactly the construction in (123)–(124): adjoin an absorbing state \(o\) with reward zero; from \(x\) or \(y\), remain at the same state with probability \(\gamma\) and move to \(o\) with probability \(1-\gamma\), under either action. The finite model is time independent, hence also belongs to the time-dependent class. Every policy is optimal. At \(x\) and \(y\), \[\begin{aligned}
\widetilde V^*=\widetilde Q^*&=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t=100,\\
V_0^*=Q_0^*&=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t
             =100(1-\gamma^H),\\
H&=\lceil200\log20\rceil=600,\\
\widetilde V^*-V_0^*=\widetilde Q^*-Q_0^*
 &=100(99/100)^{600}\approx0.2405009291>2\epsilon.\end{aligned}\] In particular, even the exact finite value is an \(\epsilon\) approximation to itself but is not a \(2\epsilon\) approximation to the infinite value. This refutes the uniform conversion asserted in (128) and (136), not merely an intermediate sufficient condition. The independently written check uses rational arithmetic for the tail and tests both inequalities; its exact fraction and numerical output are retained in `verification/0391/independent_check_output.json`.
## Alternative readings, dependency, and limited repair

Equation (126) occasionally prints a final power \(H\) although the model has \(H\) rewards. Counting one extra reward does not cure the example: its tail becomes \(100\gamma^{601}>0.2\). Lemma B.7 initially omits the factor two inside the logarithm, then uses the longer horizon above; the counterexample uses that more favorable choice. There is no stated relationship restricting \(\Gamma\) by \(1/\epsilon\), and the rewards are not normalized by \(1-\gamma\). Such changes cannot be silently supplied.

Equation reference: eq:repair. For any bounded-reward discounted model the tail is at most \(\Gamma\gamma^H\leq\Gamma e^{-H/\Gamma}\). Therefore \[
H\geq\left\lceil\Gamma\log(\Gamma/\epsilon)\right\rceil\] is a sufficient truncation condition. For the example this is \(H=691\) and the tail is about \(0.0964<0.1\). This verifies the truncation repair only. It introduces dependence on \(\log\Gamma\) absent from the asserted horizon conversion; it does not establish the exact lower bounds printed in Theorem 4.7.

Lemmas B.6 and B.7 feed directly into Theorem 4.7, Table 2, and the claimed near-optimality comparison. The invalid derivation is therefore Major even though replacing the reduction or allowing additional logarithmic factors may preserve an important result. The example is an easy MDP, so it does not refute a worst-case lower bound. The final policy paragraph on p. 35 also needs a query-preserving argument: a policy induces a value function mathematically, but its numerical evaluation is not automatically free when transitions are unknown. No independent policy lower bound is certified here.

Equation reference: eq:operator. Problem 2 (Measurement failure is not linear operator-norm error).  The first paragraphs of Appendix A.4.6, p. 21, and B.1.2, p. 24, infer from a mean-estimation failure probability \(\zeta\) an ideal deterministic encoding oracle satisfying \[
\|B^{\rm ideal}_{z_{h,s}}-B_{z_{h,s}}\|_{\rm op}\leq2A\zeta.\] They use this in a hybrid/union argument to prove the success probabilities of Theorems 3.8 and 4.3. The inference is not a property of quantum unitaries.
## Explicit check of the asserted inference

Take \(A=2\) action labels and let an extra output qubit encode the estimate. For each label, set the true scalar to zero and the tolerance below \(1/2\), so output zero is good and output one is bad. Let \[R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{1-\zeta}&-\sqrt\zeta\\
\sqrt\zeta&\sqrt{1-\zeta}\end{pmatrix},\qquad
U=I_A\otimes R_\theta,\qquad \zeta=10^{-4}.\] This is unitary. On every initialized input \(|a\rangle|0\rangle\), measurement fails with probability exactly \(\zeta\). For the clean encoding oracle \(I\), \[\|U-I\|_{\rm op}=\sqrt{2-2\sqrt{1-\zeta}}
 \approx0.0100001250>0.0004=2A\zeta.\] Moreover any ideal encoding with no bad-output amplitude is at distance at least \(\sqrt\zeta=0.01\) on this input, irrespective of its action on other inputs. Thus choosing a different unitary extension cannot establish ([eq:operator] (#eq:operator)). The same computation can be made for arbitrarily small \(\zeta\); the obstruction is the square-root scaling of amplitudes, not numerical precision.

This is a counterexample to the stated general implication used in the proof. It is not a simulation of the authors’ particular QME implementation and does not show that QVI-2 or QVI-3 necessarily returns an incorrect answer with the claimed probability. A more specialized coherent-estimation construction would require its own proof. In addition, success within an interval does not by itself yield a unique deterministic binary value oracle.
## Impact and repair scope

The probability bookkeeping is a central dependency of both speedup algorithms, so the established invalid inference is Major. Classical union bounds for actually measured estimates, such as the separate QVI-4 analysis, are not invalidated by this observation. A defensible repair would specify coherent computation/uncomputation, bound its distance on the applicable initialized subspace, amplify error sufficiently, and include QMS’s own failure probability. Algorithms 2 and 4 use \(\mathrm{QMS}_{\delta}\) at each of \(SH\) calls, while the proof’s final \(\delta/(SH)\) budget accounts only for oracle perturbation. The excerpted QMS theorem does not make this intrinsic failure disappear. Polynomially smaller subroutine failure probabilities may cost only logarithmic overhead, but the full repaired algorithm and exact advertised logarithms were not verified.
# Other checks and overall assessment

The normalized good-branch probability in QMEBO is \(\sum_i p_if_i/N=\mu/N\). Multiplying the amplitude-estimation error by \(N\) gives a term of order \(\sqrt N/T+N/T^2\), consistent with the stated \(T=O(\sqrt N/\epsilon+\sqrt{N/\epsilon})\) scaling. Conditional on correct clean estimates and maximization, the downward shift and clipping at zero yield a one-sided Bellman error at most \(\epsilon/H\); induction accumulates at most \(\epsilon\). These checks support the deterministic portion of the analysis without repairing the probability argument.

Appendix B.2’s monotonicity and variance-reduction structure was read and locally checked, but the total-variance lemma cited from prior work, gate-level arithmetic, precision implementation, all logarithmic complexity factors and optimal lower bounds were not independently reproved. Title: Technical Verification of Visual and Domain Knowledge for Professional-level Graph-of-Thought Medical Reasoning
# Identity, version and scope

The paper is by Rina Bao, Shilong Dong, Zhenfang Chen, Sheng He, Patricia Ellen Grant and Yangming Ou, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, identifier I25-43761 (0392), OpenReview `tnyxtaSve5`. The supplied published PDF has 23 physical pages; page references use one-based physical numbering, agreeing with the printed pages. All main text and Appendices A–E were read. Figures 1–10, the main performance/ablation tables and appendix input ablations were visually inspected. These images establish what is displayed, not clinical correctness of the underlying MRI annotations.

Static checks used `i3-research/HIE-Reasoning` commit `d9238f5742d9` and the reorganized `baorina/CGOT_release` commit `e8950cf327b0`, both dated 18 May 2026 in their saved manifests. The original README explicitly links the latter repository. All 30 acquired source-file hashes match their snapshots. These later releases do not establish which code generated the 2025 experiments. No patient volumes, historical prediction files or external APIs were used; no author code was executed.
# Checked evidence and necessary distinctions

Equation reference: eq:ba. The benchmark contains 133 MRI cases, but Table 6 reports only 84 outcome labels. Figure 6 gives approximately 63.1% normal and 36.9% adverse outcomes, consistent with 53 and 31 cases. Section 5.1 defines outcome performance as mean per-class accuracy, i.e., binary balanced accuracy \[
 B=\frac12\left(\frac{T_0}{N_0}+\frac{T_1}{N_1}\right),\] where \(N_c\) is the number of evaluated cases of true class \(c\) and \(T_c\) the correctly predicted number. This differs from ordinary accuracy on an imbalanced cohort.

The headline Gemini improvement is arithmetically consistent: \(71.73-56.60=15.13\) percentage points in Table 2. The GPT-series difference is \(61.11-52.16=8.95\) points. Appendix D.1 expressly explains that this series combines GPT-4o-mini’s earlier tasks with GPT-4o’s later tasks; it is not an undisclosed single-model result. Table 4 drops are \(20.79\), \(1.61\) and \(10.62\) points as printed. The smallest difference is compatible with one changed adverse-case decision (\(50/31\approx1.61\) points); without paired predictions or uncertainty estimates it does not by itself establish a general necessity claim for that component.

The prompts and current outcome code use previous model answers, not outcome labels as input. The examined outcome code uses labels to select eligible case identifiers. No direct outcome-label leakage was established. The rare-region evaluation computes a set difference from predicted anatomy and a shared common-region list. Interpretation summaries are templated from intermediate outputs, as Appendix C.4 discloses; ROUGE-L therefore measures template/content overlap and cannot independently validate clinical factuality or free-form reasoning.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (Outcome balanced accuracy omits missing predictions from its denominators).  In the reorganized release, , lines 47–83, a missing case or missing `model_answer` key enters the `KeyError` handler at lines 57–59, increments `fail`, and continues. Class counts `gt_0` and `gt_1` are incremented only afterwards at lines 70–73. Line 81 includes `fail` in ordinary accuracy; line 83 excludes it from both class denominators. The original repository’s evaluation loop is byte-identical after the loop marker. This differs from full-cohort evaluation under ([eq:ba] (#eq:ba)) whenever predictions are missing.
## Complete finite check

Consider four eligible cases, with true labels \((0,0,1,1)\) and predictions \((0,\bot,1,\bot)\), where \(\bot\) means the corresponding JSON answer key is missing. Both classes occur and both retain at least one valid answer, so the example avoids division by zero and malformed strings. The code’s class counts are \((1,1)\) and correct counts \((1,1)\); hence it prints \[B_{\rm available}=\tfrac12(1/1+1/1)=1.\] On the four-case cohort, treating an absent answer as no correct answer gives \[B_{\rm full}=\tfrac12(1/2+1/2)=\tfrac12.\] The same script’s ordinary accuracy is \(2/(2+2)=1/2\). The independent check recomputes these counts without importing or running either author script. If every answer in one true class is missing, the balanced-accuracy line instead divides by zero. More generally its estimator is \[\frac12\sum_{c=0}^1\frac{T_c}{N_c-M_c},\] with \(M_c\) the missing-answer count, rather than ([eq:ba] (#eq:ba)).
## Counterevidence, impact and repair

If \(M_0=M_1=0\), this issue has no effect. One could deliberately report selective accuracy among answered cases, but then that population, coverage by class, and abstention policy must be stated. The release prints only a global failure count, and the paper describes the class average without a conditional-population qualifier. The discrepancy is a supported local evaluation defect (Minor). Missing raw predictions prevent determining whether the paper’s 71.73% or any comparison changed; this is not evidence of fabricated results or a demonstrated failure of the core benchmark.

A precise full-cohort repair is to count \(N_c\) from all eligible ground-truth cases before answer lookup, use those fixed denominators, and give no correct-answer credit to absent or invalid predictions. Coverage and invalid-response counts should be reported separately. The independent four-case check verifies this repair’s arithmetic, not the complete evaluation pipeline or the published score.
# Unresolved source correspondence

Appendix C.4, pp. 20–21, supplies the clinical four-level score definition, with score 3 defined by cerebral hemisphere devastation. The released outcome inference file contains that clinical text but actually selects `MRI_injury_score_math_knowledge` at lines 228–231. Its lines 159–168 introduce 75% regional thresholds, including assigning score 3 when BGT, ALIC or PLIC injury exceeds 75%. This is not the same prompt as the appendix. For instance, a hypothetical isolated severe BGT injury need not constitute hemisphere devastation, so the two textual rules are not logically equivalent.

This is a verified version difference, while its relevance to historical experiments is Needs Evidence. It is not independently graded as a medical error. Saved request payloads, response files and a contemporaneous commit would establish which prompt produced Table 2 and the ablations. Those files were not in the supplied source-only packet. Current path/filename differences likewise cannot identify the historical execution. No external rerun was attempted.
# Conclusion and limits

The observed performance gains and several ablation arithmetic checks are internally consistent. Full-text reading and selected static tracing do not reproduce the clinical labels, case selection, model calls or confidence intervals. The ZADC/ROI preprocessing scripts and upstream atlas studies were not audited in full. Claims about generalization to independent institutions or causal contribution of each prompt component need evidence beyond the reported small retrospective cohort.
