Title: Technical Verification of RUN: Reversible Unfolding Network for Concealed Object Segmentation
# Identity and scope

This report reviews Chunming He, Rihan Zhang, Fengyang Xiao, Chengyu Fang, Longxiang Tang, Yulun Zhang, Linghe Kong, Deng-Ping Fan, Kai Li and Sina Farsiu, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43768 (0399), OpenReview `tiYNbKwL7T`. All 12 physical pages were read, including references, Algorithm S1 and Appendix A. All Figures 1–6 were actually viewed. Printed and physical page numbers agree. The acquired repository is `ChunmingHe/RUN`, commit `878208d5154577075fe15``156866970f2a57c2fb8`; all acquired file hashes were checked.

Complete static reading covered `Network.py`, `get_m_hat.py`, `Train.py`, `Test.py`, `data_val.py`, `utils.py`, `eval_functions.py` and the README. In `Modules.py`, the state-space wrapper, selective Mamba wrapper, REU blocks and complete REM11 were inspected (lines 1–68, 297–338, 920–1045). The remaining low-level state-space internals and unrelated utility/backbone implementations were not fully audited. No author code was executed or imported. Independent scalar calculations and static AST checks, including their command outputs, are preserved. The source is an acquired subset of a public release; neither its correspondence to historical experiments nor inaccessible separate OpenReview attachments was established.
# Supported findings

Problem 1 (The asserted optimization derivation is invalid for the specified objective).  Equation (4), p. 3, explicitly defines \(S\) as an \(\ell_1\) norm. Equations (10)–(12), p. 4, replace it by a quadratic Taylor model whose justification assumes that \(\nabla S\) is Lipschitz continuous. For the scalar restriction \(S(r)=|r|\), the derivative is undefined at zero, and for \(r=\varepsilon\) and \(s=-\varepsilon\), the derivative difference divided by \(|r-s|\) equals \(1/\varepsilon\). No finite global gradient-Lipschitz constant exists.

This obstruction is directly relevant to the proposed initialization: zero masks and the piecewise mapping in Equation (5) permit zero residuals. Choosing zero as a subgradient at zero does not supply a differentiable function or a valid tangent quadratic upper model: \(|r|>Lr^2/2\) for sufficiently small nonzero \(r\) and any finite \(L\). An additive constant that makes a quadratic a loose bound cannot restore the missing first-order equality required by the stated Taylor argument. A deliberately smoothed penalty could fix the premise, but its definition, smoothing scale, approximation error and resulting update are absent.

Even if Equation (12) is taken simply as a chosen quadratic surrogate, its printed solution is wrong. Interpret image products charitably as pointwise operations and consider one scalar pixel, freezing \(w_k,\widetilde m_k,R_{k-1}\) as stipulated. The coefficient of \(\widehat m\) in the normal equation must be \[C^2+\mu+\alpha L_S w_k^2,\] whereas Equation (13) sets \(Q_a=C^2+\mu+L_Sw_k^2\), omitting \(\alpha\). The numerator retains \(\alpha\), so a uniform redefinition of \(L_S\) does not remove the discrepancy. For \(C=1\), \(B=0\), \(\mu=1\), \(\alpha=2\), \(L_S=10\), \(m_{k-1}=0.2\), \(\widetilde m_k=0.1\), \(w_k=w_{k-1}=1\), and \(R_{k-1}=0.1\) with gradient one, Equation (12) has \[J(m)=\tfrac12(1-m)^2+\tfrac12(m-0.2)^2+10(m-0.1)^2.\] Its unique minimizer is \(3.2/22\approx0.145455\). Equation (13) instead gives \(3.2/12\approx0.266667\), where \(J'(m)=2.666667\ne0\). This scalar case already disproves the displayed closed-form claim. If one scalar mask is shared across RGB channels, the data-term coefficient additionally needs the appropriate channel sum; averaging independent channelwise solutions is not generally the same minimization.

The supplied `get_m_hat.py`, lines 39–49, differs further: its denominator adds a constant \(L_S\) without \(w_k^2\) or \(\alpha\), while its numerator retains their product. The constructor’s \(L_s\) argument is stored but the formula resets \(L_s\) to an all-ones tensor. Those choices may define a useful learned architecture, but they do not verify the claimed exact optimization correspondence.

This is Major because the paper emphasizes mathematically strict connections in Figure 3 and explicit theoretical guarantees on p. 8. It is a derivation failure, not a proof that the learned model must perform poorly. Use a valid nonsmooth proximal update or state and analyze a smooth surrogate; rederive the normal equations; define all pointwise operations, channel reductions and initial states, including \(M_{-1}\) needed at \(k=1\). If arbitrary learned blocks replace proximal maps and gradients, identify which guarantees survive and under what assumptions. Otherwise describe the method as optimization-inspired and remove unsupported convergence or optimality wording. The background scalar update in Equation (17) was checked and does solve its stated quadratic surrogate; that local correctness does not repair the mask derivation.

Problem 2 (The supplied training and inference paths omit the claimed joint unfolding mechanism).  Equation (22), p. 5, includes stage-wise reconstruction loss, and Figures 2–3 and Algorithm S1 require a refined background to influence the next segmentation stage. In the advertised `Train.py`, lines 80–82, a reconstruction quantity is computed, but line 83 sets the differentiated objective to `loss_init + loss_final + loss_edge + 2 * ual_loss`. The reconstruction quantity is absent; it is only logged afterward.

The extra uncertainty loss is defined in `utils.py`, lines 29–33, as the mean of \(1-(2\sigma(z)-1)^2\), rather than the reconstruction term in Equation (22). Moreover, in the default `Network.forward`, `Network.py` lines 646–682, the mask pipeline and selective Mamba branch modify only the coarse returned mask after `REM11` has already computed all four masks. Reconstructed backgrounds are then computed at lines 669–680, with no call returning them to another segmentation update. `REM11`, lines 998–1025 of `Modules.py`, was read to confirm the ordering and independent returned tensors. `Test.py` line 55 selects return element four, the fine mask `f1` computed before those modifications. Thus the reconstructed background branch is absent from the final forward dependency and, with the reconstruction term omitted, its own parameters have no path to the optimized loss. Auxiliary supervision on the modified coarse mask can still affect shared encoder training; this review does not claim that every added branch has no training effect.

A further implementation defect affects the central RSS component. `Network.py` line 655 creates a local `Selectivemamba()` on each call; its own forward method creates local `VSSBlock` instances at `Modules.py` lines 324 and 329. These are newly initialized module objects, not registered persistent children of the model used by the optimizer at `Train.py` line 214 or by checkpoint loading. They are therefore not learned and restored as the paper’s fixed trained RSS blocks. Calling `model.eval()` cannot turn newly created, unregistered objects into persistent evaluated submodules. This statement follows from object construction and registration, not an executed training trace.

These discrepancies constitute a Major obstacle to reproducing the central joint reconstruction/segmentation mechanism. A different historical program or accidentally released development branch could explain them; the published tables are not proved fabricated or numerically wrong. Publish the source and configurations that generated them, register state-space modules in constructors, make every intended background-to-mask dependency explicit, and include the intended reconstruction term in the training objective. Recompute the mechanism ablations with matched checkpoints and verify gradients reach the reconstruction branch. The present loss and graph cannot substantiate the claimed reconstruction-guided causal explanation merely because an intermediate image is displayed in Figure 2.

Problem 3 (The claimed experimental breadth and some universal comparisons exceed the available results).  Contribution (3), p. 3, claims validation on five COS tasks as well as salient object detection. The complete published PDF supplies comparative results for COD, polyp segmentation, tubular segmentation and transparent objects. Appendix A gives a CDS2K defect-detection protocol but no corresponding result table or figure, and no salient-object evaluation is provided. Those additional validation claims cannot be checked from the acquired paper.

Separately, the broad superiority wording on p. 6 needs metric-specific qualification. ResNet50 RUN on CAMO has \(E_\phi=0.868\), below FocusDiff’s \(0.883\), and \(S_\alpha=0.806\), below FSEL’s \(0.816\). RUN’s CORN AUC is \(0.962\), below DSCNet’s \(0.964\). These exceptions coexist with strong gains elsewhere and are not a reversal of every ranking. This Minor reporting finding requires the missing experiments or narrower scope, and wording that states the observed tradeoffs. Separate inaccessible attachments may contain additional results, but their existence and contents were not verified.
# Independent checks and remaining uncertainty

The four highlighted numerical gains in Figure 1 were checked against the relevant displayed table values: \(0.747-0.730=0.017\) for COD10K \(F_\beta\), \(0.878-0.871=0.007\) for ETIS structure score, \(0.870-0.859=0.011\) for CORN sensitivity, and \(0.952-0.944=0.008\) for GDD maximum F-score against the strongest tabulated competitor. These calculations verify differences, not experimental provenance. Table 7’s stage progression is compatible with diminishing gains in \(F_\beta\); the four-stage setting is a declared efficiency choice, although wall time, parameter counts and compute-matched stage comparisons are not reported. Small increments such as \(0.001\) in ETIS Dice need variability information before being characterized as robust improvements.

Reconstruction alone does not identify a correct mask: for any mask \(m\), choosing \(B=C(1-m)\) makes \(C-Cm-B=0\). The excluded interval in Equation (5) also gives no residual-sparsity penalty to maximally ambiguous masks. Learned semantic priors and supervised mask/edge losses may resolve that ambiguity, but the reconstruction image by itself is not evidence of segmentation correctness. The visual examples demonstrate selected successes; no random sample protocol or pixel-level recalculation was available. The paper’s term “reversible” describes foreground/background reasoning and was not misread as a formal bijection guarantee.

The released loader normalizes RGB data and uses unbounded logits on parts of the mask path; these details should be reconciled with the stated \([0,1]\) mask-domain interpretation. The published zero initialization also differs from the learned prior initialization in the release. Current default validation points to CDS2K and selects the best checkpoint by validation MAE; the test script names a path containing a COD10K validation label. These filenames do not prove which data were used historically or establish leakage. Exact split manifests and checkpoint-selection rules are needed. Likewise, the CORN “first 30% / last 70%” split requires a specified ordering and subject grouping for replication.

The full experimental metric engine is not established by the supplied utilities: the README delegates evaluation to an external MATLAB toolbox, while local utilities include both weighted and thresholded F-score routines. Appendix A’s precise F-score convention, thresholds and averaging should be tied to the actual evaluator. Baseline retraining parity, hidden tuning, raw masks, error bars and the influence of the extra pretrained dehazer in RUN+ were not independently reproduced. The latter is an additional component and does not isolate the benefit of unfolding alone.
# Repair status

The nonsmooth-gradient obstruction, missing normal-equation coefficient and scalar background solution were independently checked. Static loss/dependency evidence was verified without author execution. Two Major findings and one Minor finding are supported. Fresh independent acceptance rechecked both Major Problems and the Minor scope/comparison Problem. Scientific adjudication remains pending; human reviews remain empty.

report: Abstract: The complete published paper and embedded appendices were inspected. The scalar binary tradeoff calculation and the Gaussian limit for dense antipodal inputs withstand independent checks. Theorem 2, however, extends the latter calculation to arbitrary bounded vectors without the required dispersion condition. A fixed one-coordinate experiment embedded in every dimension disproves that extension and prevents the claimed uniform reduction of the Gaussian differential privacy parameter over the full input ball. The convergence statements also omit expectations that their proofs require; expected stationarity bounds can be recovered. Reported accuracies were not reproduced, and their privacy calibration requires a separate valid accountant. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of Noisy SIGNSGD Is More Differentially Private Than You (Might) Think
# Identity and scope

This report reviews Richeng Jin and Huaiyu Dai, ICML 2025, PMLR 267, I25-43769 (0400), OpenReview `thCqMz1ZXw`. All 22 physical pages were read, including references and Appendices A–C. Printed and physical page numbers agree. All six figures and all six tables were actually inspected, as were image renderings of the relevant theorem and proof pages. The source is the frozen published PDF; its hash and physical-page extraction records accompany this report.

No author repository was identified in the supplied bounded source search. Separate OpenReview attachments were unavailable in source preparation; this does not establish that no code or supplement exists. No author code, model or dataset was run or imported. Reviewer-authored finite hypothesis tests, scalar calculations and aggregation probabilities were computed using only the Python standard library; scripts, outputs and command receipts are preserved. Numerical grids support the analytic arguments below but are not substituted for their quantifiers.
# Supported findings

Problem 1 (The universal vector Gaussian limit and resulting uniform amplification fail).  Theorem 2, p. 6, quantifies over any vectors \(x,x'\) satisfying \(\|x\|_2,\|x'\|_2\le C\) and asserts convergence of their sign-mechanism tradeoff to \(G_\mu\) as \(d\to\infty\), with the bound in Equation (19). For fixed \(C,\sigma>0\), that bound gives \(\mu\le\mu_*=(2C/\sigma)\sqrt{2/\pi}\). Remark 2, p. 7, uses this reduction to claim \(\pi/2\) more training steps at the same overall privacy guarantee.

Equation reference: eq:binary. Set \(a=C/\sigma\), \(q=\Phi(-a)\) and, in every dimension, choose \[x_d=Ce_1,\qquad x'_d=-Ce_1.\] The first output bit has probabilities \(1-q\) and \(q\) of being positive, respectively. Every remaining output bit is an independent fair coin under both hypotheses. Those common ancillary bits contain no testing information. Thus the exact Neyman–Pearson tradeoff, for every \(d\), is \[
f_d(\alpha)=
\begin{cases}
1-\dfrac{1-q}{q}\alpha,&0\le\alpha\le q,\\[3pt]
\dfrac{q}{1-q}(1-\alpha),&q\le\alpha\le1.
\end{cases}\] In particular \(f_d(q)=q\). But the claimed limiting GDP curve satisfies \[G_{\mu_*}(q)=\Phi(a-\mu_*)>\Phi(-a)=q,\] since \(\mu_*<2a\). For \(C=\sigma=1\), the actual value is \(0.158655254\), whereas the proposed Gaussian bound requires at least \(0.275664737\). A still smaller admissible \(\mu\) only raises the required curve. The discrepancy persists as \(d\to\infty\); this is a counterexample to the theorem’s stated conclusion, not merely an absent proof detail. The piecewise linear curve also cannot become an exactly Gaussian tradeoff by appending uninformative coordinates.

More precisely, under the theorem’s comparison of all pairs in the full radius-\(C\) input ball, the smallest uniform GDP parameter remains exactly \(2C/\sigma\) for every \(d\). The raw Gaussian mechanism and post-processing give that upper bound. Conversely, [eq:binary] (#eq:binary) at \(\alpha=q\) requires \(\mu\ge2C/\sigma\). Scalar sign compression can improve the tradeoff at other test levels without improving this particular uniform GDP parameter. This observation preserves the valid information-loss result in Section 4.1 and does not deny every possible form of privacy amplification.

The proof on pp. 6 and 13–15 replaces arbitrary inputs by the dense antipodes \(x'=-x=(C/\sqrt d)\mathbf1\), then applies a central limit argument. Maximizing an extremal likelihood ratio does not establish ordering of the entire testing tradeoff for all input pairs. The Lyapunov step also needs a condition excluding a nonvanishing single-coordinate contribution to the total privacy-loss variance. The sparse sequence above violates exactly that condition. Equality of the two privacy-loss variances is valid for the symmetric antipodal pair used in the calculation, not an automatic property of every pair merely because a worst-case tradeoff is symmetric.

For the restricted dense antipodal sequence, an independent binomial calculation approaches \(G_{2\sqrt{2/\pi}}\) when \(C=\sigma=1\): the largest discrepancy over 99 interior test levels is about \(0.02290\), \(0.001781\) and \(0.0002041\) at \(d=10,100,1000\), respectively. Thus a useful restricted asymptotic theorem is plausible and its calculation is not being rejected. It must state an appropriate triangular-array dispersion condition and quantify approximation error before being used as a finite-dimensional privacy guarantee. Letting \(\sigma\to\infty\) as well makes both privacy curves tend to perfect privacy; that unscaled convergence alone does not establish the asserted nontrivial multiplicative gain.

This Major finding affects the claimed general vector amplification, the \(\pi/2\) composition argument and the privacy interpretation of the 500-versus-320-round comparison in Appendix C.2.2 and Table 3, pp. 21–22. The arithmetic \(500(2/\pi)=318.31\) is correct; its privacy premise is not supplied by Theorem 2. Repair requires either a restricted theorem with finite approximation control or a different valid worst-case accountant, followed by recalibration of the comparisons. Specify the adjacency relation, per-example clipping, mini-batch averaging, sampling and composition. Record-level sensitivity can differ from the full-input-ball comparison above. Without the actual noise scales and accountant, this review does not claim that a particular trained release violated its advertised privacy budget, or that the displayed accuracies are numerically false.

Problem 2 (The convergence bounds require expectation and stationarity qualifications).  Theorems 3 and 4, Equations (33)–(34), pp. 7–8, bound empirical averages of gradient norms at random iterates without an expectation or a probability qualifier. Their proofs, especially Equations (72)–(74) on pp. 16–17 and (82)–(84) on p. 19, start with expected descent and drop the expectation around those gradient norms. Expected descent does not imply the displayed pathwise bound.

For example, let \(F(w)=\sqrt{1+w^2}\), \(F^*=1\), \(w_0=1\), \(L=c=d=M=1\), and use its exact gradient. Assumptions 1–4 hold, including zero stochastic-gradient variance. For any finite \(T\) and \(\sigma>0\), the event that every transmitted noisy sign is negative has strictly positive probability. On that event \(w_t=1+t\eta\), so every squared gradient is at least \(1/2\). With \(\eta=T^{-1/2}\) and \(\sigma=T^{1/4}\), the stated right-hand order tends to zero. It cannot be an unconditional pathwise inequality. For Scheme II, take \(M=T\) identical workers with independent noises; the all-negative-message event still has positive probability, while the stated right-hand order also tends to zero and the \(\ell_1\) gradient remains at least \(1/\sqrt2\). Neither example contradicts an expectation bound: the exceptional event becomes very unlikely.

Equation reference: eq:expectedI, eq:expectedII. A direct repair is available. Write \(k=\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sigma\) and interpret the unbiasedness and independence assumptions conditionally on the iterate. For \(|g_i|\le c\), \[\left|\mathbb E[\operatorname{sign}(g_i+N)]-kg_i\right|
\le \frac{k|g_i|^3}{6\sigma^2},\qquad N\sim N(0,\sigma^2).\] This follows by integrating \(1-e^{-u^2/2}\le u^2/2\), without an asymptotic Taylor remainder. If \(A_t\) is the average of the transmitted bits, then \(\mathbb E[A_t\mid w_t]=k\nabla F(w_t)+e_t\) with \(\|e_t\|_2^2\le dk^2c^6/(36\sigma^4)\) and \(\|A_t\|_2^2\le d\). Smoothness and Young’s inequality yield \[
\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb E\|\nabla F(w_t)\|_2^2
\le \frac{2(F(w_0)-F^*)/(\eta T)+Ld\eta}{k}
       +\frac{dc^6}{36\sigma^4}.\] At the stated learning rate this has the leading terms in Theorem 3, with the missing expectation restored and the dimension dependence made explicit. For independent workers, each coordinate of \(A_t\) has conditional variance at most \(1/M\). Bounding the sign-decision error by its mean absolute deviation similarly gives for Scheme II \[
\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb E\|\nabla F(w_t)\|_1
\le\frac{F(w_0)-F^*}{\eta T}+\frac{Ld\eta}{2}
       +\frac{\sigma d\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt M}+\frac{dc^3}{3\sigma^2}.\] This argument avoids the variance-notation inconsistency between Assumption 3, which bounds variance by \(\sigma_{L,i}\), and Equation (80), which takes a square root of \(\sigma_{L,i}^2\). A proof following the latter route instead must distinguish variance from standard deviation. These repairs show why the omission is classified Minor rather than treated as a refutation of expected convergence.

The conclusions must concern expected stationarity, not proximity to a local optimum as stated in Remark 3: smooth nonconvex functions may have stationary saddles. Remark 4 also needs a lower growth bound on the number of workers, such as \(M=\Theta(T)\), to turn \(\sigma/\sqrt M\) with \(\sigma=O(\sqrt T/\mu_T)\) into \(O(1/\mu_T)\); the printed \(M=O(T)\) alone allows \(M=1\). A high-probability claim would require a separate concentration argument and confidence parameter. The paper explicitly excludes the effect of gradient clipping from this convergence analysis; the repaired bounds retain that restriction.
# Other checks and limits of interpretation

Theorem 1’s two-point likelihood test and the scalar Gaussian/logistic matching were checked directly. With \(|x|\le c\), the logistic scale \(s=c/\log(\Phi(c/\sigma)/\Phi(-c/\sigma))\) matches the extreme binary probabilities, hence the scalar tradeoff. The leading terms \(|x|^3/(6\sigma^2)\) and \(|x|^3/(12s^2)\) in Equations (14)–(17) describe bias of the scaled mean bit. They are not mean squared estimation errors. At \(c=\sigma=1\) and \(x=0\), both biases are zero, while the single-bit squared errors are \(\pi/2\simeq1.57080\) and \(4s^2\simeq1.43724\). The paper itself acknowledges the Gaussian variance disadvantage and that its aggregation method does not always outperform the logistic one, especially in Appendix C.2.1. Its narrower heterogeneous-data claim should retain those qualifications.

Independent convolution of the 100 Bernoulli messages in Figure 3 confirms a nonmonotone aggregation-error phenomenon under a specified tie rule. At \(\sigma=12\), the Gaussian mechanism has strictly negative-majority probability \(0.42577\) and tie probability \(0.07957\), giving \(0.46556\) with random tie-breaking. Counting a zero aggregate as wrong gives \(0.50535\) instead. The visible curve is compatible with the former value, but the displayed \(\operatorname{sign}\) formula does not specify tie handling. This needs explicit implementation documentation for even worker counts. It is not evidence that the plotted curve is fabricated. The independently computed curves were not substituted for the unavailable historical experiment.

The qualitative displays in Figures 4–6 and the six tables were checked for the stated trends. Similar test accuracies and some performance loss from majority vote are visible; those observations cannot establish equal privacy by themselves. The 32-to-1 payload calculation is correct for one binary gradient coordinate versus one 32-bit value, before framing, model broadcasts, aggregation representation and other communication costs. It should not be interpreted as a measured 32-fold end-to-end speedup. Server-side aggregation also cannot retroactively reduce the information already seen by a server in the stated local-privacy threat model.

Reported experiments specify datasets, worker counts, Dirichlet heterogeneity, clipping thresholds, a learning-rate grid, 500 rounds and ten repeats. Actual configurations, seeds, raw runs, checkpoint selection, the meaning of the reported dispersion, calibrated noise values and historical source were not available for reproduction. The Gaussian-input illustration in Appendix C is an aggregation example; its unbounded normal inputs do not themselves certify the bounded-input privacy hypothesis. No claim of complete empirical reproduction or benchmark equivalence is made.
# Repair status

One Major finding and one Minor finding are supported. The sparse counterexample is exact; finite enumeration checks it without a dimension-limit approximation. The restricted dense limit and corrected expected stationarity bounds were independently checked, so the report distinguishes surviving results from the failed generalization. Fresh independent acceptance rederived both the exact privacy counterexample and the surviving expected convergence bounds, including the Minor finding. Scientific adjudication remains pending; human reviews remain empty.
